articles.title: Forward map of the binary word residue equivalence
articles.statement:
The forward equivalence is the canonical quotient constructor applied to the polynomial
encoding.

articles.title: Remainder coefficients of an encoded binary word are its bits
articles.statement: The canonical remainder coordinates of an encoded word are exactly its low-first bits.

articles.title: Modular multiplication matches the polynomial quotient
articles.statement: Modular Horner multiplication agrees with multiplication in the polynomial quotient.

articles.title: Modular multiplication by $X$ matches the quotient root
articles.statement: Modular multiplication by `X` agrees with multiplication by the quotient root.

articles.title: Modular powering matches the polynomial quotient
articles.statement: Modular powering agrees with powering in the polynomial quotient, including width zero.

articles.title: Inverse map of the binary word residue equivalence
articles.statement:
The inverse equivalence extracts the canonical remainder's lowest `s` binary
coefficients.

articles.title: Bitwise xor corresponds to residue addition
articles.statement: Bitwise xor corresponds to quotient addition; builtin bitvector addition does not.

articles.title: Fixed-width binary words as residues modulo a monic polynomial
articles.statement:
Fixed-width binary words are in bijection with residues modulo their associated monic
polynomial. This is an ordinary equivalence because builtin bitvector addition has carries.

articles.title: Reduction of the root power in a binary residue ring
articles.statement: The defining quotient equation reduces `root ^ s` to the encoded lower coefficients.

articles.title: Coefficients of the binary polynomial of a bitvector
articles.statement:
Every coefficient of the polynomial encoding is the corresponding least-significant bit;
indices outside the fixed width have coefficient zero.

articles.title: Degree bound for a polynomial built from a coefficient list
articles.statement:
A polynomial built from a low-coefficient-first list has degree strictly less than the list
length, including for an empty list and over a trivial semiring.

articles.title: Evaluation of modular Horner multiplication
articles.statement:
Horner multiplication has its expected evaluation in every commutative ring receiving
`ZMod 2`; the second operand may have any width.

articles.title: Evaluation of modular multiplication by $X$
articles.statement:
Multiplication by `X` has its expected evaluation in every commutative ring receiving
`ZMod 2`.

articles.title: Evaluation of modular powering
articles.statement: Repeated multiplication has its expected power evaluation for positive result width.

articles.title: The binary modulus is monic
articles.statement: The binary modulus associated to a fixed-width word is monic, including at width zero.

articles.title: Degree of the binary modulus
articles.statement: The natural degree of the binary modulus is exactly the width of its lower coefficients.

articles.title: Monic binary modulus of a fixed-width word
articles.statement:
The monic polynomial obtained by adjoining the width term `X ^ s` to the encoded lower
coefficients.

articles.title: Modular multiplication of binary polynomial residues
articles.statement: Multiply binary residues by low-first Horner evaluation of the second operand's bits.

articles.title: Multiplication by $X$ of a binary polynomial residue
articles.statement: Multiply a binary residue by `X`, reducing by `X ^ s + g` when its top bit is set.

articles.title: Reconstructing a polynomial from a fixed-width coefficient list
articles.statement:
Reconstruct a polynomial from any fixed-width list containing all its possibly nonzero
coefficients.

articles.title: Modular powering of binary polynomial residues
articles.statement: Raise a binary residue to a natural power by tail-recursive repeated multiplication.

articles.title: Bitvector encoding recovers the original word
articles.statement: Extracting the coefficients of an encoded word recovers the original fixed-width word.

articles.title: Bitvector of the low coefficients of a binary polynomial
articles.statement:
Extract the lowest `s` binary coefficients of a polynomial as a fixed-width bitvector.
Coefficients at indices at least `s` are deliberately truncated.

articles.title: Polynomial encoding recovers a low-degree polynomial
articles.statement:
A polynomial whose degree is below the selected width is recovered after coefficient
extraction and fixed-width encoding.

articles.title: Bitwise xor corresponds to polynomial addition over $\mathbb{F}_2$
articles.statement:
Polynomial encoding turns bitwise xor into addition over `ZMod 2`; this is not the carried
integer addition on bitvectors.

articles.title: Binary polynomial of a bitvector
articles.statement:
The polynomial over `ZMod 2` whose coefficient of `X ^ i` is the `i`-th least-significant
bit of `w`.

articles.title: Little-endian Boolean lists are equivalent to bitvectors
articles.statement: Fixed-width little-endian Boolean lists are equivalent to bitvectors of the same width.

articles.title: Sum of a Boolean list counts its true entries
articles.statement: The sum of the natural values of a Boolean list is its number of `true` entries.

articles.title: Little-endian bits of a bitvector
articles.statement: The bits of a bitvector in little-endian order, least significant bit first.

articles.title: Radix-2 Cooley–Tukey splitting
articles.statement:
For $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$
and natural numbers $N$ and $k$, write $D_N(\omega, f, k) = \sum_{j < N} \omega^{jk} f(j)$ for the
discrete Fourier sum. Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy
$\omega^{2n} = 1$. Then for every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $K$,

$$D_{2n}(\omega, f, K) = D_n(\omega^2, f_0, K \bmod n)
  + \omega^K D_n(\omega^2, f_1, K \bmod n),$$

where $f_0(t) = f(2t)$, $f_1(t) = f(2t + 1)$, and $K \bmod n$ is the remainder of $K$ on division
by $n$ (with $K \bmod 0 = K$). So a length-$2n$ transform is two length-$n$ transforms on the
even and odd samples, combined with the twiddle factor $\omega^K$.

Proof: Split the range into even and odd indices, rewrite the powers, and use
root-of-unity periodicity to reduce the frequency modulo $n$, as in the
section "The radix-2 DIT case" of Wikipedia, "Cooley–Tukey FFT algorithm".

## Sources

- J. W. Cooley and J. W. Tukey, Math. Comp. 19 (1965) (decimation in time).

articles.title: The DFT sum at a root of unity depends only on the frequency modulo the length
articles.statement:
Let $n$
be a natural number and let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $\omega^n = 1$. Then for every
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $K$, the discrete Fourier sum of length $n$
at frequency $K$ equals the one at frequency $K \bmod n$:

$$\sum_{j < n} \omega^{jK} f(j) = \sum_{j < n} \omega^{j (K \bmod n)} f(j),$$

where $K \bmod n$ is the remainder of $K$ on division by $n$ (with $K \bmod 0 = K$).

articles.title: Even–odd splitting of the DFT sum
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, every
$\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $K$,

$$\sum_{j < 2n} \omega^{jK} f(j) = \sum_{t < n} (\omega^2)^{tK} f(2t)
  + \omega^K \sum_{t < n} (\omega^2)^{tK} f(2t + 1).$$

articles.title: Discrete Fourier sum
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$, a complex number $\omega$, a sequence
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $k$, the unnormalized discrete Fourier sum of
length $N$ at frequency $k$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \omega^{jk} f(j)$.

No condition is placed on $\omega$; the usual DFT takes $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$.

articles.title: The array FFT computes the discrete Fourier transform
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number,
$\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ a primitive $2^d$-th root of unity, $x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1}$ complex
numbers and $k < 2^d$. Then the array FFT of the array $(x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1})$ with root
$\omega$ returns an array $y$ of length $2^d$ whose entry at index $k$ is the discrete Fourier
sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2^d - 1} \omega^{jk} x_j$.

articles.title: The array FFT rejects exactly the non-powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring,
$\omega \in R$ and $x$ an array over $R$. The array FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ returns no
result if and only if the length of $x$ is different from $2^d$ for every natural number $d$.

In particular the empty array is rejected and an array of length $1 = 2^0$ is accepted.

articles.title: The array FFT agrees with the vector FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural
number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the array FFT of $x$,
viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ returns a result, namely the output of the radix-two FFT
of the length-$2^d$ vector $x$ with root $\omega$, viewed as an array.

articles.title: Exact cost of the array FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number,
$\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the cost $T$ of the array FFT of
$x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ satisfies $T + 1 = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d$.

Costs are counted in the scalar-operation and array-access model of the radix-two FFT.

articles.title: The array FFT costs the same as the vector FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a
natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the cost of the
array FFT of $x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ equals the cost of the radix-two FFT of
the length-$2^d$ vector $x$ with root $\omega$.

articles.title: Radix-two FFT on arrays
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ an array
over $R$ of length $n$, and let $d = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ (with $d = 0$ when $n = 0$). If
$n = 2^d$, the array FFT runs the radix-two FFT with root $\omega$ on $x$, viewed as a vector of
length $2^d$, and returns its output as an array, with the cost of that run. Otherwise it returns
no result, at cost $0$; the length check itself is free.

articles.title: Result of the butterfly loop
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural
number, $q = (q_0, \dots, q_{m-1})$ and $r = (r_0, \dots, r_{m-1})$ vectors over $R$, and $o$ a
vector over $R$ of length $2m$. The butterfly loop with root $\omega$ on $q$ and $r$, started
from twiddle $1$ and output vector $o$, ends with twiddle $\omega^m$ and an output vector $y$
such that $y_k = q_k + \omega^k r_k$ and $y_{k+m} = q_k - \omega^k r_k$ for every $k < m$.

articles.title: Cost of the FFT butterfly pass
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m$ a natural number. For
every $\omega \in R$, all vectors $q, r \in R^m$ and every output vector of length $2m$ over $R$,
the pass that, starting from twiddle $1$, applies one butterfly for each index $k < m$ in
increasing order costs exactly $8m$ charged operations.

articles.title: FFT butterfly pass
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\omega \in R$ and vectors
$q, r \in R^m$ and $y \in R^{2m}$, the butterfly pass starts from the state $(1, y)$, applies the
FFT butterfly with $\omega$, $q$ and $r$ at the indices $k = 0, 1, \dots, m - 1$ in increasing
order, and returns the final state; its time cost is the sum of the costs of these $m$
butterflies.

articles.title: Upper write of a butterfly step
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a
natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector
over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state
$(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $k + m$ is $q_k - w r_k$.

articles.title: Lower write of a butterfly step
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a
natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector
over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state
$(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $k$ is $q_k + w r_k$.

articles.title: A butterfly step leaves other entries unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring,
$\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle,
$o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then for every index $i < 2m$ with
$i \ne k$ and $i \ne k + m$, the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$
produces an output vector whose entry at index $i$ is $o_i$.

articles.title: Cost of one FFT butterfly
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m$ a natural number. For every
$\omega \in R$, all vectors $q, r \in R^m$, every current twiddle $w \in R$ and output vector of
length $2m$ over $R$, and every index $k < m$, one butterfly step costs exactly $8$ charged
operations: two reads, four scalar operations and two writes.

articles.title: One FFT butterfly
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\omega \in R$, vectors
$q, r \in R^m$, a state $(w, y)$ with $w \in R$ and $y \in R^{2m}$, and an index $k < m$, the
butterfly at $k$ returns the state $(w \omega, y')$, where $y'$ is obtained from $y$ by setting
entry $k$ to $q_k + w r_k$ and entry $k + m$ to $q_k - w r_k$, at a time cost of $8$.

articles.title: Rejection by array circular convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring
structure, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be arrays over $R$. The array
circular-convolution procedure with root $\omega$ returns no result on $x$ and $y$ if and only
if it is not the case that the length of $x$ is a power of two $2^k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $y$ has
the same length as $x$.

articles.title: Array circular FFT convolution agrees with the vector version
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field
with a star-ring structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$ be arbitrary, and
let $x, y$ be vectors over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then array circular FFT convolution with root
$\omega$, run on the arrays underlying $x$ and $y$, succeeds and returns the array underlying
the output of vector circular FFT convolution of $x$ and $y$ at size $2^d$ with root $\omega$.

articles.title: Output length of array circular FFT convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring
structure, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x, y$ be arrays over $R$. If array circular FFT
convolution with root $\omega$ on $x$ and $y$ returns an array $z$, then $z$ has the same
length as $x$.

articles.title: Exact cost of array circular FFT convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring
structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x, y$ be vectors over $R$
of length $2^d$. The time charged by array circular FFT convolution with root $\omega$ on the
arrays underlying $x$ and $y$, plus $2$, equals $(21d + 16) \cdot 2^d$.

articles.title: Array circular FFT convolution costs the same as the vector version
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
field with a star-ring structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let
$x, y$ be vectors over $R$ of length $2^d$. The time charged by array circular FFT convolution
with root $\omega$ on the arrays underlying $x$ and $y$ equals the time charged by vector
circular FFT convolution of $x$ and $y$ at size $2^d$ with root $\omega$.

articles.title: FFT circular convolution on arrays
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $\omega \in R$,
and $x, y$ arrays over $R$, where $x$ has length $n$. If $n = 2^d$ for some natural number $d$
and $y$ also has length $n$, the procedure returns the FFT circular convolution of $x$ and $y$
(read as vectors of length $2^d$) with root $\omega$, converted to an array, at the cost of that
convolution. Otherwise it returns no result, at cost $0$.

articles.title: Output of FFT circular convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring conjugation, let
$n = 2^d$, $\omega \in R$ and $x, y \in R^n$. The vector returned by FFT circular convolution of
$x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$ equals the vector returned by the inverse FFT with root $\omega$
applied to the vector returned by pointwise multiplication of $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$, where
$\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$ are the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of $x$ and of $y$ with
root $\omega$.

Only returned values are compared; operation counts are not.

articles.title: FFT circular convolution with root $e^{-2\pi i/n}$ computes the cyclic convolution
articles.statement:
Let
$n = 2^d$ and $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^n$. Run FFT circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root
$\omega = e^{-2\pi i/n}$, the value at $-1$ of the standard additive character of
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then for every $k < n$, entry $k$ of the returned vector equals
$\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}} x_j \, y_{k - j}$, with indices taken modulo $n$.

This root is the sign convention of the Princeton (Sedgewick–Wayne) source.

articles.title: FFT circular convolution with root $e^{2\pi i/n}$ computes the cyclic convolution
articles.statement:
Let
$n = 2^d$ and $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^n$. Run FFT circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root
$\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, the value at $1$ of the standard additive character of
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then for every $k < n$, entry $k$ of the returned vector equals
$\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}} x_j \, y_{k - j}$, with indices taken modulo $n$.

This root is the sign convention of the MIT and CLRS sources.

articles.title: Exact cost of FFT circular convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure,
let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $2^d$
over $R$. The cost charged by circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$, plus $2$,
equals $(21d + 16) \cdot 2^d$.

The cost is the sum of the costs of the two forward transforms, the pointwise product and the
inverse transform.

articles.title: Cost bound for FFT circular convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure,
let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $2^d$
over $R$. The cost charged by circular convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$ is at most
$(21d + 16) \cdot 2^d$, that is, $21 n \log_2 n + 16 n$ for the input length $n = 2^d$.

articles.title: FFT circular convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $d$ a natural number,
$\omega \in R$, and $x, y$ vectors of length $2^d$ over $R$. Circular convolution runs the timed
radix-two FFT of length $2^d$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ and then on $y$, multiplies the two
transforms pointwise, and applies the timed inverse FFT of length $2^d$ with root $\omega$ to the
product. It returns the result of the inverse transform, and its cost is the sum of the costs of
these four steps.

The definition imposes no condition on $\omega$.

articles.title: Conjugating around the FFT conjugates the root
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$, let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$
be a primitive $N$-th root of unity and let $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$. Conjugating every entry of $x$,
running the FFT procedure with root $\omega$ and conjugating every entry of the result gives the
same vector as running the FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\overline{\omega}$.

articles.title: Charged entrywise conjugation
articles.statement:
For a type with a star operation $z \mapsto \bar z$ and a
vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ of length $n$ over it, this costed computation returns
$(\bar x_0, \dots, \bar x_{n-1})$ and charges $3n$ operations: one read, one conjugation and one
write per entry.

articles.title: Correctness of the radix-two FFT
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$, every primitive $2^d$-th
root of unity $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, every vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1})$ in
$\mathbb{C}^{2^d}$ and every $k < 2^d$, the $k$-th entry of the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root
$\omega$ equals the discrete Fourier sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2^d - 1} \omega^{jk} x_j$.

articles.title: The FFT cost satisfies the radix-2 recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $C(n) = n \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ be the
closed-form FFT operation count. For every natural number $n > 0$, $C(2n) = 2\,C(n) + 2n$.

Proof: Since $n > 0$, $\lfloor \log_2 (2n) \rfloor = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$; expand the
product.

## Sources

- J. W. Cooley and J. W. Tukey, Math. Comp. 19 (1965) (`n log n` operation count).

articles.title: FFT operation count
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the closed-form FFT operation count is
$n \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, where $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ is the largest $m$ with $2^m \le n$
(taken to be $0$ when $n = 0$).

articles.title: FFT after inverse FFT is the identity at the negative-sign root
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$ and let
$\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$, the value at $-1$ of the standard additive character of
$\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For every $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, running the inverse FFT procedure on $x$
with root $\omega$ and then the FFT procedure on its output with root $\omega$ returns $x$.

articles.title: FFT after inverse FFT at the positive root is the identity
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number,
$N = 2^d$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$. For every vector $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, running the inverse
FFT with root $\omega$ on $x$ and then the radix-two FFT with root $\omega$ on its output
returns $x$.

articles.title: Rejection by array linear convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure,
let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be arrays over $R$. The array zero-padded
linear-convolution procedure with root $\omega$ returns no result on $x$ and $y$ if and only if
it is not the case that the length of $x$ is a power of two $2^k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $y$ has the
same length as $x$.

articles.title: Array linear FFT convolution agrees with the vector version
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with
a star-ring structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$ be arbitrary, and let
$x, y$ be vectors over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then array zero-padded linear FFT convolution with
root $\omega$, run on the arrays underlying $x$ and $y$, succeeds and returns the array
underlying the output (of length $2^{d+1}$) of vector zero-padded linear FFT convolution of
$x$ and $y$ at size $2^d$ with root $\omega$.

articles.title: Output length of array linear FFT convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring
structure, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x, y$ be arrays over $R$. If array zero-padded linear
FFT convolution with root $\omega$ on $x$ and $y$ returns an array $z$, then the length of $z$
is twice the length of $x$.

articles.title: Exact cost of array linear FFT convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring
structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x, y$ be vectors over $R$
of length $2^d$. The time charged by array zero-padded linear FFT convolution with root
$\omega$ on the arrays underlying $x$ and $y$, plus $2$, equals $(42d + 80) \cdot 2^d$.

articles.title: Array linear FFT convolution costs the same as the vector version
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field
with a star-ring structure, let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x, y$ be
vectors over $R$ of length $2^d$. The time charged by array zero-padded linear FFT convolution
with root $\omega$ on the arrays underlying $x$ and $y$ equals the time charged by vector
zero-padded linear FFT convolution of $x$ and $y$ at size $2^d$ with root $\omega$.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution on arrays
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $\omega \in R$,
and $x, y$ arrays over $R$, where $x$ has length $n$. If $n = 2^d$ for some natural number $d$
and $y$ also has length $n$, the procedure returns the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$
(read as vectors of length $2^d$) with root $\omega$, an array of length $2n$, at the cost of
that convolution. Otherwise it returns no result, at cost $0$.

articles.title: Output of FFT linear convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring conjugation, let
$\omega \in R$ and $x, y \in R^{2^d}$. The vector returned by FFT linear convolution of $x$ and
$y$ with root $\omega$ equals the vector returned by FFT circular convolution, at length
$2^{d+1}$ with root $\omega$, of the vectors returned by zero-padding $x$ and $y$ to length
$2^{d+1}$.

Only returned values are compared; operation counts are not.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution gives the product coefficients (Princeton sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$,
write $P_x = \sum_{j < 2^d} x_j X^j$ and $P_y = \sum_{j < 2^d} y_j X^j$, and let
$z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
which pads both vectors with zeros to length $N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then for
every $k < N$, the entry $z_k$ is the coefficient of $X^k$ in $P_x P_y$.

articles.title: The last entry of FFT linear convolution is zero (Princeton sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural
number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$, let
$z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
which pads both vectors with zeros to length $N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then the
last entry $z_{N-1}$ is $0$.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution computes the convolution sums (Princeton sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$,
extended by $x_j = y_j = 0$ for $j \ge 2^d$, let $z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT
linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$, which pads both vectors with zeros to length
$N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then for every $k < N$,

$$z_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k} x_j \, y_{k-j}.$$

articles.title: FFT linear convolution gives the product coefficients (MIT/CLRS sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$,
write $P_x = \sum_{j < 2^d} x_j X^j$ and $P_y = \sum_{j < 2^d} y_j X^j$, and let
$z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
which pads both vectors with zeros to length $N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then for
every $k < N$, the entry $z_k$ is the coefficient of $X^k$ in $P_x P_y$.

articles.title: The last entry of FFT linear convolution is zero (MIT/CLRS sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural
number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$, let
$z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
which pads both vectors with zeros to length $N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then the
last entry $z_{N-1}$ is $0$.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution computes the convolution sums (MIT/CLRS sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$,
extended by $x_j = y_j = 0$ for $j \ge 2^d$, let $z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT
linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$, which pads both vectors with zeros to length
$N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then for every $k < N$,

$$z_k = \sum_{j=0}^{k} x_j \, y_{k-j}.$$

articles.title: Exact cost of FFT linear convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure,
let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $2^d$
over $R$. The cost charged by zero-padded linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
plus $2$, equals $(42d + 80) \cdot 2^d$.

The cost is that of zero padding both inputs to length $2^{d+1}$ plus that of circular
convolution at length $2^{d+1}$.

articles.title: Cost bound for FFT linear convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star-ring structure,
let $d$ be a natural number, let $\omega \in R$, and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $2^d$
over $R$. The cost charged by zero-padded linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$
is at most $(42d + 80) \cdot 2^d$, that is, $42 n \log_2 n + 80 n$ for the input length
$n = 2^d$.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, $d$ a natural number,
$\omega \in R$, and $x, y$ vectors of length $2^d$ over $R$. Linear convolution zero-pads $x$ and
$y$ to length $2^{d+1}$ and returns the FFT circular convolution of the two padded vectors at
length $2^{d+1}$ with root $\omega$. Its cost is the cost of the two paddings plus the cost of
the circular convolution.

The root $\omega$ is used for the padded length $2^{d+1}$, twice the input length.

articles.title: Zero padding turns cyclic convolution into the polynomial product
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural
number and $N = 2^{d+1}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$, write
$P_x = \sum_{j < 2^d} x_j X^j$ and $P_y = \sum_{j < 2^d} y_j X^j$, and let $x', y' \in \mathbb{C}^N$
be their zero paddings to length $N$ ($x'_j = x_j$ for $j < 2^d$ and $x'_j = 0$ otherwise, and
likewise for $y'$), with indices of $x'$ and $y'$ read modulo $N$. Then for every $k < N$, the
coefficient of $X^k$ in $P_x P_y$ equals

$$\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}} x'_j \, y'_{k - j}.$$

articles.title: Zero padding fills the second half with zeros
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type with a zero, let $d$
be a natural number and let $x$ be a vector of length $2^d$ over $R$. For every index $i$ with
$2^d \le i < 2^{d+1}$, entry $i$ of the zero-padded vector of length $2^{d+1}$ produced from
$x$ is $0$.

articles.title: Zero padding keeps the input prefix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type with a zero, let $d$ be a natural
number and let $x$ be a vector of length $2^d$ over $R$. For every index $i < 2^d$, entry $i$
of the zero-padded vector of length $2^{d+1}$ produced from $x$ equals $x_i$.

articles.title: Zero padding to twice the length
articles.statement:
For a type $R$ with a zero, a natural number $d$ and a
vector $x$ of length $2^d$ over $R$, padding returns the vector of length $2^{d+1}$ whose $i$-th
entry is $x_i$ for $i < 2^d$ and $0$ for $2^d \le i < 2^{d+1}$, and charges $3 \cdot 2^d$ time
units.

articles.title: Entries of the pointwise product
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type with a multiplication, let $n$ be a
natural number and let $x$ and $y$ be vectors of length $n$ over $R$. For every index $i < n$,
entry $i$ of the pointwise product of $x$ and $y$ equals $x_i y_i$.

articles.title: Timed pointwise product
articles.statement:
For a type $R$ with a multiplication and vectors $x, y$ of
length $n$ over $R$, the pointwise product returns the vector of length $n$ whose $i$-th entry
is $x_i \cdot y_i$ for every $i < n$, and charges $4n$ time units: two reads, one multiplication
and one write per entry.

articles.title: Coefficients of the polynomial of a vector
articles.statement:
For every vector
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and every natural number $k$, the coefficient of
$X^k$ in the polynomial of $x$ is $x_k$ if $k < n$ and $0$ if $k \ge n$.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution returns the product polynomial (Princeton sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$,
write $P_x = \sum_{j < 2^d} x_j X^j$ and $P_y = \sum_{j < 2^d} y_j X^j$, and let
$z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
which pads both vectors with zeros to length $N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then
$\sum_{k < N} z_k X^k = P_x P_y$ as polynomials over $\mathbb{C}$.

articles.title: FFT linear convolution returns the product polynomial (MIT/CLRS sign)
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
natural number, $N = 2^{d+1}$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$. For vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$,
write $P_x = \sum_{j < 2^d} x_j X^j$ and $P_y = \sum_{j < 2^d} y_j X^j$, and let
$z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ be the output of the FFT linear convolution of $x$ and $y$ with root $\omega$,
which pads both vectors with zeros to length $N$ and convolves them circularly by FFT. Then
$\sum_{k < N} z_k X^k = P_x P_y$ as polynomials over $\mathbb{C}$.

articles.title: Zero padding preserves the polynomial
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$ and every vector
$x \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$, the zero padding of $x$ (the vector of length $2^{d+1}$ whose first
$2^d$ entries are those of $x$ and whose remaining entries are $0$) has the same polynomial
as $x$.

articles.title: Coefficients of a product beyond twice the length vanish
articles.statement:
For all vectors
$x, y \in \mathbb{C}^n$ and every natural number $k \ge 2n$, the coefficient of $X^k$ in the
product of the polynomials of $x$ and $y$ is $0$.

articles.title: Coefficients of a product of vector polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^n$, and set
$x_i = y_i = 0$ for $i \ge n$. For every natural number $k$, the coefficient of $X^k$ in the
product of the polynomials of $x$ and $y$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{k} x_j y_{k-j}$.

articles.title: The last coefficient of a doubled-length product vanishes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d$
and all vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{C}^{2^d}$, the coefficient of $X^{2 \cdot 2^d - 1}$ in the
product of the polynomials of $x$ and $y$ is $0$.

articles.title: Polynomial of a coefficient vector
articles.statement:
The polynomial of a vector
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^n$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j X^j \in \mathbb{C}[X]$, the
complex polynomial whose coefficient of $X^j$ is $x_j$ for $j < n$ and $0$ for $j \ge n$.

articles.title: High half of the FFT butterfly recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural
number, $\omega \in R$ and $x \in R^{2^{d+1}}$, with entries indexed from $0$. Let
$e, o \in R^{2^d}$ be the even- and odd-indexed subsequences of $x$ returned by the FFT split,
and let $E$ and $O$ be the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d$ with root
$\omega \cdot \omega$ on $e$ and on $o$. Then for every $k < 2^d$, entry $k + 2^d$ of the
vector returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d + 1$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ equals
$E_k - \omega^k O_k$.

articles.title: Low half of the FFT butterfly recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural
number, $\omega \in R$ and $x \in R^{2^{d+1}}$, with entries indexed from $0$. Let
$e, o \in R^{2^d}$ be the even- and odd-indexed subsequences of $x$ returned by the FFT split,
and let $E$ and $O$ be the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d$ with root
$\omega \cdot \omega$ on $e$ and on $o$. Then for every $k < 2^d$, entry $k$ of the vector
returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d + 1$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ equals
$E_k + \omega^k O_k$.

articles.title: The FFT of depth zero returns its input
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every
$\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^0}$, the vector returned by the radix-two FFT of
depth $0$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ is $x$ itself.

articles.title: Charged entrywise scaling
articles.statement:
For a type with a multiplication, a scalar $c$ and a vector
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ of length $n$ over it, this costed computation returns
$(c x_0, \dots, c x_{n-1})$ and charges $3n$ operations: one read, one multiplication and one
write per entry.

articles.title: The FFT split extracts the even-indexed entries
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type, $m$ a natural number
and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ a vector of length $2m$ over $R$. For every $k < m$, entry $k$
of the first (even) vector returned by the FFT split of $x$ is $x_{2k}$.

articles.title: The FFT split extracts the odd-indexed entries
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type, $m$ a natural number
and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ a vector of length $2m$ over $R$. For every $k < m$, entry $k$
of the second (odd) vector returned by the FFT split of $x$ is $x_{2k+1}$.

articles.title: Cost of the FFT even/odd split
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$ and every vector $x$ of length
$2m$, splitting $x$ into its even-indexed and its odd-indexed subsequences costs exactly $4m$
charged operations: two reads and two writes for each of the $m$ even/odd pairs.

articles.title: Even–odd split for the FFT
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, a natural number $m$ and a vector
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1}) \in R^{2m}$, the split returns the pair of vectors
$(x_0, x_2, \dots, x_{2m-2})$ and $(x_1, x_3, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ in $R^m$ of the entries of $x$ at
even and at odd indices, in order, at a time cost of $4m$ (the charged reads and writes).

articles.title: The radix-two FFT with root $e^{-2\pi i/n}$ computes the DFT
articles.statement:
Let $n = 2^d$ and let
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ be complex numbers, indexed by $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Run the radix-two
FFT on $x$ with sample root $\omega = e^{-2\pi i/n}$, the value at $-1$ of the standard additive
character of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then for every $k < n$, entry $k$ of the returned vector
equals the discrete Fourier transform coefficient
$\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}} e^{-2\pi i jk/n} x_j$.

articles.title: The radix-two FFT with root $e^{2\pi i/n}$, divided by $n$, computes the inverse DFT
articles.statement:
Let
$n = 2^d$ and let $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ be complex numbers, indexed by $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
Run the radix-two FFT on $x$ with sample root $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, the value at $1$ of the
standard additive character of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Then for every $k < n$, entry $k$ of
the returned vector multiplied by $1/n$ equals the inverse discrete Fourier transform coefficient
$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}} e^{2\pi i jk/n} x_j$.

articles.title: Exact cost of the radix-two FFT in terms of the input length
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x$ over $R$ of length
$n = 2^d$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs $T$ charged operations, where
$T + 1 = (7 \log_2 n + 1) \cdot n$.

articles.title: Exact cost of the radix-two FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number
$d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root
$\omega$ costs $T$ charged operations, where $T + 1 = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d$; that is,
$T = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d - 1$.

The count includes the charged reads and writes of the even/odd splits and the writes that
initialize each output vector.

articles.title: Cost bound for the radix-two FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number
$d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root
$\omega$ costs at most $8 \cdot 2^d \cdot d$ charged operations, that is, at most eight per entry
per recursion level.

articles.title: Radix-two fast Fourier transform
articles.statement:
For a commutative ring $R$, a natural number $d$, an
element $\omega \in R$ and a vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ is defined
by recursion on $d$. For $d = 0$ it returns $x$ at cost $0$. For $d + 1$ it splits $x$ into its
even- and odd-indexed subvectors $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ (cost $4 \cdot 2^d$), computes $\omega^2$
(cost $1$), computes the FFTs $q$ of $e$ and $r$ of $o$ with root $\omega^2$, writes a zero vector
$y \in R^{2^{d+1}}$ (cost $2^{d+1}$), and returns the vector part of the result of the butterfly
pass with $\omega$, $q$ and $r$ on $y$. Its time cost is the sum of the costs of all these steps.

The two transformed halves are stored once and combined with a running twiddle factor. No
assumption on $\omega$ is needed to run the algorithm; one is needed only for its correctness.

articles.title: Correctness of the inverse FFT
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$, let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ be a primitive
$N$-th root of unity and let $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$. For every $k < N$, entry $k$ of the output of
the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ equals $N^{-1}$ times the discrete Fourier sum
of length $N$ with root $\overline{\omega}$ at frequency $k$ of the sequence $j \mapsto x_j$ (set
to $0$ for $j \ge N$), that is, $N^{-1} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \overline{\omega}^{jk} x_j$.

articles.title: Inverse FFT after FFT is the identity at the negative-sign root
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$ and let
$\omega = e^{-2\pi i/N}$, the value at $-1$ of the standard additive character of
$\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For every $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, running the FFT procedure on $x$ with
root $\omega$ and then the inverse FFT procedure on its output with root $\omega$ returns $x$.

articles.title: Inverse FFT after FFT at the positive root is the identity
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number,
$N = 2^d$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$. For every vector $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, running the
radix-two FFT with root $\omega$ on $x$ and then the inverse FFT with root $\omega$ on its output
returns $x$.

articles.title: The inverse FFT is a normalized FFT at the conjugate root
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$, let
$\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ be a primitive $N$-th root of unity and let $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$. The
output of the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ is the output of the FFT procedure
on $x$ with root $\overline{\omega}$ with every entry multiplied by $N^{-1}$.

articles.title: Inverse FFT at the negative-sign root computes the inverse DFT
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$ and
$x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, and run the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $e^{-2\pi i/N}$, the value
at $-1$ of the standard additive character of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For every $k < N$, entry $k$
of its output equals the canonical inverse discrete Fourier transform of the function on
$\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ sending the class of $j < N$ to $x_j$, evaluated at the class of $k$;
that is, it equals $N^{-1} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} e^{2\pi i jk/N} x_j$.

articles.title: Inverse FFT at the positive-sign root computes the normalized forward DFT
articles.statement:
Let $N = 2^d$
and $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$, and run the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $e^{2\pi i/N}$, the
value at $1$ of the standard additive character of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. For every $k < N$,
entry $k$ of its output equals $N^{-1}$ times the canonical discrete Fourier transform of the
function on $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ sending the class of $j < N$ to $x_j$, evaluated at the class
of $k$; that is, it equals $N^{-1} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} e^{-2\pi i jk/N} x_j$.

articles.title: Exact operation count of the inverse FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star ring structure,
let $d$ be a natural number, $N = 2^d$, $\omega \in R$ arbitrary and $x \in R^N$. The number $T$ of
operations charged by the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ satisfies
$T + 1 = (7d + 10) \cdot 2^d + 1$, equivalently $T = (7d + 10) \cdot 2^d$.

Beyond the FFT, the two conjugation passes and the scaling pass each charge $3N$ operations and
computing $1/N$ charges one, for $9N + 1$ in total.

articles.title: Operation bound for the inverse FFT
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field with a star ring structure, let
$d$ be a natural number, $N = 2^d$, $\omega \in R$ arbitrary and $x \in R^N$. The number of
operations charged by the inverse FFT procedure on $x$ with root $\omega$ is at most
$8 \cdot 2^d \cdot d + 9 \cdot 2^d + 1$.

articles.title: Inverse FFT by conjugation
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a field that is a star ring, with star operation
$z \mapsto \bar z$. For a natural number $d$, an element $\omega \in R$ and a vector
$x \in R^{2^d}$, the inverse FFT conjugates every entry of $x$, applies the radix-two FFT with
root $\omega$, conjugates every entry of the result, and multiplies every entry by the inverse
$(2^d)^{-1}$ of $2^d$ in $R$ (which is $0$ when $2^d = 0$ in $R$). It charges $3 \cdot 2^d$
operations for each of the two conjugation passes and for the scaling pass, one operation for
computing $(2^d)^{-1}$, and the cost of the FFT.

articles.title: Round to nearest in a bounded format
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor
function, let $p \ge 1$, and let $q_{\min}$ and $q_{\max}$ be integers. For every $x \in K$ and
every number $f$ of the binary format with $p$-bit significands and last-place exponents in
$[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, with
$p$-bit significands satisfies $|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le |f - x|$.

articles.title: Round to nearest for floating-point numbers
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a
floor function and let $p \ge 1$. For every $x \in K$ and every binary floating-point number
$f \in K$ with a $p$-bit significand (and unbounded exponent), the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of
$x$ to nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies
$|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le |f - x|$: no floating-point number is closer to $x$ than
$\mathrm{fl}(x)$.

articles.title: The relative error bound
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and
let $p$ be a natural number. For every $x \in K$, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to
nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies
$|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| \le u\,|x|$, where $u = 2^{-p}$ is the unit roundoff.

The exponent is unbounded, so the bound holds for every $x$, with no underflow or overflow.

articles.title: Bound on the rounded significand
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor
function, let $p \ge 1$, let $x \in K$ be nonzero, and let
$e = \lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$. Then
$|\operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e)| \le 2^p$, where $\operatorname{rne}$ rounds to the nearest
integer, ties to even.

Since $|x / 2^e| < 2^p$, the value $2^p$ occurs only when rounding carries into the next
binade.

articles.title: Rounding to the nearest integer is within one half
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field
with a floor function. For every $m \in K$, the integer $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ obtained by
rounding $m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even, satisfies
$|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le 1/2$.

articles.title: Rounding error bounded by the distances to neighbouring integers
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly
ordered field with a floor function. For every $m \in K$, the integer $\operatorname{rne}(m)$
obtained by rounding $m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even, satisfies
$|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le m - \lfloor m \rfloor$ and
$|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le \lfloor m \rfloor + 1 - m$.

articles.title: Round to nearest integer
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For
every $m \in K$ and every integer $k$, the integer $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ obtained by rounding
$m$ to the nearest integer, ties to even, satisfies $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| \le |k - m|$:
no integer is closer to $m$ than $\operatorname{rne}(m)$.

articles.title: Ties to even for floating-point rounding
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor
function, let $p$ be a natural number, let $x \in K$, and let $e$ be the exponent of the last
place of $x$, which is $\lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$ for $x \ne 0$. If the rounding
$\mathrm{fl}(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, with $p$-bit significands satisfies
$|\mathrm{fl}(x) - x| = 2^e / 2$, then the integer $\operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e)$, the significand
of $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ at the last place of $x$, is even.

articles.title: Ties to even for the nearest integer
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor
function, let $m \in K$, and let $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ be the integer obtained by rounding $m$
to the nearest integer, ties to even. If $|\operatorname{rne}(m) - m| = 1/2$, that is, $m$ is
halfway between two consecutive integers, then $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is even.

articles.title: The difference of floating-point numbers within a factor of two
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly
ordered field with a floor function and let $p$ be a natural number. Let $x, y \in K$ and let
$m_x, m_y, e_x, e_y$ be integers with $|m_x| < 2^p$, $|m_y| < 2^p$, $x = m_x 2^{e_x}$ and
$y = m_y 2^{e_y}$. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then there is an integer $k$ with $|k| < 2^p$ and
$x - y = k \cdot 2^{\min(e_x, e_y)}$.

articles.title: Floating-point numbers round to themselves
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$ and let $x$ be an element of a
linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $x$ is a binary floating-point number with a
$p$-bit significand, that is, $x = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$,
then rounding $x$ to nearest, ties to even, at precision $p$ returns $x$: $\mathrm{fl}_p(x) = x$.

articles.title: Floating-point subtraction is exact under Sterbenz's condition
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$ and let $x$
and $y$ be binary floating-point numbers with $p$-bit significands in a linearly ordered field
with a floor function. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then rounding $x - y$ to nearest, ties to even,
at precision $p$ returns it exactly: $\mathrm{fl}_p(x - y) = x - y$.

articles.title: The rounding error at the scale of the last place
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be an element of a linearly
ordered field with a floor function, let $p$ be a natural number, and let $e$ be the exponent of
the last place of $x$ at precision $p$. Writing $\operatorname{rne}$ for rounding to the nearest
integer with ties to even, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, at
precision $p$ has the error
$\mathrm{fl}_p(x) - x = (\operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e) - x / 2^e) \cdot 2^e$.

articles.title: Round to nearest, ties to even
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and an element $x$ of a linearly
ordered field with a floor function, let $e$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$ at precision
$p$, and let $\operatorname{rne}$ round to the nearest integer with ties to the even one. The
rounding of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, is
$\mathrm{fl}_p(x) = \operatorname{rne}(x / 2^e) \cdot 2^e$: scale $x$ so that its last place is the
units digit, round to the nearest integer with ties to even, and scale back.

articles.title: Rounding gives a floating-point number
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$. For every element $x$ of a linearly
ordered field with a floor function, the rounding $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to
even, is a binary floating-point number with a $p$-bit significand: $\mathrm{fl}_p(x) = m \cdot 2^e$
for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$.

articles.title: In the normal range, rounding stays in the format
articles.statement:
Let $p \ge 1$, let $q_{\min}$ and
$q_{\max}$ be integers, and let $x$ be an element of a linearly ordered field with a floor
function. If $2^{q_{\min} + p - 1} \le |x|$ ($x$ is at least the smallest normal number) and
$|x| \le (2^p - 1) \cdot 2^{q_{\max}}$ ($x$ is at most the largest finite number), then the
rounding $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ of $x$ to nearest, ties to even, is a number of the binary format
with $p$-bit significands whose last place has exponent in $[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$.

Since $\mathrm{fl}_p(x)$ is also a nearest number of the format to $x$, with relative error at
most $2^{-p}$, rounding in the format in the normal range is the nearest-even rounding.

articles.title: Sterbenz's lemma in a bounded format
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number, let $q_{\min}$ and
$q_{\max}$ be integers, and let $x$ and $y$ be numbers of the binary format with $p$-bit
significands whose last place has exponent in $[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$ (subnormal numbers
included), in a linearly ordered field with a floor function. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then
$x - y$ is also a number of this format.

articles.title: Floating-point numbers of a bounded format
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ and integers
$q_{\min}$ and $q_{\max}$, an element $x$ of a linearly ordered field with a floor function is a
number of the binary format with $p$-bit significands and last-place exponents in
$[q_{\min}, q_{\max}]$ when $x = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$ and
$q_{\min} \le e \le q_{\max}$. These are zero, the subnormal numbers and the normal numbers of
the format.

In IEEE 754 terms, $q_{\min} = e_{\min} - p + 1$ and $q_{\max} = e_{\max} - p + 1$.

articles.title: Sterbenz's lemma
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number and let $x$ and $y$ be binary floating-point
numbers with $p$-bit significands (and unbounded exponent) in a linearly ordered field with a
floor function. If $y / 2 \le x \le 2y$, then $x - y$ is also a binary floating-point number
with a $p$-bit significand.

articles.title: Binary floating-point numbers
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, an element $x$ of a linearly
ordered field with a floor function is a binary floating-point number with a $p$-bit significand
and unbounded exponent when $x = m \cdot 2^e$ for some integers $m$ and $e$ with $|m| < 2^p$.

articles.title: Rounding to nearest preserves integer lower bounds
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field
with a floor function, let $m \in K$ and let $k$ be an integer. If $k \le m$, then
$k \le \operatorname{rne}(m)$, where $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is $m$ rounded to the nearest
integer with ties to even.

articles.title: Rounding to nearest preserves integer upper bounds
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field
with a floor function, let $m \in K$ and let $k$ be an integer. If $m \le k$, then
$\operatorname{rne}(m) \le k$, where $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is $m$ rounded to the nearest
integer with ties to even.

articles.title: Nearest-integer rounding with ties to even
articles.statement:
For $m$ in a linearly ordered field $K$ with a
floor function, $\operatorname{rne}(m)$ is the integer $\lfloor m \rfloor$ if
$m - \lfloor m \rfloor < 1/2$, the integer $\lfloor m \rfloor + 1$ if
$m - \lfloor m \rfloor > 1/2$, and, when $m - \lfloor m \rfloor = 1/2$, whichever of
$\lfloor m \rfloor$ and $\lfloor m \rfloor + 1$ is even.

articles.title: Bounds on the scaled significand
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor
function, let $p \ge 1$ be a natural number and let $x \in K$ be nonzero. Let
$e = \lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$ be the exponent of the last place of $x$ for
$p$-bit significands. Then $2^{p-1} \le |x / 2^e|$ and $|x / 2^e| < 2^p$.

articles.title: Exponent of the last place
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$ (the significand length) and $x$ in a
linearly ordered field $K$ with a floor function, the exponent of the last place of $x$ is the
integer $\lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor - (p - 1)$. Here $\lfloor \log_2 |x| \rfloor$ is the integer
logarithm: the largest integer $n$ with $2^n \le |x|$ when $x \ne 0$, and $0$ when $x = 0$.

articles.title: Horner evaluation of the empty coefficient list
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$
and every $x \in R$, Horner evaluation at $x$ with no coefficients ($n = 0$) returns $0$
and charges $0$ operations.

articles.title: Horner evaluation is polynomial evaluation
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$,
every $x \in R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$, the value returned by Horner
evaluation of $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ at $x$ equals $p(x)$, where
$p = a_0 + a_1 X + \dots + a_{n-1} X^{n-1} \in R[X]$ is the polynomial with these
coefficients.

articles.title: Horner evaluation computes the coefficient sum
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$,
every $x \in R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$, the value returned by Horner
evaluation of $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ at $x$ is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i x^i$.

articles.title: Horner evaluation of a constant polynomial
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$,
every $x \in R$ and every single coefficient $a_0 \in R$ ($n = 1$), Horner evaluation of
$a_0$ at $x$ returns $a_0$ and charges $2$ operations.

The two operations are the multiplication $x \cdot 0$ and the addition $a_0 + x \cdot 0$,
which are executed because the accumulator starts at zero.

articles.title: Horner evaluation uses $2n$ operations
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$, every
$x \in R$ and all coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$, Horner evaluation of
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ at $x$ charges exactly $2n$ operations, one multiplication and one
addition per coefficient.

articles.title: Horner evaluation at zero
articles.statement:
For every commutative semiring $R$ and all coefficients
$a_0, \dots, a_n \in R$ (at least one coefficient), the value returned by Horner evaluation
of $a_0, \dots, a_n$ at $x = 0$ is $a_0$.

articles.title: Horner evaluation with operation count
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let
$x \in R$, and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in R$ be coefficients listed in ascending order of
degree. Horner evaluation starts with the accumulator $v = 0$ and, for $i = n-1, \dots, 0$
in turn, replaces $v$ by $a_i + x v$, charging two operations (one multiplication and one
addition) for each step. It returns the final accumulator together with the total number of
operations charged, a natural number.

articles.title: The $n^{\log_2 3}$ bound for the Karatsuba cost recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost
recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$. For
every natural number $n \ge 1$, $T(n) \le 9\, n^{\log_2 3}$.

articles.title: Power-of-three bound on the Karatsuba cost recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost
recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$, and
let $\ell(n)$ be the least natural number $k$ with $n \le 2^k$ (so
$\ell(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for $n \ge 1$). For every natural number $n$,
$T(n) \le 3^{\ell(n) + 1}$.

The proof pads $n$ up to the next power of two.

articles.title: Karatsuba cost at powers of two
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for
$n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$. For every natural number $k$,
$T(2^k) + 2^{k+1} = 3^{k+1}$.

So at $n = 2^k$ digits the cost is exactly $3^{k+1} - 2^{k+1} = 3\, n^{\log_2 3} - 2n$.

articles.title: Karatsuba cost recurrence
articles.statement:
The function $T$ on natural numbers defined by $T(n) = 1$ for
$n \le 1$ and $T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$.

It is the cost of Karatsuba multiplication on $n$ digits: one unit for a product of single
digits, and for $n \ge 2$ three recursive calls on $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ digits plus $n$ units of
linear digit work.

articles.title: Karatsuba's middle coefficient
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a, b, c, d$, write
$P = |a - b| \cdot |c - d|$. If $b \le a$ holds exactly when $d \le c$, then
$ac + bd - P = ad + bc$, where the subtraction is truncated at $0$; otherwise
$ac + bd + P = ad + bc$.

So the cross term $ad + bc$ is recovered from the three products $ac$, $bd$ and $P$.

articles.title: Size bound for Karatsuba's recursive operands
articles.statement:
Let $B \ge 1$ and $n$ be natural numbers,
let $m = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, and let $x < B^n$ be a natural number. Then the high part
$\lfloor x / B^m \rfloor$, the low part $x \bmod B^m$, and their distance
$|\lfloor x / B^m \rfloor - x \bmod B^m|$ are all less than $B^m$.

Applied to both inputs, all six recursive operands stay within the digit model, and the base case
multiplies single digits.

articles.title: Correctness of Karatsuba multiplication
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$,
Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ returns $xy$.

The inputs need not be below $B^n$: the digit count only steers the recursion.

articles.title: The $n^{\log_2 3}$ bound for Karatsuba multiplication
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $B$, $x$,
$y$ and $n \ge 1$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in
base $B$ is at most $9\, n^{\log_2 3}$.

articles.title: Power-of-three bound on the cost of Karatsuba multiplication
articles.statement:
Let $\ell(n)$ be the least
natural number $k$ with $n \le 2^k$ (so $\ell(n) = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for $n \ge 1$). For all
natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, the cost of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as
$n$-digit numbers in base $B$ is at most $3^{\ell(n) + 1}$.

articles.title: Cost of Karatsuba multiplication
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $B$, $n$, $x$ and $y$, the cost
of Karatsuba multiplication of $x$ and $y$ as $n$-digit numbers in base $B$ equals $T(n)$, where
$T$ is the Karatsuba cost recurrence, $T(n) = 1$ for $n \le 1$ and
$T(n) = 3\,T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + n$ for $n \ge 2$.

In particular the cost depends only on the digit count $n$, not on $B$, $x$ or $y$.

articles.title: Karatsuba multiplication
articles.statement:
Karatsuba's algorithm on natural numbers $x$ and $y$, viewed as
$n$-digit numbers in base $B$, as a computation that returns a natural number together with a
cost. If $n \le 1$, it returns $xy$ at cost $1$. If $n \ge 2$, let $m = \lceil n/2 \rceil$, let
$a$ and $b$ be the natural-number quotient and remainder of $x$ by $B^m$, and let $c$ and $d$ be
those of $y$ by $B^m$. It runs itself with digit count $m$ on the pairs $(a, c)$, $(b, d)$ and
$(|a - b|, |c - d|)$, with results $e$, $f$ and $g$, and returns $B^{2m} e + B^m h + f$, where
$h = e + f - g$ (subtraction truncated at $0$) if $b \le a$ holds exactly when $d \le c$, and
$h = e + f + g$ otherwise. The cost of the call is $n$ plus the costs of the three recursive
calls.

articles.title: Square matrix accumulation computes $C + AB$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a commutative additive
monoid with a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$, stored
as vectors of rows. The matrix returned by square matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals
$C + AB$, where $AB$ is the matrix product, $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k < n} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.

articles.title: Operation count of square matrix accumulation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition
and a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$. Square matrix
accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ has cost $(n^3, n^3)$: it charges exactly $n^3$ scalar
multiplications and exactly $n^3$ scalar additions.

articles.title: Square matrix accumulation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a multiplication,
and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. Square
matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ is rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ with all
three dimensions equal to $n$: it adds $AB$ to the accumulator $C$ and returns the result with
its cost pair (scalar multiplications, scalar additions).

articles.title: Entries of rectangular matrix accumulation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a commutative additive monoid
with a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and $p \times r$
matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. For all $i < p$ and $j < r$, the $(i, j)$ entry
of the matrix returned by rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ is
$C_{ij} + \sum_{k < q} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.

articles.title: Rectangular matrix accumulation computes $C + AB$
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a commutative additive
monoid with a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and $p \times r$
matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. The matrix returned by rectangular matrix
accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the matrix product,
$(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k < q} A_{ik} B_{kj}$.

articles.title: Operation count of rectangular matrix accumulation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with an
addition and a multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and
$p \times r$ matrices over $\alpha$. Rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ has cost
$(pqr, pqr)$: it charges exactly $pqr$ scalar multiplications and exactly $pqr$ scalar
additions.

articles.title: Rectangular matrix accumulation with zero inner dimension
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with an
addition and a multiplication. If $A$ is a $p \times 0$ matrix, $B$ a $0 \times r$ matrix and $C$
a $p \times r$ matrix over $\alpha$, then rectangular matrix accumulation on $A$, $B$, $C$ returns
$C$ unchanged at cost $(0, 0)$.

articles.title: Rectangular matrix accumulation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a
multiplication, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $p \times q$, $q \times r$ and $p \times r$ matrices over
$\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. Rectangular matrix accumulation adds the product $AB$ to the
accumulator $C$: for $i < p$, then $j < r$, then $k < q$, each in increasing order, it replaces
$C_{ij}$ by $C_{ij} + A_{ik} B_{kj}$. It returns the final matrix together with a cost pair
(scalar multiplications, scalar additions), charging one of each for every such update.

articles.title: Entries of the recursive matrix multiply-accumulate
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a multiplication, let $k$ be a natural number and $n = 2^k$, and let
$A = (a_{ij})$, $B = (b_{ij})$, $C = (c_{ij})$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$, with
indices running from $0$ to $n - 1$. For all indices $i, j < n$, entry $(i, j)$ of the matrix
returned by the recursive multiply-accumulate procedure on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals
$c_{ij} + \sum_{t < n} a_{it} b_{tj}$.

articles.title: Correctness of the recursive matrix multiply-accumulate
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a multiplication, let $k$ be a natural number and $n = 2^k$, and let
$A = (a_{ij})$, $B = (b_{ij})$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$, with indices running
from $0$ to $n - 1$. Viewed as a matrix, the result returned by the recursive multiply-accumulate
procedure on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the matrix product with entries
$(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{t < n} a_{it} b_{tj}$.

articles.title: Operation count of the recursive matrix multiply-accumulate
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with
an addition and a multiplication, let $k$ be a natural number and $n = 2^k$, and let $A$, $B$,
$C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\alpha$. The recursive multiply-accumulate procedure on $A$,
$B$, $C$ performs exactly $8^k$ scalar multiplications and exactly $8^k$ accumulator additions.
Since $8^k = n^3$, each count is the cube of the dimension.

Calls, indexing and allocation are uncharged.

articles.title: Recursive matrix multiply-accumulate
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with an addition and a
multiplication, let $k$ be a natural number and $n = 2^k$, and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$
matrices over $\alpha$, stored as vectors of rows. The procedure adds the product of $A$ and $B$
to the accumulator $C$ by the eight-call recursion of CLRS. When $n = 1$, writing $a$, $b$, $c$
for the single entries of $A$, $B$, $C$, it replaces $c$ by $c + ab$. Otherwise it splits each
matrix $M$ into four $(n/2) \times (n/2)$ quadrants $M_{11}$ (top left), $M_{12}$ (top right),
$M_{21}$ (bottom left) and $M_{22}$ (bottom right), and updates, in this order,
$C_{11} \gets C_{11} + A_{11} B_{11}$, $C_{12} \gets C_{12} + A_{11} B_{12}$,
$C_{21} \gets C_{21} + A_{21} B_{11}$, $C_{22} \gets C_{22} + A_{21} B_{12}$, then
$C_{11} \gets C_{11} + A_{12} B_{21}$, $C_{12} \gets C_{12} + A_{12} B_{22}$,
$C_{21} \gets C_{21} + A_{22} B_{21}$, $C_{22} \gets C_{22} + A_{22} B_{22}$, each by a
recursive call on the accumulator left by the previous one. It returns the final accumulator
together with two counters: the number of scalar multiplications and the number of accumulator
additions.

Only these two operations are charged; calls, indexing and allocation are free.

articles.title: Quarter error bound for Miller–Rabin with several bases
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be odd and not
prime, and let $s$ be a natural number. Among the $(n - 1)^s$ lists $(b_1, \dots, b_s)$ of bases
with $0 < b_i < n$, at most $\lfloor (n - 1)/4 \rfloor^s$ make the Miller–Rabin test of $n$ with
bases $b_1, \dots, b_s$ answer *prime*.

With uniformly random bases the error probability is therefore at most $4^{-s}$.

articles.title: Half error bound for Miller–Rabin with several bases
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime,
and let $s$ be a natural number. Among the $(n - 1)^s$ lists $(b_1, \dots, b_s)$ of bases with
$0 < b_i < n$, at most $((n - 1)/2)^s$ make the Miller–Rabin test of $n$ with bases
$b_1, \dots, b_s$ answer *prime*.

With uniformly random bases the error probability is therefore at most $2^{-s}$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 31.39, in counting form.

articles.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses for a Carmichael number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a Carmichael
number: $n > 2$, $n$ is not prime, and $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $b$ coprime to $n$.
Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

The proof shows that the non-witnesses lie in a proper subgroup of
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 31.38, case 2.

articles.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$,
and suppose some $x$ coprime to $n$ has $x^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$
of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

The proof shows that the non-witnesses lie in the proper subgroup $\{y : y^{n-1} = 1\}$ of
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$.

articles.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses for a Carmichael number
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a
Carmichael number: $n > 2$, $n$ is not prime, and $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $b$
coprime to $n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for
$n$.

The proof splits $n$ into three pairwise coprime factors greater than $1$ and finds four distinct
cosets of a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ that holds the non-witnesses.

articles.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test and the modulus is not a prime power
articles.statement:
**At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test and the
modulus is not a prime power.** Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and not of the form $p^e$ with
$p$ prime and $e \ge 2$. Suppose some $z$ coprime to $n$ has $z^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Then
at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

articles.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses for an odd prime power
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
and $k \ge 2$ with $p^k$ odd. Then at most $(p^k - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, p^k - 1$ are
non-witnesses for $p^k$.

The proof shows that there are at most $p - 1$ non-witnesses: they satisfy
$a^{p^k - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^k}$, and two of them that agree modulo $p$ agree modulo $p^k$.

articles.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime. Then
at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$, so one uniformly
random base fails to expose $n$ as composite with probability at most $1/4$.

articles.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime. Then at most
$(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$; equivalently, at least
$(n - 1)/2$ of them are witnesses to the compositeness of $n$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 31.38.

articles.title: Non-witnesses pass Fermat's test and are units
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ and let $a$ be a natural number
such that the witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false. Then $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$
and $a$ is coprime to $n$.

articles.title: Miller–Rabin answers prime exactly when no base is a witness
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$n$ and every list of bases, the Miller–Rabin test on $n$ with these bases answers *prime* if and
only if, for every base $a$ in the list, the witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false,
that is, $a$ is not a witness to the compositeness of $n$.

articles.title: The Miller–Rabin test never rejects a prime when its bases lie in range
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a
prime. For every list of bases $a_1, \dots, a_s$ (possibly empty) with $0 < a_i < n$ for each
$i$, the Miller–Rabin test run on $n$ with these bases answers *prime*.

articles.title: The Miller–Rabin test
articles.statement:
Given a natural number $n$ and a list of bases
$a_1, \dots, a_s$, the test runs the witness test for $n$ on each base in turn. It answers
*composite* as soon as some base $a_i$ is a witness to the compositeness of $n$, and *prime* if
none is (in particular on the empty list). Its cost is the sum of the costs of the witness tests
it runs.

This is CLRS `MILLER-RABIN(n, s)` with the bases given explicitly instead of drawn by
`RANDOM(1, n - 1)`. A *composite* answer is guaranteed correct only when every base lies in
$1, \dots, n - 1$.

articles.title: Non-witnesses of a number
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the non-witnesses of $n$ form the
finite set of bases $a$ with $0 < a < n$ for which the Miller–Rabin witness test
$\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, that is, the bases that do not witness the compositeness
of $n$.

articles.title: With bases in range, a composite answer of the Miller–Rabin test is correct
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be
a natural number and $a_1, \dots, a_s$ a list of bases with $0 < a_i < n$ for each $i$. If the
Miller–Rabin test run on $n$ with these bases answers *composite*, then $n$ is not prime.

articles.title: A Miller–Rabin witness in range proves compositeness
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $a$ be natural numbers
with $0 < a < n$. If the witness test reports $a$ as a witness to the compositeness of $n$, then
$n$ is not prime.

articles.title: Splitting off the power of two
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m > 0$, the two-adic split of $m$
is the pair $(t, u)$ of natural numbers with $m = 2^t u$ and $u$ odd. For $m = 0$ it is
$(0, 0)$.

articles.title: What a non-witness satisfies
articles.statement:
Let $n > 1$ and write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd. If $a$ is
a natural number for which the Miller–Rabin witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false,
then $a^u \equiv 1 \pmod n$, or $a^{2^i u} \equiv -1 \pmod n$ for some $i < t$.

articles.title: A prime has no Miller–Rabin witnesses in range
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a prime and $a$ a natural
number with $0 < a < n$. Then the witness test does not report $a$ as a witness to the
compositeness of $n$.

## Sources

- CLRS Section 31.8.

articles.title: When the squaring loop finds no witness
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with
$x < n$. If the Miller–Rabin squaring loop modulo $n$, started at $x$ with $k$ squarings to
perform, reports no witness, then $x = 1$ or $x^{2^i} \equiv -1 \pmod n$ for some $i < k$.

articles.title: The squaring loop modulo a prime finds no witness when it ends at 1
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime
and let $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $x < p$ and $x^{2^k} \bmod p = 1$. Then the squaring
loop modulo $p$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining reports no witness.

articles.title: The squaring loop reports a witness when it does not end at 1
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $k$ and $x$ be
natural numbers with $n > 0$, $x < n$ and $x^{2^k} \bmod n \ne 1$. Then the squaring loop modulo
$n$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining reports a witness.

articles.title: Cost bound for the Miller–Rabin squaring loop
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$, $k$ and $x$,
the cost of the squaring loop modulo $n$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining is at most
$k$.

articles.title: The Miller–Rabin squaring loop
articles.statement:
Fix a modulus $n$. With no squarings remaining, the loop
at the current value $x$ reports a witness exactly when $x \ne 1$, at no cost. With $k + 1$
squarings remaining, it costs one modular multiplication and computes $y = x^2 \bmod n$; it
reports a witness if $y = 1$, $x \ne 1$ and $x \ne n - 1$, and otherwise continues at $y$ with
$k$ squarings remaining.

Here $x^2 \bmod 0 = x^2$, and $n - 1$ is $0$ when $n = 0$.

articles.title: Fermat witnesses are Miller–Rabin witnesses
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $n$ be natural numbers with
$n > 1$. If $a^{n-1} \bmod n \ne 1$, that is, $a^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, then the Miller–Rabin
witness test on base $a$ and modulus $n$ returns true.

articles.title: Cost of the Miller–Rabin witness test
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, write
$n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd (here $n - 1$ is truncated at $0$, and $t = u = 0$ when $n \le 1$).
The cost of the witness test on base $a$ and modulus $n$ is at most the cost of the modular
exponentiation of $a$ to the power $u$ modulo $n$ plus $t$: at most one multiplication for each
of the $t$ squarings.

articles.title: Miller–Rabin witness test
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$
odd (here $n - 1$ is truncated at $0$, and $t = u = 0$ when $n \le 1$). The test sets $x_0$ to the
result of modular exponentiation of $a$ to the power $u$ modulo $n$, which is $a^u \bmod n$ when
$u > 0$ and $1$ when $u = 0$. For $i = 1, \dots, t$ it computes $x_i = x_{i-1}^2 \bmod n$ and
returns true as soon as $x_i = 1$, $x_{i-1} \ne 1$ and $x_{i-1} \ne n - 1$. If no such step
occurs, it returns true exactly when $x_t \ne 1$. Its cost is the cost of the modular
exponentiation plus one for each squaring performed.

For a base with $0 < a < n$, the answer true proves that $n$ is composite; outside that range the
answer carries no such guarantee (for example, the test returns true for $a = n = 2$), as in CLRS,
whose bases are drawn from $1, \dots, n - 1$.

articles.title: Correctness of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with $b > 0$
and $n > 0$, the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and
modulus $n$ equals $a^b \bmod n$.

articles.title: Even step of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers with $b > 0$
and $b$ even. If modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b/2$ and modulus $n$ returns the
value $d$ using $t$ multiplications, then on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ it returns
the value $(d \cdot d) \bmod n$ using $t + 1$ multiplications.

articles.title: Modular exponentiation returns the least residue
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with
$b > 0$ and $n > 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$
and modulus $n$ satisfies $r = a^b \bmod n$ and $r < n$.

articles.title: Modular exponentiation returns a value below the modulus
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$,
