$n$ with $b > 0$ and $n > 0$, the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$,
exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is less than $n$.

articles.title: Odd step of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers with $b$ odd.
If modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b - 1$ and modulus $n$ returns the value $d$
using $t$ multiplications, then on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ it returns the value
$(a \cdot d) \bmod n$ using $t + 1$ multiplications.

articles.title: Value of the even step of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers
with $b > 0$ and $b$ even, and let $d$ be the value returned by modular exponentiation on base
$a$, exponent $b/2$ and modulus $n$. Then the value returned on base $a$, exponent $b$ and
modulus $n$ is $(d \cdot d) \bmod n$.

articles.title: Modular exponentiation returns a reduced value
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with
$b > 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and
modulus $n$ satisfies $r \bmod n = r$ (with the convention $r \bmod 0 = r$).

articles.title: Modular exponentiation with a reduced base
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$ with
$n > 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent $b$ and
modulus $n$ satisfies $r \bmod n = (a \bmod n)^b \bmod n$.

articles.title: Modular exponentiation is correct up to reduction
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$, $n$
with $n > 0$, including $b = 0$, the value $r$ returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$,
exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ satisfies $r \bmod n = a^b \bmod n$.

articles.title: Value of the odd step of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers
with $b$ odd, and let $d$ be the value returned by modular exponentiation on base $a$, exponent
$b - 1$ and modulus $n$. Then the value returned on base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is
$(a \cdot d) \bmod n$.

articles.title: Modular exponentiation returns 1 at exponent zero
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$,
modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ returns $1$.

In particular the returned value is $1$ even when $n = 1$, so it is not reduced modulo $n$.

articles.title: Multiplication count of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers
with $b > 0$, and let $\beta = \lfloor \log_2 b \rfloor + 1$ be the number of binary digits of $b$.
The number of multiplications performed by modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and
modulus $n$ is at least $\beta$ and at most $2\beta - 1$.

articles.title: Multiplication count in the even case
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $b$
positive and even. Modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ performs
exactly one more multiplication than it does with base $a$, exponent $b/2$ and modulus $n$.

articles.title: The multiplication count depends only on the exponent
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$, $a'$,
$b$, $n$ and $n'$, modular exponentiation performs the same number of multiplications with base
$a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ as with base $a'$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n'$.

articles.title: Multiplication count in the odd case
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $b$ odd.
Modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ performs exactly one more
multiplication than it does with base $a$, exponent $b - 1$ and modulus $n$.

articles.title: No multiplications at exponent zero
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$, modular
exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ performs no multiplications.

articles.title: Least residue at exponent zero
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$ with $n > 1$, the value
returned by modular exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ equals $a^0 \bmod n$
and is less than $n$.

articles.title: Unreduced result at modulus one
articles.statement:
For every natural number $a$, modular exponentiation with
base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $1$ returns $1$, whereas $a^0 \bmod 1 = 0$.

The base case of the CLRS procedure returns $1$ without reducing it modulo the modulus; this
boundary case keeps that visible.

articles.title: Base case of modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $a$ and $n$, modular
exponentiation with base $a$, exponent $0$ and modulus $n$ returns $1$ and performs no
multiplications.

articles.title: Modular exponentiation
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $n$, modular exponentiation with
base $a$, exponent $b$ and modulus $n$ is the recursive procedure that returns $1$ if $b = 0$. If
$b > 0$ is even, it computes the result $d$ for exponent $b/2$ (same base and modulus) and returns
$d \cdot d \bmod n$. If $b$ is odd, it computes the result $d$ for exponent $b - 1$ and returns
$a \cdot d \bmod n$. Each even or odd step performs one multiplication, and the cost of the
procedure is the total number of multiplications performed.

## Sources

- CLRS4 §31.6, printed page 934, `MODULAR-EXPONENTIATION`, with one tick per multiplication.

articles.title: The solver returns nothing exactly when $\gcd(a, n) \nmid b$
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a > 0$
and $n > 0$ and an integer $b$, the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ returns the
empty array if and only if $\gcd(a, n)$ does not divide $b$.

articles.title: Number of residues returned by the solver
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ and an
integer $b$, the output of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ has $\gcd(a, n)$
entries if $\gcd(a, n)$ divides $b$, and no entries otherwise.

articles.title: The solver returns exactly the solutions below $n$
articles.statement:
Let $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ be natural
numbers and $b$ an integer. A natural number $x$ occurs in the output of the modular linear
equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ if and only if $x < n$ and $a x \equiv b \pmod{n}$.

articles.title: The solver returns no repeated residues
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ and an
integer $b$, the entries of the output of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ are
pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Output of the modular linear equation solver
articles.statement:
Let $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ be natural numbers,
$b$ an integer, $d = \gcd(a, n)$, and $y$ the coefficient of $a$ in the Bézout identity
$d = n u + a y$ computed by the extended Euclidean algorithm on $(n, a)$. If $d \mid b$, the list
returned by the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ is $[x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{d-1}]$
with $x_i = \bigl((y \cdot (b / d)) \bmod n + i \cdot (n / d)\bigr) \bmod n$, where $r \bmod n$
denotes the least nonnegative residue of $r$; otherwise it is the empty list.

articles.title: Cost bounds for the modular linear equation solver
articles.statement:
Let $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ be natural
numbers, $b$ an integer and $d = \gcd(a, n)$, and put $c = 4 + 3d$ if $d \mid b$ and $c = 0$
otherwise. The cost $T$ of the modular linear equation solver on $a$, $b$, $n$ satisfies
$1 + c \le T \le 6(2 \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 2) + 1 + c$.

The cost counts arithmetic events, so this is the $O(\log n + \gcd(a, n))$ bound of the source.

articles.title: Modular linear equation solver
articles.statement:
Given natural numbers $a > 0$ and $n > 0$ and an integer
$b$, the solver solves $a x \equiv b \pmod{n}$ following CLRS. Let $d = \gcd(a, n)$ and let $y$ be
the coefficient of $a$ in the Bézout identity $d = n u + a y$ computed by the extended Euclidean
algorithm on $(n, a)$. If $d \mid b$, it returns the array $[x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{d-1}]$, where
$x_i = \bigl((y \cdot (b / d)) \bmod n + i \cdot (n / d)\bigr) \bmod n$ and $r \bmod n$ denotes the
least nonnegative residue of $r$; otherwise it returns the empty array.

Its cost is $6s + 1 + 4 + 3d$ when $d \mid b$ and $6s + 1$ otherwise, where $s$ is the number of
times the Euclidean algorithm, started from $(r, r') = (n, a)$, replaces $(r, r')$ by
$(r' \bmod r, r)$ before $r$ becomes $0$: six arithmetic operations per such step, one
divisibility test, four setup operations and three operations per returned residue.

articles.title: Entries of Strassen's matrix accumulator
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a non-unital, non-associative ring.
For every $k \ge 0$, all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$ and all indices
$i, j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the matrix returned by Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ is
$C_{ij} + \sum_{t} A_{it} B_{tj}$, the sum running over all $2^k$ indices $t$.

articles.title: Correctness of Strassen's matrix accumulator
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a non-unital, non-associative
ring. For every $k \ge 0$ and all $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, the matrix
returned by Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ equals $C + AB$, where $AB$ is the usual
matrix product, $(AB)_{ij} = \sum_t A_{it} B_{tj}$.

Multiplication in $R$ need not be commutative or associative.

articles.title: Operation counts of Strassen's matrix accumulator
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type with a zero, an
addition, a subtraction and a multiplication. For every $k \ge 0$ and all $2^k \times 2^k$
matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, Strassen's accumulator on $A$, $B$, $C$ performs exactly $7^k$
scalar multiplications and exactly $(25 \cdot 7^k - 22 \cdot 4^k)/3$ scalar additions and
subtractions.

This count does not charge allocation or bit operations.

articles.title: Strassen's matrix accumulator
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type with a zero, an addition, a subtraction
and a multiplication (no ring axioms are assumed). For $k \ge 0$ and $2^k \times 2^k$ matrices
$A$, $B$, $C$ over $R$, this procedure runs Strassen's seven-product recursion for adding $AB$ to
$C$. It returns a $2^k \times 2^k$ matrix together with a pair of counts: the number of scalar
multiplications and the number of scalar additions and subtractions it performs.
For $k = 0$, with $a$, $b$, $c$ the single entries of $A$, $B$, $C$, it performs one
multiplication and one addition and returns the $1 \times 1$ matrix with entry $c + ab$.
For $k + 1$, write $X_{11}, X_{12}, X_{21}, X_{22}$ for the top-left, top-right, bottom-left and
bottom-right $2^k \times 2^k$ blocks of a matrix $X$. The procedure forms, entrywise,
$S_1 = B_{12} - B_{22}$, $S_2 = A_{11} + A_{12}$, $S_3 = A_{21} + A_{22}$,
$S_4 = B_{21} - B_{11}$, $S_5 = A_{11} + A_{22}$, $S_6 = B_{11} + B_{22}$,
$S_7 = A_{12} - A_{22}$, $S_8 = B_{21} + B_{22}$, $S_9 = A_{11} - A_{21}$ and
$S_{10} = B_{11} + B_{12}$; obtains $P_1, \dots, P_7$ by seven recursive calls with the zero
matrix as accumulator on the pairs $(A_{11}, S_1)$, $(S_2, B_{22})$, $(S_3, B_{11})$,
$(A_{22}, S_4)$, $(S_5, S_6)$, $(S_7, S_8)$ and $(S_9, S_{10})$; and returns the matrix with
blocks $C_{11} + P_5 + P_4 - P_2 + P_6$, $C_{12} + P_1 + P_2$, $C_{21} + P_3 + P_4$ and
$C_{22} + P_5 + P_1 - P_3 - P_7$, each sum formed entrywise from left to right.
Each entrywise scalar addition or subtraction adds one to the second count and each base-case
multiplication adds one to the first; indexing, allocation, copying and zero-fill are uncharged.

articles.title: The approximate TSP tour is a tour
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a list of distinct vertices, and let $r$
and $F$ be such that $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest $F$ in preorder is a permutation
of $V$ (the tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ spans $V$). Then the list returned by
`APPROX-TSP-TOUR` on $r$ and $F$ is a tour of $V$: it is a permutation of $V$.

articles.title: Running time of `APPROX-TSP-TOUR`
articles.statement:
For every root $r$ and forest $F$, the running time of
`APPROX-TSP-TOUR` on $r$ and $F$ equals the length of the list of $r$ followed by the vertices of
$F$ in preorder: one unit per vertex of the returned tour.

articles.title: APPROX-TSP-TOUR on a given minimum spanning tree costs at most twice any tour
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a
cost function on vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid that is
symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Let $V$ be a
list of vertices, let the tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ be a minimum spanning tree of
$V$ for $d$, and let $H$ be a tour of $V$. Then the cost under $d$ of the closed tour returned by
`APPROX-TSP-TOUR` on $r$ and $F$ is at most twice the cost under $d$ of the closed tour $H$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 35.2.

articles.title: The APPROX-TSP-TOUR algorithm
articles.statement:
CLRS `APPROX-TSP-TOUR`, steps 3 and 4: given a root $r$
and a forest $F$ (the subtrees of a spanning tree with root $r$), return the tour that lists $r$
followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder. As a timed computation it charges one unit for $r$
and one unit for each vertex visited by the preorder walk of $F$.

articles.title: Forest of a parent array below a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $p$ assign to each vertex of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a vertex $v$, the
forest below $v$ of depth $k$ is empty when $k = 0$. For depth $k + 1$ it has one tree for each
child $c$ of $v$ (each vertex whose parent is $v$), in increasing order of $c$, namely $c$ with
the forest below $c$ of depth $k$ as its subtrees.

articles.title: Path as a forest
articles.statement:
The forest of a list $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ of vertices is the path
$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$: $x_1$ is its only top-level vertex and each $x_{i+1}$ is the only child
of $x_i$. The empty list gives the empty forest.

articles.title: Children in a parent array
articles.statement:
Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$
either a parent or nothing. The children of a vertex $v$ are the vertices $c$ whose parent
$p(c)$ is $v$, listed in increasing order.

articles.title: Complete graph as an ordered adjacency
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the complete graph on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ as a directed adjacency: the vertices are listed in increasing
order, and the neighbours of each vertex $u$ are all vertices other than $u$, in increasing
order.

articles.title: Every non-root vertex lies below the root
articles.statement:
Let $p$ assign to each vertex of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, forming a parent tree with root $r$, and let a
step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex without parent in place. Then every vertex
$u \ne r$ lies strictly below $r$, at most $n$ levels down: for some $j < n$, the vertex reached
from $u$ after $j$ steps up has parent $r$.

articles.title: Descendant within $k$ levels
articles.statement:
Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$
either a parent or nothing, and let a step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex
without parent in place. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, a vertex $u$ lies strictly below a vertex $v$,
at most $k$ levels down, when for some $j < k$ the vertex reached from $u$ after $j$ steps up has
parent $v$.

articles.title: Rooted forest in left-child right-sibling form
articles.statement:
A rooted forest with vertices in $\alpha$
is either empty, or consists of a first tree with root $v$, whose subtrees form a forest (the
children of $v$), followed by a forest of the remaining trees (the siblings of $v$).

articles.title: Metric cost function
articles.statement:
A cost function $d$ assigning to each pair of vertices a value in a
linearly ordered additive commutative monoid is metric when, for all vertices $x$, $y$, $z$, it
is symmetric, $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$, zero on the diagonal, $d(x, x) = 0$, nonnegative,
$0 \le d(x, y)$, and satisfies the triangle inequality $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$.

articles.title: Minimum spanning tree of a vertex list
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with
values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid. The tree with root $r$ and subtree
forest $F$ is a minimum spanning tree of a list $V$ of vertices for $d$ when it is a spanning tree
of $V$ (the vertices of $V$ are distinct and the list of $r$ followed by the vertices of $F$ in
preorder is a permutation of $V$) and, for every vertex $r'$ and forest $F'$ such that the tree
with root $r'$ and subtree forest $F'$ is a spanning tree of $V$, the weight of $F$ below $r$ is
at most the weight of $F'$ below $r'$.

articles.title: The forest of a parent tree spans all vertices
articles.statement:
Let $p$ assign to each vertex of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or nothing, forming a parent tree with root $r$. Then $r$
together with the forest below $r$ of depth $n$ built from $p$ is a spanning tree of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest in preorder lists every vertex
exactly once.

articles.title: Prim's forest spans all vertices
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero and a
commutative addition, let $d$ assign a weight in $W$ to each ordered pair of vertices of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $r$ be a vertex. Then $r$ together with Prim's forest for $d$ and
$r$ is a spanning tree of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$: $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest in
preorder lists every vertex exactly once.

articles.title: Rooted spanning tree of a vertex list
articles.statement:
The tree with root $r$ and subtree forest $F$ is a
spanning tree of a list $V$ of vertices when the vertices of $V$ are distinct and the list of $r$
followed by the vertices of $F$ in preorder is a permutation of $V$: the vertices of the tree are
those of $V$, each exactly once.

articles.title: Tour of a vertex list
articles.statement:
A list $H$ is a tour of a list $V$ of vertices when the vertices of
$V$ are distinct and $H$ is a permutation of $V$: $H$ lists each vertex of $V$ exactly once and
nothing else.

articles.title: Neighbours in the complete adjacency
articles.statement:
For all vertices $u, v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$,
$v$ is listed among the neighbours of $u$ in the complete graph as an ordered adjacency if and
only if $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in the complete simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is,
$u \ne v$.

articles.title: Prim's parent array is a parent tree
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero and
a commutative addition, let $d$ assign a weight in $W$ to each ordered pair of vertices of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $r$ be a vertex. Then Prim's parent array for $d$ from $r$ is a
parent tree with root $r$: $r$ has no parent, and every vertex reaches $r$ after finitely many
steps up, where a step up moves a vertex to its parent and leaves a vertex without parent in
place.

articles.title: Parent tree
articles.statement:
Let $p$ assign to each vertex of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ either a parent or
nothing, and let a step up move a vertex to its parent, leaving a vertex without parent in place.
The parent array $p$ is a parent tree with root $r$ when $r$ has no parent and every vertex
reaches $r$ after finitely many steps up.

articles.title: Shortcutting a closed walk through its base point
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the
vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero
on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For a vertex $p$ and lists
$A$, $B$ of vertices, the cost of the walk that starts at $p$, visits $A$ and then $B$ in order
and returns to $p$ is at most the cost of the walk from $p$ through $A$ back to $p$ plus the cost
of the walk from $p$ through $B$ back to $p$.

articles.title: Rerouting the end of a walk
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in a
linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero on the diagonal,
nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For vertices $v$, $p$ and a list $C$ of
vertices, the cost of the walk from $v$ through $C$ ending at $p$ is at most the cost of the walk
from $v$ through $C$ ending back at $v$, plus $d(v, p)$.

articles.title: Changing the starting vertex of a walk
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with
values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is symmetric, zero on the
diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For vertices $q$, $p$ and a list $L$
of vertices, the cost of the walk from $q$ through $L$ is at most $d(q, p)$ plus the cost of the
walk from $p$ through $L$.

articles.title: The closed preorder walk below a vertex costs at most twice the forest
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost
function on the vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid, which is
symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and satisfies the triangle inequality. For a forest
$F$ and a vertex $p$, let $w$ be the weight of $F$ hanging below $p$: the total cost of the edges
joining $p$ to the top-level vertices of $F$ and each vertex of $F$ to its children. Then the cost
of the walk that starts at $p$, visits the vertices of $F$ in preorder and returns to $p$ is at
most $w + w$.

articles.title: Cost of a walk
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the vertices with values in an additive
commutative monoid. For a vertex $x$ and a list $L = [y_1, \dots, y_n]$ of vertices, the cost of
the walk from $x$ through $L$ is $d(x, y_1) + d(y_1, y_2) + \dots + d(y_{n-1}, y_n)$, and $0$
when $L$ is empty.

articles.title: Preorder of a path
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of vertices, the preorder of the forest of $L$
(the path through the vertices of $L$ in order) is $L$ itself.

articles.title: Result of the preorder walk with an accumulator
articles.statement:
For every forest $F$ and every list $a$
of vertices, the preorder walk of $F$ with accumulator $a$ returns the vertices of $F$ in
preorder followed by $a$.

articles.title: Preorder walk with an accumulator
articles.statement:
For a forest $F$ and a list $a$ of vertices, this is the
timed computation defined as follows. On the empty forest it returns $a$ at no cost. On a forest
with first root $v$, children forest $C$ and sibling forest $S$, it charges one time unit, walks
$S$ with accumulator $a$ to get a list $b$, walks $C$ with accumulator $b$ to get a list $c$, and
returns $v$ followed by $c$. It thus returns the vertices of $F$ in preorder followed by $a$, at
one time unit per vertex of $F$.

The accumulator means no list is ever appended, so the untimed work is linear as well.

articles.title: Preorder walk
articles.statement:
For a forest $F$, the preorder walk of $F$ is the preorder walk of $F$ with
the empty list as accumulator: a timed computation that returns the vertices of $F$ in preorder,
at one time unit per vertex.

articles.title: Preorder of a forest
articles.statement:
The list of the vertices of a forest in preorder: empty for the empty
forest, and for a forest with first root $v$, children forest $C$ and sibling forest $S$, the
vertex $v$, followed by the preorder of $C$, followed by the preorder of $S$.

The preorder walk computes this list without appending lists.

articles.title: Forest of Prim's tree
articles.statement:
Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with
values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, take
Prim's parent array for $d$ and $r$ (Prim's algorithm run from $r$ on the complete graph with
edge weights $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$). This forest is the forest of the subtrees below $r$ in that
parent array, cut off $n$ levels below $r$, in left-child right-sibling form, with the children
of each vertex in vertex order.

articles.title: Prim's parent array on the complete graph
articles.statement:
Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition,
and a root $r$, this is the parent array returned by Prim's algorithm run from $r$ on the
complete graph on these vertices, with the weight of the edge $\{u, v\}$ equal to
$d(u,v) + d(v,u)$: it sends each vertex to its parent, or to no parent.

articles.title: Prim's tree is a minimum spanning tree
articles.statement:
Let $d(u,v)$ be real costs on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $r$ be a vertex, and weigh each edge $\{u, v\}$ by $d(u,v) + d(v,u)$.
Then Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a tree, and for every tree $H$ on these vertices the total
weight of the edges of Prim's tree is at most the total weight of the edges of $H$.

articles.title: Prim's tree is a spanning tree
articles.statement:
For costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$
with values in any linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and any root $r$,
Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a tree on all of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, that is, a spanning tree of
the complete graph.

articles.title: Prim's tree
articles.statement:
Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a
linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition, and a root $r$, Prim's tree is the
simple graph on these vertices in which distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when one of
them is the parent of the other in Prim's parent array for $d$ and $r$.

articles.title: The tour from Prim's tree is a tour
articles.statement:
For costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition,
and any root $r$, the list returned by APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is a
permutation of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$: it visits every vertex exactly once.

articles.title: APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree is a 2-approximation
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a real metric cost
on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (symmetric, zero on the diagonal, nonnegative, and
satisfying the triangle inequality), and let $r$ be a vertex. Then the cost of the closed tour
through the list returned by APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree for $d$ and $r$ is at most twice
the cost of the closed tour through $H$, for every list $H$ that visits each of
$0, 1, \dots, n-1$ exactly once.

This is CLRS Theorem 35.2, with the minimum spanning tree computed by Prim.

articles.title: APPROX-TSP-TOUR with Prim's tree
articles.statement:
Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with values in a linearly ordered type with a zero and commutative addition,
and a root $r$, the tour is $r$ followed by the vertices of the forest of Prim's tree below $r$
in preorder. Its running time counts one unit per vertex of the tour; running Prim's algorithm
and building the forest are not counted.

This is CLRS APPROX-TSP-TOUR, with the minimum spanning tree computed by Prim.

articles.title: Edge sums over a parent tree
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which the root $r$ has no parent and every chain of parents reaches
$r$, and let $w$ assign to each unordered pair $\{u, v\}$ of vertices (possibly $u = v$) a
value in a commutative additive monoid. Write $\hat p(u)$ for the parent of $u$, or $u$ itself
if $u$ has no parent. Then the sum of $w(e)$ over the edges $e$ of the parent graph (distinct
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent when one is the parent of the other) equals the sum of
$w(\{\hat p(u), u\})$ over the vertices $u$ of the forest built from $p$ below $r$, $n$ levels
deep, listed in preorder.

articles.title: Symmetrized edge weights
articles.statement:
Given costs $d(u,v)$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with
values in a type with commutative addition, the weight of an unordered pair $\{u, v\}$ is
$d(u,v) + d(v,u)$, which does not depend on the order of $u$ and $v$. When $d$ is symmetric this
is twice the cost, which leaves minimum spanning trees unchanged.

articles.title: The preorder tour costs at most twice the tree
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the
vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid that is symmetric, zero on
the diagonal, nonnegative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Let $T$ be a rooted tree with
root $r$, given by the forest $F$ of the subtrees of $r$, and let $w(T)$ be its weight, the total
cost of its edges. Then the closed tour that visits $r$, then the vertices of $F$ in preorder, and
returns to $r$ costs at most $2\,w(T)$.

## Sources

- CLRS Theorem 35.2, first half.

articles.title: Cost of a closed tour
articles.statement:
For a cost function $d$ on the vertices with values in an additive
commutative monoid, the cost of the closed tour that visits $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k$ in order and
returns to its first vertex is $\sum_{i=1}^{k} d(x_{i-1}, x_i) + d(x_k, x_0)$. The empty tour
costs $0$.

articles.title: One step up a parent array
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$,
assigning to each vertex $v$ either a parent $p(v)$ or no parent. Then $\operatorname{up}(v)$ is
the parent $p(v)$ when $v$ has one, and $v$ itself otherwise, so a root stays put.

articles.title: Weight of the forest built from a parent array
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a parent array on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $d$ be a cost on ordered pairs of vertices with values in an additive
commutative monoid, and let $\operatorname{up}(u)$ be the parent of $u$, or $u$ itself if $u$ has
no parent. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every vertex $v$, let $F$ be the forest of the subtrees
of the children of $v$ in $p$, cut off $k$ levels below $v$. Then the weight under $d$ of $F$
hanging below $v$ equals the sum of $d(\operatorname{up}(u), u)$ over the vertices $u$ of $F$ in
preorder.

articles.title: A minimum spanning tree costs at most any tour
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a cost function on the
vertices with values in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid that is symmetric, zero on
the diagonal, nonnegative and satisfies the triangle inequality. Let $V$ be a list of distinct
vertices. Let $T$ be a minimum spanning tree of $V$ for $d$: a rooted tree whose vertices are the
elements of $V$, each once, whose weight (the total cost of its edges) is at most that of every
such tree. Let $H$ be a tour of $V$, a list that is a permutation of $V$. Then the weight of $T$
is at most the cost of the closed tour $H$.

A tour minus its closing edge is a spanning path, which is a spanning tree.

## Sources

- CLRS Theorem 35.2, second half.

articles.title: Weight of a forest below a vertex
articles.statement:
For a cost function $d$ and a vertex $p$, the weight
of a forest hanging below $p$ is the total cost of its tree edges: each top-level vertex $v$ is
joined to $p$ by an edge of cost $d(p, v)$, and each vertex $u$ is joined to each of its children
$c$ by an edge of cost $d(u, c)$. The empty forest has weight $0$.

articles.title: Set with the least cost per new element
articles.statement:
Given a list $F$ of finite sets, a finite set $U$
and a rational cost $w(S)$ for each finite set $S$, this is the first set $S$ in $F$ with
$S \cap U \ne \emptyset$ that minimizes the ratio $w(S) / |S \cap U|$ among the sets of $F$ meeting
$U$, or nothing when no set of $F$ meets $U$.

articles.title: Greedy choice of a set
articles.statement:
Given a list $F$ of finite sets and a finite set $U$, the best set
of $F$ for $U$ is the first set $S$ in the list $F$ that maximizes $|S \cap U|$, or $\emptyset$
when $F$ is empty.

articles.title: Covering bound by intersections
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of finite sets and $T$ a finite set
such that every element of $T$ lies in some member of $L$. Then
$|T| \le \sum_{S \in L} |S \cap T|$, where the sum runs over the list $L$ with repetitions.

articles.title: Lower bound for a difference of harmonic numbers
articles.statement:
Write
$H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ for the $n$-th harmonic number, so $H(0) = 0$. For natural
numbers $d \le a \le k$, we have $\frac{d}{k} \le H(a) - H(a - d)$, where $\frac{d}{k}$ is read
as $0$ when $k = 0$.

Each of the $d$ reciprocals $\frac{1}{a - d + 1}, \dots, \frac{1}{a}$ is at least $\frac1k$.

articles.title: Harmonic bound in the universe size for greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite
sets, $U$ a finite set, and $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ the $n$-th harmonic number. For
every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets returned by the
greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $|C^*| \cdot H(|U|)$, where $|C^*|$
is the length of $C^*$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Corollary 35.5, in the stronger harmonic form.

articles.title: Greedy set cover is a logarithmic approximation
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets and $U$
a finite set. For every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets
returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most
$|C^*| \cdot (\ln |U| + 1)$, where $|C^*|$ is the length of $C^*$ and $\ln 0 = 0$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Corollary 35.5, via Mathlib's `harmonic_le_one_add_log`.

articles.title: Harmonic bound in the largest set size for greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite
sets each with at most $d$ elements, $U$ a finite set, and $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$
the $n$-th harmonic number. For every list $C^*$ of members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the
list of sets returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most
$|C^*| \cdot H(d)$, where $|C^*|$ is the length of $C^*$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 35.4.

articles.title: The greedy set cover is a cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets and $U$ a finite set
such that every element of $U$ lies in some set of $F$. Then every element of $U$ lies in some
set of the list returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$.

articles.title: Potential bound for greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set,
and $H(n) = 1 + \frac12 + \dots + \frac1n$ the $n$-th harmonic number. For every list $C^*$ of
members of $F$ that together cover $U$, the list of sets returned by the greedy set cover
algorithm on $F$ and $U$ has length at most $\sum_{S \in C^*} H(|S \cap U|)$, where the sum
runs over the list $C^*$ with repetitions.

articles.title: The greedy set cover has at most as many sets as elements
articles.statement:
For every list $F$ of finite
sets and every finite set $U$, the list returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and $U$
has length at most $|U|$.

articles.title: The greedy set cover draws its sets from the family
articles.statement:
For every list $F$ of finite sets and
every finite set $U$, every set in the list returned by the greedy set cover algorithm on $F$ and
$U$ is a member of $F$.

articles.title: Running time of greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets and $U$ a finite set.
The running time of greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ is at most
$(|U| + 1)(|F| + \sum_{S \in F} |S|)$, where $|F|$ is the length of the list and the sum runs
over the entries of $F$, counted with repetition.

There are at most $|U| + 1$ searches for a best set, each costing $|F| + \sum_{S \in F} |S|$.

articles.title: Greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F = [S_1, \dots, S_n]$ be a list of finite sets and $U$ a finite
set. The greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ is computed as follows. Let $T$ be the first $S_i$ in
the list that maximizes $|S_i \cap U|$, or $T = \emptyset$ when $n = 0$. If
$T \cap U = \emptyset$, the result is the empty list; otherwise it is $T$ followed by the greedy
set cover of $U \setminus T$ from $F$. Each step, including the last one, costs
$n + |S_1| + \dots + |S_n|$.

articles.title: Total cost of a list of sets
articles.statement:
For a function $w$ assigning a rational cost to each finite
set, the total cost of a list $C = [S_1, \dots, S_m]$ of finite sets is
$w(S_1) + \dots + w(S_m)$, a set that occurs several times in $C$ being counted each time.

articles.title: Chvátal's bound
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite set, $w$ a rational cost
function on finite sets with $w(S) \ge 0$ for every $S$ in $F$, and $d$ a natural number such that
every set in $F$ has at most $d$ elements. If $C^*$ is a list of sets from $F$ whose union contains
$U$, then the weighted greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ has total cost at most
$H(d)$ times the total cost of $C^*$, where $H(d) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \dots + \frac{1}{d}$ is the
$d$-th harmonic number.

articles.title: Potential bound for weighted greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a
finite set and $w$ a rational cost function on finite sets with $w(S) \ge 0$ for every $S$ in $F$.
If $C^*$ is a list of sets from $F$ whose union contains $U$, then the weighted greedy set cover of
$U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ has total cost at most $\sum_{S \in C^*} w(S)\, H(|S \cap U|)$, the sum
running over the entries of $C^*$ with repetition, where
$H(n) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \dots + \frac{1}{n}$ is the $n$-th harmonic number.

articles.title: The weighted greedy set cover is a cover
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a finite
set and $w$ any rational cost function on finite sets. If every element of $U$ lies in some set of
$F$, then every element of $U$ lies in some set chosen by the weighted greedy set cover of $U$ from
$F$ with costs $w$.

articles.title: The weighted greedy set cover uses sets of the family
articles.statement:
For every list $F$ of finite sets,
finite set $U$ and rational cost function $w$ on finite sets, every set chosen by the weighted
greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ belongs to $F$.

articles.title: Running time of weighted greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F = [S_1, \dots, S_m]$ be a list of finite
sets, $U$ a finite set and $w$ a rational cost function on finite sets. The weighted greedy set
cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ runs in time at most
$(|U| + 1)\,(m + |S_1| + \dots + |S_m|)$: at most $|U| + 1$ searches for a best set, each costing
$m$ plus the total size of the sets of $F$.

articles.title: Weighted greedy set cover
articles.statement:
Let $F = [S_1, \dots, S_n]$ be a list of finite sets, $U$ a
finite set and $w$ a function giving each finite set $S$ a rational cost $w(S)$. The weighted
greedy set cover of $U$ from $F$ with costs $w$ is computed as follows. If no $S_i$ meets $U$,
the result is the empty list. Otherwise let $T$ be the first $S_i$ in the list with
$S_i \cap U \ne \emptyset$ that minimizes $w(S_i) / |S_i \cap U|$ among the sets of $F$ meeting
$U$; the result is $T$ followed by the weighted greedy set cover of $U \setminus T$ from $F$ with
costs $w$. Each step, including the last one, costs $n + |S_1| + \dots + |S_n|$.

articles.title: At most two long jobs per machine
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $M$ be natural numbers with $M < 3p$,
and let $\ell$ be a list of natural numbers (the jobs of one machine) whose sum is at most $M$.
Then the number of entries of $\ell$ that are at least $p$, plus the number of entries that are
at least $p$ and greater than $M - p$, is at most $2$. Here $M - p$ is truncated subtraction,
equal to $0$ when $M < p$. So $\ell$ has at most two entries that are at least $p$, and at most
one if one of them is greater than $M - p$.

articles.title: The empty schedule
articles.statement:
For every number $m$ of machines, the assignment of the empty list
to each of the $m$ machines is a schedule of the empty list of jobs.

articles.title: Schedule of a list of jobs
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number. An assignment $\sigma$ of a list
$\sigma(i)$ of natural numbers (processing times) to each machine $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is a
schedule of a list $J$ of natural numbers when the sum over all machines $i$ of the multisets of
entries of $\sigma(i)$ equals the multiset of entries of $J$, that is, every number occurs in
the lists $\sigma(i)$ together exactly as often as it occurs in $J$.

articles.title: Every job is at most the makespan
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a schedule on $m$ machines of a list
$J$ of processing times. Then every entry $x$ of $J$ is at most the makespan of $\sigma$.

articles.title: Least-loaded machine
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let $L$ assign a load $L(i) \in \mathbb{N}$ to
each machine $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. The least-loaded machine for $L$ is the smallest index
$i$ at which $L(i)$ is minimal.

articles.title: Graham's bound for list scheduling
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let $J$ be a list of processing
times. Let $C$ be the makespan of the schedule that list scheduling on $m$ machines produces
from $J$, taking the jobs in the order of $J$, and let $M$ be the makespan of any schedule of $J$
on $m$ machines. Then $mC \le (2m - 1)M$, that is, $C \le (2 - 1/m)M$.

## Sources

- Graham, "Bounds for certain multiprocessing anomalies", Bell System Technical Journal 45 (1966).

articles.title: List scheduling schedules every job
articles.statement:
For $m \ge 1$ and every list $J$ of processing
times, the assignment that list scheduling on $m$ machines produces from $J$ is a schedule of
$J$.

articles.title: Invariant bound for list scheduling
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and $a, b, M \in \mathbb{N}$. Let
$\sigma$ assign job lists to the $m$ machines so that $\sigma$ is a schedule of a list $P$ of
jobs already placed, let $L(i)$ be the sum of $\sigma(i)$ for each machine $i$, and let $R$ be a
list of remaining jobs. Assume that $a$ times the makespan of $\sigma$ is at most $bM$. Assume
also that whenever $P$ followed by $R$ equals $P'$ followed by a job $p$ followed by a list
$R'$, and $\sigma'$ is any schedule of $P'$ with loads $L'(i)$ equal to the sum of
$\sigma'(i)$, we have $a(L'(k) + p) \le bM$, where $k$ is the least-loaded machine for $L'$.
Then list scheduling of $R$ started from the loads $L$ and machine lists $\sigma$ produces a
schedule whose makespan $C$ satisfies $aC \le bM$.

articles.title: List scheduling from an intermediate state
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$. Given loads $L(i)$ and job
lists $\sigma(i)$ for the machines $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ and a list of remaining jobs, list
scheduling returns $\sigma$ at cost $0$ when no jobs remain. Otherwise it charges cost $m$, takes
the first remaining job $p$, appends $p$ to $\sigma(k)$ and adds $p$ to $L(k)$ for the
least-loaded machine $k$ for $L$, and continues in the same way with the other remaining jobs.
The loads $L$ are not required to be the sums of the lists $\sigma(i)$.

articles.title: Running time of list scheduling
articles.statement:
For $m \ge 1$ and every list of $n$ jobs, list
scheduling on $m$ machines has cost exactly $nm$, in the cost model that charges $m$ for each job
placed (one unit per machine load inspected).

articles.title: Graham's list scheduling
articles.statement:
Given $m \ge 1$ identical machines and a list of job
processing times (natural numbers), start with every machine empty and take the jobs in the
given order, appending each job to the list of a currently least-loaded machine (the first one in
index order), where the load of a machine is the sum of its jobs. The result assigns to each
machine its list of jobs. The cost counted is $m$ per job, one unit for each machine load
inspected.

articles.title: Graham's bound for LPT scheduling
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let $J$ be a list of natural numbers
(job processing times). Let $C$ be the makespan of the schedule of $J$ on $m$ machines produced
by the LPT algorithm, and let $M$ be the makespan of any schedule $\tau$ of $J$ on $m$ machines.
Then $3mC \le (4m - 1)M$, that is, $C \le (4/3 - 1/(3m))M$.

## Sources

- Graham, "Bounds on multiprocessing timing anomalies", SIAM J. Appl. Math. 17 (1969).

articles.title: The LPT placement step
articles.statement:
Let $m \ge 1$ and let a list of job processing times, in
nonincreasing order, be the concatenation of a list $P$, a job $p$ and a list $R$. Let $\sigma$
be a schedule of the jobs $P$ on $m$ machines, with load $\ell_i$ on machine $i$, and let
$L = \min_i \ell_i$ be the load of a least-loaded machine. Then for every schedule $\tau$ of all
the jobs on the $m$ machines, with makespan $M$, we have $3m(L + p) \le (4m - 1)M$.

articles.title: Running time of LPT
articles.statement:
On $m \ge 1$ machines and a list of $n$ jobs, LPT costs at most
$n \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + nm$, counting merge-sort comparisons and machine load inspections.

articles.title: Longest processing time first (LPT)
articles.statement:
Given $m \ge 1$ identical machines and a list of job
processing times (natural numbers), LPT sorts the jobs into nonincreasing order by merge sort and
then applies Graham's list scheduling on $m$ machines to the sorted list. The cost counted is the
number of comparisons made by merge sort plus the cost of list scheduling, $m$ per job.

articles.title: Makespan
articles.statement:
For a schedule $\sigma$ that gives each of $m$ machines a list of processing
times, the load of a machine is the sum of its list, and the makespan of $\sigma$ is the largest
machine load ($0$ when $m = 0$).

articles.title: A least-loaded machine carries at most the average load
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a schedule of a
list $P$ of jobs on $m \ge 1$ machines, with load $\ell_i$ on machine $i$. Then $m$ times the load
of a least-loaded machine is at most the total processing time $T$ of the jobs in $P$, counted
with multiplicity: $m \min_i \ell_i \le T$.

articles.title: List-scheduling state invariant
articles.statement:
A list $P$ of jobs, machine loads $\ell_i \in \mathbb{N}$
for $i < m$, and a schedule $\sigma$ on $m$ machines satisfy the invariant when $\sigma$ is a
schedule of $P$ and, for every machine $i$, $\ell_i$ is the load of machine $i$ in $\sigma$, the
sum of the processing times assigned to it.

articles.title: Total work is at most $m$ times the makespan
articles.statement:
If $\sigma$ is a schedule of a list $P$ of
jobs on $m$ machines, then the total processing time of $P$ is at most $m$ times the makespan of
$\sigma$.

articles.title: Counting jobs when every machine is heavily loaded
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a schedule of a list
$P$ of jobs on $m$ machines, let $p$ and $M$ be natural numbers, and let $d = \max(M - p, 0)$. If
every job in $P$ is at least $p$ and every machine has load (the sum of its jobs) greater than
$d$, then $2m \le n + k$, where $n$ is the number of jobs in $P$ and $k$ is the number of jobs
$x$ in $P$ with $p \le x$ and $x > d$, both counted with multiplicity.

The reason is that each machine then holds two jobs or one job longer than $d$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the cover count in the overlays
articles.statement: More overlays cover every element at least as often.

articles.title: Cover count of an element under a family of overlays
articles.statement: The number of times the overlays `O` cover the element `i` (equation (1)).

articles.title: Weighted maximum coverage is submodular
articles.statement:
For `n = 1` (weighted maximum coverage) and nonnegative weights, the objective is
submodular.

articles.title: Submodular set function
articles.statement:
A set function is submodular if adding an element to a larger set gains at most as much
as adding it to a smaller set (the diminishing-returns form, Definition 2 of the paper).

articles.title: Monotonicity of n-times coverage for nonnegative weights
articles.statement: For nonnegative weights the `n`-times coverage function is monotone.

articles.title: The n-times coverage function
articles.statement:
The `n`-times coverage function: the total weight of the elements covered at least `n`
times by `O` (equation (2)).

articles.title: The `n`-times coverage function is not submodular
articles.statement:
**The `n`-times coverage function is not submodular** (Liu et al., Theorem 1): for every
`n ≥ 2`, take `n` overlays that each cover a single element of weight `1` once. Adding the last
overlay to the other `n - 1` gains `1`; adding it to `∅` gains `0`.

articles.title: APPROX-VERTEX-COVER covers every listed pair
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of ordered pairs of
vertices and every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$, the cover that APPROX-VERTEX-COVER returns on $L$
contains $u$ or $v$.

articles.title: APPROX-VERTEX-COVER returns a vertex cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and $L$ a list of
ordered pairs of vertices such that for every edge $uv$ of $G$, $(u, v)$ or $(v, u)$ is in $L$.
Then the cover that APPROX-VERTEX-COVER returns on $L$ is a vertex cover of $G$.

articles.title: The edges APPROX-VERTEX-COVER takes form a maximal matching of the listed pairs
articles.statement:
Let $G$
be a simple graph and $L$ a list of ordered pairs of vertices such that $u$ and $v$ are adjacent
in $G$ for every $(u, v)$ in $L$, and let $C$ be the cover that APPROX-VERTEX-COVER returns on
$L$. Then there is a sublist $A$ of $L$ such that pairs at different positions of $A$ are
vertex-disjoint, every pair in $L$ shares an endpoint with some pair in $A$, a vertex lies in $C$
exactly when it is an endpoint of some pair in $A$, and $|C| = 2|A|$, where $|A|$ is the length of
$A$.

articles.title: Running time of APPROX-VERTEX-COVER
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of ordered pairs of vertices, the
cost of APPROX-VERTEX-COVER on $L$ is the length of $L$: one unit per listed pair.

articles.title: APPROX-VERTEX-COVER is a 2-approximation
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and $L$ a list of
ordered pairs of vertices that lists exactly the edges of $G$, each in at least one orientation:
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ for every $(u, v)$ in $L$, and for every edge $uv$ of $G$,
$(u, v)$ or $(v, u)$ is in $L$. Then the cover $C$ that APPROX-VERTEX-COVER returns on $L$ is a
vertex cover of $G$ and $|C| \le 2\tau(G)$, where $\tau(G) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ is the
vertex cover number of $G$, the minimum size of a vertex cover of $G$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 35.1.

articles.title: APPROX-VERTEX-COVER
articles.statement:
Given a list $L$ of ordered pairs of vertices, APPROX-VERTEX-COVER
starts from the empty cover and goes through $L$ in order: a pair $(u, v)$ with $u$ or $v$ already
in the cover is skipped, and otherwise both $u$ and $v$ are added to the cover. It returns the
final cover, a finite set of vertices, at a cost of one unit per pair of $L$.

CLRS (third edition, Section 35.1) takes an arbitrary uncovered edge at each step; here it is the
first uncovered pair in list order.

articles.title: APPROX-VERTEX-COVER is at most twice any vertex cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph and $L$ a
list of ordered pairs of vertices such that $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ for every $(u, v)$ in
$L$. Then for every vertex cover $S$ of $G$, finite or infinite, the cover $C$ that
APPROX-VERTEX-COVER returns on $L$ satisfies $|C| \le 2|S|$, with sizes in
$\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$.

articles.title: Counting invariant of the vertex cover scan
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph, $S$ a vertex cover
of $G$, $C_0$ a finite set of vertices with $|C_0| \le 2|C_0 \cap S|$, and $L$ a list of ordered
pairs of vertices such that $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ for every $(u, v)$ in $L$. Then the
cover $C$ that the vertex cover scan returns on $L$ starting from $C_0$ satisfies
$|C| \le 2|C \cap S|$.

The invariant holds because each taken edge adds two new vertices, at least one of them in $S$.

articles.title: Matching invariant of the vertex cover scan
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph, $C_0$ a finite set
of vertices, and $L$ a list of ordered pairs of vertices such that $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$
for every $(u, v)$ in $L$, and let $C$ be the cover that the vertex cover scan returns on $L$
starting from $C_0$. Then there is a sublist $A$ of $L$ such that neither endpoint of any pair in
$A$ lies in $C_0$, pairs at different positions of $A$ are vertex-disjoint, a vertex lies in $C$
exactly when it lies in $C_0$ or is an endpoint of some pair in $A$, and $|C| = |C_0| + 2|A|$,
where $|A|$ is the length of $A$.

articles.title: The vertex cover scan only adds vertices
articles.statement:
For every finite set $C$ of vertices and every
list of pairs of vertices, the cover returned by the vertex cover scan starting from $C$ on that
list contains $C$.

articles.title: Running time of the vertex cover scan
articles.statement:
For every finite set $C$ of vertices and every list
$L$ of pairs of vertices, the running time of the vertex cover scan starting from $C$ on $L$ is
the length of $L$.

articles.title: Vertex cover scan
articles.statement:
Given a finite set $C$ of vertices and a list of pairs of vertices,
the scan processes the pairs in order, starting from the cover $C$ and charging one time unit
per pair. A pair $(u, v)$ is covered when $u$ or $v$ is already in the current cover; a covered
pair is skipped, and an uncovered pair adds both $u$ and $v$ to the cover. The scan returns the
cover reached after the last pair.

articles.title: Vertex-disjoint pairs
articles.statement:
Two pairs $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ of vertices are vertex-disjoint
when they share no endpoint: $a 
e c$, $a 
e d$, $b 
e c$ and $b 
e d$.

articles.title: Pricing scan: the total price is at most what a cover pays
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a finite
set of vertices, let $r$ be rational residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex
$v$, let $P$ be a rational number, and let $L$ be a list of edges (ordered pairs of
vertices) such that every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$ has $u \in C$ or $v \in C$. If the pricing
scan of $L$ from residual weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$
and total price $P'$, then $P' - P \le \sum_{v \in C} (r(v) - r'(v))$.

Every edge has an endpoint in $C$, which pays that edge's price.

articles.title: Pricing scan: every edge has an exhausted endpoint
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be rational residual
weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a rational number and let $L$ be
a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices). If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual
weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$, then every pair $(u, v)$
in $L$ has $r'(u) = 0$ or $r'(v) = 0$.

articles.title: Pricing scan: residual weights stay between $0$ and their start
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be rational
residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a rational number and
let $L$ be a list of edges. If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual weights $r$ and total
price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$, then $0 \le r'(v) \le r(v)$ for every vertex $v$.

articles.title: Pricing scan
articles.statement:
Given rational residual weights $r$ on the vertices, a rational total
price $P$ and a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), the pricing scan processes the
edges in order: an edge $(u, v)$ has price $\delta = \min(r(u), r(v))$, which is subtracted
from the residual weight of $u$ and of $v$ (once if $u = v$) and added to the total price.
The result is the final pair of residual weights and total price, and the scan costs one
time unit per edge.

articles.title: The pricing method covers every listed edge
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be rational weights on a finite
vertex set with $w(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, and let $L$ be a list of edges (ordered
pairs of vertices). For every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$, $u$ or $v$ belongs to the set returned
by the pricing method on $w$ and $L$.

articles.title: The pricing method returns a vertex cover
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite
vertex set, let $w$ be rational vertex weights with $w(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, and
let $L$ be a list of ordered pairs of vertices such that for every edge $uv$ of $G$, the
pair $(u, v)$ or the pair $(v, u)$ is in $L$. Then the set returned by the pricing method on
$w$ and $L$ is a vertex cover of $G$.

articles.title: Running time of the pricing method
articles.statement:
For all rational vertex weights $w$ on a finite
vertex set $V$ and every list $L$ of edges, the pricing method on $w$ and $L$ takes exactly
$|L| + |V|$ time units, where $|L|$ is the length of the list: one unit per listed edge and
one per vertex.

articles.title: The pricing method weighs at most twice any cover of the listed edges
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be
rational weights on a finite vertex set with $w(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $L$ be a
list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), and let $C$ be a set of vertices such that every
pair $(u, v)$ in $L$ has $u \in C$ or $v \in C$. Then the total weight of the set returned by
the pricing method on $w$ and $L$ is at most $2 \sum_{v \in C} w(v)$.

articles.title: Pricing method for weighted vertex cover
articles.statement:
Given rational weights $w$ on a finite vertex
set $V$ and a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), run the pricing scan on the list
starting from residual weights $w$ and total price $0$, then return the set of vertices whose
final residual weight is $0$. On top of the cost of the scan, the selection costs $|V|$ time
units.

articles.title: Pricing scan: the vertices pay at most twice the price
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite vertex set,
let $r$ be rational residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a
rational number and let $L$ be a list of edges. If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual
weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$ and total price $P'$, then
$\sum_{v \in V} (r(v) - r'(v)) \le 2 (P' - P)$.

Each edge's price is paid by its two endpoints.

articles.title: Cost of the brute-force closest-pair scan
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let
$ps$ be a list of $n$ points in $K^2$. Counting one unit of cost per squared distance computed,
twice the cost of the brute-force scan on $ps$ equals $n(n-1)$; that is, the scan computes exactly
$n(n-1)/2$ squared distances.

articles.title: Brute-force closest pair
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order, and write
$d(p, q) = (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2$ for the squared distance between points $p = (x, y)$ and
$q = (x', y')$ of $K^2$. On a list $c_1, \dots, c_n$ of points in $K^2$, the brute-force scan
returns no value if $n < 2$, and otherwise returns $\min_{i < j} d(c_i, c_j)$: for each $i$ it
computes the least squared distance from $c_i$ to the later points $c_{i+1}, \dots, c_n$, and
takes the least of these minima. It is charged one unit of cost per squared distance computed.

articles.title: Divide and conquer agrees with brute force
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field. For every
list of points in $K^2$, the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm returns the same value as
the brute-force scan (their costs may differ).

articles.title: The closest-pair algorithm returns no value exactly on fewer than two points
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
linearly ordered field. For every list of points in $K^2$, the divide-and-conquer closest-pair
algorithm returns no value if and only if the list has fewer than two entries.

articles.title: The closest-pair algorithm returns the answer
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, write
$d(p, q) = (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2$ for the squared distance between points $p = (x, y)$ and
$q = (x', y')$ of $K^2$, and let $ps$ be a list of points in $K^2$. If the divide-and-conquer
closest-pair algorithm returns a value $\delta$ on $ps$, then $\delta = d(p, q)$ for some entries
$p$, $q$ of $ps$ at different positions. For any two entries $p$, $q$ of $ps$ at different
positions, the algorithm returns a value $\delta$ with $\delta \le d(p, q)$.

articles.title: Correctness of divide-and-conquer closest pair
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and let
$ps$ be a list of at least two points in $K^2$. Then the divide-and-conquer closest-pair algorithm
returns a value $\delta$, and $\delta$ is the least squared distance between two entries of $ps$
at different positions: some two entries at different positions have squared distance $\delta$,
and any two entries at different positions have squared distance at least $\delta$.

This is the correctness of CLRS Section 33.4, with distances compared squared.

articles.title: Running time of the closest-pair algorithm
articles.statement:
For every list of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$,
the closest-pair algorithm computes at most $7 n \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + n$ squared distances,
where $\lceil \log_2 0 \rceil$ is read as $0$. In particular it computes $O(n \log n)$ distances.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Section 33.4.

articles.title: Divide-and-conquer closest pair
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order. Given a list of
points in $K^2$, the closest-pair algorithm sorts the points by first coordinate (merge sort, at
no cost) and runs the closest-pair recursion on the sorted list. It returns a squared distance or
no value, and is charged one unit of cost per squared distance computed.

This is CLRS `CLOSEST-PAIR` (Section 33.4), with distances compared squared.

articles.title: The closest-pair recursion is correct on lists sorted by first coordinate
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
linearly ordered field, write $d(u, v) = (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2$ for the squared distance between
points $u = (x, y)$ and $v = (x', y')$ of $K^2$, and let $xs$ be a list of points in $K^2$ sorted
by first coordinate: whenever an entry precedes another, its first coordinate is at most the
other's. If the closest-pair recursion returns a value $\delta$ on $xs$, then $\delta = d(p, q)$
for some entries $p$, $q$ of $xs$ at different positions. For any two entries $p$, $q$ of $xs$ at
different positions, the recursion returns a value $\delta$ with $\delta \le d(p, q)$.

articles.title: Running time of the closest-pair recursion
articles.statement:
For every list of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$
sorted by nondecreasing $x$-coordinate, the divide-and-conquer recursion of the closest-pair
algorithm computes at most $7 n \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + n$ squared distances, where
$\lceil \log_2 0 \rceil$ is read as $0$.

articles.title: Closest-pair recursion
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and $c_1, \dots, c_n$ a list
of points $c_i = (x_i, y_i)$ of $K^2$. If $n \le 3$, the recursion returns the brute-force scan of
the list. Otherwise let $m = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, and run the recursion on $c_1, \dots, c_m$ and
on $c_{m+1}, \dots, c_n$. If neither call returns a value, it returns no value. Otherwise let
$\delta$ be the least of the returned values, let $T$ be the list of the points $c_i$ with
$(x_i - x_m)^2 < \delta$ in their original order, sorted by second coordinate with a stable merge
sort, and run the strip scan with threshold $\delta$ on $T$. The recursion returns
$\min(\delta, s)$ if the strip scan returns a value $s$, and $\delta$ otherwise. In the base case
its cost is that of the brute-force scan; otherwise it is the sum of the costs of the two
recursive calls and of the strip scan when it is run, and splitting, filtering and sorting are
free.

articles.title: Squared distance in the plane
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field. The squared distance
between points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$ is $(p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$.

articles.title: Strip points
articles.statement:
Given reals $\delta$ and $x_{\mathrm{mid}}$, a tagged point $((x, y), s)$ lies
in the strip when $(x - x_{\mathrm{mid}})^2 < \delta$, and moreover $x \le x_{\mathrm{mid}}$ if its
side $s$ is left ($s$ false) and $x_{\mathrm{mid}} \le x$ if its side $s$ is right ($s$ true).

articles.title: Closest-pair answer
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and write
$d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points
$p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. For a list $c_1, \dots, c_n$ of points of $K^2$,
an optional value $r$ (an element of $K$ or no value) is an answer for the list when every value
$\delta$ that $r$ holds equals $d(c_i, c_j)$ for some $i < j$, and when for all $i < j$, $r$ holds
a value $\delta$ with $\delta \le d(c_i, c_j)$.

articles.title: Least pairwise squared distance
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and write
$d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points
$p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. For a list $c_1, \dots, c_n$ of points of $K^2$,
an element $\delta$ of $K$ is the least pairwise squared distance of the list when
$\delta = d(c_i, c_j)$ for some $i < j$ and $\delta \le d(c_i, c_j)$ for all $i < j$.

articles.title: Packing bound for the strip
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ and $x_{\mathrm{mid}}$ be reals, $p$ a tagged
point, $Z$ a list of tagged points, and $L$ the list $p$ followed by $Z$; write $y_a$ for the
$y$-coordinate of a tagged point $a$. Suppose every point of $L$ lies in the strip for $\delta$ and
$x_{\mathrm{mid}}$, any two points of $L$ at different positions with the same side are at squared
distance at least $\delta$, and every point $a$ of $Z$ satisfies $y_p \le y_a$ and
$(y_a - y_p)^2 < \delta$. Then $Z$ has at most $7$ entries.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Section 33.4, the packing argument.

articles.title: The nearest-point scan returns the least squared distance
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered
field, write $d(u, v) = (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2$ for the squared distance between points
$u = (x, y)$ and $v = (x', y')$ of $K^2$, let $p \in K^2$, and let $qs$ be a list of points in
$K^2$. If the scan for the least squared distance from $p$ to the entries of $qs$ returns a value
$\delta$, then $\delta = d(p, q)$ for some entry $q$ of $qs$. For every entry $q$ of $qs$, the
scan returns a value $\delta$ with $\delta \le d(p, q)$.

articles.title: Least squared distance from a point to a list
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and
write $d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points
$p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. For a point $p$ and a list $c_1, \dots, c_m$ of
points of $K^2$, the least squared distance from $p$ to the list is no value if $m = 0$ and
$\min_{1 \le k \le m} d(p, c_k)$ otherwise. Computing it is charged one unit of cost per point of
the list, $m$ units in total.

articles.title: Same-side points far apart
articles.statement:
For a real $\delta$, two tagged points $a$ and $b$ are
same-side far apart when, if $a$ and $b$ carry the same side, the squared distance between their
points is at least $\delta$.

articles.title: Cost of the scan from one strip point
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be a real, $q = (q_1, q_2)$ a point of
$\mathbb{R}^2$ and $L$ a list of points of $\mathbb{R}^2$. The cost of the scan from $q$ over $L$
with threshold $\delta$, one unit per squared distance computed, equals the length of the longest
initial segment of $L$ all of whose points $r = (r_1, r_2)$ satisfy $(r_2 - q_2)^2 < \delta$.

articles.title: Strip scan from a point
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, and write
$d(p, q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ for the squared distance between points
$p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ of $K^2$. Let $\delta \in K$, let $p = (p_1, p_2)$ be a
point of $K^2$ and $c_1, \dots, c_m$ a list of points $c_l = (x_l, y_l)$ of $K^2$, and let
$k \le m$ be largest such that $(y_l - p_2)^2 < \delta$ for all $1 \le l \le k$. The scan from $p$
with threshold $\delta$ returns no value if $k = 0$ and $\min_{1 \le l \le k} d(p, c_l)$
otherwise. It is charged one unit of cost per point $c_1, \dots, c_k$: it stops at the first
point whose squared vertical gap to $p$ is at least $\delta$, without computing its distance.

articles.title: The strip scan bounds every pair with a small vertical gap
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered
field, write $d(p, q) = (x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2$ for the squared distance between points
$p = (x, y)$ and $q = (x', y')$ of $K^2$, and let $\delta \in K$. Let $ys$ be a list of points in
$K^2$ sorted by second coordinate: whenever an entry precedes another, its second coordinate is at
most the other's. If $a = (a_1, a_2)$ and $b = (b_1, b_2)$ are entries of $ys$ at positions $i < j$
respectively and $(b_2 - a_2)^2 < \delta$, then the strip scan with threshold $\delta$ on $ys$
returns a value $e$ with $e \le d(a, b)$.

articles.title: Cost of the strip scan
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ and $x_{\mathrm{mid}}$ be reals and $Y$ a list of
tagged points that is sorted by nondecreasing $y$-coordinate, whose points all lie in the strip for
$\delta$ and $x_{\mathrm{mid}}$, and in which any two points at different positions with the same
side are at squared distance at least $\delta$. Then the strip scan with parameter $\delta$ over the
underlying points of $Y$ (tags forgotten) computes at most $7m$ squared distances, where $m$ is the
length of $Y$.

articles.title: Closest-pair strip scan
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, $\delta \in K$ and
$c_1, \dots, c_n$ a list of points of $K^2$. For each $i$, the strip scan runs the strip scan from
$c_i$ with threshold $\delta$ on the later points $c_{i+1}, \dots, c_n$. It returns the least of
the values these scans return, or no value if none of them returns a value, and its cost is the
sum of their costs.

articles.title: Side-tagged points
articles.statement:
A tagged point is a pair $(p, s)$ of a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and a
Boolean $s$, read as the side of the dividing line on which $p$ lies: false for left, true for
right.

articles.title: Monotone chain scan
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. Given a stack $S$ of
points of $\Bbbk^2$, listed top first, and a list of points $p_1, \dots, p_n$ of $\Bbbk^2$, the
scan processes $p_1, \dots, p_n$ in order: for each point $p = p_i$ it removes the top $a$ of the
stack as long as the stack has a second element $b$ with
$(a_x - b_x)(p_y - b_y) - (p_x - b_x)(a_y - b_y) \le 0$, and then pushes $p$. Starting from $S$,
the result is the final stack, top first. Each evaluation of this inequality costs one unit;
nothing else is counted.

articles.title: The hull polygon contains every input point
articles.statement:
Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be $n \ge 2$ points of
$\Bbbk^2$, for an ordered field $\Bbbk$, strictly increasing in the lexicographic order on $(x, y)$,
and let $v_1, \dots, v_m$ be the vertices of their convex hull computed by the monotone chain
algorithm. Then for every input point $s$ and every edge $(a, b)$ of the closed polygon
$v_1, \dots, v_m, v_1$ (that is, $a, b$ consecutive in this sequence), the cross product
$(b - a) \times (s - a)$ is nonnegative: $s$ lies on or to the left of the edge from $a$ to $b$.

articles.title: The hull's vertices are input points
articles.statement:
Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$, for an
ordered field $\Bbbk$, strictly increasing in the lexicographic order on $(x, y)$. Then every
vertex of their convex hull computed by the monotone chain algorithm is one of the $p_i$.

articles.title: The monotone chain hull makes at most $4n$ orientation tests
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with
a linear order. For every list of $n$ points of $\Bbbk^2$, computing their convex hull by the
monotone chain algorithm costs at most $4n$, where each orientation test costs one unit.

articles.title: The monotone chain hull of non-collinear points turns strictly left at every vertex
articles.statement:
Let
$\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and write $(u_1, u_2) \times (v_1, v_2) = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$
for the cross product on $\Bbbk^2$. Let $P$ be a list of points of $\Bbbk^2$ that is strictly
increasing in the lexicographic order on $(x, y)$, and suppose the points of $P$ are not all
collinear: there are points $a, b, c$ of $P$ with $(b - a) \times (c - a) \ne 0$. Let $H$ be the
list of points returned by the monotone chain convex hull algorithm on $P$. Then the list
obtained from $H$ by appending its first two points (all of $H$ if $H$ has fewer than two points)
turns strictly left: any three consecutive points $q, r, s$ of it satisfy
$(r - q) \times (s - q) > 0$.

Read cyclically, this says the hull polygon turns strictly left at every vertex, including the
two vertices where the lower and upper chains meet.

articles.title: Convex hull by the monotone chain algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order.
The convex hull of a list $P$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$ is the lower chain of $P$ followed by the
upper chain of $P$ with its first and last points removed, together with its cost: the cost of
computing the lower chain plus the cost of computing the upper chain.

For points sorted strictly in lexicographic $(x, y)$ order, the result runs counterclockwise from
the first point.

articles.title: The lower chain ends at the last point
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let
$p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic
$(x, y)$ order. If $n \ge 1$, the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ ends at $p_n$; if $n = 0$,
the lower chain is empty.

articles.title: The lower chain starts at the first point
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and
let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic
$(x, y)$ order. If $n \ge 1$, the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ starts at $p_1$; if $n = 0$,
the lower chain is empty.

articles.title: Every input point lies on or left of each lower-chain edge
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly
ordered field and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in
lexicographic $(x, y)$ order, and write $\operatorname{cross}(u, v) = u_x v_y - v_x u_y$. For
every $s \in \{p_1, \dots, p_n\}$ and every pair of consecutive vertices $a, b$ of the lower chain
of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ we have $\operatorname{cross}(b - a, s - a) \ge 0$: the point $s$ lies on or
to the left of the directed edge from $a$ to $b$.

articles.title: Correctness of the lower chain for unsorted input
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered
field, let $P$ be a list of pairwise distinct points of $\Bbbk^2$ in any order, write $\preceq$
for the lexicographic $(x, y)$ order on $\Bbbk^2$, and let $C = c_0, \dots, c_{m-1}$ be the
lower chain of the list obtained by sorting $P$ into $\preceq$-increasing order. Write
$\operatorname{cross}(u, v) = u_x v_y - v_x u_y$. Then every $c_j$ is a point of $P$; if $P$ is
nonempty then $m \ge 1$; if $m \ge 1$ then $c_0 \preceq s \preceq c_{m-1}$ for every $s \in P$;
for every $i$ with $i + 2 < m$ we have $\operatorname{cross}(c_{i+1} - c_i, c_{i+2} - c_i) > 0$;
and for every $s \in P$ and every pair of consecutive vertices $a, b$ of $C$ we have
$\operatorname{cross}(b - a, s - a) \ge 0$.

articles.title: Lower chain of unsorted points
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. For a list
$P$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$, sort $P$ by merge sort into nondecreasing lexicographic $(x, y)$
order and return the lower chain of the sorted list. Only the orientation tests of the lower
chain are counted; sorting costs nothing.

articles.title: The lower chain is a sublist of the input
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and
let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic
$(x, y)$ order. Then the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is a sublist of $p_1, \dots, p_n$: it
is $p_{i_1}, \dots, p_{i_m}$ for some indices $i_1 < \dots < i_m$.

articles.title: The lower-chain scan makes linearly many tests
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear
order. For every list of $n$ points of $\Bbbk^2$, computing its lower chain makes at most $2n$
orientation tests (cross-product evaluations).

articles.title: The lower chain turns strictly left
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let
$p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic $(x, y)$
order, with lower chain $c_0, \dots, c_{m-1}$. Writing
$\operatorname{cross}(u, v) = u_x v_y - v_x u_y$, for every $i$ with $i + 2 < m$ we have
$\operatorname{cross}(c_{i+1} - c_i, c_{i+2} - c_i) > 0$.

articles.title: Lower chain
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. The lower chain of a list of
points $p_1, \dots, p_n$ of $\Bbbk^2$ is computed by Andrew's monotone chain scan: start with an
empty stack and process $p_1, \dots, p_n$ in order; for each point $p = p_i$, remove the top $a$
of the stack as long as the stack has a second element $b$ with
$(a_x - b_x)(p_y - b_y) - (p_x - b_x)(a_y - b_y) \le 0$, then push $p$. The lower chain is the
final stack read from bottom to top. Each evaluation of the inequality costs one unit; nothing
else is counted.

The scan is meant for points sorted strictly in lexicographic $(x, y)$ order; the chain then runs
from left to right.

articles.title: Pop step of the monotone-chain scan
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field, let
$p \in \Bbbk^2$, and write $u \times v = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$ for the cross product. Given a
stack of points of $\Bbbk^2$ listed top first, while the stack has at least two points, with
top $a$ and next point $b$, and $(a - b) \times (p - b) \le 0$ (so $b \to a \to p$ is not a
strict left turn), remove $a$. The result is the first stack reached that has fewer than two
points or whose top two points $a, b$ satisfy $(a - b) \times (p - b) > 0$; that stack is
returned unchanged. Each test of the sign of $(a - b) \times (p - b)$ costs one unit, and
nothing else is charged.

articles.title: Lists of points turning strictly left
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order and write
$(u_1, u_2) \times (v_1, v_2) = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$ for the cross product on $\Bbbk^2$. A list
$q_1, \dots, q_k$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$ turns strictly left when every three consecutive points
do: $(q_{i+1} - q_i) \times (q_{i+2} - q_i) > 0$ for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le k - 2$. In
particular, every list of fewer than three points turns strictly left.

articles.title: The upper chain is a reflected lower chain
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order.
For every list $p_1, \dots, p_n$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$, the upper chain of the list is the image
under $p \mapsto -p$ of the lower chain of $-p_n, \dots, -p_1$, and the two computations have the
same cost.

articles.title: The upper chain ends at the first point
articles.statement:
Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$, for
an ordered field $\Bbbk$, strictly increasing in the lexicographic order on $(x, y)$. If $n = 0$
the upper chain is empty; otherwise its last vertex is $p_1$.

articles.title: The upper chain starts at the last point
articles.statement:
Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$,
for an ordered field $\Bbbk$, strictly increasing in the lexicographic order on $(x, y)$. If
$n = 0$ the upper chain is empty; otherwise its first vertex is $p_n$.

articles.title: Every input point lies left of the upper chain
articles.statement:
Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of
$\Bbbk^2$, for an ordered field $\Bbbk$, strictly increasing in the lexicographic order on
$(x, y)$. Then for every input point $s$ and every two consecutive vertices $a, b$ of the upper
chain, the cross product $(b - a) \times (s - a)$ is nonnegative: $s$ lies on or to the left of
the edge from $a$ to $b$.

articles.title: The upper chain is a subsequence of the reversed input
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be an ordered field and
