let $p_1, \dots, p_n \in K^2$ be strictly increasing in the lexicographic $(x, y)$ order. Then the
upper chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is a sublist of the reversed list $p_n, \dots, p_1$: it is
obtained from $p_n, \dots, p_1$ by deleting some of the entries.

articles.title: Running time of the upper chain scan
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let
$p_1, \dots, p_n \in K^2$ be any $n$ points, sorted or not. Computing the upper chain of
$p_1, \dots, p_n$ costs at most $2n$, where the cost counts one unit per orientation test (one
cross-product comparison) and nothing else.

articles.title: The upper chain turns strictly left
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be an ordered field, let
$p_1, \dots, p_n \in K^2$ be strictly increasing in the lexicographic $(x, y)$ order, and let
$c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{m-1}$ be the upper chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$. Then for every $i$ with
$i + 2 < m$, we have $(c_{i+1} - c_i) \times (c_{i+2} - c_i) > 0$, where
$(u_1, u_2) \times (v_1, v_2) = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$ is the cross product: the vertices $c_i$,
$c_{i+1}$, $c_{i+2}$ make a strict left turn.

articles.title: Upper chain
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order. The upper chain of a list of points
$p_1, \dots, p_n \in K^2$ is the lower chain of the reversed list $p_n, \dots, p_1$, together with
its cost: the same scan, counting the same orientation tests. For points sorted by $(x, y)$ it
runs from the last point back to the first.

articles.title: Collinear-endpoint step of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field,
$d \in K$ and $p_i, p_j, p_k \in K^2$. When $d = 0$, this step costs one unit and returns the value
of ON-SEGMENT$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$; when $d \neq 0$, it costs nothing and returns false.

In SEGMENTS-INTERSECT, $d$ is the direction of $p_k$ relative to $p_i$ and $p_j$.

articles.title: Cross product of plane vectors
articles.statement:
For $p = (x_p, y_p)$ and $q = (x_q, y_q)$ in $K^2$, where
$K$ is a linearly ordered field, the cross product is $p \times q = x_p y_q - x_q y_p$ (CLRS
equation (33.1)).

articles.title: Points of a segment have direction zero
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and
$p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$, then the direction
$(r - p) \times (q - p)$ is zero, that is, $r$ is collinear with $p$ and $q$.

articles.title: Direction of three points
articles.statement:
For points $p_i, p_j, p_k \in K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly
ordered field, CLRS's DIRECTION$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$ is the cross product
$(p_k - p_i) \times (p_j - p_i)$.

It is positive when $p_k$ is clockwise from $p_j$ about $p_i$, negative when counterclockwise, and
zero when the three points are collinear.

articles.title: Collinear case of segment intersection
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and
$p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. Suppose the directions $(p_1 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ and
$(p_2 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ are both zero and the closed segments $p_1 p_2$ and $p_3 p_4$
have a common point. Then $p_1$ or $p_2$ lies on the segment $p_3 p_4$, or $p_3$ or $p_4$ lies on
the segment $p_1 p_2$.

articles.title: Points with direction zero lie on the line
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and
$p, q, r \in K^2$ with $p \neq q$. If $(r - p) \times (q - p) = 0$, then $r = p + \mu (q - p)$ for
some $\mu \in K$.

One can take $\mu = \frac{(r - p) \cdot (q - p)}{(q - p) \cdot (q - p)}$, a quotient of dot
products.

articles.title: Properly crossing segments meet
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and
$p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. Suppose the directions $(p_1 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ and
$(p_2 - p_3) \times (p_4 - p_3)$ are nonzero with opposite signs, and so are
$(p_3 - p_1) \times (p_2 - p_1)$ and $(p_4 - p_1) \times (p_2 - p_1)$. Then the closed segments
$p_1 p_2$ and $p_3 p_4$ have a common point.

articles.title: A collinear point in the bounding box lies on the segment
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered
field, write $(u_1, u_2) \times (v_1, v_2) = u_1 v_2 - v_1 u_2$ for the cross product on $K^2$, and
let $p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ is collinear with $p$ and $q$, that is, the direction
$(r - p) \times (q - p)$ is zero, and ON-SEGMENT$(p, q, r)$ is true, that is, $r$ lies in the
bounding box of $p$ and $q$, then $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$.

This is the fact behind CLRS's use of ON-SEGMENT.

articles.title: Points of a segment lie in its bounding box
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and
$p, q, r \in K^2$. If $r$ lies on the closed segment from $p$ to $q$, then ON-SEGMENT$(p, q, r)$ is
true, that is, $r$ lies in the bounding box of $p$ and $q$.

articles.title: The ON-SEGMENT test
articles.statement:
For points $p_i = (x_i, y_i)$, $p_j = (x_j, y_j)$ and
$p_k = (x_k, y_k)$ in $K^2$, where $K$ is a linearly ordered field, CLRS's
ON-SEGMENT$(p_i, p_j, p_k)$ is the Boolean that is true exactly when $p_k$ lies in the bounding box
of $p_i$ and $p_j$, that is, $\min(x_i, x_j) \le x_k \le \max(x_i, x_j)$ and
$\min(y_i, y_j) \le y_k \le \max(y_i, y_j)$.

articles.title: Zero-crossing parameter of values of opposite sign
articles.statement:
If $d$ and $e$ are elements of a
linearly ordered field that straddle zero, that is, they are nonzero with opposite signs, then
$0 \le d / (d - e) \le 1$.

articles.title: Correctness of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field and let
$p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. The procedure SEGMENTS-INTERSECT$(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4)$ returns true
if and only if the closed segments $[p_1, p_2]$ and $[p_3, p_4]$ have a common point.

## Sources

- CLRS Section 33.1.

articles.title: SEGMENTS-INTERSECT as a Boolean formula
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order, let
$p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$, and write $d_1 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_1)$,
$d_2 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_2)$, $d_3 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ and
$d_4 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_4)$. The value returned by
SEGMENTS-INTERSECT$(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4)$ is true if and only if at least one of the following
holds: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are nonzero with opposite signs and $d_3$ and $d_4$ are nonzero with
opposite signs; $d_1 = 0$ and ON-SEGMENT$(p_3, p_4, p_1)$ is true; $d_2 = 0$ and
ON-SEGMENT$(p_3, p_4, p_2)$ is true; $d_3 = 0$ and ON-SEGMENT$(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ is true; or
$d_4 = 0$ and ON-SEGMENT$(p_1, p_2, p_4)$ is true.

articles.title: Running time of SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let
$p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. In the cost model that charges one unit per DIRECTION computation
and one per ON-SEGMENT test, SEGMENTS-INTERSECT$(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4)$ costs at least $4$ and at
most $8$.

The four directions are always computed, and at most four ON-SEGMENT tests run.

articles.title: The SEGMENTS-INTERSECT procedure
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and let
$p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$. CLRS's procedure SEGMENTS-INTERSECT$(p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4)$, which
tests whether the segments $p_1p_2$ and $p_3p_4$ meet, first computes, at a cost of $4$, the
directions $d_1 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_1)$, $d_2 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_2)$,
$d_3 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ and $d_4 = \mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_4)$. If $d_1$
and $d_2$ are nonzero with opposite signs and so are $d_3$ and $d_4$, it returns true. Otherwise
it tries in order the cases $d_1 = 0$ with ON-SEGMENT$(p_3, p_4, p_1)$, $d_2 = 0$ with
ON-SEGMENT$(p_3, p_4, p_2)$, $d_3 = 0$ with ON-SEGMENT$(p_1, p_2, p_3)$, and $d_4 = 0$ with
ON-SEGMENT$(p_1, p_2, p_4)$: in each case it runs the ON-SEGMENT test, at a cost of $1$, only when
the direction is $0$, and it returns true as soon as a test succeeds. If none succeeds it returns
false.

articles.title: A vanishing convex combination of nonzero values forces opposite signs
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $e$ be
nonzero elements of a linearly ordered field. If $a d + b e = 0$ for some $a, b \ge 0$ in the field
with $a + b = 1$, then $d$ and $e$ have opposite signs.

articles.title: Meeting segments cross properly or an endpoint lies on the other
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly
ordered field and $p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4 \in K^2$, and suppose the closed segments $[p_1, p_2]$ and
$[p_3, p_4]$ have a common point. Then either $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_1)$ and
$\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_3, p_4, p_2)$ are nonzero with opposite signs and
$\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ and $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p_1, p_2, p_4)$ are nonzero with
opposite signs, or $p_1 \in [p_3, p_4]$, or $p_2 \in [p_3, p_4]$, or $p_3 \in [p_1, p_2]$, or
$p_4 \in [p_1, p_2]$.

articles.title: Values of opposite sign
articles.statement:
Two elements $d$ and $e$ of a field with a linear order straddle
zero when $d > 0$ and $e < 0$, or $d < 0$ and $e > 0$; that is, $d$ and $e$ are nonzero with
opposite signs.

articles.title: Values of opposite sign have nonzero difference
articles.statement:
If $d$ and $e$ are elements of a
linearly ordered field that straddle zero, that is, they are nonzero with opposite signs, then
$d - e \ne 0$.

articles.title: Correctness of ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$ be closed segments in $\Bbbk^2$, each given by its two endpoints in either
order. Suppose no segment is vertical (its two endpoints have different $x$-coordinates) and no
point lies on three segments $s_i$, $s_j$, $s_k$ with $i$, $j$, $k$ pairwise distinct. Then
ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT returns true on these segments if and only if there are indices $i \ne j$
such that $s_i$ and $s_j$ intersect (CLRS, third edition, Theorem 33.1).

articles.title: Running time of ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. For
every $n$ segments in $\Bbbk^2$, each given by its two endpoints, ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT costs at
most $n^2 + 24n$, so it runs in time $O(n^2)$. Cost counts one unit per evaluation of DIRECTION
or ON-SEGMENT.

The bound comes from at most $n$ DIRECTION evaluations to place each segment in the list-based
status and at most three SEGMENTS-INTERSECT tests per segment.

articles.title: ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field. Given $n$ segments
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$ in $\Bbbk^2$, each given by its two endpoints, write $l_t$, the left endpoint
of $s_t$, for its endpoint with the smaller $x$-coordinate, or for its first given endpoint when
both $x$-coordinates agree, and $r_t$, the right endpoint, for the other one. The procedure sorts
the $2n$ endpoints by $x$-coordinate, left endpoints before right endpoints at equal $x$, then by
$y$-coordinate, with remaining ties in increasing order of segment index. It then sweeps a
vertical line across them, starting with an empty status list of segments, kept from bottom to
top. At the left endpoint $l_i$ of $s_i$, let $P$ be the longest initial part of the status list
consisting of segments $s_t$ with $\mathrm{DIRECTION}(l_t, r_t, l_i) < 0$. Then $s_i$ is tested
with SEGMENTS-INTERSECT first against the segment just after $P$ and then against the last
segment of $P$, when these exist, and is inserted directly after $P$. At the right endpoint of
$s_i$, the segments just before and just after $s_i$ in the status list, when both exist, are
tested against each other and $s_i$ is deleted. The procedure returns true as soon as a test
succeeds and false after the last event. Cost counts one unit per evaluation of DIRECTION or
ON-SEGMENT (CLRS, third edition, Section 33.2).

The status is kept in a list rather than CLRS's red-black tree.

articles.title: Segment strictly below a point
articles.statement:
For a segment $j$, write $l_j$ for its endpoint with the
smaller $x$-coordinate, or for its first given endpoint when both $x$-coordinates agree, and $r_j$
for its other endpoint. For a point $q$, segment $j$ is below $q$ when
$\mathrm{DIRECTION}(l_j, r_j, q) < 0$.

For a non-vertical segment this says that the line through $l_j$ and $r_j$ passes strictly below
$q$ at the abscissa of $q$.

articles.title: DIRECTION as a scaled vertical offset
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order, let
$p, q, r \in \Bbbk^2$, writing $p = (p_x, p_y)$ and likewise for $q$ and $r$, with $p_x < q_x$, and
let $y_{pq}(x)$ be the height at $x$ of the line through $p$ and $q$. Then
$\mathrm{DIRECTION}(p, q, r) = (q_x - p_x)\,(y_{pq}(r_x) - r_y)$.

articles.title: Cost charged to a sweep event
articles.statement:
For $n$ segments, the charge of an event is $n + 16$ if it
is the left endpoint of a segment and $8$ if it is the right endpoint of a segment.

These charges bound the actual costs: a left endpoint scans at most $n$ segments of the status
list and runs two SEGMENTS-INTERSECT tests, and a right endpoint runs one test.

articles.title: Sweep event
articles.statement:
For $n$ segments indexed by $0, \dots, n-1$, an event is a pair $(i, b)$ of a
segment index $i$ and a Boolean $b$; it stands for the left endpoint of segment $i$ when $b$ is
true and for its right endpoint when $b$ is false.

articles.title: Sorted sweep events
articles.statement:
For $n$ segments, each given by its two endpoints, the left endpoint
of a segment is its endpoint with the smaller $x$-coordinate, or its first given endpoint when
both $x$-coordinates agree, and the right endpoint is the other one. The event list consists of
the $2n$ events, the left and the right endpoint of each segment, sorted by the $x$-coordinate
of the endpoint, with left endpoints before right endpoints at equal $x$, and then by the
$y$-coordinate of the endpoint; events that tie appear in increasing order of segment index.
This is line 2 of CLRS ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT.

articles.title: Splitting a list at two distinct members
articles.statement:
If $a$ and $b$ are distinct members of a list
$T$, then there are elements $u$, $w$ with either $u = a$ and $w = b$, or $u = b$ and $w = a$, and
lists $A$, $M$, $B$ such that $T$ is the concatenation of $A$, the element $u$, $M$, the element
$w$ and $B$, in this order.

articles.title: A leftmost intersection point
articles.statement:
Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field, let
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$ be closed segments in $\Bbbk^2$, none of them vertical, and write $z_x$ for
the $x$-coordinate of a point $z$. If some $s_i$ and $s_j$ with $i \ne j$ meet, then there are
indices $a \ne b$ and a point $p \in s_a \cap s_b$ such that $p_x \le z_x$ for all indices
$k \ne l$ and every point $z \in s_k \cap s_l$.

articles.title: Leftmost point of the intersection of two segments
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field,
write $x_1$ for the first coordinate of a point $x \in K^2$, and let $[p, q]$ and $[p', q']$ be
segments in $K^2$ with $p_1 < q_1$ and $p'_1 < q'_1$. If $[p, q] \cap [p', q']$ is nonempty, then
it contains a point $m$ with $m_1 \le w_1$ for every $w \in [p, q] \cap [p', q']$.

articles.title: Soundness of the any-segments-intersect sweep
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a family of $n$ segments in
$K^2$, $K$ a linearly ordered field, and split the sorted list of their $2n$ endpoint events as
$P$ followed by $Q$. If running the sweep over $P$ from the empty status list succeeds with status
list $T$, and running it over $Q$ from $T$ reports an intersection, then there are two distinct
indices $i \ne j$ such that segments $i$ and $j$ meet.

In particular, when the sweep over all the events reports an intersection, two distinct segments
meet.

articles.title: Crossing of two non-vertical segments
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered field, write $z_1$ for
the first coordinate of a point $z \in K^2$, and let $[p, q]$ and $[p', q']$ be segments in $K^2$
with $p_1 < q_1$ and $p'_1 < q'_1$. For $t \in K$ let $y(t)$ be the height at $t$ of the line
through $p$ and $q$, and $y'(t)$ that of the line through $p'$ and $q'$. Let $a < b$ with
$p_1 \le a$, $p'_1 \le a$, $b \le q_1$ and $b \le q'_1$. If $y(a) < y'(a)$ and $y'(b) \le y(b)$,
then some $z \in [p, q] \cap [p', q']$ has $a < z_1 \le b$, and $z_1 < b$ if moreover
$y'(b) < y(b)$.

articles.title: First element at or above a uniquely attained height
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map a type to a linearly
ordered set, let $y$ be a value, and let $T$ be a list sorted non-strictly by $f$, that is,
$f(j) \le f(k)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$ in $T$. Suppose $b$ lies in $T$ with $f(b) = y$,
and every element $c \ne b$ of $T$ has $f(c) \ne y$. Then removing from $T$ its longest prefix of
elements $j$ with $f(j) < y$ leaves a list whose first element is $b$.

articles.title: Left endpoint events precede right endpoint events
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered set
and $S$ a family of segments in $K^2$, each given by its two endpoints. For every segment $i$ of
$S$, the left endpoint event of $i$ is strictly smaller than its right endpoint event in the sweep
order on events (by $x$-coordinate, then left endpoints before right endpoints, then by
$y$-coordinate).

articles.title: Sweep order on endpoint events
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered set and $S$ a family of
segments in $K^2$, each given by its two endpoints. An endpoint event $e$ of $S$ standing for the
point $(x, y)$ gets the key $(x, \varepsilon, y)$, compared lexicographically, where
$\varepsilon = 0$ if $e$ is a left endpoint and $\varepsilon = 1$ if it is a right endpoint. So
events are ordered by $x$; at equal $x$, left endpoints come first; then by $y$. This is the
endpoint order of CLRS.

articles.title: A sweep prefix with a right endpoint has its left endpoint
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered
set and $S$ a family of $n$ segments in $K^2$, each given by its two endpoints. If the sorted sweep
event list of $S$ is a list $P$ followed by a list $Q$, and $P$ contains the right endpoint event
of a segment $j$, then $P$ also contains the left endpoint event of $j$.

articles.title: Left endpoint of a segment
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a linearly ordered set and $S$ a family of segments
in $K^2$, segment $i$ being given by its two endpoints $(a, b)$ in either order. The left endpoint
of segment $i$ is $a$ if $a_1 \le b_1$ and $b$ otherwise, where $a_1$ and $b_1$ are the first
coordinates.

articles.title: Height of a line at an abscissa
articles.statement:
For points $p = (p_1, p_2)$ and $q = (q_1, q_2)$ in $K^2$,
$K$ a field, and $x \in K$, this is $p_2 + (x - p_1)(q_2 - p_2)/(q_1 - p_1)$, with division by
zero read as $0$. When $p_1 \ne q_1$ it is the height at $x$ of the line through $p$ and $q$.

articles.title: Meeting segments
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a linear order and $S$ a family of segments in
$K^2$, each given by its two endpoints. Segments $i$ and $j$ of $S$ meet when the closed segment
between the endpoints of $i$ and the closed segment between the endpoints of $j$ have a point in
common.

articles.title: A non-vertical segment is the graph of its line
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be points of the plane
over a linearly ordered field, where a point $z$ has coordinates $(z_1, z_2)$, and suppose
$p_1 < q_1$. A point $z$ lies on the segment from $p$ to $q$ if and only if $p_1 \le z_1 \le q_1$
and $z_2$ is the height at abscissa $z_1$ of the line through $p$ and $q$.

articles.title: The sweep order holds weakly at the leftmost intersection
articles.statement:
Let finitely many segments in
the plane over a linearly ordered field be given, where a point $z$ has coordinates $(z_1, z_2)$
and segment $j$ has left endpoint $l_j$ and right endpoint $r_j$ with $(l_j)_1 < (r_j)_1$. Write
$y_j(t)$ for the height at abscissa $t$ of the line through $l_j$ and $r_j$. Let $p_x$ be such
that every point shared by two distinct segments has abscissa at least $p_x$, let $x < p_x$, and
let $T$ be a list of segments such that $(l_j)_1 \le x$ and $p_x \le (r_j)_1$ for every $j$ in
$T$. If $y_j(x) < y_k(x)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$ in $T$, then $y_j(p_x) \le y_k(p_x)$
whenever $j$ occurs before $k$ in $T$.

articles.title: The sweep order persists before the leftmost intersection
articles.statement:
Let finitely many segments in
the plane over a linearly ordered field be given, where a point $z$ has coordinates $(z_1, z_2)$
and segment $j$ has left endpoint $l_j$ and right endpoint $r_j$ with $(l_j)_1 < (r_j)_1$. Write
$y_j(t)$ for the height at abscissa $t$ of the line through $l_j$ and $r_j$. Let $p_x$ be such
that every point shared by two distinct segments has abscissa at least $p_x$, let
$x \le x' < p_x$, and let $T$ be a list of segments such that $(l_j)_1 \le x$ and
$x' \le (r_j)_1$ for every $j$ in $T$. If $y_j(x) < y_k(x)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$ in
$T$, then $y_j(x') < y_k(x')$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$ in $T$.

articles.title: Inserting into a weakly sorted list
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map a type $\alpha$ to a linearly ordered
set, let $T$ be a list over $\alpha$ with $f(j) \le f(k)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$, let
$i \in \alpha$, and let $P$ be a predicate that holds for an element $j$ of $T$ exactly when
$f(j) < f(i)$. Insert $i$ just before the first element of $T$ not satisfying $P$: the list made
of the longest prefix of $T$ satisfying $P$, then $i$, then the rest of $T$. In this list,
$f(j) \le f(k)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$.

articles.title: Inserting into a strictly sorted list
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map a type $\alpha$ to a linearly ordered
set, let $T$ be a list over $\alpha$ with $f(j) < f(k)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$, let
$i \in \alpha$ be such that $f(j) \ne f(i)$ for every $j$ in $T$, and let $P$ be a predicate that
holds for an element $j$ of $T$ exactly when $f(j) < f(i)$. Insert $i$ just before the first
element of $T$ not satisfying $P$: the list made of the longest prefix of $T$ satisfying $P$, then
$i$, then the rest of $T$. In this list, $f(j) < f(k)$ whenever $j$ occurs before $k$.

articles.title: Endpoint of an event
articles.statement:
The point of the sweep event $(i, b)$ is the left endpoint of
segment $i$ when $b$ is true (a left-endpoint event) and the right endpoint of segment $i$ when
$b$ is false.

articles.title: Right endpoint of a segment
articles.statement:
Write $z_1$ for the abscissa of a point $z$. If segment $i$
is given by the endpoints $u$ and $v$, in this order, its right endpoint is $v$ when
$u_1 \le v_1$ and $u$ otherwise.

articles.title: Sweep completeness when the leftmost intersection is a left endpoint
articles.statement:
Let $n$ segments in
the plane over a linearly ordered field be given, where $z_1$ is the abscissa of a point $z$ and
segment $i$ has left endpoint $l_i$ and right endpoint $r_i$ with $(l_i)_1 < (r_i)_1$, and
suppose no point lies on three distinct segments. Let $a \ne b$ be segments such that $l_a$ lies
on segment $b$ and every point shared by two distinct segments has abscissa at least $(l_a)_1$.
If the left endpoint of $b$ comes before the left endpoint of $a$ in the sorted list of endpoint
events, then the sweep, run on that list from the empty status list, reports an intersection.

Inserting $a$ places it right next to $b$, so the two are tested.

articles.title: Sweep completeness when the leftmost intersection is inside both segments
articles.statement:
Let $n$
segments in the plane over a linearly ordered field be given, where $z_1$ is the abscissa of a
point $z$ and segment $i$ has left endpoint $l_i$ and right endpoint $r_i$ with
$(l_i)_1 < (r_i)_1$, and suppose no point lies on three distinct segments. Let $a \ne b$ be
segments that share a point $p$ such that every point shared by two distinct segments has
abscissa at least $p_1$, and suppose $(l_a)_1 < p_1$ and $(l_b)_1 < p_1$. Then the sweep, run on
the sorted list of endpoint events from the empty status list, reports an intersection.

Just before the sweep line reaches $p$, the segments $a$ and $b$ are neighbours on the status
list, so they were tested.

articles.title: Completeness of the segment-intersection sweep
articles.statement:
Let $n$ segments in the plane over a
linearly ordered field be given, none of them vertical (the left endpoint of each has strictly
smaller abscissa than its right endpoint), and assume, as CLRS does, that no point lies on three
distinct segments. If two distinct segments meet, then the sweep, run on the sorted list of
endpoint events from the empty status list, reports an intersection.

articles.title: Neighbours on the sweep status are disjoint
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an initial part of the sorted list
of events. If running the sweep over $P$ from the empty status list reports no intersection and
ends with status list $T$, then no two consecutive segments of $T$ meet.

articles.title: The sweep status holds the active segments
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an initial part of the sorted list
of events. If running the sweep over $P$ from the empty status list reports no intersection and
ends with status list $T$, then $T$ has no repeated entries, and a segment $j$ belongs to $T$
exactly when the left endpoint event of $j$ is in $P$ and the right endpoint event of $j$ is not.

articles.title: The status list is weakly sorted after the events left of a vertical line
articles.statement:
Fix a number
$p_x$ in the field of coordinates. Suppose no segment is vertical (each segment's left endpoint
has smaller $x$-coordinate than its right endpoint) and every point common to two distinct
segments has $x$-coordinate at least $p_x$. Split the sorted list of events as $P$ followed by
$Q$, where the endpoint of every event of $P$ has $x$-coordinate less than $p_x$ and that of every
event of $Q$ has $x$-coordinate at least $p_x$. If running the sweep over $P$ from the empty
status list reports no intersection and ends with status list $T$, then whenever segment $j$
comes before segment $k$ in $T$, the height at $p_x$ of the line through the endpoints of $j$ is
at most that of the line through the endpoints of $k$.

articles.title: Phase two: inserting left endpoints on a vertical line keeps the status weakly sorted
articles.statement:
Fix a number $p_x$ in the field of coordinates. Suppose no segment is vertical (each segment's
left endpoint has smaller $x$-coordinate than its right endpoint) and every point common to two
distinct segments has $x$-coordinate at least $p_x$. Split the sorted list of events as $P_1$,
then $P_2$, then $Q$, where the endpoint of every event of $P_1$ has $x$-coordinate less than
$p_x$, every event of $P_2$ is a left endpoint with $x$-coordinate equal to $p_x$, and the
endpoint of every event of $Q$ has $x$-coordinate at least $p_x$. If running the sweep over $P_1$
followed by $P_2$ from the empty status list reports no intersection and ends with status list
$T$, then whenever segment $j$ comes before segment $k$ in $T$, the height at $p_x$ of the line
through the endpoints of $j$ is at most that of the line through the endpoints of $k$.

articles.title: Phase one: the status list is strictly sorted between the processed and remaining events
articles.statement:
Fix a number $p_x$ in the field of coordinates. Suppose no segment is vertical (each segment's
left endpoint has smaller $x$-coordinate than its right endpoint) and every point common to two
distinct segments has $x$-coordinate at least $p_x$. Split the sorted list of events as $P$
followed by $Q$, where the endpoint of every event of $P$ has $x$-coordinate less than $p_x$, and
suppose running the sweep over $P$ from the empty status list reports no intersection and ends
with status list $T$. Let $x < p_x$ be at least the $x$-coordinate of the endpoint of every event
of $P$ and at most that of every event of $Q$. Then whenever segment $j$ comes before segment $k$
in $T$, the height at $x$ of the line through the endpoints of $j$ is less than that of the line
through the endpoints of $k$.

articles.title: Running the sweep over a list of events
articles.statement:
Starting from a status list $T$, the sweep steps
are applied to the events in order, each to the status list left by the previous one. The result
is the final status list, or no result as soon as some step reports an intersection; on the empty
list of events the result is $T$.

articles.title: One step of the sweep
articles.statement:
A step takes an event and a status list $T$ of segments, ordered
from bottom to top, and returns a new status list, or no result when an intersection is reported.
At the left endpoint $p$ of segment $i$, split $T$ as $A$ followed by $B$, where $A$ is the longest
initial part of $T$ whose segments pass strictly below $p$ by the `DIRECTION` test. If
`SEGMENTS-INTERSECT` reports that $i$ meets the first segment of $B$ or the last segment of $A$
(when these exist), there is no result; otherwise the new status list is $A$, then $i$, then $B$.
At the right endpoint of segment $i$, let $A$ be the part of $T$ before the first occurrence of
$i$ and $B$ the part after it (so $A$ is all of $T$ and $B$ is empty when $i$ does not occur). If
both the last segment of $A$ and the first segment of $B$ exist and `SEGMENTS-INTERSECT` reports
that they meet, there is no result; otherwise the new status list is $A$ followed by $B$.

articles.title: The any-segments-intersect sweep
articles.statement:
CLRS `ANY-SEGMENTS-INTERSECT`, lines 3-11: the sweep
processes a list of events with a status list $T$ of segments ordered from bottom to top, returns
true as soon as an intersection test succeeds, and returns false once the events run out. At the
left endpoint $p$ of segment $i$, split $T$ as $A$ followed by $B$, where $A$ is the longest
initial part of $T$ whose segments pass strictly below $p$ by the `DIRECTION` test; this scan
costs $\min(|A| + 1, |T|)$, one `DIRECTION` per segment scanned. Segment $i$ is tested with
`SEGMENTS-INTERSECT` against the first segment of $B$ and then against the last segment of $A$
(when these exist), and the sweep continues with $A$, then $i$, then $B$. At the right endpoint
of segment $i$, with $A$ the part of $T$ before the first occurrence of $i$ and $B$ the part
after it, the last segment of $A$ is tested against the first segment of $B$ when both exist,
and the sweep continues with $A$ followed by $B$.

articles.title: Splitting a list at the first occurrence of a member
articles.statement:
If $i$ occurs in a list $T$ of
indices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, then $T$ is the longest initial part of $T$ not containing $i$,
followed by $i$, followed by the part of $T$ after the first occurrence of $i$.

articles.title: Testing a segment against an optional neighbour
articles.statement:
Given a segment $i$ and possibly a
neighbour $j$, return the result of `SEGMENTS-INTERSECT` on segments $i$ and $j$, with its cost,
when $j$ is given, and return false at no cost when there is no neighbour.

articles.title: Testing the neighbours of a deleted segment
articles.statement:
Given $n$ segments in the plane over a
linearly ordered field and two optional segment indices $a$ and $b$ (in the sweep, the segments
just below and just above a deleted segment, when they exist), this runs the intersection test
of segments $a$ and $b$ when both indices are present, and otherwise returns `false` at no
cost.

articles.title: Intersection test for two input segments
articles.statement:
Given $n$ segments in the plane over a
linearly ordered field, each given by its two endpoints, and indices $i, j < n$, this runs CLRS
`SEGMENTS-INTERSECT` on the left and right endpoints of segment $i$ and the left and right
endpoints of segment $j$. It returns that procedure's Boolean answer together with its cost in
`DIRECTION` and `ON-SEGMENT` evaluations.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol with data is observation congruent to the buffer
articles.statement:
In the
labelled transition system of the protocol's recursive specification, the alternating-bit protocol
with data is observation congruent (rooted weakly bisimilar) to the empty one-place buffer of
bits: every transition of either process with some label is matched by the other process through
silent steps, then one actual step with the same label, then silent steps, and the two resulting
processes are weakly bisimilar.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol transmits data correctly
articles.statement:
It is weakly
bisimilar to the empty one-place buffer of bits.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The protocol process in its initial
configuration: the sender is ready to accept a data bit, to be sent with sequence bit false, the
data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and the receiver expects a frame with
sequence bit false. The four agents run in parallel, with all internal channels restricted.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol is observation congruent to a one-place buffer
articles.statement:
In the
labelled transition system of the protocol's recursive CCS specification, the data-free
alternating-bit protocol over lossy one-place channels is rooted weakly bisimilar (observation
congruent) to the one-place buffer
$\mathit{buf} = \mathit{acc}.\overline{\mathit{del}}.\mathit{buf}$.

This is stronger than weak bisimilarity; it holds because initially neither process can move
silently.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol implements a one-place buffer
articles.statement:
In the labelled transition
system of the protocol's recursive CCS specification, the data-free alternating-bit protocol over
lossy one-place channels is weakly bisimilar to the one-place buffer
$\mathit{buf} = \mathit{acc}.\overline{\mathit{del}}.\mathit{buf}$.

articles.title: The data-free alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
The process $\mathit{abp}$ is the protocol in its
initial configuration: the parallel composition of the sender, the lossy one-place data channel,
the receiver and the lossy one-place acknowledgement channel, with all eight internal channels
$\mathit{send}_b$, $\mathit{recv}_b$, $\mathit{reply}_b$ and $\mathit{ack}_b$ (for both bits $b$)
restricted, where the sender is ready to accept a message to be sent with bit $0$, both channels
are empty, and the receiver expects bit $0$.

articles.title: Acknowledgement channel of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The transitions of the
lossy one-place acknowledgement channel: when empty, it can take an input on $\mathrm{reply}_b$
for either bit $b$ and then holds $b$; when holding $b$, it can either output on $\mathrm{ack}_b$
or lose $b$ by a silent step, and in both cases it becomes empty.

articles.title: Transitions of the acknowledgement channel in the data-free alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
When
empty, the lossy one-place acknowledgement channel can, for either bit $b$, input on
$\mathit{reply}_b$ and become full with bit $b$. When full with bit $b$, it can output on
$\mathit{ack}_b$ or make a silent $\tau$ step (losing the bit), in both cases becoming empty. These
are all its transitions.

articles.title: Process constants of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
There is one process constant
for each sender state, each content of the data channel (empty, or a sequence bit with a data
bit), each receiver state, each content of the acknowledgement channel (empty, or a bit), and each
content of the one-place buffer of bits (empty, or a bit).

articles.title: Process constants of the data-free alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
There is one process constant
for each sender state, each state of the data channel, each receiver state, each state of the
acknowledgement channel, and each state of the one-place buffer (empty or full).

articles.title: The empty one-place buffer of bits
articles.statement:
The process constant of the one-place buffer of bits
with empty content.

articles.title: The data-free one-place buffer
articles.statement:
The process $\mathit{buf}$ is the one-place buffer in its
empty state. By the specification it accepts on $\mathit{acc}$ and becomes full, and the full
buffer delivers on $\mathit{del}$ and becomes empty again, so
$\mathit{buf} = \mathit{acc}.\overline{\mathit{del}}.\mathit{buf}$.

articles.title: The one-place buffer of bits with given content
articles.statement:
For a content $q$, which is either empty
or a bit, the process constant of the one-place buffer of bits holding $q$.

articles.title: Transitions of the one-place buffer of bits
articles.statement:
When empty, the buffer can take an input on
$\mathrm{acc}_d$ for either bit $d$ and then holds $d$; when holding $d$, its only transition is
an output on $\mathrm{del}_d$, after which it is empty.

articles.title: Transitions of the data-free one-place buffer
articles.statement:
The one-place buffer has two states, empty
(false) and full (true). When empty, its only transition is an input on $\mathit{acc}$ to the full
state; when full, its only transition is an output on $\mathit{del}$ to the empty state.

articles.title: The data-free one-place buffer in a given state
articles.statement:
For a Boolean $f$, $\mathit{buffer}(f)$ is
the process constant for the one-place buffer that is full if $f$ is true and empty if $f$ is
false.

articles.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate for the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
A list of 220
pairs, each a protocol configuration together with the buffer content it simulates: every
reachable configuration with the buffer content it simulates, listed so that every pair reaches
the visible actions of its buffer state through pairs listed earlier.

articles.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate for the data-free alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
The list of every
reachable protocol configuration, paired with the buffer state it simulates (full from the accept
of a message until its delivery), sorted by silent distance to the next visible action.

articles.title: States of a one-place channel
articles.statement:
A one-place channel is either empty or full, holding a single
bit.

articles.title: Configurations of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
A configuration consists of a
sender state, the content of the data channel (empty, or a pair of a sequence bit and a data
bit), a receiver state, and the content of the acknowledgement channel (empty, or a bit).

articles.title: Transitions of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
For a configuration, made of a
sender state, a data-channel content, a receiver state and an acknowledgement-channel content,
the transitions are those of the parallel composition of the sender, the data channel, the
receiver and the acknowledgement channel, where one component moves alone or two components
synchronize on complementary labels in a silent step. Of these, only the silent steps and the
actions on names that are not internal channels are kept; the internal channels are the sending,
receiving, reply and acknowledgement channels.

articles.title: Alternating-bit configuration transitions
articles.statement:
The transitions of a configuration of the
alternating-bit protocol, listed as pairs of a label and a successor configuration, are obtained
by composing the transitions of the sender, the data channel, the receiver and the
acknowledgement channel in parallel, in that order (at each stage either side moves alone, or
the two sides synchronize on an input and the complementary output on the same channel name,
giving a silent step), and then keeping only the silent steps and the steps whose channel name
is not one of the internal channel names.

articles.title: Alternating-bit configuration
articles.statement:
A configuration of the alternating-bit protocol consists
of a sender state, a state of the data channel, a receiver state and a state of the
acknowledgement channel.

articles.title: Data-channel transitions of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The data channel is a
lossy one-place channel whose content is either empty or a pair $(b, d)$ of a sequence bit $b$
and a data bit $d$. Its transitions, as a list of pairs of a label and a successor content: the
empty channel inputs on $\mathsf{send}(b, d)$ and then holds $(b, d)$, for the four pairs $(b, d)$
in the order $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$, $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true})$,
$(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$, $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true})$; a channel holding $(b, d)$
either outputs on $\mathsf{recv}(b, d)$ and becomes empty, or loses the frame by a silent step
$\tau$ and becomes empty.

articles.title: Alternating-bit data channel transitions
articles.statement:
The one-place data channel of the
alternating-bit protocol has the following transitions. When empty, it can input on
$\mathit{send}_b$ and become full with bit $b$, for each bit $b$. When full with bit $b$, it can
output on $\mathit{recv}_b$ and become empty, or lose the bit by a silent step and become empty.

articles.title: Initial configuration of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The configuration in
which the sender is in state $\mathsf{accept}(\mathrm{false})$, ready to accept a message to be
sent with sequence bit false, the data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and
the receiver is in state $\mathsf{expect}(\mathrm{false})$, expecting a frame with sequence bit
false.

articles.title: Initial alternating-bit configuration
articles.statement:
The initial configuration of the alternating-bit
protocol has the sender ready to accept a message with bit $\mathrm{false}$, both channels
empty, and the receiver expecting bit $\mathrm{false}$.

articles.title: Internal channels of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The list of the channel names
that the protocol restricts: $\mathsf{send}(b, d)$ followed by $\mathsf{recv}(b, d)$ for the pairs
$(b, d)$ in the order $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$, $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true})$,
$(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$, $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true})$, then
$\mathsf{reply}(\mathrm{false})$, $\mathsf{reply}(\mathrm{true})$, $\mathsf{ack}(\mathrm{false})$
and $\mathsf{ack}(\mathrm{true})$.

articles.title: Internal channels of the alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
The internal channel names, all of
which the protocol restricts, are $\mathit{send}_b$, $\mathit{recv}_b$, $\mathit{reply}_b$ and
$\mathit{ack}_b$ for both bits $b$, that is, every channel name except $\mathit{acc}$ and
$\mathit{del}$.

articles.title: Transition system of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The labelled transition
system whose states are the CCS processes over the protocol's channel names and process
constants, whose labels are the CCS labels over its channel names, and whose transitions are
generated by the protocol's recursive specification.

articles.title: Alternating-bit transition system
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system whose states are the
CCS processes over the alternating-bit channel names and process constants, whose labels are the
CCS labels over those names, and whose transitions are the steps of the CCS operational
semantics for the recursive specification that defines each process constant (one per state of
the sender, the data channel, the receiver, the acknowledgement channel and the one-place
buffer) as the choice of its listed transitions.

articles.title: Channel names of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
For bits $b$ and $d$, where $b$ is
a sequence bit and $d$ a data bit, the channel names are $\mathsf{acc}(d)$ (accept the data bit
$d$ from the user), $\mathsf{del}(d)$ (deliver the data bit $d$ to the user), $\mathsf{send}(b, d)$
(sender to data channel), $\mathsf{recv}(b, d)$ (data channel to receiver), $\mathsf{reply}(b)$
(receiver to acknowledgement channel) and $\mathsf{ack}(b)$ (acknowledgement channel to sender).

articles.title: Alternating-bit channel names
articles.statement:
The channel names of the alternating-bit protocol are
$\mathit{acc}$ (accept a message from the user), $\mathit{del}$ (deliver a message to the
user), and, for each bit $b$, the internal names $\mathit{send}_b$ (sender to data channel),
$\mathit{recv}_b$ (data channel to receiver), $\mathit{reply}_b$ (receiver to acknowledgement
channel) and $\mathit{ack}_b$ (acknowledgement channel to sender).

articles.title: Receiver states of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
For bits $b$ and $d$, a receiver
state is $\mathsf{expect}(b)$, expecting a frame with sequence bit $b$; $\mathsf{deliver}(b, d)$,
about to deliver the data bit $d$ of a frame with sequence bit $b$; or $\mathsf{reply}(b)$, about
to acknowledge $b$.

articles.title: Receiver transitions of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The transitions of each
receiver state, as a list of pairs of a label and a successor state, for bits $b$ and $d$:
$\mathsf{expect}(b)$ inputs on $\mathsf{recv}(b, d)$ and moves to $\mathsf{deliver}(b, d)$, or
inputs a duplicate on $\mathsf{recv}(\lnot b, d)$ and moves to the state $\mathsf{reply}(\lnot b)$,
these two for $d = \mathrm{false}$ and then for $d = \mathrm{true}$; $\mathsf{deliver}(b, d)$
outputs on $\mathsf{del}(d)$ and moves to the state $\mathsf{reply}(b)$; and the state
$\mathsf{reply}(b)$ outputs on the channel $\mathsf{reply}(b)$ and moves to
$\mathsf{expect}(\lnot b)$. So the receiver delivers the data of an expected frame and
acknowledges a duplicate again.

articles.title: Alternating-bit receiver transitions
articles.statement:
The receiver of the alternating-bit protocol has
the following transitions. Expecting bit $b$, it can input on $\mathit{recv}_b$ and become ready
to deliver $b$, or input on $\mathit{recv}_{\lnot b}$ and become ready to acknowledge $\lnot b$.
Ready to deliver $b$, it can output on $\mathit{del}$ and become ready to acknowledge $b$. Ready
to acknowledge $b$, it can output on $\mathit{reply}_b$ and then expect $\lnot b$.

articles.title: Alternating-bit receiver states
articles.statement:
A state of the alternating-bit receiver is, for a bit
$b$, either expecting a frame with bit $b$, about to deliver the message of a frame with bit
$b$, or about to acknowledge bit $b$.

articles.title: Sender states of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
For bits $b$ and $d$, a sender
state is $\mathsf{accept}(b)$, ready to accept a message to be sent with sequence bit $b$;
$\mathsf{transmit}(b, d)$, about to transmit the data bit $d$ with sequence bit $b$; or
$\mathsf{await}(b, d)$, waiting for the acknowledgement of $b$ while holding $d$ for
retransmission.

articles.title: Sender transitions of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
The transitions of each
sender state, as a list of pairs of a label and a successor state, for bits $b$ and $d$:
$\mathsf{accept}(b)$ inputs on $\mathsf{acc}(d)$ and moves to $\mathsf{transmit}(b, d)$, for
$d = \mathrm{false}$ and then $d = \mathrm{true}$; $\mathsf{transmit}(b, d)$ outputs on
$\mathsf{send}(b, d)$ and moves to $\mathsf{await}(b, d)$; and $\mathsf{await}(b, d)$ inputs on
$\mathsf{ack}(b)$ and moves to $\mathsf{accept}(\lnot b)$, inputs on $\mathsf{ack}(\lnot b)$ and
stays in $\mathsf{await}(b, d)$, or times out by a silent step $\tau$ back to
$\mathsf{transmit}(b, d)$, in this order.

articles.title: Alternating-bit sender transitions
articles.statement:
The sender of the alternating-bit protocol has the
following transitions. Ready to accept with bit $b$, it can input on $\mathit{acc}$ and become
about to transmit $b$. About to transmit $b$, it can output on $\mathit{send}_b$ and then await
the acknowledgement of $b$. Awaiting the acknowledgement of $b$, it can input on
$\mathit{ack}_b$ and become ready to accept with bit $\lnot b$, input on
$\mathit{ack}_{\lnot b}$ and keep waiting, or time out by a silent step and become about to
transmit $b$ again.

articles.title: Sender states of the data-free alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
For each bit $b$, the sender
has three states: $\mathrm{accept}(b)$, ready to accept a message to be sent with bit $b$;
$\mathrm{transmit}(b)$, about to transmit a frame tagged with bit $b$; and $\mathrm{await}(b)$,
waiting for the acknowledgement of bit $b$. These six states are all the sender states.

articles.title: Recursive specification of the alternating-bit protocol with data
articles.statement:
There is a separate
process constant $X_s$ for each state $s$ of each of five components: the sender, the lossy data
channel, the receiver, the lossy acknowledgement channel and the one-place buffer of bits. If
$(a_1, s_1), \dots, (a_n, s_n)$ are the listed transitions of $s$ in its component, then the body
of $X_s$ is the choice of prefixes $a_1.X_{s_1} + (a_2.X_{s_2} + \dots + (a_n.X_{s_n} + 0))$,
where each $X_{s_i}$ is the constant of the same component and $0$ is the inactive process; the
body is $0$ when $s$ has no listed transitions.

articles.title: Recursive specification of the data-free alternating-bit protocol
articles.statement:
The process constants
are the states of the five agents: the sender, the data channel, the receiver, the
acknowledgement channel and the one-place buffer. For a state $x$ of one of these agents, let
$(a_1, x_1), \dots, (a_n, x_n)$ be the transitions of $x$ as listed by the transition function
of its agent, let $X_i$ be the constant of the same agent at state $x_i$, and let $\mathbf{0}$
be the inactive process. The specification defines the constant of $x$ as the choice of
prefixes $a_1.X_1 + (a_2.X_2 + \cdots + (a_n.X_n + \mathbf{0}))$.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol with data in a configuration
articles.statement:
For a configuration $c$ made of
a sender state $s$, a data-channel content $d$, a receiver state $r$ and an
acknowledgement-channel content $k$, the protocol process at $c$ is
$((X_s \mid X_d) \mid X_r) \mid X_k$ with every internal channel restricted, where $X_s$, $X_d$,
$X_r$ and $X_k$ are the process constants of these states. The internal channels are all channel
names other than accepting and delivering a data bit.

articles.title: The alternating-bit protocol in a configuration
articles.statement:
Consider a configuration with sender
state $s$, data channel state $d$, receiver state $r$ and acknowledgement channel state $k$.
Write $\mathrm{Sender}(s)$, $\mathrm{Data}(d)$, $\mathrm{Receiver}(r)$ and $\mathrm{Ack}(k)$
for the constants of the four agents at these states, and let $L$ be the set of internal
channels $\mathrm{send}(b)$, $\mathrm{recv}(b)$, $\mathrm{reply}(b)$ and $\mathrm{ack}(b)$ for
both bits $b$. The protocol process is the parallel composition of these constants with every
internal channel restricted,
$(((\mathrm{Sender}(s) \mid \mathrm{Data}(d)) \mid \mathrm{Receiver}(r)) \mid \mathrm{Ack}(k))
\setminus L$.

articles.title: Removing a process from a safe sequence
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum
claims and current allocations, let $w$ be a vector of free resources (a natural number for
each resource type), and let $\sigma$ be a list of processes that is a safe sequence for $S$
from $w$. If $p$ occurs in $\sigma$, then the list obtained from $\sigma$ by deleting the first
occurrence of $p$ is a safe sequence for $S$ from $w + \mathrm{alloc}(p)$, where
$\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ is the current allocation of $p$ and the sum is taken componentwise.

In other words, letting a member of a safe sequence finish first and release its allocation
leaves the rest of the sequence safe. This is why the greedy safety check is complete.

articles.title: A safe state is not deadlocked
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum claims and
current allocations, let $w$ be a vector of free resources (a natural number for each resource
type), and let $L$ be a nonempty list of pending processes. If $S$ is safe from $w$ for $L$, then
some process $p$ in $L$ has remaining need $\mathrm{need}(p) \le w$ componentwise, so it can be
given its whole remaining need.

articles.title: Granting a request
articles.statement:
For a system $S$ of processes with maximum claims and current
allocations, a process $p$ and a resource vector $r$ (a natural number for each resource type),
the system obtained by granting $r$ to $p$ has the same maximum claims as $S$, gives $p$ the
allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p) + r$ (componentwise sum, where $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ is the current
allocation of $p$ in $S$), and leaves the allocation of every other process unchanged.

articles.title: Safe sequences are monotone in the free resources
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of processes with
maximum claims and current allocations, and let $\sigma$ be a list of processes. If $\sigma$ is a
safe sequence for $S$ from a vector $w$ of free resources (a natural number for each resource
type), and $w \le w'$ componentwise, then $\sigma$ is also a safe sequence for $S$ from $w'$.

articles.title: Remaining need after a grant
articles.statement:
For a system $S$ of processes with maximum claims and
current allocations, a process $p$ and a resource vector $r$ (a natural number for each resource
type), the remaining need of $p$ in the system obtained by granting $r$ to $p$ equals
$\mathrm{need}(p) - r$, where $\mathrm{need}(p)$ is the remaining need of $p$ in $S$ and the
subtraction is truncated subtraction of natural numbers, taken componentwise.

articles.title: Remaining need
articles.statement:
The remaining need of a process $p$ in a system $S$ is the resource
vector $\mathrm{claim}(p) - \mathrm{alloc}(p)$: the maximum claim of $p$ minus its current
allocation, computed for each resource type by truncated subtraction of natural numbers, so it
is $0$ for every resource type where the allocation exceeds the claim.

articles.title: The request algorithm grants exactly the safe requests within the claim and the free resources
articles.statement:
**The request algorithm grants exactly the safe requests within the claim
and the free resources.** Let $S$ be a system of claims and allocations with processes $P$ and a
finite set $R$ of resource types, let $a : R \to \mathbb{N}$ be the vector of free resources, $L$
a list of pending processes, $p$ a process and $r : R \to \mathbb{N}$ the resources that $p$
requests. Write $\mathrm{need}(p)$ for the remaining need of $p$ in $S$, $T$ for the system
obtained from $S$ by granting $r$ to $p$, and $a - r$ for componentwise truncated subtraction.
The resource-request algorithm grants the request and returns the free vector $a'$ and the
system $S'$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $L$, $L$ has no repetitions, both
$r \le \mathrm{need}(p)$ and $r \le a$ hold componentwise, $T$ is safe from $a - r$ for $L$,
$a' = a - r$, and $S' = T$.

articles.title: Granted requests lead to safe states
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of processes with maximum
claims and current allocations, $a$ the vector of free resources, $L$ the list of pending
processes, $p$ a process and $r$ a resource vector. If the resource-request algorithm grants the
request of $r$ by $p$, returning the free vector $a'$ and the system $S'$, then $S'$ is safe from
$a'$ for $L$.

articles.title: Resource-request algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of claims and allocations with processes
$P$ and a finite set $R$ of resource types, let $a : R \to \mathbb{N}$ be the vector of free
resources, $L$ a list of pending processes, $p$ a process and $r : R \to \mathbb{N}$ the
resources that $p$ requests. The request is granted when $p$ occurs in $L$, $L$ has no
repetitions, $r \le \mathrm{need}(p)$ and $r \le a$ componentwise, where $\mathrm{need}(p)$ is
the remaining need of $p$ in $S$, and the banker's safety algorithm succeeds for the system
obtained from $S$ by granting $r$ to $p$, from the free vector $a - r$ (componentwise truncated
subtraction) and the list $L$. A granted request returns the free vector $a - r$ and that
system; otherwise the algorithm returns no result.

No result covers the error case of the textbook algorithm (a request beyond the remaining
claim), the cases where the process must wait, and malformed input (a requester that is not
pending, or a pending list with repetitions).

articles.title: Letting a process that fits finish preserves safety
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of processes
with maximum claims and current allocations, $w$ a vector of free resources (a natural number
for each resource type) and $L$ a list of pending processes without repetitions. If $p$ occurs in
$L$ and its remaining need $\mathrm{need}(p)$ in $S$ satisfies $\mathrm{need}(p) \le w$
componentwise, then $S$ is safe from $w$ for $L$ if and only if $S$ is safe from
$w + \mathrm{alloc}(p)$ for the list obtained from $L$ by removing $p$, where
$\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ is the current allocation of $p$ and the sum is taken componentwise.

articles.title: Safe sequence
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system with processes $P$ and resource types $R$, where
process $p$ has maximum claim $\mathrm{claim}(p)$ and allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ in
$R \to \mathbb{N}$. A list $p_1, \dots, p_k$ of processes is a safe sequence from the free
resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for each $i$, the remaining need
$\mathrm{claim}(p_i) - \mathrm{alloc}(p_i)$ (truncated at zero) is at most
$w + \mathrm{alloc}(p_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{alloc}(p_{i-1})$ componentwise. In particular
the empty list is a safe sequence from every $w$.

Thus each process in turn can be given its remaining need from what is free, finish, and
release its allocation.

articles.title: Safe state
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of claims and allocations with processes $P$ and
resource types $R$. A list of pending processes is safe from the free resource vector
$w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when it has no repetitions and some permutation of it is a safe sequence
from $w$: the pending processes can all finish, one after another, in some order.

articles.title: Banker's safety algorithm with fuel
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system with processes $P$ and a
finite set $R$ of resource types, where process $p$ has maximum claim $\mathrm{claim}(p)$ and
allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ in $R \to \mathbb{N}$. Given a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a free
resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm succeeds
if the list is empty. Otherwise, if $n > 0$ and some pending process $q$ has remaining need
$\mathrm{claim}(q) - \mathrm{alloc}(q)$ (truncated at zero) at most $w$ componentwise, it takes
the first such process $p$ in the list, removes that occurrence of $p$ from the list, adds
$\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ to $w$ and continues with fuel $n - 1$; if $n = 0$ or no pending process
fits, it fails.

articles.title: Correctness of the safety algorithm
articles.statement:
For every system $S$ of claims and allocations over
a finite set $R$ of resource types, every free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ and every
list of pending processes, the banker's safety algorithm succeeds on $w$ and the list if and
only if the list is a safe state from $w$.

articles.title: Banker's safety algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a system of claims and allocations with processes
$P$ and a finite set $R$ of resource types. Given a free resource vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$
and a list of pending processes, the algorithm fails if the list has a repetition. Otherwise it
runs the safety algorithm with fuel equal to the length of the list: it repeatedly lets the
first pending process whose remaining need (claim minus allocation, truncated at zero) is at
most the free resources componentwise finish and adds its allocation to the free resources,
for at most one round per pending process, and it succeeds exactly when no pending process is
left at the end.

articles.title: Claims and allocations of processes
articles.statement:
A system with processes $P$ and resource types
$R$ consists of two maps $\mathrm{claim}, \mathrm{alloc} : P \to (R \to \mathbb{N})$, where
$\mathrm{claim}(p)$ is the maximum demand of process $p$ for each resource type and
$\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ is the amount of each resource type currently allocated to $p$. No
inequality between the two is required.

articles.title: Agreement condition (IC1)
articles.statement:
Consider the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$,
order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour of the traitors. Condition IC1 holds after $T$
rounds when any two generals $i$ and $j$, neither of which is the commander or a traitor, decide
the same value after $T$ rounds of this execution.

articles.title: The oral messages algorithm solves the Byzantine generals problem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite set
of more than $3m$ generals, at most $m$ of whom are traitors, and let the commander $c \in G$ run
$\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with the value $v$, with no superiors and with all the other generals as
lieutenants. Then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants decide the same value,
and if $c$ is loyal, every loyal lieutenant decides $v$.

This is Theorem 1 of Lamport–Shostak–Pease, applied to all the generals.

articles.title: Decision of a general
articles.statement:
In the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$, order $v$, a
set of traitors and a behaviour of the traitors, the decision of general $i$ after $T$ rounds is
the value that the decision function of $P$ assigns to $i$ in its state after $T$ rounds.

articles.title: No protocol for three generals tolerates one traitor
articles.statement:
Suppose there are at least two
possible orders. For every oral-message protocol for three generals $0$, $1$, $2$ with commander
$0$ and every number of rounds $T$, there are an order $v$, a general $t$ and a behaviour of $t$
such that, in the execution with order $v$ in which $t$ is the only traitor, the agreement
condition (IC1) or the validity condition (IC2) fails after $T$ rounds.

This is the theorem of Pease, Shostak and Lamport, proved here by a commander version of the
hexagon argument of Fischer, Lynch and Merritt.

articles.title: Messages received in a round
articles.statement:
In the execution of a protocol $P$ with commander $c$,
order $v$, a set of traitors and a behaviour $\mathrm{adv}$ of the traitors, the messages that
general $i$ receives in round $r$ form the function of the sender $j$ whose value is
$\mathrm{adv}(r, j, i)$ if $j$ is a traitor, and otherwise the message that $P$ has $j$ send to
$i$ in round $r$ from the state of $j$ after $r$ rounds.

articles.title: Initial state of a lieutenant
articles.statement:
If general $i$ is not the commander $c$, then the initial
state of $i$ when $c$ has order $v$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to $i$ as a
general other than the commander; in particular, it does not depend on $v$.

articles.title: Initial state of the commander
articles.statement:
When the commander $c$ has order $v$, the initial state of
$c$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to a commander with order $v$.

articles.title: Initial state of a general
articles.statement:
When the commander $c$ has order $v$, the initial state of
general $i$ is the initial state that the protocol assigns to a commander with order $v$ if
$i = c$, and the initial state that the protocol assigns to $i$ as a general other than the
commander if $i \ne c$.

articles.title: Majority falls back to the default value
articles.statement:
If, for every value $x$, at most half of the
elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the
majority of $s$ is the default value (retreat).

articles.title: A value filling more than half of a multiset is its majority
articles.statement:
If more than half of the
elements of a multiset $s$ of values are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity), then the
majority of $s$ is $x$.

articles.title: Majority of a multiset
articles.statement:
The majority of a finite multiset $s$ of values is the value $x$
such that more than half of the elements of $s$ are equal to $x$ (counted with multiplicity),
if there is one (there is at most one), and a fixed default value (retreat) otherwise.

articles.title: No protocol for $n$ generals tolerates $m$ traitors when $3 \le n \le 3m$
articles.statement:
Suppose there
are at least two possible orders and the set of generals is finite with $n$ elements, where
$3 \le n \le 3m$. Then for every oral-message protocol, every commander $c$ and every number of
rounds $T$, the protocol does not solve the Byzantine generals problem with commander $c$ and at
most $m$ traitors in $T$ rounds: there are an order, a set of at most $m$ traitors and a
behaviour of the traitors for which the agreement condition (IC1) or the validity condition
(IC2) fails after $T$ rounds.

This is the theorem of Lamport, Shostak and Pease, proved by reduction to three generals.

articles.title: No protocol for three generals solves the Byzantine generals problem with one traitor
articles.statement:
**No protocol for three generals solves the Byzantine generals problem with one
traitor.** Suppose there are at least two possible orders. For every oral-message protocol for
three generals $0$, $1$, $2$ with commander $0$ and every number of rounds $T$, the protocol does
not solve the Byzantine generals problem with commander $0$ and at most one traitor in $T$
rounds.

articles.title: Agreement under oral messages (IC1)
articles.statement:
Let a commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value
$v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants with $c \notin S$. If
there are more than $3m$ generals, that is $3m < |S| + 1$, and at most $m$ of the generals in
$S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal lieutenants
$p, p' \in S$ decide the same value.

This is condition IC1 of Theorem 1 of Lamport–Shostak–Pease.

articles.title: A loyal commander is obeyed under oral messages
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $k$ be natural numbers, and
let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending
to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If $2k + m < |S| + 1$ (more than $2k + m$ generals when
$c \notin S$) and at most $k$ of the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the
traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$ decides $v$.

This is Lemma 1 of Lamport–Shostak–Pease.

articles.title: Oral messages achieve interactive consistency
articles.statement:
Let a commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$
with a value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants with
$c \notin S$. If there are more than $3m$ generals, that is $3m < |S| + 1$, and at most $m$ of
the generals in $S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, any two loyal
lieutenants in $S$ decide the same value (IC1), and if $c$ is loyal, every loyal lieutenant in
$S$ decides $v$ (IC2).

This is Theorem 1 of Lamport–Shostak–Pease.

articles.title: Validity under oral messages (IC2)
articles.statement:
Let a loyal commander $c$ run $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ with a
value $v$ and any list of superiors, sending to a finite set $S$ of lieutenants. If
$3m < |S| + 1$ (more than $3m$ generals when $c \notin S$) and at most $m$ of the generals in
$S \cup \{c\}$ are traitors, then, whatever the traitors send, every loyal lieutenant $p \in S$
decides $v$.

This is condition IC2 of Theorem 1 of Lamport–Shostak–Pease.

articles.title: The oral messages algorithm
articles.statement:
Fix which generals are loyal and a strategy for the traitors,
which assigns a value to each list of generals and each recipient. Let $c$ be a commander holding
the value $v$, let $\sigma$ be the list of the commanders above $c$, and let $S$ be a finite set
of lieutenants. For a general $q$, let $r_q$ be the value $q$ receives from $c$: $v$ if $c$ is
loyal, and otherwise the value the strategy assigns to the list $\sigma c$ ($\sigma$ followed by
$c$) and the recipient $q$. The value that a general $p$ decides under $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ is defined
by recursion on $m$. Under $\mathrm{OM}(0)$, $p$ decides $r_p$. Under $\mathrm{OM}(m + 1)$, $p$
decides the majority of the multiset of values $w_q$ for $q \in S$, where $w_p = r_p$ and, for
$q \ne p$, $w_q$ is the value $p$ decides under $\mathrm{OM}(m)$ when $q$, holding $r_q$ with the
superiors $\sigma c$, sends it to the lieutenants $S \setminus \{q\}$.

articles.title: Oral-message protocol
articles.statement:
A synchronous oral-message protocol for a set $G$ of generals, with
orders in $V$, local states in $\sigma$ and messages in $M$, consists of an initial state for
each general in $G$, used by the generals other than the commander; an initial state of the
commander for each order in $V$; a sending function giving, for each round $r$, each general $j$
in each state $s$ and each general $i$, the message in $M$ that $j$ sends to $i$ in round $r$; a
transition function giving, for each round $r$, each general $i$ in each state $s$ and each
assignment of a message to every sender $j$, the state of $i$ after round $r$; and a decision
function giving the value in $V$ that each general decides in each state.

The commander is not part of the protocol: it is chosen when the protocol is run. In each round
every general sends its messages from its current state and then moves to the state given by the
transition function on the messages it received. Only the commander's initial state depends on
the order.

articles.title: A loyal commander sends its value
articles.statement:
If the commander $c$ is loyal, then for every value $v$,
every list of superiors of $c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $v$.

articles.title: A traitorous commander sends the adversary's value
articles.statement:
Fix which generals are loyal and an
adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a list of generals and a recipient.
If the commander $c$ is a traitor, then for every value $v$, every list $\sigma$ of superiors of
$c$ and every general $p$, the value $p$ receives from $c$ is $\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$, where
$\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.

articles.title: Value received from a commander
articles.statement:
Fix a predicate saying which generals are loyal and an
adversary $\mathrm{adv}$ that assigns a value to each pair of a finite sequence of generals and a
recipient. The value that lieutenant $p$ receives from commander $c$, who holds the value $v$ and
whose superiors form the sequence $\sigma$, is $v$ if $c$ is loyal, and is
$\mathrm{adv}(\sigma c, p)$ if $c$ is a traitor, where $\sigma c$ is $\sigma$ followed by $c$.

articles.title: Three generals simulating a protocol
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an oral-message protocol for the
generals $G$ with orders in $V$, states $\sigma$ and messages $M$, let $c \in G$, let
$\mathrm{grp} : G \to \{0, 1, 2\}$ split the generals into three groups and let
$\mathrm{rep} : \{0, 1, 2\} \to G$. The simulation of $P$ with $c$, $\mathrm{grp}$ and
$\mathrm{rep}$ is the oral-message protocol for the generals $\{0, 1, 2\}$ with orders in $V$,
whose states are families $(s(i))_{i \in G}$ of states of $\sigma$ and whose messages are
families $(\mu(j, i))_{j, i \in G}$ of messages of $M$, defined as follows. A general other
than the commander starts from the family of the initial states that $P$ gives each general of
$G$ as a non-commander; the commander, with order $v$, starts from the family of the initial
states of the generals of $G$ in $P$ when $c$ is the commander with order $v$. In round $r$, a
general in state $s$ sends every general the family whose entry $(j, i)$ is the message that
general $j$ of $P$, in state $s(j)$, sends to general $i$ in round $r$. In round $r$, general
$g$ in state $s$, having received $\mu_h$ from each general $h$, moves to the family that keeps
$s(i)$ for each $i$ with $\mathrm{grp}(i) \ne g$ and, for each $i$ with $\mathrm{grp}(i) = g$,
holds the state to which general $i$ of $P$ moves in round $r$ from $s(i)$ on receiving
$\mu_{\mathrm{grp}(j)}(j, i)$ from each $j \in G$. General $g$ in final state $s$ decides
what general $\mathrm{rep}(g)$ of $P$ decides in state $s(\mathrm{rep}(g))$.

articles.title: Simulation reduces many generals to three
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an oral-message protocol for a
finite set $G$ of generals, let $c \in G$ and $m, T \in \mathbb{N}$, and suppose that $P$ solves
the Byzantine generals problem with commander $c$ and at most $m$ traitors in $T$ rounds. Let
$\mathrm{grp} : G \to \{0, 1, 2\}$ and $\mathrm{rep} : \{0, 1, 2\} \to G$ satisfy
$\mathrm{grp}(c) = 0$, $\mathrm{grp}(\mathrm{rep}(g)) = g$ for every $g \ne 0$, and
$|\{i \in G : \mathrm{grp}(i) = g\}| \le m$ for every $g$. Then the simulation of $P$ with $c$,
$\mathrm{grp}$ and $\mathrm{rep}$ solves the Byzantine generals problem for the generals
$\{0, 1, 2\}$ with commander $0$ and at most one traitor in $T$ rounds.

articles.title: Solving the Byzantine generals problem
articles.statement:
An oral-message protocol $P$ for the generals
$G$ solves the Byzantine generals problem with commander $c \in G$ and at most $m$ traitors in
$T$ rounds if, for every order $v$, every set of at most $m$ traitors and every behaviour of
the traitors (the message each traitor sends to each general in each round), conditions IC1
(agreement) and IC2 (validity) hold after $T$ rounds.

articles.title: The simulation is faithful
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an oral-message protocol for a finite set $G$ of
generals with messages $M$, let $c \in G$, and let $\mathrm{grp} : G \to \{0, 1, 2\}$ and
$\mathrm{rep} : \{0, 1, 2\} \to G$ with $\mathrm{grp}(c) = 0$. Fix an order $v$, a set
$S \subseteq \{0, 1, 2\}$ of traitors and a traitor behaviour $a$ for the simulation of $P$
with $c$, $\mathrm{grp}$ and $\mathrm{rep}$: in round $r$ a traitor $h$ sends general $g$ the
family $(a_r(h, g)(j, i))_{j, i \in G}$ of messages of $M$. Compare the execution of the
simulation with commander $0$, order $v$, traitors $S$ and behaviour $a$ with the execution of
$P$ with commander $c$, order $v$ and traitors $\{j \in G : \mathrm{grp}(j) \in S\}$, in which
a traitor $j$ sends general $i$ the message $a_r(\mathrm{grp}(j), \mathrm{grp}(i))(j, i)$ in
round $r$. Then for every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $i \in G$ with $\mathrm{grp}(i) \notin S$,
the entry at $i$ of the state of general $\mathrm{grp}(i)$ after $r$ rounds of the first
execution equals the state of general $i$ after $r$ rounds of the second.

articles.title: One round of an execution
articles.statement:
In the execution of an oral-message protocol $P$ with a given
commander, order, set of traitors and traitor behaviour, for every round $r$ and every general
$i$, the state of $i$ after $r + 1$ rounds is the state to which $i$ moves by its code for round
$r$ from its state after $r$ rounds on the messages it receives in round $r$.

articles.title: The start of an execution
articles.statement:
In the execution of an oral-message protocol $P$ with
commander $c$, order $v$, any set of traitors and any traitor behaviour, every general is in
its initial state after $0$ rounds: the commander in the initial state given by the order $v$,
and every other general in its order-independent initial state.

articles.title: Executions of an oral-message protocol
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an oral-message protocol for the
generals $G$, let $c \in G$ be the commander, $v$ its order and $S \subseteq G$ a finite set of
traitors, and let $a_r(j, i)$ be the message a traitor $j$ sends general $i$ in round $r$. The
state of general $i$ after $r$ rounds is defined by recursion on $r$. After $0$ rounds it is
the initial state of $i$ for commander $c$ and order $v$. After $r + 1$ rounds it is the state
to which $i$ moves by its code for round $r$ from its state after $r$ rounds, on receiving
$a_r(j, i)$ from each traitor $j \in S$ and, from each other general $j$, the message that $P$
has $j$ send to $i$ in round $r$ from the state of $j$ after $r$ rounds.

articles.title: Local views determine states
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an oral-message protocol for the generals $G$
with states $\sigma$ and messages $M$. Let $N$ be a type of nodes, node $k$ running the code of
the general $\rho(k) \in G$, and let $L$ be a property of nodes. For each round $r$ and node
$k$, let $s_r(k), s'_r(k) \in \sigma$ be two states and $\mu_r(k), \mu'_r(k) : G \to M$ two
families of received messages. Suppose that for every $r$ and every node $k$ satisfying $L$,
$s_{r+1}(k)$ is the state to which general $\rho(k)$ of $P$ moves in round $r$ from $s_r(k)$ on
the messages $\mu_r(k)$, and $s'_{r+1}(k)$ the one to which it moves from $s'_r(k)$ on
$\mu'_r(k)$; that $s_0(k) = s'_0(k)$ for every $k$ satisfying $L$; and that for every $r$, if
$s_r(k) = s'_r(k)$ for all $k$ satisfying $L$, then $\mu_r(k) = \mu'_r(k)$ for all $k$
satisfying $L$. Then $s_r(k) = s'_r(k)$ for every $r$ and every $k$ satisfying $L$.

articles.title: Validity in the Byzantine generals problem
articles.statement:
In the execution of an oral-message protocol
with commander $c$, order $v$, a set of traitors and a traitor behaviour, condition IC2
(validity) holds after $T$ rounds if, provided the commander is loyal, every loyal general
other than the commander decides $v$ after $T$ rounds.

articles.title: Delivering a message in the Chang–Roberts ring
articles.statement:
On a ring of $n + 1$ processes with
identifiers $\mathrm{id}$, process $k$ receives the oldest message in its channel in state $s$.
If the channel of $k$ is empty there is no step. Otherwise let $j$ be the origin of that message,
which is removed from the channel: if $\mathrm{id}(k) < \mathrm{id}(j)$, process $k$ forwards it
by appending $j$ to the end of the channel of its successor on the ring; otherwise, if $j = k$,
process $k$ declares itself leader; otherwise the message is discarded. Nothing else changes.

articles.title: Forward distance on the ring
articles.statement:
For processes $j$ and $m$ on a ring of $n + 1$ processes
numbered $0, \dots, n$, the gap from $j$ to $m$ is the number of successor steps from $j$ to
$m$: it is $m - j$ if $j \le m$, and $m + (n + 1) - j$ otherwise. It lies in $[0, n]$.

articles.title: Initial state of the Chang–Roberts ring
articles.statement:
In the initial state the channel into each
process $k$ holds exactly one message, whose origin is the predecessor of $k$ on the ring (so
every process has sent its identifier to its successor), and no process is leader.

articles.title: The Chang–Roberts invariant is preserved along runs
articles.statement:
For every assignment of identifiers,
if the invariant holds in a state $s$ and the state $t$ is reached from $s$ by delivering messages
along some schedule of receiving processes (a multistep transition of the algorithm's labelled
transition system), then the invariant holds in $t$.

articles.title: The Chang–Roberts invariant holds in every reachable state
articles.statement:
For every assignment of
identifiers, every state reachable from the initial state satisfies the invariant.

articles.title: The Chang–Roberts invariant
articles.statement:
Given identifiers $\mathrm{id}$ on a ring of $n + 1$
processes, a state satisfies the invariant when two conditions hold. First, for every message
from origin $j$ waiting in the channel of process $k$, every process $m \ne j$ that the message
has already passed has a smaller identifier, $\mathrm{id}(m) < \mathrm{id}(j)$; here $m$ has been
passed when its forward distance from $j$ is less than the distance the message has travelled,
which is the forward distance from $j$ to $k$ if $k \ne j$, and $n + 1$ (the whole ring) if
$k = j$. Second, for every leader $i$ and every process $m \ne i$, we have
$\mathrm{id}(m) < \mathrm{id}(i)$.
