articles.title: Only the maximum is elected
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{id}$ assign a natural-number identifier, not
necessarily distinct, to each process $0, \dots, n$ of the Chang–Roberts ring. In every state
reachable with these identifiers, if process $i$ has declared itself leader, then
$\mathrm{id}(m) < \mathrm{id}(i)$ for every process $m \ne i$.

articles.title: There is at most one leader
articles.statement:
In every state of the Chang–Roberts algorithm reachable from
the initial state, any two processes that have declared themselves leader are equal.

articles.title: The Chang–Roberts transition system
articles.statement:
For identifiers $\mathrm{id}$, the algorithm is the
labelled transition system whose states are the global states and whose labels are processes:
there is a transition from $s$ to $t$ labelled $k$ exactly when delivering the oldest message in
the channel of process $k$ in state $s$ gives $t$.

articles.title: Predecessor on the ring
articles.statement:
On a ring of $n + 1$ processes numbered $0, \dots, n$, the
predecessor of $k$ is $k - 1$ if $k \ne 0$, and $n$ if $k = 0$.

articles.title: Reachable states of Chang–Roberts
articles.statement:
Given a natural-number identifier $\mathrm{id}(k)$ for
each process $k$ of the ring of $n + 1$ processes, a global state $s$ is reachable when the
Chang–Roberts transition system with these identifiers leads from the initial state to $s$ by a
multistep transition along some finite list of labels, that is, of receiving processes.

articles.title: Runs are multistep transitions
articles.statement:
Given a natural-number identifier $\mathrm{id}(k)$ for
each process $k$ of the ring, for all global states $s, t$ and every list $\kappa$ of processes,
running the schedule $\kappa$ from $s$ returns $t$ if and only if the Chang–Roberts transition
system with identifiers $\mathrm{id}$ has a multistep transition from $s$ to $t$ labelled by
$\kappa$.

articles.title: Running a delivery schedule
articles.statement:
Given a natural-number identifier $\mathrm{id}(k)$ for each
process $k$ of the ring, a global state $s$ and a list $k_1, \dots, k_r$ of processes, the run
applies the Chang–Roberts delivery step at $k_1$, then at $k_2$, and so on. It returns the final
state, or no state as soon as some $k_i$ has an empty channel at its turn; on the empty list it
returns $s$.

articles.title: Chang–Roberts global states
articles.statement:
For a ring of $n + 1$ processes $0, \dots, n$, a global
state assigns to each process $k$ the FIFO channel of messages waiting at $k$, oldest first,
where each message is the index of the process whose identifier it carries, and records for
each process whether it has declared itself leader.

articles.title: Successor on the Chang–Roberts ring
articles.statement:
On the ring of $n + 1$ processes $0, \dots, n$, the
successor of process $k$ is $k + 1$ when $k < n$, and $0$ when $k = n$.

articles.title: The initial messages have travelled one link
articles.statement:
For every process $k$ of the ring, the
distance travelled by a message from the predecessor of $k$ waiting at $k$ is $1$.

articles.title: Forwarding adds one link
articles.statement:
For processes $j$ and $k$ of the ring with $k \ne j$, the
distance travelled by a message from $j$ waiting at the successor of $k$ is the number of links
from $j$ forward to $k$, plus one.

articles.title: Distance travelled by a message
articles.statement:
For processes $j, k$ of the ring of $n + 1$ processes,
the distance travelled by a message from $j$ waiting at $k$ is $n + 1$, the whole ring, when
$k = j$, and otherwise the ring distance from $j$ to $k$, the number of links from $j$ forward
to $k$.

articles.title: Resource-allocation snapshot
articles.statement:
A resource-allocation snapshot, for a type $P$ of
processes and a type $R$ of resources, records for each resource the process holding it, if
any (so each resource has at most one holder), and for each process $p$ and resource $r$
whether $p$ has an outstanding request for $r$. A process never requests a resource it holds.

articles.title: A deadlocked set forces circular wait
articles.statement:
In a resource-allocation snapshot with
finitely many processes, if some set of processes is deadlocked, then the snapshot has circular
wait: some process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.

The proof follows wait-for edges inside the deadlocked set; by finiteness it must revisit a
process.

articles.title: Circular wait
articles.statement:
A resource-allocation snapshot $s$ has circular wait when some process $p$
waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges in $s$, that is, there are
processes $p = p_0, p_1, \dots, p_k = p$ with $k \ge 1$ such that $p_{i-1}$ waits for $p_i$ in
$s$ for each $1 \le i \le k$.

articles.title: Deadlock is circular wait
articles.statement:
In a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many
processes, some set of processes is deadlocked if and only if the snapshot has circular wait,
that is, some process waits for itself through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.

articles.title: Deadlocked set of processes
articles.statement:
In a resource-allocation snapshot $s$, a set $D$ of
processes is deadlocked when $D$ is nonempty and every process $p \in D$ waits in $s$ for some
process $q \in D$, that is, $p$ requests in $s$ a resource that $q$ holds in $s$.

articles.title: Circular wait yields a deadlocked set
articles.statement:
If a resource-allocation snapshot has
circular wait, that is, some process $p$ waits for itself through a chain of one or more
wait-for edges, then some set of processes is deadlocked.

One such set consists of the processes on a wait-for cycle through $p$.

articles.title: Resource ordering prevents circular wait
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number
to each resource. If a resource-allocation snapshot is ordered by $\mathrm{rank}$ (Havender's
discipline), that is, $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$ whenever some process requests
$r$ and holds $r'$, then the snapshot has no circular wait: no process waits for itself
through a chain of one or more wait-for edges.

articles.title: Resource ordering prevents deadlock
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to
each resource. If a resource-allocation snapshot with finitely many processes is ordered by
$\mathrm{rank}$ (Havender's discipline), that is, $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$
whenever some process requests $r$ and holds $r'$, then no set of processes is deadlocked.

articles.title: A process whose requests are all free waits for no one
articles.statement:
In a resource-allocation
snapshot, if no resource requested by a process $p$ has a holder, then $p$ waits for no
process $q$.

articles.title: No process waits for itself directly
articles.statement:
In a resource-allocation snapshot, no process $p$
waits for itself, that is, there is no resource that $p$ both requests and holds.

articles.title: Havender's resource ordering
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a resource-allocation snapshot and let
$\mathrm{rank}$ assign a natural number to each resource. The snapshot $s$ is ordered by
$\mathrm{rank}$ when, for every process $p$, every resource $r$ that $p$ requests in $s$ and
every resource $r'$ that $p$ holds in $s$, we have $\mathrm{rank}(r') < \mathrm{rank}(r)$:
each process requests only resources ranked strictly above every resource it holds.

articles.title: Wait-for relation
articles.statement:
In a resource-allocation snapshot $s$, a process $p$ waits for a
process $q$ when there is a resource $r$ that $p$ requests in $s$ and that $q$ holds in $s$.

articles.title: No deadlock is reported exactly when all the processes can finish
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be the free
resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. The detection
algorithm, started with $w$ free, reports no process if and only if some reordering of the pending
processes is a reduction sequence from $w$.

articles.title: Every reported process is stuck
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be the free resource vector. For every process $q$
that the detection algorithm reports, the request of $q$ is not at most $w$ plus the sum of the
allocations of the processes that the algorithm lets finish: for at least one resource type, $q$
requests more than is free even after all those processes have released their allocations.

articles.title: The detection algorithm
articles.statement:
Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending
processes, repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it
finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending
process has a request at most what is free. The processes still pending then are the ones reported
as deadlocked.

articles.title: A reduction sequence in which no process fits is empty
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a resource vector. If
$\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$ and no process of $\sigma$ has a request at most $w$,
then $\sigma$ is empty.

articles.title: Letting a process that fits finish first preserves reduction sequences
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a
resource vector and $p$ a process whose request is at most $w$. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence
from $w$, then the list obtained from $\sigma$ by removing the first occurrence of $p$, if any, is a
reduction sequence from $w$ plus the allocation of $p$.

articles.title: The processes the algorithm lets finish form a reduction sequence
articles.statement:
For every free resource
vector $w$ and every list of pending processes, the processes that the detection algorithm lets
finish, in the order it lets them finish, form a reduction sequence from $w$.

articles.title: The processes the detection algorithm lets finish
articles.statement:
Given the free resource vector $w$ and a
list of pending processes, run the detection algorithm: repeatedly take the first pending process
whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its
allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. This is
the list of the processes taken, in the order they were taken.

articles.title: Correctness of deadlock detection
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of
pending processes contain no duplicates. A process $p$ is reported by the detection algorithm if
and only if $p$ is pending and no duplicate-free reduction sequence $\sigma$ from $w$ made of
pending processes contains $p$.

articles.title: The algorithm with fuel leaves over no process of a reduction sequence
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be the free
resource vector, let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates, and let the fuel be at
least the number of pending processes. If $\sigma$ is a duplicate-free reduction sequence from $w$
all of whose processes are pending, then no process of $\sigma$ is among the processes that the
detection algorithm with that fuel leaves over.

articles.title: The detection algorithm with fuel
articles.statement:
Given the fuel, a number of steps, together with the free
resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm returns two lists: the processes
that finished, in order, and the processes left over. With fuel $0$, or when no pending process has
a request at most $w$, no process finishes and all the pending processes are left over. Otherwise
the fuel is $n + 1$ for some $n$; take the first pending process $p$ whose request is at most $w$
and run the algorithm with fuel $n$, free vector $w$ plus the allocation of $p$, and the list with
that entry of $p$ removed. The result is $p$ followed by the processes that finished there,
together with the processes left over there.

articles.title: Reduction sequences
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a type of processes and $R$ a type of resource types, and
let $S$ be a state that gives each process $p$ an allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ and a request
$\mathrm{request}(p)$, both functions $R \to \mathbb{N}$ ordered componentwise. A list of
processes $p_1, \dots, p_k$ is a reduction sequence of $S$ from the free vector
$w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for every $1 \le i \le k$, we have
$\mathrm{request}(p_i) \le w + \mathrm{alloc}(p_1) + \dots + \mathrm{alloc}(p_{i-1})$. In
particular the empty list is a reduction sequence from every $w$.

Informally: starting with $w$ free, each process in turn gets its request, finishes, and
releases its allocation.

articles.title: Resource-allocation state
articles.statement:
For a type $P$ of processes and a type $R$ of resource types,
a state consists of two functions $\mathrm{alloc}, \mathrm{request} : P \to R \to \mathbb{N}$:
$\mathrm{alloc}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of resource type $r$ that process $p$ holds,
and $\mathrm{request}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of $r$ that $p$ is waiting for.

articles.title: Under atomic acquisition every philosopher can always still eat
articles.statement:
In the dining
philosophers transition system with atomic acquisition of both forks, for each philosopher
$i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, from every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers
thinking) a state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable, in zero or more steps.

articles.title: Atomic acquisition prevents deadlock
articles.statement:
In the dining philosophers transition system with
atomic acquisition of both forks, every state reachable from the initial state (all three
philosophers thinking) has a successor: some philosopher can move.

articles.title: Dining philosophers with atomic fork acquisition
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system on the
states of the three philosophers, labelled by the philosopher that moves: there is a step
labelled $i$ from $s$ to $t$ exactly when either philosopher $i$ thinks in $s$, neither of its
forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) is held in $s$, and $t$ is $s$ with philosopher $i$ eating;
or philosopher $i$ eats in $s$ and $t$ is $s$ with philosopher $i$ thinking. A fork is held as
in the naive protocol: philosopher $j$ holds fork $j$ when it holds its first fork or eats, and
holds fork $j + 1$ when it eats.

articles.title: Mutual exclusion under atomic acquisition
articles.statement:
In the dining philosophers transition system
with atomic acquisition of both forks, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, in no state
reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) do philosopher $i$ and its
neighbour $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) both eat.

articles.title: Under a butler every philosopher can always still eat
articles.statement:
In the dining philosophers
transition system of the naive protocol under a butler, for each philosopher
$i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, from every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers
thinking) a state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable, in zero or more steps.

articles.title: A butler prevents deadlock
articles.statement:
In the dining philosophers transition system of the naive
protocol under a butler, every state reachable from the initial state (all three philosophers
thinking) has a successor: some philosopher can move.

articles.title: Dining philosophers with a butler
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system on the states of the
three philosophers, labelled by the philosopher that moves: there is a step labelled $i$ from
$s$ to $t$ exactly when philosopher $i$ can move in $s$ under the naive protocol, if
philosopher $i$ is thinking then fewer than two philosophers hold a fork in $s$, and $t$ is $s$
with philosopher $i$ advanced one phase (thinking to holding its first fork, to eating, to
thinking). Under the naive protocol each philosopher $i$ picks up the left fork $i$ first and
then the right fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$), each only when no philosopher holds it, and an eating
philosopher can always put both forks down.

articles.title: Mutual exclusion under a butler
articles.statement:
In the dining philosophers transition system of the
naive protocol under a butler, for each philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, in no state reachable
from the initial state (all three philosophers thinking) do philosopher $i$ and its neighbour
$i + 1$ (modulo $3$) both eat.

articles.title: Enabled moves under atomic acquisition
articles.statement:
Philosopher $i$ can move in state $s$ when it
thinks and neither of its forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) is held in $s$, or when it eats
(it then puts both forks down); a philosopher holding only its first fork cannot move. A fork
is held as in the naive protocol: philosopher $j$ holds fork $j$ when it holds its first fork
or eats, and holds fork $j + 1$ when it eats.

articles.title: Enabled moves under a butler
articles.statement:
Philosopher $i$ can move in state $s$ when it can move in
$s$ under the naive protocol and, if it is thinking, fewer than two philosophers hold at least
one fork in $s$. Under the naive protocol each philosopher $i$ picks up the left fork $i$ first
and then the right fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$), each only when no philosopher holds it, and an
eating philosopher can always put both forks down.

articles.title: When a philosopher can move
articles.statement:
Given a protocol and a state, philosopher $i$ can move
exactly when it is thinking (phase $0$) and its first fork is not held by any philosopher, or it
holds its first fork (phase $1$) and its second fork is not held by any philosopher, or it is
eating (phase $2$), in which case its move puts both forks down.

articles.title: The deadlock formula
articles.statement:
The CTL formula $\neg\,\mathsf{EX}\,\top$ over the philosophers as
atoms. It holds at a state exactly when the state has no successor; in the transition system of
a protocol, exactly when no philosopher can move.

articles.title: The eating valuation
articles.statement:
The valuation of the atoms $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ on the states of the
dining philosophers: atom $i$ holds at a state exactly when philosopher $i$ is eating there, that
is, when its phase is $2$.

articles.title: Held forks
articles.statement:
Given a protocol and a state, fork $f$ is held exactly when some philosopher
$i$ either has $f$ as its first fork and is in phase $1$ or $2$, or has $f$ as its second fork
and is in phase $2$ (eating).

articles.title: Initial state of the dining philosophers
articles.statement:
The state in which all three philosophers are
thinking, that is, every phase is $0$.

articles.title: Transition system of a dining-philosophers protocol
articles.statement:
For a protocol $P$, the labelled
transition system on the states whose labels are the philosophers: there is a transition from
$s$ to $t$ labelled $i$ exactly when philosopher $i$ can move in $s$ under $P$ and $t$ is the
state obtained from $s$ by the move of philosopher $i$.

articles.title: Move of a philosopher under atomic acquisition
articles.statement:
In a state $s$ (the phases of the three
philosophers), the move of philosopher $i$ changes only the phase of $i$: if $i$ is thinking, it
starts eating, picking up both forks at once; otherwise it goes back to thinking. The phases of
the other two philosophers are unchanged.

articles.title: Move of a philosopher
articles.statement:
The state obtained from $s$ when philosopher $i$ moves: the phase
of $i$ advances from thinking ($0$) to holding its first fork ($1$), from $1$ to eating ($2$),
and from eating back to thinking; the phases of the other philosophers are unchanged. Whether
the move is allowed is not checked here.

articles.title: The naive protocol can deadlock
articles.statement:
Consider the transition system of the naive protocol, in
which every philosopher $i$ picks up fork $i$ first and fork $i + 1$ second (indices modulo $3$),
with atom $i$ read as "philosopher $i$ is eating". Its initial state, where all philosophers are
thinking, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathsf{EF}$ applied to the deadlock formula: from it, a
state in which no philosopher can move is reachable.

articles.title: A deadlock state of the naive protocol
articles.statement:
In the transition system of the naive protocol,
with atom $i$ read as "philosopher $i$ is eating", the state in which every philosopher holds its
first fork (every phase is $1$) satisfies the deadlock formula: no philosopher can move there.

articles.title: Mutual exclusion under the naive protocol
articles.statement:
For every philosopher $i$, in the transition
system of the naive protocol, with atom $j$ read as "philosopher $j$ is eating", the initial
state satisfies $\mathsf{AG}$ applied to the formula that philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ (indices
modulo $3$) do not both eat: in no state reachable from the initial state, where all
philosophers are thinking, are philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ both eating.

articles.title: Naive dining-philosophers protocol
articles.statement:
The protocol in which every philosopher
$i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ picks up fork $i$ (its left fork) first and fork $i + 1$ (modulo $3$) second.

articles.title: Neighbours-apart formula
articles.statement:
For a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the CTL formula
$\neg(p_i \wedge p_{i+1})$ over the atoms $p_0, p_1, p_2$ (one per philosopher), with indices
modulo $3$. Under the valuation in which $p_j$ holds when philosopher $j$ eats, it says that the
neighbouring philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ do not eat at the same time.

articles.title: Every philosopher can still eat under resource ordering
articles.statement:
In the transition system of
the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, with the atom $p_j$ holding
when philosopher $j$ eats, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL
formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\mathrm{EF}\,p_i$ for every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$: from every
state reachable from the initial state, some state in which philosopher $i$ eats is reachable.

articles.title: Resource ordering prevents deadlock for the dining philosophers
articles.statement:
In the transition
system of the three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, the initial state,
in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula $\mathrm{AG}\,\mathrm{EX}\,\top$: every
state reachable from it has a successor, that is, some philosopher can move.

articles.title: Neighbours never eat together under resource ordering
articles.statement:
In the transition system of the
three dining philosophers under the resource-ordered protocol, with the atom $p_j$ holding when
philosopher $j$ eats, the initial state, in which everybody thinks, satisfies the CTL formula
$\mathrm{AG}\,\neg(p_i \wedge p_{i+1})$ for every philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, with indices
modulo $3$: in no state reachable from the initial state do philosophers $i$ and $i + 1$ both
eat.

articles.title: Resource-ordered dining-philosophers protocol
articles.statement:
The protocol in which every philosopher
$i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ picks up the lower-numbered of its two forks $i$ and $i + 1$ (modulo $3$)
first and the higher-numbered one second: philosophers $0$ and $1$ take fork $i$ first, and
philosopher $2$ takes fork $0$ first and fork $2$ second.

articles.title: Phase of a philosopher
articles.statement:
For a state $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2)$ of the three dining
philosophers and a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the phase of philosopher $i$ in $s$ is the
component $s_i$.

articles.title: Dining-philosophers protocol
articles.statement:
A protocol for three philosophers $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$
sitting between forks $0, 1, 2$ consists of two maps $\mathrm{first}, \mathrm{second}$ from
$\{0, 1, 2\}$ to itself, the fork philosopher $i$ picks up first and the one it picks up
second, such that for every $i$ these are its two neighbouring forks $i$ and $i + 1$
(modulo $3$) in some order: either $\mathrm{first}(i) = i$ and $\mathrm{second}(i) = i + 1$,
or $\mathrm{first}(i) = i + 1$ and $\mathrm{second}(i) = i$.

articles.title: Number of seated philosophers
articles.statement:
The number of seated philosophers in a state $s$ is the
number of philosophers that hold at least one fork in $s$, that is, whose phase is either holding
the first fork or eating.

articles.title: Updating the phase of a philosopher
articles.statement:
For a state $s = (s_0, s_1, s_2)$ of the three
dining philosophers, a philosopher $i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and a phase $p \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, setting
the phase of philosopher $i$ to $p$ gives the state obtained from $s$ by replacing the
component $s_i$ by $p$ and keeping the other two components.

articles.title: Dining-philosophers state
articles.statement:
A state of the three dining philosophers is a triple
$(s_0, s_1, s_2)$ with each $s_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ the phase of philosopher $i$: $0$ thinking,
$1$ holding the first fork, $2$ eating (holding both forks).

articles.title: Transitions of the lossy acknowledgement channel
articles.statement:
The lossy one-place acknowledgement
channel of the lossy go-back-N variant, given by its transitions in each state. When empty, it
inputs on $\mathsf{reply}_k$ and then holds $k$, for each $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. When it holds
$k$, it either outputs on $\mathsf{ack}_k$ or silently loses $k$, and in both cases it becomes
empty. It has no other transitions.

articles.title: Sender update on an acknowledgement
articles.statement:
For a go-back-N sender with window base $b$, $c$
outstanding messages and next-frame offset $o$, and an acknowledgement $k$, let
$d = \max(k + 3 - b, 0) \bmod 3$. If $1 \le d \le c$, the window slides: the new sender has
base $k$, $c - d$ outstanding messages and next-frame offset $\max(o - d, 0)$. Otherwise the
sender is unchanged.

articles.title: Process constants of the go-back-N model
articles.statement:
The process constants of the go-back-N
specification, one for each state of each component: a sender constant for each sender state, a
data-channel constant for each channel content (empty or a natural number), a receiver constant
for each receiver state, a buffer constant for each occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an
acknowledgement-channel constant for each channel content (empty or a natural number), and a
constant for each receiver state of the lossy variant.

articles.title: The empty two-place buffer
articles.statement:
The two-place buffer process of the go-back-N model with
occupancy $0$.

articles.title: The silent closure of the buffer is trivial
articles.statement:
For every occupancy $n$, every process
reachable from the go-back-N buffer with occupancy $n$ by zero or more silent steps is that
buffer itself.

articles.title: Transitions of the two-place buffer
articles.statement:
The transitions of the go-back-N two-place buffer
at occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$: if $n < 2$ it inputs on $\mathsf{acc}$ and moves to occupancy
$n + 1$, and if $n > 0$ it outputs on $\mathsf{del}$ and moves to occupancy $n - 1$. It has no
other transitions.

articles.title: Visible weak steps of the buffer
articles.statement:
For every occupancy $n$ and every visible label $a$, if
the go-back-N buffer with occupancy $n$ reaches a process $Q$ by a weak transition labelled $a$
(silent steps, one $a$-step, silent steps), then $Q$ is the buffer with some occupancy $m$ such
that the buffer at occupancy $n$ has a transition labelled $a$ to occupancy $m$.

articles.title: The two-place buffer process
articles.statement:
For an occupancy $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the process constant
of the go-back-N specification for the two-place buffer holding $n$ messages.

articles.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate for go-back-N
articles.statement:
A list of $147$ pairs, each a go-back-N
configuration together with the occupancy of the two-place buffer it simulates, namely the number
of accepted but undelivered messages. It contains every reachable configuration, and it is
ordered so that every pair can reach the visible actions of its buffer state through pairs listed
earlier.

articles.title: Transitions of go-back-N configurations
articles.statement:
The transitions of a go-back-N configuration
(sender, data channel, receiver) are those of the parallel composition of the three components,
in which one component moves alone or two components synchronize on complementary labels in a
silent step, restricted to the silent steps and the steps whose label is not on an internal
channel ($\mathsf{send}_k$, $\mathsf{recv}_k$ or $\mathsf{ack}_k$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$).

articles.title: Go-back-N configurations
articles.statement:
A configuration of the go-back-N protocol consists of a
sender state, the content of the data channel (either empty or a single frame with sequence
number $k \in \mathbb{N}$), and a receiver state.

articles.title: Transitions of the go-back-N data channel
articles.statement:
The data channel holds at most one frame.
When empty, for each sequence number $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ it can input on channel
$\mathrm{send}_k$ and then hold frame $k$. When holding frame $k$, it can either output on
channel $\mathrm{recv}_k$ or silently lose the frame by a $\tau$ step; in both cases it becomes
empty.

articles.title: Go-back-N with window 2 is observation congruent to a two-place buffer
articles.statement:
The
go-back-N protocol is observation congruent (rooted weakly bisimilar) to the empty two-place
buffer: every transition of either process is matched by a rooted weak transition of the
other with the same label (silent steps, a step with that label, silent steps), and the
resulting processes are weakly bisimilar.

articles.title: Go-back-N with window 2 implements a two-place buffer
articles.statement:
Over a lossy
one-place data channel, with timeouts and cumulative acknowledgements, the
protocol is weakly bisimilar to the empty two-place buffer.

articles.title: The go-back-N protocol
articles.statement:
The go-back-N protocol with window size $2$ and sequence
numbers modulo $3$ is the recursive CCS process in its initial configuration: the parallel
composition of the sender with an empty window based at $0$, the empty lossy one-place data
channel, and the receiver expecting $0$, with the internal channels $\mathrm{send}_k$,
$\mathrm{recv}_k$ and $\mathrm{ack}_k$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ restricted.

articles.title: Initial configuration of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The initial configuration of the go-back-N
protocol consists of the sender with window base $0$, no outstanding messages and next-frame
offset $0$; the empty data channel; and the receiver expecting sequence number $0$.

articles.title: Internal channels of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The internal channels of the go-back-N protocol are
$\mathrm{send}_k$ (sender to data channel), $\mathrm{recv}_k$ (data channel to receiver) and
$\mathrm{ack}_k$ (receiver to sender) for $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$; all of them are restricted.

articles.title: Transitions of lossy go-back-N configurations
articles.statement:
The transitions of a configuration of
the lossy go-back-N variant come from the parallel composition of the sender, the data
channel, the lossy-variant receiver and the acknowledgement channel (in each composition
either side moves alone, or the two sides synchronize on complementary input and output
labels in a silent step), keeping only the silent transitions and those whose label is not
on an internal channel $\mathrm{send}_k$, $\mathrm{recv}_k$, $\mathrm{ack}_k$ or
$\mathrm{reply}_k$, $k \in \{0, 1, 2\}$.

articles.title: Configurations of lossy go-back-N
articles.statement:
A configuration of the lossy go-back-N variant is a
go-back-N configuration (sender state, data channel content, receiver state) together with the
content of the acknowledgement channel, either empty or a single acknowledgement
$k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Lossy acknowledgements break the buffer specification
articles.statement:
With a lossy
acknowledgement channel and the deliver-then-acknowledge receiver, go-back-N is
not weakly bisimilar to the two-place buffer. Accept two messages, deliver the
first and lose its acknowledgement, and let the receiver take the second frame:
the buffer now holds one message and accepts another, but the protocol cannot
accept before it delivers.

articles.title: Go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel
articles.statement:
The process of the lossy variant of
go-back-N in its initial configuration: the sender's window is based at $0$ with no outstanding
messages and next offset $0$, the data channel and the acknowledgement channel are empty, and
the receiver expects frame $0$.

articles.title: Internal channels of lossy go-back-N
articles.statement:
The list of channels restricted in the lossy
variant: the internal channels of the reliable protocol, namely $\mathsf{send}\,k$,
$\mathsf{recv}\,k$ and $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$, followed by the channels
$\mathsf{reply}\,0$, $\mathsf{reply}\,1$ and $\mathsf{reply}\,2$ from the receiver to the
acknowledgement channel.

articles.title: Receiver transitions of lossy go-back-N
articles.statement:
The transitions of the receiver of the lossy
variant, as pairs of a label and a successor state, are those of the receiver of the reliable
protocol, except in the state about to acknowledge $k$: there the only transition is an output on
$\mathsf{reply}\,k$, to the acknowledgement channel, after which the receiver expects $k$.

articles.title: Configuration transitions are process transitions in lossy go-back-N
articles.statement:
Let $c$ and $c'$
be configurations of the lossy variant and $a$ a label. If $(a, c')$ is one of the
configuration-level transitions of $c$, then in the labelled transition system of the go-back-N
specification the lossy process in configuration $c$ has a transition labelled $a$ to the lossy
process in configuration $c'$.

articles.title: The lossy go-back-N process in a configuration
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a configuration of the lossy
variant, and let $S$, $D$, $R$ and $A$ be the process constants for its sender state, its
data-channel content, its receiver state (as a receiver of the lossy variant) and its
acknowledgement-channel content. The process of the lossy variant in $c$ is
$((S \mid D) \mid R) \mid A$ with the internal channels of the lossy variant restricted.

articles.title: Labelled transition system of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system whose states are
the CCS processes over the go-back-N channel names and process constants, whose labels are the
CCS labels over the channel names, and whose transitions are those generated by the go-back-N
recursive specification.

articles.title: Channel names of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The channel names of the go-back-N protocol are
$\mathsf{acc}$ (accept a message from the user), $\mathsf{del}$ (deliver a message to the user)
and, for every natural number $k$: $\mathsf{send}\,k$ (sender to data channel, a frame with
sequence number $k$), $\mathsf{recv}\,k$ (data channel to receiver), $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ (receiver
to sender, the cumulative acknowledgement naming $k$ as the next expected frame) and
$\mathsf{reply}\,k$ (receiver to the acknowledgement channel, in the lossy variant).

The protocol only uses the sequence numbers $0$, $1$ and $2$.

articles.title: Receiver transitions of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The transitions of the receiver, as pairs of a label
and a successor state. Expecting $e$, for each $k = 0, 1, 2$ it can input on $\mathsf{recv}\,k$
and then is about to deliver $e$ if $k = e$, and about to acknowledge $e$ otherwise. About to
deliver $e$, it outputs on $\mathsf{del}$ and is then about to acknowledge $(e + 1) \bmod 3$.
About to acknowledge $k$, it outputs on $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ and then expects $k$.

articles.title: Receiver states of go-back-N
articles.statement:
A receiver state is one of the following, for a natural
number $e$ or $k$: expecting the frame with sequence number $e$; about to deliver $e$, having
received the expected frame $e$; or about to acknowledge $k$, the next expected sequence
number.

articles.title: Sender transitions of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The transitions of a sender with window base $b$, $n$
outstanding messages and next offset $o$, as pairs of a label and a successor state, in this
order: if $n < 2$, an input on $\mathsf{acc}$ to $(b, n + 1, o)$; if $o < n$, an output on
$\mathsf{send}\,((b + o) \bmod 3)$ to $(b, n, o + 1)$; if $0 < n$, a silent timeout step to
$(b, n, 0)$; and, for each $k = 0, 1, 2$, an input on $\mathsf{ack}\,k$ to the state given by
the window update of the sender for acknowledgement $k$.

articles.title: Go-back-N sender state
articles.statement:
A state of the go-back-N sender is a triple of natural numbers:
the base of the window (the sequence number of the oldest unacknowledged frame), the number of
outstanding messages (accepted but not yet acknowledged), and the offset from the base of the
next frame to transmit.

articles.title: Recursive CCS specification of go-back-N
articles.statement:
The specification assigns to every process
constant the choice, over the transitions listed for its state, of the prefixes $a.K$, where $a$
is the label of the transition and $K$ is the process constant for its target state; an empty
list gives the inactive process. The constants are those of the sender, the data channel, the
receiver, the two-place buffer, the acknowledgement channel and the receiver of the lossy
variant, and their transitions are the sender steps, data channel steps, receiver steps, buffer
steps, acknowledgement channel steps and lossy receiver steps respectively.

articles.title: Silent closure of the stuck lossy go-back-N configuration
articles.statement:
The list of the seven
configurations of go-back-N with a lossy acknowledgement channel in which the sender's window has
base $0$ with two outstanding messages, the receiver holds frame $1$ about to deliver it, and the
acknowledgement channel is empty, while the sender's offset of the next frame to transmit and the
data channel are, in order: offset $2$ and empty, offset $0$ and empty, offset $1$ holding frame
$0$, offset $0$ holding frame $0$, offset $1$ and empty, offset $2$ holding frame $1$, and offset
$0$ holding frame $1$.

The first is the stuck configuration, reached after the acknowledgement of frame $0$ was lost; the
list is closed under silent steps (proved separately), so it contains every configuration
silently reachable from it.

articles.title: The stuck lossy go-back-N configuration refuses new messages
articles.statement:
Consider go-back-N with a
lossy acknowledgement channel in the configuration where the sender's window has base $0$ with two
outstanding messages, both transmitted (offset of the next frame $2$), the data channel and the
acknowledgement channel are empty, and the receiver holds frame $1$ about to deliver it. This
process has no weak transition labelled by accepting a message: no sequence of silent steps
followed by an accept input and further silent steps is possible from it.

articles.title: Go-back-N protocol process in a configuration
articles.statement:
For a configuration consisting of a sender
state $s$, a data channel content $d$ (empty or one frame) and a receiver state $r$, the protocol
process is the parallel composition $(S_s \mid D_d) \mid R_r$ of the process constants for the
sender in state $s$, the data channel holding $d$ and the receiver in state $r$, with the internal
channels restricted: the send, receive and acknowledgement channels for the sequence numbers $0$,
$1$ and $2$.

articles.title: The clock condition
articles.statement:
In every execution, if the event at position $a$ happened before
the event at position $b$, then the Lamport timestamp of $a$ is smaller than the Lamport
timestamp of $b$ (Lamport 1978).

articles.title: One step of the Lamport clock algorithm
articles.statement:
The state is a counter $c(p) \in \mathbb{N}$
for each process $p$ together with the timestamps assigned so far. An event $e$ of process
$p$ gets the timestamp $t = \max(c(p), s) + 1$, where $s$ is the timestamp already assigned
at the position that $e$ receives from; $s = 0$ if $e$ is not a receipt or if no timestamp
has been assigned at that position. The step sets $c(p)$ to $t$ and appends $t$ to the
timestamps.

The timestamps are kept in an array, for constant-time append and lookup.

articles.title: Event
articles.statement:
An event of an execution, for a type $P$ of processes, consists of the process
in $P$ it belongs to and, if it is a receipt, a natural number: the position in the execution
of the event whose message it receives. The structure does not require that position to be
earlier than the event itself.

articles.title: Happened-before relates positions of the execution
articles.statement:
If position $a$ happened before
position $b$ in an execution, then the execution has an event at position $a$ and an event at
position $b$.

articles.title: Happened-before
articles.statement:
Lamport's happened-before relation on the positions of an execution is
the transitive closure of one step of happened-before: $a$ happened before $b$ when there is a
chain $a = i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k = b$ with $k \ge 1$ in which each $i_m$ precedes $i_{m+1}$ by
one step.

articles.title: Happened-before goes forward in the execution
articles.statement:
If position $a$ happened before position
$b$ in an execution, then $a < b$.

articles.title: Running the Lamport clock algorithm
articles.statement:
The clock algorithm over an execution applies one
step of the algorithm to each event in order, starting from all process counters $0$ and no
timestamps. The result is the final counters together with the timestamps assigned to the
events, in order.

articles.title: One step of happened-before raises the timestamp
articles.statement:
If position $i$ precedes position $j$
by one step of happened-before in an execution, then the Lamport timestamp of $i$ is smaller
than the Lamport timestamp of $j$.

articles.title: One step of happened-before
articles.statement:
In an execution, position $i$ precedes position $j$ by one
step when $i < j$, both positions hold events, and either the two events belong to the same
process or the event at $j$ receives the message of the event at $i$.

articles.title: Process counters dominate their timestamps
articles.statement:
After the Lamport clock algorithm has run
over an execution, the counter of each process is at least the timestamp of every event of that
process in the execution.

articles.title: Lamport timestamps increase along each process
articles.statement:
Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an
execution and let $t_k$ be the Lamport timestamp of $e_k$. If $i < j < n$ and $e_i$ and $e_j$
belong to the same process, then $t_i < t_j$.

This is Lamport's clock condition C1, which his implementation rule IR1 guarantees.

articles.title: A receipt is stamped later than its send
articles.statement:
Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be a well-formed
execution and let $t_k$ be the Lamport timestamp of $e_k$. If $j < n$ and $e_j$ receives the
message sent by the event at position $i$, then $t_i < t_j$.

This is Lamport's clock condition C2, which his implementation rule IR2 guarantees.

articles.title: Appending events does not change earlier timestamps
articles.statement:
Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be an
execution, and extend it by appending further events. For every $i < n$, the Lamport timestamp
of the event at position $i$ is the same in the extended execution as in the original one.

articles.title: A timestamp depends only on a prefix containing its event
articles.statement:
Let $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ be
an execution and let $i < k \le n$. The Lamport timestamp of $e_i$ in the whole execution equals
its Lamport timestamp in the prefix $e_0, \dots, e_{k-1}$.

articles.title: Lamport timestamps
articles.statement:
The Lamport timestamps $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$ of an execution
$e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ are computed by Lamport's clock algorithm. Every process keeps a
counter, initially $0$. For $k = 0, \dots, n-1$ in turn, let $c$ be the current counter of
the process of $e_k$, and let $m = t_i$ if $e_k$ receives the message sent by the event at
position $i$ with $i < k$, and $m = 0$ otherwise. Then $t_k = \max(c, m) + 1$, and the
counter of the process of $e_k$ is set to $t_k$.

articles.title: Lamport's total order extends happened-before
articles.statement:
In every execution, if the event at
position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then position $a$ precedes position $b$
in Lamport's total order.

articles.title: Lamport's order is total
articles.statement:
In every execution, for any two distinct positions $a \ne b$
that both hold events, $a$ precedes $b$ or $b$ precedes $a$ in Lamport's total order.

Two events of the same process have different timestamps (an earlier event of a process has
a smaller timestamp), so ties only occur between different processes, which the order on
processes breaks.

articles.title: Lamport's total order
articles.statement:
Fix a linear order on the processes. In an execution
$e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ with Lamport timestamps $t_0, \dots, t_{n-1}$, position $a$ precedes
position $b$ when $a < n$, $b < n$, and either $t_a < t_b$, or $t_a = t_b$ and the process of
$e_a$ is smaller than the process of $e_b$.

articles.title: Well-formed executions
articles.statement:
An execution $e_0, \dots, e_{n-1}$ is well formed when every
receipt names an earlier event: whenever $e_j$ receives the message sent by the event at
position $i$, then $i < j$.

articles.title: An aborted participant rules out a coordinator commit
articles.statement:
In every reachable state of the
two-phase commit protocol, if some participant has aborted, then the coordinator has not decided
commit.

articles.title: Two-phase commit actions
articles.statement:
The actions of the two-phase commit protocol over a set $P$ of
participants are: a participant $p \in P$ votes yes; a participant $p$ votes no; the coordinator
decides commit; the coordinator decides abort; a participant $p$ learns the commit decision; and a
participant $p$ learns the abort decision.

articles.title: Atomicity between participants
articles.statement:
For every set $P$ of participants, in every reachable
state of the two-phase commit protocol, if some participant $p$ has committed, then no
participant $q$ has aborted.

This is the participant part of condition AC1 of Bernstein, Hadzilacos and Goodman.

articles.title: Validity for participants
articles.statement:
In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol, if
some participant has committed, then every participant voted yes, that is, every participant is
prepared or committed.

This is the participant form of condition AC3 of Bernstein, Hadzilacos and Goodman; that the
coordinator has then decided commit is the separate result that a committed participant has a
committed coordinator.

articles.title: An aborted coordinator has no committed participant
articles.statement:
In every reachable state of the
two-phase commit protocol, if the coordinator has decided abort, then no participant has
committed.

This is the coordinator–participant part of condition AC1 of Bernstein, Hadzilacos and
Goodman.

articles.title: Validity for the coordinator
articles.statement:
In every reachable state of the two-phase commit protocol,
if the coordinator has decided commit, then every participant voted yes, that is, every
participant is prepared or committed.

This is the coordinator form of condition AC3 of Bernstein, Hadzilacos and Goodman.

articles.title: A committed coordinator has no aborted participant
articles.statement:
In every reachable state of the
two-phase commit protocol, if the coordinator has decided commit, then no participant has
aborted.

This is the coordinator–participant part of condition AC1 of Bernstein, Hadzilacos and
Goodman.

articles.title: Coordinator states
articles.statement:
In two-phase commit the coordinator is in one of three states:
waiting (collecting votes), committed (it has decided commit) or aborted (it has decided abort).

articles.title: Initial state of two-phase commit
articles.statement:
The initial state of the two-phase commit protocol:
the coordinator is waiting and every participant is working.

articles.title: Multistep transitions preserve the two-phase commit invariant
articles.statement:
If a state $s$ of the
two-phase commit protocol satisfies the inductive invariant and a state $t$ is reached from $s$
by a finite sequence of transitions, then $t$ satisfies the invariant.

articles.title: The two-phase commit invariant holds in reachable states
articles.statement:
For every set $P$ of
participants, every global state of the two-phase commit protocol that is reachable from the
initial state satisfies the inductive invariant, that is, both of the following hold: if the
coordinator has committed, then every participant is prepared or committed; and every committed
participant has a committed coordinator.

articles.title: Two-phase commit invariant
articles.statement:
A global state $s$ of the two-phase commit protocol
satisfies the invariant when two conditions hold: if the coordinator has committed, then every
participant is prepared or committed; and every committed participant has a committed
coordinator.

articles.title: Two-phase commit as a transition system
articles.statement:
For a set $P$ of participants, the labelled
transition system whose states are the global states of the protocol, whose labels are the
protocol actions, and whose transitions are the protocol steps.

articles.title: A committed participant has a committed coordinator
articles.statement:
In every reachable state of the
two-phase commit protocol, if some participant has committed, then the coordinator has
committed.

This is the atomicity condition AC1 of Bernstein, Hadzilacos and Goodman between a participant
and the coordinator.

articles.title: Participant states in two-phase commit
articles.statement:
A participant is in one of four states: working
(it has not voted), prepared (it voted yes and waits for the decision), committed, or aborted
(it voted no, or learned of an abort).

articles.title: Reachable states of two-phase commit
articles.statement:
A global state $s$ is reachable when some finite
sequence of protocol actions leads by protocol steps from the initial state, in which the
coordinator is waiting and every participant is working, to $s$.

articles.title: Updating one participant's state
articles.statement:
For a global state $s$, a participant $p$ and a
participant state $x$, the updated state has the same coordinator state as $s$, gives
participant $p$ the state $x$, and leaves the state of every other participant unchanged.

articles.title: Global states of two-phase commit
articles.statement:
For a set $P$ of participants, a global state
consists of a coordinator state together with a participant state for each participant
$p \in P$.

articles.title: Reachable states are closed under steps
articles.statement:
If a global state $s$ of the two-phase commit
protocol is reachable and some action takes $s$ to $t$ in one protocol step, then $t$ is
reachable.

articles.title: Transitions of two-phase commit
articles.statement:
The protocol steps from a global state $s$ to a
global state $t$ by an action exactly in the following cases. A working participant $p$ may vote
yes, after which $p$ is prepared, or vote no, after which $p$ is aborted. If the coordinator is
waiting and every participant is prepared, the coordinator may decide commit, after which it is
committed. If the coordinator is waiting, it may decide abort, after which it is aborted. If the
coordinator has committed, a prepared participant $p$ may learn the commit, after which $p$ is
committed. If the coordinator has aborted, a prepared or working participant $p$ may learn the
abort, after which $p$ is aborted. In each step every other part of the state is unchanged.

articles.title: One step of the vector clock algorithm
articles.statement:
The state of the algorithm holds a vector
$V_q \in \mathbb{N}^P$ for each process $q$, where $P$ is the set of processes, and the
timestamps assigned so far, kept in an array for constant-time append and lookup. On an event $e$
of process $p$, the step replaces $V_p$ by the stamp $s$ of $e$ computed from the current state,
leaves the other vectors unchanged, and appends $s$ to the timestamps.

articles.title: Own-entry comparison detects happened-before
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positions of events of
an execution, and let $p$ be the process of the event at $a$. If the $p$-entry of the vector
timestamp of $a$ is at most the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $b$, then $a = b$ or $a$
happened before $b$.

articles.title: Vector clocks characterize happened-before
articles.statement:
For two events of an
execution, `a` happened before `b` exactly when `a`'s timestamp is smaller than
`b`'s in the pointwise order.

articles.title: An event's own entry is positive
articles.statement:
For every position $j$ of an event of an execution, if
$p$ is the process of that event, then the $p$-entry of the vector timestamp of $j$ is at least
$1$.

articles.title: Array lookup agrees with the timestamp list
articles.statement:
For every execution and every natural
number $i$, the entry at index $i$ of the array of timestamps built by the vector clock algorithm
on the execution equals the $i$-th vector timestamp of the execution, where an index out of range
gives the zero vector in both lookups.

articles.title: Running the vector clock algorithm
articles.statement:
The state of the vector clock algorithm after an
execution is obtained by starting from the state in which every process's vector is $0$ and no
timestamps have been assigned, and applying one step of the algorithm to each event of the
execution in order.

articles.title: Vector clock stamp of an event
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be the set of processes. Given the current
vectors $V_q \in \mathbb{N}^P$ of the processes $q$ and the timestamps $T_0, T_1, \dots$ assigned
so far, the vector clock algorithm stamps an event $e$ of process $p$ as follows. Let $m = T_i$
if $e$ receives the message sent by the event at position $i$ and $T_i$ has been assigned, and
$m = 0$ otherwise. The stamp of $e$ is the pointwise maximum of $V_p$ and $m$, with its $p$-entry
increased by $1$.

articles.title: Each process's vector dominates its events' timestamps
articles.statement:
For every execution and every
position $i$ of an event of it, the vector timestamp of $i$ is pointwise at most the vector of
that event's process in the state of the vector clock algorithm after the whole execution.

articles.title: Timestamps are stamps from the preceding state
articles.statement:
For every execution and every position
$j$ of an event $e$ of it, the vector timestamp of $j$ equals the stamp of $e$ computed from the
state of the vector clock algorithm after the first $j$ events of the execution.

articles.title: Vector timestamps of an execution
articles.statement:
The vector timestamps of an execution are the list of
vectors that the vector clock algorithm, run over the execution, assigns to its events, in
order.

articles.title: Vector timestamps are monotone along happened-before
articles.statement:
In an execution, write $V_i$ for
the vector timestamp that the vector clock algorithm gives to the event at position $i$. If the
event at position $a$ happened before the event at position $b$, then $V_a(q) \le V_b(q)$ for
every process $q$.

articles.title: Vector timestamps are monotone along one step of happened-before
articles.statement:
In an execution,
write $V_i$ for the vector timestamp that the vector clock algorithm gives to the event at
position $i$. If the event at position $j$ follows the event at position $i$ by one step of
happened-before, then $V_i(q) \le V_j(q)$ for every process $q$.

articles.title: A process's final vector is zero or one of its timestamps
articles.statement:
Run the vector clock
algorithm over an execution, starting from all vectors $0$. For every process $p$, the vector
held by $p$ at the end is either the zero vector or the vector timestamp of some event of $p$
in the execution.

articles.title: The collision experiment
articles.statement:
For a nonempty finite set $\alpha$ and a natural number $q$, the
collision experiment is the probability distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$
obtained by drawing a function $s \colon \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to \alpha$ uniformly at random
(equivalently, $q$ independent uniform samples $s(0), \dots, s(q - 1)$ from $\alpha$) and
outputting true exactly when $s$ is not injective, that is, when $s(i) = s(j)$ for some
$i \ne j$.

articles.title: The exact collision probability
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements
and $q$ a natural number. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$
contain a collision equals $1 - N (N - 1) \cdots (N - q + 1) / N^q$, where the product
$N (N - 1) \cdots (N - q + 1)$ has $q$ factors (it is $1$ for $q = 0$ and $0$ for $q > N$).

articles.title: Birthday lower bound for at most square-root many samples
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty
finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number with $q \le \sqrt{N}$. The probability that
$q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least
$q (q - 1) / (4 N)$.

articles.title: Birthday lower bound as stated in Katz and Lindell
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set
with $N$ elements and $q$ a natural number with $q \le \sqrt{2 N}$. The probability that $q$
independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $q (q - 1) / (4 N)$.

This is Lemma A.16 of Katz and Lindell (2nd ed.): "say $q \le \sqrt{2N}$ elements are chosen
uniformly and independently ... at least $q (q - 1) / (4N)$".

articles.title: Birthday lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a
natural number with $q (q - 1) \le 2 N$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples
from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $q (q - 1) / (4 N)$.

This strengthens Katz and Lindell's Lemma A.16, whose hypothesis $q \le \sqrt{2 N}$ implies
$q (q - 1) \le 2 N$.

articles.title: Birthday upper bound
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a
natural number. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a
collision is at most $q (q - 1) / (2 N)$.

This implies Katz and Lindell's Lemma A.15, which states the bound $q^2 / (2 N)$.

articles.title: Collision probability
articles.statement:
For a nonempty finite set $\alpha$ and a natural number $q$, the
collision probability is the probability, as a real number, that the collision experiment with
$q$ samples from $\alpha$ outputs true, that is, that $q$ independent uniform samples from
$\alpha$ contain two equal samples at distinct positions.

articles.title: Birthday lower bound, rational form
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$
elements, $q$ a natural number, and $x = q (q - 1) / (2 N)$. The probability that $q$ independent
uniform samples from $\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $x / (1 + x)$.

articles.title: Even odds of a collision
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$ elements and $q$ a
natural number with $2 N \le q (q - 1)$. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from
$\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $1/2$.

articles.title: Birthday lower bound, exponential form
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite set with $N$
elements and $q$ a natural number. The probability that $q$ independent uniform samples from
$\alpha$ contain a collision is at least $1 - \exp(-q (q - 1) / (2 N))$.

articles.title: Chaining value of a reversed block list
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression
function and $iv \in S$ an initial value. The chaining value of a list of blocks given last block
first is defined recursively: the empty list has chaining value $iv$, and a list with first entry
$x$ followed by a list $xs$ has chaining value $h(c, x)$, where $c$ is the chaining value of
$xs$.

articles.title: Merkle–Damgård chaining value
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression function and
$iv \in S$ an initial value. The chaining value of a list of blocks $M = (x_1, \dots, x_L)$ is
$z_L$, where $z_0 = iv$ and $z_i = h(z_{i-1}, x_i)$ for $1 \le i \le L$.

articles.title: Compression-function collision game
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression function
and let $A$ be an adversary that maps random coins $r$ from a finite nonempty type $R$ either to a
pair $(p_1, p_2)$ of compression inputs in $S \times B$ or to no output. The game is the
distribution of the Boolean outcome when $r$ is drawn uniformly from $R$: the adversary wins
(outcome true) exactly when $A(r)$ is a pair $(p_1, p_2)$ with $p_1 \ne p_2$ and
$h(p_1) = h(p_2)$, and loses when $A(r)$ is no output.

articles.title: A Merkle–Damgård hash collision yields a compression collision
articles.statement:
Let
$h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression function, $iv \in S$ an initial value and
$\ell : \mathbb{N} \to B$ a length encoding, and let $H$ be the Merkle–Damgård hash with length
strengthening they define. Write $|M|$ for the number of blocks of a list of blocks $M$. If $M$
and $M'$ are distinct lists of blocks with $H(M) = H(M')$, and $\ell(|M|) = \ell(|M'|)$ implies
$|M| = |M'|$, then the collision-finding procedure applied to $M$ and $M'$ returns a pair
$(p_1, p_2)$ of compression inputs with $p_1 \ne p_2$ and $h(p_1) = h(p_2)$.

This is a block-level form of Katz and Lindell, Theorem 5.4.

articles.title: Extracting a compression collision from a Merkle–Damgård collision
articles.statement:
Let
$h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression function, $iv \in S$ an initial value and
$\ell : \mathbb{N} \to B$ a length encoding. Let $M = (x_1, \dots, x_L)$ and
$M' = (x'_1, \dots, x'_{L'})$ be lists of blocks with chaining values $z_0 = z'_0 = iv$,
$z_i = h(z_{i-1}, x_i)$ and $z'_j = h(z'_{j-1}, x'_j)$. The procedure compares the final
compression inputs $(z_L, \ell(L))$ and $(z'_{L'}, \ell(L'))$ and returns this pair if they
differ. Otherwise, for $k = 1, 2, \dots, \min(L, L')$ in turn, it compares
$(z_{L-k}, x_{L-k+1})$ with $(z'_{L'-k}, x'_{L'-k+1})$ and returns the first such pair that
differs; if there is none, it returns no output.

articles.title: The Merkle–Damgård transform preserves collision resistance
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$
be a compression function, $iv \in S$ an initial value, $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to B$ a length
encoding and $N$ a natural number such that $\ell$ is injective on $\{0, 1, \dots, N - 1\}$. Then
for every adversary $A$ that maps random coins from a finite nonempty type $R$ to a pair of lists
of blocks, the probability that the reduction built from $A$ wins the compression-function
collision game for $h$ is at least the probability that $A$ wins the hash collision game for the
Merkle–Damgård hash defined by $h$, $iv$ and $\ell$ with messages of fewer than $N$ blocks.

articles.title: Hash collision game for Merkle–Damgård
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be the Merkle–Damgård hash with length
strengthening defined by a compression function $h : S \times B \to S$, an initial value
$iv \in S$ and a length encoding $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to B$, and let $N$ be a natural number. An
adversary $A$ maps random coins $r$ from a finite nonempty type $R$ to a pair of lists of blocks.
The game is the distribution of the Boolean outcome when $r$ is drawn uniformly from $R$: the
adversary wins (outcome true) exactly when $A(r) = (M, M')$ with $M \ne M'$, both $M$ and $M'$
have fewer than $N$ blocks, and $H(M) = H(M')$.

articles.title: Merkle–Damgård hash with length strengthening
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression
function, $iv \in S$ an initial value and $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to B$ a length encoding. The hash of
a list of blocks $M = (x_1, \dots, x_L)$ is $h(z_L, \ell(L))$, where $z_0 = iv$ and
$z_i = h(z_{i-1}, x_i)$ for $1 \le i \le L$.

articles.title: Collision of a compression function
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression function.
A pair $(p_1, p_2)$ of compression inputs in $S \times B$ is a collision of $h$ when $p_1 \ne p_2$
and $h(p_1) = h(p_2)$.

articles.title: Merkle–Damgård collision reduction
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression function,
$iv \in S$ an initial value, $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to B$ a length encoding and $A$ an adversary that
maps random coins $r$ from a finite nonempty type $R$ to a pair $(M, M')$ of lists of blocks. The
reduction is the adversary that, on coins $r$, outputs the result of the Merkle–Damgård
collision-finding procedure applied to the pair $(M, M') = A(r)$: a pair of compression inputs,
or no output.

articles.title: Backward search for a compression collision
articles.statement:
Let $h : S \times B \to S$ be a compression
function with initial value $iv$, and for a list of blocks written last block first let $z(xs)$
be its chaining value: $z([\,]) = iv$ and $z(x :: xs) = h(z(xs), x)$. Given two such lists, the
search compares their leading compression inputs: on $x :: xs$ and $y :: ys$, if
$(z(xs), x) = (z(ys), y)$ it continues with $xs$ and $ys$, and otherwise it returns the pair
$((z(xs), x), (z(ys), y))$. When either list is empty it returns no pair.

articles.title: Correctness of Diffie–Hellman key agreement
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $q$ a natural number and
$g \in G$. For $x \in G$ and $c \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ write $x^c$ for $x^n$, where $n$ is
the natural-number value of $c$: its representative in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ when $q > 0$, and
$|c|$ when $q = 0$ (in which case $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$). Then
$(g^b)^a = (g^a)^b$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Value of the Diffie–Hellman shared key
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $q$ a natural number and
$g \in G$ with $g^q = 1$. For $x \in G$ and $c \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ write $x^c$ for $x^n$,
where $n$ is the natural-number value of $c$: its representative in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ when
$q > 0$, and $|c|$ when $q = 0$ (in which case $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$). Then
$(g^b)^a = g^{ab}$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$, where $ab$ is the product in
$\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Exponentiation from a generator is a bijection
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $q$,
with $q \neq 0$, and let $g \in G$ generate $G$, that is, every element of $G$ is an integer
power of $g$. Then $a \mapsto g^a$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ to $G$, where
$g^a = g^n$ for the representative $n \in \{0, \dots, q-1\}$ of $a$. Its inverse is the
discrete logarithm to base $g$.

articles.title: Group exponentiation with modular exponents
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a group, $q$ a natural number,
$g \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$. Then $g^a$ is defined as $g^n$, where $n$ is the
natural-number value of $a$: its representative in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ when $q > 0$, and $|a|$
when $q = 0$ (in which case $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$).

articles.title: ElGamal eavesdropping adversary
articles.statement:
Given a type $G$ of public keys and messages and a type
$R$ of random coins, an eavesdropping adversary consists of a choice function, which maps a public
key $h \in G$ and coins $r \in R$ to a pair of messages in $G \times G$, and a guessing function,
which maps a public key $h \in G$, a ciphertext in $G \times G$ and coins $r \in R$ to a bit.

articles.title: Advantage of a DDH distinguisher
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group, $g \in G$ and
$q \ge 1$, and let $D$ be a distinguisher that maps three elements of $G$ and coins in a finite
nonempty type $S$ to a bit. The DDH advantage of $D$ is the real number
$|p_{\mathrm{real}} - p_{\mathrm{rand}}|$, where $p_{\mathrm{real}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{rand}}$ are
the probabilities that $D$ outputs true in the real and in the random DDH experiment for $g$ with
exponents in $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: The reduction is a fair coin on random DDH triples
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group
of order $q$ generated by $g$. For every eavesdropping adversary $A$ with random coins in a finite
nonempty type $R$, the DDH distinguisher obtained from $A$ by the reduction outputs true with
probability exactly $1/2$ in the random DDH experiment for $g$.

In that experiment the third input $g^z$, with $z$ uniform in $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$, is a group
one-time pad on the challenge message.

articles.title: Random DDH experiment
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group, $g \in G$ and $q \ge 1$ a
natural number, and let $D$ be a distinguisher that maps three elements of $G$ and coins in a
finite nonempty type $S$ to a bit. The random DDH experiment draws $x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ and
coins $s \in S$ independently and uniformly and outputs the distribution of the bit
$D(g^x, g^y, g^z, s)$, where a power $g^a$ with $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ means $g^{v(a)}$ for the
representative $v(a) \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ of $a$.

articles.title: Real DDH experiment
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group, $g \in G$ and $q \ge 1$ a
natural number, and let $D$ be a distinguisher that maps three elements of $G$ and coins in a
finite nonempty type $S$ to a bit. The real DDH experiment draws $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ and coins
$s \in S$ independently and uniformly and outputs the distribution of the bit
$D(g^x, g^y, g^{xy}, s)$, where $xy$ is the product in $\mathbb{Z}/q$ and a power $g^a$ with
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ means $g^{v(a)}$ for the representative $v(a) \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$
of $a$.

articles.title: Correctness of ElGamal
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $g \in G$ and $q$ a natural
number. For $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ and $c \in G$ write $c^a$ for
$c^{\operatorname{val}(a)}$, where $\operatorname{val}(a) \in \mathbb{N}$ is the representative
of $a$ in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ if $q \ge 1$ and $|a|$ if $q = 0$. For every secret key
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$, every message $m \in G$ and every encryption randomness
$y \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$, decrypting with $x$ the ElGamal encryption of $m$ under the
public key $g^x$ with randomness $y$ returns $m$.

articles.title: ElGamal decryption
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group and $q$ a natural number. For
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ and $c \in G$ write $c^a$ for $c^{\operatorname{val}(a)}$, where
$\operatorname{val}(a) \in \mathbb{N}$ is the representative of $a$ in $\{0, \dots, q-1\}$ if
$q \ge 1$ and $|a|$ if $q = 0$. Decrypting a ciphertext $(c_1, c_2) \in G \times G$ with the
secret key $x \in \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ gives $c_2 \cdot (c_1^x)^{-1}$.

articles.title: ElGamal eavesdropping advantage equals a DDH advantage
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative
group of order $q$ generated by $g$. For every eavesdropping adversary $A$ with random coins in a
finite nonempty type $R$, the eavesdropping advantage of $A$ against ElGamal equals the DDH
advantage of the distinguisher obtained from $A$ by the reduction.

This is the eavesdropping part of Katz and Lindell, Theorem 11.18 (ElGamal is secure if DDH is
hard), in exact, non-asymptotic form.

articles.title: DDH bounds transfer to ElGamal
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group of order $q$
generated by $g$, and let $A$ be an eavesdropping adversary with random coins in a finite nonempty
type $R$. For every real number $\varepsilon$, if the DDH advantage of the distinguisher obtained
from $A$ by the reduction is at most $\varepsilon$, then the eavesdropping advantage of $A$
against ElGamal is at most $\varepsilon$.

articles.title: Eavesdropping advantage against ElGamal
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group, $g \in G$
and $q \ge 1$. The eavesdropping advantage of an adversary $A$ with random coins in a finite
nonempty type $R$ is the real number $|p - 1/2|$, where $p$ is the probability that $A$ wins the
ElGamal eavesdropping experiment for $g$ with exponents in $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$, that is,
guesses the challenge bit correctly.

articles.title: ElGamal eavesdropping game equals the real DDH experiment of the reduction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
commutative group, $q \ge 1$ a natural number and $g \in G$ with $g^q = 1$. For every
eavesdropping adversary $A$ with coins in a finite nonempty type $R$, the output distribution of
the ElGamal eavesdropping experiment for $A$ (exponents in $\mathbb{Z}/q$) equals the output
distribution of the real DDH experiment run with the distinguisher built from $A$ by the
reduction.

articles.title: ElGamal eavesdropping experiment
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $g \in G$ and $q \ge 1$.
For an eavesdropping adversary $A$ with coins in a finite nonempty type $R$, the experiment draws
$x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/q$, coins $r \in R$ and a bit $b$ independently and uniformly. It sets the
public key $h = g^x$, lets $A$ choose messages $(m_0, m_1)$ from $h$ and $r$, and gives $A$ the
key $h$, the ElGamal ciphertext $(g^y, h^y m_b)$ and the coins $r$, where $m_b$ is $m_1$ if $b$
is true and $m_0$ otherwise; powers use the value of the exponent in $\{0, \dots, q - 1\}$. The
experiment outputs the distribution of the bit "the guess of $A$ equals $b$".

articles.title: ElGamal encryption
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group with a fixed element $g$ and let $q$ be
a natural number. The ElGamal encryption of a message $m \in G$ under the public key $h \in G$
with randomness $y \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ is the pair $(g^y, h^y m) \in G \times G$. Here a power
$k^a$ with $k \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ means $k^{v(a)}$, where $v(a) \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$
is the least nonnegative representative of $a$ if $q \ge 1$, and $v(a) = |a|$ if $q = 0$ (when
$\mathbb{Z}/0 = \mathbb{Z}$).

articles.title: Message selected by the challenge bit
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group. For a pair
of messages $(m_0, m_1) \in G \times G$ and a bit $b$, the selected message is $m_1$ if $b$ is
true and $m_0$ if $b$ is false.

articles.title: ElGamal public key
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group with a fixed element $g$ and let $q$ be
a natural number. The public key of a secret key $x \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ is $h = g^{v(x)} \in G$,
where $v(x) \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the least nonnegative representative of $x$ if $q \ge 1$,
and $v(x) = |x|$ if $q = 0$ (when $\mathbb{Z}/0 = \mathbb{Z}$).

articles.title: DDH distinguisher from an ElGamal eavesdropper
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite commutative group and
let $A$ be an eavesdropping adversary with coins in a finite nonempty type $R$. The distinguisher
built from $A$ takes three elements $X, Y, Z \in G$ and coins consisting of $r \in R$ and a bit
$b$. It lets $A$ choose messages $(m_0, m_1)$ from the public key $X$ and the coins $r$, gives $A$
the public key $X$, the ciphertext $(Y, Z m_b)$ and the coins $r$, where $m_b$ is $m_1$ if $b$ is
true and $m_0$ otherwise, and outputs true exactly when the guess of $A$ equals $b$.

articles.title: RSA-CRT decryption is correct
articles.statement:
Let $(p, q, e, d)$ be an RSA key with modulus $n = pq$, and
let $d_p, d_q \ge 1$ be natural numbers with $d_p \equiv d \pmod{p - 1}$ and
$d_q \equiv d \pmod{q - 1}$. Then for every $c \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, RSA-CRT decryption of
$c$ with the exponents $d_p$ and $d_q$ equals the RSA decryption $c^d$.

articles.title: RSA-CRT decryption with the standard exponents
articles.statement:
Let $(p, q, e, d)$ be an RSA key with
modulus $n = pq$ in which both primes are odd, that is $p > 2$ and $q > 2$. Then for every
$c \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, RSA-CRT decryption of $c$ with the exponents
$d_p = d \bmod (p - 1)$ and $d_q = d \bmod (q - 1)$ equals the RSA decryption $c^d$.

articles.title: RSA-CRT decryption
articles.statement:
Let $(p, q, e, d)$ be an RSA key with modulus $n = pq$. For natural
numbers $d_p$, $d_q$ and $c \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, let $c_p$ and $c_q$ be the images of $c$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$. RSA-CRT decryption of $c$ with the exponents
$d_p$ and $d_q$ is the element of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ that corresponds to the pair
$(c_p^{d_p}, c_q^{d_q})$ under the Chinese remainder isomorphism
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Chinese remainder isomorphism for an RSA modulus
articles.statement:
For an RSA key with distinct primes $p$,
$q$ and modulus $n = pq$, this is the ring isomorphism
$\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \cong \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ of the Chinese
remainder theorem, sending $x$ to $(x \bmod p, x \bmod q)$.

articles.title: Correctness of textbook RSA on natural numbers
articles.statement:
For an RSA key with modulus $n = pq$ and
exponents $e$, $d$, every natural number $m < n$ satisfies $(m^e \bmod n)^d \bmod n = m$.

articles.title: Correctness of textbook RSA
articles.statement:
Decryption inverts encryption on every message, including
messages that are not coprime to `n`.

articles.title: RSA decryption
articles.statement:
For an RSA key with modulus $n = pq$ and private exponent $d$, decryption is
the map $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ given by $c \mapsto c^d$.

articles.title: RSA encryption is a bijection
articles.statement:
For an RSA key with modulus $n = pq$ and public exponent
$e$, the encryption map $m \mapsto m^e$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ to itself.

articles.title: RSA encryption
articles.statement:
For an RSA key with modulus $n = pq$ and public exponent $e$, encryption is
the map $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ given by $m \mapsto m^e$.

articles.title: RSA key
articles.statement:
A textbook RSA key consists of distinct primes $p$ and $q$ and natural numbers $e$
(the public exponent) and $d$ (the private exponent) such that $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{p - 1}$ and
$ed \equiv 1 \pmod{q - 1}$.

articles.title: RSA modulus
articles.statement: The modulus of an RSA key with primes $p$ and $q$ is $n = pq$.

articles.title: RSA key from the totient condition
articles.statement:
Given distinct primes $p$ and $q$ and natural
numbers $e$ and $d$ with $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(pq)}$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient
function, this is the RSA key with primes $p$ and $q$, public exponent $e$ and private exponent
$d$. Its conditions $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{p - 1}$ and $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{q - 1}$ hold because
$\varphi(pq) = (p - 1)(q - 1)$.

articles.title: Positivity of the reduced RSA exponent
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $e$ and $d$ be natural numbers with
$p > 2$ and $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{p - 1}$. Then $d \bmod (p - 1) \ge 1$.

Otherwise $p - 1$ divides $ed$, contradicting $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{p - 1}$.

articles.title: RSA exponent identity
articles.statement:
For an RSA key with modulus $n$ and exponents $e$ and $d$, every
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $x^{ed} = x$.

articles.title: Fermat's little theorem for congruent exponents
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $a$ and $b$
be natural numbers with $a, b \ge 1$ and $a \equiv b \pmod{p - 1}$. Then $x^a = x^b$ for every
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: Checking a power identity through the Chinese remainder theorem
articles.statement:
Let an RSA key have
primes $p$ and $q$ and modulus $n$, let $k$ be a natural number and $x \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$,
