and let $(x_p, x_q) \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}$ be the image of $x$
under the Chinese remainder isomorphism. If $x_p^k = x_p$ and $x_q^k = x_q$, then $x^k = x$.

articles.title: Fermat's little theorem with exponents congruent to one
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let
$k \ge 1$ be a natural number with $k \equiv 1 \pmod{p - 1}$. Then $x^k = x$ for every
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

articles.title: The oracle algorithm that stops at once
articles.statement:
For an output $a \in \alpha$, this is the
adaptive oracle algorithm with queries in $X$ and answers in $Y$ that asks no query and stops
with output $a$.

articles.title: Adaptive oracle algorithms
articles.statement:
For a type $X$ of queries, a type $Y$ of answers and a type
$\alpha$ of outputs, an adaptive deterministic oracle algorithm is an element of CSLib's free
monad over the polynomial functor of one oracle with queries $X$ and answers $Y$. It is built
inductively: it either stops with an output in $\alpha$, or asks a query $x \in X$ and continues
with an algorithm that depends on the answer $y \in Y$.

articles.title: The signature of one oracle
articles.statement:
For types $X$ and $Y$, this is the polynomial functor whose
operations are the queries $x \in X$, each answered by an element of $Y$.

articles.title: Queries of an oracle algorithm
articles.statement:
For an oracle algorithm $c$ and a function
$O : X \to Y$, the queries of $c$ against $O$ are the list of the points of $X$ that $c$ asks,
in order, when every query $x$ is answered by $O(x)$: the empty list if $c$ stops, and otherwise
the first query $x$ followed by the queries of the continuation on the answer $O(x)$.

articles.title: Query step
articles.statement:
For a point $x \in X$ and a continuation $k$ assigning an oracle algorithm to
each answer $y \in Y$, the oracle algorithm that first queries $x$ and then continues with
$k(y)$, where $y$ is the answer.

articles.title: Running a sequential composition
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be an oracle algorithm with outputs in $\alpha$,
let $g$ map each $a \in \alpha$ to an oracle algorithm with outputs in $\beta$, and let
$O : X \to Y$. Running against $O$ the composition that first runs $c$ and then continues with
$g$ applied to its output gives the output of $g(a)$ run against $O$, where $a$ is the output
of $c$ run against $O$.

articles.title: Locality of oracle runs
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be an oracle algorithm and let $O, O' : X \to Y$ agree
at every query of $c$ against $O$. Then $c$ has the same output against $O$ as against $O'$, and
the same list of queries against $O$ as against $O'$.

articles.title: Running an oracle algorithm
articles.statement:
Given a function $O : X \to Y$, the run of an oracle
algorithm with queries in $X$, answers in $Y$ and outputs in $\alpha$ is its output when every
query $x$ is answered by $O(x)$: an algorithm that stops with output $a$ runs to $a$, and one
that queries $x$ and continues with $k(y)$ on answer $y$ runs to the run of $k(O(x))$.

articles.title: Security reduction for Lamport one-time signatures
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function on a
finite nonempty set $X$, let $\ell \ge 1$ be the message length, and let $A$ be a one-time forger
whose random coins range over a finite nonempty set $R$. Then the probability that $A$ wins the
one-time forgery game against the Lamport scheme built from $f$ is at most $2\ell$ times the
probability that the inverter built from $A$ wins the one-wayness game for $f$.

This is the reduction behind Katz and Lindell, Theorem 12.16: if $f$ is one-way, then Lamport's
scheme is one-time secure.

articles.title: One-time forgery game
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$ with $X$ finite and nonempty, and let $A$ be a
one-time forger for messages of length $\ell$ with random coins in a finite nonempty set $R$. The
one-time forgery game is the distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ obtained by drawing
a secret key $sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$ and coins $r \in R$ uniformly and
independently, and returning whether $A$ wins against $sk$ with coins $r$.

articles.title: One-time forger
articles.statement:
A one-time forger for messages of length $\ell$, with random coins in a
set $R$, consists of two maps. The first takes a public key
$pk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to Y$ and coins $r \in R$ and returns the message
$m \in \{0, 1\}^\ell$ whose signature the forger requests. The second takes a public key, a
signature $\sigma \in X^\ell$ and coins $r$ and returns a message $m' \in \{0, 1\}^\ell$ together
with a signature $\sigma' \in X^\ell$.

articles.title: One-wayness game
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$ with $X$ finite and nonempty, and let $I$ be an
inverter with random coins in a finite nonempty set $\Omega$: given $y \in Y$ and coins
$\omega \in \Omega$ it either outputs some $x' \in X$ or fails. The one-wayness game for $f$ is the
distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ obtained by drawing $x \in X$ and
$\omega \in \Omega$ uniformly and independently and returning true exactly when $I$, run on $f(x)$
with coins $\omega$, outputs some $x'$ with $f(x') = f(x)$.

articles.title: Inverter built from a forger
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$, let $A$ be a one-time forger for messages
of length $\ell$ with coins in $R$, and let $y \in Y$. The inverter's coins are a position $(i, b)$
with $i < \ell$ and $b \in \{0, 1\}$, a secret key
$sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$ and forger coins $r \in R$. It forms the
public key $pk$ with $pk(i, b) = y$ and $pk(j, c) = f(sk(j, c))$ for every other $(j, c)$, and
runs $A$ on $pk$ with coins $r$ to obtain the message $m$ whose signature $A$ requests. If
$m_i = b$ it fails. Otherwise it hands $A$ the signature $(sk(j, m_j))_{j < \ell}$ of $m$ under
$sk$ and obtains a forgery $(m', \sigma')$; it outputs $\sigma'_i$ if $m'_i = b$ and fails
otherwise.

articles.title: Planted public key
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$. Given a secret key
$sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$, a position $(i, b)$ and a value $y \in Y$, the
planted public key takes the value $y$ at $(i, b)$ and the value $f(sk(j, c))$ at every other
position $(j, c)$.

articles.title: Lamport public key
articles.statement:
For a function $f : X \to Y$ and a secret key
$sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$, the public key is the map
$pk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to Y$ with $pk(i, b) = f(sk(i, b))$.

articles.title: Lamport signing
articles.statement:
The signature of a message $m \in \{0, 1\}^\ell$ under a secret key
$sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$ is $\sigma \in X^\ell$ with
$\sigma_i = sk(i, m_i)$ for every position $i < \ell$.

articles.title: Correctness of Lamport signatures
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$. For every secret key
$sk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to X$ and every message $m \in \{0, 1\}^\ell$, the
Lamport signature of $m$ under $sk$ is valid for $m$ under the public key of $sk$.

articles.title: Lamport verification
articles.statement:
Let $f : X \to Y$. A signature $\sigma \in X^\ell$ on a message
$m \in \{0, 1\}^\ell$ is valid for a public key $pk : \{0, \dots, \ell - 1\} \times \{0, 1\} \to Y$
when $f(\sigma_i) = pk(i, m_i)$ for every position $i < \ell$.

articles.title: Winning the Lamport one-time forgery game
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a nonempty finite set, $Y$ a set
with decidable equality, $f : X \to Y$ a function, and $\ell$ a message length; messages are bit
strings $m = (m_0, \dots, m_{\ell-1})$. A one-time forger $A$ with random coins from a nonempty
finite set $R$ wins against a secret key $sk$, which assigns $sk(i, b) \in X$ to each position
$i < \ell$ and bit $b$, with coins $r \in R$ when the following holds. Let $pk$ be the public key
of $sk$, given by $pk(i, b) = f(sk(i, b))$; let $m$ be the message that $A$ chooses from $pk$ and
$r$; and let $(m', \sigma')$ be the message and signature that $A$ outputs from $pk$, the
signature $i \mapsto sk(i, m_i)$ of $m$ under $sk$, and $r$. Then $m' \ne m$, and $\sigma'$ is a
valid signature on $m'$ for $pk$: $f(\sigma'_i) = pk(i, m'_i)$ for every $i < \ell$.

articles.title: Completeness of the Schnorr identification scheme
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group,
$q \ge 1$ a natural number and $g \in G$ with $g^q = 1$; for $h \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$
write $h^a$ for $h^{\bar a}$, where $\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the representative
of $a$. For all $x, k, r \in \mathbb{Z}/q$, with public key $y = g^x$, the honest transcript
$(g^k, r, rx + k)$ is accepted, that is, $g^{rx + k} (y^r)^{-1} = g^k$.

articles.title: Schnorr verifier's acceptance condition
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q$ a natural
number and $g, y \in G$ (the base and the public key); for $h \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$
write $h^a$ for $h^{\bar a}$, where $\bar a$ is the representative of $a$ in
$\{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ (and $\bar a = |a|$ when $q = 0$, so that $\mathbb{Z}/q = \mathbb{Z}$).
The verifier accepts a transcript $(I, r, s)$ with $I \in G$ and $r, s \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ when
$g^s (y^r)^{-1} = I$.

articles.title: Special soundness
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q$ a prime and $g, y \in G$ with
$g^q = 1$ and $y^q = 1$; for $h \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ write $h^a$ for $h^{\bar a}$,
where $\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the representative of $a$. Let $I \in G$ and
$r, s, r', s' \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ with $r \ne r'$, and suppose both transcripts $(I, r, s)$ and
$(I, r', s')$ are accepted, that is, $g^s (y^r)^{-1} = I$ and $g^{s'} (y^{r'})^{-1} = I$. Then
the extracted exponent $e = (s - s')(r - r')^{-1}$ is a discrete logarithm of $y$: $g^e = y$.

articles.title: Schnorr knowledge extractor
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number. For
$r, s, r', s' \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ (the challenges and answers of two transcripts), the extracted
exponent is $(s - s')(r - r')^{-1} \in \mathbb{Z}/q$, where $u^{-1}$ is the inverse of $u$ in
$\mathbb{Z}/q$ when $u$ is a unit (and, otherwise, a conventional element of $\mathbb{Z}/q$
depending on $u$). For $q$ prime and $r \ne r'$ it is $(s - s')/(r - r')$.

articles.title: Honest Schnorr transcript
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q \ge 1$ and $g \in G$; for
$a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ write $g^a$ for $g^{\bar a}$, where $\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the
representative of $a$. For a secret key $x$, prover randomness $k$ and challenge $r$, all in
$\mathbb{Z}/q$, the honest transcript is the element $(g^k, r, rx + k)$ of
$G \times \mathbb{Z}/q \times \mathbb{Z}/q$.

articles.title: Schnorr prover's response
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be a natural number. For a secret key $x$, prover
randomness $k$ and challenge $r$, all in $\mathbb{Z}/q$, the prover's answer is
$s = rx + k \in \mathbb{Z}/q$.

articles.title: Simulated Schnorr transcript
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q \ge 1$ and $g, y \in G$;
for $h \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ write $h^a$ for $h^{\bar a}$, where
$\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the representative of $a$. For a challenge $r$ and an answer
$s$ in $\mathbb{Z}/q$, the simulated transcript is the element $(g^s (y^r)^{-1}, r, s)$ of
$G \times \mathbb{Z}/q \times \mathbb{Z}/q$.

articles.title: Schnorr simulator
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q \ge 1$ and $g, y \in G$; for
$h \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ write $h^a$ for $h^{\bar a}$, where
$\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the representative of $a$. The simulator's distribution is
the law of the simulated transcript $(g^s (y^r)^{-1}, r, s)$ when $(r, s)$ is uniform on
$\mathbb{Z}/q \times \mathbb{Z}/q$; it uses only $g$ and the public key $y$.

articles.title: Perfect honest-verifier zero knowledge
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q \ge 1$ and
$g \in G$ with $g^q = 1$; for $h \in G$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ write $h^a$ for $h^{\bar a}$,
where $\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the representative of $a$. For every secret key
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/q$, with public key $y = g^x$, the honest transcript $(g^k, r, rx + k)$ with
$(k, r)$ uniform on $\mathbb{Z}/q \times \mathbb{Z}/q$ has the same distribution as the
simulated transcript $(g^s (y^r)^{-1}, r, s)$ with $(r, s)$ uniform on
$\mathbb{Z}/q \times \mathbb{Z}/q$.

articles.title: Distribution of honest Schnorr transcripts
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a commutative group, $q \ge 1$ and
$g \in G$; for $a \in \mathbb{Z}/q$ write $g^a$ for $g^{\bar a}$, where
$\bar a \in \{0, \dots, q - 1\}$ is the representative of $a$. For a secret key
$x \in \mathbb{Z}/q$, this is the law of the honest transcript $(g^k, r, rx + k)$ when $(k, r)$ is
uniform on $\mathbb{Z}/q \times \mathbb{Z}/q$.

articles.title: Group one-time pad ciphertexts are uniform
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group. For every
message $m \in G$, the ciphertext of $m$ under the group one-time pad on $G$, whose key is
drawn uniformly from $G$, is uniformly distributed on $G$.

articles.title: The group one-time pad is perfectly secret
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group. The group
one-time pad on $G$ is perfectly secret: for every probability distribution on messages in $G$
and every ciphertext $c$ that occurs with positive probability, the conditional distribution
of the message given that the ciphertext is $c$ equals the prior distribution of the message.

## Sources

- Katz and Lindell, Lemma 11.15.

articles.title: The group one-time pad
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group. The group one-time pad on $G$ is the
private-key encryption scheme with messages, keys and ciphertexts in $G$ whose key $k$ is drawn
uniformly from $G$, which encrypts a message $m$ as $k m$, and which decrypts a ciphertext $c$
as $k^{-1} c$.

articles.title: Counting forgeries against a random function
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $T$ be finite sets and let $c$ be
an adaptive oracle algorithm that queries messages in $M$, receives tags in $T$ and outputs a pair
in $M \times T$. Call a function $f \colon M \to T$ a win for $c$ when the run of $c$ with oracle
$f$ outputs a pair $(m, t)$ with $f(m) = t$ and $m$ not among the messages queried in that run.
If $W$ is the set of functions $M \to T$ that are wins for $c$, then $|W| \cdot |T| \le |T|^{|M|}$.

Changing the tag of the fresh forged message, which the run never queries, gives $|T|$ functions
with the same run, of which exactly one is a win.

articles.title: CPA encryption from a PRF, concrete security
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $X$ and $R$ be nonempty finite sets,
$Y$ a finite additive commutative group, $q$ a natural number and $F \colon K \to X \to Y$ a keyed
function, used in the scheme $\mathrm{Enc}_k(m) = (r, F_k(r) + m)$ with uniform randomness
$r \in X$. For every CPA adversary $A$ with coins in $R$, the CPA advantage of $A$ in the
experiment whose encryption oracle answers at most $q$ queries is at most the PRF advantage of $F$
against the distinguisher built from $A$ plus $q / (2 |X|)$.

This is the reduction of Katz and Lindell, Theorem 3.31, with the sharper statistical term
$q / (2 |X|)$ in place of $q / |X|$.

articles.title: CPA advantage
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $X$ and $R$ be nonempty finite sets, $Y$ an additive commutative
group, $q$ a natural number, $F \colon K \to X \to Y$ a keyed function and $A$ a CPA adversary
with coins in $R$. The CPA advantage of $A$ is the real number $|p - 1/2|$, where $p$ is the
probability that the CPA experiment for $F$ and $A$ with at most $q$ encryption queries outputs
true, that is, that $A$ guesses the challenge bit.

articles.title: The CPA reduction is exact with the real oracle
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $X$ and $R$ be nonempty finite
sets, $Y$ an additive commutative group, $q$ a natural number and $F \colon K \to X \to Y$ a keyed
function. For every CPA adversary $A$ with coins in $R$, the CPA experiment for $F$ and $A$ with
at most $q$ encryption queries has the same output distribution as the real world of the PRF
experiment for $F$ run with the distinguisher built from $A$ for $q$ queries: with the oracle $F_k$
for a uniform key $k$, the reduction runs the CPA experiment exactly.

articles.title: The CPA experiment
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $X$ and $R$ be nonempty finite sets, $Y$ an additive
commutative group, $q$ a natural number, $F \colon K \to X \to Y$ a keyed function and $A$ a CPA
adversary with coins in $R$. The CPA indistinguishability experiment $\mathrm{PrivK}^{\mathrm{cpa}}$
for the scheme $\mathrm{Enc}_k(m) = (r, F_k(r) + m)$ draws, uniformly and independently, a key
$k \in K$, encryption randomness $\rho \colon \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to X$ for the encryption
queries, challenge randomness $r_s \in X$, a challenge bit $b$ and coins $r \in R$. It outputs true
exactly when the adversary's guess, with keyed function $F_k$, encryption randomness $\rho$,
challenge randomness $r_s$, challenge bit $b$ and the algorithm that $A$ assigns to $r$, equals $b$.
An adversary that asks more than $q$ encryption queries is stopped and guesses false.

articles.title: The adversary's guess in the CPA experiment
articles.statement:
Let $Y$ be an additive commutative group,
$f \colon X \to Y$ a function, $q$ a natural number, $\rho \colon \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to X$ the
encryption randomness, $r_s \in X$ the challenge randomness and $b$ a bit. Let $c$ be an oracle
algorithm for the encryption oracle that outputs two messages $(m_0, m_1) \in Y \times Y$ and a
second-phase algorithm. The encryption query with index $i$, counting from $0$ across both
phases, is answered for a message $m$ by $(\rho_i, f(\rho_i) + m)$. Run $c$; when it outputs
$(m_0, m_1)$, run its second phase on the challenge ciphertext $(r_s, f(r_s) + m_b)$, where $m_b$
is $m_1$ if $b$ is true and $m_0$ otherwise. The guess is the output of the second phase. If the
two phases together ask more than $q$ encryption queries, the adversary is stopped and the guess
is false.

articles.title: The PRF distinguisher built from a CPA adversary
articles.statement:
Let $X$ and $R$ be sets, $Y$ an additive
commutative group, $q$ a natural number and $A$ a CPA adversary with coins in $R$ against an
encryption oracle that takes messages in $Y$ and returns ciphertexts in $X \times Y$. With its own
coins $(\rho, r_s, b, r)$, where $\rho \colon \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to X$, $r_s \in X$, $b$ is a bit
and $r \in R$, and with oracle access to a function $O \colon X \to Y$, the distinguisher runs the
algorithm $A$ assigns to $r$. It answers the encryption query with index $i$, counting from $0$
across both phases, for a message $m$ by querying $O$ at $\rho_i$ and returning
$(\rho_i, O(\rho_i) + m)$. When the first phase outputs messages $(m_0, m_1)$, it queries $O$ at
$r_s$ and gives the second phase the challenge ciphertext $(r_s, O(r_s) + m_b)$, where $m_b$ is
$m_1$ if $b$ is true and $m_0$ otherwise. It outputs true exactly when the adversary's guess
equals $b$, where an adversary that asks more than $q$ encryption queries is stopped and guesses
false.

articles.title: CPA adversary
articles.statement:
A CPA adversary with coins in $R$, against an encryption oracle that takes
messages in $Y$ and returns ciphertexts in $X \times Y$, assigns to each $r \in R$ an adaptive
oracle algorithm with access to the encryption oracle that outputs two challenge messages
$(m_0, m_1) \in Y \times Y$ together with a second adaptive oracle algorithm, again with access to
the encryption oracle, which takes the challenge ciphertext in $X \times Y$ and outputs a guess
for the challenge bit.

articles.title: Correctness of encryption with a keyed function
articles.statement:
Let $Y$ be an additive commutative group
and $F_k \colon X \to Y$ a function. For every message $m \in Y$ and every randomness $r \in X$,
decrypting the ciphertext $\mathrm{Enc}(m) = (r, F_k(r) + m)$ gives back $m$, that is,
$\mathrm{Dec}(\mathrm{Enc}(m)) = m$ where $\mathrm{Dec}(r, c) = c - F_k(r)$.

articles.title: Decryption with a keyed function
articles.statement:
For a function $F_k \colon X \to Y$ into an additive
commutative group $Y$, the decryption of a ciphertext $(r, c) \in X \times Y$ is
$\mathrm{Dec}(r, c) = c - F_k(r)$.

articles.title: Encryption from a keyed function
articles.statement:
Let $Y$ be an additive commutative group of messages
and let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a function (in the scheme, $f = F_k$ for a key $k$). The
encryption of a message $m \in Y$ with randomness $r \in X$ is the pair
$(r, f(r) + m) \in X \times Y$.

This is Construction 3.30 of Katz and Lindell, with XOR replaced by the addition of the
message group.

articles.title: The MAC reduction in the real PRF world
articles.statement:
Let $K$ and $R$ be finite nonempty types, let
$F \colon K \to M \to T$ be a keyed function, and let $A$ be a forger: for coins $r \in R$,
$A(r)$ is an adaptive oracle algorithm with queries in $M$, answers in $T$ and output in
$M \times T$. Then the output distribution of the existential-forgery experiment for $F$ and $A$
equals the output distribution of the real world of the PRF experiment for $F$ with the
distinguisher that, on coins $r$, runs the MAC reduction on $A(r)$ starting from the empty query
log.

articles.title: The MAC from a PRF, concrete security
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $M$, $T$ and $R$ be finite types with
$K$, $T$ and $R$ nonempty, let $F \colon K \to M \to T$ be a keyed function, and let $A$ be an
adaptive chosen-message forger: for coins $r \in R$, $A(r)$ is an adaptive oracle algorithm
with queries in $M$, answers in $T$ and output in $M \times T$. Then the probability that $A$
wins the existential-forgery experiment for the MAC $\mathrm{Mac}_k(m) = F(k, m)$ is at most
the PRF advantage against $F$ of the distinguisher that, on coins $r$, runs the MAC reduction
on $A(r)$ starting from the empty query log, plus $1 / |T|$.

This is the reduction of Katz and Lindell, Theorem 4.6, stated as a concrete inequality.

articles.title: The MAC forgery experiment
articles.statement:
Let $K$ and $R$ be finite nonempty types, let
$F \colon K \to M \to T$ be a keyed function, and let $A$ be a forger: for coins $r \in R$,
$A(r)$ is an adaptive oracle algorithm with queries in $M$, answers in $T$ and output in
$M \times T$. The existential-forgery experiment under an adaptive chosen-message attack for the
MAC $\mathrm{Mac}_k(m) = F(k, m)$ draws $(k, r)$ uniformly from $K \times R$, runs $A(r)$ with
the tagging oracle $F(k, \cdot)$, and outputs true exactly when $A(r)$ wins against that oracle,
that is, outputs a pair $(m, t)$ with $F(k, m) = t$ where $m$ is not among its queries.

articles.title: The distinguisher built from a forger
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ of messages in $M$ and a forger $c$,
an adaptive oracle algorithm with queries in $M$, answers in $T$ and output in $M \times T$, the
MAC reduction is the oracle algorithm with the same queries and answers and a Boolean output,
defined by recursion on $c$. If $c$ stops with output $(m, t)$, it queries $m$ and, on answer
$t'$, stops with output true exactly when $t' = t$ and $m \notin L$. If $c$ queries $x$ and
continues with $c_y$ on answer $y$, it queries $x$ and, on answer $y$, continues as the MAC
reduction of $c_y$ with $x$ added to $L$.

Started with the empty list, it runs the forger, logging its queries, then queries the forged
message and accepts when the answer is the forged tag and the message is fresh.

articles.title: Winning the forgery game
articles.statement:
A forger $c$, an adaptive oracle algorithm with queries in $M$,
answers in $T$ and output in $M \times T$, wins against the tagging oracle $O \colon M \to T$
when, run with oracle $O$, it outputs a pair $(m, t)$ with $O(m) = t$ and $m$ is not among the
queries it asks in that run.

articles.title: Selecting the challenge message by a bit
articles.statement:
Given a pair of messages
$(m_0, m_1) \in Y \times Y$ and a challenge bit $b$, the selected message is $m_1$ when $b$ is
true and $m_0$ when $b$ is false.

articles.title: PRF advantage
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $X$, $Y$ and $S$ be finite sets with $K$, $Y$ and $S$ nonempty,
let $F : K \to X \to Y$ be a keyed function and let $D$ be a distinguisher: an oracle algorithm
with coins in $S$ that queries a function $X \to Y$ and outputs a bit. The PRF advantage of $D$
against $F$ is the real number $|p_{\mathrm{real}} - p_{\mathrm{rand}}|$, where
$p_{\mathrm{real}}$ is the probability that $D$ outputs $1$ in the real world (uniform coins
$s \in S$, oracle $F(k, \cdot)$ for a uniform key $k \in K$) and $p_{\mathrm{rand}}$ is the
probability that $D$ outputs $1$ in the random world (uniform coins, oracle a uniformly random
function $X \to Y$).

articles.title: The CPA reduction against a random function
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, $Y$ a
finite additive commutative group, $q$ a natural number and $A$ a CPA adversary with coins in a
finite nonempty set. Let $p$ be the probability that the CPA reduction built from $A$ (whose
encryption oracle answers at most $q$ queries) outputs $1$, that is, that $A$ guesses the
challenge bit, when its oracle is a uniformly random function $X \to Y$ and its coins are
uniform. Then $|p - 1/2| \le q / (2|X|)$.

The success probability is exactly $1/2$ unless the challenge randomness repeats the randomness
of one of the at most $q$ encryption queries.

articles.title: Forging against a random function
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $T$ be finite sets with $T$ nonempty, and
let $A$ be a forger: an oracle algorithm with coins in a finite nonempty set that queries tags
in $T$ of messages in $M$ and outputs a message together with a tag. When the tagging oracle is
a uniformly random function $M \to T$ and the coins are uniform, the MAC reduction built from
$A$ accepts (that is, $A$ outputs the correct tag of a message it never queried) with
probability at most $1/|T|$.

articles.title: Random world of the PRF experiment
articles.statement:
Let $X$, $Y$ and $S$ be finite sets with $Y$ and $S$
nonempty, and let $D$ be a distinguisher: an oracle algorithm with coins in $S$ that queries a
function $X \to Y$ and outputs a bit. The random world is the distribution of the output of $D$
with coins $s$ and oracle $f$, where the pair $(f, s)$ is uniform on $(X \to Y) \times S$.

articles.title: Real world of the PRF experiment
articles.statement:
Let $K$, $X$, $Y$ and $S$ be finite sets with $K$, $Y$
and $S$ nonempty, let $F : K \to X \to Y$ be a keyed function and let $D$ be a distinguisher: an
oracle algorithm with coins in $S$ that queries a function $X \to Y$ and outputs a bit. The real
world is the distribution of the output of $D$ with coins $s$ and oracle $F(k, \cdot)$, where the
pair $(k, s)$ is uniform on $K \times S$.

articles.title: The encryption oracle depends only on the encryption randomness
articles.statement:
Let $Y$ be an additive
commutative group, let $\rho_0, \dots, \rho_{q-1} \in X$ be encryption randomness and let
$f, f' : X \to Y$ satisfy $f(\rho_j) = f'(\rho_j)$ for every $j < q$. Then for every oracle
algorithm $c$ and every natural number $i$, running $c$ against the encryption oracle built from
$f$, with query indices starting at $i$, gives the same result as running it against the one
built from $f'$. Here the encryption oracle built from $f$ answers a query $m$ with index $n < q$
by $(\rho_n, f(\rho_n) + m)$, and the run fails at a query with index $n \ge q$.

articles.title: Running an algorithm against the bounded encryption oracle
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a set, $Y$ an
abelian group written additively, $f : X \to Y$ a function, $q \in \mathbb{N}$ and
$\rho : \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to X$ the encryption randomness of the queries. Run from query index
$i \in \mathbb{N}$, an oracle algorithm with messages in $Y$ as queries, answers in $X \times Y$
and outputs in $\beta$ either fails or yields its output together with the next query index: if
it stops with output $a$, the result is $(a, i)$; if it queries a message $m$ and $i < q$, the
oracle answers $(\rho(i), f(\rho(i)) + m)$ and the run continues from index $i + 1$; if it
queries a message and $i \ge q$, the run fails.

articles.title: Simulating the encryption oracle with a function oracle
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a set, $Y$ an abelian
group written additively, $q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\rho : \{0, \dots, q - 1\} \to X$ the
encryption randomness of the queries. Started at query index $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the simulation
turns an oracle algorithm with messages in $Y$ as queries, answers in $X \times Y$ and outputs in
$\beta$ into an oracle algorithm with queries in $X$ and answers in $Y$ that either fails or
outputs the original output together with the next query index: if the original algorithm stops
with output $a$, the simulation stops with $(a, i)$; if it queries a message $m$ and $i < q$, the
simulation queries $\rho(i)$ and, on answer $y$, continues by simulating the original algorithm
on the answer $(\rho(i), y + m)$ from index $i + 1$; if it queries a message and $i \ge q$, the
simulation stops with failure.

articles.title: Correctness of the union-find equivalence query
articles.statement:
Call two natural numbers $a$ and $c$
equivalent in a union-find structure when they have the same root, where a number that is not a
node is its own root. Let $U$ be a union-find structure with nodes $0, \dots, N-1$ and let
$x, y < N$. The equivalence query on $x$ and $y$, which runs FIND-SET with path compression on
$x$ and then on $y$, returns a union-find structure $U'$ and a boolean $b$ such that $U'$ has
$N$ nodes, $b$ is true if and only if $x$ and $y$ are equivalent in $U$, and for all natural
numbers $a$ and $c$, $a$ and $c$ are equivalent in $U'$ if and only if they are equivalent
in $U$.

articles.title: Connected components computes reachability
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $E$ be a
list of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. For all vertices $a, b < n$, $a$ and $b$ are
equivalent in the union-find structure returned by CONNECTED-COMPONENTS on $n$ and $E$ if and
only if $a$ and $b$ are joined by a path in the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ whose edges
are the unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ with $(u, v)$ in $E$ and $u \ne v$.

articles.title: Connected components allocates $n$ nodes
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every list
$E$ of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the union-find structure returned by
CONNECTED-COMPONENTS on $n$ and $E$ has exactly $n$ nodes.

articles.title: Operation counts of connected components
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $E$ be a list
of pairs of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $m$ be the length of $E$. Let $G$ be the
simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ whose edges are the unordered pairs $\{u, v\}$ with $(u, v)$
in $E$ and $u \ne v$, and let $k$ be the number of connected components of $G$. Running
CONNECTED-COMPONENTS on $n$ and $E$ makes exactly $n$ MAKE-SET calls, $2m$ FIND-SET calls and
$n - k$ UNION calls. Moreover, $k$ plus the number of UNION calls equals $n$, and if $n > 0$
then the number of UNION calls is at most $n - 1$.

These are the call counts recorded by the cost annotation, not bounds on parent-pointer visits.

articles.title: Connected components via union-find
articles.statement:
Given a natural number $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs
of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, CONNECTED-COMPONENTS first builds the union-find structure
with $n$ singleton nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ by $n$ MAKE-SET calls. It then processes the pairs
$(u, v)$ of $E$ in list order: it asks whether $u$ and $v$ are equivalent using two FIND-SET
calls, keeping the path compression done by the query, and if they are not equivalent it
performs UNION on $u$ and $v$ (union by rank with path compression). It returns the final
union-find structure, which has $n$ nodes, together with the numbers of MAKE-SET, FIND-SET and
UNION calls made.

articles.title: The cost-counted FIND auxiliary returns the uncounted result
articles.statement:
For a union-find
structure $S$ and a node $x < |S|$, the value returned by the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$
(the compressed node array together with the root of $x$), with its cost discarded, equals the
result of the Batteries path-compression auxiliary routine of FIND on $x$.

articles.title: Root tests exceed parent writes by one
articles.statement:
For a union-find structure $S$ and a node
$x < |S|$, if the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ has cost $(t, w)$, where $t$ counts root
tests and $w$ counts parent writes, then $t = w + 1$.

articles.title: Cost of the FIND auxiliary at a root
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure and $x < |S|$
a node. If the parent of $x$ in $S$ is $x$ itself, then the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$
has cost $(1, 0)$: one root test and no parent writes.

articles.title: Cost recurrence of the FIND auxiliary at a non-root
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure
and $x < |S|$ a node whose parent $y$ in $S$ differs from $x$. If $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the costs
of the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ and on $y$, then $c_x = (1, 0) + (c_y + (0, 1))$:
one root test at $x$, then the run on $y$, then one parent write.

articles.title: Parent writes are bounded by the rank gap
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure, let $R$
be one more than the maximum rank of a node of $S$, and let $x < |S|$ be a node. The number of
parent writes performed by the cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$ (the second coordinate of its
cost) is at most $R - \operatorname{rank}(x)$.

This is a per-call bound, not a logarithmic or amortized inverse-Ackermann bound.

articles.title: Cost-counted FIND auxiliary
articles.statement:
For a union-find structure $S$ with node array $A$ and a
node $x < |S|$, this is the recursive path-compression routine of FIND, paired with a cost in
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$. It charges $(1, 0)$ for testing whether $x$ is a root. If the
parent $y$ of $x$ in $A$ equals $x$, it returns $A$ and the root $x$. Otherwise it runs on $y$,
obtaining an array $A'$ and a root $r$, charges $(0, 1)$ for one parent write, and returns $A'$
with the parent of $x$ set to $r$, together with $r$. The first cost coordinate thus counts root
tests and the second counts parent writes.

The returned array and root are exactly those of the Batteries FIND auxiliary; only the costs
are added.

articles.title: The cost-counted FIND returns the FIND result
articles.statement:
For a union-find structure $S$ and a node
$x < |S|$, the value returned by the cost-counted FIND on $x$ (the compressed union-find
structure together with the root of $x$), with its cost discarded, equals the result of the
Batteries FIND with path compression on $x$.

articles.title: Cost-counted FIND
articles.statement:
For a union-find structure $S$ and a node $x < |S|$, this runs the
cost-counted FIND auxiliary on $x$, obtaining a node array $A'$, a root $r$ and a cost $(t, w)$.
It returns the union-find structure with node array $A'$, together with $r$ as a node of that
structure (whose size equals $|S|$), at cost $(t, w)$.

It reuses the array and root of that single run; FIND is not run a second time.

articles.title: Counted linking returns the linked array
articles.statement:
For an array $A$ of union-find nodes and
indices $x, y$ of $A$, the array returned by counted linking of $x$ and $y$ in $A$ is exactly the
array produced by the uncounted Batteries link by rank of $x$ and $y$ in $A$.

articles.title: Operation counts of linking by rank
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an array of union-find nodes, let $x, y$
be indices of $A$, and write $r_x$ and $r_y$ for the ranks stored at $x$ and $y$. Counted linking
of $x$ and $y$ in $A$ makes $(t, p, w)$ rank tests, parent writes and rank writes, where
$(t, p, w)$ is $(0, 0, 0)$ if $x = y$, is $(1, 1, 0)$ if $x \ne y$ and $r_y < r_x$, is
$(2, 1, 1)$ if $x \ne y$ and $r_x = r_y$, and is $(2, 1, 0)$ otherwise, that is, if $x \ne y$
and $r_x < r_y$.

articles.title: Linking by rank with operation counts
articles.statement:
Given an array $A$ of union-find nodes, each
storing a parent index and a rank, and indices $x, y$ of $A$, this computation returns an array
together with a count $(t, p, w)$ of rank tests $t$, parent writes $p$ and rank writes $w$. If
$x = y$ it returns $A$ with count $(0, 0, 0)$. Otherwise it makes one rank test; if the rank of $y$
is less than the rank of $x$, it sets the parent of $y$ to $x$ (one parent write). If not, it sets
the parent of $x$ to $y$ (one parent write) and makes a second rank test, and if the ranks of $x$
and $y$ are equal it also increases the rank of $y$ by one (one rank write).

The equality test $x = y$ is not counted as a rank test.

articles.title: The FIND phases of a union make two more root tests than parent writes
articles.statement:
For a
union-find structure $S$ and indices $x, y$ of $S$, in the counted union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ the
total number of root tests made by its two FIND calls equals the total number of parent writes
they make plus $2$.

articles.title: Counted union returns the union's array
articles.statement:
For a union-find structure $S$ and indices
$x, y$ of $S$, the array returned by the counted union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ equals the node array
of the Batteries union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$ (union by rank with path compression).

articles.title: Union by rank with operation counts
articles.statement:
For a union-find structure $S$ and indices $x, y$
of $S$, this computation runs counted FIND on $x$ in $S$, giving a structure $S_1$ and a root
$r_x$; then counted FIND on $y$ in $S_1$, giving a structure $S_2$ and a root $r_y$; then counted
linking of $r_x$ and $r_y$ in the node array of $S_2$. It returns the array produced by the
linking, with cost $((a, b), (t, p, w))$, where $a$ and $b$ are the total numbers of root tests
and parent writes of the two FIND calls, and $(t, p, w)$ counts the rank tests, parent writes and
rank writes of the linking.

articles.title: Equivalence after a union
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a parent forest and let $x, y, a, b$ be vertices of
$F$. Then $a$ and $b$ are equivalent in the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$
if and only if $a$ and $b$ are equivalent in $F$, or $a$ is equivalent to $x$ and $b$ is
equivalent to $y$ in $F$, or $a$ is equivalent to $y$ and $b$ is equivalent to $x$ in $F$.

Thus the union merges exactly the old classes of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Equivalent vertices of a parent forest
articles.statement:
Two vertices $x$ and $y$ of a parent forest $F$
are equivalent when find returns the same root for $x$ as for $y$ in $F$.

articles.title: The root is reached in fewer parent steps than there are nodes
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a
union-find structure with $n$ nodes and parent map $p$, and let $x < n$. Then there is $d < n$
such that $p^d(x)$ is the root of $x$ and $p^k(x)$ is not the root of $x$ for every $k < d$.

articles.title: Every vertex is equivalent to its representative
articles.statement:
For every vertex $x$ of a parent
forest $F$, the vertex $x$ is equivalent in $F$ to the root that find returns for $x$.

articles.title: Find returns a root
articles.statement:
For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, the vertex $r$ that find
returns for $x$ is a root of $F$: the parent of $r$ in $F$ is $r$ itself.

articles.title: FIND compresses exactly the original path to the root
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure
with parent map $p$ (where $p(i) = i$ for $i \ge |S|$), let $x < |S|$, and let $p'$ be the parent
map of the structure produced by FIND with path compression on $x$. Then for every natural number
$i$, $p'(i)$ is the root of $x$ if $i = p^k(x)$ for some $k \ge 0$, and $p'(i) = p(i)$
otherwise.

articles.title: Find is unchanged along a parent pointer
articles.statement:
For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$,
find returns the same root for the parent of $x$ in $F$ as for $x$.

articles.title: Union preserves the representatives of unrelated classes
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a parent forest and
let $x, y, z$ be vertices of $F$. If $z$ is not equivalent to $x$ in $F$, then find returns the
same root for $z$ in the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$ as in $F$.

No hypothesis on $y$ is needed.

articles.title: Representatives after a union
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a parent forest, let $x, y, z$ be vertices of
$F$, and let $F'$ be the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$ and $y$. If $z$ is
equivalent to $x$ in $F$, then find returns for $z$ in $F'$ the root that find returns for $y$
in $F$; otherwise find returns the same root for $z$ in $F'$ as in $F$.

articles.title: The cost of find is at most the depth certificate plus one
articles.statement:
For every vertex $x$ of a
parent forest $F$ with depth certificate $d$, the cost that find with cost charges on $x$ is at
most $d(x) + 1$.

articles.title: The cost of find is the path length plus one
articles.statement:
For every vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$,
the cost that find with cost charges on $x$ equals $\ell(x) + 1$, where $\ell(x)$ is the path
length of $x$: the number of non-root parent edges that find traverses from $x$.

articles.title: Find with cost
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ of a parent forest $F$, find with cost returns the root
that find returns for $x$, together with the cost $\ell(x) + 1$, where $\ell(x)$ is the path
length of $x$ (the number of non-root parent edges that find traverses from $x$). That is, it
charges one unit for every visited vertex, including the root.

articles.title: Root of a vertex in a parent forest
articles.statement:
For a parent forest $F$ with parent map $p$ and a
vertex $x$, the root of $x$ is found by following parent pointers from $x$: it is $x$ itself
if $p(x) = x$, and otherwise it is the root of $p(x)$.

articles.title: Parent forest with a depth certificate
articles.statement:
A parent forest on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a parent map $p$ from the vertices to themselves (a vertex $x$
with $p(x) = x$ is a root) and a depth certificate $d$ assigning a natural number to every
vertex, such that every non-root edge strictly decreases the certificate: if $p(x) \ne x$, then
$d(p(x)) < d(x)$.

articles.title: Effect of path-compressing find on each node
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a union-find structure on the
indices $0, \dots, n-1$ with parent function $p$, let $x < n$, and let $r$ be the root of $x$ in
$s$. After find with path compression is run on $x$, for every index $i < n$ the node at $i$ in
the resulting array keeps its rank from $s$, and its parent is $r$ if $i = p^k(x)$ for some
$k \ge 0$, and is its original parent $p(i)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Depth certificate after linking two roots
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a parent forest with depth
certificate $d$, and let $r$ and $s$ be vertices. The linked depth certificate assigns to a
vertex $z$ the number $d(z) + d(s) + 1$ if $z$ is equivalent to $r$ in $F$ (that is, $z$ and $r$
have the same root), and $d(z)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Parent map after linking two roots
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a parent forest with parent map $p$, and
let $r$ and $s$ be vertices. The linked parent map sends $r$ to $s$ and agrees with $p$ on every
other vertex: it maps $z$ to $s$ if $z = r$, and to $p(z)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Linking two roots of a parent forest
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a parent forest with parent map $p$ and
depth certificate $d$, and let $r \ne s$ be two distinct roots of $F$. Linking $r$ to $s$ gives
the parent forest whose parent map is the linked parent map (the parent of $r$ becomes $s$ and
all other parents are unchanged) and whose depth certificate is the linked depth certificate (the
certificate of every vertex equivalent to $r$ grows by $d(s) + 1$ and all others are unchanged).
These still satisfy the decreasing-certificate condition.

articles.title: Path length to the root
articles.statement:
For a parent forest $F$ with parent map $p$ and a vertex $x$,
the path length of $x$ is the number of parent edges followed from $x$ to its root: it is $0$ if
$p(x) = x$, and otherwise one more than the path length of $p(x)$.

articles.title: Ranks after linking two nodes of an array
articles.statement:
For an array $A$ of union-find nodes, write
$\rho_A(i)$ for the rank stored at index $i$ of $A$, or $0$ if $i$ is not an index of $A$. Let
$x, y$ be indices of $A$ and let $A'$ be the array obtained from $A$ by the Batteries link by rank
of $x$ and $y$. Then for every natural number $i$, $\rho_{A'}(i) = \rho_A(y) + 1$ if $x \ne y$,
$\rho_A(x) = \rho_A(y)$ and $i = y$, and $\rho_{A'}(i) = \rho_A(i)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Path compression preserves ranks
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure and $x$ a node of
$S$, and let $S'$ be the structure returned by FIND on $x$ with path compression. For every
natural number $i$, the rank of $i$ in $S'$ equals the rank of $i$ in $S$, where the rank of an
index that is not a node is $0$.

articles.title: Ranks after linking in a union-find structure
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure, write
$\rho(i)$ for the rank of $i$ in $S$ ($0$ if $i$ is not a node of $S$), and let $x, y$ be nodes of
$S$ such that $y$ is a root, that is, the parent of $y$ is $y$. Let $S'$ be the result of linking
$x$ and $y$ by rank. Then for every natural number $i$, the rank of $i$ in $S'$ is $\rho(y) + 1$
if $x \ne y$, $\rho(x) = \rho(y)$ and $i = y$, and is $\rho(i)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Ranks after a union
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a union-find structure, write $\rho(i)$ for the rank of
$i$ in $S$ ($0$ if $i$ is not a node of $S$) and $r(i)$ for the root of $i$ in $S$. For nodes
$x, y$ of $S$ and every natural number $i$, the rank of $i$ in the union of $x$ and $y$ in $S$
(union by rank with path compression) is $\rho(r(y)) + 1$ if $r(x) \ne r(y)$,
$\rho(r(x)) = \rho(r(y))$ and $r(y) = i$, and is $\rho(i)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Linking two roots by rank
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be a union-find structure on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and
let $x, y < n$ be roots of $U$, i.e. each is its own parent. Let $U'$ be obtained by linking $x$
and $y$ by rank: nothing changes if $x = y$; otherwise, if $\operatorname{rank}(y) <
\operatorname{rank}(x)$ then $y$ gets parent $x$, and if not then $x$ gets parent $y$ and, when
the two ranks are equal, the rank of $y$ increases by one. Then for every natural number $i$,
where the root of an index $i \ge n$ is $i$ itself: if the root of $i$ in $U$ is $x$ or $y$, the
root of $i$ in $U'$ is $x$ when $\operatorname{rank}(y) < \operatorname{rank}(x)$ and $y$
otherwise; if the root of $i$ in $U$ is neither $x$ nor $y$, its root in $U'$ is the same as in
$U$.

articles.title: Union unfolds to two finds and a link
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be a union-find structure on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $x, y < n$. Run find with path compression on $x$ in $U$, giving a
structure $U_1$ and a root $r_x$; then run find on $y$ in $U_1$ (not in $U$), giving a structure
$U_2$ and a root $r_y$. Then the node array of the union of $x$ and $y$ in $U$ equals the array
obtained from the node array of $U_2$ by linking $r_x$ and $r_y$ by rank: nothing changes if
$r_x = r_y$; otherwise, if $\operatorname{rank}(r_y) < \operatorname{rank}(r_x)$ then $r_y$ gets
parent $r_x$, and if not then $r_x$ gets parent $r_y$ and, when the two ranks are equal, the rank
of $r_y$ increases by one.

articles.title: Union of equivalent vertices changes nothing
articles.statement:
If $x$ and $y$ are equivalent vertices of a
parent forest $F$, then the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ is $F$ itself.

articles.title: Union makes its arguments equivalent
articles.statement:
For every parent forest $F$ and vertices $x$ and
$y$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are equivalent in the forest obtained from $F$ by the union of $x$
and $y$.

articles.title: Cost bound for union in a parent forest
articles.statement:
For every parent forest $F$ with depth
certificate $d$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, the cost charged for the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$
(two root searches at one unit per visited vertex, plus one unit for the link when the roots
differ) is at most $d(x) + d(y) + 3$.

articles.title: Union in a parent forest with cost
articles.statement:
For a parent forest $F$ and vertices $x$ and $y$, the
costed union returns the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ together with a cost equal to the cost of
finding the root of $x$ plus the cost of finding the root of $y$ (each one unit per visited
vertex, including the root), plus one more unit when the roots of $x$ and $y$ are distinct; when
they coincide, union performs no link and none is charged.

articles.title: Union in a union-find forest
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a union-find forest on $n$ vertices: each vertex
$z$ has a parent $p(z)$, where roots are their own parents, and a depth certificate
$d(z) \in \mathbb{N}$ with $d(p(z)) < d(z)$ whenever $p(z) \ne z$. Let $x$ and $y$ be vertices,
and let $r_x$ and $r_y$ be the roots reached from $x$ and $y$ by following parent pointers. If
$r_x = r_y$, the union of $x$ and $y$ in $F$ is $F$ itself. Otherwise it is the forest obtained
from $F$ by linking $r_x$ to $r_y$: the parent of $r_x$ becomes $r_y$, all other parent pointers
are unchanged, every vertex $z$ whose root is $r_x$ gets depth certificate $d(z) + d(r_y) + 1$,
and every other vertex keeps $d(z)$.

The operation is persistent: it returns a new forest and does not modify $F$.

articles.title: Arc sequence as the zipped Euler tour
articles.statement:
For every tree $t$, the arc sequence of $t$ is
the Euler tour of $t$ zipped with its own tail: if the Euler tour of $t$ is $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$,
then the arc sequence of $t$ is $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{k-1}, v_k)$.

articles.title: Arc sequence of the Euler tour
articles.statement:
The arc sequence of a tree $t$ is the list of consecutive
pairs of its Euler tour: if the Euler tour of $t$ is $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$, then the arc sequence
of $t$ is $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{k-1}, v_k)$.

Each tree edge occurs once in each direction.

articles.title: Induction principle for rooted trees
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a property of trees. Suppose that for
every vertex $r$ and all trees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ (with $k \ge 0$), if $P$ holds for each $c_i$, then
$P$ holds for the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$. Then $P$ holds for every
tree.

articles.title: Children of a rooted tree
articles.statement:
The children of a tree are the child subtrees of its root, as a
list in their given order.

articles.title: Cutting the last child subtree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree with root $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$. Cutting the last child subtree of $t$ gives no result when $k = 0$; when
$k \ge 1$ it gives the pair consisting of the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_{k-1}$, together with the removed subtree $c_k$.

articles.title: Linking two rooted trees
articles.statement:
Let $t_1$ be a tree with root $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$, and let $t_2$ be a tree. The link of $t_1$ and $t_2$ is the tree with root $r$
and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k, t_2$, so $t_2$ becomes the new last child subtree of the root
of $t_1$.

articles.title: The Euler tour visits exactly the vertices of the tree
articles.statement:
For every tree $t$ and every $v$,
$v$ occurs in the Euler tour of $t$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of $t$.

articles.title: Linking two copies of a single vertex is not valid
articles.statement:
For every vertex $r$, the link of the
single-vertex tree with root $r$ and another single-vertex tree with root $r$ is not valid, since
the vertex $r$ occurs twice in it. Hence the link of two valid trees need not be valid when their
vertex sets are not disjoint.

articles.title: Root of a rooted tree
articles.statement:
The root of the tree with root vertex $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$ is the vertex $r$.

articles.title: Size of a rooted tree
articles.statement:
The size of a tree is its number of nodes, counting repeated vertex
labels with multiplicity: the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ has size
$1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \operatorname{size}(c_i)$.

articles.title: Splicing two Euler tours
articles.statement:
For lists $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ of vertices and a vertex $r$,
the splice of $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ at $r$ is the list consisting of the entries of $\tau_1$,
followed by the entries of $\tau_2$, followed by $r$.

It is used with $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ the Euler tours of two trees and $r$ the root of the first
tree: walk the first tour, then the second tour, then return to $r$.

articles.title: Accumulator lemma for the Euler tour
articles.statement:
For every tree $t$ and every list $a$ of vertices,
the Euler tour of $t$ with accumulator $a$ equals the Euler tour of $t$ followed by $a$.

articles.title: Euler tour with an accumulator
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree with root $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$ in order, and let $a$ be a list of vertices. For a list $L$ of vertices, write
$r \cdot L$ for the list $L$ with $r$ put in front. The Euler tour of $t$ with accumulator $a$,
written $T(t, a)$, is $r \cdot L_1$, where $L_{k+1} = a$ and $L_i = T(c_i, r \cdot L_{i+1})$ for
$i = k, \dots, 1$.

It equals the Euler tour of $t$ followed by $a$, and computes the Euler tour without repeatedly
concatenating the tours of the child subtrees.

articles.title: Euler tour of a linked tree
articles.statement:
For trees $t_1$ and $t_2$, let $t$ be the link of $t_1$ and
$t_2$, that is, $t_1$ with $t_2$ added as the last child subtree of its root. The Euler tour of
$t$ is the Euler tour of $t_1$, followed by the Euler tour of $t_2$, followed by the root of
$t_1$.

articles.title: Recursive formula for the Euler tour
articles.statement:
For a vertex $r$ and a list of trees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$, the Euler tour of the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$
in order is $r$, followed, for each $i = 1, \dots, k$ in turn, by the Euler tour of $c_i$ and
then $r$.

articles.title: Euler tour
articles.statement:
The Euler tour of a tree $t$ with root $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$ in order is the list of vertices consisting of $r$, followed, for each
$i = 1, \dots, k$ in turn, by the Euler tour of $c_i$ and then $r$. It is the vertex sequence of
the depth-first walk that returns to the parent vertex after each child subtree.

articles.title: Rooted ordered tree
articles.statement:
A rooted ordered tree with vertices in a type $V$ consists of a root
vertex in $V$ together with an ordered list of child subtrees, each a rooted ordered tree with
vertices in $V$.

Vertex labels need not be distinct.

articles.title: Valid trees have distinct vertices
articles.statement:
A tree $t$ is valid if and only if its list of
vertices in preorder has no repeated entries.

articles.title: Linking valid trees with disjoint vertices gives a valid tree
articles.statement:
Let $t_1$ and $t_2$ be
valid trees such that no vertex of $t_1$ is a vertex of $t_2$. Then the link of $t_1$ and $t_2$,
that is, $t_1$ with $t_2$ added as the last child subtree of its root, is valid.

This is the forest precondition for reading the link as a link of two trees in a dynamic
forest.

articles.title: A single-vertex tree is valid
articles.statement:
For every vertex $r$, the tree with root $r$ and no child
subtrees is valid.

articles.title: Valid Euler-tour tree
articles.statement:
A rooted ordered tree is valid when its list of vertices in
preorder has no duplicates, that is, every vertex label occurs at most once in the tree.

Raw trees may repeat vertex labels; reading the linking of two trees as a link in a dynamic
forest requires valid trees with disjoint vertex sets.

articles.title: Accumulator preorder traversal is append
articles.statement:
For every rooted ordered tree $t$ and every
list $a$, the accumulator preorder traversal of $t$ started from $a$ equals the preorder vertex
list of $t$ followed by $a$.

articles.title: Accumulator preorder traversal
articles.statement:
For a rooted ordered tree $t$ with root $r$ and child
subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$ (in order) and a list $a$, the accumulator traversal $T(t, a)$ is
the list whose first entry is $r$ and whose remaining entries are
$T(c_1, T(c_2, \dots, T(c_k, a) \dots))$; when $k = 0$ the remaining entries are $a$.

The list $T(t, a)$ equals the preorder vertex list of $t$ followed by $a$, so the preorder list
is computed in linear time rather than by repeatedly appending child lists.

articles.title: Preorder vertex list of a node
articles.statement:
For a vertex $r$ and rooted ordered trees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$, the preorder vertex list of the tree with root $r$ and child subtrees
$c_1, \dots, c_k$ (in order) is $r$ followed by the concatenation of the preorder vertex lists
of $c_1, \dots, c_k$, in this order.

articles.title: Preorder vertex list of a rooted tree
articles.statement:
The preorder vertex list of a rooted ordered tree
$t$ is the accumulator preorder traversal of $t$ started from the empty list.

Equivalently, it is the root of $t$ followed by the preorder vertex lists of its child subtrees
in order; repeated vertex labels appear with multiplicity.

articles.title: Access preserves validity
articles.statement:
If a link-cut tree state $s$ is valid, then for every vertex
$x$ the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$ is again valid.

The new preferred edges are the retained off-path edges together with the edges of the accessed
root path; the two groups have disjoint parent endpoints (off versus on the path), so
duplicate-freeness and the at-most-one-preferred-child condition carry over.

articles.title: Access leaves the represented forest unchanged
articles.statement:
For every link-cut tree state $s$ and
every vertex $x$, accessing $x$ changes only the preferred edges: the represented forest of the
resulting state equals the represented forest of $s$.

articles.title: After access, the accessed vertex ends its preferred path
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a valid link-cut
tree state and let $x$ be a vertex of its represented forest. Then, after accessing $x$, the
preferred-path decomposition of the new state contains a path $p$ whose last vertex is $x$, and
$p$ is the path from the root down to $x$ in some tree of the represented forest of $s$.

Paths are listed from the root downward, so $x$ is the deepest vertex of $p$. No auxiliary splay
tree is modeled, so this is only the endpoint property of the accessed preferred path.

articles.title: Access in a link-cut tree
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a vertex. If $x$ is a
vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$, let $T$ be the first such tree and let $p$
be the path in $T$ from its root down to $x$. Accessing $x$ keeps the represented forest and
replaces the preferred edges by those preferred edges of $s$ whose parent endpoint is not on $p$,
followed by the edges of $p$, each directed from parent to child. If $x$ is not a vertex of the
represented forest, accessing $x$ leaves $s$ unchanged.

Thus every edge of the root-to-$x$ path becomes preferred, the previously preferred child edges
of the vertices on that path are dropped, and preferred edges hanging off the path survive: in
the tree with root $1$, whose children are $2$ and $3$, where $4$ is a child of $2$ and $5$ a
child of $3$, accessing $5$ after accessing $4$ keeps the preferred path $[2, 4]$, since the edge
from $2$ to $4$ has its parent endpoint off the path $1, 3, 5$.

articles.title: Parent-child edges are edges
articles.statement:
For every rooted tree $t$ and all vertices $a$ and $b$, if
$a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in $t$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$.

articles.title: Adjacency test
articles.statement:
For vertices $a$, $b$ and a rooted tree $t$ with root $r$ and child
subtrees $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the adjacency test of $a$ and $b$ in $t$ returns true exactly when
$r = a$ and some $c_i$ has root $b$, or $r = b$ and some $c_i$ has root $a$, or the adjacency test
of $a$ and $b$ returns true in some $c_i$.

It returns true exactly when $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$, and it is the guard checked by the
edge cut before it cuts.

articles.title: An edge cut keeps every other edge
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and let $x$ and
$y$ be adjacent in some tree of its represented forest. If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree
of the represented forest of $s$, and neither $a = x$ and $b = y$ nor $a = y$ and $b = x$, then
$a$ and $b$ are adjacent in some tree of the represented forest obtained from $s$ by cutting the
edge between $x$ and $y$.

Edges of other trees pass through untouched; edges of the cut tree survive the rerooting at $x$
and then lie on one side of the prune at $y$, and the only edge crossing the prune is the edge
between $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Edges after grafting
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $u$ be rooted trees and $y$ a vertex, and suppose that
grafting $u$ as a new child under $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$. Then for all
vertices $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are
adjacent in $t$, or adjacent in $u$, or $a = y$ and $b$ is the root of $u$, or $a$ is the root of
$u$ and $b = y$.

articles.title: Pruning keeps surviving edges
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex and $x$ a
vertex, and suppose that removing every subtree rooted at $x$ from $t$ leaves the tree $t'$ (that
is, the root of $t$ is not $x$). If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t$ and both are vertices of
$t'$, then $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$.

Together with the fact that every vertex of $t'$ is a vertex of $t$ other than $x$, this
specifies pruning at the level of edges on the surviving vertices.

articles.title: Rerooting keeps every edge
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted tree with no repeated vertex, and suppose
that rerooting $t$ at a vertex $x$ yields the tree $t'$. Then for all vertices $a$ and $b$, the
vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $t'$ if and only if they are adjacent in $t$.

articles.title: Adjacency in a rooted tree
articles.statement:
Two vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a rooted tree $t$
when they are joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in either direction: some node of $t$
labelled $a$ has a child labelled $b$, or some node of $t$ labelled $b$ has a child labelled $a$.

This is the undirected edge relation that the structural operations of the link-cut tree are
specified against.

articles.title: Connectivity via Euler tours
articles.statement:
For a link-cut tree state $s$ and vertices $x$ and $y$,
$x$ and $y$ are connected in $s$ if and only if some tree of the represented forest of $s$
contains both $x$ and $y$ in its Euler tour.

articles.title: Linking connects the endpoints
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be
vertices of its represented forest. Then in the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ to $y$,
the vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected, that is, some represented tree contains both. No
invariant on the state is needed.

articles.title: Making a vertex the root keeps its connections
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state
and let $x$ and $y$ be connected in $s$. Then $x$ and $y$ are still connected in the state
obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented tree.

Rerooting spans the same vertex set as the old tree and keeps every undirected edge; vertex
disjointness of the represented trees pins down which tree contains $x$.

articles.title: Connectivity in a link-cut tree state
articles.statement:
Two vertices $x$ and $y$ are connected in a
link-cut tree state $s$ when some tree of the represented forest of $s$ has both $x$ and $y$
among its vertices.

Connectivity is the abstraction against which the link-cut tree operations are specified.

articles.title: Cutting preserves validity
articles.statement:
If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for every vertex
$x$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting off the subtree rooted at $x$ is again valid.

Pruning splits the vertices of the cut tree into those of the remainder and those of the
detached subtree, the rest of the forest is untouched, and the preferred edges are reset.

articles.title: Edge cutting preserves validity
articles.statement:
If $s$ is a valid link-cut tree state, then for all
vertices $x$ and $y$ the state obtained from $s$ by cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ is
again valid.

On an adjacent pair the edge cut makes $x$ the root of its tree and then cuts off the subtree
rooted at $y$; otherwise it only resets the preferred edges.

articles.title: Edge cut on an adjacent pair
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be
adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and
$y$ in $s$ gives the same state as first making $x$ the root of its represented tree and then
cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$.

articles.title: Edge cut on a non-adjacent pair
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and let $x$ and $y$ be
adjacent in no tree of the represented forest of $s$. Then cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$
in $s$ leaves the represented forest unchanged and makes the list of preferred edges empty.

In particular, no other edge at $y$ is cut.

articles.title: Cutting an edge of a link-cut tree
articles.statement:
For vertices $x$ and $y$ and a link-cut tree state
$s$, cutting the edge between $x$ and $y$ works as follows. If $x$ and $y$ are adjacent in some
tree of the represented forest of $s$, the result is obtained from $s$ by first making $x$ the
root of its represented tree and then cutting off the subtree rooted at $y$. Otherwise the
represented forest is left unchanged. In both cases the list of preferred edges becomes empty.

When $x$ and $y$ are joined by an edge of a valid state, making $x$ the root turns $y$ into the
root of a child subtree of $x$, so the cut separates the two sides of the edge between $x$ and
$y$ and keeps every other edge.

The adjacency test is necessary: without it the composite would cut at $y$ regardless of $x$.
For instance, on the chain $1 \to 2$ it would detach $2$ when asked to cut the edge between
$99$ and $2$, although there is no such edge.

articles.title: Cutting off the subtree at a vertex
articles.statement:
Cutting at a vertex $x$ resets the preferred edges
of the state to the empty list and changes its forest as follows. If no tree of the forest
contains $x$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise let $T$ be the first tree containing $x$ and
$S$ the first subtree of $T$ rooted at $x$ in preorder. Every tree containing $x$ is removed from
the forest, and two trees are appended at the end: first the remainder of $T$ with every subtree
rooted at $x$ pruned off, then $S$. When $x$ is the root of $T$ nothing remains, and only $S$ is
appended.

articles.title: Access edges make the root path the downward preferred path
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a tree whose
vertex list is duplicate-free, let $x$ be a vertex of $T$ with root path $p$ (the path from the
root of $T$ down to $x$), and let $E$ be a list of directed edges such that every consecutive
pair of $p$, parent first, lies in $E$, and every edge of $E$ whose first vertex lies on $p$ is
such a consecutive pair. Then the downward preferred path of the preferred-path decomposition of
$T$ under $E$ is $p$.

articles.title: The downward preferred path starts at the root
articles.statement:
For every list of preferred edges, the
downward preferred path in the preferred-path decomposition of a tree is nonempty and its first
vertex is the root of the tree.

articles.title: Decomposition paths are paths of the tree
articles.statement:
For every list of preferred edges, in the
preferred-path decomposition of a tree $T$, the downward preferred path and every other path are
paths of $T$: any two consecutive vertices are joined by a parent-child edge of $T$, in either
direction.

articles.title: Preferred paths permute the vertex list
articles.statement:
For every list of preferred edges, the downward
preferred path of a tree followed by the concatenation of the other paths of its preferred-path
decomposition is a permutation of the vertex list of the tree.

articles.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a tree
articles.statement:
Given a list $E$ of preferred edges, each a pair
(parent, preferred child), the decomposition of a tree $T$ is a pair (down, rest): down is the
preferred path that starts at the root of $T$ and follows edges of $E$ downward, and rest is the
list of all other preferred paths of $T$. When a node has several children joined to it by edges
of $E$ (excluded in valid states, where each vertex has at most one preferred child), the first
one in child order continues the path through that node and each of the others starts its own
path in rest.

articles.title: Subtree rooted at a vertex
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ and a tree $T$, the subtree of $T$ rooted at
the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder, or nothing when $x$ does not occur in $T$.

articles.title: Tree of a forest containing a vertex
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ and a forest given as a list of
trees, the first tree whose vertices contain $x$, or nothing when no tree contains $x$.

articles.title: A root path ends at its target
articles.statement:
If $p$ is the path from the root of a tree $T$ down to a
vertex $x$ of $T$, then $p$ is nonempty and its last (deepest) vertex is $x$.

articles.title: Grafting a tree below a vertex
articles.statement:
For a vertex $y$ and trees $N$ and $T$, grafting $N$ at
$y$ in $T$ attaches $N$ as a new last child of the first node of $T$ labelled $y$ in preorder,
keeping every existing node and edge; it returns nothing when $y$ does not occur in $T$. This is
the tree surgery behind linking two trees: it adds exactly the edge from $y$ to the root of $N$.

articles.title: The root path starts at the root
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If the root path
of $x$ in $t$ (the path from the root of $t$ down to $x$) is defined and equals $p$, then $p$ is
nonempty and its first vertex is the root of $t$.

articles.title: Consecutive vertices of a root path are adjacent
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If
the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every
$i < k$ the vertices $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child
edge of $t$ in one direction or the other.

articles.title: Preferred paths of a link-cut tree state follow represented edges
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut
tree state. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in the preferred-path decomposition of $s$
and every $i < k$, some represented tree of $s$ has $p_i$ and $p_{i+1}$ adjacent, that is,
joined by a parent-child edge in one direction or the other.

This holds for every state, with no validity hypothesis.

articles.title: Preferred paths of a tree follow tree edges
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree and $E$ any list of pairs
of vertices, read as preferred (parent, child) edges. For every path $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$ in
the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$ and every $i < k$, the vertices $p_i$ and
$p_{i+1}$ are adjacent in $t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge of $t$ in one direction
or the other.

articles.title: A root path follows parent-child edges downward
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree and $x$ a vertex. If
the root path of $x$ in $t$ is defined and equals $p = (p_0, \dots, p_k)$, then for every
$i < k$ the vertex $p_i$ is the parent of $p_{i+1}$ somewhere in $t$.

articles.title: Linking in a link-cut tree preserves validity
articles.statement:
For every valid link-cut tree state $s$
and all vertices $x$ and $y$, the state obtained from $s$ by linking $x$ and $y$ is valid.

The joined tree has the union of the two old vertex lists up to permutation (rerooting and
grafting both permute), the rest of the forest is untouched, and the preferred edges are
reset.

articles.title: Linking two trees of a link-cut tree state
articles.statement:
Given vertices $x$ and $y$ and a state $s$,
the state $\operatorname{link}(x, y, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its
forest is defined as follows. If $x$ or $y$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is
unchanged. Otherwise let $t_x$ and $t_y$ be the first represented trees containing $x$ and $y$.
If $x$ is a vertex of $t_y$, the forest is unchanged. Otherwise $t_x$ is rerooted at $x$ (the
edges on its old root-to-$x$ path are reversed, so $x$ becomes its root), the result is
attached as a new last child subtree of the first node labelled $y$ in $t_y$, which adds the
edge from $y$ to $x$, and this joined tree replaces every tree containing $x$ or $y$, placed at
the end of the forest.

articles.title: Rerooting a link-cut tree state preserves validity
articles.statement:
For every valid link-cut tree state
$s$ and every vertex $x$, the state obtained from $s$ by making $x$ the root of its represented
tree is valid.

The new forest has the same flat vertex list as the old one up to permutation (the rerooted tree
replaces its original), and the preferred edges are reset.

articles.title: Making a vertex the root installs a tree rooted there
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state
and $x$ a vertex of its represented forest. After making $x$ the root, some represented tree
has root $x$ and contains $x$ as a vertex.

That tree is the rerooted old tree of $x$.

articles.title: Making a vertex the root in a link-cut tree state
articles.statement:
Given a vertex $x$ and a state $s$,
the state $\operatorname{makeRoot}(x, s)$ has no preferred edges (all edges dashed), and its
forest is defined as follows. If $x$ is not a vertex of the forest, the forest is unchanged.
Otherwise the first represented tree containing $x$ is rerooted at $x$: the edges on the path
from its old root to $x$ are reversed, and when the tree has distinct vertices every undirected
edge is kept. The rerooted tree replaces every tree containing $x$ and is placed at the end of
the forest.

articles.title: Both sides of a cut remain in the forest
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, let $x$ and
$y$ be vertices, and let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains
$x$. Suppose no vertex occurs twice in $t$, and let $T_x$ be the subtree of $t$ rooted at $x$.
If $y$ is a vertex of $t$ but not of $T_x$, then after cutting $s$ at $x$ both $x$ and $y$ are
vertices of the represented forest.

articles.title: The parent endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
articles.statement:
If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere
in a tree $t$, then $a$ is a vertex of $t$.

articles.title: The first endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
articles.statement:
If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree
$t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $a$ is a vertex of
$t$.

articles.title: Preferred paths cover exactly the vertices of the forest
articles.statement:
For every link-cut tree state
$s$ and every vertex $v$, $v$ lies on some path of the preferred-path decomposition of $s$ if
and only if $v$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$. No validity
hypothesis on $s$ is needed.

articles.title: Access makes the root path preferred
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state and $x$ a
vertex, let $t$ be the first tree of the represented forest of $s$ that contains $x$, and let
$p$ be the path in $t$ from the root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then every
edge of $p$, taken as the pair (parent, child) of consecutive vertices of $p$, is a preferred
edge of the state obtained from $s$ by accessing $x$.

articles.title: Access keeps off-path preferred edges
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state, $x$ a vertex,
and $(u, w)$ a preferred edge of $s$, directed from the parent $u$ to the child $w$. Suppose
that, if some tree of the represented forest of $s$ contains $x$, then $u$ does not lie on the
path in the first such tree from its root down to the first occurrence of $x$ in preorder. Then
$(u, w)$ is still a preferred edge after accessing $x$.

This is the edge-level fact behind the persistence of off-path preferred paths across
accesses.

articles.title: The child endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
articles.statement:
If $a$ is the parent of $b$ somewhere in
a tree $t$, then $b$ is a vertex of $t$.

articles.title: The second endpoint of a tree edge is a vertex
articles.statement:
If $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in a tree
$t$, that is, joined by a parent-child edge in either direction, then $b$ is a vertex of
$t$.

articles.title: Root paths stay inside the tree
articles.statement:
If $p$ is the path in a tree $t$ from the root down to
a vertex $x$, then every vertex of $p$ is a vertex of $t$.

articles.title: Vertices after grafting
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $C$ be trees and $y$ a vertex. If grafting $C$ at
$y$ in $t$, that is, attaching $C$ as a new last child of a node labelled $y$, produces the
tree $t'$, then for every $v$, $v$ is a vertex of $t'$ if and only if $v$ is a vertex of $t$ or
a vertex of $C$.

articles.title: Pruning keeps the vertices outside the detached subtree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted tree
whose preorder vertex list has no repeated vertex, and let $x$ be a vertex. Suppose the
subtree search finds the subtree $s$ of $t$ rooted at $x$, and pruning $t$ at $x$ leaves
the tree $t'$. Then every vertex of $t$ that is not a vertex of $s$ is a vertex of $t'$.

articles.title: Vertices of a pruned tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning
$t$ at $x$ leaves the tree $t'$, then every vertex of $t'$ is a vertex of $t$ and is
different from $x$.

articles.title: Rerooting preserves the vertex set
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted tree and $x$ a vertex. If
rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then a vertex lies in $t'$ if and only if it
lies in $t$.

articles.title: Vertex of a link-cut tree state
articles.statement:
A vertex $x$ belongs to a link-cut tree state $s$
when $x$ is a vertex of some tree of the represented forest of $s$.

articles.title: Preferred paths have distinct vertices
articles.statement:
Every preferred path of a valid state has
distinct vertices.

articles.title: Preferred paths cover each vertex at most once
articles.statement:
In a valid link-cut tree state, the
concatenation of all preferred paths of the decomposition has no repeated vertex: no vertex
occurs twice on one path or on two different paths.

Together with the fact that every vertex of the represented forest lies on some preferred
path, the preferred paths partition the vertex set.

articles.title: Root paths have distinct vertices
articles.statement:
If the preorder vertex list of a rooted tree $t$
has no repeated vertex and $p$ is the path from the root of $t$ down to a vertex $x$, then
$p$ has no repeated vertex.

articles.title: Cutting an edge separates its endpoints
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a valid link-cut tree state and
let $x$ and $y$ be adjacent in some tree of the represented forest of $s$. After the edge
cut of $x$ and $y$ in $s$, the vertices $x$ and $y$ are not connected: no represented tree
contains both.

articles.title: A cut disconnects a vertex from everything outside its subtree
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a
