link-cut tree state, let $t$ be the first tree of its represented forest containing the
vertex $x$, and let $u$ be the first subtree of $t$ in preorder whose root is $x$. After
cutting $s$ at $x$, the vertex $x$ is not connected to any vertex $y$ that is not a vertex
of $u$.

No invariant on the state is needed.

articles.title: Forest from a vertex list
articles.statement:
The forest built from the empty list is empty; the forest
built from a list $r, c_1, \dots, c_k$ consists of the single spine
$r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$, the rooted tree in which each vertex has the next one as
its only child.

articles.title: Preferred paths are pairwise vertex-disjoint
articles.statement:
In a valid link-cut tree state, any two
preferred paths at different positions of the preferred-path decomposition have no vertex in
common.

articles.title: Parent-child relation in a rooted tree
articles.statement:
For vertices $a$ and $b$ and a rooted ordered
tree $t$, $a$ is a parent of $b$ in $t$ when some node of $t$ labelled $a$ has a child subtree
whose root is $b$. Preferred edges of a link-cut tree are directed this way, from a node to its
preferred child.

articles.title: Consecutive edges of a vertex path
articles.statement:
For a list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$, its
path edges are the ordered pairs $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{n-1}, v_n)$ of consecutive
vertices, in this order; a list with at most one vertex has no path edges. For a path listed from
the root downward each pair is (parent, child), and the preferred edges installed by an access to
a vertex $x$ are the path edges of the root-to-$x$ path.

articles.title: Preferred-path decomposition of a link-cut tree state
articles.statement:
For a link-cut tree state $s$, its
preferred paths are obtained by taking, for each represented tree of $s$ in forest order, the
preferred paths of that tree under the preferred edges of $s$, and concatenating these lists.
Within a tree these are its maximal chains of preferred edges when each vertex has at most one
preferred child, each listed from its shallowest to its deepest vertex; a vertex incident to no
preferred edge forms a singleton path.

The decomposition keeps the preferred paths of every subtree, not one distinguished path, so an
access changes only the preferred edges leaving vertices of the accessed root path.

articles.title: Removing the tree containing a vertex splits the forest's vertices
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a forest of
rooted ordered trees whose concatenated vertex lists have no duplicates, let $x$ be a vertex, and
let $t$ be the first tree of $f$ containing $x$. Then the concatenated vertex list of the forest
obtained from $f$ by removing every tree containing $x$, followed by the vertex list of $t$, is a
permutation of the concatenated vertex list of $f$.

articles.title: The preferred paths of a tree rearrange its vertex list
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of directed
edges and every rooted ordered tree $t$, the concatenation of the preferred paths of $t$ under
$E$ is a permutation of the preorder vertex list of $t$.

articles.title: Grafting adds the new subtree's vertices
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $s$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$
a vertex. If grafting $s$ as a new child at $y$ in $t$ succeeds and yields the tree $t'$, then the
vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t$ followed by the vertex list of
$s$.

articles.title: Pruning a subtree splits the vertex list
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree whose vertex
list has no duplicates and let $x$ be a vertex. If $x$ occurs in $t$, with $s$ the subtree of $t$
rooted at $x$, and pruning at $x$ leaves a tree $t'$ (that is, $x$ is not the root of $t$), then
the vertex list of $t$ is a permutation of the vertex list of $t'$ followed by the vertex list
of $s$.

articles.title: Rerooting preserves the vertices
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If
rerooting $t$ at $x$ yields the tree $t'$, then the vertex list of $t'$ is a permutation of the
vertex list of $t$.

articles.title: Pruning at an absent vertex changes nothing
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a
vertex that does not occur in $t$. Then pruning the subtrees rooted at $x$ from $t$ succeeds and
returns $t$ itself.

articles.title: Pruning the subtrees rooted at a vertex
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$,
pruning $T$ at $x$ removes every subtree of $T$ whose root is labelled $x$, keeping every other
node and edge and the order of children. If the root of $T$ is $x$, nothing remains and pruning
is undefined. Otherwise the result is the tree with the same root whose children are, in their
original order, the pruned children of the root, with the children labelled $x$ dropped.

This is the tree surgery behind the remainder side of the cut operation of a link-cut tree.

articles.title: Removing the trees that contain a vertex
articles.statement:
Given a vertex $x$ and a forest, given as a list
of rooted ordered trees, removing the trees containing $x$ deletes from the list every tree that
has $x$ among its vertices and keeps the remaining trees in their original order.

articles.title: Rerooting fails at an absent vertex
articles.statement:
For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and every vertex $x$
that is not a vertex of $T$, rerooting $T$ at $x$ is undefined (it returns no tree).

articles.title: Rerooting a tree at a vertex
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$ with root $r$,
rerooting $T$ at $x$ is defined recursively. If $r = x$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise let
$C$ be the first child subtree of $r$ that contains $x$, let $p$ be the root of $C$, and let $C'$
be $C$ rerooted at $x$. The result is $C'$ with the tree formed by $r$ and its remaining
children (in their original order) attached as a new last child of the first node of $C'$, in
preorder, labelled $p$. If no child subtree of $r$ contains $x$, rerooting is undefined; thus
rerooting is defined exactly when $x$ is a vertex of $T$.

When the vertices of $T$ are distinct, this reverses the edges on the path from $r$ to $x$ and
keeps every other edge, so the undirected tree is unchanged and only the root moves to $x$. This
is the tree surgery behind making $x$ the root in a link-cut tree.

articles.title: Grafting keeps the root
articles.statement:
Let $T$ and $N$ be rooted ordered trees and $y$ a vertex. If
grafting $N$ into $T$ at $y$ is defined and yields the tree $T'$, then the root of $T'$ equals the
root of $T$.

articles.title: Root-to-vertex path
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$ and a rooted ordered tree $T$, the root path of $x$ is
defined exactly when $x$ is a vertex of $T$. It is then the list of vertices on the path from the
root of $T$ down to $x$, root first and ending with $x$; if $x$ occurs more than once, the path
leads to its first occurrence in preorder.

This is the preferred path installed by the access operation of a link-cut tree.

articles.title: Pruning keeps the root
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a rooted ordered tree and $x$ a vertex. If pruning $T$ at
$x$ yields a tree $T'$ (that is, the root of $T$ is not $x$), then the root of $T'$ equals the root
of $T$.

articles.title: Path tree on a vertex list
articles.statement:
For a vertex $r$ and a list of vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the
spine is the rooted tree $r \to c_1 \to \cdots \to c_k$: its root is $r$, each vertex has the next
one in the list as its only child, and the last vertex ($c_k$, or $r$ when $k = 0$) is a leaf.

articles.title: Link-cut tree state
articles.statement:
A state of a link-cut tree over a vertex type $V$ consists of the
represented forest, a list of rooted ordered trees with vertices in $V$, and a list of preferred
(solid) edges, each a pair $(u, v)$ of vertices meant as the edge from a node $u$ to its preferred
child $v$ in the represented forest; the structure itself does not require these pairs to be
edges of the forest. The preferred-path decomposition is derived from the preferred edges as the
maximal solid chains in each represented tree. With no preferred edges, every edge is dashed
and every vertex is its own singleton path.

articles.title: Adjacency in a tree is symmetric
articles.statement:
For every rooted ordered tree $T$ and vertices $a$ and
$b$, if $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $T$ (joined by a parent-child edge in either direction), then
$b$ and $a$ are adjacent in $T$.

articles.title: Preferred paths of a tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a rooted ordered tree and let $E$ be a list of
preferred edges, each a pair (parent, child). The preferred paths of $t$ under $E$ are listed
as follows: first the downward path of the preferred-path decomposition of $t$ under $E$, which
starts at the root of $t$ and follows preferred edges downward, and then all other paths of
that decomposition, in the order the decomposition returns them.

articles.title: Validity of states with no preferred edges
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a link-cut tree state whose list
of preferred edges is empty. If the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of the
represented forest of $s$ has no duplicates, then $s$ is valid.

This is the situation after every structural operation, which resets all edges to dashed.

articles.title: Valid link-cut tree states
articles.statement:
A link-cut tree state $s$ is valid when four conditions
hold: the concatenation of the vertex lists of the trees of its represented forest has no
duplicates (so the trees are vertex-disjoint); its list of preferred edges has no duplicates;
every preferred edge $(a, b)$ is a parent-child edge of some tree of the represented forest,
with $a$ the parent of $b$; and any two preferred edges with the same parent are equal, so each
vertex has at most one preferred child.

The duplicate-free vertex condition also pins down the parent of each vertex, so the maximal
chains of preferred edges in each tree are genuine disjoint paths.

articles.title: Bits set after inserting a list into a Bloom filter
articles.statement:
After inserting a list, bit `i` is set iff it was set before or some hash function sends
some inserted element to `i`.

articles.title: Bits set by an insertion
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a Bloom filter over $\alpha$ with $m$ bits, let
$x \in \alpha$ and let $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. Bit $i$ of the filter obtained by inserting
$x$ into $F$ is set if and only if bit $i$ of $F$ is set or some hash function $h$ of $F$
satisfies $h(x) = i$.

articles.title: Bloom filter
articles.statement:
A Bloom filter over a type $\alpha$ with $m$ bits consists of a finite list of
hash functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ and a bit vector of length $m$.

No false-positive rate is claimed because the model supplies no probability distribution.

articles.title: Number of hash outcomes leaving a given bit unset
articles.statement: Exactly `(m - 1) ^ (n * k)` outcomes of the stored hash values leave bit `i` unset.

articles.title: Bloom's formula is a lower bound
articles.statement:
**Bloom's formula is a lower bound** on the exact false-positive rate (Jensen's
inequality for `t ↦ t ^ k`).

articles.title: Empty Bloom filter
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type and $m$ a natural number. Given a list of hash
functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, the empty Bloom filter with these hash functions has
all of its $m$ bits unset.

articles.title: Exponential approximation at the optimal number of hash functions
articles.statement:
At `κ = (m / n) log 2` half of the bits are expected to be set and the approximation is
`(1 / 2) ^ κ`.

articles.title: Exponential approximation is a lower bound on the false-positive rate
articles.statement: The exponential approximation `(1 - exp (-(k n) / m)) ^ k` is also a lower bound.

articles.title: The optimal number of hash functions
articles.statement:
**The optimal number of hash functions** for the exponential approximation: on real
`κ > 0`, `(1 - exp (-κ n / m)) ^ κ` is minimal at `κ = (m / n) log 2`.

articles.title: Exponential approximation of the Bloom filter false-positive rate
articles.statement:
The exponential approximation `(1 - exp (-κ n / m)) ^ κ` of the false-positive rate, as a
function of a real number `κ` of hash functions.

articles.title: Expected fraction of set bits in a Bloom filter
articles.statement: The expected fraction of set bits is `1 - (1 - 1/m) ^ (n * k)`.

articles.title: False-positive rate as the expected k-th power of the set fraction
articles.statement: The exact false-positive rate is the expectation of `(fraction of set bits) ^ k`.

articles.title: Exact Bloom filter false-positive rate under uniform hashing
articles.statement:
The exact false-positive rate under uniform hashing: the fraction of outcomes (stored hash
values `H`, query hash values `q`) in which every query bit is set.

articles.title: Bloom filter insertion keeps the hash functions
articles.statement: Insertion keeps the hash functions.

articles.title: Inserting a list of elements into a Bloom filter
articles.statement: Insert every element of a list, left to right.

articles.title: Bloom filter insertion
articles.statement:
Inserting an element $x$ into a Bloom filter keeps its hash functions
and sets bit $h(x)$ for every hash function $h$ of the filter, leaving all other bits unchanged.

articles.title: Equality in the log-product bound holds only at $t = 1/2$
articles.statement: Equality holds only at `t = 1 / 2`.

articles.title: Bound $\log t \cdot \log(1-t) \le (\log 2)^2$ on the unit interval
The empty Bloom filter reports every element absent
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type, $m$ a
natural number and $H$ a nonempty list of hash functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. For
every element $x \in \alpha$, the empty Bloom filter with hash functions $H$ reports $x$ absent.

articles.title: Membership query in terms of bits
articles.statement:
For a Bloom filter $F$ and an element $x$, $F$ reports
that $x$ may be present if and only if bit $h(x)$ of $F$ is set for every hash function $h$ of
$F$.

articles.title: Characterization of the Bloom filter false-positive event
articles.statement:
The false-positive event: after inserting `xs` into an empty filter, `y` is reported
present iff every bit selected by `y` is selected by some stored element.

articles.title: Insertion preserves positive answers
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a Bloom filter and let $x$, $y$ be elements.
If $F$ reports that $x$ may be present, then so does the filter obtained by inserting $y$ into $F$.

Insertion never clears a bit, so an element reported present stays reported present after any
later insertion; in particular there are no false negatives under further inserts.

articles.title: An inserted element is reported present
articles.statement:
For every Bloom filter $F$ and element $x$, the
filter obtained by inserting $x$ into $F$ reports that $x$ may be present.

articles.title: Bloom filter membership query
articles.statement:
A Bloom filter reports that an element $x$ may be present
when bit $h(x)$ is set for every hash function $h$ of the filter, and reports $x$ absent
otherwise.

articles.title: A Bloom filter bit is unset iff no stored hash selects it
articles.statement: A bit is unset iff no stored hash value selects it.

articles.title: Probability that a given Bloom filter bit is unset
articles.statement: A given bit is unset with probability `(1 - 1/m) ^ (n * k)`.

articles.title: Bits set by the stored hash values
articles.statement: The bits set by the stored hash values `H a j` (element `a`, hash function `j`).

articles.title: Cuckoo hash table
articles.statement:
Given a type $K$ of keys, a type $V$ of values, a number $m$ of slots,
and two hash functions $h_1, h_2 : K \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, a cuckoo hash table consists of
two tables, each a vector of $m$ slots; every slot is either empty or holds a key–value pair
$(k, v)$ with $k \in K$ and $v \in V$. The structure itself does not require a pair $(k, v)$ to
sit at slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table or at slot $h_2(k)$ of the second.

No expected constant-time bound is claimed because the model supplies neither a probability
distribution nor an independence assumption about the hashes.

articles.title: Empty cuckoo hash table
articles.statement:
The empty cuckoo hash table has every slot of both tables
vacant.

articles.title: Cuckoo eviction loop
articles.statement:
The eviction loop takes a cuckoo hash table with hash functions $h_1$
and $h_2$, a key–value pair $(k, v)$, a choice of the first or second table, and a natural
number as fuel, and either returns a table or fails. With fuel $0$ it fails. With fuel $n + 1$
and the first table chosen, it writes $(k, v)$ into slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table; if that
slot was empty it returns the resulting table, and otherwise it repeats on the resulting table
with the evicted pair, the second table and fuel $n$. With the second table chosen it does the
same at slot $h_2(k)$ of the second table and continues with the first table.

articles.title: Cuckoo hash insertion
articles.statement:
Inserting a key $k$ with value $v$ into a cuckoo hash table with hash
functions $h_1$ and $h_2$, with fuel $n$, either returns a table or fails. If slot $h_1(k)$ of
the first table holds a binding for $k$, that slot is overwritten with $(k, v)$, and slot
$h_2(k)$ of the second table is cleared if it also holds a binding for $k$, so no stale
competing value remains. Otherwise, if slot $h_2(k)$ of the second table holds a binding for
$k$, that slot is overwritten with $(k, v)$. Otherwise the eviction loop runs on $(k, v)$,
starting with the first table, with fuel $n$, and its result is returned. Failure, when the
loop exhausts its fuel, models the rehash trigger of the classical algorithm.

articles.title: The empty cuckoo hash table is key-deterministic
articles.statement:
No key is stored with two different
values in the empty cuckoo hash table, vacuously.

articles.title: Cuckoo insertion preserves key determinism
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table that
satisfies the placement invariant and is key-deterministic. If inserting a key $k$ with value
$v$ into $T$ with some fuel succeeds with result $T'$, then $T'$ is key-deterministic. In
particular, replacement leaves no stale copy of $k$ with a different value in the other slot.

articles.title: Key determinism of a cuckoo hash table
articles.statement:
A cuckoo hash table is key-deterministic when each
key is stored with at most one value: for every key $k$ and values $v_1, v_2$, if the bindings
$k \mapsto v_1$ and $k \mapsto v_2$ are both stored in the table, then $v_1 = v_2$. Duplicate
copies of the same pair are allowed.

articles.title: Lookup in the empty cuckoo hash table
articles.statement:
Looking up any key in the empty cuckoo hash table
finds no value.

articles.title: Cuckoo lookup finds exactly the stored bindings
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table that
satisfies the placement invariant and is key-deterministic. For every key $k$ and value $v$,
looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if the binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in $T$.

articles.title: Cuckoo lookup finds every stored binding
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table that satisfies
the placement invariant and is key-deterministic. For every key $k$ and value $v$, if the
binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in $T$, then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Cuckoo lookup finds a key in its first-table slot
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash
functions $h_1$ and $h_2$, let $k$ be a key and $v$ a value. If slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table of
$T$ holds the pair $(k, v)$, then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Cuckoo lookup finds a key in its second-table slot
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash
functions $h_1$ and $h_2$, let $k$ be a key and $v$ a value. If slot $h_2(k)$ of the second table
of $T$ holds the pair $(k, v)$ and slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table of $T$ holds no pair whose key
is $k$, then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Cuckoo insertion leaves lookups of other keys unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with
hash functions $h_1$ and $h_2$ that satisfies the placement invariant and stores each key with at
most one value. If inserting (or replacing) the binding $k \mapsto v$ in $T$ with fuel $f$ succeeds
and returns the table $T'$, then for every key $k' \ne k$, looking up $k'$ in $T'$ gives the same
result as looking up $k'$ in $T$: either both return nothing or both return the same value.

articles.title: Cuckoo lookup returns an inserted value
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash functions
$h_1$ and $h_2$ that satisfies the placement invariant and stores each key with at most one value.
If inserting (or replacing) the binding $k \mapsto v$ in $T$ with fuel $f$ succeeds and returns the
table $T'$, then looking up $k$ in $T'$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Cuckoo lookup finds every stored key
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash functions $h_1$
and $h_2$ that satisfies the placement invariant, and let $k$ be a key and $v$ a value. If the
binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in some slot of either table of $T$, then looking up $k$ in $T$
returns some value.

The returned value may differ from $v$ when $k$ is stored with two different values; when $T$
stores each key with at most one value, it is $v$.

articles.title: Soundness of cuckoo lookup
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash functions $h_1$ and $h_2$,
let $k$ be a key and $v$ a value. If looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$, then the binding
$k \mapsto v$ is stored in some slot of the first or the second table of $T$.

articles.title: Cuckoo hash table lookup
articles.statement:
For a cuckoo hash table $T$ with hash functions $h_1$ and $h_2$ and a
key $k$, the lookup of $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if slot $h_1(k)$ of the first table holds a pair
$(k, v)$; otherwise it returns $v$ if slot $h_2(k)$ of the second table holds a pair $(k, v)$;
otherwise it returns nothing. No other slot is examined.

articles.title: Slot holds a key
articles.statement:
A slot of a cuckoo hash table is either empty or holds a pair $(k, v)$ of a
key and a value. For a slot $s$ and a key $k'$, this test is true when $s$ holds a pair whose key
is $k'$, and false when $s$ is empty or holds a pair with a different key.

articles.title: Cuckoo insertion preserves the bindings of other keys
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash
functions $h_1$ and $h_2$ that satisfies the placement invariant. Suppose inserting (or replacing)
the binding $k \mapsto v$ in $T$ with fuel $f$ succeeds and returns the table $T'$. Then for every
key $k' \ne k$ and every value $v'$, the binding $k' \mapsto v'$ is stored in $T'$ if and only if
it is stored in $T$.

articles.title: Cuckoo insertion stores the inserted binding
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table with hash
functions $h_1$ and $h_2$. If inserting (or replacing) the binding $k \mapsto v$ in $T$ with fuel
$f$ succeeds and returns the table $T'$, then the binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in some slot of
either table of $T'$.

articles.title: Binding stored in a cuckoo hash table
articles.statement:
A key $k$ is stored with value $v$ in a cuckoo hash
table when the pair $(k, v)$ occupies some slot of the first table or some slot of the second
table.

articles.title: The empty cuckoo hash table satisfies the placement invariant
articles.statement:
For any hash functions
$h_1, h_2$ into $m$ slots, the empty cuckoo hash table, with every slot of both tables vacant,
satisfies the placement invariant.

articles.title: Cuckoo insertion preserves the placement invariant
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a cuckoo hash table that
satisfies the placement invariant. If inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$ (which
replaces an existing binding for $k$ in place) with some fuel bound succeeds and returns the
table $T'$, then $T'$ satisfies the placement invariant.

articles.title: Placement invariant of a cuckoo hash table
articles.statement:
A cuckoo hash table with hash functions
$h_1, h_2$ satisfies the placement invariant when every pair $(k, v)$ in slot $i$ of the first
table has $i = h_1(k)$, and every pair $(k, v)$ in slot $i$ of the second table has
$i = h_2(k)$.

This is what lets lookup check only two slots.

articles.title: The empty hash table represents the empty map
articles.statement:
For every hash function $h$ and every
positive bucket count $m$, the finite map represented by the empty hash table with hash function
$h$ and $m$ buckets is the empty finite map.

articles.title: Insertion commutes with the abstraction
articles.statement:
For every valid hash table $T$, every key $k$ and
every value $v$, the finite map represented by the table obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$
into $T$ equals the finite map represented by $T$ with $k$ bound to $v$, replacing any earlier
binding of $k$.

articles.title: Finite map represented by a hash table
articles.statement:
The finite map represented by a hash table with
$m$ buckets is built from the list of all bindings of buckets $0, 1, \dots, m - 1$, concatenated
in this order: it binds exactly the keys occurring in this list, and binds each such key to the
value of its first binding in the list.

articles.title: Empty hash table
articles.statement:
For a hash function $h$ and a positive integer $m$, the empty hash table
with hash function $h$ has $m$ buckets, each holding the empty chain.

articles.title: Hash table with separate chaining
articles.statement:
For a key type $\alpha$, a value type $\beta$ and a hash
function $h : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$, a hash table with hash function $h$ consists of a positive
number $m$ of buckets and, for each bucket index $i < m$, a chain stored at bucket $i$: an
association list of key–value pairs whose keys are pairwise distinct. The structure itself does
not require keys to lie in their hash-selected bucket.

No expected constant-time bound is claimed because the model supplies neither a probability
distribution nor a probabilistic assumption about the hash function.

articles.title: Insertion into a hash table
articles.statement:
Inserting a key $k$ with value $v$ into a hash table with $m$
buckets and hash function $h$ keeps the bucket count and every bucket other than bucket
$h(k) \bmod m$, and replaces the chain at bucket $h(k) \bmod m$ by that chain with $k$ bound to
$v$: any earlier binding of $k$ in that chain is removed and the binding of $k$ to $v$ is added.

articles.title: Lookup agrees with the abstraction
articles.statement:
For every valid hash table $T$ and every key $k$,
looking up $k$ in the finite map represented by $T$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in
$T$.

articles.title: Lookup in the empty hash table
articles.statement:
For every hash function $h$, every positive bucket count
$m$ and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$
buckets finds no value.

articles.title: Insertion does not affect other keys
articles.statement:
For every hash table $T$, all keys $k \ne k'$ and
every value $v$, looking up $k'$ in the table obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ into $T$
gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $T$, also when $k$ and $k'$ lie in the same bucket.

articles.title: Hash table lookup after insertion
articles.statement:
For every hash table $T$, every key $k$ and every
value $v$, looking up $k$ in the table obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ into $T$ returns
$v$.

articles.title: Hash table lookup
articles.statement:
For a hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets, looking up
a key $k$ searches only the bucket with index $h(k) \bmod m$: the result is the value bound to
$k$ in that bucket's association list, or nothing if $k$ has no binding there.

articles.title: The empty hash table is valid
articles.statement:
For every hash function $h$ and every positive bucket
count $m$, the empty hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets is valid.

articles.title: Insertion preserves validity of a hash table
articles.statement:
If a hash table is valid, then the table
obtained from it by inserting a key $k$ with value $v$ (adding a new binding for $k$, or
replacing the existing one) is again valid.

articles.title: Valid hash table
articles.statement:
A hash table with hash function $h$ and $m$ buckets is valid when every
binding lies in its hash-selected bucket: for every bucket index $i < m$ and every key $k$, if
$k$ has a binding in bucket $i$, then $h(k) \bmod m = i$.

Keys within a single bucket are distinct automatically, since each bucket is an association list.

articles.title: Double-hashing probe sequence
articles.statement:
Given hash functions $h_1, h_2 : K \to \mathbb{N}$ and a
number of slots $m > 0$, the $i$-th probe of a key $k$ is the slot
$(h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)) \bmod m$ in $\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$.

articles.title: Empty open-addressing table
articles.statement:
The open-addressing table with $m$ slots and a given probe
sequence in which every slot is empty.

articles.title: Bounded insertion scan
articles.statement:
Given a table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, a key $k$, a
value $v$, a starting index $s$ and a budget $f$ of probes, examine the slots
$p(k, s), p(k, s + 1), \dots$ in order, for at most $f$ probes. At the first examined slot that
is empty or holds a binding for $k$, the scan returns the table with that slot overwritten by the
binding $k \mapsto v$ and every other slot unchanged; if all $f$ examined slots hold bindings for
other keys (in particular if $f = 0$), it fails and returns no table.

This is the helper behind insertion, which starts at index $0$ with budget $m$.

articles.title: Insertion into an open-addressing table
articles.statement:
To insert the binding $k \mapsto v$ into a table
with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, examine the slots $p(k, 0), p(k, 1), \dots, p(k, m - 1)$
in order. At the first one that is empty or already holds a binding for $k$, write $k \mapsto v$
there, leaving every other slot unchanged, and return the updated table. If all $m$ examined
slots hold bindings for other keys, the insertion fails and returns no table.

articles.title: Linear-probing probe sequence
articles.statement:
Given a hash function $h : K \to \mathbb{N}$ and a
number of slots $m > 0$, the $i$-th probe of a key $k$ is the slot $(h(k) + i) \bmod m$ in
$\{0, \dots, m - 1\}$.

articles.title: Bounded lookup scan
articles.statement:
Given a table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$, a key $k$, a
starting index $s$ and a budget $f$ of probes, examine the slots $p(k, s), p(k, s + 1), \dots$ in
order, for at most $f$ probes. The scan returns the value bound to $k$ in the first examined slot
that holds a binding for $k$, and returns no value if it first reaches an empty slot or exhausts
the budget.

This is the helper behind lookup, which starts at index $0$ with budget $m$.

articles.title: Lookup in the empty open-addressing table
articles.statement:
For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty
open-addressing table returns no value.

articles.title: Lookup of an absent key fails
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an open-addressing table and $k$ a key such that
no slot of $T$ stores a binding $k \mapsto v$ for any value $v$. Then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns
no value. No validity assumption on $T$ is needed.

articles.title: Lookup in a valid table returns exactly the stored binding
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a valid
open-addressing table, $k$ a key and $v$ a value. Then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and
only if the binding $k \mapsto v$ is stored in some slot of $T$.

Together with the fact that lookup after a successful insertion of $k \mapsto v$ returns $v$, this
says that a successful insertion really replaces the old binding: no other value for $k$ remains
stored afterwards.

articles.title: Insertion does not affect lookups of other keys
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a valid open-addressing table and
suppose inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$ succeeds with result $T'$. Then for every key
$k' \ne k$, looking up $k'$ in $T'$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $T$.

Together with the fact that looking up $k$ in $T'$ returns $v$, this is the map-update
specification of insertion, matching the corresponding statement for separate chaining.

articles.title: Lookup after a successful open-addressing insertion
articles.statement:
If inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$
into an open-addressing hash table $T$ succeeds and yields the table $T'$, then looking up $k$
in $T'$ returns $v$. No validity assumption on $T$ is needed.

articles.title: Open-addressing lookup succeeds exactly on stored keys
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a valid open-addressing
hash table and $k$ a key. Looking up $k$ in $T$ returns a value if and only if $T$ stores a
binding $k \mapsto v$ for some value $v$.

This membership characterization is used in place of a finite-map abstraction of the table.

articles.title: Valid open-addressing tables find every stored key
articles.statement:
If a valid open-addressing hash table
$T$ stores the binding $k \mapsto v$, then looking up $k$ in $T$ returns some value.

articles.title: Lookup in an open-addressing table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an open-addressing hash table with $m$ slots
and probe sequence $p$, and let $k$ be a key. The lookup of $k$ in $T$ inspects the slots
$p(k, 0), p(k, 1), \dots, p(k, m - 1)$ in this order. It returns the value $v$ of the first
inspected slot that holds a pair $(k, v)$, and returns nothing if an empty slot is inspected
first or if none of the $m$ inspected slots holds the key $k$.

articles.title: Failed open-addressing insertion finds every probed slot taken
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an
open-addressing hash table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$. If inserting a binding
$k \mapsto v$ into $T$ fails, then for every $i < m$ the slot $p(k, i)$ holds a pair
$(k', v')$ with $k' \neq k$.

For probe sequences that are permutations of the slots, this says that every slot of the table
holds a key other than $k$.

articles.title: Open-addressing hash table
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a type of keys, $V$ a type of values, $m$ a natural
number, and $p$ a probe sequence assigning to each key $k$ and each $i \in \mathbb{N}$ a slot
$p(k, i) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. An open-addressing hash table with $m$ slots and probe
sequence $p$ consists of $m$ slots, each either empty or holding a single pair $(k, v)$ with
$k \in K$ and $v \in V$.

No expected constant-time bound is claimed because the model supplies neither a probability
distribution nor a uniform-hashing assumption about the probe sequence.

articles.title: Open-addressing insertion leaves other keys' bindings unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an
open-addressing hash table, and suppose that inserting the binding $k \mapsto v$ into $T$
succeeds and yields the table $T'$. Then for every key $k' \neq k$ and every value $v'$, the
table $T'$ stores $k' \mapsto v'$ if and only if $T$ stores $k' \mapsto v'$.

No validity assumption is needed: the insertion writes a single slot, previously empty or
previously holding $k$, and leaves every other slot unchanged.

articles.title: Open-addressing lookup returns only stored bindings
articles.statement:
If looking up a key $k$ in an
open-addressing hash table $T$ returns the value $v$, then $T$ stores the binding $k \mapsto v$.
No validity assumption is needed.

articles.title: Bindings in a valid open-addressing table are unique
articles.statement:
If a valid open-addressing hash
table $T$ stores both $k \mapsto v_1$ and $k \mapsto v_2$, then $v_1 = v_2$.

articles.title: Stored binding in an open-addressing table
articles.statement:
An open-addressing hash table $T$ stores the
binding $k \mapsto v$ when some slot of $T$ holds the pair $(k, v)$.

articles.title: The empty open-addressing table is valid
articles.statement:
For all types $K$ and $V$, every number of
slots $m$ and every probe sequence $p$, which assigns to each key $k$ and each $i \in \mathbb{N}$
a slot $p(k, i) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, the empty table with $m$ slots and probe sequence $p$,
in which every slot is vacant, is valid: it is probe-closed and no key is stored in two
different slots.

articles.title: Insertion preserves validity of an open-addressing table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a valid table with $m$
slots and probe sequence $p$, whose keys have decidable equality. If inserting the binding
$k \mapsto v$ into $T$ (adding it, or replacing the binding already stored for $k$) succeeds and
returns the table $T'$, then $T'$ is valid: it is probe-closed and no key is stored in two
different slots.

articles.title: Valid open-addressing tables
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an open-addressing table with $m$ slots and probe
sequence $p$, where $p(k, i) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is the slot visited by the $i$-th probe of
key $k$. Then $T$ is valid when it satisfies two conditions. Probe-closedness: whenever slot $j$
holds a binding $k \mapsto v$, there is an $i < m$ with $p(k, i) = j$ such that the slots
$p(k, i')$ are occupied for all $i' < i$; this is what lets a lookup stop at the first empty
slot. Key uniqueness: if slots $j_1$ and $j_2$ hold bindings with the same key $k$, then
$j_1 = j_2$; so each key has at most one binding and insertion genuinely replaces it.

articles.title: Bucket occupancy is at most the secondary table size
articles.statement:
For every two-level perfect
hash table and every bucket $i$, the number $n_i$ of occupied slots of bucket $i$ is at most
the number $m_i$ of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$.

articles.title: Occupancy of a perfect-hashing bucket
articles.statement:
For a two-level perfect hash table and a bucket
$i$, the occupancy $n_i$ of bucket $i$ is the number of slots of the secondary table of bucket
$i$ that hold a binding. It is the $n_i$ of the Fredman–Komlós–Szemerédi analysis.

articles.title: Empty perfect hash table
articles.statement:
Given a primary hash function $h$ from keys to natural
numbers, a number of buckets $b > 0$, and for each bucket $i < b$ a secondary table size $m_i$
and a secondary hash function $h_i$, the empty table is the two-level perfect hash table with
primary hash $h$, $b$ buckets, secondary sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $h_i$ in which every
slot of every secondary table is vacant.

articles.title: The empty perfect hash table has no entries
articles.statement:
For every primary hash function, every
number of buckets $b > 0$, and all secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, the list
of entries of the empty table is the empty list.

articles.title: Entries of a perfect hash table
articles.statement:
The entries of a two-level perfect hash table form
the list of the bindings $(k, v)$ held in its occupied secondary slots, listed bucket by bucket
in increasing bucket order and, within each bucket, in increasing slot order.

A pair $(k, v)$ is a member of this list exactly when it is held in some slot of the table.

articles.title: Placement implies secondary injectivity
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table
with $b$ buckets and primary hash $h$, and for each bucket $i$ let $m_i$ be its secondary table
size and $h_i$ its secondary hash. Suppose every binding $(k, v)$ held in slot $j$ of bucket $i$
satisfies $h(k) \bmod b = i$ and $j = h_i(k) \bmod m_i$. Then for every bucket $i$ and all keys
$k_1, k_2$ that are each held, with some value, in some slot of bucket $i$, if
$h_i(k_1) \bmod m_i = h_i(k_2) \bmod m_i$, then $k_1 = k_2$.

articles.title: Lookup in the empty perfect hash table fails
articles.statement:
For every primary hash function, every
number of buckets $b > 0$, all secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, and every
key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty table returns no value.

articles.title: Lookup fails exactly on unstored keys
articles.statement:
For a valid two-level perfect hash table and
any key $k$, looking up $k$ returns no value if and only if there is no value $v$ such that the
binding $(k, v)$ is held in some slot of the table.

articles.title: Lookup finds every entry
articles.statement:
For a valid two-level perfect hash table, if the pair
$(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the table, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Lookup finds every stored binding
articles.statement:
For a valid two-level perfect hash table, if the
binding $(k, v)$ is held in some slot of the table, then looking up $k$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Lookup in a perfect hash table
articles.statement:
To look up a key $k$ in a two-level perfect hash table with
$b$ buckets, primary hash $h$, secondary sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $h_i$, let
$i = h(k) \bmod b$. If $m_i = 0$, the lookup returns nothing. Otherwise it inspects the single slot
$h_i(k) \bmod m_i$ of the secondary table of bucket $i$: if that slot holds a binding $(k, v)$, the
lookup returns $v$; if the slot is empty or holds a binding with a different key, the lookup
returns nothing.

articles.title: Entries of a perfect hash table are its stored bindings
articles.statement:
For every two-level perfect hash
table, every key $k$ and every value $v$, the pair $(k, v)$ belongs to the list of entries of the
table (the contents of its occupied secondary slots, bucket by bucket) if and only if some
secondary slot of the table holds the binding $(k, v)$.

articles.title: Successful perfect-hash lookups return entries
articles.statement:
For a two-level perfect hash table with
decidable equality on keys, if looking up a key $k$ returns a value $v$, then $(k, v)$ belongs to
the list of entries of the table. No validity hypothesis is needed.

articles.title: Placement suffices for validity of a perfect hash table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level perfect
hash table with $b$ buckets, primary hash $h$, secondary sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $h_i$.
If, whenever slot $j$ of the secondary table of bucket $i$ holds a binding $(k, v)$, we have
$h(k) \bmod b = i$ and $j = h_i(k) \bmod m_i$, then $T$ is valid.

articles.title: The empty perfect hash table stores nothing
articles.statement:
For every primary hash function, every number
$b > 0$ of buckets, every choice of secondary sizes and secondary hash functions, every key $k$
and every value $v$, no secondary slot of the empty two-level perfect hash table with these data
holds the binding $(k, v)$.

articles.title: Two-level perfect hash table
articles.statement:
Fix a type $\alpha$ of keys, a type $\beta$ of values and a
primary hash function $h : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$. A two-level (FKS) perfect hash table consists
of a number $b > 0$ of buckets and, for each bucket $i < b$, a secondary size $m_i \in \mathbb{N}$,
a secondary hash function $h_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ and a secondary table of $m_i$ slots, each
of which is empty or holds one binding $(k, v)$ with $k \in \alpha$ and $v \in \beta$.

The intended position of a key $k$ is slot $h_i(k) \bmod m_i$ of bucket $i = h(k) \bmod b$. The
structure itself imposes no condition on the hash functions and does not require bindings to sit
at their intended positions; that requirement is the separate validity condition.

articles.title: Each secondary table fits in the total secondary space
articles.statement:
In a two-level perfect hash table
with $b$ buckets and secondary sizes $m_0, \dots, m_{b-1}$, every bucket $i < b$ satisfies
$m_i \le \sum_{j < b} m_j$, the total secondary space.

articles.title: FKS square sizing rule
articles.statement:
A two-level perfect hash table with $b$ buckets is square-sized when,
for every bucket $i < b$, the size $m_i$ of its secondary table equals $n_i^2$, where $n_i$ is the
number of occupied slots of that secondary table.

articles.title: Soundness of perfect-hash lookup
articles.statement:
For a two-level perfect hash table with decidable equality
on keys, and with no validity hypothesis, if looking up a key $k$ returns a value $v$, then some
secondary slot of the table holds the binding $(k, v)$.

articles.title: Stored values in a valid perfect hash table are unique
articles.statement:
In a valid two-level perfect hash
table, if some secondary slots hold bindings $(k, v_1)$ and $(k, v_2)$ with the same key $k$, then
$v_1 = v_2$.

This is a direct consequence of placement (both bindings would occupy the one slot their shared
key hashes to), so it needs no decidable equality on keys.

articles.title: Bindings stored in a perfect hash table
articles.statement:
A key $k$ and a value $v$ are stored in a
two-level perfect hash table $T$ when some secondary slot, in some bucket of $T$, holds the
binding $(k, v)$.

articles.title: Total number of keys of a perfect hash table
articles.statement:
For a two-level perfect hash table, write
$n_i$ for the number of occupied secondary slots of bucket $i$. The total number of keys of the
table is $\sum_i n_i$, the number of occupied secondary slots over all buckets.

articles.title: Total secondary space under square sizing
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table
satisfying the FKS sizing rule, and write $n_i$ for the number of occupied secondary slots of
bucket $i$. Then the total secondary space of $T$ equals $\sum_i n_i^2$, the sum over all
buckets $i$.

articles.title: Quadratic space bound under square sizing
articles.statement:
If a two-level perfect hash table satisfies the
FKS sizing rule, then its total secondary space is at most the square of its total number of
keys.

This is weaker than the linear space bound of Fredman, Komlós and Szemerédi, which also depends
on the choice of a good primary hash function.

articles.title: Total secondary space of a perfect hash table
articles.statement:
For a two-level perfect hash table, write
$m_i$ for the number of slots of the secondary table of bucket $i$. The total secondary space of
the table is $\sum_i m_i$, the number of secondary slots over all buckets.

articles.title: The empty perfect hash table is valid
articles.statement:
For every primary hash function, every positive
number of buckets, and every choice of secondary table sizes and secondary hash functions, the
empty two-level perfect hash table with these parameters is valid: no slot is occupied, so both
conditions of validity hold vacuously.

articles.title: Valid perfect hash table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level perfect hash table with primary hash $h$,
$b$ buckets, secondary table sizes $m_i$ and secondary hashes $g_i$. Then $T$ is valid when two
conditions hold. Placement: whenever slot $j$ of bucket $i$ holds a binding $(k, v)$, we have
$i = h(k) \bmod b$ and $j = g_i(k) \bmod m_i$. Injectivity: for every bucket $i$, if keys $k_1$
and $k_2$ both occur in bindings stored in bucket $i$ and $g_i(k_1) \bmod m_i = g_i(k_2) \bmod m_i$,
then $k_1 = k_2$.

The injectivity condition follows from placement. It is recorded separately because choosing
secondary hash functions that are injective on each bucket's keys is the task of the FKS
construction.

articles.title: Collision count is at most the family size
articles.statement:
For every finite family $H$ of functions
from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ and all keys $x, y \in \alpha$, the number of
functions $h \in H$ with $h(x) = h(y)$ is at most $|H|$.

articles.title: A key collides with itself under the whole family
articles.statement:
For every finite family $H$ of
functions from a set $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ and every key $x \in \alpha$, the
collision count of $x$ with itself in $H$ equals $|H|$: $x$ collides with itself under every
function in $H$.

articles.title: Collision count
articles.statement:
For a finite family $H$ of functions from a set $\alpha$ to
$\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ and keys $x, y \in \alpha$, the collision count of $x$ and $y$ in $H$
is the number of functions $h \in H$ with $h(x) = h(y)$.

articles.title: The empty family satisfies the collision bound
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$ and all
distinct keys $x \ne y$ in a set $\alpha$, the collision count of $x$ and $y$ in the empty
family of functions from $\alpha$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$, multiplied by $m$, is at most
the size of the empty family, which is $0$.

This is the collision bound of universality without its other conditions; universality also
requires the family to be nonempty and $m > 0$, so the empty family is not universal.

articles.title: Indexed universal hash family
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a finite set of indices from a type $\iota$,
and let $h$ assign to each index $i \in \iota$ a function $h_i$ from a set $\alpha$ to
$\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$. The family $h$ is universal on $s$ if $m > 0$, $s$ is nonempty,
and for all distinct keys $x \ne y$ in $\alpha$ the number of indices $i \in s$ with
$h_i(x) = h_i(y)$, multiplied by $m$, is at most $|s|$.

Each index is counted separately, even when two indices give the same function; this is the
form in which the classical counting arguments, including the one for the mod-prime family,
are carried out. Nonemptiness is required because there is no uniform random choice from an
empty family.

articles.title: Universal hash family
articles.statement:
A finite family $H$ of functions from a set $\alpha$ to
$\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ is universal if $m > 0$, $H$ is nonempty, and for all distinct keys
$x \ne y$ in $\alpha$ the number of functions $h \in H$ with $h(x) = h(y)$, multiplied by $m$,
is at most $|H|$; that is, $x$ and $y$ collide under at most a $1/m$ fraction of the members
of $H$.

Nonemptiness makes sense of choosing a member of $H$ uniformly at random, the reading behind
the bound.

articles.title: Members of the mod-prime family
articles.statement:
Let $p > 0$ and $m > 0$. A function $h$ from
$\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ to $\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ belongs to the mod-prime family of
distinct functions exactly when $h = h_{a,b}$ for some index $(a, b)$ with
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$, where $h_{a,b}$ is the mod-prime hash
function with index $(a, b)$.

articles.title: Collision bound for the mod-prime hash functions
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $m > 0$, and
for $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a \ne 0$ let
$h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax + b) \bmod p) \bmod m$ be the mod-prime hash function. For distinct keys
$x \ne y$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the number of index pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \ne 0$ and
$h_{a,b}(x) = h_{a,b}(y)$, multiplied by $m$, is at most $p(p - 1)$, the total number of
index pairs.

This is the counting step of CLRS Theorem 11.5. The bijection
$(a, b) \mapsto (ax + b, ay + b)$ identifies the colliding index pairs with the pairs $(r, s)$
of distinct residues modulo $p$ whose representatives in $\{0, \dots, p - 1\}$ are congruent
modulo $m$.

articles.title: Mod-prime family of distinct functions
articles.statement:
For $p > 0$ and $m > 0$, the mod-prime family
is the finite set of all functions $h_{a,b}$ from $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ to
$\{0, 1, \dots, m - 1\}$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$, where
$h_{a,b}$ is the mod-prime hash function with index $(a, b)$.

Universality is proved for the indexed family of mod-prime hash functions, matching the
$p(p - 1)$ count of indices in CLRS; this set of distinct functions can be smaller, since
distinct index pairs may give the same function after the final reduction modulo $m$.

articles.title: Collisions of a mod-prime hash function
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number, $m > 0$ and
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, and write $\operatorname{val}(z)$ for the canonical
natural-number representative of $z \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ (for $p = 0$, where
$\mathbb{Z}/0\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$, its absolute value), so that the mod-prime hash
function is $h_{a,b}(x) = \operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m$. For all keys
$x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, we have $h_{a,b}(x) = h_{a,b}(y)$ exactly when
$\operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m = \operatorname{val}(ay + b) \bmod m$.

articles.title: Value of the mod-prime hash
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $m$ with $m > 0$ and elements
$a, b, x$ of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the mod-prime hash value
$h_{a,b}(x) \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, read as a natural number, equals
$\operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m$. Here $ax + b$ is computed in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, and
$\operatorname{val}(z)$ is the canonical natural-number representative of $z$: the residue in
$\{0, \dots, p - 1\}$ when $p > 0$, and $|z|$ when $p = 0$.

articles.title: Mod-prime hash function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $m$ with $m > 0$ and elements $a, b$
of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the mod-prime hash function
$h_{a,b} \colon \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is
$h_{a,b}(x) = \operatorname{val}(ax + b) \bmod m$, where $ax + b$ is computed in
$\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $\operatorname{val}(z)$ is the canonical natural-number
representative of $z$ (the residue in $\{0, \dots, p - 1\}$ when $p > 0$, and $|z|$ when
$p = 0$). This is the function $h_{a,b}(x) = ((ax + b) \bmod p) \bmod m$ of CLRS
Section 11.3.3.

articles.title: Indexed mod-prime family
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p$ and $m$ with $m > 0$, the indexed
mod-prime family assigns to each index $(a, b)$, with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and
$a \neq 0$, the mod-prime hash function
$h_{a,b} \colon \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$.

articles.title: Number of mod-prime indices
articles.statement:
For every positive natural number $p$, the set of pairs
$(a, b)$ of elements of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a \neq 0$ has exactly $p(p - 1)$
elements.

articles.title: Mod-prime index set
articles.statement:
For a natural number $p$, the index set of the mod-prime family is
the set of pairs $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$.

articles.title: Universality of the mod-prime family
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and $m$ a positive natural number.
The indexed mod-prime family, whose member at the index $(a, b)$, with
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$, is the mod-prime hash function $h_{a,b}$, is
universal over the set of all such indices: this set is nonempty, and for all distinct keys
$x \neq y$ in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, the number of indices $(a, b)$ with
$h_{a,b}(x) = h_{a,b}(y)$, multiplied by $m$, is at most the number of indices. This is CLRS
Theorem 11.5.

A uniformly random index therefore collides on any two distinct keys with probability at most
$1/m$.

articles.title: The empty hash family is not universal
articles.statement:
For every type of keys $\alpha$ and every natural
number $m$, the empty family of functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ is not universal:
universality includes nonemptiness, since its meaning is a bound on the collision probability for
a uniformly chosen member.

articles.title: The empty indexed family is not universal
articles.statement:
For every index type $\iota$, every type of
keys $\alpha$, every natural number $m$ and every family $(h_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of functions
$h_i \colon \alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, the family is not universal over the empty index
set: indexed universality includes nonemptiness of the index set, since there is no uniform
random choice from an empty family.

articles.title: The pair bijection is given by the pair map
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $x \neq y$ be
elements of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. For every index $(a, b)$ with
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$, the image of $(a, b)$ under the pair bijection
for $x, y$, viewed as an element of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, is the
value of the pair map at $(a, b)$, namely $(ax + b, ay + b)$.

articles.title: Pair bijection of the CLRS counting argument
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $x \neq y$ be
elements of the field $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. The pair bijection for $x, y$ is the bijection
from the indices $(a, b)$, with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \neq 0$, to the ordered
pairs $(r, s)$ of elements of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $r \neq s$ that sends $(a, b)$ to
the pair map value $(ax + b, ay + b)$. Its inverse solves the linear system $ax + b = r$,
$ay + b = s$: it sends $(r, s)$ to $(a, b)$ with $a = (r - s)/(x - y)$ and $b = r - ax$.

articles.title: Evaluating the pair map
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number, let $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$,
and let $(a, b)$ be an index of the mod-prime family, so that $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$
and $a \ne 0$. Then the pair map at $x$ and $y$ sends $(a, b)$ to $(ax + b, ay + b)$.

articles.title: The two values of the pair map differ
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $x \ne y$ be keys in the
field $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. For every index $(a, b)$ of the mod-prime family, that is,
$a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a \ne 0$, we have $ax + b \ne ay + b$.

Indeed, the difference $(ax + b) - (ay + b) = a(x - y)$ is a product of two nonzero factors.

articles.title: The pair map is injective
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $x \ne y$ be keys in
$\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then the pair map at $x$ and $y$, which sends an index $(a, b)$ of the
mod-prime family (so $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and $a \ne 0$) to $(ax + b, ay + b)$,
is injective.

articles.title: The pair map of the mod-prime family
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a natural number and fix two keys
$x, y \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. The pair map at $x$ and $y$ sends an index $(a, b)$ of the
mod-prime family, that is, $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ with $a \ne 0$, to the pair
$(ax + b, ay + b) \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^2$ of inner hash values at $x$ and $y$.

This is the map of the CLRS counting argument for the mod-prime family.

articles.title: Comparison bound for sift-up
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and
every natural number $i$, the number of value comparisons counted by sift-up with comparison
and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of
index $i$ in the level-order binary tree.

articles.title: Binary heap insertion leaves other multiplicities unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap
over a linearly ordered type, and let $x \ne y$ be values. Then $y$ occurs in the multiset of
elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ exactly as many times as it occurs in the
multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Binary heap insertion adds one copy of the inserted value
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap
over a linearly ordered type and $x$ a value. The multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements
of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is one more than its multiplicity in the multiset
of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Array of a binary heap after decrease-key
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly
ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap
obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ equals the result of sifting up position $i$
in the array obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry at position $i$ with $x$.

articles.title: Multiset of a binary heap after decrease-key
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a
linearly ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The
multiset of elements of the heap obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is
obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by removing one occurrence of $a_i$ and adding one
occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Decrease-key yields a heap-ordered array
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly
ordered type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap
obtained by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot
position is at least the entry at its parent position.

articles.title: Decrease-key preserves the heap size
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered
type, with level-order array $a$, let $i < |a|$ and let $x \le a_i$. The array of the heap obtained
by decreasing the key at position $i$ to $x$ has the same length as $a$.

articles.title: Decrease-key in a binary min-heap
articles.statement:
Given a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered
type, with level-order array $a$, an index $i < |a|$ and a value $x \le a_i$, decrease-key returns
the heap whose array is obtained from $a$ by replacing the entry at position $i$ with $x$ and then
sifting position $i$ up, repeatedly swapping the entry with its parent while it is strictly
smaller than the parent.

articles.title: Elements after binary heap insertion
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered
type and $x$ a value. The multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is
the multiset of elements of $h$ with one more copy of $x$ added.

articles.title: Elements of a binary min-heap
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of a binary min-heap is the
multiset of the entries of its level-order storage array, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Empty binary min-heap
articles.statement:
The empty binary min-heap is the min-heap whose level-order storage
array has no entries.

articles.title: Combined comparison and swap bound for sift-up
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly
ordered type and every natural number $i$, if sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$
at index $i$ counts $c$ comparisons and $s$ swaps, then
$c + s \le 2 \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$.

articles.title: Binary heap extraction splits off the minimum
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly
ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap
$h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ equals the multiset of elements of $h'$ with one copy
of $x$ added.

The statement is phrased by adding $x$ back, not by erasing it from the multiset of $h$.

articles.title: Binary heap extraction leaves other multiplicities unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap
over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$
and the heap $h'$, then every value $y \ne x$ occurs in the multiset of elements of $h'$ exactly
as many times as in the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Binary heap extraction removes one copy of the minimum
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over
a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and
the heap $h'$, then the multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements of $h'$ is its
multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$ minus one.

articles.title: Elements after binary heap extraction
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a linearly ordered
type. If extracting the minimum of $h$ succeeds and returns the value $x$ and the heap $h'$, then
the multiset of elements of $h'$ is obtained from the multiset of elements of $h$ by erasing one
occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap fails exactly when it is empty
articles.statement:
For a binary min-heap
$h$ over a linearly ordered type, extracting the minimum of $h$ returns no result if and only if
the level-order storage array of $h$ has size $0$.

articles.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is minimal
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over
a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value $x$
together with a heap $r$, then $x \le y$ for every value $y$ in the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Membership after extraction from a binary min-heap
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a
linearly ordered type, and suppose extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a value
$x$ together with a heap $r$. Then every value $y \ne x$ is an element of $r$ if and only if it
is an element of $h$.

articles.title: The value extracted from a binary min-heap is one of its elements
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary
min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a
value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Extraction from a binary min-heap leaves a heap-ordered array
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary
min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds and returns a
value $x$ together with a heap $r$, then the level-order array of $r$ is heap ordered: every
entry other than the root is at least its parent entry.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum of a binary min-heap
articles.statement:
For a binary min-heap $h$ over a linearly
ordered type, extraction returns nothing when the level-order array of $h$ is empty. Otherwise it
returns the root entry (the first entry of the array) together with the heap obtained from $h$ by
removing its root and restoring heap order.

articles.title: Removing the root of a nonempty binary min-heap
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a
linearly ordered type whose level-order array is nonempty. If the array has exactly one entry,
the result is the empty heap. Otherwise the last entry of the array replaces the root, the array
shrinks by one, and the result is the heap obtained by sifting this entry down from the root.

articles.title: Left child index in a level-order binary tree
articles.statement:
In a binary tree stored in level order in
an array indexed from $0$, the left child of the node at index $i$ has index $2i + 1$.

articles.title: Heap order on a level-order array
articles.statement:
An array $a$ over a type with a relation $\le$, indexed
from $0$, is heap ordered when every entry other than the root is at least its parent entry:
for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, where $|a|$ is the length of $a$, we have
$a_{\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor} \le a_i$.

articles.title: The parent of a valid nonroot index is valid
articles.statement:
For an array $a$ of length $|a|$ and an index
$i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ of $i$ is also less than
$|a|$.

articles.title: Parent index in a level-order binary tree
articles.statement:
In a binary tree stored in level order in an
array indexed from $0$, the parent index of a natural number $i$ is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$,
where $i - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers, so the root index $0$ is sent to $0$.

articles.title: Right child index in an array-backed binary tree
articles.statement:
In the level-order layout of a binary
tree in an array indexed from $0$, the right child of the node at index $i$ is at index $2i + 2$.

articles.title: The heap parent is one level up
articles.statement:
For every natural number $i > 0$, the parent index
$p = \lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$ satisfies
$\lfloor \log_2(p+1) \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$; that is, in the level-order
binary tree the parent of a nonroot index lies one level above it.

articles.title: The smaller child lies one level below its parent
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly
ordered type and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$,
then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor = \lfloor \log_2 (i+1) \rfloor + 1$; that is, in the
level-order binary tree stored in $a$, the node $c$ lies exactly one level below $i$.

articles.title: The smaller child's level is bounded by the array size
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a
linearly ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If $c$ is the
smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $\lfloor \log_2 (c+1) \rfloor \le \lfloor \log_2 |a| \rfloor$.

articles.title: Binary heap minimum lookup fails exactly when empty
articles.statement:
For a binary min-heap $h$ over a
linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns no value if and only if the storage
array of $h$ has size $0$.

articles.title: Binary min-heap
articles.statement:
A binary min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ is an array $a$
of elements of $\alpha$ (its level-order storage), of length $|a|$ and with entries
$a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1}$, that is heap ordered: for every index $i$ with $0 < i < |a|$, the entry
$a_{\lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor}$ at the parent index of $i$ is at most $a_i$.

articles.title: Binary heap minimum lookup succeeds exactly when nonempty
articles.statement:
For a binary min-heap $h$ over
a linearly ordered type, looking up the minimum of $h$ returns a value if and only if the storage
array of $h$ has positive size.

articles.title: The binary heap minimum lookup is a lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap over a
linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x \le y$ for every
element $y$ of the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: The binary heap minimum lookup returns a stored element
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a binary min-heap
over a linearly ordered type. If looking up the minimum of $h$ returns $x$, then $x$ belongs to
the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Minimum lookup in a binary heap
articles.statement:
For a binary min-heap $h$, the minimum lookup returns the
entry at index $0$ (the root) of the storage array of $h$ when that array is nonempty, and returns
no value when it is empty.

articles.title: Moving the last entry to the root removes the old root
articles.statement:
For a nonempty array $a$ over a
linearly ordered type, the multiset of entries of the array obtained from $a$ by moving its last
entry to the root equals the multiset of entries of $a$ with one occurrence of $a_0$ removed.

articles.title: Moving the last entry to the root prepares a sift-down
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be a heap-ordered array
over a linearly ordered type with at least two entries, and let $b$ be the array obtained from $a$
by moving its last entry to the root. Then $b$ is ready for sifting down at index $0$: index $0$ is
valid in $b$, and for every index $j > 0$ of $b$ whose parent index $\lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ is
not $0$, the entry of $b$ at the parent index is at most $b_j$.

articles.title: Moving the last entry to the root
articles.statement:
For a nonempty array $a$ of length $n$, this operation
swaps the entries at indices $0$ and $n - 1$ and then deletes the final entry. The result has
length $n - 1$; when $n \ge 2$ its entry at index $0$ is $a_{n-1}$ and its entry at each index
$0 < i < n - 1$ is $a_i$.

articles.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap preserves heap order
articles.statement:
For every binary min-heap $h$
over a linearly ordered type and every value $x$, the level-order array of the heap obtained
by inserting $x$ into $h$ is heap-ordered: the entry at every nonroot index $i$ is at least
the entry at its parent index $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$.

articles.title: Appending to a heap-ordered array prepares it for sift-up
articles.statement:
If an array $a$ of length $n$
over a linearly ordered type is heap-ordered and $x$ is any value, then the array obtained by
appending $x$ to $a$ satisfies the sift-up precondition at index $n$, the position of $x$: the
only edge that may violate heap order is the one entering index $n$.

articles.title: Insertion into a binary min-heap
articles.statement:
To insert a value $x$ into a binary min-heap $h$, append
$x$ at the end of the level-order array of $h$ and sift it up from its index (the old length of
the array), repeatedly swapping it with its parent while it is smaller. The result is again a
binary min-heap.

articles.title: Timed sift-down returns the sift-down result
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly
ordered type and every index $i$, the array returned by timed sift-down from $i$, with its
cost discarded, equals the array returned by sift-down from $i$.

articles.title: Counting does not change the result of sift-up
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly
ordered type and every natural number $i$, the array returned by sift-up with comparison and
swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ equals the array returned by the plain sift-up of $a$ at $i$.

articles.title: Timed child selection returns the smaller child
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly
ordered type and every index $i$, the value returned by timed child selection at $i$, with its
cost discarded, is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$ (an optional index, absent when $i$ has no
valid child).

articles.title: The root of a heap-ordered binary-heap array is minimal
articles.statement:
If an array $a$ over a linearly
ordered type is heap-ordered, then $a_0 \le a_i$ for every valid index $i$ of $a$.

articles.title: Sift-down with comparison and swap counts
articles.statement:
For an array $a$ over a linearly ordered
type and an index $i$, timed sift-down returns an array together with a cost pair
(value comparisons, array swaps), where costs add componentwise. If the left child index
$2i+1$ is not a valid index of $a$, it returns $a$ at cost $(0, 0)$. Otherwise let $c$ be the
smaller child of $i$: the left child $2i+1$, unless the right child $2i+2$ is a valid index
and $a_{2i+2} < a_{2i+1}$, in which case $c = 2i+2$. Selecting $c$ costs one comparison when
$2i+2$ is a valid index and nothing otherwise. Comparing $a_c$ with $a_i$ costs one more
comparison. If $a_c < a_i$, the entries at $i$ and $c$ are swapped at the cost of one swap,
and the result and remaining cost are those of timed sift-down from $c$ in the swapped array;
otherwise the result is $a$.

Index arithmetic, bounds checks, pattern matching and recursive calls are free.

articles.title: Sift-down makes at most two comparisons per remaining level
articles.statement:
Write $|a|$ for the size
of an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$.
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value
comparisons counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $2 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.

articles.title: Binary-heap sift-down preserves the multiset of entries
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a
linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ has
the same multiset of entries as $a$.

articles.title: Sift-down restores heap order
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type that
satisfies the sift-down precondition at a valid index $i$: the only edges that may violate heap
order are those leaving $i$, and moving either child of $i$ up to position $i$ keeps the edge
entering $i$ ordered. Then the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is heap-ordered.

articles.title: Binary-heap sift-down permutes the array
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered
type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting down $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of
$a$.

articles.title: Sift-down precondition
articles.statement:
For an array $a$ over a type ordered by $\le$, write
$p(j) = \lfloor (j-1)/2 \rfloor$ for the parent of index $j$. The array $a$ is ready for
sift-down at index $i$ when $i$ is a valid index of $a$; $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every valid index
$j > 0$ with $p(j) \ne i$; and, if $i > 0$, $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every valid index $j > 0$ with
$p(j) = i$.

Thus the only edges that may violate heap order are those leaving $i$, and moving either child
of $i$ up to position $i$ keeps the edge entering $i$ ordered.

articles.title: Sift-down performs at most one swap per remaining level
articles.statement:
Write $|a|$ for the size of an
array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$. For
every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of array swaps
counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most $\max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.

articles.title: Total sift-down cost is at most three per remaining level
articles.statement:
Write $|a|$ for the size of
an array $a$, and let $\ell(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $\ell(0) = 0$.
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the number of value
comparisons plus the number of array swaps counted by timed sift-down from $i$ is at most
$3 \max(0, \ell(|a|) - \ell(i+1))$.

articles.title: Sift-down
articles.statement:
Sifting down an array $a$ over a linearly ordered type from index $i$ works as
follows. If $i$ has a child in $a$, that is, if $2i+1$ is a valid index, let $c$ be the child of
$i$ (among $2i+1$ and $2i+2$, if valid) holding the smaller value, preferring the left child
$2i+1$ on ties. If $a_c < a_i$, swap the entries at $i$ and $c$ and continue sifting down from
$c$; otherwise, or if $i$ has no child, return the array unchanged.

articles.title: Sift-up with comparison and swap counts
articles.statement:
Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a
linearly ordered type and an index $i$, this computes the sift-up of $a$ at $i$ together
with a cost $(c, s) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $c$ counts value comparisons
and $s$ counts swaps. If $i \ge |a|$ or $i = 0$, the result is $a$ with cost $(0, 0)$.
Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of $i$. If $a_i < a_p$, the
result is this sift-up at $p$ of the array obtained from $a$ by exchanging the entries at
positions $i$ and $p$, with cost $(1, 1)$ plus the cost of that recursive sift-up;
otherwise the result is $a$ with cost $(1, 0)$.

articles.title: Binary-heap sift-up preserves the multiset of entries
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a
linearly ordered type and every index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ has the
same multiset of entries as $a$.

articles.title: Sift-up restores heap order
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and let
$i$ be an index such that $a$ is ready for sift-up at $i$. Then the array obtained by sifting
up $a$ from $i$ is heap ordered.

articles.title: Sift-up permutes the array
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every
index $i$, the array obtained by sifting up $a$ from $i$ is a permutation of $a$.

articles.title: Arrays ready for sift-up
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a type with a relation
$\le$, indexed from $0$, and for $j > 0$ let $p(j) = \lfloor (j - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of
$j$. The array $a$ is ready for sift-up at an index $i$ when $i < |a|$, when $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for
every $j \ne i$ with $0 < j < |a|$, and when, if $i > 0$, also $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every $j$
with $0 < j < |a|$ and $p(j) = i$.

articles.title: Sift-up
articles.statement:
Given an array $a$ of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed from $0$,
and an index $i$, the sift-up of $a$ from $i$ is defined by recursion on $i$. If $i = 0$ or
$i \ge |a|$, the result is $a$. Otherwise let $p = \lfloor (i - 1)/2 \rfloor$ be the parent of
$i$; if $a_i < a_p$, the result is the sift-up from $p$ of the array obtained from $a$ by
exchanging the entries at positions $i$ and $p$, and otherwise the result is $a$.

articles.title: The smaller child has a larger index
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type
and all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $i < c$.

articles.title: The smaller child is a valid index
articles.statement:
