For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and
all indices $i$ and $c$, if $c$ is the smaller child of $i$ in $a$, then $c$ is less than the
length $|a|$ of $a$.

articles.title: Smaller child
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly ordered type, indexed
from $0$, and let $i$ be an index with children $\ell = 2i + 1$ and $r = 2i + 2$. If
$\ell \ge |a|$, then $i$ has no smaller child. Otherwise the smaller child of $i$ is $r$ when
$r < |a|$ and $a_r < a_\ell$, and $\ell$ in every other case, so ties go to the left child.

articles.title: Swap bound for sift-up
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type and every
natural number $i$, the number of swaps counted by sift-up with comparison and swap counts
on $a$ at index $i$ is at most $\lfloor \log_2(i+1) \rfloor$, the depth of index $i$ in the
level-order binary tree.

articles.title: Sift-down from a leaf costs nothing
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type,
of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be an index with $|a| \le 2i+1$, so that the left child of $i$ is not
a valid index (this includes invalid indices $i$). Then timed sift-down from $i$ has cost pair
$(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.

articles.title: Sift-down from an invalid index costs nothing
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly
ordered type, of size $|a|$, and let $i$ be a natural number with $|a| \le i$. Then timed
sift-down from $i$ has cost pair $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons and no swaps.

articles.title: Sift-down from a node without children costs nothing
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a
linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no
child, then sift-down from $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps),
has cost $(0, 0)$: it makes no value comparisons and no array swaps.

articles.title: Sift-up at an out-of-range index costs nothing
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ of length $|a|$
over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $i$ with $i \ge |a|$, sift-up with
comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $i$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no comparisons
and no swaps.

articles.title: Sift-up at the root costs nothing
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ over a linearly ordered type,
sift-up with comparison and swap counts on $a$ at index $0$ has cost $(0, 0)$: it counts no
comparisons and no swaps.

articles.title: Child selection at a node without children costs nothing
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a
linearly ordered type and $i$ an index. If the smaller-child selection at $i$ in $a$ returns no
child, then the timed child selection at $i$, with cost counted as the pair (value comparisons,
array swaps), has cost $(0, 0)$.

articles.title: Cost of child selection
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$ an
index, and count cost as the pair (value comparisons, array swaps). The timed child selection at
$i$ in $a$ has cost $(1, 0)$ if the right child index $2i + 2$ is less than the size of $a$, and
cost $(0, 0)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Timed smaller-child selection
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type and $i$
an index, with left child $2i + 1$ and right child $2i + 2$; cost is counted as the pair
(value comparisons, array swaps). If both children are valid indices of $a$, the selection costs
$(1, 0)$ and returns the right child when its value is strictly less than the value at the left
child, and the left child otherwise. If only the left child is a valid index, it returns the
left child at cost $(0, 0)$. If the left child is not a valid index, it returns no child at cost
$(0, 0)$.

articles.title: Binomial heap
articles.statement:
A binomial min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ consists of a
list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ together with a proof that this list is a valid binomial
forest: every tree in it is a valid binomial tree and the tree ranks are strictly increasing
along the list.

articles.title: Binomial tree
articles.statement:
A binomial tree over a type $\alpha$ is a node that stores a rank, which is
a natural number, a root value in $\alpha$, and a list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ as its
children. The type imposes no invariant; the binomial-tree shape and heap order are expressed
by a separate validity predicate.

articles.title: Size of a valid binomial tree
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, every valid
binomial tree of rank $r$ over $\alpha$ represents a multiset of exactly $2^r$ elements, counted
with multiplicity.

articles.title: Carry insertion into a binomial forest
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type, the carry of a
binomial tree $t$ into a list $F$ of binomial trees is defined by recursion on $F$. If $F$ is
empty, the result is the one-tree list $[t]$. If $F$ starts with a tree $u$ followed by a list
$F'$ and the rank of $t$ is less than the rank of $u$, the result is $F$ with $t$ prepended.
Otherwise the result is the carry of the link of $t$ and $u$ into $F'$.

It is meant for a tree whose rank is no greater than every rank in the forest, where linking
equal-rank trees propagates like a binary carry.

articles.title: Children of a valid binomial tree are valid
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$,
every child of a valid binomial tree over $\alpha$ is itself a valid binomial tree.

articles.title: Child ranks of a valid binomial tree
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, if a
valid binomial tree over $\alpha$ has rank $r$, then the ranks of its children, listed in their
stored order, are $r - 1, r - 2, \dots, 1, 0$; there are no children when $r = 0$.

articles.title: Children of a binomial tree
articles.statement:
The children of a binomial tree are the binomial trees in
the list stored at its root node, in their stored order.

The list carries no ordering constraint in general; in a valid binomial tree of rank $r$ the
children have ranks $r - 1, \dots, 0$ in that order.

articles.title: Deleting the minimum of a binomial heap splits its multiset
articles.statement:
For a binomial heap $H$ over
a linearly ordered type, if deleting the minimum of $H$ succeeds and returns a value $m$ and a
heap $H'$, then the multiset of elements of $H$ equals the multiset of elements of $H'$ with one
more occurrence of $m$.

articles.title: Deleting the minimum of a binomial heap removes one occurrence
articles.statement:
For a binomial heap $H$
over a linearly ordered type, if deleting the minimum of $H$ succeeds and returns a value $m$
and a heap $H'$, then the multiset of elements of $H'$ is the multiset of elements of $H$ with
one occurrence of $m$ removed.

articles.title: Deleting the minimum fails only on the empty binomial heap
articles.statement:
For a binomial heap $H$ over a
linearly ordered type, deleting the minimum of $H$ returns no result if and only if the list of
trees of $H$ is empty.

articles.title: The value deleted from a binomial heap is a lower bound for its elements
articles.statement:
If deleting the
minimum of a binomial heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type succeeds and returns a value $m$
together with a remaining heap, then $m \le v$ for every value $v$ in the multiset of elements of
$H$.

articles.title: Binomial heap deletion agrees with forest deletion
articles.statement:
For every binomial heap $H$ over a
linearly ordered type, deleting the minimum of $H$ and then replacing the remaining heap by its
list of trees gives the same result as minimum deletion on the list of trees of $H$: both have no
result, or both return the same minimum value and the same list of trees.

articles.title: Minimum deletion on a binomial forest
articles.statement:
Given a list of binomial trees over a linearly
ordered type, if the list is empty there is no result. Otherwise, remove the first tree whose root
is minimal among the roots of the list; the result is the root of that tree together with the
forest obtained by melding its children, in reversed order, with the remaining trees.

articles.title: Deleting the minimum of a binomial heap
articles.statement:
If the binomial heap $H$ has no trees, there is no
result. Otherwise, remove from the list of trees of $H$ the first tree whose root is minimal; the
result is that root together with the binomial heap whose list of trees is obtained by melding
the children of the removed tree, in reversed order, with the remaining trees.

articles.title: Elements of a binomial forest
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of a list of binomial trees
$t_1, \dots, t_k$ is the multiset sum of the multisets of elements of $t_1, \dots, t_k$; for the
empty list it is the empty multiset.

articles.title: Elements of a binomial heap
articles.statement:
Over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of a
binomial heap is the multiset of elements of its list of binomial trees, that is, the multiset sum
of the multisets of elements of its trees.

articles.title: Insertion into a binomial heap adds one occurrence
articles.statement:
For every binomial heap $H$ over a
linearly ordered type and every value $v$, the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by
inserting $v$ into $H$ is the multiset of elements of $H$ with one more occurrence of $v$.

articles.title: Linking binomial trees adds their elements
articles.statement:
For any two binomial trees $s$ and $t$ over a
linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the tree obtained by linking $s$ and $t$ is
the sum of the multisets of elements of $s$ and $t$.

articles.title: Melding binomial forests adds their elements
articles.statement:
For any two lists $L$ and $R$ of binomial
trees over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the meld of $L$ and $R$ is the
sum of the multisets of elements of $L$ and $R$.

articles.title: Melding binomial heaps adds their elements
articles.statement:
For any two binomial heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ over
a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the meld of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is the sum of
the multisets of elements of $H_1$ and $H_2$.

articles.title: Elements of a binomial tree
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of a binomial tree with root value
$x$ and children $t_1, \dots, t_k$ is defined recursively as $\{x\}$ added to the multiset sum of
the multisets of elements of $t_1, \dots, t_k$; the stored rank plays no role.

articles.title: Empty binomial heap
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the empty binomial heap over
$\alpha$ is the binomial heap whose list of trees is empty.

articles.title: The minimum lookup fails exactly on the empty binomial heap
articles.statement:
For a binomial heap $H$ over a
linearly ordered type, the minimum lookup of $H$ returns no value if and only if the list of
trees of $H$ is empty.

articles.title: The minimum lookup of a binomial heap returns a lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a binomial heap over
a linearly ordered type. If the minimum lookup of $H$ returns $m$, then $m \le v$ for every
element $v$ of $H$.

articles.title: The minimum lookup of a binomial heap returns one of its elements
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a binomial
heap over a linearly ordered type. If the minimum lookup of $H$ returns $m$, then $m$ is an
element of $H$.

articles.title: Minimum of a binomial heap
articles.statement:
The minimum lookup of a binomial heap over a linearly ordered
type returns no value when the heap has no trees, and otherwise returns the least of the root
values of its trees, leaving the heap unchanged.

articles.title: Insertion into a binomial heap
articles.statement:
Inserting a value $x$ into a binomial heap $H$ over a
linearly ordered type gives the meld of the one-element binomial heap containing $x$ with $H$.

articles.title: A valid binomial forest with no elements has no trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
relation $\le$. If a list of binomial trees over $\alpha$ is a valid binomial forest and its
multiset of elements has cardinality $0$, then the list has length $0$.

articles.title: A binomial heap has logarithmically many trees
articles.statement:
If a binomial heap over a linearly ordered
type has $n$ elements, counted with multiplicity, then its number of trees is at most
$\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: A valid binomial forest has logarithmically many trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
relation $\le$. If a valid binomial forest over $\alpha$ has $n$ elements, counted with
multiplicity, then it consists of at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ trees, where
$\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Linking preserves binomial-tree validity
articles.statement:
If $s$ and $t$ are valid binomial trees
of equal rank, then the tree obtained by linking $s$ with $t$ is valid.

articles.title: Linking two binomial trees
articles.statement:
Over a linear order, the link of binomial trees $s$ and $t$
is defined as follows. If the root of $s$ is at most the root of $t$, it is the tree whose rank
is one more than the rank of $s$, whose root is the root of $s$, and whose children are $t$
followed by the children of $s$. Otherwise it is the tree whose rank is one more than the rank
of $s$, whose root is the root of $t$, and whose children are $s$ followed by the children of
$t$. In particular, the root of $s$ is kept when the two roots are equal.

articles.title: Melding preserves forest validity and rank lower bounds
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a natural number
and let $F$ and $G$ be valid binomial forests in which every tree has rank at least $r$. Then
the meld of $F$ and $G$ is a valid binomial forest in which every tree has rank at least $r$.

articles.title: Melding binomial forests
articles.statement:
Over a linear order, the meld of two lists of binomial trees
is defined by recursion on their total length. For every list $L$, the meld of the empty list
with $L$ is $L$, and the meld of $L$ with the empty list is $L$. For nonempty lists with first
trees $s$ and $t$ and remaining lists $F$ and $G$: if the rank of $s$ is less than the rank of
$t$, the meld is $s$ followed by the meld of $F$ with the second list; if the rank of $t$ is less
than the rank of $s$, it is $t$ followed by the meld of the first list with $G$; and if the ranks
are equal, it is the result of carrying the link of $s$ with $t$ into the meld of $F$ and $G$.

It is intended for forests of strictly increasing ranks, where equal-rank trees are linked and
the carries are propagated.

articles.title: Melding binomial heaps
articles.statement:
Over a linear order, the meld of two binomial heaps is the
binomial heap whose forest is the meld of the forests of the two heaps.

articles.title: Tree ranks in a valid forest are logarithmic
articles.statement:
If $F$ is a valid binomial forest and $T$
is a tree of $F$ of rank $r$, then $r \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, where $n$ is the number of
elements, counted with multiplicity, represented by $F$.

articles.title: Tree ranks in a binomial heap are logarithmic
articles.statement:
Every tree in a binomial heap holding $n$
elements, counted with multiplicity, has rank at most $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.

articles.title: The rank of a valid binomial tree is logarithmic
articles.statement:
A valid binomial tree of rank $r$
holding $n$ elements, counted with multiplicity, satisfies $r \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.

articles.title: Rank of a binomial tree
articles.statement:
The rank of a binomial tree is the natural number stored at its
root node.

articles.title: Rank lower bound for a forest
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$, a list of binomial trees has
ranks at least $r$ when every tree in it has rank at least $r$.

articles.title: Removing a minimum-root tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a list of binomial trees over a linear order, and
suppose that removing a minimum tree from $T$ returns the tree $m$ and the list $R$. Then the
multiset represented by $m$ plus the multiset represented by the forest $R$ equals the multiset
represented by the forest $T$; $m$ is a member of $T$; $R$ is a sublist of $T$; and the root of
$m$ is at most the root of every tree in $T$.

articles.title: Removing a minimum-root tree from a forest
articles.statement:
For a list $T$ of binomial trees over a linear
order, the result is nothing when $T$ is empty. Otherwise it is the first tree $m$ of $T$ whose root
is minimal among the roots of the trees of $T$, together with the list obtained from $T$ by
deleting that occurrence of $m$, the remaining trees keeping their order.

articles.title: The root of a valid binomial tree is a lower bound
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation
$\le$ and a valid binomial tree $t$ over $\alpha$, the root $a$ of $t$ satisfies $a \le v$ for
every element $v$ of the multiset represented by $t$.

articles.title: The root of a binomial tree is one of its elements
articles.statement:
For every binomial tree $t$, the root
of $t$ occurs in the multiset represented by $t$.

articles.title: Root of a binomial tree
articles.statement:
The root of the binomial tree with rank $r$, root value $a$ and
list of children $c$ is $a$.

articles.title: One-element binomial heap
articles.statement:
For a value $a$ in a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the
one-element binomial heap of $a$ is the binomial heap whose list of trees consists of exactly one
tree: the binomial tree of rank $0$ with root $a$ and no children.

articles.title: Singleton binomial heap
articles.statement:
For a value $a$ in a linear order, the binomial heap whose list of
trees consists of exactly one tree: the tree of rank $0$ with root $a$ and no children.

articles.title: Validity of binomial forests passes to sublists
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$
and lists $L$, $R$ of binomial trees over $\alpha$, if $L$ is a sublist of $R$ (obtained by
deleting entries while keeping the order of the rest) and $R$ is a valid forest, then $L$ is a valid
forest.

articles.title: Valid binomial forest
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, a list of binomial trees
over $\alpha$ is a valid forest when every tree in it is a valid binomial tree and the ranks of its
trees are strictly increasing along the list.

articles.title: The empty forest is valid
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, the empty list of
binomial trees over $\alpha$ is a valid binomial forest.

articles.title: Reversed children of a valid binomial tree form a valid forest
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered
type $\alpha$ and a valid binomial tree $t$ over $\alpha$, the children of $t$ listed in reverse
order form a valid binomial forest: every tree in the list is valid and the ranks strictly
increase along the list.

articles.title: Singleton binomial trees are valid
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and any
$a \in \alpha$, the singleton binomial tree with rank $0$, root $a$ and no children is valid.

articles.title: Valid binomial tree
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a relation $\le$, validity of binomial
trees over $\alpha$ is defined inductively: the tree with stored rank $r$, root $a$ and list of
children $c_1, \dots, c_k$ is valid when every child $c_i$ is valid, the ranks of
$c_1, \dots, c_k$ are exactly $r - 1, r - 2, \dots, 0$ in this order, the multiset of elements
of the tree (its root together with the elements of all its children) has exactly $2^r$
members counted with multiplicity, and $a \le x$ for every element $x$ of the tree.

articles.title: Arity of a $d$-ary heap built from a list
articles.statement:
For every requested arity $r \in \mathbb{N}$
and every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the $d$-ary min-heap built from $xs$ with
requested arity $r$ has arity equal to the normalized arity of $r$, namely $\max(2, r)$.

articles.title: Size of a $d$-ary min-heap
articles.statement:
For every $d$-ary min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type,
the number of elements of $h$, counted with multiplicity, equals the length of its backing
array.

articles.title: Insertion into a $d$-ary heap preserves other multiplicities
articles.statement:
For every $d$-ary min-heap
$h$ over a linearly ordered type and all values $x \ne y$, the multiplicity of $y$ among the
elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ equals the multiplicity of $y$ among the
elements of $h$.

articles.title: Insertion into a $d$-ary heap raises the multiplicity by one
articles.statement:
For every $d$-ary min-heap
$h$ over a linearly ordered type and every value $x$, the multiplicity of $x$ among the elements
of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is one more than its multiplicity among the
elements of $h$.

articles.title: Child index in a $d$-ary heap array
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$, $i$ and $k$, the child of
index $i$ with zero-based offset $k$ in a contiguous level-order $d$-ary tree is the index
$d i + k + 1$.

articles.title: $d$-ary heap order
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number and $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ an array
with entries in a type carrying a relation $\le$. The array $a$ is $d$-ary heap ordered when
$d \ge 2$ and every nonroot entry is at least the entry at its parent index:
$a_{\lfloor (i-1)/d \rfloor} \le a_i$ for every index $i$ with $0 < i < n$.

articles.title: $d$-ary min-heap
articles.statement:
A $d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ consists of a
natural number $d \ge 2$, its arity, and an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of elements of
$\alpha$, stored in level order, that is $d$-ary heap ordered:
$a_{\lfloor (i-1)/d \rfloor} \le a_i$ for every index $i$ with $0 < i < n$.

articles.title: Last-to-root move in a $d$-ary heap removes one copy of the root
articles.statement:
For every nonempty
array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of entries of the
array obtained from $a$ by the last-to-root move equals the multiset of entries of $a$ with one
occurrence of $a_0$ removed.

articles.title: Last-to-root move in a $d$-ary heap is ready for sift-down
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a natural number,
let $a$ be a $d$-ary heap ordered array with at least two entries over a linearly ordered type,
and let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ be the array obtained from $a$ by the last-to-root move.
Then $b$ is ready for a $d$-ary sift-down at index $0$: $d \ge 2$, $0 < m$, and
$b_{\lfloor (j-1)/d \rfloor} \le b_j$ for every index $j$ with $0 < j < m$ whose parent index
$\lfloor (j-1)/d \rfloor$ is not $0$.

articles.title: Last-to-root move on an array
articles.statement:
For a nonempty array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$, the
last-to-root move swaps $a_0$ and $a_{n-1}$ and then deletes the last entry, producing an array
$b = (b_0, \dots, b_{n-2})$ of length $n - 1$: when $n \ge 2$, $b_0 = a_{n-1}$ and
$b_i = a_i$ for $0 < i < n - 1$, and $b$ is empty when $n = 1$.

articles.title: The parent of a $d$-ary child
articles.statement:
Let $d$, $i$ and $k$ be natural numbers with $d \ge 2$ and
$k < d$. Then the $d$-ary parent of the child of $i$ with zero-based offset $k$, that is, of the
index $di + k + 1$, is $i$.

articles.title: The $d$-ary parent of a valid index is valid
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$ be a natural number, let $a$ be
an array over any type, write $|a|$ for its size, and let $i$ be an index with $0 < i < |a|$.
Then the $d$-ary parent of $i$ is also less than $|a|$.

articles.title: A $d$-ary parent has a smaller index
articles.statement:
Let $d$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $d \ge 2$ and
$i > 0$. Then the $d$-ary parent of $i$ is strictly less than $i$.

articles.title: Parent index in a $d$-ary tree
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $i$, the $d$-ary parent of $i$
is $\lfloor (i - 1)/d \rfloor$, computed in the natural numbers: $i - 1$ is truncated at $0$, so
the parent of $0$ is $0$, and division by $0$ gives $0$.

This is the parent index when a $d$-ary tree is stored in level order in an array with its root
at index $0$.

articles.title: Pushing onto a $d$-ary heap leaves it ready for sifting up
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type, let $d \ge 2$, and let $a$ be an array over $\alpha$ that is $d$-ary heap ordered,
with size $|a|$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the array obtained by appending $x$ to $a$ is
ready for $d$-ary sifting up at index $|a|$, the position of $x$; in particular every nonroot
entry other than $x$ is at least its $d$-ary parent.

articles.title: Sifting down in a $d$-ary heap preserves the multiset of entries
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered type, let $a$ be an array over $\alpha$, and let $i$ and $d$ be natural numbers
with $d \ge 2$. The array produced by $d$-ary sifting down from index $i$ in $a$ has the same
multiset of entries as $a$.

articles.title: Sifting down restores $d$-ary heap order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let
$d \ge 2$, and let $a$ be an array over $\alpha$ that is ready for $d$-ary sifting down at an
index $i$. Then the array produced by $d$-ary sifting down from index $i$ in $a$ is $d$-ary heap
ordered.

articles.title: Sifting down in a $d$-ary heap permutes the array
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
let $a$ be an array over $\alpha$, and let $i$ and $d$ be natural numbers with $d \ge 2$. The
array produced by $d$-ary sifting down from index $i$ in $a$ is a permutation of $a$.

articles.title: Readiness for $d$-ary sift-down
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a type with a relation $\le$,
and let $d$ and $i$ be natural numbers. Write $|a|$ for the size of $a$ and $p(j)$ for the
$d$-ary parent of an index $j$. The array $a$ is ready for $d$-ary sifting down at $i$ when
$d \ge 2$, $i < |a|$, every index $j$ with $0 < j < |a|$ and $p(j) \ne i$ satisfies
$a_{p(j)} \le a_j$, and, if $i > 0$, every index $j$ with $0 < j < |a|$ and $p(j) = i$ satisfies
$a_{p(i)} \le a_j$.

Thus the only edges that may violate heap order leave $i$, and lifting a smallest child to $i$
keeps the edge entering $i$ ordered.

articles.title: $d$-ary sift-down
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $a$ be an array over
$\alpha$, and let $i$ and $d$ be natural numbers with $d \ge 2$. Sifting down from $i$ in $a$
returns $a$ if $i$ has no valid $d$-ary child in $a$. Otherwise let $c$ be the smallest valid
$d$-ary child of $i$, with ties broken toward the lowest child offset: if $a_c < a_i$, swap the
entries at $i$ and $c$ and sift down from $c$ in the resulting array; otherwise return $a$.

articles.title: Sifting up preserves the multiset of entries
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$, let $a$ be an array over a
linearly ordered type and let $i$ be a natural number. The array obtained from $a$ by $d$-ary
sift-up from index $i$ has the same multiset of entries as $a$.

articles.title: Sift-up restores $d$-ary heap order
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type,
of length $|a|$ with entries $a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1}$, let $d$ and $i$ be natural numbers, and
write $p(j) = \lfloor (j-1)/d \rfloor$ for the parent of an index $j > 0$. Suppose $a$ is ready
for sift-up at $i$: $d \ge 2$, $i < |a|$, $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every $0 < j < |a|$ with
$j \ne i$, and, if $i > 0$, $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every $0 < j < |a|$ with $p(j) = i$. Then the
array $b$, of length $|b|$ with entries $b_0, \dots, b_{|b|-1}$, obtained from $a$ by $d$-ary
sift-up from index $i$ is $d$-ary heap ordered: $b_{p(j)} \le b_j$ for every $0 < j < |b|$.

articles.title: Sifting up permutes the array
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$, let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered
type and let $i$ be a natural number. The array obtained from $a$ by $d$-ary sift-up from index $i$
is a permutation of $a$.

articles.title: Arrays ready for $d$-ary sift-up
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1})$ be an array over a
type with a relation $\le$, let $d$ and $i$ be natural numbers, and write
$p(j) = \lfloor (j-1)/d \rfloor$ for the parent of an index $j > 0$. The array $a$ is ready for
sift-up at $i$ when $d \ge 2$, $i < |a|$, $a_{p(j)} \le a_j$ for every $0 < j < |a|$ with
$j \ne i$, and, if $i > 0$, $a_{p(i)} \le a_j$ for every $0 < j < |a|$ with $p(j) = i$.

So the only edge that may violate heap order is the one entering $i$, and the parent of $i$ is
no greater than the children of $i$.

articles.title: $d$-ary sift-up
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$, let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, of length
$|a|$ with entries $a_0, \dots, a_{|a|-1}$, let $i$ be a natural number, and write
$p(i) = \lfloor (i-1)/d \rfloor$ for the parent of $i > 0$. The sift-up of $a$ from $i$ is defined
recursively: if $0 < i < |a|$ and $a_i < a_{p(i)}$, it is the sift-up from $p(i)$ of the array
obtained from $a$ by swapping the entries at positions $i$ and $p(i)$; otherwise it is $a$.

articles.title: Smallest child among the offsets from $s$
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array over a linearly ordered
type, of length $|a|$, let $d$, $i$ and $s$ be natural numbers, and call $d i + k + 1$ the child
of $i$ at offset $k$. Scanning the offsets $s, s + 1, \dots, d - 1$, this returns the index of a
scanned child of $i$ below $|a|$ whose entry in $a$ is least among those, taking the smallest
offset among ties, or nothing if no scanned child index is below $|a|$.

articles.title: The smallest child lies after its parent
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$, let $a$ be an array over a
linearly ordered type and let $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If the smallest valid child of $i$
in the $d$-ary heap array $a$ is $c$, then $i < c$.

articles.title: The smallest child is a valid index
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly
ordered type and let $d$, $i$ and $c$ be natural numbers. If the smallest valid child of $i$ in
the $d$-ary heap array $a$ is $c$, then $c < |a|$.

articles.title: Smallest child in a $d$-ary heap array
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array of length $|a|$ over a linearly
ordered type and let $d$ and $i$ be natural numbers. The children of $i$ are the indices
$d i + k + 1$ for $0 \le k < d$, and a child is valid when it is below $|a|$. The smallest child
of $i$ is the valid child of $i$ with the least entry, taking the smallest offset $k$ among ties,
or nothing if $i$ has no valid child.

articles.title: Building a heap from a list keeps its elements
articles.statement:
For every requested arity $r$ and every
list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the multiset of elements of the min-heap of arity
$\max(2, r)$ built from $xs$ by successive insertions equals the multiset of entries of $xs$.

articles.title: Insertion into a d-ary heap adds one occurrence
articles.statement:
For a $d$-ary min-heap $h$ over a
linearly ordered type and a value $x$, the multiset of elements of the heap obtained by inserting
$x$ into $h$ is the multiset of elements of $h$ with one more occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Elements of a d-ary heap
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of a $d$-ary min-heap $h$ over a
linearly ordered type is the multiset of the entries of its level-order storage array, counted
with multiplicity.

articles.title: Empty d-ary heap
articles.statement:
For a natural number $r$ (the requested arity), the empty heap is the
$d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type with arity $d = \max(2, r)$ and an empty storage
array; a requested arity below two is thus normalized to two.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum preserves the arity of a d-ary heap
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap
over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$
and a heap $h'$, then $h'$ has the same arity as $h$.

articles.title: Extracted minimum and remaining d-ary heap recover the original elements
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a
$d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds,
returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ is the multiset of
elements of $h'$ with one more occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum of a d-ary heap lowers its multiplicity by one
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a
$d$-ary min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds,
returning a value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then the multiplicity of $x$ in the multiset of elements
of $h'$ is its multiplicity in the multiset of elements of $h$ minus one.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum of a d-ary heap removes one occurrence
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary
min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a
value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h'$ is obtained from the multiset of
elements of $h$ by removing one occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum of a d-ary heap fails exactly on the empty heap
articles.statement:
For a $d$-ary
min-heap $h$ over a linearly ordered type, extracting the minimum from $h$ returns no result if
and only if the storage array of $h$ is empty.

articles.title: The extracted minimum of a d-ary heap is a lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap
over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a value $x$
and a heap $h'$, then $x \le y$ for every element $y$ of the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: The extracted minimum of a d-ary heap is one of its elements
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary
min-heap over a linearly ordered type. If extracting the minimum from $h$ succeeds, returning a
value $x$ and a heap $h'$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum leaves a heap-ordered $d$-ary heap
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary
min-heap. If extracting the minimum of $h$ returns a value $x$ and a heap $h'$ of arity $d'$,
then $d' \ge 2$ and the storage array $a$ of $h'$ is heap-ordered: for every index $i$ with
$0 < i < |a|$, the entry $a_{\lfloor (i-1)/d' \rfloor}$ is at most $a_i$.

articles.title: Extracting the minimum of a $d$-ary min-heap
articles.statement:
For a $d$-ary min-heap $h$,
extracting the minimum returns nothing if the storage array of $h$ is empty. Otherwise it
returns the root entry (the entry at index $0$) together with the heap obtained from $h$ by
removing its root: the last entry moves to the root and sifts down along a single $d$-ary
child path.

articles.title: Removing the root of a $d$-ary heap preserves its arity
articles.statement:
For a $d$-ary min-heap $h$
with nonempty storage array, the heap obtained from $h$ by removing its root has the same
arity $d$ as $h$.

articles.title: Removing the root of a $d$-ary min-heap
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap whose storage
array $a$ is nonempty. Removing the root of $h$ gives the heap of arity $d$ whose storage array
is empty if $a$ has one entry. Otherwise the last entry of $a$ replaces the root, the last
position is dropped, and the new root is repeatedly swapped with its smallest $d$-ary child
while that child is smaller.

articles.title: The minimum query on a $d$-ary heap fails exactly when it is empty
articles.statement:
For a $d$-ary
min-heap $h$, the minimum query on $h$ (which returns the entry at index $0$ of the storage
array, if any) returns nothing if and only if the storage array of $h$ is empty.

articles.title: The minimum query on a $d$-ary heap returns a least element
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary
min-heap. If the minimum query on $h$ returns $x$, then $x \le y$ for every element $y$ of the
multiset of elements of $h$.

articles.title: The minimum query on a $d$-ary heap returns an element of the heap
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a
$d$-ary min-heap. If the minimum query on $h$ returns $x$, then $x$ belongs to the multiset of
elements of $h$.

articles.title: Minimum query on a $d$-ary min-heap
articles.statement:
The minimum query on a $d$-ary min-heap $h$
returns the entry at index $0$ (the root) of the storage array of $h$, or nothing if the array
is empty.

articles.title: Normalization leaves a valid arity unchanged
articles.statement:
For every natural number $d \ge 2$, the
normalized arity $\max(2, d)$ of $d$ equals $d$.

articles.title: Normalized arities are at least two
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$, the normalized arity
$\max(2, r)$ of $r$ is at least $2$.

articles.title: Normalized heap arity
articles.statement:
The normalized arity of a requested arity $r \in \mathbb{N}$ is
$\max(2, r)$: the requested arities $0$ and $1$ become $2$ (the binary-heap policy), and every
$r \ge 2$ is left unchanged.

articles.title: Building a $d$-ary min-heap from a list
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let
$r \in \mathbb{N}$ be a requested arity, and let $d = \max(2, r)$. The min-heap built from the
empty list is the empty min-heap of arity $d$, and the min-heap built from a list with head $x$
and tail $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$ is obtained by inserting $x$ into the min-heap built from
$xs$. Thus the min-heap built from $[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ starts from the empty min-heap of arity
$d$ and inserts $x_n$, then $x_{n-1}$, and so on, ending with $x_1$, each by $d$-ary
insertion.

articles.title: Insertion keeps a $d$-ary heap ordered
articles.statement:
Let $h$ be a $d$-ary min-heap of arity $d$ and let
$x$ be a value. Then the level-order array of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $h$ is
$d$-ary heap-ordered for the same arity $d$.

articles.title: Insertion into a $d$-ary heap
articles.statement:
Inserting a value $x$ into a $d$-ary min-heap $h$ of arity
$d$ gives the heap of the same arity $d$ whose array is obtained by appending $x$ at the end of
the level-order array of $h$ and sifting it up from that last index: while the current index
$i > 0$ holds an entry strictly smaller than the entry at its parent index
$\lfloor (i-1)/d \rfloor$, the two entries are swapped and the process continues from the
parent. Only the ancestor path of the new entry is changed.

articles.title: The root of a $d$-ary heap-ordered array is a minimum
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, let $d \ge 2$, and let $a$ be an array of elements of $\alpha$ that is $d$-ary
heap-ordered. Then $a_0 \le a_i$ for every index $i$ smaller than the size of $a$.

articles.title: Inserting a tree into a forest
articles.statement:
Given a Fibonacci tree $t$ and a list of Fibonacci
trees, the insertion of $t$ into the list is defined recursively. Inserting $t$ into the empty
list gives the one-tree list $[t]$. For a list with first tree $s$ and remaining list $L$: if
the stored degree of $t$ is less than the stored degree of $s$, the result is $t$ followed by
$s$ and then $L$; if the two stored degrees are equal, the result is the insertion of the link
of $t$ and $s$ into $L$; otherwise the result is $s$ followed by the insertion of $t$ into $L$.

On a list whose stored degrees strictly increase, this links $t$ with any tree of equal degree
and carries the linked tree forward, as in binary addition.

articles.title: Insertion increases the size of a Fibonacci heap by one
articles.statement:
For every Fibonacci heap $H$
and every value $x$, the number of elements of the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $H$,
counted with multiplicity, is the number of elements of $H$ plus one.

articles.title: Melding adds the sizes of Fibonacci heaps
articles.statement:
For Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$, the number
of elements of the meld of $H_1$ and $H_2$, counted with multiplicity, is the number of
elements of $H_1$ plus the number of elements of $H_2$.

articles.title: Fibonacci trees are nonempty
articles.statement:
Every Fibonacci tree represents at least one element: the
multiset of elements of any Fibonacci tree has positive size.

articles.title: Children of a valid Fibonacci tree are valid
articles.statement:
Every child of a valid Fibonacci tree is
itself a valid Fibonacci tree.

articles.title: Children of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
The children of the Fibonacci tree with stored degree $d$,
root value $r$ and list of subtrees $c$ are the trees of the list $c$, in order.

articles.title: Consolidation yields distinct root degrees
articles.statement:
For every list of Fibonacci trees, the trees
in its consolidation have pairwise distinct stored degrees.

articles.title: Consolidation sorts root degrees
articles.statement:
For every list of Fibonacci trees, the stored degrees
of the trees in its consolidation are strictly increasing in list order.

articles.title: Consolidation of a forest
articles.statement:
The consolidation of a list of Fibonacci trees is defined
recursively: the consolidation of the empty list is the empty list, and the consolidation of a
list with first tree $t$ and remaining list $L$ is the insertion of $t$ into the consolidation
of $L$.

Each insertion links trees of equal stored degree as in binary addition, so the result has
strictly increasing, hence distinct, stored root degrees, as in the consolidate step of CLRS.

articles.title: Cutting a subtree splits the elements of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fibonacci tree
and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves a
remainder tree $t'$, then the multiset of elements of $t$ is the sum of the multisets of
elements of $t'$ and of $s$.

articles.title: A cut without remainder extracts the whole tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fibonacci tree and $p$ a
path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves no remainder,
then $s = t$.

articles.title: The remainder of a cut from a valid tree is valid
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid Fibonacci tree
over a type with a relation $\le$, and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$
extracts a subtree and leaves a remainder tree $t'$, then $t'$ is valid: its children are
valid, its stored degree equals its number of children, and its root is $\le$ every element
of $t'$.

articles.title: The subtree extracted by a cut from a valid tree is valid
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid Fibonacci
tree over a type with a relation $\le$, and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$
extracts a subtree $s$ (with or without a remainder), then $s$ is valid.

articles.title: A cut extracts the addressed subtree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fibonacci tree and $p$ a path of
child indices. If cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ (with or without a remainder),
then $s$ is the subtree of $t$ at $p$.

articles.title: Cutting a subtree out of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
For a path $p$ of child indices and a Fibonacci
tree $t$, the cut of $t$ at $p$ is either undefined or a pair of an extracted subtree and an
optional remainder tree. For the empty path, the extracted subtree is $t$ and there is no
remainder. For a path consisting of an index $i$ followed by a path $q$, where $t$ has root $r$
and children $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$, the cut is undefined if $i \ge k$ or if the cut of $c_i$
at $q$ is undefined. Otherwise, with $s$ the subtree extracted from $c_i$, the extracted
subtree is $s$ and the remainder is the tree with root $r$ whose children are those of $t$
with $c_i$ removed (if the cut of $c_i$ left no remainder) or with $c_i$ replaced by that
remainder (otherwise), and whose stored degree is its new number of children.

When the cut is defined, there is no remainder exactly when $p$ is empty.

articles.title: Cutting a subtree splits the elements of a Fibonacci forest
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a forest of
Fibonacci trees, $i$ an index and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $F$ at the $i$-th tree
and path $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves the forest $F'$, then the multiset of elements
of $F$ is the sum of the multisets of elements of $F'$ and of $s$.

articles.title: Every addressed subtree of a forest can be cut out
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a forest of Fibonacci
trees whose tree at position $i$ is $t$, and let $p$ be a path of child indices such that the
subtree of $t$ at $p$ is $s$. Then cutting $F$ at index $i$ and path $p$ is defined and extracts
$s$, together with some remaining forest.

articles.title: Cutting a valid forest leaves valid parts
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a valid forest of Fibonacci trees
over a type with a relation $\le$, $i$ an index and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting $F$
at index $i$ and path $p$ extracts a subtree $s$ and leaves the forest $F'$, then $s$ is a valid
tree and $F'$ is a valid forest.

articles.title: Cutting a subtree out of a Fibonacci forest
articles.statement:
For a forest given as a list of Fibonacci
trees, an index $i$ and a path $p$ of child indices, the cut is undefined if the list has no
tree at position $i$ (counting from $0$) or if cutting that tree $t$ at $p$ is undefined.
Otherwise, if cutting $t$ at $p$ extracts the subtree $s$, the result is $s$ together with the
list in which the tree at position $i$ is removed (if the cut of $t$ left no remainder) or
replaced by the remainder (otherwise).

articles.title: Decrease-key preserves the number of elements
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root
index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$
out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that
$k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then the multiset represented by the heap obtained from $H$ by
decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ has the same number of elements,
counted with multiplicity, as the multiset represented by $H$.

articles.title: Decrease-key replaces one key, stated by address
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, let $T$ be
the $i$-th tree of its root list, and let $S$ be the subtree of $T$ at the path $p$ of child
indices. If the key $k$ is at most the root of $S$, then the multiset represented by the heap
obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ is the multiset
represented by $H$ with one occurrence of the root of $S$ removed and one occurrence of $k$
added.

articles.title: Decrease-key replaces one key
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index, $p$ a path
of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th
tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is at most the
root of $S$. Then the multiset represented by the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at
root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ is the multiset represented by $H$ with one occurrence of the
root of $S$ removed and one occurrence of $k$ added.

articles.title: Decrease-key at an unresolved address does nothing
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a
root index and $p$ a path of child indices. If cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th
tree of the root list of $H$ fails, then for every key $k$, decreasing the key at root index $i$
and path $p$ to $k$ returns $H$ unchanged.

articles.title: Decrease-key with a larger key does nothing
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index,
$p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of
the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is
not at most the root of $S$ (keys are linearly ordered, so $k$ is greater than that root). Then
decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ returns $H$ unchanged.

articles.title: Minimum after decrease-key
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap whose minimum, as returned by
find-min, is $m$, and let $i$ be a root index, $p$ a path of child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose
that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$ succeeds and
extracts the subtree $S$, and that $k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then find-min on the heap
obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ returns
$\min(k, m)$.

articles.title: Root list after decrease-key
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap, $i$ a root index, $p$ a path of
child indices and $k$ a key. Suppose that cutting the subtree at path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree
of the root list of $H$ succeeds, extracting the subtree $S$ and leaving the forest $R$, and that
$k$ is at most the root of $S$. Then the root list of the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing
the key at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ consists of $S$ with its root replaced by $k$,
followed by the trees of $R$ in order.

articles.title: Decrease-key yields a valid forest
articles.statement:
For every Fibonacci heap $H$, root index $i$, path $p$
of child indices and key $k$, the root list of the heap obtained from $H$ by decreasing the key
at root index $i$ and path $p$ to $k$ is a valid forest, that is, every tree in it is valid.

This holds by construction: every Fibonacci heap carries a valid forest.

articles.title: Decrease-key in a Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
Given a Fibonacci heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type,
a root index $i$, a path $p$ of child indices and a key $k$, decrease-key cuts the subtree $S$ at
path $p$ out of the $i$-th tree of the root list of $H$, replaces the root of $S$ by $k$, and
puts the resulting tree in front of the remaining forest (the root list with the $i$-th tree
replaced by what is left of it after the cut, or removed when $S$ is that whole tree). The
cached minimum of the result is the smaller of $k$ and the previous cached minimum, computed
without rescanning the root list. When the cut fails (the address does not resolve) or $k$ is
greater than the root of $S$, the heap $H$ is returned unchanged.

Unlike CLRS decrease-key, this performs no cascading cuts: the trees carry no mark field.

articles.title: Lowering the root keeps a Fibonacci tree valid
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a valid Fibonacci tree over a
preordered type and let $k$ be a key that is at most the root of $T$. Then the tree obtained
from $T$ by replacing its root by $k$, keeping its degree and children, is valid: the new root
is still no greater than every represented element.

articles.title: Replacing the root key of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
For a Fibonacci tree $t$ and a key $k$, this
is the tree whose root value is $k$ and whose stored degree and list of children are those of $t$.

It is used on an extracted subtree with a key no larger than the old root.

articles.title: The degree of a valid Fibonacci tree is its number of children
articles.statement:
For every valid Fibonacci
tree, its stored degree equals the number of its children.

articles.title: Degree of the link of two trees of equal degree
articles.statement:
If two Fibonacci trees $s$ and $t$
over a linearly ordered type have the same degree $d$, then their link has degree $d + 1$.

articles.title: The degree of a valid Fibonacci tree is less than its size
articles.statement:
For every valid Fibonacci
tree over a type with a relation $\le$, the degree of the tree is strictly less than the
number of elements, counted with multiplicity, of the multiset the tree represents, since
every child contributes at least one element.

articles.title: Degree of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
The degree of the Fibonacci tree with stored degree $d$,
root value $r$ and list of children $c$ is the stored natural number $d$; it is not computed
from the children.

articles.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion splits off the minimum
articles.statement:
If deleting the minimum of a
Fibonacci heap $H$ succeeds and returns the value $m$ and the heap $H'$, then the multiset of
elements of $H$ is the multiset of elements of $H'$ with one copy of $m$ added.

articles.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion removes one copy of the minimum
articles.statement:
If deleting the
minimum of a Fibonacci heap $H$ succeeds and returns the value $m$ and the heap $H'$, then the
multiset of elements of $H'$ is the multiset of elements of $H$ with one occurrence of $m$
removed.

articles.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion fails exactly on the empty heap
articles.statement:
Deleting the minimum
of a Fibonacci heap fails if and only if the heap's list of root trees is empty.

articles.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion returns a lower bound
articles.statement:
If deleting the minimum of a
Fibonacci heap $H$ succeeds and returns the value $m$, then $m \le v$ for every element $v$
of $H$.

articles.title: After minimum deletion a Fibonacci heap has at most as many roots as elements
articles.statement:
If
deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap succeeds and returns the heap $H'$, then the number
of root trees of $H'$ is at most the number of elements of $H'$, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Minimum deletion leaves a Fibonacci heap with strictly increasing root degrees
articles.statement:
If
deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap succeeds and returns the heap $H'$, then the degrees
of the root trees of $H'$, in list order, are strictly increasing; consolidation is what
makes them so.

articles.title: Fibonacci heap minimum deletion agrees with its root-list version
articles.statement:
For every Fibonacci
heap $H$, deleting the minimum of $H$ and keeping only the returned value and the root list
of the resulting heap gives the same result as the root-list minimum deletion applied to the
root list of $H$: either both fail, or both return the same value and the same list of
trees.

articles.title: Minimum deletion on a forest
articles.statement:
Given a list of Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered type,
the result is nothing if the list is empty. Otherwise the first tree whose root is minimal is
removed, and the result is its root value together with the consolidation of the forest made of
the removed tree's children followed by the remaining trees.

This is the forest-level computation behind deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap, without the
validity proofs.

articles.title: Deleting the minimum of a Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
If the root list of the heap is empty, the result
is nothing. Otherwise the first tree of the root list whose root is minimal is removed, and the
result is its root value together with the heap whose root list is the consolidation of the
removed tree's children followed by the remaining trees, and whose cached minimum is the minimum
root of this consolidated forest.

articles.title: Multiset of a Fibonacci forest
articles.statement:
Write $M(t)$ for the multiset of values stored in a
Fibonacci tree $t$. The multiset represented by a Fibonacci forest, a list of Fibonacci trees
$t_1, \dots, t_k$, is the sum $M(t_1) + \cdots + M(t_k)$; the empty forest represents the empty
multiset.

articles.title: Multiset of a Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
The multiset represented by a Fibonacci heap over a linearly
ordered type is the multiset of its list of trees: the sum, over the trees in the list, of the
multisets of values stored in them. The cached minimum plays no role.

articles.title: Elements of a concatenated forest
articles.statement:
For any two lists $L$ and $R$ of Fibonacci trees, the
forest made of the trees of $L$ followed by the trees of $R$ represents the sum of the multisets
represented by $L$ and by $R$.

articles.title: Consolidation preserves the elements
articles.statement:
For every list of Fibonacci trees over a linearly
ordered type, its consolidation represents the same multiset as the original list.

articles.title: Elements after replacing the root key
articles.statement:
For a Fibonacci tree $t$ and any key $k$, the
multiset of elements represented by the tree obtained from $t$ by replacing its root value with $k$
equals the multiset of elements of $t$ with one occurrence of the root of $t$ removed and $k$
added.

articles.title: The empty Fibonacci heap has no elements
articles.statement:
The empty Fibonacci heap represents the empty
multiset.

articles.title: Insertion adds one occurrence
articles.statement:
For every Fibonacci heap $H$ over a linearly ordered type
and every value $x$, the heap obtained by inserting $x$ into $H$ represents the multiset of $H$
with one more occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Linking adds the elements
articles.statement:
For any two Fibonacci trees $S$ and $T$ over a linearly ordered
type, the tree obtained by linking $S$ and $T$ represents the sum of the multisets represented by
$S$ and by $T$.

articles.title: Melding adds the elements
articles.statement:
For any two Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ over a linearly
ordered type, the meld of $H_1$ and $H_2$ represents the sum of the multisets represented by
$H_1$ and by $H_2$.

articles.title: Multiset of a singleton Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
For every value $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the
singleton Fibonacci heap on $x$, whose only tree is the single-node tree with root $x$, represents
the multiset $\{x\}$.

articles.title: The union of Fibonacci heaps adds their multisets
articles.statement:
For Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ over
a linearly ordered type, the multiset represented by the union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is the sum of
the multisets represented by $H_1$ and by $H_2$.

articles.title: Multiset of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
The multiset $M(t)$ of values stored in a Fibonacci tree $t$,
defined recursively: if $t$ has root value $r$ and children $t_1, \dots, t_k$, then
$M(t) = \{r\} + M(t_1) + \cdots + M(t_k)$. The stored degree plays no role.

articles.title: Empty Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
The Fibonacci heap over a linearly ordered type whose list of trees
is empty and whose cached minimum is absent.

articles.title: Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
A Fibonacci min-heap over a linearly ordered type consists of a list of
Fibonacci trees, each valid (heap-ordered, and at every node the stored degree equals the number
of children), together with a cached minimum equal to the least root value of these trees,
absent when the list is empty.

articles.title: Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
A Fibonacci tree over a type $\alpha$ is a rose tree: a node carrying a
stored degree $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a root value in $\alpha$, and a finite list of child Fibonacci
trees.

Heap order and the equality of the stored degree with the number of children are not part of
the type; they are imposed by the validity predicate on trees.

articles.title: Find-min fails exactly on the empty Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
For a Fibonacci heap $H$ over a
linearly ordered type, find-min on $H$ returns no value if and only if $H$ has no trees.

articles.title: Find-min returns a lower bound of the Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap over a
linearly ordered type. If find-min on $H$ returns $m$, then $m \le v$ for every value $v$ in the
multiset represented by $H$.

articles.title: Find-min returns an element of the Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a Fibonacci heap over a
linearly ordered type. If find-min on $H$ returns $m$, then $m$ belongs to the multiset
represented by $H$.

articles.title: Find-min for Fibonacci heaps
articles.statement:
Find-min on a Fibonacci heap returns its cached minimum
without modifying the heap: the least root value of its trees, or no value when the heap has no
trees.

articles.title: Insertion into a Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
Inserting a value $x$ into a Fibonacci heap $H$ gives
the meld of the one-element Fibonacci heap containing $x$ with $H$, the one-element heap coming
first.

articles.title: Degree-sorted forests have at most as many trees as elements
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a valid forest
of Fibonacci trees whose degrees are strictly increasing along the list. Then the number of
trees in $F$ is at most the number of elements, counted with multiplicity, that $F$ represents.

Every degree is smaller than the total element count and the degrees are distinct.

articles.title: Linking preserves validity of Fibonacci trees
articles.statement:
If $s$ and $t$ are valid Fibonacci trees
over a linearly ordered type, then the link of $s$ and $t$ is a valid Fibonacci tree.

articles.title: Linking two Fibonacci trees
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be Fibonacci trees over a linearly ordered
type. If the root of $s$ is at most the root of $t$, the link of $s$ and $t$ is the tree with the
root of $s$, stored degree one more than that of $s$, and children $t$ followed by the children
of $s$. Otherwise it is the tree with the root of $t$, stored degree one more than that of $t$,
and children $s$ followed by the children of $t$.

articles.title: Melding Fibonacci heaps
articles.statement:
The meld of Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ is the Fibonacci heap
whose root list is the root list of $H_1$ followed by that of $H_2$, and whose cached minimum is
the smaller of the two cached minima when both heaps have one, and otherwise the cached minimum
of whichever heap has one (none if neither does).

No linking happens until the next minimum deletion.

articles.title: Minimum of two optional values
articles.statement:
For optional values $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered
type, their combined minimum is defined as follows: if $x$ and $y$ are both present, with values
$a$ and $b$, it is $\min(a, b)$; if exactly one of $x$ and $y$ is present, it is that value; and
if both are absent, it is absent.

articles.title: Minimum root of a concatenated forest
articles.statement:
For forests $F$ and $G$ of Fibonacci trees over a
linearly ordered type, the minimum root of $F$ followed by $G$ is the combined minimum of the
optional minimum roots of $F$ and of $G$: their minimum if both exist, the one that exists if
only one does, and absent if neither does.

articles.title: Only the empty forest has no minimum root
articles.statement:
A forest of Fibonacci trees over a linearly
ordered type has no minimum root exactly when it is empty.

articles.title: The minimum root is a least root
articles.statement:
If a forest $F$ of Fibonacci trees over a linearly
ordered type has minimum root $m$, then $m$ is the root of some tree of $F$ and $m$ is at most
the root of every tree of $F$.

articles.title: Minimum root of a forest
articles.statement:
The minimum root of a forest of Fibonacci trees over a linearly
ordered type is an optional value: it is absent for the empty forest, and for a nonempty forest
it is the least of the roots of its trees.

articles.title: Minimum-tree removal in a Fibonacci forest
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a list of Fibonacci trees over a
linearly ordered type. If removing a minimum tree from $T$ returns a tree $m$ and a list $R$, then
the multiset of elements of $m$ plus the multiset of elements of $R$ equals the multiset of elements
of $T$, the tree $m$ belongs to $T$, the list $R$ is a sublist of $T$, and the root of $m$ is at
most the root of every tree in $T$.

articles.title: Removing a minimum tree from a Fibonacci forest
articles.statement:
For a list of Fibonacci trees over a
linearly ordered type, this returns nothing on the empty list. Otherwise it returns the first tree
whose root is minimal among all roots in the list, so earlier trees win ties, together with the list
of the remaining trees in their original order.

articles.title: Roots of valid Fibonacci trees are lower bounds
articles.statement:
The root of a valid Fibonacci tree is no
greater than every element of the multiset the tree represents.

articles.title: The root of a Fibonacci tree is one of its elements
articles.statement:
For every Fibonacci tree, its root
value belongs to the multiset of elements the tree represents.

articles.title: Root of a Fibonacci tree
articles.statement:
The root of a Fibonacci tree is the value stored at its top
node.

articles.title: Singleton Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the singleton
Fibonacci heap on $x$ has as its only tree the single-node tree with root $x$, stored degree $0$
and no children, and its cached minimum is $x$.

articles.title: One-element Fibonacci heap
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the one-element
Fibonacci heap on $x$ has as its only tree the single-node tree with root $x$, and its cached
minimum is $x$.

articles.title: Forests with strictly increasing degrees
articles.statement:
A Fibonacci forest, a list of Fibonacci trees
$t_1, \dots, t_k$, has sorted degrees when the stored degrees of its trees strictly increase along
the list: $\deg t_i < \deg t_j$ whenever $i < j$.

articles.title: Sublists of valid Fibonacci forests are valid
articles.statement:
If a list of Fibonacci trees is a valid
forest, then every sublist of it (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous) is a valid forest.

articles.title: Subtrees of a valid Fibonacci tree are valid
articles.statement:
If a Fibonacci tree $t$ is valid and a path
$p$ of child indices addresses a subtree $s$ of $t$, then $s$ is valid.

articles.title: Every addressed subtree can be cut out
articles.statement:
If a path $p$ of child indices addresses a subtree
$s$ of a Fibonacci tree $t$, then cutting $t$ at $p$ succeeds and extracts exactly $s$, together
with some remainder, which may be absent.

articles.title: Subtree of a Fibonacci tree at a path
articles.statement:
For a list $p = (i_1, \dots, i_n)$ of natural
numbers and a Fibonacci tree $t$, the subtree of $t$ at $p$ is found by starting at the root and
moving to the child with zero-based index $i_1$, then to its child with index $i_2$, and so on.
The result is absent when some index is at least the number of children of the current node.
The empty path addresses the whole tree $t$.

articles.title: Union of Fibonacci heaps
articles.statement:
The union of Fibonacci heaps $H_1$ and $H_2$ is their meld: the
heap whose trees are those of $H_1$ followed by those of $H_2$, and whose cached minimum is the
smaller of the two cached minima (the one that exists if a heap is empty, none if both are).

CLRS calls this operation union.

articles.title: Valid Fibonacci forests
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. A Fibonacci forest,
a list of Fibonacci trees with values in $\alpha$, is valid when every tree in it is a valid
Fibonacci tree.

Root degrees may repeat; consolidation is what makes them distinct.

articles.title: Concatenation preserves validity of Fibonacci forests
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ carry a relation
$\le$. If $F$ and $G$ are valid Fibonacci forests with values in $\alpha$, then the forest
consisting of the trees of $F$ followed by the trees of $G$ is valid.

articles.title: Consolidation preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a
Fibonacci forest with values in $\alpha$ is valid, then its consolidation is valid.

articles.title: The empty Fibonacci forest is valid
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. The empty
forest, containing no Fibonacci trees with values in $\alpha$, is valid.

articles.title: Singleton Fibonacci trees are valid
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every
$v \in \alpha$, the Fibonacci tree of degree $0$ with root $v$ and no children is valid.

articles.title: Valid Fibonacci trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ carry a relation $\le$. A Fibonacci tree with
stored degree $d$, root $r \in \alpha$ and list of children $c$ is valid when every tree in $c$ is
valid, $d$ equals the length of $c$, and $r \le x$ for every element $x$ of the multiset
represented by the tree (the root together with the elements of all children).

articles.title: Decrease-key fails exactly on absent identities and non-decreases
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an
indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be
an identity and let $k \in W$. Decreasing the key of $v$ to $k$ in $q$ returns no queue if and
only if either the position vector of $q$ records no slot for $v$, or it records a slot $i$
for $v$ with $i$ less than the size of the heap array of $q$ and $k$ is not strictly less, in
$W \cup \{\top\}$, than the key of the heap entry at index $i$.

articles.title: Successful decrease-key
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with
identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be an identity and let $k \in W$, and suppose that
decreasing the key of $v$ to $k$ in $q$ returns the queue $q'$. Let $a$ be the heap array of
$q$. Then the position vector of $q$ records a slot $i$ for $v$ with $i$ less than the size of
$a$, $k$ is strictly less, in $W \cup \{\top\}$, than the key of the entry $a_i$, and the heap
array of $q'$ is obtained by sifting up from index $i$ the array that agrees with $a$ except
that $a_i$ is replaced by $(k, v)$. Moreover, every identity has a recorded slot in $q'$ if and
only if it has one in $q$.

articles.title: Logarithmic event bound for indexed-queue decrease-key
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered
type and let $W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined. Let $q$ be an
indexed minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$ with keys in $W \cup \{\top\}$ whose
heap has $s$ entries, let $v < n$ be an identity and let $k \in W$ be a key. For each of the five
counted events (comparisons, swaps, position reads, position writes, and entry appends, pops or
replacements), the number of times that event occurs when decreasing the key of $v$ to $k$ in
$q$ is at most $20 (\lfloor \log_2 (s + 1) \rfloor + 1)$.

articles.title: Decrease-key in an indexed minimum queue
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type and let
$W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined. Costs are counted as five
event counts: comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector,
and entry appends, pops or replacements. Given an indexed minimum queue $q$ over the identities
$0, \dots, n-1$ with keys in $W \cup \{\top\}$, whose heap entries (pairs of a key and an
identity) are ordered lexicographically, first by key and then by identity, an identity $v < n$
and a finite key $k \in W$, decrease-key fails (returns nothing) when the position vector of $q$
assigns no index to $v$, at the cost of one position read, and when $k$ is not strictly smaller
than the current key of $v$, at the cost of one position read and one comparison. Otherwise it
replaces the entry of $v$ by $(k, v)$ in the same slot and sifts it up: while it is not at the
root and is smaller than its parent, it is swapped with its parent and the positions of both
swapped identities are updated. It returns the resulting queue, at the cost of one position
read, one comparison and one entry replacement, plus one comparison for each comparison with a
parent and one swap and two position writes for each swap.

articles.title: The empty indexed min queue has no present identity
articles.statement:
For every linear order $W$, every
$n$ and every identity $v \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the position vector of the empty indexed min
queue over $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ records no slot for $v$.

articles.title: Empty indexed minimum queue
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered type $W$ and every natural number
$n$, the empty indexed minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$, with keys in $W$ with a
new greatest element adjoined, has the empty min-heap and a position vector that assigns nothing
to each of the $n$ identities, so no identity is present.

articles.title: Extraction from an indexed min queue fails exactly when it is empty
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an
indexed min queue over a linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Extracting
the minimum of $q$ returns no result if and only if the heap array of $q$ has size $0$.

articles.title: Successful extraction from an indexed min queue
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a
linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and suppose that extracting the
minimum of $q$ returns the heap entry $e = (k, u)$, with key $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$ and
identity $u$, together with the queue $q'$. Then binary min-heap extraction on the heap of $q$
returns $e$ together with the heap of $q'$; the position vector of $q'$ records no slot for
$u$; and every identity $w \neq u$ has a recorded slot in $q'$ if and only if it has one in
$q$.

articles.title: Logarithmic event bound for indexed-queue extract-min
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed minimum
queue whose heap has $s$ entries. For each of the five counted events (comparisons, swaps,
position reads, position writes, and entry appends, pops or replacements), the number of times
that event occurs when extracting the minimum of $q$ is at most
$20 (\lfloor \log_2 (s + 1) \rfloor + 1)$.

articles.title: Extract-min in an indexed minimum queue
articles.statement:
Costs are counted as five event counts:
comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry
appends, pops or replacements. Given an indexed minimum queue $q$, extract-min fails (returns
nothing) exactly when the heap of $q$ is empty, at zero cost. Otherwise let $(k, v)$ be the root
entry of the heap. If the heap has one entry, extract-min returns $(k, v)$ together with the
queue whose heap is empty and in which $v$ has no position, at the cost of one position write
and one entry pop. If the heap has at least two entries, the root is swapped with the last entry
and the positions of both are updated, the last slot is removed, the position of $v$ is cleared,
and the new root is sifted down: while it has a child, let $c$ be its smaller child (the left
one on ties); if $c$ is smaller than it, the two are swapped and the positions of both are
updated, otherwise the sift stops. It returns $(k, v)$ together with the resulting queue, at the
cost of one swap, three position writes and one entry pop, plus, at each sift-down step, one
comparison between the two children when both exist, one comparison with $c$, and one swap and
two position writes when a swap is made.

articles.title: Indexed minimum queue
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type, let $W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$
with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined, and let $n$ be a natural number. An indexed
minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$ consists of a binary min-heap whose entries are
pairs $(k, v)$ of a key $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$ and an identity $v < n$, ordered lexicographically
(first by key, then by identity), together with a position vector assigning to each identity
$v < n$ either nothing or an index $i < n$. It is required that the heap has at most $n$ entries
and that, for all identities $v < n$ and indices $i < n$, the position of $v$ is $i$ exactly
when $i$ is a slot of the heap whose entry has identity $v$.

articles.title: Insertion fails exactly on present identities
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a
linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be an identity and let
$k \in W \cup \{\top\}$. Inserting $v$ with key $k$ into $q$ returns no queue if and only if
the position vector of $q$ records a slot for $v$.

articles.title: Successful insertion into an indexed min queue
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a
linear order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $v$ be an identity and let
$k \in W \cup \{\top\}$, and suppose that inserting $v$ with key $k$ into $q$ returns the
queue $q'$. Then the heap of $q'$ is the binary min-heap push of the entry $(k, v)$ onto the
heap of $q$; the position vector of $q'$ records a slot $i$ for $v$, with $i$ less than the
size of the heap array of $q'$, and that array holds $(k, v)$ at index $i$; and every identity
$w \neq v$ has a recorded slot in $q'$ if and only if it has one in $q$.

articles.title: Logarithmic event bound for indexed-queue insertion
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type
and let $W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined. Let $q$ be an
indexed minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$ with keys in $W \cup \{\top\}$ whose
heap has $s$ entries, let $v < n$ be an identity and let $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$ be a key. For
each of the five counted events (comparisons, swaps, position reads, position writes, and entry
appends, pops or replacements), the number of times that event occurs when inserting $v$ with
key $k$ into $q$ is at most $20 (\lfloor \log_2 (s + 1) \rfloor + 1)$.

articles.title: Insertion into an indexed minimum queue
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type and let
$W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined. Costs are counted as five
event counts: comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector,
and entry appends, pops or replacements. Given an indexed minimum queue $q$ over the identities
$0, \dots, n-1$ with keys in $W \cup \{\top\}$, whose heap entries (pairs of a key and an
identity) are ordered lexicographically, first by key and then by identity, an identity $v < n$
and a key $k \in W \cup \{\top\}$, insertion fails (returns nothing) when the position vector of
$q$ assigns an index to $v$, at the cost of one position read. Otherwise it appends the entry
$(k, v)$ at the end of the heap, sets the position of $v$ to that slot, and sifts the entry up:
while it is not at the root and is smaller than its parent, it is swapped with its parent and
the positions of both swapped identities are updated. It returns the resulting queue, at the
cost of one position read, one position write and one entry append, plus one comparison for
each comparison with a parent and one swap and two position writes for each swap.

articles.title: Membership reads the position vector
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear
order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $v$ be an identity. The membership
test for $v$ in $q$ returns true if and only if the position vector of $q$ records a slot for
$v$.

articles.title: Membership costs one position read
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear
order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $v$ be an identity. The cost of the
membership test for $v$ in $q$, counted in five event classes (comparisons, swaps,
position-vector reads, position-vector writes, and entry appends, pops or replacements), is
exactly one position-vector read and no event of any other class.

articles.title: Membership test in an indexed minimum queue
articles.statement:
Costs are counted as five event counts:
comparisons, swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry
appends, pops or replacements. For an indexed minimum queue $q$ over the identities
$0, \dots, n-1$ and an identity $v < n$, the membership test returns true exactly when the
position vector of $q$ assigns an index to $v$, and its cost is one position read and no other
event.

articles.title: Absent identities carry no heap entry
articles.statement:
Let $q$ be an indexed min queue over a linear
order $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $v$ be an identity. The position
vector of $q$ records no slot for $v$ if and only if no entry of the heap array of $q$ has
identity $v$.

articles.title: Recorded positions lie inside the heap
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type and let $q$
