be an indexed min-queue over $W$ with identities in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. If the position
table of $q$ records slot $i$ for an identity $v$, then $i$ is less than the number of
entries currently stored in the heap array of $q$.

articles.title: Event bound for building an indexed queue by repeated insertion
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly
ordered type and let $W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined. Let
$q_0, \dots, q_n$ be indexed minimum queues over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$ with keys in
$W \cup \{\top\}$, and let $k_0, \dots, k_{n-1}$ be keys in $W \cup \{\top\}$. Suppose $q_0$ is
the empty queue and, for each $i < n$, inserting identity $i$ with key $k_i$ into $q_i$ succeeds
and returns $q_{i+1}$. Then for each of the five counted events (comparisons, swaps, position
reads, position writes, and entry appends, pops or replacements), the total number of times that
event occurs over these $n$ insertions is at most $20 n (\lfloor \log_2 (n + 1) \rfloor + 1)$.

articles.statement: The multi-pass cost bound (15.2) for equally sized heaps.

articles.title: Cost bound for one adjacent merging pass
articles.statement: One adjacent pass costs at most the number of pairs times the merge bound.

articles.title: Lower bound on all elements of a heap
articles.statement: All elements in heap are ≥ x (for heap ordering)

Graded theorem: correctness of lheap_list2 and complexity equivalence.

articles.statement: List construction satisfies min-heap ordering.

articles.title: Min-heap ordering of every heap in a list
articles.statement: Every heap in the list satisfies the min-heap ordering predicate.

articles.title: Min-heap property
articles.statement: Min-heap property: root ≤ all in subtrees

articles.statement: A reusable per-input form of the three construction-correctness conjuncts.

lheap_list2: convert list to leftist heap via merge_all2 (tail-recursive adj).

articles.statement: Leftist heap: Empty or Node rank value left right

articles.statement: Every heap in the list has correct stored ranks and is leftist.

Node constructor restoring the leftist property

Helper to restore leftist property.

articles.title: Accumulator characterization of tail-recursive adjacent merging
articles.statement:
The accumulator is a reversed prefix; newly merged pairs follow it in
input order. This additional output characterization is not required by the
original exercise. Append appears only in the specification, not the algorithm.

articles.title: Tail-recursive adjacent merging with an accumulator
articles.statement:
Tail-recursive merge_adj2 with accumulator, no use of List.append.
   Genuinely tail-recursive: uses an accumulator and reverse at base case.
   Does not use List.append (avoids append operator).
   Complexity model: only merge steps counted, so `T_merge_adj2 acc ts = T_merge_adj ts`
   should hold; accumulator reversal overhead is intentionally excluded
   per textbook convention that only merge calls are counted.

articles.title: Cost of merging leftist heaps
articles.statement: Cost of merge: number of merge steps (only merge calls counted)

articles.title: Increment costs at most the width
articles.statement:
For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits,
lowest bit first), the cost of incrementing $b$ is at most $k$.

articles.title: Incrementing the all-ones counter costs the full width
articles.statement:
For every $k$, the cost of
incrementing the $k$-bit counter whose $k$ bits are all $1$ is exactly $k$.

articles.title: Exact cost of an increment
articles.statement:
Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter stored
lowest bit first, and let $t$ be the length of its initial run of $1$ bits, that is, the largest
$t \le k$ with $b_0 = \dots = b_{t-1} = 1$. The cost of incrementing $b$ is $t + 1$ if $t < k$,
and $t$ if $t = k$.

articles.title: Increment adds one with wraparound
articles.statement:
Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter
stored lowest bit first, with bits $b_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and unsigned value
$v(b) = \sum_{i < k} b_i 2^i$. If $b'$ is the counter returned by incrementing $b$, then
$v(b') = (v(b) + 1) \bmod 2^k$.

articles.title: Binary counter increment
articles.statement:
A $k$-bit counter is a vector $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ of bits
stored lowest bit first. Incrementing $b$ changes the initial run of $1$ bits $b_0, \dots, b_{t-1}$
to $0$ and then changes the first $0$ bit $b_t$, if there is one, to $1$; if every bit is $1$, all
bits become $0$ and no new bit is added. The result is again a $k$-bit counter, and the cost of
the increment is the number of bits changed, one unit per changed bit.

articles.title: Potential identity for reset
articles.statement:
For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the
cost of resetting $b$ plus the number of $1$ bits in the returned counter equals the number of
$1$ bits in $b$.

articles.title: Reset is idempotent
articles.statement:
For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter returned by
resetting $b$ returns the same counter as resetting $b$ once.

articles.title: A second reset costs nothing
articles.statement:
For every $k$-bit counter $b$, resetting the counter
returned by resetting $b$ has cost $0$.

articles.title: Reset cost is the Hamming distance
articles.statement:
Let $b = (b_0, \dots, b_{k-1})$ be a $k$-bit counter
and $b' = (b'_0, \dots, b'_{k-1})$ the counter returned by resetting $b$. The cost of resetting
$b$ equals the number of indices $i < k$ with $b_i \ne b'_i$.

articles.title: Reset costs at most the width
articles.statement:
For every $k$-bit counter $b$ (a vector of $k$ bits), the
cost of resetting $b$ is at most $k$.

articles.title: Resetting the all-false counter costs nothing
articles.statement:
For every width $k$, resetting the
all-false bit vector of width $k$ has cost $0$.

articles.title: Resetting a width-zero counter costs nothing
articles.statement:
Resetting a bit vector of width $0$ has
cost $0$.

articles.title: Cost of resetting a binary counter
articles.statement:
For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the cost of
resetting $b$ equals the number of positions of $b$ that hold true.

articles.title: Reset returns the all-false counter
articles.statement:
For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits
returned by resetting $b$ are, in order, $k$ copies of false.

articles.title: Reset yields the value zero
articles.statement:
For every bit vector $b$ of width $k$, the bits returned
by resetting $b$, read low-order bit first as an unsigned binary numeral, have value $0$.

articles.title: Resetting a binary counter
articles.statement:
Resetting a bit vector $b$ of width $k$ returns the
all-false bit vector of width $k$ and charges cost $1$ for each position of $b$ that holds
true, that is, for each bit it changes from true to false.

articles.title: Flip counts of the individual bits
articles.statement:
Let $k$, $i$ and $n$ be natural numbers
with $i < k$, and for each $t$ let $c_t$ be the bit vector returned by running $t$ increments
from the all-false bit vector of width $k$. Then the number of $t < n$ such that the bit at
position $i$ of $c_t$ (counting from the low-order bit, starting at $0$) differs from the bit at
position $i$ of $c_{t+1}$ is $\lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.

articles.title: One more increment
articles.statement:
For every bit vector $b$ and every natural number $n$, the bit vector
returned by running $n + 1$ increments from $b$ is the increment of the bit vector returned by
running $n$ increments from $b$.

articles.title: Exact cost of increments from zero
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $n$, running
$n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$ costs exactly
$\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \lfloor n / 2^i \rfloor$.

articles.title: Lower bound on the cost of increments from zero
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$
and $n$ with $k > 0$, running $n$ increments from the all-false bit vector of width $k$
costs at least $n$.

articles.title: Aggregate cost bound for the binary counter
articles.statement:
For every width $k$ and every $n > 0$,
performing $n$ successive increments on the $k$-bit counter that starts with all bits zero
costs strictly fewer than $2n$ bit changes in total.

articles.title: Cost recurrence for the binary counter run
articles.statement:
For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter
$b$ and every $n$, the cost of running $n + 1$ successive increments from $b$ equals the cost of
running $n$ increments from $b$ plus the cost of incrementing the counter that the $n$-step run
returns.

articles.title: Counter value after successive increments
articles.statement:
For every width $k$, every $k$-bit counter $b$
and every $n$, let $v$ be the value of $b$ read as an unsigned binary number with the least
significant bit first. After $n$ successive increments starting from $b$, the counter read the
same way has value $(v + n) \bmod 2^k$.

articles.title: Running zero increments
articles.statement:
For every width $k$ and every $k$-bit counter $b$, running zero
increments from $b$ returns $b$ unchanged at cost zero.

articles.title: Running the binary counter
articles.statement:
For a width $k$, a $k$-bit counter $b$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
the run of $n$ increments from $b$ is defined recursively. The run of $0$ increments returns $b$
at cost zero. The run of $n + 1$ increments performs the run of $n$ increments, then increments
the counter it returned and returns the result; its cost is the cost of the $n$-step run plus
the cost of that increment.

articles.title: Popping the back of a deque
articles.statement:
If popping the back of a deque $d$ succeeds and returns an
element $x$ and a deque $d'$, then the sequence represented by $d$ is the sequence represented by
$d'$ followed by $x$.

articles.title: Popping the front of a deque
articles.statement:
If popping the front of a deque $d$ succeeds and returns an
element $x$ and a deque $d'$, then the sequence represented by $d$ is $x$ followed by the sequence
represented by $d'$.

articles.title: Pushing at the back of a deque
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$ and element $x$, the sequence
represented by the deque obtained by pushing $x$ at the back of $d$ is the sequence represented by
$d$ followed by $x$.

articles.title: Pushing at the front of a deque
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$ and element $x$, the sequence
represented by the deque obtained by pushing $x$ at the front of $d$ is $x$ followed by the
sequence represented by $d$.

articles.title: Represented sequence of a deque
articles.statement:
The sequence represented by a deque with front list $f$
and back list $b$ is $f$ followed by the reverse of $b$; it lists the elements from front to
back.

articles.title: Two-list deque
articles.statement:
A deque with elements in a type $\alpha$ consists of two lists of elements
of $\alpha$, the front list and the back list. The front list holds the front part of the
sequence in order and the back list holds the back part in reverse order.

articles.title: The empty deque
articles.statement:
The empty deque is the deque whose front list and back list are both
empty.

articles.title: Correctness of the deque emptiness test
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$, the emptiness test of $d$
returns true if and only if the sequence represented by $d$ is empty.

articles.title: Emptiness test for a deque
articles.statement:
The emptiness test of a deque returns true exactly when both
its front list and its back list are empty.

articles.title: Peeking at the back of a deque
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$, peeking at the back of $d$ returns
the last element of the sequence represented by $d$ when that sequence is nonempty, and returns
nothing when it is empty.

articles.title: Peek at the back of a deque
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$,
where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Peeking at the back of $d$ returns, without removing it,
the first element of $b$ when $b$ is nonempty, and otherwise the last element of $f$; when both
lists are empty it returns no element.

articles.title: Peeking at the front gives the first element
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$, peeking at the front of
$d$ returns the first element of the sequence represented by $d$, and returns no element when
that sequence is empty.

articles.title: Peek at the front of a deque
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$,
where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Peeking at the front of $d$ returns, without removing it,
the first element of $f$ when $f$ is nonempty, and otherwise the last element of $b$; when both
lists are empty it returns no element.

articles.title: Popping the back fails exactly on empty deques
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$, popping the back of
$d$ returns no result if and only if the sequence represented by $d$ is empty.

articles.title: Pop the back of a deque
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$, where
$b$ is stored in reverse order. If $b$ has first element $v$ and remaining list $b'$, popping the
back of $d$ returns $v$ together with the deque with front list $f$ and back list $b'$. If $b$ is
empty and the reverse of $f$ has first element $v$ and remaining list $r$, it returns $v$ together
with the deque with empty front list and back list $r$. If both lists are empty, it returns no
result.

articles.title: Popping the front fails exactly on empty deques
articles.statement:
For every deque $d$, popping the front of
$d$ returns no result if and only if the sequence represented by $d$ is empty.

articles.title: Pop the front of a deque
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$, where
$b$ is stored in reverse order. If $f$ has first element $v$ and remaining list $f'$, popping the
front of $d$ returns $v$ together with the deque with front list $f'$ and back list $b$. If $f$ is
empty and the reverse of $b$ has first element $v$ and remaining list $r$, it returns $v$ together
with the deque with front list $r$ and empty back list. If both lists are empty, it returns no
result.

articles.title: Push at the back of a deque
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$,
where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Pushing an element $x$ at the back of $d$ gives the deque
with front list $f$ and back list consisting of $x$ followed by the entries of $b$.

articles.title: Push at the front of a deque
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a deque with front list $f$ and back list $b$,
where $b$ is stored in reverse order. Pushing an element $x$ at the front of $d$ gives the deque
with front list consisting of $x$ followed by the entries of $f$, and back list $b$.

articles.title: Empty circular list with a sentinel
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ slots indexed by
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, each either empty or holding a node with a payload and optional next and
previous indices, and let $s$ be an index. Then $S$ represents the empty circular list with
sentinel $s$ if and only if slot $s$ holds a node whose next index and previous index are both
$s$.

articles.title: Circular doubly linked list with a sentinel
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ slots indexed by
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, each either empty or holding a node with a payload and optional next and
previous indices. The store $S$ represents a circular list with sentinel $s$ and data nodes
$x_1, \dots, x_k$ (a list of indices) when the $x_i$ are pairwise distinct and all differ from
$s$; slot $s$ holds a node whose next index is $x_1$ and whose previous index is $x_k$ (both
are $s$ when $k = 0$); and for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le k$, slot $x_i$ holds a node whose
previous index is $x_{i-1}$ and whose next index is $x_{i+1}$, where $x_0 = x_{k+1} = s$.

articles.title: Deletion from a doubly linked list allocates and frees nothing
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$
cells, each empty or holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or
NIL), let $h$ be a header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose
cell holds a node $X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor
$X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ be the store returned
by List Delete on $S$, $h$ and $x$. Then for every index $z$, the cell $S'(z)$ holds a node if and
only if $S(z)$ does.

articles.title: The deleted node keeps its record
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding
a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$ be a header (an
index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a node $X$ such that
the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor $X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes
whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ be the store returned by List Delete on $S$, $h$
and $x$. Then $S'(x) = S(x)$: the deleted node stays allocated with its payload and both of its
pointers unchanged.

articles.title: Deletion preserves lists avoiding the deleted node's neighbors
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$
cells, each empty or holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or
NIL), let $h$ be a header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose
cell holds a node $X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor
$X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ be the store returned
by List Delete on $S$, $h$ and $x$. Let $h_0$ be a header and $L$ a list of indices such that $S$
with header $h_0$ represents $L$: the entries of $L$ are distinct, $h_0$ is the first entry of
$L$ (NIL if $L$ is empty), and the cell of each entry of $L$ holds a node whose previous and next
pointers are the adjacent entries of $L$, NIL at the ends. If neither $X.\mathrm{prev}$ nor
$X.\mathrm{next}$ is an entry of $L$, then $S'$ with header $h_0$ also represents $L$.

articles.title: Deletion changes only the cells of the neighbors
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each
empty or holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$
be a header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a
node $X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor
$X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ be the store returned
by List Delete on $S$, $h$ and $x$. Then $S'(z) = S(z)$ for every index $z$ with
$X.\mathrm{prev} \ne z$ and $X.\mathrm{next} \ne z$.

articles.title: Cellwise result of doubly linked list deletion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each
empty or holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$
be a header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a
node $X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor
$X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ be the store returned
by List Delete on $S$, $h$ and $x$. For an index $z$, let $C$ be the cell $S(z)$ with the next
pointer of its node set to $X.\mathrm{next}$ if $X.\mathrm{prev} = z$, and $C = S(z)$ otherwise.
Then $S'(z)$ is $C$ with the previous pointer of its node set to $X.\mathrm{prev}$ if
$X.\mathrm{next} = z$, and $S'(z) = C$ otherwise; an empty cell stays empty. So the write at the
predecessor is applied before the write at the successor.

articles.title: Header after doubly linked list deletion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or
holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$ be a
header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a node
$X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor $X.\mathrm{next}$
hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $h'$ be the header returned by List Delete on
$S$, $h$ and $x$. Then $h' = h$ if $X.\mathrm{prev}$ is not NIL, and $h' = X.\mathrm{next}$ if
$X.\mathrm{prev}$ is NIL.

articles.title: Deletion preserves payloads
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a node
(a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$ be a header (an index
in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a node $X$ such that the
cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor $X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes
whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ be the store returned by List Delete on $S$, $h$
and $x$. Then for every index $z$, either $S'(z)$ and $S(z)$ are both empty, or both hold nodes
and these two nodes have the same payload.

articles.title: Correctness of doubly linked list deletion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or
holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$ be a
header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a node
$X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor $X.\mathrm{next}$
hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $S'$ and $h'$ be the store and header
returned by List Delete on $S$, $h$ and $x$. Let $L$ be a list of indices such that $S$ with
header $h$ represents $L$: the entries of $L$ are distinct, $h$ is the first entry of $L$ (NIL if
$L$ is empty), and the cell of each entry of $L$ holds a node whose previous and next pointers
are the adjacent entries of $L$, NIL at the ends. If $x$ is an entry of $L$, then $S'$ with
header $h'$ represents the list obtained from $L$ by removing $x$.

articles.title: Result of doubly linked list deletion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or
holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL), let $h$ be a
header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell holds a node
$X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor $X.\mathrm{next}$
hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Let $T$ be $S$ if $X.\mathrm{prev}$ is NIL, and
otherwise $S$ with the next pointer of the node in cell $X.\mathrm{prev}$ set to
$X.\mathrm{next}$. Then List Delete on $S$, $h$ and $x$ returns the store equal to $T$ if
$X.\mathrm{next}$ is NIL, and otherwise to $T$ with the previous pointer of the node in cell
$X.\mathrm{next}$ of $T$ set to $X.\mathrm{prev}$, together with the header $h$ if
$X.\mathrm{prev}$ is not NIL and $X.\mathrm{next}$ if it is NIL. The successor's node is read
from $T$, so when $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and $X.\mathrm{next}$ are the same index (not NIL), both
pointer updates apply to its node.

articles.title: Doubly linked list deletion costs at most four events
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells,
each empty or holding a node (a payload with next and previous pointers, each an index or NIL),
let $h$ be a header (an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL), and let $x$ be an index whose cell
holds a node $X$ such that the cells at the predecessor $X.\mathrm{prev}$ and the successor
$X.\mathrm{next}$ hold nodes whenever these pointers are not NIL. Then List Delete on $S$, $h$
and $x$ costs at most $4$, counting NIL tests and executed pointer and header assignments.

articles.title: Running time of doubly linked list deletion
articles.statement:
Let the store be an array of cells, each
either empty or holding a node with optional next and previous pointers, let $h$ be the optional
head pointer, and let $x$ be a cell holding a node such that each cell named by its previous or
next pointer also holds a node. Counting one unit per NIL test and per executed pointer or head
assignment, deleting $x$ from the list with head $h$ costs exactly $4$ units if the node at $x$
has a next pointer, and exactly $3$ units otherwise.

articles.title: Deletion from a doubly linked list
articles.statement:
Let the store be an array of cells, each either empty
or holding a node with a payload and optional next and previous pointers to cells, let $h$ be
the optional head pointer, and let $x$ be a cell holding a node such that each cell named by its
previous or next pointer also holds a node. Following CLRS `LIST-DELETE`, deleting $x$ returns a
new store and head as follows. If the node at $x$ has a previous pointer $p$, the next pointer of
the node at $p$ is set to the next pointer of $x$ and the head stays $h$; otherwise the head
becomes the next pointer of $x$. Then, if the node at $x$ has a next pointer $s$, the previous
pointer of the node at $s$ in the store from the first step is set to the previous pointer of $x$.
The computation is charged one unit for each of the two NIL tests and one unit for each executed
pointer or head assignment, so three or four units in total.

The record stored at $x$ is kept and no cell is freed; list consistency is needed only for
correctness, not to run the procedure.

articles.title: Doubly-linked-list insertion neither allocates nor frees cells
articles.statement:
For a store $S$ and
allocated cells $x$ and $y$ such that the successor of $y$ in $S$, if any, is allocated, every
cell $z$ of the store returned by inserting $x$ after $y$ is allocated if and only if cell $z$ of
$S$ is allocated. No distinctness of $x$, $y$ and the successor of $y$ is assumed.

articles.title: Doubly-linked-list insertion preserves disjoint lists
articles.statement:
Suppose the store $S$ with head
$h$ represents the list of cells $(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$ and with head $h'$ represents a list
$L'$ of cells, and that the two lists have no cell in common. Let $k < m$, let $x$ be an
allocated cell not in $L'$, and assume that cell $i_k$ and its successor in $S$, if any, are
allocated. Then the store returned by inserting $x$ after $i_k$, with head $h'$, still
represents $L'$.

articles.title: Frame property of doubly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
For a store $S$ and allocated cells $x$
and $y$ such that the successor of $y$ in $S$, if any, is allocated, let $z$ be a cell with
$z \ne x$, $z \ne y$, and $z$ not the successor of $y$ in $S$. Then cell $z$ of the store
returned by inserting $x$ after $y$ equals cell $z$ of $S$.

articles.title: Cells after doubly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
For a store $S$, allocated cells $x$ and $y$
such that the successor of $y$ in $S$, if any, is allocated, and any cell $z$, let $s$ be the
next pointer of $y$ in $S$. Let $c_1$ be the node of $x$ in $S$ with next pointer replaced by
$s$ and previous pointer replaced by $y$ if $z = x$, and the content of cell $z$ in $S$
otherwise. Let $c_2$ be $c_1$ with previous pointer replaced by $x$ if $s = z$, and $c_1$
otherwise. Then cell $z$ of the store returned by inserting $x$ after $y$ is $c_2$ with next
pointer replaced by $x$ if $z = y$, and $c_2$ otherwise (an empty cell stays empty).

No distinctness of $x$, $y$ and $s$ is assumed.

articles.title: Doubly-linked-list insertion preserves payloads
articles.statement:
For a store $S$ and allocated cells $x$
and $y$ such that the successor of $y$ in $S$, if any, is allocated, every cell $z$ of the store
returned by inserting $x$ after $y$ is empty exactly when cell $z$ of $S$ is empty, and
otherwise holds a node with the same payload as the node in cell $z$ of $S$.

No hypothesis on the payloads, such as distinct keys, is needed.

articles.title: Insertion into a represented doubly-linked list
articles.statement:
Suppose the store $S$ with head $h$
represents the list of distinct cells $(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$. Let $k < m$, let $x$ be an
allocated cell not among $i_0, \dots, i_{m-1}$, and assume that cell $i_k$ and its successor in
$S$, if any, are allocated. Then the store returned by inserting $x$ after $i_k$, with the same
head $h$, represents the list $(i_0, \dots, i_k, x, i_{k+1}, \dots, i_{m-1})$.

The hypothesis that $x$ is not in the list is used only in the proof; the insertion itself runs
without it.

articles.title: Result of doubly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
For a store $S$ and allocated cells $x$ and $y$
such that the successor of $y$ in $S$, if any, is allocated, let $s$ be the next pointer of $y$
in $S$. Let $S_1$ be $S$ with cell $x$ replaced by the node of $x$ with next pointer $s$ and
previous pointer $y$. Let $S_2 = S_1$ if $s$ is NIL; if $s$ is a cell $z$, let $S_2$ be $S_1$
with the previous pointer of the node in cell $z$ of $S_1$ replaced by $x$. Then the store
returned by inserting $x$ after $y$ is $S_2$ with the next pointer of the node in cell $y$ of
$S_2$ replaced by $x$.

No distinctness or representation hypothesis is assumed.

articles.title: Cost of doubly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
For a store $S$ and allocated cells $x$ and $y$
such that the successor of $y$ in $S$, if any, is allocated, the cost of inserting $x$ after
$y$, counting one unit per pointer assignment and per NIL test, is $5$ if $y$ has a successor
in $S$ and $4$ if the next pointer of $y$ in $S$ is NIL.

No distinctness of $x$ and $y$ is assumed.

articles.title: Doubly-linked-list insertion (LIST-INSERT)
articles.statement:
A store is an array of $n$ cells, each
either empty or holding a node with a payload and optional next and previous pointers to cells.
Given allocated cells $x$ and $y$ such that the successor of $y$, if any, is allocated,
inserting $x$ after $y$ performs the five lines of LIST-INSERT in order, each reading the store
as updated so far: set the next pointer of $x$ to the next pointer of $y$; set the previous
pointer of $x$ to $y$; test whether the next pointer of $y$ is NIL; if it is some cell $z$, set
the previous pointer of $z$ to $x$; set the next pointer of $y$ to $x$. The result is the
updated store, with cost one unit per pointer assignment and per NIL test.

articles.title: Doubly-linked list prepend preserves allocation
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on $s$,
$\mathrm{head}$ and $x$. Then for every identity $z$, $s'(z)$ is a node if and only if $s(z)$ is a
node.

articles.title: Doubly-linked list prepend preserves disjoint lists
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a
store assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Suppose moreover that $s$ with some head $o$ represents a
list $L = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k)$ of identities, that is, the $\ell_i$ are distinct, $o$ is
$\ell_1$ (NIL if $k = 0$), and each $s(\ell_i)$ is a node with previous pointer $\ell_{i-1}$ and
next pointer $\ell_{i+1}$ (NIL past the ends of $L$), that $x$ is not in $L$, and that
$\mathrm{head}$ is NIL or an identity not in $L$. Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on
$s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$. Then $s'$ with head $o$ also represents $L$.

articles.title: Doubly-linked list prepend leaves other cells unchanged
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a
store assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on $s$,
$\mathrm{head}$ and $x$. Then $s'(z) = s(z)$ for every identity $z$ with $z \ne x$ and
$\mathrm{head} \ne z$.

articles.title: Cells after doubly-linked list prepend
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store assigning
to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an identity, and
let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an identity,
$s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$
and $x$. For every identity $z$, let $c$ be the node $s(x)$ with next pointer $\mathrm{head}$ and
previous pointer NIL if $z = x$, and $c = s(z)$ otherwise. Then $s'(z)$ is $c$ with previous pointer
$x$ (nothing, if $c$ is nothing) when $\mathrm{head} = z$, and $s'(z) = c$ otherwise.

articles.title: Prepending makes the supplied node the head
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Then the head returned by List Prepend on $s$,
$\mathrm{head}$ and $x$ is $x$.

articles.title: Pointers of the node prepended to a doubly-linked list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a
store assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Suppose moreover that $\mathrm{head}$ is not $x$ (it may be
NIL). Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$. Then $s'(x)$
is the node $s(x)$ with next pointer $\mathrm{head}$ and previous pointer NIL.

articles.title: Old head after doubly-linked list prepend
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Suppose moreover that $\mathrm{head}$ is an identity $h$
with $h \ne x$. Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$.
Then $s'(h)$ is the node $s(h)$ with previous pointer $x$.

articles.title: Doubly-linked list prepend preserves payloads
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Let $s'$ be the store returned by List Prepend on $s$,
$\mathrm{head}$ and $x$. Then for every identity $z$, either $s(z)$ and $s'(z)$ are both nothing, or
both are nodes with the same payload.

articles.title: Correctness of doubly-linked list prepend
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an
identity, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an
identity, $s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Suppose moreover that $s$ with head $\mathrm{head}$
represents a list $L = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k)$ of identities, that is, the $\ell_i$ are distinct,
$\mathrm{head}$ is $\ell_1$ (NIL if $k = 0$), and each $s(\ell_i)$ is a node with previous pointer
$\ell_{i-1}$ and next pointer $\ell_{i+1}$ (NIL past the ends of $L$), and that $x$ is not in $L$.
Let $s'$ and $h'$ be the store and head returned by List Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$.
Then $s'$ with head $h'$ represents the list $(x, \ell_1, \dots, \ell_k)$.

articles.title: Result of doubly-linked list prepend
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store assigning to
each identity $i < n$ either a node or nothing, let $\mathrm{head}$ be NIL or an identity, and let
$x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node and, when $\mathrm{head}$ is an identity,
$s(\mathrm{head})$ is a node. Let $u$ be $s$ with the cell at $x$ replaced by the node $s(x)$ with
next pointer $\mathrm{head}$ and previous pointer NIL. Then List Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and
$x$ returns the head $x$ together with the store $u$ when $\mathrm{head}$ is NIL, and, when
$\mathrm{head}$ is an identity $h$, together with the store obtained from $u$ by replacing its cell
at $h$ with the node $u(h)$ with previous pointer $x$ (leaving the cell empty if $u(h)$ is
nothing).

This holds also when $h = x$.

articles.title: Uniform cost bound for doubly linked list prepend
articles.statement:
Let a store assign to each identity
below $n$ either nothing or a doubly linked list node, let the head be an identity below $n$ or
NIL, and let $x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node, where the store entry of the head is
also a node when the head is not NIL. Then prepending $x$ costs at most $5$ time units, counting
one unit per pointer assignment and per NIL test of the old head.

articles.title: Exact cost of doubly linked list prepend
articles.statement:
Let a store assign to each identity below $n$
either nothing or a doubly linked list node, let the head be an identity below $n$ or NIL, and let
$x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node, where the store entry of the head is also a node
when the head is not NIL. Then prepending $x$ costs exactly $5$ time units if the head is not NIL
and exactly $4$ if it is NIL, counting one unit per pointer assignment and per NIL test of the
old head.

articles.title: Prepending a node to a doubly linked list
articles.statement:
Let a store assign to each identity below $n$
either nothing or a doubly linked list node whose pointers are identities below $n$ or NIL, let
the head be an identity below $n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node,
where the store entry of the head is also a node when the head is not NIL. The procedure sets the
next pointer of $x$ to the head, then sets the previous pointer of $x$ to NIL, then tests whether
the head is NIL; if it is not, it sets the previous pointer of the node at the head (read after
the two writes at $x$) to $x$. Finally it makes $x$ the new head and returns the updated store
together with the head $x$. One time unit is charged for each pointer assignment and for the NIL
test, so the cost is $4$ when the head is NIL and $5$ otherwise.

articles.title: Sentinel search preserves the circular list
articles.statement:
If a store circularly represents the list $L$
of data nodes with sentinel $s$, then for every key $k$ the store returned by sentinel search for
$k$ still circularly represents $L$ with sentinel $s$.

articles.title: Sentinel search changes only the sentinel's key
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be the sentinel of some list of
data nodes that a store circularly represents, and let $k$ be a key. In the store returned by
sentinel search for $k$, the cell $s$ holds the original sentinel node with its key replaced by
$k$ and its satellite data and next and prev links unchanged, and every cell $z \ne s$ holds
exactly what it held in the input store.

articles.title: Sentinel search returns the first matching node
articles.statement:
If a store circularly represents the list
$L$ of data nodes with sentinel $s$, then sentinel search for a key $k$ returns the first node of
$L$ (in list order, which starts at the successor of $s$) whose key in the input store is $k$, and
returns no node if no node of $L$ has key $k$. In particular, the sentinel is never returned.

articles.title: Cost of sentinel search
articles.statement:
If a store circularly represents the list $L$ of $n$ data nodes
with sentinel $s$, then sentinel search for a key $k$ costs exactly $2i + 4$, where $i$ is the
position, counting from $0$, of the first node of $L$ whose key is $k$, and $i = n$ if no node of
$L$ has key $k$.

That is, two units for each mismatching data node before the match plus four fixed units; an
unsuccessful search scans all $n$ data nodes.

articles.title: Search in a circular list with a sentinel
articles.statement:
Let a store have cells indexed by
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$, each empty or holding a node that carries a key, satellite data and optional
next and prev links, and let the cell $s$ be the sentinel of some list of data nodes that the
store circularly represents. Sentinel search for a key $k$ first overwrites the key of the
sentinel with $k$, keeping its satellite data and links, then starts at the successor of $s$ and
follows next links until it reaches a node whose key is $k$. It returns the modified store
together with that node, or no node if the scan stopped at $s$.

Only the sentinel key is overwritten, and its old key is not restored. The cost charges one unit
for the key write, one for initializing the cursor, one for each key comparison, one for each
advance past a mismatching node and one for the final test against $s$; reads and result
construction are free, and physical storage or bit operations are not counted.

articles.title: Doubly linked list node
articles.statement:
A doubly linked list node with payloads in $\alpha$ and identities
in $\iota$ consists of a payload in $\alpha$ (the key together with any satellite data), a next
pointer and a previous pointer, each of which is either an identity in $\iota$ or NIL.

articles.title: Store representing a doubly linked list
articles.statement:
Let a store assign to each identity below $n$
either nothing or a doubly linked list node whose pointers are identities below $n$ or NIL, and
let the head be an identity below $n$ or NIL. The store and head represent the list of identities
$i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$ when these identities are pairwise distinct, the head is $i_0$ (and NIL
when $k = 0$), and for each $j < k$ the store entry at $i_j$ is a node whose previous pointer is
NIL if $j = 0$ and $i_{j-1}$ otherwise, and whose next pointer is $i_{j+1}$ if $j + 1 < k$ and
NIL otherwise.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion preserves allocation
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an address whose
cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells at $p$ and $n$
are nonempty. For every address $z$, the cell at $z$ after sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ is
nonempty if and only if the cell of $S$ at $z$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion removes a node from its circular list
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$
an address whose cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the
cells at $p$ and $n$ are nonempty. If $S$ represents a circular doubly linked list with sentinel
$s$ and data addresses $\ell$, and $x$ occurs in $\ell$, then the store returned by sentinel
deletion of $x$ from $S$ represents a circular doubly linked list with sentinel $s$ and the
list of data addresses obtained from $\ell$ by removing the first occurrence of $x$.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion keeps the deleted node
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an address
whose cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells at $p$
and $n$ are nonempty. The cell at $x$ after sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ equals the cell of
$S$ at $x$, so the deleted node stays allocated and unchanged.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion preserves disjoint circular lists
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an
address whose cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells
at $p$ and $n$ are nonempty. Suppose $S$ represents a circular doubly linked list with sentinel
$s$ and data addresses $\ell$, with $x$ in $\ell$, and also one with sentinel $t$ and data
addresses $m$, such that no address occurs both among $s$ and $\ell$ and among $t$ and $m$.
Then the store returned by sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ still represents the circular
doubly linked list with sentinel $t$ and data addresses $m$.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion changes only the two neighbours
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an
address whose cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells
at $p$ and $n$ are nonempty. For every address $z$ with $z \ne p$ and $z \ne n$, the cell at $z$
after sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ equals the cell of $S$ at $z$.

articles.title: Cells after sentinel deletion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an address whose cell
holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells at $p$ and $n$ are
nonempty. For every address $z$, let $C$ be the cell of $S$ at $z$ if $z \ne p$, and that cell
with its next address set to $n$ if $z = p$. Then after sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ the
cell at $z$ is $C$ if $z \ne n$, and $C$ with its previous address set to $p$ if $z = n$.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion preserves payloads
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an address whose
cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells at $p$ and $n$
are nonempty. For every address $z$, the cell at $z$ after sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$
and the cell of $S$ at $z$ are either both empty or both hold nodes with the same payload.

The payload includes any key and satellite data.

articles.title: The store returned by sentinel deletion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an address
whose cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells at $p$
and $n$ are nonempty. Let $S_1$ be $S$ with the node at $p$ replaced by a copy whose next
address is $n$. Then sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ returns $S_1$ with the node of $S_1$ at
$n$ replaced by a copy whose previous address is $p$.

articles.title: Sentinel deletion takes two pointer assignments
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store and $x$ an
address whose cell holds a node with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells
at $p$ and $n$ are nonempty. Then sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ has cost exactly $2$, one
for each pointer assignment.

This includes the alias cases in which $p$, $n$ and $x$ are not pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Deletion from a circular list with a sentinel
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a node store with $c$ cells,
each either empty or holding a node (a payload, an optional next address and an optional
previous address in $\{0, \dots, c-1\}$). Let $x$ be an address whose cell holds a node $\nu$
with previous address $p$ and next address $n$, where the cells at $p$ and $n$ are nonempty.
Sentinel deletion of $x$ from $S$ is the timed computation that first sets the next address of
the node at $p$ to $n$, at cost $1$, then sets the previous address of the node at $n$ in the
resulting store to $p$, at cost $1$, and returns the store obtained.

These dereferences are its only preconditions: it does not check that $x$ is not the sentinel
or that $x$ lies on a represented list.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion preserves allocation
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or
holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL,
and the cell it points to is allocated. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel insertion of
$x$ after $y$. Then every cell $z$ is allocated in $S'$ if and only if it is allocated in $S$.

No distinctness of $x$, $y$, $z$ and the successor of $y$ is assumed.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion preserves the circular list
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each
empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is
not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Suppose $S$ circularly represents the list $L$
of cells with sentinel $s$, that $L$ is the concatenation of lists $B$ and $A$, and that $y$ is
the last element of $B$, or $y = s$ if $B$ is empty. If $x \ne s$ and $x$ does not occur in $L$,
then the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$ circularly represents, with
sentinel $s$, the list consisting of the elements of $B$, then $x$, then the elements of $A$.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion preserves a disjoint circular list
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$
cells, each empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next
pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Suppose $S$ circularly
represents the list $L$ with sentinel $s$, that $L$ is the concatenation of lists $B$ and $A$,
and that $y$ is the last element of $B$, or $y = s$ if $B$ is empty. Suppose $S$ also circularly
represents the list $M$ with sentinel $t$, that no cell among $s$ and the elements of $L$ equals
$t$ or an element of $M$, and that $x \ne t$ and $x$ does not occur in $M$. Then the store
returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$ still circularly represents $M$ with sentinel
$t$.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion leaves other cells unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each
empty or holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is
not NIL, and the cell it points to is allocated. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel
insertion of $x$ after $y$. If a cell $z$ differs from $x$ and from $y$, and the next pointer of
$y$ in $S$ is not $z$, then $z$ has the same content in $S'$ as in $S$.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion, cell by cell
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding a
node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the
cell it points to is allocated; write $S[c]$ for the node at an allocated cell $c$. Let $S'$ be
the store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$. Then for every cell $z$, the content of
$z$ in $S'$ is obtained from its content in $S$ by three steps in order: if $z = x$, replace the
content by the node $S[x]$ with next pointer equal to the next pointer of $S[y]$ and previous
pointer $y$; if the next pointer of $S[y]$ is $z$, set the previous pointer to $x$; if $z = y$,
set the next pointer to $x$. The last two steps leave an empty cell empty.

No distinctness of $x$, $y$, $z$ and the successor of $y$ is assumed.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion preserves payloads
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or
holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL,
and the cell it points to is allocated. Let $S'$ be the store returned by sentinel insertion of
$x$ after $y$. Then for every cell $z$, either $z$ is empty in both $S$ and $S'$, or it holds a
node in both and the two nodes have the same payload, including keys and satellite data.

articles.title: The store after sentinel insertion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding
a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the
cell $w$ it points to is allocated; write $S[c]$ for the node at an allocated cell $c$. Then the
store returned by sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$ is obtained from $S$ by three updates, each
applied to the result of the previous one: replace the content of $x$ by the node $S[x]$ with next
pointer equal to the next pointer of $S[y]$ and previous pointer $y$; set the previous pointer of
the node at $w$ to $x$; set the next pointer of the node at $y$ to $x$.

No freshness or distinctness of $x$, $y$ and $w$ is assumed.

articles.title: Sentinel insertion takes four steps
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or holding
a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not NIL, and the
cell it points to is allocated. Then sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$ in $S$ costs exactly $4$
time units, one per pointer assignment.

This counts logical pointer assignments, not full RAM cost.

articles.title: Sentinel list insertion (LIST-INSERT′)
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store of $n$ cells, each empty or
holding a node, in which the cells $x$ and $y$ are allocated, the next pointer of $y$ is not
NIL, and the cell $w$ it points to is allocated. Sentinel insertion of $x$ after $y$ performs four
pointer assignments in order, each costing one time unit, and returns the resulting store: set
the next pointer of $x$ to the next pointer of $y$; set the previous pointer of $x$ to $y$; set
the previous pointer of the successor $w$ of $y$ to $x$; set the next pointer of $y$ to $x$.

Each assignment reads the store left by the previous ones, so aliased cells see earlier writes.
Unlike LIST-INSERT, there is no NIL test.

articles.title: Formula for the contents of a dynamic table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The contents of
$T$ is the array obtained from the prefix $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$ by skipping the empty slots and
keeping the items of the occupied ones, in order.

articles.title: Contents of a dynamic table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$,
each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The contents of $T$ is the array of the
items held by the occupied slots among $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, in order; empty slots in this
prefix are skipped.

The insertion procedure never consults the contents.

articles.title: The empty dynamic table has no slots and no items
articles.statement:
The empty dynamic table has an empty
slot array, so capacity $0$, and item count $0$.

articles.title: Empty dynamic table
articles.statement:
The empty dynamic table is the table with no slots (capacity $0$)
and item count $0$. It models a table before its first allocation.

articles.title: Lookup at the vacated position after deletion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count
$n$, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. After applying deletion to $T$, the lookup at
logical position $n - 1$ returns no value.

articles.title: Deletion preserves lookups below the last position
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic
table holding $n$ items, and let $i$ be a natural number with $i < n - 1$. After applying
deletion to $T$, the lookup at logical position $i$ returns the same result as the lookup at
position $i$ in $T$.

articles.title: Lookup beyond the item count returns nothing
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count
$n$. For every natural number $i \ge n$, the lookup at logical position $i$ in $T$ returns no
value.

articles.title: Lookup succeeds exactly below the item count
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table
holding $n$ items. For every natural number $i$, the lookup at logical position $i$ in $T$
returns a value if and only if $i < n$.

articles.title: Lookup in a dynamic table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$,
each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. The lookup at logical position $i$
returns the item held by $s_i$ when $i < n$ and $s_i$ is occupied; it returns no value when
$i < n$ and $s_i$ is empty, and when $i \ge n$.

articles.title: Deletion removes the last item from the contents
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table.
The contents of the table obtained by applying deletion to $T$ is the contents of $T$ with its
last entry removed; when the contents of $T$ is empty, it stays empty.

articles.title: Item count after deletion
articles.statement:
Applying deletion to a dynamic table with item count $n$ gives
a table with item count $n - 1$ when $n \ge 1$, and item count $0$ when $n = 0$.

articles.title: Capacity after deletion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with capacity $m$ and item count $n$,
and apply deletion to $T$. If $n = 0$, the capacity stays $m$. If $n \ge 1$ and $4(n-1) < m$, the
new capacity is $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor$. Otherwise the capacity stays $m$.

articles.title: Slots after deletion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table with slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ holding $n \ge 1$ items, and let $m'$ be the capacity of the table obtained
by applying deletion to $T$. The slots of that table are the first $n - 1$ slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-2}$ of $T$ followed by $m' - (n - 1)$ empty slots.

articles.title: Deletion preserves well-formedness
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table, that is, its
occupied slots are exactly its first $n$ slots, where $n$ is its item count. Then the table
obtained by applying deletion to $T$ is again well-formed.

articles.title: Deletion from a dynamic table
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$,
each empty or holding an item, and item count $n \le m$. Deleting the last item of $T$ gives the
following table. If $n = 0$, the result is $T$ itself. Otherwise, if $4(n-1) < m$, that is, the
load factor after deletion is strictly below $1/4$, the table contracts: the result has slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-2}$ followed by $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor - (n-1)$ empty slots, so capacity
$\lfloor m/2 \rfloor$, and item count $n-1$. Otherwise the result has the slots of $T$ with
$s_{n-1}$ made empty, and item count $n-1$.

articles.title: Amortized cost of dynamic-table insertion
articles.statement:
For a dynamic table $T$ with item count $n$
and capacity (number of slots) $m$, let $\Phi(T) = 2n - m$, an integer that may be negative.
If inserting an item $x$ into $T$ has cost $c$ and returns the table $T'$, then
$c + \Phi(T') - \Phi(T) \le 3$. Here the cost of an insertion is one unit for writing $x$ plus
one unit for each old slot copied when a full table is doubled.

articles.title: Insertion appends to the contents
articles.statement:
If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x$ is an
item, then the contents of the table obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ are the contents of $T$
followed by $x$.

articles.title: Inserting an array appends it to the contents
articles.statement:
If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table
and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ is an array of items, then inserting $x_1, \dots, x_k$ into $T$ one at a
time, in this order, gives a table whose contents are the contents of $T$ followed by
$x_1, \dots, x_k$.

articles.title: Capacity after inserting into the empty table
articles.statement:
Starting from the empty dynamic table
and inserting the items of an array of length $k$ one at a time, the resulting table has
capacity (number of slots) at most $2k$.

articles.title: Total cost of insertions into the empty table
articles.statement:
Starting from the empty dynamic table
and inserting the items of an array of length $k$ one at a time, the total cost is at most
$3k$, where each insertion costs one unit for writing the new item plus one unit for each old
slot copied when a full table is doubled.

articles.title: Strict cost bound for nonempty insertion sequences
articles.statement:
Starting from the empty dynamic
table and inserting the items of a nonempty array of length $k$ one at a time, the total cost
is less than $3k$.

The bound is strict because the first insertion, which allocates the first slot, has amortized
cost $2$ rather than $3$.

articles.title: Repeated insertion preserves well-formedness of a dynamic table
articles.statement:
Call a dynamic table
with item count $n$ well formed when, for every slot index $i$, slot $i$ is occupied exactly
when $i < n$. If a dynamic table $T$ is well formed, then for every array $xs$, the table
obtained from $T$ by inserting the entries of $xs$ one at a time with TABLE-INSERT, in array
order, is again well formed.

articles.title: Inserting an array of items into a dynamic table
articles.statement:
Given a dynamic table $T$ and an array
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of items, the result of inserting the array into $T$ is obtained by starting
from $T$ and inserting $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ one at a time with TABLE-INSERT, in array
order. Its cost is the sum of the costs of the $k$ insertions; for an empty array the result is
$T$ at cost $0$.

articles.title: Insertion increases the item count by one
articles.statement:
For every dynamic table $T$ with item count $n$
and every item $x$, the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT has item count
$n + 1$.

articles.title: Capacity after an insertion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with item count $n$ and capacity
(number of slots) $m$, and let $x$ be an item. The table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with
TABLE-INSERT has capacity $1$ if $m = 0$, capacity $2m$ if $m > 0$ and $n = m$, and capacity $m$
otherwise.

articles.title: Slots after an insertion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a well-formed dynamic table with slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n$, let $x$ be an item, and let $T'$ be the table returned
by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT, with capacity $m'$. Then the slots of $T'$ are
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, followed by a slot holding $x$, followed by $m' - (n + 1)$ empty slots.

articles.title: Cost of an insertion
Insertion preserves well-formedness
articles.statement:
If $T$ is a well-formed dynamic table and $x$ is an
item, then the table returned by inserting $x$ into $T$ with TABLE-INSERT is well formed.

articles.title: TABLE-INSERT
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count
$n \le m$, and let $x$ be an item. Inserting $x$ into $T$ proceeds as follows. If $m = 0$, first
replace the slots by a single empty slot. Then, if the table is full, that is, $n$ equals the
current capacity $c$, allocate $2c$ empty slots and copy the $c$ old slots into the first $c$ of
them, at cost $1$ per copied slot. Finally write $x$ into slot $n$, at cost $1$, and set the item
count to $n + 1$. The result is the new table together with the total cost.

articles.title: Dynamic table
articles.statement:
A dynamic table with items of type $\alpha$ consists of an array of slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$, each either empty or holding an item of type $\alpha$, together with an
item count $n$ satisfying $n \le m$. The number $m$ of slots is the capacity of the table.

articles.title: Characterization of well-formed dynamic tables
articles.statement:
A dynamic table with slots
$s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count $n$ is well formed if and only if, for every $i < m$, slot
$s_i$ is occupied exactly when $i < n$.

articles.title: Well-formed dynamic table
articles.statement:
A dynamic table with slots $s_0, \dots, s_{m-1}$ and item count
$n$ is well formed when, for every $i < m$, slot $s_i$ is occupied if and only if $i < n$; that is,
the occupied slots are exactly the first $n$.

The items held in the occupied slots are not constrained.

articles.title: Catenable heap
articles.statement:
A catenable heap over a type $\alpha$ is a persistent unsorted heap,
represented as a join list (catenation tree): it is either the empty heap, an element of $\alpha$
added in front of a catenable heap, or the join of two catenable heaps.

articles.title: Cost and result of insertion into a catenable heap
articles.statement:
For every element $x$ and catenable
heap $h$, inserting $x$ into $h$ returns the heap with $x$ added in front of $h$, at cost
exactly $1$.

articles.title: Insertion into a catenable heap
articles.statement:
For an element $x$ and a catenable heap $h$, inserting
$x$ into $h$ returns the heap with $x$ added in front of $h$ and charges cost $1$, for the one
front node it allocates.

articles.title: Cost and result of creating a catenable heap
articles.statement:
Creating a catenable heap returns the empty
heap, at cost $0$.

articles.title: Creating an empty catenable heap
articles.statement:
The operation that creates a catenable heap returns the
empty heap and charges cost $0$, since it allocates no node.

articles.title: Result of insertion into a catenable heap
articles.statement:
For every element $x$ and catenable heap $h$,
the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the heap with $x$ added in front of $h$.

articles.title: Result of creating a catenable heap
articles.statement:
The heap returned by the operation that creates a
catenable heap is the empty heap.

articles.title: Result of the union of catenable heaps
articles.statement:
For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the heap
returned by their union is the join of $h_1$ and $h_2$, with $h_1$ as left child and $h_2$ as
right child, both unchanged.

articles.title: Size of a heap with an element added in front
articles.statement:
For every element $a$ and catenable heap
$t$, the size of the heap obtained by adding $a$ in front of $t$ is the size of $t$ plus one.

articles.title: The empty catenable heap has size zero
articles.statement: The empty catenable heap has size $0$.

articles.title: Size of a catenable heap as a multiset cardinality
articles.statement:
For every catenable heap $h$, the size
of $h$ equals the cardinality of the multiset of its elements.

articles.title: Insertion into a catenable heap increases its size by one
articles.statement:
For every element $x$ and
catenable heap $h$, the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ has size one more than the size
of $h$.

articles.title: Size of a catenable heap join
articles.statement:
For catenable heaps $\ell$ and $r$, the size of the join
node with left child $\ell$ and right child $r$ is the size of $\ell$ plus the size of $r$.

articles.title: A newly made catenable heap has size zero
articles.statement:
The heap returned by the operation that
creates an empty catenable heap has size $0$.

articles.title: Size of a catenable heap union
articles.statement:
For catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the heap returned by
the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ has size equal to the size of $h_1$ plus the size of $h_2$.

articles.title: Size of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
The size of a catenable heap is the length of its left-to-right
list of elements, that is, the number of its elements counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Insertion into a catenable heap costs one
articles.statement:
For every element $x$ and catenable heap $h$,
inserting $x$ into $h$ has time cost exactly $1$.

articles.title: Creating an empty catenable heap costs nothing
articles.statement:
The operation that creates an empty
catenable heap has time cost $0$.

articles.title: Union of catenable heaps costs one
articles.statement:
For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the union of
$h_1$ and $h_2$ has time cost exactly $1$, independently of $h_1$ and $h_2$.

articles.title: Accumulator flattening of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
For every catenable heap $h$ and list $a$,
flattening $h$ from left to right in front of the accumulator $a$ gives the naive left-to-right
flattening of $h$ followed by $a$.

articles.title: Accumulating flattening of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
Given a catenable heap $h$ and a list $s$, the
accumulating flattening of $h$ onto $s$ is defined by recursion on $h$: for the empty heap it is
$s$; for the heap with an element $x$ added in front of a heap $t$ it is $x$ followed by the
accumulating flattening of $t$ onto $s$; for the join of heaps $l$ and $r$ it is the accumulating
flattening of $l$ onto the accumulating flattening of $r$ onto $s$.

Each node of $h$ is visited once.

articles.title: Flattening a front node of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
For an element $x$ and a catenable heap $t$,
the flattening of the heap with $x$ added in front of $t$ is $x$ followed by the flattening of
$t$.

articles.title: Flattening the empty catenable heap
articles.statement:
The flattening of the empty catenable heap is the
empty list.

articles.title: Flattening of a catenable heap equals its naive flattening
articles.statement:
For every catenable heap $h$,
the flattening of $h$ equals the naive flattening of $h$.

articles.title: Flattening after insertion into a catenable heap
articles.statement:
For an element $x$ and a catenable heap
$h$, the flattening of the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ is $x$ followed by the
flattening of $h$.

articles.title: Flattening a join of catenable heaps
articles.statement:
For catenable heaps $l$ and $r$, the flattening of
the join of $l$ and $r$ is the flattening of $l$ followed by the flattening of $r$.

articles.title: A newly created catenable heap flattens to the empty list
articles.statement:
The flattening of the heap
returned by the operation that creates a catenable heap is the empty list.

articles.title: Naive flattening of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
The naive flattening of a catenable heap is defined
by recursion: the empty heap flattens to the empty list, the heap with an element $x$ added in
front of a heap $t$ flattens to $x$ followed by the naive flattening of $t$, and the join of
heaps $l$ and $r$ flattens to the naive flattening of $l$ followed by that of $r$.

It is the reference against which the accumulating flattening is checked.

articles.title: Flattening a union of catenable heaps
articles.statement:
For catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the flattening
of the heap returned by the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ is the flattening of $h_1$ followed by the
flattening of $h_2$.

articles.title: Flattening of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
The flattening of a catenable heap $h$ is the list of its
elements from left to right, computed as the accumulating flattening of $h$ onto the empty list.

articles.title: Multiset of a front node
articles.statement:
For every element $a$ and every catenable heap $t$, the multiset
of elements of the heap obtained by adding $a$ in front of $t$ is the multiset of elements of $t$
with one more copy of $a$.

articles.title: The empty catenable heap has no elements
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of the empty catenable
heap is the empty multiset.

articles.title: Insertion adds one copy of the element
articles.statement:
For every element $x$ and every catenable heap $h$,
the multiset of elements of the heap returned by inserting $x$ into $h$ is the multiset of
elements of $h$ with one more copy of $x$.

articles.title: Multiset of a join node
articles.statement:
For all catenable heaps $L$ and $R$, the multiset of elements of
the join node with left child $L$ and right child $R$ is the multiset sum of the multisets of
elements of $L$ and $R$ (multiplicities add).

articles.title: A newly made catenable heap has no elements
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of the heap returned
by the make operation is the empty multiset.

articles.title: Union adds the multisets of elements
articles.statement:
For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the multiset
of elements of the heap returned by the union of $h_1$ and $h_2$ is the multiset sum of the
multisets of elements of $h_1$ and $h_2$ (multiplicities add).

articles.title: Multiset of elements of a catenable heap
articles.statement:
The multiset of elements of a catenable heap $h$
is the multiset of the entries of the left-to-right list of elements of $h$.

articles.title: Union allocates one join node
articles.statement:
For all catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, the union of $h_1$
and $h_2$ returns the join node whose left child is $h_1$ and whose right child is $h_2$, at
cost $1$.

articles.title: Union of catenable heaps
articles.statement:
The union of catenable heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ allocates one join
node, at cost $1$, and returns that join node, whose left child is $h_1$ and whose right child is
$h_2$; neither operand is traversed or changed.

articles.title: Empty LRU cache
articles.statement:
For every capacity $c$, the empty LRU cache of capacity $c$ is the cache
with no entries.

articles.title: Erasing a key from a list of entries
articles.statement:
Given a key $k$ and a list of key–value pairs,
erasing $k$ deletes every pair whose key is $k$ and keeps the other pairs in their original
order. When the keys in the list are pairwise distinct, at most one pair is deleted.

articles.title: The evicted key is the least recently used one
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be an LRU cache of capacity $c$,
let $k'$ be a key not stored in $C$, and let $k$ be a key stored in $C$. If $k$ is no longer
stored after putting $k'$ with any value $v$ into $C$, then $C$ held exactly $c$ entries and $k$
is the last key of $C$, that is, the least recently used one.

articles.title: Extensionality of LRU caches
articles.statement:
Two LRU caches with the same key type, value type and
capacity are equal if their lists of entries are equal.

articles.title: A lookup of a stored key returns its value
articles.statement:
If an LRU cache stores the pair $(k, v)$,
then looking up $k$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Lookups keep keys distinct
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the keys of the cache
obtained by looking up $k$ are pairwise distinct.

articles.title: A lookup of an absent key misses
articles.statement:
If the key $k$ is not stored in an LRU cache, then
looking up $k$ returns no value and leaves the cache unchanged.

articles.title: A lookup permutes the entries
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the list of
entries of the cache after looking up $k$ is a permutation of the list of entries before.

articles.title: A successful lookup moves the entry to the front
articles.statement:
If an LRU cache stores the pair
$(k, v)$, then after looking up $k$ the most recently used (first) entry of the cache is
$(k, v)$.

articles.title: A put without eviction preserves lookups of other keys
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be an LRU cache of
capacity $c$ that holds fewer than $c$ entries or already stores the key $k$. Then for every
key $k' \ne k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k'$ in the cache obtained by putting the binding
$(k, v)$ into $C$ returns the same optional value as looking up $k'$ in $C$.

articles.title: Lookup after insertion into an LRU cache
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache of positive capacity, every key
$k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$
returns $v$.

articles.title: Lookup respects the capacity
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache of capacity $c$ and every key
$k$, the cache after looking up $k$ holds at most $c$ entries.

articles.title: Lookup preserves the size
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache and every key $k$, the cache after
looking up $k$ holds exactly as many entries as before.

articles.title: LRU cache lookup
articles.statement:
Looking up a key $k$ in an LRU cache returns an optional value
together with a cache. If the cache stores a binding $(k, v)$, the result is $v$ together
with the cache in which that binding is moved to the front and the other entries keep their
order; otherwise the result is no value together with the unchanged cache.

articles.title: Keys of an LRU cache are distinct
articles.statement:
The keys stored in any LRU cache are pairwise
distinct.

articles.title: Key list of an LRU cache
articles.statement:
The key list of an LRU cache is the list of the keys of its
entries in the order of the cache, so the most recently used key comes first.

articles.title: Least-recently-used cache
articles.statement:
For a type $K$ of keys, a type $V$ of values and a
natural number $c$, an LRU cache of capacity $c$ is a list of key-value pairs in $K \times V$,
ordered from most to least recently used, whose keys are pairwise distinct and whose length
is at most $c$.

articles.title: Lookup preserves the stored bindings
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache and every key $k$, a
key-value pair is stored in the cache after looking up $k$ if and only if it was stored in
the cache before the lookup.

articles.title: Insertion without eviction
articles.statement:
Let an LRU cache of capacity $c$ hold fewer than $c$
entries or already store a binding for the key $k$, and let $v$ be a value. Then a key-value
pair $p$ is stored in the cache after putting the binding $(k, v)$ if and only if $p = (k, v)$,
or $p$ was stored before and the key of $p$ differs from $k$.

articles.title: Entries after insertion
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache, key $k$ and value $v$, every
key-value pair $p$ stored in the cache after putting the binding $(k, v)$ either equals
$(k, v)$, or was stored before and has a key different from $k$.

articles.title: With positive capacity, the inserted binding becomes the most recent entry
articles.statement:
Let $C$
be an LRU cache of positive capacity, $k$ a key and $v$ a value. After the binding $(k, v)$
is put into $C$, the first entry of the resulting cache, its most recently used entry, is
$(k, v)$.

articles.title: Insertion keeps the keys of an LRU cache distinct
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache $C$, key $k$
and value $v$, the keys of the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ are
pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Insertion respects the capacity of an LRU cache
articles.statement:
For every LRU cache $C$ of capacity
$c$, key $k$ and value $v$, the cache obtained by putting the binding $(k, v)$ into $C$ has
size at most $c$.

articles.title: Insertion into an LRU cache
articles.statement:
Putting the binding $(k, v)$ into an LRU cache of capacity $c$
removes any entry with key $k$, places $(k, v)$ at the front as the most recently used entry,
and then keeps only the first $c$ entries, so the least recently used entries beyond the
capacity are evicted.

articles.title: An LRU cache never exceeds its capacity
articles.statement:
Every LRU cache of capacity $c$ has size at most
$c$.

articles.title: Size of an LRU cache
articles.statement: The size of an LRU cache is the number of entries it stores.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix has a hit iff the list does
articles.statement: The inclusive first-hit prefix has a hit exactly when the source list has one.

articles.title: Equality of uniformly split lists from equal block extracts
articles.statement: Lists of the same uniform-block length are equal when every block extract agrees.

articles.title: Every equal-length list family is realized by its concatenation
articles.statement: Every finite family of equal-length lists is realized by their concatenation.

articles.title: Extracting a member from a uniform-width concatenation
articles.statement: A uniform-width extract of a concatenated family recovers that family member.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix commutes with filter-map
articles.statement:
Filtering selected elements from an inclusive prefix commutes with taking the corresponding
inclusive prefix of the selected elements.

articles.title: First-witness fold over the inclusive first-hit prefix
articles.statement:
Folding the first-witness update over the inclusive tested prefix returns the first witness in
the whole source list.

articles.title: Named chunk lookup uses the first occurrence
articles.statement: Looking up a named chunk uses the first occurrence of its name.

articles.title: Splitting a list at a repeated width
articles.statement: Splitting at a repeated width recovers the corresponding uniform chunk.

articles.title: Start position of a chunk in a split list
articles.statement: A valid indexed chunk begins after the total length of the preceding chunks.

articles.title: List positions agree with values of an increasing map
articles.statement: In a list along which `f` increases, position order agrees with value order.

articles.title: Length of a concatenation of equal-length lists
articles.statement: Concatenating `count` lists of length `width` has length `count * width`.

articles.title: Chunks of a list have length at most the chunk size
articles.statement:
Let $n > 0$ and let $L$ be a list.
Split $L$ from left to right into consecutive chunks of size $n$: elements go into the current
chunk until it holds $n$ elements, then a new chunk is started. Every chunk produced has at most
