$n$ elements.

articles.title: Members of an accumulator-stopped prefix lie in the list
articles.statement: Every member of an accumulator-stopped prefix belongs to the source list.

articles.title: Members of an inclusive first-hit prefix lie in the list
articles.statement: Every member of an inclusive first-hit prefix belongs to the source list.

articles.title: Members after ordered insertion
articles.statement:
Over a linearly ordered type, for all elements $x$, $y$
and every list $\ell$, the element $y$ belongs to the ordered insertion of $x$ into $\ell$ if and
only if $y = x$ or $y$ belongs to $\ell$.

articles.title: Inserting a present element into a strictly increasing list
articles.statement:
Over a linearly ordered
type, if every element of a list $\ell$ is smaller than every later element of $\ell$ and $x$
belongs to $\ell$, then the ordered insertion of $x$ into $\ell$ is $\ell$ itself.

Without strict increase this fails: inserting $2$ into $[3, 2]$ gives $[2, 3, 2]$.

articles.title: Ordered insertion into a list
articles.statement:
For an element $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the ordered
insertion of $x$ into the empty list is $[x]$. For a list with head $a$ and tail $\ell$, it is
$x$ followed by the whole list if $x < a$; it is $a$ followed by the ordered insertion of $x$
into $\ell$ if $a < x$; and it is the list unchanged if $a = x$.

On a strictly increasing list a key that is already present is therefore ignored. On an unsorted
list a later duplicate is not detected: inserting $2$ into $[3, 2]$ gives $[2, 3, 2]$.

articles.title: Pairwise relations on list products in lexicographic order
articles.statement:
The Cartesian product of two pairwise-related lists is pairwise-related in lexicographic
order.

articles.title: Accumulator-stopped prefix when the head update continues
articles.statement:
If the accumulator continues after the head update, the same updated accumulator processes the
tail.

articles.title: Accumulator-stopped prefix when the head update stops
articles.statement: If the accumulator stops after the head update, the prefix contains only the head.

articles.title: Accumulator-stopped prefix as a first-hit prefix of a scan
articles.statement:
The recursive ETH operation is the ordinary inclusive first-hit prefix of the elements paired
with their updated accumulators.

articles.title: First-witness accumulator gives the inclusive first-hit prefix
articles.statement:
Accumulating a projection of the first witness in an `Option` gives the ordinary inclusive
first-hit prefix.

articles.title: Accumulator-stopped prefix of the empty list
articles.statement: An empty list has an empty accumulator-stopped prefix.

articles.title: Disjunction accumulator gives the inclusive first-hit prefix
articles.statement: Accumulating disjunction from `false` gives the ordinary inclusive first-hit prefix.

articles.title: Accumulator-stopped list is a prefix of its source
articles.statement: The accumulator-stopped list is a prefix of its source list.

articles.title: Accumulator-stopped inclusive prefix of a list
articles.statement:
The prefix through the first element after whose update the accumulator satisfies `stop`,
including that element. The initial accumulator is not tested. If no updated accumulator satisfies
`stop`, this is the whole list.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of an append with no hit on the left
articles.statement: If the left list has no hit, the prefix contains all of it and continues into the right list.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of an append with a hit on the left
articles.statement: Once the left list has a hit, appending another list does not change the prefix.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix when the head is not a hit
articles.statement: If the head does not satisfy the predicate, the search continues through the tail.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix when the head is a hit
articles.statement: If the head satisfies the predicate, it is the whole inclusive first-hit prefix.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of a list with no hit
articles.statement: If no element satisfies the predicate, the inclusive first-hit prefix is the whole list.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of the empty list
articles.statement: The inclusive first-hit prefix of an empty list is empty.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of a range of naturals
articles.statement: On `range n`, the prefix ends one past the first hit, or at `n` if there is no hit.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of a singleton
articles.statement: A singleton is its own inclusive first-hit prefix.

articles.title: Inclusive first-hit prefix of a list
articles.statement:
The prefix through the first element satisfying `p`, including that element. If no element
satisfies `p`, this is the whole list.

articles.title: The payload list depends only on the listed cells
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ and $s'$
be stores assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node. If $L$
is a list of identities below $n$ and $s'(i) = s(i)$ for every $i$ in $L$, then the contents of
$s'$ at $L$ equal the contents of $s$ at $L$.

articles.title: The payload list has one entry per identity
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node. For every list
$L$ of identities below $n$, the contents of $s$ at $L$ have the same length as $L$.

articles.title: Payload list of a singly linked list store
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node (a payload
together with a next pointer that is an identity below $n$ or NIL). For a list of identities
$i_0, \dots, i_{m-1}$ below $n$, the contents of $s$ at this list are the list
$c_0, \dots, c_{m-1}$, where $c_j$ is the payload of $s(i_j)$ when $s(i_j)$ is a node and $c_j$ is
nothing (marking an unallocated cell) when $s(i_j)$ is nothing.

articles.title: Contents after deleting a successor
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning to
each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let
$L = (i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$ be a list of identities below $n$, and let $k < m$ be such that
$s(i_k)$ is a node. Let $s'$ be the store obtained from $s$ by deleting the successor of $i_k$.
Then the contents of $s'$ at the list obtained from $L$ by removing the entry at position $k + 1$
equal the list obtained from the contents of $s$ at $L$ by removing the entry at position $k + 1$.
Positions count from $0$, and nothing is removed when $k + 1 = m$.

articles.title: Deleting a successor leaves other cells unchanged
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $y$ be an
identity such that $s(y)$ is a node, and let $s'$ be the store obtained from $s$ by deleting the
successor of $y$. Then $s'(z) = s(z)$ for every identity $z \ne y$.

articles.title: Cells after deleting a successor
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $y$ be an identity such that
$s(y)$ is a node, and let $s'$ be the store obtained from $s$ by deleting the successor of $y$.
Let $c$ be the node $s(y)$ with its next pointer replaced by the next pointer of $s(m)$ if the
next pointer of $s(y)$ is an identity $m$ such that $s(m)$ is a node, and by NIL otherwise. Then
for every identity $z$, $s'(z)$ is the node $c$ if $z = y$, and $s'(z) = s(z)$ if $z \ne y$.

articles.title: Deleting a successor preserves payloads
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning
to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $y$ be an identity
such that $s(y)$ is a node, and let $s'$ be the store obtained from $s$ by deleting the successor
of $y$. Then for every identity $z$, either $s(z)$ and $s'(z)$ are both nothing, or both are nodes
with the same payload.

articles.title: Deleting a successor removes it from the represented list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a
store assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and
suppose that $s$ with head $h$ represents the list of identities $L = (i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$. Let
$k < m$ be such that $s(i_k)$ is a node, and let $s'$ be the store obtained from $s$ by deleting
the successor of $i_k$. Then $s'$ with the same head $h$ represents the list obtained from $L$ by
removing the entry at position $k + 1$. Positions count from $0$, and at the tail ($k + 1 = m$)
the list is unchanged.

articles.title: Deleting the successor in a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node whose next
pointer is an identity below $n$ or NIL, and let $y$ be an identity such that $s(y)$ is a node.
Deleting after $y$ returns the store that agrees with $s$ except at $y$, where it holds the node
$s(y)$ with its next pointer replaced as follows: if the next pointer of $s(y)$ is an identity $m$
and $s(m)$ is a node, the new next pointer is the next pointer of $s(m)$; otherwise it is NIL.

The removed node stays allocated in the store; at the tail the links are unchanged.

articles.title: Deleting the head removes the first identity
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and suppose that
$s$ with head $h$ represents the list of identities $L$, where $h$ is an identity below $n$ or NIL.
Let $(s', h')$ be the store and head returned by deleting the head of $s$ with head $h$. Then $s'$
with head $h'$ represents $L$ with its first entry removed, which is the empty list when $L$ is
empty.

articles.title: Deleting the head of a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Let a store assign to each identity below $n$
either nothing or a singly linked list node whose next pointer is an identity below $n$ or NIL,
and let the head be an identity below $n$ or NIL. Deleting the head returns the store unchanged
together with a new head: NIL if the head is NIL or the store entry at the head is empty, and
otherwise the next pointer of the node stored at the head.

articles.title: Contents after singly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store assigning to each identity
below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$ be a list of
identities below $n$, let $k < m$, and let $x$ be an identity such that the store entries of $x$
and $i_k$ are nodes, the node of $x$ having payload $a$. Then the contents of the store obtained
by inserting $x$ after $i_k$ at the list $(i_0, \dots, i_k, x, i_{k+1}, \dots, i_{m-1})$ equal
the contents of $S$ at $(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$ with the present payload $a$ inserted as entry
$k + 1$ (counting from $0$).

No representation or distinctness hypothesis is assumed.

articles.title: Frame property of singly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store assigning to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and let $x$ and $y$ be identities
whose store entries are nodes. For every identity $z$ with $z \ne y$ and $z \ne x$, cell $z$ of
the store obtained by inserting $x$ after $y$ equals cell $z$ of $S$.

articles.title: Cells after singly-linked-list insertion
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store assigning to each identity
below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $x$ and $y$ be identities whose store
entries are nodes, and let $z$ be any identity. Let $c$ be the node of $x$ in $S$ with next
pointer replaced by the next pointer of $y$ in $S$ if $z = x$, and the content of cell $z$ in $S$
otherwise. Then cell $z$ of the store obtained by inserting $x$ after $y$ is $c$ with next pointer
replaced by $x$ if $z = y$, and $c$ otherwise.

No distinctness of $x$ and $y$ is assumed.

articles.title: Singly-linked-list insertion preserves payloads
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store assigning to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and let $x$ and $y$ be identities
whose store entries are nodes. For every identity $z$, cell $z$ of the store obtained by inserting
$x$ after $y$ is empty exactly when cell $z$ of $S$ is empty, and otherwise holds a node with the
same payload as the node in cell $z$ of $S$.

articles.title: Insertion into a represented singly linked list
articles.statement:
Suppose the store $S$ with head $h$
represents the list of distinct identities $(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$. Let $k < m$, assume that the
store entry of $i_k$ is a node, and let $x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node and which
is not among $i_0, \dots, i_{m-1}$. Then the store obtained by inserting $x$ after $i_k$, with
the same head $h$, represents the list $(i_0, \dots, i_k, x, i_{k+1}, \dots, i_{m-1})$.

articles.title: Inserting a node after another in a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Let a store $S$ assign to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node whose next pointer is an identity
below $n$ or NIL, and let $x$ and $y$ be identities whose store entries are nodes. Inserting $x$
after $y$ first replaces cell $x$ by the node of $x$ with next pointer replaced by the next
pointer of $y$ in $S$, then, in the store so obtained, replaces the next pointer of the node in
cell $y$ by $x$, and returns the resulting store.

articles.title: Singly linked list node
articles.statement:
A singly linked list node with payloads in $\alpha$ and identities
in $\iota$ consists of a payload in $\alpha$ (the key together with any satellite data) and a next
pointer, which is either an identity in $\iota$ or NIL.

articles.title: Contents after prepending to a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store assigning to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $h$ be an identity below $n$
or NIL, let $x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node with payload $a$, and let
$(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$ be a list of identities below $n$ not containing $x$. Then the contents,
at the list $(x, i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$, of the store obtained by prepending $x$ to the list with
head $h$ are the present payload $a$ followed by the contents of $S$ at the list
$(i_0, \dots, i_{m-1})$.

articles.title: Frame property of prepending to a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store assigning to
each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $h$ be an identity below
$n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node. For every identity
$z \ne x$, cell $z$ of the store obtained by prepending $x$ to the list with head $h$ equals
cell $z$ of $S$.

articles.title: Store after prepending to a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let
$\mathrm{head}$ be an identity below $n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a
node. Then for every identity $z$ below $n$, the entry at $z$ of the store returned by Prepend on
$s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$ is the node $s(x)$ with its next pointer replaced by $\mathrm{head}$
when $z = x$, and is $s(z)$ when $z \ne x$.

articles.title: Prepending makes the node the head
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning to
each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let $\mathrm{head}$ be an
identity below $n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a node. Then the head
returned by Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$ is $x$.

articles.title: The prepended node points at the old head
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let
$\mathrm{head}$ be an identity below $n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a
node. Then the entry at $x$ of the store returned by Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$ and $x$ is the
node $s(x)$ with its payload kept and its next pointer replaced by $\mathrm{head}$.

articles.title: Prepending conses onto the represented list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let
$\mathrm{head}$ be an identity below $n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity such that $s(x)$ is a
node. If $s$ and $\mathrm{head}$ represent the list of identities $i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$ and $x$ is
none of $i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$, then the store and head returned by Prepend on $s$, $\mathrm{head}$
and $x$ represent the list $x, i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$.

articles.title: Prepending a node to a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let a store assign to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, let the head be an identity below
$n$ or NIL, and let $x$ be an identity whose store entry is a node. Prepending $x$ replaces the
store entry at $x$ by the same node with its next pointer set to the head, leaves every other entry
unchanged, and returns the updated store together with the new head $x$.

articles.title: Represented identities hold nodes
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning to
each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and let $\mathrm{head}$ be an
identity below $n$ or NIL. If $s$ and $\mathrm{head}$ represent the list of identities
$i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$, then for every identity $i$ in this list the store entry $s(i)$ is a
node.

articles.title: Represented lists have no missing contents
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and let
$\mathrm{head}$ be an identity below $n$ or NIL. If $s$ and $\mathrm{head}$ represent the list of
identities $i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$, then every entry of the contents of $s$ at $i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$
is a payload rather than nothing.

articles.title: Represented lists fit in the store
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let $s$ be a store assigning to
each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node, and let $\mathrm{head}$ be an
identity below $n$ or NIL. If $s$ and $\mathrm{head}$ represent the list of identities
$i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$, then $k \le n$.

The identities are pairwise distinct and there are only $n$ of them.

articles.title: Representation of the empty singly linked list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$ and let $s$ be any store
assigning to each identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node. Then $s$ with
head NIL represents the empty list of identities.

articles.title: Store representing a singly linked list
articles.statement:
Fix a capacity $n$, let a store assign to each
identity below $n$ either nothing or a singly linked list node whose next pointer is an identity
below $n$ or NIL, and let the head be an identity below $n$ or NIL. The store and head represent
the list of identities $i_0, \dots, i_{k-1}$ when these identities are pairwise distinct, the head
is $i_0$ (and NIL when $k = 0$), and for each $j < k$ the store entry at $i_j$ is a node whose next
pointer is $i_{j+1}$ if $j + 1 < k$ and NIL otherwise.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded search finds the first matching represented identity
articles.statement:
Suppose a node pool
represents, from the head $h$, the list of distinct identities $\ell$. Then for every target
payload $t$ and every fuel $f$ with $f \ge |\ell|$, fuel-bounded search for $t$ from $h$ with
fuel $f$ returns the first identity in $\ell$ whose cell holds a node with payload $t$, and
returns nothing if no identity in $\ell$ has this property.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded search in a singly-linked list
articles.statement:
Given a node pool with $n$ cells, a target
payload $t$, a fuel $f \in \mathbb{N}$ and a start $h$ that is either an identity in
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL, fuel-bounded search for $t$ from $h$ with fuel $f$ returns nothing
if $f = 0$ or $h$ is NIL. Otherwise $h$ is an identity $i$: the search returns nothing if cell
$i$ is unallocated, returns $i$ if the node in cell $i$ has payload $t$, and otherwise continues
from the next pointer of that node with fuel $f - 1$.

articles.title: Search finds the first matching represented identity
articles.statement:
If a node pool represents, from the
head $h$, the list of distinct identities $\ell$, then for every target payload $t$ the search
for $t$ from $h$ returns the first identity in $\ell$ whose cell holds a node with payload $t$,
and returns nothing if no identity in $\ell$ has this property.

articles.title: Search fails exactly when no represented node has the target payload
articles.statement:
If a node pool
represents, from the head $h$, the list of distinct identities $\ell$, then for every target
payload $t$ the search for $t$ from $h$ returns nothing if and only if no identity in $\ell$ has
a cell holding a node with payload $t$.

articles.title: A successful search returns a matching represented identity
articles.statement:
If a node pool represents,
from the head $h$, the list of distinct identities $\ell$, and the search for a target payload
$t$ from $h$ returns an identity $x$, then $x$ belongs to $\ell$ and cell $x$ holds a node with
payload $t$.

articles.title: Search in a singly-linked list
articles.statement:
Given a node pool with $n$ cells, a head $h$ that is
either an identity in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or NIL, and a target payload $t$, the search for $t$
from $h$ is fuel-bounded search for $t$ from $h$ with fuel $n$. It follows next pointers from
$h$ and returns the first visited identity whose node has payload $t$, returning nothing if it
reaches NIL or an unallocated cell first, or if $n$ steps run out.

articles.title: Cost balance for stack operation sequences
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$ and every finite sequence
$\sigma$ of stack operations, if running $\sigma$ on $S$ succeeds with final stack $F$, then the
cost of the run plus the number of elements of $F$ equals the number of elements of $S$ plus
twice the number of PUSH operations in $\sigma$.

articles.title: Running a POP agrees with the standalone POP
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$ and every finite
sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, running POP followed by $\sigma$ on $S$ has the same result
and cost as first performing the standalone POP on $S$ and then, if it reports underflow,
stopping with an error at no further cost, or, if it removes the top element and leaves the stack
$S'$, running $\sigma$ on $S'$, the two costs being added.

articles.title: Running a PUSH agrees with the standalone PUSH
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$, every value $x$ and
every finite sequence $\sigma$ of stack operations, running PUSH $x$ followed by $\sigma$ on $S$
has the same result and cost as first performing the standalone PUSH of $x$ on $S$ and then
running $\sigma$ on the resulting stack, the two costs being added.

articles.title: Aggregate cost of stack operation sequences
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$ and every sequence of
$n$ stack operations (PUSH, POP and MULTIPOP), if running the sequence on $S$ succeeds, that is,
no POP meets an empty stack, then its cost is at most $|S| + 2n$, where $|S|$ is the number of
elements of $S$.

articles.title: Running a sequence of stack operations
articles.statement:
Given a stack $S$ and a finite sequence of
operations, each a PUSH of a value, a POP or a MULTIPOP with an integer count, the operations are
applied to $S$ in order. PUSH of $x$ puts $x$ on top at cost $1$; POP removes the top element at
cost $1$; MULTIPOP with count $k$ is MULTIPOP with an integer count, costing one unit per element
removed. If a POP meets an empty stack, the run stops and reports an error, that POP is not
charged, and the cost is that of the operations before it. Otherwise the run returns the final
stack, and its cost is the sum of the costs of all operations.

articles.title: Result of MULTIPOP
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$, stored as a list with its top first, and every
natural number $k$, the stack returned by MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ is $S$ with its top $k$
elements removed, or the empty stack if $S$ has fewer than $k$ elements.

articles.title: MULTIPOP with a nonpositive count does nothing
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$ and every integer
$k \le 0$, MULTIPOP with integer count $k$ applied to $S$ returns $S$ at cost $0$.

articles.title: MULTIPOP with an integer count
articles.statement:
For a stack $S$ and an integer $k$, MULTIPOP with integer
count $k$ is MULTIPOP of $S$ with the natural count $\max(k, 0)$, with the same result and cost.
In particular, a count $k \le 0$ removes nothing.

articles.title: Cost of MULTIPOP
articles.statement:
For every stack $S$ and every natural number $k$, the cost of MULTIPOP
of $S$ with count $k$ is $\min(|S|, k)$, where $|S|$ is the number of elements of $S$.

articles.title: MULTIPOP
articles.statement:
For a stack $S$, stored as a list with its top first, and a natural number $k$,
MULTIPOP of $S$ with count $k$ repeatedly removes the top element while the stack is nonempty and
fewer than $k$ elements have been removed, and returns the remaining stack. Each removed element
costs one unit, and nothing else is charged.

This is MULTIPOP from CLRS, fourth edition, Section 16.1.

articles.title: Stack operations for the MULTIPOP aggregate analysis
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ of stack
entries, a stack operation is one of the following: $\mathrm{PUSH}(x)$ for an element
$x \in \alpha$, $\mathrm{POP}$, or $\mathrm{MULTIPOP}(k)$ for an integer count $k$.

These are the operations whose sequences CLRS analyse in Section 16.1.

articles.title: Result and cost of the stack operations
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $s$ be a stack over
$\alpha$ (a list of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top) and let $v \in \alpha$.
Pushing $v$ onto $s$ returns the stack with top $v$ followed by the elements of $s$, at cost $1$.
Popping $s$ returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$ if $s$ is empty, and returns the pair
$(h, t)$ at cost $1$ if $s$ has top $h$ and remaining stack $t$. Reading the top of $s$ returns
underflow (no value) at cost $0$ if $s$ is empty, and returns $h$ at cost $1$ if $s$ has top $h$.

articles.title: Result and cost of stack pop
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a stack over a type $\alpha$ (a list of elements
of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top). If $s$ is empty, popping $s$ returns underflow (no
value) at cost $0$. If $s$ has top $h$ and remaining stack $t$, popping $s$ returns the pair
$(h, t)$ at cost $1$.

This holds for every type $\alpha$; no element of $\alpha$ is assumed to exist.

articles.title: Stack pop
articles.statement:
Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first
element as the top. Popping the empty stack returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. Popping a
stack with top $v$ and remaining stack $t$ returns the pair $(v, t)$ at cost $1$ (one successful
pop event).

articles.title: Stack push
articles.statement:
Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first
element as the top. Pushing $v \in \alpha$ onto a stack $s$ returns the stack with top $v$
followed by the elements of $s$, at cost $1$ (one successful push event).

articles.title: Result and cost of reading the stack top
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a stack over a type $\alpha$ (a list
of elements of $\alpha$ whose first element is the top). If $s$ is empty, reading the top of $s$
returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$. If $s$ has top $h$, reading the top of $s$ returns $h$
at cost $1$.

This holds for every type $\alpha$; no element of $\alpha$ is assumed to exist.

articles.title: Stack top
articles.statement:
Stacks over a type $\alpha$ are lists of elements of $\alpha$, with the first
element as the top. Reading the top of the empty stack returns underflow (no value) at cost $0$.
Reading the top of a stack with top $v$ returns $v$ at cost $1$ (one successful top event); the
stack itself is not returned or changed.

articles.title: Amortized charge of a queue operation
articles.statement:
The potential-method charge of a queue operation is
$2$ for an enqueue and $1$ for a dequeue.

articles.title: Enqueueing appends to the contents
articles.statement:
For every queue $q$ and value $v$, the contents of
the queue obtained by enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ are the contents of $q$ followed by $v$.

articles.title: A successful dequeue splits off the first element
articles.statement:
If dequeueing a queue $q$ succeeds
and returns an element $a$ and a queue $r$, then the contents of $q$ are $a$ followed by the
contents of $r$.

articles.title: Contents of a two-list queue
articles.statement:
A queue is stored as a dequeue list and an enqueue list
whose most recently enqueued element comes first. Its contents are its elements in FIFO
order: the dequeue list followed by the reverse of the enqueue list.

articles.title: Amortized cost of dequeueing
articles.statement:
For every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of dequeueing
from $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $1$. This
includes the case where $q$ is empty.

articles.title: Modeled cost of a dequeue
articles.statement:
For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the
modeled cost of dequeueing is $1$ when the dequeue list is nonempty, and $m + 1$ when the dequeue
list is empty, where $m$ is the length of the enqueue list (the number of elements reversed when
they are moved to the dequeue list).

articles.title: Dequeueing fails exactly on empty queues
articles.statement:
For every queue $q$, dequeueing $q$ returns
nothing if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.

articles.title: Timed dequeue
articles.statement:
Dequeueing from a two-list queue $q$ returns the next element in first-in,
first-out order together with the remaining queue, or returns no element together with $q$ itself
when $q$ is empty. In both cases the recorded cost is the modeled dequeue cost of $q$.

articles.title: Amortized cost of enqueueing
articles.statement:
For every two-list queue $q$ and every value $v$, the modeled
cost of enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of
$q$ plus $2$.

articles.title: Timed enqueue
articles.statement:
Enqueueing a value $v$ onto a two-list queue $q$ returns the queue
obtained from $q$ by adding $v$ at the back, that is, by prepending $v$ to the enqueue list,
together with a recorded cost of $1$.

articles.title: The queue emptiness test matches the contents
articles.statement:
For every queue $q$, the emptiness test
of $q$ returns true if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.

articles.title: Queue operation
articles.statement:
A queue operation over a type $\alpha$ is either a request to enqueue a
value $v \in \alpha$ or a request to dequeue. Sequences of such operations are used to state
aggregate cost bounds.

articles.title: Potential of a two-list queue
articles.statement:
For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the
potential is the length of the enqueue list: the number of elements that will be reversed when
they are moved to the dequeue list.

articles.title: Amortized cost of a sequence of queue operations
articles.statement:
For every list of queue operations and
every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting
at $q$, plus the potential of the final queue, equals the potential of $q$ plus the total charge
of the operations.

articles.title: Linear bound on the cost of queue operations
articles.statement:
For every list of $n$ queue operations and
every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting
at $q$ is at most the potential of $q$ plus $2n$.

articles.title: Running a sequence of queue operations
articles.statement:
Running a list of queue operations from a
queue $q$ performs the operations one step at a time from left to right, starting at $q$.
The result is the final queue, and the cost is the sum of the costs of the individual
steps; running the empty list returns $q$ at cost $0$.

articles.title: Amortized cost of one queue operation
articles.statement:
For every queue $q$ and every queue operation
$o$, the modeled cost of performing $o$ on $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals
the potential of $q$ plus the charge of $o$.

articles.title: One step of a queue operation
articles.statement:
For a queue $q$, an enqueue operation with value $v$
performs the costed enqueue of $v$ onto $q$. A dequeue operation performs the costed dequeue
of $q$ and keeps the remaining queue and the cost, discarding the removed value; on an empty
queue the remaining queue is $q$ itself.

articles.title: Array conversion lists the contents
articles.statement:
For every queue $q$, the array obtained from $q$,
read as a list, equals the contents of $q$.

articles.title: Total charge of a sequence of queue operations
articles.statement:
For a list of queue operations, the
total charge is the sum of the amortized charges of its operations, where an enqueue is charged
$2$ and a dequeue is charged $1$.

articles.title: Ball tree
articles.statement:
For a dimension $d$, a ball tree over the integer points $\mathbb{Z}^d$
(functions $\{0, \dots, d-1\} \to \mathbb{Z}$) is either empty, a leaf holding one point,
or a node holding a center point $c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, a natural number $b$ (the squared-radius
bound of the node's sphere) and two child ball trees.

That the sphere around $c$ actually contains the points below the node is a separate validity
invariant, not part of this definition.

articles.title: Building a ball tree by halving
articles.statement:
The ball tree built from a list of points of
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ is defined by recursion on the list. The empty list gives the empty tree and a
one-point list $[p]$ gives the leaf $p$. A list $L = [x_1, \dots, x_n]$ with $n \ge 2$ gives a
node whose center is $x_1$, whose bound is the squared radius of $L$ around $x_1$ (the largest
squared distance from $x_1$ to a point of $L$), whose left child is the tree built from the
first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ points of $L$, and whose right child is the tree built from the
remaining points of $L$.

articles.title: Symmetry of squared distance
articles.statement:
For all points $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the squared
distance from $p$ to $q$ equals the squared distance from $q$ to $p$.

articles.title: Points lie within the squared radius
articles.statement:
Let $c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $L$ be a list
of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. For every point $p$ of $L$, the squared distance from $c$ to $p$
is at most the squared radius of $L$ around $c$, the largest squared distance from $c$ to a
point of $L$.

articles.title: Relaxed triangle inequality for squared distance
articles.statement:
For all points
$a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, writing $\delta(x, y)$ for the squared distance from $x$ to $y$,
we have $\delta(a, c) \le 2\,(\delta(a, b) + \delta(b, c))$.

The factor $2$ comes from $(x + y)^2 \le 2(x^2 + y^2)$ applied coordinatewise. This is the
estimate that makes bounding-sphere pruning sound without square roots.

articles.title: Squared Euclidean distance
articles.statement:
For points $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the squared distance
from $p$ to $q$ is the natural number $\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} (p_i - q_i)^2$, computed in
$\mathbb{Z}$ and then converted to $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Number of points of a ball tree
articles.statement:
For every ball tree $t$, the list of points stored in
$t$, read from left to right, has length equal to the size of $t$.

articles.title: Search of a built ball tree
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, let
$q, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $r$ be a natural number. Then $p$ is returned by the similarity
search with query $q$ and squared radius $r$ on the ball tree built from $L$ if and only if $p$
occurs in $L$ and the squared distance from $q$ to $p$ is at most $r$.

articles.title: Search of a valid ball tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a ball tree satisfying the bounding-sphere
invariant. For all $q, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every natural number $r$, $p$ is returned by the
similarity search of $t$ with query $q$ and squared radius $r$ if and only if $p$ is one of the
points stored in $t$ and the squared distance from $q$ to $p$ is at most $r$.

articles.title: Points of a built ball tree
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and every
point $p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $p$ is one of the points stored in the ball tree built from $L$ if
and only if $p$ occurs in $L$.

articles.title: Squared covering radius
articles.statement:
For a center $c \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and a list $P$ of points of
$\mathbb{Z}^d$, the squared covering radius of $P$ about $c$ is the largest squared distance from
$c$ to a point of $P$, or $0$ if $P$ is empty.

articles.title: Accumulating ball-tree search
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a dimension and write $\delta(x, y)$ for the
squared distance from $x$ to $y$ in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. For a ball tree $T$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$, a
query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, a squared radius $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $A$ of points,
the accumulating search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ with accumulator $A$ is $A$ when $T$ is empty;
when $T$ is a leaf holding $p$, it is $p$ followed by $A$ if $\delta(q, p) \le r$ and $A$
otherwise; when $T$ is a node with center $c$, squared-radius bound $b$ and children $L$ and $R$,
it is $A$ if $2(b + r) < \delta(c, q)$, and otherwise the accumulating search of $L$ for $q$ and
$r$ whose accumulator is the accumulating search of $R$ for $q$ and $r$ with accumulator $A$.

When $T$ satisfies the bounding-sphere invariant, this pruning is sound by the relaxed triangle
inequality $\delta(x, z) \le 2(\delta(x, y) + \delta(y, z))$ for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z}^d$,
and the result is the points of $T$ within squared distance $r$ of $q$, from left to right,
followed by $A$.

articles.title: Ball-tree search of a built tree, up to order
articles.statement:
For every list $P$ of points of
$\mathbb{Z}^d$, every query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, the search of
the ball tree built from $P$ for $q$ and $r$ is a permutation of the sublist of $P$ consisting of
the points $p$ whose squared distance from $q$ is at most $r$, kept with their multiplicities.

articles.title: Ball-tree search of a built tree
articles.statement:
For every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, every
query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, let $T$ be the ball tree built from
$P$. The search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ equals the list of points of $T$, from left to right,
filtered to the points $p$ whose squared distance from $q$ is at most $r$, in their order.

articles.title: Ball-tree search is exact
articles.statement:
For every ball tree $T$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ satisfying the
bounding-sphere invariant, every query point $q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, the
search of $T$ for $q$ and $r$ equals the list of points of $T$, from left to right, filtered to
the points $p$ whose squared distance from $q$ is at most $r$, in their order. Pruning against
the bounding spheres loses no point.

articles.title: Ball-tree similarity search
articles.statement:
The search of a ball tree $T$ for a query point
$q \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ and a squared radius $r \in \mathbb{N}$ is the accumulating search of $T$ for
$q$ and $r$ started with the empty accumulator.

When $T$ satisfies the bounding-sphere invariant, the search lists exactly the points of $T$
within squared distance $r$ of $q$, from left to right.

articles.title: Size of a built ball tree
articles.statement:
For every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the size of
the ball tree built from $P$ equals the length of $P$, that is, the number of entries of $P$
counted with repetition.

articles.title: Size of a ball tree
articles.statement:
The size of a ball tree is the number of points held in its leaves:
it is $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and the sum of the sizes of the two children for a
node; the center of a node is not counted.

articles.title: Accumulating traversal of a ball tree
articles.statement:
For a ball tree $T$ and a list $A$ of points, the
accumulating traversal returns $A$ when $T$ is empty, the point $p$ followed by $A$ when $T$ is a
leaf holding $p$, and, when $T$ is a node with children $L$ and $R$, the accumulating traversal of
$L$ whose accumulator is the accumulating traversal of $R$ with accumulator $A$.

The result is the leaf points of $T$, from left to right, followed by $A$.

articles.title: A built ball tree stores a permutation of its input
articles.statement:
For every list $P$ of points of
$\mathbb{Z}^d$, the list of points of the ball tree built from $P$, from left to right, is a
permutation of $P$.

articles.title: Point list of a ball tree
articles.statement:
The point list of a ball tree is the list of the points held
at its leaves, from left to right: the empty tree gives the empty list, a leaf holding $p$ gives
the list $[p]$, and a node gives the point list of its left subtree followed by the point list of
its right subtree. The centers stored at nodes are not included.

articles.title: Ball trees built by halving are valid
articles.statement:
For every list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the
ball tree built from it by recursive halving satisfies the bounding-sphere invariant.

articles.title: Bounding-sphere invariant of a ball tree
articles.statement:
Validity of a ball tree is defined inductively:
the empty tree and every leaf are valid, and a node with center $c$ and squared-radius bound $b$
is valid when both of its subtrees are valid and every point in the point list of either subtree
lies within squared Euclidean distance $b$ of $c$.

articles.title: Out-of-range point updates leave a Fenwick tree unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree
over a commutative additive monoid $\alpha$, and let $n$ be its size (the length of its stored
array minus one). For every natural number $i \ge n$ and every $\delta \in \alpha$, the point
update of $t$ adding $\delta$ at position $i$ returns $t$ itself.

articles.title: Point update of a Fenwick tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over a commutative additive
monoid $\alpha$, let $n$ be its size (the length of its stored array minus one), let $i$ be a
natural number and let $\delta \in \alpha$. Adding $\delta$ at underlying position $i$ adds
$\delta$ to the stored entries at the one-indexed positions $j_1 = i + 1$ and
$j_{k+1} = j_k + \operatorname{lowbit}(j_k)$, for as long as $j_k \le n$, where
$\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$; every other stored entry
is left unchanged. In particular, if $i \ge n$ the tree is unchanged.

Each write is constant-time only when the stored array is uniquely referenced, since a shared
array is copied by the first persistent write. The walk is fuelled by the size, which always
suffices because the visited positions strictly increase.

articles.title: Interval sum read from an array
articles.statement:
For an array $a$ of elements of a commutative additive
monoid $\alpha$ and a natural number $j$, this is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$
entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the
largest power of two dividing $j$ (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$) and entries past the
end of $a$ count as $0$.

It has the same value as the list-based interval sum but reads each entry in constant time;
Fenwick-tree construction uses it, so building takes $O(n \log n)$ reads rather than quadratic
list indexing.

articles.title: Fenwick-tree interval sum of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $a$ of elements of a commutative additive
monoid $\alpha$ and a natural number $j$, the interval sum at the one-indexed position $j$ is
the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at zero-indexed position
$j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$ (with
$\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$) and entries past the end of $a$ count as $0$.

articles.title: Building a Fenwick tree from a list
articles.statement:
For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a commutative
additive monoid $\alpha$, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ stores the array of length $n + 1$
whose entry at index $0$ is $0$ and whose entry at each one-indexed position $j$ with
$1 \le j \le n$ is the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ entries of $a$ ending at
zero-indexed position $j - 1$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two
dividing $j$.

The input is converted to an array once, so each entry read is constant-time and construction
is $O(n \log n)$.

articles.title: Fenwick tree
articles.statement:
A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over a commutative additive monoid
$\alpha$ is an array of elements of $\alpha$, read as one-indexed interval sums with an unused
dummy entry at index $0$. The structure itself imposes no condition on the entries, and the
underlying array it represents is not stored; the relation saying that a tree represents a
given array is defined separately.

articles.title: Dividing out the lowest set bit leaves an odd number
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > 0$,
the quotient $n / \operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is odd, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the
value of the lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.

articles.title: The lowest set bit divides the number
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > 0$,
$\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ divides $n$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the
lowest set bit of $n$ in binary.

articles.title: The lowest set bit is at most the number
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$,
$\operatorname{lowbit}(n) \le n$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest
set bit of $n$ in binary (with $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$).

articles.title: The lowest set bit of a positive number is positive
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > 0$,
$\operatorname{lowbit}(n) > 0$, where $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the value of the lowest set
bit of $n$ in binary.

articles.title: The lowest set bit is a power of two
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n > 0$,
$\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is a power of two: $\operatorname{lowbit}(n) = 2^k$ for some natural
number $k$.

articles.title: Lowbit of zero
articles.statement: By convention, $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Lowest set bit
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n > 0$, $\operatorname{lowbit}(n)$ is the largest
power of two dividing $n$; for $n = 0$ it is defined as $\operatorname{lowbit}(0) = 0$.

articles.title: Prefix sums after a point update
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a$ of
elements of an additive commutative monoid, let $i < |a|$ be a position, let $\delta$ be an
element of the monoid, and let $k$ be any natural number, possibly larger than $|a|$. Then the
prefix sum of length $k$ of the tree obtained from $t$ by adding $\delta$ at position $i$ equals
the prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ plus $\delta$ if $i < k$, and equals the prefix sum of
length $k$ of $t$ if $k \le i$.

articles.title: Prefix sums of a built Fenwick tree
articles.statement:
For every list $a$ of elements of an additive
commutative monoid and every natural number $k$, the prefix sum of length $k$ of the Fenwick tree
built from $a$ equals the sum of the first $\min(k, |a|)$ entries of $a$.

articles.title: Correctness of Fenwick tree prefix sums
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list $a$
of elements of an additive commutative monoid. Then for every natural number $k$, including
$k > |a|$, the prefix sum of length $k$ of $t$ equals the sum of the first $\min(k, |a|)$ entries
of $a$.

articles.title: The empty prefix sum is zero
articles.statement:
For every Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative
monoid, the prefix sum of length $0$ of $t$ is $0$.

articles.title: Fenwick tree prefix sum
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over an additive commutative monoid
with $n$ underlying entries, let $k$ be a natural number and let $m = \min(k, n)$. The prefix sum
of length $k$ of $t$ is the sum of the stored entries of $t$ at the positions $j_0 = m$,
$j_{r+1} = j_r - \operatorname{lowbit}(j_r)$, taken for as long as $j_r > 0$.

When $t$ represents a list, this is the sum of its first $m$ entries, so queries past the end
are clamped.

articles.title: Correctness of Fenwick tree range sums
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree representing a list
$a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of elements of an additive commutative group. Then for all natural
numbers $\mathit{lo}$ and $\mathit{hi}$, the range sum of $t$ over $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$
equals $\sum_{\mathit{lo} \le i < \min(\mathit{hi}, n)} a_i$; in particular it is $0$ when
$\mathit{hi} \le \mathit{lo}$.

articles.title: Fenwick tree range sum
articles.statement:
For a Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative group and
natural numbers $\mathit{lo}$ and $\mathit{hi}$, the range sum of $t$ over
$[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$ is $0$ if $\mathit{hi} \le \mathit{lo}$, and otherwise the prefix sum
of length $\mathit{hi}$ of $t$ minus the prefix sum of length $\mathit{lo}$ of $t$.

When $t$ represents a list, this is the sum of its entries with indices in
$[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$. This is the only Fenwick tree operation that needs additive
inverses.

articles.title: Size of a built Fenwick tree
articles.statement:
For every list $a$ over an additive commutative monoid,
the Fenwick tree built from $a$ has size equal to the length of $a$.

articles.title: A Fenwick tree has the length of the list it represents
articles.statement:
If a Fenwick tree $t$ over an
additive commutative monoid represents a list $a$, then the size of $t$ equals the length of
$a$.

articles.title: Size of a Fenwick tree
articles.statement:
The size of a Fenwick tree is the length of its stored array
minus one, truncated at $0$; the one accounts for the dummy entry at index $0$. It is read off
the stored array in constant time.

articles.title: Point update preserves representation
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a Fenwick tree over an additive
commutative monoid that represents a list $a$ of length $n$. For every index $i < n$ (counting
from $0$) and every element $\delta$, the tree obtained from $t$ by adding $\delta$ at position
$i$ represents the list obtained from $a$ by replacing its entry $a_i$ with $a_i + \delta$.

articles.title: Building a Fenwick tree yields a valid representation
articles.statement:
For every list $a$ over an
additive commutative monoid, the Fenwick tree built from $a$ represents $a$.

articles.title: Fenwick tree representing a list
articles.statement:
A Fenwick tree $t$ over an additive commutative monoid
represents a list $a$ of length $n$ when its stored array has length $n + 1$ (a dummy entry at
index $0$ plus one entry per element of $a$) and, for every $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$, the stored
entry at index $j$ equals the block sum of $a$ at $j$: the sum of the $\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$
entries of $a$ ending at position $j - 1$ (positions counted from $0$), where
$\operatorname{lowbit}(j)$ is the largest power of two dividing $j$.

The underlying list itself is not stored at runtime; it appears only in this specification
relation.

articles.title: Augmenting a catalog by the head of a list
articles.statement:
Given a catalog $c$ and a list $L$ of
catalogs, the result is $c$ itself if $L$ is empty, and otherwise the sorted merge of $c$
with the sample (every other element, starting with the first) of the first catalog of $L$.

articles.title: Augmenting a catalog by the next one
articles.statement:
For catalogs $c$ and $a$, the augmentation of $c$
by $a$ is the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$ (every other element of $a$, starting
with the first). In fractional cascading, $a$ is the next augmented catalog.

articles.title: Augmenting a single catalog
articles.statement:
For every catalog $c$, the list of augmented catalogs of the
one-element list $[c]$ is $[c]$: the only augmented catalog is $c$ itself.

articles.title: Augmented catalogs
articles.statement:
For a list of catalogs $c_1, \dots, c_k$, the augmented catalogs
$A_1, \dots, A_k$ are built from the last one backwards: $A_k = c_k$, and for $i < k$, $A_i$ is
the sorted merge of $c_i$ with the sample (every other element, starting with the first) of
$A_{i+1}$. The empty list of catalogs has no augmented catalogs.

articles.title: Bridge pointers are at most the catalog length
articles.statement:
For every catalog $L$ and value $v$, the
bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$ is at most the length of $L$.

articles.title: Bridge pointer
articles.statement:
For a catalog $L$ and a value $v$, the bridge pointer of $v$ into $L$ is
the number of elements of $L$ that are $\le v$.

When $L$ is sorted, this is the index just past the elements of $L$ that are $\le v$.

articles.title: Bridge pointer list
articles.statement:
For catalogs $C$ and $L$, the bridge pointers of $C$ into $L$ form the
list obtained by replacing each entry $v$ of $C$, in order, by the bridge pointer of $v$ into
$L$.

articles.title: The scan count equals the lower bound
articles.statement:
For every value $x$ and every catalog $L$, the scan
count of elements of $L$ that are $< x$ equals the lower bound of $x$ in $L$.

articles.title: Scan count of smaller elements
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$, the scan count of $x$ in
$L$ is the number of elements of $L$ that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan: it is $0$ for
the empty catalog, and for a catalog with head $a$ and tail $L'$ it is the scan count of $x$ in
$L'$, plus $1$ if $a < x$.

articles.title: Search positions are lower bounds, index by index
articles.statement:
For every value $x$, list of catalogs
$C_0, \dots, C_{k-1}$ and index $i$: if $i < k$, the $i$-th position returned by searching all
catalogs for $x$ is the lower bound of $x$ in $C_i$; if $i \ge k$, the search result has no
$i$-th entry.

articles.title: Bridge pointers are at most the next catalog's length
articles.statement:
For lists $c$ and $d$ over a
linearly ordered type, every entry $p$ of the list of bridge pointers of $c$ into $d$ satisfies
$p \le |d|$, where $|d|$ is the length of $d$; so every recorded bridge pointer is a boundary
index of $d$.

articles.title: Length bound for one augmented catalog
articles.statement:
For lists $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered
type, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample of $a$ has length at most
$|c| + \lfloor (|a| + 1)/2 \rfloor$, the length of $c$ plus half the length of $a$ rounded up.

articles.title: Length of one augmented catalog
articles.statement:
For lists $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the
augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample $s(a)$ of $a$ has length
$|c| + |s(a)|$.

articles.title: Number of augmented catalogs
articles.statement:
For every list $cs$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered
type, the list of augmented catalogs built from $cs$ has the same length as $cs$: there is one
augmented catalog per catalog.

articles.title: Number of bridge pointers
articles.statement:
For lists $c$ and $d$ over a linearly ordered type, the list
of bridge pointers of $c$ into $d$ has the same length as $c$: there is one bridge pointer per
entry of $c$.

articles.title: Augmented catalogs are bounded by the total input size
articles.statement:
For every list
$cs = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of catalogs over a linearly ordered type, every augmented catalog built
from $cs$ has length at most $|c_1| + \dots + |c_k|$.

articles.title: The sample is no longer than the list
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ (over any type), the sample
of $xs$, every other element starting with the first, has length at most the length of $xs$.

articles.title: The sample has at most half the length, rounded up
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ (over any
type), the sample of $xs$ has length at most $\lfloor (|xs| + 1)/2 \rfloor$, half the length of
$xs$ rounded up: for an even length $2m$ the bound is $m$, and for an odd length $2m + 1$ it is
$m + 1$.

articles.title: One search position per catalog
articles.statement:
For every value $x$ and every list $cs$ of catalogs
over a linearly ordered type, searching each catalog of $cs$ for $x$ gives a list of positions
of the same length as $cs$.

articles.title: One augmented search position per catalog
articles.statement:
For every value $x$ and every list $cs$ of
catalogs over a linearly ordered type, searching each augmented catalog built from $cs$ for $x$
gives a list of positions of the same length as $cs$.

articles.title: Length of a sorted merge
articles.statement:
For catalogs (finite lists) $L$ and $M$ over a linearly ordered
type, the sorted merge of $L$ and $M$ has length equal to the length of $L$ plus the length of
$M$.

articles.title: Lower bound in an augmented catalog is at most the sum
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and catalogs $c$
and $a$ over a linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the augmented catalog of $c$ with
$a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) is at most the lower bound of $x$ in $c$
plus the lower bound of $x$ in $a$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of
its entries less than $x$.

articles.title: Lower bound in an augmented catalog splits
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a
linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted
merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) equals the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ plus the lower bound of
$x$ in the sample of $a$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog is the number of its entries
less than $x$.

articles.title: Lower bound is at most the catalog length
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a catalog $L$ over a
linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ (the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$)
is at most the length of $L$.

articles.title: Lower bound in a sample is at most the lower bound in the catalog
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a
catalog $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the number of entries less than $x$ in the sample of
$L$ (every other entry of $L$, starting with the first) is at most the number of entries of $L$
less than $x$.

articles.title: Lower bound in a sorted merge splits
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and catalogs $L$ and $M$ over a
linearly ordered type, the lower bound of $x$ in the sorted merge of $L$ and $M$ equals the lower
bound of $x$ in $L$ plus the lower bound of $x$ in $M$, where the lower bound of $x$ in a catalog
is the number of its entries less than $x$.

articles.title: Lower bound of a value in a catalog
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a catalog
(finite list) $L$, the lower bound of $x$ in $L$ is the number of entries of $L$ that are less
than $x$, counted with multiplicity. For a sorted catalog this is the first index whose entry is
not less than $x$, or the length of $L$ if there is none.

articles.title: Membership in an augmented catalog
articles.statement:
For catalogs $c$ and $a$ over a linearly ordered type,
a value $v$ is an entry of the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted merge of $c$ with the
sample of $a$) if and only if $v$ is an entry of $c$ or an entry of the sample of $a$.

articles.title: Entries of an augmented catalog come from the two catalogs
articles.statement:
For catalogs $c$ and $a$ over
a linearly ordered type, every entry $v$ of the augmented catalog of $c$ with $a$ (the sorted
merge of $c$ with the sample of $a$) is an entry of $c$ or an entry of $a$.

articles.title: Entries of a sample are entries of the catalog
articles.statement:
For a catalog (finite list) $L$, every
entry of the sample of $L$ (every other entry of $L$, starting with the first) is an entry of
$L$.

articles.title: Elements of a sorted merge
articles.statement:
For lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order and any
element $v$, $v$ belongs to the sorted merge of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ if and only if $v$ belongs
to $\ell_1$ or to $\ell_2$.

articles.title: One augmentation step yields a sorted list
articles.statement:
For any lists $c$ and $a$ over a linear order,
sorted or not, the augmented catalog obtained by merging $c$ with the sample of $a$ is sorted in
nondecreasing order.

articles.title: The augmented catalogs of sorted catalogs are sorted
articles.statement:
If every catalog in a list of
catalogs over a linear order is sorted in nondecreasing order, then every augmented catalog built
from that list is sorted in nondecreasing order.

articles.title: The sample of a sorted list is sorted
articles.statement:
If a list over a linear order is sorted in
nondecreasing order, then so is its sample.

articles.title: A sorted merge is sorted
articles.statement:
For any lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linear order, sorted
or not, their sorted merge is sorted in nondecreasing order.

articles.title: A sorted merge rearranges the concatenation
articles.statement:
For any lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a
linear order, the sorted merge of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ is a permutation of the concatenation of
$\ell_1$ followed by $\ell_2$.

articles.title: Alternating selection gives a sublist
articles.statement:
For every flag $b$ (true or false) and every list
$\ell$, the alternating selection of $\ell$ with initial flag $b$ is a sublist of $\ell$: it is
obtained from $\ell$ by deleting some elements and keeping the rest in order.

articles.title: Alternating selection with a flag
articles.statement:
For a flag $b$ (true or false) and a list $\ell$, the
alternating selection of $\ell$ with initial flag $b$ is defined by recursion on $\ell$: the empty
list gives the empty list; for a list with head $a$ and tail $\ell'$, if $b$ is true it keeps $a$
and continues on $\ell'$ with flag false, and if $b$ is false it drops $a$ and continues on
$\ell'$ with flag true.

articles.title: The sample is a sublist
articles.statement:
For every list $\ell$, the sample of $\ell$ is a sublist of
$\ell$: it is obtained from $\ell$ by deleting some elements and keeping the rest in order.

articles.title: Sample of a catalog
articles.statement:
The sample of a list $[x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is the list
$[x_0, x_2, x_4, \dots]$ of every other element, starting with the first, in their original
order.

articles.title: Searching a nonempty list of catalogs
articles.statement:
For a value $x$, a catalog $c$ and a list of
catalogs $cs$, searching $c$ followed by $cs$ for $x$ gives first the direct-scan count of the
elements of $c$ that are $< x$, followed by the positions obtained by searching $cs$ for $x$.

articles.title: Correctness of searching every catalog
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs
$c_1, \dots, c_k$, searching every catalog for $x$ returns the list whose $i$-th entry is the
lower bound of $x$ in $c_i$, that is, the number of elements of $c_i$ that are $< x$.

articles.title: Search positions are boundary indices
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a value and let $cs$ be a list of
catalogs whose entry at index $i$ is the catalog $c$. Then searching every catalog of $cs$ for
$x$ gives, at index $i$, the lower bound of $x$ in $c$ (the number of elements of $c$ that are
$< x$), and this lower bound is at most the length of $c$.

articles.title: Searching no catalogs
articles.statement:
Searching the empty list of catalogs for any value $x$ gives the
empty list of positions.

articles.title: Searching every catalog
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs, the search returns, for
each catalog in order, the number of its elements that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan of
that catalog. This is the lower-bound position of $x$ in each catalog.

articles.title: Correctness of augmented search
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs $cs$, searching
every augmented catalog of $cs$ for $x$ returns, for each augmented catalog in order, the lower
bound of $x$ in it, that is, the number of its elements that are $< x$.

articles.title: Searching every augmented catalog
articles.statement:
For a value $x$ and a list of catalogs, the augmented
search builds the augmented catalogs and returns, for each augmented catalog in order, the number
of its elements that are $< x$, computed by a direct scan of that catalog.

articles.title: Sorted merge of two catalogs
articles.statement:
For lists $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ over a linearly ordered
type, their sorted merge is the result of merge sort, with respect to $\le$, applied to the
concatenation of $\ell_1$ followed by $\ell_2$.

This models the merge of two sorted catalogs; the linear-time merge itself is not part of this statement.

articles.title: Doubled sample length bound
articles.statement:
For every catalog $L$, twice the length of the sample of $L$
is at most the length of $L$ plus one.

articles.title: Keyed deletion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree that
is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint
and a natural-number identifier). The tree $T'$ returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the
tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) is again AVL balanced with exact stored
heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.

articles.title: Keyed insertion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree that
is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $e$ be an entry. The tree $T'$ returned by keyed
insertion of $e$ into $T$ (which replaces an entry with the same key, if there is one; we take the
tree component of the result and ignore the cost) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights,
and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one more.

articles.title: Rebalancing a rebuilt interval-tree node restores AVL balance
articles.statement:
Let $L$ and $R$ be interval
trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ satisfying
$h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$, and let $e$ be an entry. Let $B$ be the tree obtained by
rebalancing the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ (the tree component
of the result; the cost is ignored). Then $B$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, the
height of $B$ is $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$ or $\max(h_L, h_R)$, and it is $\max(h_L, h_R)$ only if
$h_L = h_R + 2$ or $h_R = h_L + 2$.

articles.title: Rebalancing an interval-tree node with exact stored height restores AVL balance
articles.statement:
Let $L$
and $R$ be interval trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and
$h_R$ satisfying $h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$. Let $N$ be a node with left subtree $L$,
entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose stored height is $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$ (its stored size and
stored maximum are arbitrary), and let $B$ be the tree obtained by rebalancing $N$ (the tree
component of the result; the cost is ignored). Then $B$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights,
the height of $B$ is $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$ or $\max(h_L, h_R)$, and it is $\max(h_L, h_R)$ only if
$h_L = h_R + 2$ or $h_R = h_L + 2$.

articles.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance in an interval tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree
that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds and
returns an entry $m$, a remaining tree $R$ and a cost $c$, then $R$ is AVL balanced with exact
stored heights, and the height of $R$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.

articles.title: AVL balance of an interval tree
articles.statement:
An interval tree is AVL balanced with exact stored heights
when it is empty, or when it is a node such that, writing $h_L$ and $h_R$ for the stored heights
of its left and right subtrees (the empty tree has height $0$), the node's stored height equals
$\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and both subtrees are again AVL
balanced with exact stored heights.

articles.title: Boolean AVL balance check for interval trees
articles.statement:
The balance check returns true on the empty
tree. On a node whose left and right subtrees have stored heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ (the empty tree
has height $0$), it returns true exactly when the node's stored height equals
$\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and the check returns true on both
subtrees.

articles.title: Keyed deletion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree
satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and
let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree
returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is
ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes keys that do not occur in $T$.

articles.title: Keyed insertion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree
satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and
let $e$ be an entry. The tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (the tree component of
the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes the case where
an entry with the same key is replaced.

articles.title: The interval-tree smart constructor preserves the cache invariant
articles.statement:
If interval trees $L$
and $R$ satisfy the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is
exact), then for every entry $e$ the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$
also satisfies the cache invariant.

articles.title: The executable cache check implies the cache invariant
articles.statement:
If the executable cache check
returns true on an interval tree $t$, then $t$ satisfies the cache invariant.

articles.title: Rebalancing preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
If an interval tree $t$
satisfies the cache invariant, then the tree returned by the rebalancing step at the root of $t$
also satisfies the cache invariant.

articles.title: Removing the minimum preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be an interval
tree that satisfies the cache invariant. If removing the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds and
returns an entry, a tree $t'$ and an operation cost, then $t'$ satisfies the cache invariant.

articles.title: Left-right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
If an interval tree $t$
satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left-right double rotation of $t$, which leaves
$t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty left subtree whose right subtree is nonempty.

articles.title: Left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
If an interval tree $t$
satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged
when $t$ is empty or has an empty right subtree.

articles.title: Right-left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
If an interval tree $t$
satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right-left double rotation of $t$, which leaves
$t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty right subtree whose left subtree is nonempty.

articles.title: Right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
articles.statement:
If an interval tree $t$
satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged
when $t$ is empty or has an empty left subtree.

articles.title: Cache invariant of an interval tree
articles.statement:
An interval tree satisfies the cache invariant when
every cached field is exact, recursively. The empty tree satisfies it. A node with stored height
$h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$
satisfies it when $L$ and $R$ satisfy it, $m$ is at least the high endpoint of every entry of
$L$, of $e$ and of every entry of $R$, $m$ equals the high endpoint of one of these entries,
$h = \max(\operatorname{height} L, \operatorname{height} R) + 1$ and
$s = \operatorname{size} L + \operatorname{size} R + 1$. Here the height and size of a subtree
are its stored fields, and the empty tree has height and size $0$.

articles.title: Executable cache check for interval trees
articles.statement:
The Boolean cache check returns true on the
empty tree. On a node with stored height $h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree
$L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ it returns true exactly when
$h = \max(\operatorname{height} L, \operatorname{height} R) + 1$,
$s = \operatorname{size} L + \operatorname{size} R + 1$, $m$ is the largest of the high endpoint
of $e$ and the cached maxima of those of $L$ and $R$ that are nonempty, and the check returns
true on both $L$ and $R$. Here the height and size of a subtree are its stored fields, and the
empty tree has height and size $0$.

It is used only by the executable invariant checker.

articles.title: Cached maximum of an interval tree
articles.statement:
The cached maximum of an interval tree is no value
when the tree is empty, and when the tree is a node it is the integer stored in the node's cached
maximum-high-endpoint field.

It is read in constant time. The tree type itself does not require this field to equal the
largest high endpoint of an interval in the subtree.

articles.title: Representation check for the indexed interval tree
articles.statement:
For an indexed interval tree, the
check returns true exactly when all of the following hold: at every node the cached height and size
agree with the values recomputed from its children's cached heights and sizes, and the cached
maximum high endpoint equals the largest of the node's own high endpoint and its children's cached
maxima; the tree is AVL-balanced (sibling heights differ by at most one) with exact stored heights;
the entry keys (low endpoint, identifier), ordered lexicographically, are strictly ordered as a
binary search tree and every stored interval has low endpoint at most its high endpoint; the
identifiers of the stored entries are pairwise distinct; the identifier index maps the identifier of
every stored entry to that entry's low endpoint; and every identifier and low endpoint paired by the
index belong to some stored entry.

articles.title: Lexicographic comparison of keys
articles.statement:
For keys $(a, i)$ and $(b, j)$ in
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ (a low endpoint and an occurrence identifier), the comparison
returns less-than if $a < b$, or if $a = b$ and $i < j$; greater-than if $a > b$, or if $a = b$
and $i > j$; and equal if $a = b$ and $i = j$.

articles.title: Operation cost counters for interval trees
articles.statement:
A cost record for the interval tree consists
of seven natural-number counters, each defaulting to $0$: node visits, key comparisons, endpoint
comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations, and identifier-index operations.

The cached-maximum counter is deliberately narrow: it counts only the reads made by search
pruning, one per visited node where the left subtree's cached maximum decides the descent. Node
construction, rebalancing and the rotations read cached heights, sizes and maxima while rebuilding
nodes; those reads are not counted separately, and maintenance work is reported through the cache
write, rotation and remaining counters instead.

articles.title: Interval tree entry
articles.statement:
An entry of the interval tree consists of an identifier, which is a
natural number, and an interval with integer low and high endpoints.

Identifiers, rather than endpoints, are meant to be unique among stored entries; this is required
by the indexed tree's representation invariant, not by the entry itself.

articles.title: Keyed erasure removes exactly the entries with that key
articles.statement:
The key of an entry is the pair
$(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ of its low endpoint $\ell$ and identifier $i$; keys are
compared lexicographically. Let $T$ be an interval tree whose keys are strictly ordered (every key
in a left subtree is lexicographically below its node's key and every key in a right subtree is
above it), and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the in-order list of entries
of the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $T$ is a permutation of the in-order list of entries of $T$
with every entry of key $k$ removed.

articles.title: Keyed erasure with cost
articles.statement:
Erasing a key $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ from an
interval tree returns a new tree together with its cost; the key of an entry is the pair of its low
endpoint and identifier, and keys are compared lexicographically. The empty tree is returned
unchanged at a cost of one node visit. At a node with entry $x$, the key $k$ is compared with the
key of $x$. If $k$ is smaller, $k$ is erased from the left subtree; if it is larger, from the right
subtree; in both cases the node is rebuilt with the new subtree and rebalanced, and the cost is the
subtree's cost plus one node visit, one key comparison, one cache write and the rebalancing cost.
If $k$ equals the key of $x$ and the right subtree is empty (so it has no leftmost entry to
remove), the result is the left subtree at a cost of one node visit and one key comparison.
Otherwise the leftmost entry of the right subtree is removed and takes the place of $x$, the node
is rebuilt and rebalanced, and the cost is the removal's cost plus one node visit, one key
comparison, one cache write and the rebalancing cost.

articles.title: Correctness of erasure from the indexed interval tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree
satisfying the representation invariant, and let $i$ be a natural number. Then the tree obtained by
erasing identifier $i$ from $T$ again satisfies the invariant, and an entry is stored in it if and
only if it is stored in $T$ and its identifier differs from $i$.

In particular, if no stored entry has identifier $i$, the stored entries are unchanged.

articles.title: Erasure by identifier with cost
articles.statement:
To erase identifier $i$ from an indexed interval tree,
look $i$ up in the identifier index. If it is absent, the tree is returned unchanged at a cost of
one index operation. If the index maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key
$(\ell, i)$ is erased from the underlying interval tree, $i$ is removed from the index, and the
cost is the cost of the keyed erasure plus two index operations.

When the representation invariant holds, this deletes exactly the stored entry with identifier
$i$.

articles.title: Backward identifier-index check
articles.statement:
For an indexed interval tree, the backward index check
returns true exactly when, for every identifier $i$ that the identifier index maps to a low endpoint
$\ell$, some stored entry has identifier $i$ and an interval with low endpoint $\ell$.

articles.title: Forward identifier-index check
