articles.statement:
For an indexed interval tree, the forward index check
returns true exactly when the identifier index maps the identifier of every stored entry to the low
endpoint of that entry's interval.

articles.title: Indexed interval tree
articles.statement:
An indexed interval tree consists of a root interval tree together
with an identifier index: a finite map, implemented as a balanced search tree, from natural-number
identifiers to integer low endpoints.

articles.title: Entries after keyed insertion
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree whose entries are strictly ordered by key,
and let $x$ be an entry. The in-order list of entries of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$
by key is a permutation of the list consisting of $x$ followed by those entries of $t$ whose key
differs from the key of $x$.

articles.title: Keyed insertion with cost
articles.statement:
Inserting an entry $x$ into a tree returns a new tree together
with an operation cost; keys (low endpoint, then identifier) are compared lexicographically. Into
the empty tree, $x$ is inserted as a single node, at a cost of one node visit and one cache write.
At a node with entry $y$: if the key of $x$ equals the key of $y$, then $y$ is replaced by $x$, at a
cost of one node visit, one key comparison and one cache write; if the key of $x$ is smaller
(respectively larger), then $x$ is inserted recursively into the left (respectively right)
subtree, the node is rebuilt with recomputed metadata and rebalanced, and the cost is the cost of
the recursive insertion, plus one node visit, one key comparison and one cache write, plus the
cost of rebalancing.

articles.title: Correctness of insertion into an indexed interval tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree
satisfying the representation invariant, and let $x$ be an entry whose interval is valid (its low
endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If inserting $x$ into $T$ succeeds with result $T'$, then
$T'$ satisfies the representation invariant, $x$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$, and an entry
$e$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$ if and only if either $e = x$, or $e$ is stored in the root
tree of $T$ and the identifier of $e$ differs from the identifier of $x$.

articles.title: Insertion by identifier with cost
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree and let $e$ be an
entry with identifier $i$ and interval $[a, b]$. Inserting $e$ into $T$ first tests $a \le b$. If
$a > b$, it returns no tree, at a cost of one endpoint comparison. Otherwise, if the identifier
index of $T$ maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the
root tree of $T$ by keyed erasure; if $i$ is not in the index, the root tree is kept, at zero
cost. Then $e$ is inserted into the resulting tree by keyed insertion. The result is the indexed
interval tree with this new root tree and with the index updated to map $i$ to $a$, and the cost
is the cost of the erasure plus the cost of the insertion plus one endpoint comparison and two
index operations.

articles.title: Interval
articles.statement:
An interval is a pair of integers, its low endpoint and its high endpoint, read as
the closed interval from the low to the high endpoint. The structure itself imposes no order on the
endpoints; the public update operations accept an interval only when its low endpoint is at most
its high endpoint.

articles.title: Soundness of the invariant checker
articles.statement:
If the executable checker returns true on an indexed
interval tree $T$, then $T$ satisfies the representation invariant.

articles.title: Representation invariant of an indexed interval tree
articles.statement:
An indexed interval tree $T$
satisfies the representation invariant when its root tree has exact cached metadata (heights,
sizes, and attained maximum high endpoints), is strictly ordered by the composite key (low
endpoint, then identifier), is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and stores only valid
intervals; the identifiers of the stored entries are pairwise distinct; the identifier index maps
the identifier of every stored entry to that entry's low endpoint; and every pair $(i, \ell)$ in
the identifier index is the identifier and low endpoint of some stored entry.

The ordering of low endpoints used by search follows from the strict key ordering.

articles.title: Key between optional bounds
articles.statement:
Given an optional lower bound, an optional upper bound and a
key $k$ (a pair of an integer and a natural number), this test returns true exactly when the lower
bound is absent or strictly below $k$, and the upper bound is absent or strictly above $k$. Keys
are compared lexicographically: first by the integer, then by the natural number.

articles.title: Strictly key-ordered trees have distinct keys
articles.statement:
If a tree is strictly ordered by key, then
the keys of its stored entries are pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Deletion from an interval tree preserves key ordering
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval
tree and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the tree returned by the
cost-instrumented keyed deletion of $k$ from $t$ (the reported cost is discarded) is again
key-ordered.

articles.title: Insertion into an interval tree preserves key ordering
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval
tree and let $e$ be an entry. Then the tree returned by the cost-instrumented keyed insertion of
$e$ into $t$ (which replaces the entry with the same key, if there is one; the reported cost is
discarded) is again key-ordered.

articles.title: The executable ordering check implies key ordering
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be an interval tree and let
$\ell$ and $u$ be optional keys in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$. If the executable ordering check
of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is key-ordered, and every
entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$ when $\ell$ is present and
$\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the lexicographic order on keys
(low endpoint first, then identifier).

articles.title: Removing the minimum from an interval tree preserves key ordering
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a
key-ordered interval tree. If the cost-instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds,
returning that entry, a remaining tree $t'$ and a cost, then $t'$ is key-ordered.

articles.title: Key-ordered interval tree
articles.statement:
The empty tree is key-ordered, and a node is key-ordered when
both of its subtrees are key-ordered, the key of every entry in the left subtree is strictly less
than the key of the node's entry, and the key of the node's entry is strictly less than the key of
every entry in the right subtree. Keys are compared lexicographically: low endpoint first, then
identifier.

articles.title: Search key of an interval entry
articles.statement:
The key of an entry is the pair
$(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $\ell$ is the low endpoint of the entry's
interval and $i$ is the entry's identifier.

articles.title: The executable ordering check implies low-endpoint ordering
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be an interval tree
and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional keys in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$. If the executable
ordering check of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is
low-endpoint ordered, and every entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$
when $\ell$ is present and $\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the
lexicographic order on keys (low endpoint first, then identifier).

articles.title: Low-endpoint ordered interval tree
articles.statement:
The empty tree is low-endpoint ordered, and a node is
low-endpoint ordered when both of its subtrees are low-endpoint ordered, every interval in the
left subtree has low endpoint at most the low endpoint of the node's interval, and the node's
low endpoint is at most the low endpoint of every interval in the right subtree.

articles.title: Maximum with an optional value
articles.statement:
For an integer $a$ and an optional integer $v$, the value
is $a$ when $v$ is absent and $\max(a, v)$ when $v$ is present. It combines a value with an
optional subtree maximum without using a sentinel value.

articles.title: Node construction with repaired metadata
articles.statement:
For an interval tree $T$ write $h(T)$ and $|T|$
for its cached height and size, both $0$ for the empty tree. Given interval trees $L$ and $R$ and
an entry $e$, this builds the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose
cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$, whose cached size is $|L| + |R| + 1$, and whose cached
maximum high endpoint is the largest of the high endpoint of $e$ and the cached maxima of the
nonempty subtrees among $L$ and $R$.

It is the sole ordinary node constructor.

articles.title: Maximum high endpoint at a node
articles.statement:
For subtrees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, the node
maximum is the largest of the high endpoint of the interval of $e$, the cached maximum high
endpoint stored at the root of $L$, and the one stored at the root of $R$, where an empty subtree
stores no cached maximum and contributes nothing.

articles.title: Linear-scan overlap search
articles.statement:
For a tree $T$ and a query interval $q$, the oracle search
returns the first entry, in the in-order list of entries of $T$, whose interval overlaps $q$ as
closed intervals, and returns nothing when no entry's interval overlaps $q$.

It is a separate full-traversal oracle used only by specifications and tests.

articles.title: Ordered-and-valid check for interval trees
articles.statement:
Keys of entries are pairs (low endpoint,
identifier), ordered lexicographically. Given optional lower and upper key bounds $\ell$ and $u$,
the check accepts the empty tree, and accepts a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right
subtree $R$ exactly when the key $k$ of $e$ is strictly greater than $\ell$ if $\ell$ is present
and strictly less than $u$ if $u$ is present, the interval of $e$ has low endpoint at most its
high endpoint, $L$ is accepted with bounds $\ell$ and $k$, and $R$ is accepted with bounds $k$
and $u$.

articles.title: Overlap test for closed intervals
articles.statement:
For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high
endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the overlap test of
$I$ against $J$ returns true exactly when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; it compares $a$ with $d$ first
and returns false without the second comparison when $a > d$.

articles.title: The instrumented overlap test returns the plain result
articles.statement:
For intervals $I$ and $J$, the
Boolean component of the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ equals the overlap test of
$I$ against $J$.

articles.title: Comparison count of the overlap test
articles.statement:
For intervals $I$ and $J$, the instrumented overlap
test of $I$ against $J$ reports $2$ endpoint comparisons when the low endpoint of $I$ is at most
the high endpoint of $J$, and $1$ comparison otherwise.

articles.title: Overlap test with comparison count
articles.statement:
For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high
endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the instrumented
overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns the pair (false, $1$) when $a > d$, the pair (false, $2$)
when $a \le d$ and $c > b$, and the pair (true, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; the number
is the count of endpoint comparisons evaluated.

articles.title: Overlapping closed intervals
AVL rebalancing step with cost
articles.statement:
Rebalancing a tree $T$ returns a tree and a cost, where
heights are the stored heights. If $T$ is empty, or neither subtree of its root is more than one
taller than the other, it returns $T$ unchanged with zero cost. If the left subtree $L$ is more
than one taller than the right subtree, it applies a right rotation, costing $2$ cache writes and
one rotation, when the left child of $L$ is at least as tall as the right child of $L$, and
otherwise a left-right double rotation, costing $3$ cache writes and two rotations. If the right
subtree $R$ is more than one taller than the left subtree, it applies a left rotation, costing
$2$ cache writes and one rotation, when the right child of $R$ is at least as tall as the left
child of $R$, and otherwise a right-left double rotation, costing $3$ cache writes and two
rotations. All other cost counters are zero.

articles.title: Removing the minimum preserves the other entries
articles.statement:
If removing the leftmost entry of a tree
$T$ returns an entry $m$, a tree $T'$ and a cost, then the list consisting of $m$ followed by the
in-order entries of $T'$ is a permutation of the in-order entries of $T$.

articles.title: The removed minimum has the least key
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a key-ordered interval tree: at every
node, the keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and those in the right subtree strictly
larger than the node's key, where the key of an entry is the pair (low endpoint, identifier)
compared lexicographically. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ returns the entry $m$ (together
with the remaining tree and a cost record), then every entry $e$ stored in $T$ is either $m$
itself or has a key strictly larger than the key of $m$.

articles.title: Removing the leftmost entry, with its cost
articles.statement:
Removing the leftmost entry of an interval
tree $T$ returns nothing when $T$ is empty. When the root's left subtree is empty, it returns the
root entry, the right subtree, and a cost of one node visit. Otherwise it removes the leftmost
entry $m$ of the left subtree recursively (returning nothing if that fails), rebuilds the root
node over the new left subtree with recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint, and
rebalances that node; it returns $m$, the rebalanced tree, and the cost of the recursive call plus
one node visit and one cache write plus the cost of rebalancing.

articles.title: Left-right double rotation
articles.statement:
Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree
$L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left-right rotation sends
$\langle\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle, z, d\rangle$ to
$\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the
result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this
shape is returned unchanged.

articles.title: Left rotation
articles.statement:
Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$
and right subtree $R$. The left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$ to
$\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly
recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned
unchanged.

articles.title: Right-left double rotation
articles.statement:
Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree
$L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right-left rotation sends
$\langle a, x, \langle\langle b, y, c\rangle, z, d\rangle\rangle$ to
$\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the
result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this
shape is returned unchanged.

articles.title: Right rotation
articles.statement:
Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$
and right subtree $R$. The right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$ to
$\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly
recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned
unchanged.

articles.title: Completeness of indexed interval search
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying
its representation invariant, and let $Q$ be a valid query interval (low endpoint at most high
endpoint). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps $Q$ (each interval's low
endpoint is at most the other's high endpoint), then searching $T$ for $Q$ returns some entry.

articles.title: Completeness of interval-tree search
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree whose cached height, size
and maximum high endpoint are exact at every node, and whose low endpoints respect the search
order (at every node, low endpoints in the left subtree are at most the node's, and those in the
right subtree at least the node's). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps the
query interval $Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's high endpoint), then
searching $T$ for $Q$ returns some entry.

articles.title: Interval-tree search fails exactly when nothing overlaps
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree
whose cached height, size and maximum high endpoint are exact at every node, and whose low
endpoints respect the search order (at every node, low endpoints in the left subtree are at most
the node's, and those in the right subtree at least the node's). Then searching $T$ for a query
interval $Q$ returns nothing if and only if no entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps
$Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's high endpoint).

articles.title: Soundness of indexed interval-tree search
articles.statement:
The search of an indexed interval tree $T$ for
a query interval $q = [c, d]$ returns nothing when $c > d$, and otherwise returns the entry, if
any, found by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the root tree of $T$. For every indexed
interval tree $T$, every query interval $q$ and every entry $e$, if this search returns $e$, then
$e$ is one of the entries stored in the root tree of $T$ and the interval of $e$ overlaps $q$.

The representation invariant of $T$ is not needed.

articles.title: Instrumented search in the empty tree
articles.statement:
For every query interval $q$, the instrumented
overlap search of $q$ in the empty interval tree returns no entry, and its cost record counts
one node visit and zero for every other counter (key comparisons, endpoint comparisons,
cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations and index operations).

articles.title: Instrumented search in a one-entry tree
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be an entry whose interval is $[a, b]$,
let $q = [c, d]$ be a query interval, and let $k = 2$ if $a \le d$ and $k = 1$ otherwise.
Consider the single-node tree built from $e$ with empty subtrees and exact cached fields. If
$[a, b]$ and $[c, d]$ overlap (that is, $a \le d$ and $c \le b$), the instrumented overlap search
of $q$ in this tree returns $e$ with a cost record of one node visit and $k$ endpoint
comparisons. Otherwise it returns no entry with a cost record of two node visits (the root and
its empty right subtree) and $k$ endpoint comparisons. All other counters are zero in both
cases.

articles.title: Instrumented overlap search
articles.statement:
Given a query interval $q = [c, d]$ and an interval tree
$T$, the instrumented overlap search returns an optional entry together with a cost record,
defined by recursion on $T$. On the empty tree it returns no entry and records one node visit.
At a node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ with interval $[a, b]$ and right subtree $R$, it
first tests overlap by evaluating $a \le d$ and, only if that holds, $c \le b$; let
$k \in \{1, 2\}$ be the number of relations evaluated. If both hold, it returns $e$ and records
one node visit and $k$ endpoint comparisons. Otherwise, if $L$ is empty, it returns the result of
searching $R$, adding one node visit and $k$ endpoint comparisons to that search's cost. If $L$
is nonempty with cached maximum high endpoint $m$, it returns the result of searching $L$ when
$c \le m$ and of searching $R$ otherwise, adding one node visit, $k + 1$ endpoint comparisons and
one cached-maximum read to that search's cost. No other counter is ever incremented.

articles.title: Interval-tree overlap search
articles.statement:
The overlap search of a query interval $q$ in an interval
tree $T$ returns the optional entry produced by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in $T$,
discarding its cost record.

articles.title: Interval tree
articles.statement:
An interval tree is either empty or a node consisting of a left subtree,
an entry, a right subtree and three cached fields: a height and a size (natural numbers) and a
maximum high endpoint (an integer). The type imposes no balance or consistency condition on
these fields; it is the carrier on which the AVL interval-tree operations act.

articles.title: Boolean interval validity test
articles.statement:
For an interval $[a, b]$ with integer endpoints, the
Boolean validity test returns true exactly when $a \le b$.

articles.title: Keyed erasure preserves interval validity
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every
stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then for every key $(\ell, i)$ with $\ell$ an
integer and $i$ a natural number, the tree returned by keyed erasure of $(\ell, i)$ from $T$ also
has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.

articles.title: Keyed insertion preserves interval validity
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every
stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, and let $e$ be an entry whose interval $[a, b]$
satisfies $a \le b$. Then the tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ also has every
stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.

articles.title: Stored intervals of a valid tree are valid
articles.statement:
If an interval tree $T$ satisfies the validity
invariant, then every entry stored in $T$ has an interval $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$.

articles.title: Node construction preserves interval validity
articles.statement:
If $L$ and $R$ are interval trees
satisfying the validity invariant and $e$ is an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies
$a \le b$, then the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$, built by the
node constructor that recomputes the cached fields, satisfies the validity invariant.

articles.title: The ordering check implies interval validity
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree and let
$\ell$ and $u$ be optional lower and upper key bounds. If the executable check of $T$ with
bounds $\ell$ and $u$, which tests that every key lies strictly between its bounds and that every
stored interval passes the Boolean validity test, returns true, then every interval stored in
$T$ is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.

articles.title: Removing the minimum preserves interval validity
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an interval tree in which
every stored interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If the
instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds, returning that entry $m$, the
remaining tree $T'$ and a cost record $c$, then every interval stored in $T'$ is valid.

articles.title: Validity invariant of an interval tree
articles.statement:
A tree satisfies the validity invariant when
every interval stored in it is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.
Recursively, the empty tree satisfies it, and a node satisfies it when its left subtree does,
the interval of its entry is valid, and its right subtree does.

articles.title: Valid interval
articles.statement:
A closed interval with integer endpoints $a$ (low) and $b$ (high) is
valid when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint, $a \le b$.

articles.title: Kd-tree construction from the first axis
articles.statement:
For $d \ge 1$ and a list of points in
$\mathbb{Z}^d$, this is the kd-tree built from the list by alternating-axis median splits,
starting with split axis $0$.

articles.title: Kd-tree construction by median splits
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$, let $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$ be
an axis and let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. The kd-tree built from $P$ starting at
axis $a$ is the empty tree if $P$ is empty and the leaf holding $p$ if $P = [p]$. If $P$ has
$n \ge 2$ points, sort $P$ by $a$-coordinate with merge sort, let $L$ be the first
$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ points of the sorted list and $R$ the remaining ones. The result is the
split node with axis $a$ whose split value is the $a$-coordinate of the first point of $R$, whose
left subtree is built from $L$ and whose right subtree is built from $R$, both starting at the
next axis $(a + 1) \bmod d$.

articles.title: First-point coordinate
articles.statement:
For an axis $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$ and a list of points in
$\mathbb{Z}^d$, this is the $a$-coordinate of the first point of the list, or $0$ if the list
is empty.

articles.title: Membership in an axis-aligned box
articles.statement:
For $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the point $p$ lies
in the closed axis-aligned box $[lo, hi]$ when $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate
$i \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$.

articles.title: Kd-trees
articles.statement:
A kd-tree over points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is either empty, a leaf holding one
point of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, or a split node holding a split axis $a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, a split
value $s \in \mathbb{Z}$ and two kd-trees, its left and right subtrees.

articles.title: Length of the point list of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
For every kd-tree $t$, the list of the points
stored in $t$, read from left to right, has length equal to the size of $t$, the number of
points stored in $t$.

articles.title: Membership in the range report of a built kd-tree
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$, let
$a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$, let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and let
$lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$. Then $p$ occurs in the range report, for the box $[lo, hi]$, of the
kd-tree built from $P$ by median splits starting at axis $a$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $P$ and
$lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Range report of a kd-tree built from the first axis
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$, let $P$ be a list
of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and let $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$. Then $p$ occurs in the range
report, for the box $[lo, hi]$, of the kd-tree built from $P$ by median splits starting at
axis $0$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $P$ and $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate
$i$.

articles.title: Range report of a valid kd-tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a kd-tree over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ that
satisfies the kd invariant, and let $lo, hi, p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$. Then $p$ occurs in the range
report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ if and only if $p$ is one of the points stored in $t$ and
$lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: A built kd-tree holds the same points as its input
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$, let
$a \in \{0, \dots, d-1\}$ and let $P$ be a list of points in $\mathbb{Z}^d$. A point
$p \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ is stored in the kd-tree built from $P$ by median splits starting at axis
$a$ if and only if $p$ occurs in $P$.

articles.title: Next split axis of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
For a dimension $d \ge 1$ and an axis
$a \in \{0, \dots, d - 1\}$, the next split axis is $(a + 1) \bmod d$, so the axes are
visited cyclically.

articles.title: Accumulator range report of a valid kd-tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid kd-tree over
$\mathbb{Z}^d$, let $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $acc$ be a list of points. The
accumulator range report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ onto $acc$ equals the list of points
of $t$, in left-to-right order, that lie in the box (the points $p$ with
$lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$), followed by $acc$.

articles.title: Accumulator range report of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
Points are vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with
coordinates $p_0, \dots, p_{d-1}$; the box $[lo, hi]$ consists of the points $p$ with
$lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every $i$. For a kd-tree $t$ and a list $acc$ of points, the
accumulator report of $t$ for $[lo, hi]$ onto $acc$ is defined by recursion on $t$. For the
empty tree it is $acc$. For a leaf $p$ it is $p$ followed by $acc$ if $p$ lies in the box,
and $acc$ otherwise. For a split node with axis $a$, split value $s$, left child $L$ and
right child $R$, let $acc'$ be $acc$ if $hi_a < s$ and the report of $R$ onto $acc$
otherwise; the result is $acc'$ if $s < lo_a$ and the report of $L$ onto $acc'$ otherwise.

The accumulator avoids repeatedly appending the results of left subtrees, so building the
output list costs work linear in the number of reported points; the traversal still visits
every node that pruning does not cut, which can be the whole tree even for an empty report.
No complexity bound is formalized.

articles.title: Range report of a built kd-tree up to order
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$. For every starting axis $a$,
every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and all $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the range report
for the box $[lo, hi]$ of the kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$ is a permutation of
the list of entries of $P$ that lie in the box, that is, the points $p$ with
$lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Range report of a built kd-tree as a filter
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$. For every starting axis
$a$, every list $P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and all $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, let $T$ be
the kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$. The range report of $T$ for the box
$[lo, hi]$ equals the list of points of $T$, in left-to-right order, that lie in the box,
that is, the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Correctness of the kd-tree range report
articles.statement:
For every valid kd-tree $t$ over
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ and all $lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the range report of $t$ for the box
$[lo, hi]$ equals the list of points of $t$, in left-to-right order, that lie in the box,
that is, the points $p$ with $lo_i \le p_i \le hi_i$ for every coordinate $i$.

articles.title: Orthogonal range report of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
For a kd-tree $t$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and
$lo, hi \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the range report of $t$ for the box $[lo, hi]$ is the accumulator
range report of $t$ for $[lo, hi]$ onto the empty list.

articles.title: Size of a built kd-tree
articles.statement:
Let $d \ge 1$. For every starting axis $a$ and every list
$P$ of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the size of the kd-tree built from $P$ starting at axis $a$
equals the length of $P$ (repeated points counted with multiplicity).

articles.title: Size of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
The size of a kd-tree is defined by recursion: the empty tree has
size $0$, a leaf has size $1$, and a split node has the sum of the sizes of its two
children. Since points are stored only at leaves, this is the number of points stored in the
tree, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Accumulator traversal of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
For every kd-tree $t$ over $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and
every list $acc$ of points, the accumulator traversal of $t$ onto $acc$ equals the list of
points of $t$ in left-to-right order followed by $acc$.

articles.title: Kd-tree point traversal with an accumulator
articles.statement:
For a kd-tree $t$ over points of
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of such points, the accumulator traversal of $t$ onto
$\mathit{acc}$ is $\mathit{acc}$ when $t$ is empty, the point $p$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$ when
$t$ is a leaf holding $p$, and, when $t$ is a split node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree
$R$, the traversal of $L$ onto the traversal of $R$ onto $\mathit{acc}$.

Threading the output suffix avoids repeatedly appending (and copying) left-subtree results.

articles.title: Building a kd-tree preserves its points
articles.statement:
For $d \ge 1$, every axis $a$ and every list of
points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the point list of the kd-tree built from the list by median splits
starting at axis $a$ is a permutation of the list.

articles.title: Building a kd-tree from axis 0 preserves its points
articles.statement:
For $d \ge 1$ and every list of
points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the point list of the kd-tree built from the list by median splits
starting at axis $0$ is a permutation of the list.

articles.title: Point list of a kd-tree split node
articles.statement:
For a split node with axis $a$, split value $s$, left
subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, the point list of the node is the point list of $L$ followed
by the point list of $R$.

articles.title: Point list of a kd-tree
articles.statement:
The point list of a kd-tree is the list of the points stored at
its leaves, from left to right.

articles.title: Kd-trees built from axis 0 satisfy the kd invariant
articles.statement:
For $d \ge 1$ and every list of
points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the kd-tree built from the list by median splits starting at axis $0$
satisfies the kd invariant.

articles.title: Median-split kd-trees satisfy the kd invariant
articles.statement:
For $d \ge 1$, every axis $a$ and every
list of points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the kd-tree built from the list by median splits starting at
axis $a$ satisfies the kd invariant.

articles.title: Kd invariant
articles.statement:
A kd-tree satisfies the kd invariant when at every split node, with axis $a$
and split value $s$, every point of the left subtree has $a$-coordinate at most $s$ and every
point of the right subtree has $a$-coordinate at least $s$.

articles.title: The cached bounds of a nonempty bounds-valid range tree are leaf values
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a
bounds-valid range tree with at least one leaf. Then the cached lower bound of $t$ and the cached
upper bound of $t$ are both leaf values of $t$.

Together with the fact that every leaf value lies between the cached bounds, this shows that the
cached interval is exactly the interval spanned by the leaves, not merely an enclosing one.

articles.title: Leaf values of a bounds-valid tree lie between the cached bounds
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a
bounds-valid range tree, and write $t_{\min}$ and $t_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper
bounds. Then every leaf value $x$ of $t$ satisfies $t_{\min} \le x \le t_{\max}$.

articles.title: Built range trees are bounds-valid
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of integers, the range tree built
from $L$ by recursive halving is bounds-valid.

articles.title: Bounds-valid range trees
articles.statement:
For a range tree $s$, write $s_{\min}$ and $s_{\max}$ for its
cached lower and upper bounds: the stored interval endpoints at a node, the value itself at a
leaf, and $0$ for the empty tree. Bounds-validity is defined inductively: the empty tree and every
leaf are bounds-valid, and a node with cached interval $[a, b]$, left child $\ell$ and right child
$r$ is bounds-valid when $\ell$ and $r$ are bounds-valid, each of them has at least one leaf,
$a = \min(\ell_{\min}, r_{\min})$ and $b = \max(\ell_{\max}, r_{\max})$.

The children must be nonempty because the empty tree has cached bounds $0$: with an empty child
the node cache would only enclose the leaves (a node over an empty child and the single leaf $5$
could cache $[0, 5]$), not equal their true interval. In a bounds-valid tree every leaf value lies
in the cached interval, and if the tree has a leaf, both cached bounds are leaf values.

articles.title: Building a range tree from a list
articles.statement:
For a range tree $s$, write $s_{\min}$ and $s_{\max}$
for its cached lower and upper bounds. The range tree built from a list $L$ of integers of length
$n$ is defined by recursion on $n$: the empty list gives the empty tree, a one-element list $[x]$
gives the leaf $x$, and for $n \ge 2$ it is the node whose left child $\ell$ is the tree built from
the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries of $L$, whose right child $r$ is the tree built from the
remaining entries, and whose cached interval is
$[\min(\ell_{\min}, r_{\min}), \max(\ell_{\max}, r_{\max})]$.

The entries of $L$ are kept in their given order; $L$ is not sorted first.

articles.title: Range counting on a built tree
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of integers and all integers $a$ and
$b$, the range count over $[a, b]$ of the range tree built from $L$ equals the number of entries
of $L$, counted with multiplicity, that lie in $[a, b]$.

articles.title: Range count of a bounds-valid tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree and let $a$ and
$b$ be integers. Then the range count of $t$ over $[a, b]$ equals the number of leaves of $t$
whose value lies in $[a, b]$.

articles.title: Range count
articles.statement:
For a range tree $t$ and integers $a$ and $b$, the range count of $t$ over
$[a, b]$ is the length of the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$.

On a bounds-valid tree this is the number of leaves whose value lies in $[a, b]$.

articles.title: Length of the leaf list of a range tree
articles.statement:
For every range tree $t$, the list of leaf values
of $t$ read from left to right has length equal to the number of leaves of $t$.

articles.title: Range report membership on a built tree
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of integers and all integers
$a$, $b$ and $x$, the value $x$ occurs in the range report for $[a, b]$ on the range tree built
from $L$ if and only if $x$ is an entry of $L$ and $a \le x \le b$.

articles.title: Membership in a range report
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a range tree satisfying the bounds-correctness
predicate: every node has two subtrees with at least one leaf each and caches the least and the
greatest leaf value of its subtree. For all integers $a$, $b$ and $x$, the value $x$ occurs in the
range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ if and only if $x$ is a leaf value of $t$ and $a \le x \le b$.

articles.title: Valid range trees have sorted leaves
articles.statement:
If a range tree $t$ is valid, then its list of leaf
values, read from left to right, is sorted in nondecreasing order.

articles.title: Range tree
articles.statement:
A one-dimensional range tree over the integers is either empty, a single leaf
holding an integer, or a binary node made of two integers $l$ and $h$ together with a left and a
right subtree. The integers $l$ and $h$ are meant to cache the interval $[l, h]$ spanned by the
leaf values of the node's subtree; the type does not enforce this, the bounds-correctness
predicate does.

articles.title: Accumulator range report of a bounds-valid range tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range
tree, let $a$ and $b$ be integers and let $\mathit{acc}$ be a list of integers. Then the
accumulator range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ starting from $\mathit{acc}$ is the list of the leaf
values $x$ of $t$ with $a \le x \le b$, in left-to-right order and with repetitions, followed by
$\mathit{acc}$.

articles.title: Accumulator range report
articles.statement:
For integers $a$, $b$ and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of integers, the
accumulator range report of a range tree for $[a, b]$ starting from $\mathit{acc}$ is defined by
recursion on the tree. The empty tree returns $\mathit{acc}$. A leaf with value $x$ returns $x$
followed by $\mathit{acc}$ if $a \le x \le b$, and $\mathit{acc}$ otherwise. A node with cached
interval $[l, h]$ returns $\mathit{acc}$ if $h < a$ or $b < l$; otherwise, if $a \le l$ and
$h \le b$, it returns the node's leaf values from left to right followed by $\mathit{acc}$;
otherwise it returns the report of the left child starting from the report of the right child
starting from $\mathit{acc}$.

The cached bounds make each pruning test constant-time.

articles.title: Range report on a built tree
articles.statement:
For every list $\mathit{xs}$ of integers and all integers $a$
and $b$, the range report for $[a, b]$ on the range tree built from $\mathit{xs}$ equals the list
of elements $x$ of $\mathit{xs}$ with $a \le x \le b$, in their original order.

articles.title: Correctness of the range report
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a range tree satisfying the bounds-correctness
predicate: every node has two subtrees with at least one leaf each and caches the least and the
greatest leaf value of its subtree. For all integers $a$ and $b$, the range report of $t$ for
$[a, b]$ equals the list of leaf values $x$ of $t$ with $a \le x \le b$, in left-to-right order.

articles.title: Range report
articles.statement:
The range report of a range tree $t$ for integers $a$ and $b$ is the
accumulator range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ starting from the empty list.

articles.title: Size of a built range tree
articles.statement:
For every list $\mathit{xs}$ of integers, the range tree built
from $\mathit{xs}$ has exactly as many leaves as $\mathit{xs}$ has elements.

articles.title: Number of leaves of a range tree
articles.statement:
The size of a range tree is its number of leaves: $0$ for
the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and the sum of the sizes of the two children for a node.

articles.title: Cached upper bound of a range tree
articles.statement:
For a range tree $t$, $\operatorname{tmax}(t)$ is
$0$ if $t$ is empty, $x$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and the stored upper bound
$hi$ if $t$ is a node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$ and two subtrees.

The value $0$ for the empty tree is a sentinel without meaning.

articles.title: Cached lower bound of a range tree
articles.statement:
For a range tree $t$, $\operatorname{tmin}(t)$ is
$0$ if $t$ is empty, $x$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and the stored lower bound
$lo$ if $t$ is a node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$ and two subtrees.

The value $0$ for the empty tree is a sentinel without meaning. Computing
$\operatorname{tmin}(t)$ takes constant time: it reads the bound cached at the root and does not
traverse the tree.

articles.title: Range-tree leaf traversal appends to its accumulator
articles.statement:
For every range tree $t$ and every
list $a$ of integers, the accumulator leaf traversal of $t$ started from $a$ equals the leaf list
of $t$ followed by $a$.

articles.title: Leaf traversal of a range tree with an accumulator
articles.statement:
For a range tree $t$ and a list $a$
of integers, $\operatorname{aux}(t, a)$ is $a$ if $t$ is empty, the list $x$ followed by $a$ if
$t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and $\operatorname{aux}(L, \operatorname{aux}(R, a))$ if $t$
is a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$.

Equivalently, $\operatorname{aux}(t, a)$ is the leaf list of $t$ followed by $a$, so the leaf list
is computed in linear time rather than by repeatedly appending left leaf lists.

articles.title: Building a range tree preserves the list
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of integers, the leaf list
of the range tree built from $xs$ is $xs$.

articles.title: Leaf list of a range-tree node
articles.statement:
For all integers $lo$, $hi$ and range trees $L$, $R$, the
leaf list of the node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is
the leaf list of $L$ followed by the leaf list of $R$.

articles.title: Leaf list of a range tree
articles.statement:
The leaf list of a range tree $t$ is the list of the integers
stored at its leaves, read from left to right and with repetitions.

articles.title: Building from a sorted list gives a valid range tree
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of integers that
is sorted in nondecreasing order, the range tree built from $xs$ is valid.

Without the sortedness hypothesis the built tree still has correct cached bounds, but it need not
be valid.

articles.title: Valid range tree
articles.statement:
A range tree $t$ is valid when it has correct cached bounds (every node
has two subtrees with nonempty leaf lists, and its stored lower and upper bounds are the minimum
of the lower bounds and the maximum of the upper bounds of its two subtrees, recursively) and
its leaf list is sorted in nondecreasing order.

articles.title: Quadtree complementation preserves compression
articles.statement: Complementation preserves compression of the input.

articles.title: Local compression of compressed children is compressed
articles.statement: Four compressed children produce a compressed result.

articles.title: Quadtree difference preserves compression
articles.statement: Difference preserves compression when both inputs are compressed.

articles.title: Quadtree union preserves compression
articles.statement: Union preserves compression when both inputs are compressed.

articles.title: Six-part correctness of Boolean quadtree operations
articles.statement:
The original graded six-part correctness statement, under its original
name.

articles.title: Quadtree complementation negates lookup at sufficient scale
articles.statement: Complementation negates each lookup whenever the scale bounds height.

articles.title: Local compression preserves lookup at positive scales
articles.statement:
Compression preserves positive-scale lookup. Scale zero is excluded:
collapsing four `true` leaves changes a branch's zero-scale default.

articles.title: Quadtree difference is pointwise set difference at sufficient scale
articles.statement:
Difference is pointwise conjunction with the second region's complement,
provided the scale bounds both heights.

articles.title: Quadtree union is pointwise disjunction at sufficient scale
articles.statement: Union is pointwise Boolean disjunction at a scale bounding both heights.

articles.title: Boolean quadtree lookup
articles.statement:
Boolean lookup with `false` on a nonleaf at scale zero.
Leaves ignore coordinates; positive scales use the shared quadrant order.

articles.title: Quadtree complementation does not increase height
articles.statement: Complementation does not increase height.

articles.title: Local compression does not increase quadtree height
articles.statement: Local compression never increases a branch's height.

articles.title: Height bound for quadtree difference
articles.statement: Difference height is bounded by the maximum input height.

articles.title: Height bound for quadtree union
articles.statement: Union height is bounded by the maximum input height.

articles.title: Complement of a Boolean quadtree
articles.statement: Complements every leaf, compressing the rebuilt branches.

articles.title: Compressing branch constructor for Boolean quadtrees
articles.statement:
A branch constructor that collapses four identical Boolean leaves.
This is local compression, not recursive normalization of its arguments.

articles.title: Difference of Boolean quadtrees
articles.statement:
Ordered Boolean difference: cells in the first region but not the second.
A full first region complements the second; an empty second returns the
first.

articles.title: Union of Boolean quadtrees
articles.statement:
Boolean union, short-circuiting constant regions and compressing
branches when both inputs are branches.

articles.title: Correctness of function reconstruction by quadtrees
articles.statement: The original graded reconstruction theorem, under its original name.

articles.title: Sampled quadtree recovers the function on the represented square
articles.statement:
Reading a sampled function recovers its value within the represented
square.

articles.title: Polymorphic quadtree lookup
articles.statement:
Polymorphic lookup. A leaf is constant; at zero scale a branch follows
its first child at `(0, 0)`. Positive scales select quadrants by the split.

articles.title: Height of the quadtree sampled from a function
articles.statement: Reconstruction builds exactly the requested number of branch levels.

articles.title: Membership in the represented square
articles.statement: Membership in the represented square is a pair of strict bounds.

articles.title: Full quadtree sampled from a function
articles.statement:
Samples `f` into a full tree. Every branch splits its coordinate square
into four equal quadrants, without compressing equal leaves.

articles.title: Square region represented by a quadtree
articles.statement: The represented square: both natural coordinates are below `2 ^ n`.

articles.title: Compressed quadtree
articles.statement:
Every subtree is compressed and no branch has four identical leaves.
Identical nonleaf children are allowed: they need not represent a constant.

articles.title: Height bound for the children of a quadtree branch
articles.statement: A bound on branch height bounds all four child heights one level lower.

articles.title: Height of a quadtree
articles.statement: The maximum number of branches from the root to a leaf.

articles.title: Region quadtree
articles.statement: A finite region quadtree with a value leaf or four ordered quadrants.

articles.title: Quadrant selection by coordinate flags
articles.statement:
Selects low/low, low/high, high/low, or high/high, respectively, when
`(x, y)` is `(true, true)`, `(true, false)`, `(false, true)`, or
`(false, false)`.
In lookup, `true` means that the corresponding coordinate is below the split.

articles.title: Aggregate of a built segment tree
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ with entries in an additive
monoid, the aggregate of the segment tree built from $L$ equals the sum of the entries of $L$,
taken from left to right.

articles.title: Aggregate of a valid segment tree
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid segment tree with values in an
additive monoid, then the aggregate of $t$ equals the sum of the leaf values of $t$, taken from
left to right.

articles.title: Aggregate after a point update of a built segment tree
articles.statement:
Let $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$
be a list with entries in an additive monoid, let $i < n$, and let $y$ be an element of the
monoid. Applying the point update at index $i$ with value $y$ to the segment tree built from $L$
gives a tree whose aggregate is the sum, taken from left to right, of the list obtained from $L$
by replacing $x_i$ with $y$.

articles.title: Aggregate of a segment tree
articles.statement:
The aggregate of a segment tree with values in an additive
monoid is $0$ for the empty tree, $x$ for a single leaf with value $x$, and the aggregate cached at
the root for an internal node.

articles.title: Building a segment tree from a list
articles.statement:
The segment tree built from a list $L$ with entries
in an additive monoid is the empty tree if $L$ is empty, and a single leaf with value $x$ if
$L = (x)$. If $L$ has length $n \ge 2$, it is the internal node whose left child is the tree built
from the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries of $L$, whose right child is the tree built from the
remaining entries, and which caches the aggregate of the left child plus the aggregate of the
right child, in that order, and the sum of the sizes of its children.

articles.title: Size of a valid segment tree
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid segment tree with values in an additive
monoid, then the length of the list of leaf values of $t$, read from left to right, equals the
size of $t$.

articles.title: Range queries on a built segment tree
articles.statement:
Let $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list with
entries in an additive monoid and let $l, r$ be natural numbers. The range query over $[l, r)$ on
the segment tree built from $L$ returns $\sum_{l \le k < \min(r, n)} x_k$, the sum taken in
increasing order of $k$; it is $0$ when $\min(r, n) \le l$.

articles.title: Correctness of range queries on a valid segment tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid segment tree with
values in an additive monoid, let $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be its leaf values from left to right,
and let $l, r$ be natural numbers. The range query over $[l, r)$ on $t$ returns
$\sum_{l \le k < \min(r, n)} x_k$, the sum taken in increasing order of $k$; it is $0$ when
$\min(r, n) \le l$.

articles.title: Range queries after a point update of a built segment tree
articles.statement:
Let $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$
be a list with entries in an additive monoid, let $i < n$, let $y$ be an element of the monoid,
and let $L'$ be the list obtained from $L$ by replacing $x_i$ with $y$, with entries
$x'_0, \dots, x'_{n-1}$. Apply the point update at index $i$ with value $y$ to the segment tree
built from $L$. For all natural numbers $l, r$, the range query over $[l, r)$ on the result
returns $\sum_{l \le k < \min(r, n)} x'_k$, the sum taken in increasing order of $k$; it is $0$
when $\min(r, n) \le l$.

articles.title: Range query on a segment tree
articles.statement:
For a segment tree $t$ with values in an additive monoid
and natural numbers $l, r$, the range query over $[l, r)$, with positions counted from the start
of the segment of $t$, is defined recursively. On the empty tree it is $0$. On a leaf with value
$x$ it is $x$ if $l = 0 < r$, and $0$ otherwise. On an internal node with cached aggregate $a$,
cached size $s$ and children $t_1, t_2$, it is $0$ if $r \le l$ or $s \le l$; otherwise it is $a$
if $l = 0$ and $s \le r$; and in all remaining cases it is the query over $[l, r)$ on $t_1$ plus
the query over $[l - m, r - m)$ on $t_2$, where $m$ is the size of $t_1$ and subtraction is
truncated at $0$.

An empty range and a node disjoint from the range contribute $0$ without descending, and a fully
covered node contributes its cached aggregate.

articles.title: Segment tree
articles.statement:
A segment tree with values in $\alpha$ is either empty, a leaf holding a
value in $\alpha$, or an internal node holding a cached segment aggregate in $\alpha$, a cached
segment length in $\mathbb{N}$, a left child and a right child, both segment trees.

articles.title: Size of a built segment tree
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ with entries in an additive monoid, the
segment tree built from $xs$ has size equal to the length of $xs$.

articles.title: Point update preserves the size of a segment tree
articles.statement:
For every segment tree $t$ over an
additive monoid, every index $i$ and every value $y$, the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$
has the same size as $t$.

Every node on the update path keeps its cached segment length.

articles.title: Size of a segment tree
articles.statement:
The size of a segment tree is $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a
leaf, and, for an internal node, the segment length cached at that node.

When every cached length is the sum of the sizes of the node's children, this is the number of
leaves, and internal nodes answer in constant time.

articles.title: Accumulator traversal prepends the leaf list
articles.statement:
For every segment tree $t$ and every list
$acc$, the accumulator traversal of $t$ starting from $acc$ returns the leaf list of $t$ followed
by $acc$.

articles.title: Accumulator traversal of a segment tree
articles.statement:
Given a segment tree and a list $acc$, the
accumulator traversal returns $acc$ for the empty tree, the list $acc$ with $x$ prepended for a
leaf with value $x$, and, for an internal node with left child $L$ and right child $R$, the
traversal of $L$ starting from the result of the traversal of $R$ starting from $acc$.

Threading the output suffix this way collects the leaves of an $n$-leaf tree in linear time
instead of repeatedly appending (and copying) left-subtree results.

articles.title: Building a segment tree preserves the list
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ with entries in an
additive monoid, the leaf list of the segment tree built from $xs$ is $xs$.

articles.title: Leaf list of an internal node
articles.statement:
For every internal node of a segment tree, with any cached
aggregate, any cached length, left child $L$ and right child $R$, its leaf list is the leaf list
of $L$ followed by the leaf list of $R$.

With the accumulator definition of the leaf list this is a theorem, not a definitional
unfolding.

articles.title: Point update of a built segment tree
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ with entries in an additive
monoid, every index $i$ smaller than the length of $xs$ and every value $y$, the leaf list of the
segment tree built from $xs$, after the point update at $i$ with $y$, is $xs$ with its entry at
position $i$ (counting from $0$) replaced by $y$.

articles.title: Out-of-range point update leaves the leaf list unchanged
articles.statement:
For every valid segment tree $t$
over an additive monoid, every index $i$ at least the size of $t$ and every value $y$, the point
update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ has the same leaf list as $t$.

articles.title: Leaf list after an in-range point update
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid segment tree over an
additive monoid and let $i$ be a natural number less than the size of $t$. Then for every value
$y$, the leaf list of the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ is the leaf list of $t$ with its
entry at position $i$ (counting from $0$) replaced by $y$.

Validity is what ties the cached sizes used for routing to the leaf list.

articles.title: Leaf list of a segment tree
articles.statement:
The leaf list of a segment tree is the list of its leaf
values from left to right: the empty list for the empty tree, $[x]$ for a leaf with value $x$,
and the leaf list of the left child followed by the leaf list of the right child for an
internal node.

articles.title: Point update preserves validity
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid segment tree over an additive monoid,
then for every natural number $i$ and every value $y$, the point update of $t$ at $i$ with $y$ is
valid.

articles.title: Point update of a segment tree
articles.statement:
The point update of a segment tree over an additive
monoid at an index $i \in \mathbb{N}$, relative to the tree's segment, with a value $y$ is
defined recursively. The empty tree stays empty. A leaf becomes a leaf with value $y$ if $i = 0$
and is unchanged otherwise. At an internal node with left child $L$ and right child $R$: if $i$
is less than the size of $L$, then $L$ is replaced by its point update at $i$ with $y$, and
otherwise $R$ is replaced by its point update at $i$ minus the size of $L$ with $y$; the node
keeps its cached length, and its cached aggregate becomes the aggregate of the new left child
plus the aggregate of the new right child.

articles.title: Built segment trees are valid
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over an additive monoid, the segment
tree built from $xs$ is valid.

articles.title: Valid segment trees
articles.statement:
Validity of a segment tree over an additive monoid is defined
inductively: the empty tree and every leaf are valid, and an internal node with valid left child
$L$ and valid right child $R$ is valid when its cached aggregate is the aggregate of $L$ plus
the aggregate of $R$ and its cached length is the size of $L$ plus the size of $R$. Here the
aggregate and size of the empty tree are $0$ and $0$, of a leaf with value $x$ are $x$ and $1$,
and of an internal node are its cached aggregate and cached length.

articles.title: One step of the sparse-table construction
articles.statement:
Work over a type with a minimum operation
$\min$. Given a pair $(r, L)$ of a current row $r$ (an array of length $|r|$) and an array $L$
of the rows recorded so far, and a natural number $k$, the build step returns the pair
$(r', L')$, where $L'$ is $L$ with $r$ appended at the end, and $r'$ is the array whose
entry $i$ is $\min(r_i, r_{i+2^k})$ for each $i$ with $i + 2^k < |r|$.

articles.title: Built sparse tables are valid
articles.statement:
For every list $a$ over a type with a minimum operation,
the sparse table built from $a$ is valid: its stored rows are exactly the levels
$0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ of $a$, in this order, where $n$ is the length of $a$
and $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.

articles.title: Building a sparse table
articles.statement:
For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a type with a minimum
operation $\min$, the sparse table built from $a$ has data $a$ and
$\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ stored rows, where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.
The rows are produced by iterating the build step for $k = 0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$,
starting from the current row $a$ and no recorded rows. So row $0$ is $a$, and entry $i$ of
row $k + 1$ is $\min(x_i, x_{i+2^k})$, where $x$ is row $k$ and $i + 2^k$ is less than the
length of $x$. Each row is computed once, from its predecessor.

articles.title: Entries of a built sparse table are interval minima
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be
a list over a linearly ordered type, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with
$i + 2^k \le n$. Then the entry of the sparse table built from $a$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is
defined and equals $\min(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+2^k-1})$.

No separate bound on $k$ is needed: $i + 2^k \le n$ already implies
$k \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.

articles.title: Entries of a valid sparse table are interval minima
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid sparse table
over a linearly ordered type, with data $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{n-1})$, and let $k$ and $i$ be
natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is
defined and equals $\min(d_i, d_{i+1}, \dots, d_{i+2^k-1})$.

articles.title: Rows of a valid sparse table are its levels
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a type
with a minimum operation, with data $d$ of length $n$, and let $k \le \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$,
where $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$. Then for every index $i$, the entry of $t$
at row $k$ and index $i$ is defined exactly when level $k$ of $d$ has an element at index $i$,
and in that case the two are equal.

articles.title: Sparse-table entries
articles.statement:
For a sparse table $t$ and natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the entry
of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is element $i$ of the $k$-th stored row of $t$ (both counted
from $0$) when $t$ has a $k$-th row and that row has an element at index $i$; otherwise the
entry is undefined. Both lookups are random-access array lookups.

articles.title: Levels hold interval minima
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a linearly
ordered type, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then level $k$ of $a$
has an element at index $i$, and it equals $\min(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+2^k-1})$.

articles.title: Length of a level
articles.statement:
For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a type with a minimum operation
and a natural number $k$, level $k$ of $a$ has length $\max(n + 1 - 2^k, 0)$: one element for
each start index $i$ with $i + 2^k \le n$.

articles.title: Levels of a sparse table
articles.statement:
For a list $a$ over a type with a minimum operation $\min$, the
levels of $a$ are defined recursively: level $0$ is $a$, and if level $k$ is
$\ell = (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{m-1})$, then level $k + 1$ is the list of the values
$\min(\ell_i, \ell_{i+2^k})$ for $0 \le i < m - 2^k$ (empty when $m \le 2^k$).

Over a linear order, element $i$ of level $k$ is the minimum of the $2^k$ consecutive elements
of $a$ starting at index $i$, and only start indices whose interval fits in $a$ get an element.

articles.title: Next level of a sparse table row
articles.statement:
For a type with a minimum operation, an array
$(r_0, \dots, r_{n-1})$ and a natural number $k$, the next level is the array of length
$n - 2^k$ (empty when $2^k \ge n$) whose entry $i$ is $\min(r_i, r_{i + 2^k})$.

The construction of a sparse table computes each level once from the previous one this way.

articles.title: Idempotence of the option minimum
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every
optional value $a$ (an element of $\alpha$ or none), the option minimum of $a$ with itself is $a$.

This is what lets two overlapping query intervals count their overlap twice.

articles.title: Option minimum
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a minimum operation, the option minimum extends
$\min$ to optional values (elements of $\alpha$ or none): on two elements $a, b$ of $\alpha$ it
returns $\min(a, b)$, and none is a neutral element on either side.

articles.title: Whole-range sparse table query
articles.statement:
For every list $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered
type, the range-minimum query over $[0, n)$ on the sparse table built from $a$ returns the
minimum of $a$ (none when $a$ is empty).

articles.title: Correctness of sparse table queries
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a
linearly ordered type and let $l, r$ be natural numbers with $r \le n$. Then the range-minimum
query over $[l, r)$ on the sparse table built from $a$ returns the minimum of the slice
$(a_l, \dots, a_{r-1})$ (none when $r \le l$, where the slice is empty).

No ordering premise $l \le r$ is needed.

articles.title: Correctness of queries on valid sparse tables
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a
linearly ordered type whose data is the list $(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$, and let $l, r$ be natural
numbers with $r \le n$. Then the range-minimum query over $[l, r)$ on $t$ returns the minimum of
the slice $(a_l, \dots, a_{r-1})$ (none when $r \le l$, where the slice is empty).

Only the premise $r \le n$ is needed: for reversed bounds $r \le l$ both sides are none.

articles.title: Sparse table range-minimum query
articles.statement:
For a sparse table $t$ over a type with a minimum operation
and natural numbers $l, r$, the query over $[l, r)$ returns none when $r \le l$. Otherwise, with
$k = \lfloor \log_2 (r - l) \rfloor$, it returns the option minimum (the minimum, with none as a
neutral element on either side) of the entries of $t$ at level $k$ and indices $l$ and $r - 2^k$,
in this order, where an entry not stored in $t$ counts as none.

articles.title: Sparse table
articles.statement:
A sparse table over a type $\alpha$ consists of an array of elements of
$\alpha$, called its data, and an array of arrays of elements of $\alpha$, called its levels.

The intended meaning is that level $k$ stores the minima of the length-$2^k$ slices of the data;
data and levels are stored as arrays so that entry lookup is random access. Arbitrary values need
not relate data and levels at all; validity ties every stored level to this specification, tables
produced by the construction are valid, and query correctness is stated for valid tables.

articles.title: Valid sparse table
articles.statement:
A sparse table over a type with a minimum operation, whose data is a
list $a$ of length $n$, is valid when it has exactly $m + 1$ levels, where
$m = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ for $n \ge 1$ and $m = 0$ for $n = 0$, and for each $k \le m$ its
level $k$ is the list $L_k$ defined by $L_0 = a$ and, for $x = L_j$, $L_{j+1}$ is the list of
length $|x| - 2^j$ (empty when $2^j \ge |x|$) whose entry $i$ is $\min(x_i, x_{i + 2^j})$. For a
linear order, $L_k$ is the list of minima of the length-$2^k$ slices of $a$.

Tables produced by the construction are valid, an arbitrary value such as data $(1)$ with the
single level $(99)$ is not, and query correctness is stated only for valid tables.

articles.title: All-keys predicate agrees with the flattening on 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$
on keys and every 2-3 tree $t$ of height $h$, every key stored at a node of $t$ satisfies $p$
if and only if every element of the inorder flattening of $t$ satisfies $p$.

articles.title: All-keys predicate agrees with membership on 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on
keys and every 2-3 tree $t$ of height $h$, the recursive predicate requiring $p$ at every key
stored at a node of $t$ holds if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every member $x$ of $t$, where
$x$ is a member of $t$ when it equals one of the keys stored at some node of $t$.

articles.title: Predicate on all keys of a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
For a predicate $p$ on keys and a 2-3 tree $t$,
$\mathrm{All}_p(t)$ states that every separator key stored at a node of $t$ satisfies $p$: it
is true at a leaf, and at a node it requires $p$ of each key of the node and
$\mathrm{All}_p$ of each of its subtrees.

articles.title: Every height-indexed 2-3 tree is balanced
articles.statement:
For every height $h$, every 2-3 tree of
height $h$ satisfies the balance invariant: at every node, the subtrees are balanced and have
equal computed heights.

articles.title: Every rooted 2-3 tree is balanced
articles.statement:
For every root, that is, a 2-3 tree packaged with its
height, the underlying height-indexed tree satisfies the balance invariant.

articles.title: Balance invariant for 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
A leaf is balanced, and a node is balanced when all of
its subtrees are balanced and have the same computed height, where the computed height of a
tree is the length of its leftmost path from the root down to a leaf. Hence all leaves of a
balanced tree lie at the same depth.

articles.title: Search in a rooted 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, searching a root (a 2-3
tree packaged with its height) for a key $x$ returns the Boolean result of the 2-3 tree search
for $x$ in the underlying height-indexed tree.

articles.title: Search in a rooted 2-3 tree is correct
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly ordered and let $t$ be
a root (a 2-3 tree packaged with its height) whose underlying tree satisfies the ordering
invariant. Then searching $t$ for a key $x$ returns true if and only if $x$ occurs in the
inorder flattening of $t$.

articles.title: Search in an ordered 2-3 tree is correct
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly ordered and let $t$ be
a 2-3 tree of height $h$ that satisfies the ordering invariant. Then searching $t$ for a key
$x$ returns true if and only if $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $t$.

articles.title: Search in a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, searching a 2-3 tree for a key
$x$ returns false at a leaf. At a 2-node with key $a$, it searches the left subtree if $x < a$,
otherwise the right subtree if $a < x$, and otherwise returns true. At a 3-node with keys $a$
and $b$, it searches the left subtree if $x < a$; otherwise, if $a < x$, it searches the
middle subtree if $x < b$, otherwise the right subtree if $b < x$, and otherwise returns true;
if neither $x < a$ nor $a < x$, it returns true.

articles.title: Empty 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
The empty 2-3 tree is the root of height $0$ whose underlying tree is
the leaf.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a 2-3 tree root
articles.statement:
The flattening of a 2-3 tree root is the
flattening of its underlying tree, that is, the list of its keys in inorder.

articles.title: The accumulated traversal appends the suffix
articles.statement:
For every 2-3 tree $t$ (of any height)
and every list $s$, the accumulated inorder traversal of $t$ onto $s$ equals the flattening of
$t$ followed by $s$.

articles.title: Accumulated inorder traversal of a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
For a 2-3 tree $t$ and a list $s$, the
accumulated traversal $F(t, s)$ is defined by recursion on $t$: for a leaf, $F(t, s) = s$; for
a 2-node with key $a$ and children $l, r$, $F(t, s)$ is $F(l, s')$ where $s'$ is $a$ prepended
to $F(r, s)$; for a 3-node with keys $a, b$ and children $l, m, r$, $F(t, s)$ is $F(l, s')$
where $s'$ is $a$ prepended to $F(m, s'')$ and $s''$ is $b$ prepended to $F(r, s)$.

The result is the inorder traversal of $t$ followed by $s$. It is built without recopying the
traversals of left subtrees.

articles.title: Insertion into a 2-3 tree is ordered insertion into its traversal
articles.statement:
Let the keys be
linearly ordered, let $t$ be an ordered 2-3 tree root and let $x$ be a key. Then the flattening
of the root obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ equals the ordered insertion of $x$ into the
flattening of $t$.

articles.title: The traversal of an ordered 2-3 tree has no duplicates
articles.statement:
If the keys are linearly ordered
and a 2-3 tree $t$ (of any height) is ordered, then no key occurs twice in the flattening of
$t$.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
The flattening of a 2-3 tree $t$ is the accumulated
inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list. Equivalently, the flattening of a leaf is empty;
that of a 2-node with key $a$ and children $l, r$ is the flattening of $l$, then $a$, then the
flattening of $r$; and that of a 3-node with keys $a, b$ and children $l, m, r$ is the flattening
of $l$, then $a$, then the flattening of $m$, then $b$, then the flattening of $r$.

articles.title: Building a 2-3 tree from a list
articles.statement:
For linearly ordered keys, the 2-3 tree root built from
a list is defined by recursion: the empty list gives the empty 2-3 tree, and a list with head $x$
and tail $xs$ gives the result of inserting $x$ into the root built from $xs$. Thus the elements
are inserted into the empty tree from the last to the first.

articles.title: Computed height equals the height index
articles.statement:
For every 2-3 tree $t$ with height index $h$,
the height of $t$ computed along its leftmost spine equals $h$.

articles.title: Insertion raises the height of a 2-3 tree by at most one
articles.statement:
For linearly ordered keys,
every key $x$ and every 2-3 tree root $t$, the stored height of the root obtained by inserting
$x$ into $t$ is at most the stored height of $t$ plus one.

articles.title: The stored height of a 2-3 tree root is its computed height
articles.statement:
For every root $t$, that
is, a 2-3 tree together with its height index, the height of the underlying tree computed along
its leftmost spine equals the stored height of $t$.

articles.title: Height of a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
The height of a 2-3 tree is computed along its leftmost spine:
a leaf has height $0$, and a 2-node or a 3-node has height one more than the height of its
leftmost child.

articles.title: Correctness of 2-3 tree insertion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let $x \in \alpha$,
and let $t$ be an ordered 2-3 tree of height $h$. Then inserting $x$ into $t$ meets the insertion
specification. If the insertion returns a single tree $t'$ of height $h$, then $t'$ is ordered
and its inorder traversal is the ordered insertion of $x$ into the inorder traversal of $t$. If
it returns a split into trees $l$ and $r$ of height $h$ around a promoted key $k$, then $l$ and
$r$ are ordered, every key of $l$ is less than $k$, every key of $r$ is greater than $k$, and
the traversal of $l$ followed by $k$ and then the traversal of $r$ is the ordered insertion of
$x$ into the inorder traversal of $t$.

Balance is automatic from the height index.

articles.title: Insertion specification for 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let
$x \in \alpha$, and let $t$ be a 2-3 tree of height $h$. An insertion result of height $h$ meets
the specification for inserting $x$ into $t$ when the following holds. If it is a single tree
$t'$ of height $h$, then $t'$ is ordered and its inorder traversal equals the ordered insertion
of $x$ into the inorder traversal of $t$. If it is a split into trees $l$ and $r$ of height $h$
around a promoted key $k$, then $l$ and $r$ are ordered, every key of $l$ is less than $k$,
every key of $r$ is greater than $k$, and the traversal of $l$ followed by $k$ and then the
traversal of $r$ equals the ordered insertion of $x$ into the inorder traversal of $t$.

articles.title: Insertion into a height-indexed 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
Inserting a key $x$ into a 2-3 tree of
height $h$ yields either a single tree of height $h$ or a split into two trees of height $h$
around a promoted key. Inserting into a leaf gives the split of two leaves around $x$. At a
2-node with key $a$, insertion recurses into the left child if $x < a$ and into the right child
if $a < x$; a returned tree replaces that child, and a returned split around $k$ is absorbed by
turning the node into a 3-node with keys $k, a$ (left) or $a, k$ (right). At a 3-node with keys
$a, b$, insertion recurses into the left child if $x < a$, the middle child if $a < x < b$, and
the right child if $a < x$ and $b < x$; a returned tree replaces that child, and a returned split
makes the node split into two 2-nodes, promoting $a$, the child's promoted key, or $b$
respectively. In the remaining cases $x$ equals a key of the node and the tree is returned
unchanged.

articles.title: Insertion into a 2-3 tree root
articles.statement:
To insert a key $x$ into a root, that is, a 2-3 tree
together with its height $h$, insert $x$ into the underlying tree. If this returns a single tree
of height $h$, that tree is the new root, of height $h$. If it returns a split into trees $l$
and $r$ around a key $k$, the new root is the 2-node with key $k$ and children $l$ and $r$, of
height $h + 1$.

articles.title: Keys after insertion into a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered and let $t$ be an
ordered 2-3 tree root over $\alpha$. For all $x, y \in \alpha$, $y$ occurs in the inorder
traversal of the root obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ occurs in
the inorder traversal of $t$.

articles.title: The inorder traversal lists exactly the keys of a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
For every 2-3 tree $t$ of
height $h$ and every key $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a
member of $t$, that is, one of the separator keys stored at its nodes.

articles.title: Keys of a 2-3 tree built from a list
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered. For every list
$L$ over $\alpha$ and every $x \in \alpha$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of the 2-3 tree
built from $L$ (by inserting its elements from right to left into the empty tree) if and only
if $x$ occurs in $L$.

articles.title: Membership in a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
A key $x$ is a member of a 2-3 tree when it is one of the
separator keys stored at its nodes: nothing is a member of a leaf; $x$ is a member of a 2-node
with key $a$ and children $l, r$ when it is a member of $l$, equals $a$, or is a member of $r$;
and $x$ is a member of a 3-node with keys $a, b$ and children $l, m, r$ when it is a member of
$l$, equals $a$, is a member of $m$, equals $b$, or is a member of $r$.

Membership is structural and does not use the ordering invariant.

articles.title: Ordering invariant for 2-3 trees of unspecified height
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
relation $<$. A 2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ is ordered when its underlying
height-indexed 2-3 tree satisfies the ordering invariant.

articles.title: The empty 2-3 tree is ordered
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $<$, the empty
2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ (the leaf, of height $0$) satisfies the ordering
invariant.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of an ordered 2-3 tree is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered type. For every natural number $h$ and every ordered 2-3 tree $t$ over $\alpha$
of height $h$, the flattening (inorder traversal) of $t$ is strictly increasing: whenever a key
$x$ occurs before a key $y$ in it, $x < y$.

articles.title: Building a 2-3 tree from a list gives an ordered tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type. For every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the 2-3 tree of unspecified height built from
$L$, by inserting the elements of $L$ from right to left into the empty tree, is ordered.

articles.title: Insertion preserves the ordering of 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type.
If $t$ is an ordered 2-3 tree of unspecified height over $\alpha$ and $x \in \alpha$, then the
tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.

articles.title: Ordering invariant for 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. The leaf is
ordered. A 2-node with separator $a$ and children $l$, $r$ is ordered when $l$ and $r$ are
