ordered, $y < a$ for every key $y$ stored in $l$, and $a < y$ for every key $y$ stored in $r$. A
3-node with separators $a$, $b$ and children $l$, $m$, $r$ is ordered when $l$, $m$ and $r$ are
ordered, $a < b$, $y < a$ for every key $y$ stored in $l$, $a < y$ and $y < b$ for every key $y$
stored in $m$, and $b < y$ for every key $y$ stored in $r$.

articles.title: Insertion results for 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ and a natural number $h$, an
insertion result at height $h$ is either a 2-3 tree over $\alpha$ of height $h$, or a split:
two 2-3 trees $l$ and $r$ over $\alpha$ of height $h$ together with a promoted key $k \in \alpha$.

It records the outcome of inserting a key into a tree of height $h$.

articles.title: 2-3 trees of unspecified height
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$, a 2-3 tree of unspecified height
over $\alpha$ is a pair $(h, t)$ of a natural number $h$ and a height-indexed 2-3 tree $t$ over
$\alpha$ of height $h$.

It serves as a standalone search tree.

articles.title: Turning an insertion result into a 2-3 tree
articles.statement:
An insertion result at height $h$ becomes a
2-3 tree of unspecified height as follows: a tree $t$ of height $h$ gives $t$ itself, of height
$h$, and a split into trees $l$, $r$ of height $h$ around a key $k$ gives the 2-node with
separator $k$, left child $l$ and right child $r$, of height $h + 1$.

articles.title: Height-indexed 2-3 trees
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ of keys, the 2-3 trees over $\alpha$ indexed
by height are generated as follows. The leaf is a tree of height $0$ and stores no key. For a
natural number $h$, a key $a$ and trees $l$, $r$ of height $h$, the 2-node with separator $a$
and children $l$, $r$ is a tree of height $h + 1$. For a natural number $h$, keys $a$, $b$ and
trees $l$, $m$, $r$ of height $h$, the 3-node with separators $a$, $b$ and children $l$, $m$,
$r$ is a tree of height $h + 1$. Hence all leaves of a tree of height $h$ lie at depth $h$.

articles.title: The all-keys predicate in terms of membership (AVL trees)
articles.statement:
For a predicate $p$ on keys and
a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every
$x \in t$, where $x \in t$ means that $x$ is the key of some node of $t$.

articles.title: Keys left after removing the minimum exceed it
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a
linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, and suppose $t$ is ordered: at every node,
all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys in the right subtree are strictly
larger than the key at that node. Let $m$ be the leftmost key of $t$, or an arbitrary default
value if $t$ is empty. Then every key of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key,
rebalancing on the way back up, is strictly greater than $m$.

articles.title: The all-keys predicate is unchanged by erasing height caches
articles.statement:
For a predicate $p$ on keys
and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p$ holds at every
key of the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights. This holds by
definition.

articles.title: Every key of an AVL tree satisfies a predicate
articles.statement:
For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$
with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds when $p$ holds at the key of every node of $t$. It
is defined as the corresponding predicate on the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing
its cached heights.

articles.title: Rebalancing when the heights of the children differ by at most one
articles.statement:
Let $l$ and $r$ be
trees with cached heights, let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root
of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 1$, then
$\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is the node with left subtree $l$, key $x$, right subtree $r$ and
cached height $\max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$; no rotation is performed.

articles.title: Left-right double rotation in AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the
root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with
cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node
$\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $R$ be trees with cached
heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(R) + 1 < c$ and
$h(A) < c'$, then $\mathrm{balance}(\langle c; A, y, \langle c'; B, z, C \rangle \rangle, x, R) =
N(N(A, y, B), z, N(C, x, R))$.

articles.title: Single right rotation in AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root
of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached
height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node
$\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $R$ be trees with cached heights,
let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(R) + 1 < c$ and $h(B) \le h(A)$, then
$\mathrm{balance}(\langle c; A, y, B \rangle, x, R) = N(A, y, N(B, x, R))$.

articles.title: Right-left double rotation in AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the
root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with
cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node
$\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$, $C$ be trees with cached
heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(L) + 1 < c$ and
$h(C) < c'$, then $\mathrm{balance}(L, x, \langle c; \langle c'; A, z, B \rangle, y, C \rangle) =
N(N(L, x, A), z, N(B, y, C))$.

articles.title: Single left rotation in AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of
a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height
$c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node
$\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$ be trees with cached heights,
let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(L) + 1 < c$ and $h(A) \le h(B)$, then
$\mathrm{balance}(L, x, \langle c; A, y, B \rangle) = N(N(L, x, A), y, B)$.

articles.title: AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
For trees $l$, $r$ with cached heights and a key $x$, write $h(T)$ for
the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree) and $N(A, y, B)$ for the
node with left subtree $A$, key $y$, right subtree $B$ and cached height $\max(h(A), h(B)) + 1$.
The node $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is defined by cases. If $h(l) > h(r) + 1$ and $l$ has left
subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, it is the single right rotation $N(A, y, N(B, x, r))$
when $h(B) \le h(A)$, and otherwise, when $B$ has left subtree $B_1$, key $z$ and right subtree
$B_2$, the left-right double rotation $N(N(A, y, B_1), z, N(B_2, x, r))$. Symmetrically, if
$h(l) \le h(r) + 1$, $h(r) > h(l) + 1$ and $r$ has left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$,
it is the single left rotation $N(N(l, x, A), y, B)$ when $h(A) \le h(B)$, and otherwise, when
$A$ has left subtree $A_1$, key $z$ and right subtree $A_2$, the right-left double rotation
$N(N(l, x, A_1), z, N(A_2, y, B))$. In every other case it is $N(l, x, r)$.

For balanced children with correct cached heights whose heights differ by at most two, the result
is balanced again.

articles.title: AVL rebalancing yields a balanced tree
articles.statement:
Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are
correct at every node and which are balanced (at every node the cached heights of the two
subtrees differ by at most one), let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the
root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 2$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 2$,
then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is balanced.

One insertion step maintains this precondition.

articles.title: Minimum deletion preserves AVL balance
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at
each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights
of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion
(removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) is again balanced.

articles.title: Deleting a key preserves AVL balance
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly
ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is
balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for
every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is
again balanced.

articles.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height
at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached
heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its
leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, is again balanced.

articles.title: Deletion preserves AVL balance
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered
type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at
every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$,
the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.

articles.title: AVL trees built from a list are balanced
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered
type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion satisfies the AVL balance invariant.

articles.title: AVL insertion preserves balance
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be an
AVL tree over $\alpha$ and let $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ has correct cached heights and satisfies
the AVL balance invariant, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also satisfies the
AVL balance invariant.

articles.title: The AVL node constructor preserves balance
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$ and $r$ be AVL trees that satisfy
the AVL balance invariant, and write $h(\ell)$ and $h(r)$ for the heights cached at their roots
(with height $0$ for the empty tree). If $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, then
for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores
the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, satisfies the AVL balance invariant.

articles.title: AVL balance invariant
articles.statement:
The empty tree is balanced. A node with left subtree $\ell$ and
right subtree $r$ is balanced when $\ell$ and $r$ are balanced and $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and
$h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the
empty tree). Equivalently, at every node the balance factor $h(\ell) - h(r)$ lies in
$\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

articles.title: AVL rebalancing preserves cached heights
articles.statement:
If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct
cached heights, then for every key $k$ the tree produced by the rebalancing function from
$\ell$, $k$ and $r$ also has correct cached heights.

articles.title: Minimum deletion keeps cached heights correct
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height
at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the
cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of
the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way
back up) are again correct.

articles.title: Deleting a key keeps cached heights correct
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a
linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node
stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having
height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting
$x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.

articles.title: Removing the minimum keeps cached heights correct
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached
height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of
the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights
of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, are
again correct.

articles.title: Deletion keeps cached heights correct
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly
ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores
one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height
$0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$,
rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.

articles.title: AVL trees built from a list have correct cached heights
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a
linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion has correct cached
heights.

articles.title: AVL insertion preserves cached heights
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If an
AVL tree $t$ over $\alpha$ has correct cached heights, then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree
obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also has correct cached heights.

articles.title: The AVL node constructor preserves cached heights
articles.statement:
If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have
correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the
smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$ where $h$ denotes the height
cached at the root (and $0$ for the empty tree), also has correct cached heights.

articles.title: Correct cached heights
articles.statement:
The empty tree has correct cached heights. A node storing the
height $c$, with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$, has correct cached heights when
$\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights and $c = \max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, where $h$ denotes
the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree).

articles.title: Correctness of AVL search
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an
ordered AVL tree over $\alpha$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, searching for $x$ in $t$ by
following comparisons from the root returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.

articles.title: Membership search in an AVL tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and a key $x$,
the search for $x$ returns false on the empty tree; at a node with key $k$ it searches the left
subtree if $x < k$, searches the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise. The cached
heights are ignored.

articles.title: Minimum deletion in an AVL tree
articles.statement:
Minimum deletion maps a binary tree with cached heights to
the tree obtained by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up. It is the
operation of removing the minimum, under the name used for the successor step of deletion, where a
deleted node with two children is replaced by the minimum of its right subtree.

articles.title: AVL tree deletion under its alternative name
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a
key $x \in \alpha$ and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$ is defined to be
$\mathrm{erase}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$.

articles.title: Removing the leftmost key of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
For a tree $t$ with cached heights, the tree
obtained by removing the leftmost key of $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree stays
empty. A node whose left subtree is empty is replaced by its right subtree. A node with nonempty
left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ is replaced by $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where
$l'$ is $l$ with its leftmost key removed and $\mathrm{balance}$ is the AVL rebalancing function.

articles.title: AVL tree deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. Deleting $x$
from a tree with cached heights is defined by recursion on the tree, where $\mathrm{balance}$
denotes the AVL rebalancing function. The empty tree stays empty. For a node with left subtree
$l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where
$l'$ is $l$ with $x$ deleted; if $k < x$, the result is $\mathrm{balance}(l, k, r')$, where $r'$
is $r$ with $x$ deleted; if $x = k$, the node is replaced by $r$ when $l$ is empty, by $l$ when
$r$ is empty, and otherwise by $\mathrm{balance}(l, m, r'')$, where $m$ is the leftmost key of
$r$ and $r''$ is $r$ with its leftmost key removed.

articles.title: Building an AVL tree from a list
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the tree built
from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$ and tail
$xs$ is obtained by AVL insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$. Thus the list is
inserted from right to left, starting from the empty tree.

articles.title: Upper bound on height after AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached
heights are correct at every node, and write $h$ for the cached height. Then for every key $k$,
the rebalanced node $b$ built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ satisfies $h(b) \le \max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$.

articles.title: Deletion does not increase the height of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of
the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$.

articles.title: Removing the leftmost key does not increase the height of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a tree
whose cached heights are correct, then the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing
its leftmost key is at most the cached height of $t$.

articles.title: Upper bound on height after AVL insertion
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if a tree
$t$ has correct cached heights at every node, then for every key $x$ the cached height of the
tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$ plus one.

articles.title: Cached height of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
The cached height of the empty tree is $0$, and the cached
height of a node is the height value stored at that node, so it is read off the root in
constant time.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree onto a suffix
articles.statement:
Given a tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is
the list of keys of $t$ in inorder (left subtree, root key, right subtree, recursively)
followed by $s$. It is computed in linear time by the binary search tree traversal of $t$ with
its cached heights erased.

articles.title: AVL rebalancing preserves the inorder traversal
articles.statement:
For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every
key $k$, the inorder traversal of the rebalanced node built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ is the
inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.

articles.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion, alternative name
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of
$\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$ under its alternative name, is the
inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the
traversal is unchanged.

articles.title: The inorder traversal begins with the leftmost key
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a nonempty tree with
cached heights and $m$ its leftmost key. Then the inorder traversal of $t$ is $m$ followed by the
inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.

The leftmost key is computed by a function that takes a default value for the empty tree; the
identity holds for every choice of default.

articles.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
$x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by
deleting $x$ from $t$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed;
if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.

articles.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree has no duplicates
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered
type $\alpha$, if an AVL tree is ordered, then its inorder traversal contains no key twice.

articles.title: AVL inorder traversal agrees with the erased binary search tree
articles.statement:
For every AVL tree
$t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary search tree inorder traversal of the binary
tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights; this holds by definition.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
The inorder traversal of a tree $t$ lists its keys with
the left subtree first, then the root key, then the right subtree, recursively. It is the
binary search tree inorder traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased, computed in linear
time.

articles.title: Insertion into an AVL tree
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly ordered, and write
$\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and
right subtree $R$. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives the node with key $x$, two empty
children and cached height $1$. Inserting $x$ into a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right
subtree $R$ gives $\mathrm{balance}(L', k, R)$, where $L'$ is the result of inserting $x$ into $L$,
when $x < k$; it gives $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R')$, where $R'$ is the result of inserting $x$
into $R$, when $k < x$; and otherwise it returns the node unchanged.

articles.title: Rebalancing does not drop below the taller child
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the
root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$
for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. If $L$
and $R$ are trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, then for every key $k$ we have
$\max(h(L), h(R)) \le h(\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R))$.

articles.title: Removing the leftmost key lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a
tree whose cached heights are correct and which is balanced, then the cached height of $t$ is at
most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.

articles.title: Deletion lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a balanced tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the
cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting
$x$ from $t$.

articles.title: Insertion does not lower the height
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a
tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Let the keys be linearly ordered, and let $T$ be
a tree whose cached heights are correct at every node and which satisfies the AVL balance
invariant at every node. Then for every key $x$, if $T'$ is the tree obtained by inserting $x$
into $T$, we have $h(T) \le h(T')$.

articles.title: Membership after AVL rebalancing
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing
of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. For trees $L$ and $R$ and keys
$k$ and $x$, the key $x$ lies in $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ if and only if $x$ lies in $L$,
$x = k$, or $x$ lies in $R$.

articles.title: AVL deletion keeps every other key
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights whose keys
come from a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs in
$T$, then $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$. No search-tree ordering of
$T$ is assumed.

articles.title: Keys of an ordered AVL tree after deletion
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights
over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller,
and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for all keys $x$
and $y$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ if and only if $y$ occurs in
$T$ and $y \ne x$.

articles.title: Membership in an AVL tree built from a list
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key lies
in the tree obtained by inserting the entries of a list one at a time, from last to first, into
the empty tree exactly when it is in the list.

articles.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
A key $x$ occurs in the inorder
traversal of a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in $T$.

articles.title: Membership after insertion into an AVL tree
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key $y$
lies in the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into a tree $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ lies
in $T$.

articles.title: AVL membership is membership in the underlying binary tree
articles.statement:
A key $x$ lies in a tree $T$ if
and only if $x$ lies in the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights.

This holds by definition.

articles.title: Membership in an AVL tree
articles.statement:
A key $x$ belongs to a tree $T$ when $x$ belongs to the binary
tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights. Equivalently, no key belongs to the empty
tree, and $x$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when
$x$ belongs to $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ belongs to $R$.

articles.title: The leftmost key lies in the tree
articles.statement:
For every nonempty binary tree $T$ with cached heights
and every default value $d$, the leftmost key of $T$ computed with default $d$ occurs in $T$.

articles.title: Leftmost key of a tree
articles.statement:
Given a default value $d$ and a binary tree $T$ with cached
heights, the leftmost key of $T$ with default $d$ is $d$ when $T$ is empty; when $T$ has left
subtree $L$ and root key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $L$ with default $k$. Thus for a
nonempty tree it is the key of the node reached from the root by following left children as
far as possible, and it does not depend on $d$.

articles.title: AVL node with computed height
articles.statement:
Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree
$T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Given trees $L$ and $R$ and a key $k$, this is the
node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is
$\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$.

articles.title: Deletion removes the deleted key from an ordered AVL tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with
cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree. Then for every key $x$,
$x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$.

articles.title: Rebalancing an AVL node preserves the search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type, let $k \in \alpha$, and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered trees with cached heights
over $\alpha$ such that every key of $L$ is less than $k$ and every key of $R$ is greater
than $k$. Then the tree that rebalancing produces from left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right
subtree $R$ is ordered.

articles.title: Successor-step minimum removal preserves search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with
cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the
tree obtained by the minimum-removal step used for the successor in deletion, which removes the
leftmost key of $T$ and rebalances on the way back up.

articles.title: Deleting a key from an ordered AVL tree keeps it ordered
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with
cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then for every
key $x$ the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search
tree.

articles.title: Removing the leftmost key preserves search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached
heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree
obtained from $T$ by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up.

articles.title: AVL deletion preserves search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over
a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and
every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for every key $x$, the
tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.

articles.title: AVL trees built from a list are ordered
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For
every list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting
the elements of $xs$ one at a time, from the last element to the first, is ordered.

articles.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered type. If a tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered, then in
the inorder traversal of $t$ every key is less than every key that comes after it.

articles.title: AVL insertion preserves the search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type.
For every key $x \in \alpha$ and every ordered tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$, the
tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.

articles.title: Order of an AVL tree via its underlying binary tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
relation $<$. A tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered if and only if the
binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing the cached heights is an ordered binary search
tree.

articles.title: Ordered AVL trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree with cached
heights over $\alpha$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached heights
is an ordered binary search tree: the empty tree is ordered, and a node with key $k$ is
ordered when its left and right subtrees are ordered, every key of the left subtree is less
than $k$, and every key of the right subtree is greater than $k$.

articles.title: Erasing the cached heights of an AVL tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type. Erasing the cached
heights sends a tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ to a binary tree over $\alpha$: the empty
tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with height $h$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and
right subtree $R$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are
the erasures of $L$ and $R$.

articles.title: Binary trees with cached heights
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$, a tree with cached heights over
$\alpha$ (the underlying type of AVL trees) is either empty, or a node made of a natural
number $h$ (its cached height), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right subtree.

The type does not require $h$ to equal the actual height of the node.

articles.title: Borrowing a key from the left sibling
articles.statement:
Given a tree $s$ (the left sibling), a separator key
$k$ and a tree $c$ (the child) such that $s$ and $c$ are both leaves or both internal nodes, $s$
has at least one key, and, when they are internal nodes, $s$ has at least one child: the last key
of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the new separator, $k$ becomes the first key of $c$, and,
for internal nodes, the last child of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the first child of $c$.
The result is the triple of the new sibling, the new separator and the new child. In every other
case the result is the unchanged triple $(s, k, c)$.

articles.title: Borrowing a key from the right sibling
articles.statement:
Given a tree $c$ (the child), a separator key $k$
and a tree $s$ (the right sibling) such that $c$ and $s$ are both leaves or both internal nodes,
$s$ has at least one key, and, when they are internal nodes, $s$ has at least one child: $k$
becomes the last key of $c$, the first key of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the new
separator, and, for internal nodes, the first child of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the
last child of $c$. The result is the triple of the new child, the new separator and the new
sibling. In every other case the result is the unchanged triple $(c, k, s)$.

articles.title: Raw B-trees
articles.statement:
A raw B-tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is either a leaf, holding a list
of keys, or an internal node, holding a list of separator keys and a list of child raw B-trees.
The type imposes no invariant: that an internal node with $k$ keys has $k + 1$ children, the
bounds on key counts, the balance of the tree and the ordering of the keys are imposed
separately by the structural and ordering invariants of B-trees.

articles.title: Search after top-down deletion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$
over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, searching for $y$ in the tree obtained
by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ succeeds if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ is a
key of $T$.

articles.title: Search after rebuilding deletion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree
$t$, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys. The B-tree search for $y$ in the rebuilding deletion of $x$
from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ returns true if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ is stored in $T$.

articles.title: Correctness of B-tree search
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered and let $T$ be a B-tree
of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$. For every key $x \in \alpha$, the search procedure
returns true on $x$ and $T$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $T$, that is, $x$ occurs in the
inorder flattening of $T$.

articles.title: B-tree search
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, the search for a key $x$ in a raw B-tree
proceeds as follows. At a leaf, report whether $x$ is in the leaf's key list. At an internal
node with separators $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and children $c_0, c_1, \dots$, scan the separators in
order. On reaching $k_i$, report failure if the node has no child $c_{i-1}$; otherwise search
$c_{i-1}$ if $x < k_i$, report success if $x = k_i$, and move on to the next separator if
$k_i < x$. If every separator is less than $x$, search the child $c_m$, or report failure if
the node has no such child.

articles.title: Height-indexed B-tree deletion
articles.statement:
Given a height $h$, a minimum degree $t$, a key $x$ of a
linearly ordered key type and a tree $T$, the result is defined as follows. If $T$ is a leaf, the
result is the leaf whose key list is that of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ erased,
whatever $h$ is. If $T$ is an internal node and $h = 0$, the result is $T$. If $T$ is an internal
node and $h = n + 1$, the result is the internal node whose separator and child lists are
obtained by deletion of $x$ within the node of $T$ (with minimum degree $t$), where deletion from
a child is height-indexed deletion with minimum degree $t$ at height $n$.

The correctness specification only covers heights that match the shape of the tree.

articles.title: Deletion within a B-tree node
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an operation that deletes a key from a tree, let
$t$ be a natural number, let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered key type, and write $|c|$ for the
number of keys stored at the root of a tree $c$. Deleting $x$ within a node with separator list
$K$ and child list $C$, using $D$ on children, produces a new separator list and a new child list.
Write $k$ for the first separator, $c$ for the first child, and $K'$ and $C'$ for the remaining
separators and children.

If $K$ is empty and $C$ is nonempty, $D$ deletes $x$ from the first child and nothing else
changes; if both are empty, so is the result.

If $x < k$ and either $|c| \ge t$ or $C'$ is empty, $D$ deletes $x$ from $c$. Otherwise let $s$
be the first tree of $C'$. If $|s| \ge t$, borrowing for $c$ from its right sibling $s$ with
separator $k$ gives $(c', k', s')$, which replace $c$, $k$ and $s$, and $D$ deletes $x$ from $c'$.
If $|s| < t$, the trees $c$ and $s$ are merged with $k$ into one tree, which replaces $c$ and $s$,
$k$ is dropped from the separators, and $D$ deletes $x$ from the merged tree.

If $k < x$, $K'$ is empty and $C'$ consists of a single tree $l$: if $|l| \ge t$, $D$ deletes $x$
from $l$; otherwise, if $|c| \ge t$, borrowing for $l$ from its left sibling $c$ with separator
$k$ gives $(c', k', l')$, which replace $c$, $k$ and $l$, and $D$ deletes $x$ from $l'$;
otherwise the result has no separators and a single child, obtained by applying $D$ to delete $x$
from the merge of $c$ and $l$ with $k$. If $k < x$ and $K'$ is nonempty, $k$ and $c$ are kept
and the deletion continues recursively within $K'$ and $C'$.

If $x = k$ and $C'$ is nonempty with first tree $r$: if $|c| \ge t$, the key $p$ found by
descending the rightmost spine of $c$ (following last children down to a leaf or to an internal
node without children, and taking the last key there) replaces $k$ and $D$ deletes $p$ from $c$;
otherwise, if $|r| \ge t$, the key $q$ found by descending the leftmost spine of $r$ (following
first children in the same way and taking the first key there) replaces $k$ and $D$ deletes $q$
from $r$; otherwise $c$ and $r$ are merged with $k$ into one tree, which replaces $c$ and $r$,
$k$ is dropped from the separators, and $D$ deletes $x$ from the merged tree.

In every remaining case (a shape of the separator and child lists not covered above, or a spine
descent that ends at a node with no keys) the lists are returned unchanged.

articles.title: Top-down deletion preserves the B-tree invariant
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of
minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by
deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is again a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

articles.title: Rebuilding deletion yields a B-tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$,
whether or not $T$ is itself a B-tree, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum
degree $t$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

articles.title: Rebuilding deletion unfolds to erase and rebuild
articles.statement:
For every minimum degree $t$, key $x$
and tree $T$, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ equals the tree
built from the list obtained by removing the first occurrence of $x$ from the flattening of $T$,
by inserting its keys from right to left into the empty tree with minimum degree $t$.

articles.title: Rebuilding deletion yields a root-valid tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$. For every key $x$ and every
tree $T$, there is a height $h$ such that the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum
degree $t$ is root-valid of minimum degree $t$ and height $h$: all leaves sit at depth $h$, every
node holds at most $2t - 1$ keys, every non-root node holds at least $t - 1$ keys, an internal
root holds at least one key, and an internal node with $k$ keys has $k + 1$ children.

No relation between $h$ and the height of $T$ is claimed.

articles.title: B-tree deletion by rebuilding
articles.statement:
For a minimum degree $t$, a key $x$ and a tree $T$, the
rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ is the tree obtained by inserting the keys of the list $L$,
from right to left, into the empty tree with B-tree insertion of minimum degree $t$, where $L$ is
the inorder flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed ($L$ is the flattening
itself when $x$ does not occur in it).

This is a reference implementation, not the single-pass borrow-and-merge deletion of CLRS
Section 18.3, which is formalized separately.

articles.title: Top-down deletion yields a root-valid tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of
minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by
deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ satisfies the root invariant of B-trees of minimum
degree $t$ at some height.

articles.title: Top-down deletion lowers the height by at most one
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be an
ordered tree over a linearly ordered key type (its inorder flattening is strictly increasing)
that satisfies the root invariant of B-trees of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$. For every key
$x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ satisfies the root
invariant of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$ or at height $h - 1$, where $h - 1$ is truncated
subtraction, so equal to $0$ when $h = 0$.

articles.title: Top-down B-tree deletion
articles.statement:
Deleting a key $x$ of a linearly ordered key type from a tree $T$
with minimum degree $t$ applies height-indexed deletion of $x$ with minimum degree $t$ to $T$ at
the height of $T$, where the height of a leaf, or of an internal node without children, is $0$,
and the height of any other internal node is one more than the height of its first child. If the
outcome is an internal node with no keys and exactly one child, the result is that child;
otherwise the result is the outcome itself.

This follows the top-down deletion of CLRS Section 18.3.

articles.title: The empty tree is a B-tree
articles.statement:
For every key type equipped with a binary relation $<$ and
every natural number $t \ge 2$, the empty B-tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

articles.title: The empty B-tree
articles.statement: The empty B-tree is the leaf with no keys.

articles.title: B-trees satisfy the root invariant
articles.statement:
If $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then there
is a height $h$ such that $T$ satisfies the root structural invariant of minimum degree $t$ at
height $h$.

articles.title: The accumulating B-tree flattening is correct
articles.statement:
For every raw B-tree $T$ and every list
$s$, the accumulating flattening of $T$ with suffix $s$ equals the inorder flattening of $T$
followed by $s$.

articles.title: Accumulating flattening of a B-tree
articles.statement:
Given a raw B-tree $T$ and a list $s$, this returns
the inorder traversal of $T$ followed by $s$. For a leaf it is the leaf's key list followed by
$s$. For an internal node with separator keys $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and children $c_0, \dots, c_n$
it is the sequence $c_0, k_1, c_1, k_2, \dots$, in which children and keys alternate starting
with a child until one of the two lists runs out, then the remaining keys or children in
order, and finally $s$; each key contributes itself, and each child contributes its own
accumulating flattening with everything after it as the suffix. In particular every key of
the tree occurs in the result.

The result is built from right to left, so each key is copied only once.

articles.title: Repeated top-down deletion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$
over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, deleting $x$ from $T$ twice with minimum
degree $t$ gives a tree with the same inorder flattening as deleting $x$ from $T$ once.

articles.title: Rebuilding deletion of the same key twice
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree (its
flattening is strictly increasing) and let $x$ be a key. Deleting $x$ twice by rebuilding with
minimum degree $t$ gives a tree with the same flattening as deleting $x$ once.

articles.title: Rebuilding deletion of an absent key
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree and let
$x$ be a key that does not occur in the flattening of $T$. Then the rebuilding deletion of $x$
from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ has the same flattening as $T$.

The tree itself may be rebuilt to a different shape with the same flattening.

articles.title: Flattening after rebuilding deletion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree and let
$x$ be a key. The flattening of the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$
is the flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not
occur).

No occupancy hypothesis on $T$ is needed.

articles.title: Deletion from a B-tree erases the key from its flattening
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a
B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the inorder
flattening of the tree obtained from $T$ by top-down deletion of $x$ with minimum degree $t$ is
the flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

articles.title: Building a B-tree from a strictly increasing list
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$. For every strictly
increasing list $L$ of keys, the tree built from $L$ by inserting its keys from right to left
into the empty tree with minimum degree $t$ has flattening exactly $L$.

articles.title: B-tree insertion as sorted list insertion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let
$t \ge 2$, and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$. For every key
$x \in \alpha$, the inorder flattening of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ with
minimum degree $t$ equals the sorted insertion of $x$ into the inorder flattening of $T$.

articles.title: Key count after rebuilding deletion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree with
flattening of length $n$, and let $x$ be a key. The flattening of the rebuilding deletion of $x$
from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ has length $n - 1$ if $x$ occurs in the flattening of $T$, and
length $n$ otherwise.

articles.title: Deletion shortens the flattening by one exactly when the key is present
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$,
let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type, and let $x$ be a key.
If $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$, the flattening of the tree obtained from $T$ by
deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) has length one less than the flattening of $T$; otherwise
the two flattenings have the same length.

articles.title: Size of a B-tree after insertion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let $t \ge 2$, let
$T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, and let $x \in \alpha$. Let $T'$ be
the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ with minimum degree $t$. If $x$ occurs in the
inorder flattening of $T$, then the flattening of $T'$ has the same length as that of $T$;
otherwise it is one longer.

articles.title: Splitting a node's flattening at a separator
articles.statement:
Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be lists of keys, $m$ a
key, and $C_1$ and $C_2$ lists of raw B-trees such that $C_1$ has exactly one more element than
$K_1$. Then the flattening of the node whose key list is $K_1$ followed by $m$ followed by $K_2$
and whose child list is $C_1$ followed by $C_2$ equals the flattening of the node with keys $K_1$
and children $C_1$, followed by $m$, followed by the flattening of the node with keys $K_2$ and
children $C_2$.

articles.title: Flattening a childless node, one key at a time
articles.statement:
For a key $k$ and a list of keys $K$, the
flattening of the node with key list $k$ followed by $K$ and no children is $k$ followed by the
flattening of the node with key list $K$ and no children.

This covers nodes with more keys than a well-formed node would have.

articles.title: Flattening a keyless node, one child at a time
articles.statement:
For a raw B-tree $c$ and a list $C$ of
raw B-trees, the flattening of the node with no keys and child list $c$ followed by $C$ is the
flattening of $c$ followed by the flattening of the node with no keys and child list $C$.

This covers nodes with more children than a well-formed node would have.

articles.title: Flattening of the empty node
articles.statement:
The flattening of the internal node with no keys and no
children is the empty list.

articles.title: An ordered B-tree has no duplicate keys
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, the flattening
of an ordered raw B-tree has no duplicate entries.

articles.title: Inorder flattening of a B-tree
articles.statement:
The flattening of a raw B-tree is the list of its keys
defined recursively: for a leaf it is the leaf's key list, and for an internal node with keys
$k_1, k_2, \dots$ and children $c_1, c_2, \dots$ it is the flattening of $c_1$, then $k_1$, then
the flattening of $c_2$, then $k_2$, and so on, alternating while both lists last; whatever
remains of the longer list is then appended in order, each surplus child contributing its
flattening and each surplus key contributing itself. In particular every key of the tree occurs
in the flattening.

The flattening is computed in linear time by an accumulator-passing auxiliary function.

articles.title: Building from a list yields a B-tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, every natural
number $t \ge 2$ and every list $L$ of keys, the tree obtained by inserting the elements of $L$
from right to left into the empty tree, each insertion with minimum degree $t$, is a B-tree of
minimum degree $t$.

articles.title: B-tree built from a list
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type and a natural number $t$, the
tree built from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$
and tail $L$ is the result of inserting $x$, with minimum degree $t$, into the tree built from
$L$. Thus the elements are inserted from right to left.

articles.title: Flattening of a B-tree insertion result
articles.statement:
The flattening of an insertion result that is a
single tree is the flattening of that tree; for a result that splits into a left tree $\ell$, a
promoted median key $m$ and a right tree $r$, it is the flattening of $\ell$, followed by $m$,
followed by the flattening of $r$.

articles.title: Insertion into a B-tree leaf
articles.statement:
Over a linearly ordered key type, let $t$ be a natural
number, $x$ a key, $K$ the key list of a leaf, and $K'$ the result of ordered insertion of $x$
into $K$. If $K'$ has at most $2t - 1$ keys, the insertion result is the single leaf with keys
$K'$. Otherwise the leaf is split: the result consists of the leaf holding the first $t - 1$ keys
of $K'$, the next key of $K'$ promoted as the median, and the leaf holding the remaining keys.
Here subtraction of natural numbers is truncated at $0$.

articles.title: Result of inserting into a B-tree subtree
articles.statement:
An insertion result over a key type $\alpha$
is either a single tree over $\alpha$, or a triple $(\ell, m, r)$ of two trees $\ell$ and $r$
over $\alpha$ and a key $m$ of $\alpha$. In insertion, the first form is a subtree that did not
split, and the second form is an overflowing node split into two trees of the same height, with
the median key $m$ promoted between them; the type itself does not record heights.

articles.title: Split-returning insertion into a B-tree subtree
articles.statement:
For minimum degree $t$ and a key $x$,
insertion of $x$ into a tree returns an insertion result and is defined by recursion. At a leaf
with key list $K$, it is leaf insertion of $x$ into $K$. At an internal node, the separator list
and the child list are scanned together from the left. If $x$ is smaller than the current
separator, or no separator is left but a child is, $x$ is inserted into the current child. If $x$
is larger than the current separator, the scan moves on to the next separator and child. If $x$
equals the current separator, or no child is left, the remaining lists are kept unchanged. When
the child that received $x$ returns a single tree, that tree replaces the child; when it returns
two trees $\ell$, $r$ with a median $m$, the child is replaced by $\ell$ and $r$ with $m$ inserted
as a separator between them. The rebuilt separator and child lists are then turned into a node by
the internal-node rebuilding step: kept as one node if there are at most $2t - 1$ separators, and
split otherwise.

articles.title: Insertion preserves the B-tree invariant
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let the keys come from a
linearly ordered type. If $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then for every key $x$ the tree
obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ is again a B-tree of minimum degree $t$: it is ordered and
root-valid at some height.

articles.title: B-tree insertion
articles.statement:
For minimum degree $t$, the tree obtained by inserting a key $x$ into a
tree $T$ is computed from the split-returning insertion of $x$ into $T$: if that returns a single
tree, this tree is the result; if it returns two trees $\ell$ and $r$ with a promoted median key
$m$, the result is a new root node with the single separator $m$ and the two children $\ell$ and
$r$.

When $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, inserting a key already present in $T$ returns a tree
with the same flattening.

articles.title: B-trees of a given minimum degree
articles.statement:
A tree $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ when
$t \ge 2$ (the CLRS Chapter 18 minimum-degree requirement), $T$ is ordered, and $T$ is
root-valid at some height. This is the invariant preserved by insertion and by building a tree
from a list.

articles.title: Number of keys at the root of a B-tree
articles.statement:
For a raw B-tree $T$, this is the length of the
key list stored at the root of $T$: the number of keys of $T$ if $T$ is a leaf, and the number of
separator keys of $T$ if $T$ is an internal node. Keys in the children are not counted.

articles.title: Rightmost key of a B-tree
articles.statement:
For a tree $T$, the rightmost key of $T$ is an optional key
defined by descending the rightmost spine: for a leaf it is the last of its keys (none if the
leaf has no keys); for an internal node with at least one child it is the rightmost key of its
last child; for an internal node with no children it is the last of its separator keys (none
if there are none).

If $T$ satisfies the structural B-tree invariant for a minimum degree $t \ge 2$ and has at least
one key at its root, the rightmost key exists and is the last key of the inorder flattening of
$T$, so on an ordered tree it is the greatest key. Each step splits a child list of length at
most $2t$, so on a valid tree of height $h$ the descent costs $O(t h)$, without computing the
flattening.

articles.title: Membership after rebuild deletion from a B-tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of
minimum degree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, the key $y$
lies in the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (erasing $x$ from the inorder
flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) if and
only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ lies in $T$.

articles.title: Membership after deletion from a B-tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum
degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ belongs to the tree
obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$
belongs to $T$.

articles.title: Membership in a B-tree built from a list
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $xs$ be a list over a
linearly ordered key type. A key $x$ belongs to the tree of minimum degree $t$ built from $xs$
(by inserting the elements of $xs$ into the empty tree, from right to left) if and only if $x$
is an element of $xs$.

articles.title: Membership after B-tree insertion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum
degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ belongs to the tree
obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ belongs to $T$.

articles.title: Membership in a B-tree
articles.statement:
A key $x$ belongs to a tree $T$ when $x$ occurs in the inorder
flattening of $T$.

Structurally, a key belongs to an internal node exactly when it is one of the node's separator
keys or belongs to one of its children.

articles.title: Merging two B-tree nodes around a separator
articles.statement:
Given a key $s$ and trees $L$ and $R$, the
merge of $L$ and $R$ around $s$ is defined as follows. If $L$ and $R$ are leaves with key lists
$k_1$ and $k_2$, it is the leaf with keys $k_1$, then $s$, then $k_2$. If $L$ and $R$ are internal
nodes with key lists $k_1, k_2$ and child lists $c_1, c_2$, it is the internal node with keys
$k_1$, then $s$, then $k_2$, and children $c_1$ followed by $c_2$. In every other case it is $L$.

In deletion from a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, it is applied to two trees of the same height
that each hold $t - 1$ keys at the root, so the merged node holds $2t - 1$ keys.

articles.title: Leftmost key of a B-tree
articles.statement:
For a tree $T$, the leftmost key of $T$ is an optional key
defined by descending the leftmost spine: for a leaf it is the first of its keys (none if the
leaf has no keys); for an internal node with at least one child it is the leftmost key of its
first child; for an internal node with no children it is the first of its separator keys (none
if there are none).

If $T$ satisfies the structural B-tree invariant for a minimum degree $t \ge 2$ and has at least
one key at its root, the leftmost key exists and is the first key of the inorder flattening of
$T$, so on an ordered tree it is the least key.

articles.title: Rebuilding an internal node after insertion
articles.statement:
For minimum degree $t$, a separator list $K$
and a child list $C$, the result is the internal node with separators $K$ and children $C$, kept
as a single tree when $K$ has at most $2t - 1$ keys, and otherwise split by node splitting into
two nodes and a promoted median key.

articles.title: The separator keys of an ordered node are sorted
articles.statement:
If an internal node with separator list
$K$ is ordered, then $K$ is strictly increasing: every key of $K$ is smaller than every key that
comes after it in $K$.

articles.title: The deleted key is absent after rebuild deletion
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of
minimum degree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained
from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (erasing $x$ from the inorder flattening of $T$ and
rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) does not contain $x$.

articles.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion from a B-tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a
B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, $x$ does not
belong to the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$).

articles.title: B-trees are ordered
articles.statement:
If a tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then it is ordered:
each key of its inorder flattening is less than every key that comes after it.

articles.title: Rebuild deletion yields an ordered tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let keys come from a linearly
ordered type. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, not necessarily ordered, the tree obtained
from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (removing the first occurrence of $x$, if any, from the
inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys)
is ordered: its inorder flattening is strictly increasing.

articles.title: Deletion from a B-tree yields an ordered tree
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of
minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained from $T$
by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) is ordered: its inorder flattening is strictly
increasing.

articles.title: Ordered B-tree
articles.statement:
A B-tree over a type with a relation $<$ is ordered when its inorder
flattening is strictly increasing, that is, each key of the flattening is less than every
key that comes after it. This single condition packages sortedness of the keys at each node
and the separator bounds between a node's keys and the keys stored in its subtrees.

articles.title: Separator bounds in an ordered B-tree node
articles.statement:
Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be lists of keys,
$k$ a key, and $C_1$ and $C_2$ lists of B-trees such that $C_1$ has exactly one more tree
than $K_1$ has keys. If the internal node whose key list is $K_1$ followed by $k$ followed
by $K_2$, and whose child list is $C_1$ followed by $C_2$, is ordered, then every key in the
flattening of the node with keys $K_1$ and children $C_1$ is less than $k$, and $k$ is less
than every key in the flattening of the node with keys $K_2$ and children $C_2$.

Here the last tree of $C_1$ is the subtree immediately left of $k$ and the first tree of
$C_2$ the one immediately right of it; in particular, every key in a child of an ordered
node lies strictly between the separators adjacent to it.

articles.title: Splitting off the last element of a list
articles.statement:
For a nonempty list $l$, the result is the pair
consisting of $l$ with its last element removed and the last element of $l$; for the empty list
there is no result.

articles.title: Splitting a B-tree node
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a minimum degree, $s = t - 1$ (so $s = 0$ when
$t = 0$), $k_1, \dots, k_m$ a list of keys and $c_1, \dots, c_n$ a list of B-trees. If
$m > s$, splitting returns the pair of internal nodes formed by the keys $k_1, \dots, k_s$
with the first $t$ children (all of them if $n < t$) and by the keys $k_{s+2}, \dots, k_m$
with the children after the first $t$, together with the key $k_{s+1}$ promoted between
them. If $m \le s$, it returns the single internal node with keys $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and
children $c_1, \dots, c_n$ unchanged.

On an overfull node with $2t$ keys and $t \ge 1$, the promoted key $k_t$ is the median key.

articles.title: Height of a B-tree along first children
articles.statement:
The height of a B-tree is computed by
following first children: a leaf has height $0$, an internal node with no children has height
$0$, and an internal node whose first child is $c$ has height one more than the height of $c$.

If a tree satisfies the B-tree structural invariant (or the root invariant) at height $h$,
then this height equals $h$.

articles.title: The minimum degree of a B-tree is at least two
articles.statement:
If a tree is a B-tree of minimum
degree $t$, then $t \ge 2$.

articles.title: Root-valid B-trees are valid
articles.statement:
If a tree satisfies the root invariant for minimum
degree $t$ at height $h$, then for some natural number $m$ it satisfies the structural
invariant for minimum degree $t$, minimum top-node key count $m$ and height $h$.

articles.title: Root invariant of a B-tree
articles.statement:
For a minimum degree $t$ and a height $h$, a tree
satisfies the root invariant when either $h = 0$ and the tree is a leaf with at most
$2t - 1$ keys (possibly none, for the empty tree), or $h = h' + 1$ and the tree is an
internal node with between $1$ and $2t - 1$ keys and exactly one more child than keys,
every child satisfying the structural invariant for minimum degree $t$, minimum top-node
key count $t - 1$ and height $h'$. Here $2t - 1$ and $t - 1$ are truncated at $0$.

articles.title: Structural invariant of a B-tree
articles.statement:
For a minimum degree $t$ and a minimum key count $m$
for the top node, the invariant is defined inductively over the height: a leaf with $k$ keys
satisfies it at height $0$ when $m \le k \le 2t - 1$, and for every natural number $h$, an
internal node with $k$ keys satisfies it at height $h + 1$ when $m \le k \le 2t - 1$, the
node has exactly $k + 1$ children, and every child satisfies the invariant with minimum key
count $t - 1$ at height $h$. Here $2t - 1$ and $t - 1$ are truncated at $0$.

Consequently all leaves of a valid tree sit at the same depth, every node has at most
$2t - 1$ keys, and every node other than the top one has at least $t - 1$ keys. Non-root
trees are used with $m = t - 1$; the root of a B-tree satisfies the root invariant instead.

articles.title: A predicate holds at all keys of a binary tree iff it holds at all its members
articles.statement:
For a
type $\alpha$, a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, every key
of $t$ satisfies $p$ in the recursive sense (the empty tree qualifies, and a node qualifies when
its left subtree qualifies, its key satisfies $p$ and its right subtree qualifies) if and only if
$p(x)$ holds for every $x$ that is a member of $t$.

articles.title: A predicate holding at every key of a binary tree
articles.statement:
For a predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$,
the empty binary tree satisfies "every key satisfies $p$", and a node with key $k$, left subtree
$L$ and right subtree $R$ satisfies it exactly when $L$ satisfies it, $p(k)$ holds and $R$
satisfies it.

articles.title: Search in a binary search tree is correct
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key
$x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered (recursively, every
key in the left subtree of a node is strictly smaller than the node's key and every key in its
right subtree is strictly larger), the comparison search for $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only
if $x$ is a member of $t$.

articles.title: Search in a binary search tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and
a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, the search for $x$ in $t$ returns a Boolean: false if $t$
is empty, and if $t$ is a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, the search
for $x$ in $L$ when $x < k$, the search for $x$ in $R$ when $k < x$, and true otherwise.

Unlike the index of a key in a binary tree, which encodes the root-to-node path as a positive
binary number, this search returns only whether the key was found.

articles.title: Deletion from a binary search tree
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type. Deleting $x$
from the empty tree gives the empty tree. Deleting $x$ from a tree with root key $k$, left subtree
$L$ and right subtree $R$ gives the tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ with $x$ deleted and
right subtree $R$ if $x < k$; the tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$
with $x$ deleted if $k < x$; and the join of $L$ and $R$ otherwise, that is, if $x = k$.

articles.title: Binary search tree built from a list
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the binary tree
built from a list $[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ of elements of $\alpha$ is obtained from the empty tree by
inserting $x_n$, then $x_{n-1}$, and so on down to $x_1$, using binary search tree insertion; the
empty list gives the empty tree.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a binary tree with an accumulator
articles.statement:
For a binary tree $t$ and a list
$s$, the accumulated traversal of the empty tree onto $s$ is $s$, and the accumulated traversal of
a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ onto $s$ is the accumulated traversal
of $L$ onto the list consisting of $k$ followed by the accumulated traversal of $R$ onto $s$.

Unfolding the recursion, the result is the inorder traversal of $t$ followed by $s$.

articles.title: Inorder traversal after deletion
articles.statement:
If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly
ordered type and $x$ is a key, then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$
from $t$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (and is the
inorder traversal of $t$ itself if $x$ does not occur in it).

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a join
articles.statement:
For binary trees $L$ and $R$, the inorder traversal of the join
of $L$ and $R$ is the inorder traversal of $L$ followed by the inorder traversal of $R$.

articles.title: The inorder traversal of a binary search tree has no duplicates
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered
type $\alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered (recursively, every key
in the left subtree of a node is strictly smaller than the node's key and every key in its right
subtree is strictly larger), the inorder traversal of $t$ is a list with no repeated entries.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a binary tree
articles.statement:
The inorder traversal of a binary tree $t$ is the
accumulated inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list. Equivalently, the empty tree gives the
empty list, and a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ gives the inorder
traversal of $L$, then $k$, then the inorder traversal of $R$.

articles.title: Insertion into a binary search tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key
$x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives
the single node with key $x$ and empty subtrees; inserting $x$ into a node with key $k$, left
subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ inserts $x$ into $L$ when $x < k$, inserts $x$ into $R$ when
$k < x$, and returns the node unchanged when $x = k$.

articles.title: Join of two binary trees
articles.statement:
The join of the empty tree and a tree $R$ is $R$. The join of a tree
with root key $k$, left subtree $L_1$ and right subtree $L_2$ and a tree $R$ is the tree with root
key $k$, left subtree $L_1$ and right subtree the join of $L_2$ and $R$. Thus, when the first tree
is nonempty, $R$ becomes the right subtree of its rightmost node.

In the inorder traversal of the join, every key of the first tree comes before every key of the
second tree.

articles.title: Deletion keeps the other keys
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree over a linearly ordered type, not
necessarily ordered, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs in $t$, then $y$
occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.

articles.title: Membership after deletion
articles.statement:
If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly ordered
type, then for all keys $x$ and $y$, the key $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from
$t$ if and only if $y$ occurs in $t$ and $y \ne x$.

articles.title: Members of the binary search tree built from a list
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$,
a key $x \in \alpha$ and a list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, $x$ is a member of the binary tree
built from $xs$ by successive binary search tree insertion if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.

articles.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of a binary tree
articles.statement:
For every binary tree $T$ and every
key $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in $T$.

articles.title: Membership after insertion into a binary search tree
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly ordered.
For all keys $x, y$ and every binary tree $T$, $y$ lies in the tree obtained by inserting $x$
into $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ lies in $T$.

articles.title: Membership in a join
articles.statement:
For binary trees $L$ and $R$, a key $x$ occurs in the join of $L$ and
$R$ if and only if $x$ occurs in $L$ or $x$ occurs in $R$.

articles.title: Membership in a binary tree
articles.statement:
A key $x$ belongs to a binary tree $T$ when it is the key
of some node of $T$: no key belongs to the empty tree, and $x$ belongs to a node with key $k$,
left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $x$ belongs to $L$, $x = k$, or $x$
belongs to $R$.

This membership does not use the search-tree ordering.

articles.title: The deleted key is gone
articles.statement:
If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a linearly ordered type
and $x$ is a key, then $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.

articles.title: The length of the inorder traversal of a binary tree is its number of nodes
articles.statement:
For every
binary tree $T$, the number of nodes of $T$ (each node carries one key, and the empty tree has
none) equals the length of the inorder traversal of $T$.

articles.title: Inserting a present key into a binary search tree leaves its size unchanged
articles.statement:
Let the
keys be linearly ordered, and let $T$ be an ordered binary tree. If a key $x$ lies in $T$, then
the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ has the same number of nodes as $T$.

articles.title: Inserting an absent key into a binary search tree adds one node
articles.statement:
Let the keys be
linearly ordered. For every binary tree $T$ and every key $x$ that does not lie in $T$, the tree
obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ has one more node than $T$.

articles.title: Deletion preserves the search-tree order
articles.statement:
If $t$ is an ordered binary search tree over a
linearly ordered type, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is
ordered.

articles.title: Binary search trees built from a list are ordered
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type. For every list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, the tree obtained from the empty tree by
inserting the elements of $xs$ one at a time, from the last element to the first, is ordered.

articles.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered binary tree is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be
a linearly ordered type. If a binary tree $T$ over $\alpha$ is ordered, then in the inorder
traversal of $T$ every key is less than every key that comes after it.

articles.title: Binary search tree insertion preserves order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type.
For every key $x \in \alpha$ and every ordered binary tree $T$ over $\alpha$, the tree obtained
by inserting $x$ into $T$ is ordered.

articles.title: Joining separated ordered trees
articles.statement:
Let $L$ and $R$ be ordered binary search trees over a type
with a relation $<$. If $a < b$ for every key $a$ of $L$ and every key $b$ of $R$, then the join
of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.

articles.title: Ordered binary trees
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. The empty tree is
ordered, and a binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is ordered
when $L$ and $R$ are ordered, every key of $L$ is less than $k$, and $k$ is less than every key
of $R$.

articles.title: Rank counts the smaller inorder entries
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key
$x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, the rank of $x$ in $t$ equals the
length of the list obtained from the inorder traversal of $t$ by keeping exactly the entries
strictly less than $x$.

articles.title: The rank of a selected key is its index
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and
let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in $\alpha$, that is, at every node each key of the
left subtree is strictly smaller and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger than the
node's key. If selecting index $i$ in $t$ returns a key $x$, then the rank of $x$ in $t$
equals $i$.

articles.title: Rank of a key in a binary tree
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key
$x \in \alpha$ and a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, the rank of $x$ in $t$ is the number
of positions of the inorder traversal of $t$ whose entry is strictly less than $x$.

articles.title: Selection is indexing into the inorder traversal
articles.statement:
For a binary tree $t$ and a natural
number $i$, selecting index $i$ in $t$ gives the same result as looking up zero-based position
$i$ of the inorder traversal of $t$: the entry at that position when $i$ is less than the length
of the traversal, and nothing otherwise.

articles.title: Selecting the rank of a key returns the key
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type
and let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in $\alpha$, that is, at every node each key of the
left subtree is strictly smaller and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger than the
node's key. If $x$ is a key of $t$, then selecting, in $t$, the index equal to the rank of $x$
in $t$ returns $x$.

articles.title: Inorder selection in a binary tree
articles.statement:
For a binary tree $t$ and a natural number $i$,
selecting index $i$ in $t$ returns the entry at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal
of $t$ when $i$ is less than the length of that traversal, and returns nothing otherwise.

articles.title: A predicate holds on every key iff it holds along the inorder traversal
articles.statement:
For every
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every binary tree $T$ with keys in $\alpha$, every key of $T$
satisfies $p$ if and only if every element of the inorder traversal of $T$ satisfies $p$.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded Cartesian tree construction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For a natural
number $n$ (the fuel) and a list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the tree built from $xs$ with fuel $n$ is
the empty tree if $n = 0$ or $xs$ is empty. Otherwise $n = k + 1$ and $xs$ is nonempty; let $m$
be the minimum of $xs$, and let $L$ and $R$ be the parts of $xs$ before and after the first
occurrence of $m$. Then the tree has root $m$, its left subtree is built from $L$ with fuel $k$,
and its right subtree is built from $R$ with fuel $k$.

Each split produces strictly shorter lists, so a fuel of at least the length of $xs$ never runs
out.

articles.title: Cartesian tree of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $xs$ over a linear order, the Cartesian tree of $xs$
is the result of the fuel-bounded Cartesian tree construction on $xs$ with fuel equal to the
length of $xs$. So the empty list gives the empty tree, and otherwise the root is the minimum $m$
of $xs$, the left subtree is built in the same way from the elements before the first occurrence
of $m$, and the right subtree from the elements after that occurrence.

Its inorder traversal is $xs$ and it is min-heap ordered.

articles.title: Cartesian trees are heap-ordered
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the Cartesian
tree of $xs$ is min-heap ordered.

articles.title: Min-heap ordered binary tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $\le$. A binary tree
with keys in $\alpha$ is min-heap ordered when, at every node, the key $k$ of that node satisfies
$k \le y$ for every key $y$ in its left subtree and every key $y$ in its right subtree. The empty
tree is min-heap ordered.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a Cartesian tree
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the
inorder traversal of the Cartesian tree of $xs$ is $xs$.

articles.title: Minimum of a nonempty list
articles.statement:
For an element $a$ and a list $as$ over a linear order, the
left-fold minimum of $a$ and $as$ is the minimum of the list with head $a$ and tail $as$. It is
computed from the head: it equals $a$ when $as$ is empty, and when $as$ has head $b$ and tail $bs$
it equals the left-fold minimum of $\min(a, b)$ and $bs$.

articles.title: Keys of a Cartesian tree
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linear order and every element $x$,
$x$ is a key of the Cartesian tree of $xs$ if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.

articles.title: The root of a binary tree is one of its keys
articles.statement:
For every binary tree $T$ and every key $k$,
