if $T$ is nonempty with root key $k$, then $k$ is a key of $T$.

articles.title: The keys of a Cartesian tree permute its input
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linear order,
the inorder traversal of the Cartesian tree of $xs$ is a permutation of $xs$.

articles.title: The Cartesian tree of a nonempty list has a root
articles.statement:
For every nonempty list $xs$ over a
linearly ordered type, the Cartesian tree of $xs$ has a root key $m$.

articles.title: The root of a Cartesian tree is a minimum of the list
articles.statement:
Let $xs$ be a list over a
linearly ordered type. If the Cartesian tree of $xs$ has root key $m$, then $m$ occurs in $xs$
and $m \le y$ for every element $y$ of $xs$.

articles.title: The root of a heap-ordered tree is below every key
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a binary tree over a
preordered type that is heap-ordered (in min-heap order). If $T$ has root key $k$, then
$k \le x$ for every key $x$ occurring in $T$.

articles.title: Optional root key of a binary tree
articles.statement:
For a binary tree $T$ with keys in $\alpha$, the
root key of $T$ is an optional element of $\alpha$: it is absent (none) when $T$ is empty, and it
is $k$ when the top node of $T$ holds the key $k$.

articles.title: Splitting at the first occurrence leaves the value out of the left part
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an
element of a type with decidable equality and let $xs$ be a list in which $m$ occurs. When $xs$ is
split at the first occurrence of $m$, the left part does not contain $m$.

Together with the reconstruction property (the left part, then $m$, then the right part give back
$xs$), this characterizes the split point, including how duplicates of $m$ are handled when
building Cartesian trees; reconstruction alone would hold for a split at any occurrence.

articles.title: Splitting a list at the first occurrence of a value
articles.statement:
For a value $m$ of a type with
decidable equality and a list $xs$, the split of $xs$ at $m$ is the pair of the part of $xs$
before the first occurrence of $m$ and the part after it; that occurrence itself is dropped. If
$m$ does not occur in $xs$, the split is the pair of $xs$ and the empty list.

Only equality on the element type is needed, not the linear order required to build Cartesian
trees.

articles.title: Order-statistic deletion preserves cache correctness
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $k \in \alpha$ a key and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$. If the cached subtree size
at every node of $T$ equals the number of nodes in that node's subtree, then the same holds for the
tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$.

articles.title: Order-statistic trees built from a list have correct size caches
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered type. For every list $\ell$ of elements of $\alpha$, the order-statistic tree
obtained by inserting the elements of $\ell$ into the empty tree, from right to left, has correct
cached subtree sizes at every node.

articles.title: Insertion preserves correct size caches
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let
$k \in \alpha$, and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ whose cached subtree sizes
are correct at every node. Then the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ also has correct
cached subtree sizes at every node.

articles.title: Order-statistic merge preserves cache correctness
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be order-statistic trees
whose cached subtree size at every node equals the number of nodes in that node's subtree. Then
the merge of $A$ and $B$ has the same property. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is
assumed.

articles.title: The cache-computing node constructor preserves correct size caches
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a key and
let $L$ and $R$ be order-statistic trees whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node.
Then the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, whose root cache is the
cached root size of $L$ plus the cached root size of $R$ plus one, also has correct cached
subtree sizes at every node.

articles.title: Correct size caches
articles.statement:
An order-statistic tree has correct size caches when, at every
node, the cached subtree size equals the number of nodes of the left subtree plus the number of
nodes of the right subtree plus one, that is, the number of nodes of the subtree rooted at that
node. The empty tree has correct size caches.

articles.title: Correct caches give the tree size
articles.statement:
If an order-statistic tree $T$ has correct cached
subtree sizes at every node, then the cached root size of $T$ (zero for the empty tree) equals
the number of nodes of $T$.

articles.title: Cached root size
articles.statement:
The cached root size of an order-statistic tree is the subtree size
stored in the entry of its root node, and is $0$ for the empty tree.

articles.title: Search misses a key deleted from an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys
of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's
key). Comparison search for $k$ in the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ returns false.

articles.title: Search in an ordered order-statistic tree is correct
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered: after forgetting the cached
sizes, at every node all keys in the left subtree are smaller than the node's key and all keys in
the right subtree are larger. Then for every $q \in \alpha$, comparison search for $q$ in $T$
returns true if and only if $q$ is the key of some node of $T$.

articles.title: Search in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and
$q \in \alpha$. Searching for $q$ in the empty tree returns false. At a node with key $k$, the
search continues in the left subtree if $q < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < q$, and
returns true otherwise.

articles.title: Deletion from an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Deleting a key $k$ from an order-statistic tree over a
linearly ordered type follows the comparison path from the root. The empty tree stays empty. At a
node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$: if $k < x$, the result is the node with
key $x$, left subtree the deletion of $k$ from $L$ and right subtree $R$; if $x < k$, it is the
node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree the deletion of $k$ from $R$; otherwise
($k = x$) it is the merge of $L$ and $R$. Each rebuilt node gets as cached size the sum of the
cached root sizes of its children plus one, an empty child counting as zero.

If $k$ does not occur in the tree, the result has the same keys.

articles.title: Order-statistic tree node entry
articles.statement:
A node entry of an order-statistic tree over a type
$\alpha$ consists of a key in $\alpha$ and a natural number, the cached number of nodes in the
subtree rooted at that node.

articles.title: Insertion commutes with forgetting the size caches
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$. Forgetting the cached sizes
of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ gives the same binary tree as inserting $k$, by
ordinary binary-search-tree insertion, into $T$ with its cached sizes forgotten.

articles.title: Erasing the size caches of an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
The erasure of an order-statistic
tree is the binary tree of the same shape whose node keys are the keys of the original nodes:
the empty tree is sent to the empty tree, and a node is sent to the node with the same key
whose left and right subtrees are the erasures of the original left and right subtrees, so
every cached subtree size is dropped.

articles.title: Order-statistic tree built from a list
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, the
order-statistic tree built from a list of keys is obtained by inserting the keys into the empty
tree from right to left: the empty list gives the empty tree, and a list with head $k$ and
tail $l$ gives the insertion of $k$ into the tree built from $l$.

articles.title: Inorder traversal after order-statistic deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
$k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of
the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key).
The inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ is the inorder traversal of
$T$ with every occurrence of $k$ removed.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of an order-statistic merge
articles.statement:
For order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$, the
inorder traversal of the merge of $A$ and $B$ is the inorder traversal of $A$ followed by the
inorder traversal of $B$. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
The inorder traversal of an
order-statistic tree is the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached
subtree sizes: the traversal of the left subtree, then the root key, then the traversal of the
right subtree, and the empty list for the empty tree.

articles.title: Insertion into an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Inserting a key $k$ of a linearly ordered type
into the empty tree gives a single node with key $k$ and cached size $1$. For a nonempty tree
with root key $r$: if $k < r$, the key is inserted into the left subtree; if $r < k$, it is
inserted into the right subtree; in both cases the root is rebuilt with key $r$ and cached size
equal to the cached root sizes of its two subtrees plus one (an empty subtree counts as zero).
Otherwise $k = r$ and the tree is returned unchanged.

articles.title: Keys of an order-statistic tree after deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
$k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of
the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key).
For every $y \in \alpha$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ if and only
if $y$ is a key of $T$ and $y \ne k$.

articles.title: Keys of an order-statistic tree built from a list
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, a
key $k$ and a list $l$ of keys, $k$ is a key of some node of the order-statistic tree built
from $l$ by successive insertion if and only if $k$ occurs in $l$.

articles.title: Keys of an order-statistic merge
articles.statement:
For order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$ over a type $\alpha$
and any $x \in \alpha$, $x$ is a key of the merge of $A$ and $B$ if and only if $x$ is a key of $A$
or a key of $B$. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.

articles.title: Merging order-statistic trees
articles.statement:
The merge of order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$ is defined by
recursion on $A$. If $A$ is empty, it is $B$. If $A$ has root key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right
subtree $R$, it is the node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree the merge of $R$ and
$B$, whose cached size is the sum of the cached root sizes of its children plus one, an empty
child counting as zero. Thus $B$ is attached below the rightmost path of $A$, and every node on
that path gets a recomputed cache.

The merge is intended for trees in which every key of $A$ is smaller than every key of $B$, but it
is defined for all pairs of trees.

articles.title: Order-statistic tree node with computed cache
articles.statement:
Given a key $k$ and order-statistic
trees $L$ and $R$, the node built from them has key $k$, left subtree $L$, right subtree $R$,
and cached subtree size equal to the cached root size of $L$ plus the cached root size of $R$
plus one, where the empty tree has cached root size zero.

articles.title: Deleted key is absent from an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys
of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's
key). Then $k$ is not a key of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$.

articles.title: Deletion preserves order in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, after its
cached sizes are removed, every key in a left subtree is strictly smaller than the key of its node
and every key in a right subtree is strictly larger. Then for every key $k$, the tree obtained
from $T$ by deleting $k$ is again ordered.

articles.title: Order-statistic trees built from lists are ordered
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ of keys from a
linearly ordered type, the order-statistic tree built from $l$ by successive insertion is
ordered: after its cached sizes are erased, at every node each key of the left subtree is
strictly smaller than the node's key and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger.

articles.title: Insertion preserves ordering of order-statistic trees
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an order-statistic
tree over a linearly ordered key type that is ordered, meaning that after its cached sizes are
erased, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's key and
each key of the right subtree is strictly larger. Then for every key $k$, the tree obtained by
inserting $k$ into $T$ is again ordered.

articles.title: Merging separated ordered order-statistic trees preserves order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered type and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered order-statistic trees over $\alpha$ such
that $x < y$ for every key $x$ of $L$ and every key $y$ of $R$. Then the merge of $L$ and $R$
is ordered.

articles.title: Ordered order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
An order-statistic tree over a type equipped with a
relation $<$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached sizes is an ordered
binary search tree: at every node, each key of the left subtree is $<$ the node's key, the
node's key is $<$ each key of the right subtree, and both subtrees are ordered.

articles.title: Rank after deletion in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type
and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered and whose cached subtree
sizes are correct. Let $k$ and $q$ be keys and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by
deleting $k$. Then the rank of $q$ in $T'$, computed by navigation with cached sizes, equals the
number of entries strictly smaller than $q$ in the inorder traversal of $T'$ with its cached
sizes removed.

articles.title: Cached rank agrees with traversal rank
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a
linearly ordered key type whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node and which is
ordered. Then for every query $q$, the rank of $q$ computed by descending $T$ with cached
left-subtree sizes equals the number of entries strictly smaller than $q$ in the inorder
traversal of the binary tree obtained by erasing the caches of $T$.

articles.title: Rank inverts select in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree
over a linearly ordered type whose cached subtree sizes are correct and which satisfies the
binary-search-tree ordering. If select at zero-based index $i$ in $T$ returns a key $k$, then
the rank of $k$ in $T$ equals $i$.

articles.title: Rank in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
For a key $q$ of a linearly ordered type, the rank of
$q$ in an order-statistic tree is computed by descending from the root. It is $0$ for the empty
tree. At a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is the rank of $q$ in
$L$ if $q < k$; it is $s(L) + 1$ plus the rank of $q$ in $R$ if $k < q$; and it is $s(L)$ if
$q = k$. Here $s(L)$ is the subtree size cached at the root of $L$, and $0$ if $L$ is empty.

When the cached sizes are correct and the tree is ordered, this is the number of keys in the
tree strictly smaller than $q$.

articles.title: Selection after deletion in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct.
Let $k$ be a key and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. Then for every
natural number $i$, selecting position $i$ in $T'$ by navigation with cached sizes returns the
entry at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of $T'$ with its cached sizes removed,
and returns nothing when that traversal has at most $i$ entries.

articles.title: Cached select agrees with inorder select
articles.statement:
For every order-statistic tree $T$ whose
cached subtree sizes are correct and every natural number $i$, select at index $i$ in $T$
(descending with the cached sizes) returns the same result as taking the element at zero-based
position $i$ of the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached
sizes; in particular both return nothing when that position does not exist.

articles.title: Selecting the rank of a surviving key after deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered and whose cached subtree
sizes are correct, let $k$ be a key, and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$.
If $y$ is a key of $T'$, then selecting, with cached sizes, the position in $T'$ given by the
cached rank of $y$ in $T'$ returns $y$.

articles.title: Select inverts rank in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over
a linearly ordered type whose cached subtree sizes are correct and which satisfies the
binary-search-tree ordering. For every key $k$ in $T$, select in $T$ at the index equal to the
rank of $k$ in $T$ returns $k$.

articles.title: Select in an order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
For an order-statistic tree $T$ and a natural number
$i$, select at index $i$ in $T$ is computed by descending from the root. It returns nothing for
the empty tree. At a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is select at
index $i$ in $L$ if $i < s(L)$; it returns $k$ if $i = s(L)$; and it is select at index
$i - s(L) - 1$ in $R$ if $i > s(L)$. Here $s(L)$ is the subtree size cached at the root of $L$,
and $0$ if $L$ is empty.

When the cached sizes are correct, this returns the key at zero-based position $i$ of the
inorder traversal, and nothing if $T$ has at most $i$ nodes.

articles.title: Order-statistic tree
articles.statement:
An order-statistic tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is a binary
tree, possibly empty, each of whose nodes carries a key in $\alpha$ together with a natural
number, meant as the cached number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node. That these
caches are correct is a separate condition.

articles.title: All keys of a red-black tree via its color erasure
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$
and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if
$p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors. This holds
by definition.

articles.title: All keys versus members of a red-black tree
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every
red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p(x)$ holds
for every $x \in \alpha$ that is a (structural) member of $t$.

articles.title: Predicate holding at every key of a red-black tree
articles.statement:
For a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and a
red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ when $p$ holds at every key
of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors.

articles.title: Red invariant away from the root
articles.statement:
A red-black tree satisfies the relaxed red invariant
when it is empty, or when its left and right subtrees both satisfy the red invariant (no red node
has a red child). The root itself is unconstrained, so a red root may have a red child.

This is the intermediate invariant of Okasaki's unchecked insertion.

articles.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the left subtree
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a tree whose
root may be double black, $k$ a key and $R$ a red-black tree. If $L$ is a genuine red-black tree,
the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$.
Otherwise the double black of $L$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty
tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The result is
then the left-deficit repair (Fix Left) applied to the color $c$, the absorbed tree, the key $k$
and the sibling $R$; it may again have a double-black root.

articles.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the right subtree
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a red-black
tree, $k$ a key and $R$ a tree whose root may be double black. If $R$ is a genuine red-black
tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree
$R$. Otherwise the double black of $R$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the
empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The
result is then the right-deficit repair (Fix Right) applied to the color $c$, the sibling $L$, the
key $k$ and the absorbed tree; it may again have a double-black root.

articles.title: Okasaki's rebalancing
articles.statement:
Given a color $c$, red-black trees $l$ and $r$, and a key $k$,
rebalancing produces a tree as follows. Suppose $c$ is black and one of these configurations
occurs, taking the first that applies: $l$ is a red node with a red left child; $l$ is a red node
with a red right child; $r$ is a red node with a red left child; $r$ is a red node with a red
right child. The black root and the two red nodes then hold three keys and leave four subtrees,
which read in inorder as $t_1, x, t_2, y, t_3, z, t_4$. The result is a red node with key $y$, left
child the black node with subtrees $t_1, t_2$ and key $x$, and right child the black node with
subtrees $t_3, t_4$ and key $z$. In every other case the result is the node with color $c$, left
subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.

articles.title: Black-height balance of a possibly double-black tree
articles.statement:
A tree whose root may be double
black is balanced when it is a genuine red-black tree that is balanced, when it is the
double-black empty tree, or when it is a double-black node whose left and right subtrees are both
balanced and have the same black height.

articles.title: Double-black deletion keeps a valid tree balanced
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $x \in \alpha$, and $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$. Then the tree obtained from
$T$ by double-black deletion of $x$ is balanced.

articles.title: Deletion by rebuilding is black-height balanced
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered type of
keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the tree obtained
from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black-height balanced.

articles.title: Red-black insertion preserves black-height balance
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type.
If a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same
number of black nodes), then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is
balanced.

articles.title: Black-height balanced red-black tree
articles.statement:
A red-black tree is balanced when every root-to-leaf
path contains the same number of black nodes. Recursively: the empty tree is balanced, and a node
is balanced when both of its subtrees are balanced and have the same black height (the number of
black nodes on the leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the leaf).

articles.title: Trees with a possibly double-black root
articles.statement:
A tree with a possibly double-black root over a
type $\alpha$ is one of the following: a genuine red-black tree over $\alpha$; the double-black
empty tree; or a double-black node consisting of a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right
subtree, where both subtrees are genuine red-black trees. Hence a double black can occur only at
the root.

articles.title: Extended root colors
articles.statement:
An extended color is one of three values: red, black or double
black.

Double black marks the root of a tree after a deletion and counts as two black nodes in its black
height.

articles.title: Black height of a possibly double-black tree
articles.statement:
The black height of a genuine red-black tree
is its usual black height. The double-black empty tree has black height $2$, and a double-black
node with left subtree $L$ has black height $h(L) + 2$, where $h(L)$ is the usual black height of
$L$. Thus a double-black root counts as two black nodes, where the usual black height counts the
empty tree as one.

For an ordered, balanced red-black tree satisfying the red invariant, deleting any key by the
double-black descent, before the root is blackened, yields a tree whose black height in this sense
equals the black height of the original tree.

articles.title: Black height after double-black deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
$x \in \alpha$, $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$, and $T'$ the tree obtained from $T$ by
double-black deletion of $x$. Then the black height of $T'$ either equals the black height of $T$
or is one less than it.

The black height drops by one when a double black left by the deletion is absorbed at the root.

articles.title: Insertion raises the black height by at most one
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type.
For every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ and every $x \in \alpha$, the black height of the
tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ equals either the black height of $t$ or the black height of
$t$ plus one.

Any increase comes from recoloring the root black at the end of insertion.

articles.title: Black height
articles.statement:
The black height of a red-black tree is the number of black nodes on its
leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the empty leaf as one black node: the empty tree has black
height $1$, a red node has the black height of its left subtree, and a black node has the black
height of its left subtree plus $1$.

articles.title: Absorbing a double-black root
articles.statement:
Blackening sends a tree whose root may be double black to
a genuine red-black tree by changing only its root: a genuine tree has its root recolored black
(the empty tree stays empty), the double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a
double-black node becomes the black node with the same subtrees and key.

articles.title: Extended root color
articles.statement:
The extended color of a tree whose root may be double black is the
color of its root, red or black, when it is a genuine red-black tree, where the empty tree counts
as black; it is double black for the double-black empty tree and for every double-black node.

articles.title: Double-black deletion leaves a black root
articles.statement:
For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type
and every red-black tree $t$, valid or not, the root of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$
by the double-black method is black, where the empty tree counts as black.

articles.title: Deletion by rebuilding gives a black root
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered type of keys,
every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the root of the tree
obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black, where the empty tree counts as having
a black root.

articles.title: Root color
articles.statement:
The root color of a red-black tree is the color of its root node; the empty
tree has root color black.

articles.title: Red-black node colors
articles.statement:
The colors of red-black tree nodes are the two values red and
black.

articles.title: Search in an ordered red-black tree is correct
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a red-black tree over a
linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger,
recursively). Then for every key $x$, the search for $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$
is a key of some node of $t$.

articles.title: Search in a red-black tree
articles.statement:
Searching a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type for a
key $x$ returns a Boolean, ignoring colors: the empty tree gives false, and at a node with key $k$
the search continues in the left subtree if $x < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < x$,
and returns true otherwise.

articles.title: Double-black deletion
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, deleting $x$ from a
red-black tree returns a tree whose root may be double black, by recursion on the tree. The
empty tree gives the empty tree. At a node of color $c$ with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right
subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the left reassembly of color $c$, the deletion of $x$
from $l$, key $k$ and $r$; if $k < x$, it is the right reassembly of color $c$, $l$, key $k$ and
the deletion of $x$ from $r$. A reassembly rebuilds the node when the recursive result is a
genuine tree, and otherwise repairs the double-black child against its sibling. If $x = k$ and
$l$ is empty, the result is $r$ when $c$ is red and $r$ with one black added at its root when
$c$ is black; otherwise, if $r$ is empty, the same with $l$ in place of $r$. If $x = k$ and both
subtrees are nonempty, let $s$ be the leftmost key of $r$; the result is the right reassembly of
color $c$, $l$, key $s$ and the deletion of $s$ from $r$. Thus a node with two children is
deleted by promoting its successor, the minimum key of its right subtree.

articles.title: Unbalanced red-black tree deletion
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, unbalanced
deletion of $x$ from a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree stays
empty. At a node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the
result is the node with color $c$, left subtree the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$
and right subtree $r$; if $k < x$, it is the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and
right subtree the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $r$; otherwise (so $x = k$) it is the splice of
$l$ with $r$.

Colors are kept, so the result need not satisfy the red invariant or be black-height balanced.

articles.title: Red-black tree deletion by the double-black method
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered
type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ runs the double-black deletion of $x$ from
$t$, which returns a tree whose root may be double black, and then absorbs a remaining double
black at the root and recolors the root black.

When $t$ is ordered, has no red node with a red child and has the same number of black nodes on
every root-to-leaf path, the result is a valid red-black tree; when $t$ is only ordered, the
inorder traversal of the result is that of $t$ with $x$ erased.

articles.title: Red-black tree deletion by rebuilding
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a
red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ by rebuilding first forms the unbalanced deletion of
$x$ from $t$, then rebalances it: starting from the empty tree, it inserts the keys of the inorder
traversal of that tree one at a time, from the last key to the first.

articles.title: Recoloring the root black does not change the color erasure
articles.statement:
For every red-black
tree $t$, the color erasure of the tree obtained from $t$ by recoloring its root black (the empty
tree is left unchanged) equals the color erasure of $t$.

articles.title: Color erasure
articles.statement:
The color erasure of a red-black tree is the binary tree obtained by
forgetting the node colors: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with key $k$
and subtrees $l$ and $r$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose subtrees are the color
erasures of $l$ and $r$.

articles.title: Left repair after double-black deletion
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and
black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right
subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $D$, a key $k$ and a tree $S$, the left repair returns a
tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. If
$S = N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3))$ or, failing that,
$S = N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2), z, T_3)$, it returns
$N(c, N(\mathrm{B}, D, k, T_1), y, N(\mathrm{B}, T_2, z, T_3))$. Otherwise, if
$S = N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, T_2)$, it returns $N(\mathrm{B}, D, k, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2))$ when
$c$ is red, and the double-black node with left child $D$, key $k$ and right child
$N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2)$ when $c$ is black. In the next three cases $c$ is not used. If
$S = N(\mathrm{R}, N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3)), w, T_4)$ or, failing that,
$S = N(\mathrm{R}, N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2), z, T_3), w, T_4)$, it returns
$N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, N(\mathrm{B}, D, k, T_1), y, N(\mathrm{B}, T_2, z, T_3)), w, T_4)$.
Otherwise, if $S = N(\mathrm{R}, N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, T_2), w, T_3)$, it returns
$N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{B}, D, k, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2)), w, T_3)$. In every remaining case
it returns $N(c, D, k, S)$.

The repair is meant for a deficient left subtree $D$ whose double black has been absorbed, so
that $D$ has one black node fewer than its sibling $S$ on every root-to-leaf path.

articles.title: Right repair after double-black deletion
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and
black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right
subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $S$, a key $k$ and a tree $D$, the right repair returns a
tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. If
$S = N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2), z, T_3)$ or, failing that,
$S = N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3))$, it returns
$N(c, N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, T_2), z, N(\mathrm{B}, T_3, k, D))$. Otherwise, if
$S = N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, T_2)$, it returns $N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2), k, D)$ when
$c$ is red, and the double-black node with left child $N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2)$, key $k$ and
right child $D$ when $c$ is black. In the next three cases $c$ is not used. If
$S = N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3), w, T_4))$ or, failing that,
$S = N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{B}, T_2, z, N(\mathrm{R}, T_3, w, T_4)))$, it returns
$N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{R}, N(\mathrm{B}, T_2, z, T_3), w, N(\mathrm{B}, T_4, k, D)))$.
Otherwise, if $S = N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{B}, T_2, z, T_3))$, it returns
$N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3), k, D))$. In every remaining case
it returns $N(c, S, k, D)$.

The repair is the mirror image of the left repair, meant for a deficient right subtree $D$ whose
double black has been absorbed, so that $D$ has one black node fewer than its sibling $S$ on
every root-to-leaf path.

articles.title: Red-black tree from a list
articles.statement:
The red-black tree built from a list over a linearly ordered
type inserts the elements of the list into the empty tree from right to left: the empty list
gives the empty tree, and a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ gives the insertion of $x$ into the
tree built from $xs$.

articles.title: Adding a black to the root
articles.statement:
Add one black to the root of a red-black tree, producing a
tree whose root may be double black: the empty tree becomes the double-black empty tree, a red
root becomes black, and a black root becomes double black.

articles.title: Inorder traversal onto a suffix
articles.statement:
For a red-black tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the
accumulator form of the binary-search-tree inorder traversal applied to the color erasure of $t$:
for the empty tree it returns $s$, and for a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ it returns
the result for $l$ with suffix the list $k$ followed by $u$, where $u$ is the result for $r$ with
suffix $s$.

Thus the result lists the keys of $t$ in inorder followed by $s$, in time linear in the size
of $t$.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a possibly double-black tree
articles.statement:
The inorder traversal of a red-black
tree whose root may be double black ignores the double-black mark: a genuine tree gives its
inorder traversal, the double-black empty tree gives the empty list, and a double-black node with
left child $l$, key $k$ and right child $r$ gives the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$,
followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.

articles.title: Double-black deletion erases the key from the inorder traversal
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ of a
linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of the tree
obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is the inorder traversal of $t$
with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

articles.title: Inorder traversal after deletion by rebuilding
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered
type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from
$t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$
removed (it is unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

articles.title: Inorder traversal ignores colors
articles.statement:
For every red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of
$t$ equals the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$; this holds by
definition.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a splice
articles.statement:
For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type,
the inorder traversal of the splice of $t$ with $s$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ followed by the
inorder traversal of $s$.

articles.title: Ordered red-black trees have duplicate-free inorder traversals
articles.statement:
For a red-black tree $t$
over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key
larger, recursively), the inorder traversal of $t$ contains no key twice.

articles.title: Inorder traversal of a red-black tree
articles.statement:
The inorder traversal of a red-black tree $t$ is
the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$, computed in linear time
with an accumulator starting from the empty list. It lists the keys of $t$ from left to right:
the empty tree gives the empty list, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ gives the
traversal of $l$, then $k$, then the traversal of $r$.

articles.title: Unchecked red-black insertion
articles.statement:
For keys from a linearly ordered type, the unchecked
insertion of $x$ into a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. Inserting $x$ into the
empty tree gives a red node with key $x$ and two empty subtrees. Inserting $x$ into a node with
color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ gives: if $x < k$, Okasaki's
rebalancing of color $c$, left subtree the insertion of $x$ into $l$, key $k$ and right subtree
$r$; if $k < x$, Okasaki's rebalancing of color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree
the insertion of $x$ into $r$; otherwise the node itself, unchanged.

The result may have a red root with a red child, so it need not satisfy the red invariant.

articles.title: Red-black tree insertion
articles.statement:
For keys from a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into a
red-black tree $t$ gives the unchecked insertion of $x$ into $t$ with its root recolored black.

articles.title: Splicing two red-black trees
articles.statement:
The splice of a red-black tree $t$ with a red-black tree $s$ is
defined by recursion on $t$. The splice of the empty tree with $s$ is $s$. The splice of the node
with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ with $s$ is the node with color
$c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree the splice of $r$ with $s$.

So $s$ becomes the right subtree of the rightmost node of $t$, and all existing colors are kept.

articles.title: Blackening the root
articles.statement:
Recoloring the root of a red-black tree black leaves the empty tree
unchanged and turns a node with any color, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ into the
black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.

articles.title: Keys after double-black deletion
articles.statement:
For keys $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type and an
ordered red-black tree $t$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the
double-black method if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$ and $y \ne x$.

articles.title: Membership after deletion by rebuilding
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $y$ be keys of a linearly ordered
type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $y$ belongs to the tree obtained from $t$ by
deleting $x$ by rebuilding if and only if $y$ belongs to $t$ and $y \ne x$.

articles.title: Red-black membership is membership in the underlying binary tree
articles.statement:
For every red-black tree
$t$ and every $x$, $x$ is a member of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained
from $t$ by erasing its colors.

This holds by definition.

articles.title: Membership in a red-black tree built from a list
articles.statement:
For keys from a linearly ordered type and
every list $xs$, a key $x$ is a member of the red-black tree built from $xs$ by successive
insertion if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.

articles.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of a red-black tree
articles.statement:
For every red-black tree $t$ and
every $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.

articles.title: Membership after insertion into a red-black tree
articles.statement:
For keys from a linearly ordered type, a
key $y$ is a member of the red-black tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$
or $y$ is a member of $t$.

articles.title: Membership in a splice
articles.statement:
For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, a key $x$
belongs to the splice of $t$ with $s$ if and only if $x$ belongs to $t$ or $x$ belongs to $s$.

articles.title: Membership in a red-black tree
articles.statement:
An element $x$ is a member of a red-black tree $t$ when $x$
is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors, that is, when $x$ equals
the key of some node of $t$.

Membership is structural: it does not use the search-tree ordering.

articles.title: Leftmost key of a red-black tree
articles.statement:
For a red-black tree $t$ over a type $\alpha$, the
leftmost key of $t$ is either a key in $\alpha$ or undefined. It is undefined when $t$ is empty.
When $t$ is a node, of either color, with left subtree $l$ and key $k$, it is the leftmost key of
$l$ if that is defined, and $k$ otherwise. Hence the leftmost key is defined exactly when $t$ is
nonempty.

Under the search-tree invariant the leftmost key is the minimum key of the tree.

articles.title: The deleted key is absent after double-black deletion
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every
node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are
strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the key $x$ does not occur in
the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method.

articles.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion by rebuilding
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a key of a linearly
ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $x$ does not belong to the tree
obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding.

articles.title: Double-black deletion preserves the search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every
node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are
strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting
$x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again ordered.

articles.title: Red-black deletion yields an ordered tree
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered key type, every key
$x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is ordered: at every
node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's key and all keys in the
right subtree are strictly larger. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.

articles.title: A red-black tree is ordered exactly when its underlying binary tree is
articles.statement:
For keys with a
relation $<$, a red-black tree $t$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by
erasing its colors is an ordered binary search tree.

This holds by definition.

articles.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered red-black tree is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
For keys from a
linearly ordered type, if a red-black tree $t$ is ordered, then every entry of the inorder
traversal of $t$ is strictly smaller than every later entry.

articles.title: Red-black insertion preserves the search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If $t$ is ordered (at
every node with key $k$, every key in the left subtree is less than $k$ and every key in the right
subtree is greater than $k$), then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.

articles.title: Joining separated ordered trees preserves order
articles.statement:
Let $<$ be a relation on the keys, and let
$L$ and $R$ be red-black trees that are ordered for $<$ such that $a < b$ for every key $a$ of $L$
and every key $b$ of $R$. Then the join of $L$ and $R$, obtained by putting $R$ in place of the
empty right subtree of the rightmost node of $L$ (or $R$ itself if $L$ is empty) and keeping all
colors, is ordered.

articles.title: Ordered red-black tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with
keys in $\alpha$ is ordered when, at every node with key $k$, every key $y$ in the left subtree
satisfies $y < k$ and every key $z$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < z$.

Equivalently, the binary tree obtained by erasing the colors is an ordered binary search tree.

articles.title: Rebuilding a red-black tree from its keys
articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, the rebuild of
a red-black tree $t$ is the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the keys of the inorder
traversal of $t$ one at a time with Okasaki insertion, starting from the last key.

The result is a valid red-black tree whose keys are exactly the keys of $t$.

articles.title: Red invariant for trees with a possibly double-black root
articles.statement:
A tree whose root may be
double black satisfies the red invariant in the following cases: a genuine red-black tree
satisfies it when it satisfies the usual red invariant (no red node has a red child); the
double-black empty tree always satisfies it; and a double-black node with left subtree $l$ and
right subtree $r$ satisfies it when both $l$ and $r$ satisfy the usual red invariant.

articles.title: Double-black deletion from a valid tree keeps the red invariant
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered,
satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every
$x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method satisfies
the red invariant: no red node has a red child.

articles.title: Red-black deletion yields a tree with no red-red edge
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered key
type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$
satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.

articles.title: Red-black insertion preserves the red property
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
$x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If no red node of $t$ has a
red child, then no red node of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ has a red child.

articles.title: Red property of red-black trees
articles.statement:
A red-black tree satisfies the red property when no red
node has a red child, where empty subtrees count as black.

articles.title: Recoloring the root black
articles.statement:
For a red-black tree $t$, this is the tree obtained from $t$
by coloring its root black: the empty tree stays empty, and a node with left subtree $l$, key
$k$ and right subtree $r$, of either color, becomes the black node with left subtree $l$, key
$k$ and right subtree $r$.

articles.title: Red-black tree data type
articles.statement:
A red-black tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is either empty or
a node consisting of a color (red or black), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$, and a right
subtree.

No ordering, color or balance invariant is imposed by the type itself.

articles.title: Double-black deletion yields a valid tree from the structural invariants
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$
be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered,
satisfies the red invariant (no red node has a red child), and is black-height balanced (all
root-to-leaf paths contain the same number of black nodes). Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the
tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is a valid red-black tree.

The root of $t$ need not be black, since the deletion recolors the root of its result black.

articles.title: Double-black deletion preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and
$t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is
black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by
deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again a valid red-black tree.

The proof uses only that $t$ is ordered, satisfies the red invariant and is balanced.

articles.title: Red-black deletion yields a valid red-black tree
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered key type,
every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is a valid
red-black tree: it is ordered, no red node has a red child, every root-to-leaf path contains the
same number of black nodes, and its root is black (the empty tree counts as black). No hypothesis
on $t$ is needed.

The result is valid because deletion rebuilds the tree by repeated insertion, which always
produces a valid red-black tree.

articles.title: The empty red-black tree is valid
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $<$, the empty
red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is a valid red-black tree.

articles.title: Red-black trees built from a list are valid
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For
every list $l$ of elements of $\alpha$, the red-black tree obtained from the empty tree by
inserting the elements of $l$ one at a time, from the last to the first, is valid.

articles.title: Red-black insertion yields a valid tree from the invariants
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is
ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), and is balanced (every
root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes). Then the tree obtained by inserting
$x$ into $t$ is valid.

The root of $t$ need not be black, since insertion recolors the root black.

articles.title: Red-black insertion preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and
$x \in \alpha$. If $t$ is a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$, then the tree obtained by
inserting $x$ into $t$ is also valid.

articles.title: Valid red-black tree
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with
keys in $\alpha$ is valid when it is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red
child), is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), and its
root is black, where the empty tree counts as black.

articles.title: Keys of a valid skip list are distinct
articles.statement:
If a skip list is valid, then the keys of the
pairs in its bottom-level abstraction, read in order, form a list without duplicates.

articles.title: Bottom-level abstraction of a skip list
articles.statement:
The bottom-level abstraction of a skip list is
the association list obtained from its bottom-level nodes, in order, by keeping the key-value
pair $(k, v)$ of each node and forgetting its tower height.

articles.title: One search step returns a suffix
articles.statement:
For every search key, every level $i$ and every list
$L$ of skip-list nodes, advancing the search at level $i$ on $L$ returns a suffix of $L$.

articles.title: One level of skip-list search
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a search key, $i$ a zero-based level and $L$
a list of skip-list nodes. Let $P$ be the longest prefix of $L$ whose nodes all have keys less
than $k$. If some node of $P$ has tower height greater than $i$ (so it is visible at level
$i$), advancing at level $i$ returns the part of $L$ after the last such node; otherwise it
returns $L$ unchanged.

The returned suffix is the window that every lower level continues to scan.

articles.title: Empty skip list
articles.statement: The empty skip list is the skip list with no nodes.

articles.title: Skip-list node
articles.statement:
A skip-list node consists of a key, a value and a natural number, the
height of its tower. The node itself does not require the height to be positive; positivity is
part of the validity invariant of skip lists.

articles.title: Erasing the key of the first entry
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of
entries, and consider the skip list whose entry list is $e$ followed by $L$. If a key $k$ equals
the key of $e$, then erasing $k$ from this skip list leaves the entry list $L$.

articles.title: Erasing past a smaller first entry
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of
entries. If the key of $e$ is less than a key $k$, then erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry
list $e$ followed by $L$ gives the entry list consisting of $e$ followed by the entry list obtained
by erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry list $L$.

articles.title: Erasing a key below the first entry
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be a skip-list entry and $L$ a list of
entries. If a key $k$ is less than the key of $e$, then erasing $k$ from the skip list with entry
list $e$ followed by $L$ leaves the entry list $e$ followed by $L$ unchanged.

articles.title: Erasing from the empty skip list
articles.statement:
For every key $k$, erasing $k$ from the empty skip list
gives the empty skip list.

articles.title: Erasure on a valid skip list filters out the key
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$ is
a key, then the entry list of the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the entry list of
$S$ with every entry whose key equals $k$ removed, the remaining entries kept in their order.

articles.title: Skip-list erasure
articles.statement:
Given a key $k$ from a linearly ordered type and a skip list $S$, the
erasure of $k$ from $S$ is the skip list obtained by scanning the entries of $S$ in order: an
entry whose key is less than $k$ is kept and the scan continues; at the first entry whose key is
greater than $k$ the scan stops, and that entry and all later ones are kept; at the first entry
whose key equals $k$ that entry is removed, the scan stops, and all later entries are kept. Every
kept entry keeps its key, value and tower height.

articles.title: Erasure preserves the heights of other keys
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$, $k'$
are keys with $k' \ne k$, then the stored tower height of $k'$ in the skip list obtained by
erasing $k$ from $S$ is the same as in $S$; in particular $k'$ has no stored height in one exactly
when it has none in the other.

articles.title: The erased key has no stored height
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$ is a key, then
after erasing $k$ from $S$ the key $k$ has no stored tower height.

articles.title: Height of a newly inserted key
articles.statement:
If a key $k$ does not occur in a skip list $S$, then
after inserting $k$ into $S$ with any value and requested height $h$, the stored tower height
of $k$ is $\max(1, h)$.

articles.title: Reinsertion preserves tower height
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a valid skip list in which the key $k$
has stored tower height $h_0$. Then after inserting $k$ into $S$ with any value and any
requested height, the stored tower height of $k$ is still $h_0$.

articles.title: Stored tower height of a key
articles.statement:
For a key $k$ and a skip list $S$, the stored tower height
of $k$ in $S$ is the tower height of the first bottom-level node of $S$ whose key equals $k$
under the given Boolean equality test on keys; it is undefined when no node has key $k$.

articles.title: Skip-list insertion
articles.statement:
To insert key $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ into a
skip list, scan its bottom-level nodes in order, keeping every node whose key is less than $k$.
At the first node whose key is not less than $k$: if its key equals $k$, its value is replaced
by $v$ and its tower height is kept; if its key is greater than $k$, a new node with key $k$,
value $v$ and tower height $\max(1, h)$ is placed before it. If every key is less than $k$, the
new node is appended at the end.

articles.title: Erasure removes the key from every level
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a valid skip list, $k$ is a key and
$i$ is a natural number, then the level-$i$ list of key-value pairs (levels numbered from $0$) of
the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ is the level-$i$ list of $S$ with every pair whose
key equals $k$ removed, the remaining pairs kept in their order.

articles.title: Keys on each skip-list level are distinct
articles.statement:
If a skip list is valid, then for every level
index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), no key occurs twice in the list of
key-value pairs visible at level $i$.

articles.title: Skip-list levels are sorted by key
articles.statement:
If a skip list is valid, then for every level index
$i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), the keys in the list of key-value pairs visible
at level $i$ are strictly increasing: every pair has a strictly smaller key than every pair after
it.

articles.title: Each skip-list level is a subsequence of the level below
articles.statement:
For every skip list and every
level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$ at the bottom), the list of key-value pairs visible
at level $i + 1$ is a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous, of the list of key-value pairs
visible at level $i$.

articles.title: Level of a skip list
articles.statement:
For a skip list and a level index $i$ (levels are numbered from $0$
at the bottom), level $i$ is the list of key-value pairs $(k, v)$ of the stored nodes whose tower
height $h$ satisfies $i < h$, in the order in which these nodes appear in the bottom-level list
of the skip list.

articles.title: Skip-list search agrees with bottom-level lookup
articles.statement:
For every skip list and every key $k$,
the top-down skip-list lookup of $k$ returns the same result as looking up $k$ in the
bottom-level abstraction, the list of key-value pairs of all stored nodes in order: the value of
the first pair with key $k$, or no value if there is none.

articles.title: Erasure preserves lookups of other keys
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a valid skip list and $k$, $k'$ are
keys with $k' \ne k$, then looking up $k'$ in the skip list obtained by erasing $k$ from $S$ gives
the same result as looking up $k'$ in $S$: the same value, or no value in both.

articles.title: Erased keys are absent from a skip list
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a valid skip list, that is, its keys
are strictly increasing and every stored tower has positive height. For every key $k$, looking
up $k$ in the skip list obtained from $L$ by erasing $k$ returns no value.

articles.title: Skip-list insertion does not change lookup of other keys
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly
ordered type. For every skip list $S$ with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, all keys $k$
and $k'$ in $\alpha$ with $k' \ne k$, every value $v \in \beta$ and every requested height
$h \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k'$ in the skip list obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and
requested height $h$ into $S$ gives the same result as looking up $k'$ in $S$.

articles.title: Lookup after insertion returns the inserted value
articles.statement:
For every skip list, key $k$, value
$v$ and requested height $h$, looking up $k$ after inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested
height $h$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Skip-list lookup
articles.statement:
The lookup of a key $k$ in a skip list computes the search window for
$k$, the suffix of the bottom-level nodes reached by descending from the highest level to level
$0$, and returns the value of the first node in the window whose key is $k$, or no value if the
window has no such node.

articles.title: The search window is a suffix of the bottom level
articles.statement:
For every skip list and every key $k$,
the search window for $k$ is a suffix of the list of the skip list's bottom-level nodes.

articles.title: Skip-list search window
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a key and let $H$ be the greatest tower height in a
skip list ($H = 0$ if the list is empty or every tower has height $0$). Start with the full list
of bottom-level nodes, and for each level $i$ from $H - 1$ down to $0$ in turn (no levels when
$H = 0$) replace the current list by the result of advancing at level $i$: within the longest
initial segment of the current list whose keys are all less than $k$, take the last node whose
tower height exceeds $i$ and keep only the nodes after it, leaving the list unchanged if there is
no such node. The search window for $k$ is the list that remains after these steps.

articles.title: Skip list
articles.statement:
A deterministic skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is
represented by the list of its bottom-level nodes, each node an entry carrying a key in $\alpha$,
a value in $\beta$ and a tower height, a natural number. No ordering or height condition is
imposed by this structure.

articles.title: The empty skip list is valid
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every type
$\beta$, the empty skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid.

articles.title: Erasure preserves skip-list validity
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a valid skip list, that is, its keys are
strictly increasing and every stored tower has positive height. For every key $k$, the skip list
obtained from $L$ by erasing $k$ is again valid.

articles.title: Insertion preserves skip-list validity
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and
$\beta$ a type. If a skip list with keys in $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid, then for every
key $k \in \alpha$, value $v \in \beta$ and requested height $h \in \mathbb{N}$ (including
$h = 0$), inserting $k$ with value $v$ and requested height $h$ yields a valid skip list. This
covers both a new key and a key already present, whose value is replaced.

articles.title: Valid skip list
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. A skip list with keys in
$\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is valid when the keys of its bottom-level nodes are strictly
increasing along the list and every node has a tower of positive height.

articles.title: The tree returned by a splay-tree access
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a
linearly ordered type, the tree component of the access of $x$ in $t$ is the tree obtained by
splaying $x$ in $t$.

articles.title: Splay-tree access
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the
access of $x$ in $t$ is the pair $(b, t')$, where $t'$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in
$t$ and $b$ is true exactly when $t'$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.

articles.title: Splitting an ordered tree separates the keys around the split key
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be an ordered
binary tree over a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. When $t$ is split at $x$, every
key of the left part is strictly less than $x$ and every key of the right part is strictly
greater than $x$.

articles.title: Correctness of the splay-tree membership test
articles.statement:
For an ordered binary tree $t$ over a
linearly ordered type and a key $x$, the splay-tree membership test of $x$ in $t$ returns true
if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.

articles.title: Splay-tree membership test
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered
type, the membership test of $x$ in $t$ is the Boolean component of the access of $x$ in $t$:
it is true exactly when the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key
is $x$.

articles.title: Splaying preserves the inorder traversal
articles.statement:
For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$
over a linearly ordered type, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$
equals the inorder traversal of $t$. No search-tree ordering of $t$ is assumed.

articles.title: Splay-tree insertion
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type,
inserting $x$ into $t$ splays $x$ in $t$, splits the resulting tree at $x$ into a left part and
a right part, and returns the tree whose root key is $x$, whose left subtree is the left part
and whose right subtree is the right part.

In an ordered tree that already contains $x$, the key is splayed to the root and dropped by the
split, so no duplicate is created.

articles.title: Keys after splay-tree insertion
articles.statement:
For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a
linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$
if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a key of $t$.

articles.title: Splay-tree split parts contain only original keys
articles.statement:
For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary
tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, if $y$ is a key of the left part or of the right part of
the split of $t$ at $x$, then $y$ is a key of $t$.

articles.title: Splaying preserves membership
articles.statement:
For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly
ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ if and only if $y$ is a
key of $t$.

articles.title: Keys other than the split key survive a split
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a
linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs as a key of $t$,
then $y$ occurs as a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$.
The tree $t$ need not be a binary search tree.

articles.title: Splaying preserves the number of nodes
articles.statement:
For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly
ordered type and every key $x$, the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ has the same number of
nodes as $t$.

articles.title: Splay-tree insertion preserves the search-tree property
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys
in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node,
every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly
larger than the key of the node), then the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is again a binary
search tree.

articles.title: Splaying preserves the search-tree property
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a
linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every
key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger
than the key of the node), then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is again a binary search
tree.

articles.title: Both parts of a split search tree are search trees
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a
linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every
key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger
than the key of the node), then the left part and the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$ are
both binary search trees.

articles.title: Splay-tree insertion puts the inserted key at the root
articles.statement:
For every binary tree $t$ with keys
in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is a
nonempty tree whose root key is $x$.

articles.title: Root key after splaying a present key
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a
linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every
key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that
occurs in $t$. Then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.

articles.title: Splaying a present key brings it to the root
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in
a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and
every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key
that occurs in $t$. Then there are binary trees $l$ and $r$ such that splaying $x$ in $t$ gives
the tree whose root holds $x$, with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$.

articles.title: Root key of a splay tree
articles.statement:
The optional root key of a binary tree is undefined (none) for
the empty tree, and is the key $k$ for a tree whose root node holds $k$.

articles.title: Splaying the empty tree
articles.statement:
For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, splaying $x$ in the
empty binary tree gives the empty tree.

articles.title: Splay operation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary
tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. For $x \in \alpha$, the splay
$S_x(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree
splays to itself, and $t = (k; L, R)$ is left unchanged if $x = k$, if $x < k$ and $L$ is empty,
or if $x > k$ and $R$ is empty. If $x < k$ and $L = (a; A, B)$, then: if $x = a$, the result is
the zig $(a; A, (k; B, R))$; if $x < a$ and $S_x(A) = (d; A_1, A_2)$, the result is the zig-zig
$(d; A_1, (a; A_2, (k; B, R)))$; if $x > a$ and $S_x(B) = (d; B_1, B_2)$, the result is the
zig-zag $(d; (a; A, B_1), (k; B_2, R))$; and if the splayed subtree $S_x(A)$, respectively
$S_x(B)$, is empty, the result is the zig $(a; A, (k; B, R))$. The case $x > k$ with
$R = (b; C, D)$ is the mirror image: if $x = b$, the result is the zig $(b; (k; L, C), D)$; if
$x > b$ and $S_x(D) = (d; D_1, D_2)$, it is the zig-zig $(d; (b; (k; L, C), D_1), D_2)$; if
$x < b$ and $S_x(C) = (d; C_1, C_2)$, it is the zig-zag $(d; (k; L, C_1), (b; C_2, D))$; and if
the splayed subtree is empty, it is the zig $(b; (k; L, C), D)$.

The search path for $x$ runs from the root to the node with key $x$, or to the last node visited
if $x$ is absent. Each recursive step consumes two edges of this path, starting at the root, so
when the path has an odd number of edges the single rotation is performed on its last edge, the
one farthest from the root.

articles.title: Search-path split at a key
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $x \in \alpha$, and
write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$.
The split of a binary tree with keys in $\alpha$ at $x$ is the pair of trees defined by
recursion: the empty tree splits into two empty trees; if $x < k$ and $L$ splits into
$(L_1, L_2)$, then $(k; L, R)$ splits into $(L_1, (k; L_2, R))$; if $k < x$ and $R$ splits into
$(R_1, R_2)$, then $(k; L, R)$ splits into $((k; L, R_1), R_2)$; and if $x = k$, then
$(k; L, R)$ splits into $(L, R)$.

When the tree is a binary search tree (at every node, the keys of the left subtree are strictly
smaller and those of the right subtree strictly larger than the node's key), the first part
holds the keys below $x$ and the second part the keys above $x$; the key $x$, if present, is
dropped.

articles.title: Treap all-nodes predicate via node membership
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value
and a natural-number priority, and let $t$ be a tree. Then $p$ holds at every node of $t$ if and
only if $p(k, v, n)$ holds for every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ such that the entry
$(k, v, n)$ occurs as a node of $t$.

articles.title: Treap all-nodes predicate on keys via key membership
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a predicate on keys and
let $t$ be a tree. Then the key of every node of $t$ satisfies $p$ if and only if $p(k)$ holds
for every key $k$ that occurs in $t$.

articles.title: Treap predicate holding at every node
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a predicate on a key, a value and a
natural-number priority. A tree satisfies $p$ at every node when $p(k, v, n)$ holds for the key
$k$, value $v$ and priority $n$ of each of its nodes. By recursion, this holds for the empty
tree, and holds for a node exactly when it holds for the left subtree, $p$ holds at the node's
key, value and priority, and it holds for the right subtree.

articles.title: Treap inorder traversal onto a suffix
articles.statement:
For a tree $t$ and a list $s$ of key-value pairs,
the traversal of $t$ onto $s$ is defined by recursion: for the empty tree it is $s$, and for a
node with left subtree $l$, key $k$, value $v$ and right subtree $r$ it is the traversal of $l$
onto the list obtained by putting $(k, v)$ in front of the traversal of $r$ onto $s$. The result
is the key-value pairs of $t$ in inorder, priorities dropped, followed by $s$.

No ancestor recopies a completed traversal, so the traversal takes linear time.

articles.title: Treap inorder contents after erasure
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type, let
$t$ be a tree and $k$ a key, and let $L$ and $G$ be the lower and upper trees produced by
splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value pairs of the tree obtained by erasing
$k$ from $t$ is the inorder list of $L$ followed by the inorder list of $G$.

articles.title: Treap inorder contents after insertion
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type,
let $t$ be a tree, $k$ a key, $v$ a value and $n$ a natural-number priority, and let $L$ and $G$
be the lower and upper trees produced by splitting $t$ at $k$. Then the inorder list of key-value
pairs of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $n$ into $t$ is the
inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $G$.

articles.title: Treap merge concatenates inorder contents
articles.statement:
For trees $l$ and $r$, the inorder list of
key-value pairs of the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is the inorder list of $l$ followed
by the inorder list of $r$.

articles.title: Treap inorder contents of a node
articles.statement:
For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a
natural-number priority $n$, the inorder list of key-value pairs of the node with left subtree
$l$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $n$ and right subtree $r$ is the inorder list of $l$, followed
by $(k, v)$, followed by the inorder list of $r$.

articles.title: Treap inorder contents split at a pivot
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type,
let $t$ be a tree and $k$ a pivot key, and let splitting $t$ at $k$ produce a lower tree $L$, an
optional value-priority pair found at $k$, and an upper tree $G$. Then the inorder list of
key-value pairs of $t$ is the inorder list of $L$, followed by $(k, v)$ if the split found a pair
with value $v$ (and by nothing if it found none), followed by the inorder list of $G$.

articles.title: Treap inorder contents
articles.statement:
The contents of a tree $t$ is the list of its key-value pairs in
inorder (left subtree, then node, then right subtree), with priorities dropped. It is defined as
the inorder traversal of $t$ onto the empty list, which takes linear time.

articles.title: Treap deletion
articles.statement:
For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type and a tree $t$, deleting
$k$ from $t$ splits $t$ at $k$ and returns the priority-guided merge of the part of the split
below $k$ with the part above $k$; the entry the split finds at $k$, if any, is dropped.

articles.title: Merging preserves heap order
articles.statement:
If two trees $l$ and $r$ are both heap-ordered in their
priorities, then the priority-guided merge of $l$ and $r$ is heap-ordered.

articles.title: Treap split preserves heap order
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linearly ordered type and let
$t$ be a heap-ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the upper tree
produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both heap-ordered.

articles.title: Heap order of treap priorities
articles.statement:
A tree is heap-ordered when the priority of every
node is at most the priority of every node below it. Recursively, the empty tree is
heap-ordered, and a node with priority $p$ is heap-ordered when its left and right subtrees
are heap-ordered and every node in them has priority at least $p$.

articles.title: The root of a heap-ordered tree has minimal priority
articles.statement:
If a nonempty tree whose root
has priority $p$ is heap-ordered, then every node of the tree, the root included, has
priority at least $p$.

articles.title: Treap insertion
articles.statement:
For a key $k$ of a linearly ordered key type, a value $v$, a priority
$p$ and a tree $t$, inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ splits $t$ at $k$,
drops the entry the split finds at $k$ if any, merges the part below $k$ with the single node
$(k, v, p)$, and then merges the result with the part above $k$; all merges are
priority-guided.

articles.title: Keys occurring in the inorder contents
articles.statement:
For a key $k$ and a tree $t$, some pair
$(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$ if and only if $k$ is the key
of some node of $t$.

articles.title: Inorder keys of a node
articles.statement:
For trees $l$ and $r$, a key $k$, a value $v$ and a priority
$p$, the inorder key list of the node with left subtree $l$, entry $(k, v, p)$ and right
subtree $r$ is the inorder key list of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder key list
of $r$.

articles.title: Treap keys are distinct
