articles.statement:
For a linearly ordered key type, if a tree is ordered as a
binary search tree (at every node, every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in
the right subtree is larger than the node's key), then its inorder key list has no
duplicates.

articles.title: Inorder key list of a treap
articles.statement:
The inorder key list of a tree $t$ is the list of first
components of the inorder list of key-value pairs of $t$, that is, the keys of $t$ in
inorder.

articles.title: Treap lookup agrees with the inorder contents
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly
ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and
every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$,
looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder
key-value list of $t$.

articles.title: Treap lookup finds exactly the stored entries
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a tree with keys in a linearly
ordered type that is ordered as a binary search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller and
every key in a right subtree is larger than the node's key). For every key $k$ and value $v$,
looking up $k$ in $t$ returns $v$ if and only if $t$ has a node with key $k$ and value $v$, for
some priority.

articles.title: Erased keys are not found
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered type,
that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For every
key $k$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from $t$ returns no value.

articles.title: Treap lookup after insertion
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid treap with keys in a linearly ordered
type, that is, $t$ is ordered as a binary search tree by key and as a min-heap by priority. For
every key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p \in \mathbb{N}$, looking up $k$ in the tree obtained by
inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $p$ into $t$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Lookup cost is at most the tree size
articles.statement:
For every tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered
type and every key $k$, the number of nodes visited by the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$ is at most
the number of nodes of $t$.

articles.title: Costed lookup returns the ordinary lookup result
articles.statement:
For every tree $t$ with keys in a
linearly ordered type and every key $k$, the value component of the costed lookup of $k$ in $t$
(ignoring the visit count) equals the result of looking up $k$ in $t$.

articles.title: Lookup with cost
articles.statement:
The costed lookup of a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly
ordered type returns a possibly absent value together with a natural number counting the
visited nodes. On the empty tree it returns no value and cost $0$. At a node with key $r$ and
value $v$, if $k < r$ it returns the result of the costed lookup of $k$ in the left subtree
with cost increased by $1$; if $r < k$ it does the same with the right subtree; otherwise it
returns $v$ with cost $1$.

articles.title: Treap lookup
articles.statement:
Looking up a key $k$ in a tree with keys in a linearly ordered type follows
the binary search tree comparisons. The empty tree gives no value. At a node with key $r$ and
value $v$, the lookup continues in the left subtree if $k < r$, continues in the right subtree
if $r < k$, and otherwise returns $v$.

articles.title: Inorder contents list the treap's entries
articles.statement:
For every tree $t$, key $k$ and value $v$,
the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the inorder key-value list of $t$ if and only if $t$ has a node
with key $k$ and value $v$, for some priority.

articles.title: Keys of a merged treap
articles.statement:
For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, $k$ is the key of
some node of the merge of $l$ and $r$ if and only if $k$ is the key of some node of $l$ or of
some node of $r$.

articles.title: Entry membership implies key membership in a treap
articles.statement:
If a key $k$, value $v$ and
priority $p$ form an entry of a treap tree $t$, that is, some node of $t$ stores exactly $k$,
$v$ and $p$, then $k$ is a key of $t$.

articles.title: Key membership in a treap tree
articles.statement:
A key $k$ is a key of a treap tree when it is stored
at some node: no key belongs to the empty tree, and $k$ belongs to a node with left subtree
$L$, root key $r$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $k$ belongs to $L$, or $k = r$, or $k$
belongs to $R$.

Membership is structural and does not assume the search-tree or heap invariants.

articles.title: The inorder key list lists exactly the keys of a treap
articles.statement:
For every treap tree $t$ and
key $k$, $k$ occurs in the inorder key list of $t$ if and only if $k$ is a key of $t$.

articles.title: Entry membership in a treap tree
articles.statement:
A key $k$, value $v$ and priority $p$ form an entry
of a treap tree when some node stores exactly $k$, $v$ and $p$: the empty tree has no
entries, and $(k, v, p)$ is an entry of a node with left subtree $L$, root key $r$, root value
$w$, root priority $q$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when it is an entry of $L$, or $k = r$,
$v = w$ and $p = q$, or it is an entry of $R$.

articles.title: Treap merge
articles.statement:
The merge of two treap trees is defined recursively. Merging the empty
tree with a tree $T$, or $T$ with the empty tree, gives $T$. If both trees are nodes, with
root priorities $p$ for the first and $q$ for the second, then when $p \le q$ the result keeps
the root of the first tree and its left subtree, and its right subtree is the merge of the
first tree's right subtree with the second tree; otherwise the result keeps the root of the
second tree and its right subtree, and its left subtree is the merge of the first tree with
the second tree's left subtree.

articles.title: Inorder keys of an ordered treap are strictly increasing
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a
linearly ordered type. If a treap tree $t$ is ordered, then its inorder key list is strictly
increasing: each key in the list is smaller than every key after it.

articles.title: Treap merge preserves search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linearly ordered
type. If treap trees $L$ and $R$ are both ordered and every key of $L$ is smaller than every
key of $R$, then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.

articles.title: Treap split preserves search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linearly ordered
type and let $t$ be an ordered treap tree. For every pivot key $k$, the lower tree and the
upper tree produced by splitting $t$ at $k$ are both ordered.

articles.title: Ordered treap tree
articles.statement:
For a key type equipped with a relation $<$, a treap tree is
ordered when it is empty, or when it is a node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are
both ordered, every key $x$ in the left subtree satisfies $x < k$, and every key $y$ in the
right subtree satisfies $k < y$.

articles.title: Root priority of a treap tree
articles.statement:
The root priority of a treap tree is an optional
natural number: it is absent for the empty tree, and for a node it is the priority stored at
that node.

articles.title: Separated treap trees
articles.statement:
For keys equipped with a binary relation $<$, two trees $L$
and $R$ are separated when $a < b$ for every key $a$ occurring at a node of $L$ and every
key $b$ occurring at a node of $R$.

articles.title: Size of a treap tree
articles.statement:
The size of a tree is its number of nodes, computed recursively:
the empty tree has size $0$, and a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ has size
equal to the size of $L$ plus one plus the size of $R$.

articles.title: Split bounds for an ordered treap
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linear order and let $T$ be
an ordered tree. For every pivot $p$, every key of the lower tree obtained by splitting $T$ at
$p$ is strictly less than $p$, and every key of the upper tree is strictly greater than $p$.

articles.title: Result of a treap split
articles.statement:
For key type $\kappa$ and value type $\nu$, a split result
consists of a lower tree, an optional entry given by a value in $\nu$ together with a
natural-number priority, and an upper tree, where both trees are treap trees with keys in
$\kappa$ and values in $\nu$.

The structure imposes no constraint; on an ordered tree, splitting at a pivot fills the lower
tree with the keys below the pivot, the upper tree with the keys above it, and the entry with
the pivot's value and priority when the pivot occurs.

articles.title: Treap split
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linear order, and write $(L, k, v, q, R)$ for the
node with left subtree $L$, key $k$, value $v$, priority $q$ and right subtree $R$. Splitting
a tree at a pivot $p$ returns a split result, defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree
splits into two empty trees and no entry. For a node $(L, k, v, q, R)$: if $k < p$, split $R$
at $p$ into a lower tree $R_1$, an optional entry $e$ and an upper tree $R_2$, and return the
lower tree $(L, k, v, q, R_1)$, the entry $e$ and the upper tree $R_2$; if $p < k$, split $L$
at $p$ into $L_1$, $e$ and $L_2$, and return the lower tree $L_1$, the entry $e$ and the upper
tree $(L_2, k, v, q, R)$; otherwise $k = p$, and return the lower tree $L$, the entry
$(v, q)$ and the upper tree $R$.

On an ordered tree, the lower tree holds the keys below $p$, the upper tree holds the keys
above $p$, and the entry is the value and priority stored at $p$ when $p$ occurs.

articles.title: Treap trees
articles.statement:
For a type $\kappa$ of keys and a type $\nu$ of values, a treap tree is
either empty or a node made of a left subtree, a key in $\kappa$, a value in $\nu$, a
natural-number priority and a right subtree. Trees are finite, and no ordering of keys or
priorities is imposed; the treap invariants are stated separately.

articles.title: Erasing from a treap preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linear order. If a
tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its
priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$ the tree obtained by erasing $k$ from
it is again a valid treap.

articles.title: Inserting into a treap preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linear order. If a
tree is a valid treap, that is, its keys are in strict binary-search-tree order and its
priorities are in min-heap order, then for every key $k$, value $v$ and natural-number
priority $q$, the tree obtained by inserting $k$ with value $v$ and priority $q$ is again a
valid treap.

articles.title: Merging separated treaps preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linear order. If
$L$ and $R$ are valid treaps and every key of $L$ is strictly less than every key of $R$, then
the merge of $L$ and $R$ is a valid treap.

articles.title: Splitting a treap preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let the keys come from a linear order. If a tree
is a valid treap, then for every pivot $p$, both the lower tree and the upper tree obtained by
splitting it at $p$ are valid treaps.

articles.title: Valid treap
articles.statement:
A binary tree whose nodes each carry a key, a value and a natural-number
priority, with keys compared by a relation $<$ (any `LT` instance; no order axioms are
assumed), is a valid treap when it satisfies both of the following at every node: every key in
the left subtree is less than the node's key and the node's key is less than every key in the
right subtree (search-tree order with respect to $<$), and the node's priority is at most the
priority of every node in its left and right subtrees (min-heap order on priorities).

articles.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing
articles.statement:
For binary trees $L$, $R$ and a key $k$, write $|t|$ for
the number of keys of a tree $t$, $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight, $w = w(L) + w(R)$, and
$\langle X, x, Y \rangle$ for the node with key $x$, left subtree $X$ and right subtree
$Y$. The rebalanced node $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ is defined as follows.
If $3w < 4\,w(L)$, then $L = \langle A, a, B \rangle$ is a node; if $|B| \le 2|A|$, the
result is the single rotation $\langle A, a, \langle B, k, R \rangle \rangle$, and
otherwise $B = \langle B_1, b, B_2 \rangle$ is a node and the result is the double
rotation $\langle \langle A, a, B_1 \rangle, b, \langle B_2, k, R \rangle \rangle$.
Otherwise, if $3w < 4\,w(R)$, then $R = \langle C, c, D \rangle$ is a node; if
$|C| \le 2|D|$, the result is $\langle \langle L, k, C \rangle, c, D \rangle$, and
otherwise $C = \langle C_1, d, C_2 \rangle$ is a node and the result is
$\langle \langle L, k, C_1 \rangle, d, \langle C_2, c, D \rangle \rangle$.
In all remaining cases the result is $\langle L, k, R \rangle$.

articles.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing restores balance
articles.statement:
Let $L$ and $R$ be weight-balanced trees
and $k$ a key, and write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$. If
$4(|L| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2) + 1$ and $4(|R| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2) + 1$, then the
rebalanced node $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ is weight-balanced.

These hypotheses are the two inequalities of the weight-balance invariant for the node with
children $L$ and $R$, each with its right-hand side increased by $1$; this is the precondition that
one insertion step maintains.

articles.title: Weight-balanced trees built by insertion are balanced
articles.statement:
For every list
$x_1, \dots, x_n$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, the tree obtained from the empty
tree by inserting $x_n, x_{n-1}, \dots, x_1$ in this order with weight-balanced insertion
is weight-balanced.

articles.title: Weight-balanced insertion preserves balance
articles.statement:
For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered
type and every weight-balanced tree $t$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ with
weight-balanced insertion is weight-balanced.

articles.title: Weight form of the balance condition at a node
articles.statement:
Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of
a tree $t$ and $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight. Let $N$ be the node with key $k$, left subtree
$L$ and right subtree $R$. Then $N$ is weight-balanced if and only if $L$ and $R$ are
weight-balanced, $4\,w(L) \le 3\,w(N)$ and $4\,w(R) \le 3\,w(N)$. This is the classical
$\mathrm{BB}[1/4]$ invariant: each child has weight at most three quarters of the weight of
the node.

articles.title: Building a weight-balanced node
articles.statement:
Let $L$ and $R$ be weight-balanced trees and $k$ a
key, and write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$. If
$4(|L| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2)$ and $4(|R| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2)$, then the node with
key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is weight-balanced.

articles.title: Weight-balanced trees
articles.statement:
Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a binary tree $t$ and
$w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight. A binary tree is weight-balanced, or satisfies the
invariant $\mathrm{BB}[1/4]$, when it is empty, or when it is a node with left subtree $L$
and right subtree $R$ such that $L$ and $R$ are weight-balanced,
$4\,w(L) \le 3(w(L) + w(R))$ and $4\,w(R) \le 3(w(L) + w(R))$. Since the weight of a node
is $w(L) + w(R)$, this says that each child has weight at most three quarters of the
weight of the node.

articles.title: Weight-balanced tree from a list
articles.statement:
The tree built from a list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of
elements of a linearly ordered type is obtained from the empty tree by inserting
$x_n, x_{n-1}, \dots, x_1$ in this order with weight-balanced insertion; the empty list
gives the empty tree.

articles.title: Height of a weight-balanced tree is logarithmic
articles.statement:
Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a
binary tree $t$ and $h(t)$ for its height, where the empty tree has height $0$ and a node has
height one more than the larger height of its two subtrees. If $t$ is weight-balanced, then
$h(t) \le \lfloor \log_2 ((|t| + 1)^3) \rfloor + 1$.

The proof passes from the exponential weight lower bound in base $4/3$ to base $2$, using
$(4/3)^3 > 2$.

articles.title: Weight-balanced insertion
articles.statement:
For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the insertion
$\mathrm{insert}(x, t)$ of $x$ into a binary tree $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. Into the
empty tree it gives the single node with key $x$. Into the node $N$ with key $k$, left subtree
$L$ and right subtree $R$ it gives $\mathrm{balance}(\mathrm{insert}(x, L), k, R)$ if $x < k$,
$\mathrm{balance}(L, k, \mathrm{insert}(x, R))$ if $k < x$, and $N$ itself if $x = k$, where
$\mathrm{balance}$ is weight-balanced rebalancing.

articles.title: Weight-balanced insertion does not decrease the number of keys
articles.statement:
Let the keys
carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$, the number of nodes of $t$ is
at most the number of nodes of the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$.

articles.title: Membership after weight-balanced rebalancing
articles.statement:
For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$,
an element $x$ occurs in the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ exactly when $x$ occurs
in $l$, $x = k$, or $x$ occurs in $r$. Membership is structural: $x$ is the key of some node.

articles.title: Membership in a weight-balanced tree built from a list
articles.statement:
Let the keys carry a linear
order. For every key $x$ and every list $xs$, $x$ occurs in the weight-balanced tree built from
$xs$ by repeated insertion exactly when $x$ is an element of $xs$.

articles.title: Membership after weight-balanced insertion
articles.statement:
Let the keys carry a linear order. For all
keys $x$, $y$ and every binary tree $t$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained from $t$ by
weight-balanced insertion of $x$ exactly when $y = x$ or $y$ occurs in $t$.

articles.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing preserves the number of keys
articles.statement:
Write $|t|$ for the number of
nodes of a binary tree $t$. For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, the weight-balanced
rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ has exactly $|l| + |r| + 1$ nodes.

articles.title: Number of keys of the empty tree
articles.statement: The empty binary tree has $0$ nodes.

articles.title: Weight-balanced insertion adds at most one key
articles.statement:
Let the keys carry a linear order. For
every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$, the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion
of $x$ has at most one more node than $t$.

articles.title: Number of keys of a node
articles.statement:
Write $|t|$ for the number of nodes of a binary tree $t$. For
binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, the node with key $k$, left subtree $l$ and right subtree
$r$ has $|l| + |r| + 1$ nodes.

articles.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing preserves ordering
articles.statement:
Let the keys carry a linear order, let $l$
and $r$ be ordered binary trees (strict binary search trees), and let $k$ be a key such that every
key of $l$ is less than $k$ and every key of $r$ is greater than $k$. Then the weight-balanced
rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ is ordered.

articles.title: Weight-balanced trees built from a list are ordered
articles.statement:
Let the keys carry a linear order.
For every list $xs$, the weight-balanced tree built from $xs$ by repeated insertion is ordered,
that is, a strict binary search tree.

articles.title: Weight-balanced insertion preserves the search-tree order
articles.statement:
Let the keys be linearly
ordered. If a binary tree $t$ is ordered as a search tree (at every node, every key of the left
subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key at
the node), then the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of any key $x$ is again
ordered.

articles.title: Exponential weight lower bound for weight-balanced trees
articles.statement:
Write $w(t)$ for the
weight of a binary tree $t$ (its number of keys plus one), and measure height so that the empty
tree has height $0$ and a node has height one more than the taller of its children. If $t$ is
weight balanced with parameter $1/4$ (at every node, each child has weight at most three
quarters of the weight of the node) and has height $k + 1$ for a natural number $k$, then
$w(t) \ge (4/3)^k$; in integer form, $4^k \le 3^k \, w(t)$.

The proof uses the weight form of the invariant: the taller child has weight at most three
quarters of the weight of the node.

articles.title: Weight of a binary tree
articles.statement:
The Nievergelt–Reingold weight $w(t)$ of a binary tree $t$
is its number of keys plus one. Equivalently, it counts the external leaves: the empty tree
has weight $1$, and the weight of a node is the sum of the weights of its two children.

articles.title: A list is its common prefix with another list followed by the rest
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be
lists over a type with decidable equality, and let $p$ be the longest common prefix of $s$ and
$t$. Then $s$ is $p$ followed by the list obtained by dropping the first $|p|$ elements of $s$,
where $|p|$ is the length of $p$.

articles.title: When the common prefix is the second list, the first list extends it
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be
lists over a type with decidable equality. If the longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$ is $t$,
then $s$ is $t$ followed by the list obtained by dropping the first $|t|$ elements of $s$, where
$|t|$ is the length of $t$.

articles.title: Radix trie built from a list of key-value pairs
articles.statement:
The trie built from the empty list is the
empty trie, and the trie built from a list with head $(k, v)$ and tail $L$ is the trie built from
$L$ with the value $v$ inserted at the key $k$. Later pairs in the list are thus inserted first,
so on duplicate keys the head-most value wins.

articles.title: A shared prefix factors out of the longest common prefix
articles.statement:
Write $uv$ for the list $u$
followed by the list $v$. For lists $p$, $s$ and $t$ over a type with decidable equality, the
longest common prefix of $ps$ and $pt$ is $p$ followed by the longest common prefix of $s$ and
$t$.

articles.title: Longest common prefix in terms of dropped remainders
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type
with decidable equality, let $p$ be their longest common prefix, of length $n$, and let $s'$ and
$t'$ be the lists obtained from $s$ and $t$ by dropping their first $n$ elements. Then $s$ is $p$
followed by $s'$, $t$ is $p$ followed by $t'$, and either $s'$ is empty, or $t'$ is empty, or
$s'$ and $t'$ are both nonempty with different first elements.

articles.title: The longest common prefix of a list and its prefix
articles.statement:
Let $s$, $t$ and $u$ be lists over a
type with decidable equality. If $s$ is $t$ followed by $u$, then the longest common prefix of
$s$ and $t$ is $t$.

articles.title: Longest common prefix of a list with itself
articles.statement:
For every list $s$ over a type with decidable
equality, the longest common prefix of $s$ and $s$ is $s$.

articles.title: Characterization of the longest common prefix
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type with
decidable equality, with longest common prefix $p$. Then there are lists $s'$ and $t'$ such that
$s$ is $p$ followed by $s'$, $t$ is $p$ followed by $t'$, and either $s'$ is empty, or $t'$ is
empty, or $s'$ and $t'$ are both nonempty with different first elements.

articles.title: Longest common prefix
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with decidable equality, the
longest common prefix of $s$ and $t$ is defined by recursion: it is empty if $s$ or $t$ is
empty; if $s$ has first element $a$ and rest $s'$, and $t$ has first element $b$ and rest $t'$,
it is $a$ followed by the longest common prefix of $s'$ and $t'$ when $a = b$, and empty when
$a \ne b$.

articles.title: The empty radix trie is valid
articles.statement:
For all types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the empty radix trie whose
keys are lists over $\alpha$ and whose values lie in $\beta$ is valid.

articles.title: Empty radix trie
articles.statement:
The empty radix trie is the single node that stores no value and has no
child edges; it contains no key-value entries.

articles.title: Entries of a radix trie
articles.statement:
The entries of a radix trie are its key-value pairs, listed
recursively. For a node with child edges $(\ell_1, t_1), \dots, (\ell_n, t_n)$ in stored order,
the list starts with the pair $(\varepsilon, v)$, where $\varepsilon$ is the empty key, if the
node stores a value $v$; it continues with the entries of $t_1$ with $\ell_1$ prepended to
every key, then the entries of $t_2$ with $\ell_2$ prepended, and so on up to $t_n$.

articles.title: Edge search by first symbol
articles.statement:
Given a symbol $c$ and a list of edges, each a pair of a
label (a list of symbols) and a subtree, this returns the first edge in the list whose label
starts with $c$, or nothing if no label starts with $c$.

articles.title: Prefix search is correct on valid radix tries
articles.statement:
For a valid radix trie $t$ and a list $p$
of symbols, prefix search for $p$ in $t$ succeeds if and only if some stored key $k$ of $t$ has
$p$ as a prefix.

articles.title: Prefix search in a radix trie
articles.statement:
For a radix trie $t$ and a pattern $p$ (a list of symbols),
prefix search returns a boolean computed as follows. If $p$ is empty, it is true exactly when
$t$ stores at least one key. Otherwise let $c$ be the first symbol of $p$ and take the first
child edge of the root whose label starts with $c$; if there is none, the answer is false. If
that edge has label $\ell$ and subtree $s$, then: when $p$ is a prefix of $\ell$, the answer is
whether $s$ stores at least one key; otherwise, when $\ell$ is a prefix of $p$, the search
continues in $s$ with $p$ minus its first $|\ell|$ symbols; otherwise the answer is false.

On valid radix tries this decides whether some stored key has $p$ as a prefix.

articles.title: Insertion preserves validity of radix tries
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid radix trie, then for every
key $k$ and value $v$, the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k$ in $t$ is valid.

articles.title: Insertion into a radix trie
articles.statement:
Inserting a value $v$ at a key $k$ (a list of symbols) into a
radix trie works as follows. If $k$ is empty, the root's value becomes $v$. Otherwise let $c$ be
the first symbol of $k$. If no child edge of the root has a label starting with $c$, a new edge
labelled $k$ leading to a leaf storing $v$ is added after the existing edges. Otherwise take the
first such edge, with label $\ell$ and subtree $s$, let $q$ be the longest common prefix of $k$
and $\ell$, and replace that edge in place. If $k = \ell = q$, the edge keeps label $\ell$ and
leads to $s$ with its root value set to $v$. If $k = q$ but $\ell$ is longer, the edge is
labelled $q$ and leads to a new node storing $v$ whose only edge is the rest of $\ell$ leading
to $s$. If $\ell = q$ but $k$ is longer, the edge keeps label $\ell$ and leads to $s$ with $v$
inserted at the rest of $k$. If both are longer than $q$, the edge is labelled $q$ and leads to
a new node with no value and two edges: the rest of $\ell$ leading to $s$, then the rest of $k$
leading to a leaf storing $v$.

articles.title: Stored keys of a valid radix trie are distinct
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid radix trie, then its
list of stored keys has no duplicates.

articles.title: Stored keys of a radix trie
articles.statement:
The stored keys of a radix trie form the list of the keys of
its entries, in the same order.

articles.title: Every listed key is present in the built radix trie
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ of key-value pairs, if
$(k, v)$ belongs to $L$, then looking up $k$ in the radix trie built from $L$ returns some
value.

articles.title: Lookup in a radix trie built from a list with distinct keys
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of
key-value pairs, whose keys are lists over $\gamma$, in which no key occurs twice. If the pair
$(k, v)$ occurs in $L$, then looking up $k$ in the radix trie built from $L$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Lookup in the empty radix trie
articles.statement:
For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty radix
trie returns no value.

articles.title: Lookup agrees with the entries of a valid radix trie
articles.statement:
For a valid radix trie $T$, every
key $k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$
occurs in the list of entries of $T$.

articles.title: Insertion into a radix trie leaves lookups of other keys unchanged
articles.statement:
For every radix
trie $T$, all keys $k \ne k'$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$
by inserting $v$ at $k'$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T$.

articles.title: Lookup of a key just inserted into a radix trie
articles.statement:
For every radix trie $T$, key $k$ and
value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$ by inserting $v$ at $k$ returns $v$.

articles.title: Radix trie lookup of a nonempty key at a node
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a nonempty key with first symbol
$c$, and consider a node with children $C$ (a list of edges, each a label with a subtree),
whatever value the node stores. If no edge of $C$ has a label starting with $c$, looking up $k$
at the node returns no value. Otherwise let $(\ell, T')$ be the first such edge of $C$: if the
longest common prefix of $k$ and $\ell$ is $\ell$, the lookup returns the lookup in $T'$ of the
key obtained from $k$ by dropping its first $|\ell|$ symbols, and otherwise it returns no value.

articles.title: Radix trie lookup
articles.statement:
Looking up a key, a list over $\alpha$, in a radix trie returns an
optional value. At a node, the empty key returns the value stored at the node, if any. A
nonempty key $k$ with first symbol $c$ goes to the first child edge whose label starts with $c$.
If there is no such edge, or its label $\ell$ is not a prefix of $k$, the lookup returns no
value; otherwise it continues in the subtree of that edge with $k$ minus its first $|\ell|$
symbols.

articles.title: Keys of a radix trie built from a list
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of key-value pairs and every
key $k$, $k$ is a stored key of the radix trie built from $L$ if and only if the pair $(k, v)$
occurs in $L$ for some value $v$.

articles.title: Stored keys of a valid radix trie are the keys with a successful lookup
articles.statement:
For a valid
radix trie $T$ and every key $k$, $k$ is a stored key of $T$ if and only if looking up $k$ in
$T$ returns some value.

articles.title: Lookups in a radix trie built from a list come from the list
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of
key-value pairs, if looking up a key $k$ in the radix trie built from $L$ returns a value $v$,
then the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in $L$.

articles.title: Sibling edge labels start with distinct symbols
articles.statement:
If a radix-trie node with child edges
$(\ell_1, t_1), \dots, (\ell_n, t_n)$ is valid, then the first symbols of the labels
$\ell_1, \dots, \ell_n$ are pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Radix trie
articles.statement:
For types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, a radix trie with keys that are lists over
$\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is a node made of an optional value in $\beta$ and a finite list of
child edges, each a pair of a label, which is a list over $\alpha$, and a radix trie (the
subtree at the end of the edge).

No invariant is built into the type: labels may be empty and sibling labels may share first
symbols. The radix-trie invariant is imposed separately.

articles.title: Replacing the child edge for a symbol
articles.statement:
Given a symbol $c$, an edge $e$ (a pair of a label
and a radix trie) and a list of child edges, this operation replaces the first edge of the list
whose label starts with $c$ by $e$ and keeps all other edges in order. If no label in the list
starts with $c$, it appends $e$ at the end of the list.

articles.title: Children of a valid node are path-compressed
articles.statement:
If a radix-trie node is valid, then for each
of its child edges, the subtree at the end of that edge is path-compressed at its root: its root
stores a value or has at least two child edges.

articles.title: Path-compressed root
articles.statement:
A radix trie is path-compressed at its root when its root node stores
a value or has at least two child edges.

A value-free node with at most one child could be merged into the edge above it, which a radix
trie rules out for every node reached by an edge; the root of the whole trie has no incoming edge
and is exempt.

articles.title: Valid radix trie
articles.statement:
Validity of radix tries is defined inductively: a node is valid when every
label of its child edges is nonempty, the first symbols of the labels of its child edges are
pairwise distinct, and for each child edge the subtree at its end is valid and path-compressed at
its root (its root stores a value or has at least two child edges).

Thus every value-free node other than the root has at least two children, so no unary value-free
node remains to be merged into its parent edge.

articles.title: Longest-common-prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ and a list of indices
$i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k$, this is the list of length $k$ whose $t$-th entry, for $t < k$, is the
length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes of $s$ starting at $i_t$ and at $i_{t+1}$,
where the suffix starting at an index at or past the end of $s$ is the empty list. It has one
entry per adjacent pair of indices, and it is empty for an empty index list.

articles.title: The LCP array
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the LCP array of $s$ is
the list of longest-common-prefix lengths of adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order: if the
suffix array of $s$ is $i_0, i_1, \dots, i_k$, then the LCP array has length $k$ and its $t$-th
entry, for $t < k$, is the length of the longest common prefix of the suffixes of $s$ starting
at $i_t$ and at $i_{t+1}$. It is empty when $s$ is empty.

articles.title: Longest common prefix length
articles.statement:
For lists $x$ and $y$, $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ is the length
of the longest common prefix of $x$ and $y$: the number of positions, counted from the start, at
which $x$ and $y$ agree before they first differ or one of them ends.

Only equality of letters is tested, so no order on the alphabet is needed.

articles.title: Characterization of the longest common prefix length
articles.statement:
For lists $x$ and $y$, let
$\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of the longest common prefix of $x$ and $y$. For every natural
number $q$, we have $q \le \mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ if and only if $q$ is at most the lengths of both
$x$ and $y$ and the first $q$ elements of $x$ and of $y$ agree.

In particular $\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ is the largest such $q$.

articles.title: Binary search is correct
articles.statement:
If `p` holds on an initial segment of `[lo, hi)` (whenever it
holds at `j`, it holds at every `i` with `lo ≤ i ≤ j`), then `lowerBound p lo hi` is the end `k` of
that segment: `lo ≤ k ≤ hi`, `p` holds on `[lo, k)` and fails on `[k, hi)`.

articles.title: Binary search is logarithmic
articles.statement: At most `⌊log₂ (hi - lo)⌋ + 1` probes, for any predicate.

articles.title: Number of probes made by the binary search
articles.statement: The number of probes `lowerBound p lo hi` makes.

articles.title: Binary search for the boundary of a predicate
articles.statement:
Binary search for the boundary of a predicate on `[lo, hi)`: the first index at which `p`
is false, assuming `p` holds on an initial segment of `[lo, hi)` (`lowerBound_spec`). Each call
probes the midpoint and recurses on one half.

articles.title: The suffix array sorts the suffixes
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ over a linearly ordered alphabet,
the suffixes of $s$ taken in suffix-array order are sorted lexicographically: whenever an index
$i$ comes before an index $j$ in the suffix array of $s$, the suffix of $s$ starting at $i$ is
lexicographically less than or equal to the suffix of $s$ starting at $j$.

articles.title: Prefix classes are lexicographic intervals
articles.statement:
If `x ≤ y ≤ z` and `P` is a prefix of both
`x` and `z`, then `P` is a prefix of `y`.

articles.title: The occurrences of a pattern are contiguous in the suffix array
articles.statement:
If rows `r₁ ≤ r₂ ≤ r₃`
of the suffix array of `s` are in range and the suffixes of rows `r₁` and `r₃` start with `P`,
so does the suffix of row `r₂`.

articles.title: Truncated suffix of a suffix-array row
articles.statement:
The suffix of row `r` of the (precomputed) suffix array `sa` of `s`, truncated to
`m` letters: the key compared with the pattern during the search. `sa` is computed once
by `saSearch` and passed in, so probes do not rebuild the suffix array.

articles.title: Suffix-array search returns a valid row interval
articles.statement: The search returns a genuine interval of rows: `sp ≤ ep ≤ |s|`.

articles.title: Suffix-array search is correct
articles.statement:
A row `r < |s|` lies in `[sp, ep)` exactly when the suffix
of row `r` starts with `P`.

articles.title: Suffix-array search for a pattern's row interval
articles.statement:
Suffix-array search (Manber and Myers 1993): the row interval `[sp, ep)` of the suffixes of
`s` that start with `P`, found by two binary searches over the rows `[0, |s|)`. The suffix
array is computed once and shared by both searches.

articles.title: The suffix array is a permutation of the indices
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a
linearly ordered alphabet, the suffix array of $s$ is a permutation of the list
$0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ of all indices below $n$.

articles.title: Suffix array
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the suffix
array of $s$ is the list of the indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$, sorted so that the suffixes of $s$
starting at them appear in lexicographic order.

Distinct indices below $n$ give suffixes of different lengths, so these suffixes are pairwise
distinct and the sorted order is unique.

articles.title: Suffix of a list at an index
articles.statement:
For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over a linearly
ordered alphabet and a natural number $i$, the suffix of $s$ at $i$ is the list obtained from
$s$ by dropping its first $i$ entries: it is $(s_i, \dots, s_{n-1})$ when $i < n$ and the empty
list when $i \ge n$.

articles.title: Suffixes of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered alphabet, the
list of suffixes of $s$ is the list, for $i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ in this order, of the lists
obtained from $s$ by dropping its first $i$ entries. It starts with $s$ itself and ends with the
empty list.

articles.title: Common prefixes of every shorter length
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $y$ be lists and let
$\mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of their longest common prefix. For every natural number
$q \le \mathrm{lcp}(x, y)$, the first $q$ elements of $x$ and of $y$ agree.

articles.title: Two lists agree on their longest common prefix
articles.statement:
For lists $x$ and $y$ over a type with
decidable equality, let $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ be the length of their longest common prefix.
Then the first $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$ elements of $x$ and the first $\operatorname{lcp}(x, y)$
elements of $y$ form the same list.

articles.title: Truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order
articles.statement: Truncation is monotone for the lexicographic order: `x ≤ y → x.take m ≤ y.take m`.

articles.title: Lookup in the suffix tree returns starting indices
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$, let
$k$ be a list over $\alpha$ extended by a fresh terminator symbol, and let $i$ be a natural number.
If looking up $k$ in the suffix tree of $s$ returns $i$, then $i \le |s|$ and $k$ is the
terminated string of $s$ with its first $i$ symbols removed.

articles.title: Suffix-tree search finds exactly the prefixes of suffixes
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $p$ over
$\alpha$, prefix search for $p$ (each symbol viewed in the alphabet extended by the terminator) in
the suffix tree of $s$ succeeds if and only if there is a natural number $i$ such that $p$ is a
prefix of the list obtained from $s$ by removing its first $i$ symbols.

articles.title: Suffix-tree search finds exactly the infixes
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $p$ over $\alpha$, prefix
search for $p$ (each symbol viewed in the alphabet extended by the terminator) in the suffix tree
of $s$ succeeds if and only if $p$ occurs in $s$ as a contiguous sublist (an infix).

articles.title: Infixes are prefixes of suffixes
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $p$, $p$ is an infix (a contiguous
sublist) of $s$ if and only if there is a natural number $i$ such that $p$ is a prefix of the list
obtained from $s$ by removing its first $i$ symbols.

articles.title: A tagged pattern cannot reach past the terminator
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ and $q$ over $\alpha$,
view their symbols in $\alpha$ extended by a fresh terminator symbol. If $p$ is a prefix of $q$
followed by the terminator, then $p$ is a prefix of $q$.

The terminator differs from every symbol of $\alpha$, so the pattern cannot reach past it.

articles.title: Lookup of a suffix returns its starting index
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$ and $i$ a
natural number with $i \le |s|$. Looking up, in the suffix tree of $s$, the terminated string of
$s$ with its first $i$ symbols removed returns $i$.

articles.title: The stored keys of a suffix tree are its terminated suffixes
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a list over
$\alpha$. A key $k$ is stored in the suffix tree of $s$ if and only if there is a natural number
$i \le |s|$ such that $k$ is the terminated string of $s$ with its first $i$ symbols removed.

articles.title: Terminated suffixes are distinct
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a list over $\alpha$. The lists obtained from
the terminated string of $s$ by removing its first $i$ symbols, for $i$ ranging over
$0, 1, \ldots, |s|$, are pairwise distinct.

They are distinct because their lengths differ.

articles.title: The suffix tree stores one key per suffix
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ over $\alpha$, the list of
stored keys of the suffix tree of $s$ has length $|s| + 1$.

There is one key for each terminated suffix.

articles.title: Stored keys of the suffix tree
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ over $\alpha$, the stored keys of $s$ form
the list of keys stored in the suffix tree of $s$, in stored sibling order.

They are exactly the terminated suffixes. This concerns stored keys, not structural trie leaves:
a valid radix trie may carry values at internal nodes, and no leaf characterization is claimed.

articles.title: Suffix entries of a string
articles.statement:
For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, let
$\hat s = (\mathrm{some}\,s_0, \dots, \mathrm{some}\,s_{n-1}, \mathrm{none})$ be its
terminated string. The suffix entries of $s$ are the list of pairs $(\hat s_{\ge i}, i)$ for
$i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ in increasing order, where $\hat s_{\ge i}$ is $\hat s$ with its first
$i$ entries removed: each nonempty suffix of $\hat s$ paired with its starting index.

articles.title: Suffix tree
articles.statement:
For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, let
$\hat s = (\mathrm{some}\,s_0, \dots, \mathrm{some}\,s_{n-1}, \mathrm{none})$ be its
terminated string over $\mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$. The suffix tree of $s$ is the radix trie
with keys over $\mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$ and natural-number values obtained from the empty
trie by inserting, for $i = n, n - 1, \dots, 0$ in this order, the suffix of $\hat s$
starting at index $i$ with value $i$.

articles.title: Suffixes of the terminated string
articles.statement:
For a list $s$ over $\alpha$ and a natural number
$i \le |s|$, removing the first $i$ entries of the terminated string of $s$ gives the suffix
of $s$ starting at index $i$ with every symbol tagged $\mathrm{some}$, followed by
$\mathrm{none}$.

articles.title: Terminated string
articles.statement:
For a list $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, the terminated
string of $s$ is the list $(\mathrm{some}\,s_0, \dots, \mathrm{some}\,s_{n-1}, \mathrm{none})$
over $\mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$: every symbol of $s$ tagged $\mathrm{some}$, followed by the
terminator $\mathrm{none}$.

articles.title: Deletion preserves trie validity
articles.statement:
If a trie $t$ is valid, that is, every node has distinct
child keys and valid child tries, then for every key $k$ the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting
$k$ is valid.

articles.title: Deletion from a trie
articles.statement:
Deleting a key $k$ (a list of letters) from a trie $t$ works by
recursion on $k$. If $k$ is empty, the root of $t$ loses its value and keeps its children. If
$k$ consists of a first letter $a$ followed by a key $k'$ and the root of $t$ has no child at
$a$, then $t$ is unchanged. Otherwise $k'$ is deleted from the first child at $a$. If the
result has neither value nor children, every entry at $a$ is removed from the root's child
list; if not, the first entry at $a$ is replaced by the result and any later entries at $a$
are removed. The root's value and the other children, in their order, are kept.

Deleting an absent key leaves every lookup unchanged.

articles.title: Validity of the empty trie
articles.statement: The empty trie is valid.

articles.title: Empty trie
articles.statement:
The empty trie is the trie consisting of a single root node that stores no
value and has no children, so it contains no key-value entries.

articles.title: Entries of a trie
articles.statement:
The entries of a trie are the list of its key-value pairs, where a key
is a list of letters. If the root stores a value $v$, the list begins with the pair consisting of
the empty key and $v$; it continues, for each child in the stored sibling order, with the entries
$(k, w)$ of that child, in order, each rewritten as $(a k, w)$, where $a$ is the letter labelling
the child and $a k$ is the key $k$ with $a$ prepended.

articles.title: Insertion preserves trie validity
articles.statement:
If a trie $T$ is valid, then for every key $k$ (a list
of letters) and every value $v$, the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k$ in $T$ is valid.

articles.title: Insertions at distinct keys commute in a trie
articles.statement:
For every trie $T$, all keys $k_1 \ne k_2$
and all values $v_1, v_2$, inserting $v_1$ at $k_1$ and then $v_2$ at $k_2$ gives a trie that is
lookup-equivalent to the one obtained by inserting $v_2$ at $k_2$ and then $v_1$ at $k_1$.

articles.title: Trie insertion
articles.statement:
Inserting a value $v$ at a key $k$ (a list of letters) in a trie stores $v$
at the node reached by following $k$ from the root, replacing any value stored there. Along the
way, a missing child is created as an empty trie and appended after its siblings, an existing
child is updated in place, and all other values and children are unchanged.

articles.title: Characterization of empty nodes
articles.statement:
The empty-node test is true on a trie $t$ exactly when
$t$ is the node with no value and no children, that is, the empty trie.

articles.title: Empty trie nodes
articles.statement:
The empty-node test is true on a trie node exactly when the node
carries no value and has no children; when deletion leaves a child in this state, the child is
removed from its parent.

articles.title: Deletion does not affect other keys
articles.statement:
For every trie $t$ and all keys $k \ne k'$, looking
up $k$ in the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k'$ gives the same result as looking up $k$
in $t$.

articles.title: A deleted key is absent
articles.statement:
For every trie $t$ and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the
trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k$ finds no value.

articles.title: Lookup in the empty trie
articles.statement:
For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty trie returns no
value.

articles.title: Trie lookup agrees with the entries
articles.statement:
For every valid trie $T$, every key $k$ and every
value $v$, looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if $(k, v)$ is one of the entries of
$T$.

articles.title: Lookup equivalence of tries
articles.statement:
Two tries $T$ and $T'$ are lookup-equivalent when, for every
key $k$, looking up $k$ in $T$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T'$.

articles.title: Trie insertion leaves other keys unchanged
articles.statement:
For every trie $T$, all keys $k \ne k'$ and
every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k'$ in $T$ gives the
same result as looking up $k$ in $T$.

articles.title: Lookup after insertion in a trie
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with decidable equality. For
every trie $T$ with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, every key $k$ and
every value $v \in \beta$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$ by inserting $v$ at $k$
returns $v$.

articles.title: Setting a child leaves the other children unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie
pairs, $c$ a trie and $a \ne b$ letters, and let $L'$ be obtained from $L$ by setting the child
at $b$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $b$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children).
Then looking up $a$ in $L'$ gives the same result as looking up $a$ in $L$.

articles.title: Looking up a child just set
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs, $a$ a letter and
$c$ a trie, and let $L'$ be obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the
entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children). Looking up $a$ in $L'$ finds
nothing when $c$ has neither value nor children, and finds $c$ otherwise.

articles.title: Trie lookup
articles.statement:
The lookup of a key (a list over $\alpha$) in a trie returns an optional
value in $\beta$, by recursion on the key. For the empty key it is the optional value stored at
the root. For a key with first letter $a$ followed by the key $k$, it fails if no child of the
root is labelled $a$, and otherwise it is the lookup of $k$ in the first child labelled $a$.

articles.title: Lookup-equivalent valid tries have the same entries
articles.statement:
Let $T$ and $T'$ be valid tries
with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, and suppose $T$ and $T'$ are
lookup-equivalent. Then for every key $k$ and every value $v \in \beta$, the pair $(k, v)$
occurs in the entry list of $T$ if and only if it occurs in the entry list of $T'$.

articles.title: Valid trie nodes have distinct child keys
articles.statement:
If a trie node with optional value $v$ and
child list $c$ is valid, then the letters labelling the children in $c$ are pairwise distinct.

articles.title: Reflexivity of trie lookup equivalence
articles.statement: Every trie is lookup-equivalent to itself.

articles.title: Setting a child preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let a trie node with value $v$ and child list $L$ be
valid, let $c$ be a valid trie and $a$ a letter. Then the node with value $v$ whose child list
is obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead
when $c$ has neither value nor children) is valid.

articles.title: Setting a child preserves the child-list part of validity
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of
letter–trie pairs whose letters are pairwise distinct and whose tries are all valid, let $c$
be a valid trie and $a$ a letter. Then the list obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$
to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children) again has
pairwise distinct letters, and every trie in it is valid.

articles.title: Setting a child in a trie's child list
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of pairs $(k, c)$ of a key $k$
in $\alpha$ and a trie $c$ (the children of a trie node), let $a$ be a key and $t$ a trie, and
call $t$ empty when it carries no value and has no children. Setting the child at $a$ to $t$
in $L$ gives the following list. If no entry of $L$ has key $a$, the result is $L$ itself when
$t$ is empty, and $L$ with $(a, t)$ appended at the end otherwise. If some entry of $L$ has key
$a$, the entries before the first such entry are kept; that entry is replaced in place by
$(a, t)$, or removed when $t$ is empty; and every later entry with key $a$ is removed, while
later entries with other keys are kept in their order.

Thus the order of the surviving entries is preserved and at most one entry with key $a$
remains, even when $L$ has repeated keys. Deletion from a trie uses this operation to prune
empty nodes.

articles.title: Symmetry of trie lookup equivalence
articles.statement:
If a trie $T$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T'$,
then $T'$ is lookup-equivalent to $T$.

articles.title: Transitivity of trie lookup equivalence
articles.statement:
If a trie $T_1$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie
$T_2$ and $T_2$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T_3$, then $T_1$ is lookup-equivalent to $T_3$.

articles.title: Trie
articles.statement:
A trie with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is a node
consisting of an optional value in $\beta$ and a finite list of children, each child being a pair
of a letter in $\alpha$ and a trie. The letters labelling the children need not be distinct.

articles.title: Valid trie
articles.statement:
Validity of tries is defined inductively: a trie node with optional value $v$
and child list $c$ is valid when the letters labelling the children in $c$ are pairwise distinct
and every child trie in $c$ is valid.

articles.title: Contents of the empty van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$, the set of
stored elements of the empty van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$
is empty.

articles.title: Contents after insertion into a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number, let
$t$ be a van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an
element of the universe. The set of stored elements of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into
$t$ is the set of stored elements of $t$ together with $x$. No validity assumption on $t$ is
needed.

articles.title: Set of stored elements of a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number. For a van
Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the set of stored elements of
$t$ is the finite set of those elements of the universe that are members of $t$.

articles.title: Empty van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, the empty van Emde Boas tree over
the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ is the tree in which all $m$ summary bits and all
$m^2$ cluster bits ($m$ clusters of $m$ bits each) are unset.

articles.title: Insertion into a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number, let $t$ be a van Emde
Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an element of the
universe. Inserting $x$ into $t$ gives the tree obtained from $t$ by setting bit $x \bmod m$ of
cluster $\lfloor x / m \rfloor$ and summary bit $\lfloor x / m \rfloor$, leaving every other bit
unchanged.

articles.title: Maximum query on the empty van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$, the
maximum query on the empty van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$
returns no element.

articles.title: When the van Emde Boas maximum query returns nothing
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number and let
$t$ be a valid van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. The maximum query
on $t$ returns no element if and only if no element of the universe is a member of $t$.

articles.title: Correctness of the van Emde Boas maximum query
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number, let $t$ be a
valid van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an element of
the universe. The maximum query on $t$ returns $x$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$ and
$y \le x$ for every member $y$ of $t$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas maximum query bounds every member
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number and let
$t$ be a valid van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If the maximum
query on $t$ returns $x$, then $y \le x$ for every member $y$ of $t$.

articles.title: Maximum query on a one-element van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a natural number and let
$x$ be an element of the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. The maximum query on the tree
obtained by inserting $x$ into the empty van Emde Boas tree over this universe returns $x$.

articles.title: The maximum query of a van Emde Boas tree returns a member
articles.statement:
For every two-level van Emde
Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every $x$ in that universe, if the
maximum query of $t$ returns $x$, then $x$ is a member of $t$. No validity hypothesis on $t$ is
needed.

articles.title: Maximum query of a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For a two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the
universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the maximum query first finds the greatest index $i < m$ whose
summary bit is set, and then the greatest index $j < m$ whose bit is set in cluster $i$; it returns
the element $i m + j$. It returns no element if no summary bit is set, or if no bit of cluster $i$
is set. When the summary bits record exactly the nonempty clusters, this is the greatest stored
element.

articles.title: The contents of a van Emde Boas tree are its members
articles.statement:
For every two-level van Emde Boas
tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every $x$ in that universe, $x$ belongs
to the finite set of stored elements of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.

articles.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree has no members
articles.statement:
For every $m$ and every $x$ in the universe
$\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, $x$ is not a member of the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree over that
universe.

articles.title: Insertion into a van Emde Boas tree keeps existing members
articles.statement:
For every two-level van Emde
Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and all $x, y$ in that universe, if $y$
is a member of $t$, then $y$ is a member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$.

articles.title: Insertion into a van Emde Boas tree leaves other elements unchanged
articles.statement:
For every two-level
van Emde Boas tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and all $x \ne y$ in that
universe, $y$ is a member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y$ is a
member of $t$.

articles.title: An inserted element is a member of a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For every two-level van Emde Boas
tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every $x$ in that universe, $x$ is a
member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$.

articles.title: Membership after insertion into a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For every two-level van Emde Boas
tree $t$ over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and all $x, y$ in that universe, $y$ is a
member of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a member
of $t$.

articles.title: Membership in a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
An element $x$ of the universe
$\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ is a member of a two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ when bit
$x \bmod m$ of cluster $\lfloor x / m \rfloor$ of $t$ is set. The summary bits are not consulted.

articles.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree has no minimum
articles.statement:
For every $m$, the minimum query of the empty
two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, 1, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ returns no element.

articles.title: Empty minimum query in a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. The minimum query on $t$ returns no element if and
only if no element of the universe is stored in $t$.

articles.title: Characterization of the van Emde Boas minimum
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$ be in the universe. The minimum query
on $t$ returns $x$ if and only if $x$ is stored in $t$ and $x \le y$ for every $y$ stored in $t$.

articles.title: Minimum of a one-element van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For every $x$ in the universe
$\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the minimum query on the two-level van Emde Boas tree obtained by
inserting $x$ into the empty tree returns $x$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas minimum is a lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If the minimum query on $t$ returns $x$, then
$x \le y$ for every $y$ stored in $t$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas minimum is stored
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the
universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If the minimum query on $t$ returns $x$, then $x$ is stored in
$t$.

articles.title: Minimum query of a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the
universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$. If some summary bit of $t$ is set, let $h$ be the least cluster
index whose summary bit is set; if cluster $h$ has a set position, let $\ell$ be the least one.
The minimum query on $t$ then returns the element $h \cdot m + \ell$. If no summary bit is set,
or cluster $h$ has no set position, it returns no element.

In a valid tree this is the least stored element.

articles.title: Predecessor queries in the empty van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For every $x$ in the universe
$\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, the predecessor query for $x$ in the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree
returns no element.

articles.title: Empty predecessor query in a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$ be in the universe. The predecessor
query for $x$ in $t$ returns no element if and only if $x \le z$ for every $z$ stored in $t$.

articles.title: Characterization of the van Emde Boas predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde
Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$ and $y$ be in the universe. The
predecessor query for $x$ in $t$ returns $y$ if and only if $y$ is stored in $t$, $y < x$, and
$z \le y$ for every $z$ stored in $t$ with $z < x$.

articles.title: Maximality of the van Emde Boas predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, and let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be in the universe. If the
predecessor query for $x$ in $t$ returns $y$, and $z$ is stored in $t$ with $z < x$, then
$z \le y$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas predecessor is strictly smaller than its argument
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level
van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$
and $y$ be elements of the universe. If the predecessor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $y < x$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas predecessor is stored
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the
universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the
universe. If the predecessor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $y$ is a member of $T$.

articles.title: Predecessor query in a two-level van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x = hm + \ell$ with $0 \le h, \ell < m$, so
that $x$ sits at position $\ell$ of cluster $h$. If cluster $h$ has a set position before $\ell$,
the predecessor of $x$ in $T$ is $hm + \ell'$ for the greatest such position $\ell'$. Otherwise,
let $h'$ be the greatest cluster index with $h' < h$ whose summary bit is set; the predecessor is
$h'm + \ell''$ for the greatest position $\ell''$ set in cluster $h'$. If there is no such $h'$, or
cluster $h'$ has no set position, $x$ has no predecessor.

In a valid tree, the predecessor of $x$ is the greatest member of $T$ less than $x$.

articles.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree has no successors
articles.statement:
For every $m$ and every element $x$ of the
universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, $x$ has no successor in the empty two-level van Emde Boas tree
over that universe.

articles.title: A van Emde Boas successor is missing exactly when nothing larger is stored
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ be an
element of the universe. Then $x$ has no successor in $T$ if and only if every member $z$ of $T$
satisfies $z \le x$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas successor is the least larger member
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a valid two-level van
Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the
universe. Then the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$ if and only if $y$ is a member of $T$, $x < y$,
and $y \le z$ for every member $z$ of $T$ with $x < z$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas successor is strictly larger than its argument
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level
van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$
and $y$ be elements of the universe. If the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $x < y$.

articles.title: No member lies strictly between an element and its van Emde Boas successor
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
valid two-level van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x$, $y$, $z$
be elements of the universe. If the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$ and $z$ is a member of $T$ with
$x < z$, then $y \le z$.

articles.title: The van Emde Boas successor is stored
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas tree over the
universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$, not necessarily valid, and let $x$ and $y$ be elements of the
universe. If the successor of $x$ in $T$ is $y$, then $y$ is a member of $T$.

articles.title: Successor query in a two-level van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a two-level van Emde Boas
tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and let $x = hm + \ell$ with $0 \le h, \ell < m$, so
that $x$ sits at position $\ell$ of cluster $h$. If cluster $h$ has a set position after $\ell$, the
successor of $x$ in $T$ is $hm + \ell'$ for the least such position $\ell'$. Otherwise, let $h'$ be
the least cluster index with $h < h'$ whose summary bit is set; the successor is $h'm + \ell''$ for
the least position $\ell''$ set in cluster $h'$. If there is no such $h'$, or cluster $h'$ has no
set position, $x$ has no successor.

In a valid tree, the successor of $x$ is the least member of $T$ greater than $x$.

articles.title: The empty van Emde Boas tree is valid
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$, the empty two-level
van Emde Boas tree over the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ satisfies the summary invariant: each
summary bit is set exactly when its cluster is nonempty.

articles.title: Insertion preserves validity of van Emde Boas trees
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$, every
element $x$ of the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ and every two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ over
that universe that satisfies the summary invariant (each summary bit is set exactly when its
cluster is nonempty), the tree obtained from $t$ by inserting $x$ also satisfies the summary
invariant.

articles.title: Summary invariant of a van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
A two-level van Emde Boas tree $t$ with $m$
clusters is valid when, for every cluster index $i < m$, summary bit $i$ of $t$ is set exactly when
cluster $i$ of $t$ is nonempty, that is, when some bit $j < m$ of cluster $i$ is set.

articles.title: Two-level van Emde Boas tree
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, a two-level van Emde Boas tree over
the universe $\{0, \dots, m^2 - 1\}$ consists of a summary bit vector of length $m$ and, for each
$i < m$, a cluster bit vector of length $m$; bit $j$ of cluster $i$ records whether the element
$im + j$ is stored. Unlike the fully recursive van Emde Boas tree over universes of size
$2^{2^k}$, the summary and the clusters here are plain bit vectors, not van Emde Boas trees.

articles.title: Keys of an x-fast trie after insertion
articles.statement:
For every x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and
every $w$-bit key $x$, the set of keys stored in the trie obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is
the set of keys stored in $t$ with $x$ added.

articles.title: Keys of a y-fast trie
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, let $R$ be the set of
keys stored in the representative x-fast trie of $t$, and for each $r \in R$ let $B(r)$ be the
bucket owned by $r$. The set of keys stored in $t$ is the union of the buckets of its
representatives, $\bigcup_{r \in R} B(r)$.

It is computed from the representatives alone, not by filtering all $2^w$ possible keys.

articles.title: The empty x-fast trie
articles.statement:
The empty x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys stores no keys, and the
prefix set at each of its levels $0, 1, \dots, w$ is empty.

articles.title: Level probes of a valid x-fast trie
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys,
let $0 \le l \le w$ and let $x$ be a $w$-bit key. The probe of level $l$ of $t$ at $x$ succeeds if
and only if some key $y$ stored in $t$ has the same $l$-bit prefix as $x$.

articles.title: Level probe of an x-fast trie
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys, a level
$0 \le l \le w$ and a $w$-bit key $x$, the probe of level $l$ of $t$ at $x$ returns true exactly
when the $l$-bit prefix of $x$ belongs to the prefix set stored at level $l$ of $t$.

When $t$ is valid, this holds exactly when some key stored in $t$ has the same $l$-bit prefix
as $x$.

articles.title: Insertion into an x-fast trie
articles.statement:
Inserting a $w$-bit key $x$ into an x-fast trie $t$ adds $x$
to the keys stored in $t$ and, for each level $0 \le l \le w$, adds the $l$-bit prefix of $x$ to
the prefix set at level $l$.

articles.title: Keys of a valid y-fast trie are the keys in buckets
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid y-fast trie over
$w$-bit keys, then a $w$-bit key $x$ is stored in $t$ if and only if $x$ lies in the bucket owned
by some $w$-bit key $r$ (such an owner $r$ is then necessarily a representative).

articles.title: Membership in a y-fast trie via representatives' buckets
articles.statement:
For every y-fast trie $t$ over
$w$-bit keys and every $w$-bit key $x$, $x$ is stored in $t$ if and only if $x$ lies in the bucket
owned by some representative of $t$, that is, by some key stored in the representative x-fast
trie of $t$.

articles.title: The membership test of a valid x-fast trie is exact
articles.statement:
For a valid x-fast trie $t$ over
$w$-bit keys and a $w$-bit key $x$, the membership test of $t$ at $x$, which probes the deepest
level $w$, returns true if and only if $x$ is stored in $t$.

articles.title: An inserted key passes the membership test
articles.statement:
For every x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys
and every $w$-bit key $x$, the membership test at $x$ of the trie obtained by inserting $x$ into
$t$ returns true.

No validity assumption on $t$ is needed: insertion puts the full-length prefix of $x$ directly
into the deepest level, which is the level the membership test probes.

articles.title: Membership query in an x-fast trie
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys
and a key $x < 2^w$, the membership query of $x$ in $t$ answers true exactly when the
length-$w$ prefix of $x$, which is $x$ itself, lies in the prefix set that $t$ stores
for level $w$: a single probe of the deepest level, as in the classical structure.

articles.title: When an x-fast trie has no predecessor
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys
and a key $x < 2^w$, the predecessor query of $x$ in $t$ returns no key if and only if
no key stored in $t$ is smaller than $x$.

articles.title: Characterization of the x-fast trie predecessor
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over
$w$-bit keys and keys $x, y < 2^w$, the predecessor query of $x$ in $t$ returns $y$ if and
only if $y$ is stored in $t$, $y < x$, and every key $z$ stored in $t$ with $z < x$
satisfies $z \le y$.

articles.title: Predecessor query in an x-fast trie
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and
a key $x < 2^w$, the predecessor of $x$ in $t$ is the greatest key stored in $t$ that is
smaller than $x$, if such a key exists; otherwise the query returns no key.

articles.title: The full-length prefix of a key is the key
articles.statement:
For every $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$, the
length-$w$ prefix of $x$ equals $x$.

articles.title: A prefix fits in its length
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l \le w$ and a $w$-bit key
$x < 2^w$, the length-$l$ prefix of $x$ is less than $2^l$.

articles.title: The empty prefix is zero
articles.statement:
For every $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$, the length-$0$ prefix
of $x$ (the trie root) is $0$.

articles.title: Bit prefix of a key
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $l$ and $w$ and a $w$-bit key $x < 2^w$,
the length-$l$ prefix of $x$ is the natural number $\lfloor x / 2^{w-l} \rfloor$, where
$w - l$ is truncated subtraction (it is $0$ when $l > w$). For $l \le w$ these are the top
$l$ bits of $x$, a number below $2^l$.

articles.title: Representatives of a valid y-fast trie are stored keys
articles.statement:
If a y-fast trie $t$ over
$w$-bit keys is valid, then every key of the representative x-fast trie of $t$ is a stored
key of $t$.

articles.title: When an x-fast trie has no successor
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys
and a key $x < 2^w$, the successor query of $x$ in $t$ returns no key if and only if no
key stored in $t$ is greater than $x$.

articles.title: Characterization of the x-fast trie successor
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be an x-fast trie over $w$-bit
keys and let $x$ and $y$ be keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$. The successor of $x$ in $t$ exists
and equals $y$ if and only if $y$ is a stored key of $t$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every stored
key $z$ of $t$ with $x < z$.

articles.title: Successor in an x-fast trie
articles.statement:
For an x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys and a key
$x \in \{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$, the successor of $x$ in $t$ is the least stored key of $t$ that is
greater than $x$ when some stored key is greater than $x$; otherwise $x$ has no successor in $t$.

It is computed directly from the stored key set rather than by the classical binary search over
the levels, so no $O(\log w)$ time bound is claimed.

articles.title: Valid y-fast trie skeleton
articles.statement:
A y-fast trie skeleton $t$ over $w$-bit keys, with bucket $B_r$
owned by each key $r$, is valid when its representative x-fast trie is valid, a key $r$ is stored
in the representative x-fast trie exactly when its bucket $B_r$ is nonempty, and every key $r$
stored in the representative x-fast trie lies in its own bucket $B_r$.

So the representatives are sampled from the stored keys: a representative $0$ whose bucket is
$\{1\}$ is not valid. The classical bucket ordering invariant (the keys of bucket $B_r$ lie in
the interval ending at $r$) is not required, so this is the invariant of the skeleton only.

articles.title: The empty x-fast trie is valid
articles.statement:
For every $w$, the empty x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys,
which has no stored keys and every level empty, is valid.

articles.title: Insertion preserves validity of an x-fast trie
articles.statement:
If $t$ is a valid x-fast trie over
$w$-bit keys and $x \in \{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$, then the x-fast trie obtained from $t$ by
inserting $x$ is valid.

articles.title: Valid x-fast trie
articles.statement:
An x-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit keys is valid when, for every level
$l \in \{0, \dots, w\}$, the level-$l$ set of $t$ equals the set of $l$-bit prefixes (top $l$
bits) of the stored keys of $t$.

articles.title: x-fast trie
articles.statement:
An x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys consists of a finite set of stored keys in
$\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$ together with, for each level $l \in \{0, \dots, w\}$, a finite set of
natural numbers, intended to hold the $l$-bit prefixes of the stored keys.

The classical per-level hash tables are modeled as finite sets, so no $O(\log w)$ successor bound
(or any other running-time bound) is claimed.

articles.title: y-fast trie skeleton
articles.statement:
A y-fast trie skeleton over $w$-bit keys consists of an x-fast trie
over $w$-bit keys, whose stored keys are the representatives, together with a bucket $B_r$, a
finite set of keys, for every key $r \in \{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$.

In the classical structure each bucket is a balanced search tree of $\Theta(w)$ keys; here buckets
are plain finite sets, the bucket ordering invariant and the split and merge maintenance are not
modeled, and no complexity bound is claimed.

articles.title: Fuel-bounded chunking
articles.statement:
Given a bound $B$, a fuel $n$ and a list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, the
fuel-bounded chunking is the empty list of chunks when $n = 0$ or $l$ is empty; otherwise it is
the chunk formed by the first $\min(B, |l|)$ elements of $l$, followed by the fuel-bounded
chunking with bound $B$ and fuel $n - 1$ of the remaining elements of $l$.

articles.title: Chunks of a sorted list
articles.statement:
Let $B > 0$ and let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of
$w$-bit keys. Then every chunk of the chunking of $l$ into groups of at most $B$ keys is
nonempty, has at most $B$ elements, and is strictly increasing.

articles.title: Chunking with bound zero
articles.statement:
For every nonempty list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, the chunking of
$l$ with bound $B = 0$ consists of the single chunk $l$.

articles.title: Chunking a list into groups
articles.statement:
Given a bound $B$ and a list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, when
$B > 0$ the chunking of $l$ cuts $l$ from the left into consecutive chunks of exactly $B$
elements each, except that the last chunk holds the remaining one to $B$ elements; there are no
chunks when $l$ is empty. When $B = 0$, the chunking has no chunks if $l$ is empty and is the
single chunk $l$ otherwise.

So every chunk has at most $B$ elements when $B > 0$, but not when $B = 0$ and $l$ is
nonempty.

articles.title: Keys of the trie of representatives
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of $w$-bit keys, the x-fast
trie obtained by inserting the elements of $L$ one by one into the empty x-fast trie stores
exactly the elements of $L$: its key set is the set of elements of $L$.

articles.title: Keys of the grouped y-fast trie built from a list
articles.statement:
For every group bound $B$ (including
$B = 0$) and every list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, sorted or not, the key set of the grouped y-fast
trie built from $l$ with group bound $B$ is exactly the set of elements of $l$.

articles.title: Keys of a grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
The key set of a grouped y-fast trie $t$ is the finite
set of all keys that occur in some group of $t$.

articles.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
For every key length $w$ and group bound $B$, the empty
grouped y-fast trie has the empty x-fast trie as its trie of representatives and has no
groups.

articles.title: Group of a representative
articles.statement:
For a grouped y-fast trie $t$ and a key $r$, the group of $r$
