is the first group of $t$, in the order of the groups, whose last element is $r$, or the empty
list if no group of $t$ ends with $r$.

In a valid trie every group is strictly increasing, so its last element is its maximum.

articles.title: Chunking preserves the list
articles.statement:
For every bound $B$ (including $B = 0$) and every list $l$
of $w$-bit keys, concatenating the chunks of the chunking of $l$ with bound $B$, in order,
gives back $l$.

articles.title: Chunks of a sorted list are ordered
articles.statement:
Let $B$ be a natural number and let $l$ be a
strictly increasing list of $w$-bit keys. Then the chunk groups of $l$ with bound $B$ are group
ordered: every key of an earlier chunk is smaller than every key of a later chunk.

articles.title: Ordered list of groups
articles.statement:
A list of groups, each a list of $w$-bit keys, is group ordered
when every key of an earlier group is smaller than every key of a later group.

articles.title: Grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $w$ and $B$, a grouped y-fast trie over $w$-bit
keys with group bound $B$ consists of an x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys, which holds the
representatives, and a list of groups, each a list of $w$-bit keys. The structure itself imposes
no condition on these fields; the intended invariants (the representative trie is a valid x-fast
trie whose keys are exactly the group maxima, every group is nonempty, strictly sorted and of
length at most $B$, and the groups are in increasing order) are imposed by the validity
predicate.

Each group is a sorted list standing in for a balanced search tree; no complexity bound is
claimed.

articles.title: Stored keys are the keys of the groups
articles.statement:
For every grouped y-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit
keys and every key $x$, $x$ lies in the contents of $t$ if and only if $x$ belongs to some group
of $t$.

articles.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie has no members
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $w$ and $B$ and
every $w$-bit key $x$, the membership query on the empty grouped y-fast trie over $w$-bit keys
with group bound $B$ returns false at $x$.

articles.title: Correctness of the y-fast trie membership query
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid grouped y-fast trie
over $w$-bit keys. Then for every key $x$, the membership query on $t$ (locate the least
representative at least $x$, then scan its group) returns true at $x$ if and only if $x$ lies in
the contents of $t$.

articles.title: Membership in a trie built from a sorted list
articles.statement:
Let $B > 0$ and let $l$ be a strictly
increasing list of $w$-bit keys. Then for every key $x$, the membership query on the grouped
y-fast trie built from $l$ with group bound $B$ returns true at $x$ if and only if $x$ belongs
to $l$.

articles.title: Membership query of a grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
Given a grouped y-fast trie $t$ over $w$-bit
keys and a key $x$, the query first finds a representative $r$: $r = x$ if the membership probe of
the representative x-fast trie accepts $x$, and otherwise $r$ is the successor of $x$ in the
representative trie. If there is no such $r$, the query returns false. Otherwise it returns
whether $x$ belongs to the group owned by $r$, namely the first group of $t$ whose last element is
$r$ (the empty list if there is none).

articles.title: Representative trie of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $rs$ of $w$-bit keys, the representative
x-fast trie of $rs$ is obtained from the empty x-fast trie over $w$-bit keys by inserting the
elements of $rs$ one at a time, from first to last.

articles.title: Building from a nonempty list with group bound zero gives an invalid trie
articles.statement:
For every
natural number $w$ and every nonempty list $l$ of $w$-bit keys, the grouped y-fast trie with
group bound $B = 0$ built from $l$ is not valid.

With $B = 0$ the only group is $l$ itself, which has more than $0$ keys. For $B > 0$ and strictly
increasing $l$, the grouped y-fast trie built from $l$ is valid.

articles.title: Grouped y-fast trie from a list of groups
articles.statement:
For a list of groups $g_1, \dots, g_k$,
each a list of $w$-bit keys, and any group-size bound $B$, this is the grouped y-fast trie
whose groups are $g_1, \dots, g_k$ in this order and whose representative x-fast trie is
obtained from the empty x-fast trie by inserting the last element of each nonempty group,
in order. No condition on the groups is checked here; when a group is sorted, its last
element is its maximum.

articles.title: Grouped y-fast trie from a sorted list
articles.statement:
For a group bound $B$ and a list $l$ of
$w$-bit keys, this is the grouped y-fast trie whose groups, in order, are consecutive pieces of
$l$ that together make up $l$, and whose representative x-fast trie is obtained from the empty
x-fast trie by inserting the last element of each group, in order. If $B > 0$, the groups are
obtained by repeatedly cutting off the first $B$ keys, so every group has exactly $B$ keys
except possibly the last, which has between one and $B$ keys. If $B = 0$, the only group is $l$
itself. In both cases there are no groups when $l$ is empty.

The construction is intended for strictly increasing $l$. It yields a valid trie when $B > 0$
and $l$ is strictly increasing, and an invalid one when $B = 0$ and $l$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Least representative at or above a key
articles.statement:
For a grouped y-fast trie $t$ and a key $x$,
the result is $x$ itself if the membership test of the representative x-fast trie of $t$ (a
single probe of its deepest level) reports $x$ as present. Otherwise it is the successor of $x$
in the representative x-fast trie, that is, the least representative greater than $x$, or
nothing if there is none.

When $t$ is valid, the result is the least representative $r$ with $x \le r$, and nothing
when there is no such representative.

articles.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie has no successors
articles.statement:
For every key $x$, the successor query
for $x$ in the empty grouped y-fast trie returns nothing.

articles.title: Successor query fails exactly when no larger key is stored
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid grouped
y-fast trie and $x$ a key. The successor query for $x$ in $t$ returns nothing if and only if no
key stored in $t$ is greater than $x$.

articles.title: Successor query returns the least larger stored key
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a valid grouped y-fast
trie and let $x$, $y$ be keys. The successor query for $x$ in $t$ returns $y$ if and only if
$y$ is stored in $t$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every key $z$ stored in $t$ with $x < z$.

articles.title: Successor in the trie built from a sorted list
articles.statement:
Let $B > 0$, let $l$ be a strictly
increasing list of $w$-bit keys, and let $x$, $y$ be keys. The successor query for $x$ in the
grouped y-fast trie built from $l$ with group bound $B$ returns $y$ if and only if $y$ belongs
to $l$, $x < y$, and $y \le z$ for every $z$ in $l$ with $x < z$.

articles.title: Successor query in a grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
For a grouped y-fast trie $t$ and a key
$x$, let $r$ be the least key greater than $x$ stored in the representative x-fast trie of
$t$; if there is none, the query returns nothing. Otherwise let $g$ be the first group of $t$
whose last element is $r$, or the empty list if no group has last element $r$. The query then
returns the first key of $g$ greater than $x$, or nothing if $g$ has no such key.

articles.title: The empty grouped y-fast trie is valid
articles.statement:
For every key width $w$ and group bound $B$,
the empty grouped y-fast trie satisfies the grouped y-fast trie invariant.

articles.title: Inserting a list of keys into the empty x-fast trie gives a valid trie
articles.statement:
For every list
of $w$-bit keys, the x-fast trie obtained from the empty x-fast trie by inserting the keys of
the list one at a time satisfies the x-fast trie invariant: each level holds exactly the
prefixes of that length of the stored keys.

articles.title: Assembling a valid grouped y-fast trie from groups
articles.statement:
Let $w$ and $B$ be natural numbers
and let $g_1, \dots, g_k$ be a list of groups, each a list of keys in $\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$.
Suppose every group is nonempty, has at most $B$ keys, and is strictly increasing, and the
groups are ordered: every key of an earlier group is smaller than every key of a later group.
Then the grouped y-fast trie with group bound $B$ assembled from these groups, whose
representatives are the last elements of the groups, is valid.

articles.title: Building from a sorted list gives a valid grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
Let $w$ and $B$ be
natural numbers with $0 < B$, and let $l$ be a strictly increasing list of keys in
$\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$. Then the grouped y-fast trie with group bound $B$ built from $l$ by
cutting it into consecutive groups of at most $B$ keys is valid.

articles.title: Validity of a grouped y-fast trie
articles.statement:
A grouped y-fast trie $t$ over keys in
$\{0, \dots, 2^w - 1\}$ with group bound $B$ is valid when its representative trie is a valid
x-fast trie; a key $r$ is stored in the representative trie exactly when $r$ is the last element
of some group of $t$; every group of $t$ is nonempty, has at most $B$ keys, and is strictly
increasing; and the groups of $t$ are ordered, that is, every key of an earlier group is smaller
than every key of a later group.

articles.title: Read or write access
articles.statement:
The kind of access an operation makes to its data item is one of
two values: a read or a write.

articles.title: Serializing along a topological order preserves conflict equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a
schedule in which no operation occurs twice, and let $L$ be a topological order of the
precedence graph of $s$. Then the schedule obtained from $s$ by stably sorting its operations
by the first position of their transaction in $L$ is conflict-equivalent to $s$.

articles.title: Conflict equivalence
articles.statement:
A schedule $s'$ is conflict-equivalent to a schedule $s$ when $s'$
is a permutation of $s$ and, for any two operations $a$ and $b$ that belong to the same
transaction or conflict, an occurrence of $a$ comes before an occurrence of $b$ in $s$ if and
only if the same holds in $s'$.

articles.title: The serializability theorem
articles.statement:
A schedule without duplicate operations is
conflict-serializable exactly when its precedence graph is acyclic.

articles.title: A rank increasing along precedence edges gives conflict serializability
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a
schedule in which no operation occurs twice. If $r$ is a function from the transactions to the
natural numbers with $r(i) < r(j)$ whenever the precedence graph of $s$ has an edge from $i$ to
$j$, then $s$ is conflict-serializable.

articles.title: Conflict-serializable schedule
articles.statement:
A schedule $s$ is conflict-serializable when some serial
schedule is conflict-equivalent to $s$.

articles.title: Conflicting operations
articles.statement:
Two operations of a schedule conflict when they belong to different
transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of the two accesses is a write.

articles.title: A conflict-serializable schedule has an acyclic precedence graph
articles.statement:
If a schedule $s$ in
which no operation occurs twice is conflict-serializable, then the precedence graph of $s$ is
acyclic.

In a conflict-equivalent serial schedule, the position of the first operation of each
transaction increases along every edge of the precedence graph.

articles.title: Serializing along a complete transaction order gives a serial schedule
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a
schedule and $L$ a list in which every transaction occurs. Then the schedule obtained from $s$
by stably sorting its operations by the first position of their transaction in $L$ is serial.

articles.title: Serial schedule
articles.statement:
A schedule $s$ is serial when, for any two distinct transactions $i$ and
$j$, either every operation of $i$ in $s$ occurs before every operation of $j$ in $s$, or every
operation of $j$ in $s$ occurs before every operation of $i$ in $s$.

articles.title: Operation of a schedule
articles.statement:
For $n$ transactions, numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, and data items
of type $X$, an operation consists of a transaction $t \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, an occurrence
identifier $k \in \mathbb{N}$, an access, which is a read or a write, and a data item $x \in X$:
transaction $t$ reads or writes $x$, and $k$ makes repeated accesses of $t$ to an item distinct
operations.

articles.title: Operations whose relative order matters
articles.statement:
Two operations $a$ and $b$ are order-relevant when
they belong to the same transaction or they conflict. These are the pairs whose relative order a
conflict-equivalent schedule must keep.

articles.title: Edge of the precedence graph
articles.statement:
For a schedule $s$ and transactions $i$ and $j$, there is a
precedence edge from $i$ to $j$ in $s$ when some operation of $i$ occurs in $s$ before some
operation of $j$ in $s$ that conflicts with it.

articles.title: Precedence graph
articles.statement:
The precedence (serialization) graph of a schedule $s$ of $n$
transactions is the directed adjacency graph whose vertices are the transactions
$0, \dots, n - 1$, listed in increasing order, and whose adjacency list at a transaction $i$ lists,
in increasing order, the transactions $j$ such that there is a precedence edge from $i$ to $j$
in $s$.

articles.title: Serialization of a schedule along a transaction order
articles.statement:
For a list $\sigma$ of transactions
and a schedule $s$, the serialization of $s$ along $\sigma$ sorts the operations of $s$ by the
position of the first occurrence of their transaction in $\sigma$, where a transaction that does
not occur in $\sigma$ gets the length of $\sigma$ as its position. The sort is stable: operations
with the same position keep their relative order in $s$.

articles.title: One transaction before another in a schedule
articles.statement:
For a schedule $s$ and transactions $i$ and
$j$, transaction $i$ precedes transaction $j$ in $s$ when every operation of $i$ in $s$ occurs in
$s$ before every operation of $j$ in $s$.

articles.title: Attribute closure
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of attributes, $F$ a finite set of functional
dependencies over $A$ and $X \subseteq A$. The attribute closure $X^+$ of $X$ under $F$ is
computed by the closure algorithm: starting from $X$, repeat closure rounds (each adds the right
side of every dependency of $F$ whose left side is already included) until nothing changes, for
at most $|A|$ rounds.

articles.title: Iterated closure rounds
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies, $n$ a
natural number and $Y$ a finite set of attributes. The loop returns $Y$ if $n = 0$ or if one
closure round for $F$ leaves $Y$ unchanged; otherwise it returns the loop with $n - 1$ rounds
started from the result of one closure round applied to $Y$. Thus it repeats closure rounds from
$Y$ until nothing changes, for at most $n$ rounds.

articles.title: The attribute closure is a fixed point of a closure round
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of
attributes, $F$ a finite set of functional dependencies over $A$ and $X \subseteq A$. Applying
one closure round for $F$ to the attribute closure $X^+$ of $X$ under $F$ returns $X^+$.

articles.title: One round of the attribute-closure algorithm
articles.statement:
For a finite set $F$ of functional
dependencies and a finite set $Y$ of attributes, one closure round returns $Y$ together with the
right side of every dependency of $F$ whose left side is contained in $Y$, that is, the set
$Y \cup \bigcup \{R : (L \to R) \in F,\ L \subseteq Y\}$.

articles.title: Closure witness relation
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of attributes, $F$ a finite set of
functional dependencies over $A$ and $X \subseteq A$. The closure witness relation for $X$ is the
relation with values in $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ whose tuples are the tuple that is
$\mathrm{true}$ on every attribute and the tuple that is $\mathrm{true}$ exactly on the attribute
closure $X^+$ of $X$ under $F$. These two tuples agree exactly on $X^+$, and they coincide when
$X^+ = A$.

articles.title: Decomposition rule
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies and $X$, $Y$, $Z$
finite sets of attributes with $Z \subseteq Y$. If $X \to Y$ is derivable from $F$ with
Armstrong's axioms, then so is $X \to Z$.

articles.title: Armstrong's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of attributes, $F$ a finite set of
functional dependencies over $A$ and $f$ a functional dependency over $A$. Then $f$ is
derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's axioms if and only if $F$ entails $f$, that is, $f$ holds
in every relation (with values in any type) that satisfies every dependency of $F$. In other
words, Armstrong's axioms are sound and complete for functional dependencies.

articles.title: The closure algorithm decides derivability
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of attributes, $F$ a
finite set of functional dependencies over $A$ and $X, Y \subseteq A$. Then $X \to Y$ is
derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's axioms if and only if $Y \subseteq X^+$, where $X^+$ is the
attribute closure of $X$ under $F$ computed by the closure algorithm.

articles.title: Completeness of Armstrong's axioms, two-tuple form
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite set of
attributes, $F$ a finite set of functional dependencies over $A$ and $f$ a functional
dependency over $A$. If $f$ holds in every relation with values in
$\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ that has at most two tuples and satisfies every dependency
of $F$, then $f$ is derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's axioms.

articles.title: Derivability with Armstrong's axioms
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies over a set $A$ of attributes. Derivability from $F$ is the least property of
functional dependencies over $A$ such that, for all finite sets $X$, $Y$, $Z$ of attributes:
every dependency of $F$ is derivable; $X \to Y$ is derivable whenever $Y \subseteq X$
(reflexivity); if $X \to Y$ is derivable, then so is $X \cup Z \to Y \cup Z$ (augmentation);
and if $X \to Y$ and $Y \to Z$ are derivable, then so is $X \to Z$ (transitivity).

articles.title: Entailment of functional dependencies
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a type of attributes. A finite set $F$
of functional dependencies on $A$ entails a functional dependency $f$ on $A$ when, for every
type $V$ and every relation $r$ with values in $V$ (a set of tuples $A \to V$) that satisfies
$F$, the dependency $f$ holds in $r$.

articles.title: Tuples that agree on a superkey are equal
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies on a finite set of attributes $A$, and let $K$ be a superkey for $F$. Let $V$ be a
type of values. If a relation $r$, a set of tuples $A \to V$, satisfies $F$, then any two tuples
$t, u \in r$ that agree on every attribute of $K$ are equal.

articles.title: Every superkey contains a candidate key
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies on a finite set of attributes $A$. Every superkey $K$ for $F$ has a subset
$K' \subseteq K$ that is a candidate key for $F$.

articles.title: Functional dependency
articles.statement:
A functional dependency $X \to Y$ over a type $A$ of attributes
consists of two finite sets of attributes $X, Y \subseteq A$: the determining attributes $X$
(its left side) and the determined attributes $Y$ (its right side).

articles.title: The key-finding algorithm returns a candidate key
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies on a finite set of attributes $A$, and let $l$ be a list in which every attribute
of $A$ occurs. Then the output of the key-finding algorithm on $F$ and $l$, which starts from the
set of all attributes and goes through $l$ in order, removing each listed attribute whenever
what remains is still a superkey, is a candidate key for $F$.

articles.title: Key-finding algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies on a finite set
of attributes $A$, and let $l$ be a list of attributes. The key-finding algorithm starts from the
set $K = A$ of all attributes and goes through $l$ in order: for each listed attribute $a$, it
replaces $K$ by $K \setminus \{a\}$ when the attribute closure of $K \setminus \{a\}$ under $F$ is
all of $A$, and keeps $K$ otherwise. It returns the final set $K$.

articles.title: The closure witness satisfies the dependencies
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies on a finite set of attributes $A$. For every set $X \subseteq A$ of attributes, the
closure witness relation for $X$ under $F$ satisfies $F$.

articles.title: A functional dependency holds in a relation
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a type of attributes and $V$ a
type of values. A functional dependency $X \to Y$ on $A$ holds in a relation $r$, a set of tuples
$A \to V$, when any two tuples $t, u \in r$ that agree on every attribute of $X$ also agree on
every attribute of $Y$.

articles.title: Candidate keys are the superkeys minimal under single removals
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set
of functional dependencies on a finite set of attributes $A$. A set $K \subseteq A$ of attributes
is a candidate key for $F$ if and only if $K$ is a superkey for $F$ and, for every $a \in K$, the
set $K \setminus \{a\}$ is not a superkey for $F$.

articles.title: Candidate key
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies on a finite set of
attributes $A$. A set $K \subseteq A$ of attributes is a candidate key for $F$ when $K$ is a
superkey for $F$ and no proper subset of $K$ is a superkey for $F$.

articles.title: Superkey
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies over a finite set of
attributes $A$. A set of attributes $K$ is a superkey for $F$ when the dependency $K \to A$ is
derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's axioms, that is, $K$ determines every attribute.

articles.title: The closure algorithm computes the attribute closure
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of
functional dependencies over a finite set of attributes and $X$ a set of attributes. An
attribute $a$ lies in the attribute closure $X^+$ of $X$ under $F$, as computed by the closure
algorithm, if and only if the dependency $X \to \{a\}$ is derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's
axioms.

articles.title: Supersets of superkeys are superkeys
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies
over a finite set of attributes. If $K$ is a superkey for $F$ and $K \subseteq K'$, then $K'$ is a
superkey for $F$.

articles.title: Pseudotransitivity rule
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies and
$X, Y, W, Z$ finite sets of attributes. If $X \to Y$ and $Y \cup W \to Z$ are derivable from $F$
with Armstrong's axioms, then so is $X \cup W \to Z$.

articles.title: The attribute closure is closed under the dependencies
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of
functional dependencies over a finite set of attributes, $X$ a set of attributes and $X^+$ its
attribute closure under $F$. For every dependency $Y \to Z$ in $F$ with $Y \subseteq X^+$, also
$Z \subseteq X^+$.

articles.title: A relation satisfies a set of dependencies
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies over attributes $A$, and let $r$ be a relation, given as a set of tuples $A \to V$
with values in a type $V$. Then $r$ satisfies $F$ when every dependency of $F$ holds in $r$.

articles.title: Shrinking a key along a list
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies over a
finite set of attributes. Given a list $l$ of attributes and a set of attributes $K$, go through
$l$ in order and, for each attribute $a$, remove $a$ from the current set whenever the attribute
closure under $F$ of the current set without $a$ is the set of all attributes (that is, the set
without $a$ is still a superkey); the result is the set reached at the end of the list.

articles.title: Armstrong's axioms are sound
articles.statement:
A derivable dependency holds in every relation satisfying
`F`.

articles.title: Adding the left side to the right side
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies
and $X, Y$ finite sets of attributes. If $X \to Y$ is derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's axioms,
then so is $X \to X \cup Y$.

articles.title: Union rule
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies and $X, Y, Z$ finite sets
of attributes. If $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$ are derivable from $F$ with Armstrong's axioms, then so
is $X \to Y \cup Z$.

articles.title: Candidate BCNF violations
articles.statement:
Given a list $l$ of attributes and a set $S$ of attributes, the
candidate violations of BCNF in $S$ are all subsets of the set of attributes that occur in $l$ and
lie in $S$, listed once each. Duplicates in $l$ are removed first, so there are $2^k$ candidates
when $k$ distinct attributes of $l$ lie in $S$.

articles.title: BCNF decomposition with bounded depth
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, $l$ a
list of attributes, $n$ a natural number and $S$ a scheme. For $n = 0$ the result is the list $[S]$.
For $n > 0$, the candidate violations of BCNF in $S$ built from $l$ are searched in order for the
first $X$ that violates BCNF in $S$ for $F$. If there is none, the result is $[S]$. Otherwise, with
$X^+$ the attribute closure of $X$ under $F$, the result is the decomposition of $X^+ \cap S$
followed by the decomposition of $S \setminus (X^+ \setminus X)$, both computed with depth bound
$n - 1$.

articles.title: The BCNF decomposition is lossless
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, $l$ a list
of attributes and $S$ a set of attributes, and let $r$ be a relation over $S$ that satisfies every
dependency $X \to Y$ derivable from $F$ with $X, Y \subseteq S$. Then $r$ is the natural join of
its projections onto the schemes of the BCNF decomposition of $S$ for $F$ and $l$.

articles.title: BCNF decomposition
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies, $l$ a list of attributes
and $S$ a scheme. The BCNF decomposition of $S$ for $F$ and $l$ is the BCNF decomposition with
bounded depth run on $S$ with depth bound $|S|$. At each step, if some candidate violation of BCNF
in the current scheme $T$ built from $l$ violates BCNF in $T$ for $F$, the first such $X$ is used:
with $X^+$ the attribute closure of $X$ under $F$, $T$ is replaced by the decomposition of
$X^+ \cap T$ followed by the decomposition of $T \setminus (X^+ \setminus X)$. Otherwise, or once
the depth bound is reached, $T$ is kept as it is.

articles.title: Dependency-preserving decompositions
articles.statement:
A list $l$ of schemes is dependency-preserving for a
set $F$ of functional dependencies when every dependency of $F$ is derivable from the union, over
the schemes $S$ of $l$, of the sets of dependencies $X \to Y$ derivable from $F$ with
$X, Y \subseteq S$.

articles.title: Converse of the lossless-join test for two schemes
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a set of functional
dependencies, let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be schemes whose union is the set of all attributes, and let
$D$ be a value type containing at least two distinct elements. If the decomposition of
$R_1 \cup R_2$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless for $F$ with values in $D$, then $F$ derives
$R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ or $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$.

articles.title: Equivalent sets of functional dependencies
articles.statement:
Two sets $F$ and $G$ of functional dependencies
are equivalent when $F$ derives every dependency of $G$ and $G$ derives every dependency of $F$.

articles.title: The BCNF decomposition produces BCNF schemes
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies
and $l$ a list containing every attribute. Then for every scheme $S$, every scheme in the BCNF
decomposition of $S$ for $F$ and $l$ is in Boyce–Codd normal form for $F$.

articles.title: Boyce–Codd normal form
articles.statement:
A scheme $S$ is in Boyce–Codd normal form for a set $F$ of
functional dependencies when, for every dependency $X \to Y$ derivable from $F$ with
$X, Y \subseteq S$, either $Y \subseteq X$ or $F$ derives $X \to S$ (that is, $X$ is a superkey of
$S$).

articles.title: BCNF violations
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a set of functional dependencies and $S$ a scheme, and write
$X^+$ for the attribute closure of a set $X$ of attributes under $F$. A set $X \subseteq S$
violates BCNF in $S$ when $S \not\subseteq X^+$ and $X^+ \cap S \not\subseteq X$, that is, when
the closure $X^+ \cap S$ of $X$ within $S$ is neither $X$ nor $S$.

articles.title: Heath's theorem
articles.statement:
If the dependency `R₁ ∩ R₂ → R₁` holds in a relation `r` over
`R₁ ∪ R₂`, then `r` is the natural join of its projections onto `R₁` and `R₂`.

articles.title: Join of the projections of a relation
articles.statement:
For a relation $r$ (a finite set of tuples) and a
list of schemes $S_1, \dots, S_n$, this is the natural join of the projections
$\pi_{S_1} r, \dots, \pi_{S_n} r$, computed as
$\pi_{S_1} r \bowtie (\pi_{S_2} r \bowtie (\cdots \bowtie (\pi_{S_n} r \bowtie U)))$, where $U$ is
the relation containing only the empty tuple; for the empty list it is $U$.

articles.title: Unit relation of the natural join
articles.statement: The relation containing only the empty tuple, the unit of the natural join.

articles.title: Lossless binary decompositions
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies, let
$R_1$ and $R_2$ be sets of attributes whose union is the set of all attributes, and suppose that
the value type $D$ has two distinct elements. Then the decomposition into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is
lossless for $F$ with values in $D$ if and only if $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ or
$R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$ is derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms.

articles.title: Lossless binary decompositions from derivable dependencies
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of
functional dependencies and let $R_1$, $R_2$ be sets of attributes. If $R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_1$ or
$R_1 \cap R_2 \to R_2$ is derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms, then for every value type $D$
the decomposition of $R_1 \cup R_2$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless for $F$ with values in $D$.

articles.title: Lossless decomposition into two schemes
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional
dependencies, let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be finite sets of attributes, and let $D$ be a type of values.
The decomposition of $R_1 \cup R_2$ into $R_1$ and $R_2$ is lossless for $F$ with values in $D$
when every relation $r$ over $R_1 \cup R_2$ with values in $D$ that satisfies $F$ on
$R_1 \cup R_2$ (every dependency $X \to Y$ with $X, Y \subseteq R_1 \cup R_2$ that is derivable
from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms holds in $r$) is the natural join of its projections:
$\pi_{R_1}(r) \bowtie \pi_{R_2}(r) = r$.

articles.title: Membership in a join of projections
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a relation over a schema $R$ and let
$S_1, \dots, S_n$ be a list of schemes, each contained in $R$. A tuple $t$ belongs to the natural
join of the projections $\pi_{S_1} r, \dots, \pi_{S_n} r$ if and only if $t$ is a tuple over
$S_1 \cup \dots \cup S_n$ and, for every $i$, the restriction of $t$ to $S_i$ belongs to
$\pi_{S_i} r$.

articles.title: Projection of the dependency closure onto a scheme
articles.statement:
For a finite set $F$ of functional
dependencies and a set $S$ of attributes, this is the finite set of all dependencies $X \to Y$
with $X, Y \subseteq S$ that are derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms, that is, the projection
onto $S$ of the closure $F^+$ of $F$.

articles.title: Satisfying a set of dependencies on a scheme
articles.statement:
A relation $r$ satisfies a finite set $F$ of
functional dependencies on a set $S$ of attributes when every dependency $X \to Y$ with
$X, Y \subseteq S$ that is derivable from $F$ by Armstrong's axioms holds in $r$.

articles.title: Union of a list of schemes
articles.statement:
For a list $S_1, \dots, S_n$ of schemes (finite sets of
attributes), this is the union $S_1 \cup \dots \cup S_n$; for the empty list it is the empty set.

articles.title: Synthesis is dependency-preserving
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of functional dependencies and
$G$ a list of functional dependencies equivalent to $F$ (each derives every dependency of the
other). Then for every set of attributes $K$, the decomposition synthesized from $G$ and $K$,
with one scheme $X \cup Y$ for each dependency $X \to Y$ of $G$ together with the scheme $K$, is
dependency-preserving for $F$.

articles.title: Synthesis is lossless
articles.statement:
For a cover `G` of `F` and a superkey `K` of all attributes, every
relation over all attributes satisfying `F` is the join of its projections onto the synthesized
schemes.

articles.title: Synthesis
articles.statement:
Given a list $G$ of functional dependencies and a set of attributes $K$, the
synthesized decomposition is the list of schemes consisting of $K$ followed by, for each
dependency $X \to Y$ of $G$ in order, the scheme $X \cup Y$.

articles.title: Attributes of a selection condition
articles.statement:
The set of attributes mentioned by a selection
condition, defined by recursion: it is empty for the always-true condition; for the comparison
$a = d$ of an attribute $a$ with a constant $d$ it is $\{a\}$; for the comparison $a = b$ of
attributes $a$ and $b$ it is $\{a, b\}$; for the negation $\neg \varphi$ of a condition $\varphi$
it is the set of attributes of $\varphi$; and for the conjunction $\varphi \land \psi$ of
conditions $\varphi$ and $\psi$ it is the union of the attributes of $\varphi$ and of $\psi$.

articles.title: Compatibility with a merge, grouped from the left
articles.statement:
For tuples $t$, $u$, $v$: $t$ and $u$
are compatible and the merge of $t$ and $u$ is compatible with $v$ if and only if $t$, $u$, $v$
are pairwise compatible, that is, $t$ and $u$, $t$ and $v$, and $u$ and $v$ are compatible.

articles.title: Compatibility with a merge, grouped from the right
articles.statement:
For tuples $t$, $u$, $v$: $u$ and $v$
are compatible and $t$ is compatible with the merge of $u$ and $v$ if and only if $t$, $u$, $v$
are pairwise compatible, that is, $t$ and $u$, $t$ and $v$, and $u$ and $v$ are compatible.

articles.title: Compatible tuples
articles.statement:
Two tuples $t$ and $u$ are compatible (joinable) when they agree on
every attribute where both are defined: for every attribute $a$, either $t$ is undefined at $a$,
or $u$ is undefined at $a$, or $t(a) = u(a)$.

articles.title: Selection conditions
articles.statement:
The selection conditions over attributes $A$ and values $D$ are
generated by: the condition that always holds; the equality $a = c$ of an attribute $a$ with a
constant $c \in D$; the equality $a = b$ of two attributes $a$ and $b$; the negation of a
condition; and the conjunction of two conditions.

articles.title: Databases conforming to a schema
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a set of relation names. A database
schema assigns to each name $n \in N$ a finite set of attributes $\mathrm{sch}(n)$, and a
database assigns to each name $n$ a finite set of tuples $\mathrm{db}(n)$. The database
$\mathrm{db}$ conforms to the database schema $\mathrm{sch}$ when, for every name $n$, the
set $\mathrm{db}(n)$ is a relation over $\mathrm{sch}(n)$.

articles.title: Query equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{sch}$ be a database schema, assigning a finite set of
attributes to each relation name. Two queries $e$ and $e'$ are equivalent with respect to
$\mathrm{sch}$ when there is a finite set of attributes $S$ such that the inferred schemas of
$e$ and of $e'$ with respect to $\mathrm{sch}$ are both $S$ (in particular both queries are
well-formed), and $e$ and $e'$ evaluate to the same relation on every database that conforms
to $\mathrm{sch}$.

articles.title: Value of a query
articles.statement:
Given a database $\mathrm{db}$, which assigns a finite set of tuples
$\mathrm{db}(n)$ to each relation name $n$, the value of a relational algebra query on
$\mathrm{db}$ is the finite set of tuples defined by recursion on the query: the base relation
$n$ has value $\mathrm{db}(n)$; for a query $e$ with value $v$, the selection $\sigma_c(e)$ by a
selection condition $c$, the projection $\pi_T(e)$ onto a finite set $T$ of attributes and the
renaming $\rho_f(e)$ along a permutation $f$ of the attributes have values $\sigma_c(v)$,
$\pi_T(v)$ and $\rho_f(v)$; and the natural join, the union and the difference of queries $e$
and $e'$ with values $v$ and $v'$ have values $v \bowtie v'$, $v \cup v'$ and
$v \setminus v'$.

articles.title: Typing is sound
articles.statement:
A well-formed query evaluates, on every conforming database, to a
relation over its inferred schema.

articles.title: Selection conditions depend only on their attributes
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a selection condition,
$t$ a tuple and $T$ a finite set of attributes containing every attribute of $c$. Then $c$ has
the same truth value on the restriction of $t$ to $T$ as on $t$.

articles.title: Truth value of a selection condition
articles.statement:
The truth value of a selection condition on a
tuple $t$ is defined by recursion: the always-true condition holds; $a = c$ holds when $t$ is
defined at $a$ with value $c$; $a = b$ holds when $t(a) = t(b)$ as possibly undefined values,
so it also holds when $t$ is undefined at both $a$ and $b$; a negation holds when the negated
condition fails; and a conjunction holds when both conditions hold.

articles.title: Relational algebra queries
articles.statement:
The relational algebra queries over base relations named
by $N$, with attributes $A$ and values $D$, are generated by: the base relation named $n$ for
each $n \in N$; the selection $\sigma_c(e)$ of a query $e$ by a selection condition $c$; the
projection $\pi_T(e)$ of a query $e$ on a finite set of attributes $T$; the natural join of two
queries; the union of two queries; the difference of two queries; and the renaming
$\rho_f(e)$ of a query $e$ along a permutation $f$ of $A$.

articles.title: Relation over a schema
articles.statement:
A finite set $r$ of tuples is a relation over the schema $S$, a
finite set of attributes, when every tuple $t \in r$ is over $S$, that is, $t$ is defined exactly
on the attributes of $S$.

articles.title: Tuple over a schema
articles.statement:
A tuple $t$ is over the schema $S$, a finite set of attributes, when
$t$ is defined exactly on the attributes of $S$: for every attribute $a$, the value $t(a)$ is
defined if and only if $a \in S$.

articles.title: Associativity of the natural join
articles.statement:
For all finite sets $r$, $s$ and $w$ of tuples,
$(r \bowtie s) \bowtie w = r \bowtie (s \bowtie w)$, where $\bowtie$ is the natural join.

articles.title: Commutativity of the natural join
articles.statement:
For all finite sets $r$ and $s$ of tuples,
$r \bowtie s = s \bowtie r$, where $\bowtie$ is the natural join.

articles.title: The natural join on a common schema is the intersection
articles.statement:
If $r$ and $s$ are relations
over the same schema $S$, that is, finite sets of tuples each over $S$, then their natural join
is their intersection: $r \bowtie s = r \cap s$.

articles.title: Natural join
articles.statement:
The natural join $r \bowtie s$ of finite sets of tuples $r$ and $s$ is the
set of merges of $t$ and $u$ over all pairs of tuples $t \in r$ and $u \in s$ that are
compatible, that is, agree on every attribute where both are defined. The merge of $t$ and $u$
takes the value of $t$ where $t$ is defined and the value of $u$ otherwise.

articles.title: Membership in a join
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a relation over the schema $S$ and $s$ a relation over
the schema $S'$, that is, finite sets of tuples each over $S$, respectively each over $S'$. A
tuple $t$ belongs to the natural join $r \bowtie s$ if and only if $t$ is over $S \cup S'$, the
restriction of $t$ to $S$ belongs to $r$, and the restriction of $t$ to $S'$ belongs to $s$.

articles.title: Merge of two tuples
articles.statement:
The merge of tuples $t$ and $u$ is the tuple whose value at each
attribute $a$ is $t(a)$ if $t$ is defined at $a$, and $u(a)$ otherwise; it is undefined at $a$
when neither $t$ nor $u$ is.

articles.title: Cascade of projections as a query rewrite
articles.statement:
Fix a database schema $\mathrm{sch}$
assigning a finite set of attributes to each base relation name. Let $e$ be a well-formed query
with schema $S$, and let $T \subseteq T' \subseteq S$ be finite sets of attributes. Then the
query $\pi_T(\pi_{T'}(e))$, the projection onto $T$ of the projection of $e$ onto $T'$, is
equivalent to the query $\pi_T(e)$, the projection of $e$ onto $T$: both are well-formed with
the same schema, and they have equal values on every database conforming to $\mathrm{sch}$.

articles.title: Cascade of projections onto a subset
articles.statement:
Assume the set of attributes is finite. For finite
sets of attributes $T \subseteq T'$ and every finite set $r$ of tuples,
$\pi_T(\pi_{T'}(r)) = \pi_T(r)$, where $\pi_T$ is projection onto $T$.

articles.title: Cascade of projections
articles.statement:
Assume the set of attributes is finite. For all finite sets of
attributes $T$ and $T'$ and every finite set $r$ of tuples,
$\pi_T(\pi_{T'}(r)) = \pi_{T \cap T'}(r)$, where $\pi_T$ is projection onto $T$.

articles.title: Projection distributes over union
articles.statement:
For every finite set $T$ of attributes and all finite
sets $r$ and $s$ of tuples, the projection onto $T$ of $r \cup s$ is the union of the projections
onto $T$ of $r$ and of $s$: $\pi_T(r \cup s) = \pi_T(r) \cup \pi_T(s)$.

articles.title: Projection of a relation
articles.statement:
For a finite set $T$ of attributes and a finite set $r$ of
tuples, the projection $\pi_T(r)$ is the finite set of the restrictions to $T$ of the tuples of
$r$: $\pi_T(r) = \{ t|_T : t \in r \}$.

articles.title: Renaming of attributes
articles.statement:
For a permutation $f$ of the attributes and a finite set $r$ of
tuples, the renaming $\rho_f(r)$ is the finite set of the tuples $t \circ f^{-1}$ for $t \in r$:
each tuple keeps its values, and its value at an attribute $a$ moves to the attribute $f(a)$.

articles.title: Restriction of a tuple
articles.statement:
For a finite set $T$ of attributes and a tuple $t$, the
restriction $t|_T$ is the tuple that agrees with $t$ on every attribute in $T$ and is undefined
on every attribute outside $T$.

articles.title: Schema of a query
articles.statement:
Given a database schema assigning a finite set $\mathrm{sch}(n)$ of
attributes to each base relation name $n$, the schema of a relational algebra query is either a
finite set of attributes or undefined (the query is ill-formed), defined by recursion on the
query: the base relation $n$ has schema $\mathrm{sch}(n)$; if $e$ has schema $S$, then the
selection $\sigma_c(e)$ has schema $S$ when every attribute of the condition $c$ lies in $S$, the
projection $\pi_T(e)$ has schema $T$ when $T \subseteq S$, and the renaming $\rho_f(e)$ along a
permutation $f$ of the attributes has schema $f(S)$; if $e$ and $e'$ have schemas $S$ and $S'$,
then the natural join of $e$ and $e'$ has schema $S \cup S'$, and their union and their
difference have schema $S$ when $S = S'$. In every other case, including when an operand is
ill-formed, the schema is undefined.

articles.title: Selections commute
articles.statement:
For all selection conditions $c$ and $c'$ and every finite set $r$ of
tuples, selecting by $c'$ and then by $c$ gives the same result as selecting by $c$ and then by
$c'$: $\sigma_c(\sigma_{c'}(r)) = \sigma_{c'}(\sigma_c(r))$.

articles.title: Selection pushdown into the left operand of a join
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a relation over a schema
$S$, that is, a finite set of tuples each defined exactly on the attributes of $S$, and let $s$ be
any finite set of tuples. If every attribute of the selection condition $c$ lies in $S$, then
$\sigma_c(r \bowtie s) = \sigma_c(r) \bowtie s$, where $\sigma_c$ is selection by $c$ and
$\bowtie$ is the natural join.

articles.title: Selection pushdown into the right operand of a join
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a relation over a schema
$S'$, that is, a finite set of tuples each defined exactly on the attributes of $S'$, and let $r$
be any finite set of tuples. If every attribute of the selection condition $c$ lies in $S'$, then
$\sigma_c(r \bowtie s) = r \bowtie \sigma_c(s)$, where $\sigma_c$ is selection by $c$ and
$\bowtie$ is the natural join.

articles.title: Selection pushdown as a query rewrite
articles.statement:
Fix a database schema $\mathrm{sch}$ assigning a
finite set of attributes to each base relation name. Let $e$ and $e'$ be well-formed queries with
schemas $S$ and $S'$, and let $c$ be a selection condition all of whose attributes lie in $S$.
Then the query $\sigma_c(e \bowtie e')$, the selection by $c$ of the natural join of $e$ and $e'$,
is equivalent to the query $\sigma_c(e) \bowtie e'$: both are well-formed with the same schema,
and they have equal values on every database conforming to $\mathrm{sch}$.

articles.title: Selection commutes with projection
articles.statement:
Assume the set of attributes is finite. Let $c$ be a
selection condition, $T$ a finite set of attributes containing every attribute of $c$, and $r$ a
finite set of tuples. Then $\sigma_c(\pi_T(r)) = \pi_T(\sigma_c(r))$, where $\sigma_c$ is
selection by $c$ and $\pi_T$ is projection onto $T$.

articles.title: Selection distributes over difference
articles.statement:
Assume the set of attributes is finite. Let $c$
be a selection condition and write $\sigma_c$ for selection by $c$. For finite sets $r$ and $s$
of tuples, $\sigma_c(r \setminus s) = \sigma_c(r) \setminus \sigma_c(s)$.

articles.title: Cascade of selections as a query rewrite
articles.statement:
Fix a database schema $\mathrm{sch}$
assigning a finite set of attributes to each base relation name. Let $e$ be a well-formed query
with schema $S$, and let $c$ and $c'$ be selection conditions all of whose attributes lie in
$S$. Then the query $\sigma_c(\sigma_{c'}(e))$, the selection by $c$ of the selection of $e$ by
$c'$, is equivalent to the query $\sigma_{c' \land c}(e)$, the selection of $e$ by the
conjunction $c' \land c$: both are well-formed with the same schema, and they have equal values
on every database conforming to $\mathrm{sch}$.

articles.title: Cascade of selections
articles.statement:
Write $\sigma_c$ for selection by a selection condition $c$. For
selection conditions $c$ and $c'$ and a finite set $r$ of tuples,
$\sigma_c(\sigma_{c'}(r)) = \sigma_{c' \land c}(r)$: selecting by $c'$ and then by $c$ is the same
as selecting once by the conjunction $c' \land c$.

articles.title: Selection distributes over union
articles.statement:
Assume the set of attributes is finite. Let $c$ be a
selection condition and write $\sigma_c$ for selection by $c$. For finite sets $r$ and $s$ of
tuples, $\sigma_c(r \cup s) = \sigma_c(r) \cup \sigma_c(s)$.

articles.title: Selection
articles.statement:
For a selection condition $c$ and a finite set $r$ of tuples, the selection
$\sigma_c(r)$ is the set of tuples $t \in r$ on which $c$ evaluates to true.

articles.title: Tuple
articles.statement:
For a type $A$ of attributes and a type $D$ of values, a tuple is a partial
assignment of values to attributes: a function that assigns to each attribute $a \in A$ either a
value in $D$ or no value, in which case the tuple is undefined at $a$.

articles.title: Action of a locked schedule
articles.statement:
For $n$ transactions, numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, and a type $X$
of data items, an action of a locked schedule is one of three kinds: a read or write operation; a
lock request, in which a transaction $t$ acquires a lock on an item $x \in X$ in a lock mode $m$
(shared or exclusive); or a release, in which a transaction $t$ releases its lock on an item
$x \in X$.

articles.title: Strict two-phase locking theorem
articles.statement:
If the reads and writes of a locked schedule are
distinct, are covered by locks, and the schedule is legal and strict two-phase, then its reads and
writes form a conflict-serializable schedule.

articles.title: The two-phase locking theorem
articles.statement:
If the reads and writes of a locked schedule are distinct,
are covered by locks, and the schedule is legal and two-phase, then its reads and writes form a
conflict-serializable schedule.

articles.title: Lock mode coverage
articles.statement:
A lock mode $m'$ covers a lock mode $m$ when a lock in mode $m'$
permits what a lock in mode $m$ permits: an exclusive lock covers both modes, and a shared lock
covers only the shared mode.

articles.title: Holding a lock
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a locked schedule, $t$ a transaction, $x$ a data item, $m$ a
lock mode and $p$ a natural number. Transaction $t$ holds a lock on $x$ covering mode $m$ just
before position $p$ of $s$ when there is a position $q < p$ at which $s$ has a lock request by $t$
on $x$ in some mode $m'$ that covers $m$, and for no position $r$ with $q < r < p$ is the action
of $s$ at $r$ a release of $x$ by $t$.

articles.title: Release test
articles.statement:
For a transaction $t$, this Boolean test on the actions of a locked schedule
returns true exactly when the action is a release by $t$ of its lock on some item.

articles.title: Lock compatibility at a point
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ is legal just before position $p$
when, for every data item $x$, all distinct transactions $t \ne t'$ and all lock modes $m$, $m'$:
if $t$ holds a lock on $x$ covering $m$ and $t'$ holds a lock on $x$ covering $m'$ just before
position $p$ of $s$, then $m$ and $m'$ are both the shared mode. In words, two transactions do not
both hold locks on the same item unless both locks are shared.

articles.title: Legal locked schedule
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ of length $\ell$ is legal when it satisfies
lock compatibility at every point $p \le \ell$: just before position $p$, no two distinct
transactions both hold locks on the same item unless both locks are shared.

After the last action the locks no longer change, so the points $p \le \ell$ are all the points.

articles.title: Lock mode
articles.statement:
A lock is held in one of two modes: shared (a read lock) or exclusive (a write
lock).

articles.title: Locked items
articles.statement:
The list of data items locked in a locked schedule $s$: for each lock request
of $s$, in order, the item it locks, so an item appears once for each lock request on it.

articles.title: Lock coverage at a position
articles.statement:
For a locked schedule $s$ and a position $p$: if $s$ has at
position $p$ a read or write $o$ by transaction $t$ on item $x$, then just before position $p$
transaction $t$ holds a lock on $x$ whose mode covers the mode $o$ requires (shared for a read,
exclusive for a write; an exclusive lock covers both modes). If position $p$ holds a lock request
or a release, or lies beyond the end of $s$, the condition holds trivially.

articles.title: Schedules covered by locks
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ is covered by locks when every read or
write is protected by a lock of its transaction: whenever $s$ has at position $p$ a read or write
$o$ by transaction $t$ on item $x$, just before position $p$ transaction $t$ holds a lock on $x$
(acquired at an earlier position and not released since) whose mode covers the mode $o$ requires,
namely shared for a read and exclusive for a write; an exclusive lock covers both modes.

articles.title: Lock mode required by an access
articles.statement:
The lock mode an access requires: shared for a read,
exclusive for a write.

articles.title: Reads and writes of a locked schedule
articles.statement:
For a locked schedule $s$, the schedule of reads and
writes of $s$: its reads and writes in order, with the lock requests and releases erased.

articles.title: Release of the lock requested at a position
articles.statement:
For a locked schedule $s$ and a position $q$:
if $s$ has at position $q$ a lock request (in either mode) by transaction $t$ on item $x$, then
there is a position $r$ with $q < r$ and $r$ less than the length of $s$ at which $s$ has a release
by $t$ of $x$. If position $q$ holds a read, a write or a release, or lies beyond the end of $s$,
the condition holds trivially.

articles.title: Schedules that release every lock
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ releases its locks when every lock
request is followed by a matching release: whenever $s$ has at position $q$ a lock request (in
either mode) by transaction $t$ on item $x$, there is a position $r > q$ at which $s$ has a
release by $t$ of $x$.

In particular, transactions end holding no locks.

articles.title: Strictness at a pair of positions
articles.statement:
For a locked schedule $s$ and positions $p$ and $q$: if
$s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ of item $x$, just before position $p$
transaction $t$ holds an exclusive lock on $x$, and $s$ has at position $q$ a read or write by
$t$, then $q < p$. For every other pair of positions, including positions beyond the end of $s$,
the condition holds trivially.

articles.title: Strict two-phase schedules
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ is strict two-phase when it is two-phase
and every transaction releases its exclusive locks only after its last read or write: whenever
$s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ of item $x$ and just before position $p$
transaction $t$ holds an exclusive lock on $x$, every read or write of $t$ in $s$ occurs at a
position before $p$.

articles.title: Two-phase condition at a pair of positions
articles.statement:
For a locked schedule $s$ and positions $p$ and
$q$: if $s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ and at position $q$ a lock request by
the same transaction $t$, then $q < p$. For every other pair of positions, including positions
beyond the end of $s$, the condition holds trivially.

articles.title: Two-phase schedules
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ is two-phase when every lock request of a
transaction precedes every release of that transaction: whenever $s$ has at position $p$ a release
by transaction $t$ and at position $q$ a lock request by $t$ (on any items, in any mode), then
$q < p$.

articles.title: Well-formed locked schedules
articles.statement:
A locked schedule $s$ (a list of reads, writes, lock
requests and lock releases of transactions) is well formed when its accesses are covered by
locks and it releases its locks: every read or write in $s$ is preceded by a lock request of its
own transaction on its item, in a mode covering the access (shared or exclusive for a read,
exclusive for a write), with no release of that item by that transaction in between; and every
lock request in $s$ by a transaction on an item is followed later in $s$ by a release of that
item by the same transaction.

articles.title: Correctness of the longest common subsequence algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type whose
boolean equality test agrees with equality, let $x$ and $y$ be lists over $\alpha$, and let
$(k, w)$ be the pair returned by the dynamic-programming longest common subsequence algorithm on
$x$ and $y$. Then $w$ has length $k$, $w$ is a subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of both
$x$ and $y$, and every common subsequence of $x$ and $y$ has length at most the length of $w$.

articles.title: Running time of the longest common subsequence algorithm
articles.statement:
For lists $x$ and $y$ of
lengths $m$ and $n$ over a type with a boolean equality test, the abstract time of the
dynamic-programming longest common subsequence algorithm on $x$ and $y$ (its number of table
and reconstruction transitions) is at most $mn + (m + n)$.

articles.title: Longest common subsequence by dynamic programming
articles.statement:
Given lists $x = x_1 \cdots x_m$ and
$y = y_1 \cdots y_n$ over a type with a boolean equality test, fill a table $c_{i,j}$ for
$0 \le i \le m$ and $0 \le j \le n$ by $c_{i,0} = c_{0,j} = 0$, by $c_{i,j} = c_{i-1,j-1} + 1$ when
the test reports $x_i = y_j$, and by $c_{i,j} = \max(c_{i-1,j}, c_{i,j-1})$ otherwise. Then build
a witness $w$ by walking back from $(m, n)$ until $i = 0$ or $j = 0$: when the test reports
$x_i = y_j$, put $x_i$ in front of $w$ and move to $(i-1, j-1)$; otherwise move to $(i-1, j)$ if
$c_{i-1,j} \ge c_{i,j-1}$ and to $(i, j-1)$ if not. The algorithm returns the pair $(c_{m,n}, w)$.

The abstract time counts one step for each table entry $c_{i,j}$ with $i, j \ge 1$ and one for
each backward step taken from a position with $i, j \ge 1$; everything else is free.

articles.title: A subsequence starting with $y$ starts at an occurrence of $y$
articles.statement:
For an element $y$ and lists
$zs$ and $l$, if the list $y$ followed by $zs$ is a subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of $l$,
then there is a list $s$ such that $y$ followed by $s$ is a suffix of $l$ and $zs$ is a subsequence
of $s$.

articles.title: The step of the LIS recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be an element, $rest$ a list, and $t$ a table of
triples $(y, k, zs)$ that satisfies the invariant of the LIS table for $rest$. Let $(b, w)$ be the
result of the scan of $t$ for entries above $x$. Then $(b + 1, w)$ is a table cell for $x$ followed
by $rest$: $w$ is a subsequence of $rest$, the list $x$ followed by $w$ is strictly increasing and
has length $b + 1$, and every strictly increasing list $x$ followed by a subsequence of $rest$ has
length at most $b + 1$.

articles.title: Table cell of the LIS dynamic program
articles.statement:
For an element $x$, lists $s$ and $zs$, and a
natural number $k$, the pair $(k, zs)$ is a table cell for $x$ followed by $s$ when $zs$ is a
subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of $s$, the list $x$ followed by $zs$ is strictly
increasing (each element strictly less than every later one) and has length $k$, and for every
subsequence $zs'$ of $s$ such that $x$ followed by $zs'$ is strictly increasing, the list $x$
followed by $zs'$ has length at most $k$. So $x$ followed by $zs$ is a longest strictly increasing
subsequence of $x$ followed by $s$ that starts with this $x$.

articles.title: The quadratic LIS program attains the optimal length
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a preorder,
the length of the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ is
the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.

articles.title: Length of a longest increasing subsequence
articles.statement:
For a list $xs$ over a preorder and a natural
number $k$, $k$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ when some
strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has length $k$ and every strictly increasing subsequence
of $xs$ has length at most $k$. Here a subsequence need not be contiguous, and strictly increasing
means that each element is strictly less than every later one.

articles.title: Correctness of the quadratic LIS program, by length
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a preorder
and every natural number $k$, the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence
program on $xs$ has length $k$ if and only if $k$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing
subsequence of $xs$.

articles.title: Table of the quadratic LIS program
articles.statement:
The table of a list is a list of triples $(y, k, zs)$,
built from the right: the empty list has the empty table, and the table of $x$ followed by $rest$
is the table $t$ of $rest$ with the entry $(x, b + 1, w)$ put in front, where $(b, w)$ is the
result of the scan of $t$ for entries above $x$. Building the table costs the total cost of these
scans.

articles.title: Invariant of the LIS table
articles.statement:
A table $t$ of triples $(y, k, zs)$ satisfies the invariant for
a list $l$ when every entry $(y, k, zs)$ of $t$ has a list $s$ such that $y$ followed by $s$ is a
suffix of $l$ and $(k, zs)$ is a table cell for $y$ followed by $s$, and conversely, for every
element $y$ and list $s$ such that $y$ followed by $s$ is a suffix of $l$, some entry $(y, k, zs)$
of $t$ makes $(k, zs)$ a table cell for $y$ followed by $s$.

articles.title: Correctness of the quadratic LIS program
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a preorder, the list
returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ is a subsequence of $xs$,
is strictly increasing (each element strictly less than every later one), and is at least as long
as every strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.

articles.title: Running time of the quadratic LIS program
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a
preorder, twice the cost of the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ equals
$n(n + 1)$, so the program costs exactly $n(n + 1)/2$.

The cost model charges one unit for each table entry inspected.

articles.title: Longest increasing subsequence by dynamic programming
articles.statement:
Given a list
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ of elements of a preorder with decidable $<$, this timed computation
builds, from the right, a table recording for each position $i$ a length and a strictly
increasing subsequence starting with $x_i$ (the longest one, by the recurrence
$L_i = 1 + \max \{ L_j : i < j,\ x_i < x_j \}$ with $\max \emptyset = 0$), and returns the
stored subsequence of an entry of largest length, or the empty list when $n = 0$. The cost
is one unit for each table entry inspected: building the entry for position $i$ scans the
entries to its right, and the final scan inspects each entry once.

articles.title: Cost of the scan for the best entry above a value
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a preorder with
decidable $<$. For every value $x \in \alpha$ and every list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where
$y \in \alpha$, $k$ is a natural number and $zs$ is a list over $\alpha$, the scan of $t$ for the
best table entry above $x$ costs exactly the length of $t$.

articles.title: Best table entry above a value
articles.statement:
Given a value $x$ and a list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$,
where $y$ is a value, $k$ a natural number and $zs$ a list of values, this timed computation
returns the pair of $k$ and the list $y$ followed by $zs$ for an entry of $t$ with $x < y$ whose
$k$ is largest among such entries, provided that $k$ is positive; if no entry with $x < y$ has
$k > 0$, it returns $0$ and the empty list. It costs one unit per entry of $t$.

articles.title: Table entry of largest length
articles.statement:
Given a list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where $k$ is a
natural number and $zs$ is a list with elements of the same type as $y$, this timed computation
returns the pair of $k$ and the list $y$ followed by $zs$ for an entry of $t$ whose $k$ is
largest, provided that this $k$ is positive, and returns $0$ and the empty list otherwise (in
particular when $t$ is empty). It costs one unit per entry of $t$.

articles.title: Patience sorting invariant
articles.statement:
For lists $P$ and $t = (t_0, \dots, t_{m-1})$ over a linear
order, the invariant holds for the processed prefix $P$ and the tails $t$ when three conditions
hold: $t$ is strictly increasing; for every $k < m$ some strictly increasing subsequence of $P$ of
length $k + 1$ has last element $t_k$; and every nonempty strictly increasing subsequence of $P$,
of length $\ell$ and with last element $y$, satisfies $\ell \le m$ and $t_{\ell - 1} \le y$.

articles.title: Patience sorting agrees with the quadratic dynamic program
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a
linear order, the value returned by patience sorting on $xs$ equals the length of the list
returned on $xs$ by the quadratic dynamic program for a longest strictly increasing subsequence.

articles.title: Correctness of patience sorting
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the value
returned by patience sorting on $xs$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of
$xs$: some strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has this length, and no strictly increasing
subsequence of $xs$ is longer.

articles.title: Comparison bound for patience sorting
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear
order, patience sorting on $xs$ uses at most $n \lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ comparisons.

articles.title: Patience sorting
articles.statement:
Given a list $xs$ over a linear order, patience sorting runs the patience
scan of $xs$ starting from the empty array of tails and returns the size of the resulting array.
Its cost is the number of comparisons made by the scan.

articles.title: Patience scan
articles.statement:
Given an array of tails and a list over a linear order, the patience scan
applies the patience step to the elements of the list in order: on the empty list it returns the
tails unchanged, and on a list $x$ followed by $xs$ it applies the patience step for $x$ to the
tails and then runs the patience scan of $xs$ from the result. Its cost is the total cost of the
steps.

articles.title: A patience step grows the tails by at most one
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For every
array $t$ over $\alpha$ and every element $x \in \alpha$, the array returned by the patience step
for $x$ on $t$ has size at most the size of $t$ plus $1$.

articles.title: Patience step
articles.statement:
Given an array $t$ of tails and an element $x$ over a linear order, let $i$
be the index returned by the lower-bound binary search for $x$ in $t$. If $i$ is less than the
size of $t$, the step replaces the entry of $t$ at index $i$ by $x$; otherwise it appends $x$ to
$t$. Its cost is the number of comparisons made by the binary search.

When $t$ is sorted increasingly, as it stays throughout the patience scan from the empty array,
$i$ is the first index whose entry is at least $x$, so the step replaces the first entry $\ge x$,
or appends $x$ if there is none. On unsorted input $i$ need not be the first such index.

articles.title: The patience scan preserves the invariant
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a list and $t$ an array of tails over
a linear order such that the patience sorting invariant holds for $P$ and the entries of $t$. Then
for every list $xs$, the invariant holds for $P$ followed by $xs$ and the entries of the array
returned by the patience scan of $xs$ from $t$.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the longest increasing subsequence length
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of elements
of a preorder and all natural numbers $k$ and $k'$, if both $k$ and $k'$ are the length of a
longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$, then $k = k'$.

articles.title: Column count of a parenthesization
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural
numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. The
column count of a parenthesization of $n$ matrices with respect to $p$ is $p_{i+1}$ for a single
leaf naming matrix $i$, and the column count of the right factor for a product node.

articles.title: Matrix-chain cost
articles.statement:
A matrix-chain cost is a pair of natural numbers counting the abstract
events charged by matrix-chain ordering and reconstruction: the number of split candidates
evaluated by the dynamic program, and the number of tree nodes emitted during reconstruction.

articles.title: Dimension-compatible parenthesization
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural
numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. A
parenthesization of $n$ matrices is dimension-compatible with $p$ when, at every product node, the
column count of the left factor equals the row count of the right factor, where row and column
counts are taken with respect to $p$. A single leaf is always dimension-compatible.

articles.title: Valid parenthesization
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural numbers,
regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. A
parenthesization of $n$ matrices is valid for $p$ when its leaf indices, read left to right, are
exactly $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$, and it is dimension-compatible with $p$.

articles.title: Split candidates evaluated by matrix-chain ordering
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural
numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, the matrix-chain ordering algorithm run on the dimensions
$p_0, \dots, p_n$ evaluates exactly $\binom{n+1}{3}$ split candidates.

This is the number of triples $i \le k < j < n$, so the dynamic program evaluates one candidate
for every interval split.

articles.title: Matrix-chain ordering reports the cost of its parenthesization
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and
all natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, the scalar-multiplication cost of the parenthesization
returned by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ equals the
optimal cost it reports.

articles.title: Reported matrix-chain cost is a lower bound
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$, all natural numbers
$p_0, \dots, p_n$ and every parenthesization $T$ of $n$ matrices that is valid for these
dimensions, the optimal cost reported by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm on the dimensions
$p_0, \dots, p_n$ is at most the scalar-multiplication cost of $T$.

articles.title: Matrix-chain ordering returns a valid parenthesization
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and all
natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, the parenthesization returned by the matrix-chain ordering
algorithm on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ is valid: its leaves are the matrices
$0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in order, each exactly once, and at every multiplication node the column
count of the left factor equals the row count of the right factor, where matrix $i$ has $p_i$
rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns.

articles.title: Reconstruction size in matrix-chain ordering
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural numbers
$p_0, \dots, p_n$, the matrix-chain ordering algorithm run on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$
charges exactly $2n - 1$ reconstruction events.

This is the number of nodes of a full binary tree with $n$ leaves.

articles.title: Cubic bound for matrix-chain ordering
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural numbers
$p_0, \dots, p_n$, the total number of events charged by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm run
on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ is at most $3n^3$.

articles.title: Exact event count of matrix-chain ordering
articles.statement:
For every $n \ge 1$ and all natural numbers
$p_0, \dots, p_n$, the total number of events charged by the matrix-chain ordering algorithm run
on the dimensions $p_0, \dots, p_n$ is $\binom{n+1}{3} + (2n - 1)$.

The first term counts evaluated split candidates and the second the nodes of the reconstructed
tree.

articles.title: Matrix-chain ordering
articles.statement:
Given $n \ge 1$ and natural numbers $p_0, \dots, p_n$, where matrix
$i$ of the chain ($0 \le i < n$) has $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns, the algorithm computes,
bottom-up by interval length, values $m_{i,j}$ for $0 \le i \le j < n$: $m_{i,i} = 0$ and, for
$i < j$, $m_{i,j}$ is the least value of $m_{i,k} + m_{k+1,j} + p_i p_{k+1} p_{j+1}$ over
$i \le k < j$, and the first split point $k$ attaining it is recorded. It then rebuilds a
parenthesization of the whole chain from the recorded split points and returns $m_{0,n-1}$
together with this parenthesization. One event is charged per evaluated split candidate and one
per reconstructed tree node.

articles.title: Leaf indices of a parenthesization
articles.statement:
The leaf indices of a parenthesization of $n$ matrices
form the list of indices in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ obtained by reading its leaves from left to
right: $[i]$ for a single leaf naming matrix $i$, and the concatenation of the lists of the left
and right factors for a product node.

articles.title: Parenthesization
articles.statement:
A parenthesization of $n$ matrices is a full binary tree whose leaves are
labeled by indices in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$: either a single leaf naming matrix $i$, or a product
node with a left and a right parenthesization as factors. Labels may be repeated, omitted, or out
of order.

articles.title: Matrix-chain result
articles.statement:
A matrix-chain result for $n$ matrices pairs a natural number, the
reported optimal scalar multiplication count, with a parenthesization of $n$ matrices, the
reported optimal parenthesization. The structure itself does not require the count to be minimal
or to be attained by the parenthesization.

articles.title: Row count of a parenthesization
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector of natural
numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$ columns. The
row count of a parenthesization of $n$ matrices with respect to $p$ is $p_i$ for a single leaf
naming matrix $i$, and the row count of the left factor for a product node.

articles.title: Scalar multiplication count of a parenthesization
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_n)$ be a vector
of natural numbers, regarding matrix $i$ (for $0 \le i < n$) as having $p_i$ rows and $p_{i+1}$
columns, and let $r(T)$ and $c(T)$ be the row and column counts of a parenthesization $T$ with
respect to $p$. The scalar multiplication count of a single leaf is $0$, and that of a product
node with factors $L$ and $R$ is the sum of the counts of $L$ and $R$ plus $r(L)\,c(L)\,c(R)$.

articles.title: Total matrix-chain cost
articles.statement:
The total of a matrix-chain cost is its number of candidate
evaluations plus its number of reconstruction nodes.

articles.title: Maximum subarray sum of a concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear
order such that $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$, and let $L$ and $R$ be
lists over $\alpha$. Suppose that $l$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of $L$, $r$
is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of $R$, $s$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty
suffix of $L$, and $p$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty prefix of $R$. Then
$\max(\max(l, r), s + p)$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of the concatenation of
$L$ followed by $R$.

articles.title: Maximum subarray sum after appending an element
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid
with a linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. Let $p$ be a list over
$\alpha$, let $e$ be the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix of $p$, and let $b$ be the maximum sum
of a nonempty contiguous sublist of $p$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the maximum sum of a
nonempty contiguous sublist of the list obtained by appending $x$ to $p$ is
$\max(b, \max(x, e + x))$.

articles.title: Maximum suffix sum after appending an element
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a
linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. If $e$ is the maximum sum of a
nonempty suffix of a list $p$ over $\alpha$, then for every $x \in \alpha$ the maximum sum of a
nonempty suffix of the list obtained by appending $x$ to $p$ is $\max(x, e + x)$.

Such a suffix is either $[x]$ alone or a nonempty suffix of $p$ followed by $x$.

articles.title: Kadane's algorithm returns an attained sum
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a
linear order such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. If Kadane's algorithm returns a value
$m$ on a list $L$ over $\alpha$, then some nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$.

articles.title: Maximum prefix sum
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. For a list $xs$
over $\alpha$ and $p \in \alpha$, $p$ is the maximum prefix sum of $xs$ when some nonempty prefix
of $xs$ has sum $p$ and every nonempty prefix of $xs$ has sum at most $p$.

articles.title: Being the maximum subarray sum
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a
linear order, an element $m \in \alpha$ is the maximum subarray sum of $L$ when some nonempty
contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$ and every nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum at
most $m$.

articles.title: Being the maximum suffix sum
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a
linear order, an element $e \in \alpha$ is the maximum suffix sum of $L$ when some nonempty suffix
of $L$ has sum $e$ and every nonempty suffix of $L$ has sum at most $e$. A nonempty suffix is a
contiguous run ending at the last element of $L$.

Kadane's scan maintains its first accumulator as the maximum suffix sum of the elements read
so far.

articles.title: Invariant of Kadane's scan
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order such
that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. Let $p$ be a list over $\alpha$, let $e$ be the maximum
sum of a nonempty suffix of $p$, and let $b$ be the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous sublist
of $p$. Then for every list $r$ over $\alpha$, the value that Kadane's scan from the accumulators
$e$ and $b$ returns on $r$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous sublist of the list $p$
followed by $r$.

articles.title: Cost of Kadane's scan
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. For all
accumulators $e, b \in \alpha$ and every list $L$ over $\alpha$ of length $n$, Kadane's scan of
$L$ from the accumulators $e$ and $b$ costs exactly $3n$.

articles.title: Kadane's scan
articles.statement:
Given accumulators $e, b$ in an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear
order, the scan over the empty list returns $b$ at cost $0$. Over a list with first element $x$
and remaining elements $L$, it sets $e' = \max(x, e + x)$ and returns the result of the scan of
$L$ from the accumulators $e'$ and $\max(b, e')$, at cost $3$ plus the cost of that scan.

Here $e$ is the best sum of a nonempty run ending at the last element read and $b$ is the best
sum of any nonempty run read so far.

articles.title: Divide-and-conquer core of maximum subarray
articles.statement:
For lists over an additive monoid with a
linear order: on the empty list it returns $0$ and on a one-element list $[x]$ it returns $x$,
both at no cost. On a list of length $n \ge 2$, let $m = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, let $l$ and $r$ be
its results on the first $m$ elements and on the remaining $n - m$ elements, let $s$ be the best
nonempty suffix sum of the first $m$ elements as computed by the suffix scan, and let $p$ be the
prefix scan of the remaining elements. It returns $\max(\max(l, r), s + p)$, at the cost of
these four computations plus $3$.

articles.title: Cost recurrence of divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
articles.statement:
The function
$T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $T(n) = 0$ for $n \le 1$ and
$T(n) = T(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + T(n - \lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + 2n + 3$ for $n \ge 2$.

articles.title: Divide and conquer agrees with Kadane's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with
a linear order such that $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$. For every list
$xs$ over $\alpha$, the divide-and-conquer maximum subarray algorithm and Kadane's algorithm
return the same result on $xs$.

articles.title: Correctness of divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid
