with a linear order such that $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$. For every
list $xs$ over $\alpha$ and every $m \in \alpha$, the divide-and-conquer algorithm returns $m$ on
$xs$ if and only if $m$ is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of $xs$.

articles.title: Running time of divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid
with a linear order. On a nonempty list over $\alpha$ of length $n$, the cost $T$ of the
divide-and-conquer maximum subarray algorithm satisfies
$T + 3 \le 2n\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 3n$, that is, $T \le 2n\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 3(n - 1)$.

articles.title: Divide-and-conquer maximum subarray
articles.statement:
The CLRS algorithm FIND-MAXIMUM-SUBARRAY over an
additive monoid with a linear order, returning only the sum. On the empty list it returns no
value, at no cost. On a nonempty list it returns the value of the divide-and-conquer core on that
list, at the same cost; the core splits a list of length $n \ge 2$ after its first
$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ elements and returns the largest of its results on the two parts and the
best nonempty suffix sum of the first part plus the prefix scan of the second part.

When $b \le c$ implies $a + b \le a + c$ and $b + a \le c + a$, the value returned on a nonempty
list is the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous run of the list.

articles.title: Correctness of Kadane's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order
such that $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$. For every list $L$ over $\alpha$ and every
$m \in \alpha$, Kadane's algorithm returns $m$ on $L$ if and only if $m$ is the maximum sum of a
nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$: some nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum $m$, and
every nonempty contiguous sublist of $L$ has sum at most $m$.

articles.title: Cost of Kadane's algorithm
articles.statement:
Over an additive monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, Kadane's
algorithm on a list of length $n \ge 1$ costs exactly $3(n - 1)$ operations, and on the empty
list it costs $0$.

articles.title: Kadane's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type with an additive monoid
structure. On the empty list, Kadane's algorithm returns no value. On a list
$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ of elements of $\alpha$ with $n \ge 1$, it sets $e = b = x_1$; then for
$i = 2, \dots, n$ in turn it replaces $e$ by $\max(x_i, e + x_i)$ and then $b$ by $\max(b, e)$;
finally it returns $b$. Each of the steps $i = 2, \dots, n$ is charged three operations, and
nothing else is charged.

When $u \le v$ implies $u + w \le v + w$ for all $u, v, w \in \alpha$, after each step $e$ is the
largest sum of a nonempty contiguous run ending at the element just read, and $b$ is the largest
sum of a nonempty contiguous run among the elements read so far.

articles.title: A list with a maximum subarray sum is nonempty
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a
linear order. If an element $m \in \alpha$ is the maximum subarray sum of a list $L$ over
$\alpha$, then $L$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Prefix scan
articles.statement:
For lists over an additive monoid with a linear order, the prefix scan returns
$0$ on the empty list at no cost, and $x$ on a one-element list $[x]$ at cost $2$. On a list with
first element $x$ and nonempty tail $t$ it returns $\max(x, x + b)$, where $b$ is the prefix scan
of $t$, at the cost of the scan of $t$ plus $2$.

When $u \le v$ implies $a + u \le a + v$, the value on a nonempty list is the maximum sum of a
nonempty prefix of the list.

articles.title: Correctness of the suffix scan
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid with a linear order. For
every nonempty list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the suffix scan of $xs$ returns a pair whose first
component is the sum of $xs$ and whose second component is the maximum sum of a nonempty suffix
of $xs$.

articles.title: Right-to-left suffix scan
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive monoid carrying a linear order.
For a nonempty list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ in $\alpha$, this timed computation returns the pair
$(x_1 + \dots + x_n, s)$, where $s$ is the maximum of the suffix sums $x_i + \dots + x_n$ over
$1 \le i \le n$. It scans from the right: the step for $x_i$ forms $x_i + (x_{i+1} + \dots + x_n)$
and takes its maximum with the best suffix sum found so far, at a cost of $2$ time units per
element, $2n$ in total. On the empty list it returns $(0, 0)$ at no cost.

articles.title: Kadane's algorithm bounds every nonempty run
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type
with an additive monoid structure in which $b \le c$ implies $b + a \le c + a$. If Kadane's
algorithm returns the value $m$ on a list $L$ over $\alpha$, then every nonempty contiguous run
of $L$ has sum at most $m$.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the maximum subarray sum
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type with an
additive monoid structure, and let $L$ be a list over $\alpha$. If $m, m' \in \alpha$ are both
maximum subarray sums of $L$, meaning that each is the sum of some nonempty contiguous run of $L$
and bounds the sum of every nonempty contiguous run of $L$, then $m = m'$.

articles.title: Covering recurrence is bottom iff no selection reaches the target
articles.statement: The covering recurrence is `⊥` exactly when no selection reaches the target.

articles.title: Covering recurrence for multiple-choice knapsack
articles.statement:
The covering recurrence: the best total value of a selection with total weight at least
`L`, `⊥` if none exists. The residual target `L - weight` is truncated subtraction.

articles.title: Packing recurrence is bottom iff no selection fits the capacity
articles.statement: The packing recurrence is `⊥` exactly when no selection fits the capacity.

articles.title: Packing recurrence for multiple-choice knapsack
articles.statement:
The packing recurrence: the best total value of a selection with total weight at most `c`,
`⊥` if none exists.

articles.title: Covering recurrence is attained by a covering selection
articles.statement:
The covering recurrence is attained: a finite value is the value of a selection of total
weight at least `L`.

articles.title: Packing recurrence is attained by a feasible selection
articles.statement: The packing recurrence is attained: a finite value is the value of a feasible selection.

articles.title: Multiple-choice knapsack selection
articles.statement: A selection chooses exactly one item from each group, in group order.

articles.title: Knapsack item with weight and value
articles.statement: A knapsack item with a natural weight and a value in `β`.

articles.title: Covering recurrence bounds every covering selection's value
articles.statement:
The covering recurrence is an upper bound: every selection of total weight at least `L` has
value at most `bestCovering`.

articles.title: Packing recurrence bounds every feasible selection's value
articles.statement:
The packing recurrence is an upper bound: every feasible selection's value is at most
`bestPacking`.

articles.title: Packing table computes the packing recurrence
articles.statement: The table computes the recurrence at every capacity `0, …, capacity`.

articles.title: Bottom-up packing table for multiple-choice knapsack
articles.statement:
The bottom-up packing table: for each suffix of the groups, the row of best values at
capacities `0, …, capacity`, each row computed from the next one by one scan of its group per
cell.

articles.title: Total value of a knapsack selection
articles.statement: The total value of a selection.

articles.title: Total weight of a knapsack selection
articles.statement: The total weight of a selection.

articles.title: Expected search cost of a binary search tree
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be an additive commutative monoid,
let $n$ be a natural number, and let $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1} \in R$ (key weights) and
$q_0, \dots, q_n \in R$ (dummy-key weights) be given. Let $T$ be a binary tree whose nodes are
labelled by elements of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and whose inorder traversal is $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, so
each key labels exactly one node and $T$ has exactly $n + 1$ empty subtrees. The depth of a node
or empty subtree is its distance from the root, the root having depth $0$; write $d(k)$ for the
depth of the node labelled $k$ and $\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n$ for the depths of the empty subtrees
listed from left to right. The expected search cost of $T$ is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (d(k) + 1) \cdot p_k + \sum_{i=0}^{n} (\ell_i + 1) \cdot q_i,$$

where $m \cdot x$ denotes the $m$-fold sum of $x$ in $R$.

articles.title: Optimal BST with no keys
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid in
which addition is monotone. For $n = 0$ keys and a single dummy weight $q_0 \in R$, the optimal
binary search tree procedure returns the $1 \times 1$ cost table whose only entry is $q_0$, the
empty $0 \times 0$ root table, and running time $0$.

articles.title: The optimal BST procedure finds the minimum expected search cost
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly
ordered additive commutative monoid in which addition is monotone, let $n$ be a natural number,
and let $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}, q_0, \dots, q_n \in R$. Let $e$ be the cost table returned by the
optimal binary search tree procedure on these weights. Then $e[0][n]$ is the least expected
search cost, with key weights $p$ and dummy-key weights $q$, of a binary tree whose nodes are
labelled by elements of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and whose inorder traversal is $0, 1, \dots, n-1$:
some such tree has expected search cost $e[0][n]$, and every such tree has expected search cost
at least $e[0][n]$.

articles.title: Optimal BST table recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid
in which addition is monotone, let $n$ be a natural number, let
$p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}, q_0, \dots, q_n \in R$, and let $e$ and $\rho$ be the cost table and the
root table returned by the optimal binary search tree procedure on these weights. For
$a \le b \le n$ write $w(a, b) = \sum_{i=a}^{b-1} p_i + \sum_{i=a}^{b} q_i$. Then
$e[a][a] = q_a$ for every $a \le n$, and for all $a < b \le n$ there is an $r$ with
$a \le r < b$ such that $\rho[a][b-1] = r$, $e[a][b] = e[a][r] + e[r+1][b] + w(a, b)$, and for
every $t$ with $a \le t < b$

$$e[a][b] \le e[a][t] + e[t+1][b] + w(a, b),$$

with strict inequality when $t < r$. So $e[a][b]$ is the minimum of
$e[a][t] + e[t+1][b] + w(a, b)$ over $a \le t < b$, and $r$ is the earliest $t$ attaining it.

articles.title: Cubic running time of the optimal BST procedure
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered additive
commutative monoid in which addition is monotone. For every natural number $n$ and all
$p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}, q_0, \dots, q_n \in R$, the running time $T$ of the optimal binary search
tree procedure on these weights, which is the number of candidate roots it examines, satisfies
$n^3 \le 6T$ and $T \le n^3$.

articles.title: Exact running time of the optimal BST procedure
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered additive
commutative monoid in which addition is monotone. For every natural number $n$ and all
$p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}, q_0, \dots, q_n \in R$, the running time of the optimal binary search tree
procedure on these weights, which is the number of candidate roots it examines, equals
$\binom{n+2}{3}$.

articles.title: Optimal binary search tree procedure
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered additive commutative
monoid in which addition is monotone, let $n$ be a natural number, and let
$p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}, q_0, \dots, q_n \in R$. The procedure (CLRS OPTIMAL-BST, with keys indexed
from $0$) fills a cost table $e$ of size $(n+1) \times (n+1)$, an auxiliary weight table $w$ of
the same size, and a root table of size $n \times n$ with entries in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ or
empty; all entries start as $0$ or empty. First it sets $e[a][a] = w[a][a] = q_a$ for
$a = 0, \dots, n$. Then for $\ell = 1, \dots, n$ in increasing order and, for each $\ell$, for
$a = 0, \dots, n - \ell$ in increasing order, with $b = a + \ell$, it sets
$w[a][b] = w[a][b-1] + p_{b-1} + q_b$ and examines the candidate roots $r = a, \dots, b-1$ in
increasing order, replacing the current best only when the candidate value
$e[a][r] + e[r+1][b] + w[a][b]$ is strictly smaller. It stores the resulting minimum in $e[a][b]$
and the earliest minimizing $r$ at position $(a, b-1)$ of the root table. The procedure returns
the cost table $e$ and the root table, with running time equal to the total number of candidate
roots examined.

articles.title: Correctness of bottom-up rod cutting
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
linear order in which addition is monotone, and let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ be prices in $\alpha$,
$p_i$ being the price of a piece of length $i$. The value returned by bottom-up rod cutting on $p$
is the greatest revenue of a composition of $n$: it equals $p_{b_1} + \dots + p_{b_m}$ for some
composition $(b_1, \dots, b_m)$ of $n$ into positive parts, and it is at least this sum for every
such composition.

Prices may be negative; every piece of the rod must be sold, so there is no option to discard
material.

articles.title: Bottom-up rod cutting takes quadratic time
articles.statement:
For prices $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ in an
additive commutative monoid with a linear order, the cost $T$ of bottom-up rod cutting on $p$, the
number of first-piece candidates it evaluates, satisfies $n^2 \le 2T$ and $T \le n^2$.

articles.title: Cost of bottom-up rod cutting as a sum over rows
articles.statement:
For prices $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ in an
additive commutative monoid with a linear order, the cost of bottom-up rod cutting on $p$ (the
number of first-piece candidates it evaluates) equals $\sum_{j=0}^{n} j$.

Row $j$ of the table contributes the $j$ candidates of its scan.

articles.title: Twice the cost of bottom-up rod cutting
articles.statement:
For prices $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ in an additive
commutative monoid with a linear order, the cost $T$ of bottom-up rod cutting on $p$ (the number of
first-piece candidates it evaluates) satisfies $2T = n(n + 1)$.

articles.title: Exact cost of bottom-up rod cutting
articles.statement:
For prices $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ in an additive
commutative monoid with a linear order, the cost of bottom-up rod cutting on $p$ (the number of
first-piece candidates it evaluates) is the triangular number $n(n + 1)/2$, whatever the prices.

articles.title: Bottom-up rod cutting on the empty rod
articles.statement:
For the empty price vector ($n = 0$) over an
additive commutative monoid with a linear order, bottom-up rod cutting returns $0$ at cost $0$.

articles.title: Bottom-up rod cutting
articles.statement:
Given prices $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ in an additive commutative
monoid $\alpha$ with a linear order, $p_i$ being the price of a piece of length $i$, bottom-up rod
cutting fills a table $r_0, \dots, r_n$ in increasing order by $r_0 = 0$ and
$r_j = \max_{1 \le i \le j} (p_i + r_{j-i})$ for $1 \le j \le n$, and returns $r_n$. Its cost is
the number of candidates $p_i + r_{j-i}$ it evaluates, one for each pair $1 \le i \le j \le n$.

articles.title: Revenue is additive under concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ be prices in an
additive commutative monoid, and define the revenue of a composition $(b_1, \dots, b_m)$ of some
$k \le n$ to be $p_{b_1} + \dots + p_{b_m}$. If $c$ is a composition of $k$ and $d$ is a
composition of $l$ with $k + l \le n$, then the revenue of their concatenation, a composition of
$k + l$, is the revenue of $c$ plus the revenue of $d$.

articles.title: Revenue of an uncut rod
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ be prices in an additive commutative
monoid, $p_i$ being the price of a piece of length $i$. For $0 < k \le n$, the revenue of the
one-part composition $(k)$ of $k$ is $p_k$.

articles.title: The empty rod earns nothing
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n)$ be prices in an additive
commutative monoid. Every composition of $0$, namely the empty one, has revenue $0$ with respect
to $p$.

articles.title: Revenue of a rod composition
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_{n-1})$ be a price vector with
entries in an additive commutative monoid, where $p_{\ell - 1}$ is the price of a piece of length
$\ell$. For $k \le n$ and a composition $(b_1, \dots, b_m)$ of $k$ into positive parts, its revenue
is $p_{b_1 - 1} + \dots + p_{b_m - 1}$, the total price of its pieces.

articles.title: Reconstructed pieces are the saved first cuts
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a price vector of length $n$
with entries in an additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order. Let $s$ be the vector of
saved first cuts computed by the extended bottom-up rod-cutting algorithm, of length $n$, whose
entry $j - 1$ is the cut saved for length $j$, and let $(b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ be the composition
of $n$ returned by the rod-cutting reconstruction. For every $i < m$, the index
$n - (b_0 + \dots + b_{i-1}) - 1$ lies within $s$ and the entry of $s$ at this index is $b_i$:
the $i$-th piece is the first cut saved for the remaining length $n - (b_0 + \dots + b_{i-1})$.

articles.title: Rod-cutting reconstruction is optimal
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a price vector of length $n$ with
entries in a linearly ordered additive commutative monoid (addition is monotone). The composition
of $n$ returned by the rod-cutting reconstruction has the greatest revenue among all compositions
of $n$: its revenue is at least the revenue of every composition of $n$.

articles.title: Reconstruction earns the final saved revenue
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a price vector of length $n$
with entries in an additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order, and let
$r = (r_0, \dots, r_n)$ be the revenue table computed by the extended bottom-up rod-cutting
algorithm. The revenue of the composition of $n$ returned by the rod-cutting reconstruction
equals $r_n$.

articles.title: Cost of rod-cutting reconstruction
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a price vector of length $n$ with entries
in an additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order. The rod-cutting reconstruction charges
exactly $n(n+1)/2 + m$ events, where $m$ is the number of pieces of the composition of $n$ it
returns: one event per evaluated first-cut candidate and one per emitted piece.

articles.title: Rod-cutting reconstruction on the empty rod
articles.statement:
For the empty price vector (rod length
$0$) with entries in an additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order, the rod-cutting
reconstruction returns the empty composition of $0$ and charges no events.

articles.title: Rod cutting with reconstruction
articles.statement:
Given a price vector $p$ of length $n$ with entries in an
additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order, where entry $\ell - 1$ is the price of a
piece of length $\ell$, first run the extended bottom-up rod-cutting algorithm to obtain the saved
first cuts $s_1, \dots, s_n$ (with $s_j$ stored as entry $j - 1$ of its cut vector). Then,
starting from the remaining length $L = n$, repeatedly emit a piece of length $s_L$ and replace
$L$ by $L - s_L$ until $L = 0$. The result is the composition of $n$ formed by the emitted pieces
in order. Its cost is the cost of the extended algorithm plus one event per emitted piece;
allocation and arithmetic are free.

articles.title: Saved revenues are optimal
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a price vector of length $n$ with entries in a
linearly ordered additive commutative monoid (addition is monotone), and let
$r = (r_0, \dots, r_n)$ be the revenue table computed by the extended bottom-up rod-cutting
algorithm. For every $j \le n$, $r_j$ is the greatest revenue of a composition of $j$: some
composition of $j$ has revenue $r_j$, and every composition of $j$ has revenue at most $r_j$.

articles.title: The saved first cut attains the saved revenue
articles.statement:
Let $p = (p_0, \dots, p_{n-1})$ be a
price vector with entries in an additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order, where
$p_{\ell - 1}$ is the price of a piece of length $\ell$. Let $r = (r_0, \dots, r_n)$ be the
revenue table and $s = (s_1, \dots, s_n)$ the saved first cuts computed by the extended bottom-up
rod-cutting algorithm, with $s_j$ stored as entry $j - 1$ of the cut vector. For every $j$ with
$0 < j \le n$, the cut $\ell = s_j$ satisfies $1 \le \ell \le j$ and
$p_{\ell - 1} + r_{j - \ell} = r_j$, and every $\ell'$ with $1 \le \ell' < \ell$ satisfies
$p_{\ell' - 1} + r_{j - \ell'} < r_j$.

articles.title: The extended algorithm computes the same revenue
articles.statement:
For every price vector of length $n$
with entries in an additive commutative monoid carrying a linear order, the last entry $r_n$ of
the revenue table computed by the extended bottom-up rod-cutting algorithm equals the value
returned by the bottom-up rod-cutting algorithm.

articles.title: Running time of extended bottom-up rod cutting
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative
monoid with a linear order. For every vector of $n$ prices in $\alpha$, the extended bottom-up
rod-cutting algorithm has cost exactly $n(n+1)/2$, whatever the prices are.

articles.title: Extended bottom-up rod cutting on the empty rod
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative
monoid with a linear order. On the empty price vector (rod length $0$), the extended bottom-up
rod-cutting algorithm returns the revenue table whose single entry is $0$ together with the empty
first-cut table, at cost $0$.

articles.title: Extended bottom-up rod cutting
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
linear order, and let $p_1, \dots, p_n \in \alpha$ be the prices of pieces of length
$1, \dots, n$ (the price vector's entry $i - 1$ is $p_i$). The algorithm fills a revenue table
$r_0, \dots, r_n$ and a first-cut table $s_1, \dots, s_n$ for the lengths $j = 0, 1, \dots, n$ in
increasing order: $r_0 = 0$, and for $j \ge 1$ it scans the candidates $p_i + r_{j-i}$ for
$i = 1, \dots, j$ in increasing order of $i$, starting from the candidate for $i = 1$ and moving
to a later candidate only when it is strictly larger than the current one. Then $r_j$ is the
largest candidate and $s_j$ is the least $i$ whose candidate equals $r_j$. The result is the pair
of tables, where $r_j$ is the revenue vector's entry $j$ and $s_j$ is the cut vector's entry
$j - 1$, and the cost is one tick per evaluated candidate, so $j$ ticks for length $j$.

articles.title: The memoized auxiliary fills the cache up to the requested length
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linearly ordered additive commutative monoid (that is, $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$), let
$p = (p_1, \dots, p_n) \in \alpha^n$ be prices, where $p_i$ is the price of a piece of length $i$,
and let $j \le n$. If the memoized rod-cutting auxiliary is run on length $j$ with the cache
$(c_0, \dots, c_n)$ whose entries are all unknown, then for every $k \le j$ entry $k$ of the
returned cache is a known value, and that value is the greatest composition revenue over
compositions of $k$.

articles.title: Correctness of the memoized rod-cutting auxiliary
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
additive commutative monoid (that is, $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$) and let
$p = (p_1, \dots, p_n) \in \alpha^n$ be prices, where $p_i$ is the price of a piece of length $i$.
Call a cache $c = (c_0, \dots, c_n)$, whose entries are each unknown or a value in $\alpha$, valid
if for every known entry $c_k = v$ the value $v$ is the greatest composition revenue over
compositions of $k$. If $c$ is valid, $j \le n$, and the memoized rod-cutting auxiliary on length
$j$ and cache $c$ returns the value $q$ and the cache $c'$, then $q$ is the greatest composition
revenue over compositions of $j$, the cache $c'$ is valid, and $c'_j = q$.

articles.title: A cache hit in memoized rod cutting returns at once
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative
monoid with a linear order, let $p \in \alpha^n$ be a vector of prices, let $c = (c_0, \dots, c_n)$
be a cache whose entries are each unknown or a value in $\alpha$, and let $j \le n$. If $c_j$ is a
known value $v$, then the memoized rod-cutting auxiliary on length $j$ and cache $c$ returns $v$
and the unchanged cache $c$, and charges exactly one event.

articles.title: The memoized auxiliary preserves known and higher cache entries
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a linear order, let $p \in \alpha^n$ be a vector of prices, let
$c = (c_0, \dots, c_n)$ be a cache whose entries are each unknown or a value in $\alpha$, let
$j \le n$, and let $c'$ be the cache returned by the memoized rod-cutting auxiliary on length $j$
and cache $c$. Then for every $k \le n$, if $c_k$ is a known value $v$, then $c'_k = v$; and for
every $k$ with $j < k \le n$, $c'_k = c_k$.

articles.title: Memoized rod-cutting auxiliary (CLRS MEMOIZED-CUT-ROD-AUX)
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a linear order, let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n) \in \alpha^n$ be prices, where
$p_i$ is the price of a piece of length $i$, and let $c = (c_0, \dots, c_n)$ be a cache whose
entries are each either unknown or a value in $\alpha$. For $j \le n$ the procedure returns a value
and an updated cache, and counts events, as follows. It first charges one event for probing $c_j$.
If $c_j$ is a known value $v$, it returns $v$ and the unchanged cache $c$. Otherwise, if $j = 0$,
it charges one event for a write and returns $0$ with $c_0$ set to $0$. If $j \ge 1$, then for
$i = 1, \dots, j$ in turn it calls itself on length $j - i$ with the cache returned by the previous
call (starting from $c$), obtaining a value $q_i$, and charges one event for the candidate
$p_i + q_i$. It then charges one event for a write and returns
$q = \max(p_1 + q_1, \dots, p_j + q_j)$ with entry $j$ of the last returned cache set to $q$. The
event count is the total over the whole recursion.

Known entries are returned as they are, whatever their sign, including at length zero.

articles.title: Correctness of memoized rod cutting
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered additive commutative
monoid (that is, $a \le b$ implies $a + c \le b + c$) and let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n) \in \alpha^n$
be prices, where $p_i$ is the price of a piece of length $i$. The value returned by the memoized
cut-rod procedure on $p$ is the greatest composition revenue over compositions of $n$: it is the
revenue of some composition of $n$, and it is at least the revenue of every composition of $n$.

articles.title: Event count of memoized rod cutting
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
linear order and let $p \in \alpha^n$ be a vector of prices. The memoized cut-rod procedure on $p$
charges exactly $n^2 + 2n + 2$ events, where one event is charged per cache probe, per first-cut
candidate, and per cache write.

Allocation, initialization, arithmetic, comparisons and control are not charged.

articles.title: Memoized rod cutting on the empty rod
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with
a linear order. For the empty price vector ($n = 0$), the memoized cut-rod procedure returns $0$
and charges exactly $2$ events: one cache probe and one cache write.

articles.title: The memoized cut-rod procedure (CLRS MEMOIZED-CUT-ROD)
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive
commutative monoid with a linear order and let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_n) \in \alpha^n$ be prices, where
$p_i$ is the price of a piece of length $i$. The procedure runs the memoized rod-cutting auxiliary
on length $n$ with the cache $(c_0, \dots, c_n)$ whose entries are all unknown, and returns the
value it computes, discarding the final cache. Its event count is that of the auxiliary call.

articles.title: Correctness of recursive CUT-ROD
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
linear order for which addition is monotone, and let $p_1, \dots, p_n \in \alpha$ be prices,
$p_i$ being the price of a piece of length $i$. The value returned by recursive CUT-ROD on these
prices is the greatest revenue of a composition of $n$: it equals the revenue
$p_{i_1} + \dots + p_{i_k}$ of some composition $n = i_1 + \dots + i_k$ into positive parts,
and it is at least the revenue of every such composition.

Every piece is sold: negative prices do not create an option to discard part of the rod.

articles.title: Running time of recursive CUT-ROD
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with a
linear order, and let $p_1, \dots, p_n \in \alpha$ be prices. Recursive CUT-ROD on these prices,
which charges one tick per invocation, makes exactly $2^n$ invocations, counting the root call
and every call on an empty rod, whatever the prices are.

articles.title: Recursive CUT-ROD
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an additive commutative monoid with a linear order,
and let $p_1, \dots, p_n \in \alpha$ be prices, $p_i$ being the price of a piece of length $i$.
Recursive CUT-ROD returns $r(n)$, where $r(0) = 0$ and, for $1 \le j \le n$,
$r(j) = \max(p_1 + r(j - 1), p_2 + r(j - 2), \dots, p_j + r(0))$. The first cuts
$i = 1, \dots, j$ are scanned in increasing order and every $r(j - i)$ is recomputed by a fresh
recursive call, without memoization. One cost tick is charged at every invocation, including
the root call and every call on an empty rod.

articles.title: Optimality of exact subset sum for distinct positive inputs
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a list of
distinct positive natural numbers, $t$ a positive natural number, and $r$ the value returned by
the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$. Then $r$ is the sum of some sublist of
$x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous), $r \le t$, and every sublist of $x$ whose sum
is at most $t$ has sum at most $r$.

These are the hypotheses of CLRS, Section 35.5; the proof does not use them.

articles.title: Optimality of exact subset sum
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a list of natural numbers, $t$ a natural
number, and $r$ the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$ with target $t$.
Then $r$ is the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous),
$r \le t$, and every sublist of $x$ whose sum is at most $t$ has sum at most $r$.

The entries of $x$ may be zero or repeated.

articles.title: Exact subset sum returns the maximum of the computed sums
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of natural
numbers and every natural number $t$, the value returned by the exact subset sum algorithm on $x$
with target $t$ equals $\max(\cdots\max(\max(0, s_1), s_2)\cdots, s_k)$, where $s_1, \dots, s_k$
is the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$.

articles.title: The number of computed sums is at most two to the power of the input length
articles.statement:
For every
list $x$ of natural numbers, of length $n$, and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums
computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $2^n$.

articles.title: The number of computed sums is at most the input total plus one
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of
natural numbers with sum $S$ and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the
exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $S + 1$.

articles.title: The number of computed sums is at most the target plus one
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of
natural numbers and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset
sum traversal on $x$ with target $t$ has length at most $t + 1$.

articles.title: Characterization of the exact subset sum list
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a list of natural numbers,
$t$ a natural number, and $L$ the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal
on $x$ with target $t$. A natural number $z$ belongs to $L$ if and only if $z \le t$ and $z$ is
the sum of some sublist of $x$ (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous).

articles.title: Prefixes of the powers of two attain every sum
articles.statement:
Let $i \le n$ be natural numbers. On the
list $1, 2, 4, \dots, 2^{i-1}$ (the first $i$ entries of $1, 2, \dots, 2^{n-1}$) with target
$2^n - 1$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal is exactly
$0, 1, 2, \dots, 2^i - 1$ in increasing order.

articles.title: The exact subset sum list is strictly increasing
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of natural numbers
and every natural number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal
on $x$ with target $t$ is strictly increasing; in particular it has no repeated entries.

articles.title: Zero is always a computed sum
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of natural numbers and every natural
number $t$, the final list of sums computed by the exact subset sum traversal on $x$ with target
$t$ contains $0$.

articles.title: Attainable sums in exact subset sum
articles.statement:
Given a list $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of natural
numbers and a target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, this timed procedure starts from the list $L_0 = (0)$
and, for $i = 1, \dots, n$ in order, forms $L_i$ from $L_{i-1}$ in four steps: add $x_i$ to
every entry of $L_{i-1}$; merge $L_{i-1}$ with this shifted list (the standard merge of two
lists, comparing entries with $\le$); delete adjacent repeated values; and keep only the values
at most $t$. It returns $L_n$. The counted events are the initial assignment and, in each
phase, one event per addition, one per merge comparison, one per comparison of adjacent
values, one per comparison with $t$, and one for the phase assignment.

articles.title: Exponential lower bound for exact subset sum on powers of two
articles.statement:
For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on the list $(2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{n-1})$
(empty when $n = 0$) with target $2^n - 1$ makes at least $2^n - 1$ counted events.

articles.title: Exponential upper bound for exact subset sum
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of $n$ natural numbers
and every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most
$1 + n + 7(2^n - 1) + 2^n$ counted events.

articles.title: Pseudo-polynomial bound for exact subset sum
articles.statement:
For every list $x$ of $n$ natural numbers
with sum $s$ and every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$
makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)\min(t + 1, s + 1)$ counted events.

articles.title: Polynomial event bound for exact subset sum with a polynomially bounded target
articles.statement:
Let $x$
be a list of $n$ natural numbers and let $t, d \in \mathbb{N}$ with $t \le n^d$. Then the exact
subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)(n^d + 1)$ counted events.

articles.title: Polynomial event bound for exact subset sum with polynomially bounded inputs
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be
a list of $n$ natural numbers and let $d \in \mathbb{N}$ be such that every entry of $x$ is at
most $n^d$. Then for every target $t \in \mathbb{N}$ the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and
$t$ makes at most $1 + n + (7n + 1)(n \cdot n^d + 1)$ counted events.

articles.title: Event count of exact subset sum
articles.statement:
Let $x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ be a list of natural
numbers and $t \in \mathbb{N}$ a target. For $0 \le i \le n$ let $L_i$ be the list of attainable
sums of the prefix $(x_1, \dots, x_i)$ with target $t$. For $i < n$ let $M_i$ be the merge of
$L_i$ with the list obtained by adding $x_{i+1}$ to every entry of $L_i$, let $c_i$ be the
number of comparisons this merge makes, and let $D_i$ be $M_i$ with adjacent repeated values
deleted. Then the number of counted events of the exact subset-sum procedure on $x$ and $t$ is

$$1 + n + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \bigl(|L_i| + c_i + (|M_i| - 1) + |D_i|\bigr) + |L_n|,$$

where $|\cdot|$ denotes length and $|M_i| - 1$ is truncated subtraction of natural numbers.

articles.title: Exact subset sum procedure
articles.statement:
Given a list $x$ of natural numbers and a target
$t \in \mathbb{N}$, the procedure first computes the list $L = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m)$ of
attainable sums of $x$ with target $t$, then scans it from left to right, keeping a running
maximum that starts at $0$, and returns $\max(0, \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m)$. Its counted events
are those of computing $L$ plus one per entry of $L$.

articles.title: Feasible knapsack selection
articles.statement:
For knapsack items $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ with weights $w_i$
and a capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of item indices is
feasible when its total weight $\sum_{i \in S} w_i$ is at most $W$.

articles.title: Knapsack item
articles.statement:
A zero-one knapsack item consists of a weight $w \in \mathbb{N}$ and a value
$v \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Knapsack result
articles.statement:
For a list of $n$ knapsack items, a knapsack result consists of a set
$S \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of item indices, the chosen items, and a natural number, the
reported total value.

articles.title: Correctness of the zero-one knapsack algorithm
articles.statement:
For every list of knapsack items and every
capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$, let $S$ and $v$ be the index set and the reported value returned by
the bottom-up knapsack algorithm. Then $S$ is feasible for $W$, $v$ is the total value of $S$,
and every feasible set $T$ of item indices has total value at most $v$.

articles.title: Pseudo-polynomial cost bound for knapsack
articles.statement:
For every list of $n$ knapsack items and every
capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$ with $W \ge 1$, the bottom-up knapsack algorithm costs at most $3nW$
ticks.

articles.title: Exact cost of the knapsack algorithm
articles.statement:
For every list of $n$ knapsack items and every
capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$, the bottom-up knapsack algorithm costs exactly $n(W + 1) + n$ ticks:
one for each of the $n(W + 1)$ table cells it computes and one for each of the $n$ item rows it
inspects during reconstruction.

articles.title: Bottom-up zero-one knapsack algorithm
articles.statement:
Given knapsack items $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ with
weights $w_i$ and values $v_i$ and a capacity $W \in \mathbb{N}$, the algorithm fills a table
$V(i, c)$ for $0 \le i \le n$ and $0 \le c \le W$ by $V(0, c) = 0$ and, for $i < n$,
$V(i + 1, c) = \max(V(i, c), V(i, c - w_i) + v_i)$ if $w_i \le c$ and $V(i + 1, c) = V(i, c)$
otherwise. Starting from $c = W$, it then inspects the rows $i = n, n - 1, \dots, 1$: if
$V(i, c) = V(i - 1, c)$ it skips item $i - 1$, and otherwise it selects index $i - 1$ and
replaces $c$ by $c - w_{i-1}$. It returns the selected index set together with the value
$V(n, W)$. Each of the $n(W + 1)$ cells of rows $1, \dots, n$ costs one tick, and each of the
$n$ inspected rows costs one tick.

articles.title: Total value of a knapsack selection
articles.statement:
For knapsack items $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ with values
$v_i$ and a set $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of item indices, the total value of $S$ is
$\sum_{i \in S} v_i$.

articles.title: Total weight of a knapsack selection
articles.statement:
For knapsack items $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ with weights
$w_i$ and a set $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of item indices, the total weight of $S$ is
$\sum_{i \in S} w_i$.

articles.title: The counted matrix copy returns its input
articles.statement:
For every $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with entries
in any type, the value returned by the counted copy of $A$ is $A$ itself.

articles.title: Cost of the counted matrix copy
articles.statement:
For every $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with entries in any
type, the counted copy of $A$ has total cost $(n^2, (0, 0))$: exactly $n^2$ logical assignments
in the first cost coordinate and zero in the other two.

articles.title: Counted copy of a square matrix
articles.statement:
Given an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ (a vector of $n$ rows,
each a vector of $n$ entries), this computation returns the matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is
$A_{ij}$, traversing the entries row by row and charging a cost of $(1, (0, 0))$ for each entry,
that is, one logical assignment in the first cost coordinate and nothing in the other two.

articles.title: FASTER-APSP computes shortest-path weights
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be an $n \times n$ matrix with
entries in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, read as edge weights of a directed graph on the
vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ (weight $\infty$ meaning no edge), such that $W_{ii} = 0$ for every
$i$ and $W$ has no negative cycle. Run FASTER-APSP on $W$ over the min-plus semiring, whose
addition is $\min$ and whose multiplication is $+$. Then for all vertices $i$ and $j$, the
returned entry $d$ at $(i, j)$ is the shortest-path weight from $i$ to $j$: $d$ is at most the
weight of every path from $i$ to $j$ all of whose edges have finite weight, and either
$d = \infty$ or $d$ is the weight of such a path. Paths are nonempty vertex sequences and may
repeat vertices.

articles.title: FASTER-APSP computes edge-bounded shortest-path weights
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be an $n \times n$
matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, read as edge weights of a directed graph on
the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ (weight $\infty$ meaning no edge), with $W_{ii} = 0$ for every
$i$, and let $k = \lceil \log_2 (n - 1) \rceil$ be the least natural number with
$n - 1 \le 2^k$. Run FASTER-APSP on $W$ over the min-plus semiring, whose addition is $\min$
and whose multiplication is $+$. Then for all vertices $i$ and $j$, the returned entry $d$ at
$(i, j)$ is at most the weight of every path from $i$ to $j$ with at most $2^k$ edges, all of
finite weight, and either $d = \infty$ or $d$ is the weight of such a path. Paths are
nonempty vertex sequences and may repeat vertices; no assumption on negative cycles is made.

articles.title: FASTER-APSP returns a power of the input matrix
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a semiring, let $W$ be
an $n \times n$ matrix over $\alpha$, and let $k = \lceil \log_2 (n - 1) \rceil$ be the least
natural number with $n - 1 \le 2^k$ (so $k = 0$ when $n \le 2$). The matrix returned by
FASTER-APSP on $W$ is the matrix power $W^{2^k}$, with products computed in $\alpha$.

articles.title: Asymptotic operation count of FASTER-APSP
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with addition,
multiplication and zero, and for each $n$ let $W_n$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over $\alpha$. The
total number of copy and fill assignments, scalar additions and scalar multiplications that
FASTER-APSP performs on $W_n$ is $\Theta(n^3 \log n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Operation counts of FASTER-APSP
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with addition, multiplication and
zero, let $W$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over $\alpha$, and let $k = \lceil \log_2 (n - 1) \rceil$ be
the least natural number with $n - 1 \le 2^k$. On input $W$, FASTER-APSP performs exactly
$n^2 + 2 k n^2$ copy and fill assignments, $k n^3$ scalar additions and $k n^3$ scalar
multiplications.

Assignments count the matrix cells copied or filled with zero; the accumulator vector updates
inside the matrix multiplications are not counted.

articles.title: FASTER-APSP
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over a type with addition, multiplication
and zero. FASTER-APSP copies $W$ into a matrix $L$ and sets $r = 1$. While $r < n - 1$, it fills
a new $n \times n$ matrix $M$ with zeros, sets each entry to
$M_{ij} = 0 + L_{i0} L_{0j} + \dots + L_{i,n-1} L_{n-1,j}$ (adding the terms from left to right),
copies $M$ into $L$ and doubles $r$. It returns the final $L$. The run also records three counts:
one assignment for each matrix cell copied or filled with zero, and one scalar addition and one
scalar multiplication for each term added to an entry of $M$.

articles.title: The counted zero initialization returns the zero matrix
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a
zero element and every natural number $n$, the counted zero initialization of size $n$ over
$\alpha$ returns the $n \times n$ matrix all of whose entries are $0$.

articles.title: Cost of the counted zero initialization
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a zero element and
every natural number $n$, the counted zero initialization of size $n$ over $\alpha$ has total
cost $(n^2, (0, 0))$: exactly $n^2$ logical assignments in the first cost coordinate and zero in
the other two.

articles.title: Counted zero initialization of a square matrix
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a zero element
and a natural number $n$, this computation returns the $n \times n$ matrix over $\alpha$ all of
whose entries are $0$, producing the entries row by row and charging a cost of $(1, (0, 0))$ for
each entry, that is, one logical assignment in the first cost coordinate and nothing in the
other two.

articles.title: Characterization of the shortest path weight with at most $r$ edges
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be an
$n \times n$ matrix of weights in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $r$ be a natural number, let $i$ and $j$ be vertices, and let
$d \in \mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$. For a weighted path $p$, write $w(p)$ for its weight. Then $d$
is the shortest weight of a path from $i$ to $j$ with at most $r$ edges if and only if
$d \le w(p)$ for every weighted path $p$ from $i$ to $j$ with at most $r$ edges, and either
$d = \infty$ or $d = w(p)$ for some weighted path $p$ from $i$ to $j$ with at most $r$ edges.

articles.title: Shortest path weight with at most $r$ edges
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be an $n \times n$ matrix of
weights in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $r$ be a natural
number, let $i$ and $j$ be vertices, and let $d \in \mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$. A weighted path
from $i$ to $j$ is a nonempty list $p$ of vertices that starts at $i$, ends at $j$ and has finite
weight on each pair of consecutive vertices; its number of edges is its length minus one, and its
weight $w(p)$ is the sum of the weights of its edges. Then $d$ is the shortest weight of a path
from $i$ to $j$ with at most $r$ edges when $d \le w(p)$ for every weighted path $p$ from $i$ to
$j$ with at most $r$ edges, and either $d = \infty$ or $d = w(p)$ for some weighted path $p$ from
$i$ to $j$ with at most $r$ edges.

Paths may repeat vertices; no absence-of-negative-cycles hypothesis is needed.

articles.title: One min-plus multiplication extends shortest paths by one edge
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be
$n \times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, viewed in the min-plus
semiring, and let $r$ be a natural number. Suppose that $B_{jj} = 0$ for every $j$, and that for
all $i$ and $j$ the entry $A_{ij}$ is the shortest weight of a path from $i$ to $j$ with at most
$r$ edges for the weight matrix $B$. Then for all $i$ and $j$, the entry $(i, j)$ of the matrix
returned by the matrix accumulator on $A$, $B$ and the accumulator whose entries are all $\infty$
is the shortest weight of a path from $i$ to $j$ with at most $r + 1$ edges for the weight
matrix $B$.

Paths may repeat vertices and edge weights may be negative.

articles.title: Entries of the min-plus matrix accumulator
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be $n \times n$
matrices with entries in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, viewed in the min-plus semiring. For all
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the entry $(i, j)$ of the matrix returned by the matrix
accumulator on $A$, $B$ and the accumulator $C$ equals
$\min\bigl(C_{ij}, \min_{k} (A_{ik} + B_{kj})\bigr)$, where $k$ ranges over
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

articles.title: Min-plus matrix powers give shortest path weights with at most $r$ edges
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be an
$n \times n$ matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, viewed in the min-plus
semiring, with $W_{ii} = 0$ for every $i$. Then for every natural number $r$ and all $i$ and $j$,
the entry $(W^r)_{ij}$ of the $r$-th min-plus power of $W$ is the shortest weight of a path from
$i$ to $j$ with at most $r$ edges for the weight matrix $W$.

Paths may repeat vertices.

articles.title: SLOW-APSP computes shortest-path weights
articles.statement:
Let $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ be $n \times n$ matrices
over the min-plus semiring on $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $w_{xy}$ be the underlying value
in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ of $W_{xy}$. Suppose that $w_{ii} = 0$ for every $i$, that the
underlying value of $L^{(0)}_{ij}$ is $0$ if $i = j$ and $\infty$ otherwise, and that $w$ has no
negative cycle. Then for all $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the underlying value $d$ of the
$(i, j)$ entry of the matrix returned by SLOW-APSP on $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ is at most the weight of
every path from $i$ to $j$, and $d$ is either $\infty$ or the weight of some path from $i$ to $j$.
Here a path from $i$ to $j$ is a nonempty sequence of vertices that starts at $i$, ends at $j$ and
has $w_{xy} \ne \infty$ for each pair of consecutive vertices $x, y$; its weight is the sum of
these $w_{xy}$. A negative cycle is a path from a vertex to itself with at least two vertices,
negative weight, and no repeated vertex once its last vertex is removed.

articles.title: Bounded-edge shortest weights from SLOW-APSP
articles.statement:
Let $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ be
$n \times n$ matrices over the min-plus semiring on $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $w_{xy}$
be the underlying value in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ of $W_{xy}$. Suppose that $w_{ii} = 0$ for
every $i$ and that the underlying value of $L^{(0)}_{ij}$ is $0$ if $i = j$ and $\infty$ otherwise.
Then for all $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the underlying value $d$ of the $(i, j)$ entry of the
matrix returned by SLOW-APSP on $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ is at most the weight of every path from $i$ to
$j$ with at most $n - 1$ edges, and $d$ is either $\infty$ or the weight of such a path. Here a
path from $i$ to $j$ is a nonempty sequence of vertices that starts at $i$, ends at $j$ and has
$w_{xy} \ne \infty$ for each pair of consecutive vertices $x, y$; vertices may repeat, its number
of edges is its number of vertices minus one, and its weight is the sum of these $w_{xy}$.

articles.title: SLOW-APSP returns a min-plus matrix power
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ over
the min-plus semiring on $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, in which addition is $\min$ and
multiplication is $+$, the matrix returned by SLOW-APSP on $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ equals the
min-plus matrix product $L^{(0)} W^{n-1}$.

articles.title: SLOW-APSP takes quartic time
articles.statement:
For any choice, for each $n$, of $n \times n$ matrices $W_n$
and $L^{(0)}_n$ over the min-plus semiring on $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, the total cost of
SLOW-APSP on $W_n$ and $L^{(0)}_n$, that is the number of cell assignments (copies and fills)
plus the number of scalar additions plus the number of scalar minimums, is $\Theta(n^4)$ as
$n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Exact operation counts of SLOW-APSP
articles.statement:
For all $n \times n$ matrices $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ over
the min-plus semiring on $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, the cost of SLOW-APSP on $W$ and $L^{(0)}$
is the triple $(n^2 + 2(n-1)n^2,\ (n-1)n^3,\ (n-1)n^3)$ of cell assignments (copies and fills),
scalar additions and scalar minimums, where $n - 1$ means $\max(n - 1, 0)$.

The assignment count excludes the accumulator updates inside the min-plus accumulation loop.

articles.title: Slow all-pairs shortest paths (SLOW-APSP)
articles.statement:
Let $W$ and $L^{(0)}$ be $n \times n$ matrices
over the min-plus semiring on $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, in which addition is $\min$ and
multiplication is $+$. SLOW-APSP copies $L^{(0)}$ cell by cell and then runs $\max(n - 1, 0)$
phases. Phase $r$ fills a fresh $n \times n$ matrix $M$ with $\infty$, then for each triple
$(i, j, k)$ in increasing $i$-$j$-$k$ order sets $M_{ij} \leftarrow \min(M_{ij}, L^{(r-1)}_{ik} +
W_{kj})$, and finally copies $M$ cell by cell to give $L^{(r)}$; the result is $L^{(n-1)}$. The
cost is a triple of natural numbers: the first coordinate counts one assignment for each cell
copied or filled, and the second and third coordinates count one scalar addition and one scalar
minimum for each update $M_{ij} \leftarrow \min(M_{ij}, L^{(r-1)}_{ik} + W_{kj})$.

Accumulator updates inside the loop are not charged as assignments.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford spends no witness steps when it returns distances
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of
weighted edges on $n$ vertices and every source $s$, if Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns
distances rather than a negative cycle, then the run charges zero negative-cycle witness
reconstruction steps.

articles.title: Witness cost of a returned negative cycle
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of weighted edges on $n$
vertices and every source $s$, if Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns a reachable negative
cycle whose cycle has $c$ edges and whose path from $s$ to the cycle has $q$ edges, then the run
charges exactly $n + c + q$ negative-cycle witness reconstruction steps.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford spends at most $3n$ witness steps
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of weighted edges on
$n$ vertices and every source $s$, Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ charges at most $3n$
negative-cycle witness reconstruction steps.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford leaves exactly the unreachable vertices at infinite distance
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a
list of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a
vertex. If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$, with $\infty$ marking a vertex
that has no finite distance, then for every vertex $t$, $d(t) = \infty$ if and only if $t$ is not
reachable from $s$ in the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting the weights.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford distances are lower bounds on walk weights
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex.
If Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$, the distance $d(t)$ of a vertex $t$
is a finite integer $\delta$, and $P$ is a walk from $s$ to $t$ along edges of $E$ (vertices may
repeat), then $\delta$ is at most the total weight of $P$.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford distances are realized by walks
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run
on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$ and the distance $d(t)$ of a vertex $t$ is a finite integer
$\delta$, then there is a walk from $s$ to $t$ along edges of $E$ whose total weight is
$\delta$.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford path reconstruction fails exactly at infinite distances
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If
Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$, with $\infty$ marking a vertex that has
no finite distance, together with predecessor edges, then for every vertex $t$, reconstructing a
path to $t$ (following predecessor edges back from $t$ for at most $n$ steps until $s$ is
reached) fails if and only if $d(t) = \infty$.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford reconstructed paths are simple and realize the distances
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list
of integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex.
Suppose Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$ together with predecessor edges,
and that reconstructing a path to a vertex $t$ (following predecessor edges back from $t$ for at
most $n$ steps until $s$ is reached) yields the edge sequence $P$. Then $P$ is a walk from $s$
to $t$ along edges of $E$, $d(t)$ is finite and equals the total weight of $P$, the vertex $s$
and the targets of the edges of $P$ are pairwise distinct, and $P$ has fewer than $n$ edges.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford predecessor edges are tight
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed
edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. Suppose Bellman-Ford run on
$E$ from $s$ returns distances $d$ together with predecessor edges, and the predecessor edge of a
vertex $t$ is an edge $e$ from $u$ to $v$ of weight $w$. Then $e$ belongs to $E$, $v = t$, and
$d(u)$ and $d(t)$ are both finite with $d(t) = d(u) + w$.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford makes exactly $n \cdot |E|$ relaxation checks
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of weighted
edges on $n$ vertices and every source $s$, Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ charges exactly
$n \cdot |E|$ relaxation checks, where $|E|$ is the length of $E$ counting repeated edges.

articles.title: Relaxation checks of Bellman-Ford pass by pass
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of weighted edges on
$n$ vertices and every source $s$, Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ charges exactly
$(n - 1) \cdot |E| + |E|$ relaxation checks, where $|E|$ is the length of $E$.

The two terms count one check per edge occurrence in each of the $n - 1$ ordinary passes and in
the final pass.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford succeeds exactly when no negative cycle is reachable
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex.
Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns distances if and only if there is no negative cycle
reachable from $s$, that is, no simple path from $s$ to a vertex $b$ together with a nonempty
cycle through $b$ along edges of $E$ whose edge sources are pairwise distinct and whose total
weight is negative.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford reports a negative cycle exactly when one is reachable
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex.
Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ returns a reachable negative cycle witness if and only if a
negative cycle is reachable from $s$, that is, there are a simple path from $s$ to a vertex $b$
and a nonempty cycle through $b$ along edges of $E$ whose edge sources are pairwise distinct and
whose total weight is negative.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford gives the source no predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. If Bellman-Ford run
on $E$ from $s$ returns distances together with predecessor edges, then $s$ has no predecessor
edge.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford makes at most $4 n |E|$ counted steps
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of weighted edges
on $n$ vertices and every source $s$, the total cost of Bellman-Ford run on $E$ from $s$ (its
relaxation checks plus its negative-cycle witness reconstruction steps) is at most
$4 \cdot n \cdot |E|$, where $|E|$ is the length of $E$.

articles.title: Bellman–Ford algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed edges on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ be a vertex. Bellman–Ford run on $E$ from $s$ starts
with distance $d(s) = 0$ and $d(v) = \infty$ for every other vertex $v$, and makes $n - 1$ passes
over $E$ followed by one final pass. A pass goes through the edges of $E$ in list order, charging
one relaxation check per edge occurrence; an edge from $u$ to $v$ of weight $w$ with $d(u)$ finite
sets $d(v)$ to $d(u) + w$ and records the edge as the predecessor edge of $v$ when $d(v) = \infty$
or $d(u) + w < d(v)$. If the final pass changes no distance, the result is the distances and
predecessor edges. Otherwise, starting from the vertex whose distance the final pass changed
last, the algorithm follows $n$ predecessor edges back to a vertex $b$; it then collects the
cycle of predecessor edges through $b$, following at most $n$ predecessor edges back from $b$
until it reaches an edge with source $b$, and collects a path from $s$ to $b$ of at most $n - 1$
edges by following back from $b$ the edges by which vertices first received a finite distance.
Each lookup of a recorded edge in these three steps is charged as one witness step, also when
no edge is recorded. If all three steps succeed and give a reachable negative cycle witness for
$E$ and $s$, that witness is the result; otherwise the result is the distances and predecessor
edges.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford cost counters
articles.statement:
The cost of a Bellman-Ford run is a pair of natural numbers:
the number of edge occurrences checked by relaxation passes, and the number of predecessor edges
read or emitted while reconstructing a negative-cycle witness.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford distance table
articles.statement:
For a graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, the output of a
successful Bellman-Ford run consists of a source vertex $s$, for every vertex a distance that is
either an integer or $\infty$, and for every vertex an optional predecessor edge (a weighted
directed edge, or none).

The structure only records these values; that they are shortest-path data is proved separately.

articles.title: Edges of the weight-forgetting graph
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of weighted directed edges on the
vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and vertices $u$, $v$, the graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights
has an edge from $u$ to $v$ if and only if some edge in $E$ has source $u$ and target $v$.

articles.title: Weighted directed edge
articles.statement:
A weighted directed edge on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ consists
of a source vertex, a target vertex and an integer weight.

Bellman-Ford takes a list of such edges, so each entry is one edge occurrence.

articles.title: Existence of a reachable negative cycle
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on
the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and $s$ a vertex. Then $E$ has a negative cycle reachable from $s$
when there is a reachable negative cycle witness for $E$ and $s$: a base vertex $b$, a weighted
path in $E$ from $s$ to $b$ that visits no vertex twice, and a nonempty weighted path in $E$ from
$b$ to $b$ whose edge sources are pairwise distinct and whose total weight is negative.

articles.title: Appending an edge to a weighted path
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the
vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $s$, $m$ and $t$ be vertices. If $P$ is a weighted path in $E$
from $s$ to $m$ and $e$ is an edge belonging to $E$ with source $m$ and target $t$, then the list
$P$ followed by $e$ is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Tail of a weighted path
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If the list consisting of an edge $e$ followed by
a list $R$ of edges is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$, then $R$ is a weighted path in $E$
from the target of $e$ to $t$.

articles.title: Weighted paths give walks of the same length
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed
edges on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If a list $P$ of $k$ edges
is a weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$, then there is a walk of length $k$ from $s$ to $t$ in
the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting the weights.

articles.title: Weighted path in an edge list
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of weighted directed edges on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$. A list $P = (e_1, \dots, e_k)$ of weighted directed edges is a weighted path in $E$
from $s$ to $t$ when every $e_i$ belongs to $E$, the target of $e_i$ is the source of $e_{i+1}$ for
every $i < k$, and either $k = 0$ and $s = t$, or $k \ge 1$, the source of $e_1$ is $s$ and the
target of $e_k$ is $t$.

articles.title: Predecessor paths realize the distances under a decreasing rank
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
distances record on $n$ vertices with source $s$, distance table $d$ (each $d(v)$ is an integer
or infinite) and predecessor table $p$; let $E$ be a list of weighted edges; and let $r$ assign to
each vertex $v$ a natural number $r(v) < n$. Suppose that $d(s) = 0$, that every vertex $v$ with
$d(v)$ infinite has no predecessor, that every vertex $v \ne s$ with $d(v)$ finite has a
predecessor, and that whenever $p(v) = e$, the edge $e$ occurs in $E$, ends at $v$, and its start
$u$ has $d(u)$ finite, $d(v) = d(u) + w(e)$ where $w(e)$ is the weight of $e$, and $r(u) < r(v)$.
Then for every vertex $t$, following predecessors from $t$ back to $s$ for at most $n$ edges fails
exactly when $d(t)$ is infinite; and whenever it returns a path $P$ and $d(t)$ is finite, $P$ is a
path from $s$ to $t$ made of edges of $E$, its total weight is $d(t)$, and it has fewer than $n$
edges.

articles.title: Bellman-Ford path reconstruction
articles.statement:
Let the output of a Bellman-Ford run on $n$ vertices
have source $s$. The path to a vertex $t$ is built backwards from $t$: at a vertex $v \ne s$, take
the recorded predecessor edge $e$ of $v$, put it in front of the edges collected so far, and
continue from the source of $e$. When $s$ is reached within at most $n$ such steps, the result is
the collected list of edges (empty if $t = s$). If some vertex on the way has no predecessor edge,
or $s$ is not reached within $n$ steps, there is no result.

articles.title: Vertices of a path
articles.statement:
For a vertex $s$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a list of weighted edges
$e_1, \dots, e_k$ on these vertices, the vertices of the path from $s$ along this list are the
list $s, t_1, \dots, t_k$, where $t_i$ is the target of $e_i$.

The edges are not required to be consecutive.

articles.title: Weight of a path with an edge appended
articles.statement:
For every list $P$ of weighted directed edges on
the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and every weighted directed edge $e$ on these vertices, the weight of
the list $P$ followed by $e$ is the weight of $P$ plus the weight of $e$.

articles.title: Bellman–Ford path weight
articles.statement:
The weight of a list of integer-weighted edges is the sum of the
weights of its entries, an edge occurring several times being counted each time.

articles.title: Reachability by weighted paths
articles.statement:
For a list of weighted edges on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the vertex $t$ is reachable from $s$ in the directed
graph obtained from the list by forgetting the weights if and only if there is a weighted path
from $s$ to $t$ using edges of the list.

articles.title: Reachable negative cycle witness
articles.statement:
For a list of weighted edges on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a source vertex $s$, a reachable negative cycle consists of a base
vertex $b$, a weighted path $p$ from $s$ to $b$ using edges of the list whose vertices along $p$
from $s$ are pairwise distinct, and a nonempty weighted path $c$ from $b$ to $b$ using edges of
the list whose edges have pairwise distinct sources and whose weight is negative.

articles.title: Bellman–Ford result
articles.statement:
For a list of weighted edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and
a source vertex $s$, a Bellman–Ford result is either a distance record (a source vertex, an
optional integer distance for each vertex and an optional predecessor edge for each vertex) or a
reachable negative cycle witness for the list and $s$.

The type itself does not require the distances to be correct.

articles.title: Weight-forgetting directed graph
articles.statement:
For a list of weighted edges on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the associated ordered directed graph enumerates its vertices as
$0, 1, \dots, n-1$, and the outgoing neighbor list of a vertex $u$ is the list of targets of the
edges of the list with source $u$, in the order in which they occur and with repetitions.

articles.title: Total Bellman–Ford cost
articles.statement:
The total of a Bellman–Ford cost record is its number of edge
relaxation checks plus its number of negative-cycle witness reconstruction steps.

articles.title: Adjacency entry count
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ given by an out-neighbour list
$\mathrm{adj}(v)$ for each vertex $v$, the adjacency entry count of $G$ is the total length
$\sum_{v} |\mathrm{adj}(v)|$ of these lists over all vertices $v$, so repeated entries and
self-loops are counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Cost of dense Dijkstra
articles.statement:
A Dijkstra cost is a pair of natural numbers that counts two
kinds of events separately: the number of vertex entries inspected during minimum selection,
and the number of adjacency-list entries inspected during relaxation.

articles.title: Dijkstra's distance is infinite exactly at unreachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every
ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. The distance to $t$ output by
Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$ with weights $w$ from source $s$ is infinite if and only if $t$ is
not reachable from $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: Dijkstra's finite distances are lower bounds on walk weights
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph
on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every ordered pair
of vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$ with weights $w$
from source $s$ outputs a finite distance $d$ for $t$, then $d \le d'$ for every walk
$s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t$ in $G$ (with an edge from each $v_{i-1}$ to $v_i$) of weight
$d' = \sum_{i=1}^{k} w(v_{i-1}, v_i)$.

articles.title: Dijkstra's finite distances are realized by walks
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the
vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every ordered pair of
vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$ with weights $w$ from
source $s$ outputs a finite distance $d$ for $t$, then $G$ has a walk
$s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t$, with an edge from each $v_{i-1}$ to $v_i$, of weight
$\sum_{i=1}^{k} w(v_{i-1}, v_i) = d$.

articles.title: Relaxation count of dense Dijkstra
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every ordered pair of vertices,
and let $s$ be a vertex. The number of adjacency-list entries that Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$
with weights $w$ from source $s$ inspects during relaxation equals the adjacency entry count
of $G$, the total length of all out-neighbour lists.

articles.title: Minimum-selection count of dense Dijkstra
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every ordered pair of vertices,
and let $s$ be a vertex. Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$ with weights $w$ from source $s$ inspects
exactly $n^2$ vertex entries during minimum selection.

articles.title: Dijkstra's path reconstruction fails exactly at infinite distance
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every
ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. Reconstructing a path from $s$ to
$t$ by following, for at most $n$ steps, the predecessor pointers output by Dijkstra's
algorithm on $G$ with weights $w$ from source $s$ fails if and only if the distance output
for $t$ is infinite.

articles.title: Reconstructed Dijkstra paths are simple and have the output weight
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every
ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. Suppose that following the
predecessor pointers output by Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$ with weights $w$ from source $s$
reconstructs a list of vertices $P$ for $t$. Then $P$ is nonempty, say $P = v_0, \dots, v_k$,
with $v_0 = s$ and $v_k = t$; there is an edge from each $v_{i-1}$ to $v_i$; the $v_i$ are
pairwise distinct; and the distance $d$ output for $t$ is finite with
$d = \sum_{i=1}^{k} w(v_{i-1}, v_i)$.

articles.title: Dijkstra's predecessor pointers satisfy the distance equation
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w(u, v)$ be a natural-number weight for every
ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$, $t$ and $p$ be vertices. If Dijkstra's algorithm on $G$
with weights $w$ from source $s$ outputs $p$ as the predecessor of $t$, then $G$ has an edge
from $p$ to $t$, the distances $d(p)$ and $d(t)$ output for $p$ and $t$ are both finite, and
$d(t) = d(p) + w(p, t)$.

articles.title: Output of Dijkstra's algorithm
articles.statement:
For vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, a Dijkstra result consists
of a source vertex $s$, a distance entry $d(v)$ for each vertex $v$ that is either a natural
number or $\infty$, and a predecessor entry $p(v)$ for each vertex $v$ that is either a vertex or
undefined. The entries are stored as arrays of length $n$; $d(v)$ is meant as the computed
distance from $s$ to $v$ and $p(v)$ as the vertex before $v$ on a shortest path from $s$.

articles.title: Running time of dense Dijkstra
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$ given by adjacency lists, let $w(u, v) \in \mathbb{N}$ be a weight for each
ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ be a vertex. For dense Dijkstra from $s$, the number of
vertex entries inspected by minimum selection plus the number of adjacency entries inspected by
relaxation is exactly $n^2 + m$, where $m$ is the number of adjacency-list entries of $G$,
counting duplicates and self-loops.

articles.title: Dense Dijkstra's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$
given by a fixed enumeration of its vertices and adjacency lists, let $w(u, v) \in \mathbb{N}$ be
a weight for each ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ be a source vertex. The algorithm starts
with $d(s) = 0$, $d(v) = \infty$ for $v \ne s$, no predecessors and no settled vertices, and runs
$n$ rounds. In each round it scans all vertices in the order of the enumeration of $G$ and
selects the first unsettled vertex $u$ in that order whose value $d(u)$ is minimal among
unsettled vertices; if every vertex is settled the round does nothing. Otherwise it marks $u$
settled and, for each entry $v$ of the adjacency list of $u$ in order, if $v$ is unsettled,
$d(u)$ is finite and $d(u) + w(u, v) < d(v)$, it sets $d(v) := d(u) + w(u, v)$ and makes $u$ the
predecessor of $v$. The result is $s$ together with the final distances and predecessors. The
cost charges one minimum-selection step for each vertex inspected during selection and one
relaxation step for each adjacency entry inspected during relaxation.

articles.title: Walks of a given weight
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph given by adjacency lists, let
$w(u, v) \in \mathbb{N}$ be a weight for each ordered pair of vertices, let $s$ and $t$ be
vertices and let $d$ be a natural number. Then $s$ reaches $t$ with weight $d$ when there is a
nonempty list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_0 = s$, $v_k = t$ and each $v_{i+1}$ in
the adjacency list of $v_i$, such that $w(v_0, v_1) + \dots + w(v_{k-1}, v_k) = d$.

articles.title: Path recovery from Dijkstra predecessors
articles.statement:
Let a Dijkstra result on $n$ vertices have
source $s$ and predecessor entries $p$. The path to a vertex $t$ follows predecessors backwards:
starting from $u_0 = t$, as long as $u_i \ne s$ it sets $u_{i+1} = p(u_i)$. If $u_k = s$ for
some $k \le n$, the result is the list $u_k, u_{k-1}, \dots, u_0$ from $s$ to $t$. If some
$p(u_i)$ is undefined before $s$ is reached, or $s$ is not reached within $n$ steps, there is no
result.

articles.title: Endpoint-weight sum along a vertex list
articles.statement:
Given a weight $w(u, v) \in \mathbb{N}$ for each
ordered pair of vertices, the weight of a list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ is
$w(v_0, v_1) + w(v_1, v_2) + \dots + w(v_{k-1}, v_k)$. In particular the empty list and every
one-vertex list have weight $0$.

articles.title: Reachability via weighted walks
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph given by adjacency lists and
let $w(u, v) \in \mathbb{N}$ be a weight for each ordered pair of vertices. For vertices $s$ and
$t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G$ if and only if there is a natural number $d$ such that $s$
reaches $t$ with weight $d$ with respect to $w$.

articles.title: Total Dijkstra cost
articles.statement:
The total of a Dijkstra cost record is its number of vertex entries
inspected by minimum selection plus its number of adjacency entries inspected by relaxation.

articles.title: Floyd–Warshall cost record
articles.statement:
A cost record for the Floyd–Warshall algorithm is a pair of
natural numbers: the number of initialization events (input matrix cells copied into the initial
distance table) and the number of min-plus transition events (table entries updated).

articles.title: Floyd–Warshall reports $\infty$ exactly for unreachable pairs
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign a weight
in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ to each ordered pair of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $D$
be the distance matrix computed by Floyd–Warshall from $w$. For all vertices $s$ and $t$,
$D(s, t) = \infty$ if and only if there is no weighted path from $s$ to $t$, that is, no nonempty
vertex sequence from $s$ to $t$ in which every consecutive pair has finite weight.

articles.title: No path is shorter than the Floyd–Warshall distance
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign a weight in
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ to each ordered pair of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, suppose that
$w$ has no negative cycle, and let $D$ be the distance matrix computed by Floyd–Warshall from $w$.
Then for all vertices $s$ and $t$ and every weighted path $p$ from $s$ to $t$ (a nonempty vertex
sequence from $s$ to $t$ in which every consecutive pair has finite weight), $D(s, t)$ is at most
the weight of $p$, the sum of the weights of its consecutive pairs.

articles.title: Finite Floyd–Warshall distances are attained
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign a weight in
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ to each ordered pair of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $D$
be the distance matrix computed by Floyd–Warshall from $w$. If $D(s, t) = d$ for vertices $s$, $t$
and an integer $d$, then there is a weighted path from $s$ to $t$ (a nonempty vertex sequence from
$s$ to $t$ in which every consecutive pair has finite weight) whose weight, the sum of the weights
of its consecutive pairs, is $d$.

articles.title: Floyd–Warshall computes shortest-path distances
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign a weight in
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ to each ordered pair of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, suppose that
$w$ has no negative cycle, and let $D$ be the distance matrix computed by Floyd–Warshall from $w$.
Then for all vertices $s$ and $t$, $D(s, t)$ is at most the weight of every weighted path from $s$
to $t$, and either $D(s, t) = \infty$ or $D(s, t)$ is the weight of some weighted path from $s$ to
$t$. Here a weighted path is a nonempty vertex sequence in which every consecutive pair has finite
weight, and its weight is the sum of these weights.

Formally this is the stage-$n$ characterization, which considers only paths whose intermediate
vertices are all below $n$; every path qualifies.

articles.title: Without negative cycles, Floyd–Warshall finds no negative diagonal entry
articles.statement:
Let $w$
assign a weight in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ to each ordered pair of vertices in
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $D$ be the distance matrix computed by Floyd–Warshall from $w$. If $w$
