has no negative cycle, then the negative-diagonal check on $D$ returns false, that is,
$D(v, v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$.

articles.title: A negative diagonal entry in Floyd–Warshall reveals a negative cycle
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign a
weight in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$ to each ordered pair of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and
let $D$ be the distance matrix computed by Floyd–Warshall from $w$. If $D(v, v) < 0$ for some vertex
$v$, then $w$ has a negative cycle: a vertex sequence $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_m$ with $m \ge 1$ and
$v_m = v_0$, whose vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{m-1}$ are pairwise distinct, in which every consecutive
pair has finite weight, and whose total weight is negative.

articles.title: Initialization count of Floyd–Warshall
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every $n \times n$ matrix of
weights in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$, the Floyd–Warshall algorithm performs exactly $n^2$
initialization events, one for each ordered pair of vertices.

articles.title: Floyd–Warshall performs $n^2 + n^3$ steps
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every $n \times n$ matrix of
weights in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$, the total number of events counted by the Floyd–Warshall
algorithm, initialization events plus min-plus transition events, is exactly $n^2 + n^3$.

articles.title: Transition count of Floyd–Warshall
articles.statement:
For every $n$ and every $n \times n$ matrix of weights
in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$, the Floyd–Warshall algorithm performs exactly $n^3$ min-plus
transition events, one for each triple $(k, i, j)$ of vertices.

articles.title: Floyd–Warshall algorithm
articles.statement:
Given an $n \times n$ matrix $w$ of weights in
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$ indexed by the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$, the Floyd–Warshall
algorithm starts from the table with $d^{(0)}_{ii} = \min(w_{ii}, 0)$ and $d^{(0)}_{ij} = w_{ij}$
for $i \ne j$, and for $k = 0, \dots, n - 1$ computes the table
$d^{(k+1)}_{ij} = \min\bigl(d^{(k)}_{ij}, d^{(k)}_{ik} + d^{(k)}_{kj}\bigr)$. It returns the
matrix $d^{(n)}$ together with its cost: one initialization event for each entry of $d^{(0)}$
and one transition event for each entry of each table $d^{(k+1)}$.

articles.title: Matrices with a negative cycle
articles.statement:
An $n \times n$ matrix $w$ of weights in
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$ has a negative cycle when some list of vertices is a negative
cycle for $w$.

articles.title: Characterization of the negative-diagonal test
articles.statement:
For every $n \times n$ matrix $d$ with
entries in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$, the negative-diagonal test on $d$ returns true if and
only if $d_{vv} < 0$ for some vertex $v$.

articles.title: Negative-diagonal test
articles.statement:
For an $n \times n$ matrix $d$ with entries in
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$, the negative-diagonal test on $d$ is the Boolean value that is
true exactly when $d_{vv} < 0$ for some vertex $v$.

articles.title: Intermediate vertices below a bound
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a list of vertices in
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ has all its intermediate vertices below $k$ when every entry of the list
other than its first and its last is less than $k$.

articles.title: Negative cycles
articles.statement:
For an $n \times n$ matrix $w$ of weights in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{+\infty\}$,
a list of vertices $v_0, \dots, v_m$ is a negative cycle when $m \ge 1$, $v_m = v_0$, every
weight $w_{v_i v_{i+1}}$ with $i < m$ is finite, the vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{m-1}$ are
pairwise distinct, and the path weight $\sum_{i < m} w_{v_i v_{i+1}}$ is negative.

articles.title: Stage-$k$ shortest-path weight
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign to each ordered pair of vertices in
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a weight in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, let $k$ be a natural number, let
$s$ and $t$ be vertices and let $d \in \mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$. A weighted path from $s$ to
$t$ is a nonempty list of vertices that starts at $s$, ends at $t$ and has $w(u, v) \ne \infty$
for every pair of consecutive vertices $u, v$; its weight is the sum of these values $w(u, v)$,
and its intermediate vertices are all its entries except the first and the last. Then $d$ is the
stage-$k$ shortest-path weight from $s$ to $t$ when $d$ is at most the weight of every weighted
path from $s$ to $t$ whose intermediate vertices are all less than $k$, and either $d = \infty$ or
some such path has weight exactly $d$.

articles.title: Finite-weight vertex path in a weight matrix
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign to each ordered pair of
vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a weight in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, and let $s$ and $t$ be
vertices. A list of vertices $p$ is a weighted path from $s$ to $t$ when $p$ is nonempty, its
first entry is $s$, its last entry is $t$, and $w(u, v) \ne \infty$ for every pair of consecutive
entries $u, v$ of $p$.

articles.title: Weight matrices without negative cycles
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign to each ordered pair of vertices
in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a weight in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$. Then $w$ has no negative cycle
when there is no list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_m$ with $m \ge 1$ such that $v_m = v_0$,
the vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{m-1}$ are pairwise distinct, $w(v_{i-1}, v_i) \ne \infty$ for
$1 \le i \le m$, and $w(v_0, v_1) + \cdots + w(v_{m-1}, v_m) < 0$.

articles.title: Weight of a vertex path in an extended-integer weight matrix
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign to each
ordered pair of vertices in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ a weight in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$. The
weight of a list of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_m$ with $m \ge 1$ is
$w(v_0, v_1) + w(v_1, v_2) + \cdots + w(v_{m-1}, v_m)$, computed in $\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$
where adding $\infty$ gives $\infty$. The empty list and every single-vertex list have
weight $0$.

articles.title: Total Floyd–Warshall cost
articles.statement:
The total of a Floyd–Warshall cost record is its number of
initialization events plus its number of min-plus transition events.

articles.title: Correctness of Johnson's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of directed edges on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with integer weights, and suppose Johnson's algorithm on $E$ returns a
table $d$. Then for all vertices $s$ and $t$, $d(s, t) = \infty$ if and only if $t$ is not
reachable from $s$ along edges of $E$. Moreover, if $d(s, t)$ is an integer $x$, then some
weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to $t$ has weight $x$, and every weighted path in $E$ from $s$ to
$t$ has weight at least $x$.

articles.title: Johnson's algorithm fails exactly on reachable negative cycles
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of
directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with integer weights, Johnson's algorithm on
$E$ returns no table if and only if there is a vertex $s$ from which a negative cycle of $E$ is
reachable.

articles.title: Cost bound for Johnson's algorithm
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of $m$ directed edges on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with integer weights, the counted cost of Johnson's algorithm on
$E$, including the case where it extracts a negative cycle, is at most
$n^3 + nm + (n+1)(m+n) + 2n^2 + 4m + 5n + 1 + 3(n+1)$.

articles.title: Exact cost of a successful run of Johnson's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of $m$ directed
edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with integer weights. If Johnson's algorithm on $E$
returns a table, then its counted cost is exactly
$n^3 + nm + (n+1)(m+n) + 2n^2 + 4m + 5n + 1$.

articles.title: Johnson's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of directed edges on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with integer weights. Johnson's algorithm adds a new vertex $s$ with an
edge of weight $0$ to every original vertex and runs Bellman–Ford from $s$. If Bellman–Ford
reports a negative cycle, the algorithm returns no table. Otherwise let $h(v)$ be the
Bellman–Ford distance of $v$ (taken to be $0$ if $v$ is unreached). Each edge from $u$ to $v$ of
weight $w$ gets the new weight $\max(0, w + h(u) - h(v))$.
For each original vertex $u$ the algorithm runs Dijkstra from $u$ on the original vertices,
where the weight from $x$ to $y$ is the least new weight of an edge from $x$ to $y$. It
returns the table whose entry at $(u, v)$ is $\infty$ if Dijkstra does not reach $v$, and
$d'(u, v) + h(v) - h(u)$ otherwise, where $d'(u, v)$ is the Dijkstra distance.

The cost counts the selected construction, scan, relaxation and decoding actions, not full RAM
or bit complexity.

articles.title: Cost of the DAG shortest-path pass
articles.statement:
The cost of the one-pass relaxation in topological
order consists of three natural-number counters: the number of vertices taken from the order, the
number of edge occurrences checked for relaxation, and the number of distance installations
(strict improvements or first finite distances).

Preparation and topological sorting are not counted.

articles.title: Unreachable vertices are exactly those at infinite DAG distance
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and $s$ a source vertex.
If the DAG shortest-path algorithm on $E$ from $s$ succeeds, then for every vertex $t$ the
returned distance to $t$ is infinite if and only if $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the directed
graph with an edge $u \to v$ for each edge of $E$ from $u$ to $v$.

articles.title: DAG shortest-path distances are shortest-path weights
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and $s$ a source vertex.
Suppose the DAG shortest-path algorithm on $E$ from $s$ succeeds and returns a finite distance
$d \in \mathbb{Z}$ for a vertex $t$. Then some path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ has weight $d$, and
every path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ has weight at least $d$. Here a path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ is a
list of edges of $E$, each starting where the previous one ends, the first starting at $s$ and
the last ending at $t$ (the empty list when $t = s$), and its weight is the sum of its edge
weights.

articles.title: Failure output of DAG shortest paths
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of integer-weighted edges on $n$
vertices, a source $s$, and lists $P$ and $R$ of vertices, the DAG shortest-path algorithm on $E$
from $s$ returns the error $(P, R)$ if and only if Kahn's topological sort of the directed graph
obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights fails after processing $P$ and leaving $R$.

articles.title: Successful output of DAG shortest paths
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of integer-weighted edges on $n$
vertices, a source $s$, and a distance record $D$, the DAG shortest-path algorithm on $E$ from $s$
returns $D$ if and only if there is a topological order $\sigma$ of the directed graph obtained
from $E$ by forgetting weights such that Kahn's topological sort of that graph succeeds with
$\sigma$ and $D$ is the result of the one-pass relaxation from $s$ in the order $\sigma$.

articles.title: A failed DAG shortest-path run exhibits a cycle
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and $s$ a source vertex. If the DAG
shortest-path algorithm on $E$ from $s$ fails, reporting the processed vertices and the list $R$
of remaining vertices of its topological sort, then the directed graph with an edge $u \to v$ for
each edge of $E$ from $u$ to $v$ contains a nonempty directed cycle without repeated vertices
whose vertices all lie in $R$.

articles.title: Extracted DAG shortest paths are shortest paths
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and $s$ a source vertex. Suppose the DAG
shortest-path algorithm on $E$ from $s$ succeeds, and following its predecessor edges back from a
vertex $t$ reaches $s$ within $n$ steps, giving the path $P$. Then $P$ is a path from $s$ to $t$
in $E$, the returned distance to $t$ is finite and equals the weight of $P$, $P$ has fewer than
$n$ edges, and every path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ has weight at least the weight of $P$. Here a
path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ is a list of edges of $E$, each starting where the previous one ends,
the first starting at $s$ and the last ending at $t$ (the empty list when $t = s$), and its weight
is the sum of its edge weights.

articles.title: The DAG shortest-path algorithm succeeds exactly on acyclic graphs
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and $s$ a source vertex. The
DAG shortest-path algorithm on $E$ from $s$ succeeds if and only if the directed graph with an
edge $u \to v$ for each edge of $E$ from $u$ to $v$ has no directed cycle.

This includes disconnected graphs: a cycle unreachable from $s$ still causes failure.

articles.title: Shortest paths in a DAG with a topology check
articles.statement:
Given a list $E$ of integer-weighted edges
on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and a source $s$, run Kahn's topological sort on the directed graph
obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights. If it succeeds with order $\sigma$, start from distance
$0$ at $s$ and $\infty$ elsewhere, relax the outgoing edge occurrences of each vertex in the order
$\sigma$, and return the resulting distances and predecessor edges. If it fails after processing
the list $P$ of vertices and leaving the list $R$, return the error $(P, R)$. Only the relaxation
pass is charged in the recorded cost.

Failure preserves the sorter's processed and remaining lists; it does not return a cycle list.

articles.title: Infinite DAG distances are exactly unreachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted edges on $n$ vertices, $s$ a source, and $\sigma$ a topological order of the
directed graph $G$ obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights. For every vertex $t$, the one-pass
relaxation from $s$ in the order $\sigma$ leaves the distance of $t$ infinite if and only if $t$ is
not reachable from $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: Finite DAG distances are at most every path weight
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
edges on $n$ vertices, $s$ a source, and $\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph
obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights. If the one-pass relaxation from $s$ in the order $\sigma$
gives a vertex $t$ the finite distance $d$, then $d \le w(p)$ for every path $p$ from $s$ to $t$
made of edge occurrences of $E$, where $w(p)$ is the sum of the weights of the edges of $p$.

articles.title: Finite DAG distances are path weights
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted edges on $n$
vertices, $s$ a source, and $\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$ by
forgetting weights. If the one-pass relaxation from $s$ in the order $\sigma$ gives a vertex $t$
the finite distance $d$, then there is a path from $s$ to $t$ made of edge occurrences of $E$
whose edge weights sum to $d$.

articles.title: Distance updates are bounded by edge relaxations
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
edges on $n$ vertices, $s$ a source, and $\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph
obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights. In the cost of the one-pass relaxation from $s$ in the
order $\sigma$, the number of distance installations is at most the number of edge relaxations.

Only actual strict improvements or first finite estimates install a predecessor.

articles.title: Edge relaxation count of the DAG pass
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted edges on $n$
vertices, $s$ a source, and $\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$ by
forgetting weights. In the cost of the one-pass relaxation from $s$ in the order $\sigma$, the
number of edge relaxations equals the length of $E$, with identical duplicate edges counted
separately.

articles.title: Finite non-source vertices have predecessors
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted edges on
$n$ vertices, $s$ a source, and $\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$
by forgetting weights. If the one-pass relaxation from $s$ in the order $\sigma$ gives a vertex
$t \ne s$ a finite distance, then it records a predecessor edge for $t$.

articles.title: Unreached vertices have no DAG shortest-path predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a
source vertex, and let $\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$
by forgetting weights. If the one-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the
order $\sigma$ ends with an infinite distance estimate at a vertex $v$, then it records no
predecessor edge for $v$.

articles.title: Predecessor extraction fails exactly at infinite distances
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $s$ a source vertex, and
$\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph with an edge $u \to v$ for each edge of $E$
from $u$ to $v$. After the one-pass relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order $\sigma$, for every
vertex $t$, following the predecessor edges back from $t$ fails to reach $s$ within $n$ steps if
and only if the computed distance to $t$ is infinite.

articles.title: Paths extracted after topological relaxation are shortest paths
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edges on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $s$ a source vertex, and
$\sigma$ a topological order of the directed graph with an edge $u \to v$ for each edge of $E$
from $u$ to $v$. After the one-pass relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order $\sigma$, suppose
following the predecessor edges back from a vertex $t$ reaches $s$ within $n$ steps, giving the
path $P$. Then $P$ is a path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$, the computed distance to $t$ is finite and
equals the weight of $P$, $P$ has fewer than $n$ edges, and every path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ has
weight at least the weight of $P$. Here a path from $s$ to $t$ in $E$ is a list of edges of $E$,
each starting where the previous one ends, the first starting at $s$ and the last ending at $t$
(the empty list when $t = s$), and its weight is the sum of its edge weights.

articles.title: Predecessor edges of the DAG shortest-path pass
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a source vertex, and
let $\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting
weights. Suppose the one-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order $\sigma$
records an edge occurrence $e$ from $u$ to $w$ with weight $c$ as the predecessor of a vertex
$v$. Then $e$ occurs in $E$, $w = v$, and there is an integer $d$ such that the final distance
estimate at $u$ is $d$, the final distance estimate at $v$ is $d + c$, and the position of $u$
in $\sigma$ is less than the position of $v$ in $\sigma$.

articles.title: The DAG shortest-path pass gives the source distance zero
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a
source vertex, and let $\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$
by forgetting weights. The one-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order
$\sigma$ ends with distance estimate $0$ at $s$.

This holds even when edges of negative weight enter $s$.

articles.title: The source has no DAG shortest-path predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a source vertex, and
let $\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting
weights. The one-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order $\sigma$ records
no predecessor edge for $s$.

articles.title: The DAG shortest-path pass keeps its source
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted
directed edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a source vertex, and
let $\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting
weights. The result of the one-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order
$\sigma$ records $s$ as its source.

articles.title: The DAG shortest-path pass is charged one vertex visit per vertex
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
integer-weighted directed edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a
source vertex, and let $\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$
by forgetting weights. The one-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation of $E$ from $s$ in the order
$\sigma$ is charged exactly $n$ vertex visits.

articles.title: One-pass DAG shortest-path relaxation
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of integer-weighted directed
edge occurrences on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ be a source vertex, and let
$\sigma$ be a topological order of the directed graph obtained from $E$ by forgetting weights.
The relaxation starts from distance estimate $0$ at $s$, infinite estimates at every other
vertex and no predecessor edges. It then takes the vertices $u$ of $\sigma$ in turn and relaxes
each occurrence $e$ in $E$ from $u$ to some $v$ with weight $c$, in the order of $E$: if the
estimate $d$ at $u$ is finite and the estimate at $v$ is infinite or greater than $d + c$, it
sets the estimate at $v$ to $d + c$ and the predecessor of $v$ to $e$. The result records $s$ as
its source together with the final estimates and predecessors. Its cost counts one vertex visit
per vertex of $\sigma$, one edge relaxation per occurrence relaxed, and one distance update per
estimate set.

The original edge occurrences are retained, so every parallel occurrence is checked. The proof
that $\sigma$ is a topological order is not used by the computation.

articles.title: Arc flow of an integer flow
articles.statement:
For an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$, its arc flow is the natural-number matrix whose entry at $(u, v)$ is the positive
part $\max(f(u, v), 0)$ of $f(u, v)$.

articles.title: Augmentation within residual capacities preserves feasibility
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a
capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$
and $t$ be vertices, and let $f$ be a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$. Let
$P = (v_0, \dots, v_k)$ be a nonempty list of pairwise distinct vertices with $v_0 = s$ and
$v_k = t$, and let $a$ be an integer with $0 \le a$ and
$a \le c(v_i, v_{i+1}) - f(v_i, v_{i+1})$ for every $i < k$. Then the augmentation of $f$
along $P$ by $a$ is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$.

articles.title: Bottleneck augmentation preserves feasibility
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with
natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be vertices,
and let $f$ be a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$. If $P$ is a path from $s$ to $t$
in the residual graph of $f$, that is, a nonempty list of pairwise distinct vertices
starting at $s$ and ending at $t$ whose consecutive pairs are residual edges, then the
augmentation of $f$ along $P$ by the bottleneck of $P$ is again feasible for $c$, $s$,
$t$.

articles.title: Augmenting a flow along a path
articles.statement:
Given an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, a list of vertices $P$ and an integer $a$, the augmentation of $f$
along $P$ by $a$ is the matrix whose entry at $(u, v)$ is $f(u, v) + a \cdot d$, where $d$
is the number of consecutive pairs of $P$ equal to $(u, v)$ minus the number of
consecutive pairs of $P$ equal to $(v, u)$, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Two-sided capacity bounds for a feasible flow
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with
natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be vertices,
and let $f$ be a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$. Then for all vertices $u$ and
$v$, we have $-c(v, u) \le f(u, v) \le c(u, v)$.

The lower bound follows from skew symmetry and the upper bound on the reverse entry.

articles.title: No $s$-$t$ cut is smaller than the Edmonds–Karp residual cut
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity
function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities,
and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Let $S_0$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual
graph of the flow computed by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$. Then for every $s$-$t$
cut $S$, the capacity of $S_0$ is at most the capacity of $S$.

articles.title: Cut capacity
articles.statement:
For a capacity matrix $c$ with natural-number entries on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a set $S$ of vertices, the capacity of the cut $S$ is the integer
$\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \notin S} c(u, v)$.

articles.title: Edge delta of a path
articles.statement:
For a list $P$ of elements of a set $V$ and elements $u, v$
of $V$, the edge delta of $P$ at $(u, v)$ is the integer obtained as the number of
consecutive pairs of $P$ equal to $(u, v)$ minus the number of consecutive pairs of $P$
equal to $(v, u)$, counted with multiplicity. It is $0$ when $P$ has fewer than two
elements.

articles.title: The Edmonds–Karp flow is feasible
articles.statement:
For every capacity matrix $c$ with
natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$,
the flow $f$ returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ is feasible for $c$,
$s$, $t$: it is skew-symmetric, satisfies $f(u, v) \le c(u, v)$ for all vertices $u, v$,
and has zero net outflow at every vertex other than $s$ and $t$.

articles.title: Edmonds-Karp computes a maximum flow and a minimum cut
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function on
the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let
$s \ne t$ be vertices. Let $f$ be the real arc flow of the flow computed by the Edmonds-Karp
algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ (its positive part, viewed as real numbers), and let $S_0$ be the set
of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of that flow. Then $f$ is a feasible $s$-$t$
flow for $c$; every feasible real-valued $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ has value at most the value of $f$;
the value of $f$ is at most the capacity of every $s$-$t$ cut; $S_0$ is an $s$-$t$ cut; and the
value of $f$ equals the capacity of $S_0$.

articles.title: Maximality of the Edmonds–Karp flow
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with
natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be distinct
vertices, and let $f$ be the flow returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$.
Then every integer flow $g$ that is feasible for $c$, $s$, $t$ has value at $s$ at most
the value of $f$ at $s$, where the value of a flow at $s$ is its net flow out of $s$.

articles.title: The Edmonds–Karp flow value equals its residual cut capacity
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity
matrix with natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be
distinct vertices, and let $f$ be the flow returned by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$,
$s$, $t$. Then the net flow of $f$ out of $s$ equals the capacity of the cut formed by the
vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of $f$.

articles.title: No augmenting path remains after Edmonds–Karp
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with
natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $s$ and $t$ be distinct
vertices. Then $t$ is not reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow returned
by the Edmonds–Karp algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$.

articles.title: Edmonds–Karp maximum flow
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function assigning a natural number
$c(u, v)$ to each ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If $s = t$, the
Edmonds–Karp flow is the zero flow. Otherwise it is the result of running at most $C + 1$ rounds
of bottleneck augmentation from the zero flow, where $C = \sum_v c(s, v)$ is the total capacity
leaving $s$: each round looks for a shortest path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual graph, stops if
there is none, and otherwise augments the flow along that path by its bottleneck.

articles.title: Integral flow theorem
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$
with natural-number values, viewed as real capacities, and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. Then there
is a natural-number valued function $f$ on pairs of vertices which, viewed as a real function, is
a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$ whose value is at least the value of every feasible real-valued
$s$-$t$ flow for $c$.

The proof takes $f$ to be the arc flow of the flow computed by the Edmonds-Karp algorithm.

articles.title: A skew flow is the difference of its arc flows
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be an integer flow matrix on the
vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ that is skew-symmetric, $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u, v$, and let
$a(u, v) = \max(f(u, v), 0)$ be its arc flow. Then $f(u, v) = a(u, v) - a(v, u)$ for all
vertices $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Augmenting along a path changes the flow value by the amount
articles.statement:
Let $s \ne t$ be vertices,
$f$ a flow, $a$ an integer, and $p$ a nonempty list of vertices whose first entry is $s$ and whose
last entry is $t$. Then the net flow leaving $s$ under the flow obtained by augmenting $f$ along
$p$ by $a$ equals the net flow leaving $s$ under $f$, plus $a$.

No feasibility of $f$, no edge condition on consecutive entries of $p$, and no duplicate-freeness
of $p$ is needed.

articles.title: Weak max-flow min-cut duality
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function, $s$ and $t$ vertices, and
$f$ a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$ and $t$. For every set $S$ of vertices with $s \in S$
and $t \notin S$, the net flow leaving $s$ under $f$ is at most the capacity of the cut $S$,
namely $\sum_{u \in S} \sum_{v \notin S} c(u, v)$.

articles.title: The augmentation loop never decreases the flow value
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function and
$s \ne t$ vertices. For every flow $f$ and every natural number $k$, the net flow leaving $s$
after running at most $k$ rounds of bottleneck augmentation from $f$ is at least the net flow
leaving $s$ under $f$.

articles.title: The flow value is at most the source capacity
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function, $s$ and
$t$ vertices, and $f$ a flow that is feasible for $c$, $s$ and $t$. Then the net flow leaving $s$
under $f$ is at most $\sum_v c(s, v)$, the total capacity leaving $s$.

articles.title: One augmentation step keeps or strictly raises the flow value
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity
function and $s \ne t$ vertices. For every flow $f$, the flow obtained from $f$ by one step of
bottleneck augmentation either has the same net flow leaving $s$ as $f$, or a strictly larger
one.

articles.title: Flow value
articles.statement:
For a flow $f$ on $n$ vertices and a vertex $s$, the value of $f$ at $s$ is
the net flow leaving $s$, namely the integer $\sum_v f(s, v)$, where $v$ runs over all vertices.

articles.title: Flow
articles.statement:
A flow on $n$ vertices, labelled $0, \dots, n-1$, is an integer matrix: it assigns
an integer $f(u, v)$ to each ordered pair of vertices $(u, v)$.

No condition is imposed here; skew symmetry, capacity bounds and conservation are required by
feasibility.

articles.title: A feasible skew flow gives a feasible flow
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values and let $s, t$ be vertices. If an integer flow matrix
$f$ is a feasible skew-symmetric $s$-$t$ flow for $c$, then its arc flow
$(u, v) \mapsto \max(f(u, v), 0)$, viewed as a real function, is a feasible $s$-$t$ flow for $c$
viewed as real capacities.

articles.title: Feasible flow
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function assigning a natural number $c(u, v)$ to
each ordered pair of vertices, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. A flow $f$ is feasible for $c$,
$s$ and $t$ when it is skew symmetric, $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u$ and $v$; it respects
the capacities, $f(u, v) \le c(u, v)$ for all $u$ and $v$; and it is conserved: for every vertex
$v$ other than $s$ and $t$, the net flow $\sum_w f(v, w)$ leaving $v$ is $0$.

articles.title: Directed path
articles.statement:
In a directed graph $G$, a list $p$ of vertices is a path from $s$ to $t$
when it is nonempty, its first entry is $s$, its last entry is $t$, every pair of consecutive
entries $u, v$ forms a directed edge of $G$ from $u$ to $v$, and no vertex occurs twice in $p$.

articles.title: The Edmonds-Karp residual cut separates source and sink
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity function
on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with natural-number values and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. The set
of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph of the flow computed by the Edmonds-Karp
algorithm on $c$, $s$, $t$ is an $s$-$t$ cut: it contains $s$ and not $t$.

articles.title: Unit skew flow along an oriented edge
articles.statement:
For vertices $a$, $b$, $u$, $v$,
the unit skew flow of the oriented edge $(a, b)$ at the ordered pair $(u, v)$ is the integer
$[u = a \text{ and } v = b] - [u = b \text{ and } v = a]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds
and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Augmenting paths have positive bottleneck
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with
natural-number entries and $f$ any integer matrix (the flow) on the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$,
and let $s \ne t$ be vertices. If $p$ is a duplicate-free path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual
graph of $c$ and $f$, then the bottleneck of $p$, the minimum of $c(u, v) - f(u, v)$ over
consecutive vertices $u, v$ of $p$, is positive.

articles.title: Bottleneck of a path
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries and $f$
an integer matrix (the flow) on the same vertices. The bottleneck of a list of vertices
$v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $k \ge 1$ is the integer
$\min_{i < k} \bigl(c(v_i, v_{i+1}) - f(v_i, v_{i+1})\bigr)$, the least residual capacity of a
consecutive pair; a list with at most one vertex has bottleneck $0$.

articles.title: Edges of a path
articles.statement:
The edges of a list $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ are the list of its
consecutive ordered pairs $(v_0, v_1), (v_1, v_2), \dots, (v_{k-1}, v_k)$, in this order; the
empty list and one-element lists have no edges.

articles.title: Soundness of distance-guided path reconstruction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on
a type $V$ whose Boolean test $\equiv$ on pairs of vertices holds exactly for equal vertices, let
$d$ be a partial labelling of the vertices by natural numbers, let $t$ and $u$ be vertices, and let
$k$ be a natural number. If the distance-guided reconstruction for $G$, $d$ and $t$ from $u$ with
$k$ steps left succeeds and returns a list $p$, then $p$ is a walk from $u$ to $t$ in $G$ (it is
nonempty, its first entry is $u$, its last entry is $t$, and every pair of consecutive entries is
an edge of $G$) and $p$ has exactly $k + 1$ entries.

articles.title: Distance-guided path reconstruction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered adjacency
lists, $d$ a partial labelling of its vertices by natural numbers, $t$ a vertex, and $\equiv$ a
given Boolean test on pairs of vertices (not required to be equality). The reconstruction from
a vertex $u$ with $k$ steps left returns the one-element list $[u]$ when $k = 0$ and $u \equiv t$
holds, and fails when $k = 0$ and $u \equiv t$ fails. When $k \ge 1$, it takes the first
out-neighbour $w$ of $u$ in adjacency order with $d(w) = k - 1$; it fails if there is none, and
otherwise returns $u$ followed by the reconstruction from $w$ with $k - 1$ steps left, failing
if that fails.

articles.title: Real capacities
articles.statement:
For a capacity function $c$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with
natural-number values, the real capacities are the same values viewed as real numbers,
$(u, v) \mapsto c(u, v) \in \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Real arc flow
articles.statement:
For an integer flow matrix $f$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, its real
arc flow is the function $(u, v) \mapsto \max(f(u, v), 0)$, the arc flow of $f$, viewed as real
numbers.

articles.title: Residual capacity
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries and $f$ an
integer matrix (the flow) on the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$. The residual capacity of an ordered
pair of vertices $(u, v)$ is the integer $c(u, v) - f(u, v)$.

articles.title: Residual cut
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix assigning a natural number $c(u, v)$ to each
ordered pair of vertices among $0, \dots, n - 1$, let $f$ be a flow on these vertices, and let $s$
be a vertex. The residual cut of $c$, $f$ and $s$ is the set of vertices visited by breadth-first
search from $s$ in the residual graph of $c$ and $f$, that is, the set of vertices reachable from
$s$ in that residual graph.

articles.title: Edges of the residual graph
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries and
$f$ an integer matrix (the flow) on the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$. For all vertices $u$ and $v$,
the residual graph of $c$ and $f$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$ if and only if
$f(u, v) < c(u, v)$.

articles.title: Residual graph
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix assigning a natural number $c(u, v)$ to each
ordered pair of vertices among $0, \dots, n - 1$, and let $f$ be a flow on these vertices. The
residual graph of $c$ and $f$ is the directed adjacency graph whose vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ are
enumerated in increasing order and in which the adjacency list of $u$ consists of the vertices $v$
with $f(u, v) < c(u, v)$, that is, with positive residual capacity $c(u, v) - f(u, v)$, in
increasing order.

articles.title: The iteration stops when there is no augmenting path
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with
natural-number entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, let $s$ and $t$ be vertices, and let
$f$ be a flow (an integer-valued matrix on pairs of vertices). If the breadth-first shortest-path
search finds no path from $s$ to $t$ in the residual graph of $f$ with respect to $c$, then for
every fuel bound $k$, the augmenting-path iteration started at $f$ with fuel $k$ returns $f$.

articles.title: Augmenting-path iteration with fuel
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number
entries on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, let $s$ be a source and $t$ a sink, let $k$ be a fuel
bound and let $f$ be a flow (an integer-valued matrix on pairs of vertices). The iteration returns
$f$ if $k = 0$ or $s = t$. Otherwise it runs the breadth-first shortest-path search from $s$ to $t$
in the residual graph of $f$ with respect to $c$. If the search finds no path, the iteration returns
$f$. If it returns a path $P$, let $b$ be the bottleneck of $P$, the least residual capacity
$c(u, v) - f(u, v)$ over the edges $(u, v)$ of $P$; the iteration augments $f$ along $P$ by $b$,
adding $b$ to $f(u, v)$ and subtracting $b$ from $f(v, u)$ for each edge $(u, v)$ of $P$, and
continues from the augmented flow with fuel $k - 1$.

articles.title: The shortest-path search fails exactly when the sink is unreachable
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite
directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. The
breadth-first shortest-path search in $G$ from $s$ to $t$ returns no path if and only if $t$ is not
reachable from $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: The shortest-path search succeeds exactly when the sink is reachable
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite
directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. The
breadth-first shortest-path search in $G$ from $s$ to $t$ returns some path if and only if $t$ is
reachable from $s$ in $G$ (every vertex counts as reachable from itself).

articles.title: Soundness of the shortest-path search
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices. If the breadth-first shortest-path search in
$G$ from $s$ to $t$ returns a list $P$ of vertices, then $P$ is a directed path in $G$ from $s$ to
$t$ without repeated vertices, and breadth-first search in $G$ from $s$ assigns $t$ a distance $d$
such that $P$ has exactly $d + 1$ vertices.

articles.title: Shortest path via breadth-first search
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with ordered adjacency lists, and let $s$ be a source and $t$ a sink. Run
breadth-first search from $t$ in the reverse graph of $G$; it labels each vertex $v$ from which $t$
is reachable with the distance from $v$ to $t$ in $G$. If $s$ has no label, the search returns no
path. Otherwise, starting at $s$ with label $d$, take $d$ steps, each time moving to the first
out-neighbour (in adjacency order) whose label is one less than that of the current vertex. The
search returns the list of visited vertices, from $s$ to the last one, if every step succeeds and
the last vertex is $t$, and no path otherwise.

articles.title: Source capacity
articles.statement:
For a capacity matrix $c$ with natural-number entries on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and a source $s$, the source capacity is the total capacity leaving $s$,
namely $\sum_{v} c(s, v)$, where $v$ ranges over all vertices, including $s$ itself.

articles.title: One augmenting-path step
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a capacity matrix with natural-number entries on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, let $s$ be a source and $t$ a sink, and let $f$ be a flow (an
integer-valued matrix on pairs of vertices). Run the breadth-first shortest-path search from $s$ to
$t$ in the residual graph of $f$ with respect to $c$. If it finds no path, the step returns $f$. If
it returns a path $P$, let $b$ be the bottleneck of $P$, the least residual capacity
$c(u, v) - f(u, v)$ over the edges $(u, v)$ of $P$ (and $b = 0$ if $P$ has no edges); the step
returns $f$ augmented along $P$ by $b$, that is, $b$ is added to $f(u, v)$ and subtracted from
$f(v, u)$ for each edge $(u, v)$ of $P$.

articles.title: Net outflow in the arc representation
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a skew-symmetric integer flow matrix on
the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, so $f(u, v) = -f(v, u)$ for all $u, v$, and let
$a(u, v) = \max(f(u, v), 0)$ be its arc flow, viewed as real numbers. Then for every vertex $v$,
$\sum_w a(v, w) - \sum_u a(u, v) = \sum_w f(v, w)$, the net flow leaving $v$.

articles.title: The zero flow is feasible
articles.statement:
For every capacity matrix $c$ with natural-number entries on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, the zero flow is feasible for $c$ with
source $s$ and sink $t$.

articles.title: Zero flow
articles.statement:
The zero flow on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ is the integer-valued matrix
$f$ with $f(u, v) = 0$ for all vertices $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Choosing the next proposer
articles.statement:
In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with proposers
$0, 1, \dots, n-1$, the chooser returns the least proposer $m$ who is free in $s$ and has made
fewer than $n$ proposals in $s$, or no proposer if there is none.

articles.title: A proposer's final partner is his last proposal
articles.statement:
Let each proposer $m$ rank the $n$
receivers by a permutation $\sigma_m$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, where $\sigma_m(k)$ is his choice
of rank $k$, let each receiver rank the $n$ proposers, and let $p_m$ be the number of proposals
$m$ has made in the final state of deferred acceptance. Then $p_m \ge 1$, and the Gale-Shapley
partner $\mu(m)$ of $m$ has rank $p_m - 1$ in his ranking, that is,
$\sigma_m^{-1}(\mu(m)) = p_m - 1$.

articles.title: Gale-Shapley serves every preference profile with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers
articles.statement:
Let
the $n$ proposers and the $n$ receivers both be numbered $0, \dots, n-1$. Let each proposer $m$
have a strict total order $\lt _m$ of preference on the receivers and each receiver $w$ a strict
total order $\lt _w$ of preference on the proposers, where $x \lt _m y$ means that $m$ prefers $x$ to
$y$, and likewise for $\lt _w$. Then there are permutations $\sigma_m$ (one for each proposer $m$)
and $\tau_w$ (one for each receiver $w$) of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read as rankings, such that
$w \lt _m w'$ exactly when $\sigma_m^{-1}(w) < \sigma_m^{-1}(w')$ and $a \lt _w b$ exactly when
$\tau_w^{-1}(a) < \tau_w^{-1}(b)$, and the Gale-Shapley matching $\mu$ of the rankings $\sigma$
and $\tau$ is stable for these preferences and proposer-optimal: for every perfect matching $\nu$
that is stable for these preferences and every proposer $m$, it is not the case that
$\nu(m) \lt _m \mu(m)$.

articles.title: Every strict total order on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is given by a ranking
articles.statement:
For every strict
total order $\prec$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$
such that, for all $a$ and $b$, $a \prec b$ holds exactly when $\sigma^{-1}(a) < \sigma^{-1}(b)$.

Hence the Gale-Shapley algorithm on rankings applies to every preference on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

articles.title: Free proposer
articles.statement:
A proposer $m$ is free in a state $s$ of deferred acceptance when no
receiver holds $m$ in $s$.

articles.title: Deferred acceptance
articles.statement:
Let each of $n$ proposers rank the $n$ receivers, and each receiver
rank the $n$ proposers, with rank $0$ the best. Deferred acceptance is the state reached from the
initial state, in which no one has proposed and no receiver holds anyone, by repeating the
following step at most $n^2$ times, stopping early once no proposer is both free and has made
fewer than $n$ proposals: the least such proposer, having made $p$ proposals so far, proposes to
the receiver of rank $p$ in his ranking, and she then holds whichever of him and her current
holder she ranks better, or him if she held no one.

These $n^2$ steps always suffice: in the resulting state no proposer is both free and has made
fewer than $n$ proposals.

articles.title: Proposer-optimality
articles.statement:
No stable matching gives a proposer a partner he prefers to his
Gale-Shapley partner.

articles.title: Receiver-pessimality
articles.statement:
No stable matching gives a receiver a partner she likes less than
her Gale-Shapley partner.

articles.title: The Gale-Shapley matching
articles.statement: Each proposer with the receiver who holds him at the end.

articles.title: When deferred acceptance stops, every proposer is held
articles.statement:
Fix rankings of the $n$ receivers
by each of $n$ proposers and of the proposers by each receiver. Let $s$ be a state of deferred
acceptance that satisfies the invariant of deferred acceptance for these rankings, and suppose
that no proposer is both free in $s$ and has made fewer than $n$ proposals in $s$. Then every
proposer is held by some receiver in $s$.

articles.title: Every receiver holds someone once every proposer is held
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a state of deferred
acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers. If every proposer is held by some receiver in
$s$, then every receiver holds some proposer in $s$.

articles.title: Initial state of deferred acceptance
articles.statement:
The initial state with $n$ proposers and
$n$ receivers: every proposer has made $0$ proposals and no receiver holds anyone.

articles.title: Invariant of deferred acceptance
articles.statement:
Let each proposer $m$ have a ranking $\sigma_m$ of the
$n$ receivers and each receiver $w$ a ranking $\tau_w$ of the $n$ proposers, where $\sigma_m(k)$
is the choice of $m$ of rank $k$ (rank $0$ is the best) and $\tau_w^{-1}(x)$ is the rank of $x$
for $w$. A state $s$ of deferred acceptance satisfies the invariant when: every proposer has made
at most $n$ proposals; if $w$ holds $m$, then $m$ has made $k + 1$ proposals for some rank $k$
with $\sigma_m(k) = w$; no proposer is held by two different receivers; for every proposer $m$
and every rank $k$ less than the number of proposals of $m$, the receiver $w = \sigma_m(k)$ holds
some $m'$ with $\tau_w^{-1}(m') \le \tau_w^{-1}(m)$; and for such $m$ and $k$, if $\sigma_m(k)$
does not hold $m$, then no perfect matching that is stable for the preferences given by the
rankings matches $m$ with $\sigma_m(k)$.

articles.title: The Gale-Shapley matching is stable
articles.statement:
For $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, each with a
ranking of the other side, the perfect matching computed by deferred acceptance is stable for the
strict preferences given by these rankings.

articles.title: Rejected proposals bound stable partners
articles.statement:
Let each proposer $m$ have a ranking
$\sigma_m$ of the $n$ receivers ($\sigma_m(k)$ is the choice of $m$ of rank $k$, rank $0$ the
best), and each receiver a ranking of the $n$ proposers. Let $s$ be a state of deferred
acceptance satisfying the invariant, let $\nu$ be a perfect matching that is stable for the
preferences given by the rankings, let $m$ be a proposer, and let $b$ be a natural number at most
the number of proposals $m$ has made in $s$. If for every rank $k < b$ the receiver $\sigma_m(k)$
does not hold $m$ in $s$, then $\sigma_m^{-1}(\nu(m)) \ge b$.

articles.title: Proposers' preferences from rankings
articles.statement:
Given for each proposer $m$ a ranking $\sigma_m$ of
the $n$ receivers ($\sigma_m(k)$ is the choice of $m$ of rank $k$, rank $0$ the best), the
proposers' preference profile assigns to $m$ the strict total order in which $m$ prefers $w$ to
$w'$ when $\sigma_m^{-1}(w) < \sigma_m^{-1}(w')$.

articles.title: Cases of the receiver's new holder
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a state of deferred acceptance, $m$ a
proposer and $w$ a receiver with ranking $\tau_w$ of the proposers ($\tau_w^{-1}(x)$ is the rank
of $x$, rank $0$ the best). Then one of the following holds: $w$ holds nobody in $s$ and holds $m$
after $m$ proposes to her; or $w$ holds some $y$ in $s$ with $\tau_w^{-1}(m) < \tau_w^{-1}(y)$
and holds $m$ after $m$ proposes to her; or $w$ holds some $y$ in $s$ with
$\tau_w^{-1}(m) \ge \tau_w^{-1}(y)$ and holds $y$ after $m$ proposes to her.

articles.title: Receiver's holder after a proposal
articles.statement:
In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance, the proposer
whom receiver $w$ holds after proposer $m$ proposes to her is $m$ if she holds nobody in $s$ or
ranks $m$ strictly better than her current holder $m'$ in her ranking, and $m'$ otherwise.

articles.title: A stable matching has no blocking pair
articles.statement:
Let each proposer $m$ have a ranking $\sigma_m$ of
the $n$ receivers and each receiver $w$ a ranking $\tau_w$ of the $n$ proposers, where
$\sigma_m^{-1}(x)$ and $\tau_w^{-1}(x)$ are ranks ($0$ the best). If $\nu$ is a perfect matching
that is stable for the preferences given by these rankings, there are no proposer $m$ and
receiver $w$ with $\sigma_m^{-1}(w) < \sigma_m^{-1}(\nu(m))$ and
$\tau_w^{-1}(m) < \tau_w^{-1}(\nu^{-1}(w))$.

articles.title: Rank under a strict total order
articles.statement:
For a strict total order $<$ on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the
rank of an element $a$ is the number of elements $b$ with $b < a$ (the elements preferred to $a$),
as an element of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

articles.title: Proposer's partner
articles.statement:
In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$
receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, the partner of a proposer $m$ is the lowest-numbered
receiver that holds $m$ in $s$; if no receiver holds $m$, it is the receiver numbered $m$
(a default value).

articles.title: Receiver's partner
articles.statement:
In a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$
receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, the partner of a receiver $w$ is the proposer she holds
in $s$; if she holds nobody, it is the proposer numbered $w$ (a default value).

articles.title: A proposal
articles.statement:
Fix, for each proposer, a ranking of the $n$ receivers and, for each receiver,
a ranking of the $n$ proposers (rank $0$ is the first choice). Let $s$ be a state of deferred
acceptance in which proposer $m$ has made $k$ proposals. If $k < n$, then $m$ proposes to the
receiver $w$ of rank $k$ in his ranking: his number of proposals becomes $k + 1$, and $w$ now
holds $m$ if she held nobody or ranks $m$ strictly above the proposer she held, and keeps her old
holder otherwise; all other counts and holders are unchanged. If $k \ge n$, the state is
unchanged.

articles.title: Remaining proposals
articles.statement:
For a state $s$ of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$
receivers, in which each proposer $m$ has made $k_m$ proposals, the number of proposals still
available is $\sum_{m} \max(n - k_m, 0)$, the sum running over all $n$ proposers.

articles.title: Running deferred acceptance
articles.statement:
Fix rankings for $n$ proposers and $n$ receivers, both
numbered $0, \dots, n-1$. Starting from a state $s$ with a budget of $f$ proposals: if $f = 0$, or
if no proposer is both free (held by no receiver) and has made fewer than $n$ proposals, the run
returns $s$; otherwise the lowest-numbered such proposer makes a proposal, and the run continues
from the resulting state with budget $f - 1$.

articles.title: Deferred-acceptance state
articles.statement:
A state of deferred acceptance with $n$ proposers and $n$
receivers, both numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, records for each proposer a natural number, the number of
proposals he has made (his next proposal goes to his choice of that rank), and for each receiver
either the proposer she currently holds or that she holds nobody.

articles.title: Deferred acceptance makes at most n² proposals
articles.statement:
For any rankings of the $n$ receivers by
each of the $n$ proposers and of the proposers by each receiver, in the final state of deferred
acceptance the numbers of proposals made by the proposers sum to at most $n \cdot n$.

No proposer proposes more than $n$ times.

articles.title: A proposal adds one to the proposal count
articles.statement:
Fix rankings for $n$ proposers and $n$
receivers. If proposer $m$ has made fewer than $n$ proposals in a state $s$ of deferred
acceptance, then after $m$ proposes, the total number of proposals made by all proposers is one
more than in $s$.

articles.title: Preference order of a ranking
articles.statement:
A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read as a
ranking ($\sigma(k)$ is the $k$-th choice, $\sigma(0)$ the best), gives the strict total order on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which $a$ is preferred to $b$ when $\sigma^{-1}(a) < \sigma^{-1}(b)$.

articles.title: Receivers' preference profile from rankings
articles.statement:
Given for each receiver $w$ a ranking
$\sigma_w$ of the $n$ proposers (a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with $\sigma_w(0)$ her first
choice), the receivers' preference profile assigns to $w$ the preference order of $\sigma_w$: $w$
prefers $a$ to $b$ when $\sigma_w^{-1}(a) < \sigma_w^{-1}(b)$.

articles.title: Acyclicity of a newest-first edge list
articles.statement:
A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges
on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, read newest first, is newest-first acyclic when, for
every $i$, the endpoints of $e_i$ are not connected by the later list $e_{i+1}, \dots, e_k$
in the sense of connectivity by a newest-first edge list.

articles.title: Acyclic edge list
articles.statement:
A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is acyclic when, for every $i$, the endpoints of $e_i$ are not connected
by the preceding edges $e_1, \dots, e_{i-1}$, in the sense of connectivity by an edge list.

articles.title: Connectivity by a newest-first edge list
articles.statement:
Connectivity of vertices $u$ and $v$ of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ by a list of validated edges, read newest first, is defined by recursion
on the list. By the empty list, $u$ and $v$ are connected exactly when $u = v$. By a list
whose first edge $e$ has source $a$ and target $b$ and whose remaining edges form the list
$L$, the vertices $u$ and $v$ are connected when $u$ and $v$ are connected by $L$, or $u$ is
connected to $a$ and $v$ is connected to $b$ by $L$, or $u$ is connected to $b$ and $v$ is
connected to $a$ by $L$.

articles.title: Connectivity by an edge list
articles.statement:
Vertices $u$ and $v$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ are
connected by a list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges when they are connected by the
reversed list $e_k, \dots, e_1$ in the sense of connectivity by a newest-first edge list.

articles.title: Decoding a raw edge at an ordinal
articles.statement:
Given natural numbers $n$ and $i$ and a raw edge
with source $s$, target $t$ and weight $w$, decoding at ordinal $i$ returns the validated
edge on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with ordinal $i$, source $s$, target $t$ and
weight $w$ when $s < n$ and $t < n$, and returns no edge otherwise.

articles.title: Kruskal input graph
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, an input graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of a list of raw edges, kept in input order; the same pair of
endpoints may occur on several edges.

The endpoints of a raw edge are natural numbers and are not required to be below $n$.

articles.title: Greedy cut property of Kruskal's scan
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an input graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, give each valid edge with weight $w$ and input ordinal $o$ the key
$(w, o)$, and compare keys lexicographically. The graph $G$ has the greedy cut property when
the following holds for every way of splitting the valid edges of $G$, sorted by key, into an
initial segment, an edge $e$ and a final segment. Let $P$ be the union-find partition obtained
by scanning the initial segment from the discrete parent forest with no accepted edges. If the
endpoints of $e$ lie in different classes of $P$, then the key of $e$ is at most the key of
every valid edge of $G$ whose endpoints lie in different classes of $P$.

articles.title: Discrete parent forest
articles.statement:
The initial forest on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is
the parent forest in which every vertex is its own parent, so every vertex is a root, and
whose depth certificate is $0$ at every vertex.

articles.title: Ordered spanning forest
articles.statement:
For an input graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$,
a list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of validated edges is an ordered spanning forest of $G$ when it is a
spanning forest of $G$ and its keys are nondecreasing: for all $i < j$, the key of $e_i$ is
at most the key of $e_j$, where the key of an edge with weight $w$ and input ordinal $o$ is
the pair $(w, o)$ and keys are compared lexicographically.

articles.title: Spanning forest of an input graph
articles.statement:
For an input graph $G$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, a list $F$ of validated edges is a spanning forest of $G$ when every
edge of $F$ is a valid edge of $G$, $F$ is acyclic, and $F$ spans $G$: for every valid edge
of $G$, its endpoints are connected by $F$.

articles.title: Lexicographic order on edge keys
articles.statement:
For pairs of natural numbers $(w, i)$ and $(w', i')$,
$(w, i) \preceq (w', i')$ holds when $w < w'$, or $w = w'$ and $i \le i'$. This is the
non-strict lexicographic order on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$; Kruskal's algorithm applies it to
keys (weight, input ordinal).

articles.title: Sorting key of a weighted edge
articles.statement:
The sorting key of a weighted edge $e$ is the pair
$(w(e), i(e)) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of its weight $w(e)$ and its input ordinal $i(e)$,
the zero-based position of $e$ in the original input edge list.

Keys are compared lexicographically.

articles.title: Kruskal's output is acyclic
articles.statement:
For every graph $G$, the edge list returned by Kruskal's
algorithm on $G$ is acyclic: each edge in it joins two vertices that are not connected by the
edges before it in the list.

articles.title: Kruskal selects only valid input edges
articles.statement:
For every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, every edge
in the list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a valid edge of $G$: an input edge whose
two endpoints are both below $n$, carrying its input ordinal.

articles.title: Kruskal's greedy cut property
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph and let $e_1, \dots, e_m$ be its valid
edges sorted lexicographically by key (weight, then input ordinal). For a position $k$, let
$P_k$ be the partition of the vertices given by the union-find forest after Kruskal's scan,
started from the discrete forest, has processed $e_1, \dots, e_{k-1}$. If the endpoints of $e_k$
lie in different classes of $P_k$, then for every valid edge $c$ of $G$ whose endpoints lie in
different classes of $P_k$, the key of $e_k$ is lexicographically at most the key of $c$: either
$e_k$ has smaller weight than $c$, or the same weight and input ordinal at most that of $c$.

articles.title: Kruskal's output is a sorted spanning forest
articles.statement:
For every graph $G$, the edge list returned
by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a spanning forest of $G$ (its edges are valid edges of $G$, it
is acyclic, and it connects the endpoints of every valid edge of $G$), and whenever an edge $e$
comes before an edge $f$ in it, the key (weight, input ordinal) of $e$ is lexicographically at
most that of $f$.

articles.title: Kruskal's output is a spanning forest
articles.statement:
For every graph $G$, the edge list returned by
Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is a spanning forest of $G$: every edge in it is a valid edge of $G$,
it is acyclic, and it connects the two endpoints of every valid edge of $G$.

articles.title: Kruskal accepts light edges
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph and let $e_1, \dots, e_m$ be its valid
edges sorted lexicographically by key (weight, then input ordinal). For a position $k$, let
$P_k$ be the partition of the vertices given by the union-find forest after Kruskal's scan,
started from the discrete forest, has processed $e_1, \dots, e_{k-1}$. If the endpoints of $e_k$
lie in different classes of $P_k$, then the weight of $e_k$ is at most the weight of every valid
edge of $G$ whose endpoints lie in different classes of $P_k$.

articles.title: Kruskal's algorithm gives a minimum spanning forest
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph with
natural-number edge weights, and let $F$ be any spanning forest of $G$: a list of valid edges of
$G$ that is acyclic and connects the endpoints of every valid edge of $G$. Then the total weight
of the edge list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$ is at most the total weight of $F$.

Total weights count parallel edge occurrences separately, and $G$ need not be connected.

## Sources

- CLRS, fourth edition, §21.2, cut-exchange argument.

articles.title: Kruskal's output is sorted by key
articles.statement:
For every graph $G$, if an edge $e$ comes before an
edge $f$ in the list returned by Kruskal's algorithm on $G$, then $e$ has smaller weight than
$f$, or the same weight as $f$ and input ordinal at most that of $f$.

articles.title: Kruskal's selected edges span the graph
articles.statement:
For every finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, given by its list of input edges, and every valid input edge of $G$
(one whose endpoints are both less than $n$), the two endpoints of that edge are connected by the
edges that Kruskal's algorithm selects on $G$.

The graph $G$ need not be connected.

articles.title: Kruskal's algorithm
articles.statement:
For a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, Kruskal's algorithm starts from the partition of the vertices into
singletons and processes the valid input edges of $G$ (those whose endpoints are both less than
$n$) in lexicographic order of (weight, input position). An edge whose endpoints lie in different
classes of the current partition is accepted and its two classes are merged; an edge whose
endpoints lie in the same class is skipped. The result is the list of accepted edges in the order
in which they were processed.

articles.title: Valid edges in Kruskal order
articles.statement:
For a finite weighted multigraph $G$ on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the ordered edges of $G$ are its valid input edges (those whose endpoints
are both less than $n$), sorted by merge sort in lexicographic order of (weight, input position):
by nondecreasing weight, with edges of equal weight in input order.

articles.title: Raw input edge
articles.statement:
A raw edge is an undirected weighted input edge given by three natural
numbers: two endpoints, which are not yet checked to be vertices of the graph, and a weight.

articles.title: Scanning a list of edges
articles.statement:
Starting from a Kruskal scan state $s$, scanning a list of
validated edges $e_1, \dots, e_k$ applies one Kruskal step to each edge in list order: the scan
of the empty list returns $s$, and the scan of $e_1, \dots, e_k$ is the scan of $e_2, \dots, e_k$
from the state obtained by processing $e_1$ in $s$.

articles.title: Sorting edges by weight and input position
articles.statement:
Sorting a list of validated edges is merge
sort with the comparison $(w, i) \preceq (w', i')$ if $w < w'$, or $w = w'$ and $i \le i'$, applied
to the pairs (weight, input position) of the edges.

articles.title: Edge lists spanning a graph
articles.statement:
A list $L$ of validated edges spans a finite weighted
multigraph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ when, for every valid input edge of $G$ (one
whose endpoints are both less than $n$), the two endpoints of that edge are connected using the
edges of $L$.

articles.title: Kruskal scan state
articles.statement:
A state of the Kruskal scan on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$
consists of a union-find parent forest on these vertices, which records the current partition,
and the list of edges accepted so far, newest first.

articles.title: One Kruskal step
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a Kruskal scan state and $e$ a validated edge with endpoints
$u$ and $v$. If $u$ and $v$ are equivalent in the union-find forest of $s$, processing $e$ leaves
$s$ unchanged. Otherwise $e$ is accepted: the new forest is the union of $u$ and $v$ in the forest
of $s$, and $e$ is put at the front of the list of accepted edges.

articles.title: Total weight of a Kruskal edge list
articles.statement:
The total weight of a list of validated edges is the
sum of the weights of its entries, each entry counted once, so parallel edges and repeated
entries each contribute their weight.

articles.title: Validating an edge list from a given ordinal
articles.statement:
Given $n$, a starting ordinal $o$ and a
list of raw edges $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{m-1}$, this returns, in input order, the weighted edges on
the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ obtained from those $e_k$ whose two endpoints are both less than
$n$; each keeps the endpoints and weight of $e_k$ and carries the ordinal $o + k$. Edges with an
endpoint at least $n$ are omitted, but they still count towards the ordinals of later edges.

articles.title: Valid edges of an input graph
articles.statement:
For a graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ given
by its list of raw edges $e_0, e_1, \dots, e_{m-1}$, the valid edges of $G$ are, in input order,
the weighted edges obtained from those $e_k$ whose two endpoints are both less than $n$; each
keeps the endpoints and weight of $e_k$ and carries its zero-based input ordinal $k$. Edges with an
endpoint at least $n$ are omitted.

articles.title: Weighted edge
articles.statement:
A weighted edge on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ consists of an ordinal,
a natural number recording its zero-based position in the original input list, two endpoints in
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, and a natural-number weight.

articles.title: Alternating path
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array, giving each right vertex at most one left
vertex as its partner, let $k$ be a natural number and $j$ a right vertex. A list $P$ of pairs
$(i, j')$ of a left vertex $i$ and a right vertex $j'$ is an alternating path from $j$ within
round $k$ when all of the following hold: $P$ is nonempty and its first pair has right vertex
$j$; for every pair $(i, j')$ of $P$, $j'$ is a neighbour of $i$ but $i$ is not the partner of
$j'$; for every pair $(i, j')$ of $P$, the alternating search from the unmatched left vertices
reaches $i$ within $k$ rounds and $j'$ within $k + 1$ rounds; no left vertex and no right vertex
occurs twice in $P$; for any two consecutive pairs $(i, j')$ and $(i', j'')$ of $P$, $i$ is the
partner of $j''$; and the left vertex of the last pair of $P$ is the partner of no right vertex.

When $j$ is unmatched as well, $P$ is an augmenting path.

articles.title: A failed augmentation reaches no unmatched right vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array on a
bipartite graph with $a$ left vertices. If the augmentation step on $\mu$ fails, then no unmatched
right vertex is reached within $a + 1$ rounds of the alternating search from the unmatched left
vertices.

articles.title: A successful augmentation grows the matching by one edge
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array
that describes a matching. If the augmentation step on $\mu$ returns a partner array $\mu'$, then
$\mu'$ also describes a matching, and $\mu'$ has exactly one more matched right vertex than
$\mu$.

articles.title: One augmentation step
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array on a bipartite graph with $a$ left
vertices and $b$ right vertices. Run the alternating search from the unmatched left vertices for
$a + 1$ rounds and take the first right vertex $j$, in the order $0, \dots, b - 1$, that is
unmatched and reached. If there is none, the step fails. Otherwise it returns the partner array
obtained from $\mu$ by flipping the path found by walking back from $j$ through the search
layers: every right vertex $j'$ on the path gets as partner the left vertex paired with it on the
path, and every other right vertex keeps its partner.

articles.title: One round of the layered search bounds the deficit
articles.statement:
If no unmatched right vertex is reached
by round `k + 1`, every matching has at most as many edges as the current one plus the right
vertices first reached in round `k + 1`: the unreached left vertices and the right vertices reached
by round `k + 1` cover every edge.

articles.title: Closing a deficit of $f$ in $f$ Hopcroft–Karp phases
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array,
$M$ a matching of the bipartite graph and $f \in \mathbb{N}$. If $M$ has at most $f$ more pairs
than the matched pairs of $\mu$, then $M$ has at most as many pairs as the matched pairs of the
partner array returned by the Hopcroft–Karp phase loop with fuel $f$ from $\mu$.

Each phase that finds a path adds at least one edge, and a phase that finds none leaves a maximum
matching.

articles.title: Hopcroft and Karp's bound on the number of phases
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with $b$ right
vertices, run at most $2 \lfloor \sqrt{b} \rfloor + 2$ Hopcroft–Karp phases from the empty
matching, stopping early when a phase finds no augmenting path. Then no matching of the graph has
more edges than the resulting one.

After the first $\lfloor \sqrt{b} \rfloor + 1$ phases every augmenting path has more than
$\lfloor \sqrt{b} \rfloor$ pairs, so the deficit against any matching is at most
$\lfloor \sqrt{b} \rfloor$, and each further phase adds an edge.

articles.title: Correctness of Hopcroft–Karp
articles.statement: No matching is larger than the result.

articles.title: Optimality of the augmenting-path matching algorithm
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with $b$ right
vertices, start from the empty matching and repeat the augmentation step until it fails, at most
$b + 1$ times. No matching of the graph has more edges than the resulting matching.

articles.title: Kőnig's certificate
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array on a bipartite graph with $a$ left
vertices that describes a matching. If no unmatched right vertex is reached within $a + 1$ rounds
of the alternating search from the unmatched left vertices, then no matching has more edges than
the matching of $\mu$: the unreached left vertices and the reached right vertices cover every
edge, and each of them is matched, to distinct matching edges.

articles.title: Flipping disjoint augmenting paths matches at least one more vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a
partner array and let $P_1, \dots, P_n$, with $n \ge 1$, be augmenting paths for $\mu$, all for
the same number $k$ of search rounds, such that no right vertex occurs twice in the concatenation
$P_1 P_2 \cdots P_n$. Then flipping this concatenation in $\mu$ gives a partner array with at
least one more matched right vertex than $\mu$: the right vertices matched before stay matched,
and so does the start of the first path.

articles.title: Flipping an augmenting path adds one matched vertex
articles.statement:
If $P$ is an augmenting path for a
partner array $\mu$, then flipping $P$ in $\mu$ gives a partner array with exactly one more
matched right vertex than $\mu$.

articles.title: Matched pairs and matched right vertices are equinumerous
articles.statement:
For every partner array
$\mu$, the number of matched pairs $(i, j)$ of $\mu$, those with $\mu(j) = i$, equals the number
of matched right vertices of $\mu$.

articles.title: Shortest chains from a vertex whose level a phase keeps were chains before it
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$
be a valid partner array whose first free round is defined, and let $\mu'$ be obtained from $\mu$
by flipping all the paths of the phase of $\mu$. Let $z$ be a right vertex and $m$ a natural
number such that $z$ is first reached in round $m + 1$ of the layered search both for $\mu$ and
for $\mu'$, and let $S$ be an alternating chain for $\mu'$ from $z$ to an unmatched left vertex
with exactly $m + 1$ pairs. Then $S$ is also an alternating chain for $\mu$ from $z$ to an
unmatched left vertex, and for every pair of $S$ after the first, its right vertex is not the
right vertex of any pair on the paths of the phase.

A flipped edge would step back a round, which a chain of this length cannot afford.

articles.title: Exact level of a right vertex
articles.statement:
For a partner array $\mu$, a natural number $m$ and a
right vertex $z$, $z$ has exact level $m$ when $z$ is first reached in round $m + 1$ of the
layered search for $\mu$: it is reached within $m + 1$ rounds but not within $m$ rounds.

articles.title: Matched reached left vertices are reached through a partner
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array
and $k$ a natural number. If a left vertex $i$ is reached within $k$ rounds of the layered search
and is matched (some right vertex has partner $i$), then some right vertex $j$ reached within $k$
rounds has partner $i$, that is, $\mu(j) = i$.

articles.title: When there is no first free round
articles.statement:
For a partner array $\mu$ of a bipartite graph with
$a$ left vertices, the first free round of $\mu$ is undefined if and only if no unmatched right
vertex is reached within $a + 1$ rounds of the layered search.

articles.title: Characterization of the first free round
articles.statement:
For a partner array $\mu$ of a bipartite graph
with $a$ left vertices and a natural number $d$, the first free round of $\mu$ equals $d$ if and
only if $d \le a$, some unmatched right vertex is reached within $d + 1$ rounds of the layered
search, and for every $k < d$ no unmatched right vertex is reached within $k + 1$ rounds.

articles.title: Each phase lengthens the shortest augmenting paths
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array
and $c$ a natural number such that the first free round of $\mu$, if defined, is at least $c$.
For every natural number $f$, running at most $f$ Hopcroft–Karp phases from $\mu$, stopping
early when a phase finds no path, gives a valid partner array whose first free round, if
defined, is at least $c + f$.

articles.title: First free round
articles.statement:
For a partner array $\mu$ of a bipartite graph with $a$ left vertices,
the first free round of $\mu$ is the least $d \le a$ such that some unmatched right vertex is
reached within $d + 1$ rounds of the layered search; it is undefined if there is no such $d$.

articles.title: Flipping a list of pairs
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array, assigning to each right vertex
either a left partner or none, and let $P$ be a list of pairs $(i, j)$ of a left vertex $i$ and a
right vertex $j$. The flip of $\mu$ along $P$ sends each right vertex $j$ to the left vertex of
the first pair in $P$ whose right vertex is $j$, and to $\mu(j)$ (a partner or none) when no pair
of $P$ has right vertex $j$.

articles.title: A phase leaves no new unmatched left vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (a
matching of the graph) whose first free round is defined, equal to some $d$. If a left vertex $i$
is unmatched in the flip of $\mu$ along the concatenation of all the paths of the phase of $\mu$,
then $i$ is unmatched in $\mu$.

The first pair of each path starts at an unmatched right vertex, and every other right vertex of a
path had the previous left vertex as partner, which the phase rematches.

articles.title: Unmatched left vertex
articles.statement:
Given a partner array $\mu$, which assigns to each right vertex $j$
either a left vertex $\mu(j)$ as partner or no partner, a left vertex $i$ is unmatched (free) when
no right vertex $j$ has $\mu(j) = i$.

articles.title: A Hopcroft–Karp step that finds nothing
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (a matching of
the graph, whose left vertices number $a$). If the Hopcroft–Karp step on $\mu$ returns nothing,
then no right vertex without a partner in $\mu$ is reached within $a + 1$ rounds of the
alternating breadth-first layers of $\mu$.

articles.title: A successful Hopcroft–Karp step grows the matching
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (a
matching of the graph). If the Hopcroft–Karp step on $\mu$ returns a partner array $\mu'$, then
$\mu'$ is valid and $|\mathrm{matched}(\mu)| + 1 \le |\mathrm{matched}(\mu')|$, where
$\mathrm{matched}(\nu)$ is the set of right vertices that have a partner in $\nu$.

articles.title: Hopcroft–Karp step
articles.statement:
Given a partner array $\mu$, consider the phase of $\mu$, a list of
paths, each a list of pairs. If the phase is empty, the step returns nothing; otherwise it returns
the flip of $\mu$ along the concatenation of all the paths of the phase.

articles.title: Fuel adds up in the phase loop
articles.statement:
For all $f, g \in \mathbb{N}$ and every partner array
$\mu$, the Hopcroft–Karp phase loop with fuel $f + g$ from $\mu$ returns the same partner array as
the loop with fuel $g$ run from the result of the loop with fuel $f$ from $\mu$.

articles.title: The phase loop stops when a step finds nothing
articles.statement:
If the Hopcroft–Karp step on a partner
array $\mu$ returns nothing, then for every fuel $f \in \mathbb{N}$ the Hopcroft–Karp phase loop
with fuel $f$ from $\mu$ returns $\mu$.

articles.title: Correctness of the phase loop
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (a matching of the
graph) on $b$ right vertices, and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ be a fuel with
$b < |\mathrm{matched}(\mu)| + n$, where $\mathrm{matched}(\mu)$ is the set of right vertices with
a partner in $\mu$; so $n$ exceeds the number of unmatched right vertices. Let $\mu'$ be the
result of the Hopcroft–Karp phase loop with fuel $n$ from $\mu$. Then $\mu'$ is valid, and every
