matching $M$ of the graph satisfies $|M| \le |\mathrm{pairs}(\mu')|$, where $\mathrm{pairs}(\mu')$
is the set of pairs $(i, j)$ with $\mu'(j) = i$.

articles.title: Hopcroft–Karp phase loop
articles.statement:
Given a fuel $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a partner array $\mu$, the
loop returns $\mu$ when $n = 0$ or when the Hopcroft–Karp step on $\mu$ returns nothing; when
$n \ge 1$ and the step returns a partner array $\mu'$, it returns the loop with fuel $n - 1$ run
from $\mu'$. So it runs Hopcroft–Karp steps while they find paths, at most $n$ times.

articles.title: Hopcroft–Karp
articles.statement:
Let a bipartite graph have left vertices $0, \dots, a-1$, right
vertices $0, \dots, b-1$ and an adjacency list for each left vertex. Starting from the empty
matching, the Hopcroft–Karp algorithm runs phases, at most $b + 1$ of them, and stops early at
the first phase that finds no path: each phase computes the layered search once, collects
vertex-disjoint augmenting paths from the unmatched right vertices reached in the earliest round
that reaches any, and flips all of them at once. The result is the final matching, given as the
partner (or the absence of one) of each right vertex.

The result is a maximum matching.

articles.title: Augmenting path
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array, $k$ a natural number and $j$ a right
vertex. A list $P$ of pairs of a left vertex and a right vertex is an augmenting path from $j$
within round $k$ when $P$ is an alternating path from $j$ within round $k$ and $j$ is unmatched:
$\mu$ gives $j$ no partner.

Since the last left vertex of an alternating path is unmatched, both endpoints of an augmenting
path are unmatched.

articles.title: Alternating chain to an unmatched left vertex
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph, let each right vertex
have at most one partner, a left vertex (the partners need not form a matching), and let $z$ be a
right vertex. A list $Q$ of pairs (left vertex, right vertex) is an alternating chain from $z$
when its first pair has right vertex $z$, each of its pairs $(i, j)$ is an edge with $i$ not the
partner of $j$, each right vertex after the first is the partner of the preceding left vertex,
and its last left vertex is the partner of no right vertex.

Unlike an augmenting path, $z$ may be matched, the vertices need not lie in the layers of the
search, and a vertex may occur more than once.

articles.title: Hopcroft–Karp returns a matching
articles.statement:
For every bipartite graph with left vertices
$0, \dots, a-1$, right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$ and an adjacency list for each left vertex, the
pairs $(i, j)$ such that the Hopcroft–Karp algorithm makes $i$ the partner of $j$ form a matching
of the graph: each pair is an edge, and no two distinct pairs share a left or a right vertex.

articles.title: The augmenting-path algorithm returns a matching
articles.statement:
For every bipartite graph with left
vertices $0, \dots, a-1$, right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$ and an adjacency list for each left
vertex, the pairs $(i, j)$ such that the augmenting-path maximum matching algorithm (from the
empty matching, repeatedly flip an augmenting path found by the layered search) makes $i$ the
partner of $j$ form a matching of the graph: each pair is an edge, and no two distinct pairs
share a left or a right vertex.

articles.title: A valid partner array gives a matching
articles.statement:
Let each right vertex $j$ of a bipartite graph
have at most one partner, a left vertex. If the partners are valid for the graph (each partner of
$j$ is adjacent to $j$, and no left vertex is the partner of two right vertices), then the set of
pairs $(i, j)$ with $i$ the partner of $j$ is a matching of the graph.

articles.title: Matching in a bipartite graph
articles.statement:
Let a bipartite graph have left vertices $0, \dots, a-1$,
right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$ and an adjacency list for each left vertex. A finite set $M$ of
pairs $(i, j)$ of a left vertex $i$ and a right vertex $j$ is a matching when every pair in $M$ is
an edge ($j$ is in the adjacency list of $i$), no two distinct pairs of $M$ have the same left
vertex, and no two distinct pairs of $M$ have the same right vertex.

articles.title: Distances do not decrease across a phase
articles.statement:
Let the partner array of a bipartite graph with
$a$ left vertices be valid, and suppose that some round $r \le a + 1$ of the layered search
reaches an unmatched right vertex, so that a phase runs from the earliest such round. After
flipping all the paths that phase finds, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ the left vertices and the
right vertices reached within $k$ rounds of the layered search were already reached within $k$
rounds before the flip.

This is a step of Hopcroft and Karp's analysis.

articles.title: The left layers stop growing once two consecutive ones agree
articles.statement:
For any partner array, if
the layered search reaches the same left vertices within $k$ rounds as within $k + 1$ rounds,
then for every $m \ge k$ it reaches exactly those left vertices within $m$ rounds.

articles.title: Rounds $a$ and $a + 1$ reach the same left vertices
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with $a$ left
vertices, for every partner array $\mu$, the alternating layered search for $\mu$ reaches the same
left vertices within $a + 1$ rounds as within $a$ rounds.

articles.title: Alternating breadth-first layers
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ give each right vertex $j$ of a bipartite
graph at most one partner $\mu(j)$ among the left vertices. The layers are pairs $(Z_k, R_k)$ of a
set $Z_k$ of left vertices and a set $R_k$ of right vertices, defined by recursion on $k$: $Z_0$ is
the set of unmatched left vertices (those that are the partner of no right vertex) and
$R_0 = \emptyset$; $R_{k+1}$ is the set of right vertices $j$ adjacent to some $i \in Z_k$ with
$\mu(j) \ne i$, and $Z_{k+1}$ is $Z_k$ together with the left vertices $\mu(j)$ for $j \in R_{k+1}$.

The layers are cumulative on both sides: $Z_k$ holds the left vertices reached within $k$ rounds
and $R_k$ the right vertices reached within $k$ rounds. The round where a vertex is first reached
is its breadth-first level.

articles.title: The first free round does not decrease across a phase
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner
assignment of a bipartite graph (a matching), and let $\mu'$ be obtained from $\mu$ by flipping
all the paths of the phase of $\mu$ at once. If the first free round of $\mu$ is $d$ and the first
free round of $\mu'$ is $d'$, then $d \le d'$.

articles.title: No augmenting path is shorter than a phase's
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ give each right vertex of a
bipartite graph at most one partner among the left vertices. If the first free round of $\mu$ is
$d$, then every augmenting path for $\mu$ has at least $d + 1$ pairs.

articles.title: Phases use shortest augmenting paths
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner assignment of a
bipartite graph (a matching) whose first free round is $d$. Then every path of the phase of $\mu$
has exactly $d + 1$ pairs.

Every augmenting path for $\mu$ has at least $d + 1$ pairs, so these paths are shortest
augmenting paths.

articles.title: The next phase's paths are strictly longer
articles.statement:
**The next phase's paths are strictly longer** (Hopcroft and Karp). Let $\mu$ be a valid
partner assignment of a bipartite graph (a matching), and let $\mu'$ be obtained from $\mu$ by
flipping all the paths of the phase of $\mu$ at once. If the first free round of $\mu$ is $d$ and
the first free round of $\mu'$ is $d'$, then $d < d'$.

A shortest augmenting path for $\mu'$ of the same length would be a shortest augmenting chain for
$\mu$ that is disjoint from the paths of the phase, contradicting the maximality of the phase.

articles.title: Marking a right vertex dead
articles.statement:
Given a set $D$ of right vertices, represented by its
indicator function, and a right vertex $j$, the result is the indicator function of
$D \cup \{j\}$.

articles.title: Marking the left vertices of a path used
articles.statement:
Given a set $U$ of left vertices, represented
by its indicator function, and a list $P$ of pairs $(i, j)$ of a left vertex $i$ and a right
vertex $j$, the result is the indicator function of $U$ together with the left vertices of the
pairs of $P$.

articles.title: Marking the right vertices of a path used
articles.statement:
Given a set $U$ of right vertices,
represented by its indicator function, and a list $P$ of pairs $(i, j)$ of a left vertex $i$ and
a right vertex $j$, the result is the indicator function of $U$ together with the right vertices
of the pairs of $P$.

articles.title: Flipping an alternating path matches its first vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ give each right
vertex of a bipartite graph at most one partner among the left vertices, and let $P$ be an
alternating path for $\mu$ starting at the right vertex $j$. Then the right vertices matched after
flipping $P$ are exactly $j$ and the right vertices matched under $\mu$.

The other right vertices of $P$ change partners but stay matched.

articles.title: Matched right vertices
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ give each right vertex $j$ of a bipartite graph at
most one partner $\mu(j)$ among the left vertices. The matched right vertices of $\mu$ are the
right vertices $j$ that have a partner $\mu(j)$.

articles.title: Enough augmentations reach a maximum matching
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with right vertices
$0, \dots, b-1$, let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (it assigns to each right vertex at most one
left partner, partners are neighbours, and no left vertex is the partner of two right vertices).
Let $f \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $b < |\mathrm{matched}(\mu)| + f$, where $\mathrm{matched}(\mu)$ is
the set of right vertices with a partner, and let $\mu'$ be the result of the augmentation loop
from $\mu$ with fuel $f$. Then $\mu'$ is valid, and every matching $M$ of the graph satisfies
$|M| \le |\mathrm{pairs}(\mu')|$, where $\mathrm{pairs}(\mu')$ is the set of pairs $(i, j)$ with
$\mu'(j) = i$.

articles.title: Augmentation loop
articles.statement:
Given a fuel $f \in \mathbb{N}$ and a partner array $\mu$ (assigning to
each right vertex at most one left partner), the loop returns $\mu$ when $f = 0$. When $f \ge 1$ it
performs one augmentation step on $\mu$: if the layered search reaches no unmatched right vertex,
the loop returns $\mu$; otherwise it runs with fuel $f - 1$ on the array that this step returns,
obtained by flipping the pairs walked back through the layers from the least-indexed unmatched
right vertex that the search reaches. Thus it augments while possible, at most $f$ times.

articles.title: The augmenting-path maximum matching
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with right vertices
$0, \dots, b-1$, the partner array obtained by running the augmentation loop with fuel $b + 1$ from
the empty matching, in which no right vertex has a partner.

articles.title: The start of an alternating chain of $L$ pairs is reached within $L$ rounds
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be
a partner array, let $L \ge 1$, and let $(i_1, j_1), \dots, (i_L, j_L)$ be pairs of a left and a
right vertex such that each $j_t$ is adjacent to $i_t$ with $\mu(j_t) \ne i_t$, each $j_{t+1}$ has
partner $\mu(j_{t+1}) = i_t$ for $t < L$, and $i_L$ is unmatched. Then $j_1$ is among the right
vertices reached within $L$ rounds of the alternating layered search for $\mu$.

From the unmatched end, each pair advances one round.

articles.title: A matched right vertex is reached no later than its partner
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner
array (partners are neighbours, and no left vertex is the partner of two right vertices), let $j$
be a right vertex with partner $\mu(j) = i$, and let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. If $i$ is among the left
vertices reached within $k$ rounds of the alternating layered search for $\mu$, then $j$ is among
the right vertices reached within $k$ rounds.

articles.title: The deficit is at most $b / d$
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$,
let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (partners are neighbours, and no left vertex is the partner of
two right vertices), let $M$ be any matching of the graph, and let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose that
for every $k < d$, no unmatched right vertex is among the right vertices reached within $k + 1$
rounds of the alternating layered search for $\mu$. Then $d \cdot \max(|M| - |P_\mu|, 0) \le |R_d|$,
where $P_\mu$ is the set of pairs $(i, j)$ with $\mu(j) = i$ and $R_d$ is the set of right vertices
reached within $d$ rounds.

This is the counting step of Hopcroft and Karp's bound: since $R_d$ has at most $b$ elements, the
deficit of the current matching against any matching is at most $b / d$ when $d \ge 1$.

articles.title: No shortest escape
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array, $U$ a set of left vertices, $D$ a set of
right vertices and $z$ a right vertex. Then $z$ has no escape avoiding $U$ and $D$ when there are
no $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and no list of pairs $(i_1, j_1), \dots, (i_{m+1}, j_{m+1})$ such that $z$ is
first reached in round $m + 1$ of the alternating layered search for $\mu$, the list is an
alternating chain from $z$, no $i_t$ lies in $U$, and no $j_t$ with $t \ge 2$ lies in $D$. Here
the list is an alternating chain from $z$ when $j_1 = z$, each $j_t$ is adjacent to $i_t$ with
$\mu(j_t) \ne i_t$, $\mu(j_{t+1}) = i_t$ for $t \le m$, and $i_{m+1}$ is unmatched.

A phase gives this property to every right vertex it marks dead after a failed search.

articles.title: Shortest chains avoiding earlier paths contain no dead vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner
array, $U$ a set of left vertices and $D$ a set of right vertices, and let $L$ be a set of left
vertices and $R$ a set of right vertices such that every vertex of $U$ lies in $L$ and every
vertex of $D$ lies in $R$ or has no escape avoiding $U$ and $D$. Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$, let $z$ be
a right vertex first reached in round $m + 1$ of the alternating layered search for $\mu$, and let
$S$ be an alternating chain from $z$ with $m + 1$ pairs such that no left vertex of $S$ lies in $L$
and no right vertex of $S$ lies in $R$. Then no right vertex of $S$ lies in $D$.

In a phase, $L$ and $R$ are the left and right vertices of the paths found so far.

articles.title: Levels along a shortest alternating chain
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array, let
$m \in \mathbb{N}$, let $z$ be a right vertex first reached in round $m + 1$ of the alternating
layered search for $\mu$, and let $S$ be an alternating chain from $z$ with $m + 1$ pairs. Then
for every pair $(i, j)$ of $S$ there is $m' \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $j$ is first reached in round
$m' + 1$ and $i$ is reached within $m'$ rounds.

articles.title: Levels of the pairs of a phase
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with left vertices $0, \dots, a-1$, let
$\mu$ be a valid partner array (partners are neighbours, and no left vertex is the partner of two
right vertices), and let $d \le a$ be such that round $d + 1$ of the alternating layered search for
$\mu$ reaches an unmatched right vertex and no earlier round does. Then for every pair $(i, j)$ on
a path of the Hopcroft–Karp phase for $\mu$ there is $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $j$ is first
reached in round $m + 1$ and $i$ is among the left vertices reached within $m$ rounds.

articles.title: Matched pairs of a partner assignment
articles.statement:
Given a partner assignment $\mathrm{mate}$ that
sends each right vertex $j < b$ to a left vertex $i < a$ or to nothing, the matched pairs of
$\mathrm{mate}$ form the set of all pairs $(i, j)$ of a left vertex $i < a$ and a right vertex
$j < b$ with $\mathrm{mate}(j) = i$.

articles.title: Partner of a left vertex
articles.statement:
Given a partner assignment $\mathrm{mate}$ that sends each right
vertex $j < b$ to a left vertex $i < a$ or to nothing, the partner of a left vertex $i$ is the
least right vertex $j$ with $\mathrm{mate}(j) = i$; it is undefined when there is no such $j$,
that is, when $i$ is unmatched.

articles.title: Partners of predecessors lie one level earlier
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{mate}$ be a valid partner
assignment for the bipartite graph with adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}$. Let $z$ be a right
vertex first reached in round $k + 2$ of the alternating layered search, let $i$ be a left vertex
reached within $k + 1$ rounds with $z \in \mathrm{adj}(i)$ and $\mathrm{mate}(z) \ne i$, and let
$j'$ be a right vertex with $\mathrm{mate}(j') = i$. Then $j'$ is first reached in round
$k + 1$.

articles.title: The walk back from an unmatched reached vertex is an augmenting path
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid
partner array, $k$ a natural number and $j$ a right vertex that is unmatched and is reached within
$k + 1$ rounds of the alternating layered search for $\mu$. Then the walk back from $j$ at level
$k$ is an augmenting path from $j$ within round $k$.

articles.title: The walk back is an alternating path
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{mate}$ be a valid partner assignment.
For every level $k$ and every right vertex $j$ reached within $k + 1$ rounds of the alternating
layered search, the walk back from $j$ at level $k$ is an alternating path from $j$ at level $k$:
it starts at $j$, its pairs are non-matching edges, its left vertices are reached within $k$
rounds and its right vertices within $k + 1$ rounds, no vertex occurs twice, each right vertex
after the first is the partner of the previous left vertex, and the last left vertex is
unmatched.

articles.title: Walking the layers back
articles.statement:
Given the adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}$ of a bipartite graph, a
partner assignment $\mathrm{mate}$, a level $k$ and a right vertex $j$, the walk back from $j$ at
level $k$ is a list of pairs defined by recursion on $k$. At level $0$ it is $[(i, j)]$ for the
least unmatched left vertex $i$ with $j \in \mathrm{adj}(i)$ and $\mathrm{mate}(j) \ne i$, and
empty if there is none. At level $k + 1$, if $j$ is reached within $k + 1$ rounds of the
alternating layered search, it is the walk back from $j$ at level $k$. Otherwise take the least
left vertex $i$ reached within $k + 1$ rounds with $j \in \mathrm{adj}(i)$ and
$\mathrm{mate}(j) \ne i$ (the walk is empty if there is none): if no right vertex has partner $i$
the walk is $[(i, j)]$, and otherwise it is $(i, j)$ followed by the walk back at level $k$ from
the least right vertex $j'$ with $\mathrm{mate}(j') = i$.

When $j$ is reached within $k + 1$ rounds, the walk descends to the round where $j$ is first
reached and lists the pairs to match, $j$ first.

articles.title: Length bound for phase paths
articles.statement:
For every partner assignment $\mathrm{mate}$, level $k$,
list of candidate right vertices and sets of used left and right vertices, every path that the
phase search at level $k$ collects from these candidates has at most $k + 1$ pairs.

articles.title: Invariant of a phase
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{mate}$ be a valid partner assignment, let $j$ be a
right vertex first reached in round $d + 1$ of the alternating layered search, and let $Q$ be an
alternating chain from $j$ with $d + 1$ pairs. Let $J$ be a list of right vertices each first
reached in round $d + 1$, $U$ a set of left vertices, $D$ a set of right vertices and $F$ a list of
paths, such that every vertex in $U$ is a left vertex of a path in $F$, and every vertex in $D$
either has no escape avoiding $U$ and $D$ or is a right vertex of a path in $F$. If $j$ is in $J$
or in $D$, then some path in $F$, or among the paths that the phase search at level $d$ collects
from $J$ with used left vertices $U$ and used right vertices $D$, shares a left vertex or a right
vertex with $Q$.

articles.title: Phase paths are disjoint augmenting paths
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{mate}$ be a valid partner
assignment, $k$ a level, $J$ a list of right vertices each unmatched and reached within $k + 1$
rounds of the alternating layered search, and $U_L$, $U_R$ sets of left and right vertices. Then
every path that the phase search at level $k$ collects from $J$ with used left vertices $U_L$ and
used right vertices $U_R$ is an augmenting path from some right vertex, with left vertices reached
within $k$ rounds and right vertices within $k + 1$ rounds; no left vertex and no right vertex
occurs twice among all pairs of all these paths; and every pair $(i, j)$ of these paths has
$i \notin U_L$ and $j \notin U_R$.

articles.title: Phase search over candidates
articles.statement:
Given a partner assignment $\mathrm{mate}$, a level $k$, a
list of candidate right vertices, a set $U$ of used left vertices and a set $D$ of used or dead
right vertices, the phase search tries the candidates in order. For a candidate $j$ it runs the
layered depth-first search from $j$ at level $k$ with used left vertices $U$ and dead set $D$,
which returns an optional path and an enlarged dead set $D'$. If it finds no path, the phase
search continues with the remaining candidates, $U$ and $D'$; if it finds a path $P$, it records
$P$ and continues with the remaining candidates, $U$ together with the left vertices of $P$, and
$D'$ together with the right vertices of $P$. The result is the list of the recorded paths.

articles.title: Phases are maximal
articles.statement:
Suppose the partner array describes a matching and $d$ is the earliest
round such that round $d + 1$ of the alternating breadth-first search reaches an unmatched right
vertex. Then for every $k$, every augmenting path $Q$ at level $k$ with exactly $d + 1$ pairs
shares a vertex with some path $P$ of the phase: some pair of $Q$ has its left vertex among the
left vertices of $P$ or its right vertex among the right vertices of $P$.

Every augmenting path has at least $d + 1$ pairs, so these are the shortest augmenting paths, and
the phase's vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths form a maximal set, as Hopcroft and Karp
require.

articles.title: A phase finds a path when an unmatched right vertex is reached
articles.statement:
If the partner array
describes a matching and some unmatched right vertex is reached within $a + 1$ rounds of the
alternating breadth-first search, where $a$ is the number of left vertices, then the phase finds
at least one path.

The search from the first candidate always yields a path.

articles.title: The paths of a phase are vertex-disjoint augmenting paths
articles.statement:
Suppose the partner array
describes a matching and $d$ is the earliest round such that round $d + 1$ of the alternating
breadth-first search reaches an unmatched right vertex. Then every path of the phase is an
augmenting path at level $d$ from some right vertex, and no left vertex and no right vertex occurs
twice among the pairs of all the paths of the phase.

articles.title: Hopcroft–Karp phase
articles.statement:
If no round of the alternating breadth-first search reaches an
unmatched right vertex, the phase finds no path. Otherwise let $d$ be the earliest round such that
round $d + 1$ reaches one. The phase runs the search at level $d$ from each unmatched right vertex
reached within $d + 1$ rounds, in increasing order, starting with no left vertex used and no right
vertex dead, and lists the paths found. After each search, the left vertices of the path found
become used and its right vertices become dead, and right vertices that the search marked dead
stay dead for the later searches.

articles.title: Dead vertices have no escape
articles.statement:
Suppose the partner array describes a matching. Run the
search at level $k$ from a right vertex $z$ first reached in round $k + 1$, with a set $U$ of used
left vertices and an initial set $D$ of dead right vertices, and let $D'$ be the dead set after
it. Then every right vertex $y$ in $D'$ but not in $D$ has no escape avoiding $U$ and $D'$: if $y$
is first reached in round $m + 1$, no alternating chain from $y$ to an unmatched left vertex with
$m + 1$ pairs has all its left vertices outside $U$ and all its right vertices after $y$ outside
$D'$.

So Hopcroft and Karp's pruning loses no path.

articles.title: Searches from reached vertices succeed when nothing is used or dead
articles.statement:
If the partner array
describes a matching, then for every $k$ and every right vertex $j$ reached within $k + 1$ rounds
of the alternating breadth-first search, the search at level $k$ from $j$, with no left vertex
used and no right vertex dead, finds a path.

articles.title: Length bound for search paths
articles.statement:
For every set of used left vertices, every level $k$,
every right vertex $j$ and every set of dead right vertices, a path found by the search at level
$k$ from $j$ has at most $k + 1$ pairs.

articles.title: The dead set of a search only grows
articles.statement:
For every set of used left vertices, every level
$k$, every right vertex $j$ and every set of dead right vertices, each right vertex that is dead
before the search at level $k$ from $j$ is still dead after it.

articles.title: A failed search marks its start dead
articles.statement:
For every set of used left vertices, every level
$k$, every right vertex $z$ and every set of dead right vertices, if the search at level $k$ from
$z$ finds no path, then $z$ is dead after it.

articles.title: Search paths are alternating paths through unused vertices
articles.statement:
Suppose the partner array
describes a matching, $k$ is a level and $j$ is a right vertex reached within $k + 1$ rounds of the
alternating breadth-first search. For every set of used left vertices and every set of dead right
vertices, if the search at level $k$ from $j$ finds a path $P$, then $P$ is an alternating path at
level $k$ from $j$, no left vertex of $P$ is used, and no right vertex of $P$ was dead before the
search.

articles.title: Depth-first search of a Hopcroft–Karp phase
articles.statement:
Fix a partner array $\mu$ assigning each right
vertex at most one left partner, and a set $U$ of used left vertices. Write $L_n$ and $R_n$ for
the left and right vertices reached within $n$ rounds of the alternating breadth-first layers of
$\mu$ (so $R_0 = \emptyset$). A left vertex $i$ is unmatched if no right vertex has partner $i$;
otherwise its partner is the least right vertex $j'$ with $\mu(j') = i$. The search from a right
vertex $j$ with bound $n$ and a set $D$ of dead right vertices returns an optional path (a list of
pairs of a left and a right vertex) together with a new dead set:

* if $j \in D$, it fails and returns $D$ unchanged;
* otherwise, if $j \in R_n$, it is the search from $j$ with bound $n - 1$ and dead set $D$;
* otherwise it goes through the candidates, the left vertices $i \in L_n$ in increasing order with
  $j$ adjacent to $i$, $\mu(j) \ne i$ and $i \notin U$. For an unmatched candidate $i$ it returns
  the path $[(i, j)]$ and the current dead set. For a matched candidate $i$ it searches from the
  partner of $i$ with bound $n - 1$ and the current dead set (when $n = 0$ this search fails and
  returns the dead set unchanged); if that search finds a path $P$, it returns $(i, j)$ followed
  by $P$, with the dead set that search returned, and otherwise it moves on to the next candidate
  with the dead set that search returned. If every candidate fails, it fails and returns the
  current dead set with $j$ added.

This is the pruning of Hopcroft and Karp: a right vertex from which the search fails is marked
dead and not searched again.

articles.title: The second pair of a shortest alternating chain
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a partner array and $z$ a
right vertex first reached in round $m + 1$ of the alternating breadth-first layers of $\mu$, and
let $Q$ be an alternating chain for $\mu$ from $z$ ending at an unmatched left vertex, with exactly
$m + 1$ pairs, at least two of them. Let $(i', j')$ be the second pair of $Q$. Then $m \ge 1$, the
right vertex $j'$ is first reached in round $m$, and $Q$ without its first pair is an alternating
chain for $\mu$ from $j'$ ending at an unmatched left vertex.

articles.title: Where newly dead vertices come from
articles.statement:
For a right vertex $j$, a test $\mathrm{ok}$ on left vertices, a map $\pi$ giving each left vertex
an optional right vertex, and a search $s$ taking a right vertex and a dead set (a set of right
vertices) to an optional path and a new dead set, write $T(l, D)$ for the optional path and the
dead set returned by trying the left vertices of the list $l$ as predecessors of $j$, starting from
the dead set $D$.
Suppose $s$ never shrinks the dead set: for every right vertex $j'$ and every dead set $d$, the
dead set returned by $s(j', d)$ contains $d$.
Let $E$ be the dead set of $T(l, D)$ and let $y$ be a right vertex in $E$ but not in $D$. Then
either $T(l, D)$ finds no path and $y = j$, or there are a vertex $i$ of $l$ passing
$\mathrm{ok}$, a right vertex $j'$ and a dead set $d$ containing $D$ such that $\pi(i) = j'$,
$y \notin d$, $y$ is in the dead set returned by $s(j', d)$, and that dead set is contained in
$E$.

articles.title: When trying candidates finds a path
articles.statement:
For a right vertex $j$, a test $\mathrm{ok}$ on left vertices, a map $\pi$ giving each left vertex
an optional right vertex, and a search $s$ taking a right vertex and a dead set (a set of right
vertices) to an optional path and a new dead set, write $T(l, D)$ for the optional path and the
dead set returned by trying the left vertices of the list $l$ as predecessors of $j$, starting from
the dead set $D$.
Suppose some vertex of $l$ passes $\mathrm{ok}$, and for every vertex $i$ of $l$ passing
$\mathrm{ok}$ and every right vertex $j'$ with $\pi(i) = j'$, the search $s(j', D)$ finds a path.
Then $T(l, D)$ finds a path.

Only the initial dead set matters: it does not change before the first vertex passing
$\mathrm{ok}$.

articles.title: Trying candidates keeps dead vertices dead
articles.statement:
For a right vertex $j$, a test $\mathrm{ok}$ on left vertices, a map $\pi$ giving each left vertex
an optional right vertex, and a search $s$ taking a right vertex and a dead set (a set of right
vertices) to an optional path and a new dead set, write $T(l, D)$ for the optional path and the
dead set returned by trying the left vertices of the list $l$ as predecessors of $j$, starting from
the dead set $D$.
Suppose $s$ never shrinks the dead set: for every right vertex $j'$ and every dead set $d$, the
dead set returned by $s(j', d)$ contains $d$.
Then for every list $l$ of left vertices and every dead set $D$, the dead set of $T(l, D)$
contains $D$.

articles.title: When trying candidates fails
articles.statement:
For a right vertex $j$, a test $\mathrm{ok}$ on left vertices, a map $\pi$ giving each left vertex
an optional right vertex, and a search $s$ taking a right vertex and a dead set (a set of right
vertices) to an optional path and a new dead set, write $T(l, D)$ for the optional path and the
dead set returned by trying the left vertices of the list $l$ as predecessors of $j$, starting from
the dead set $D$.
Suppose $s$ never shrinks the dead set: for every right vertex $j'$ and every dead set $d$, the
dead set returned by $s(j', d)$ contains $d$.
If $T(l, D)$ finds no path, then $j$ is in the dead set $E$ of $T(l, D)$, and for every vertex $i$
of $l$ passing $\mathrm{ok}$ there are a right vertex $j'$ and a dead set $d$ such that
$\pi(i) = j'$, $s(j', d)$ finds no path, and the dead set returned by $s(j', d)$ is contained in
$E$.

articles.title: A path found by trying candidates comes from one candidate
articles.statement:
For a right vertex $j$, a test $\mathrm{ok}$ on left vertices, a map $\pi$ giving each left vertex
an optional right vertex, and a search $s$ taking a right vertex and a dead set (a set of right
vertices) to an optional path and a new dead set, write $T(l, D)$ for the optional path and the
dead set returned by trying the left vertices of the list $l$ as predecessors of $j$, starting from
the dead set $D$.
Suppose $s$ never shrinks the dead set: for every right vertex $j'$ and every dead set $d$, the
dead set returned by $s(j', d)$ contains $d$.
If $T(l, D)$ returns a path $P$, then there are a vertex $i$ of $l$ with $\mathrm{ok}(i)$ and a
dead set $D_0$ containing $D$ such that either $\pi(i)$ is undefined and $P = [(i, j)]$, or
$\pi(i) = j'$ for a right vertex $j'$ and $s(j', D_0)$ returns a path $P'$ with $P$ equal to
$(i, j)$ followed by $P'$.

articles.title: Trying the candidate predecessors of a right vertex
articles.statement:
Let $j$ be a right vertex,
$\mathrm{ok}$ a test on left vertices, $\pi$ a map giving each left vertex an optional right vertex
(its partner, if any), and $s$ a search taking a right vertex and a dead set (a set of right
vertices) to an optional path, a list of pairs of a left and a right vertex, and a new dead set.
Given a list of left vertices and a dead set $D$, the procedure goes through the list in order,
skipping the vertices that fail $\mathrm{ok}$. At the first remaining vertex $i$: if $\pi(i)$ is
undefined, it returns the path $[(i, j)]$ and $D$; if $\pi(i) = j'$ and $s(j', D)$ finds a path
$P$, it returns the path $(i, j)$ followed by $P$, with the dead set returned by $s$; if
$s(j', D)$ finds no path, it continues with the rest of the list from the dead set returned by
$s$. When the list is exhausted, it fails and returns the current dead set with $j$ added.

articles.title: Flipping disjoint alternating paths at once keeps a matching
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner
array (partners are neighbours and no left vertex is the partner of two right vertices), $k$ a
natural number, and $P_1, \dots, P_r$ paths each of which is an alternating path for $\mu$, with
round bound $k$, from some right vertex. Suppose no left vertex and no right vertex occurs twice in
the concatenation $P_1 \cdots P_r$. Then the partner array obtained from $\mu$ by matching each
pair of the concatenation and keeping the other partners is valid.

articles.title: Flipping an alternating path keeps a matching
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a valid partner array (partners
are neighbours and no left vertex is the partner of two right vertices), and let $P$ be an
alternating path for $\mu$ from a right vertex $j$ with round bound $k$. Then the partner array
obtained from $\mu$ by matching each pair of $P$ and keeping the other partners is valid.

articles.title: Partner arrays that describe a matching
articles.statement:
Consider a bipartite graph with left vertices
$\{0, \dots, a-1\}$, right vertices $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$ and, for each left vertex $i$, a list of
its neighbours. A partner array assigns to each right vertex $j$ either no partner or a left
vertex as its partner. It is valid when every partner is a neighbour (if $i$ is the partner of
$j$, then $j$ is in the list of neighbours of $i$) and no left vertex is the partner of two
different right vertices (if $i$ is the partner of both $j$ and $j'$, then $j = j'$).

articles.title: Adjacency inspections of Prim's algorithm on a simple graph
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly
ordered type with a zero element, let $G$ be a simple graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let
$D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the same vertices with adjacency lists $A(u)$, let $w$
assign a weight in $W$ to every unordered pair of vertices, not necessarily distinct, and let
$r$ be a vertex. Suppose that for all vertices $u$ and $v$, $v$ occurs in $A(u)$ exactly when
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$, and that no list $A(u)$ has repeated entries. Then the number
of adjacency entries inspected by Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$ is twice the number of
edges of $G$.

articles.title: Logarithmic heap cost of Prim's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero
element, let $D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with adjacency
lists $A(u)$, let $w$ assign a weight in $W$ to every unordered pair of vertices, not necessarily
distinct, let $r$ be a vertex, and let $a$ be the sum of the lengths $|A(u)|$ over all vertices
$u$. Each of the five heap event counts of Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$ (comparisons,
swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry appends, pops or
replacements) is at most $20(2n + a)(\lfloor \log_2(n + 1) \rfloor + 1) + a$.

articles.title: Number of adjacency inspections in Prim's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type
with a zero element, let $D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$
with adjacency lists $A(u)$, let $w$ assign a weight in $W$ to every unordered pair of vertices,
not necessarily distinct, and let $r$ be a vertex. The number of adjacency entries inspected by
Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$ equals the sum of the lengths $|A(u)|$ over all vertices
$u$.

articles.title: Prim's algorithm returns a tree
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a zero element,
let $G$ be a connected simple graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $D$ be a directed
adjacency structure on the same vertices with adjacency lists $A(u)$ such that for all vertices
$u$ and $v$, $v$ occurs in $A(u)$ exactly when $u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$, let $w$ assign
a weight in $W$ to every unordered pair of vertices, not necessarily distinct, and let $r$ be a
vertex. Let $T$ be the simple graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ in which two distinct
vertices are adjacent when one of them is the parent of the other in the output of Prim's
algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$. Then $T$ is a tree.

articles.title: Bound on key comparisons in Prim's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a
zero element, let $D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ with
adjacency lists $A(u)$, let $w$ assign a weight in $W$ to every unordered pair of vertices, not
necessarily distinct, and let $r$ be a vertex. The number of inspected adjacency entries that
Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$ finds still in the queue, which is its number of key
comparisons, is at most the sum of the lengths $|A(u)|$ over all vertices $u$.

articles.title: Prim's algorithm returns a minimum spanning tree
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a connected simple graph on
the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the same vertices with
adjacency lists $A(u)$ such that for all vertices $u$ and $v$, $v$ occurs in $A(u)$ exactly when
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$, let $w$ assign a real weight $w(e)$ to every unordered pair $e$
of vertices, not necessarily distinct, and let $r$ be a vertex. Let $T$ be the simple graph on
the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ in which two distinct vertices are adjacent when one of them is the
parent of the other in the output of Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$, and write $E(H)$ for
the edge set of a graph $H$. Then every edge of $T$ is an edge of $G$, $T$ is a tree, and every
graph $H$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ that is a tree and whose edges are all edges of $G$
satisfies $\sum_{e \in E(T)} w(e) \le \sum_{e \in E(H)} w(e)$.

Weights are arbitrary signed real numbers, and ties are allowed.

articles.title: Parents returned by Prim's algorithm are adjacency-list neighbors
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly
ordered type with a zero element, let $D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$ with adjacency lists $A(u)$, let $w$ assign a weight in $W$ to every unordered
pair of vertices, not necessarily distinct, and let $r$ be a vertex. For all vertices $u$ and
$v$, if Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$ returns $u$ as the parent of $v$, then $v$ occurs
in $A(u)$.

articles.title: The root has no parent in Prim's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a
zero element, let $D$ be a directed adjacency structure on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, let $w$
assign a weight in $W$ to every unordered pair of vertices, not necessarily distinct, and let
$r$ be a vertex. In the output of Prim's algorithm on $D$, $w$ and $r$, the vertex $r$ has no
parent.

articles.title: Prim's algorithm with an indexed binary heap
articles.statement:
Let $W$ be a linearly ordered type with a
zero element, let $W \cup \{\top\}$ be $W$ with a new greatest element $\top$ adjoined, let $D$
be a directed adjacency structure on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, with vertex list $L$ and
adjacency lists $A(u)$, let $w$ assign a weight $w(\{u, v\}) \in W$ to every unordered pair
$\{u, v\}$ of vertices, not necessarily distinct, and let $r$ be a vertex. Prim's algorithm
starts with no vertex having a parent and inserts the vertices, in the order of $L$, into an
empty indexed minimum queue over the identities $0, \dots, n-1$, with key $0$ for $r$ and key
$\top$ for every other vertex. It then repeats the following at most $n$ times, stopping early
when the queue is empty: it extracts the entry of minimum key, ties broken by the smaller
vertex, say with vertex $u$, and for each entry $v$ of $A(u)$ in order, if $v$ is still in the
queue and $w(\{u, v\})$ is strictly smaller than the current key of $v$, it sets the parent of
$v$ to $u$ and decreases the key of $v$ to $w(\{u, v\})$. It returns, for each vertex, its
parent or nothing.

Costs are counted as seven numbers: the five event counts of the queue operations (comparisons,
swaps, reads of the position vector, writes to the position vector, and entry appends, pops or
replacements), the number of adjacency entries inspected, and the number of inspected entries
found still in the queue, which is the number of key comparisons. On a disconnected graph every
vertex is still extracted and the parents form a forest.

articles.title: Erasing an edge leaves the other out-neighbour lists unchanged
articles.statement:
For every
directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$ and $u$ with $u \ne s$, the out-neighbour
list of $u$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ equals the
out-neighbour list of $u$ in $G$.

articles.title: Out-neighbours of the source after erasing an edge
articles.statement:
For every directed-adjacency graph
$G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, the out-neighbour list of $s$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by
erasing the edge $s \to t$ is the out-neighbour list of $s$ in $G$ with every occurrence of $t$
removed, the remaining entries kept in their original order.

articles.title: Concatenation of walks
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on $V$ and let
$s, m, t \in V$. If $G$ has a walk of length exactly $a$ from $s$ to $m$ and a walk of length
exactly $b$ from $m$ to $t$, then $G$ has a walk of length exactly $a + b$ from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Directed adjacency graph
articles.statement:
A directed adjacency graph on a type $V$ consists of a list of
vertices that has no duplicates and contains every element of $V$ (so $V$ is finite), together
with, for each vertex $v$, an ordered list of the out-neighbors of $v$, in which entries may
repeat.

articles.title: Edges after erasing an edge
articles.statement:
For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$,
$t$, $u$ and $v$, there is an edge from $u$ to $v$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing
the edge $s \to t$ if and only if there is an edge from $u$ to $v$ in $G$ and it is not the case
that both $u = s$ and $v = t$.

articles.title: Edges of the transpose graph
articles.statement:
Let $V$ have decidable equality and let $G$ be a directed
adjacency graph on $V$. For all $s, t \in V$, the transpose of $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$
if and only if $G$ has an edge from $t$ to $s$.

articles.title: Edge of a directed adjacency graph
articles.statement:
For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and
vertices $s, t \in V$, there is an edge from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ when $t$ occurs in the adjacency
list of $s$.

articles.title: Erasing an edge twice gives the same out-neighbour lists
articles.statement:
For every directed-adjacency
graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$, erasing the edge $s \to t$ from $G$ and then erasing it
again gives, at every vertex, the same out-neighbour list as erasing it once.

articles.title: Erasing a directed edge
articles.statement:
Given a directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and $t$,
erasing the edge $s \to t$ gives the directed-adjacency graph with the same vertex enumeration as
$G$ whose out-neighbour list at $s$ is the out-neighbour list of $s$ in $G$ with every occurrence
of $t$ removed (the remaining entries keep their order), and whose out-neighbour list at every
other vertex is the same as in $G$.

articles.title: The Boolean edge test is correct
articles.statement:
For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a directed
adjacency graph $G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, the Boolean edge test of $G$ at $(s, t)$
returns true if and only if $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: The erased edge is absent
articles.statement:
For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$ and
$t$, the Boolean edge lookup for $s \to t$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge
$s \to t$ returns false.

articles.title: Boolean edge test
articles.statement:
For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a directed adjacency graph
$G$ on $V$ and vertices $s, t \in V$, the edge test of $G$ at $(s, t)$ is the Boolean value
that is true exactly when $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.

articles.title: Reachability after erasing an edge implies reachability in the original graph
articles.statement:
For
every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, if $v$ is reachable from
$u$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$, then $v$ is reachable from $u$
in $G$.

articles.title: Reachability by walks
articles.statement:
In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from
a vertex $s$ if and only if there is a natural number $n$ such that $G$ has a walk of length
exactly $n$ from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Reachability in the associated transition system
articles.statement:
In a directed adjacency graph $G$, a
vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if, in the unit-labelled labelled
transition system of $G$, there is a finite list of labels along which $s$ reaches $t$ by a
multistep transition.

articles.title: Reachability is the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation
articles.statement:
In a directed
adjacency graph $G$, a vertex $t$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ if and only if $(s, t)$ lies
in the reflexive-transitive closure of the edge relation of $G$.

articles.title: Semantically equivalent graphs have the same reachability
articles.statement:
If two directed adjacency
graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on $V$ are semantically equivalent, then for all $s, t \in V$, $t$ is
reachable from $s$ in $G_1$ if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G_2$.

articles.title: Reachability in the transpose graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph on a vertex
type with decidable equality, and let $G^{\mathsf{T}}$ be its transpose. For all vertices $s$ and
$t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ in $G^{\mathsf{T}}$ if and only if $s$ is reachable from $t$ in
$G$.

articles.title: Reachability in a directed graph
articles.statement:
For a directed adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$
and $t$, $t$ is reachable from $s$ when the pair $(s, t)$ lies in the reflexive-transitive
closure of the edge relation of $G$: either $s = t$, or a finite sequence of edges of $G$ leads
from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every directed adjacency
graph $G$ is semantically equivalent to itself.

articles.title: Transposing twice gives a semantically equivalent graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency
graph on a vertex type with decidable equality. The transpose of the transpose of $G$ is
semantically equivalent to $G$, that is, it has exactly the same edges as $G$.

articles.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs
articles.statement:
Two directed adjacency graphs $G_1$
and $G_2$ on the same vertex type are semantically equivalent when they have the same edges: for
all vertices $s$ and $t$, $G_1$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$ if and only if $G_2$ does.

articles.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is symmetric
articles.statement:
If a directed adjacency
graph $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to a directed adjacency graph $G_2$, then $G_2$ is
semantically equivalent to $G_1$.

articles.title: Adjacency in the associated digraph
articles.statement:
For a directed adjacency graph $G$ and vertices $s$
and $t$, $s$ is adjacent to $t$ in the digraph associated with $G$ if and only if $G$ has an edge
from $s$ to $t$, that is, $t$ occurs in the adjacency list of $s$.

articles.title: The digraph of a directed adjacency graph
articles.statement:
The digraph associated with a directed
adjacency graph $G$ on a vertex type $V$ is the directed graph on $V$ in which $s$ is adjacent to
$t$ exactly when $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$. It forgets the order of the adjacency lists and
the multiplicity of their entries.

articles.title: The transition system of a directed adjacency graph
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system of a
directed adjacency graph $G$ has the vertices of $G$ as states and a single label, and it has a
transition from $s$ to $t$ exactly when $G$ has an edge from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Semantic equivalence of directed adjacency graphs is transitive
articles.statement:
If a directed adjacency
graph $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to $G_2$, and $G_2$ is semantically equivalent to $G_3$,
then $G_1$ is semantically equivalent to $G_3$.

articles.title: Transposition preserves semantic equivalence
articles.statement:
For directed adjacency graphs $G_1$ and
$G_2$ on a vertex type with decidable equality, if $G_1$ and $G_2$ are semantically
equivalent, then their transposes are semantically equivalent.

articles.title: Transpose of a directed adjacency graph
articles.statement:
For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a
vertex type with decidable equality, the transpose of $G$ has the same vertex enumeration as
$G$, and the adjacency list of a vertex $v$ consists of the vertices $u$ such that $v$ occurs
in the adjacency list of $u$ in $G$, each listed once and in the order of the vertex
enumeration.

articles.title: Erasing an edge keeps the vertex enumeration
articles.statement:
For every directed-adjacency graph $G$ and
vertices $s$ and $t$, the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge $s \to t$ has the same
vertex enumeration as $G$: the same list of vertices, in the same order.

articles.title: Walks after erasing an edge are walks in the original graph
articles.statement:
For every
directed-adjacency graph $G$, vertices $s$, $t$, $u$ and $v$, and natural number $n$, if there
is a walk of length $n$ from $u$ to $v$ in the graph obtained from $G$ by erasing the edge
$s \to t$, then there is a walk of length $n$ from $u$ to $v$ in $G$.

articles.title: Semantically equivalent graphs have the same walks
articles.statement:
If two directed adjacency graphs
$G_1$ and $G_2$ are semantically equivalent, then for every natural number $n$ and all
vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G_1$ if and only if
there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G_2$.

articles.title: Splitting off the first edge of a walk
articles.statement:
In a directed adjacency graph $G$, for every
natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n + 1$ from $s$ to
$t$ if and only if there is a vertex $v$ such that $(s, v)$ is an edge of $G$ and there is a
walk of length $n$ from $v$ to $t$.

articles.title: Walks in the transpose are reversed walks
articles.statement:
For a directed adjacency graph $G$ on a
vertex type with decidable equality, every natural number $n$ and all vertices $s$ and $t$,
there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in the transpose of $G$ if and only if there is
a walk of length $n$ from $t$ to $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: Walks of length zero
articles.statement:
In a directed adjacency graph, there is a walk of length $0$ from
a vertex $s$ to a vertex $t$ if and only if $s = t$.

articles.title: Walks of a given length
articles.statement:
For a directed adjacency graph $G$, a natural number $n$ and
vertices $s$ and $t$, there is a walk of length $n$ from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ when there are
vertices $v_0, \dots, v_n$ with $v_0 = s$ and $v_n = t$ such that $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an edge
of $G$ for every $i < n$.

articles.title: Edge insertion in an adjacency matrix
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i$ and $j$, adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ gives the adjacency
matrix that has an edge from $i$ to $j$ and agrees with $m$ on every other ordered pair of
vertices.

articles.title: Adjacency matrix
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, an adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices is a
directed graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ given by a Boolean-valued function
$\mathrm{adj}$ on ordered pairs of vertices: $\mathrm{adj}(i, j)$ is true exactly when there is a
directed edge from $i$ to $j$.

articles.title: Empty adjacency matrix
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the empty adjacency matrix on $n$
vertices is the directed graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with no edges: its adjacency function is
false on every ordered pair of vertices.

articles.title: Edge deletion in an adjacency matrix
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i$ and $j$, removing the edge from $i$ to $j$ gives the adjacency
matrix that has no edge from $i$ to $j$ and agrees with $m$ on every other ordered pair of
vertices.

articles.title: Extensionality of adjacency matrices
articles.statement:
Two adjacency matrices $m$ and $m'$ on the same $n$
vertices are equal if, for all vertices $i$ and $j$, $m$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$ exactly when
$m'$ does.

articles.title: Edges after inserting an edge
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices
$i$, $j$, $a$, $b$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge
from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $a = i$ and $b = j$, or $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.

articles.title: Inserting an edge leaves other pairs unchanged
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$
vertices and vertices $i$, $j$, $a$, $b$ with $a \ne i$ or $b \ne j$, the matrix obtained from $m$
by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $m$ does.

articles.title: An inserted edge is present
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$
and $j$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from $i$ to
$j$.

articles.title: The empty adjacency matrix has no edges
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and all vertices $i$
and $j$ among the $n$ vertices, the empty adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices has no edge from $i$ to
$j$.

articles.title: Edges after deleting an edge
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on $n$ vertices and vertices $i$,
$j$, $a$, $b$, the matrix obtained from $m$ by removing the edge from $i$ to $j$ has an edge from
$a$ to $b$ if and only if $(a, b) \ne (i, j)$ and $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.

articles.title: Deleting an edge leaves the other entries unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the
vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j, a, b$ be vertices with $(a, b) \ne (i, j)$, that is,
$a \ne i$ or $b \ne j$. Then the graph obtained from $m$ by deleting the edge from $i$ to $j$ has
an edge from $a$ to $b$ if and only if $m$ has an edge from $a$ to $b$.

articles.title: Deleting an edge removes it
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then the graph obtained from $m$ by deleting the
edge from $i$ to $j$ has no edge from $i$ to $j$.

articles.title: Edge query of an adjacency matrix
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and vertices $i, j$, the edge query of $m$ at $(i, j)$ is the Boolean value
that is true exactly when $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.

articles.title: Out-neighbors after adding an edge
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j, b$ be vertices. Then $b$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of
$i$ in the graph obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$ if and only if $b = j$ or
$b$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of $i$ in $m$.

articles.title: Adding an edge makes its target an out-neighbor
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the
vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then $j$ belongs to the out-neighbor
list of $i$ in the graph obtained from $m$ by adding the edge from $i$ to $j$.

articles.title: The out-neighbor list matches the edge query
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an adjacency matrix on the vertex
set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and let $i, j$ be vertices. Then $j$ belongs to the out-neighbor list of
$i$ if and only if $m$ has a directed edge from $i$ to $j$.

articles.title: Out-neighbor lists of the empty graph
articles.statement:
In the graph with no edges on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the out-neighbor list of every vertex $i$ is the empty list.

articles.title: Out-neighbor lists have no duplicates
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, no vertex occurs twice in the out-neighbor list of $i$.

articles.title: Out-neighbor lists are strictly increasing
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a vertex $i$, the out-neighbor list of $i$ is strictly increasing: every
vertex in it is smaller than every vertex that comes after it.

articles.title: Out-neighbor list
articles.statement:
For an adjacency matrix $m$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and a
vertex $i$, the out-neighbor list of $i$ is the list of all vertices $j$ such that $m$ has a
directed edge from $i$ to $j$, in increasing order.

articles.title: Deleting an edge removes the out-neighbor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$, given by its adjacency matrix, and let $i$ and $j$ be vertices. After the edge
from $i$ to $j$ is deleted from $G$ (whether or not $G$ had that edge), $j$ is not an
out-neighbor of $i$.

articles.title: Vertices of the empty graph have out-degree zero
articles.statement:
For every $n$, every vertex of the
empty directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ has out-degree $0$.

articles.title: Out-degree
articles.statement:
The out-degree of a vertex $i$ of a directed graph given by an adjacency
matrix is the number of its out-neighbors, that is, the number of vertices $j$ such that there is
an edge from $i$ to $j$.

articles.title: The executable BFS agrees with the list model
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ with
ordered adjacency lists and every source vertex $s$, the result of the executable breadth-first
search from $s$ equals the result of the list model of breadth-first search from $s$: both
report the same distance (or none) for every vertex and the same first-discovery order.

articles.title: Breadth-first search on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$
articles.statement:
Given a natural number $n$, an
adjacency function assigning to each vertex $i < n$ an ordered list of vertices among
$0, \dots, n-1$, and a source vertex $s < n$, this is the result of breadth-first search from $s$
on the finite directed graph with vertex enumeration $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ and these adjacency
lists.

articles.title: List model of breadth-first search
articles.statement:
Given a finite directed graph $G$ with ordered
adjacency lists and a source vertex $s$, the list model keeps a list of processed pairs and a
queue of pairs $(v, d)$ of a vertex and a distance, starting with no processed pairs and the
queue $[(s, 0)]$. It performs one round per vertex of $G$: if the queue is empty, nothing
changes; otherwise the front pair $(u, d)$ is removed from the queue and recorded as processed,
and then each entry $w$ of the adjacency list of $u$, from left to right, is appended to the
queue as $(w, d + 1)$ unless $w$ already occurs in a processed or queued pair. The reported
distance of a vertex $v$ is the distance in the first pair for $v$ in the list of processed pairs
in processing order followed by the queue, or none if there is no such pair; the reported order
lists the processed vertices in processing order.

The model can be evaluated by kernel reduction, which is used to check concrete results.

articles.title: Breadth-first search with parents returns the ordinary BFS result
articles.statement:
For every finite
directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and every source vertex $s$, the output of
breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$, with its cost and its predecessor table
forgotten, equals the result of ordinary FIFO breadth-first search from $s$ in $G$: the same
distance table and the same first-discovery order.

articles.title: Linear bound on the cost of BFS with parents
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with
vertex list $V$ and adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}(u)$, and let $s$ be a vertex. The cost of
breadth-first search with parents from $s$, counting dequeue attempts, adjacency checks, enqueues
and parent writes, is at most $3|V| + \sum_{u \in V} |\mathrm{adj}(u)|$, where adjacency lists
are counted with repetitions.

articles.title: Exact cost of BFS with parents
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with vertex list $V$
and adjacency lists $\mathrm{adj}(u)$, let $s$ be a vertex, and let $L$ be the list of vertices in
the order in which breadth-first search from $s$ discovers them. The cost of breadth-first search
with parents from $s$, counting dequeue attempts, adjacency checks, enqueues and parent writes,
equals $|V| + \sum_{u \in L} |\mathrm{adj}(u)| + |L| + (|L| - 1)$, where adjacency lists are
counted with repetitions and $|L| - 1$ is truncated at $0$.

articles.title: Breadth-first search with parent pointers
articles.statement:
Given a finite directed graph $G$ on a vertex
type $V$, with ordered adjacency lists, and a source vertex $s$, this runs first-in-first-out
breadth-first search from $s$ for $|V|$ rounds. The queue starts with $s$ at distance $0$. Each
round tries to dequeue a vertex $u$; if it succeeds, it scans the neighbors of $u$ in
adjacency-list order, and each neighbor not yet discovered gets distance one more than $u$,
records $u$ as its parent and is enqueued. An already discovered vertex keeps its distance and
parent. The result is the search forest: the distance of each discovered vertex, the vertices in
the order they were dequeued, and the parent of each discovered vertex other than $s$. The cost
counts one unit for each dequeue attempt, each check of an adjacency entry against the
discovered set, each enqueue (including that of $s$) and each parent write.

articles.title: Breadth-first search
articles.statement:
Given a finite directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and a
source vertex $s$, breadth-first search keeps a FIFO queue of pairs $(v, d)$ of a vertex and a
distance and a table of discovered vertices with their distances, starting with the queue
$[(s, 0)]$ and $s$ discovered at distance $0$. It performs one round per vertex of $G$: if the
queue is empty, nothing changes; otherwise it dequeues the front pair $(u, d)$, records $u$ as
processed, and scans the adjacency list of $u$ from left to right, enqueueing each entry $w$ that
is not yet discovered as $(w, d + 1)$ and discovering it at distance $d + 1$. The result reports
for each vertex its discovered distance, or none if it was never discovered, and lists the
processed vertices in processing order.

The table is a hash map, so the search runs in expected time linear in the number of vertices
plus the total length of the adjacency lists.

articles.title: Breadth-first search forest
articles.statement:
A breadth-first search forest on a vertex type $V$ consists
of a breadth-first search result, namely a partial distance function from $V$ to the natural
numbers and a list of vertices, together with a partial predecessor function from $V$ to $V$.
For a search from a source vertex $s$, these are meant to give the distance from $s$ of each
reachable vertex, the reachable vertices in first-discovery order, and the vertex from which
each reachable vertex other than $s$ was first discovered, with $s$ and the unreachable vertices
having no predecessor; the structure itself imposes none of these properties.

articles.title: Result of breadth-first search
articles.statement:
A breadth-first search result on a vertex type $V$
consists of a distance function, assigning to each vertex either a natural number or none,
and a list of vertices. They are meant to record the shortest distance from the source (none
when the vertex is unreachable) and the vertices in first-discovery order.

articles.title: BFS reports exactly the shortest walk length
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ with
ordered adjacency lists, all vertices $s$ and $v$, and every natural number $d$, breadth-first
search from $s$ reports distance $d$ for $v$ if and only if there is a walk of exactly $d$ edges
from $s$ to $v$ in $G$ and $d \le k$ for every natural number $k$ such that there is a walk of
exactly $k$ edges from $s$ to $v$.

articles.title: BFS reports a distance exactly for the reachable vertices
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph
$G$ with ordered adjacency lists and all vertices $s$ and $v$, breadth-first search from $s$
reports some distance for $v$ (rather than none) if and only if $v$ is reachable from $s$
in $G$.

articles.title: BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ with
ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$, the distances reported by breadth-first search
from $s$, listed along its first-discovery order, form a nondecreasing sequence, where a vertex
without a reported distance counts as $0$.

articles.title: BFS lists exactly the reachable vertices
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered
adjacency lists and all vertices $s$ and $v$, the vertex $v$ occurs in the first-discovery order
of breadth-first search from $s$ if and only if $v$ is reachable from $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: BFS discovers each vertex at most once
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ with ordered
adjacency lists and every vertex $s$, no vertex occurs twice in the first-discovery order of
breadth-first search from $s$.

articles.title: Path reconstruction fails exactly at unreachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed
graph given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. Following the saved parents of the
breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ towards $s$ returns no path if and only
if $v$ is not reachable from $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: Path reconstruction at the source
articles.statement:
For every breadth-first search forest $F$ and every
vertex $s$, following the saved parents of $F$ from $s$ back to $s$ returns the one-vertex path
$[s]$. This holds for every forest, including one whose discovery order is empty.

articles.title: Reconstructed BFS paths are shortest paths
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by
adjacency lists, let $s$ and $v$ be vertices, and suppose that following the saved parents of the
breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ returns a list $P$ of vertices. Then $P$
starts at $s$ and ends at $v$, each vertex of $P$ after the first has the preceding vertex as its
saved parent, $G$ has an edge from each vertex of $P$ to the next, no vertex occurs twice in $P$,
breadth-first search from $s$ reports a distance $d$ for $v$ and $P$ has $d + 1$ vertices, and
every list of vertices from $s$ to $v$ such that $G$ has an edge from each of its vertices to the
next has at least as many vertices as $P$.

articles.title: Cost of path reconstruction for an unreachable vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph
given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices with $v$ not reachable from $s$ in $G$.
Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from $s$ back from $v$ costs
exactly $2$, counting one unit for each comparison with $s$, each parent lookup and each vertex
prepended to the path: one comparison of $v$ with $s$ and one lookup of the missing parent of
$v$.

articles.title: Cost of path reconstruction for a reachable vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph
given by adjacency lists, let $s$ and $v$ be vertices, and suppose breadth-first search from $s$
reports distance $d$ for $v$. Following the saved parents of the breadth-first search forest of
$G$ from $s$ back from $v$ costs exactly $3d + 2$, counting one unit for each comparison with $s$,
each parent lookup and each vertex prepended to the path.

articles.title: Path reconstruction from BFS parents
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be the predecessor function of a
breadth-first search forest, let $n$ be the length of its discovery order, and let $s$ and $t$ be
vertices. Starting from $v_k = t$, this walks back along $p$, setting $v_{i-1} = p(v_i)$,
until it reaches a vertex $v_0$ that tests equal to $s$, and returns the list
$v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$. It returns no list if the walk meets a vertex that does not test equal to
$s$ and has no predecessor, or if none of the first $n + 1$ vertices $t, p(t), \dots$ of the walk
tests equal to $s$. The cost counts one unit for each test against $s$, each predecessor lookup
and each vertex prepended to the list.

The bound $n$ makes the walk terminate even when the predecessor table contains a cycle.

articles.title: Saved-parent chains are simple
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by adjacency
lists and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. If a list of vertices starts at $s$, ends at $v$, and each
of its vertices after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent in the breadth-first
search forest of $G$ from $s$, then no vertex occurs twice in the list.

articles.title: Each reachable vertex has a unique saved-parent chain
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph
given by adjacency lists, and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices with $v$ reachable from $s$ in $G$.
There is exactly one list of vertices that starts at $s$, ends at $v$, and in which each vertex
after the first has the preceding vertex as its saved parent in the breadth-first search forest
of $G$ from $s$.

articles.title: A BFS parent is one step closer to the source
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with
ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first
search with parents from $s$ in $G$. If $F$ records $p$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then
there is a natural number $d$ such that $F$ records distance $d$ for $p$ and distance $d + 1$
for $v$.

articles.title: BFS parents are joined by graph edges
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with ordered
adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by breadth-first search
with parents from $s$ in $G$. If $F$ records $p$ as the predecessor of a vertex $v$, then $G$ has
a directed edge from $p$ to $v$, that is, $v$ occurs in the adjacency list of $p$.

articles.title: The BFS parent is the first discovered in-neighbour
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph
with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest computed by
breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. For every vertex $v \ne s$, the predecessor
that $F$ records for $v$ is the first vertex $u$, in the first-discovery order of ordinary FIFO
breadth-first search from $s$ in $G$, whose adjacency list contains $v$; if no vertex in that
order has $v$ in its adjacency list, $F$ records no predecessor for $v$.

articles.title: Exactly the source and the unreachable vertices have no BFS parent
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite
directed graph with ordered adjacency lists, $s$ a vertex, and $F$ the predecessor forest
computed by breadth-first search with parents from $s$ in $G$. A vertex $v$ has no recorded
predecessor in $F$ if and only if $v = s$ or $v$ is not reachable from $s$ along directed edges
of $G$.

articles.title: The saved-parent relation is acyclic
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by
adjacency lists and let $s$ and $v$ be vertices. In the breadth-first search forest of $G$ from
$s$, there is no sequence $v = x_0, x_1, \dots, x_k = v$ with $k \ge 1$ in which each $x_i$ is
the saved parent of $x_{i+1}$.

articles.title: Breadth-first search places the source at distance zero
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph
$G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $s$ of $G$, breadth-first search in $G$
from $s$ reports a distance for $s$ itself, and that distance is $0$ edges.

articles.title: Occurring before in a list
articles.statement:
For elements $x$ and $y$ and a list $xs$, $x$ occurs before
$y$ in $xs$ when there are lists $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $xs$ is the concatenation of $a$, the
element $x$, $b$, the element $y$ and $c$; that is, some occurrence of $x$ lies at a strictly
earlier position than some occurrence of $y$.

articles.title: A DFS child finishes before its parent
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph with ordered
adjacency lists and fix an ordered list of roots. If $(c, p)$ is one of the (child, parent) pairs
recorded by the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots, then $c$ occurs before $p$
in the postorder (finish order) of that search.

articles.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices
articles.statement:
For every directed graph
$G$ with ordered adjacency lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order of $G$ contains no
vertex twice.

articles.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency
lists, the whole-graph decreasing finish order is the decreasing finish order of the left-first
depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's vertex
enumeration order; its vertices are listed from the latest finished to the earliest finished.

articles.title: Decreasing finish order has no repeated vertices
articles.statement:
For every directed graph $G$ with
ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order of the
depth-first search of $G$ from those roots contains no vertex twice.

articles.title: Decreasing finish order
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists and an
ordered list of roots, the decreasing finish order is the reverse of the postorder of the
left-first depth-first search of $G$ from those roots: the vertices that search visits, listed
from the latest finished to the earliest finished.

articles.title: Exact transition count of whole-graph depth-first search
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed
graph whose vertices are listed without repetition as $v_1, \dots, v_n$, with ordered adjacency
lists $N(v)$ whose entries may repeat. Run the depth-first search machine with roots
$v_1, \dots, v_n$ in this order (each transition drops a pending vertex that is already visited,
discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Then there is a terminal machine state, with no
work left, whose recorded output is the whole-graph depth-first traversal of $G$ and which is
reached from the initial state in exactly $2n + \sum_{i=1}^{n} |N(v_i)|$ transitions, where
$|N(v)|$ is the length of the adjacency list of $v$, counting repeated entries and self-loops.

articles.title: Depth-first search of the whole graph
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency
lists, the whole-graph traversal is the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all
vertices of $G$, taken in the graph's fixed vertex enumeration order.

articles.title: Exact transition count of depth-first search
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph with
ordered adjacency lists $N(v)$, whose entries may repeat, and let $R$ be a list of roots, possibly
with repetitions. Run the depth-first search machine from $R$ (each transition drops a pending
vertex that is already visited, discovers a new vertex, or finishes a vertex). Let
$v_1, \dots, v_k$ be the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$. Then there is a
terminal machine state, with no work left, whose recorded output is the depth-first traversal of
$G$ from $R$ and which is reached from the initial state in exactly
$|R| + k + \sum_{i=1}^{k} |N(v_i)|$ transitions, where $|R|$ is the length of $R$ and $|N(v)|$
is the length of the adjacency list of $v$.

articles.title: Executable DFS meets the left-first specification
articles.statement:
For every directed graph $G$ with
ordered adjacency lists and every ordered list of roots, the traversal computed by left-first
depth-first search of $G$ from these roots conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots.

articles.title: Left-first depth-first search
articles.statement:
Given a directed graph $G$ with ordered adjacency lists
and an ordered list of roots, depth-first search processes the roots from left to right,
skipping roots already visited. Visiting an unvisited vertex $v$ marks it visited and records its
discovery, then processes the out-neighbours of $v$ in adjacency-list order, visiting each one
not yet visited at that moment and recording $v$ as its parent, and finally records that $v$ has
finished. The result is the traversal consisting of the vertices in discovery order (preorder),
the vertices in finish order (postorder), and the (child, parent) pairs in the order the children
were discovered.

articles.title: The left-first DFS specification determines the traversal
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph
with ordered adjacency lists, fix an ordered list of roots, and let $T$ be a traversal. If $T$
conforms to left-first DFS for $G$ and these roots, then $T$ equals the traversal computed by
left-first depth-first search of $G$ from these roots.

articles.title: A DFS forest root has no parent
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered
adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ and $p$ be vertices. If $v$ is a
forest root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $(v, p)$ is not among the
(child, parent) pairs recorded by that search.

articles.title: DFS forest roots are scheduled roots
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered
adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$ be a vertex. If $v$ is a forest
root of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$, then $v$ occurs in $r$.

articles.title: DFS forest roots are distinct
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered
adjacency lists and every list $r$ of root vertices, the list of forest roots of the left-first
depth-first search of $G$ from $r$ contains no vertex twice.

articles.title: Roots of a DFS forest
articles.statement:
The forest roots of a traversal $T$ are the vertices of the preorder
