of $T$ that do not occur as the child in any (child, parent) pair recorded by $T$, listed in the
order in which they occur in the preorder.

articles.title: Left-first depth-first traversals
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph given by ordered
adjacency lists and let $r = (r_1, \dots, r_k)$ be a list of root vertices. A traversal $T$ is a
left-first DFS of $G$ from $r$ when some finite run of the following machine ends with an empty
work list and with recorded preorder, postorder and (child, parent) list equal to those of $T$.

The machine holds a work list of frames, each either "enter $v$ with parent $p$" (where the parent
$p$ may be absent) or "exit $v$", a set of visited vertices, and the three recorded lists. It starts
with the frames "enter $r_1$ with no parent", ..., "enter $r_k$ with no parent", no visited vertex
and empty recorded lists. A step removes the first frame of the work list. For "exit $v$" it
appends $v$ to the postorder. For "enter $v$ with parent $p$" it does nothing more if $v$ is
visited; otherwise it marks $v$ visited, appends $v$ to the preorder, appends $(v, p)$ to the
(child, parent) list if $p$ is present, and puts in front of the remaining work the frames
"enter $w$ with parent $v$" for the entries $w$ of the adjacency list of $v$, in order, followed by
"exit $v$".

articles.title: Whole-graph decreasing finish order contains every vertex
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph
$G$ given by ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the whole-graph
decreasing finish order of $G$, that is, the decreasing finish order of the left-first
depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.

articles.title: Decreasing finish order lists exactly the vertices reachable from the roots
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
finite directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let
$v$ be a vertex. Then $v$ occurs in the decreasing finish order of the left-first depth-first
search of $G$ from $r$ if and only if $v$ is reachable in $G$ from some vertex of $r$.

articles.title: Whole-graph DFS finishes every vertex
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ given by ordered
adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the postorder of the whole-graph
depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all
vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.

articles.title: Whole-graph DFS discovers every vertex
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$ given by
ordered adjacency lists and every vertex $v$ of $G$, $v$ occurs in the preorder of the whole-graph
depth-first search of $G$, that is, the left-first depth-first search of $G$ whose roots are all
vertices of $G$ in the graph's vertex order.

articles.title: Every discovered vertex is a forest root or has a unique parent
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite
directed graph given by ordered adjacency lists, let $r$ be a list of root vertices, and let $v$
be a vertex in the preorder of the left-first depth-first search of $G$ from $r$. Then $v$ is a
forest root of that search, or there is exactly one vertex $p$ such that $(v, p)$ is among the
(child, parent) pairs recorded by the search.

articles.title: Depth-first search finishes exactly the reachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed
graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the finish order (postorder) of the
depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$ is
reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.

articles.title: Depth-first search discovers exactly the reachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed
graph and $R$ a list of root vertices. A vertex $v$ occurs in the discovery order (preorder) of
the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ if and only if there is a root $r$ in $R$ from which $v$
is reachable in $G$ by a directed path of length zero or more.

articles.title: In decreasing finish order, a DFS parent precedes its child
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed
graph and $R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair
$(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs
strictly before $c$ in the decreasing finish order, the reverse of the finish order.

articles.title: In preorder, a DFS parent precedes its child
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a
list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in
the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $p$ occurs strictly before $c$ in
the discovery order (preorder) of the search.

articles.title: Parent chains in a DFS forest end at a forest root
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and
$R$ a list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded
parent of $c$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the
search, and call a discovered vertex with no recorded parent a forest root. Then for every
vertex $v$ in the discovery order (preorder) there are $k \ge 0$ and vertices
$v = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ such that each $v_{i+1}$ is a recorded parent of $v_i$ and $v_k$ is a
forest root.

articles.title: No vertex is recorded twice as a DFS child
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a
list of root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. In the list of
(child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, no vertex occurs as the child of more than one
entry; that is, the list of children has no repeated entries.

articles.title: DFS parent pairs are graph edges
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of root
vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. If the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of
(child, parent) pairs recorded by the search, then $G$ has a directed edge from $p$ to $c$.

articles.title: Parent relation of a list of pairs
articles.statement:
Given a list $P$ of (child, parent) pairs, $p$ is a
parent of $c$ in $P$ when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in $P$.

articles.title: The DFS parent relation is acyclic
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of
root vertices, and run depth-first search on $G$ from $R$. Say that $p$ is a recorded parent of $c$
when the pair $(c, p)$ occurs in the list of (child, parent) pairs recorded by the search. Then
there are no $k \ge 1$ and vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_k = v_0$ such that each
$v_{i+1}$ is a recorded parent of $v_i$.

articles.title: DFS finishes each vertex at most once
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of
root vertices. The finish order (postorder) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no
vertex twice.

articles.title: Depth-first search discovers every reachable vertex
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph
given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. If a vertex $v$ is reachable in
$G$ from some root in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero), then $v$ occurs in the
preorder (discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$.

articles.title: Depth-first search discovers each vertex at most once
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$
given by ordered adjacency lists and every list $R$ of roots, the preorder (discovery order) of
the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ contains no vertex twice.

articles.title: Depth-first search discovers only reachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph
given by ordered adjacency lists and let $R$ be a list of roots. Every vertex in the preorder
(discovery order) of the depth-first search of $G$ from $R$ is reachable in $G$ from some root
in $R$ by a directed path (possibly of length zero).

articles.title: Sequences of depth-first search machine steps
articles.statement: Zero or more independent DFS machine steps.

articles.title: Depth-first traversal record
articles.statement:
A traversal over a vertex type $V$ consists of three lists: a
preorder (discovery order) list of vertices, a postorder (finish order) list of vertices, and a
list of parent pairs in $V \times V$, each stored as $(\text{child}, \text{parent})$.

No condition relating the three lists is imposed by the record itself.

articles.title: Balanced edge list
articles.statement:
A list $E$ of ordered pairs of vertices, read as directed edge
occurrences, is balanced when every vertex $x$ occurs as the first component of exactly as many
entries of $E$ as it occurs as the second component, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Edge list of an adjacency function
articles.statement:
Given a directed adjacency graph $G$ and a function
$R$ assigning to each vertex $u$ a list $R(u)$ of vertices, the edge list of $R$ is the list of
pairs $(u, w)$, one for each entry $w$ of $R(u)$, taken over the vertices $u$ in the order of the
vertex enumeration of $G$ and, for each $u$, in the order of $R(u)$. A repeated entry gives a
repeated pair.

articles.title: Edge list of a directed graph
articles.statement:
The edge list of a directed adjacency graph $G$ is the list
of pairs $(u, w)$, one for each entry $w$ of the adjacency list of $u$, taken over the vertices
$u$ in the order of the vertex enumeration of $G$ and, for each $u$, in adjacency-list order. A
repeated adjacency entry gives a repeated pair, so $G$ is read as a multigraph with one edge
occurrence per entry.

articles.title: Multiplicity of a vertex in an unordered edge
articles.statement:
For a vertex $x$, this assigns to an
unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ the number $[x = a] + [x = b]$ of its endpoints equal to $x$, where
$[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise; in particular a loop $\{x, x\}$ gives $2$.

articles.title: Degrees of an undirected Euler path
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite list of edges of an undirected
multigraph and let $W$ be an Euler path of $E$ from $s$ to $t$. Then every vertex other than $s$
and $t$ has even degree in $E$ (a loop counts twice); if $s \ne t$, then $s$ and $t$ have odd
degree, and if $s = t$, every vertex has even degree.

articles.title: Degrees along a walk
articles.statement:
Let $W = (w_0, \dots, w_n)$ be a nonempty sequence of vertices with
$w_0 = s$ and $w_n = t$, and consider the multigraph whose edges are the consecutive pairs
$(w_{i-1}, w_i)$ for $1 \le i \le n$. In it every vertex other than $s$ and $t$ has even degree
(a loop counts twice); if $s \ne t$, then $s$ and $t$ have odd degree, and if $s = t$, every
vertex has even degree.

articles.title: Degree parity condition for two endpoints
articles.statement:
For a finite list $R$ of edges of an
undirected multigraph and vertices $v$, $t$, the condition holds when for every vertex $x$ the
number $\deg_R(x) + [x = v] + [x = t]$ is even, where $\deg_R$ is the degree in $R$ (a loop counts
twice) and $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. Thus if $v \ne t$, exactly $v$ and $t$
have odd degree, and if $v = t$, every degree is even.

articles.title: Euler circuit criterion for directed multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph,
read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ be a vertex such that the
source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then $G$ has an Euler circuit from $s$ if and
only if $G$ is balanced, that is, every vertex is the source of exactly as many edge occurrences
as it is the target of.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Problem 22-3; strong connectivity is weakened to reachability from $s$ of the source of every edge.

articles.title: Euler path criterion for directed multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read
as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices such that the
source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then $G$ has an Euler path from $s$ to $t$ if
and only if $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$: at $s$ one more edge occurrence leaves than
enters, at $t$ one more enters than leaves, and every other vertex is the source of exactly as
many edge occurrences as it is the target of (every vertex, when $s = t$).

articles.title: Euler's theorem for undirected multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite list of edges of an
undirected multigraph (parallel edges and loops allowed), each given as a pair $(a, b)$, and let
$s$, $t$ be vertices such that the first endpoint $a$ of every edge is reachable from $s$ along
edges of $E$ traversed in either direction. Then $E$ has an Euler path from $s$ to $t$ if and only
if, when $s \ne t$, exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree, and, when $s = t$, every vertex has even
degree (a loop counts twice towards the degree).

This is the algorithmic form: the proof shows that Hierholzer's algorithm started at $s$ finds
such a path.

articles.title: Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler circuits in directed multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, that is balanced (every
vertex is the source of exactly as many edge occurrences as it is the target of), and let $s$ be a
vertex such that the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then the vertex sequence
returned by Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ is an Euler circuit of $G$ from $s$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Problem 22-3, sufficiency with the algorithm; strong connectivity is weakened to reachability from $s$ of the source of every edge.

articles.title: Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler paths in directed multigraphs
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be
vertices such that $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$ (at $s$ one more edge occurrence leaves
than enters, at $t$ one more enters than leaves, and at every other vertex as many leave as enter;
at every vertex when $s = t$) and the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then the
vertex sequence returned by Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ is an Euler path of $G$ from $s$
to $t$.

articles.title: Running time of Hierholzer's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a
multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be vertices such that $G$ is
semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$ and the source of every edge of $G$ is reachable from $s$. Then
Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ costs exactly $|E|$ units, where $|E|$ is the number of
edge occurrences of $G$, that is, the length of its edge list.

The cost model charges one unit per edge traversal (removing the head of an adjacency list);
reading an adjacency list and emitting a vertex are free.

articles.title: Hierholzer's algorithm returns a trail in a directed multigraph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed
adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with one edge per adjacency entry, and let $s$ and $t$ be
vertices such that $G$ is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$. Then the vertex sequence $W$ returned by
Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$ starts at $s$ and ends at $t$, and the edge list of $G$ is a
permutation of the list of consecutive pairs of $W$ followed by some further list of pairs. So $W$
is a walk from $s$ to $t$ that uses each edge occurrence at most once; reachability is not
assumed.

articles.title: Hierholzer's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed adjacency graph, read as a multigraph with
one edge occurrence per adjacency entry, let $s$ be a vertex, and let $m$ be the number of edge
occurrences of $G$, that is, the length of its edge list. Hierholzer's algorithm on $G$ from $s$
runs Hierholzer's recursion from $s$ with fuel $m + 1$, with the adjacency list of each vertex as
its list of remaining out-neighbours and the empty list as accumulator, and returns the list of
vertices produced by the recursion, at the cost of the recursion.

articles.title: A directed multigraph with an Euler circuit is balanced
articles.statement:
If a finite directed multigraph
has an Euler circuit from some vertex $s$, then it is balanced: every vertex is the source of as
many edge occurrences as it is the target of.

This is the necessity direction of CLRS Problem 22-3.

articles.title: Balanced directed multigraph
articles.statement:
A finite directed multigraph, read from its adjacency lists
with each entry $w$ in the list of $u$ counted as one occurrence of the edge $u \to w$, is
balanced when every vertex is the source of as many edge occurrences as it is the target of.

articles.title: Euler circuit in a directed multigraph
articles.statement:
In a finite directed multigraph, a list of
vertices $W$ is an Euler circuit from a vertex $s$ when it is an Euler path from $s$ to $s$: it
starts and ends at $s$, and its list of consecutive pairs is a permutation of the list of edge
occurrences of the graph.

articles.title: Euler path in a directed multigraph
articles.statement:
In a finite directed multigraph, a list of vertices
$W = (w_0, \dots, w_k)$ is an Euler path from $s$ to $t$ when $w_0 = s$, $w_k = t$, and its list
of steps $(w_0, w_1), \dots, (w_{k-1}, w_k)$ is a permutation of the list of edge occurrences of
the graph, so that each edge occurrence, counted with multiplicity, is traversed exactly once.

articles.title: A directed multigraph with an Euler path is semi-balanced
articles.statement:
If a finite directed
multigraph has an Euler path from $s$ to $t$, then it is semi-balanced for $s$ and $t$: counting
edge occurrences, $s$ has one more outgoing than incoming edge, $t$ one more incoming than
outgoing, and every other vertex is balanced (every vertex, when $s = t$).

articles.title: Semi-balanced directed multigraph
articles.statement:
A finite directed multigraph is semi-balanced for
vertices $s$ and $t$ when, for every vertex $x$, the number of edge occurrences leaving $x$ plus
$[x = t]$ equals the number entering $x$ plus $[x = s]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$
otherwise. So for $s \ne t$, one more edge occurrence leaves $s$ than enters it, one more enters
$t$ than leaves it, and every other vertex is balanced; for $s = t$ every vertex is balanced.

articles.title: Euler path in an undirected multigraph
articles.statement:
For a finite list $E$ of edges of an undirected
multigraph and vertices $s$, $t$, a sequence of vertices $W = (w_0, \dots, w_n)$ is an Euler path
of $E$ from $s$ to $t$ when $w_0 = s$, $w_n = t$, and the multiset of unordered pairs
$\{w_{i-1}, w_i\}$ for $1 \le i \le n$ equals the multiset of the edges of $E$ taken as unordered
pairs. Thus every edge is traversed exactly once, in either direction.

articles.title: Other endpoint of an edge
articles.statement:
For an edge $e = (a, b)$ and a vertex $v$, the other endpoint
of $e$ at $v$ is $b$ if $a = v$, and $a$ otherwise; in particular a loop $(v, v)$ gives $v$.

articles.title: Moving a block of a list in front of an element is a permutation
articles.statement:
For an element $e$ and
lists $A$, $B$, $C$ of the same type, the list $e \cdot A \cdot B \cdot C$ is a permutation of
$B \cdot e \cdot A \cdot C$, where $\cdot$ denotes concatenation and $e$ stands for the
one-element list.

This is how a sub-tour $B$ is spliced in front of the edge $e$.

articles.title: Semi-balanced edge list
articles.statement:
A list $E$ of ordered pairs of vertices is semi-balanced for
vertices $v$ and $t$ when, for every vertex $x$, the number of pairs in $E$ with first component
$x$ plus $[x = t]$ equals the number with second component $x$ plus $[x = v]$, where $[P]$ is $1$
if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. So for $v \ne t$, $v$ has one more outgoing than incoming
occurrence, $t$ one more incoming than outgoing, and every other vertex is balanced; for $v = t$
every vertex is balanced.

articles.title: Degrees depend only on the unordered edges
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be finite lists of edges of an
undirected multigraph such that the multiset of edges of $A$, taken as unordered pairs, equals that
of $B$. Then every vertex has the same degree in $A$ as in $B$.

articles.title: Degree after removing an edge
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a finite list of edges of an undirected
multigraph, each an ordered pair of vertices, let $e = (a, b)$ be an edge in $R$, and let $x$ be a
vertex. Then the degree of $x$ in $R$ equals the degree of $x$ in the list obtained from $R$ by
removing the first occurrence of $e$, plus $[x = a] + [x = b]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds
and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Degree in an undirected edge list
articles.statement:
For a finite list $R$ of edges of an undirected
multigraph, each given as a pair $(a, b)$, the degree of a vertex $x$ is the number of edges in
$R$ whose first component is $x$ plus the number whose second component is $x$; parallel edges
count separately and a loop $(x, x)$ counts twice.

articles.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler circuits
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of undirected
edges (ordered pairs of vertices) in which every vertex has even degree, and let $s$ be a vertex
such that the first endpoint of every edge of $E$ is reachable from $s$ through edges of $E$. Then
the vertex sequence returned by the undirected Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ is an Euler
path of $E$ from $s$ to $s$, that is, an Euler circuit at $s$.

articles.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm finds Euler paths
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges
(ordered pairs of vertices) and $s$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree in
$E$ (no vertex has odd degree when $s = t$), and suppose the first endpoint of every edge of $E$ is
reachable from $s$ through edges of $E$. Then the vertex sequence returned by the undirected
Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ is an Euler path of $E$ from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Cost of the undirected Hierholzer algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges and
$s$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree in $E$ (no vertex has odd degree
when $s = t$), and suppose the first endpoint of every edge of $E$ is reachable from $s$ through
edges of $E$. Then the undirected Hierholzer algorithm on $E$ from $s$ costs exactly $|E|$, the
number of edges of $E$, in the cost model that charges one unit per removed edge.

articles.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm returns a trail
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of undirected edges
and $s$, $t$ vertices such that exactly $s$ and $t$ have odd degree in $E$ (no vertex has odd
degree when $s = t$). Then the vertex sequence $W$ returned by the undirected Hierholzer algorithm
on $E$ from $s$ starts at $s$ and ends at $t$, and the consecutive pairs of $W$, as unordered
pairs, form a sub-multiset of the edges of $E$ as unordered pairs: no edge is traversed more often
than it occurs in $E$.

articles.title: Undirected Hierholzer's algorithm
articles.statement:
Given a list $E$ of undirected edges (ordered pairs of
vertices) and a start vertex $s$, run the undirected Hierholzer recursion from $s$ on $E$ with an
empty accumulator and fuel $|E| + 1$, and return the list of emitted vertices; its cost is the
cost of that recursion.

articles.title: Reachability in an undirected multigraph
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of edges (ordered pairs of
vertices), a vertex $x$ is reachable from a vertex $s$ when there are vertices
$s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n = x$ with $n \ge 0$ such that for each $i < n$, $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ or
$(v_{i+1}, v_i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: An edge at a vertex joins it to its other endpoint
articles.statement:
If an ordered pair $e = (a, b)$ of
vertices has $a = v$ or $b = v$, then the unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ equals $\{v, w\}$, where $w$
is the other endpoint of $e$ at $v$.

articles.title: Unordered edge of an ordered pair
articles.statement:
The ordered pair $(a, b)$ of vertices, viewed as the
unordered pair $\{a, b\}$, so that $(a, b)$ and $(b, a)$ give the same unordered edge.

articles.title: Invariant of the undirected Hierholzer recursion
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a list of edges, $v$, $t$
vertices such that exactly $v$ and $t$ have odd degree in $R$ (no vertex when $v = t$), $A$ a list
of vertices, and $f > |R|$ a fuel bound. Run the undirected Hierholzer recursion with fuel $f$
from $v$ on $R$ with accumulator $A$, and let $R'$ be the remaining edge list it returns and $c$
its cost. Then there is a vertex sequence $W$ starting at $v$ and ending at $t$ such that the
returned vertex list is $W$ followed by $A$; the edges of $R$, as unordered pairs, are a
permutation of the consecutive pairs of $W$ followed by the edges of $R'$, all as unordered pairs;
every vertex has even degree in $R'$; every vertex of $W$ has degree $0$ in $R'$; $R'$ is a
sublist of $R$; and $c + |R'| = |R|$.

articles.title: Undirected Hierholzer recursion
articles.statement:
The recursion takes a fuel $f \in \mathbb{N}$, a vertex
$v$, a list $R$ of remaining edges and an accumulator list $A$ of vertices, and returns a list of
vertices and a list of remaining edges. With fuel $0$ it returns $A$ and $R$ unchanged. With fuel
$f + 1$: if no edge of $R$ has $v$ as an endpoint, it returns $v$ prepended to $A$, together with
$R$; otherwise, with $e$ the first such edge, it removes $e$ from $R$ at a cost of one unit,
recurses with fuel $f$ from the other endpoint of $e$ at $v$ on the shortened list with
accumulator $A$, obtaining a vertex list $A'$ and remaining edges $R'$, and then recurses with fuel
$f$ from $v$ on $R'$ with accumulator $A'$.

articles.title: Contract of Hierholzer's recursion
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed multigraph, let $R$
assign to each vertex $u$ a list $R(u)$ of remaining out-neighbours, and let $E(R)$ be the list
of remaining edge occurrences, one pair $(u, w)$ for each entry $w$ of $R(u)$. Let $v$ and $t$ be
vertices, $\mathit{acc}$ a list of vertices and $n$ a natural number with $|E(R)| < n$, and
suppose $E(R)$ is semi-balanced for $v$ and $t$: for every vertex $x$, the number of pairs in
$E(R)$ with first component $x$ plus $[x = t]$ equals the number with second component $x$ plus
$[x = v]$, where $[P]$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise. Let $(L, R')$ be the result and $c$
the cost of Hierholzer's recursion with fuel $n$ from $v$ on $R$ with accumulator $\mathit{acc}$.
Then there is a list of vertices $W$ such that $L$ is $W$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$; $W$ starts
at $v$ and ends at $t$; $E(R)$ is a permutation of the steps (consecutive pairs) of $W$ followed
by $E(R')$; every vertex is the first component of as many pairs of $E(R')$ as it is the second
component of; $R'(x)$ is empty for every vertex $x$ of $W$; $R'(x)$ is a suffix of $R(x)$ for
every vertex $x$; and $c + |E(R')| = |E(R)|$.

articles.title: Hierholzer's recursion
articles.statement:
Given a fuel $n$, a vertex $v$, an assignment $R$ of a list of
remaining out-neighbours to each vertex, and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of vertices, the recursion
returns a list of vertices and a new assignment, with a cost. With fuel $0$ it returns
$(\mathit{acc}, R)$ at cost $0$. With fuel $n + 1$: if $R(v)$ is empty, it returns $v$ followed by
$\mathit{acc}$ together with $R$, at cost $0$; otherwise $R(v)$ is $w$ followed by a list
$\mathit{rest}$, and it replaces $R(v)$ by $\mathit{rest}$, runs the recursion with fuel $n$ from
$w$ on the new assignment with accumulator $\mathit{acc}$, obtaining $(L_1, R_1)$, and returns the
result of the recursion with fuel $n$ from $v$ on $R_1$ with accumulator $L_1$, at cost $1$ plus
the costs of the two calls.

This follows unused edges depth first and splices sub-tours in; too little fuel can stop it
early. Hierholzer's algorithm runs it with fuel one more than the number of edge occurrences.

articles.title: Steps of a concatenated walk
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty vertex sequences, where $A$
ends at the vertex $a$ and $B$ starts at the vertex $b$. Then the steps of the concatenation
$A B$ are the steps of $A$, followed by the step $(a, b)$, followed by the steps of $B$.

articles.title: Steps of a walk
articles.statement:
For a finite sequence of vertices $W = (w_0, w_1, \dots, w_n)$, the
steps of $W$ are the list of consecutive pairs $((w_0, w_1), (w_1, w_2), \dots, (w_{n-1}, w_n))$,
in order. A sequence with at most one vertex has no steps.

articles.title: Each computed component is a full mutual-reachability class
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph,
let $B$ be one of the blocks returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$, and
let $m$ be a vertex of $B$. Then for every vertex $v$ of $G$, the vertices $m$ and $v$ are strongly
connected (each is reachable from the other) if and only if $v$ lies in $B$.

articles.title: Reachability between components
articles.statement:
In a directed graph $G$, a list $S$ of vertices reaches
a list $T$ of vertices when some vertex of $S$ reaches some vertex of $T$ by a directed path in
$G$, possibly of length zero.

articles.title: The condensation of the computed components is acyclic
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph and
let $S$ and $T$ be blocks returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$. If some
vertex of $S$ reaches some vertex of $T$ and some vertex of $T$ reaches some vertex of $S$, then
$S = T$.

Equivalently, the condensation relation has no nontrivial directed cycle.

articles.title: The computed components form the SCC partition
articles.statement:
For every directed graph $G$, the list of
blocks returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ is an SCC partition of $G$:
every block is nonempty and contains no vertex twice, blocks at different positions of the list
are disjoint, every vertex of $G$ lies in some block, two vertices lie in a common block exactly
when they are strongly connected, and for every vertex $m$ of a block $B$ and every vertex $v$,
the vertices $m$ and $v$ are strongly connected exactly when $v$ lies in $B$.

articles.title: Computed components have no repeated vertices
articles.statement:
For every directed graph $G$, each block
returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ contains no vertex more than
once.

articles.title: Computed components are nonempty
articles.statement:
For every directed graph $G$, each block returned by the
strongly connected components algorithm on $G$ contains at least one vertex.

articles.title: Computed components are pairwise disjoint
articles.statement:
For every directed graph $G$, any two blocks at
different positions of the list returned by the strongly connected components algorithm on $G$
have no vertex in common.

articles.title: Strongly connected components algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph and let
$v_1, \dots, v_n$ be its vertices in decreasing order of finishing time in a depth-first search of
the whole graph that takes its roots in the vertex order of $G$. For each $i$, let $C_i$ be the
list of those $v_j$, in increasing order of $j$, such that $v_i$ and $v_j$ are strongly connected
(tested by two depth-first searches). The output is the list $C_1, \dots, C_n$ with repeated
blocks removed, keeping the last occurrence of each.

The result is deterministic: within a block, vertices appear in decreasing finish order.

articles.title: Acyclic condensation
articles.statement:
A list $\mathcal{B}$ of vertex lists of a directed graph $G$ has an
acyclic condensation when, for all $S, T \in \mathcal{B}$, if some vertex of $S$ reaches some
vertex of $T$ in $G$ and some vertex of $T$ reaches some vertex of $S$, then $S = T$. That is,
reachability between the blocks is antisymmetric.

articles.title: SCC partition
articles.statement:
A list $\mathcal{B}$ of vertex lists is an SCC partition of a directed graph
$G$ when every block of $\mathcal{B}$ is nonempty and contains no vertex twice, blocks at different
positions of $\mathcal{B}$ are disjoint, a vertex lies in some block exactly when it is a vertex of
$G$, two vertices lie in a common block exactly when they are strongly connected (each is
reachable from the other), and for every block $B$, every $m \in B$ and every vertex $v$, the
vertices $m$ and $v$ are strongly connected exactly when $v \in B$.

articles.title: The computed components cover the vertex list
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ and a vertex
$v$, $v$ belongs to some block of the computed strongly connected components of $G$ if and only
if $v$ occurs in the vertex enumeration of $G$.

articles.title: The mutual-reachability test is correct
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$,
the executable mutual-reachability test on $u$ and $v$ returns true if and only if $u$ and $v$ are
strongly connected in $G$.

articles.title: Executable mutual-reachability test
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the
test returns true exactly when $v$ occurs in the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from
the single root $u$, and $u$ occurs in the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from the
single root $v$.

articles.title: Vertices share a computed component exactly when strongly connected
articles.statement:
For a directed graph
$G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, some block of the computed strongly connected components of $G$
contains both $u$ and $v$ if and only if $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected in $G$.

articles.title: Strong connectivity is reflexive
articles.statement:
In a directed graph $G$, every vertex is strongly
connected to itself.

articles.title: Strong connectivity as an equivalence relation
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$, the relation on
the vertices of $G$ that holds between $u$ and $v$ exactly when $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected
in $G$, packaged as an equivalence relation.

articles.title: Strongly connected vertices
articles.statement:
In a directed adjacency graph $G$, vertices $u$ and $v$ are
strongly connected when $v$ is reachable from $u$ and $u$ is reachable from $v$ in $G$.

articles.title: Strong connectivity is symmetric
articles.statement:
In a directed graph $G$, if $u$ is strongly connected to
$v$, then $v$ is strongly connected to $u$.

articles.title: Strong connectivity is transitive
articles.statement:
In a directed graph $G$, if $u$ is strongly connected to
$v$ and $v$ is strongly connected to $w$, then $u$ is strongly connected to $w$.

articles.title: Kahn's algorithm succeeds on acyclic graphs
articles.statement:
If a finite directed graph $G$, given by a
vertex enumeration and adjacency lists, is acyclic, then deterministic FIFO Kahn topological
sorting of $G$ returns success with some vertex order.

articles.title: Characterization of directed cycles within a vertex list
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed
graph and let $R$ and $c = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ be lists of vertices. Then $c$ is a directed cycle
of $G$ in $R$ if and only if $k \ge 1$, the vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are pairwise distinct,
$G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for every $1 \le i < k$, $G$ has an edge from $c_k$ to
$c_1$, and every $c_i$ lies in $R$.

articles.title: Directed cycle within a vertex list
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph and $R$ a list of
vertices. A list $c = [c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of vertices is a directed cycle of $G$ in $R$ when
$k \ge 1$, the vertices $c_1, \dots, c_k$ are pairwise distinct, $G$ has an edge from $c_i$ to
$c_{i+1}$ for each $1 \le i < k$ and an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$, and every $c_i$ lies in $R$.

articles.title: A failed Kahn run leaves a directed cycle
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If
deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after processing the vertex list $P$
and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then $G$ has a directed cycle in $R$: a nonempty
list of pairwise distinct vertices of $R$ in which each vertex has an edge to the next and the
last vertex has an edge to the first.

articles.title: Unprocessed vertices of a failed Kahn run have positive indegree among the unprocessed
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails
after processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then for every
vertex $v$ in $R$ the indegree of $v$ within $R$, the number of entries $u$ of $R$ such that $G$
has an edge from $u$ to $v$, is positive.

articles.title: A failed Kahn run splits the vertices into processed and unprocessed ones
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
finite directed graph. If deterministic FIFO Kahn topological sorting of $G$ fails after
processing the vertex list $P$ and leaving the vertex list $R$ unprocessed, then $R$ is nonempty,
neither $P$ nor $R$ has repeated entries, a vertex lies in the vertex list of $G$ if and only if
it lies in $P$ or in $R$, and no vertex lies in both $P$ and $R$.

articles.title: Indegree within a vertex list
articles.statement:
For a finite directed graph $G$, a list $R$ of vertices and
a vertex $v$, the indegree of $v$ within $R$ is the number of entries $u$ of $R$, counted with
multiplicity, such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$.

articles.title: Indegree
articles.statement:
The indegree of a vertex $v$ in a finite directed graph $G$ is the number of
vertices $u$ such that $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$; repeated entries in adjacency lists
count once.

articles.title: Acyclicity means having no directed cycle
articles.statement:
A finite directed graph $G$ is acyclic if and
only if there is no directed cycle of $G$ in its vertex list, that is, no nonempty list of
pairwise distinct vertices in which each vertex has an edge to the next and the last vertex has
an edge to the first.

articles.title: Acyclic directed graph
articles.statement:
A finite directed graph $G$ is acyclic when it has no directed
cycle, that is, no nonempty list $[c_1, \dots, c_k]$ of pairwise distinct vertices such that $G$
has an edge from $c_i$ to $c_{i+1}$ for each $1 \le i < k$ and an edge from $c_k$ to $c_1$.

articles.title: Topological order
articles.statement:
A list $L$ of vertices of a finite directed graph $G$ is a topological
order of $G$ when $L$ has no duplicates, a vertex lies in $L$ exactly when it lies in the vertex
enumeration of $G$, and for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$ the first position of $u$ in $L$ is strictly
smaller than the first position of $v$ in $L$.

articles.title: Outcome of Kahn's topological sort
articles.statement:
The result of Kahn's topological sorting algorithm on a
graph with vertices of type $\alpha$ is either a success, carrying a list of vertices, or a failure,
carrying the list of vertices processed before the queue emptied and the list of vertices that
remain.

articles.title: Kahn's topological sort
articles.statement:
Run Kahn's algorithm with a first-in first-out queue on a finite
directed graph $G$ whose vertices are enumerated as $v_1, \dots, v_n$. Initially every vertex is
remaining, the counter of each vertex is its number of in-neighbours, and the queue holds the
vertices with no in-neighbours in enumeration order. At each of $n$ steps, if the queue is nonempty,
its front vertex $x$ is removed from the queue and from the remaining vertices and appended to the
output; then each distinct out-neighbour $y$ of $x$ that is still remaining, taken in order of first
occurrence in the adjacency list of $x$, has its counter decreased by one and joins the back of the
queue if that counter was $1$. If no vertices remain after the $n$ steps, the result is a success
with the output list; otherwise it is a failure with the output list as the processed vertices and
the remaining vertices in enumeration order.

articles.title: Kahn's algorithm succeeds exactly on acyclic graphs
articles.statement:
For every finite directed graph $G$,
Kahn's topological sort on $G$ returns a success if and only if $G$ is acyclic.

articles.title: A successful topological sort lists every vertex
articles.statement:
If Kahn's topological sort on a finite
directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then a vertex lies in $L$ if and only if it
lies in the vertex enumeration of $G$.

articles.title: A successful topological sort points every edge forward
articles.statement:
If Kahn's topological sort on a
finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then for every edge $u \to v$ of $G$ the
first position of $u$ in $L$ is strictly smaller than the first position of $v$ in $L$.

articles.title: Success of Kahn's algorithm implies acyclicity
articles.statement:
If Kahn's topological sort on a finite
directed graph $G$ returns a success, then $G$ is acyclic.

articles.title: A successful topological sort is a topological order
articles.statement:
If Kahn's topological sort on a
finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then $L$ is a topological
order of $G$.

articles.title: A successful topological sort has no repeated vertex
articles.statement:
If Kahn's topological sort on a
finite directed graph $G$ returns a success with list $L$, then $L$ has no duplicates.

articles.title: Correctness of the transitive-closure algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Boolean adjacency matrix
of a directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$. For all vertices $i$ and $j$, the entry
$(i, j)$ of the matrix returned by the transitive-closure algorithm on $A$ is true if and only if
$j$ is reachable from $i$ by a sequence of zero or more edges of the graph.

articles.title: Cost of initializing the transitive-closure matrix
articles.statement:
For every Boolean adjacency matrix on
$n$ vertices, the staged transitive-closure computation with no pivot stages (only the
initialization of the $n \times n$ matrix) charges exactly $n^2$ time units, one for each cell
assignment.

articles.title: Cost of one transition stage
articles.statement:
For every Boolean adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices and every
$k < n$, the time charged by the staged transitive-closure computation with $k + 1$ pivot stages
minus the time charged with $k$ pivot stages equals $n^2$: one time unit for each cell assignment
of the new stage.

articles.title: Invariant of the transitive-closure stages
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Boolean adjacency matrix of a
directed graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $k \le n$. For all vertices $i$ and $j$, the
entry $(i, j)$ of the matrix produced by the staged transitive-closure computation after its first
$k$ pivot stages is true if and only if there are vertices $i = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_m = j$ with
$m \ge 0$ such that each $A_{v_t v_{t+1}}$ is true and every intermediate vertex
$v_1, \dots, v_{m-1}$ is less than $k$.

articles.title: Transition recurrence of the transitive-closure stages
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Boolean adjacency
matrix on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, and for $m \le n$ let $T^{(m)}$ be the matrix produced by
the staged transitive-closure computation on $A$ after its first $m$ pivot stages. For every
$k < n$ and all vertices $i$ and $j$,

$$T^{(k+1)}_{ij} = T^{(k)}_{ij} \lor \bigl(T^{(k)}_{ik} \land T^{(k)}_{kj}\bigr).$$

Every operand of stage $k + 1$ is read from the complete matrix saved after stage $k$.

articles.title: Initial matrix of the transitive-closure computation
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Boolean adjacency
matrix on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$. For all vertices $i$ and $j$, the entry $(i, j)$ of the
matrix produced by the staged transitive-closure computation with no pivot stages is true if and
only if $i = j$ or $A_{ij}$ is true.

articles.title: Staged transitive-closure computation
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Boolean adjacency matrix on the
vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and let $k \le n$. The computation first builds the $n \times n$ Boolean
matrix $T^{(0)}$ whose entry $(i, j)$ is true exactly when $i = j$ or $A_{ij}$ is true. Then, for
$p = 0, \dots, k - 1$, it builds a new matrix $T^{(p+1)}$ from the saved matrix $T^{(p)}$ by
$T^{(p+1)}_{ij} = T^{(p)}_{ij} \lor (T^{(p)}_{ip} \land T^{(p)}_{pj})$, and it returns $T^{(k)}$.
One time unit is charged for each cell assignment.

articles.title: Cost of transitive closure on one vertex
articles.statement:
For every Boolean adjacency matrix on a single
vertex, the transitive-closure algorithm charges exactly $2$ time units: one cell assignment for
the initialization and one for the single transition stage.

articles.title: Cost of transitive closure on the empty graph
articles.statement:
For the graph with no vertices, the
transitive-closure algorithm charges $0$ time units: it performs no cell assignments.

articles.title: Running time of the transitive-closure algorithm
articles.statement:
For every Boolean adjacency matrix on
$n$ vertices, the transitive-closure algorithm charges exactly $n^2 + n^3$ time units: $n^2$ cell
assignments to initialize the matrix and $n^2$ in each of the $n$ transition stages.

articles.title: Cost of the transition stages of transitive closure
articles.statement:
Charge one time unit for each cell
assignment. For every Boolean adjacency matrix on $n$ vertices, let $a$ be the cost of running the
initialization of the saved-matrix transitive-closure algorithm followed by all $n$ of its
stages, and let $b$ be the cost of running the initialization alone. Then $a - b = n^3$, where the
subtraction is subtraction of natural numbers, truncated at $0$. That is, the $n$ transition
stages together perform exactly $n^3$ cell assignments.

articles.title: Saved-matrix transitive-closure algorithm
articles.statement:
Given a Boolean adjacency matrix $A$ on the
vertices $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, the algorithm first builds the matrix $t^{(0)}$ with $t^{(0)}_{ij}$
true exactly when $i = j$ or $A_{ij}$ is true. Then, for $k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1$ in turn, it
builds a new matrix $t^{(k+1)}$ with
$t^{(k+1)}_{ij} = t^{(k)}_{ij} \lor (t^{(k)}_{ik} \land t^{(k)}_{kj})$ for all $i, j$, reading
every operand from the saved matrix $t^{(k)}$, and it returns $t^{(n)}$. One time unit is
charged for each cell assignment; reads, Boolean operations and matrix allocation are free.

This is the saved-matrix recurrence of CLRS for the reflexive transitive closure.

articles.title: Frontier occurrences satisfy the resource invariant
articles.statement: Every frontier occurrence satisfies the resource invariant at some budgets.

articles.title: Branch-split properties hold at the root iff at some leaf
articles.statement: A property split by branches holds at the root iff it holds at some frontier occurrence.

articles.title: Deepening the cut past a terminal frontier changes nothing
articles.statement: Increasing a depth cut beyond a terminal frontier leaves the list unchanged.

articles.title: Depth-cut frontiers are nonempty
articles.statement: Every depth-cut frontier is nonempty.

articles.title: Commuting maps transport the ordered frontier
articles.statement: A map commuting with both steps transports the ordered frontier, preserving multiplicity.

articles.title: Invariant-restricted step transport of the frontier
articles.statement:
Step transport restricted to a preserved invariant transports the frontier and
records that all its occurrences satisfy the invariant.

articles.title: Depth-cut frontier of a binary branching step
articles.statement:
The frontier below `s`, left to right, cut at depth `k`. At depth zero it is `[s]`,
even when `step s` branches. Duplicate occurrences are retained.

articles.title: Binomial bound on the frontier size under depth and heavy budgets
articles.statement:
With at most `d` further depth steps and `h` further heavy steps, the frontier has
at most `∑ j ∈ range (h + 1), d.choose j` occurrences. The source budget hypotheses
are retained, including the strict heavy-budget inequality.

articles.title: Stack invariants hold for every collected leaf
articles.statement: A property of every state ever on the stack holds of each collected leaf.

articles.title: Final count of counting rounds is the frontier weight
articles.statement: With a terminal frontier and enough rounds, the final count is its total weight.

articles.title: Counting rounds project list-output rounds
articles.statement: Counting rounds are the projection of list-output rounds to the sum of output weights.

articles.title: Weight-counting depth-first round
articles.statement:
One stack round accumulating natural weights rather than a list of terminal states.
The previous count is retained, and each terminal occurrence contributes its weight.

articles.title: Commuting maps transport any number of rounds
articles.statement: A commuting node map transports any number of rounds. No injectivity is required.

articles.title: Enough rounds empty the stack and collect the frontier
articles.statement:
After at least `2 * length - 1` rounds from `[s]`, the stack is empty and all
terminal frontier occurrences have been collected in reverse order.

articles.title: Exact round count for traversing a terminal frontier
articles.statement:
If every frontier occurrence is terminal, exactly `2 * length - 1` rounds process
the tree below `s`, preserving the tail `r` and prepending its reversed frontier to `out`.
The terminal-frontier hypothesis is essential: a depth cut may contain branching states.

articles.title: Commuting maps transport one depth-first round
articles.statement: A commuting node map transports one stack round and its accumulated output.

articles.title: An empty work stack is fixed by every round
articles.statement: An empty work stack is fixed by any number of rounds.

articles.title: One depth-first round of binary branching
articles.statement:
One depth-first round on `(stack, output)`. Terminal states are prepended to the output;
a branching state is replaced by its left child followed by its right child.

articles.title: Depth budget bounds the depth-first stack size
articles.statement:
The depth budget bounds the stack by `D + 1` at every round; each pending state
satisfies the resource invariant. This is a list-size bound, not a machine-space model.

articles.title: A large enough depth cut yields only terminal states
articles.statement: A depth allowance covering the remaining depth budget produces only terminal states.

articles.title: Additive weight of the root is the sum over the frontier
articles.statement:
A natural-valued weight additive across each branch equals the sum of the frontier
weights, even when the frontier is cut before termination.

articles.title: Pending plus collected occurrences are bounded by the frontier length
articles.statement:
With a terminal frontier, pending and collected occurrences together never exceed
its length, including before traversal is complete.

articles.title: A round does not decrease pending plus collected occurrences
articles.statement: One round does not decrease the combined number of pending and collected occurrences.

articles.title: Cache events
articles.statement:
A cache event over a type $\alpha$ of blocks records how one request is
served: either a hit on the requested block $r \in \alpha$, or a miss on the requested block $r$
together with an optional evicted block $v \in \alpha$, absent when nothing is evicted.

articles.title: Legal cache traces preserve valid caches
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity and suppose a finite
sequence of cache events leads from the cache $C$ to the cache $C'$ by legal cache transitions
for capacity $k$. If $C$ has no duplicate entries and length at most $k$, then $C'$ has no
duplicate entries and length at most $k$.

articles.title: Legal cache transitions preserve valid caches
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity and let $C \to C'$
be a legal cache transition for capacity $k$, labelled by any cache event. If $C$ has no
duplicate entries and length at most $k$, then $C'$ has no duplicate entries and length at
most $k$.

articles.title: Legal cache transitions
articles.statement:
For a capacity $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the labelled
transition system whose states are lists of blocks (the cache contents, in any order) and whose
labels are cache events. Write $|C|$ for the length of a list $C$, $x :: C$ for $C$ with $x$
prepended, and $C \setminus v$ for $C$ with the first occurrence of $v$ removed. There is a
transition from $C$ to $C'$ labelled by a hit on $r$ when $r \in C$ and $C'$ is a permutation of
$C$; labelled by a miss on $r$ with no eviction when $r \notin C$ and either $k = 0$ and $C$ and
$C'$ are both empty, or $|C| < k$ and $C'$ is a permutation of $r :: C$; and labelled by a miss on
$r$ evicting $v$ when $k > 0$, $r \notin C$, $|C| = k$, $v \in C$ and $C'$ is a permutation of
$r :: (C \setminus v)$.

articles.title: One step of the furthest-in-future manager
articles.statement:
Write $x :: L$ for the list $L$ with $x$
prepended, $[\,]$ for the empty list, $|L|$ for the length of $L$, and $L \setminus v$ for $L$
with the first occurrence of $v$ removed. Write $\mathrm{FIF}_k(R, C) = (E, D)$ when the
furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ on the requests $R$ from the initial cache $C$ emits
the events $E$ and ends with the cache $D$. Write $\mathrm{hit}(r)$ for a hit on $r$,
$\mathrm{miss}(r)$ for a miss on $r$ with no eviction, and $\mathrm{miss}(r, v)$ for a miss on
$r$ evicting $v$. Let $C$ be a duplicate-free list of blocks with $|C| \le k$, let $r$ be a block
and $f$ a list of blocks, and for a block $b$ let $\nu(b) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ be the
position of the first occurrence of $b$ in $f$, or $\infty$ if $b$ does not occur in $f$.
If $r \in C$, then $\mathrm{FIF}_k(r :: f, C) = (\mathrm{hit}(r) :: E, D)$ where
$(E, D) = \mathrm{FIF}_k(f, C)$. If $k = 0$, then
$\mathrm{FIF}_k(r :: f, C) = (\mathrm{miss}(r) :: E, D)$ where $(E, D) = \mathrm{FIF}_k(f, [\,])$.
If $r \notin C$ and $|C| < k$, then $\mathrm{FIF}_k(r :: f, C) = (\mathrm{miss}(r) :: E, D)$
where $(E, D) = \mathrm{FIF}_k(f, r :: C)$. If $r \notin C$, $k > 0$ and $|C| = k$, and $v$ is
the first entry of $C$ at which $\nu$ is maximal on $C$, then
$\mathrm{FIF}_k(r :: f, C) = (\mathrm{miss}(r, v) :: E, D)$ where
$(E, D) = \mathrm{FIF}_k(f, r :: (C \setminus v))$.

articles.title: The furthest-in-future manager produces legal traces
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $R$ a list
of requested blocks and $C$ a duplicate-free list of blocks of length at most $k$. Let $E$ be the
events and $D$ the final cache produced by the furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ on
$R$ from the initial cache $C$. Then $E$ leads from $C$ to $D$ by legal cache transitions for
capacity $k$, the blocks requested by the events of $E$ are, in order, exactly $R$, and $D$ is
duplicate-free of length at most $k$.

articles.title: Optimality of furthest-in-future caching
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $R$ a list of requested
blocks and $C$ a duplicate-free list of blocks of length at most $k$. Let $E'$ be any list of
cache events that leads from $C$ to some final cache by legal cache transitions for capacity $k$
and whose events request, in order, exactly the blocks of $R$. Then the furthest-in-future
manager with capacity $k$ on $R$ from the initial cache $C$ emits at most as many miss events as
$E'$ contains.

Legal transitions may reorder the list representing the cache, so a competing trace need not
keep the manager's order.

articles.title: Furthest-in-future caching has the fewest misses
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $R$ a list of
requested blocks and $C$ a duplicate-free list of blocks of length at most $k$. Let $E'$ be any
list of cache events that leads from $C$ to some final cache by legal cache transitions for
capacity $k$ and whose events serve, in order, exactly the blocks of $R$. Then the number of
misses among the events emitted by the furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ on $R$ from
the initial cache $C$ is at most the number of misses of $E'$.

articles.title: Furthest-in-future on no requests
articles.statement:
For every capacity $k$ and every list $C$ of blocks,
the furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ on the empty request list from the initial
cache $C$ emits no events and ends with the cache $C$, unchanged.

articles.title: Furthest-in-future serves exactly the requests
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $R$ a list of
requested blocks and $C$ a duplicate-free list of blocks of length at most $k$. Then the events
emitted by the furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ on $R$ from the initial cache $C$
serve, in order, exactly the blocks of $R$.

articles.title: Furthest-in-future caching with zero capacity
articles.statement:
Run with capacity $0$ on a request
sequence $r_1, \dots, r_n$ from the empty cache, the furthest-in-future manager emits exactly
the events $\mathrm{miss}(r_1), \dots, \mathrm{miss}(r_n)$, one miss per request in order and
each evicting no page, and its final cache is empty.

articles.title: Furthest-in-future caching
articles.statement:
Given a capacity $k$, a sequence of requested pages and an
initial cache (a list of pages), the furthest-in-future manager serves the requests in order
and returns the list of emitted cache events together with the final cache. A request for a
page $r$ already in the cache is a hit and leaves the cache unchanged. Otherwise it is a miss:
if $k = 0$, nothing is evicted and the cache becomes empty; if the cache holds fewer than $k$
pages, nothing is evicted and $r$ is added at the front; otherwise the manager evicts the cached
page whose next occurrence among the later requests is furthest away (a page never requested
again counts as infinitely far, and ties go to the page listed first in the cache), removes it
and adds $r$ at the front.

articles.title: Miss indicator
articles.statement:
The miss indicator of a cache event is true if the event is a miss and
false if it is a hit.

articles.title: Number of misses in a trace
articles.statement:
The number of misses of a finite list of cache events is the
number of events in the list that are misses.

articles.title: A legal trace misses at least once
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity and $C$ a cache listing at most
$k$ pages, and consider a legal trace of cache events for capacity $k$ that starts from $C$. Let
$p$ be a page in $C$. If at least $k + 1$ distinct pages are each equal to $p$ or served by some
event of the trace, then the trace contains at least one miss.

articles.title: A legal trace without misses serves only cached pages
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity. If a legal
trace of cache events for capacity $k$ starts from a cache $C$ and contains no miss, then every
page served by an event of the trace lies in $C$.

articles.title: A legal step caches the served page
articles.statement:
Let $k > 0$ be a capacity. If a legal transition for
capacity $k$ takes a cache $C$ to a cache $C'$ by a cache event, then the page served by that
event lies in $C'$.

articles.title: Page served by a cache event
articles.statement:
The page served by a cache event is the page it requests,
whether the event is a hit or a miss.

articles.title: Characterization of the bridge test
articles.statement:
On a finite vertex set, let $S$ be a finite set of
unordered pairs of vertices and let $u$, $v$ be vertices. The bridge test of $S$ on the pair
$\{u, v\}$ returns true if and only if $u$ and $v$ are not connected by a path in the graph whose
edges are the non-loop pairs of $S \setminus \{\{u, v\}\}$.

articles.title: Bridge test for an edge set
articles.statement:
On a finite vertex set, for a finite set $S$ of unordered
pairs of vertices and a pair $e = \{u, v\}$, the bridge test returns true exactly when $u$ and $v$
are not connected by a path in the graph whose edges are the non-loop pairs of $S \setminus \{e\}$.
When $e \in S$ is not a loop, this says that $e$ is a bridge of $S$: deleting it disconnects its
endpoints.

articles.title: Deleting a bridge adds one component
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set
and let $ab$ be an edge of $H$. If $a$ and $b$ are not connected in the graph obtained from $H$
by deleting the edge $ab$, then that graph has exactly one more connected component than $H$.

articles.title: Graph of a finite edge set
articles.statement: The graph of a finite edge set, with decidable adjacency.

articles.title: Augmentation property of forests
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, and
let $I$ and $J$ be sets of edges of $G$ that each form an acyclic graph. If $|I| < |J|$, then there
is an edge $e \in J$ with $e \notin I$ such that $I \cup \{e\}$ still forms an acyclic graph.

articles.title: The forest oracle decides graphic-matroid independence
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a
finite vertex set and a finite set $S$ of unordered pairs of vertices, the forest oracle of $G$
accepts $S$ if and only if $S$ is independent in the graphic matroid of $G$.

articles.title: Forest oracle
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the forest oracle accepts a
finite set $S$ of unordered pairs of vertices exactly when every $e \in S$ is an edge of $G$ and
passes the bridge test in $S$: its endpoints are not connected in the graph formed by the other
pairs of $S$. It serves as the independence oracle of the graphic matroid of $G$, since a graph
is a forest if and only if every edge is a bridge.

articles.title: Graphic matroid
articles.statement:
For a simple graph $G$ on a finite vertex set, the graphic matroid of $G$
is the matroid on unordered pairs of vertices whose ground set is the edge set of $G$ and whose
independent sets are the forests of $G$, that is, the sets of edges of $G$ that form an acyclic
graph.

That these sets form a matroid is CLRS Theorem 16.5.

articles.title: Forests of a graph
articles.statement:
A set $I$ of unordered pairs of vertices is a forest of a simple graph
$G$ when every element of $I$ is an edge of $G$ and the graph with edge set $I$ has no cycles.

articles.title: Kruskal's algorithm returns a maximal forest
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex
set and let $L$ be a list of unordered pairs of vertices such that a pair is an edge of $G$ if and
only if it occurs in $L$. Then the matroid greedy algorithm run with the forest oracle of $G$ on
$L$ returns a base of the graphic matroid of $G$, that is, a maximal forest of $G$.

articles.title: Kruskal's algorithm returns a forest
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type
$V$. For every list $L$ of unordered pairs of vertices, the matroid greedy algorithm run on $L$
with the forest oracle of $G$ returns a forest of $G$: a set of edges of $G$ without cycles.

This is Kruskal's algorithm in the form of CLRS Section 16.4, the greedy algorithm on the graphic
matroid.

articles.title: Optimality of Kruskal's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex type
$V$, let $w$ assign a natural number to each unordered pair of vertices, and let $L$ be a list
of unordered pairs of vertices in nonincreasing order of $w$ (each entry weighs at least as much
as every later one). Let $T$ be the set returned by the matroid greedy algorithm run on $L$ with
the forest oracle of $G$. Then every forest $I$ of $G$ all of whose edges occur in $L$ satisfies
$\sum_{x \in I} w(x) \le \sum_{x \in T} w(x)$.

This is CLRS Theorem 16.11 on the graphic matroid.

articles.title: Edges plus components of a forest
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite vertex set. For every natural
number $n$ and every forest (acyclic simple graph) $F$ on $V$ with exactly $n$ edges, the number
of edges of $F$ plus the number of connected components of $F$ equals $|V|$. So a forest on $V$
with $e$ edges has $|V| - e$ connected components.

articles.title: Compatible activities
articles.statement:
Let each activity $a$ have a start time $s(a)$ and a finish time
$f(a)$ in a linearly ordered type, thought of as the closed-open interval $[s(a), f(a))$. Two
activities $a$ and $b$ are compatible when $f(a) \le s(b)$ or $f(b) \le s(a)$; in particular,
activities whose intervals only touch at an endpoint are compatible.

articles.title: Correctness and optimality of earliest-finish interval scheduling
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $f$ assign
start and finish times in a linear order to activities, and let $L$ be a list of activities with
$s(a) < f(a)$ for every $a$ in $L$. Let $S$ be the list returned by the earliest-finish schedule
of $L$. Then $S$ is a subpermutation of $L$ (each activity occurs in $S$ at most as often as in
$L$), any two entries of $S$ at distinct positions are compatible, and every subpermutation $M$
of $L$ whose entries at distinct positions are pairwise compatible has length at most the length
of $S$.

articles.title: Comparison bound for earliest-finish interval scheduling
articles.statement:
For any start and finish times
and any list of $n$ activities, the earliest-finish schedule charges at most
$n \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + (n - 1)$ comparisons when $n \ge 1$, and none when $n = 0$.

articles.title: Earliest-finish greedy interval scheduling
articles.statement:
Given start and finish times $s$ and $f$ in a
linear order and a list $L$ of activities, sort $L$ by finish time with merge sort, then scan the
sorted list: the first activity is selected, and each later activity $a$ is selected exactly when
$s(a)$ is at least the finish time of the last selected activity. The result is the list of
selected activities in sorted order, together with a cost that counts one for each finish-time
comparison made by the merge sort and one for each scanned activity after the first.

articles.title: Symmetry of interval compatibility
articles.statement:
For any start and finish times and any activities $a$
and $b$, if $a$ is compatible with $b$, then $b$ is compatible with $a$.

articles.title: Greedy optimality gives the augmentation axiom
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let
$\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ for which the greedy
algorithm is optimal. If $I$ and $J$ are independent sets with $|I| < |J|$, then some element
$e \in J$ with $e \notin I$ makes $I \cup \{e\}$ independent.

articles.title: Threshold counts of the matroid greedy result
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$, let
$O$ be an oracle that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is independent in
$M$, and let $w : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ be a weight function. Let $L$ be a list of elements of
$\alpha$ in nonincreasing order of weight (whenever $a$ occurs before $b$ in $L$, $w(b) \le w(a)$),
and let $G$ be the set returned by the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$. Then for every
finite independent set $I$ of $M$ whose elements all occur in $L$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the
number of $x \in I$ with $w(x) > t$ is at most the number of $x \in G$ with $w(x) > t$.

articles.title: Greedy-optimal independence systems are matroids
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let
$\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ for which the greedy
algorithm is optimal. Then there is a matroid $M$ on $\alpha$ whose ground set is all of
$\alpha$ such that a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is independent in $M$ exactly when $S$ is
independent under $\mathrm{indep}$.

articles.title: Rado–Edmonds theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an
independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$. The greedy algorithm is optimal for
$\mathrm{indep}$ if and only if there is a matroid $M$ on $\alpha$ whose ground set is all of
$\alpha$ such that a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is independent in $M$ exactly when $S$ is
independent under $\mathrm{indep}$.

articles.title: Greedy optimality
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an
independence oracle on the finite subsets of $\alpha$. The greedy algorithm is optimal for
$\mathrm{indep}$ when, for every weight function $w : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ and every list $L$
that contains every element of $\alpha$ exactly once, in nonincreasing order of $w$, the set $T$
returned by the matroid greedy algorithm on $L$ with oracle $\mathrm{indep}$ satisfies
$\sum_{x \in I} w(x) \le \sum_{x \in T} w(x)$ for every finite set $I$ independent under
$\mathrm{indep}$.

Finiteness of $\alpha$ keeps this from holding vacuously: on an infinite type no list contains
every element.

articles.title: Independence system
articles.statement:
A predicate $\mathrm{indep}$ on the finite subsets of a type
$\alpha$ is an independence system when the empty set is independent and every subset of an
independent set is independent.

articles.title: The matroid greedy result is independent
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$ and let
$O$ be an oracle that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is independent in
$M$. For every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the set returned by the greedy algorithm with
oracle $O$ on $L$ is independent in $M$, and each of its elements occurs in $L$.

articles.title: The matroid greedy result is a base
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$ with ground set
$E$, and let $O$ be an oracle that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is
independent in $M$. For every list $L$ in which an element of $\alpha$ occurs if and only if it lies
in $E$, the set returned by the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$ is a base of $M$.

articles.title: Optimality of the matroid greedy algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$, let $O$
be an oracle that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is independent in $M$,
and let $w : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ be a weight function. Let $L$ be a list of elements of $\alpha$
in nonincreasing order of weight (whenever $a$ occurs before $b$ in $L$, $w(b) \le w(a)$), and let
$G$ be the set returned by the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on $L$. Then every finite
independent set $I$ of $M$ whose elements all occur in $L$ satisfies
$\sum_{x \in I} w(x) \le \sum_{x \in G} w(x)$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 16.11.

articles.title: The greedy scan over a concatenation
articles.statement:
For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type
$\alpha$, every finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and all lists $P$ and $Q$ of elements of $\alpha$,
the set returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $P$ followed by $Q$ equals the
set returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ over $Q$ starting from the set that the scan with
oracle $O$ from $S$ over $P$ returns.

articles.title: A scan that accepts nothing
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $\mathrm{indep}$ be an
independence oracle on the finite subsets of $\alpha$, let $S$ be a finite subset of $\alpha$
and let $L$ be a list of elements of $\alpha$ such that $\mathrm{indep}$ rejects $S \cup \{e\}$
for every $e$ in $L$. Then the greedy scan of $L$ starting from $S$ returns $S$.

articles.title: A scan inside an independent set keeps everything
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type, let
$\mathrm{indep}$ be an independence system on the finite subsets of $\alpha$ and let $I$ be an
independent set. For every list $L$ of elements of $I$ and every finite set $S \subseteq I$, the
greedy scan of $L$ starting from $S$ returns $S$ together with all elements of $L$.

articles.title: Invariant of the greedy scan
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a matroid on a type $\alpha$, let $O$ be an oracle
that accepts a finite set $A \subseteq \alpha$ exactly when $A$ is independent in $M$, let $S$ be a
finite independent set of $M$ and $L$ a list of elements of $\alpha$, and let $T$ be the set
returned by the greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $L$. Then $T$ is independent in $M$, and
for every element $e$ of $L$ with $e \notin T$, the set $T \cup \{e\}$ is not independent in $M$.

articles.title: Running time of the greedy scan
articles.statement:
For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a type
$\alpha$, every finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the
greedy scan with oracle $O$ from $S$ over $L$ takes time exactly the length of $L$.

articles.title: Greedy scan with an independence oracle
articles.statement:
Given an oracle $O$ that accepts or rejects each
finite subset of a type $\alpha$, a finite set $S \subseteq \alpha$ and a list $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of
elements of $\alpha$, the greedy scan processes $e_1, \dots, e_n$ in order, starting with $S$ as
the current set: it replaces the current set $T$ by $T \cup \{e_i\}$ if $O$ accepts
$T \cup \{e_i\}$, and leaves it unchanged otherwise. It returns the final current set and charges
one unit of time per element processed.

articles.title: Running time of the matroid greedy algorithm
articles.statement:
For every oracle $O$ on finite subsets of a
type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy algorithm with oracle $O$ on
$L$ takes time exactly the length of $L$, one oracle query per element.

articles.title: Greedy algorithm on a matroid
articles.statement:
Given an oracle $O$ that accepts or rejects each finite
subset of a type $\alpha$ and a list $L$ of elements of $\alpha$, the greedy algorithm starts from
the empty set, processes the elements of $L$ in order, adds an element $e$ to the current set $T$
when $O$ accepts $T \cup \{e\}$ and leaves $T$ unchanged otherwise, and returns the final set. It
charges one unit of time per element processed.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Section 16.4, procedure GREEDY, without its sorting step.

articles.title: A\* leaves exactly the unreachable vertices at infinity
articles.statement:
**A\* leaves exactly the unreachable vertices at infinity.** Let $G$ be a directed graph on the
vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be any heuristic with natural
values and let $s$ be a source vertex. The path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a vertex
$v$ is infinite if and only if $v$ is not reachable from $s$ in $G$.

articles.title: A\* with a consistent heuristic is optimal
articles.statement:
**A\* with a consistent heuristic is optimal.** Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural
values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If the path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a
vertex $v$ is finite, then $g(v) \le d$ for every weight $d$ of a path in $G$ from $s$ to $v$.

articles.title: A\*'s finite path weights are realized by paths
articles.statement:
**A\*'s finite path weights are realized by paths.** Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural
values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If the path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a
vertex $v$ is finite, then some path in $G$ from $s$ to $v$ has weight exactly $g(v)$.

articles.title: The final keys of A\*
articles.statement:
**The final keys of A\*.** Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with
natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a
source vertex. If the path weight $g(v)$ that A* from $s$ returns for a vertex $v$ is finite, then
the distance $g'(v)$ that Dijkstra's algorithm from $s$ computes for $v$ on the reduced weights
$w(x, y) + h(y) - h(x)$ (subtraction truncated at $0$) is finite as well, and
$g(v) + h(v) = g'(v) + h(s)$; that is, the key $g'(v)$ is A*'s value $f(v) = g(v) + h(v)$ shifted
down by $h(s)$.

articles.title: A\*'s predecessor paths are simple and realize its path weights
articles.statement:
**A\*'s predecessor paths are simple and realize its path weights.** Let $G$ be a directed graph
on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic
with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If following the predecessor pointers that A*
from $s$ returns, back from a vertex $v$, yields the vertex list $p$ (listed from $s$ to $v$), then
the path weight $g(v)$ that A* returns for $v$ is finite, $p$ starts at $s$ and ends at $v$,
$G$ has an edge from each vertex of $p$ to the next one, no vertex occurs twice in $p$, and the
weight of $p$ (the sum of $w$ over its consecutive pairs) equals $g(v)$.

articles.title: A\*'s predecessor edges are tight
articles.statement:
**A\*'s predecessor edges are tight.** Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural
values and let $s$ be a source vertex. If A* from $s$ records $u$ as the predecessor of a vertex
$v$, then $G$ has an edge from $u$ to $v$, the path weights $g(u)$ and $g(v)$ that A* returns are
both finite, and $g(v) = g(u) + w(u, v)$.

articles.title: Cost of A\*
articles.statement:
**Cost of A\*.** Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural
edge weights $w$, let $h$ be any heuristic with natural values and let $s$ be a source vertex. In
Dijkstra's dense cost model, which counts the vertex entries inspected by minimum selection and
the adjacency entries inspected by relaxation, A* from $s$ charges exactly $n^2 + m$ events in
total, where $m$ is the number of entries in the adjacency lists of $G$, counting duplicates and
self-loops.

articles.title: A\* search
articles.statement:
**A\* search.** Given a directed graph $G$ on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural
edge weights $w$, a heuristic $h$ with natural values and a source vertex $s$, A* runs Dijkstra's
algorithm from $s$ on the reduced weights $w(u, v) + h(v) - h(u)$ at Dijkstra's cost, and returns
Dijkstra's result (its distances $g'$ and predecessor pointers) together with the path weights
$g(v) = g'(v) + h(s) - h(v)$, where both subtractions are truncated at $0$ and $g(v)$ is infinite
when $g'(v)$ is.

For a consistent heuristic, Dijkstra's distances on the reduced weights are A*'s values
$f = g + h$ shifted by $h(s)$.

articles.title: A consistent heuristic that vanishes at the goal is admissible
articles.statement: **A consistent heuristic that vanishes at the goal is admissible.**

articles.title: Admissible heuristic
articles.statement:
For a directed graph $G$ with natural edge weights $w$, a heuristic
$h$ with natural values is admissible for a goal vertex $t$ when it never overestimates the weight
of a path to $t$: $h(v) \le d$ for every vertex $v$ and every weight $d$ of a path in $G$ from $v$
to $t$.

articles.title: Output of A-star search
articles.statement:
An A* result on $n$ vertices consists of a Dijkstra result on $n$
vertices (the underlying search, with its source, final keys and predecessor pointers) and a
vector that assigns to each vertex $v$ a value $g(v) \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$. In the
output of A* from a source $s$ with a consistent heuristic $h$, the underlying search runs on the
reduced weights, its keys are $f(v) - h(s)$ where $f = g + h$, and $g(v)$ is the least weight of
a path from $s$ to $v$, with $\infty$ when there is none.

articles.title: Consistent heuristic
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and
let $w$ assign a natural number $w(u, v)$ to each pair of vertices. A heuristic $h$ assigning a
natural number to each vertex is consistent (monotone) if $h(u) \le w(u, v) + h(v)$ for every
edge $u \to v$ of $G$.
