articles.title: Path recovered from an A-star result
articles.statement:
Given an A* result $r$ on $n$ vertices and a vertex
$v$, follow the predecessor pointers of the underlying Dijkstra search backward from $v$, at most
$n$ times, until the source is reached, and return the visited vertices in order from the source
to $v$. There is no result if a vertex without a predecessor is met before the source, or if the
source is not reached within $n$ steps.

articles.title: Reduced weights telescope along paths
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a directed graph on the vertices
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ with natural edge weights $w$, let $h$ be a consistent heuristic with natural
values, and let $w_h(x, y) = w(x, y) + h(y) - h(x)$ be the reduced weight, with the subtraction
truncated at $0$. For all vertices $u$ and $v$ and every nonempty list of vertices
$v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ with $v_0 = u$, $v_k = v$ and an edge of $G$ from each $v_i$ to $v_{i+1}$,
the sum of $w_h(v_i, v_{i+1})$ over $i < k$, plus $h(u)$, equals the sum of $w(v_i, v_{i+1})$
over $i < k$, plus $h(v)$.

articles.title: Reduced weight
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign a natural number $w(u, v)$ to each pair of vertices and let
$h$ assign a natural number to each vertex. The reduced weight of the pair $(u, v)$ is the
natural number $w(u, v) + h(v) - h(u)$, computed with truncated subtraction, so it is $0$ when
$h(u) > w(u, v) + h(v)$.

articles.title: AC-3 on the whole problem
articles.statement:
For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables and
domains $\mathrm{dom}$, AC-3 on the whole problem is AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with the queue
initialized to the arc list of $P$; it returns the final domains together with the number of
revisions performed.

articles.title: AC-3 only shrinks domains
articles.statement:
For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains
$\mathrm{dom}$, a queue $q$ of pairs of variables and a variable $v$, the domain of $v$ returned
by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$ is a subset of $\mathrm{dom}(v)$.

articles.title: AC-3 revisions are bounded by the potential
articles.statement:
For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many
variables, domains $\mathrm{dom}$ and a queue $q$ of pairs of variables, the number of revisions
AC-3 performs from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$ is at most the potential
$\ell + \sum_x |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x)$, where $\ell$ is the length of $q$ and
$\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the number of entries of the arc list of $P$ ending at $x$.

Each revision lowers the potential by at least $1$.

articles.title: Bound on the number of AC-3 revisions
articles.statement:
For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables
and initial domains $\mathrm{dom}$, AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with every arc of $P$ queued
performs at most $m + \sum_x |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x)$ revisions, where $m$ is
the length of the arc list of $P$ and $\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the number of entries of that list
ending at $x$.

This is $O(e d)$ for $e$ arcs and domains of size $d$.

articles.title: The AC-3 algorithm
articles.statement:
Given a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains
$\mathrm{dom}$ and a queue $q$ of pairs of variables, AC-3 returns $\mathrm{dom}$ when $q$ is
empty. Otherwise it removes the first pair $(x, y)$ of $q$ and revises it: the revised domain of
$x$ consists of the values $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for which some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ has the
arc $(x, y)$ allowing $x = a$ together with $y = b$. If the revised domain equals
$\mathrm{dom}(x)$, AC-3 continues from $\mathrm{dom}$ with the rest of $q$; otherwise it replaces
the domain of $x$ by the revised domain and continues with the rest of $q$ followed by the arcs
$(z, x)$ of $P$ with $z \ne y$, in the order of the arc list of $P$. Each revision costs one unit
of time.

articles.title: Arc consistency invariant of AC-3
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary CSP with finitely many variables
whose constraints are symmetric, that is the arc $(x, y)$ allows $(a, b)$ exactly when the arc
$(y, x)$ allows $(b, a)$, and whose arcs all join two distinct variables. Let $\mathrm{dom}$ be
domains and $q$ a queue whose entries are arcs of $P$, such that every arc of $P$ not in $q$ is
consistent with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$. Then every arc of $P$ is consistent with respect to the
domains returned by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$.

The invariant: every arc of the problem outside the queue stays consistent, and at the end the
queue is empty.

articles.title: AC-3 makes every arc consistent
articles.statement:
**AC-3 makes every arc consistent**, for constraints given symmetrically on both
orientations of an arc and arcs between distinct variables.

articles.title: Arc consistency after one AC-3 revision
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary CSP whose constraints are
symmetric, that is the arc $(x, y)$ allows $(a, b)$ exactly when the arc $(y, x)$ allows $(b, a)$.
Let $\mathrm{dom}$ be domains, let $x \ne y$ be variables, let $R$ be the set of values
$a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for which some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ has the arc $(x, y)$ allowing
$x = a$ together with $y = b$, and let $\mathrm{dom}'$ be $\mathrm{dom}$ with the domain of $x$
replaced by $R$. Let $e$ be an arc of $P$ with two distinct endpoints such that $e = (x, y)$ or
$e$ is consistent with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$, and such that, if $R \ne \mathrm{dom}(x)$, then
$e$ is not of the form $(z, x)$ with $z \ne y$. Then $e$ is consistent with respect to
$\mathrm{dom}'$.

articles.title: Arc consistency
articles.statement:
Given a binary CSP $P$ and domains $\mathrm{dom}$, an arc $(x, y)$ is
consistent when for every value $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ there is a value $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$
such that the arc $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$.

articles.title: Binary constraint satisfaction problem
articles.statement:
A binary constraint satisfaction problem with
variables in $X$ and values in $D$ consists of a finite list of directed arcs $(x, y)$ with
$x, y \in X$, and, for all variables $x, y$ and values $a, b \in D$, a Boolean saying whether the
arc $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$.

articles.title: In-degree of a variable
articles.statement:
For a binary constraint satisfaction problem $P$ and a variable
$x$, the in-degree of $x$ is the number of arcs $(z, x)$ of $P$ ending at $x$, counted with
multiplicity in the list of arcs of $P$.

articles.title: No solution is lost
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely
many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, and $q$ a queue of arcs each of
which is an arc of $P$. Then every solution $\sigma$ of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$ is also a
solution of $P$ within the domains returned by AC-3 started from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$.

articles.title: Solution of a binary CSP within given domains
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint
satisfaction problem with variables $X$ and values $D$, and give each variable $x$ a finite
domain $\mathrm{dom}(x) \subseteq D$. An assignment $\sigma : X \to D$ is a solution of $P$ within
$\mathrm{dom}$ when $\sigma(x) \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for every variable $x$ and, for every arc
$(x, y)$ of $P$, the arc $(x, y)$ allows the pair $(\sigma(x), \sigma(y))$.

articles.title: Solutions survive AC-3
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with
finitely many variables and $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables. If $\sigma$ is a
solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$, then for every variable $v$ the value $\sigma(v)$ lies in
the domain of $v$ returned by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with all arcs of $P$ queued.

articles.title: Revision keeps solution values
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem,
$\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables and $\sigma$ a solution of $P$ within
$\mathrm{dom}$. For every arc $(x, y)$ of $P$, the value $\sigma(x)$ lies in the revision of the
arc $(x, y)$ with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$.

articles.title: An emptied domain rules out solutions
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction
problem with finitely many variables and $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables. If AC-3,
run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with all arcs of $P$ queued, returns the empty domain for some variable
$v$, then no assignment $\sigma$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$.

articles.title: A shrinking revision lowers the potential
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction
problem with finitely many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, $x$ and
$y$ variables and $q$ a queue of arcs. Suppose the revision $R$ of the arc $(x, y)$ with respect
to $\mathrm{dom}$ differs from $\mathrm{dom}(x)$, and let $\mathrm{dom}'$ agree with
$\mathrm{dom}$ except that $\mathrm{dom}'(x) = R$. Then the potential of $\mathrm{dom}'$ with the
queue $q$ followed by the arcs requeued after revising $(x, y)$ is strictly less than the
potential of $\mathrm{dom}$ with the queue $(x, y)$ followed by $q$.

articles.title: Termination potential of AC-3
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with
finitely many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables and $q$ a queue of arcs.
The potential of $\mathrm{dom}$ and $q$ is

$$|q| + \sum_{x} |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x),$$

where $|q|$ is the length of the queue, the sum runs over all variables $x$, and
$\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the in-degree of $x$ in $P$.

articles.title: Arcs requeued after a revision
articles.statement:
For a binary constraint satisfaction problem $P$ and
variables $x$ and $y$, the arcs requeued after revising $(x, y)$ are the arcs $(z, x)$ of $P$
with $z \neq y$, in their order in the list of arcs of $P$.

AC-3 queues these arcs when revising $(x, y)$ shrinks the domain of $x$.

articles.title: Revision of an arc
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with values $D$,
$\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, and $x$, $y$ variables. The revision of the arc
$(x, y)$ is the set of values $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ that have a support in the domain of $y$:
some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ such that the arc $(x, y)$ allows the pair $(a, b)$.

articles.title: Symmetric binary CSP
articles.statement:
A binary constraint satisfaction problem is symmetric when, for
all variables $x, y$ and values $a, b$, the constraint on the ordered pair $(x, y)$ allows
$x = a$ together with $y = b$ exactly when the constraint on $(y, x)$ allows $y = b$ together
with $x = a$.

The condition concerns the allowed pairs for every ordered pair of variables; it does not
require the reverse of a listed arc to be listed.

articles.title: Alpha-beta with the full window returns the minimax value
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a game tree whose
values lie in a bounded linear order with least element $\bot$ and greatest element $\top$. For
either player $p$ to move, alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[\bot, \top]$
returns exactly the minimax value of $t$ for $p$.

articles.title: Alpha-beta is exact inside the window
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a game tree with values in a bounded
linear order, $p$ the player to move and $a, b$ values. If the minimax value $v$ of $t$ for $p$
satisfies $a < v < b$, then alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the window $[a, b]$ returns
exactly $v$.

articles.title: Alpha-beta fails low when the minimax value is at most the lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a game
tree with values in a bounded linear order, $p$ the player to move and $a < b$ values. If the
minimax value of $t$ for $p$ is at most $a$, then alpha-beta pruning run on $t$ for $p$ with the
window $[a, b]$ returns a value at most $a$.

articles.title: The minimizer's alpha-beta scan stays at or below its upper bound
articles.statement:
For all values $a, b$ in
a linear order and every list $ts$ of game trees, the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of
$ts$ for the minimizer with lower bound $a$ and upper bound $b$ is at most $b$.

articles.title: Correctness of the alpha-beta scan
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be the player to move, $ts$ a list of game
trees with values in a bounded linear order, and $a \le b$. Let $r$ be the value returned by the
alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for $p$ with window $[a, b]$, and let $m$ be the best value for $p$ among
$ts$: the maximum of the minimax values of the trees in $ts$ for the minimizer ($\bot$ if $ts$ is
empty) when $p$ is the maximizer, and the minimum of their minimax values for the maximizer
($\top$ if $ts$ is empty) when $p$ is the minimizer. Then $\max(a, \min(b, r)) =
\max(a, \min(b, m))$.

articles.title: Cost of the alpha-beta scan
articles.statement:
For either player $p$, all values $a, b$ in a linear order
and every list $ts$ of game trees, the alpha-beta scan of $ts$ for $p$ with lower bound $a$ and
upper bound $b$ evaluates at most as many leaves as the trees in $ts$ have in total, each leaf
evaluation costing one unit.

articles.title: Alpha-beta scan of the children
articles.statement:
Given the player $p$ to move, values $a$ and $b$ in a
linear order and a list of game trees (the children of a position), the scan runs alpha-beta
pruning for the other player on the children in order, each time with the current bounds $a$ and
$b$. The maximizer replaces $a$ by $\max(a, v)$, where $v$ is the child's returned value, and
stops as soon as $b \le a$, returning the new $a$; if it never stops early it returns the final
$a$ ($a$ itself for an empty list). The minimizer replaces $b$ by $\min(b, v)$ and stops as soon
as $b \le a$, returning the new $b$; if it never stops early it returns the final $b$ ($b$ itself
for an empty list). The cost of the scan is the total cost of the children it evaluates.

articles.title: Alpha-beta is correct
articles.statement:
**Alpha-beta is correct** (Knuth and Moore 1975, Theorem 1): for `a ≤ b`, the result of
alpha-beta agrees with the minimax value after clamping both to the window `[a, b]`.

articles.title: Alpha-beta never evaluates more leaves than the tree has
articles.statement:
For either player $p$ to move
and all values $a, b$ in a linear order, alpha-beta pruning run on a game tree $t$ for $p$ with
window $[a, b]$ evaluates at most as many leaves as $t$ has, each leaf evaluation costing one
unit.

articles.title: Alpha-beta pruning
articles.statement:
For a player $p$ to move and values $a$ and $b$ in a linear order,
alpha-beta pruning with window $[a, b]$ returns the value of a leaf at a cost of one unit (one
leaf evaluation), and on an inner node runs the alpha-beta scan of its children for $p$ with
window $[a, b]$.

articles.title: Game tree
articles.statement:
A game tree with values in a type $\alpha$ is either a leaf, which carries a
value in $\alpha$ (the value of a terminal position), or an inner node, which carries a finite
list of game trees (the positions reachable in one move; the list may be empty). Game trees are
built inductively, so every game tree is finite.

articles.title: Lower bound for the maximizer's scan
articles.statement:
Let values lie in a linear order. For all values $a$
and $b$ and every finite list of game trees, the value returned by the alpha-beta scan of the list
with the maximizer to move and window $[a, b]$ is at least $a$.

articles.title: Alpha-beta at or above the top of the window
articles.statement:
Let values lie in a bounded linear order, let
$t$ be a game tree, let $p$ be a player, and let $a < b$. If the minimax value of $t$ with $p$ to
move is at least $b$, then the value returned by alpha-beta pruning on $t$ with $p$ to move and
window $[a, b]$ is at least $b$.

articles.title: Number of leaves of a list of game trees
articles.statement:
The number of leaves of a finite list of game
trees is the sum of the numbers of leaves of its members ($0$ for the empty list).

articles.title: Number of leaves
articles.statement:
The number of leaves of a game tree is defined recursively: a leaf counts
$1$, and an inner node counts the total number of leaves of its children (so an inner node without
children counts $0$).

articles.title: Minimax value of a list of positions
articles.statement:
Let values lie in a bounded linear order. For a player
$p$ and a finite list of game trees, the value for $p$ is the best of their minimax values with the
other player to move: for the maximizer, the maximum of these values, or $\bot$ if the list is
empty; for the minimizer, the minimum of these values, or $\top$ if the list is empty.

articles.title: Minimax value
articles.statement:
Let values lie in a bounded linear order. The minimax value of a game tree
with player $p$ to move (the maximizer or the minimizer) is defined recursively: a leaf is worth
the value it carries; an inner node is worth, for the maximizer, the maximum of the minimax values
of its children with the minimizer to move, and for the minimizer, the minimum of the minimax
values of its children with the maximizer to move. An inner node without children is worth $\bot$
to the maximizer and $\top$ to the minimizer.

articles.title: Policy improvement step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of states
$S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards $r(s, a)$ and stochastic transition
probabilities $P(s' \mid s, a)$, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. The improvement of a deterministic
policy $\pi : S \to A$ is a fixed choice of policy greedy for the value $V^\pi$ of $\pi$: in each
state $s$ it takes a chosen action $a$ maximizing
$r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) V^\pi(s')$ over $A$ (ties broken arbitrarily).

articles.title: Values below their Bellman image lie below the policy value
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision
process with a finite set of states $S$, real rewards and stochastic transition probabilities,
and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Let $\pi$ be a deterministic policy, with Bellman operator $T^\pi$ and
value $V^\pi$. If $V : S \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $V(s) \le (T^\pi V)(s)$ for every state $s$,
then $V(s) \le V^\pi(s)$ for every state $s$.

articles.title: Policy iteration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of states $S$, a
finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic transition probabilities, and let
$0 \le \gamma < 1$. Policy iteration run for $n$ steps from a deterministic policy $\pi : S \to A$
is the policy obtained from $\pi$ by applying the policy improvement step $n$ times.

articles.title: Improvement stalls exactly at optimal policies
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a
finite set of states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic
transition probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Write $V^\pi$ for the value of a
deterministic policy $\pi : S \to A$ and $V^*$ for the optimal value. For every deterministic
policy $\pi$, with improved policy $\pi'$, we have $V^{\pi'} = V^\pi$ if and only if
$V^\pi = V^*$ (as functions on $S$).

articles.title: Away from optimality, improvement changes the value
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process
with a finite set of states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic
transition probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Write $V^\pi$ for the value of a
deterministic policy $\pi : S \to A$ and $V^*$ for the optimal value. If $V^\pi \ne V^*$, then the
improved policy $\pi'$ satisfies $V^{\pi'} \ne V^\pi$ (as functions on $S$).

articles.title: Policy improvement theorem
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of
states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic transition
probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Write $V^\pi$ for the value of a deterministic policy
$\pi : S \to A$. For every deterministic policy $\pi$, the improved policy $\pi'$, which is greedy
for $V^\pi$, satisfies $V^\pi(s) \le V^{\pi'}(s)$ for every state $s$.

articles.title: Policy iteration never decreases the value
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a
finite set of states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic
transition probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Write $V^\pi$ for the value of a
deterministic policy $\pi : S \to A$, and $\pi_k$ for the policy after $k$ steps of policy
iteration from $\pi$. If $i \le j$, then $V^{\pi_i}(s) \le V^{\pi_j}(s)$ for every state $s$.

articles.title: Once optimal, policy iteration stays optimal
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a
finite set of states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic
transition probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Write $V^\pi$ for the value of a
deterministic policy $\pi : S \to A$, $V^*$ for the optimal value, and $\pi_k$ for the policy
after $k$ steps of policy iteration from $\pi$. If $i \le j$ and $V^{\pi_i} = V^*$, then
$V^{\pi_j} = V^*$.

articles.title: Policy iteration terminates
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of
states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, real rewards and stochastic transition
probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Write $V^\pi$ for the value of a deterministic policy
$\pi : S \to A$, $V^*$ for the optimal value, and $N = |A|^{|S|}$ for the number of deterministic
policies. For every deterministic policy $\pi$, the policy $\pi_N$ obtained after $N$ steps of
policy iteration from $\pi$ is optimal: $V^{\pi_N} = V^*$.

articles.title: The Bellman operator contracts by $\gamma$
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with
finitely many states, a nonempty finite set of actions, and rewards and stochastic transition
probabilities in a linearly ordered field $K$, let $\gamma \ge 0$ in $K$, and let $T$ be the
Bellman optimality operator of $M$ with discount $\gamma$. If two functions $V, W$ from states
to $K$ satisfy $|V(s) - W(s)| \le d$ for every state $s$, where $d \in K$, then
$|(TV)(s) - (TW)(s)| \le \gamma d$ for every state $s$.

articles.title: Bellman's operator is a contraction
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely
many states, a nonempty finite set of actions, real rewards and stochastic transition
probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Then the Bellman optimality operator $T$ of $M$ with
discount $\gamma$, acting on real-valued functions on the states with the sup metric, is a
contraction with constant $\gamma$: for all such functions $V$ and $W$,
$\|TV - TW\|_\infty \le \gamma \|V - W\|_\infty$.

## Sources

- Puterman, Theorem 6.2.3.

articles.title: The optimal value solves the Bellman optimality equation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision
process with finitely many states, a nonempty finite set of actions, real rewards and stochastic
transition probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. Then the optimal value $V^*$ of $M$ with
discount $\gamma$ is a fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator $T$ of $M$ with discount
$\gamma$: $T V^* = V^*$.

articles.title: Bellman optimality operator
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely many
states $s$, a nonempty finite set of actions $a$, rewards $r(s, a)$ and transition probabilities
$p(s, a, s')$ in a field $K$ carrying a linear order, and let $\gamma \in K$ be a discount factor.
The Bellman optimality operator $T$ sends a function $V$ from states to $K$ to the function

$$(TV)(s) = \max_a \Big( r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s, a, s') V(s') \Big),$$

the largest action value in state $s$.

articles.title: Stopping test
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely many states,
a nonempty finite set of actions, real rewards and stochastic transition probabilities, let
$0 \le \gamma < 1$, and let $T$ be the Bellman optimality operator and $V^*$ the optimal value of
$M$ with discount $\gamma$. For every real-valued function $V$ on the states,
$\|V - V^*\|_\infty \le \|V - TV\|_\infty / (1 - \gamma)$, where $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the sup
norm. So if one Bellman update moves $V$ by at most $\varepsilon$, then $V$ is within
$\varepsilon / (1 - \gamma)$ of the optimal value.

articles.title: A priori error bound for value iteration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with
finitely many states, a nonempty finite set of actions, real rewards and stochastic transition
probabilities, let $0 \le \gamma < 1$, and let $T$ be the Bellman optimality operator and $V^*$
the optimal value of $M$ with discount $\gamma$. For every real-valued function $V$ on the states
and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the result $T^n V$ of $n$ steps of value iteration from $V$ satisfies
$\|T^n V - V^*\|_\infty \le \|V - TV\|_\infty \, \gamma^n / (1 - \gamma)$, where
$\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the sup norm.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the solution of the Bellman optimality equation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov
decision process with finitely many states, a nonempty finite set of actions, real rewards and
stochastic transition probabilities, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. If a real-valued function $V$ on
the states satisfies $TV = V$, where $T$ is the Bellman optimality operator of $M$ with discount
$\gamma$, then $V$ is the optimal value of $M$ with discount $\gamma$.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the solution of a policy's Bellman equation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision
process with finitely many states, real rewards and stochastic transition probabilities, let
$0 \le \gamma < 1$, and let $\pi$ be a deterministic stationary policy, a map from states to
actions. If a real-valued function $V$ on the states satisfies $T_\pi V = V$, where $T_\pi$ is the
Bellman operator of $\pi$ in $M$ with discount $\gamma$, then $V$ is the value of $\pi$.

articles.title: Greedy policy
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely many states, a nonempty
finite set of actions, and rewards $r(s, a)$ and transition probabilities $p(s, a, s')$ in a field
$K$ carrying a linear order, let $\gamma \in K$, and let $V$ be a function from states to $K$. The
greedy policy for $V$ chooses in each state $s$ an action $a$ maximizing the action value
$r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s, a, s') V(s')$; when several actions attain the maximum, one of
them is fixed by choice.

articles.title: Markov decision process
articles.statement:
A Markov decision process with states in $S$, actions in $A$ and
values in $K$ consists of a reward $r(s, a) \in K$ for taking action $a$ in state $s$ and, for all
states $s, s'$ and actions $a$, a value $p(s, a, s') \in K$, the probability of moving from $s$ to
$s'$ under action $a$.

No condition is imposed here: finiteness of the states and actions, an order on $K$ and the
stochasticity of $p$ are hypotheses of the results that use them.

articles.title: Optimal value of a discounted Markov decision process
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision
process with finitely many states $S$, finitely many actions (at least one), real rewards
$r(s,a)$, and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ that are nonnegative and sum to $1$ over
$s'$, and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$. The optimal value of $M$ with discount $\gamma$ is the unique
function $V^* : S \to \mathbb{R}$ that is a fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, that
is, $V^*(s) = \max_a \bigl(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') \, V^*(s')\bigr)$ for every
state $s$. It exists and is unique because this operator is a $\gamma$-contraction in the sup
metric.

articles.title: A policy's Bellman update is at most the optimal one
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision
process with a finite set of states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions $A$, and rewards
$r(s,a)$ and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ in a field $K$ with a linear order, let
$\gamma \in K$, and let $\pi : S \to A$ be a deterministic stationary policy. For every
$V : S \to K$ and every state $s$, the Bellman operator of $\pi$ applied to $V$ is at most the
Bellman optimality operator applied to $V$ at $s$:
$r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,\pi(s),s') \, V(s') \le
\max_a \bigl(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') \, V(s')\bigr)$.

articles.title: A policy's value satisfies its Bellman equation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process
with finitely many states, real rewards $r(s,a)$, and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ that
are nonnegative and sum to $1$ over $s'$, let $0 \le \gamma < 1$, and let $\pi$ be a
deterministic stationary policy with value $V^\pi$. Then $V^\pi$ is a fixed point of the
Bellman operator of $\pi$: for every state $s$,
$V^\pi(s) = r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,\pi(s),s') \, V^\pi(s')$.

articles.title: Bellman operator of a policy
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of
states $S$, a set of actions $A$, and rewards $r(s,a)$ and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$
in a field $K$, let $\gamma \in K$ be a discount factor, and let $\pi : S \to A$ be a
deterministic stationary policy. The Bellman operator of $\pi$ sends a value estimate
$V : S \to K$ to the function
$s \mapsto r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,\pi(s),s') \, V(s')$.

articles.title: A greedy policy for the optimal value is optimal
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process
with finitely many states, finitely many actions (at least one), real rewards $r(s,a)$, and
transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ that are nonnegative and sum to $1$ over $s'$, let
$0 \le \gamma < 1$, and let $V^*$ be the optimal value. Let $\pi$ be the greedy policy for
$V^*$, which in each state $s$ chooses an action $a$ maximizing
$r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') \, V^*(s')$. Then the value of $\pi$ equals $V^*$.

articles.title: No policy beats the optimal value
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely
many states, finitely many actions (at least one), real rewards $r(s,a)$, and transition
probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ that are nonnegative and sum to $1$ over $s'$, and let
$0 \le \gamma < 1$. For every deterministic stationary policy $\pi$, the value $V^\pi$ of $\pi$
is at most the optimal value $V^*$ in every state: $V^\pi(s) \le V^*(s)$ for all states $s$.

articles.title: Value of a policy
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of states $S$,
a set of actions $A$, real rewards $r(s,a)$, and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ that are
nonnegative and sum to $1$ over $s'$, let $0 \le \gamma < 1$, and let $\pi : S \to A$ be a
deterministic stationary policy. The value of $\pi$ is the unique function
$V^\pi : S \to \mathbb{R}$ that is a fixed point of the Bellman operator of $\pi$, that is,
$V^\pi(s) = r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,\pi(s),s') \, V^\pi(s')$ for every state $s$.
It exists and is unique because this operator is a $\gamma$-contraction in the sup metric.

articles.title: The greedy action attains the Bellman maximum
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process
with a finite set of states $S$, a finite nonempty set of actions, and rewards $r(s,a)$ and
transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ in a field $K$ with a linear order, and let $\gamma \in K$.
For every $V : S \to K$ and every state $s$, the action $g$ that the greedy policy for $V$
chooses in $s$ satisfies
$r(s,g) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,g,s') \, V(s') =
\max_a \bigl(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') \, V(s')\bigr)$, so its action value equals
the value of the Bellman optimality operator applied to $V$ at $s$.

articles.title: Q-value of an action
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with a finite set of states
$S$ and with rewards $r(s,a)$ and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ in a field $K$, and let
$\gamma \in K$. The Q-value of action $a$ in state $s$ against a value estimate
$V : S \to K$ is $r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') \, V(s')$.

articles.title: Stochastic Markov decision process
articles.statement:
A Markov decision process with finitely many states
and transition probabilities $P(s,a,s')$ in a field $K$ with a linear order is stochastic when
$0 \le P(s,a,s')$ for all states $s, s'$ and actions $a$, and
$\sum_{s'} P(s,a,s') = 1$ for every state $s$ and action $a$.

articles.title: Value iteration converges
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely many states
$S$, a nonempty finite set of actions, real rewards and stochastic transition probabilities
(nonnegative, each row summing to $1$), and let $0 \le \gamma < 1$ be a discount factor. Let $T$ be
the Bellman optimality operator of $M$ with discount $\gamma$. Then for every initial value
function $V : S \to \mathbb{R}$, the value iterates $T^n V$ converge to the optimal value of $M$
with discount $\gamma$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Tabulated value iteration is correct
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with states
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$, a nonempty finite set of actions and values in a field $K$ with a linear
order, let $\gamma \in K$, and let $T$ be the Bellman optimality operator of $M$ with discount
$\gamma$. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every vector $v \in K^m$ and every state $s$, entry $s$ of
the vector computed by $n$ steps of tabulated value iteration from $v$ equals $(T^n v)(s)$, where
$v$ is read as a function on states.

articles.title: Tabulated value iteration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with states
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$, a nonempty finite set of actions, and rewards and transition probabilities
in a field $K$ carrying a linear order, let $\gamma \in K$, and let $T$ be the Bellman optimality
operator of $M$ with discount $\gamma$. Tabulated value iteration takes a number of steps
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a vector $v \in K^m$, read as a function on states: with $0$ steps it
returns $v$, and with $k + 1$ steps it computes the vector $\bigl((Tv)(0), \dots, (Tv)(m-1)\bigr)$
and then runs $k$ steps from that vector.

Each update is stored as a vector, so update $k + 1$ reads the stored values of update $k$.

articles.title: Value iteration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Markov decision process with finitely many states, a
nonempty finite set of actions, and rewards and transition probabilities in a field $K$ carrying
a linear order, let $\gamma \in K$, and let $T$ be the Bellman optimality operator of $M$ with
discount $\gamma$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a function $V$ from states to $K$, $n$ steps of
value iteration from $V$ give the $n$-fold iterate $T^n V$, where $T^0 V = V$.

Evaluated directly, this definition recomputes earlier iterates; tabulated value iteration
stores each update instead.

articles.title: Bayes posterior kernel
articles.statement:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a countable measurable space with measurable
singletons, $\kappa$ a kernel from a measurable space $\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$, and $\mu$ a measure
on $\Theta$. The Bayes posterior kernel is the kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $\Theta$ that sends each
observation $x \in \mathcal X$ to the Bayes posterior of the prior $\mu$ after observing $x$ under
the likelihood $\kappa$.

articles.title: Bayes' rule for countably many hypotheses
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ be a countable measurable space and
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space, both with measurable singletons, let $\kappa$ be a kernel from
$\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$ (the likelihood) and $\mu$ a measure on $\Theta$ (the prior). For every
observation $x \in \mathcal X$ and every $\theta \in \Theta$, the Bayes posterior $\pi_x$ of $\mu$
after observing $x$ satisfies

$$\pi_x(\{\theta\}) = \frac{\mu(\{\theta\}) \, \kappa_\theta(\{x\})}
{\sum_{\theta' \in \Theta} \mu(\{\theta'\}) \, \kappa_{\theta'}(\{x\})},$$

where the quotient is taken in $[0, \infty]$ with $0 / 0 = 0$ and $a / \infty = 0$ for every $a$.
The denominator is the evidence of $x$.

articles.title: Bayes posterior
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a kernel from a measurable space $\Theta$ of hypotheses to
a measurable space $\mathcal X$ of observations (the likelihood) and $\mu$ a measure on $\Theta$
(the prior). The Bayes posterior after observing $x \in \mathcal X$ is the measure $\pi_x$ on
$\Theta$ with

$$\pi_x(s) = E(x)^{-1} \int_s \kappa_\theta(\{x\}) \, d\mu(\theta)$$

for every measurable $s \subseteq \Theta$, where $E(x) = (\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\})$ is the evidence
of $x$: the mass of $\{x\}$ under the composition $\kappa \circ \mu$ of $\mu$ with $\kappa$, the
marginal law of the observation. The inverse is taken in $[0, \infty]$, with $0^{-1} = \infty$,
$\infty^{-1} = 0$ and $\infty \cdot 0 = 0$; in particular $\pi_x$ is the zero measure when the
evidence is zero.

articles.title: The evidence as a sum over hypotheses
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ be a countable measurable space and
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space, both with measurable singletons, let $\kappa$ be a kernel from
$\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$ and $\mu$ a measure on $\Theta$. For every $x \in \mathcal X$,

$$(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\}) = \sum_{\theta \in \Theta} \mu(\{\theta\}) \, \kappa_\theta(\{x\}),$$

where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of $\mu$ with $\kappa$ (the marginal law of the
observation) and the sum is taken in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: The evidence is the integral of the likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a kernel from a measurable
space $\Theta$ to a measurable space $\mathcal X$ with measurable singletons, and $\mu$ a measure on
$\Theta$. For every $x \in \mathcal X$,

$$(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\}) = \int_\Theta \kappa_\theta(\{x\}) \, d\mu(\theta),$$

where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of $\mu$ with $\kappa$ (the marginal law of the
observation) and the right side is the Lebesgue integral of a $[0, \infty]$-valued function.

articles.title: The evidence from a factorization of densities
articles.statement:
Let $\nu$ be an s-finite measure on a
measurable space $\Theta$ and $\rho$ an s-finite measure on a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$. Let
$p : \Theta \to [0, \infty]$, $q : \Theta \times \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty]$,
$c : \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty]$ and $r : \mathcal{X} \times \Theta \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable
functions such that $\int r(x, \theta) \, d\nu(\theta) = 1$ for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and
$p(\theta) \, q(\theta, x) = c(x) \, r(x, \theta)$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ and
$x \in \mathcal{X}$. If the prior $\mu$ is the measure on $\Theta$ with density $p$ with respect
to $\nu$, and the likelihood $\kappa$ is a kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathcal{X}$ such that each
$\kappa(\theta)$ has density $q(\theta, \cdot)$ with respect to $\rho$, then the marginal law of
the data, the measure $\kappa \circ \mu$ on $\mathcal{X}$ given by
$(\kappa \circ \mu)(s) = \int \kappa(\theta)(s) \, d\mu(\theta)$ for measurable $s$, has density
$c$ with respect to $\rho$.

articles.title: Evidence times posterior is the joint mass
articles.statement:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a measurable space with
measurable singletons, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel from a measurable space $\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$
and $\mu$ a finite measure on $\Theta$. Let $x \in \mathcal X$ and write $\pi_x$ for the Bayes
posterior of $\mu$ after observing $x$ under $\kappa$. Then for every measurable set
$s \subseteq \Theta$,

$$(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\}) \cdot \pi_x(s) = \int_s \kappa_\theta(\{x\}) \, d\mu(\theta),$$

where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of $\mu$ with $\kappa$, so that the first factor is the
evidence of $x$.

articles.title: Disintegration of the joint law from a factorization of densities
articles.statement:
Let $\nu$ be an
s-finite measure on a measurable space $\Theta$ and $\rho$ an s-finite measure on a measurable
space $\mathcal{X}$. Let $p : \Theta \to [0, \infty]$,
$q : \Theta \times \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty]$, $c : \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty]$ and
$r : \mathcal{X} \times \Theta \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable functions such that
$\int r(x, \theta) \, d\nu(\theta) = 1$ for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and
$p(\theta) \, q(\theta, x) = c(x) \, r(x, \theta)$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ and
$x \in \mathcal{X}$. Let the prior $\mu$ be an s-finite measure on $\Theta$ with density $p$ with
respect to $\nu$, let the likelihood $\kappa$ be an s-finite kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathcal{X}$
such that each $\kappa(\theta)$ has density $q(\theta, \cdot)$ with respect to $\rho$, and let
$\eta$ be an s-finite kernel from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\Theta$ such that each $\eta(x)$ has density
$r(x, \cdot)$ with respect to $\nu$. Write $\kappa \circ \mu$ for the marginal law of the data,
$(\kappa \circ \mu)(s) = \int \kappa(\theta)(s) \, d\mu(\theta)$, and $\mu \otimes \kappa$ for the
joint law on $\Theta \times \mathcal{X}$,
$(\mu \otimes \kappa)(t) = \int \kappa(\theta)(\{x : (\theta, x) \in t\}) \, d\mu(\theta)$, and
similarly $(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \eta$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \Theta$. Then
$(\kappa \circ \mu) \otimes \eta$ is the image of $\mu \otimes \kappa$ under the swap
$(\theta, x) \mapsto (x, \theta)$.

articles.title: Under a uniform prior, MAP is maximum likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ and $\mathcal X$ be countable
measurable spaces with measurable singletons, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel from $\Theta$ to
$\mathcal X$, and $\mu$ a finite measure on $\Theta$ that is uniform: there is $c \in [0, \infty]$,
$c \neq 0$, with $\mu(\{\theta\}) = c$ for every $\theta \in \Theta$. Let $x \in \mathcal X$ be an
observation with $(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\}) \neq 0$, where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of
$\mu$ with $\kappa$. Then a hypothesis $\theta \in \Theta$ is a MAP hypothesis for $x$ under the
prior $\mu$ and the likelihood $\kappa$ if and only if it is a maximum-likelihood hypothesis for
$x$ under $\kappa$.

articles.title: MAP hypotheses through the posterior kernel
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ be a nonempty countable standard
Borel space, $\mathcal X$ a countable measurable space with measurable singletons, $\kappa$ a Markov
kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\Theta$, and $x \in \mathcal X$ an
observation with $(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\}) \neq 0$, where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of
$\mu$ with $\kappa$. Write $\kappa^\dagger_\mu$ for the posterior kernel from $\mathcal X$ to
$\Theta$, the fixed disintegration of the joint law of hypothesis and observation along the
observation. Then $\theta \in \Theta$ is a MAP hypothesis for $x$ under the prior $\mu$ and the
likelihood $\kappa$ if and only if
$\kappa^\dagger_\mu(x)(\{\theta'\}) \le \kappa^\dagger_\mu(x)(\{\theta\})$ for every
$\theta' \in \Theta$.

articles.title: MAP hypotheses maximize prior times likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ and $\mathcal X$ be countable
measurable spaces with measurable singletons, $\kappa$ a Markov kernel from $\Theta$ to
$\mathcal X$, $\mu$ a finite measure on $\Theta$, and $x \in \mathcal X$ an observation with
$(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\}) \neq 0$, where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the composition of $\mu$ with
$\kappa$. Then $\theta \in \Theta$ is a MAP hypothesis for $x$ under the prior $\mu$ and the
likelihood $\kappa$ if and only if
$\mu(\{\theta'\}) \, \kappa_{\theta'}(\{x\}) \le \mu(\{\theta\}) \, \kappa_\theta(\{x\})$ for every
$\theta' \in \Theta$.

The evidence $(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\})$ is a common factor of all posterior masses.

articles.title: Maximum a posteriori hypothesis
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ and $\mathcal X$ be countable measurable
spaces with measurable singletons, $\kappa$ a kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$ and $\mu$ a
measure on $\Theta$, and write $\pi_x$ for the Bayes posterior of the prior $\mu$ after observing
$x \in \mathcal X$ under the likelihood $\kappa$. A hypothesis $\theta \in \Theta$ is a maximum a
posteriori (MAP) hypothesis for $x$ when $\pi_x(\{\theta'\}) \le \pi_x(\{\theta\})$ for every
$\theta' \in \Theta$.

articles.title: Maximum-likelihood hypothesis for a discrete observation
articles.statement:
Let $\kappa$ be a kernel from a
parameter space $\Theta$ to a countable observation space $\mathcal X$ with measurable singletons,
assigning to each hypothesis $\theta$ a measure $\kappa_\theta$ on $\mathcal X$. A hypothesis
$\theta \in \Theta$ is a maximum-likelihood hypothesis for the observation $x \in \mathcal X$ when
no hypothesis gives $x$ higher likelihood: $\kappa_{\theta'}(\{x\}) \le \kappa_\theta(\{x\})$ for
every $\theta' \in \Theta$.

articles.title: Bayes' rule for densities
articles.statement:
Let $\Theta$ be a nonempty standard Borel space, $\nu$ an
s-finite measure on $\Theta$ and $\rho$ an s-finite measure on a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$.
Let $p : \Theta \to [0, \infty]$, $q : \Theta \times \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty]$,
$c : \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty]$ and $r : \mathcal{X} \times \Theta \to [0, \infty]$ be measurable
functions such that $\int r(x, \theta) \, d\nu(\theta) = 1$ for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and
$p(\theta) \, q(\theta, x) = c(x) \, r(x, \theta)$ for all $\theta \in \Theta$ and
$x \in \mathcal{X}$. Let the prior $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\Theta$ with density $p$ with
respect to $\nu$, and let the likelihood $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel from $\Theta$ to
$\mathcal{X}$ such that each $\kappa(\theta)$ has density $q(\theta, \cdot)$ with respect to
$\rho$. Then for almost every $x$ with respect to the marginal law of the data
$\kappa \circ \mu$, given by $(\kappa \circ \mu)(s) = \int \kappa(\theta)(s) \, d\mu(\theta)$, the
posterior $\kappa^\dagger_\mu(x)$ of $\kappa$ with respect to $\mu$ is the measure with density
$r(x, \cdot)$ with respect to $\nu$.

articles.title: Bayes' rule for Mathlib's posterior kernel with countably many hypotheses and observations
articles.statement:
**Bayes' rule for Mathlib's posterior kernel with countably many hypotheses and
observations.** Let the parameter space $\Theta$ be a nonempty countable standard Borel space and
the observation space $\mathcal X$ be countable, both with measurable singletons. Let $\kappa$ be
a Markov kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$ (the likelihood), writing $\kappa_\theta$ for the
probability measure it assigns to $\theta \in \Theta$, let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\Theta$
(the prior), and let $\kappa^\dagger\mu$ be Mathlib's posterior kernel from $\mathcal X$ to
$\Theta$. If the observation $x \in \mathcal X$ has nonzero evidence $(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\})$,
where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the law of the observation under the prior, then for every
$\theta \in \Theta$

$$
\kappa^\dagger\mu(x)(\{\theta\}) = \frac{\mu(\{\theta\})\,\kappa_\theta(\{x\})}
{\sum_{\theta' \in \Theta} \mu(\{\theta'\})\,\kappa_{\theta'}(\{x\})}.
$$

articles.title: Bayes' rule for discrete observations
articles.statement:
Let the parameter space $\Theta$ be a nonempty
standard Borel space and the observation space $\mathcal X$ be countable with measurable
singletons. Let $\kappa$ be a Markov kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathcal X$ (the likelihood),
writing $\kappa_\theta$ for the probability measure it assigns to $\theta \in \Theta$, let $\mu$
be a finite measure on $\Theta$ (the prior), and let $\kappa^\dagger\mu$ be Mathlib's posterior
kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $\Theta$. If the observation $x \in \mathcal X$ has nonzero evidence
$(\kappa \circ \mu)(\{x\})$, where $\kappa \circ \mu$ is the law of the observation under the
prior, then the posterior measure $\kappa^\dagger\mu(x)$ equals the Bayes posterior after
observing $x$: the prior $\mu$ reweighted by the likelihood $\theta \mapsto \kappa_\theta(\{x\})$
and divided by the evidence.

articles.title: Prior times likelihood factors as evidence times posterior
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$,
let $s_0, \sigma^2 \ge 0$ be nonzero, let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $w \in \mathbb{R}$.
Write $\varphi(t; \mu, \tau)$ for the Gaussian density with mean $\mu$ and variance $\tau$ at $t$,
$L(y \mid w) = \prod_i \varphi(y_i; w x_i, \sigma^2)$ for the likelihood density, $m$ and $v$ for
the posterior mean and variance of the weight, and $Z(y)$ for the evidence density. Then
$\varphi(w; m_0, s_0) \, L(y \mid w) = Z(y) \, \varphi(w; m, v)$.

articles.title: Completing the square for linear regression
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, let
$s_0, \sigma^2 \ge 0$ be nonzero, and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Write $\varphi(t; \mu, \tau)$
for the Gaussian density with mean $\mu$ and variance $\tau$ at $t$, $p(w) = \varphi(w; m_0, s_0)$
for the prior density, $L(y \mid w) = \prod_i \varphi(y_i; w x_i, \sigma^2)$ for the likelihood
density, $m$ and $v$ for the posterior mean and variance of the weight, and
$r(w) = \varphi(w; m, v)$ for the posterior density. Then for every weight $w \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$p(w) \, L(y \mid w) \, r(m) = p(m) \, L(y \mid m) \, r(w).$$

articles.title: Precisions add in Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
Let $s_0, \sigma^2 \ge 0$ be nonzero and
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Then the posterior variance $v$ of the weight for prior variance $s_0$, noise
variance $\sigma^2$ and inputs $x$ satisfies $1 / v = 1 / s_0 + (\sum_i x_i^2) / \sigma^2$.

articles.title: The evidence density of Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
For $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$,
$s_0, \sigma^2 \ge 0$ and $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, let $m$ and $v$ be the posterior mean and
variance of the weight, write $\varphi(t; \mu, \tau) = (2\pi\tau)^{-1/2} e^{-(t - \mu)^2 / (2\tau)}$
for the Gaussian density with mean $\mu$ and variance $\tau$ at $t$ (read as $0$ when $\tau = 0$),
and let $L(y \mid w) = \prod_i \varphi(y_i; w x_i, \sigma^2)$ be the likelihood density. The
evidence density at $y$ is

$$Z(y) = \frac{\varphi(m; m_0, s_0) \, L(y \mid m)}{\varphi(m; m, v)},$$

prior density times likelihood divided by the posterior density, all at the posterior mean (a
quotient by $0$ is read as $0$).

For $s_0 \ne 0$ and $\sigma^2 \ne 0$ the ratio does not depend on the point where it is evaluated,
and $Z$ is the Lebesgue density of the marginal law of the data. It is not a density of the
evidence in the degenerate cases.

articles.title: The linear regression likelihood is a product of Gaussians
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma^2 \ge 0$ be
nonzero, $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}$. Given the weight $w$, the linear regression
likelihood with noise variance $\sigma^2$ and inputs $x$ is the product measure
$\bigotimes_i \mathcal{N}(w x_i, \sigma^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

articles.title: The evidence of Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, let
$s_0, \sigma^2 \ge 0$ be nonzero, and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$. If the weight has prior
$\mathcal{N}(m_0, s_0)$ and the responses follow the linear regression likelihood with noise
variance $\sigma^2$ and inputs $x$, then the marginal law of the responses is the measure on
$\mathbb{R}^n$ whose density with respect to Lebesgue measure is the evidence density $Z$ for
$m_0$, $s_0$, $\sigma^2$ and $x$.

articles.title: The extended-real linear regression likelihood density
articles.statement:
For $\sigma^2 \ge 0$,
$x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $w \in \mathbb{R}$, it is $\prod_i \varphi(y_i; w x_i, \sigma^2)$ as an
extended nonnegative real, where $\varphi(t; \mu, \tau)$ is the Gaussian density with mean $\mu$
and variance $\tau$ at $t$, read as $0$ when $\tau = 0$. It is the likelihood density for
$\sigma^2 \ne 0$ or $n = 0$, and it is $0$ for $\sigma^2 = 0$ and $n > 0$.

articles.title: The linear regression likelihood density
articles.statement:
For $\sigma^2 \ge 0$, $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$
and $w \in \mathbb{R}$, it is the real number $\prod_i \varphi(y_i; w x_i, \sigma^2)$, where
$\varphi(t; \mu, \tau) = (2\pi\tau)^{-1/2} e^{-(t - \mu)^2 / (2\tau)}$ is the Gaussian density
with mean $\mu$ and variance $\tau$ at $t$, read as $0$ when $\tau = 0$. For $\sigma^2 \ne 0$ it
is the Lebesgue density of the responses $y$ given the weight $w$, independent with
$y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(w x_i, \sigma^2)$. With no data ($n = 0$) it is the empty product $1$, the
density of the unit mass on the single empty response. For $\sigma^2 = 0$ and $n > 0$ the
responses are deterministic and have no density, and this formula is $0$.

articles.title: The noiseless linear regression likelihood
articles.statement:
For $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and
$w \in \mathbb{R}$, the linear regression likelihood with noise variance $0$ and inputs $x$, given
the weight $w$, is the Dirac measure at the vector $(w x_i)_i$: the responses are exactly
$y_i = w x_i$.

articles.title: The likelihood of Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
**The likelihood of Bayesian linear regression** with one feature and known noise variance
$\sigma^2 \ge 0$, for fixed inputs $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$: the kernel from the weight
$w \in \mathbb{R}$ to the responses in $\mathbb{R}^n$ under which, given $w$, the responses are
independent with $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(w x_i, \sigma^2)$. For $\sigma^2 \ne 0$ it is given by the
density $\prod_i \varphi(y_i; w x_i, \sigma^2)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure, where
$\varphi(t; \mu, \tau)$ is the Gaussian density with mean $\mu$ and variance $\tau$ at $t$; for
$\sigma^2 = 0$ it sends $w$ to the Dirac measure at $(w x_i)_i$.

articles.title: Posterior mean in Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
For a prior mean $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$,
a prior variance $s_0 \ge 0$, a noise variance $\sigma^2 \ge 0$, inputs $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$
and responses $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the posterior mean of the weight is the real number
$(\sigma^2 m_0 + s_0 \sum_i x_i y_i) / (\sigma^2 + s_0 \sum_i x_i^2)$, read as $0$ when
the denominator is $0$.

articles.title: Posterior variance in Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
For a prior variance $s_0 \ge 0$,
a noise variance $\sigma^2 \ge 0$ and inputs $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the posterior variance
of the weight is the nonnegative real number
$s_0 \sigma^2 / (\sigma^2 + s_0 \sum_i x_i^2)$, read as $0$ when the denominator is $0$.

articles.title: Posterior predictive at a new input
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, let $s_0 > 0$ and
$\sigma^2 > 0$, and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $x' \in \mathbb{R}$. Put the prior
$N(m_0, s_0)$ (mean $m_0$, variance $s_0$) on a scalar weight $w$, and let the responses be
independent given $w$ with $y_i \sim N(w x_i, \sigma^2)$. Then for Lebesgue-almost every
response vector $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, integrating the law $N(w x', \sigma^2)$ of the response
at $x'$ against the posterior of $w$ given $y$ gives the Gaussian
$N(x' m, x'^2 v + \sigma^2)$, where
$m = (\sigma^2 m_0 + s_0 \sum_i x_i y_i) / (\sigma^2 + s_0 \sum_i x_i^2)$ and
$v = s_0 \sigma^2 / (\sigma^2 + s_0 \sum_i x_i^2)$ are the posterior mean and variance.

articles.title: Predictive law of a linear-regression response
articles.statement:
For a noise variance $\sigma^2 \ge 0$
and a new input $x' \in \mathbb{R}$, the predictive kernel sends a weight $w \in \mathbb{R}$
to the Gaussian law $N(w x', \sigma^2)$ of the response at $x'$, which is the point mass at
$w x'$ when $\sigma^2 = 0$.

articles.title: Measurability of the posterior mean in Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
For a prior mean
$m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, a prior variance $s_0 \ge 0$, a noise variance $\sigma^2 \ge 0$ and inputs
$x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the posterior mean of the weight, as a function of the responses
$y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, is a measurable map from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Bayesian linear regression
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, let $s_0 > 0$ and $\sigma^2 > 0$,
and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be fixed inputs. Put the prior $N(m_0, s_0)$ (mean $m_0$, variance
$s_0$) on a scalar weight $w$, and let the responses be independent given $w$ with
$y_i \sim N(w x_i, \sigma^2)$. Then for Lebesgue-almost every response vector
$y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the posterior of $w$ given $y$ is Gaussian with mean
$(\sigma^2 m_0 + s_0 \sum_i x_i y_i) / (\sigma^2 + s_0 \sum_i x_i^2)$ and variance
$s_0 \sigma^2 / (\sigma^2 + s_0 \sum_i x_i^2)$.

articles.title: Recurrence for the beta function in the first argument
articles.statement:
For real $a > 0$ and $b > 0$, the
beta function $B(a, b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a + b)$ satisfies
$B(a + 1, b) = B(a, b) \cdot \frac{a}{a + b}$.

articles.title: Beta prior times binomial likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ be real, $n, k$ natural numbers,
$m = n - k$ if $k \le n$ and $m = 0$ otherwise, and $\theta$ real. Write $f_{a,b}$ for the
$\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ density (zero outside $(0, 1)$) and $B$ for the beta function. Then the
density $f_{a,b}(\theta)$ times the probability that the binomial kernel at $\theta$ gives exactly
$k$ successes in $n$ trials equals
$\binom{n}{k} \frac{B(a + k, b + m)}{B(a, b)} f_{a + k, b + m}(\theta)$, as an identity in
$[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Conjugacy of the beta density
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ be real, $k, m$ natural numbers and
$\theta$ real. Write $f_{a,b}$ for the $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ density (zero outside $(0, 1)$) and
$B(a, b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a + b)$ for the beta function. Then
$f_{a,b}(\theta) \, \theta^k (1 - \theta)^m =
\frac{B(a + k, b + m)}{B(a, b)} f_{a + k, b + m}(\theta)$.

articles.title: The beta-binomial distribution
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ be real, $n, k$ natural numbers and
$B(x, y) = \Gamma(x)\Gamma(y)/\Gamma(x + y)$ the beta function. Under a $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$
prior on the success probability, the marginal probability (the evidence) that the binomial kernel
gives exactly $k$ successes in $n$ trials is $\binom{n}{k} \frac{B(a + k, b + n - k)}{B(a, b)}$,
where $n - k$ is truncated at $0$.

articles.title: Prior predictive probability of a success
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ be real. Under a
$\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ prior on the success probability, the probability that a single trial of the
binomial kernel succeeds is the prior mean $a / (a + b)$.

articles.title: Binomial likelihood kernel
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the binomial kernel sends a real
$\theta$ to the binomial distribution $\mathrm{Bin}(n, p)$ on $\mathbb{N}$, the law of the number of
successes in $n$ independent coin flips with success probability $p$, where $p$ is $\theta$
clipped to $[0, 1]$.

articles.title: Prior predictive of the Dirichlet–categorical model
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$
with $\alpha_i > 0$ for every $i$. Drawing a parameter $\theta$ from the Dirichlet
distribution $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$ and then one label from the categorical likelihood with
parameter $\theta$ gives the label $i \in \{0, \dots, n\}$ with probability
$\alpha_i / \sum_j \alpha_j$, which is the mean of $\theta_i$ under $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$.

articles.title: The categorical likelihood
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the categorical likelihood is the
kernel from parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ to labels $\{0, \dots, n\}$ that sends a
probability vector $\theta$ (all $\theta_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i \theta_i = 1$) to the law of one
label drawn with probability $\theta_i$ for label $i$, and sends every other $\theta$ to the
point mass at label $0$.

Parameters outside the probability vectors form a null set under a Dirichlet prior.

articles.title: The multinomial sampling model
articles.statement:
For $n, N \in \mathbb{N}$, the multinomial sampling
model is the kernel from parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ to sequences
$s = (s_0, \dots, s_{N-1})$ of $N$ labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$ that sends a probability vector
$\theta$ (all $\theta_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i \theta_i = 1$) to the law of $N$ independent draws
from $\theta$, which gives $s$ probability $\prod_{m < N} \theta_{s_m}$, and sends every other
$\theta$ to the point mass at the all-zero sequence.

articles.title: Disintegration of the Normal–Normal joint law
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v_0, v > 0$,
and write $N(\mu, s)$ for the Gaussian law with mean $\mu$ and variance $s$. Let $\pi = N(m_0, v_0)$
be the prior on the parameter $\theta$, let $K$ be the Gaussian likelihood with noise variance $v$,
so that $K(\theta) = N(\theta, v)$, and let $Q$ be the normal posterior kernel,
$Q(x) = N(\mu(x), s)$ with $\mu(x) = (v m_0 + v_0 x)/(v_0 + v)$ and $s = v_0 v/(v_0 + v)$. For a
measure $\rho$ and a kernel $L$, write $L \circ \rho = \int L(y)\,d\rho(y)$ and $\rho \otimes L$ for
the law of $(y, z)$ when $y \sim \rho$ and $z \sim L(y)$. Then $(K \circ \pi) \otimes Q$ is the
image of $\pi \otimes K$ under $(\theta, x) \mapsto (x, \theta)$: the joint law of $(x, \theta)$ is
the marginal law $K \circ \pi$ of $x$ followed by the posterior kernel.

articles.title: Label counts
articles.statement:
For a sequence $s = (s_0, \dots, s_{N-1})$ of labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$
and a label $i$, the count $n_i(s)$ is the number of positions $m < N$ with $s_m = i$.

articles.title: The marginal of the data
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v_0, v > 0$, and write
$N(\mu, s)$ for the Gaussian law with mean $\mu$ and variance $s$. If the parameter $\theta$ has
prior $N(m_0, v_0)$ and the observation given $\theta$ has law $N(\theta, v)$ (the Gaussian
likelihood with noise variance $v$), then the marginal law of the observation is $N(m_0, v_0 + v)$.

Applied with the posterior in place of the prior, this also gives the posterior predictive law.

articles.title: Normal–Normal posterior predictive
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v_0, v > 0$, and write
$N(\mu, s)$ for the Gaussian law with mean $\mu$ and variance $s$. Take the prior $N(m_0, v_0)$ on
the parameter $\theta$ and the Gaussian likelihood $\theta \mapsto N(\theta, v)$, and let
$\mu(x) = (v m_0 + v_0 x)/(v_0 + v)$ and $s = v_0 v/(v_0 + v)$. For Lebesgue-almost every
observation $x$, a new observation drawn from the likelihood, with $\theta$ distributed according
to the posterior given $x$, has law $N(\mu(x), s + v)$.

articles.title: Noiseless Gaussian likelihood
articles.statement:
With noise variance $0$, the Gaussian likelihood sends each
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ to the Gaussian law with mean $\theta$ and variance $0$, which is the point
mass at $\theta$: the observation is the parameter.

articles.title: Gaussian likelihood with known variance
articles.statement:
For a noise variance $v \ge 0$, the Gaussian
likelihood is the kernel from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ that sends a parameter $\theta$ to the
law of the observation $x \sim N(\theta, v)$, the Gaussian with mean $\theta$ and variance $v$: for
$v > 0$ it is the measure with the $N(\theta, v)$ density with respect to Lebesgue measure, and for
$v = 0$ it is the point mass at $\theta$.

articles.title: Completing the square
articles.statement:
Let $m_0, \theta, x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v_0, v > 0$, and write
$\varphi_{\mu, s}(y) = (2 \pi s)^{-1/2} \exp(-(y - \mu)^2 / (2 s))$ for the density of the Gaussian
with mean $\mu$ and variance $s$. With $\mu(x) = (v m_0 + v_0 x)/(v_0 + v)$ and
$s = v_0 v/(v_0 + v)$,

$$
\varphi_{m_0, v_0}(\theta)\,\varphi_{\theta, v}(x) =
\varphi_{m_0, v_0 + v}(x)\,\varphi_{\mu(x), s}(\theta):
$$

the prior density at $\theta$ times the likelihood of $x$ is the marginal density of $x$ times the
posterior density at $\theta$.

articles.title: Precisions add
articles.statement:
For variances $v_0, v > 0$, the posterior variance $s = v_0 v/(v_0 + v)$
satisfies $s^{-1} = v_0^{-1} + v^{-1}$.

articles.title: Measurability of the Gaussian density in its mean and argument
articles.statement:
For a variance $v \ge 0$,
write $\varphi_{\theta, v}(x) = (2 \pi v)^{-1/2} \exp(-(x - \theta)^2 / (2 v))$ for the density
at $x$ of the Gaussian with mean $\theta$ and variance $v$, read as $0$ when $v = 0$, with values
in $[0, \infty]$. Then $(\theta, x) \mapsto \varphi_{\theta, v}(x)$ is a measurable map on
$\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Posterior mean as a gain update
articles.statement:
Let $m_0, x \in \mathbb{R}$, $v_0 > 0$ and $v \ge 0$. The
posterior mean $(v m_0 + v_0 x)/(v_0 + v)$ equals $m_0 + \frac{v_0}{v_0 + v}(x - m_0)$: it moves
from the prior mean $m_0$ toward the observation $x$ by the gain $v_0/(v_0 + v)$.

articles.title: Posterior mean of the Normal–Normal model
articles.statement:
For a prior mean $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, a prior
variance $v_0 \ge 0$, a noise variance $v \ge 0$ and an observation $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the
posterior mean is $(v m_0 + v_0 x)/(v_0 + v)$, taken to be $0$ when $v_0 = v = 0$. When
$v_0 + v > 0$ it is the precision-weighted average of $m_0$ and $x$.

articles.title: Posterior variance of the normal–normal model
articles.statement:
For variances $v_0, v \ge 0$, the posterior
variance is $\frac{v_0 v}{v_0 + v}$, taken to be $0$ when $v_0 = v = 0$. In the normal–normal model
with prior variance $v_0$ and known noise variance $v$, this is the variance of the posterior of the
mean after one observation.

articles.title: Candidate posterior kernel of the normal–normal model
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and
$v_0, v \ge 0$, let $s = \frac{v_0 v}{v_0 + v}$ be the posterior variance and, for
$x \in \mathbb{R}$, let $\mu(x) = \frac{v m_0 + v_0 x}{v_0 + v}$ be the posterior mean (with
$0 / 0 = 0$). The kernel from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ sends $x$ to the measure with density
$\theta \mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi s}} e^{-(\theta - \mu(x))^2 / (2 s)}$ with respect to Lebesgue
measure. For $v_0, v > 0$ this is the normal law $N(\mu(x), s)$. If $v_0 = 0$ or $v = 0$, then
$s = 0$, the density is taken to be $0$, and the kernel is the zero measure at every $x$.

articles.title: Beta–binomial conjugacy
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ be real and $k \le n$ natural numbers. For the
binomial kernel and a $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ prior, the posterior distribution (Mathlib's posterior
kernel) after observing $k$ successes in $n$ trials is $\mathrm{Beta}(a + k, b + n - k)$.

articles.title: Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with $\alpha_i > 0$
for every $i$, and let $s$ be a sequence of $N$ labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$ with label counts
$n_i(s)$. Under the multinomial sampling model with the Dirichlet prior $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$,
the posterior distribution of the parameter after observing $s$ is the Dirichlet distribution
with parameters $\alpha_i + n_i(s)$.

articles.title: Normal–Normal conjugacy with known variance
articles.statement:
Let $m_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $v_0, v > 0$. Take
the prior $N(m_0, v_0)$ on the mean $\theta$ and the likelihood under which an observation $x$ has
law $N(\theta, v)$. Then for Lebesgue-almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the posterior distribution of
$\theta$ given $x$ is the normal law with mean $\frac{v m_0 + v_0 x}{v_0 + v}$ and variance
$\frac{v_0 v}{v_0 + v}$.

articles.title: Posterior predictive of the beta-binomial model
articles.statement:
Let $a, b > 0$ be real and $k \le n$
natural numbers. Under a $\mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$ prior on the success probability, after observing
$k$ successes in $n$ trials of the binomial kernel, the posterior predictive probability that one
further trial succeeds is $(a + k) / (a + b + n)$.

For $a = b = 1$ this is Laplace's rule of succession, $(k + 1) / (n + 2)$.

articles.title: Posterior predictive of the Dirichlet–multinomial model
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$
with $\alpha_i > 0$ for every $i$, and let $s$ be a sequence of $N$ labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$
with label counts $n_i(s)$. Under the multinomial sampling model with the Dirichlet prior
$\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$, drawing a parameter from the posterior after observing $s$ and then one
label from the categorical likelihood gives the label $i$ with probability
$(\alpha_i + n_i(s)) / (\sum_j \alpha_j + N)$.

This is the Dirichlet–multinomial analogue of Laplace's rule of succession.

articles.title: Probability vectors
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the probability vectors are the
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with $\theta_i \ge 0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_i \theta_i = 1$; they
form the parameter space of the categorical model.

articles.title: The sequence likelihood depends only on the label counts
articles.statement:
For every
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and every sequence $s$ of $N$ labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$ with
label counts $n_i(s)$, the likelihood $\prod_{m < N} \theta_{s_m}^+$ of $s$ equals
$\prod_{i = 0}^{n} (\theta_i^+)^{n_i(s)}$ as extended nonnegative reals, where
$x^+ = \max(x, 0)$.

articles.title: Likelihood of a label sequence
articles.statement:
For $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and a sequence
$s = (s_0, \dots, s_{N-1})$ of labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$, the likelihood of $s$ is the
extended nonnegative real $\prod_{m < N} \theta_{s_m}^+$, where $x^+ = \max(x, 0)$.

articles.title: Evidence-weighted Dirichlet prior
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with $\alpha_i > 0$
for every $i$, and let $s$ be a sequence of $N$ labels in $\{0, \dots, n\}$ with label counts
$n_i(s)$. The Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$ weighted by the density
$\theta \mapsto P_\theta(s)$, the probability of $s$ under the multinomial sampling model with
parameter $\theta$, equals $B(\alpha + n(s)) / B(\alpha)$ times $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha + n(s))$,
where $B$ is the multivariate Beta function and $\alpha + n(s)$ has entries $\alpha_i + n_i(s)$.

articles.title: The evidence lower bound
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set, let $p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers
indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values $z \in Z$, with
$p_\theta(x, z) > 0$ for all $\theta$, $x$, $z$, and let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data. For every
parameter $\theta$ and all probability distributions $q_1, \dots, q_N$ on $Z$,

$$
\sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} q_n(z) \bigl(\log p_\theta(x_n, z) - \log q_n(z)\bigr) \le
\sum_{n=1}^N \log \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x_n, z),
$$

that is, the evidence lower bound of $q_1, \dots, q_N$ at $\theta$ is at most the log-likelihood
of the data at $\theta$. Terms with $q_n(z) = 0$ count as $0$.

articles.title: The ELBO at the posterior is the EM objective plus the entropy
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set,
let $p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent
values $z \in Z$, let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data, and write
$p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ for the posterior,
$Q(\theta' \mid \theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_{\theta'}(x_n, z)$
for the EM objective and
$H(\theta) = -\sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_\theta(z \mid x_n)$ for the
entropy of the posteriors. For all parameters $\theta'$ and $\theta$, the evidence lower bound at
$\theta'$ of the posteriors $q_n = p_\theta(\cdot \mid x_n)$ satisfies

$$
\sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} q_n(z) \bigl(\log p_{\theta'}(x_n, z) - \log q_n(z)\bigr) =
Q(\theta' \mid \theta) + H(\theta),
$$

that is, it splits as the EM objective $Q(\theta' \mid \theta)$ plus the posterior entropy.

articles.title: The bound is tight at the posterior
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a nonempty finite set, let
$p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values
$z \in Z$, with $p_\theta(x, z) > 0$ for all $\theta$, $x$, $z$, and let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data.
For every parameter $\theta$, the posteriors
$q_n(z) = p_\theta(z \mid x_n) = p_\theta(x_n, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x_n, z')$ satisfy

$$
\sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} q_n(z) \bigl(\log p_\theta(x_n, z) - \log q_n(z)\bigr) =
\sum_{n=1}^N \log \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x_n, z),
$$

that is, the evidence lower bound at $\theta$ of the posteriors equals the log-likelihood of the
data at $\theta$.

articles.title: Evidence lower bound of latent distributions
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set, let
$p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values
$z \in Z$, and let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data. For a parameter $\theta$ and functions
$q_1, \dots, q_N : Z \to \mathbb{R}$ (one latent distribution per data point), the evidence lower
bound is $\sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} q_n(z) \bigl(\log p_\theta(x_n, z) - \log q_n(z)\bigr)$.

articles.title: The EM inequality
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a nonempty finite set, let $p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers
indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values $z \in Z$, with
$p_\theta(x, z) > 0$ for all $\theta$, $x$, $z$, and let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data. Write
$p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ for the posterior,
$Q(\theta' \mid \theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_{\theta'}(x_n, z)$
for the EM objective and $\ell(\theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \log \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x_n, z)$ for the
log-likelihood. For all parameters $\theta'$ and $\theta$,
$Q(\theta' \mid \theta) - Q(\theta \mid \theta) \le \ell(\theta') - \ell(\theta)$: the
log-likelihood gains at least as much as $Q(\cdot \mid \theta)$.

articles.title: The EM objective
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set, let $p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers indexed by
parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values $z \in Z$, let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data,
and write $p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ for the posterior.
For parameters $\theta'$ and $\theta$, the EM objective is
$Q(\theta' \mid \theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_{\theta'}(x_n, z)$
(maximized over $\theta'$ in the M-step).

articles.title: Posteriors are probability distributions
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a nonempty finite set and let
$p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values
$z \in Z$, with $p_\theta(x, z) > 0$ for all $\theta$, $x$, $z$. For every parameter $\theta$ and
observation $x$, the posterior $z \mapsto p_\theta(x, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ is a
probability distribution on $Z$: its values are nonnegative and sum to $1$.

articles.title: Probability distributions on a finite latent space
articles.statement:
A function $q : Z \to \mathbb{R}$ on a
finite set $Z$ is a probability distribution when $q(z) \ge 0$ for every $z \in Z$ and
$\sum_{z \in Z} q(z) = 1$.

articles.title: EM iterates have monotone likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a nonempty finite set, let
$p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values
$z \in Z$, with $p_\theta(x, z) > 0$ for all $\theta$, $x$, $z$, and let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data.
Write $p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ for the posterior,
$Q(\theta' \mid \theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_{\theta'}(x_n, z)$
for the EM objective and $\ell(\theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \log \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x_n, z)$ for the
log-likelihood. Let $M$ be a map on parameters, with $k$-th iterate $M^k$ ($M^0$ the identity),
such that $Q(M\theta \mid \theta) \ge Q(\theta \mid \theta)$ for every $\theta$ (in particular if
$M\theta$ maximizes $Q(\cdot \mid \theta)$, or $M$ is a generalized-EM step). Then for every
$\theta_0$ the sequence $k \mapsto \ell(M^k \theta_0)$ is nondecreasing.

articles.title: The EM theorem
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a nonempty finite set, let $p_\theta(x, z)$ be real numbers
indexed by parameters $\theta$, observations $x$ and latent values $z \in Z$, with
$p_\theta(x, z) > 0$ for all $\theta$, $x$, $z$, and let $x_1, \dots, x_N$ be data. Write
$p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x, z) / \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ for the posterior,
$Q(\theta' \mid \theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_{\theta'}(x_n, z)$
for the EM objective and $\ell(\theta) = \sum_{n=1}^N \log \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x_n, z)$ for the
log-likelihood. For parameters $\theta$ and $\theta'$, if
$Q(\theta \mid \theta) \le Q(\theta' \mid \theta)$, then $\ell(\theta) \le \ell(\theta')$: a step
that does not decrease $Q(\cdot \mid \theta)$ does not decrease the log-likelihood.

articles.title: Log-likelihood of a latent-variable model
articles.statement:
For a joint model $p$ with finite latent space
$Z$ and data $x_0, \dots, x_{N-1}$, the log-likelihood at the parameter $\theta$ is
$\ell(\theta) = \sum_{n < N} \log p_\theta(x_n)$, where
$p_\theta(x) = \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x, z)$ is the marginal.

articles.title: Marginal of a latent-variable model
articles.statement:
For a joint model $p$ assigning a real number
$p_\theta(x, z)$ to each parameter $\theta$, observation $x$ and latent value $z$ in a finite
latent space $Z$, the marginal is $p_\theta(x) = \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(x, z)$.

articles.title: Posterior entropy
articles.statement:
For a joint model $p$ with finite latent space $Z$, data
$x_0, \dots, x_{N-1}$ and a parameter $\theta$, the posterior entropy is
$-\sum_{n < N} \sum_{z \in Z} p_\theta(z \mid x_n) \log p_\theta(z \mid x_n)$, where
$p_\theta(z \mid x)$ is the posterior of $z$ given $x$.

articles.title: Posterior of a latent-variable model
articles.statement:
For a joint model $p$ with finite latent space $Z$,
the posterior of the latent value $z$ given the observation $x$ at the parameter $\theta$ is
$p_\theta(z \mid x) = p_\theta(x, z) / p_\theta(x)$, where
$p_\theta(x) = \sum_{z' \in Z} p_\theta(x, z')$ is the marginal (the quotient is read as $0$
when the marginal is $0$). Computing it is the E-step of expectation-maximization.

articles.title: Equality case of Gibbs' inequality
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite nonempty set, let
$p : Z \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $p(z) > 0$ for all $z$, and write $P = \sum_{z \in Z} p(z)$. Then

$$\sum_{z \in Z} \frac{p(z)}{P} \left(\log p(z) - \log \frac{p(z)}{P}\right) = \log P,$$

that is, the bound of Gibbs' inequality is attained at the distribution $q = p / P$.

articles.title: Gibbs' inequality (evidence lower bound form)
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set, let
$p : Z \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $p(z) > 0$ for all $z$, and let $q$ be a probability distribution
on $Z$. Then $\sum_{z \in Z} q(z) (\log p(z) - \log q(z)) \le \log \sum_{z \in Z} p(z)$.

This is the log-sum inequality with $\sum_{z} q(z) = 1$; terms with $q(z) = 0$ contribute $0$.

articles.title: Detailed balance gives a stationary distribution
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite set, $\pi$ a
probability distribution on $\alpha$ and $P$ a transition rule assigning to each $x \in \alpha$ a
probability distribution $P(x, \cdot)$ on $\alpha$. If $\pi(x) P(x, y) = \pi(y) P(y, x)$ for all
$x, y \in \alpha$, then one step of $P$ started from $\pi$ is again distributed as $\pi$: for every
$y \in \alpha$, $\sum_{x \in \alpha} \pi(x) P(x, y) = \pi(y)$.

articles.title: Conditional law of a coordinate
articles.statement:
Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the
configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite, such that $\pi(x) \neq 0$ for every
$x$. For a coordinate $i \in \iota$ and a configuration $x$, the conditional law of coordinate $i$
given the others is the probability distribution on $S$ that gives $s \in S$ the mass
$\pi(x[i \mapsto s]) / Z_i(x)$, where $x[i \mapsto s]$ is $x$ with coordinate $i$ set to $s$ and
$Z_i(x) = \sum_{t \in S} \pi(x[i \mapsto t])$. In the usual notation this is
$\pi(x_i = s \mid x_{-i})$, where $x_i$ is coordinate $i$ of $x$ and $x_{-i}$ is the family of
its other coordinates.

articles.title: Normalizer of the conditional law
articles.statement:
Let $\pi$ be a probability distribution on the
configurations $x : \iota \to S$, with $\iota$ and $S$ finite. For a coordinate $i \in \iota$ and a
configuration $x$, the normalizer is $Z_i(x) = \sum_{s \in S} \pi(x[i \mapsto s]) \in [0, \infty]$,
where $x[i \mapsto s]$ is $x$ with coordinate $i$ set to $s$. It normalizes the conditional law of
coordinate $i$ given the other coordinates of $x$.

articles.title: The systematic-scan Gibbs sampler converges to its target
articles.statement:
If the sweep visits every
