$m \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and a covariance matrix $P$, an arbitrary real $n \times n$ matrix. It
describes the Gaussian distribution $N(m, P)$ when $P$ is positive semidefinite (the belief is
valid); for other matrices Mathlib's multivariate Gaussian is a junk value. Prediction with
positive semidefinite process noise, update with positive definite observation noise, and a filter
step with both preserve validity.

articles.title: One filter step is the exact posterior
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $w$ be measurable random vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and $v$ a measurable random vector in $\mathbb{R}^p$ on a probability space, with
$x$ independent of $w$ and the pair $(x, w)$ independent of $v$. Suppose $x$ has the law
$N(m, P)$ of a belief with mean $m$ and positive semidefinite covariance $P$, $w$ has law
$N(0, Q)$ and $v$ has law $N(0, R)$, with $Q$ and $R$ positive semidefinite. Let $F$ be a real
$n \times n$ matrix and $H$ a real $p \times n$ matrix with $H (F P F^\top + Q) H^\top + R$
invertible, and put $x' = F x + w$ and $Y = H x' + v$. Then for almost every $y$ with respect to
the law of $Y$, the conditional distribution of $x'$ given $Y = y$ is the law of the belief
obtained from $(m, P)$ by one filter step with $F$, $Q$, $H$, $R$ and the observation $y$.

articles.title: The update step is the exact posterior
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a measurable random vector in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and $v$ a measurable random vector in $\mathbb{R}^p$ on a probability space, with
$x$ independent of $v$. Suppose $x$ has the law $N(m, P)$ of a belief with mean $m$ and positive
semidefinite covariance $P$, and $v$ has law $N(0, R)$ with $R$ positive semidefinite. Let $H$ be
a real $p \times n$ matrix with $H P H^\top + R$ invertible, and put $Y = H x + v$. Then for
almost every $y$ with respect to the law of $Y$, the conditional distribution of $x$ given
$Y = y$ is the law of the belief obtained from $(m, P)$ by the update with $H$, $R$ and the
observation $y$.

articles.title: Kalman gain
articles.statement:
For a real $p \times n$ matrix $H$, a real $p \times p$ matrix $R$ and a
belief with covariance $P$, the Kalman gain is the real $n \times p$ matrix
$K = P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1}$, where the inverse is taken to be $0$ when
$H P H^\top + R$ is singular.

articles.title: Law of a belief
articles.statement:
The law of a belief with mean $m$ and covariance $P$ is Mathlib's
multivariate Gaussian measure $N(m, P)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. It is the Gaussian distribution with
mean $m$ and covariance $P$ when $P$ is positive semidefinite (the belief is valid); otherwise it
is the point mass at $m$.

articles.title: The predict step is exact
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $w$ be measurable, independent random vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^n$ on a probability space. If $x$ has the law $N(m, P)$ of a belief with mean $m$ and
positive semidefinite covariance $P$, and $w$ has law $N(0, Q)$ with $Q$ positive semidefinite,
then for every real $n \times n$ matrix $F$ the random vector $F x + w$ has the law of the
predicted belief, $N(F m, F P F^\top + Q)$.

articles.title: Prediction preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let $F$ and $Q$ be real $n \times n$ matrices with $Q$
positive semidefinite. If a belief is valid, that is, its covariance $P$ is positive
semidefinite, then the predicted belief, with covariance $F P F^\top + Q$, is valid.

articles.title: Kalman prediction
articles.statement:
Given real $n \times n$ matrices $F$ and $Q$, the prediction of a
belief with mean $m$ and covariance $P$ is the belief with mean $F m$ and covariance
$F P F^\top + Q$. It models the dynamics $x' = F x + w$ with process noise $w \sim N(0, Q)$.

articles.title: A filter step preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let $F$ and $Q$ be real $n \times n$ matrices with $Q$
positive semidefinite, $H$ a real $p \times n$ matrix, $R$ a positive definite real $p \times p$
matrix and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$. If a belief is valid (its covariance is positive semidefinite),
then so is the belief obtained from it by one filter step with $F$, $Q$, $H$, $R$ and the
observation $y$.

articles.title: Kalman filter step
articles.statement:
Given real $n \times n$ matrices $F$ and $Q$, a real $p \times n$
matrix $H$, a real $p \times p$ matrix $R$ and an observation $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$, one filter
step sends a belief to the update, with $H$, $R$ and $y$, of its prediction with $F$ and $Q$.

articles.title: Schur form of the updated covariance
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a real $p \times n$ matrix, $R$ a real
$p \times p$ matrix and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$, and let a belief have covariance $P$. Then the
covariance of the belief updated with $H$, $R$ and $y$ equals
$P - P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1} H P$. Here $M^{-1}$ is the matrix inverse, taken to be $0$
when $M$ is singular, so no invertibility is assumed.

With the Kalman gain $K = P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1}$ this says $(I - K H) P =
P - P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1} H P$.

articles.title: The Kalman update preserves validity
articles.statement:
Let $H$ be a real $p \times n$ matrix, $R$ a
symmetric positive definite real $p \times p$ matrix and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$. If a belief is
valid, then the belief updated with $H$, $R$ and $y$ is valid.

articles.title: Kalman filter update
articles.statement:
Given a real $p \times n$ observation matrix $H$, a real $p \times p$
matrix $R$, an observation $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a belief with mean $m$ and covariance $P$,
the updated belief has mean $m + K (y - H m)$ and covariance $(I - K H) P$, where
$K = P H^\top (H P H^\top + R)^{-1}$ is the Kalman gain and the matrix inverse is taken to be
$0$ when $H P H^\top + R$ is singular.

It corresponds to observing a state $x$ as $y = H x + v$ with Gaussian noise $v \sim N(0, R)$.

articles.title: Valid Gaussian beliefs
articles.statement:
A belief is valid when its covariance matrix is positive
semidefinite.

articles.title: Adjacent vertices in a network structure
articles.statement: `u` and `w` are adjacent (joined by an edge in either direction).

articles.title: BDe family score as a ratio of marginal likelihoods
articles.statement: With BDe hyperparameters, a family score is a ratio of set marginal likelihoods.

articles.title: Bayesian–Dirichlet family score
articles.statement:
The Bayesian–Dirichlet score of a family `F` with parent set `P ⊆ F` and hyperparameters
`α` on the configurations of `F`.

articles.title: Bayesian–Dirichlet network score
articles.statement:
The BD score of the structure `Pa` with family hyperparameters `α`: the product of the
family scores.

articles.title: BDe hyperparameters
articles.statement:
BDe hyperparameters (Heckerman, Geiger and Chickering): `ess` times the weight
`∑_{x ↦ c} p x` of the configuration `c` of `S`. When `∑ x, p x = 1`, `p` is a prior joint
distribution and this is the prior probability of `c`.

articles.title: Covered-edge reversal preserves the BDe score
articles.statement:
**Covered-edge reversal preserves the BDe score** (for a positive weight function `p` —
a prior when `∑ x, p x = 1` — and positive equivalent sample size).

articles.title: Covered-edge reversals preserve the BDe score
articles.statement: Structures connected by a sequence of covered-edge reversals have the same BDe score.

articles.title: BDe network score
articles.statement: The BDe score of the structure `Pa`.

articles.title: Joint configurations of a set of variables
articles.statement: The joint values of the variables in `S`.

articles.title: Count of cases matching a configuration
articles.statement: The number of cases in `D` that take the values `c` on the variables `S`.

articles.title: Covered-edge reversal
articles.statement:
`Pa'` is obtained from `Pa` by reversing a covered edge `x → y` (Chickering 1995): `x` is a
parent of `y` and `y`'s other parents are exactly `x`'s parents (`Pa y = insert x (Pa x)`);
after the reversal `y` has parents `Pa x` and `x` has parents `insert y (Pa x)`. Acyclicity
is not required: the score identity holds for any parent-set maps (on a DAG, `x ∉ Pa x` and
`y ∉ Pa x` hold automatically).

articles.title: Acyclic network structure
articles.statement: The structure has no directed cycle.

articles.title: V-structure in a directed graph
articles.statement: `u → w ← z` is a v-structure: two non-adjacent distinct parents of a common child.

articles.title: BDe marginal likelihood of a variable set
articles.statement:
The (unnormalized) marginal likelihood of the data restricted to the variables `S` under
the BDe Dirichlet prior on the joint values of `S`. `p` is treated as generalized weights
here: the total Dirichlet mass over configurations is `ess * ∑ x, p x`, so the omitted
normalizing factor is `1 / rising (ess * ∑ x, p x) D.length`, the same for every `S`. When
`p` is normalized (`∑ x, p x = 1`) this is `1 / rising ess D.length`, and `p` is a prior
joint distribution.

articles.title: Sequential Pólya–Dirichlet prediction factor
articles.statement:
The sequential Pólya–Dirichlet prediction factor for the case `x` after the cases `D`:
`∏_v (α_{v,c} + n_{v,c}) / (α_{v,j} + n_{v,j})`, with `c`, `j` the family and parent values of
`x` and `n` the counts in `D`. This is a genuine conditional probability only when `Pa` is a
DAG; for arbitrary parent maps (e.g. cycles or self-parents) the factors over all cases need
not sum to one.

articles.title: Chickering's transformational characterization
articles.statement:
**Chickering's transformational characterization** (1995): two acyclic structures on a finite
set of vertices with the same skeleton and the same v-structures (Markov equivalent by Verma
and Pearl) are connected by a sequence of covered-edge reversals.

articles.title: Rising factorial
articles.statement: The rising factorial `a (a + 1) ⋯ (a + n - 1)`, equal to `Γ(a + n) / Γ(a)` for `a > 0`.

articles.title: Sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product after prior cases
articles.statement:
The sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product for the cases `D`, in order, after the cases `E`:
each case contributes its `predictive` factor given all cases before it. A genuine probability
of the data only when `Pa` is a DAG (see `predictive`).

articles.title: The BD score is the sequential prediction product
articles.statement:
**The BD score is the sequential prediction product** of the data (hence it does not
depend on the order of the cases). This is an identity for all real hyperparameters.
Positivity of the hyperparameters only makes every predictive denominator positive; it does
not make this product a probability. The product is a genuine probability of the data only
when `Pa` is a DAG with no self-parents: for cyclic parent maps the predictive factors over
all cases need not sum to one.

articles.title: Sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product of the data
articles.statement:
The sequential Pólya–Dirichlet product for the cases of `D`, in order. A genuine probability
of the data only when `Pa` is a DAG (see `predictive`).

articles.title: Parent configuration counts sum over family configurations
articles.statement:
The number of cases matching a parent configuration is the sum over the family
configurations extending it (`N_j = ∑_k N_jk`).

articles.title: Belief at the root is the root message
articles.statement:
For every tree model over a finite set of values,
the belief of the root, vertex $0$, is the root message computed by variable elimination: the two
agree at every value.

articles.title: Sum-product belief
articles.statement:
The belief of each vertex of a tree model over a finite set of values,
computed by sum-product message passing: the product of its unary factor, the messages from its
subtree and the message from its parent. Recursively, in a model with a single vertex the belief
of that vertex is its unary factor; in a model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ the belief of the
last vertex at a value $b$ is its unary factor at $b$ times the downward message to the last
vertex at $b$, and the belief of every other vertex is its belief in the model with the last
vertex summed out.

articles.title: Max-product decoding
articles.statement:
An assignment of a tree model over a finite nonempty set of values,
defined by recursion on the number of vertices. For a single vertex, its value is one that
maximizes its unary factor. For vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, the vertices $0, \dots, n$ get the
decoding of the model with the last vertex maximized out, and the last vertex gets a value $b$
maximizing $\psi(b, a)\, \phi(b)$, where $a$ is the decoded value of its parent, $\psi$ is the
factor of the edge between the last vertex and its parent and $\phi$ is the unary factor of the
last vertex; that is, $b$ attains the max-product message of the last vertex at $a$.

articles.title: Downward message to the last vertex
articles.statement:
For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ over
a finite set of values, the message from the parent $p$ of the last vertex to the last vertex at
a value $b$ is the sum over all values $a$ of $\psi(b, a)\, \beta(a)$, where $\psi$ is the factor
of the edge between the last vertex and $p$ (last vertex first) and $\beta(a)$ is the belief of
$p$ at $a$ in the model without the last vertex.

articles.title: Removing the last vertex
articles.statement:
For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, the tree model
on $0, \dots, n$ with the same parents, unary factors and edge factors: the last vertex, which is
a leaf, is removed together with its unary factor and the factor of its edge.

articles.title: Eliminating the last vertex of a tree model
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite, let $m$ be a pairwise
tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with parents $p$, unary factors $\varphi_i$ and
pairwise factors $\psi_k$, and let $\mu$ be the message from the last vertex $n + 1$ to its
parent $q = p(n + 1)$. Eliminating the last vertex gives the pairwise tree model on the vertices
$0, \dots, n$ in which vertex $k + 1$ has parent $p(k + 1)$ and edge factor $\psi_k$ for each
$k < n$, and whose unary factors are $\varphi'_q(a) = \varphi_q(a) \, \mu(a)$ and
$\varphi'_i = \varphi_i$ for every vertex $i \le n$ with $i \ne q$.

articles.title: Parent of the last vertex
articles.statement:
In a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, this
is the parent of the last vertex $n + 1$, regarded as one of the vertices $0, \dots, n$ of the tree
with the last vertex removed.

articles.title: Beliefs are the unnormalized marginals
articles.statement:
For every tree model over a finite set of values,
every vertex $v$ and every value $a$, the belief of $v$ at $a$ is the unnormalized marginal of $v$
at $a$: the sum of the weights of all assignments $x$ with $x_v = a$.

articles.title: Maximizing out the last vertex
articles.statement:
For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ over a
finite nonempty set of values, the tree model on $0, \dots, n$ with the same parents and edge
factors whose unary factor at the parent of the last vertex is multiplied by the max-product
message of the last vertex; the other unary factors are unchanged.

articles.title: Max-product message
articles.statement:
For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ over a finite
nonempty set of values, the max-product message from the last vertex to its parent at a value $a$
is the maximum over all values $b$ of $\psi(b, a)\, \phi(b)$, where $\psi$ is the factor of the
edge between the last vertex and its parent and $\phi$ is the unary factor of the last vertex.

articles.title: Max-product value
articles.statement:
For a tree model over a finite nonempty set of values, the value
computed by maximizing out the vertices from the last one down: for a single vertex it is the
maximum of its unary factor over all values, and for more vertices it is the max-product value of
the model with the last vertex maximized out.

When all factors are nonnegative, this is the largest weight of an assignment.

articles.title: Message from the last vertex
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite and consider a pairwise tree model on
the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with unary factors $\varphi_i$ and pairwise factors $\psi_k$. The
message from the last vertex $n + 1$ to its parent is the function $\mu : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$
given by $\mu(a) = \sum_{b \in \alpha} \psi_n(b, a) \, \varphi_{n+1}(b)$, where $\psi_n$ is the
factor of the edge between vertex $n + 1$ and its parent.

articles.title: Nonnegative factors
articles.statement:
A tree model has nonnegative factors when all its unary factors and
all its edge factors take only nonnegative values.

articles.title: Parent of a vertex
articles.statement:
In a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$, for $k < n$ the
parent of vertex $k + 1$ is the parent recorded by the model, an element of $\{0, \dots, k\}$,
regarded as one of the vertices $0, \dots, n$.

articles.title: Variable elimination computes the partition function
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$
be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message
$r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then the partition function of $m$ is the total root message:
$\sum_x w(x) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} r(a)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments
$\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.

articles.title: Variable elimination computes the unnormalized root marginal
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite and
let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message
$r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then for every $a \in \alpha$ the unnormalized marginal of the root
at $a$ equals $r(a)$, that is, $\sum_x w(x) = r(a)$, where $x$ ranges over the assignments
$\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$ with $x_0 = a$.

articles.title: Root message of a tree model
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite. The root message of a pairwise tree
model $m$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ is the function $r_m : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
recursion on $n$: if $n = 0$, it is the unary factor of the root $0$; if $m$ is a model on the
vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, it is $r_{m'}$, where $m'$ is the model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$
obtained from $m$ by eliminating the last vertex.

By variable elimination, $r_m(a)$ is the unnormalized marginal of the root at $a$.

articles.title: Summing out the last vertex preserves weighted sums at the other vertices
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a
pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with values in a finite type $\alpha$, and
let $m'$ be the model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ obtained from $m$ by summing out its last
vertex. Write $w_m$ and $w_{m'}$ for their unnormalized weights. Then for every vertex $v \le n$
and every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$,

$$\sum_x w_m(x)\, g(x_v) = \sum_y w_{m'}(y)\, g(y_v),$$

where $x$ and $y$ range over all assignments of values in $\alpha$ to the vertices of $m$ and of
$m'$.

articles.title: One step of variable elimination
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite, let $m$ be a pairwise tree model
on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with weight $w$, and let $m'$ be the model on the vertices
$0, \dots, n$ obtained from $m$ by eliminating the last vertex, with weight $w'$. Then for every
function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ we have $\sum_x w(x) \, g(x_0) = \sum_y w'(y) \, g(y_0)$,
where $x$ ranges over all assignments $\{0, \dots, n + 1\} \to \alpha$ and $y$ over all
assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.

articles.title: Belief propagation is exact on trees
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices
$0, \dots, n$ with values in a finite type $\alpha$, let $w$ be its unnormalized weight, and let
$b_v$ be the belief of vertex $v$ computed by sum-product message passing. Then for every vertex
$v$ and every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$,

$$\sum_x w(x)\, g(x_v) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} b_v(a)\, g(a),$$

where $x$ ranges over all assignments of values in $\alpha$ to the vertices.

articles.title: Variable elimination is exact
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model
on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then
for every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ of the root value,
$\sum_x w(x) \, g(x_0) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} r(a) \, g(a)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments
$\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.

articles.title: Pairwise model on a tree
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ of values and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a pairwise
tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ consists of a parent $p(k + 1) \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ for
each vertex $k + 1$ with $k < n$ (so vertex $0$ is the root and every vertex comes after its
parent), a unary factor $\varphi_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ for each vertex $i \le n$, and for each
$k < n$ a pairwise factor $\psi_k(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}$ on the edge between vertex $k + 1$ and its
parent, defined for all $a, b \in \alpha$, where $a$ is the value at vertex $k + 1$ and $b$ the
value at its parent.

articles.title: Max-product decoding attains the max-product value
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model with
values in a finite nonempty type, and let $M$ be its max-product value, obtained by maximizing out
the vertices from the last one down. Then the weight of the assignment produced by max-product
decoding equals $M$.

articles.title: The max-product value bounds every weight
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model with values in
a finite nonempty type $\alpha$ whose unary and pairwise factors are all nonnegative, and let $M$
be its max-product value, obtained by maximizing out the vertices from the last one down. Then
every assignment of values in $\alpha$ to the vertices has weight at most $M$.

articles.title: Max-product decoding finds a MAP assignment
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model with values
in a finite nonempty type $\alpha$ whose unary and pairwise factors are all nonnegative. Then every
assignment of values in $\alpha$ to the vertices has weight at most the weight of the assignment
produced by max-product decoding.

articles.title: Weight of an assignment in a tree model
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type and let $m$ be a pairwise
model on a tree with vertices $0, \dots, n$, with unary factors $\varphi_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$
for each vertex $i$, and with factor $\psi_k : \alpha \times \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ on the edge
between vertex $k + 1$ and its parent $p(k + 1)$ for each $k < n$. The unnormalized weight of an
assignment $x : \{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$ is the real number

$$w(x) = \prod_{i=0}^{n} \varphi_i(x_i) \cdot \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} \psi_k(x_{k+1}, x_{p(k+1)}),$$

the product of all factors evaluated at $x$.

articles.title: The backward pass is the vector-Jacobian product
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a feedforward network with
layers $f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, let
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write
$N_j : \mathbb{R}^{d_0} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_j}$ for the forward pass through the first $j$ layers. If
$f_j$ is differentiable at $N_j(x)$ for every $j < n$, then for every $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^{d_n}$
the backward pass from $\delta$ at input $x$ through the first $n$ layers equals
$DN_n(x)^* \, \delta$, where $DN_n(x)$ is the Fréchet derivative of $N_n$ at $x$ and $^*$ denotes
the adjoint.

articles.title: The backward pass
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a feedforward network with layers
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, let
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ be an input, and write $a_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ for the forward pass of
$x$ through the first $k$ layers. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the backward pass at $x$ sends a
vector $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^{d_n}$ to $B_n(\delta) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$, defined by
$B_0(\delta) = \delta$ and $B_{n+1}(\delta) = B_n(Df_n(a_n)^* \, \delta)$, where $Df_n(a_n)$ is the
Fréchet derivative of $f_n$ at $a_n$ (taken to be $0$ if $f_n$ is not differentiable there) and
$^*$ denotes the adjoint. Thus
$B_n(\delta) = Df_0(a_0)^* \cdots Df_{n-1}(a_{n-1})^* \, \delta$: the adjoints of the layer
Jacobians are applied from the last layer to the first.

articles.title: Differentiable layers are differentiable along every forward pass
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a
feedforward network with layers $f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between
Euclidean spaces. If every $f_k$ is differentiable on all of $\mathbb{R}^{d_k}$, then for every
input $x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the layer $f_j$ is differentiable at
the forward pass of $x$ through the first $j$ layers for every $j < n$.

articles.title: Differentiability along the forward pass
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a feedforward network with layers
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, let
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write $a_j \in \mathbb{R}^{d_j}$ for the
forward pass of $x$ through the first $j$ layers. The network is differentiable along the forward
pass of $x$ through its first $n$ layers when $f_j$ is differentiable at $a_j$ for every
$j < n$.

articles.title: Differentiability of the forward pass
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a feedforward network with layers
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, let
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write
$N_j : \mathbb{R}^{d_0} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_j}$ for the forward pass through the first $j$ layers. If
$f_j$ is differentiable at $N_j(x)$ for every $j < n$, then $N_n$ is differentiable at $x$.

articles.title: Splitting the forward pass
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a feedforward network with layers
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, write $N_n$ for its
forward pass through the first $n$ layers, and for $j \in \mathbb{N}$ write $N^{(j)}_m$ for the
forward pass through the first $m$ layers of the shifted network with layers
$f_j, f_{j+1}, \dots$. Then for all $j, m \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$,
$N_{j+m}(x) = N^{(j)}_m(N_j(x))$.

articles.title: The forward pass
articles.statement:
For a feedforward network with layers
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, the forward pass
through the first $n$ layers is the map $N_n : \mathbb{R}^{d_0} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_n}$ given by
$N_0(x) = x$ and $N_{n+1}(x) = f_n(N_n(x))$, that is, $N_n = f_{n-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_0$.

articles.title: Backpropagation computes the input gradient
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a feedforward network with layers
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ between Euclidean spaces, let
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and write $N_j$ for the forward pass through the
first $j$ layers. Assume that $f_j$ is differentiable at $N_j(x)$ for every $j < n$, and let
$\ell : \mathbb{R}^{d_n} \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $N_n(x)$. Then
$\nabla(\ell \circ N_n)(x)$ is the backward pass of $\nabla \ell(N_n(x))$ at input $x$ through
the first $n$ layers, that is,
$\nabla(\ell \circ N_n)(x) = Df_0(N_0(x))^* \cdots Df_{n-1}(N_{n-1}(x))^* \, \nabla \ell(N_n(x))$,
where $Df_j(N_j(x))$ is the Fréchet derivative of $f_j$ at $N_j(x)$ and $^*$ denotes the
adjoint.

articles.title: Backpropagation computes the parameter gradients
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a network with parameters
whose layer $i$ is a map $g_i : \mathbb{R}^{p_i} \times \mathbb{R}^{d_i} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{i+1}}$
of the parameters and the input (all spaces Euclidean). Fix parameters $\theta = (\theta_i)_i$
with $\theta_i \in \mathbb{R}^{p_i}$, let $N$ be the network with layers
$f_i = g_i(\theta_i, \cdot)$, let $x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}$ and $k, m \in \mathbb{N}$, set
$L = k + 1 + m$, and write $a_j$ for the forward pass of $x$ through the first $j$ layers of $N$.
Assume that $f_{k+1+i}$ is differentiable at $a_{k+1+i}$ for every $i < m$, that
$h(t) = g_k(t, a_k)$ is differentiable at $\theta_k$, and that
$\ell : \mathbb{R}^{d_L} \to \mathbb{R}$ is differentiable at $a_L$. For
$t \in \mathbb{R}^{p_k}$ let $\Phi(t)$ be the forward pass of $x$ through the first $L$ layers of
the network obtained by replacing $\theta_k$ with $t$. Then

$$\nabla(\ell \circ \Phi)(\theta_k) = Dh(\theta_k)^* \, \delta,$$

where $\delta = Df_{k+1}(a_{k+1})^* \cdots Df_{L-1}(a_{L-1})^* \, \nabla \ell(a_L)$ (so
$\delta = \nabla \ell(a_L)$ when $m = 0$) is the backward pass of $\nabla \ell(a_L)$ through
layers $k + 1, \dots, L - 1$ of $N$, $D$ denotes the Fréchet derivative and $^*$ the adjoint.

articles.title: The network at fixed parameters
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a network with parameters whose layer $k$ is a
map $g_k : \mathbb{R}^{p_k} \times \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$ of the parameters
and the input (all spaces Euclidean). For parameters $\theta = (\theta_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ with
$\theta_k \in \mathbb{R}^{p_k}$, the network at $\theta$ is the feedforward network whose layer
$k$ is $g_k(\theta_k, \cdot) : \mathbb{R}^{d_k} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_{k+1}}$.

articles.title: Feedforward network
articles.statement:
Given layer widths $d : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, a feedforward
network with widths $d$ is a sequence of arbitrary maps
$f_k : \mathbb{R}^{d(k)} \to \mathbb{R}^{d(k+1)}$, one for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, where $f_k$ is
the map computed by layer $k$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ carries its Euclidean structure.

articles.title: Parametrized feedforward network
articles.statement:
Given layer widths $d : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and
parameter dimensions $p : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, a parametrized network is a sequence of
arbitrary maps $f_k : \mathbb{R}^{p(k)} \times \mathbb{R}^{d(k)} \to \mathbb{R}^{d(k+1)}$, one for
each $k \in \mathbb{N}$: layer $k$ sends parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{p(k)}$ and an input
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{d(k)}$ to $f_k(\theta, x)$.

articles.title: Shifted network
articles.statement:
For a feedforward network $N$ with layer widths $d$ and a natural number
$j$, the shifted network has layer widths $i \mapsto d(j + i)$, and its layer $i$ is layer
$j + i$ of $N$. It is made of the layers of $N$ from layer $j$ on.

articles.title: A posterior argmax classifier has minimal 0-1 risk
articles.statement:
Let the set $C$ of classes be countable
and nonempty with measurable singletons, let $P$ be a finite kernel from $C$ to the observation
space $\mathcal X$ and $\pi$ a finite measure on $C$, and let $\ell(c, y)$ be the 0-1 loss
($0$ if $y = c$, $1$ otherwise). For a kernel $\kappa$ from $\mathcal X$ to $C$, its average 0-1
risk is $\int_C \int_C \ell(c, y)\,(\kappa \circ P)(c)(dy)\,\pi(dc)$, where
$(\kappa \circ P)(c) = \int_{\mathcal X} \kappa(x)\,P(c)(dx)$. If $f : \mathcal X \to C$ is a
posterior argmax classifier for $P$ and $\pi$, then for every Markov kernel $\kappa$ from
$\mathcal X$ to $C$ (a randomized classifier), the average 0-1 risk of the deterministic kernel
$x \mapsto \delta_{f(x)}$ is at most the average 0-1 risk of $\kappa$.

articles.title: The 0-1 risk of a deterministic classifier
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a measurable space of classes with
measurable singletons, $P$ a kernel from $C$ to the observation space $\mathcal X$, $\pi$ a
measure on $C$, $f : \mathcal X \to C$ a measurable map, and $\ell(c, y)$ the 0-1 loss ($0$ if
$y = c$, $1$ otherwise). Then the average 0-1 risk of the deterministic kernel
$\delta_f : x \mapsto \delta_{f(x)}$,
$\int_C \int_C \ell(c, y)\,(\delta_f \circ P)(c)(dy)\,\pi(dc)$ with
$(\delta_f \circ P)(c) = \int_{\mathcal X} \delta_{f(x)}\,P(c)(dx)$, equals
$\int_C P(c)(\{x \in \mathcal X : f(x) \ne c\})\,\pi(dc)$.

When each $P(c)$ is a probability measure, $P(c)(\{x : f(x) \ne c\})$ is the probability that
$f$ misclassifies an observation of class $c$.

articles.title: The Bayes risk for the 0-1 loss
articles.statement:
Let the set $C$ of classes be finite and nonempty with
measurable singletons, let $P$ be a finite kernel from $C$ to the observation space $\mathcal X$
and $\pi$ a finite measure on $C$, and let $\ell(c, y)$ be the 0-1 loss ($0$ if $y = c$, $1$
otherwise). Write $P \circ \pi$ for the marginal measure on $\mathcal X$ and $P^\dagger_\pi$ for
the posterior kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $C$. For a kernel $\kappa$ from $\mathcal X$ to $C$,
write $(\kappa \circ P)(c) = \int_{\mathcal X} \kappa(x)\,P(c)(dx)$. Then the Bayes risk for the
0-1 loss, the infimum over all Markov kernels $\kappa$ from $\mathcal X$ to $C$ of the average
0-1 risk $\int_C \int_C \ell(c, y)\,(\kappa \circ P)(c)(dy)\,\pi(dc)$, equals
$\int_{\mathcal X} \inf_{y \in C} P^\dagger_\pi(x)(C \setminus \{y\})\,(P \circ \pi)(dx)$: the
average over the observations of the posterior probability of error of the best guess.

articles.title: Existence of a posterior argmax classifier
articles.statement:
Let the set $C$ of classes be finite and
nonempty with measurable singletons, let $P$ be a finite kernel from $C$ to the observation space
$\mathcal X$ and $\pi$ a finite measure on $C$. Then there is a posterior argmax classifier
$f : \mathcal X \to C$ for $P$ and $\pi$.

The classifier constructed takes, at each observation, the first maximizer of the posterior
probability in an enumeration of the classes.

articles.title: A posterior argmax classifier is an argmin estimator for the 0-1 loss
articles.statement:
Let the set $C$ of
classes be countable and nonempty with measurable singletons, let $P$ be a finite kernel from $C$
to the observation space $\mathcal X$ and $\pi$ a finite measure on $C$, write $P \circ \pi$ for
the marginal measure on $\mathcal X$, $P^\dagger_\pi$ for the posterior kernel from $\mathcal X$
to $C$, and $\ell(c, y)$ for the 0-1 loss ($0$ if $y = c$, $1$ otherwise). If
$f : \mathcal X \to C$ is a posterior argmax classifier for $P$ and $\pi$, then $f$ is an argmin
estimator for $\ell$: it is measurable and, for $(P \circ \pi)$-almost every $x$,
$\int_C \ell(c, f(x))\,P^\dagger_\pi(x)(dc)$ equals
$\inf_{y \in C} \int_C \ell(c, y)\,P^\dagger_\pi(x)(dc)$.

articles.title: The Bayes classifier is optimal
articles.statement:
A posterior argmax classifier attains the Bayes risk
for the 0-1 loss.

articles.title: Posterior argmax classifiers are exactly the argmin estimators for the 0-1 loss
articles.statement:
Let the
set $C$ of classes be countable and nonempty with measurable singletons, let $P$ be a finite
kernel from $C$ to the observation space $\mathcal X$ and $\pi$ a finite measure on $C$, write
$P \circ \pi$ for the marginal measure on $\mathcal X$, $P^\dagger_\pi$ for the posterior kernel
from $\mathcal X$ to $C$, and $\ell(c, y)$ for the 0-1 loss ($0$ if $y = c$, $1$ otherwise). A
map $f : \mathcal X \to C$ is a posterior argmax classifier for $P$ and $\pi$ if and only if it
is an argmin estimator for $\ell$: $f$ is measurable and, for $(P \circ \pi)$-almost every $x$,
$\int_C \ell(c, f(x))\,P^\dagger_\pi(x)(dc)$ equals
$\inf_{y \in C} \int_C \ell(c, y)\,P^\dagger_\pi(x)(dc)$.

articles.title: MAP classifiers are posterior argmax classifiers
articles.statement:
Let the set $C$ of classes be countable
and nonempty with measurable singletons, let the observation space $\mathcal X$ be countable with
measurable singletons, let $P$ be a Markov kernel from $C$ to $\mathcal X$ and $\pi$ a finite
measure on $C$, and write $P \circ \pi$ for the marginal measure on $\mathcal X$. If
$f : \mathcal X \to C$ assigns to every observation $x$ with $(P \circ \pi)(\{x\}) \ne 0$ a
maximum a posteriori class for $x$ under $P$ and $\pi$, then $f$ is a posterior argmax
classifier for $P$ and $\pi$.

Since posterior argmax classifiers attain the Bayes risk for the 0-1 loss, MAP classification is
Bayes optimal; observations of zero evidence may be classified arbitrarily.

articles.title: Posterior argmax classifier
articles.statement:
Let the set $C$ of classes be countable and nonempty with
measurable singletons, let $P$ be a finite kernel from $C$ to the observation space $\mathcal X$
and $\pi$ a finite measure on $C$, write $P \circ \pi$ for the marginal measure on $\mathcal X$
and $P^\dagger_\pi$ for the posterior kernel from $\mathcal X$ to $C$. A map
$f : \mathcal X \to C$ is a posterior argmax classifier for $P$ and $\pi$ if $f$ is measurable
and, for $(P \circ \pi)$-almost every $x$,
$P^\dagger_\pi(x)(\{y\}) \le P^\dagger_\pi(x)(\{f(x)\})$ for every $y \in C$.

Countably many classes with measurable singletons make the posterior masses of classes
meaningful, and give the standard Borel structure the posterior needs.

articles.title: Integrating the 0-1 loss over the prediction
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a measurable space with
measurable singletons, $\nu$ a measure on $C$ and $c \in C$, and let $\ell(c, y)$ be the 0-1
loss of predicting $y$ when the true class is $c$ ($0$ if $y = c$, $1$ otherwise). Then
$\int_C \ell(c, y)\,\nu(dy) = \nu(C \setminus \{c\})$.

When $\nu$ is the law of a random prediction, this is its expected 0-1 loss when the true class
is $c$.

articles.title: Expected 0-1 loss of a fixed prediction
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a measurable space in which every
singleton is measurable, let $\nu$ be a measure on $C$, and let $y \in C$. Writing $\ell(c, y)$
for the 0-1 loss of predicting $y$ when the true class is $c$, we have
$\int \ell(c, y) \, d\nu(c) = \nu(C \setminus \{y\})$.

articles.title: The 0-1 loss
articles.statement:
For elements $c$ and $y$ of a type $C$ of classes, the 0-1 loss of
predicting $y$ when the true class is $c$ is the extended nonnegative real number that equals
$0$ if $y = c$ and $1$ if $y \ne c$.

articles.title: Absolute loss
articles.statement:
The absolute loss of predicting $y \in \mathbb{R}$ when the true value is
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ is $|\theta - y|$, regarded as an element of $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: A posterior median is a Bayes estimator for absolute loss
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite kernel from
$\mathbb{R}$ to a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$, sending a parameter $\theta$ to the measure
$P_\theta$ on $\mathcal{X}$, let $\pi$ be a finite prior measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and let
$f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a measurable choice of posterior medians. Then the
deterministic estimator $x \mapsto f(x)$ is a Bayes estimator for the absolute loss
$\ell(\theta, y) = |\theta - y|$: its average risk
$\int \int |\theta - f(x)| \, dP_\theta(x) \, d\pi(\theta)$ equals the Bayes risk, the infimum
of the average risks of all Markov kernels from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$, where risks take
values in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: The posterior mean is a Bayes estimator for squared loss
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite kernel from
$\mathbb{R}$ to a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$, sending a parameter $\theta$ to the measure
$P_\theta$ on $\mathcal{X}$, let $\pi$ be a finite prior measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and let
$f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a measurable version of the posterior mean. Then the
deterministic estimator $x \mapsto f(x)$ is a Bayes estimator for the squared loss
$\ell(\theta, y) = (\theta - y)^2$: its average risk
$\int \int (\theta - f(x))^2 \, dP_\theta(x) \, d\pi(\theta)$ equals the Bayes risk, the infimum
of the average risks of all Markov kernels from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$, where risks take
values in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Measurable versions of the posterior mean
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite kernel from $\mathbb{R}$ to
a measurable space $\mathcal{X}$, sending $\theta$ to the measure $P_\theta$, let $\pi$ be a
finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and write $P^\dagger\pi$ for the posterior kernel from
$\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. A function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a measurable version
of the posterior mean if $f$ is measurable and $f(x) = \int \theta \, d(P^\dagger\pi)(x)(\theta)$
(the posterior mean, taken to be $0$ when the posterior has no finite first moment) for almost
every $x$ with respect to the marginal distribution of the data, the measure
$A \mapsto \int P_\theta(A) \, d\pi(\theta)$ on $\mathcal{X}$.

articles.title: Measurable choices of posterior medians
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite kernel from $\mathbb{R}$ to a
measurable space $\mathcal{X}$, sending $\theta$ to the measure $P_\theta$, let $\pi$ be a finite
measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and write $P^\dagger\pi$ for the posterior kernel from $\mathcal{X}$ to
$\mathbb{R}$. A function $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a measurable choice of posterior
medians if $f$ is measurable and, for almost every $x$ with respect to the marginal distribution
$A \mapsto \int P_\theta(A) \, d\pi(\theta)$ of the data, $f(x)$ is a median of the posterior
distribution $(P^\dagger\pi)(x)$.

articles.title: The expected absolute loss is minimized at every median
articles.statement:
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure
on $\mathbb{R}$ and let $m$ be a median of $\nu$. Then for every $y \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$\int |\theta - m| \, d\nu(\theta) \le \int |\theta - y| \, d\nu(\theta),$$

where both integrals are taken in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: The mean minimizes the expected squared loss
articles.statement:
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ with mean $m = \int t \, d\nu(t)$ (taken to be $0$ when $\nu$ has no finite first
moment). Then for every $y \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$\int (\theta - m)^2 \, d\nu(\theta) \le \int (\theta - y)^2 \, d\nu(\theta),$$

where both integrals are taken in $[0, \infty]$.

When the right side is infinite the inequality is trivial; otherwise $\nu$ has a second moment and
the variance decomposition applies.

articles.title: Posterior mean
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a finite kernel from $\mathbb{R}$ to a measurable space
$\mathcal{X}$, let $\pi$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and write $P^\dagger\pi$ for the
posterior kernel from $\mathcal{X}$ to $\mathbb{R}$. The posterior mean is the function on
$\mathcal{X}$ sending $x$ to $\int \theta \, d(P^\dagger\pi)(x)(\theta)$, the mean of the posterior
distribution given the observation $x$ (taken to be $0$ when that distribution has no finite
first moment).

articles.title: Squared loss
articles.statement:
The squared loss of predicting $y \in \mathbb{R}$ when the true value is
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ is $(\theta - y)^2$, regarded as an element of $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: The bias-variance decomposition
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mu)$ be a probability space, with
expectation $\mathbb{E}$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}$ taken with respect to $\mu$. Let $f$ be
a real number, and let $\varepsilon$ (the noise) and $\hat Y$ (the predictor) be square-integrable
real random variables on $\Omega$ such that $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$ and $\varepsilon$ is
independent of $\hat Y$. Then the expected squared error of $\hat Y$ for the response
$\varepsilon + f$ is the noise variance plus the squared bias plus the variance of the predictor:
$\mathbb{E}[(\varepsilon + f - \hat Y)^2] = \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) +
(f - \mathbb{E}[\hat Y])^2 + \operatorname{Var}(\hat Y)$.

articles.title: Expected squared error of independent random variables
articles.statement:
Let $(\Omega, \mu)$ be a
probability space, with expectation $\mathbb{E}$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}$ taken with
respect to $\mu$. If $Y$ and $\hat Y$ are independent square-integrable real random variables on
$\Omega$, then $\mathbb{E}[(Y - \hat Y)^2] = \operatorname{Var}(Y) + \operatorname{Var}(\hat Y) +
(\mathbb{E}[Y] - \mathbb{E}[\hat Y])^2$.

articles.title: Cross-entropy loss via the likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a probabilistic classifier, assigning
to each input $x \in X$ a probability distribution $f(x)$ on a finite set of labels, and let
$D = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_N, y_N))$ be a labelled sample with $f(x_n)(y_n) \ne 0$ for every $n$.
Then the cross-entropy loss of $f$ on $D$ equals $-\log_2(L) / N$, where
$L = \prod_{n=1}^{N} f(x_n)(y_n)$ is the likelihood of the sample and the division is computed in
$[0, \infty]$, so that both sides are $0$ when $N = 0$.

articles.title: The cross-entropy loss is infinite exactly when a label is ruled out
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a
probabilistic classifier, assigning to each input $x \in X$ a probability distribution $f(x)$ on
a finite set of labels, and let $D = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_N, y_N))$ be a labelled sample with
$N \ge 1$. The cross-entropy loss of $f$ on $D$ is $\infty$ if and only if $f(x_n)(y_n) = 0$ for
some $n$.

articles.title: The cross-entropy loss is the average negative log-likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a probabilistic
classifier, assigning to each input $x \in X$ a probability distribution $f(x)$ on a finite set
of labels, and let $D = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_N, y_N))$ be a labelled sample. The cross-entropy
loss of $f$ on $D$ equals the average surprisal of the labels,

$$\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{N} s\big(f(x_n)(y_n)\big)\Big) / N,$$

where $s(q) = -\log_2 q$ is the surprisal of a probability $q$, with $s(0) = \infty$, and the
average is computed in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Comparing cross-entropy losses of classifiers that rule out no label
articles.statement:
Let $f$ and $g$ be
probabilistic classifiers, each assigning to every input $x \in X$ a probability distribution on
a finite set of labels, and let $D = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_N, y_N))$ be a labelled sample with
$N \ge 1$ such that $f(x_n)(y_n) \ne 0$ and $g(x_n)(y_n) \ne 0$ for every $n$. Then the
cross-entropy loss of $f$ on $D$ is at most that of $g$ if and only if
$\prod_{n=1}^{N} g(x_n)(y_n) \le \prod_{n=1}^{N} f(x_n)(y_n)$.

articles.title: Minimizing cross-entropy is maximum likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $f$ and $g$ be probabilistic
classifiers, each assigning to every input $x \in X$ a probability distribution on a finite set of
labels, and let $D = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_N, y_N))$ be a labelled sample with $N \ge 1$. Then
the cross-entropy loss of $f$ on $D$ is at most that of $g$ if and only if
$\prod_{n=1}^{N} g(x_n)(y_n) \le \prod_{n=1}^{N} f(x_n)(y_n)$, that is, $f$ gives the labels at
least as large a likelihood as $g$.

A label predicted to be impossible gives likelihood $0$ and loss $\infty$.

articles.title: Cross-entropy loss
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a probabilistic classifier, assigning to each input
$x \in X$ a probability distribution $f(x)$ on a finite set of labels, and let
$D = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_N, y_N))$ be a labelled sample. The cross-entropy (log) loss of $f$
on $D$, in bits, is the value in $[0, \infty]$

$$\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{N} H\big(\delta_{y_n}, f(x_n)\big)\Big) / N,$$

where $H$ is the cross-entropy and $\delta_y$ is the point mass at $y$; it is $0$ when $N = 0$.

articles.title: The Gaussian-process posterior
articles.statement:
Let $k : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a kernel, let
$x^* = (x^*_i)_{i \in \tau}$ (test inputs) and $x = (x_j)_{j \in \nu}$ (training inputs) be
finite families in $X$, and write $K(a, b)$ for the kernel matrix $(k(a_i, b_j))_{i, j}$. Assume
that the kernel matrix of the combined family $(x^*, x)$, indexed by $\tau \sqcup \nu$, is
positive semidefinite, and let $\sigma^2 > 0$. Let $V$ be a measurable random vector in
$\mathbb{R}^{\tau \sqcup \nu}$ on a probability space whose law is the Gaussian $N(0, \Sigma)$,
where $\Sigma$ is the joint covariance of $k$, $\sigma^2$, $x^*$ and $x$, and let $F$ (the test
values) and $Y$ (the training targets), random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{\tau}$ and
$\mathbb{R}^{\nu}$, be the test and training blocks of $V$. Then for almost every $y$ with respect
to the law of $Y$, the conditional distribution of $F$ given $Y = y$ is the Gaussian with mean
$K(x^*, x) (K(x, x) + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y$ and covariance
$K(x^*, x^*) - K(x^*, x) (K(x, x) + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} K(x, x^*)$.

articles.title: Regularized kernel matrices are invertible
articles.statement:
Let $k : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a kernel
and $x = (x_j)_{j \in \nu}$ a finite family of inputs whose kernel matrix
$K = (k(x_i, x_j))_{i, j \in \nu}$ is positive semidefinite. Then for every $\sigma^2 > 0$ the
matrix $K + \sigma^2 I$ has nonzero determinant, so it is invertible.

articles.title: The joint covariance as a kernel matrix plus noise
articles.statement:
For a kernel
$k : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$, a real number $\sigma^2$, test inputs $x^* = (x^*_i)_{i \in \tau}$
and training inputs $x = (x_j)_{j \in \nu}$, the joint covariance of $k$, $\sigma^2$, $x^*$ and $x$
equals $K + D$, where $K$ is the kernel matrix of the combined family $(x^*, x)$ indexed by
$\tau \sqcup \nu$ and $D$ is the diagonal matrix with entry $0$ at each test index and $\sigma^2$
at each training index.

articles.title: The joint covariance is positive semidefinite
articles.statement:
Let $k : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a
kernel, let $x^* = (x^*_i)_{i \in \tau}$ and $x = (x_j)_{j \in \nu}$ be families of test and
training inputs, and let $\sigma^2 \ge 0$. If the kernel matrix of the combined family $(x^*, x)$,
indexed by $\tau \sqcup \nu$, is positive semidefinite, then the joint covariance of $k$,
$\sigma^2$, $x^*$ and $x$ is positive semidefinite.

articles.title: Joint prior covariance in Gaussian-process regression
articles.statement:
The joint prior covariance of the test values `f(x*)` and the noisy training targets
`y = f(x) + ε`, `ε ~ N(0, σ² I)`: `[[K(x*, x*), K(x*, x)], [K(x, x*), K(x, x) + σ² I]]`.

articles.title: Training blocks of positive semidefinite kernel matrices
articles.statement:
Let
$k : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a kernel and let $x^* = (x^*_i)_{i \in \tau}$ and
$x = (x_j)_{j \in \nu}$ be families of inputs. If the kernel matrix of the combined family
$(x^*, x)$, indexed by $\tau \sqcup \nu$, is positive semidefinite, then so is the kernel matrix
$(k(x_i, x_j))_{i, j \in \nu}$ of $x$.

articles.title: Kernel matrix
articles.statement:
For a kernel $k : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ and two families of inputs
$a = (a_i)_{i \in \alpha}$ and $b = (b_j)_{j \in \beta}$ in $X$, the kernel (Gram) matrix
$K(a, b)$ is the $\alpha \times \beta$ real matrix with entries $K(a, b)_{ij} = k(a_i, b_j)$.

articles.title: Training-target projection
articles.statement:
For finite index sets $	au$ (test inputs) and $
u$
(training inputs), the training-target projection is the $
u 	imes (	au \sqcup 
u)$ real
matrix with a zero block on the columns indexed by $	au$ and the identity matrix on the columns
indexed by $
u$. It sends a joint vector $(u, y)$ with $u \in \mathbb{R}^{	au}$ and
$y \in \mathbb{R}^{
u}$ to its block of training targets $y$.

articles.title: Test-value projection
articles.statement:
For finite index sets $\tau$ (test inputs) and $\nu$ (training
inputs), the test-value projection is the $\tau \times (\tau \sqcup \nu)$ real matrix with the
identity matrix on the columns indexed by $\tau$ and a zero block on the columns indexed by $\nu$.
It sends a joint vector $(u, y)$ with $u \in \mathbb{R}^{\tau}$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ to its
block of test values $u$.

articles.title: Zero information gain means independence
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite sets carrying
σ-algebras in which singletons are measurable, and let $p$ be a joint probability law on
$\alpha \times \beta$. The information gain of $p$ is zero if and only if $p$, as a measure, equals
the product of its marginal law on $\alpha$ and its marginal law on $\beta$; that is, exactly when
the attribute (first coordinate) and the label (second coordinate) are independent.

articles.title: Information gain in terms of entropies
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a joint probability law on
$\alpha \times \beta$ with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ finite, and let $p_X$ and $p_Y$ be its marginal
laws on $\alpha$ and on $\beta$. Writing $H$ for Shannon entropy in bits, the information gain of
$p$ equals $H(p_X) + H(p_Y) - H(p)$.

articles.title: No split has negative information gain
articles.statement:
For every joint probability law $p$ on
$\alpha \times \beta$ with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ finite, the information gain of $p$ is at least
$0$.

articles.title: Information gain of a split
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a joint probability law on $\alpha \times \beta$
with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ finite, the law of an attribute $X$ (first coordinate) and a label $Y$
(second coordinate). The information gain of splitting on $X$ for predicting $Y$ is the real
number $H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$, where $H(Y)$ is the Shannon entropy in bits of the marginal law of
$Y$ and $H(Y \mid X)$ is the conditional entropy in bits of $Y$ given $X$ under $p$.

articles.title: Information gain is mutual information
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be finite sets carrying
σ-algebras in which singletons are measurable, and let $p$ be a joint probability law on
$\alpha \times \beta$. The information gain of $p$, regarded as an element of $[0, \infty]$, equals
the mutual information in bits of $p$ viewed as a probability measure on $\alpha \times \beta$.

articles.title: The GBLUP posterior
articles.statement:
If the genetic values `Z' β` of individuals with genotypes `Z'` and
the phenotypes `y = Z β + ε` of the training individuals are jointly Gaussian with the covariance
of the marker kernel (marker-effect variance `s > 0`, residual variance `σ² > 0`), then given `y`
the genetic values are Gaussian with mean `Z' Zᵀ (ZZᵀ + (σ²/s) I)⁻¹ y`, which is the RR-BLUP
prediction `Z' β̂` (`gpMean_markerKernel_mulVec`), and covariance
`s (Z' Z'ᵀ - Z' Zᵀ (ZZᵀ + (σ²/s) I)⁻¹ Z Z'ᵀ)`.

articles.title: GP posterior mean = RR-BLUP
articles.statement:
With the marker kernel, the GP predictive mean at genotypes
`Z'` is `Z' β̂` for the ridge marker effects `β̂` with `λ = σ²/s`.

articles.title: GP posterior mean = GBLUP
articles.statement:
For the marker kernel with variance `s > 0` and noise variance
`σ² > 0`, the predictive-mean matrix `K(Z', Z) (K(Z, Z) + σ² I)⁻¹` of Gaussian-process
regression is `Z' Zᵀ (ZZᵀ + (σ²/s) I)⁻¹`.

articles.title: Positive semidefiniteness of the marker kernel matrix
articles.statement:
For `s ≥ 0` the marker kernel is a covariance kernel: its kernel matrix on any inputs is
positive semidefinite.

articles.title: Kernel matrix of the marker kernel
articles.statement: The kernel matrix of the marker kernel between genotypes `Z'` and `Z` is `s Z' Zᵀ`.

articles.title: Kernel ridge regression = GBLUP = RR-BLUP
articles.statement:
In a real RKHS whose kernel has Gram matrix
`ZZᵀ` at the training inputs, the kernel ridge fit (the minimizer of
`∑ᵢ (yᵢ - f xᵢ)² + λ ‖f‖²`, `kernelRidgeRisk_kernelRidgeFit_le`) has fitted values `Z β̂`.

articles.title: Formula for the linear marker kernel
articles.statement: Unfolding `markerKernel`.

articles.title: Linear marker kernel on genotype vectors
articles.statement:
The linear marker kernel `k(a, b) = s ⟪a, b⟫ = s ∑ⱼ aⱼ bⱼ` on genotype vectors: the
covariance of genetic values `aᵀβ` and `bᵀβ` when the marker effects `β` are independent with
variance `s`.

articles.title: RR-BLUP = GBLUP
articles.statement: **RR-BLUP = GBLUP** (fitted values): `Z (ZᵀZ + λI)⁻¹ Zᵀ = ZZᵀ (ZZᵀ + λI)⁻¹` for `λ > 0`.

articles.title: RR-BLUP = GBLUP
articles.statement:
**RR-BLUP = GBLUP** (predictions): for any genotypes `Z'` (training or new individuals),
`Z' β̂ = Z' Zᵀ (ZZᵀ + λI)⁻¹ y`.

articles.title: Positive definiteness of the GBLUP matrix
articles.statement: For `λ > 0` the GBLUP matrix `ZZᵀ + λI` is positive definite.

articles.title: Ridge marker effects are back-solved from GBLUP
articles.statement:
The ridge marker effects are back-solved from GBLUP:
`(ZᵀZ + λI)⁻¹ Zᵀ y = Zᵀ (ZZᵀ + λI)⁻¹ y`.

articles.title: Push-through identity for ridge regression
articles.statement: The **push-through identity** `(ZᵀZ + λI)⁻¹ Zᵀ = Zᵀ (ZZᵀ + λI)⁻¹` for `λ > 0`.

articles.title: Convexity of the lasso objective
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns
indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and let $\lambda \ge 0$. Then the lasso
objective $\theta \mapsto \sum_k (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \in \iota} |\theta_i|$
is a convex function on all of $\mathbb{R}^\iota$.

articles.title: Convexity of the residual sum of squares
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and
columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$, and let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then the residual sum of
squares $\theta \mapsto \sum_k (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2$ is a convex function on all of
$\mathbb{R}^\iota$.

articles.title: Existence of the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimate
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$
rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $v > 0$, and let $L$
be the Gaussian likelihood of linear regression with noise variance $v$. Then $L$ attains its
maximum on $\mathbb{R}^\iota$: there is $\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ with
$L(\theta) \le L(\theta_0)$ for every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$.

articles.title: Least-squares estimates exist
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed
by a finite set $\iota$, and let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then there is $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$
with $X^\top X \theta = X^\top y$: the normal equations always have a solution, whatever the rank
of $X$.

The reason is that the range of $X^\top X$ is contained in that of $X^\top$ and the two matrices
have the same rank, so their ranges coincide.

articles.title: The Gaussian likelihood decreases with the residual sum of squares
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real
matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and
$v > 0$, let $L$ be the Gaussian likelihood of linear regression with noise variance $v$, and let
$\mathrm{RSS}(\theta) = \sum_k (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2$ be the residual sum of squares. Then for all
$\theta, \theta' \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, $L(\theta) \le L(\theta')$ if and only if
$\mathrm{RSS}(\theta') \le \mathrm{RSS}(\theta)$.

articles.title: Gaussian likelihood of linear regression
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and
columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and let $v \ge 0$. The Gaussian
likelihood with noise variance $v$ is the function of $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ given by

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi v}}
\exp\left(-\frac{(y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2}{2 v}\right).
$$

This is the likelihood of $y$ when $y_k = (X\theta)_k + \varepsilon_k$ with independent
$\varepsilon_k \sim N(0, v)$.

For $v = 0$ each factor is the zero function (with the convention $1/0 = 0$), not a Dirac kernel;
the results about this likelihood assume $v \neq 0$.

articles.title: Least squares is maximum likelihood
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns
indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $v > 0$, and let $L$ be the Gaussian
likelihood of linear regression with noise variance $v$. Then $\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$
maximizes $L$ over $\mathbb{R}^\iota$ if and only if it solves the normal equations
$X^\top X \theta_0 = X^\top y$.

articles.title: The ridge estimate maximizes the ridge posterior
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real design matrix with $m$
rows and columns indexed by a finite type $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and let $v$ and $\tau$
be positive reals. Let $p$ be the posterior kernel of linear regression with Gaussian noise of
variance $v$ and independent $N(0, \tau)$ priors on the coordinates of the parameter, and let
$\hat\theta = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y$ be the ridge estimate with $\lambda = v / \tau$.
Then $\hat\theta$ maximizes $p$: for every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ we have
$p(\theta) \le p(\hat\theta)$.

articles.title: Laplace density
articles.statement:
For a scale $b \ge 0$, the density of the Laplace distribution with
location $0$ and scale $b$ is the function on $\mathbb{R}$

$$
f_b(x) = \frac{1}{2b} \exp\left(-\frac{|x|}{b}\right).
$$

For $b = 0$ this is read with the convention $1/0 = 0$ and gives the zero function; the results
about this density assume $b \neq 0$.

articles.title: Lasso is MAP estimation
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a
finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and let $v > 0$ and $b > 0$. Let $P$ be the
posterior kernel of linear regression with Gaussian noise of variance $v$ and the Laplace prior
with scale $b$ on each coordinate, and let $\ell$ be the lasso objective with $\lambda = 2v/b$,
$\ell(\theta) = \sum_k (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \in \iota} |\theta_i|$. Then for all
$\theta, \theta' \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, $P(\theta) \le P(\theta')$ if and only if
$\ell(\theta') \le \ell(\theta)$.

articles.title: Lasso posterior kernel
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a
finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and let $v \ge 0$ and $b \ge 0$. The lasso posterior
kernel at $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ is

$$\prod_{k=1}^{m} \varphi_v\bigl(y_k - (X\theta)_k\bigr) \cdot \prod_{i \in \iota} p_b(\theta_i),$$

where $\varphi_v(x) = e^{-x^2/(2v)} / \sqrt{2\pi v}$ is the density of the normal distribution with
mean $0$ and variance $v$ and $p_b(x) = e^{-|x|/b} / (2b)$ is the density of the Laplace
distribution with location $0$ and scale $b$: the Gaussian likelihood of $y$ with noise variance
$v$ times the Laplace prior density of $\theta$.

It is a meaningful kernel for $v \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$; for $v = 0$ (respectively $b = 0$) the
normal (respectively Laplace) density is the zero function.

articles.title: Lasso with an orthonormal design
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed
by a finite set $\iota$ such that $X^\top X = I$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and let $\lambda \ge 0$.
Let $\hat\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ be given by $\hat\theta_i = S_{\lambda/2}((X^\top y)_i)$,
where $S_t$ is soft thresholding at $t$. Then $\hat\theta$ minimizes the lasso objective: for every
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$,
$\sum_{k=1}^m (y_k - (X\hat\theta)_k)^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \in \iota} |\hat\theta_i| \le
\sum_{k=1}^m (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \in \iota} |\theta_i|$.

articles.title: Lasso objective
articles.statement:
For a real matrix $X$ with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a finite set
$\iota$, responses $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and a real number $\lambda$, the lasso objective at
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ is
$\sum_{k=1}^m (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2 + \lambda \sum_{i \in \iota} |\theta_i|$, the residual sum of
squares plus $\lambda$ times the $\ell^1$ norm of $\theta$.

articles.title: Closed-form solution of the normal equations
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and
columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$ such that $X^\top X$ is invertible, and let
$y \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then $\hat\theta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$ solves the normal equations
$X^\top X \hat\theta = X^\top y$.

articles.title: The ridge matrix is positive definite
articles.statement:
For every real matrix $X$ with $m$ rows and columns
indexed by a finite set $\iota$ and every real $\lambda > 0$, the matrix $X^\top X + \lambda I$ is
positive definite.

articles.title: Density of independent centred Gaussian coordinates
articles.statement:
For a finite set $\iota$, a variance
$\tau \ge 0$ and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, the product over $i \in \iota$ of the densities of
the normal distribution $N(0, \tau)$ at $\theta_i$ equals
$\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\tau}}\right)^{|\iota|} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\tau}
\sum_{i \in \iota} \theta_i^2\right)$.

This also holds at $\tau = 0$, where the normal density is the zero function, with the
convention $1/0 = 0$.

articles.title: Expansion of the ridge objective around a solution of its normal equations
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a
real matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$
and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm and
$R(\theta) = \|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta\|^2$ for the ridge objective. If
$\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ satisfies $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\theta_0 = X^\top y$, then for
every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$,
$R(\theta) = R(\theta_0) + \|X(\theta - \theta_0)\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta - \theta_0\|^2$.

articles.title: Ridge estimate
articles.statement:
For a real matrix $X$ with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a finite set
$\iota$, responses $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and a real number $\lambda$, the ridge estimate is
$(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$.

The inverse of a singular matrix is taken to be $0$; for $\lambda > 0$ the matrix
$X^\top X + \lambda I$ is always invertible.

articles.title: Solutions of the ridge normal equations minimize the ridge objective
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real
matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and
$\lambda \ge 0$, and write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm. If $\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$
satisfies $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\theta_0 = X^\top y$, then for every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$,
$\|y - X\theta_0\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta_0\|^2 \le \|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta\|^2$.

articles.title: Closed form of ridge regression
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real matrix with $m$ rows and columns indexed
by a finite set $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\lambda > 0$, and write $\|\cdot\|$ for the
Euclidean norm. The ridge estimate $\hat\theta = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y$ minimizes
the ridge objective: for every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$,
$\|y - X\hat\theta\|^2 + \lambda \|\hat\theta\|^2 \le \|y - X\theta\|^2 + \lambda \|\theta\|^2$.

articles.title: Ridge regression is MAP estimation
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real design matrix with $m$ rows and
columns indexed by a finite type $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and let $v$ and $\tau$ be
positive reals. Let $p$ be the posterior kernel of linear regression with Gaussian noise of
variance $v$ and independent $N(0, \tau)$ priors on the coordinates of the parameter, and let $R$
be the ridge objective with $\lambda = v / \tau$. Then for all
$\theta, \theta' \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ we have $p(\theta) \le p(\theta')$ if and only if
$R(\theta') \le R(\theta)$.

So the posterior kernel is a decreasing function of the ridge objective.

articles.title: Posterior kernel of ridge regression
articles.statement:
For $s \ge 0$ let $\varphi_s$ be the density of
$N(0, s)$, $\varphi_s(x) = (2 \pi s)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2 / (2 s)}$, with $\varphi_0$ the zero function.
For a real design matrix $X$ with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a finite type $\iota$, responses
$y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, variances $v, \tau \ge 0$ and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, the posterior
kernel is the Gaussian likelihood of $y$ times the prior density of $\theta$:

$$p(\theta) = \prod_{k=1}^{m} \varphi_v(y_k - (X\theta)_k) \prod_{i} \varphi_\tau(\theta_i).$$

This is the posterior kernel of linear regression with Gaussian noise of variance $v$ and
independent $N(0, \tau)$ priors on the coordinates of $\theta$; it is meaningful for
$v, \tau > 0$.

articles.title: Ridge objective
articles.statement:
For a real design matrix $X$ with $m$ rows and columns indexed by a
finite type $\iota$, responses $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, a real number $\lambda$ and
$\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, let $S(\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2$ be the
residual sum of squares. The ridge objective is $S(\theta) + \lambda \sum_{i} \theta_i^2$.

articles.title: Expansion of the residual sum of squares
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real design matrix with $m$ rows
and columns indexed by a finite type $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and write
$S(\theta) = (y - X\theta) \cdot (y - X\theta)$ for the residual sum of squares. Then for all
$\theta, v \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$,

$$S(\theta + v) = S(\theta) - 2\, v \cdot \bigl(X^\top (y - X\theta)\bigr) + (Xv) \cdot (Xv).$$

articles.title: Pythagoras for least squares
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real design matrix with $m$ rows and columns
indexed by a finite type $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, write $S$ for the residual sum of
squares, and let $\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ solve the normal equations
$X^\top X \theta_0 = X^\top y$. Then for every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$,

$$S(\theta) = S(\theta_0) + (X(\theta - \theta_0)) \cdot (X(\theta - \theta_0)).$$

articles.title: Least squares and the normal equations
articles.statement:
Let $X$ be a real design matrix with $m$ rows and
columns indexed by a finite type $\iota$, let $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$, and write $S$ for the residual
sum of squares. A vector $\theta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ satisfies $S(\theta_0) \le S(\theta)$ for
every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$ if and only if $X^\top X \theta_0 = X^\top y$.

articles.title: Residual sum of squares
articles.statement:
For a real design matrix $X$ with $m$ rows and columns indexed
by a finite type $\iota$, responses $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^\iota$, the
residual sum of squares is
$S(\theta) = (y - X\theta) \cdot (y - X\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{m} (y_k - (X\theta)_k)^2$.

articles.title: Soft thresholding solves the one-dimensional lasso
articles.statement:
Let $t \ge 0$ and $z \in \mathbb{R}$,
and let $S_t(z)$ be the soft thresholding of $z$ at $t$. Then for every $s \in \mathbb{R}$,

$$(z - S_t(z))^2 + 2t\,|S_t(z)| \le (z - s)^2 + 2t\,|s|,$$

so $S_t(z)$ minimizes $(z - s)^2 + 2t\,|s|$ over $s \in \mathbb{R}$.

articles.title: Soft thresholding
articles.statement:
For real numbers $t$ and $z$, the soft thresholding of $z$ at $t$ is
$S_t(z) = z - t$ if $z > t$; otherwise $S_t(z) = z + t$ if $z < -t$; and $S_t(z) = 0$ in the
remaining case.

For $t \ge 0$ this shrinks $z$ towards $0$ by $t$ and sets it to $0$ when $|z| \le t$.

articles.title: Backward-selection chain at a nonempty set
articles.statement: Unfolding `chain` at a nonempty set.

articles.title: Backward-selection chain at the empty set
articles.statement: Unfolding `chain` at the empty set (the chain stops).

articles.title: Backward-selection chain of remaining feature sets
articles.statement:
Backward selection: the list of remaining sets `R₀ = R, R₁, …, ∅`, where `R_{t+1}` is
`R_t` with the feature chosen by `pick` masked.

articles.title: Existence of greedy backward-selection rules
articles.statement: Greedy rules exist for every `g`.

articles.title: Proposition 1 (second part)
articles.statement:
**Proposition 1 (second part)** of Carter et al.: among the sets met during backward
selection, the returned SIS has the smallest cardinality among the sufficient ones.

articles.title: Proposition 1 (first part)
articles.statement:
**Proposition 1 (first part)** of Carter et al.: no feature of the returned SIS can be
additionally masked while keeping the prediction at or above the threshold.

articles.title: FindSIS returns a set when the start reaches the threshold
articles.statement: If the prediction on the starting set reaches the threshold, `findSIS` returns a set.

articles.title: Minimality of FindSIS for monotone set functions
articles.statement:
For a monotone set function (masking more features never raises the prediction), the
returned SIS is inclusion-minimal: no proper subset is sufficient. (Derived; the paper states
only Proposition 1.)

articles.title: FindSIS returns a sufficient subset of the features
articles.statement: Criterion (1): the returned SIS is a subset of the starting features and is sufficient.

articles.title: FindSIS procedure for sufficient input subsets
articles.statement:
`FindSIS`: un-mask features in reverse order of masking (start from `∅`) and return the
first set on which the prediction reaches the threshold, or `none`. The paper's procedure does
not test `∅` itself; the two agree whenever `g ∅ < τ`, the case the paper considers.

articles.title: Greedy backward-selection rule
articles.statement:
`pick` is a greedy backward-selection rule for `g`: from a nonempty remaining set `R` it
masks a feature `i ∈ R` maximizing `g (R.erase i)`.

articles.title: Starting set begins the backward-selection chain
articles.statement: The starting set is the first set of the chain.

articles.title: Sets of the SIS-collection are pairwise disjoint
articles.statement: The sets of the SIS-collection are pairwise disjoint.

articles.title: Proposition 2
articles.statement:
**Proposition 2** of Carter et al.: if the fully masked input is below the threshold,
masking every set of the SIS-collection leaves the prediction below the threshold.

articles.title: Sets of the SIS-collection are nonempty and sufficient
articles.statement: Every set of the SIS-collection is a nonempty sufficient subset of the starting features.

articles.title: SIS-collection procedure
articles.statement:
`SIScollection`: while the remaining features `R` are sufficient (`τ ≤ g R`), find a SIS
among them, record it and mask it. Stops if `findSIS` returns an empty set (only possible
when `τ ≤ g ∅`).

articles.title: Sets in the backward-selection chain are subsets of the start
articles.statement: Every set in the backward-selection chain is a subset of the starting set.

articles.title: Existence of an archetype minimizer on the hull boundary
articles.statement:
If the RSS has a feasible minimizer with `p ≥ 2` archetypes, it has one with every
archetype on the boundary of the convex hull of the data.

articles.title: Feasible archetypes can be moved to the boundary of the hull
articles.statement:
Cutler–Breiman Proposition 1(ii): for at least two archetypes, any feasible archetypes can
be replaced by feasible archetypes on the boundary of the convex hull of the data whose convex
hull contains the original one; in particular the RSS does not increase.

articles.title: Feasible archetypes
articles.statement: Archetypes are feasible if each is a mixture of the data points.

articles.title: Sample mean of the data
articles.statement: The sample mean of the data.

articles.title: The sample mean is the optimal single archetype
articles.statement:
Cutler–Breiman Proposition 1(i): with a single archetype, the sample mean is feasible and
minimizes the RSS.

articles.title: The RSS vanishes when the archetypes' convex hull contains the data
articles.statement:
Cutler–Breiman Proposition 1(iii): if every data point is a mixture of the archetypes, the
RSS vanishes. Requires `0 < p`: for `p = 0` the hull is empty, so `rss` is `0` vacuously
and the vanishing would not witness a fit.

articles.title: Residual sum of squares in archetypal analysis
articles.statement:
The residual sum of squares of archetypes `z` for the data `x`: each data point is
replaced by the closest point of the convex hull of the archetypes. This is only meaningful
for `0 < p`: for `p = 0` the hull is empty and `infDist` to the empty set is `0` by
convention, so `rss` is `0` vacuously and must not be read as a perfect fit.

articles.title: The cost never increases along a run of Lloyd's algorithm
articles.statement: **The cost never increases along a run of Lloyd's algorithm.**

articles.title: The centroid update step
articles.statement:
Let $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) be points in a real
inner product space and let $a$ assign each point $i$ to a cluster $a(i) \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$.
The updated centers send each cluster $j$ to the centroid of the points $x_i$ with $a(i) = j$.
A cluster with no points gets the center $0$, which does not affect the $k$-means cost of $a$.

articles.title: Centroid
articles.statement:
Let $x_i$ be points in a real inner product space and $s$ a finite set of
indices. The centroid of the points indexed by $s$ is $\frac{1}{|s|} \sum_{i \in s} x_i$; when $s$
is empty it is the zero vector.

articles.title: The update step never increases the cost
articles.statement:
For a fixed assignment, the centroids are the
best centers.

articles.title: The cost as a sum over clusters
articles.statement:
For points $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) in a
normed additive commutative group, an assignment $a$ of each point $i$ to a cluster
$a(i) \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ and centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$, the $k$-means cost equals
$\sum_{j} \sum_{i : a(i) = j} \lVert x_i - c_j \rVert^2$: for each cluster $j$, add up the squared
distances from the points assigned to $j$ to its center $c_j$.

articles.title: One round of Lloyd's algorithm never increases the cost
articles.statement:
Recompute the centers, then
reassign every point to a nearest new center.

articles.title: The assignment step never increases the cost
articles.statement:
For fixed centers, nearest-center
assignment is optimal.

articles.title: The k-means cost
articles.statement:
For points $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) in a normed additive
commutative group, an assignment $a$ of each point $i$ to a cluster $a(i) \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}$
and centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$, the $k$-means cost is
$\sum_{i \in \iota} \lVert x_i - c_{a(i)} \rVert^2$, the sum of the squared distances from the
points to their assigned centers.

articles.title: Nearest-center assignments exist
articles.statement:
For any points $x_i$ in a normed additive commutative
group and any centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1}$ with $k \ge 1$, there is an assignment that sends
every point to a nearest center.

articles.title: Runs of Lloyd's algorithm exist
articles.statement:
Let $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite type) be points in a
real inner product space and let $k \ge 1$. Every starting assignment $a_0$ of the points to
clusters $0, \dots, k-1$ and every choice of starting centers $c_0$ extend to a run of Lloyd's
algorithm: there are assignments $a_t$ and centers $c_t$ for $t \in \mathbb{N}$, equal to $a_0$
and $c_0$ at $t = 0$, that form a run.

articles.title: Run of Lloyd's algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$, a finite index set) be points in a
real inner product space $E$. Sequences of assignments $a_t : \iota \to \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ and of
centers $c_t : \{0, \dots, k-1\} \to E$, indexed by $t \in \mathbb{N}$, form a run of Lloyd's
algorithm when for every $t$: for each $j < k$ the center $c_{t+1}(j)$ is the centroid of the
cluster $\{i : a_t(i) = j\}$ (the zero vector if this cluster is empty), and $a_{t+1}$ assigns
every point to a nearest center of $c_{t+1}$. The initial assignment $a_0$ and centers $c_0$ are
arbitrary.

articles.title: Ratio of isotropic Gaussian densities with a common variance
articles.statement:
For all points
$\mu, \nu, x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and every real $v > 0$, writing $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, vI)$ for
the isotropic Gaussian density with mean $\mu$ and covariance $vI$,

$$
\frac{\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, vI)}{\mathcal{N}(x \mid \nu, vI)}
= \exp\left(\frac{\|x - \nu\|^2 - \|x - \mu\|^2}{2v}\right).
$$

articles.title: The k-means assignment step is the zero-variance limit of the E-step
articles.statement:
Let
$x_1, \dots, x_N$ be points of $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be means
with positive weights $w_1, \dots, w_K$, and let $a$ assign to each $n$ a component $a(n)$ such
that $\|x_n - \mu_{a(n)}\| < \|x_n - \mu_k\|$ for every $k \ne a(n)$. Then $a$ is a nearest-center
assignment, that is, $\|x_n - \mu_{a(n)}\| \le \|x_n - \mu_k\|$ for all $n$ and $k$, and for all
$n$ and $k$ the common-variance responsibility $r_v(x_n, k)$ of component $k$ at $x_n$ for these
weights and means tends to $1$ if $k = a(n)$ and to $0$ otherwise as $v \to 0^+$.

articles.title: Nearest-center assignment
articles.statement:
Given points $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$) in a normed additive
commutative group $E$ and centers $c_0, \dots, c_{k-1} \in E$, an assignment
$a : \iota \to \{0, \dots, k-1\}$ assigns every point to a nearest center when
$\|x_i - c_{a(i)}\| \le \|x_i - c_j\|$ for every index $i \in \iota$ and every $j < k$.

articles.title: The Gaussian-mixture M-step mean is the common-variance M-step mean
articles.statement:
Let $\theta$ be valid
parameters of an isotropic Gaussian mixture with $K$ components on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with weights
