$w_k$, means $\mu_k$ and variances all equal to a real number $v$. Then for data
$x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and every component $k$, the M-step mean of component $k$ under
$\theta$ equals the common-variance M-step mean of component $k$ for the weights $w$, means $\mu$,
variance $v$ and data $x_1, \dots, x_N$.

articles.title: The Gaussian-mixture responsibilities are the common-variance responsibilities
articles.statement:
Let
$\theta$ be valid parameters of an isotropic Gaussian mixture with $K$ components on
$\mathbb{R}^d$, with weights $w_k$, means $\mu_k$ and variances all equal to a real number $v$.
Then for every point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and every component $k$, the responsibility of $k$ at
$x$ under $\theta$ equals the common-variance responsibility $r_v(x, k)$ for the weights $w$ and
means $\mu$.

articles.title: Common-variance responsibilities relative to a fixed component
articles.statement:
For weights
$w_1, \dots, w_K \in \mathbb{R}$, means $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $v > 0$,
a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and components $j$ and $k$, the common-variance responsibility
$r_v(x, k)$ of component $k$ at $x$ for these weights and means satisfies

$$
r_v(x, k) = \frac{w_k \exp\bigl((\|x - \mu_j\|^2 - \|x - \mu_k\|^2) / (2v)\bigr)}
{\sum_i w_i \exp\bigl((\|x - \mu_j\|^2 - \|x - \mu_i\|^2) / (2v)\bigr)}.
$$

articles.title: Responsibilities with a common variance
articles.statement:
Given weights $w_1, \dots, w_K \in \mathbb{R}$,
means $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real $v$, the common-variance responsibility
of component $k$ at a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is

$$
r_v(x, k) = \frac{w_k \, \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_k, vI)}
{\sum_i w_i \, \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_i, vI)},
$$

where, for $v > 0$, $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, vI)$ is the isotropic Gaussian density with mean
$\mu$ and covariance $vI$, and for $v \le 0$ it is $1$ if $d = 0$ and $0$ if $d \ge 1$. A quotient
with denominator $0$ is $0$.

articles.title: Common-variance M-step mean
articles.statement:
Given weights $w_1, \dots, w_K \in \mathbb{R}$, means
$\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $v$ and data $x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$,
the common-variance M-step mean of component $k$ is

$$
\Bigl(\sum_n r_v(x_n, k)\Bigr)^{-1} \sum_n r_v(x_n, k) \, x_n,
$$

where $r_v(x, k)$ is the common-variance responsibility of component $k$ at $x$ for these
weights and means, and $0^{-1} = 0$.

articles.title: Sum of squared distances about the centroid
articles.statement:
Let $x_i$ ($i \in \iota$) be points in a
real inner product space $E$, let $s$ be a finite set of indices, and let $\mu$ be the centroid of
the points $x_i$ with $i \in s$. Then for every point $c \in E$,

$$
\sum_{i \in s} \|x_i - c\|^2 = \sum_{i \in s} \|x_i - \mu\|^2 + |s| \, \|\mu - c\|^2.
$$

Consequently the centroid minimizes the sum of squared distances to the points $x_i$, $i \in s$.

articles.title: Exponential decay as the variance tends to zero
articles.statement:
For every real $c < 0$,
$\exp(c / (2v)) \to 0$ as $v \to 0^+$.

articles.title: Responsibilities in the zero-variance limit
articles.statement:
Let $w_1, \dots, w_K$ be positive weights,
$\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$ means and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ a point, and suppose that
$\mu_j$ is the unique nearest mean to $x$: $\|x - \mu_j\| < \|x - \mu_k\|$ for every $k \ne j$.
Then for every component $k$, the common-variance responsibility $r_v(x, k)$ of $k$ at $x$ for
these weights and means tends to $1$ if $k = j$ and to $0$ otherwise as $v \to 0^+$.

## Sources

- Bishop, *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*, Section 9.3.2.

articles.title: The M-step in the zero-variance limit
articles.statement:
Let $x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be data, let
$\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be means with positive weights $w_1, \dots, w_K$, and let
$a$ assign to each $n$ a component $a(n)$ with $\|x_n - \mu_{a(n)}\| < \|x_n - \mu_k\|$ for
every $k \ne a(n)$. Then for every component $k$ such that $a(n) = k$ for some $n$, the
common-variance M-step mean of component $k$ for these weights, means and data tends, as
$v \to 0^+$, to the k-means centroid of cluster $k$ under $a$, the mean of the points $x_n$ with
$a(n) = k$.

articles.title: Essential uniqueness of NMF when both factors are separable
articles.statement:
Suppose `X = W * H`, where
`W` has a pure row for every factor (`IsSeparable Wᵀ`: for each `a` a row `i` with
`W i · = e • e_a`, `e > 0`) and `H` has a pure column for every factor (`IsSeparable H`). Then
every factorization `X = W' * H'` with `W', H' ≥ 0` and the same inner dimension agrees with
`(W, H)` up to a permutation `σ` and positive scalings `d` of the factors:
`W' · a = d a • W · (σ a)` and `H' a · = (d a)⁻¹ • H (σ a) ·`. The signs of `W` and `H` are not
used. Proof: the anchor rows and columns of `X` form a positive diagonal block, so the matching
block of `W'` is a nonnegative matrix with a nonnegative inverse, hence monomial
(`exists_perm_of_mul_eq_one`).

articles.title: Existence of a minimizer
articles.statement:
For every real matrix `X` and every finite inner index type
`k`, the objective attains its infimum over pairs `W, H ≥ 0` (entrywise).

articles.title: Existence of a factorization of nonnegative-rank inner dimension
articles.statement: A nonnegative matrix has a nonnegative factorization of inner dimension `nonnegRank X`.

articles.title: A nonnegative matrix with a nonnegative inverse is monomial
articles.statement:
If `G * K = 1` with `G` and
`K` entrywise nonnegative, then there are a permutation `σ` and positive weights `d` with
`G a b = d b` if `a = σ b` and `0` otherwise.

articles.title: Gradient of the NMF objective with respect to H
articles.statement: The gradient of the objective with respect to `H`: `2 (Wᵀ W H - Wᵀ X)`.

articles.title: Gradient of the NMF objective with respect to W
articles.statement: The gradient of the objective with respect to `W`: `2 (W H Hᵀ - X Hᵀ)`.

articles.title: Partial derivative of the NMF objective in an entry of H
articles.statement: `gradH X W H a j` is the partial derivative of the objective in the entry `H a j`.

articles.title: Partial derivative of the NMF objective in an entry of W
articles.statement: `gradW X W H i a` is the partial derivative of the objective in the entry `W i a`.

articles.title: Positive fixed points are KKT points
articles.statement:
A fixed point of the Lee–Seung sweep with all
entries of `W` and `H` positive has both gradients zero, so it satisfies the KKT conditions.

articles.title: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker point of nonnegative matrix factorization
articles.statement:
The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions of `min ‖X - W H‖_F²` subject to `W, H ≥ 0`: primal
feasibility, dual feasibility (nonnegative gradients) and complementary slackness.

articles.title: Separable factor matrix
articles.statement:
`H` is separable: every factor `a` has a pure column, a column `j` of `H` equal to a
positive multiple of the unit vector `e_a`. For `X = W * H` this makes column `j` of `X` a
positive multiple of column `a` of `W` (a sample containing only factor `a`). Applied to `Wᵀ`
it says that every factor has a pure row of `W` (an "anchor" feature of factor `a` alone).

articles.title: Gene-expression deconvolution
articles.statement:
Write the bulk matrix (genes × samples) as `C * P`, the
cell-type profiles `C` times the cell-type proportions `P`. If the proportions of sample `j` are
nonnegative and sum to `1` and every cell type expresses gene `g` at a level in `[lo, hi]`, then
the bulk level of `g` in sample `j` lies in `[lo, hi]`.

articles.title: Complementary slackness at a fixed point of the `H` update
articles.statement:
If `updateH X W H = H`,
then `H a j * gradH X W H a j = 0` for every entry.

articles.title: Complementary slackness at a fixed point of the `W` update
articles.statement: **Complementary slackness at a fixed point of the `W` update**.

articles.title: Nonnegative rank is at most the number of columns
articles.statement: The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is at most its number of columns.

articles.title: A nonnegative factorization bounds the nonnegative rank
articles.statement: A nonnegative factorization with inner dimension `r` bounds the nonnegative rank by `r`.

articles.title: Nonnegative rank of a matrix
articles.statement:
The nonnegative rank of `X`: the least `r` such that `X = W * H` with `W : m × r` and
`H : r × n` entrywise nonnegative (Cohen and Rothblum 1993). If `X` has a negative entry no
such factorization exists and the value is the junk value `sInf ∅ = 0`.

articles.title: Nonnegativity of the NMF objective
articles.statement: The objective is nonnegative.

articles.title: The objective is non-increasing along the Lee–Seung iterates
articles.statement:
**The objective is non-increasing along the Lee–Seung iterates** started from `W, H ≥ 0`,
for `X ≥ 0`.

articles.title: One Lee–Seung sweep does not increase the objective
articles.statement: **One Lee–Seung sweep does not increase the objective**, for `X, W, H ≥ 0`.

articles.title: The NMF objective is invariant under transposition
articles.statement: Transposing exchanges the roles of `W` and `H`: `‖Xᵀ - Hᵀ Wᵀ‖² = ‖X - W H‖²`.

articles.title: Lee–Seung, `H` step
articles.statement:
**Lee–Seung, `H` step** (Lee and Seung 2001, Theorem 1): for `W, H ≥ 0`, the multiplicative
update of `H` does not increase `‖X - W H‖_F²`. The proof is the auxiliary-function argument:
the quadratic term of the exact expansion is bounded by Lee and Seung's diagonal majorant
(here through a weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality), and the update minimizes the majorant.
`X` may have any sign.

articles.title: Lee–Seung, `W` step
articles.statement:
For `W, H ≥ 0`, the multiplicative update of `W` does not increase
`‖X - W H‖_F²`.

articles.title: Objective of nonnegative matrix factorization
articles.statement:
The NMF objective: the squared Frobenius distance `‖X - W H‖_F² = ∑ i j, (X i j - (W H) i j)²`
between the data `X` and the product `W * H`.

articles.title: The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is at least its rank
articles.statement: **The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is at least its rank.**

articles.title: Mutational signatures
articles.statement:
**Mutational signatures** (Alexandrov et al. 2013). Write the mutation-count matrix
(mutation types × samples) as `W * H`, signatures (columns of `W`) times exposures `H`. If every
signature is a probability vector over mutation types, the total mutation count of sample `j`
equals the sum of its exposures.

articles.title: Column sums of a matrix product
articles.statement: Column sums of a product: `∑ i, (W H) i j = ∑ a, (∑ i, W i a) H a j`.

articles.title: A Lee–Seung sweep preserves nonnegativity
articles.statement: One sweep keeps both factors nonnegative when `X ≥ 0`.

articles.title: One sweep of the Lee–Seung algorithm
articles.statement: One sweep of the Lee–Seung algorithm: update `H`, then update `W` using the new `H`.

articles.title: The Lee–Seung H update preserves nonnegativity
articles.statement: The `H` update keeps `H` nonnegative when `X`, `W`, `H` are nonnegative.

articles.title: Lee–Seung multiplicative update of H
articles.statement:
The Lee–Seung multiplicative update of `H` (Lee and Seung 2001, Theorem 1):
`H a j ← H a j * (Wᵀ X) a j / (Wᵀ W H) a j`. An entry with a zero denominator becomes `0`
(Lean's `x / 0 = 0`).

articles.title: The W update is the H update of the transposed problem
articles.statement: The `W` update is the `H` update of the transposed problem.

articles.title: The Lee–Seung W update preserves nonnegativity
articles.statement: The `W` update keeps `W` nonnegative when `X`, `W`, `H` are nonnegative.

articles.title: Lee–Seung multiplicative update of W
articles.statement:
The Lee–Seung multiplicative update of `W` (Lee and Seung 2001, Theorem 1):
`W i a ← W i a * (X Hᵀ) i a / (W H Hᵀ) i a`. An entry with a zero denominator becomes `0`.

articles.title: Characteristic function of a linear image
articles.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\mathbb{R}^q$
and $W$ a real $d \times q$ matrix, and write
$\varphi_\nu(t) = \int e^{i\langle x, t\rangle}\,d\nu(x)$ for the characteristic function of a
measure $\nu$. Then the pushforward $W_*\mu$ of $\mu$ under $z \mapsto Wz$ satisfies
$\varphi_{W_*\mu}(t) = \varphi_\mu(W^\top t)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

articles.title: The factor-analysis marginal
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ and $E$ be independent random vectors on a
probability space, with values in $\mathbb{R}^q$ and $\mathbb{R}^d$, such that $Z$ has the
standard Gaussian law $N(0, I_q)$ and $E$ has law $N(0, \operatorname{diag}\psi)$ for a vector
$\psi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\psi_i \ge 0$ for all $i$. Then for every real $d \times q$ matrix
$W$ and every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the random vector $WZ + \mu + E$ has law
$N(\mu, WW^\top + \operatorname{diag}\psi)$.

articles.title: The transpose of a real matrix is its adjoint
articles.statement:
For every real $d \times q$ matrix $W$ and
all $z \in \mathbb{R}^q$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the Euclidean inner products satisfy
$\langle Wz, t\rangle = \langle z, W^\top t\rangle$.

articles.title: Probabilistic PCA MLE when the sample covariance has the model form
articles.statement:
Let
$x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be data with sample mean $\bar{x}$ and sample covariance $S$.
If $W_0$ is a real $d \times q$ matrix and $\sigma_0^2 > 0$ is a real number with
$S = W_0 W_0^\top + \sigma_0^2 I$, then $(\bar{x}, W_0, \sigma_0^2)$ is a probabilistic PCA
maximum-likelihood estimate for the data.

articles.title: Probabilistic PCA maximum-likelihood estimate
articles.statement:
Given data
$x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a triple $(\mu_0, W_0, \sigma_0^2)$ of a mean
$\mu_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $d \times q$ loading matrix $W_0$ and a real number $\sigma_0^2$
is a probabilistic PCA maximum-likelihood estimate when $\sigma_0^2 > 0$ and, for every
$\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, every real $d \times q$ matrix $W$ and every real $\sigma^2 > 0$, the
probabilistic PCA log-likelihood of the data at $(\mu, W, \sigma^2)$ is at most its value at
$(\mu_0, W_0, \sigma_0^2)$.

articles.title: The probabilistic PCA likelihood is at most the unconstrained Gaussian maximum
articles.statement:
Let
$x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be data whose sample covariance $S$ is positive definite, and
let $\bar{x}$ be their sample mean. Then for every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, every real
$d \times q$ matrix $W$ and every real $\sigma^2 > 0$, the probabilistic PCA log-likelihood of the
data at $(\mu, W, \sigma^2)$ is at most $\sum_{n=1}^N \log \mathcal{N}(x_n \mid \bar{x}, S)$,
where $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \bar{x}, S)$ is the multivariate Gaussian density with mean $\bar{x}$
and covariance $S$.

The sample covariance is positive definite, for example, when the data do not all lie in an
affine hyperplane.

articles.title: The mean MLE is the sample mean
articles.statement:
Let $x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be data with
sample mean $\bar{x}$. For every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, every real $d \times q$ loading matrix
$W$ and every real $\sigma^2 > 0$, the probabilistic PCA log-likelihood of the data at
$(\mu, W, \sigma^2)$ is at most its value at $(\bar{x}, W, \sigma^2)$.

articles.title: The log-likelihood of no data is zero
articles.statement:
For the empty data set ($N = 0$), the
probabilistic PCA log-likelihood at every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, every real $d \times q$ matrix
$W$ and every real number $\sigma^2$ is $0$.

articles.title: No latent factors: the noise-variance MLE is the average sample variance
articles.statement:
Let
$x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be data with sample mean $\bar{x}$ and sample covariance $S$,
and suppose $\operatorname{tr} S > 0$. Then for every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and every real
$\sigma^2 > 0$, the probabilistic PCA log-likelihood of the data with the zero $d \times q$
loading matrix at $(\mu, 0, \sigma^2)$ is at most its value at
$(\bar{x}, 0, \operatorname{tr} S / d)$.

Here $\operatorname{tr} S / d$ is the average sample variance (Tipping and Bishop's $\sigma^2$
estimate with no retained components).

articles.title: Probabilistic PCA log-likelihood
articles.statement:
For data $x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a mean
$\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $d \times q$ loading matrix $W$ and a real number $\sigma^2$, the
probabilistic PCA log-likelihood of the data is

$$
\sum_{n=1}^N \log \mathcal{N}(x_n \mid \mu, W W^\top + \sigma^2 I),
$$

where, for a real $d \times d$ matrix $\Sigma$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$,

$$
\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \Sigma) = (2\pi)^{-d/2} \bigl(\sqrt{\det \Sigma}\bigr)^{-1}
\exp\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2} (x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\bigr)
$$

is the multivariate Gaussian density formula, read with the conventions $\sqrt{t} = 0$ for
$t < 0$, $0^{-1} = 0$, $\Sigma^{-1} = 0$ for singular $\Sigma$ and $\log 0 = 0$. These conventions
matter only when $W W^\top + \sigma^2 I$ is not positive definite. When $\sigma^2 > 0$ the matrix
$W W^\top + \sigma^2 I$ is positive definite, and this is the density of the Gaussian with mean
$\mu$ and covariance $W W^\top + \sigma^2 I$.

articles.title: The marginal of probabilistic PCA and factor analysis is Gaussian
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ and $E$ be
independent random vectors on a probability space, with values in $\mathbb{R}^q$ and
$\mathbb{R}^d$, such that $Z$ has the standard Gaussian law $N(0, I_q)$ and $E$ has law
$N(0, \Psi)$ for a positive semidefinite real $d \times d$ matrix $\Psi$. Then for every real
$d \times q$ matrix $W$ and every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the random vector $WZ + \mu + E$ has
law $N(\mu, WW^\top + \Psi)$.

This is the marginal of Tipping and Bishop's model: probabilistic PCA is the case
$\Psi = \sigma^2 I$, factor analysis the case of a diagonal $\Psi$.

articles.title: Probabilistic PCA covariance
articles.statement:
For a real $d \times q$ matrix $W$ and a real number
$\sigma^2$, the probabilistic PCA covariance is the $d \times d$ matrix $W W^\top + \sigma^2 I$.

articles.title: The density of the probabilistic PCA observation
articles.statement:
Let $z$ and $\varepsilon$ be
independent random vectors on a probability space, with $z$ standard Gaussian in $\mathbb{R}^q$
and $\varepsilon$ Gaussian in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with mean $0$ and covariance $\sigma^2 I$, where
$\sigma^2 > 0$. Then for every real $d \times q$ matrix $W$ and every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the
law of $x = W z + \mu + \varepsilon$ has density $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, W W^\top + \sigma^2 I)$
with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \Sigma)$ is the
multivariate Gaussian density with mean $\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$.

articles.title: The probabilistic PCA marginal
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ and $E$ be independent random vectors on a
probability space, with values in $\mathbb{R}^q$ and $\mathbb{R}^d$, such that $Z$ has the
standard Gaussian law $N(0, I_q)$ and $E$ has the isotropic law $N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)$ for a real
$\sigma^2 \ge 0$. Then for every real $d \times q$ matrix $W$ and every $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the
random vector $WZ + \mu + E$ has law $N(\mu, WW^\top + \sigma^2 I_d)$.

articles.title: Sample covariance
articles.statement:
For data $x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with sample mean
$\bar{x}$, the sample covariance is the $d \times d$ matrix
$S = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N (x_n - \bar{x})(x_n - \bar{x})^\top$, taken to be $0$ when
$N = 0$.

articles.title: Sample mean
articles.statement:
For data points $x_1, \dots, x_N \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the sample mean is
$\bar x = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} x_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

When $N = 0$ the sample mean is $0$.

articles.title: Equality case of the sub-convex combination norm bound
articles.statement:
Gillis–Vavasis Lemma 1 (`f = ‖·‖²`), equality case: for linearly independent vectors of
norm at most `M > 0`, a sub-convex combination of norm `M` is a vertex `w k` with
`‖w k‖ = M`.

articles.title: Existence of successive projection runs of every length
articles.statement: SPA runs of every length exist (on a nonempty set of columns).

articles.title: Run of the successive projection algorithm
articles.statement:
`S` (most recent pick first) is a run of the successive projection algorithm: each pick
maximizes the residual norm given the earlier picks (ties broken arbitrarily).

articles.title: SPA recovers archetypes
articles.statement:
**SPA recovers archetypes** (Gillis–Vavasis Theorem 1, noiseless case): in the first `r`
picks of any SPA run on a separable matrix with `r` archetypes, the picked columns are
pairwise distinct.

articles.title: SPA recovers archetypes
articles.statement:
**SPA recovers archetypes** (Gillis–Vavasis Theorem 1, noiseless case): each of the first
`r` picks of any SPA run is an archetype.

articles.title: Norm bound for a sub-convex combination of vectors
articles.statement:
Gillis–Vavasis Lemma 1 (`f = ‖·‖²`), bound: a sub-convex combination of vectors of norm
at most `M` has norm at most `M`.

articles.title: Successive projection finds every archetype after r picks
articles.statement: After exactly `r` picks, SPA has found every archetype.

articles.title: Residual of a column in the successive projection algorithm
articles.statement:
The residual of column `j`: its projection onto the orthogonal complement of the span of
the columns indexed by `S`.

articles.title: Separable data matrix
articles.statement:
A separable data matrix: columns `m j` are sub-convex combinations of `r` linearly
independent archetypes `w k`, and every archetype is a column (Gillis–Vavasis Assumption 1).

articles.title: The adversary forces $n$ misses while the optimum misses at most $k + \lceil n / k \rceil$ times
articles.statement:
**The adversary forces $n$ misses while the optimum misses at most $k + \lceil n / k \rceil$
times.** Let $k \ge 1$ and let $A$ be a deterministic online pager with cache size $k$ on the
$k + 1$ pages $0, \dots, k$. For every $n$, on the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests started
from the initial state of $A$, the pager $A$ started in its initial state misses exactly $n$
times, and the furthest-in-future strategy with capacity $k$ started with an empty cache misses
at most $k + \lceil n / k \rceil$ times.

articles.title: The paging adversary
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a deterministic online pager with cache size $k$ on the
$k + 1$ pages $0, \dots, k$. From a state $q$ of $A$, the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests is
empty for $n = 0$; for $n + 1$ it first requests the smallest page not in the cache of $q$ (page
$0$ if there is none) and then continues with the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests from the
state that $A$ reaches from $q$ by serving that request.

articles.title: Deterministic online paging algorithm
articles.statement:
A deterministic online paging algorithm with cache size `k`: a state machine whose cache
never holds more than `k` pages. Its moves need not be legal transitions; the lower bound holds
for any such machine.

articles.title: FIFO keeps the cache legal on every request sequence
articles.statement:
If a list $c$ of pages has no
duplicates and at most $k$ entries, then for every finite request sequence $\sigma$ the cache
obtained from $c$ by serving the requests of $\sigma$ in order, each with one FIFO step of
capacity $k$, also has no duplicates and at most $k$ entries.

articles.title: FIFO is `k`-competitive against the offline optimum
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $\sigma$ be a
finite request sequence, and let $c_0$ be a list of at most $k$ distinct pages. Let $m$ be the
number of misses of the furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ serving $\sigma$ from the
cache $c_0$. Then the FIFO online pager with capacity $k$, started in any legal cache (at most
$k$ distinct pages), misses at most $k m + k$ of the requests of $\sigma$.

articles.title: FIFO is `k`-competitive
articles.statement:
**FIFO is `k`-competitive** (Sleator and Tarjan). Let $k \ge 1$, and let $\tau$ be a legal
trace of the caching system with capacity $k$ that starts from a cache $c_0$ of at most $k$
distinct pages; let $m$ be its number of misses. Then the FIFO online pager with capacity $k$,
started in any legal cache (at most $k$ distinct pages) and serving the requests of $\tau$ in
order, misses at most $k m + k$ times.

articles.title: FIFO misses at most `k` times per phase
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a list of at most $k$ distinct pages
(the pages already in the current phase), let $c$ be any list of pages (a FIFO cache, oldest page
first), and let $L$ be a list of distinct pages, each of them in $S$, that is a suffix of $c$. For
every request sequence $\sigma$, let $P$ be the phase split off from $\sigma$ given $S$: the
longest prefix of $\sigma$ whose distinct pages, together with those of $S$, number at most $k$.
Then the number of misses of the FIFO step policy with capacity $k$ serving $P$ from $c$, plus the
length of $L$, is at most $k$.

The pages loaded so far in the phase ($L$, in load order) stay at the back of the queue: each
miss appends one, and an eviction removes the front, which is not among them while at most $k$
pages have been loaded. So a page of the phase is missed at most once, and a phase has at most
$k$ distinct pages.

articles.title: The ratio `k` is tight for FIFO
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and let $c$ and $d$ be natural numbers
with $c < k d$. For every natural number $b$ there is a finite request sequence $\sigma$ over
$k + 1$ pages with $c \cdot m + b < d \cdot f$, where $m$ is the number of misses of the
furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$ serving $\sigma$ from the empty cache, and $f$ is
the number of misses of the FIFO online pager with capacity $k$ serving $\sigma$ from its initial,
empty cache.

So no ratio $c / d < k$ makes FIFO $c / d$-competitive, whatever the additive constant.

articles.title: FIFO as an online pager misses as often as the FIFO step policy
articles.statement:
For every legal cache
$q$ of capacity $k$ (at most $k$ distinct pages) and every request sequence $\sigma$, the number
of misses of the FIFO online pager started in $q$ and serving $\sigma$ equals the number of misses
of the policy given by the FIFO step with capacity $k$ serving $\sigma$ from the cache $q$.

articles.title: FIFO paging as an online pager
articles.statement:
The online pager with capacity $k$ whose states are the
legal caches of capacity $k$ (lists of at most $k$ distinct pages, oldest first), whose initial
state is the empty cache, whose cache in a state is that list itself, and which serves a request
$p$ by one FIFO step with capacity $k$.

articles.title: One FIFO step keeps the cache legal
articles.statement:
If a list $c$ of pages has no duplicates and at most
$k$ entries, then for every page $p$ the cache produced from $c$ by one FIFO step with capacity
$k$ on request $p$ also has no duplicates and at most $k$ entries.

articles.title: One step of FIFO paging
articles.statement:
The cache is a list of pages, oldest first, and $k$ is the
capacity. On a request for a page $p$ already in the cache $c$, the cache stays $c$. Otherwise
$p$ is appended at the back of $c$; if $c$ had fewer than $k$ pages, that is the new cache, and
if not, the front page, the one loaded earliest, is removed as well.

articles.title: A full cache has a page outside the next $k - 1$ requests
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $c$ be a
list of $k$ distinct pages and let $f$ be any list of requests. Then the search through $c$ for
the first page that does not occur among the first $k - 1$ entries of $f$ succeeds; in
particular, some page of $c$ does not occur there.

articles.title: Legal cache
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ of pages and a capacity $k \in \mathbb{N}$, a legal cache
is a list of pages of $\alpha$ with no duplicates and at most $k$ entries.

articles.title: LRU as an online pager
articles.statement: LRU as an online pager.

articles.title: Cache after LRU serves a request sequence
articles.statement:
For a capacity $k$, a cache $c$ (a list of
pages, most recently used first) and a request sequence $\sigma$, this is the cache obtained from
$c$ by applying one LRU step with capacity $k$ for each request of $\sigma$, in order.

articles.title: The event of an LRU step
articles.statement:
For a capacity $k$, a cache $c$ (a list of pages, most recently
used first) and a requested page $p$, the LRU event is a hit on $p$ if $p \in c$. Otherwise it is
a miss on $p$ that evicts the last page of $c$ (the least recently used one) if $c$ is nonempty,
$k > 0$ and $c$ has at least $k$ pages, and a miss on $p$ without eviction in all other cases.

articles.title: LRU is $k$-competitive against the offline optimum
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, and let $c$ and $c_0$
be duplicate-free caches with at most $k$ pages each. For every request sequence $\sigma$, the
trace that LRU with capacity $k$ emits when serving $\sigma$ from $c$ has at most $k m + k$
misses, where $m$ is the number of misses of the furthest-in-future manager with capacity $k$
serving $\sigma$ from $c_0$.

Furthest-in-future misses no more often than any legal trace serving the same requests from the
same cache, so it is the offline optimum.

articles.title: LRU is $k$-competitive
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and let $c$ be a duplicate-free cache with at most
$k$ pages. Let $e$ be a legal trace of the cache system with capacity $k$ that starts from a
duplicate-free cache with at most $k$ pages, and let $m$ be its number of misses. Then the trace
that LRU with capacity $k$ emits when serving, from $c$, the requests of $e$ in order has at most
$k m + k$ misses.

This is the bound of Sleator and Tarjan for an online and an offline cache of the same size.

articles.title: LRU misses at most $k - |S|$ times in the rest of a phase
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $c$ a
cache (most recently used first) and $S$ a duplicate-free list of at most $k$ pages equal to the
first $|S|$ pages of $c$. For every request sequence $\sigma$, let $\pi$ be the phase that the
phase split cuts from $\sigma$ with $S$ as the pages already in the phase: the longest prefix of
$\sigma$ whose distinct pages, together with those of $S$, number at most $k$. Then the number of
LRU misses with capacity $k$ serving $\pi$ from $c$, plus $|S|$, is at most $k$.

articles.title: Number of LRU misses
articles.statement:
For a capacity $k$, a cache $c$ and a request sequence $\sigma$, this
is the number of requests of $\sigma$ that are not in the current cache when they are served,
where the cache starts at $c$ and after each request is updated by one LRU step with capacity
$k$.

articles.title: LRU as an online pager has LRU's miss count
articles.statement:
For every cache $c$ of at most $k$ pages and
every request sequence $\sigma$, the number of misses of LRU with capacity $k$, viewed as an
online pager and started in the state with cache $c$, on $\sigma$ equals the number of misses of
LRU with capacity $k$ started with cache $c$ on $\sigma$.

articles.title: The recency invariant for a repeated page
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $c$ a cache (most
recently used first) and $S$ a list of at most $k$ pages equal to the first $|S|$ pages of $c$.
If $p \in S$, then after one LRU step with capacity $k$ serving $p$, the first $|S|$ pages of the
cache are $p$ followed by $S$ with the first occurrence of $p$ removed.

articles.title: The recency invariant for a new page
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $c$ a cache (most recently
used first) and $S$ a list with $|S| + 1 \le k$ equal to the first $|S|$ pages of $c$. If
$p \notin S$, then after one LRU step with capacity $k$ serving $p$, the first $|S| + 1$ pages of
the cache are $p$ followed by $S$.

articles.title: One LRU step
articles.statement:
For a capacity $k$, a cache $c$ (a list of pages, most recently used first)
and a requested page $p$, the LRU step removes the first occurrence of $p$ from $c$ (if any), puts
$p$ at the front, and keeps the first $k$ pages of the result. On a miss with a cache of exactly
$k \ge 1$ pages, this evicts the last page, the least recently used one.

articles.title: Each LRU step is a legal transition
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity and $c$ a duplicate-free cache
with at most $k$ pages. For every page $p$, the cache system with capacity $k$ has a transition
from $c$, labelled by the LRU event for $p$ at $c$, to the cache produced by one LRU step with
capacity $k$ serving $p$.

articles.title: LRU is a legal cache manager
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, $c$ a cache given as a list of pages
without repetitions with at most $k$ pages, and $\sigma$ a request sequence. Then the sequence of
events that LRU emits when serving $\sigma$ from $c$ is a run of the cache system with capacity
$k$ from $c$ to the cache LRU holds after serving $\sigma$; the pages requested by these events are
exactly $\sigma$, in order; and the number of misses among these events equals the number of
misses of LRU on $\sigma$ from $c$.

articles.title: The LRU trace
articles.statement:
Given a capacity $k$, a cache $c$ and a request sequence $\sigma$, the
events LRU emits on $\sigma$ from $c$: nothing on the empty sequence, and on a sequence $p$
followed by $\sigma'$, the event LRU emits when serving $p$ from $c$, followed by the events LRU
emits on $\sigma'$ from the cache after one LRU step with capacity $k$ serving $p$ from $c$.

articles.title: After a miss on a full cache, every page except the evicted one is present
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a
list of $k$ distinct pages among the $k + 1$ pages $0, \dots, k$, let $p$ be a page not in $c$,
and let $v$ be any page. Then every page $x \neq v$ lies in the cache obtained from $c$ by
removing $v$ and adding $p$.

articles.title: The pager misses every request
articles.statement: **The pager misses every request** of the adversary's sequence.

articles.title: Hits do not change the offline strategy's misses
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, let $c$ be a
cache and let $w$ be a request sequence all of whose requests lie in $c$. Then for every request
sequence $\tau$, the offline strategy with capacity $k$ (on a miss with a full cache, evict the
first cached page not among the next $k - 1$ requests, if there is one) started with cache $c$
misses as many times on $w$ followed by $\tau$ as on $\tau$ alone.

articles.title: The offline trace misses at most once every $k$ requests
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and consider the
$k + 1$ pages $0, 1, \dots, k$. Let $N$ be a natural number, $\sigma$ a sequence of $n \le N$
requests to these pages, and $c$ a cache of $|c| \le k$ distinct pages. Then the number of misses
of the offline trace with cache size $k$ from $c$ on $\sigma$ is at most
$(k - |c|) + \lfloor (n + k - 1) / k \rfloor = (k - |c|) + \lceil n / k \rceil$: after at most
$k - |c|$ misses filling the cache, at most one miss every $k$ requests.

articles.title: Misses of an online pager
articles.statement:
For an online pager $A$, a state $q$ and a request sequence
$\sigma$, the number of misses of $A$ from $q$ on $\sigma$ counts the requests of $\sigma$ that
are not in the cache of the current state, where the run starts at $q$ and each request moves
$A$ to its next state.

articles.title: No deterministic online pager is better than $k$-competitive
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and let $A$
be a deterministic online pager with cache size $k$ on the $k + 1$ pages $0, \dots, k$. For a
request sequence $\sigma$, write $A(\sigma)$ for the number of misses of $A$ started in its
initial state on $\sigma$, and $\mathrm{OPT}(\sigma)$ for the number of misses of the
furthest-in-future strategy with capacity $k$ started with an empty cache on $\sigma$. Then for
all natural numbers $c$, $d$ with $c < kd$ and every natural number $b$, there is a request
sequence $\sigma$ with $c \cdot \mathrm{OPT}(\sigma) + b < d \cdot A(\sigma)$. That is, the pager
misses more than $c / d$ times the optimum plus $b / d$.

articles.title: Each offline step is a legal transition
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $c$ be a cache of at most $k$
distinct pages, let $p$ be a requested page and let $f$ be the list of future requests. Then the
event and the new cache produced by the offline step with cache size $k$ on $c$, $p$ and $f$
form a legal transition from $c$ of the caching system with capacity $k$.

articles.title: Offline paging step
articles.statement:
Given a cache size $k$, a cache $c$ (a list of pages), a requested
page $p$ and the list $f$ of future requests, the offline step returns an event and a new cache.
If $p \in c$, it is a hit on $p$ and the cache is unchanged. Otherwise, if $c$ has fewer than $k$
pages, it is a miss on $p$ with no eviction and the new cache is $p$ followed by $c$. Otherwise,
if some page of $c$ does not occur among the first $k - 1$ entries of $f$ (no entries at all when
$k = 0$, and all of $f$ when $f$ is shorter), it is a miss on $p$ evicting the first such page $v$
in $c$, and the new cache is $p$ followed by $c$ with the first occurrence of $v$ removed. If
there is no such page, it is a miss on $p$ with no eviction and the new cache is $p$ followed by
$c$.

articles.title: The offline trace is legal
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$, let $c$ be a cache of at most $k$ distinct
pages and let $\sigma$ be a list of requests. Then the offline trace with cache size $k$ from
$c$ on $\sigma$ is a legal run of the caching system with capacity $k$ from $c$ to some final
cache, and the pages served by its events are, in order, exactly $\sigma$.

articles.title: Offline paging trace
articles.statement:
Given a cache size $k$, the offline trace from a cache $c$ on a list
of requests is defined by recursion on the list: on the empty list it is empty, and on a list
with first request $p$ and remaining requests $r$ it is the event of the offline step with cache
size $k$ on $c$, $p$ and $r$, followed by the offline trace on $r$ from the new cache of that
step.

articles.title: The outside page is not cached
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number and let $c$ be a list of at
most $k$ pages from $\{0, \dots, k\}$. Then the outside page of $c$ does not occur in $c$.

articles.title: Outside page of a cache
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$ and a list $c$ of pages from
$\{0, \dots, k\}$, the outside page of $c$ is the smallest $x \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ that does not
occur in $c$, or $0$ if every page of $\{0, \dots, k\}$ occurs in $c$.

articles.title: A phase ends only on a $(k + 1)$-st distinct page
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a capacity, let $s$ be a
list of pages without repetitions with at most $k$ pages (the pages already in the current
phase), and let $\sigma$ be a request sequence. If the remainder left after splitting off a phase
from $\sigma$ given $s$ starts with a page $q$, then there is a list $S$ of exactly $k$ pairwise
distinct pages, none equal to $q$, each of which lies in $s$ or in that phase.

articles.title: Splitting off a phase
articles.statement:
Given a capacity $k$ and a list $s$ of pages (the pages already in
the current phase, most recent first), a request sequence $\sigma$ is split into a phase and a
remainder as follows. The empty sequence splits into two empty parts. For a sequence $p$
followed by $\sigma'$: if $p$ is in $s$, then $p$ joins the phase and $\sigma'$ is split with $s$
replaced by $p$ followed by $s$ with its first occurrence of $p$ removed; if $p$ is not in $s$
and $s$ has fewer than $k$ entries, then $p$ joins the phase and $\sigma'$ is split with $p$
added at the front of $s$; otherwise the phase is empty and the remainder is the whole sequence.

When $s$ has no repetitions and at most $k$ pages, the phase is the longest prefix of $\sigma$
whose distinct pages, together with those of $s$, number at most $k$.

articles.title: A policy that misses at most $k$ times per phase is $k$-competitive
articles.statement:
Let $k \ge 1$ and
consider a paging policy on list caches, given by its step function. Suppose that, started from
any cache, the policy misses at most $k$ times on the first phase of every request sequence (the
longest prefix of the sequence with at most $k$ distinct pages). Let $T$ be a legal trace of
caching with capacity $k$ (a run of the cache transition system) whose initial cache is a list of
at most $k$ pages with no page repeated, and let $m$ be the number of misses in $T$. Then, started
from any cache, the policy misses at most $km + k$ times on the sequence of requests served by
$T$.

articles.title: LRU as a policy on list caches
articles.statement:
For every capacity $k$, the misses of the paging policy
whose step is the LRU step with capacity $k$ coincide with the LRU misses with capacity $k$, from
every starting cache and on every request sequence.

articles.title: Misses of a paging policy on list caches
articles.statement:
Let a paging policy be given by its step
function, which maps a cache (a list of pages) and a requested page to the next cache. Starting
from a cache $c$, the policy serves a request sequence $p_1, \dots, p_n$ by setting $c_0 = c$ and
$c_i = \mathrm{step}(c_{i-1}, p_i)$ for each $i$; its number of misses is the number of indices
$i$ with $p_i \notin c_{i-1}$.

articles.title: Positions in a list and in its reverse
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a list of length $\ell$ with no
repeated entries and $x$ is an entry of $L$, then the access cost of $x$ in $L$ plus the access
cost of $x$ in the reverse of $L$ equals $\ell + 1$: the positions of $x$ in $L$ and in its
reverse, counting from $1$, add up to $\ell + 1$.

articles.title: Access cost
articles.statement:
The cost of accessing an item $x$ in a list $L$ is its position in $L$,
counting from $1$: one more than the index of the first occurrence of $x$ in $L$. If $x$ does not
occur in $L$, the cost is the length of $L$ plus one.

articles.title: Online and offline costs on the adversary's sequence
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a nonempty list of $\ell$
distinct items, let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$, let
$d$ be an item and $n$ a natural number, and let $\sigma$ be the adversary's sequence of $n$
requests against $A$ from its initial state, with default item $d$. Then the cost of $A$ on
$\sigma$ from its initial state is $n \ell$, and there are lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, each a
rearrangement of $M$, with $L_0 = M$ such that the offline cost $C$ of this sequence of lists on
$\sigma$ satisfies $2 C \le n (\ell + 1) + 2 (\ell + \ell^2)$.

articles.title: The list-update adversary
articles.statement:
Given a deterministic online list-update algorithm $A$, a
default item $d$, a number $n$ and a state $q$ of $A$, the adversary's sequence is the sequence of
$n$ requests that starts in state $q$, always requests the last item of $A$'s current list, and
then moves $A$ to its next state on that request. If the current list is empty, the default item
$d$ is requested instead.

articles.title: Counting the entries before an entry
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a list with no repeated entries and $x$
is an entry of $L$, then the number of entries of $L$ whose index is less than the index of $x$
equals the index of $x$ (indices counted from $0$).

articles.title: The adversary makes every access cost the full length of the list
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a nonempty
list of $\ell$ distinct items and let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the
items of $M$. For every default item $d$, every natural number $n$ and every state $q$ of $A$,
the cost of $A$ from state $q$ on the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests from $q$ with default
item $d$ is $n \ell$.

articles.title: Cost of an online list-update algorithm
articles.statement:
The cost of a deterministic online list-update
algorithm $A$ on a request sequence $x_1, \dots, x_m$ from a state $q_0$ is
$c_1 + \dots + c_m$, where $q_i$ is the state $A$ moves to from $q_{i-1}$ on request $x_i$ and
$c_i$ is the access cost of $x_i$ in the list of state $q_{i-1}$. The empty sequence costs $0$.

articles.title: Deterministic online list-update algorithm
articles.statement:
A deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of `M`: a state machine whose list
is always a rearrangement of `M`. Its rearrangements are free, which only strengthens the lower
bound.

articles.title: A free move rearranges the list
articles.statement:
If $x$ is an item of a list $L$, then for every index
$j$ (counting from $0$), the list obtained from $L$ by the free move of $x$ to index $j$ is a
rearrangement (permutation) of $L$.

articles.title: Free move
articles.statement:
A free exchange (Sleator and Tarjan): right after accessing $x$ in a list $L$,
move $x$ forward to index $j$ (indices counted from $0$), at no charge. If the index of $x$ in
$L$ is at most $j$, the list is unchanged, so $x$ never moves backward for free; otherwise the
result is obtained by erasing the first occurrence of $x$ from $L$ and inserting $x$ back so that
it has index $j$.

articles.title: Indices after erasing an entry
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list with no repeated entries and let
$a \ne x$ be entries of $M$. After erasing $x$ from $M$, the index of $a$ is unchanged if $a$
comes before $x$ in $M$, and is one less if $a$ comes after $x$ (indices counted from $0$).

articles.title: Move-to-front keeps the relative order of the other items
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list without
duplicates, $x$ an item of $M$, and let $M'$ be the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the
front. For any items $a \ne x$ and $b \ne x$ of $M$, $a$ comes before $b$ in $M'$ if and only if
$a$ comes before $b$ in $M$.

articles.title: Free moves never add inversions against a list headed by the moved item
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list
without duplicates, $x$ an item of $L$, and $N$ a list that is empty or starts with $x$, all of
whose items occur in $L$. For every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $L'$ be the list obtained from $L$ by
moving $x$ forward for free so that exactly $j$ items precede it, where $L' = L$ if at most $j$
items already precede $x$ in $L$. Then the number of inversions of $L'$ against $N$ is at most the
number of inversions of $L$ against $N$.

This applies to move-to-front's list right after accessing $x$.

articles.title: Inversions are at most the squared length
articles.statement:
For any lists $M$ and $L$, the number of
inversions of $L$ against $M$ is at most $\ell^2$, where $\ell$ is the length of $M$.

articles.title: Inversion set of two lists
articles.statement:
For lists $M$ and $L$, the inversion set is the set of pairs
$(a, b)$ of items of $M$ with $a$ before $b$ in $M$ and $b$ before $a$ in $L$, that is, the pairs
that $M$ and $L$ order differently. Here the position of an item in a list is the index of its
first occurrence, and an item that does not occur in the list sits at the position equal to the
length of the list.

articles.title: Triangle inequality for inversions
articles.statement:
Let $M$, $L$ and $L'$ be lists with $L$ a
rearrangement of $M$. Then the number of inversions of $L'$ against $M$ is at most the number of
inversions of $L$ against $M$ plus the number of inversions of $L'$ against $L$.

articles.title: Number of inversions between two lists
articles.statement:
For lists $M$ and $L$, the number of inversions
of $L$ against $M$ is the size of their inversion set: the number of pairs $(a, b)$ of items of
$M$ with $a$ before $b$ in $M$ and $b$ before $a$ in $L$, where the position of an item in a list
is the index of its first occurrence, or the length of the list if it does not occur.

When $L$ is a rearrangement of a list $M$ without duplicates, this is the Kendall tau distance
between them.

articles.title: The list of an algorithm on a nonempty list is never empty
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a deterministic
online list-update algorithm on the items of a nonempty list $M$. Then in every state of $A$, the
list of $A$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Members of the inversion set
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $L$ be lists. If a pair $(a, b)$ belongs to the
inversion set of $M$ and $L$, then $a$ and $b$ are items of $M$, $a$ comes before $b$ in $M$, and
$b$ comes before $a$ in $L$. Here the position of an item in a list is the index of its first
occurrence, and an item that does not occur in the list sits at the position equal to the length
of the list.

articles.title: Amortized bound for move-to-front over a request sequence, with free exchanges
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be
a list without duplicates, $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$, $L_0, L_1,
\dots$ lists that are each a rearrangement of $M$, and $J_0, J_1, \dots$ natural numbers.
Accessing the item at position $i$ of a list, counting from $1$, costs $i$. Let $C$ be the total
access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, $F$ the list it ends with, and $D$
the cost on $\sigma$ of the offline algorithm with free exchanges that serves the $t$-th request
(counting from $0$) with list $L_t$, paying its access cost, then moves the accessed item forward
for free so that exactly $J_t$ items precede it (no move if at most $J_t$ items already precede
it), and finally rearranges the resulting list into $L_{t+1}$, paying one for each pair of items
whose relative order changes. Writing $\mathrm{inv}(N, K)$ for the number of inversions of $K$
against $N$,

$$C + \mathrm{inv}(F, L_m) + m \le 2D + \mathrm{inv}(M, L_0).$$

articles.title: Amortized bound for move-to-front over a request sequence
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list without
duplicates, $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$, and $L_0, L_1, \dots$ lists
that are each a rearrangement of $M$. Accessing the item at position $i$ of a list, counting from
$1$, costs $i$. Let $C$ be the total access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$,
$F$ the list it ends with, and $D$ the cost on $\sigma$ of the offline algorithm without free
exchanges that serves the $t$-th request (counting from $0$) with list $L_t$, paying its access
cost, and then rearranges it into $L_{t+1}$, paying one for each pair of items whose relative
order changes. Writing $\mathrm{inv}(N, K)$ for the number of inversions of $K$ against $N$,

$$C + \mathrm{inv}(F, L_m) + m \le 2D + \mathrm{inv}(M, L_0).$$

articles.title: Move-to-front is 2-competitive
articles.statement:
In the model of Sleator and Tarjan (1985) with free
exchanges, let $M$ be a list of distinct items and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an
item of $M$. Consider an offline algorithm given by lists $L_0, L_1, \ldots$, each a
rearrangement of $M$ with $L_0 = M$, and natural numbers $J_0, J_1, \ldots$. It serves request
$t$ (counting from $0$) with the list $L_t$ and pays the position of the request in $L_t$
(counting from $1$). If more than $J_t$ items precede the request in $L_t$, it then moves the
request forward for free so that exactly $J_t$ items precede it, keeping the order of the other
items. Finally it pays one for each pair of items whose relative order differs between the
resulting list and $L_{t+1}$. Then the access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from
$M$, plus $m$, is at most twice the total cost of the offline algorithm.

articles.title: Move-to-front against a static list
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list of distinct items, $L$ a
rearrangement of $M$, and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$. Then the
access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, plus $m$, is at most twice the cost
of serving $\sigma$ with the fixed list $L$ (the sum over the requests of their positions in $L$,
counting from $1$), plus the number of inversions between $M$ and $L$ (the pairs of items that
$M$ and $L$ order differently).

articles.title: Move-to-front is 2-competitive without free exchanges
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list of distinct
items and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$. Consider an offline
algorithm that serves request $t$ with a list $L_t$, where every $L_t$ is a rearrangement of
$M$ and $L_0 = M$: it pays the position of the request in $L_t$ (counting from $1$), and then
one for each pair of items whose relative order differs between $L_t$ and $L_{t+1}$. Then the
access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, plus $m$, is at most twice the
total cost of the offline algorithm.

This is the special case of the model with free exchanges in which no free exchange is made.

articles.title: Cost of move-to-front
articles.statement:
Starting from a list $L$, move-to-front serves a request sequence
$\sigma$ one request at a time: a request $x$ costs the position of $x$ in the current list,
counting from $1$ (an item not in the list costs its length plus one), and then $x$ is moved to
the front (inserted at the front if absent). The cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is
the sum of these access costs.

articles.title: Final list of move-to-front
articles.statement:
Starting from a list $L$ and serving a request sequence
$\sigma$, move-to-front moves each request $x$ in turn to the front of the current list
(inserting it at the front if it is absent). The final list of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from
$L$ is the list it ends with.

articles.title: Online move-to-front pays the move-to-front cost
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list and $\sigma$ a
request sequence whose requests are all items of $M$. From any state of online move-to-front
on $M$, its access cost on $\sigma$ equals the cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from
the list of that state.

articles.title: Online move-to-front
articles.statement:
For a list $M$, online move-to-front is the online list-update
algorithm on the items of $M$ whose states are the rearrangements of $M$, starting from $M$
itself: on a request $x$ that is in the current list it moves $x$ to the front, and it ignores
requests that are not in the current list.

articles.title: Move-to-front rearranges the list
articles.statement:
If $x$ is an item of a list $M$, then the list
obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front is a rearrangement (permutation) of $M$.

articles.title: The amortized cost of a move-to-front step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list of distinct items, $L$ a
rearrangement of $M$ (the offline list), and $x$ an item of $M$ at position $k$ in $M$ and
position $i$ in $L$, counting from $1$. Let $\Phi$ be the number of inversions between $M$ and
$L$ (the pairs of items that the two lists order differently), and $\Phi'$ the number of
inversions between the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front and $L$. Then
$k + \Phi' \le \Phi + 2i - 1$.

This is the amortized step of Sleator and Tarjan's analysis, with potential $\Phi$.

articles.title: Move-to-front
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ and an item $x$, moving $x$ to the front gives the list
consisting of $x$ followed by $L$ with its first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not
occur in $L$, this is $x$ followed by $L$.

articles.title: No deterministic online list-update algorithm beats $2 - 2/(\ell + 1)$
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
nonempty list of $\ell$ distinct items and let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update
algorithm on the items of $M$. Let $c$, $d$ and $b$ be natural numbers with
$c (\ell + 1) < 2 \ell d$ (so $d \ge 1$ and $c / d < 2\ell / (\ell + 1) = 2 - 2/(\ell + 1)$).
Then there are a request sequence $\sigma$, each request an item of $M$, and lists
$L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, each a rearrangement of $M$, with $L_0 = M$, such that
$c \cdot C + d \cdot b < d \cdot K$, where $C$ is the offline cost without free exchanges of
$L_0, L_1, \dots$ on $\sigma$ and $K$ is the cost of $A$ on $\sigma$ from its initial state.

The offline lists make no free exchanges, so the same holds with the offline cost with free
exchanges in place of $C$.

## Sources

- Karp and Raghavan, see Irani, *Two results on the list update problem*, IPL 38, 1991; Borodin and El-Yaniv, Chapter 1.

articles.title: The static cost is the offline cost of a constant list
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ and every
request sequence $\sigma$, the offline cost (without free exchanges) of serving $\sigma$ with the
constant sequence of lists $L, L, L, \dots$ equals the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $L$.

articles.title: Without free moves the two offline costs agree
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a natural number and let
$L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$ be lists, each of length at most $K$. Take every free-exchange target to be
$K$; this moves nothing, since every item already has index at most $K$. Then for every request
sequence $\sigma$, the offline cost with free exchanges of serving $\sigma$ with $L_0, L_1, \dots$
equals the offline cost without free exchanges of serving $\sigma$ with $L_0, L_1, \dots$.

articles.title: Offline cost with free exchanges
articles.statement:
Given lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, target indices
$J_0, J_1, J_2, \dots$ and a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$, let $L_t'$ be the
list obtained from $L_t$ by the free exchange that moves $x_t$ forward to index $J_t$ (counting
from $0$); it equals $L_t$ if $x_t$ already has index at most $J_t$. The offline cost with free
exchanges of $\sigma$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in $L_t$ (its position,
counting from $1$) plus the number of inversions between $L_t'$ and $L_{t+1}$.

This is the model of Sleator and Tarjan: the free exchange costs nothing, and each pair of items
whose relative order changes from $L_t'$ to $L_{t+1}$ costs one. With no free moves it is the
offline cost without free exchanges.

articles.title: Switching lists after the first request
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a list of length $\ell$ and $R$ a list,
and write $\mathrm{inv}(M, R)$ for the number of inversions between $M$ and $R$. For every request
sequence $\sigma$ of items of $M$, the offline cost (without free exchanges) of serving $\sigma$
with the lists $M, R, R, R, \dots$ is at most $\ell + \mathrm{inv}(M, R)$ plus the static cost of
serving $\sigma$ with $R$.

articles.title: Offline cost without free exchanges
articles.statement:
Given lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, the offline cost
of a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost
of $x_t$ in $L_t$ (its position, counting from $1$) plus the number of inversions between $L_t$
and $L_{t+1}$. That is, the algorithm serves request $t$ with $L_t$ and then rearranges it into
$L_{t+1}$, paying one for each pair of items whose relative order it changes.

Adding free exchanges gives the offline cost with free exchanges.

articles.title: A list or its reverse serves any sequence at average cost at most $(\ell + 1)/2$
articles.statement:
Let $L$
be a list of $\ell$ distinct items. For every request sequence $\sigma$ of $m$ items of $L$, the
static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $L$ plus the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with the reverse
of $L$ equals $m(\ell + 1)$.

In particular, one of the two static costs is at most $m(\ell + 1)/2$.

articles.title: Static cost
articles.statement:
The static cost of serving a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$
with a fixed list $L$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in $L$, its position in
$L$ counting from $1$.

articles.title: The adversary's offline matching
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an online matcher, $h$ a list of earlier
neighbour lists and $ps$ a list of gadgets, pairs $(u, v)$ of left vertices. The list
$\mathrm{opt}(A, h, ps)$ of left vertices is empty when $ps$ is empty. Otherwise, for the first
gadget $(u, v)$, let $x = v$ if $A$, after the history $h$, proposes $v$ for an arrival with
neighbour list $[u, v]$, and $x = u$ otherwise; the list starts with $u, v$ in the first case and
with $v, u$ in the second, and continues with $\mathrm{opt}(A, h', ps')$, where $h'$ is $h$
extended by the neighbour lists $[u, v]$ and $[x]$ and $ps'$ is the list of remaining gadgets.

articles.title: The adversary for online bipartite matching
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an online matcher, $h$ a list of
earlier neighbour lists and $ps$ a list of gadgets, pairs $(u, v)$ of left vertices. The
adversary's sequence of arrivals is empty when $ps$ is empty. Otherwise, for the first gadget
$(u, v)$, let $x = v$ if $A$, after the history $h$, proposes $v$ for an arrival with neighbour
list $[u, v]$, and $x = u$ otherwise (a proposal of $u$, of no vertex, or of a non-neighbour).
The sequence is an arrival with neighbour list $[u, v]$, then an arrival with neighbour list
$[x]$, then the adversary's sequence for $A$, the history $h$ extended by $[u, v]$ and $[x]$, and
the remaining gadgets.

articles.title: Greedy online matching is `1/2`-competitive
articles.statement:
Every matching has at most twice as many
edges as the greedy one. An edge of the matching whose right vertex the greedy algorithm matched
is charged to that right vertex, any other edge to its left vertex, which the greedy algorithm
matched by maximality; a matching charges each greedy edge at most once on each side.

articles.title: Greedy online matching is within a factor $2$ of the maximum
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph, the
maximum matching computed by augmenting paths has at most twice as many edges as the greedy online
matching, in which the right vertices arrive in increasing order.

articles.title: Done right vertices
articles.statement:
Given a partner array, which assigns to each right vertex its partner
on the left if it has one, the right vertices of a list $S$ are done when, for every right vertex
$j$ of $S$ and every left vertex $i$ adjacent to $j$, $j$ is matched or $i$ is matched.

articles.title: The $1/2$ lower bound with a matching of the arrivals' graph
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
and every online matcher $A$ with $2n$ left vertices, there is a sequence $\sigma$ of arrivals
(neighbour lists) such that the bipartite graph of $\sigma$, in which left vertex $i$ is adjacent
to arrival $j$ when $i$ lies in the $j$-th neighbour list, has a matching with $2n$ edges, while
$A$, run on $\sigma$ from the empty history with no left vertex matched, matches at most $n$
arrivals.

articles.title: Perfect matchings of the arrivals are matchings of their graph
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a sequence
of arrivals (neighbour lists) and $m$ a perfect matching of $\sigma$. Then the bipartite graph of
$\sigma$, in which left vertex $i$ is adjacent to arrival $j$ when $i$ lies in the $j$-th
neighbour list, has a matching with as many edges as $\sigma$ has arrivals.

articles.title: No deterministic online bipartite matching algorithm beats `1/2`
articles.statement:
**No deterministic online bipartite matching algorithm beats `1/2`** (Karp, Vazirani and
Vazirani): against every algorithm with `2 n` left vertices, some sequence of `2 n` arrivals has
a perfect matching while the algorithm matches at most `n` of them.

articles.title: Gadgets with distinct vertices
articles.statement:
A list of gadgets, pairs $(u, v)$ of left vertices, has
distinct vertices when $u 
e v$ for every gadget $(u, v)$ of the list, and any two gadgets
$(u, v)$ and $(u', v')$ at different positions of the list share no vertex:
$u 
e u'$, $u 
e v'$, $v 
e u'$ and $v 
e v'$.

articles.title: The $n$ gadgets on $2n$ left vertices
articles.statement:
For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of gadgets
$(0, 1), (2, 3), \dots, (2n - 2, 2n - 1)$ of left vertices in $\{0, \dots, 2n - 1\}$, that is, the
pairs $(2k, 2k + 1)$ for $k = 0, \dots, n - 1$ in increasing order of $k$.

articles.title: The greedy matching is maximal
articles.statement: Every edge has a matched endpoint.

articles.title: The greedy online matching
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with left vertices $0, \dots, a - 1$ and
right vertices $0, \dots, b - 1$, the greedy online matching is the partner array obtained by
starting from the empty matching and letting the right vertices arrive in the order
$0, 1, \dots, b - 1$, each arriving vertex being matched to its first free left neighbour in the
order $0, \dots, a - 1$, or left unmatched if no neighbour is free.

It is computed on arrays, with one array write per arrival.

articles.title: Greedy run on an array
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with left vertices $0, \dots, a - 1$ and right
vertices $0, \dots, b - 1$, start from an array whose entry $k$ holds the partner of the right
vertex $k$, a missing entry meaning no partner, and let the right vertices of a list $L$ arrive one
after another in the order of $L$. Each arrival performs the greedy step on the array: the entry of
the arriving vertex $j$ is set to the first left neighbour of $j$, in the order $0, \dots, a - 1$,
that is free, that is, the partner of none of the right vertices $0, \dots, b - 1$ in the current
array, or to none if no neighbour of $j$ is free; if the array has no entry $j$, it is unchanged.

articles.title: Invariants of the greedy run
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of distinct right vertices, all unmatched
in a valid partner array $m$, and let $S$ be a list of right vertices that are done for $m$. Then
the partner array obtained from $m$ by the greedy run along $L$ is valid, and every right vertex
of $L$ or of $S$ is done for it.

articles.title: Greedy online bipartite matching
articles.statement:
Consider a bipartite graph with left vertices
$0, \dots, a-1$ and right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$, an assignment $m$ giving each right vertex
either a left partner or none, and a list $j_1, \dots, j_n$ of right vertices, the arrivals in
order. The greedy matching from $m$ on these arrivals is the assignment obtained from $m$ by
applying the greedy step of online bipartite matching for the arrival of $j_1$, then of $j_2$,
and so on up to $j_n$; if the list is empty, it is $m$.

articles.title: The greedy online matching is a matching
articles.statement:
The set of pairs $(i, j)$ such that the greedy
online matching assigns the left vertex $i$ to the right vertex $j$ is a matching of the bipartite
graph.

articles.title: The adversary's arrivals have a perfect matching
articles.statement:
For every online matcher $A$, every
list $h$ of earlier neighbour lists and every list of gadgets with distinct vertices, the
adversary's offline matching for $A$, $h$ and the gadgets is a perfect matching of the
adversary's arrivals for $A$, $h$ and the gadgets. In each gadget, the first arrival takes the
vertex the second one does not.

articles.title: Perfect matchings of a sequence of arrivals
articles.statement:
A list $m$ of left vertices is a perfect
matching of a sequence $\sigma$ of arrivals (neighbour lists) when $m$ and $\sigma$ have the same
length, the entries of $m$ are pairwise distinct, and for each $j$ the $j$-th entry of $m$ lies
in the $j$-th neighbour list of $\sigma$.

articles.title: The adversary holds every algorithm to one match per gadget
articles.statement:
For every online matcher
$A$, every list $h$ of earlier neighbour lists, every list $U$ of left vertices and every list of
$k$ gadgets, the run of $A$ on the adversary's arrivals for $A$, $h$ and the gadgets, after the
history $h$ and with the left vertices of $U$ already matched, matches at most $k$ arrivals.

articles.title: Number of arrivals an online matcher matches
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an online matcher with $a$ left
vertices, $h$ a history (the neighbour lists of earlier arrivals), $U$ a list of left vertices
already matched, and $\sigma$ a sequence of arrivals, each given by its list of left neighbours.
The run of $A$ on $\sigma$ takes the arrivals in order: on an arrival with neighbour list $N$,
$A$ proposes a left vertex, or none, from the current history and $N$; a proposal $i$ with
$i \in N$ and $i \notin U$ is accepted, counting the arrival as matched and adding $i$ to $U$,
and otherwise the arrival stays unmatched; then $N$ is appended to the history. The value is the
number of arrivals matched.

articles.title: Finite-size lower bound for deterministic online matching
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be
natural numbers with $d < 2c$ and $b < n$. For every online matcher $A$ with $2n$ left vertices
there are a sequence $\sigma$ of arrivals and a perfect matching $m$ of $\sigma$ such that
$d \cdot \mathrm{ALG} + b < c \cdot |m|$, where $\mathrm{ALG}$ is the number of arrivals of
$\sigma$ that $A$ matches when run from the empty history with no left vertex matched, and $|m|$
is the length of $m$.

At a fixed size some additive constant always suffices, which is why $b$ is bounded by $n$;
letting the size grow removes the bound.

articles.title: No deterministic online matcher beats ratio $1/2$, with any additive constant
articles.statement:
Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of online matchers, $A_n$ having $2n$ left vertices, and
let $b$, $c$, $d$ be natural numbers with $d < 2c$. Then for some $n$ there are a sequence
$\sigma$ of arrivals on the left vertices of $A_n$ and a perfect matching $m$ of $\sigma$ such
that $d \cdot \mathrm{ALG} + b < c \cdot |m|$, where $\mathrm{ALG}$ is the number of arrivals of
$\sigma$ that $A_n$ matches when run from the empty history with no left vertex matched, and
$|m|$ is the length of $m$.

For $d > 0$ this says that the family is not $c/d$-competitive, whatever the additive constant.

articles.title: Deterministic online bipartite matching algorithm
articles.statement:
A deterministic online bipartite
matching algorithm with $a$ offline (left) vertices $0, \dots, a - 1$ is given by a proposal
rule: on each arrival it receives the neighbour lists (lists of left vertices) of all earlier
arrivals, in order, and the neighbour list of the current arrival, and proposes a left vertex to
match the arrival to, or none.

articles.title: Greedy step on an array
articles.statement:
In a bipartite graph with left vertices $0, \dots, a - 1$ and right
vertices $0, \dots, b - 1$, take an array whose entry $k$ holds the partner of the right vertex $k$,
a missing entry meaning no partner. On the arrival of a right vertex $j$, entry $j$ is set to the
first left neighbour of $j$, in the order $0, \dots, a - 1$, that is free, that is, the partner of
none of the right vertices $0, \dots, b - 1$ in the array, or to none if no neighbour of $j$ is
free; if the array has no entry $j$, it is unchanged.

Storing the partners in an array computes each choice once per arrival; evaluating the composed
function updates of the specification directly would recompute every earlier choice at each
lookup, a cost exponential in the number of right vertices.

articles.title: Earlier partners survive an arrival
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be an assignment giving each right vertex of
a bipartite graph either a left partner or none, and let $j$ be a right vertex with no partner
in $m$. If a right vertex $j'$ has partner $i$ in $m$, then $j'$ still has partner $i$ after
the greedy step for the arrival of $j$.

articles.title: Greedy step of online bipartite matching
articles.statement:
Consider a bipartite graph with left vertices
$0, \dots, a-1$ and right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$, and an assignment $m$ giving each right
vertex either a left partner or none. On the arrival of a right vertex $j$, the greedy step
returns the assignment that agrees with $m$ at every right vertex other than $j$, and gives $j$
the smallest left neighbour of $j$ that is free in $m$ (the partner of no right vertex), or no
partner if $j$ has no free neighbour.

articles.title: Graph of a sequence of arrivals
articles.statement:
For a sequence $\sigma = (\sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_{k-1})$
of arrivals, each a list of left vertices in $\{0, \dots, a - 1\}$, the bipartite graph of $\sigma$
is given by adjacency lists: left vertex $i$ is sent to the list, in increasing order, of the
arrivals $j < k$ with $i \in \sigma_j$.

articles.title: Partner assignment from an array
articles.statement:
An array $A$ whose entries are each a left vertex or
none is read as an assignment of partners to the right vertices $0, \dots, b-1$: right vertex
$j$ gets the entry of $A$ at index $j$ when $j$ is less than the length of $A$, and no partner
otherwise.

articles.title: Break-even strategy
articles.statement:
For a purchase price $B$, the break-even strategy is the deterministic
strategy that buys on day $B$.

articles.title: The break-even strategy pays at most twice the optimum
articles.statement:
For every purchase price $B \ge 1$
and every season length $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d)$ of
the break-even strategy for a season of $d$ days is at most $2 \cdot \mathrm{opt}_B(d)$, twice
the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$. In particular, the break-even strategy is
$2$-competitive.

articles.title: Ski-rental upper bound for the break-even strategy
articles.statement:
For every purchase price $B \ge 1$ and
every season length $d$, the break-even strategy $\mathrm{breakEven}_B$ pays at most $2 - 1/B$
times the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$: its cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d)$
for a season of $d$ days satisfies
$B \cdot \mathrm{cost}_B(\mathrm{breakEven}_B, d) \le (2B - 1) \cdot \mathrm{opt}_B(d)$.

articles.title: Cost of a ski-rental strategy
articles.statement:
Renting skis costs $1$ per day and buying them costs a
natural number $B$. The cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(s, d) \in \mathbb{N}$ of a strategy $s$ for a season
of $d \in \mathbb{N}$ days is $(t - 1) + B$ if $s$ buys on a day $t$ with $1 \le t \le d$ (rent for
$t - 1$ days, then buy), and $d$ otherwise, that is, if $s$ rents forever or buys on a day $t$
with $t = 0$ or $t > d$ (rent every day).

articles.title: Lower bound
articles.statement:
Every deterministic strategy pays at least `(2 - 1/B)` times the optimum on
some season, `(2 B - 1) * opt ≤ B * cost`.

articles.title: The offline optimum bounds every strategy's cost
articles.statement:
For every purchase price $B$, every
deterministic strategy $s$ and every season length $d$, the offline optimum $\mathrm{opt}_B(d)$ is
at most the cost $\mathrm{cost}_B(s, d)$ of $s$ for a season of $d$ days.

articles.title: Offline optimum for ski rental
articles.statement:
For a purchase price $B \in \mathbb{N}$ and a season of
$d \in \mathbb{N}$ days, the offline optimum is $\mathrm{opt}_B(d) = \min(d, B)$: rent every day
or buy on day one, whichever is cheaper.

articles.title: Deterministic ski-rental strategy
articles.statement:
A deterministic strategy is either a day
$t \in \mathbb{N}$ on which to buy the skis, after renting on the days before it, or the choice to
rent forever. Days are numbered from $1$; the value $t = 0$ is also a strategy, and the cost
treats it as renting forever.

articles.title: Initial state of pointer jumping
articles.statement:
For a successor map $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes
$0, \dots, n-1$, where $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ is either a node or undefined (at the end of a list), the
initial pointer-jumping state gives each node $v$ the pointer $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ and the distance
$0$ if $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ is undefined and $1$ otherwise.

articles.title: Initial state of pointer jumping for suffix sums
articles.statement:
Given nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ with a
partial successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ and values $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$, the
initial state gives each node $v$ the pointer $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ (undefined at the end of a
list) and the sum $x_v$.

articles.title: The characteristic property of the rank
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the
nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. For every node $v$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
following $\mathrm{succ}$ for $k$ steps from $v$ runs off the end of the list if and only if
$k > \operatorname{rank}(v)$.

articles.title: Iterated successor
articles.statement:
For a successor map $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$, where
$\mathrm{succ}(v)$ is either a node or undefined, the $k$-step jump from $v$ is the node reached by
applying $\mathrm{succ}$ $k$ times starting at $v$, and is undefined if some step is undefined: the
$0$-step jump from $v$ is $v$, and the $(k+1)$-step jump is $\mathrm{succ}$ of the $k$-step jump.

articles.title: Pointer jumping ranks every list in ⌈log₂ n⌉ rounds
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map
on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. Then for every node $v$, entry $v$ of the table
returned by list ranking by pointer jumping, which runs $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds, is the
rank of $v$.

articles.title: List ranking by pointer jumping
articles.statement:
For a successor map $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes
$0, \dots, n-1$, list ranking by pointer jumping runs $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds of pointer
jumping on arrays, starting from the initial state, and returns the resulting array of distances,
whose entry $v$ is the distance of node $v$.

When the lists terminate, entry $v$ is the rank of node $v$.

articles.title: Pointer jumping computes all suffix sums in $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{succ}$ be a partial successor function on nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ under which every list
ends, that is, from every node, the node reached in $n$ steps along $\mathrm{succ}$ is undefined,
and let $x_v$ be values in an additive monoid $M$. Then for every node $v$, entry $v$ of the
array of sums computed by $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds of pointer jumping on arrays is the
suffix sum of $v$: the sum, in list order, of the values from $v$ to the end of its list.

articles.title: Suffix sums by pointer jumping on arrays
articles.statement:
Given a partial successor function
$\mathrm{succ}$ on nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ and values $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$, this is
the array of sums obtained after $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds (the least $k$ with
$n \le 2^k$) of pointer jumping on arrays, starting from the pointers $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ and the
sums $x_v$.

When every list ends, entry $v$ is the suffix sum of node $v$.

articles.title: Rank decreases along jumps
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes
$0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. If following $\mathrm{succ}$ for $a$ steps from a node $v$
reaches the node $u$, then $a \le \operatorname{rank}(v)$ and
$\operatorname{rank}(u) = \operatorname{rank}(v) - a$.

articles.title: Rank of a node in a linked list
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map on the nodes
$0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate. The rank of a node $v$ is the least $k$ such that following
$\mathrm{succ}$ for $k + 1$ steps from $v$ runs off the end of the list, that is, the number of
nodes after $v$ in its list.

articles.title: One round of pointer jumping
articles.statement:
In one parallel round, every node $v$ whose pointer is a node
$u$ adds the distance of $u$ to its own distance and moves its pointer to the pointer of $u$
(undefined if that of $u$ is); a node whose pointer is undefined keeps its distance and its
undefined pointer.

articles.title: One pointer-jumping round on arrays
articles.statement:
Given an array $P$ of pointers (each a node among
$0, \dots, n-1$ or undefined) and an array $D$ of natural-number distances, one round returns
arrays $P'$ and $D'$ of length $n$ where, for each node $v$, $P'[v]$ is $P[u]$ if $P[v] = u$ and is
undefined if $P[v]$ is undefined, and $D'[v] = D[v] + D[u]$ if $P[v] = u$ and $D'[v] = D[v]$ if
$P[v]$ is undefined. Entries missing from the input arrays are read as undefined pointers and
distance $0$.

articles.title: One round of pointer jumping on arrays
articles.statement:
Given an array $P$ of pointers (each a node
among $0, \dots, n-1$ or undefined) and an array $S$ of sums in an additive monoid $M$, one
