round returns arrays $P'$ and $S'$ of length $n$ where, for each node $v$: if $P[v]$ is
undefined, then $P'[v]$ is undefined and $S'[v] = S[v]$; if $P[v] = u$, then $P'[v] = P[u]$ and
$S'[v] = S[v] + S[u]$. A read outside an array gives an undefined pointer or the sum $0$.

articles.title: One round of pointer jumping for suffix sums
articles.statement:
Given a state in which each node $v$ has
a pointer $p(v)$, either a node or undefined, and a sum $s(v)$ in an additive monoid $M$, one
round produces a new state as follows. If $p(v)$ is undefined, the pointer of $v$ stays
undefined and its sum stays $s(v)$. If $p(v) = u$, the new pointer of $v$ is $p(u)$ and its new
sum is $s(v) + s(u)$, with $s(u)$ added on the right so that list order is kept.

articles.title: The list-ranking state after $t$ rounds
articles.statement:
For a successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ on the
nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$, the pointer-jumping state after $t$ rounds is defined by recursion on
$t$: after $0$ rounds it is the initial state of $\mathrm{succ}$, and after $t + 1$ rounds it is
one round of pointer jumping applied to the state after $t$ rounds.

articles.title: Pointer-jumping sums are the suffix sums once $n \le 2^t$
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a
partial successor function on nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ under which every list ends, that is, from
every node, the node reached in $n$ steps along $\mathrm{succ}$ is undefined, and let $x_v$ be
values in an additive monoid $M$. If $t \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $n \le 2^t$, then for every
node $v$ the sum of $v$ after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping is the suffix sum of $v$: the sum, in
list order, of the values from $v$ to the end of its list.

articles.title: After enough rounds, the distances are the ranks
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a successor map
on the nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ whose lists terminate, and let $t$ be a natural number with
$n \le 2^t$. Then after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping from the initial state, the distance of
every node $v$ is the rank of $v$.

articles.title: The invariant of pointer jumping for list ranking
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ map each of the
nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ to its successor or to nothing, and suppose the lists terminate: from
every node, $n$ steps run off the end. Write $\mathrm{rank}(v)$ for the number of nodes after
$v$. Then for every $t \ge 0$ and every node $v$, after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping, the
pointer of $v$ is the node $2^t$ steps down the list from $v$ (no node if the list ends before
that), and the distance of $v$ is $\min(2^t, \mathrm{rank}(v))$.

articles.title: The invariant of pointer jumping for suffix sums
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a partial
successor function on nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ and $x_v$ values in an additive monoid $M$. For
every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every node $v$, after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping the pointer of
$v$ is the node reached from $v$ in $2^t$ steps along $\mathrm{succ}$ (undefined if the list
ends sooner), and the sum of $v$ is the sum, in list order, of the values of the nodes reached
from $v$ in $0, 1, \dots, 2^t - 1$ steps (a missing node contributes $0$).

articles.title: List-ranking rounds on arrays
articles.statement:
For a successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes
$0, \dots, n - 1$ and $t \ge 0$, the arrays after $t$ rounds are a pair of arrays (pointers and
distances) defined by recursion on $t$: after $0$ rounds they are the tabulation of the initial
state of $\mathrm{succ}$, and after $t + 1$ rounds they are one round on arrays applied to the
arrays after $t$ rounds.

articles.title: Arrays after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping for suffix sums
articles.statement:
Given a partial successor
function $\mathrm{succ}$ on nodes $0, \dots, n-1$ and values $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$,
the pair of arrays after $0$ rounds stores the pointers $\mathrm{succ}(v)$ and the sums $x_v$,
and the pair after $t + 1$ rounds is one round of pointer jumping on arrays applied to the pair
after $t$ rounds.

articles.title: State after $t$ rounds of pointer jumping for suffix sums
articles.statement:
Given a partial successor
function $\mathrm{succ}$ on nodes $0, \dots, n-1$, values $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$ and
$t \in \mathbb{N}$, the state after $t$ rounds is obtained from the initial state (pointers
$\mathrm{succ}(v)$, sums $x_v$) by applying one round of pointer jumping $t$ times.

articles.title: Segment sums add up
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{succ}$ be a partial successor function on nodes
$0, \dots, n-1$ and $x_v$ values in an additive monoid $M$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ write
$S_k(v)$ for the sum, in list order, of the values of the nodes reached from $v$ in
$0, 1, \dots, k - 1$ steps along $\mathrm{succ}$ (a missing node contributes $0$). Then for all
$a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and every node $v$, $S_{a+b}(v) = S_a(v) + S_b(u)$ if the node $u$ reached
from $v$ in $a$ steps exists, and $S_{a+b}(v) = S_a(v)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Segment sums of unit values count nodes
articles.statement:
Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a
partial successor function such that, starting from any node, $n$ steps run off the end of its
list, and give every node the value $1 \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and
every node $v$, the segment sum of length $k$ from $v$ (the sum of the values of the first $k$
nodes from $v$, fewer at the end of the list) is $\min(k, \operatorname{rank}(v) + 1)$, where
$\operatorname{rank}(v)$ is the number of nodes after $v$ in its list.

articles.title: Segment sums
articles.statement:
Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor function, and
let each node $v$ carry a value $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$ (not necessarily commutative).
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a node $v$, the segment sum of length $k$ from $v$ is the sum, in
list order, of the values of the first $k$ nodes of the list starting at $v$ (fewer if the list
ends sooner); for $k = 0$ it is $0$.

articles.title: Pointer-jumping state for list ranking
articles.statement:
A pointer-jumping state on the nodes
$0, \dots, n - 1$ assigns to each node a pointer, which is either a node or empty (once it points
past the end of the list), and a distance in $\mathbb{N}$, the distance covered by the pointer.

articles.title: State of pointer jumping for suffix sums
articles.statement:
For $n$ nodes and a type $M$, a state assigns
to each node $v$ a pointer, which is either a node or none (past the end of the list), and an
accumulated value in $M$. The accumulated value is meant to be the sum of the node values from
$v$ up to, but not including, the pointer's target.

articles.title: The value $k$ steps ahead
articles.statement:
Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor
function, each node $u$ carrying a value $x_u$ in an additive monoid $M$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$
and a node $v$, this is $x_u$ where $u$ is the node $k$ steps after $v$ along its list, and $0$
if the list ends before $k$ steps.

articles.title: The characteristic property of suffix sums
articles.statement:
Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a
partial successor function such that, starting from any node, $n$ steps run off the end of its
list, and let each node $v$ carry a value $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$. Then for every node
$v$, the suffix sum of $v$ is $x_v$ plus the suffix sum of the successor of $v$, or just $x_v$
if $v$ has no successor.

articles.title: List ranking is the special case of unit values
articles.statement:
Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by
a partial successor function such that, starting from any node, $n$ steps run off the end of
its list. If every node has value $1 \in \mathbb{N}$, then the suffix sum of every node $v$ is
$\operatorname{rank}(v) + 1$, where $\operatorname{rank}(v)$ is the number of nodes after $v$ in
its list.

articles.title: Suffix sums
articles.statement:
Let $n$ nodes be linked into lists by a partial successor function, each
node $v$ carrying a value $x_v$ in an additive monoid $M$. The suffix sum of a node $v$ is the
segment sum of length $n$ from $v$: the sum, in list order, of the values of the first $n$ nodes
of the list starting at $v$ (fewer if it ends sooner).

When the list from $v$ ends, it has at most $n$ nodes, so this is the sum of the values from $v$
to the end of its list.

articles.title: Tabulating a list-ranking state
articles.statement:
The tabulation of a pointer-jumping state $s$ on the
nodes $0, \dots, n - 1$ is the pair of arrays of length $n$ whose entries at $v$ are the pointer
and the distance of $v$ in $s$.

Evaluating the state after $t$ rounds directly re-reads earlier rounds' pointers at every query,
a cost growing exponentially with the number of rounds; the tabulated rounds cost $O(n)$ array
operations each.

articles.title: Pointer-jumping state as arrays
articles.statement:
A suffix-sum pointer-jumping state on $n$ nodes is
stored as a pair of arrays of length $n$: the array whose entry $v$ is the pointer of node $v$,
and the array whose entry $v$ is the accumulated value of node $v$.

Evaluating the rounds of pointer jumping directly re-reads earlier rounds at every query, a
cost exponential in the number of rounds; on arrays each round costs $O(n)$ operations.

articles.title: Terminating successor functions
articles.statement:
A successor function $\mathrm{succ}$ on the nodes
$0, \dots, n - 1$, mapping each node to its successor or to nothing, terminates when from every
node $v$ the walk of $n$ steps along $\mathrm{succ}$ runs off the end, that is, there is no node
$n$ steps down the list from $v$.

articles.title: Blelloch's scan computes the exclusive prefix products
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid, $k$ a
natural number and $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ a sequence in $M$. For every $j < 2^k$, the value at
position $j$ of Blelloch's scan of $x$ on $2^k$ positions is the exclusive prefix product
$x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{j-1}$ (equal to $1$ when $j = 0$).

articles.title: Blelloch's scan on lists
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid. For a natural number $k$ and a list
$xs = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ in $M$, the list scan $L_k(xs)$ is defined by recursion on $k$:
$L_0(xs)$ is the one-element list $(1)$, and $L_{k+1}(xs)$ is obtained from the list scan
$z = L_k(p)$ of the pair products $p = (x_0 x_1, x_2 x_3, \dots)$ of $xs$ (a trailing unpaired
entry is dropped) by interleaving: $L_{k+1}(xs) = (z_0, z_0 x_0, z_1, z_1 x_2, \dots)$, where
each $z_i$ is followed by $z_i x_{2i}$ and the list stops at the first $i$ for which $z_i$ or
$x_{2i+1}$ does not exist.

On a list of length $2^k$ this takes $O(2^k)$ time.

articles.title: Blelloch's scan has logarithmic span
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the span of
Blelloch's scan on $n = 2^k$ positions is $2k = 2 \log_2 n$.

articles.title: Parallel steps of Blelloch's scan
articles.statement:
The span $S(k)$ of Blelloch's scan on $2^k$
positions is defined by $S(0) = 0$ and $S(k+1) = S(k) + 2$: one parallel step for the pair
products, the recursive scan, and one parallel step for the odd positions.

articles.title: Blelloch's scan is work-efficient
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the number $W(k)$ of
monoid multiplications Blelloch's scan performs on $n = 2^k$ positions satisfies
$W(k) + 2 = 2^{k+1}$, so $W(k) = 2^{k+1} - 2 < 2n$.

articles.title: Work of Blelloch's scan
articles.statement:
The number $W(k)$ of monoid multiplications Blelloch's scan
performs on $2^k$ positions is defined by $W(0) = 0$ and $W(k+1) = 2^k + W(k) + 2^k$: on
$2^{k+1}$ positions, $2^k$ pair products, the recursive scan on the $2^k$ pair products, and
$2^k$ products for the odd positions.

articles.title: Blelloch's scan
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid. For a natural number $k$ and a sequence
$x = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ in $M$, the scan $B_k(x)$ is the sequence in $M$ defined by recursion
on $k$: $B_0(x)$ is constantly $1$, and $B_{k+1}(x)$ is obtained from the scan $y = B_k(p)$ of
the pair products $p_i = x_{2i} x_{2i+1}$ by setting $B_{k+1}(x)_{2i} = y_i$ and
$B_{k+1}(x)_{2i+1} = y_i x_{2i}$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Interleaving step of Blelloch's list scan
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid. For lists
$z = (z_0, z_1, \dots)$ and $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots)$ in $M$, the expansion of $z$ along $x$ is
the list $(z_0, z_0 x_0, z_1, z_1 x_2, z_2, z_2 x_4, \dots)$: each $z_i$ is followed by
$z_i x_{2i}$, and the list stops at the first $i$ for which $z_i$ or $x_{2i+1}$ does not
exist.

articles.title: The list implementation computes the exclusive prefix products
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid,
$k$ a natural number and $xs = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^k - 1})$ a list in $M$ of length $2^k$. For
every $j < 2^k$, the entry at position $j$ of Blelloch's list scan of $xs$ in $k$ rounds is
the exclusive prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{j-1}$ (equal to $1$ when $j = 0$).

articles.title: The list implementation computes Blelloch's scan
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid, $k$ a natural
number and $xs = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^k - 1})$ a list in $M$ of length $2^k$. For every $j < 2^k$,
the entry at position $j$ of Blelloch's list scan of $xs$ in $k$ rounds equals the value at
position $j$ of Blelloch's scan on $2^k$ positions of the sequence
$x_0, \dots, x_{2^k - 1}, 1, 1, \dots$ obtained by extending $xs$ by $1$.

articles.title: The tabulated scan computes all prefix products
articles.statement:
Let $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ be a list of
elements of a monoid $M$ and let $K$ be a natural number with $n \le 2^K$. Then for every $i < n$,
entry $i$ of the list produced by $K$ rounds of the tabulated scan equals the prefix product
$x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$.

articles.title: The tabulated scan agrees with the round recursion
articles.statement:
Let $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ be a list of
elements of a monoid $M$, extended to a sequence by $x_j = 1$ for $j \ge n$. For every number of
rounds $K$ and every position $i < n$, entry $i$ of the list produced by $K$ rounds of the
tabulated scan equals the value at position $i$ after $K$ rounds of the Kogge–Stone scan applied
to the sequence $x$.

articles.title: The scan computes all prefixes in logarithmically many rounds
articles.statement:
Let $x_0, x_1, \dots$ be a
sequence in a monoid $M$ and let $n$ be a natural number. After $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ rounds of
the Kogge–Stone scan (the least $K$ with $n \le 2^K$), every position $i < n$ holds the prefix
product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$.

articles.title: The scan computes all prefix products
articles.statement:
Let $x_0, x_1, \dots$ be a sequence in a monoid $M$
and let $n$ and $K$ be natural numbers with $n \le 2^K$. After $K$ rounds of the Kogge–Stone scan,
every position $i < n$ holds the prefix product $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$.

articles.title: What the scan holds after each round
articles.statement:
Let $x_0, x_1, \dots$ be a sequence in a monoid
$M$, let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers, and let $m = \min(i + 1, 2^k)$. After $k$ rounds of the
Kogge–Stone scan, position $i$ holds the product $x_{i+1-m} \cdots x_i$ of the $m$ consecutive
inputs ending at $i$, taken in increasing order of index.

articles.title: The Kogge–Stone scan
articles.statement:
Given a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots$ in a monoid $M$, the value
$s_k(i)$ at position $i$ after $k$ rounds is defined by $s_0(i) = x_i$ and, for each $k$,
$s_{k+1}(i) = s_k(i - 2^k) \, s_k(i)$ if $2^k \le i$ and $s_{k+1}(i) = s_k(i)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Adjacent pair products of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $[a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1}]$ of
elements of a monoid $M$, the list of adjacent pair products is $[a_0 a_1, a_2 a_3, \ldots]$:
it has length $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, its $i$-th entry is $a_{2i} a_{2i+1}$, and when $n$ is odd
the last element $a_{n-1}$ is dropped.

articles.title: Adjacent pair products of a sequence
articles.statement:
For a sequence $x \colon \mathbb{N} \to M$ in a
monoid $M$, the sequence of adjacent pair products is the sequence whose term at $i$ is
$x(2i) \cdot x(2i+1)$.

articles.title: Prefix product
articles.statement:
For a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots$ in a monoid $M$ and a natural number $i$,
the prefix product at $i$ is $x_0 x_1 \cdots x_i$, the factors taken in increasing order of
index.

articles.title: One round of the scan on a list
articles.statement:
Given a list $y_0, \dots, y_{n-1}$ in a monoid $M$ and a
natural number $k$, one round produces the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is
$y_{i - 2^k} \, y_i$ when $2^k \le i$ and $y_i$ when $i < 2^k$.

The list is traversed in lockstep with its own suffix starting at position $2^k$, so a round
costs $O(n)$.

articles.title: The work of a round counts its combining positions
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the
work of round $k$ on $n$ positions equals the number of positions $i$ with $2^k \le i < n$.

articles.title: Work of a scan round
articles.statement:
The work of round $k$ on $n$ positions is $\max(n - 2^k, 0)$, the
number of positions $i < n$ with $i \ge 2^k$, each of which performs one multiplication.

articles.title: Tabulated Kogge–Stone scan
articles.statement:
For a list $y = (y_0, \dots, y_{n-1})$ in a monoid $M$, the
list after $K$ rounds is defined by recursion on $K$: after $0$ rounds it is $y$, and after
$K + 1$ rounds it is round $K$ applied to the list after $K$ rounds. Here round $k$ sends a list
$(z_0, \dots, z_{n-1})$ to the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is $z_i$ for $i < 2^k$ and
$z_{i - 2^k} z_i$ for $2^k \le i < n$.

articles.title: Products of adjacent windows
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a monoid and $x : \mathbb{N} \to M$ a sequence,
and for $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ let $x_{[a, b)}$ be the ordered product $x_a x_{a+1} \cdots x_{b-1}$
(equal to $1$ if $b \le a$). For all $a \le b \le c$, $x_{[a, b)} \, x_{[b, c)} = x_{[a, c)}$.

articles.title: Window product
articles.statement:
For a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to M$ in a monoid $M$ and
$a, b \in \mathbb{N}$, the window product is the ordered product $x_a x_{a+1} \cdots x_{b-1}$ of
the terms with indices $a \le j < b$; it is the empty product $1$ when $b \le a$.

articles.title: Span of the Kogge–Stone scan
articles.statement:
The span of $K$ rounds of the scan is $K$: each round is
one parallel step.

articles.title: Work bound for the Kogge–Stone scan
articles.statement:
For all $n, K \in \mathbb{N}$, the total work of $K$
rounds of the scan on $n$ positions is at most $nK$.

articles.title: Work of the Kogge–Stone scan
articles.statement:
The total work of $K$ rounds on $n$ positions is
$\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \max(n - 2^k, 0)$, the sum over the rounds $k < K$ of the work
$\max(n - 2^k, 0)$ of round $k$.

articles.title: Brent's theorem with the work and span laws
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG on $n$
unit-time tasks with span $D$, and let $p \ge 1$. Then some schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors
has length $T$ with $pT \le n + (p - 1)D$, and every schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors has a
length $T'$ with $n \le pT'$ (the work law) and $D \le T'$ (the span law).

articles.title: Computation DAG
articles.statement:
A computation DAG on $n$ unit-time tasks, numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$,
assigns to each task $v$ a list of predecessors (the tasks $v$ waits for), each numbered below
$v$; so the numbering is a topological order.

articles.title: No step of Brent's level schedule mixes levels
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG and
$p \ge 1$. If two tasks $u$ and $v$ run in the same step of Brent's level-by-level schedule on
$p$ processors, then $u$ and $v$ have the same depth.

articles.title: Depth bounds the step of a task
articles.statement:
For every schedule of a computation DAG on $p$
processors, with steps numbered from $0$, every task $v$ runs in a step $t$ with
$\operatorname{depth}(v) \le t + 1$.

articles.title: Predecessors have smaller depth
articles.statement:
In a computation DAG, if $u$ is a predecessor of $v$,
then the depth of $u$ is strictly less than the depth of $v$.

articles.title: Table of depths
articles.statement:
The list of the depths of tasks $0, \dots, n - 1$ of a computation DAG on
$n$ tasks, computed once each in topological order: the entry for task $k$ is $1$ plus the largest
entry at a predecessor of $k$, or $1$ if $k$ has no predecessors.

With lists (appending and indexed reads take linear time) this costs $O(n^2 + n|E|)$, where $|E|$
is the total number of predecessor entries; evaluating the depth directly from its recursive
definition instead recomputes shared subpaths exponentially often.

articles.title: Depth of a task in a computation DAG
articles.statement:
The depth of a task $v$ is the number of tasks on a
longest path ending at $v$: it is $1$ plus the largest depth of a predecessor of $v$, or $1$ if
$v$ has no predecessors.

articles.title: Depths of an initial segment of tasks
articles.statement:
For $k \le n$, the list of the depths of tasks
$0, \dots, k - 1$ of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, computed in topological order: the empty
list for $k = 0$, and for $k + 1$ the list for $k$ followed by $1$ plus the largest entry of that
list at a predecessor of task $k$ (or $1$ if task $k$ has no predecessors).

articles.title: Every step of a schedule has a task running at or after it
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a schedule of a
computation DAG on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps, numbered from $0$. For every step $t < T$
there is a task that $S$ runs at step $t$ or later.

articles.title: The table of depths is correct
articles.statement:
For every task $v$ of a computation DAG, the entry of the
table of depths at position $v$ equals the depth of $v$.

articles.title: Greediness need only be checked at the steps of the schedule
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a schedule of a
computation DAG on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then $S$ is greedy if and only if, for every
step $t < T$ and every task $v$ that is ready at step $t$, exactly $p$ tasks run in step $t$.

This holds because a task is never ready at or after the last step.

articles.title: The greedy scheduling bound
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and
let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then
$pT \le n + (p - 1)D$.

Each complete step runs $p$ tasks, and each of the at most $D$ incomplete steps runs at least one.

## Sources

- the unit-task case of Graham's list-scheduling argument, Graham, *Bounds for certain multiprocessing anomalies*, Bell System Tech. J. 45, 1966.

articles.title: The work-span bound for greedy schedules
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and
span $D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then
$pT \le n + pD$, that is, $T \le n/p + D$ when $p \ge 1$.

This is a weakening of the greedy scheduling bound $pT \le n + (p - 1)D$.

## Sources

- CLRS, third edition, Theorem 27.1.

articles.title: Greedy schedule
articles.statement:
A schedule $S$ of a computation DAG on $p$ processors is greedy if, for
every step $t$ and every task that is ready at step $t$, exactly $p$ tasks run in step $t$: a step
leaves a ready task waiting only when all $p$ processors are busy.

articles.title: A greedy schedule has at most $D$ incomplete steps
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG with span
$D$, and let $S$ be a greedy schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. Then at most $D$
of the steps $t < T$ are incomplete, that is, run fewer than $p$ tasks.

articles.title: Each incomplete step advances the critical path
articles.statement:
In a greedy schedule, fewer than
`depth v` incomplete steps precede the step of task `v`.

articles.title: Number of incomplete steps
articles.statement:
For a schedule $S$ of a computation DAG on $p$ processors and
a natural number $t$, the number of incomplete steps before step $t$ is the number of steps
$s < t$ in which $S$ runs fewer than $p$ tasks.

articles.title: Length of a schedule
articles.statement:
The length of a schedule is the number of steps it takes: one more
than the latest step in which a task runs (steps are numbered from $0$), or $0$ if there are no
tasks.

articles.title: Level $0$ is empty
articles.statement:
In every computation DAG no task has depth $0$, so the number of
tasks of depth $0$ is $0$.

articles.title: Level size
articles.statement:
For a computation DAG and a natural number $d$, the size of level $d$ is the
number of tasks of depth $d$.

articles.title: Brent's theorem
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks and span $D$, and let
$p \ge 1$. If Brent's level schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors takes $T$ steps, then
$pT \le n + (p - 1) D$, that is, $T \le (n - D)/p + D$.

articles.title: Brent's level schedule
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p \ge 1$. For each $d$ let
$L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$ and $o_d = \sum_{e < d} \lceil L_e / p \rceil$, and for
each task $v$ let $r(v)$ be the number of tasks of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number.
Brent's level schedule is the schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors that runs each task $v$ at step
$o_{\operatorname{depth}(v)} + \lfloor r(v) / p \rfloor$.

It runs the tasks level by level, in order of depth, each level of $L_d$ tasks in
$\lceil L_d / p \rceil$ steps of at most $p$ tasks.

articles.title: Steps of a level
articles.statement:
For a computation DAG and natural numbers $p$ and $d$, let $L_d$ be the
number of tasks of depth $d$. The number of steps of level $d$ on $p$ processors is
$\lceil L_d / p \rceil$ if $p \ge 1$, and $0$ if $p = 0$.

articles.title: Step of a task in Brent's schedule
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG and $p$ a natural number.
If $p \ge 1$, for each $d$ let $L_d$ be the number of tasks of depth $d$ and
$o_d = \sum_{e < d} \lceil L_e / p \rceil$, and for each task $v$ let $r(v)$ be the number of tasks
of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number; the step of a task $v$ is
$o_{\operatorname{depth}(v)} + \lfloor r(v) / p \rfloor$. If $p = 0$, the step of every task is $0$.

For $p \ge 1$ this runs the tasks level by level, each level of $L_d$ tasks in
$\lceil L_d / p \rceil$ steps of at most $p$ tasks.

articles.title: Load of a step
articles.statement:
The load of step $t$ in a schedule $S$ of a computation DAG is the number
of tasks that $S$ runs in step $t$.

articles.title: Complete steps are bounded by the work
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a computation DAG with $n$ tasks, and
let $S$ be a schedule of $G$ on $p$ processors taking $T$ steps. If $C$ is the number of steps
$t < T$ in which $S$ runs at least $p$ tasks (the complete steps, where all $p$ processors are
busy), then $pC \le n$.

articles.title: First step of a level
articles.statement:
For a computation DAG and natural numbers $p$ and $d$, let $s_e$
be the number of steps of level $e$ on $p$ processors: $\lceil L_e / p \rceil$ if $p \ge 1$ and
$0$ if $p = 0$, where $L_e$ is the number of tasks of depth $e$. The first step of level $d$ is
$\sum_{e < d} s_e$.

articles.title: A greedy schedule never idles
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a greedy schedule of a task graph on $p$
processors that takes $T$ steps, numbered $0, \dots, T - 1$. Then every step $t < T$ of $S$
runs at least one task.

The task that runs earliest among those not run before step $t$ has all its predecessors done
before step $t$. If step $t$ ran no task, this task would be ready at step $t$, while a greedy
step with a ready task keeps all $p$ processors busy.

articles.title: Ranks increase within a level
articles.statement:
In a computation DAG, if tasks $u$ and $v$ have the same
depth and $u$ has a smaller number than $v$, then the rank of $u$ is smaller than the rank of
$v$, where the rank of a task is the number of tasks of the same depth with a smaller number.
In particular, ranks are distinct within a level.

articles.title: Rank within a level
articles.statement:
In a computation DAG, the rank of a task $v$ is the number of tasks
of the same depth as $v$ with a smaller number than $v$. Taken in numbering order, the tasks of a
level have ranks $0, 1, 2, \dots$

articles.title: Ready task
articles.statement:
In a schedule $S$ of a task graph, a task $v$ is ready at step $t$ if $v$
runs in a step later than $t$ and every predecessor of $v$ runs in a step earlier than $t$.

articles.title: Schedule of a computation DAG
articles.statement:
A schedule of a computation DAG on $n$ tasks on $p$
processors assigns to each task $v$ a step $t(v) \in \mathbb{N}$ in which it runs, such that
$t(u) < t(v)$ whenever $u$ is a predecessor of $v$, and for every step $s$ at most $p$ tasks $v$
have $t(v) = s$.

articles.title: The span law
articles.statement: No schedule is shorter than the span.

articles.title: Span of a computation DAG
articles.statement:
The span of a computation DAG is the number of tasks on a
longest path, that is, the largest depth of a task, and $0$ when there are no tasks.

articles.title: The step loads add up to the number of tasks
articles.statement:
For a schedule $S$ of a task graph with $n$
tasks that takes $T$ steps, the numbers of tasks run in the steps $0, 1, \dots, T - 1$ add up
to $n$.

articles.title: The work law
articles.statement:
For a computation DAG on $n$ tasks, every schedule of it on $p$ processors
that takes $T$ steps satisfies $n \le p T$. In particular, for $p > 0$ the schedule takes at
least $n / p$ steps.

articles.title: Prepending a silent step to the silent closure
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system with a
silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the silent closure, the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. If $s \xrightarrow{\tau} m$ is a transition and
$m \Rightarrow t$, then $s \Rightarrow t$.

articles.title: Bisimilar states enable the same labels
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be bisimilar states of a
labelled transition system. Then for every label $\mu$, $s$ has a transition labelled $\mu$ if
and only if $t$ has a transition labelled $\mu$.

articles.title: Weakly bisimilar states enable the same weak labels
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system
with a silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. The weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ are the trivial ones $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$
and the composites $s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$; the saturated
system has the same states and has the weak transitions as its transitions. Two states are
weakly bisimilar if some bisimulation of the saturated system relates them.
If $s$ and $t$ are weakly bisimilar, then for every label $\mu$, there is a weak transition
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} s'$ for some $s'$ if and only if there is a weak transition
$t \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t'$ for some $t'$.

articles.title: Weak transitions with a visible label
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system with a silent
label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive closure of the
$\tau$-transition relation. A weak transition $s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ is either
the trivial one $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$ or a composite
$s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$. For a label $\mu \ne \tau$,
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ holds if and only if there are states $s_1, s_2$ with
$s \Rightarrow s_1$, $s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2$ and $s_2 \Rightarrow t$.

articles.title: Weak bisimilarity is bisimilarity of the saturated system
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition
system with a silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. The weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ are the trivial ones $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$
and the composites $s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$; the saturated
system has the same states and has the weak transitions as its transitions. Two states are
weakly bisimilar if some bisimulation of the saturated system relates them.
Thus two states are weakly bisimilar if and only if they are bisimilar in the saturated
system; this holds by definition.

articles.title: Bisimilarity transfers multistep transitions
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be bisimilar states of a
labelled transition system, and suppose $s$ reaches a state $s'$ by a multistep transition along
a finite (possibly empty) list of labels $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$. Then there is a state $t'$ such
that $t$ reaches $t'$ by a multistep transition along the same list of labels, and $s'$ and $t'$
are bisimilar.

articles.title: A silent step lies in the silent closure
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system with a silent
label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the silent closure, the reflexive-transitive closure of
the $\tau$-transition relation. If $s \xrightarrow{\tau} t$ is a transition, then
$s \Rightarrow t$.

articles.title: Bisimilar states have equal sets of outgoing labels
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be bisimilar states
of a labelled transition system. Then the set of labels $\mu$ for which $s$ has a transition
labelled $\mu$ equals the set of labels $\mu$ for which $t$ has a transition labelled $\mu$.

articles.title: Weakly bisimilar states have the same set of weak labels
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition
system with a silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. The weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ are the trivial ones $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$
and the composites $s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$; the saturated
system has the same states and has the weak transitions as its transitions. Two states are
weakly bisimilar if some bisimulation of the saturated system relates them.
If $s$ and $t$ are weakly bisimilar, then the set of labels $\mu$ with
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} s'$ for some $s'$ equals the set of labels $\mu$ with
$t \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t'$ for some $t'$.

articles.title: Weak bisimilarity transfers weak transitions
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system with a
silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. The weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ are the trivial ones $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$
and the composites $s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$; the saturated
system has the same states and has the weak transitions as its transitions. Two states are
weakly bisimilar if some bisimulation of the saturated system relates them.
If $s$ and $t$ are weakly bisimilar and $s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} s'$, then there is a
state $t'$ with $t \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t'$ such that $s'$ and $t'$ are weakly
bisimilar.

articles.title: Weak bisimilarity transfers weak traces
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system with a
silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. The weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ are the trivial ones $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$
and the composites $s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$; the saturated
system has the same states and has the weak transitions as its transitions. Two states are
weakly bisimilar if some bisimulation of the saturated system relates them.
Suppose $s$ and $t$ are weakly bisimilar and $s$ reaches $s'$ by a multistep transition of
the saturated system with label list $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$, that is, by weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu_1}{\Longrightarrow} \cdots \stackrel{\mu_n}{\Longrightarrow} s'$. Then $t$
reaches some $t'$ by a multistep transition of the saturated system with the same label list,
and $s'$ and $t'$ are weakly bisimilar.

articles.title: The silent closure is made of runs of silent steps
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system
with a silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the silent closure, the
reflexive-transitive closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. Then $s \Rightarrow t$ if and
only if, for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there is a multistep transition from $s$ to $t$ whose
list of labels consists of $n$ copies of $\tau$.

articles.title: Strong bisimilarity implies weak bisimilarity
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system with a
silent label $\tau$, write $\Rightarrow$ for the reflexive-transitive
closure of the $\tau$-transition relation. The weak transitions
$s \stackrel{\mu}{\Longrightarrow} t$ are the trivial ones $s \stackrel{\tau}{\Longrightarrow} s$
and the composites $s \Rightarrow s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2 \Rightarrow t$; the saturated
system has the same states and has the weak transitions as its transitions. Two states are
weakly bisimilar if some bisimulation of the saturated system relates them.
If two states are bisimilar in the original system, then they are weakly bisimilar.

articles.title: Strong traces are weak traces
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a labelled transition system with a silent
label $\tau$. A weak $\tau$-transition is a sequence of zero or more $\tau$-steps, and for
$\mu \ne \tau$ a weak $\mu$-transition is zero or more $\tau$-steps, one $\mu$-step and zero or
more $\tau$-steps; the saturation of $L$ is the system on the same states whose
$\mu$-transitions are the weak $\mu$-transitions of $L$. If $L$ moves from a state $s$ to a
state $t$ by a sequence of transitions labelled $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$, then the saturation of
$L$ moves from $s$ to $t$ by a sequence of transitions with the same labels
$\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n$.

articles.title: Weak bisimilarity answers a strong step with a weak step
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a labelled
transition system with a silent label $\tau$. A weak $\tau$-transition is a sequence of zero or
more $\tau$-steps, and for $\mu \ne \tau$ a weak $\mu$-transition is zero or more $\tau$-steps,
one $\mu$-step and zero or more $\tau$-steps. Two states are weakly bisimilar when some
bisimulation of the system whose $\mu$-transitions are the weak $\mu$-transitions of $L$ relates
them. If $p$ and $q$ are weakly bisimilar and $L$ has a transition from $p$ to $p'$ labelled
$\mu$, then there is a state $q'$ with a weak $\mu$-transition from $q$ to $q'$ such that $p'$
and $q'$ are weakly bisimilar.

articles.title: Silent steps before a weak transition
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a labelled transition system with a
silent label $\tau$. A weak $\tau$-transition is a sequence of zero or more $\tau$-steps, and for
$\mu \ne \tau$ a weak $\mu$-transition is zero or more $\tau$-steps, one $\mu$-step and zero or
more $\tau$-steps. If a state $s$ reaches a state $m$ by zero or more $\tau$-steps and there is a
weak $\mu$-transition from $m$ to $t$, then there is a weak $\mu$-transition from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Silent steps after a weak transition
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a labelled transition system with a
silent label $\tau$. A weak $\tau$-transition is a sequence of zero or more $\tau$-steps, and for
$\mu \ne \tau$ a weak $\mu$-transition is zero or more $\tau$-steps, one $\mu$-step and zero or
more $\tau$-steps. If there is a weak $\mu$-transition from a state $s$ to a state $m$ and $m$
reaches a state $t$ by zero or more $\tau$-steps, then there is a weak $\mu$-transition from $s$
to $t$.

articles.title: Actions permitted by a restriction
articles.statement:
Given a finite list $L$ of blocked channel names, the
silent action $\tau$ is always permitted, and an input or an output on a channel $a$ is permitted
exactly when $a \notin L$.

articles.title: Applying a relabelling to a channel name
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a finite relabelling whose table lists
the entries $(a_1, \ell_1), \dots, (a_k, \ell_k)$, where each $a_i$ is a channel name and each
$\ell_i$ a visible label. The image of a channel name $a$ under $f$ is $\ell_i$ for the first index
$i$ with $a_i = a$, and the input label on $a$ when no entry has name $a$.

articles.title: Lifting relations through choice
articles.statement:
Given relations $R$ and $S$ on finite CCS processes,
write $P_1 + P_2$ for the nondeterministic choice of $P_1$ and $P_2$. The choice lift of $R$
and $S$ relates $P$ to $Q$ exactly when $R(P, Q)$ holds, or $S(P, Q)$ holds, or $P = P_1 + P_2$
and $Q = Q_1 + Q_2$ with $R(P_1, Q_1)$ and $S(P_2, Q_2)$.

articles.title: Choice preserves strong bisimilarity in CCS with communication
articles.statement:
For CCS processes $P_1$,
$P_2$, $Q_1$, $Q_2$ with labels over a set of names: if $P_1$ and $P_2$ are strongly bisimilar and
$Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of CCS with
communication, then the choices $P_1 + Q_1$ and $P_2 + Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar there.

articles.title: Labelled transition system of CCS with communication
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system whose
states are CCS processes with labels over a set of names, whose labels are CCS labels over those
names, and whose transition relation is the CCS transition relation with communication.

articles.title: Transitions of a parallel composition
articles.statement:
For CCS processes $P$, $Q$, $R$ and a CCS label $a$,
the parallel composition $P \mid Q$ has a transition labelled $a$ to $R$ in the CCS transition
relation with communication if and only if one of the following holds: $P$ has a transition
labelled $a$ to some $P'$ and $R = P' \mid Q$; or $Q$ has a transition labelled $a$ to some $Q'$
and $R = P \mid Q'$; or $a = \tau$ and there are processes $P'$, $Q'$ and complementary labels
$b$, $c$ such that $P$ has a transition labelled $b$ to $P'$, $Q$ has a transition labelled $c$
to $Q'$, and $R = P' \mid Q'$.

articles.title: Prefix preserves strong bisimilarity in CCS with communication
articles.statement:
For every CCS label $a$ and
all CCS processes $P$ and $Q$: if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition
system of CCS with communication, then so are the prefixed processes $a.P$ and $a.Q$.

articles.title: CCS transition relation with communication
articles.statement:
The transition relation on CCS processes with
labels over a set of names given by the raw step relation for the synchronization function under
which an input and an output on the same name, in either order, synchronize to the silent label
$\tau$, and no other pair of labels synchronizes.

articles.title: Complement of a visible label
articles.statement:
The complement of the input label on a channel $a$ is the
output label on $a$, and the complement of the output label on $a$ is the input label on $a$.

articles.title: Complementary labels
articles.statement:
Two CCS labels are complementary when one is the input on a name $a$
and the other is the output on the same name $a$, in either order. No other pair of labels is
complementary; in particular the silent label $\tau$ has no complement.

articles.title: Constant occurrences of a process
articles.statement:
The constant occurrences of a recursive CCS
process $P$ are the list of the process constants occurring in $P$, from left to right and
with repetitions: the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$ has none; a constant $A$ has the single
occurrence $A$; a prefix $\alpha.Q$, a restriction $Q \setminus L$ and a relabelling $Q[f]$
have the occurrences of $Q$; and a choice $Q + R$ or a parallel composition $Q \mid R$ has
the occurrences of $Q$ followed by those of $R$.

articles.title: Constants of a process
articles.statement:
Assuming equality of process constants is decidable, the
constants of a recursive CCS process $P$ are the list obtained from the constant occurrences
of $P$ by removing duplicates, so that every process constant occurring in $P$ appears in it
exactly once.

articles.title: Reflexive closure of a relation on processes
articles.statement:
Given a relation $E$ on finite CCS processes,
its equation closure relates $P$ to $Q$ exactly when $P = Q$ or $E(P, Q)$; that is, it is the
reflexive closure of $E$.

It is used to prove the algebraic laws of nondeterministic choice up to strong bisimilarity.

articles.title: Guarded recursive specification
articles.statement:
A recursive specification $\Delta$, which assigns
to each process constant $A$ a body $\Delta(A)$, is guarded when for every constant $A$ the
body $\Delta(A)$ is a guarded process.

articles.title: Renaming constants preserves guardedness
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a recursive CCS process, let
$\rho$ be a map from its process constants to another set of constants, and let $P\rho$ be
the process obtained from $P$ by renaming its constants by $\rho$. Then for each Boolean flag
$b$, $P\rho$ is guarded under $b$ if and only if $P$ is guarded under $b$.

articles.title: Every process is guarded beneath a prefix
articles.statement:
Every recursive CCS process $P$ is guarded
under the flag $\mathrm{true}$: once an action prefix has been crossed, every constant
occurrence counts as guarded.

articles.title: Guardedness under a prefix flag
articles.statement:
For a Boolean flag $b$, recording whether an action
prefix has already been crossed, guardedness of a recursive CCS process under $b$ is defined
recursively: the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$ is guarded under $b$; a constant $A$ is guarded
under $b$ exactly when $b$ is true; a prefix $\alpha.Q$ is guarded under $b$ when $Q$ is guarded
under true; a choice $Q + R$ or a parallel composition $Q \mid R$ is guarded under $b$ when
both $Q$ and $R$ are; and a restriction $Q \setminus L$ or a relabelling $Q[f]$ is guarded
under $b$ when $Q$ is.

Thus under the flag false a process is guarded exactly when every constant occurrence lies
beneath an action prefix. Static operators and parallel/choice contexts do not themselves
guard recursion.

articles.title: Guarded process
articles.statement:
A recursive CCS process is guarded when all of its constant
occurrences lie beneath an action prefix.

articles.title: CCS labels
articles.statement:
For a set of names, a CCS label is either the silent action $\tau$, the input
on a name $a$, or the output on a name $a$.

articles.title: Labelled transition system of a recursive specification
articles.statement:
Assuming equality of names
is decidable, for a recursive specification $\Delta$ the labelled transition system generated
by $\Delta$ has the recursive CCS processes as states and the CCS labels as labels, and its
transitions $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ are exactly the steps of the structural operational
semantics relative to $\Delta$.

articles.title: Transition system of CCS with restriction and relabelling
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system
of finite CCS with static operators has the finite CCS processes with restriction and relabelling
as states and the CCS labels as labels, and its transitions are the steps of the structural
operational semantics of these processes.

articles.title: Labelled transition system of finite CCS
articles.statement:
The labelled transition system whose states are
the finite CCS processes, whose labels are the actions, and whose transitions $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$
are those of the communication-free operational semantics of finite CCS.

articles.title: Renaming process constants
articles.statement:
Given a map $\rho$ from one set of process constants to
another, renaming the constants of a recursive CCS process $P$ by $\rho$ replaces each
occurrence of a constant $A$ by $\rho(A)$ and leaves $P$ otherwise unchanged: the inactive
process, prefixes, choices, parallel compositions, restrictions and relabellings are kept as
they are.

articles.title: Embedding finite CCS into CCS with static operators
articles.statement:
Each finite CCS process over CCS
labels is sent to the process with static operators of the same shape: the inactive process goes
to the inactive process, the prefix of an action $\alpha$ to a process $P$ goes to the prefix of
$\alpha$ to the image of $P$, and a choice or a parallel composition of $P$ and $Q$ goes to the
choice or the parallel composition of the images of $P$ and $Q$.

articles.title: Parallel composition is commutative up to strong bisimilarity
articles.statement:
For all CCS processes $P$
and $Q$ with labels over a set of names, $P \mid Q$ and $Q \mid P$ are strongly bisimilar in the
labelled transition system of CCS with communication.

articles.title: Parallel composition preserves strong bisimilarity
articles.statement:
For CCS processes $P_1$, $P_2$, $Q_1$,
$Q_2$ with labels over a set of names: if $P_1$ and $P_2$ are strongly bisimilar and $Q_1$ and
$Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of CCS with communication, then
the parallel compositions $P_1 \mid Q_1$ and $P_2 \mid Q_2$ are strongly bisimilar there.

articles.title: Parallel lift of two relations
articles.statement:
Given two relations $R$ and $S$ on CCS processes with
labels over a set of names, their parallel lift relates a process $U$ to a process $V$ exactly
when $R$ relates $U$ to $V$, or $S$ relates $U$ to $V$, or $U = P_1 \mid Q_1$ and
$V = P_2 \mid Q_2$ where $R$ relates $P_1$ to $P_2$ and $S$ relates $Q_1$ to $Q_2$.

articles.title: The inactive process is a left unit for parallel composition
articles.statement:
Let the names form a type
with decidable equality. For every CCS process $P$ over input, output and silent labels on these
names, the parallel composition $0 \mid P$ of the inactive process $0$ with $P$ is strongly
bisimilar to $P$ in the communication labelled transition system.

articles.title: The inactive process is a right unit for parallel composition
articles.statement:
Let the names form a type
with decidable equality. For every CCS process $P$ over input, output and silent labels on these
names, the parallel composition $P \mid 0$ of $P$ with the inactive process $0$ is strongly
bisimilar to $P$ in the communication labelled transition system.

articles.title: Prefix preserves strong bisimilarity
articles.statement:
For every action $a$ and all finite CCS processes
$P$ and $Q$, if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled transition system of finite
CCS, then the prefixed processes $a.P$ and $a.Q$ are strongly bisimilar there as well.

articles.title: Recursive CCS processes
articles.statement:
Given a set of names and a set of process constants, the
recursive CCS processes are generated by the following constructors: the inactive process
$\mathbf{0}$; a process constant $A$; a prefix $\alpha.P$ for a CCS label $\alpha$ and a
process $P$; a choice $P + Q$; a parallel composition $P \mid Q$; a restriction
$P \setminus L$ for a finite list $L$ of names; and a relabelling $P[f]$ for a CCS
relabelling $f$.

articles.title: Finite CCS processes
articles.statement:
For a type $A$ of actions, the finite CCS processes over $A$ are
built from the inactive process $\mathbf{0}$ by action prefix $a.P$ (an action $a \in A$
followed by a process $P$), nondeterministic choice $P + Q$, and parallel composition
$P \mid Q$.

articles.title: Operational semantics of finite CCS with a synchronization function
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a
partial function that assigns to some pairs of actions $(a, b)$ an action $\sigma(a, b)$. The
transition relation $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ on finite CCS processes (built from prefix $a.P$,
choice $P + Q$ and parallel composition $P \mid Q$) determined by $\sigma$ is the least relation
such that $a.P \xrightarrow{a} P$; if $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ then $P + Q \xrightarrow{a} P'$,
$Q + P \xrightarrow{a} P'$, $P \mid Q \xrightarrow{a} P' \mid Q$ and
$Q \mid P \xrightarrow{a} Q \mid P'$; and if $P \xrightarrow{a} P'$, $Q \xrightarrow{b} Q'$ and
$\sigma(a, b) = c$, then $P \mid Q \xrightarrow{c} P' \mid Q'$.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves complementary actions
articles.statement:
For every relabelling $f$ and all CCS labels
$\alpha$ and $\beta$, if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complementary, then the actions obtained by
relabelling $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $f$ are complementary.

articles.title: Relabelling an action
articles.statement:
For a relabelling $f$, the silent action $\tau$ is relabelled to
$\tau$, an input on a channel $a$ is relabelled to the image of $a$ under $f$, and an output on
$a$ is relabelled to the complement of the image of $a$ under $f$, each viewed as a CCS label.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves strong bisimilarity
articles.statement:
For every relabelling $f$ and all finite CCS
processes $P$ and $Q$ with static operators, if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the
labelled transition system of finite CCS with static operators, then the relabellings of $P$
and of $Q$ by $f$ are strongly bisimilar there.

articles.title: Closure of a relation under one relabelling
articles.statement:
Given a relabelling $f$ and a relation $R$
on finite CCS processes with static operators, the lifted relation is the least relation that
relates $P$ to $Q$ and relates the relabelling of $P$ by $f$ to the relabelling of $Q$ by $f$
whenever $R$ relates $P$ to $Q$.

articles.title: Relabelling
articles.statement:
A finite CCS relabelling over channel names is a finite list of entries
$(a, \ell)$, each pairing a channel name $a$ with a visible label $\ell$, that is, an input or an
output on some channel. The entry $(a, \ell)$ gives $\ell$ as the image of the input on $a$; the
image of the output on $a$ is then the complement of $\ell$. The first entry with name $a$ is
used, and a name occurring in no entry is mapped to itself.

articles.title: Restriction preserves strong bisimilarity
articles.statement:
For every finite list $L$ of channel names and
all static CCS processes $P$ and $Q$, if $P$ and $Q$ are strongly bisimilar in the labelled
transition system of finite CCS with static operators, then so are the restricted processes
$P \setminus L$ and $Q \setminus L$.

articles.title: Lifting a relation through a restriction
articles.statement:
Given a finite list $L$ of channel names and a
relation $R$ on static CCS processes, the lifted relation relates $P$ to $Q$ exactly when either
$R$ relates $P$ to $Q$, or $P = P' \setminus L$ and $Q = Q' \setminus L$ for some processes $P'$
and $Q'$ that $R$ relates.

articles.title: Recursive CCS specification
articles.statement:
Given a type of channel names and a type of process constants,
a recursive specification assigns to each process constant $A$ a defining body: a CCS process
expression over those names, which may itself mention process constants (including $A$).

articles.title: Static CCS processes
articles.statement:
Finite CCS processes with the static operators, over a type of
channel names, are built from the inactive process $0$ by the prefix $\alpha.P$ of a CCS action
$\alpha$ (silent, an input or an output) and a process $P$, the choice $P + Q$, the parallel
composition $P \mid Q$, the restriction $P \setminus L$ of $P$ by a finite list $L$ of names, and
the relabelling $P[f]$ of $P$ by a finite relabelling $f$.

Unlike function-valued operators, finite lists and tables preserve decidable
equality of processes and cannot express relabellings that alter the silent action $\tau$ or fail
to preserve complementary visible actions.

articles.title: Transitions of recursive CCS
articles.statement:
Let the channel names have decidable equality and let
$\Delta$ be a recursive specification, assigning to each process constant $A$ its defining body
$\Delta(A)$. The labelled transition relation $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ relative to $\Delta$ on
recursive CCS processes, with actions $\alpha$ the CCS labels (silent $\tau$, inputs and outputs),
is the least relation closed under the following rules, where $\alpha.P$ is the prefix, $P + Q$
the choice, $P \mid Q$ the parallel composition, $P \setminus L$ the restriction of $P$ by a
finite list $L$ of channel names, and $P[f]$ the relabelling of $P$ by a finite relabelling $f$.
If $\Delta(A) \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, then $A \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$. The prefix has the
transition $\alpha.P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P$. If $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, then
$P + Q \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, $Q + P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$,
$P \mid Q \xrightarrow{\alpha} P' \mid Q$ and $Q \mid P \xrightarrow{\alpha} Q \mid P'$. If
$P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ and $Q \xrightarrow{\beta} Q'$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
complementary (an input and an output on the same channel), then
$P \mid Q \xrightarrow{\tau} P' \mid Q'$. If $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ and $\alpha$ is $\tau$ or
its channel is not in $L$, then $P \setminus L \xrightarrow{\alpha} P' \setminus L$. If
$P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, then $P[f] \xrightarrow{f(\alpha)} P'[f]$, where $f(\tau) = \tau$, an
input on a channel $a$ is sent to the visible label $f(a)$ that $f$ assigns to $a$, and an output
on $a$ is sent to the complement of $f(a)$.

articles.title: Transitions of static CCS
articles.statement:
The labelled transition relation $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ on
static CCS processes, with actions $\alpha$ the CCS labels (silent $\tau$, inputs and outputs), is
the least relation closed under the following rules, where $\alpha.P$ is the prefix, $P + Q$ the
choice, $P \mid Q$ the parallel composition, $P \setminus L$ the restriction of $P$ by a finite
list $L$ of channel names, and $P[f]$ the relabelling of $P$ by a finite relabelling $f$. The
prefix has the transition $\alpha.P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P$. If $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, then
$P + Q \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, $Q + P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$,
$P \mid Q \xrightarrow{\alpha} P' \mid Q$ and $Q \mid P \xrightarrow{\alpha} Q \mid P'$. If
$P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ and $Q \xrightarrow{\beta} Q'$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
complementary (an input and an output on the same channel), then
$P \mid Q \xrightarrow{\tau} P' \mid Q'$. If $P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$ and $\alpha$ is $\tau$ or
its channel is not in $L$, then $P \setminus L \xrightarrow{\alpha} P' \setminus L$. If
$P \xrightarrow{\alpha} P'$, then $P[f] \xrightarrow{f(\alpha)} P'[f]$, where $f(\tau) = \tau$, an
input on a channel $a$ is sent to the visible label $f(a)$ that $f$ assigns to $a$, and an output
on $a$ is sent to the complement of $f(a)$.

articles.title: Transitions of finite CCS without communication
articles.statement:
The transition relation
$P \xrightarrow{a} P'$ on finite CCS processes is the operational semantics of finite CCS whose
synchronization function is undefined on every pair of actions. Thus prefix and choice move as
usual, and a parallel composition $P \mid Q$ moves only by letting one of $P$ and $Q$ move;
there are no communication steps.

articles.title: Synchronization of CCS labels
articles.statement:
Let the names form a type with decidable equality. For
labels $a$ and $b$, the synchronization of $a$ with $b$ is the silent action $\tau$ when $a$ is
the input on a name $n$ and $b$ is the output on the same name $n$, or when $a$ is the output on
$n$ and $b$ is the input on $n$. For every other pair of labels, including any pair involving
$\tau$, there is no result.

This partial function supplies the communication rule of the CCS operational semantics.

articles.title: Visible labels as CCS labels
articles.statement:
The inclusion of visible labels into CCS labels sends the
input on a channel $a$ to the input on $a$, and the output on $a$ to the output on $a$.

articles.title: Visible CCS label
articles.statement: A visible CCS label, excluding the silent action.

articles.title: Locally closed processes at a binder depth
articles.statement:
Every variable refers to an enclosing input/restriction binder.
`ClosedAt 0` permits free constants, but no dangling de Bruijn variables.

articles.title: Name scoped at a binder depth
articles.statement:
A name refers only to the `depth` surrounding binders or to a free
constant. At depth zero, no variable is permitted.

articles.title: Lifting preserves process scoping
articles.statement:
Shifting a process past a new binder preserves scoping. Inner input
and restriction binders increase the cutoff as in `Basic.liftProc`.

articles.title: Lifting fixes an in-scope name
articles.statement: Lifting above the ambient binder depth fixes an in-scope name.

articles.title: Lifting fixes a locally closed process
articles.statement:
Lifting above the surrounding binders fixes a locally closed process.
At depth zero, insertion under a fresh binder cannot capture its names.

articles.title: Lifting preserves name scoping
articles.statement:
Inserting a binder at any cutoff preserves name scoping in the
larger environment.

articles.title: Instantiating the innermost binder preserves process scoping
articles.statement: Instantiating the innermost binder preserves process scoping.

articles.title: Substitution at any cutoff preserves process scoping
articles.statement:
Capture-avoiding substitution removes one ambient binder while
preserving every name's scope, including under input and restriction.

articles.title: Name substitution preserves scoping
articles.statement:
Removing the binder at `k ≤ n` preserves name scoping when its
replacement is scoped in the remaining environment.

articles.title: Barbed bisimilar processes have the same barbs
articles.statement: Bisimilar processes have the same immediate free-channel barbs.

articles.title: Structural congruence preserves immediate barbs
articles.statement: Structural congruence preserves immediate barbs.

articles.title: Barbs of an input prefix
articles.statement: Waiting inputs are observable, despite being unable to reduce alone.

articles.title: The inactive process has no barbs
articles.statement: The inactive process has no barb, even after structural rearrangement.

articles.title: Barbs of a restricted output prefix
articles.statement:
A restricted output is visible exactly when its subject is free.
Sending the private name on a free subject remains observable.

articles.title: Barbs of an output prefix
articles.statement:
Output readiness sees only its free subject and direction, not its
object or guarded continuation.

articles.title: Immediate free-channel barb
articles.statement:
Immediate free-channel readiness, up to the existing structural
congruence. A witness performs no `Step`.

articles.title: Structurally congruent processes are barbed bisimilar
articles.statement:
Every structural law of `Basic` is sound for strong barbed
bisimilarity, including scope extrusion and replication unfolding.

articles.title: Strong barbed bisimilarity
articles.statement:
Strong barbed bisimilarity, using the canonical CSLib bisimulation API.
No context closure is built into this relation.

articles.title: Labels for reductions and barb observations
articles.statement: Labels for reductions and observation-only self-loops.

articles.title: Structural congruence is a strong barbed bisimulation
articles.statement:
Structural congruence is a strong barbed bisimulation: reductions
match one for one, while free-channel observations match immediately.

articles.title: Every reduction source has an unguarded output
articles.statement:
Every reduction needs an unguarded output in its source, even when
communication is private or structural congruence is used arbitrarily.

articles.title: Structural congruence preserves unguarded outputs
articles.statement:
Structural rearrangement cannot expose an output from an input-guarded
process. This includes arbitrary uses of replication and scope laws.

articles.title: Unguarded output in a process
articles.statement:
An output not behind a prefix, on any subject (including bound names).
This is an overapproximation for arbitrary unguarded sums, not a barb.

articles.title: Free-channel input is not barbed bisimilar to nil
articles.statement:
Waiting for input is not equivalent to doing nothing. Reduction-only
bisimilarity would miss this distinction.

articles.title: Decorated-LTS bisimulations are exactly strong barbed bisimulations
articles.statement:
The decorated LTS has precisely the strong reduction-matching and
immediate-barb-preservation clauses of a strong barbed bisimulation.

articles.title: Barbed bisimilarity preserves may-barbs
articles.statement: Strong barbed bisimilarity preserves finite may observations.

articles.title: May-barb after finitely many reductions
articles.statement:
A free-channel barb reachable by finitely many existing reductions,
possibly zero. This is a may observation, not a weak equivalence.

articles.title: Processes without unguarded output cannot reduce
articles.statement:
Outputless processes cannot reduce. Input guards may still have
observable input barbs; this theorem does not identify them with `nil`.

articles.title: Free-channel input and output observables
articles.statement:
A visible input or output subject. Restricted variables are not subjects
of these free-channel observations.

articles.title: Reduction LTS decorated with barb observations
articles.statement:
The existing reduction semantics decorated with barb tests. The
observation transitions do not consume a prefix or transmit a name.

articles.title: Exposed guards are barbs
articles.statement:
A directly exposed guard is a barb, with the reflexive structural
representative as witness.

articles.title: Free-channel guard offered without reduction
articles.statement:
A selected free-channel guard exposed without reduction. Restrictions
hide bound subjects but do not hide free constants.

articles.title: Barbed bisimilarity transfers finite reduction paths
articles.statement: A finite reduction path transfers across strong barbed bisimilarity.

articles.title: Barbed bisimilarity matches each reduction by one reduction
articles.statement:
A reduction from the first process is matched by one reduction,
with strong barbed bisimilar derivatives.

articles.title: Contextual barbed equivalence implies barbed bisimilarity
articles.statement: Contextual barbed equivalence implies standalone barbed bisimilarity.

articles.title: Composition of process contexts
articles.statement: Substitute a context into the hole of another context.

articles.title: One-hole lexical process contexts
articles.statement: One-hole lexical contexts, including guards, choice and replication.

articles.title: Structural congruence implies contextual barbed equivalence
articles.statement:
Structural congruence is sound under every observer context, with
one-for-one reduction matching and immediate input/output barbs.

articles.title: Contextual strong barbed equivalence
articles.statement:
Strong barbed equivalence in every lexical process context. For
capture-avoiding use, both hole processes must satisfy `Proc.ClosedAt 0`.

articles.title: Structural congruence is closed under contexts
articles.statement: Structural congruence survives every one-hole lexical context.

articles.title: Contextual barbed equivalence is closed under contexts
articles.statement: Contextual barbed equivalence survives filling a context.

articles.title: Structural laws are barbed sound in capture-avoiding contexts
articles.statement:
Every structural law is strongly barbed sound under capture-avoiding
contexts, for locally closed hole processes.

articles.title: Capture-avoiding and lexical filling agree on locally closed holes
articles.statement:
Lexical and capture-avoiding filling agree for locally closed holes.
This is the explicit admissibility condition for the contextual theorem.

articles.title: Capture-avoiding filling of a process context
articles.statement:
Capture-avoiding filling: each context binder shifts dangling names
of the hole, while binders internal to the hole remain untouched.

articles.title: Filling a composed context is iterated filling
articles.statement: Context composition agrees with iterated filling.

articles.title: Lexical filling of a process context
articles.statement:
Fill the lexical hole. Free constants are never captured; locally
closed hole processes have no references into surrounding binders.

articles.title: Structural congruence of π-calculus processes
articles.statement:
Structural congruence: `|` is commutative and associative with
unit `nil`, `ν` extrudes over `|` (lifting the other side, which cannot
mention the fresh name), restriction of `nil` is `nil`, nested
restrictions commute (swapping the two bound indices), and replication
unfolds.

articles.title: Lifting free de Bruijn indices of a π-calculus name
articles.statement:
Shift free variables at or above `cutoff` up by one, e.g. when
pushing a process under a binder.

articles.title: Lifting free de Bruijn indices of a π-calculus process
articles.statement:
Shift free variables of a process, entering binders with an
increased cutoff.

articles.title: Channel name in the π-calculus
articles.statement:
A channel name: a free channel `const n`, or the `i`-th enclosing
binder `var i`.

articles.title: Processes of the π-calculus
articles.statement:
Processes of the π-calculus. `inp a p` binds variable `0` in `p`;
`nu p` binds variable `0` in `p` as a fresh channel.

articles.title: Guarded-choice resolution in the π-calculus
articles.statement:
Guarded-choice resolution: discard sum branches to reach a
guarded process. Transitivity handles nested sums.

articles.title: Reduction relation of the π-calculus
articles.statement:
Reduction: communication (substituting the sent channel for the
input variable) between any selected output and input guards,
reduction under `|` and `ν`, and reduction up to structural
congruence.

articles.title: Substitution of a name into a π-calculus name
articles.statement:
Substitute the name `n` for the variable at `cutoff`: variables
below the cutoff are bound by inner binders and untouched, the variable
at the cutoff is replaced by `n`, and variables above shift down by
one.

articles.title: Substitution leaves constant channels and the empty process unchanged
articles.statement:
Substitution leaves a process with no `var 0` untouched: a
constant channel stays constant, and the empty process stays empty.

articles.title: Substitution of a name into a π-calculus process at a cutoff
articles.statement:
Substitute the name `n` for the variable at `cutoff` in a
process. Under a binder, `n` is lifted by one at cutoff `0` so it
keeps referring to the same outer names: every free index of `n`
refers to a binder above the substitution point, so all of them shift.
Lifting at the current cutoff would leave indices below the cutoff
captured by the new binder.

articles.title: Substitution for the innermost bound variable of a process
articles.statement: Substitute the name `n` for the innermost bound variable of `p`.

articles.title: Swapping adjacent de Bruijn indices in a name
articles.statement:
Swap the two de Bruijn indices `cutoff` and `cutoff + 1` in a name:
the two binders at that depth exchange places.

articles.title: Swapping adjacent binders throughout a process
articles.statement:
Swap the two binders at depth `cutoff` throughout a process,
incrementing the cutoff under binders.

articles.title: Boolean restriction test
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ of blocked names, the test returns true on a
label exactly when the label is the silent action $\tau$, or an input or an output on a name
that does not occur in $L$. It is the Boolean form of the condition that restriction by $L$
allows the label.

articles.title: Backward certificate check
articles.statement:
Let $s$ list the labelled transitions $(a, x')$ of each
implementation code $x$, let $t$ list those of each specification code $y$, and let $R$ be a
finite list of code pairs. The backward check succeeds when for every pair $(x, y)$ in $R$ and
every entry $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$, at least one of the following holds: $a = \tau$ and
$(x, y')$ is in $R$; some entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ with the same label has $(x', y')$ in $R$;
or some entry $(\tau, x'')$ of $s(x)$ has $(x'', y)$ in $R$, and the first occurrence of
$(x'', y)$ in $R$ comes strictly before the first occurrence of $(x, y)$.

articles.title: Weak-bisimulation certificate check
articles.statement:
For transition lists $s$ of implementation codes
and $t$ of specification codes and a finite list $R$ of code pairs, the certificate check
succeeds when both the forward check and the backward check succeed on $s$, $t$ and $R$.

articles.title: Constants listing their transitions realize them
articles.statement:
Fix a recursive specification, a map
$\iota$ from codes to process constants and a function $s$ listing labelled transitions for
each code. Suppose that for every code $x$, writing $(a_1, y_1), \dots, (a_n, y_n)$ for the
entries of $s(x)$ in order, the body of the constant $\iota(x)$ is
$a_1.\iota(y_1) + (a_2.\iota(y_2) + \dots + (a_n.\iota(y_n) + 0))$, which is $0$ when $n = 0$.
Then the processes $\iota(x)$, indexed by codes $x$, realize $s$.

articles.title: Forward certificate check
articles.statement:
Let $s$ list the labelled transitions $(a, x')$ of each
implementation code $x$, let $t$ list those of each specification code $y$, and let $R$ be a
finite list of code pairs. The forward check succeeds when for every pair $(x, y)$ in $R$ and
every entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$, either $a = \tau$ and $(x', y)$ is in $R$, or some entry
$(a, y')$ of $t(y)$ with the same label has $(x', y')$ in $R$.

articles.title: Code-level parallel composition
articles.statement:
Given functions $s$ and $t$ listing the labelled
transitions of codes $x$ and $y$, the transitions of the pair $(x, y)$ are listed in three
blocks: $(a, (x', y))$ for each entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$; then $(a, (x, y'))$ for each entry
$(a, y')$ of $t(y)$; then $(\tau, (x', y'))$ for each entry $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ and each entry
$(b, y')$ of $t(y)$ whose labels are complementary, that is, one is the input and the other the
output on the same name.

articles.title: Parallel composition preserves realization
articles.statement:
Fix a recursive specification. If the
processes $P_x$ realize $s$ and the processes $Q_y$ realize $t$, then the parallel compositions
$P_x \mid Q_y$, indexed by pairs $(x, y)$, realize the code-level parallel composition of $s$
and $t$.

articles.title: Realization of a code-level transition system
articles.statement:
Fix a recursive specification. A family
of processes $P_x$ indexed by codes $x$ realizes a function $s$ that lists, for each code $x$,
labelled transitions $(a, y)$ with $a$ a label and $y$ a code, when for every code $x$, every
label $a$ and every process $q$, the process $P_x$ has a transition with label $a$ to $q$
exactly when $s(x)$ contains an entry $(a, y)$ with $P_y = q$.

articles.title: Code-level restriction
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ of blocked names and a function $s$ listing the
labelled transitions of each code, the restricted transitions of a code $x$ are the entries
$(a, y)$ of $s(x)$, in order, whose label $a$ is the silent action $\tau$ or an input or an
output on a name that does not occur in $L$.

articles.title: Restriction preserves realization
articles.statement:
Fix a recursive specification and a list $L$ of
blocked names. If the processes $P_x$ realize $s$, then the restricted processes
$P_x \setminus L$ realize the code-level restriction of $s$ by $L$.

articles.title: Direct check of the root condition
articles.statement:
Given code-level transition functions $s$ on codes
$\alpha$ and $t$ on codes $\beta$, each listing labelled steps to codes, a relation $R$ given as
a list of code pairs, and codes $x$ and $y$, the root check succeeds exactly when every listed
step $(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ is matched by some listed step $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$ with the same label
and $(x', y') \in R$, and every listed step $(a, y')$ of $t(y)$ is matched by some listed step
$(a, x')$ of $s(x)$ with the same label and $(x', y') \in R$.

This is a sufficient check of the root condition of observation congruence at $(x, y)$. Rooted
weak bisimilarity also allows silent steps around the matching step, so the check is incomplete.

articles.title: Certificate checks give rooted observation congruence
articles.statement:
Let $f$ realize the code-level
transition function $s$ and $g$ realize $t$ for a recursive specification, and let $R$ be a list
of code pairs on which the certificate check of $s$, $t$ and $R$ succeeds. If the root check of
$s$, $t$ and $R$ succeeds at codes $x$ and $y$, then the processes $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ are rooted
weakly bisimilar (observation congruent) in the labelled transition system of the specification
(Milner, Chapter 7).

articles.title: Transitions of a sum of prefixes
articles.statement:
For every recursive specification, every list $l$ of
pairs of a label and a process, every label $a$ and every process $q$, the sum of the prefixes
listed in $l$ has a transition labelled $a$ to $q$ exactly when $(a, q)$ belongs to $l$.

articles.title: Sum of prefixes
articles.statement:
For a list $l$ of pairs $(a, q)$ of a label and a process, the process
that chooses among the prefixes $a.q$ listed in $l$: the empty list gives the inactive process
$\mathbf{0}$, and the list with head $(a, q)$ and tail $r$ gives the choice $a.q + P$ between the
prefix $a.q$ and the process $P$ built in the same way from $r$.

articles.title: Certificate checks give weak bisimilarity
articles.statement:
Let $f$ realize the code-level transition
function $s$ and $g$ realize $t$ for a recursive specification, and let $R$ be a list of code
pairs on which the certificate check of $s$, $t$ and $R$ succeeds. Then for every pair $(x, y)$
in $R$, the processes $f(x)$ and $g(y)$ are weakly bisimilar in the labelled transition system
of the specification.

articles.title: Finite run
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system, a sequence of states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$
is a finite run of length $k$ when for every $i < k$ there is a label $a$ such that there is a
transition from $s_i$ to $s_{i+1}$ labelled $a$.

The states after index $k$ are unconstrained.

articles.title: Invariant principle for infinite runs
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a predicate on the states of a labelled
transition system such that, whenever $P(s)$ holds and there is a transition from $s$ to $t$ with
some label, $P(t)$ holds. Then for every infinite run $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ with $P(s_0)$, the
predicate $P(s_k)$ holds for every $k$.

articles.title: Infinite state runs lift to labeled executions
articles.statement: Select a witnessing label at each step of an infinite state run.

articles.title: Labeled infinite executions give state runs
articles.statement: Forget the labels of a canonical infinite execution.

articles.title: Infinite run
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system, a sequence of states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$
is an infinite run when for every $i$ there is a label $a$ such that there is a transition from
$s_i$ to $s_{i+1}$ labelled $a$.

articles.title: Shifted function sequences agree with ω-sequence drop
articles.statement: Function-sequence suffixes agree with canonical `ωSequence.drop`.

articles.title: Shifted sequence
articles.statement:
For a sequence $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$ and a natural number $k$, the shift
of the sequence by $k$ is the sequence whose $i$-th term is $s_{i+k}$; that is, the suffix
starting at index $k$, re-indexed from $0$.

articles.title: Reachability in a labelled transition system is transitive
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition
system, say that a state $s$ can reach a state $t$ when there is a finite list of labels along
which $s$ makes a multistep transition to $t$. If $s$ can reach $m$ and $m$ can reach $t$, then
$s$ can reach $t$.

The witnessing list of labels is the concatenation of the two given lists.

articles.title: Observation congruence matches rooted weak transitions
articles.statement:
In a labelled transition system
with a silent label $\tau$, if $p$ and $q$ are rooted weakly bisimilar and there is a rooted weak
