respect to $I$, and that every state satisfying $I$ in which $b$ evaluates to false satisfies
$Q$. Then $I$ entails the weakest liberal precondition of the loop
$\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ with respect to $Q$.

articles.title: Loop runs with a given number of iterations
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression and $c$ a
command. For a natural number $n$ and states $s$, $s'$, the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$
runs from $s$ to $s'$ in $n$ iterations when, started in $s$, it exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$
executions of the body $c$. This is the least relation such that the loop runs from $s$ to $s$ in
$0$ iterations whenever $b$ evaluates to false in $s$, and the loop runs from $s$ to $s'$ in
$n + 1$ iterations whenever $b$ evaluates to true in $s$, the body $c$ has a terminating big-step
execution from $s$ to some state $t$, and the loop runs from $t$ to $s'$ in $n$ iterations.

articles.title: The iteration count of a nonterminating loop is zero
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a
command and $s$ a state. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ has no terminating
big-step execution from $s$ to any state, then the iteration count of the loop from $s$ is
$0$.

articles.title: The iteration count of a terminating loop run
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a
command, $n$ a natural number and $s$, $s'$ states. If the loop $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$,
started in $s$, exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$ executions of the body $c$, then the iteration
count of the loop from $s$ is $n$.

articles.title: Loop iteration count
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ a command and $s$ a state. If
there are a natural number $n$ and a state $s'$ such that the loop
$\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, started in $s$, exits in $s'$ after exactly $n$ executions of
the body $c$, then the iteration count of the loop from $s$ is such an $n$; otherwise it is $0$.

Such an $n$ is unique because IMP is deterministic, so the iteration count is the number of body
executions the loop performs from $s$ before exiting.

articles.title: Total-correctness weakest precondition implies the weakest liberal precondition
articles.statement:
For
every command $c$, postcondition $Q$ and state $s$, if $s$ satisfies the total-correctness
weakest precondition $\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)$, then $s$ satisfies the weakest liberal precondition
$\mathrm{wlp}(c, Q)$.

articles.title: Soundness of total-correctness Hoare logic
articles.statement:
For all assertions $P$ and $Q$ and every
command $c$, if the triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic, then
it is valid for total correctness: every state satisfying $P$ has a terminating big-step
execution of $c$ ending in a state that satisfies $Q$.

articles.title: Soundness of Hoare logic for partial correctness
articles.statement:
Every partial-correctness Hoare triple
$\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ that is derivable in the partial-correctness proof system is valid: for all
states $s$ and $s'$, if $s$ satisfies $P$ and $c$ has a terminating big-step execution from $s$ to
$s'$, then $s'$ satisfies $Q$.

articles.title: Precondition strengthening for total correctness
articles.statement:
Let $P$, $P'$ and $Q$ be assertions and
$c$ a command. If $P$ entails $P'$ (every state satisfying $P$ satisfies $P'$) and the triple
$\{P'\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic, then so is
$\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$.

articles.title: Precondition strengthening for partial correctness
articles.statement:
Let $P$, $P'$ and $Q$ be assertions
and $c$ a command. If $P$ entails $P'$ (every state satisfying $P$ satisfies $P'$) and the
partial-correctness triple $\{P'\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the partial-correctness proof
system, then so is $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$.

articles.title: Substitution in an assertion
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be an assertion, $x$ a variable and $e$ an
arithmetic expression. The assertion $P[e/x]$ holds in a state $s$ exactly when $P$ holds in
the state obtained from $s$ by setting the value of $x$ to the value of $e$ in $s$.

articles.title: Total-correctness Hoare logic is sound and complete for the denotational semantics
articles.statement:
For
all assertions $P$, $Q$ (predicates on states) and every IMP command $c$, the triple
$\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the total-correctness Hoare logic if and only if for every
state $s$ satisfying $P$ there is a state $s'$ such that $(s, s')$ lies in the relational
denotation of $c$ and $s'$ satisfies $Q$.

articles.title: Soundness and relative completeness of total-correctness Hoare logic
articles.statement:
For all assertions
$P$, $Q$ (predicates on states) and every IMP command $c$, the triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is
derivable in the total-correctness Hoare logic if and only if it is totally valid.

articles.title: The weakest-precondition triple is derivable in total-correctness Hoare logic
articles.statement:
For every
IMP command $c$ and every assertion $Q$ (a predicate on states), the triple
$\{\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ is derivable in the total-correctness Hoare logic. Here
$\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)$ is the semantic weakest precondition: it holds in a state $s$ exactly when
there is a terminating execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state satisfying $Q$.

articles.title: Total-correctness Hoare logic
articles.statement:
Derivability of total-correctness Hoare triples
$\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$, for assertions $P$, $Q$ (predicates on states) and IMP commands $c$, is the
least relation closed under the following rules. In an assertion, $b$ for a boolean expression
means that $b$ evaluates to true and $\neg b$ that it evaluates to false. Skip:
$\{Q\}\,\mathtt{skip}\,\{Q\}$. Assignment: for a variable $x$ and an arithmetic expression $a$,
$\{Q[a/x]\}\,x := a\,\{Q\}$, where $Q[a/x]$ holds in a state $s$ iff $Q$ holds in $s$ updated at
$x$ to the value of $a$ in $s$. Sequencing: from $\{P\}\,c_1\,\{R\}$ and $\{R\}\,c_2\,\{Q\}$
derive $\{P\}\,c_1; c_2\,\{Q\}$. Conditional: from $\{P \wedge b\}\,c_1\,\{Q\}$ and
$\{P \wedge \neg b\}\,c_2\,\{Q\}$ derive
$\{P\}\,\mathtt{if}\ b\ \mathtt{then}\ c_1\ \mathtt{else}\ c_2\,\{Q\}$. Loop (variant rule): for an
assertion $I$ and a map $V$ from states to natural numbers, if for every natural number $n$ the
triple $\{I \wedge b \wedge V = n\}\,c\,\{I \wedge V < n\}$ is derivable, derive
$\{I\}\,\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c\,\{I \wedge \neg b\}$. Consequence: if $P$ entails $P'$,
$\{P'\}\,c\,\{Q'\}$ is derivable and $Q'$ entails $Q$, derive $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$, where entailment
is pointwise implication.

articles.title: Total correctness gives a terminating small-step run
articles.statement:
If the total-correctness Hoare
triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid and a state $s$
satisfies $P$, then there is a state $t$ such that $c$, started in $s$, reaches
$\mathtt{skip}$ with state $t$ in finitely many small steps, and $t$ satisfies $Q$.

articles.title: Total-correctness tag for Hoare triples
articles.statement:
An empty type used only as a label: derivability
of Hoare triples in the total-correctness Hoare logic is registered as an inference system under
this tag, while partial-correctness derivability is the default inference system on Hoare
triples.

articles.title: Hoare triples
articles.statement:
A Hoare triple $\{P\}\,c\,\{Q\}$ consists of a precondition $P$ and a
postcondition $Q$, both assertions (predicates on states), and an IMP command $c$. It is the
judgement form of both the partial-correctness and the total-correctness Hoare logic.

articles.title: Validity of total-correctness Hoare triples
articles.statement:
For assertions $P$ and $Q$ on states and a
command $c$, the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and
postcondition $Q$ is valid when every state $s$ satisfying $P$ has a terminating big-step
execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state $t$ that satisfies $Q$.

articles.title: Total correctness implies partial correctness
articles.statement:
For assertions $P$, $Q$ and a command
$c$, if the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and
postcondition $Q$ is valid, then the partial-correctness Hoare triple with the same
precondition, command and postcondition is valid.

articles.title: Validity of a Hoare triple
articles.statement:
For assertions $P$ and $Q$ and a command $c$, the
partial-correctness Hoare triple $\lbrace P \rbrace\ c\ \lbrace Q \rbrace$ is valid when, for all
states $s$ and $t$, if $s$ satisfies $P$ and executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $t$ under the
big-step semantics, then $t$ satisfies $Q$.

articles.title: Weakest-precondition unfolding of a while loop
articles.statement:
For a Boolean guard $b$, a loop body
$c$, a postcondition $Q$ and a state $s$, the state $s$ satisfies the total-correctness weakest
precondition $\mathrm{wp}(\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c, Q)$ if and only if either $b$
evaluates to false in $s$ and $s$ satisfies $Q$, or $b$ evaluates to true in $s$ and $s$
satisfies $\mathrm{wp}(c, \mathrm{wp}(\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c, Q))$.

articles.title: Weakest liberal precondition unfolding of a while loop
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression,
$c$ a command and $Q$ an assertion. Write $\mathrm{wlp}(d, R)$ for the weakest liberal
precondition of a command $d$ with respect to an assertion $R$, and let $W$ be the loop
$\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$. Then $\mathrm{wlp}(W, Q)$ is the assertion that holds in a
state $s$ exactly when both of the following hold: if $b$ evaluates to false in $s$, then $Q$
holds in $s$; and if $b$ evaluates to true in $s$, then $\mathrm{wlp}(c, \mathrm{wlp}(W, Q))$
holds in $s$.

articles.title: Invariant rule for while loops
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be an assertion, $b$ a Boolean expression and
$c$ a command. Write $I \wedge b$ for the assertion that $I$ holds and $b$ evaluates to true,
and $I \wedge \neg b$ for the assertion that $I$ holds and $b$ evaluates to false. If the
partial-correctness Hoare triple $\lbrace I \wedge b \rbrace\ c\ \lbrace I \rbrace$ is valid,
then so is the triple
$\lbrace I \rbrace\ \mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c\ \lbrace I \wedge \neg b \rbrace$.

articles.title: Variant rule for while loops
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be an assertion (the invariant), $V$ a function
from states to natural numbers (the variant), $b$ a Boolean guard and $c$ a command. Suppose
that for every state $s$ satisfying $I$ in which $b$ evaluates to true, there is a terminating
big-step execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state $s'$ that satisfies $I$ with
$V(s') < V(s)$. Then the total-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $I$, command
$\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ and postcondition "$I$ holds and $b$ evaluates to false"
is valid.

articles.title: Weakest liberal precondition
articles.statement:
For a command $c$ and an assertion $Q$, the weakest
liberal precondition of $c$ with respect to $Q$ is the assertion that holds in a state $s$
exactly when every state $t$ in which an execution of $c$ from $s$ terminates, under the
big-step semantics, satisfies $Q$.

It is liberal because no termination claim is made: a state from which $c$ has no terminating
execution satisfies it for every $Q$.

articles.title: Weakest precondition for total correctness
articles.statement:
For a command $c$ and a postcondition $Q$,
the weakest precondition $\mathrm{wp}(c, Q)$ is the assertion that holds at a state $s$ exactly
when there is a terminating big-step execution of $c$ from $s$ ending in a state that satisfies
$Q$.

articles.title: Membership in a diagonal test relation
articles.statement: Membership in a diagonal test.

articles.title: A one-step simulation lifts to finite iteration
articles.statement:
A one-step simulation lifts to arbitrary finite iteration.
The simulator `p` need not be invertible or a test.

articles.title: Postcondition absorption characterizes partial correctness
articles.statement:
A postcondition can be absorbed on the right exactly when it holds
on every execution starting in the precondition.

articles.title: Verification inequality characterizes partial correctness
articles.statement:
The verification inequality is precisely universal partial
correctness: every execution from `P` ends in `Q`.

articles.title: Partial correctness as unreachability of the negated postcondition
articles.statement:
Classically, verification means that no execution from `P` can
reach the complement of `Q`.

articles.title: Test of a negated assertion is the complement within identity
articles.statement:
Boolean test negation is complement relative to identity, not the
full relation-algebra complement (which includes off-diagonal pairs).

articles.title: Test of the false assertion is the zero relation
articles.statement: The false assertion is the zero relation.

articles.title: Diagonal tests are subidentities
articles.statement: A test is a subidentity, not an arbitrary relation.

articles.title: Composing diagonal tests conjoins their assertions
articles.statement: Sequential tests conjoin their assertions without changing state.

articles.title: Test of a union of assertions is the union of tests
articles.statement: Union of assertions is union of their diagonal tests.

articles.title: Test of the true assertion is the identity relation
articles.statement: The true assertion is the identity relation.

articles.title: Diagonal test relation of an assertion
articles.statement: The diagonal relation restricted to an assertion.

articles.title: Tests preserved by one step are preserved by iteration
articles.statement:
An idempotent subidentity preserved by one step is preserved by
iteration. This is a corollary of `star_simulation`; the test assumptions
are explicit, with no additional algebraic structure.

articles.title: Assignment rule with a store-irrelevant heap assertion
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $y$ be variables,
let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on stores, and let $H$ be a store-irrelevant heap assertion.
Write $s[x := n]$ for the store that agrees with $s$ except that it maps $x$ to $n$. If every
store $s$ satisfying $p$ has $q(s[x := s(y)])$, then the separation-logic triple for the
assignment $x := y$ is valid with precondition "$p(s)$ and $H(s, h)$" and postcondition
"$q(s)$ and $H(s, h)$", where $s$ is the store and $h$ the heap.

An assignment leaves the heap untouched, so no framing is needed.

articles.title: Empty-heap assertion
articles.statement:
The heap assertion $\mathrm{emp}$ holds of a store $s$ and a heap
$h$ exactly when $h$ is the empty heap, whatever the store $s$ is.

articles.title: Entailment of heap assertions
articles.statement:
A heap assertion $P$ entails a heap assertion $Q$ when, for
every store $s$ and every heap $h$, if $P$ holds of $s$ and $h$, then $Q$ holds of $s$ and $h$.

articles.title: Existential rule for separation-logic triples
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a heap command, let $\iota$ be
an arbitrary index (any type or proposition), and let $P_i$ and $Q_i$ be heap assertions for
each $i$ in $\iota$. If for every $i$ the triple with precondition $P_i$, command $c$ and
postcondition $Q_i$ is valid, then the triple with precondition "there is $i$ with $P_i$",
command $c$ and postcondition "there is $i$ with $Q_i$" is valid.

articles.title: Store-irrelevant frames satisfy the frame-rule side condition
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
store-irrelevant heap assertion and $c$ a heap command. For all stores $s, s'$ and every heap
$h$, if $R(s, h)$ holds and $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of variables
that $c$ may assign to, then $R(s', h)$ holds.

This is the side condition on the frame in the frame rule.

articles.title: Frame rule
articles.statement:
Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be heap assertions and $c$ a heap command. Suppose the
separation-logic triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid, and
suppose that whenever $R$ holds of a store $s$ and a heap $h$, it also holds of $s'$ and $h$ for
every store $s'$ that agrees with $s$ on every variable outside the set of variables that $c$ may
assign to. Then the triple with precondition $P \star R$, command $c$ and postcondition
$Q \star R$ is valid, where $\star$ denotes separating conjunction.

articles.title: Conjunction of heap assertions
articles.statement:
For heap assertions $P$ and $Q$, the assertion
$P \wedge Q$ holds of a store $s$ and a heap $h$ exactly when $P$ holds of $s$ and $h$ and $Q$
holds of $s$ and the same heap $h$.

articles.title: Heap assertion
articles.statement:
A heap assertion is a predicate on a store and a heap: it assigns a
proposition to every store $s$ and every heap $h$. Heap assertions serve as the preconditions
and postconditions of separation logic.

articles.title: Existential heap assertion
articles.statement:
For a function $p$ assigning a heap assertion $p(n)$ to each
natural number $n$ (an address or a value), the assertion $\exists n,\ p(n)$ holds of a store $s$
and a heap $h$ exactly when $p(n)$ holds of $s$ and $h$ for some natural number $n$.

articles.title: Framed embedding of Hoare validity
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be store assertions, $R$ a heap
assertion and $c$ a command of plain IMP, and write $\hat c$ for the embedding of $c$ into heap
IMP. Suppose the partial-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and
postcondition $Q$ is valid, and suppose that whenever $R$ holds of a store $s$ and a heap $h$, it
also holds of $s'$ and $h$ for every store $s'$ that agrees with $s$ on every variable outside the
set of variables that $\hat c$ may assign to. Write $\tilde P$ and $\tilde Q$ for the heap
assertions that hold of a store $s$ and any heap exactly when $P(s)$, respectively $Q(s)$, holds.
Then the separation-logic triple with precondition $\tilde P \star R$, command $\hat c$ and
postcondition $\tilde Q \star R$ is valid, where $\star$ denotes separating conjunction.

articles.title: Hoare validity embeds into separation validity
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be store assertions and
$c$ a command of plain IMP. If the partial-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command
$c$ and postcondition $Q$ is valid, then the separation-logic triple for the embedding of $c$ into
heap IMP is valid with the precondition that holds of a store $s$ and any heap exactly when $P(s)$
holds and the postcondition that holds of a store $s$ and any heap exactly when $Q(s)$ holds.

Embedded commands are always safe, never change the heap, and terminate exactly when the plain
command does.

articles.title: Points-to assertion
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $a$ and $v$, the assertion $a \mapsto v$ holds of
a store $s$ and a heap $h$ exactly when $h$ is the singleton heap that maps the address $a$ to the
value $v$ and allocates no other address.

articles.title: Pure assertion
articles.statement:
For a proposition $p$, the pure assertion of $p$ holds of a store $s$ and
a heap $h$ exactly when $h$ is the empty heap and $p$ is true.

articles.title: Local rule for a heap read
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $y$ be variables, let $a$ and $v$ be natural
numbers, and let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on stores. Write $s[x := n]$ for the store that agrees
with $s$ except that it maps $x$ to $n$, and $a \mapsto v$ for the heap assertion that holds when
the heap is the single cell at address $a$ holding $v$. If every store $s$ satisfying $p$ has
$s(y) = a$ and $q(s[x := v])$, then the separation-logic triple for the heap read $x := [y]$
(which loads into $x$ the value stored at the address held in $y$) is valid with precondition
"$p(s)$ and $a \mapsto v$ holds at $(s, h)$" and postcondition "$q(s)$ and $a \mapsto v$ holds at
$(s, h)$", where $s$ is the store and $h$ the heap.

articles.title: Separation-logic triple validity
articles.statement:
For heap assertions $P$, $Q$ and a heap command $c$,
the triple $\lbrace P \rbrace\ c\ \lbrace Q \rbrace$ is valid (in the fault-avoiding sense)
when, for every store $s$ and heap $h$ with $P(s, h)$, the configuration $(c, s, h)$ is safe
(no configuration reachable from it is stuck at a command other than $\mathtt{skip}$), and
whenever $(c, s, h)$ reaches $(\mathtt{skip}, s', h')$ in finitely many heap steps,
$Q(s', h')$ holds.

articles.title: Pulling a store fact out of a separating conjunction
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a predicate on
stores and $P$, $R$ heap assertions. Write $A \star B$ for the separating conjunction of heap
assertions $A$ and $B$ (the heap splits into two disjoint parts satisfying $A$ and $B$,
respectively, at the same store), and $p \land P$ for the heap assertion that holds at store
$s$ and heap $h$ when $p(s)$ and $P(s, h)$ both hold. Then
$(p \land P) \star R = p \land (P \star R)$.

This lets framed local triples be stated with the store facts kept outside the separating
conjunction.

articles.title: Rearranging a separating conjunction
articles.statement:
For heap assertions $P$, $Q$ and $R$, write
$A \star B$ for the separating conjunction of heap assertions $A$ and $B$ (the heap splits into
two disjoint parts satisfying $A$ and $B$, respectively, at the same store). Then
$P \star (Q \star R)$ entails $(P \star R) \star Q$: every store and heap satisfying the first
assertion satisfy the second.

articles.title: Separating conjunction
articles.statement:
For heap assertions $P$ and $Q$, the assertion $P \star Q$ holds
of a store $s$ and a heap $h$ when there are disjoint heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ with
$h = h_1 \cup h_2$ such that $P(s, h_1)$ and $Q(s, h_2)$.

articles.title: Store-irrelevant heap assertions
articles.statement:
A heap assertion $P$ is store-irrelevant when for all
stores $s, s'$ and every heap $h$, $P(s, h)$ implies $P(s', h)$; that is, whether $P$ holds
does not depend on the store.

The empty-heap and points-to assertions are store-irrelevant, and so is the separating
conjunction of two store-irrelevant assertions.

articles.title: Separation-logic while rule
articles.statement:
Let $I$ be a heap assertion, $b$ a Boolean expression and
$c$ a heap command. Write $I \wedge b$ for the assertion that holds of a store $s$ and a heap
$h$ when $I(s, h)$ holds and $b$ evaluates to true in $s$, and $I \wedge \neg b$ for the one
that holds when $I(s, h)$ holds and $b$ evaluates to false in $s$. If the triple
$\lbrace I \wedge b \rbrace\ c\ \lbrace I \rbrace$ is valid, then so is the triple
$\lbrace I \rbrace\ \mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c\ \lbrace I \wedge \neg b \rbrace$.

articles.title: Annotated commands
articles.statement:
An annotated command is built like an IMP command, from skip,
assignments $x := a$ of an arithmetic expression $a$ to a variable $x$ (a natural number),
sequential composition $C_1;\,C_2$ and conditionals
$\mathrm{if}\ b\ \mathrm{then}\ C_1\ \mathrm{else}\ C_2$ on a boolean expression $b$, except that
every while loop $\{I\}\ \mathrm{while}\ b\ \mathrm{do}\ C$ also carries an assertion $I$, its
invariant.

articles.title: Weakening the postcondition of an annotated command
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be an annotated command and
$Q$, $Q'$ assertions such that $Q$ entails $Q'$, and write $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$ and
$\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ for the precondition and the verification condition of $C$ for the
postcondition $Q$. If $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ holds, then $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$ entails
$\mathrm{pre}(C, Q')$ and $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q')$ holds.

articles.title: Precondition of an annotated command
articles.statement:
For an annotated command $C$ and an assertion $Q$
(the postcondition), the precondition $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$ is the assertion computed backwards
as follows: $\mathrm{pre}(\mathrm{skip}, Q) = Q$; $\mathrm{pre}(x := a, Q)$ holds in a state $s$
iff $Q$ holds in the state obtained from $s$ by giving $x$ the value of $a$ in $s$;
$\mathrm{pre}(C_1;\,C_2, Q) = \mathrm{pre}(C_1, \mathrm{pre}(C_2, Q))$; the precondition of
$\mathrm{if}\ b\ \mathrm{then}\ C_1\ \mathrm{else}\ C_2$ for $Q$ holds in a state $s$ iff
$\mathrm{pre}(C_1, Q)$ holds in $s$ when $b$ is true in $s$, and $\mathrm{pre}(C_2, Q)$ holds in
$s$ when $b$ is false in $s$; and the precondition of a loop
$\{I\}\ \mathrm{while}\ b\ \mathrm{do}\ C$ is its invariant $I$, whatever $Q$ is.

articles.title: Erasing annotations
articles.statement:
The IMP command $\mathrm{strip}(C)$ underlying an annotated command
$C$ is obtained by deleting the invariant of every while loop: skip, assignments, sequential
composition and conditionals are kept with their parts stripped, and
$\{I\}\ \mathrm{while}\ b\ \mathrm{do}\ C'$ becomes
$\mathrm{while}\ b\ \mathrm{do}\ \mathrm{strip}(C')$.

articles.title: Completeness of verification conditions for valid triples
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be an IMP command and
$P$, $Q$ assertions such that the partial-correctness Hoare triple $\{P\}\ c\ \{Q\}$ is valid.
Then there is an annotated command $C$ such that erasing its loop invariants gives $c$, that is
$\mathrm{strip}(C) = c$, the verification condition $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ holds, and $P$ entails
the precondition $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$.

The proof goes through relative completeness of the Hoare logic.

articles.title: Completeness of verification conditions for derivable triples
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be an IMP command
and $P$, $Q$ assertions such that the Hoare triple $\{P\}\ c\ \{Q\}$ is derivable in the
partial-correctness Hoare logic. Then there is an annotated command $C$ such that erasing its
loop invariants gives $c$, that is $\mathrm{strip}(C) = c$, the verification condition
$\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ holds, and $P$ entails the precondition $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$.

articles.title: Soundness of verification conditions
articles.statement:
For an annotated command $C$ and an assertion $Q$,
write $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$ and $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ for the precondition and the verification
condition of $C$ for the postcondition $Q$, and $\mathrm{strip}(C)$ for the IMP command obtained
from $C$ by erasing its loop invariants. For every such $C$ and $Q$, if $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$
holds, then the Hoare triple $\{\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)\}\ \mathrm{strip}(C)\ \{Q\}$ is derivable in
the partial-correctness Hoare logic.

articles.title: Verification conditions yield valid Hoare triples
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be an annotated command, let
$\mathrm{strip}(C)$ be the IMP command obtained from $C$ by erasing its loop invariants, and let
$P$, $Q$ be assertions. If the verification condition $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ holds and $P$ entails
the precondition $\mathrm{pre}(C, Q)$, then the partial-correctness Hoare triple
$\{P\}\ \mathrm{strip}(C)\ \{Q\}$ is valid.

articles.title: Verification condition of an annotated command
articles.statement:
For an annotated command $C$ and an
assertion $Q$ (the postcondition), the verification condition $\mathrm{vc}(C, Q)$ is the
proposition defined as follows, where $\mathrm{pre}$ is the precondition of an annotated
command: $\mathrm{vc}(\mathrm{skip}, Q)$ and $\mathrm{vc}(x := a, Q)$ are true;
$\mathrm{vc}(C_1;\,C_2, Q)$ holds iff $\mathrm{vc}(C_1, \mathrm{pre}(C_2, Q))$ and
$\mathrm{vc}(C_2, Q)$ hold; the verification condition of
$\mathrm{if}\ b\ \mathrm{then}\ C_1\ \mathrm{else}\ C_2$ for $Q$ holds iff $\mathrm{vc}(C_1, Q)$
and $\mathrm{vc}(C_2, Q)$ hold; and for a loop $\{I\}\ \mathrm{while}\ b\ \mathrm{do}\ C'$, the
verification condition for $Q$ holds iff every state satisfying $I$ in which $b$ is true
satisfies $\mathrm{pre}(C', I)$, every state satisfying $I$ in which $b$ is false satisfies
$Q$, and $\mathrm{vc}(C', I)$ holds.

articles.title: Code accessors implement the extended closure environment
articles.statement:
Let $v$ be a source value
related to a target value $w$ by the value relation of closure conversion, and let $\rho$ and $ws$
be lists of source and target values of the same length such that, for every index $i$ below that
length, the entry of $\rho$ at $i$ is related to the entry of $ws$ at $i$. Then the code accessors
implement the source environment $v :: \rho$ ($\rho$ with $v$ added at index $0$) in the
one-element target environment whose entry is the pair of $w$ and the encoding of $ws$ as nested
pairs ending in $\mathsf{unit}$.

articles.title: Accessors implementing a source environment
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a list of source values,
$\rho_t$ a list of target values and $\mathit{acc}$ a family of target terms indexed by the
natural numbers. The accessors $\mathit{acc}$ implement $\rho$ in $\rho_t$ when, for every index
$i$ less than the length of $\rho$, there is a target value $w$ such that $\mathit{acc}(i)$
evaluates to $w$ in the environment $\rho_t$ and the entry of $\rho$ at index $i$ is related to
$w$ by the value relation of closure conversion.

articles.title: Variables captured by a lambda
articles.statement:
For a raw term $b$, the captured variables of $b$ form
the list of free indices of $b$ at binder depth $1$ with duplicates removed: the de Bruijn
indices $j$ such that variable $j + 1$ occurs free in $b$, that is, the free variables of the
abstraction $\lambda.\,b$, each listed once.

articles.title: Correctness of closure conversion in the empty environment
articles.statement:
If a source term $t$
evaluates to a source value $v$ in the empty environment, then there is a target value $w$ such
that the closure conversion of $t$ evaluates to $w$ in the empty environment and $v$ is related to
$w$ by the value relation of closure conversion.

articles.title: Correctness of flat closure conversion for closed programs
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a closed raw
term, that is, one with no free variables. If $t$ evaluates to a source value $v$ in the empty
environment, then the flat closure conversion of $t$ evaluates in the empty target environment
to some target value $w$ related to $v$ by the flat value relation.

articles.title: Flat closure conversion of a closed term is well scoped
articles.statement:
If a raw term $t$ is closed,
then its flat closure conversion is scoped in $0$: it has no free variables, and every code
body in it is scoped in $1$, so refers only to its parameter.

articles.title: Flat closure conversion of a program
articles.statement:
The flat closure conversion of a raw term $t$ is
the flat conversion of $t$ with the accessors $i \mapsto \mathsf{var}\,i$, which send each free
variable $i$ of $t$ to the target variable $i$. It is meant for closed terms.

articles.title: Closure conversion of a closed term is well scoped
articles.statement:
If a source term $t$ is closed (it
has no free variables), then its closure conversion is scoped in $0$: it has no free variables,
and every code body in it is scoped in $1$, so refers only to its parameter.

articles.title: Closure conversion of a program
articles.statement:
The closure conversion of a source term $t$ is the
conversion of $t$ in a scope of $0$ variables with the accessors that send each index $i$ to the
target variable $i$. It is intended for closed terms.

articles.title: Accessors inside converted code
articles.statement:
Write $\#0$ for the target variable $0$ and
$\mathsf{snd}^i$ for $i$ applications of the second projection. The code accessor for index $0$
is $\mathsf{fst}\,\#0$, and the code accessor for index $i + 1$ is
$\mathsf{fst}\,(\mathsf{snd}^i\,(\mathsf{snd}\,\#0))$. When the code parameter $\#0$ is the pair
of the argument and an environment encoded as nested pairs, accessor $0$ fetches the argument and
accessor $i + 1$ fetches entry $i$ of the environment.

articles.title: Correctness of closure conversion
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a list of source values, $\ell$ its
length, and $t$ a source term that evaluates to a source value $v$ in the environment $\rho$. Let
$\rho_t$ be a list of target values and $\mathit{acc}$ a family of target terms indexed by the
natural numbers that implement $\rho$ in $\rho_t$. Then there is a target value $w$ such that the
conversion of $t$ in a scope of $\ell$ variables with accessors $\mathit{acc}$ evaluates to $w$
in the environment $\rho_t$, and $v$ is related to $w$ by the value relation of closure
conversion.

articles.title: Correctness of flat closure conversion
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a source environment, $\rho_t$ a
target environment, $\mathrm{acc}$ a map from natural numbers to target terms, and $t$ a raw term
that evaluates to a source value $v$ in $\rho$. Suppose that for every free variable $i$ of $t$,
$i$ is less than the length of $\rho$ and $\mathrm{acc}(i)$ evaluates in $\rho_t$ to a target
value related by the flat value relation to the entry $\rho_i$ of $\rho$ at index $i$ (counting
from $0$). Then the flat conversion of $t$ with accessors $\mathrm{acc}$ evaluates in $\rho_t$ to
some target value related to $v$ by the flat value relation.

articles.title: Flat closure conversion preserves scoping
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a raw term, $m$ a natural number
and $\mathrm{acc}$ a map from natural numbers to target terms. If $\mathrm{acc}(i)$ is scoped in
$m$ for every free variable $i$ of $t$, then the flat conversion of $t$ with accessors
$\mathrm{acc}$ is scoped in $m$. In particular every code body it contains is scoped in $1$, so
refers only to its parameter.

articles.title: Flat closure conversion
articles.statement:
Given accessors $\mathrm{acc}$, a map from natural numbers to
target terms, the flat conversion $C_{\mathrm{acc}}(t)$ of a raw term $t$ is defined by recursion
on $t$. A variable $i$ becomes $\mathrm{acc}(i)$. A lambda $\lambda.\,b$, whose parameter type is
ignored, becomes the pair $(\mathsf{code}\,C_{\mathrm{acc}'}(b), e)$. Here $i_1, \dots, i_n$ are
the captured variables of $b$, the environment $e$ is
$(\mathrm{acc}(i_1), (\mathrm{acc}(i_2), \dots, (\mathrm{acc}(i_n), \mathsf{unit})\dots))$, and
$\mathrm{acc}'$ sends $0$ to $\mathsf{fst}\,(\mathsf{var}\,0)$ and $j + 1$ to
$\mathsf{fst}\,(\mathsf{snd}^{k+1}\,(\mathsf{var}\,0))$, where $k$ is the position of $j$ in that
list, counting from $0$ (the length $n$ if $j$ does not occur). An application $f\,a$ becomes
$\mathsf{let}\ C_{\mathrm{acc}}(f)\ \mathsf{in}\ (\mathsf{fst}\,(\mathsf{var}\,0))\,
(C_{\mathrm{acc}^{+}}(a), \mathsf{snd}\,(\mathsf{var}\,0))$, where $\mathsf{var}\,0$ is the
variable bound by the $\mathsf{let}$ and $\mathrm{acc}^{+}(i)$ is the shift of $\mathrm{acc}(i)$.

articles.title: Converted terms are well scoped
articles.statement:
Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers and $t$ a source term
whose list of free indices at binder depth $n$ is empty, that is, $t$ is scoped in $n$ variables.
If $\mathit{acc}$ is a family of target terms indexed by the natural numbers such that
$\mathit{acc}(i)$ is scoped in $m$ for every $i < n$, then the conversion of $t$ in a scope of
$n$ variables with accessors $\mathit{acc}$ is scoped in $m$; in particular, every code body it
contains is scoped in $1$.

articles.title: Closure conversion with accessors
articles.statement:
Let $\mathit{acc}$ be a family of target terms indexed
by the natural numbers (accessor $i$ fetches source variable $i$) and $n$ a natural number (the
number of source variables in scope). The conversion $\mathcal{C}(\mathit{acc}, n, t)$ of a
source term $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. A variable $i$ converts to $\mathit{acc}(i)$. A
lambda with body $b$ (whatever its parameter type) converts to the pair of
$\mathsf{code}\,\mathcal{C}(c, n + 1, b)$, where $c$ is the family of code accessors, and the
target term packing $\mathit{acc}(0), \dots, \mathit{acc}(n - 1)$ as nested pairs ending in
$\mathsf{unit}$. An application $f\,a$ converts to
$\mathsf{let}\ \mathcal{C}(\mathit{acc}, n, f)\ \mathsf{in}\ (\mathsf{fst}\,\#0)\,
(\mathcal{C}(\mathit{acc}', n, a), \mathsf{snd}\,\#0)$, where $\#0$ is the target variable $0$
and $\mathit{acc}'(i)$ is the shift of $\mathit{acc}(i)$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Source evaluation is deterministic
articles.statement:
For every environment $\rho$ of source values and
every raw term $t$, if $t$ evaluates in $\rho$ to source values $v$ and $w$, then $v = w$.

articles.title: Encoding a list of target values
articles.statement:
The encoding of a list of target values as nested pairs
sends the empty list to the unit value and a list with head $w$ and tail $ws$ to the pair of $w$
and the encoding of $ws$. Thus $[w_0, \dots, w_{k-1}]$ is encoded as
$(w_0, (w_1, \dots (w_{k-1}, \mathsf{unit})))$.

articles.title: Length of an evaluated flat environment
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{acc}$ be a map from natural numbers
to target terms and $i_1, \dots, i_n$ a list of natural numbers. If the flat environment
$(\mathrm{acc}(i_1), (\dots, (\mathrm{acc}(i_n), \mathsf{unit})\dots))$ evaluates in some target
environment to the encoding $(w_1, (\dots, (w_k, \mathsf{unit})\dots))$ of a list of target values
$w_1, \dots, w_k$, then $k = n$.

articles.title: Flat closure environment
articles.statement:
For a map $\mathrm{acc}$ from natural numbers to target terms
and a list $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of natural numbers, the flat environment is the target term
$(\mathrm{acc}(i_1), (\mathrm{acc}(i_2), \dots, (\mathrm{acc}(i_n), \mathsf{unit})\dots))$, which
packs $\mathrm{acc}(i)$ for each $i$ in the list, in order, as nested pairs ending in
$\mathsf{unit}$; the empty list gives $\mathsf{unit}$.

articles.title: Packed accessors evaluate to an encoded related environment
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a list of
source values, $\rho_t$ a list of target values and $\mathit{acc}$ a map from natural numbers
to target terms, and suppose the accessors $\mathit{acc}$ implement $\rho$ in $\rho_t$: for
every $i < |\rho|$, the term $\mathit{acc}(i)$ evaluates in $\rho_t$ to a target value related
to $\rho_i$ by the value relation. Then there is a list $ws$ of target values with
$|ws| = |\rho|$ and $\rho_i$ related to $ws_i$ for every $i < |\rho|$, such that the target
term packing $\mathit{acc}(0), \dots, \mathit{acc}(|\rho| - 1)$ as nested pairs ending in
$\mathsf{unit}$ evaluates in $\rho_t$ to the encoding of $ws$ as nested pairs ending in the
unit value.

articles.title: Environment-packing term
articles.statement:
For a map $\mathit{acc}$ from natural numbers to target terms
and a natural number $n$, the environment-packing term of $\mathit{acc}$ and $n$ is the target
term $(\mathit{acc}(0), (\mathit{acc}(1), \dots (\mathit{acc}(n - 1), \mathsf{unit})\dots))$
packing $\mathit{acc}(0), \dots, \mathit{acc}(n - 1)$ as nested pairs ending in $\mathsf{unit}$.
Recursively, it is $\mathsf{unit}$ for $n = 0$, and for $n + 1$ it is the pair of
$\mathit{acc}(0)$ and the environment-packing term of $i \mapsto \mathit{acc}(i + 1)$ and $n$.

articles.title: Big-step semantics of the closure-conversion target
articles.statement:
Evaluation $\rho \vdash e \Downarrow v$
of a target term $e$ to a target value $v$ in an environment $\rho$ (a list of values, where
variable $n$ refers to the entry of $\rho$ at index $n$, counting from $0$) is the least relation
closed under the following rules. A variable $n$ evaluates to the entry of $\rho$ at index $n$,
when that entry exists. Code evaluates to itself: $\rho \vdash \mathsf{code}\,b \Downarrow
\mathsf{code}\,b$. If $\rho \vdash f \Downarrow \mathsf{code}\,b$, $\rho \vdash a \Downarrow v$ and
$[v] \vdash b \Downarrow w$, then $\rho \vdash f\,a \Downarrow w$; so a code body runs in the
one-element environment $[v]$ and never sees $\rho$. The unit term evaluates to the unit value.
If $\rho \vdash a \Downarrow v$ and $\rho \vdash b \Downarrow w$, then
$\rho \vdash (a, b) \Downarrow (v, w)$. If $\rho \vdash e \Downarrow (v, w)$, then
$\rho \vdash \mathsf{fst}\,e \Downarrow v$ and $\rho \vdash \mathsf{snd}\,e \Downarrow w$. If
$\rho \vdash e \Downarrow v$ and $v :: \rho \vdash b \Downarrow w$, where $v :: \rho$ is $\rho$
with $v$ added at index $0$, then $\rho \vdash \mathsf{let}\ e\ \mathsf{in}\ b \Downarrow w$.

articles.title: Evaluating a flat environment
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a source environment, $\rho_t$ a target
environment, $\mathrm{acc}$ a map from natural numbers to target terms, and $i_1, \dots, i_n$ a
list of natural numbers. Write $\rho_i$ for the entry of $\rho$ at index $i$, counting from $0$.
Suppose every $i$ in the list is less than the length of $\rho$ and $\mathrm{acc}(i)$ evaluates
in $\rho_t$ to a target value related to $\rho_i$ by the flat value relation. Then there are
target values $w_1, \dots, w_n$ such that the flat environment
$(\mathrm{acc}(i_1), (\dots, (\mathrm{acc}(i_n), \mathsf{unit})\dots))$ evaluates in $\rho_t$ to
$(w_1, (\dots, (w_n, \mathsf{unit})\dots))$, and for each $k$ the index $i_k$ is less than the
length of $\rho$ and $w_k$ is related to $\rho_{i_k}$ by the flat value relation.

articles.title: Iterated second projections of an encoded environment
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a list of target
values, $e$ a target term and $ws = [w_0, \dots, w_{m-1}]$ a list of target values, and suppose
$e$ evaluates in $\rho$ to the encoding of $ws$, the nested pairs
$(w_0, (w_1, \dots (w_{m-1}, \mathsf{unit})\dots))$. Then for every natural number $k \le m$, the
term obtained by applying the second projection $k$ times to $e$ evaluates in $\rho$ to the
encoding of $[w_k, \dots, w_{m-1}]$, the list $ws$ with its first $k$ entries dropped.

articles.title: Big-step semantics of the closure-conversion source
articles.statement:
Evaluation
$\rho \vdash t \Downarrow v$ of a raw term $t$ to a source value $v$ in an environment $\rho$ (a
list of source values, where variable $n$ refers to the entry of $\rho$ at index $n$, counting
from $0$) is the least relation closed under the following rules, a call-by-value environment
semantics that ignores the type annotations of lambdas. A variable $n$ evaluates to the entry of
$\rho$ at index $n$, when that entry exists. A lambda $\lambda. b$ evaluates to the closure of $b$
over $\rho$. If $f$ evaluates in $\rho$ to the closure of $b$ over $\rho'$, if
$\rho \vdash a \Downarrow v$, and if $v :: \rho' \vdash b \Downarrow w$, where $v :: \rho'$ is
$\rho'$ with $v$ added at index $0$, then $\rho \vdash f\,a \Downarrow w$.

articles.title: Flat accessors implement the variables of a closure body
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a raw term, let
$c = (c_0, \dots, c_{m-1})$ be the list of variables captured by $\lambda. b$, let $\rho$ be a list
of source values of length $|\rho|$, write $\rho_n$ for the entry of $\rho$ at index $n$ (counting
from $0$), and let $w_0, \dots, w_{m-1}$ be target values such that $c_k < |\rho|$ and $\rho_{c_k}$
is related to $w_k$ by the flat value relation for every $k < m$. If a source value $v$ is related
to a target value $w$ by the flat value relation, then the flat accessors for $c$ implement the
free variables of $b$ for the source environment $v :: \rho$ (the list $\rho$ with $v$ added at
index $0$) in the one-entry target environment $[(w, \mathrm{enc}(w_0, \dots, w_{m-1}))]$, where
$\mathrm{enc}$ encodes a list of target values as nested pairs ending in $\mathsf{unit}$. That is,
for every free variable $i$ of $b$, $i < |\rho| + 1$ and the flat accessor for $i$ evaluates in
that target environment to a target value related to the entry of $v :: \rho$ at index $i$ by the
flat value relation.

articles.title: Accessors implementing the free variables of a term
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a list of source
values of length $|\rho|$, $\rho_t$ a list of target values, $\mathrm{acc}$ a map assigning a target
term to each natural number, and $t$ a raw term. The accessors $\mathrm{acc}$ implement $t$ for
$\rho$ in $\rho_t$ when, for every free variable $i$ of $t$, $i < |\rho|$ and $\mathrm{acc}(i)$
evaluates in the target environment $\rho_t$ to a target value that is related, by the flat value
relation, to the entry of $\rho$ at index $i$ (counting from $0$).

articles.title: Accessors inside flat code
articles.statement:
For a list $L$ of natural numbers, the flat accessors for $L$
assign a target term to each variable: variable $0$ is sent to $\mathsf{fst}\,\#0$, and variable
$j + 1$ is sent to $\mathsf{fst}\,(\mathsf{snd}^k\,(\mathsf{snd}\,\#0))$. Here $\#0$ is target
variable $0$, $\mathsf{snd}^k$ applies the second projection $k$ times, and $k$ is the index of the
first occurrence of $j$ in $L$, or the length of $L$ if $j$ does not occur in $L$.

Inside flat code the parameter $\#0$ is the pair of the argument and the environment, so variable
$0$ is the argument and variable $j + 1$ is the entry of the environment at the position of $j$
in $L$.

articles.title: Flat value relation
articles.statement:
The flat value relation between source values and target values is
the least relation with the following property. Let $b$ be a raw term, $\rho$ a list of source
values of length $|\rho|$, $c = (c_0, \dots, c_{m-1})$ the list of variables captured by
$\lambda. b$, and $w_0, \dots, w_{m-1}$ target values, as many as there are captured variables. If,
for every $k < m$, $c_k < |\rho|$ and the entry of $\rho$ at index $c_k$ (counting from $0$) is
related to $w_k$, then the source closure of $b$ over $\rho$ is related to the target value
$(\mathsf{code}\,B, \mathrm{enc}(w_0, \dots, w_{m-1}))$, where $B$ is the flat closure conversion
of $b$ with the flat accessors for $c$, and $\mathrm{enc}$ encodes a list of target values as
nested pairs ending in $\mathsf{unit}$.

articles.title: Lifting a renaming under a binder, for the closure-conversion target
articles.statement:
The lift
$r^{\uparrow}$ of a renaming $r : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of de Bruijn indices sends $0$ to $0$
and $i + 1$ to $r(i) + 1$.

articles.title: Free variables one binder deeper
articles.statement:
For every raw term $t$ and natural numbers $d$ and $j$,
$j$ is a free index of $t$ at binder depth $d + 1$ if and only if $j + 1$ is a free index of $t$
at binder depth $d$.

articles.title: Evaluation is stable under renaming
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ and $\rho'$ be environments and
$r : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ a renaming such that, for every index $i$ and value $w$, if $\rho$
has entry $w$ at index $i$ then $\rho'$ has entry $w$ at index $r(i)$. If a target term $e$
evaluates to $v$ in $\rho$, then the renaming of $e$ by $r$ evaluates to $v$ in $\rho'$.

articles.title: Renaming target terms
articles.statement:
For $r : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the renaming $t[r]$ of a target
term $t$ replaces each variable $i$ by $r(i)$, leaves code $\mathsf{code}\,b$ unchanged (its body
$b$ is not renamed), fixes $\mathsf{unit}$, commutes with application, pairing and the two
projections, and sends $\mathsf{let}\ e\ \mathsf{in}\ b$ to
$\mathsf{let}\ e[r]\ \mathsf{in}\ b[r^{\uparrow}]$, where $r^{\uparrow}$, the lift of $r$ under
one binder, sends $0$ to $0$ and $i + 1$ to $r(i) + 1$.

articles.title: Well-scoped target terms
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m$, a target term $e$ is scoped in $m$
when every free variable of $e$ is less than $m$ and every code body in $e$ is closed, that is,
scoped in $1$. Inductively: a variable $i$ is scoped in $m$ when $i < m$; $\mathsf{code}\,b$ is
scoped in every $m$ when $b$ is scoped in $1$; $\mathsf{unit}$ is scoped in every $m$; an
application, a pair or a projection is scoped in $m$ when its immediate subterms are; and
$\mathsf{let}\ e\ \mathsf{in}\ b$ is scoped in $m$ when $e$ is scoped in $m$ and $b$ is scoped in
$m + 1$.

articles.title: Evaluation of a shifted term
articles.statement:
If a target term $e$ evaluates to $v$ in an environment
$\rho$, then for every value $x$ the shift of $e$ evaluates to $v$ in the environment $x :: \rho$
obtained from $\rho$ by adding $x$ at index $0$.

articles.title: Shifting preserves scoping
articles.statement:
If a target term $e$ is scoped in $m$, then its shift is scoped
in $m + 1$.

articles.title: Shifting a target term
articles.statement:
The shift of a target term $e$ is its renaming by the successor map
$i \mapsto i + 1$: every free variable of $e$ goes up by one, and code bodies are left unchanged.

articles.title: Iterated second projection
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$ and a target term $e$, the term
$\mathsf{snd}^k\,e$ applies the second projection $k$ times to $e$: $\mathsf{snd}^0\,e = e$ and
$\mathsf{snd}^{k+1}\,e = \mathsf{snd}\,(\mathsf{snd}^k\,e)$.

articles.title: Target terms of closure conversion
articles.statement:
The terms of the closure-conversion target language,
with variables as de Bruijn indices, are: a variable $n$ for each natural number $n$; code
$\mathsf{code}\,b$ of one parameter, whose body $b$ is evaluated with only its parameter in scope,
as variable $0$; application $f\,a$ of code to an argument; the unit term $\mathsf{unit}$ (the
empty tuple); pairs $(a, b)$; the projections $\mathsf{fst}\,e$ and $\mathsf{snd}\,e$; and
$\mathsf{let}\ e\ \mathsf{in}\ b$, which binds the value of $e$ as variable $0$ in $b$.

articles.title: Value relation for closure conversion
articles.statement:
The relation between source values and target
values of closure conversion is the least relation such that, for every source lambda body $b$,
every list $\rho$ of source values and every list $ws$ of target values with $|\rho| = |ws|$
and $\rho_i$ related to $ws_i$ for every $i < |\rho|$, the source closure of $b$ over $\rho$ is
related to the target pair $(\mathsf{code}\,c, E)$. Here $c$ is the closure conversion of $b$ in
a scope of $|\rho| + 1$ variables with the code accessors, which read variable $0$ as
$\mathsf{fst}\,\#0$ and variable $i + 1$ as $\mathsf{fst}\,(\mathsf{snd}^i\,(\mathsf{snd}\,\#0))$,
where $\#0$ is the code parameter and $\mathsf{snd}^i$ applies the second projection $i$ times;
and $E$ is the encoding of $ws$ as nested pairs ending in the unit value.

articles.title: Target values of closure conversion
articles.statement:
A value of the closure-conversion target language is
code $\mathsf{code}\,b$ for a target term $b$, the unit value $\mathsf{unit}$, or a pair $(v, w)$
of values.

articles.title: Source values of closure conversion
articles.statement:
A source value is a closure of a raw term $b$ (the
body of a lambda) over an environment $\rho$, which is a list of source values.

articles.title: Instruction count of an arithmetic expression
articles.statement:
The instruction count $\ell(a)$ of an
arithmetic expression $a$ is defined by recursion on $a$: a constant or a variable has count $1$,
and if $a$ is the sum, difference or product of $a_1$ and $a_2$, then
$\ell(a) = \ell(a_1) + \ell(a_2) + 1$.

It is the number of stack-machine instructions generated when $a$ is compiled.

articles.title: Instruction count of a Boolean expression
articles.statement:
The instruction count $\ell(b)$ of a Boolean
expression $b$ is defined by recursion on $b$, using the instruction count $\ell(a)$ of
arithmetic expressions $a$: a truth value has count $1$; the tests $a_1 = a_2$ and $a_1 \le a_2$
have count $\ell(a_1) + \ell(a_2) + 1$; the negation of $b_1$ has count $\ell(b_1) + 1$; and the
conjunction of $b_1$ and $b_2$ has count $\ell(b_1) + \ell(b_2) + 1$.

It is the number of stack-machine instructions generated when $b$ is compiled.

articles.title: Instruction count of a command
Compiled arithmetic code pushes the value of the expression
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an arithmetic
expression with compiled code $C(a)$ and instruction count $\ell(a)$, let $P$ and $Q$ be lists of
instructions, $\sigma$ a stack and $s$ a state, and write $|P|$ for the length of $P$. The stack
machine running the program $P \, C(a) \, Q$ (the concatenation of $P$, $C(a)$ and $Q$) goes in
finitely many steps from program counter $|P|$, stack $\sigma$ and state $s$ to program counter
$|P| + \ell(a)$, the stack obtained from $\sigma$ by pushing the value of $a$ in $s$, and the
same state $s$.

articles.title: Compilation of arithmetic expressions
articles.statement:
The compiled code of an arithmetic expression is
the list of stack-machine instructions defined by recursion: a constant $n$ compiles to the
single instruction push $n$, a variable $x$ to the single instruction load $x$, and the sum,
difference or product of $a_1$ and $a_2$ to the code of $a_1$, then the code of $a_2$, then the
single instruction add, sub or mul respectively.

Running this code leaves the value of the expression on top of the stack.

articles.title: Compiled Boolean code pushes the truth value of the expression
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean
expression with compiled code $C(b)$ and instruction count $\ell(b)$, let $P$ and $Q$ be lists of
instructions, $\sigma$ a stack and $s$ a state, and write $|P|$ for the length of $P$. The stack
machine running the program $P \, C(b) \, Q$ (the concatenation of $P$, $C(b)$ and $Q$) goes in
finitely many steps from program counter $|P|$, stack $\sigma$ and state $s$ to program counter
$|P| + \ell(b)$, the stack obtained from $\sigma$ by pushing $1$ if $b$ evaluates to true in $s$
and $0$ otherwise, and the same state $s$.

articles.title: Compilation of Boolean expressions
articles.statement:
The compiled code of a Boolean expression is the list
of stack-machine instructions defined by recursion, using the compiled code of arithmetic
expressions: the truth value true compiles to the single instruction push $1$ and false to push
$0$; the test $a_1 = a_2$ (respectively $a_1 \le a_2$) compiles to the code of $a_1$, then the
code of $a_2$, then the equality (respectively order) test instruction; the negation of $b_1$
compiles to the code of $b_1$ followed by the negation instruction; and the conjunction of $b_1$
and $b_2$ compiles to the code of $b_1$, then the code of $b_2$, then the conjunction instruction.

Running this code leaves $1$ (true) or $0$ (false) on top of the stack.

articles.title: Correctness of compilation to the stack machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a command and $s$, $s'$ states
such that $c$ run from $s$ terminates in $s'$ under the big-step semantics. Let $C_0(c)$ be the
compiled code of $c$ at base program counter $0$ and $\ell(c)$ the instruction count of $c$.
Then the stack machine running $C_0(c)$ goes in finitely many steps from program counter $0$,
the empty stack and state $s$ to program counter $\ell(c)$, the empty stack and state $s'$.

Since $C_0(c)$ has exactly $\ell(c)$ instructions, no step is possible at program counter
$\ell(c)$, so the machine halts there. Only this forward simulation is claimed, not its
converse.

articles.title: Compiled command code simulates big-step execution
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a command and $s$, $s'$
states such that $c$ run from $s$ terminates in $s'$ under the big-step semantics. Let $P$ and
$Q$ be lists of instructions, $\sigma$ a stack, $|P|$ the length of $P$, $C_p(c)$ the compiled
code of $c$ at base program counter $p$, and $\ell(c)$ the instruction count of $c$. Then the
stack machine running the program $P \, C_{|P|}(c) \, Q$ (the concatenation of $P$,
$C_{|P|}(c)$ and $Q$) goes in finitely many steps from program counter $|P|$, stack $\sigma$ and
state $s$ to program counter $|P| + \ell(c)$, the same stack $\sigma$ and state $s'$.

articles.title: Compilation of commands
articles.statement:
The compiled code $C_p(c)$ of an IMP command $c$ at base program
counter $p$ is the list of stack-machine instructions defined by recursion on $c$, where jump
targets are absolute program counters and $\ell$ denotes instruction counts:
$C_p(\mathbf{skip})$ is empty; $C_p(x := a)$ is the code of $a$ followed by the instruction
store $x$; $C_p(c_1; c_2)$ is $C_p(c_1)$ followed by $C_{p + \ell(c_1)}(c_2)$. For the
conditional $\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2$, put $q = p + \ell(b) + 1$
and $r = q + \ell(c_1) + 1$; its code is the code of $b$, then jump-if-zero to $r$, then
$C_q(c_1)$, then jump to $r + \ell(c_2)$, then $C_r(c_2)$. For the loop
$\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c_1$, put $q = p + \ell(b) + 1$; its code is the code of $b$,
then jump-if-zero to $q + \ell(c_1) + 1$, then $C_q(c_1)$, then jump to $p$.

articles.title: Stack machine configurations
articles.statement:
A configuration of the stack machine is a triple
$(pc, \sigma, s)$ of a program counter $pc \in \mathbb{N}$, a stack $\sigma$, which is a finite list
of natural numbers whose head is the top of the stack, and a state $s$ assigning a natural number
to each variable.

articles.title: Determinism of the stack machine
articles.statement:
For every program $P$, the step relation of the stack
machine running $P$ is deterministic: if a configuration $x$ steps to $y$ and to $z$, then
$y = z$. The fetched instruction and the shape of the stack determine the next configuration.

articles.title: Fetching from an embedded code segment
articles.statement:
Let $B$, $S$ and $A$ be lists of instructions and
let $i < |S|$ be a natural number. Then the instruction at position $|B| + i$ of the concatenation
$B\,S\,A$ of the three lists equals the instruction at position $i$ of $S$, positions being
counted from $0$.

articles.title: Stack machine instructions
articles.statement:
An instruction of the stack machine is one of
$\mathsf{push}\ n$, $\mathsf{load}\ x$ and $\mathsf{store}\ x$ for natural numbers $n$ and $x$;
the arithmetic instructions $\mathsf{add}$, $\mathsf{sub}$ and $\mathsf{mul}$; the comparison and
Boolean instructions $\mathsf{eq}$, $\mathsf{le}$, $\mathsf{not}$ and $\mathsf{and}$; and the
jumps $\mathsf{jump}\ t$ and $\mathsf{jumpIfZero}\ t$ for a natural number $t$. Jump targets are
absolute program counters.

articles.title: No step past the end of the program
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a program, that is a list of instructions,
and let $(pc, \sigma, s)$ be a configuration with $|P| \le pc$. Then the stack machine running $P$
has no step from $(pc, \sigma, s)$ to any configuration, since there is no instruction at
position $pc$ to fetch.

Hence the length of the code compiled from a command at base address $0$ is a halt address for
that code.

articles.title: Step relation of the stack machine
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a program, that is a list of instructions,
and write $a :: \sigma$ for the stack with top $a$ above the stack $\sigma$. A configuration
$(pc, \sigma, s)$ steps to a configuration $c'$ under $P$ exactly when $pc < |P|$ and, for the
instruction at position $pc$ of $P$ (counted from $0$), one of the following holds, where
$s[x \mapsto v]$ is the state $s$ with variable $x$ set to $v$.

- $\mathsf{push}\ n$: $c' = (pc + 1, n :: \sigma, s)$.
- $\mathsf{load}\ x$: $c' = (pc + 1, s(x) :: \sigma, s)$.
- $\mathsf{store}\ x$: $\sigma = v :: \tau$ and $c' = (pc + 1, \tau, s[x \mapsto v])$.
- $\mathsf{add}$, $\mathsf{sub}$, $\mathsf{mul}$: $\sigma = a :: b :: \tau$ and
  $c' = (pc + 1, r :: \tau, s)$, where $r$ is $b + a$, $\max(b - a, 0)$ or $b \cdot a$ respectively.
- $\mathsf{eq}$, $\mathsf{le}$: $\sigma = a :: b :: \tau$ and $c' = (pc + 1, r :: \tau, s)$,
  where $r$ is $1$ if $b = a$, respectively $b \le a$, and $r = 0$ otherwise.
- $\mathsf{not}$: $\sigma = a :: \tau$ and $c' = (pc + 1, r :: \tau, s)$, where $r = 1$ if $a = 0$
  and $r = 0$ otherwise.
- $\mathsf{and}$: $\sigma = a :: b :: \tau$ and $c' = (pc + 1, r :: \tau, s)$, where $r = 1$ if
  $b \ne 0$ and $a \ne 0$, and $r = 0$ otherwise.
- $\mathsf{jump}\ t$: $c' = (t, \sigma, s)$.
- $\mathsf{jumpIfZero}\ t$: either $\sigma = 0 :: \tau$ and $c' = (t, \tau, s)$, or
  $\sigma = (n + 1) :: \tau$ for some $n$ and $c' = (pc + 1, \tau, s)$.

For binary instructions the top of the stack $a$ is thus the right operand and the value below it
$b$ is the left operand.

articles.title: Multi-step execution of the stack machine
articles.statement:
For a program $P$, the multi-step relation on
configurations is the reflexive transitive closure of the step relation of the stack machine
running $P$: it relates $c$ to $c'$ when $c'$ is obtained from $c$ by zero or more steps.

articles.title: Related computations in the call-by-name CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an
interpretation $I$ of the base types; write $D(A)$ for the set of values of a simple type $A$,
$A^\ast$ for its call-by-name CPS translation, $C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$, and $\sim_A$ for
the call-by-name logical relation between $D(A)$ and $D(A^\ast)$. A computation $c \in D(C(A))$
is related to a value $a \in D(A)$ when there is $v \in D(A^\ast)$ with $a \sim_A v$ such that
$c\,k = k\,v$ for every continuation $k \in D(A^\ast \to R)$.

articles.title: Computation types of the call-by-name CPS translation
articles.statement:
For an answer type $R$ and a simple
type $A$, the type of call-by-name computations of type $A$ is $C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$,
where $A^\ast$ is the call-by-name CPS translation of $A$.

articles.title: Denotational correctness of the call-by-name CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and
an interpretation of the base types; write $D(A)$ for the set of values of a simple type $A$,
$A^\ast$ for its call-by-name CPS translation, and $\sim_A$ for the call-by-name logical
relation. Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ be an environment
for $\Gamma$ and $\eta'$ an environment for the translated context such that $\eta$ and $\eta'$
are related. Let $a \in D(A)$ be the denotation of $t$ in $\eta$, and let $c$ be the denotation
in $\eta'$ of the call-by-name CPS translation $\overline{t}$ of $t$. Then there is
$v \in D(A^\ast)$ with $a \sim_A v$ such that $c\,k = k\,v$ for every continuation
$k \in D(A^\ast \to R)$.

articles.title: Running the call-by-name CPS translation with the identity continuation
articles.statement:
Fix an
interpretation of the base types. Let $t$ be a term of a base type $b$ in a context $\Gamma$, take
the answer type to be $b$, let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Gamma$, and let $\eta'$ be an
environment for the translated context related to $\eta$. Then the denotation in $\eta'$ of the
call-by-name CPS translation $\overline{t}$ of $t$, applied to the identity function on the values
of type $b$, equals the denotation of $t$ in $\eta$.

articles.title: The call-by-name CPS translation at base types
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an
interpretation of the base types. Let $t$ be a term of a base type $b$ in a context $\Gamma$, let
$\eta$ be an environment for $\Gamma$, and let $\eta'$ be an environment for the translated
context related to $\eta$. Then for every continuation $k$ from the values of type $b$ to the
values of type $R$, the denotation in $\eta'$ of the call-by-name CPS translation $\overline{t}$
of $t$, applied to $k$, equals $k$ applied to the denotation of $t$ in $\eta$.

articles.title: Related environments for the call-by-name CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an
interpretation of the base types, and write $C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$, where $A^\ast$ is the
call-by-name CPS translation of a simple type $A$. Let $\eta$ be an environment for a context
$\Gamma = A_1, \dots, A_n$, assigning to each variable $x$ of type $A$ a value $\eta(x)$ of type
$A$, and let $\eta'$ be an environment for the translated context $C(A_1), \dots, C(A_n)$. Then
$\eta$ and $\eta'$ are related when for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, of type $A$ say, the
value that $\eta'$ assigns to the variable at the same position as $x$ in the translated context
is a computation of type $C(A)$ related to $\eta(x)$.

articles.title: Call-by-name evaluation is preserved by the CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$,
and write $\overline{M}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term $M$ and $T^*$ for the
translation of a type $T$. Let $M$ and $V$ be closed terms of type $T$ such that $M$ evaluates
to $V$ under call-by-name big-step evaluation. Then for every closed value $K$ of type
$T^* \to R$ and every closed term $w$ of type $R$, the application $\overline{M}\,K$ evaluates to
$w$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation if and only if $\overline{V}\,K$ does.

articles.title: The call-by-name CPS translation commutes with instantiation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and
write $\overline{t}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term $t$. Let $N$ be a term of type
$B$ in a context $A, \Gamma$ whose newest variable $x$ has type $A$, and let $a$ be a term of type
$A$ in context $\Gamma$. Then translating the instantiation $N[a/x]$ of $x$ by $a$ gives the
instantiation of the newest variable of $\overline{N}$ by $\overline{a}$:
$\overline{N[a/x]} = \overline{N}[\overline{a}/x]$.

articles.title: Logical relation for the call-by-name CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an
interpretation $I$ of the base types. Write $D(A)$ for the set of values of a simple type $A$
($D(b) = I(b)$ for a base type $b$, and $D(A \to B)$ is the set of functions from $D(A)$ to
$D(B)$), $A^\ast$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of $A$, and
$C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$. The relation $a \sim_A a'$ between $a \in D(A)$ and
$a' \in D(A^\ast)$ is defined by recursion on $A$. At a base type $b$, $a \sim_b a'$ holds when
$a = a'$. At a function type, $f \sim_{A \to B} g$ holds when for every $a \in D(A)$ and every
$c \in D(C(A))$: if there is $v$ with $a \sim_A v$ and $c\,k = k\,v$ for every
$k \in D(A^\ast \to R)$, then there is $w$ with $f\,a \sim_B w$ and $g\,c\,k = k\,w$ for every
$k \in D(B^\ast \to R)$.

articles.title: The call-by-name CPS translation of a renaming
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$. The translation
of a context $\Gamma$ replaces each type $A$ in it by the computation type $(A^* \to R) \to R$,
where $A^*$ is the call-by-name translation of $A$, and a variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ becomes the
variable $\overline{x}$ at the same position of the translated context. A renaming $\rho$ from
$\Gamma$ to $\Delta$, a type-preserving map from the variables of $\Gamma$ to those of $\Delta$,
is transported to the renaming $\overline{\rho}$ of the translated contexts with
$\overline{\rho}(\overline{x}) = \overline{\rho(x)}$ for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$.

articles.title: The call-by-name CPS translation commutes with renaming
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$\overline{t}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term $t$. For a renaming $\rho$ from a
context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, let $\overline{\rho}$ be the renaming of the translated
contexts that sends the translation of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the translation of
$\rho(x)$. Then for every term $t$ in context $\Gamma$, the translation of the renamed term
$t[\rho]$ is the renaming of $\overline{t}$ by $\overline{\rho}$:
$\overline{t[\rho]} = \overline{t}[\overline{\rho}]$.

articles.title: Plotkin's simulation theorem for the call-by-name CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type
$R$, and write $\overline{M}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term $M$ and $T^*$ for
the translation of a type $T$. Let $M$ be a closed term of type $A \to B$ that evaluates to
$\lambda x.\,N$ under call-by-name big-step evaluation. Then for every closed value $K$ of type
$(A \to B)^* \to R$ and every closed term $w$ of type $R$, the application $\overline{M}\,K$
evaluates to $w$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation if and only if
$K\,(\lambda x.\,\overline{N})$ does.

This is the big-step form of the theorem, for the simply typed calculus.

articles.title: The call-by-name CPS translation commutes with substitution
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and
write $\overline{t}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term $t$ and $\overline{x}$ for the
translation of a variable $x$, the variable at the same position of the translated context. Let
$\sigma$ be a substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ (assigning to each
variable of $\Gamma$ a term of the same type in context $\Delta$), and let $\tau$ be a
substitution from the translated context of $\Gamma$ to that of $\Delta$ such that
$\tau(\overline{x}) = \overline{\sigma(x)}$ for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$. Then for every
term $t$ in context $\Gamma$, $\overline{t[\sigma]} = \overline{t}[\tau]$.

articles.title: Call-by-name CPS translation of types
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ of the simply typed lambda
calculus. The call-by-name CPS translation $A^\ast$ of a simple type $A$ is defined by recursion
on $A$: a base type is translated to itself, $b^\ast = b$, and a function type is translated by
$(A \to B)^\ast = ((A^\ast \to R) \to R) \to ((B^\ast \to R) \to R)$.

articles.title: The translation of a closed term is a value
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$. For every closed term
$t$, the call-by-name CPS translation of $t$ is a value, that is, a $\lambda$-abstraction.

articles.title: Call-by-name CPS translation of variables
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$, where $A^\ast$ is the call-by-name CPS translation of a simple
type $A$. A variable of type $A$ in a context $A_1, \dots, A_n$ is translated to the variable at
the same position in the translated context $C(A_1), \dots, C(A_n)$, where it has type $C(A)$.

articles.title: The call-by-name CPS translation commutes with weakening
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$\overline{t}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term $t$. For every term $t$ in a context
$\Gamma$ and every type $B$, translating the weakening of $t$ to the context $B, \Gamma$ (which
adds a fresh newest variable of type $B$) gives the weakening of $\overline{t}$ to the translated
context, which adds a fresh newest variable of the translated type
$(B^* \to R) \to R$, where $B^*$ is the call-by-name translation of $B$.

articles.title: Call-by-name CPS translation of terms
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$C(A) = (A^\ast \to R) \to R$, where $A^\ast$ is the call-by-name CPS translation of a simple
type $A$. A term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $A_1, \dots, A_n$ is translated to a term
$\overline{t}$ of type $C(A)$ in the context $C(A_1), \dots, C(A_n)$, by recursion on $t$: a
variable $x$ is translated to the variable at the same position; an abstraction by
$\overline{\lambda x.\, M} = \lambda k.\, k\,(\lambda x.\, \overline{M})$; and an application by
$\overline{M\,N} = \lambda k.\, \overline{M}\,(\lambda m.\, m\,\overline{N}\,k)$, where $k$ and
$m$ are fresh variables.

articles.title: CPS computation type
articles.statement:
For an answer type $R$ and a simple type $A$, the type of CPS
computations returning a value of type $A$ is $(\overline{A} \to R) \to R$, where $\overline{A}$
is the call-by-value CPS translation of $A$ for answer type $R$.

articles.title: Denotational correctness of the CPS translation (Meyer–Wand)
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$
and an interpretation $I$ of the base types; write $D(A)$ for the set interpreting a type $A$,
$\overline{A}$, $\overline{\Gamma}$ and $\overline{t}$ for the call-by-value CPS translations of
types, contexts and terms, and $[t]_\eta$ for the denotation of a term $t$ in an environment
$\eta$. Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ and $\eta'$ be related
environments for $\Gamma$ and $\overline{\Gamma}$. Then there is a value $v' \in D(\overline{A})$,
related to $[t]_\eta$ by the CPS logical relation at $A$, such that $[\overline{t}]_{\eta'}(k) =
k(v')$ for every continuation $k \colon D(\overline{A}) \to D(R)$.

articles.title: CPS translation at a base type with the identity continuation
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$
of the base types, let $t$ be a term of base type $b$ in context $\Gamma$, and take the answer
type to be $b$; write $\overline{\Gamma}$ and $\overline{t}$ for the call-by-value CPS
translations of $\Gamma$ and $t$, and $[t]_\eta$ for the denotation of $t$ in an environment
$\eta$. If $\eta$ and $\eta'$ are related environments for $\Gamma$ and $\overline{\Gamma}$, then
$[\overline{t}]_{\eta'}(\mathrm{id}) = [t]_\eta$, where $\mathrm{id}$ is the identity on $I(b)$.

articles.title: CPS translation at a base type
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an interpretation $I$ of the
base types; write $D(A)$ for the set interpreting a type $A$, $\overline{\Gamma}$ and
$\overline{t}$ for the call-by-value CPS translations of contexts and terms, and $[t]_\eta$ for
the denotation of a term $t$ in an environment $\eta$. Let $t$ be a term of base type $b$ in
context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ and $\eta'$ be related environments for $\Gamma$ and
$\overline{\Gamma}$. Then $[\overline{t}]_{\eta'}(k) = k([t]_\eta)$ for every continuation
$k \colon I(b) \to D(R)$.

articles.title: The CPS translation commutes with instantiation by a value or variable
articles.statement:
Fix an answer
type $R$ and write $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of types,
contexts (entrywise) and terms. Let $N$ be a term of type $B$ in a context $A, \Gamma$, let $v$
be a term of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, and let $p$ be a term of type $\llbracket A \rrbracket$ in
$\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ related to $v$ by the value translation $\Psi$ (a variable is related
to the corresponding variable, $\lambda x. M$ to $\lambda x. \llbracket M \rrbracket$). Writing
$N[u]$ for $N$ with its newest free variable replaced by $u$, we have
$\llbracket N[v] \rrbracket = \llbracket N \rrbracket[p]$.

articles.title: Translated renaming
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write $\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ for the
context obtained by applying the call-by-value CPS type translation to every entry of $\Gamma$. A
renaming $\rho$ from $\Gamma$ to $\Delta$ induces the renaming from $\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$
to $\llbracket \Delta \rrbracket$ that sends the translation of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ (the
variable at the same position) to the translation of $\rho(x)$.

articles.title: The call-by-value CPS translation commutes with renaming
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and
write $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of types, contexts
(entrywise) and terms. For every renaming $\rho$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and
every term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the translation of the renamed term $t[\rho]$ equals the
renaming of $\llbracket t \rrbracket$ along the translated renaming from
$\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ to $\llbracket \Delta \rrbracket$, which sends the translation of
each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the translation of $\rho(x)$.

articles.title: Simulation for terms evaluating to an abstraction
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of types, contexts (entrywise)
and terms. If a term $M$ of type $A \to B$ in a context $\Gamma$ evaluates to $\lambda x. N$ under
call-by-value big-step evaluation, then for every value $K$ of type
$\llbracket A \to B \rrbracket \to R$ in $\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ and every term $w$ of type
$R$, the application $\llbracket M \rrbracket\, K$ evaluates to $w$ if and only if
$K\, (\lambda x. \llbracket N \rrbracket)$ evaluates to $w$.

articles.title: Plotkin's simulation theorem, big-step form
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of types, contexts (entrywise)
and terms. If a term $M$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ evaluates to $V$ under call-by-value
big-step evaluation, then there is a term $p$ related to $V$ by the value translation $\Psi$ (a
variable is related to the corresponding variable, $\lambda x. N$ to
$\lambda x. \llbracket N \rrbracket$) such that for every value $K$ of type
$\llbracket A \rrbracket \to R$ in $\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ and every term $w$, the
application $\llbracket M \rrbracket\, K$ evaluates to $w$ if and only if $K\, p$ evaluates
to $w$.

articles.title: The CPS translation commutes with substitution of values and variables
articles.statement:
Fix an answer
type $R$ and write $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of types,
contexts (entrywise) and terms; for a variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, $\llbracket x \rrbracket$ is the
variable of $\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ at the same position. Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from
$\Gamma$ to $\Delta$ and $\tau$ a substitution from $\llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$ to
$\llbracket \Delta \rrbracket$ such that for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, the term
$\tau(\llbracket x \rrbracket)$ is related to $\sigma(x)$ by the value translation $\Psi$ (a
variable is related to the corresponding variable, $\lambda y. N$ to
$\lambda y. \llbracket N \rrbracket$). Then for every term $M$ in $\Gamma$, writing $M[\sigma]$
for the result of applying $\sigma$ to $M$, we have
$\llbracket M[\sigma] \rrbracket = \llbracket M \rrbracket[\tau]$.

articles.title: Call-by-value CPS translation of types
articles.statement:
For a fixed answer type $R$, the translation
$\overline{A}$ of a simple type $A$ is defined by recursion on $A$: $\overline{b} = b$ for a base
type $b$, and $\overline{A \to B} = \overline{A} \to ((\overline{B} \to R) \to R)$.

articles.title: CPS translation of variables
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write $\overline{A}$ for the
call-by-value CPS translation of a type $A$. A de Bruijn variable of type $A$ in a context
$A_1, \ldots, A_n$ is sent to the variable at the same position in the translated context
$\overline{A_1}, \ldots, \overline{A_n}$, which has type $\overline{A}$.

articles.title: The CPS translation commutes with weakening
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write
$\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of types, contexts (entrywise)
and terms. For every term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ and every type $B$, the translation
of the weakening of $t$ to the context $B, \Gamma$ is the weakening of $\llbracket t \rrbracket$ to
the context $\llbracket B \rrbracket, \llbracket \Gamma \rrbracket$.

articles.title: Call-by-value CPS translation of terms
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and write $\overline{A}$
for the call-by-value CPS translation of a type $A$ and $\overline{\Gamma}$ for the context
obtained by translating each type of a context $\Gamma$. A term $M$ of type $A$ in context
$\Gamma$ is sent to a term $\overline{M}$ of type $(\overline{A} \to R) \to R$ in context
$\overline{\Gamma}$, defined by recursion on $M$ by $\overline{x} = \lambda k.\,k\,x$,
$\overline{\lambda x.\,M} = \lambda k.\,k\,(\lambda x.\,\overline{M})$ and
$\overline{M\,N} = \lambda k.\,\overline{M}\,(\lambda m.\,\overline{N}\,(\lambda n.\,m\,n\,k))$,
where $k$, $m$ and $n$ are fresh variables.

articles.title: Related environments
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an interpretation $I$ of the base types,
and write $\overline{\Gamma}$ for the context obtained by translating each type of a context
$\Gamma$ by the call-by-value CPS translation. An environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ and an
environment $\eta'$ for $\overline{\Gamma}$ are related when, for every variable $x$ of type $A$
in $\Gamma$, the value $\eta(x)$ is related at type $A$, by the CPS logical relation, to the value
that $\eta'$ assigns to the variable at the same position in $\overline{\Gamma}$.

articles.title: Evaluation of an application depends on the function only through its results
articles.statement:
Let $F$
and $F'$ be terms of type $C \to D$ in a context $\Xi$ such that, for every term $u$, $F$ evaluates
to $u$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation if and only if $F'$ does. Then for every term $a$ of
type $C$ and every term $w$ of type $D$ in $\Xi$, the application $F\, a$ evaluates to $w$ if and
only if $F'\, a$ evaluates to $w$.

articles.title: A β-redex with a value argument evaluates as its contractum
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a term of type $D$
in a context $C, \Xi$ and let $v$ be a value of type $C$ in $\Xi$. Writing $N[v]$ for $N$ with its
