newest free variable replaced by $v$, for every term $w$ of type $D$ the application
$(\lambda x. N)\, v$ evaluates to $w$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation if and only if $N[v]$
evaluates to $w$.

articles.title: The translation of an abstraction passes the translated function to its continuation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$, and write $\overline{t}$ for the call-by-name CPS translation of a term
$t$, $T^*$ for the translation of a type $T$, and $\Gamma^*$ for the context obtained from
$\Gamma$ by replacing each type $C$ with $(C^* \to R) \to R$. Let $N$ be a term of type $B$ in
context $A, \Gamma$, let $K$ be a value of type $(A \to B)^* \to R$ in context $\Gamma^*$, and
let $w$ be a term of type $R$ in context $\Gamma^*$. Then $\overline{\lambda x.\,N}\,K$
evaluates to $w$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation if and only if
$K\,(\lambda x.\,\overline{N})$ does.

articles.title: Call-by-name big-step evaluation
articles.statement:
Call-by-name big-step evaluation $M \Downarrow_n V$
of the simply typed $\lambda$-calculus relates two terms of the same type in the same context
$\Gamma$. It is the least relation closed under two rules: every abstraction $\lambda x.\,N$
evaluates to itself, and if $f \Downarrow_n \lambda x.\,N$ and $N[a/x] \Downarrow_n v$, then
$f\,a \Downarrow_n v$. The argument $a$ is substituted for $x$ without being evaluated.

articles.title: Administrative step of the call-by-name translation of an application
articles.statement:
Let $\Xi$ be a
context and $W$, $V$, $Z$ types, and write $t^{\uparrow}$ for the weakening of a term $t$ by one
new newest variable. Let $F$ be a term of type
$((W \Rightarrow ((V \Rightarrow Z) \Rightarrow Z)) \Rightarrow Z) \Rightarrow Z$, $N$ a term of
type $W$ and $K$ a term of type $V \Rightarrow Z$, all in context $\Xi$. In the context $\Xi$
extended by a newest variable $k$ of type $V \Rightarrow Z$, consider the term
$F^{\uparrow}\,(\lambda p.\; p\; N^{\uparrow\uparrow}\; k)$. Here $p$ is the bound variable, of type
$W \Rightarrow ((V \Rightarrow Z) \Rightarrow Z)$, with de Bruijn index $0$, and $k$ has index $1$
under the binder. Instantiating $k$ with $K$ in this term gives
$F\,(\lambda p.\; p\; N^{\uparrow}\; K^{\uparrow})$.

articles.title: Instantiating a return to the continuation
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a term of type $X$ and $K$ a term
of type $X \to Z$ in a context $\Xi$. In the context $X \to Z, \Xi$, let $k$ be the newest
variable (of type $X \to Z$) and $V'$ the weakening of $V$. Replacing $k$ by $K$ in the term
$k\, V'$ gives $K\, V$.

articles.title: Plotkin's value translation $\Psi$
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$, and write $A^*$ for the
call-by-value CPS translation of a type $A$, $\Gamma^*$ for the context obtained by translating
each type of a context $\Gamma$, and $\overline{M}$ for the CPS translation of a term $M$. The
relation $\Psi$ between terms of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and terms of type $A^*$ in context
$\Gamma^*$ holds in exactly two cases: a variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ is related to the variable at
the same position in $\Gamma^*$, and an abstraction $\lambda x.\, N$ is related to
$\lambda x.\, \overline{N}$.

articles.title: Logical relation for the CPS translation
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$ and an interpretation
$I$ of the base types; write $D(A)$ for the set interpreting a simple type $A$ under $I$ and
$\overline{A}$ for the call-by-value CPS translation of $A$. The relation $a \sim_A a'$ between
$a \in D(A)$ and $a' \in D(\overline{A})$ is defined by recursion on $A$: at a base type $b$,
$a \sim_b a'$ means $a = a'$; at a function type, $f \sim_{A \to B} f'$ means that for all
$a \sim_A a'$ there is a $b' \in D(\overline{B})$ with $f(a) \sim_B b'$ and $f'(a')(k) = k(b')$
for every continuation $k \in D(\overline{B} \to R)$.

articles.title: The value translation preserves values
articles.statement:
Fix an answer type $R$. If a term $v$ of type $A$
in context $\Gamma$ is related by Plotkin's value translation $\Psi$ to a term $p$ (of the
translated type in the translated context), and $v$ is a value, that is, a $\lambda$-abstraction,
then $p$ is a value.

articles.title: Denotational executions are big-step executions
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and all
states $s$ and $s'$, if the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s'$, then executing $c$
from $s$ terminates in $s'$ according to the big-step semantics.

articles.title: Big-step executions are denotational executions
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and all
states $s$ and $s'$, if executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $s'$ according to the big-step
semantics, then the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s'$.

articles.title: Relational denotational semantics of IMP
articles.statement:
The denotation of an IMP command is a binary
relation on states, defined by recursion on the command. The command $\mathtt{skip}$ relates
$s$ to $s'$ iff $s' = s$. For a variable identifier $x$ and an arithmetic expression $a$, the
assignment $x := a$ relates $s$ to $s'$ iff $s'$ is $s$ with $x$ updated to the value of $a$
in $s$. The sequence $c_1; c_2$ relates $s$ to $s'$ iff there is a state $m$ such that $c_1$
relates $s$ to $m$ and $c_2$ relates $m$ to $s'$. For a Boolean expression $b$, the conditional
$\mathtt{if}\ b\ \mathtt{then}\ t\ \mathtt{else}\ e$ relates $s$ to $s'$ iff either $b$
evaluates to true in $s$ and $t$ relates $s$ to $s'$, or $b$ evaluates to false in $s$ and $e$
relates $s$ to $s'$. The denotation of $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ is the least fixed
point, for inclusion of relations, of the one-step unfolding functional of a while loop with
guard $b$ and body relation the denotation of $c$.

articles.title: The denotational semantics of IMP is deterministic
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and all
states $s$, $s_1$ and $s_2$, if the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s_1$ and $s$
to $s_2$, then $s_1 = s_2$.

The proof goes through the agreement with the deterministic big-step semantics.

articles.title: Agreement of the denotational and big-step semantics of IMP
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$
and all states $s$ and $s'$, the relational denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to $s'$ if and only
if executing $c$ from $s$ terminates in $s'$ according to the big-step semantics.

articles.title: The while denotation is a fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression and $c$ an IMP
command, let $W$ be the relational denotation of $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, and let
$\Phi$ be the one-step unfolding functional of a while loop with guard $b$ and body relation the
denotation of $c$. Then $W = \Phi(W)$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the while-loop unfolding functional
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $B$
a binary relation on states, and $\Phi$ the one-step unfolding functional of a while loop with
guard $b$ and body relation $B$. Then $\Phi$ is monotone for inclusion of relations: for all
relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ on states with $R_1 \subseteq R_2$, we have
$\Phi(R_1) \subseteq \Phi(R_2)$.

articles.title: One-step unfolding functional of a while loop
articles.statement:
Given a Boolean expression $b$ (the guard)
and a binary relation $B$ on states (the body relation), the functional sends a relation $R$ on
states to the relation that relates $s$ to $s'$ exactly when either $b$ evaluates to false in
$s$ and $s' = s$, or $b$ evaluates to true in $s$ and there is a state $m$ with $B$ relating
$s$ to $m$ and $R$ relating $m$ to $s'$.

articles.title: Unfolding equation for the while denotation
articles.statement:
For every Boolean expression $b$, IMP command
$c$ and states $s$ and $s'$, the relational denotation of $\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$
relates $s$ to $s'$ if and only if either $b$ evaluates to false in $s$ and $s' = s$, or $b$
evaluates to true in $s$ and there is a state $m$ such that the denotation of $c$ relates $s$ to
$m$ and the denotation of the loop relates $m$ to $s'$.

articles.title: Park induction for while loops
articles.statement:
Let $b$ be a Boolean expression, $c$ an IMP command and
$P$ a binary relation on states, and let $\Phi$ be the one-step unfolding functional of a while
loop with guard $b$ and body relation the denotation of $c$. If $\Phi(P) \subseteq P$, then
for all states $s$ and $s'$ related by the relational denotation of
$\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$, $P$ relates $s$ to $s'$.

articles.title: The while-loop functional as a monotone map
articles.statement:
For a boolean guard $b$ and a relation $B$
between states (the body denotation), this is the map $\Phi$ on relations between states, ordered
by inclusion, where $\Phi(R)$ relates $s$ to $s'$ exactly when either $b$ is false in $s$ and
$s' = s$, or $b$ is true in $s$ and there is a state $m$ with $B(s, m)$ and $R(m, s')$. The map
$\Phi$ is monotone: $R_1 \subseteq R_2$ implies $\Phi(R_1) \subseteq \Phi(R_2)$.

articles.title: Frame decomposition of a single heap step
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap
command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step. If
$(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h'')$, then there is a heap $h_1$, disjoint
from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to $(c', s', h_1)$ and $h'' = h_1 \cup h_f$.

The step-existence hypothesis forces any address the step touches to lie in $h$.

articles.title: Frame decomposition of heap executions
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps, $c$ a heap
command and $s$ a store, and suppose that the configuration $(c, s, h)$ is safe. If
$(c, s, h \cup h_f)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h'')$ by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then
there is a heap $h_2$, disjoint from $h_f$, such that $(c, s, h)$ reaches $(c'', s'', h_2)$ by
finitely many small steps, $h'' = h_2 \cup h_f$, and $(c'', s'', h_2)$ is safe.

Safety supplies the step-existence that single-step decomposition needs at each stage.

articles.title: The empty heap is disjoint from every heap
articles.statement:
For every heap $h$, the empty heap is
disjoint from $h$ (with the empty heap as the first heap).

articles.title: Every heap is disjoint from the empty heap
articles.statement:
For every heap $h$, $h$ is disjoint from
the empty heap (with the empty heap as the second heap).

articles.title: Erasing an address preserves disjointness
articles.statement:
If heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint, then
for every address $a$, the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$ (removing the address $a$
and its value) is disjoint from $h_2$.

articles.title: Inserting an address the other heap lacks preserves disjointness
articles.statement:
If heaps $h_1$ and
$h_2$ are disjoint and the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then for every value $v$, the
heap obtained from $h_1$ by inserting $a$ with value $v$ (overwriting any value $h_1$ stores at
$a$) is disjoint from $h_2$.

articles.title: Disjointness from a singleton heap
articles.statement:
For every address $a$, value $v$ and heap $h$, the
singleton heap that stores $v$ at $a$ and allocates no other address is disjoint from $h$ if and
only if $a$ is not allocated in $h$.

articles.title: Disjoint heaps
articles.statement:
Two heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$ are disjoint when no address is allocated in
both: every address allocated in $h_1$ is not allocated in $h_2$.

articles.title: Erasing an address that the right heap of a union lacks
articles.statement:
For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, let
$h_1 \cup h_2$ be their left-biased union (at an address allocated in both it keeps the value from
$h_1$). If the address $a$ is not allocated in $h_2$, then erasing $a$ from $h_1 \cup h_2$ gives
the union of $h_2$ with the heap obtained from $h_1$ by erasing $a$, taken with that heap on the
left.

articles.title: Every heap has a free address
articles.statement:
For every heap $h$ there is an address that is not
allocated in $h$.

articles.title: Adding a frame heap preserves the ability to step
articles.statement:
Let $h$ and $h_f$ be disjoint heaps,
$c$ a heap command and $s$ a store. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ can take a small step, then
so can $(c, s, h \cup h_f)$.

Allocation may choose a different fresh address on the larger heap.

articles.title: Heap configurations
articles.statement:
A heap configuration is a triple $(c, s, h)$ of a heap command $c$,
a store $s$ and a heap $h$.

articles.title: Heap commands
articles.statement:
Heap commands extend the commands of IMP with heap operations. A heap
command is one of: $\mathbf{skip}$; an assignment $x := a$; a sequence $c_1; c_2$; a
conditional $\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2$; a loop
$\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$; a heap read $x := [a]$; a heap write $[a] := e$; an
allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; or a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$. Here $x$ is a variable
(a natural number), $a$ and $e$ are arithmetic expressions, $b$ is a Boolean expression, and $c$,
$c_1$, $c_2$ are heap commands.

articles.title: Heap
articles.statement:
A heap is a finite partial map from addresses to values, where addresses and values
are natural numbers: it stores a value $v \in \mathbb{N}$ at each address of a finite set of
addresses in $\mathbb{N}$, called the addresses allocated in the heap.

articles.title: Small-step semantics of heap commands
articles.statement:
The single-step relation
$(c, s, h) \to (c', s', h')$ on heap configurations is the least relation closed under the rules
below. Here $a(s)$ is the value of an expression $a$ in the store $s$, $s[x \mapsto n]$ is $s$
with variable $x$ set to $n$, $h[\ell \mapsto n]$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ set to $n$, and
$h \setminus \ell$ is $h$ with address $\ell$ removed.

- Assignment: $(x := a, s, h) \to (\mathbf{skip}, s[x \mapsto a(s)], h)$.
- Sequence: $(\mathbf{skip}; c_2, s, h) \to (c_2, s, h)$, and if
  $(c_1, s, h) \to (c_1', s', h')$ then $(c_1; c_2, s, h) \to (c_1'; c_2, s', h')$.
- Conditional: $(\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2, s, h)$ steps to
  $(c_1, s, h)$ if $b(s)$ is true and to $(c_2, s, h)$ if $b(s)$ is false.
- Loop: $(\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c, s, h)$ steps to
  $(\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ d\ \mathbf{else}\ \mathbf{skip}, s, h)$, where $d$ is the
  sequence $c; \mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c$.
- Read: if $h$ maps the address $a(s)$ to $v$, then
  $(x := [a], s, h) \to (\mathbf{skip}, s[x \mapsto v], h)$.
- Write: if $a(s)$ is allocated in $h$, then
  $([a] := e, s, h) \to (\mathbf{skip}, s, h[a(s) \mapsto e(s)])$.
- Allocation: for every address $\ell$ not allocated in $h$,
  $(x := \mathbf{alloc}(e), s, h) \to (\mathbf{skip}, s[x \mapsto \ell], h[\ell \mapsto e(s)])$.
- Deallocation: if $a(s)$ is allocated in $h$, then
  $(\mathbf{free}(a), s, h) \to (\mathbf{skip}, s, h \setminus a(s))$.

articles.title: Multi-step heap execution
articles.statement:
The relation $(c, s, h) \to^* (c', s', h')$ on heap
configurations is the reflexive-transitive closure of the small-step relation: it holds when the
first configuration reaches the second by a finite, possibly empty, sequence of small steps.

articles.title: Reinserting an erased value restores the heap
articles.statement:
If a heap $h$ stores the value $v$ at the
address $a$, then erasing $a$ from $h$ and then inserting $a$ with value $v$ gives back $h$.

articles.title: Steps do not enlarge the modified variables
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ for the set of
variables a heap command $c$ may assign to. If the configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes a small step to
$(c', s', h')$, then $\mathrm{mod}(c') \subseteq \mathrm{mod}(c)$.

articles.title: Modified variables of a heap command
articles.statement:
The set $\mathrm{mod}(c)$ of variables a heap command
$c$ may assign to is defined by recursion on $c$. It is empty for $\mathbf{skip}$, a heap write
$[a] := e$ and a deallocation $\mathbf{free}(a)$; it is $\{x\}$ for an assignment $x := a$, a heap
read $x := [a]$ and an allocation $x := \mathbf{alloc}(e)$; it is $\mathrm{mod}(c_1) \cup
\mathrm{mod}(c_2)$ for a sequence $c_1; c_2$ and for a conditional
$\mathbf{if}\ b\ \mathbf{then}\ c_1\ \mathbf{else}\ c_2$; and it is $\mathrm{mod}(c_0)$ for a loop
$\mathbf{while}\ b\ \mathbf{do}\ c_0$.

articles.title: Safety is preserved along executions
articles.statement:
If a heap configuration is safe and reaches a second
configuration by finitely many (possibly zero) small steps, then the second configuration is
safe.

articles.title: Executions of embedded commands are plain executions
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a plain IMP command,
$s$ a store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$
into the heap language. If $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches a heap configuration $(c_2, s_2, h_2)$
in zero or more heap steps, then $h_2 = h$ and there is a plain command $c_2'$ with
$c_2 = \overline{c_2'}$ such that $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2', s_2)$ in zero or more plain small
steps.

articles.title: Embedded plain commands are safe
articles.statement:
For every plain IMP command $c$ with embedding
$\overline{c}$ into the heap language, every store $s$ and every heap $h$, the heap
configuration $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ is safe.

This holds because plain IMP never gets stuck except at $\mathtt{skip}$.

articles.title: Safe heap configurations
articles.statement:
A heap configuration, consisting of a heap command, a store and
a heap, is safe when every heap configuration reachable from it in zero or more heap steps
either has command $\mathtt{skip}$ or can take a further heap step.

articles.title: Heap executions only change assignable variables
articles.statement:
If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$
reaches a heap configuration $(c', s', h')$ in zero or more heap steps, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for
every variable $x$ outside the set of variables that $c$ may assign to.

articles.title: A heap step only changes assignable variables
articles.statement:
If a heap configuration $(c, s, h)$ takes
one heap step to $(c', s', h')$, then $s'(x) = s(x)$ for every variable $x$ outside the set of
variables that $c$ may assign to.

articles.title: Symmetry of heap disjointness
articles.statement:
For heaps $h_1$ and $h_2$, if $h_1$ and $h_2$ are
disjoint, then $h_2$ and $h_1$ are disjoint.

articles.title: Embedding preserves termination
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a plain IMP command with embedding
$\overline{c}$ into the heap language, let $s, s'$ be stores and let $h$ be a heap. Then $c$
terminates from $s$ with final store $s'$ if and only if $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches
$(\mathtt{skip}, s', h)$ in zero or more heap steps.

articles.title: Heap steps of embedded commands are plain steps
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a plain IMP command, $s$ a
store and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the
heap language. Then $(\overline{c}, s, h)$ takes a heap step to a heap configuration $K$ if and
only if there are a plain command $c'$ and a store $s'$ such that $(c, s)$ takes a plain small
step to $(c', s')$ and $K = (\overline{c'}, s', h)$.

articles.title: Plain executions lift to the heap language
articles.statement:
Let $c, c_2$ be plain IMP commands, $s, s_2$
stores and $h$ a heap, and write $\overline{d}$ for the embedding of a plain command $d$ into the
heap language. If $(c, s)$ reaches $(c_2, s_2)$ in zero or more plain small steps, then
$(\overline{c}, s, h)$ reaches $(\overline{c_2}, s_2, h)$ in zero or more heap steps.

articles.title: Embedding of IMP into the heap language
articles.statement:
The embedding sends each plain IMP command to
the heap command of the same shape: $\mathtt{skip}$ goes to $\mathtt{skip}$, an assignment of an
arithmetic expression to a variable goes to the same assignment, a sequence goes to the
sequence of the embeddings of its parts, and a conditional or while loop goes to the conditional
or while loop with the same guard and with each subcommand replaced by its embedding.

articles.title: Abstraction of an element at a bound atom
articles.statement: The abstraction `[a]x`.

articles.title: Equality of abstractions is α-equivalence
articles.statement: Equality of abstractions is α-equivalence.

articles.title: Abstractions with the same bound atom have equal bodies
articles.statement: An abstraction with the same bound atom determines its body.

articles.title: Reflexivity of α-equivalence
articles.statement: **Reflexivity of α-equivalence.** α-equivalence is reflexive.

articles.title: Symmetry of α-equivalence
articles.statement:
**Symmetry of α-equivalence.** α-equivalence is symmetric. Symmetry uses equivariance of support
(`supp_smul`).

articles.title: Transitivity of α-equivalence
articles.statement:
**Transitivity of α-equivalence.** α-equivalence is transitive. Transitivity uses the fact that two
permutations agreeing on `supp y` act equally on `y`
(`smul_eq_of_agree_on_supp`).

articles.title: α-equivalence relation on atom–element pairs
articles.statement:
**α-equivalence relation on atom–element pairs.** α-equivalence: equal pairs, or a renaming of the bound atom by a fresh
transposition.

articles.title: Setoid of α-equivalence
articles.statement: The setoid of α-equivalence.

articles.title: Permutation action on abstractions
articles.statement: The action of a permutation on abstractions, applied to a representative.

articles.title: Atom abstraction of a nominal set
articles.statement: Atom abstraction: `[a]x`, the quotient of `Atom × X` by α-equivalence.

articles.title: Existence of fresh atoms
articles.statement: Every element has a fresh atom: choose one outside any of its supports.

articles.title: Existence of a least finite support
articles.statement:
A least finite support exists: among the supports of `x`, one is
contained in every support. The proof is by strong induction on a chosen
support `S₀`: either every element of `S₀` lies in every support (so `S₀`
itself is least), or some `a ∈ S₀` is missing from a support `Sₐ`, and the
induction hypothesis applies to the strictly smaller support `Sₐ ∩ S₀`.

articles.title: Subgroup of finitely supported permutations of atoms
articles.statement:
The subgroup of finitely supported permutations of `Atom`: permutations
that fix all atoms outside some finite set.

articles.title: Group of finitely supported permutations
articles.statement: The group of finitely supported permutations of `Atom`.

articles.title: Freshness is non-membership in the least support
articles.statement: Freshness is exactly non-membership in the least support.

articles.title: Freshness of an atom for an element
articles.statement:
`a` is *fresh* for `x`, written `a # x` in the nominal literature, when
some finite support of `x` does not contain `a`.

articles.title: Permutation image of a support
articles.statement: A permutation moves a support of `x` to a support of `π • x`.

articles.title: Intersection of two supports is a support
articles.statement:
The intersection of two supports is a support: a permutation fixing the
intersection fixes `x`, since every atom it can move (outside some finite
support of the permutation, and outside the intersection) is fresh for `x`.

articles.title: Equivariant elements of a nominal set
articles.statement: An element fixed by every permutation has the empty set as a support.

articles.title: Membership in the least support
articles.statement:
Membership in the least support: `a ∈ supp (Atom := Atom) x` iff `a` lies in every
support of `x`.

articles.title: Enlarging a support
articles.statement:
A support can be enlarged: fixing a larger set pointwise is a stronger
hypothesis.

articles.title: Nominal set
articles.statement:
A type with an action of finite permutations in which every element has a
finite support: a *nominal set*.

articles.title: A pair is supported by the union of its components' supports
articles.statement: A pair is supported by the union of supports of its components.

articles.title: Permutation action on abstractions computed on representatives
articles.statement: A permutation applied to an abstraction, on representatives.

articles.title: Permutations agreeing on the support act equally
articles.statement:
Two permutations that agree on the support of `x` act equally on `x`:
their ratio fixes the support pointwise, hence fixes `x`.

articles.title: Permutations moving only fresh atoms fix the element
articles.statement:
A permutation that fixes every atom outside a finite set `F` of fresh
atoms fixes `x`, by induction on `F`. If `π a = a` we apply the induction
hypothesis to `π`; otherwise we factor `π = swap a b * π'` with `b = π a`,
where `π'` fixes `a` and has support inside `F \ {a}`, and `swap a b` fixes
`x` since `a` and `b` are fresh.

articles.title: Support of an atom abstraction
articles.statement: The support of an abstraction is the body's support minus the bound atom.

articles.title: Support of an atom
articles.statement: The support of an atom is its singleton.

articles.title: Equivariant elements have empty support
articles.statement: An equivariant element has empty support.

articles.title: Equivariance of the least support
articles.statement: Support is equivariant: permuting `x` permutes its support.

articles.title: Minimality of the least support
articles.statement: The least support is contained in every support: minimality.

articles.title: Least support is a support
articles.statement: The least support is a support.

articles.title: Least finite support of an element
articles.statement:
The *least* finite support of `x`: a support contained in every support
of `x`.

articles.title: Equivariant elements are supported by the empty set
articles.statement: An equivariant element is supported by the empty set.

articles.title: Abstractions are supported by the body's support minus the atom
articles.statement:
The action of a permutation on an abstraction fixes it when the
permutation fixes `supp x \ {a}` pointwise.

articles.title: Supporting set of atoms for an element
articles.statement: `S` supports `x` when every finite permutation fixing `S` pointwise fixes `x`.

articles.title: Symmetry of transpositions
articles.statement: Transpositions are symmetric.

articles.title: Conjugation of a transposition
articles.statement: Conjugation of a transposition: `σ * swap b c * σ⁻¹ = swap (σ b) (σ c)`.

articles.title: A transposition is its own inverse
articles.statement: A transposition is its own inverse.

articles.title: A transposition squares to the identity
articles.statement: A transposition is an involution, stated for the `FinPerm` group.

articles.title: Transposition of an atom with itself is the identity
articles.statement: A transposition of an atom with itself is the identity.

articles.title: Swapping two fresh atoms fixes the element
articles.statement:
Swapping two fresh atoms fixes `x`. The proof uses a third atom `c` fresh
for both witnessing supports, and the conjugation identity
`swap a b = swap a c * swap b c * swap a c`.

articles.title: Transposition fixes atoms other than the swapped pair
articles.statement: A transposition fixes every atom distinct from its two swapped atoms.

articles.title: Transposition of atoms outside a support fixes the element
articles.statement: A transposition of two atoms both outside a support of `x` fixes `x`.

articles.title: Action of a transposition
articles.statement: Applying a transposition is applying the underlying `Equiv.swap`.

articles.title: Transposition of two atoms
articles.statement: The transposition of two atoms, as a finite permutation.

articles.title: Arithmetic expressions of IMP
articles.statement:
The arithmetic expressions of IMP are built inductively
from the constants $n$, one for each natural number $n$, and the variables $x_i$, one for each
natural number $i$: if $a_1$ and $a_2$ are arithmetic expressions, then so are $a_1 + a_2$,
$a_1 - a_2$ and $a_1 \cdot a_2$.

articles.title: Boolean expressions of IMP
articles.statement:
The Boolean expressions of IMP are built inductively from the
constants true and false and the comparisons $a_1 = a_2$ and $a_1 \le a_2$ of arithmetic
expressions $a_1, a_2$: if $b$, $b_1$ and $b_2$ are Boolean expressions, then so are the negation
$\neg b$ and the conjunction $b_1 \wedge b_2$.

articles.title: Big-step semantics of IMP
articles.statement:
The big-step relation says when running a command $c$ from a
state $s$ terminates in a state $t$; we then say that $c$ takes $s$ to $t$. It is the least
relation satisfying the following rules. The command $\mathtt{skip}$ takes $s$ to $s$. The
assignment $x := a$ takes $s$ to the state $s[x \mapsto a(s)]$, which agrees with $s$ except that
$x$ has the value $a(s)$ of the arithmetic expression $a$ in $s$. If $c_1$ takes $s$ to $u$ and
$c_2$ takes $u$ to $t$, then the sequence $c_1 ; c_2$ takes $s$ to $t$. If the Boolean expression
$b$ is true in $s$ and $c_1$ takes $s$ to $t$, then
$\mathtt{if}\ b\ \mathtt{then}\ c_1\ \mathtt{else}\ c_2$ takes $s$ to $t$; if $b$ is false in $s$
and $c_2$ takes $s$ to $t$, then it also takes $s$ to $t$. If $b$ is false in $s$, then the loop
$\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c$ takes $s$ to $s$; if $b$ is true in $s$, $c$ takes $s$ to $u$
and the loop takes $u$ to $t$, then the loop takes $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: Commands of IMP
articles.statement:
The commands of the while-language IMP are built inductively from skip
and the assignments $x_i := a$ of an arithmetic expression $a$ to the variable $x_i$ with index
$i \in \mathbb{N}$: if $c$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are commands and $b$ is a Boolean expression, then so
are the sequential composition $c_1 ; c_2$, the conditional if $b$ then $c_1$ else $c_2$, and the
loop while $b$ do $c$.

articles.title: IMP configuration
articles.statement:
A configuration of IMP is a pair $(c, \sigma)$ of a command $c$ and a
state $\sigma$.

articles.title: Small-step termination is deterministic
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$, $s_1$,
$s_2$, if $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s_1$ and also terminates by small steps
in $s_2$, then $s_1 = s_2$.

articles.title: Determinism of IMP small-step semantics
articles.statement:
For all IMP configurations $x$, $y$, $z$, if
$x$ steps to $y$ and $x$ steps to $z$ in one small step, then $y = z$.

articles.title: Determinism of IMP big-step semantics
articles.statement:
For every command $c$ and every state $s$, if $c$
run from $s$ terminates in a state $t_1$ and also in a state $t_2$ under the big-step semantics,
then $t_1 = t_2$.

articles.title: Evaluation of IMP Boolean expressions
articles.statement:
The truth value of a Boolean expression in a
state $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by recursion on the expression: the
constants true and false have values true and false; for arithmetic expressions $a_1$ and $a_2$,
the comparison $a_1 = a_2$ is true exactly when the values of $a_1$ and $a_2$ in $\sigma$ are
equal, and $a_1 \le a_2$ is true exactly when the value of $a_1$ is at most the value of $a_2$;
for Boolean expressions $b$, $b_1$ and $b_2$, the negation $\neg b$ is true exactly when $b$ is
false, and the conjunction $b_1 \wedge b_2$ is true exactly when both $b_1$ and $b_2$ are true.

articles.title: Evaluation of IMP arithmetic expressions
articles.statement:
The value of an arithmetic expression in a state
$\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is the natural number defined by recursion on the expression:
a constant $n$ has value $n$, the variable $x_i$ with index $i$ has value $\sigma(i)$, and for
arithmetic expressions $a_1$ and $a_2$, the expressions $a_1 + a_2$, $a_1 - a_2$ and
$a_1 \cdot a_2$ have as value the sum, the truncated difference and the product of the values of
$a_1$ and $a_2$. The truncated difference of natural numbers $m$ and $n$ is $\max(m - n, 0)$.

articles.title: Hoare validity via small-step termination
articles.statement:
For assertions $P$ and $Q$ on states and an IMP
command $c$, the partial-correctness Hoare triple with precondition $P$, command $c$ and
postcondition $Q$ is valid if and only if, for all states $s$ and $s'$, whenever $P$ holds in $s$
and $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$, $Q$ holds in $s'$.

articles.title: Big-step executions terminate in small steps
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$ and
$s'$, if $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics, then $c$ started in $s$
terminates by small steps in $s'$: finitely many small steps lead from the configuration $(c, s)$
to $(\mathrm{skip}, s')$.

articles.title: Prepending one small step to a big-step execution
articles.statement:
Let $x = (c, s)$ and $y = (d, t)$ be
configurations and $s'$ a state. If $x$ moves to $y$ in one small step and $d$ evaluates from $t$
to $s'$ in the big-step semantics, then $c$ evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step
semantics.

articles.title: Prepending finitely many small steps to a big-step execution
articles.statement:
Let $x = (c, s)$ and
$y = (d, t)$ be configurations and $s'$ a state. If $x$ reaches $y$ in finitely many (possibly
zero) small steps and $d$ evaluates from $t$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics, then $c$
evaluates from $s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics.

articles.title: Small-step termination implies big-step evaluation
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$
and $s'$, if $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$, then $c$ evaluates from $s$ to
$s'$ in the big-step semantics.

articles.title: IMP program states
articles.statement:
A state of an IMP program is a function
$\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ assigning a natural-number value $\sigma(i)$ to each variable,
where variables are identified by natural numbers $i$.

articles.title: IMP small-step relation
articles.statement:
The single-step relation $\to$ on IMP configurations is the
smallest relation satisfying the following rules, for all variables $x$, arithmetic expressions
$a$, Boolean expressions $b$, commands $c, c_1, c_1', c_2$ and states $\sigma, \sigma'$.
Assignment: $(x := a, \sigma) \to (\mathtt{skip}, \sigma[x \mapsto v])$, where $v$ is the value
of $a$ in $\sigma$. Sequencing: $(\mathtt{skip}; c_2, \sigma) \to (c_2, \sigma)$, and if
$(c_1, \sigma) \to (c_1', \sigma')$ then $(c_1; c_2, \sigma) \to (c_1'; c_2, \sigma')$.
Conditional: $(\mathtt{if}\ b\ \mathtt{then}\ c_1\ \mathtt{else}\ c_2, \sigma)$ steps to
$(c_1, \sigma)$ if $b$ evaluates to true in $\sigma$ and to $(c_2, \sigma)$ if it evaluates to
false. Loop: $(\mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c, \sigma)$ steps to $(W, \sigma)$, where $W$ is
the command $\mathtt{if}\ b\ \mathtt{then}\ (c; \mathtt{while}\ b\ \mathtt{do}\ c)$
$\mathtt{else}\ \mathtt{skip}$.

articles.title: IMP multi-step relation
articles.statement:
The relation $\to^*$ on IMP configurations is the reflexive,
transitive closure of the small-step relation: $x \to^* y$ when $y$ is reached from $x$ by a
finite sequence of zero or more small steps.

articles.title: Equivalence of small-step and big-step semantics
articles.statement:
For every IMP command $c$ and states $s$
and $s'$, $c$ started in $s$ terminates by small steps in $s'$ if and only if $c$ evaluates from
$s$ to $s'$ in the big-step semantics.

articles.title: Termination of an IMP command
articles.statement:
A command $c$ terminates from an initial state $\sigma$
in a final state $\tau$ when the configuration $(c, \sigma)$ reaches $(\mathtt{skip}, \tau)$ in
finitely many small steps.

articles.title: Computational adequacy for PCF
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a closed PCF term of ground type
$\mathsf{nat}$ and let $n$ be a natural number. If the denotation of $t$ in the empty environment
is defined with value $n$, then $t$ evaluates to the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n(\mathsf{zero})$.

articles.title: The least element approximates every term
articles.statement:
For every PCF type $A$ and every closed term
$t$ of type $A$, the least element $\bot$ of the domain of $A$ formally approximates $t$.

articles.title: Fundamental lemma of formal approximation
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $A$ in a context
$\Gamma$, let $\eta$ be a semantic environment for $\Gamma$, and let $\sigma$ assign to each
variable of $\Gamma$ a closed term of the same type. Suppose that for every variable $x$ of
$\Gamma$, of type $B$ say, the value of $x$ in $\eta$ formally approximates the closed term
$\sigma(x)$ at type $B$. Then the denotation of $t$ in $\eta$ formally approximates, at type $A$,
the closed term $\sigma(t)$ obtained by simultaneously substituting $\sigma(x)$ for each
variable $x$ in $t$.

articles.title: Formal approximation is closed under head expansion
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a PCF type, let $t$ and
$t'$ be closed terms of type $A$, and let $d$ be an element of the domain of $A$. If $t$
evaluates to every closed term $v$ to which $t'$ evaluates, and $d$ formally approximates $t'$,
then $d$ formally approximates $t$.

articles.title: Formal approximation is closed under suprema of chains
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a PCF type, $t$ a
closed term of type $A$ and $(c_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ a chain in the domain of $A$. If every
$c_i$ formally approximates $t$, then the supremum $\bigsqcup_i c_i$ formally approximates $t$.

articles.title: Formal approximation relation
articles.statement:
For each PCF type $A$, the relation "$d$ formally
approximates $t$" between an element $d$ of the domain of $A$ and a closed term $t$ of type $A$
is defined by recursion on $A$. At the ground type, whose domain is the flat domain of partial
natural numbers, $d$ formally approximates $t$ when, for every natural number $n$ such that $d$
is defined with value $n$, the term $t$ evaluates to the numeral $n$. At a function type
$A \to B$, $f$ formally approximates $t$ when, for every element $d$ of the domain of $A$ and
every closed term $s$ of type $A$ such that $d$ formally approximates $s$, the element $f(d)$
formally approximates the application $t\,s$ at type $B$.

articles.title: Associativity of PCF context composition
articles.statement:
For one-hole contexts $C$ and $D$ such that the
hole of $C$ takes terms of the type and typing context that $D$ produces, write $C \circ D$ for
the context obtained from $C$ by replacing its hole by $D$. For PCF one-hole contexts $C_1$, $C_2$
and $C_3$ such that the hole of $C_1$ takes terms of the type and typing context that $C_2$
produces, and the hole of $C_2$ takes terms of the type and typing context that $C_3$ produces,
composition is associative: $(C_1 \circ C_2) \circ C_3 = C_1 \circ (C_2 \circ C_3)$.

articles.title: Composition of PCF contexts
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a one-hole context whose hole takes terms of type
$B$ in typing context $\Delta$ and which produces terms of type $B'$ in typing context $\Theta$,
and let $D$ be a one-hole context whose hole takes terms of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$
and which produces terms of type $B$ in typing context $\Delta$. The composite $C \circ D$ is the
context obtained from $C$ by replacing its hole by $D$; its hole takes terms of type $A$ in
typing context $\Gamma$, and it produces terms of type $B'$ in typing context $\Theta$.

articles.title: Contextual equivalence in PCF is a congruence
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $u$ be PCF terms of type $A$ in
typing context $\Gamma$. If $t$ and $u$ are contextually equivalent, then for every one-hole
context $D$ whose hole takes terms of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$, the terms $D[t]$ and
$D[u]$ obtained by plugging $t$ and $u$ into the hole of $D$ are contextually equivalent.

articles.title: Extending a PCF substitution by a term
articles.statement:
Given a substitution $\sigma$ from a context
$\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and a term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Delta$, the extended substitution
goes from $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ to $\Delta$: it sends the newest
variable to $a$ and every older variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\sigma(x)$.

articles.title: Denotational approximation implies contextual approximation in PCF
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $u$ be
PCF terms of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$, and write $[\![s]\!]$ for the denotation of a
term $s$. If $[\![t]\!]\eta \le [\![u]\!]\eta$ in the domain denoted by $A$ for every environment
$\eta$ for $\Gamma$, then $t$ contextually approximates $u$.

articles.title: Contextual approximation in PCF
articles.statement:
Write $C[s]$ for the term obtained by plugging $s$ into
the hole of a one-hole context $C$. For PCF terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in typing context
$\Gamma$, $t$ contextually approximates $u$ when, for every one-hole context $C$ whose hole takes
terms of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$ and which produces closed terms of the ground type
of natural numbers, and for every natural number $n$: if $C[t]$ evaluates to the numeral $n$,
then $C[u]$ evaluates to the numeral $n$. Evaluation is big-step call-by-name evaluation.

articles.title: Contextual equivalence is mutual contextual approximation in PCF
articles.statement:
PCF terms $t$ and $u$
of the same type in the same typing context are contextually equivalent if and only if $t$
contextually approximates $u$ and $u$ contextually approximates $t$.

articles.title: Equal denotations imply contextual equivalence in PCF
articles.statement:
If two PCF terms $t$ and $u$ of
the same type in the same typing context have the same denotation, as continuous maps from
environments to the domain of their type, then $t$ and $u$ are contextually equivalent.

articles.title: Contextual equivalence in PCF
articles.statement:
Write $C[s]$ for the term obtained by plugging $s$ into
the hole of a one-hole context $C$. PCF terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$
are contextually equivalent when, for every one-hole context $C$ whose hole takes terms of type
$A$ in typing context $\Gamma$ and which produces closed terms of the ground type of natural
numbers, and for every natural number $n$, $C[t]$ evaluates to the numeral $n$ if and only if
$C[u]$ evaluates to the numeral $n$. Evaluation is big-step call-by-name evaluation.

articles.title: One-hole contexts of PCF
articles.statement:
Fix a typing context $\Gamma$ and a type $A$. A one-hole context
to $(\Delta, B)$ has a hole that takes a term of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$ and turns it
into a term of type $B$ in typing context $\Delta$. These contexts are generated by the following
rules, for typing contexts $\Delta$, $\Delta'$ and types $B$, $C$, with $\mathbb{N}$ the ground
type of natural numbers. The hole itself is a context to $(\Gamma, A)$. If $\Delta \cdot B$
extends $\Delta$ by a new innermost variable of type $B$, a context to $(\Delta \cdot B, C)$
gives by $\lambda$-abstraction a context to $(\Delta, B \to C)$. A context to
$(\Delta, B \to C)$ applied to a term of type $B$ in $\Delta$, and a term of type $B \to C$ in
$\Delta$ applied to a context to $(\Delta, B)$, are contexts to $(\Delta, C)$. Successor and
predecessor of a context to $(\Delta, \mathbb{N})$ are contexts to $(\Delta, \mathbb{N})$, and so
is the zero test with a context to $(\Delta, \mathbb{N})$ in any one of its three argument
positions and terms of type $\mathbb{N}$ in $\Delta$ in the other two. The fixed-point operator
applied to a context to $(\Delta, B \to B)$ is a context to $(\Delta, B)$. Finally, a
type-preserving renaming of variables from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$ applied to a context to
$(\Delta, B)$ is a context to $(\Delta', B)$, which renames the term the inner context builds.

articles.title: Soundness of the PCF denotational semantics
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a PCF type and let $t$ and $v$
be closed terms of type $A$. If $t$ evaluates to $v$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation,
then for every environment $\eta$ of the empty context, the denotations of $t$ and $v$ at
$\eta$ are equal.

articles.title: Fixed-point equation for the PCF denotation of fix
articles.statement:
For every PCF term $t$ of type
$A \to A$ in a context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the denotation of
$\mathsf{fix}\,t$ at $\eta$ equals the denotation of the application $t\,(\mathsf{fix}\,t)$ at
$\eta$.

articles.title: PCF denotation of instantiation
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$
extended by a newest variable of type $A$, let $a$ be a term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and
let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Gamma$. Writing $[\![s]\!]\eta$ for the denotation of a term $s$
at $\eta$, the denotation at $\eta$ of the term obtained from $t$ by substituting $a$ for the newest
variable equals $[\![t]\!](\eta, [\![a]\!]\eta)$, the denotation of $t$ at the extension of $\eta$
that gives the newest variable the value $[\![a]\!]\eta$.

articles.title: Closed PCF terms that evaluate to a numeral denote its value
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a closed PCF
term of the ground type of natural numbers and let $n$ be a natural number. If $t$ evaluates
to the numeral for $n$, then for every environment $\eta$ of the empty context, the denotation
of $t$ at $\eta$ is the defined element $n$ of the flat domain of partial natural numbers.

articles.title: Equal denotations are preserved by plugging into PCF contexts
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $u$ be PCF
terms of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$ with the same denotation, and let $C$ be a one-hole
context whose hole takes terms of type $A$ in typing context $\Gamma$. Then the terms $C[t]$ and
$C[u]$ obtained by plugging $t$ and $u$ into the hole of $C$ have the same denotation.

articles.title: Plugging into a PCF context is monotone in the denotation
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a one-hole context
that turns terms of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ into terms of type $B$ in context $\Delta$, and
let $t$ and $u$ be terms of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$. Write $C[s]$ for the term obtained by
plugging a term $s$ into the hole of $C$, and $[\![ s ]\!]\,\eta$ for the denotation of a term $s$
in an environment $\eta$, ordered in the domain of its type. If
$[\![ t ]\!]\,\eta \le [\![ u ]\!]\,\eta$ for every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, then
$[\![ C[t] ]\!]\,\eta \le [\![ C[u] ]\!]\,\eta$ for every environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$.

articles.title: PCF denotation of a renamed term
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a type-preserving renaming of the
variables of a context $\Gamma$ into a context $\Delta$, let $t$ be a PCF term of type $A$ in
context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Delta$. Then the denotation at $\eta$ of
the renaming of $t$ along $\rho$ equals the denotation of $t$ at the environment for $\Gamma$ that
gives each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ the value of the variable $\rho(x)$ in $\eta$.

articles.title: PCF denotation of a substituted term
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a type-preserving substitution
assigning to each variable of a context $\Gamma$ a PCF term in a context $\Delta$, let $t$ be a
term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, and let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Delta$. Then the
denotation at $\eta$ of the term obtained by applying $\sigma$ to $t$ equals the denotation of $t$
at the environment for $\Gamma$ that gives each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ the value at $\eta$ of the
denotation of $\sigma(x)$.

articles.title: Weakening preserves the PCF denotation
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $A$ in a context
$\Gamma$, let $\eta$ be an environment for $\Gamma$, and let $b$ be an element of the domain of a
type $B$. The denotation of the weakening of $t$ (the same term in the context $\Gamma$ extended by
a newest variable of type $B$) at the extended environment $(\eta, b)$ equals the denotation of $t$
at $\eta$.

articles.title: Denotation of PCF terms
articles.statement:
The denotation of a PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$
is the Scott-continuous map $[\![t]\!]$ from environments for $\Gamma$ to the domain of $A$,
defined by recursion on $t$: a variable denotes its lookup map; $[\![\lambda t]\!]$ is the
currying of $[\![t]\!]$; $[\![f\,a]\!]\eta = [\![f]\!]\eta\,([\![a]\!]\eta)$;
$[\![\mathsf{zero}]\!]$ is constantly the defined value $0$; $[\![\mathsf{succ}\,t]\!]\eta$ and
$[\![\mathsf{pred}\,t]\!]\eta$ apply $n \mapsto n + 1$ and the predecessor map (with $0 \mapsto 0$)
to the partial natural number $[\![t]\!]\eta$, and are undefined where it is undefined;
$[\![\mathsf{ifz}\,t\,s_1\,s_2]\!]$ is the strict zero test of $[\![t]\!]$, $[\![s_1]\!]$,
$[\![s_2]\!]$; and $[\![\mathsf{fix}\,t]\!]\eta$ is the least fixed point of the continuous map
$[\![t]\!]\eta$.

articles.title: Determinism of PCF call-by-name reduction
articles.statement:
One-step call-by-name reduction of closed PCF
terms is deterministic: if a closed term $t$ of type $A$ reduces in one step to $t_1$ and also
reduces in one step to $t_2$, then $t_1 = t_2$.

articles.title: Determinism of PCF big-step evaluation
articles.statement:
For closed PCF terms $t$, $v$, $w$ of the same
type, if $t \Downarrow v$ and $t \Downarrow w$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation, then
$v = w$.

articles.title: Domain of a PCF type
articles.statement:
The ω-complete partial order denoted by a PCF type is defined by
recursion on the type: the ground type denotes the flat domain of partial natural numbers, and a
function type $A \to B$ denotes the ω-complete partial order of Scott-continuous maps from the
domain of $A$ to the domain of $B$.

articles.title: Semantic environments for PCF
articles.statement:
The ω-complete partial order of environments for a context
$\Gamma$ (a list of PCF types) is defined by recursion on $\Gamma$: the empty context has the
one-point order, and the environments for $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ are
the pairs $(\eta, a)$ of an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ and an element $a$ of the domain of
$A$, ordered componentwise.

articles.title: Closed values of ground type are numerals
articles.statement:
If a closed PCF term $v$ of the ground type of
natural numbers is a value, then $v$ is the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$ for some
natural number $n$.

articles.title: Backward reduction preserves evaluation in PCF
articles.statement:
Let $t$, $t'$ and $v$ be closed PCF terms
of type $A$. If $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-name step and $t'$ evaluates to $v$ in the
big-step call-by-name semantics, then $t$ evaluates to $v$.

articles.title: Reduction to a value implies big-step evaluation in PCF
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $v$ be closed PCF
terms of type $A$. If $t$ reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) call-by-name steps and
$v$ is a value, then $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics.

articles.title: Big-step evaluation agrees with small-step reduction in PCF
articles.statement:
For closed PCF terms $t$ and
$v$ of type $A$, $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics if and only if $t$
reduces to $v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) call-by-name steps and $v$ is a value.

articles.title: Evaluation to a numeral agrees with the denotation
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, a
closed PCF term $t$ of ground type evaluates to the numeral $n$ if and only if the denotation
of $t$ is the defined value $n$.

articles.title: Big-step call-by-name evaluation of PCF
articles.statement:
Write $\underline{n}$ for the numeral
$\mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$. For closed PCF terms $t$ and $v$ of the same type,
$t \Downarrow v$ ($t$ evaluates to $v$) is the least relation closed under the following rules,
where all terms are closed and $n$ ranges over natural numbers.
Every $\lambda$-abstraction evaluates to itself, and $\mathsf{zero} \Downarrow \mathsf{zero}$.
If $t \Downarrow \underline{n}$, then $\mathsf{succ}\,t \Downarrow \underline{n+1}$.
If $t \Downarrow \mathsf{zero}$, then $\mathsf{pred}\,t \Downarrow \mathsf{zero}$; if
$t \Downarrow \underline{n+1}$, then $\mathsf{pred}\,t \Downarrow \underline{n}$.
For the zero test, if $t \Downarrow \mathsf{zero}$ and $s_1 \Downarrow v$, then
$\mathsf{ifz}\,t\,s_1\,s_2 \Downarrow v$; if $t \Downarrow \underline{n+1}$ and $s_2 \Downarrow v$,
then $\mathsf{ifz}\,t\,s_1\,s_2 \Downarrow v$. If $f \Downarrow \lambda x.\,b$ and
$b[a/x] \Downarrow v$, then $f\,a \Downarrow v$, where $b[a/x]$ substitutes the unevaluated
argument $a$ for $x$ in $b$. If $t\,(\mathsf{fix}\,t) \Downarrow v$, then
$\mathsf{fix}\,t \Downarrow v$.

articles.title: Identity PCF substitution
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$, the identity substitution from
$\Gamma$ to $\Gamma$ sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the term consisting of $x$ alone.

articles.title: Strict zero test as a continuous map
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an ω-complete partial order and let
$t$, $s_1$, $s_2$ be Scott-continuous maps from $\alpha$ to the flat domain of partial natural
numbers. Their strict zero test is the Scott-continuous map sending $x \in \alpha$ to $s_1(x)$ if
$t(x)$ is defined and equal to $0$, to $s_2(x)$ if $t(x)$ is defined and nonzero, and to the
undefined value if $t(x)$ is undefined.

articles.title: Instantiation after substitution under a binder
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from a
context $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, let $b$ be a term of type $B$ in $\Gamma$ extended by a
newest variable of type $A$, and let $a$ be a term of type $A$ in $\Delta$. Applying the lift of
$\sigma$ to $b$ and then instantiating the newest variable with $a$ gives the same term as
applying to $b$ the extension of $\sigma$ by $a$, which sends the newest variable to $a$ and
every older variable $x$ to $\sigma(x)$.

articles.title: Instantiating the newest variable of a PCF term
articles.statement:
Given a term $b$ of type $B$ in a context
$\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and a term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the
instantiation of $b$ with $a$ is the term of type $B$ in $\Gamma$ obtained by applying to $b$ the
substitution that sends the newest variable to $a$ and every older variable to itself.

articles.title: Lifting a PCF substitution under a binder
articles.statement:
Given a substitution $\sigma$ from a context
$\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ and a type $A$, the lift of $\sigma$ is the substitution from
$\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ to $\Delta$ extended by a newest variable of
type $A$ that sends the newest variable to the newest variable and every older variable $x$ to
the weakening of $\sigma(x)$ by one variable.

articles.title: Variable lookup in a PCF environment
articles.statement:
For a variable $x$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$,
the lookup of $x$ is the Scott-continuous map from environments for $\Gamma$ to the domain of $A$
defined by recursion on $x$: if $x$ is the newest variable, it sends an environment $(\eta, a)$ to
$a$; if $x$ is the shift of a variable $y$ of the older context, it sends $(\eta, a)$ to the lookup
of $y$ at $\eta$.

articles.title: Natural number type of PCF
articles.statement:
The ground type $\mathsf{nat}$ of natural numbers is the unique
base type of PCF, whose types are the simple types over a single base type.

articles.title: PCF values are normal forms
articles.statement:
If $v$ is a closed PCF value of type $A$ (an abstraction or a
numeral), then there is no closed term $t'$ such that $v$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-name
step.

articles.title: PCF numerals
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$ and natural number $n$, the numeral of $n$ is the
term $\mathsf{succ}^n(\mathsf{zero})$ of type $\mathsf{nat}$ in $\Gamma$: the numeral of $0$ is
$\mathsf{zero}$, and the numeral of $n + 1$ is $\mathsf{succ}$ applied to the numeral of $n$.

articles.title: Injectivity of PCF numerals
articles.statement:
In every context, the map sending a natural number $n$ to
the numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n(\mathsf{zero})$ of type $\mathsf{nat}$ is injective: distinct
natural numbers give distinct numerals.

articles.title: PCF numerals are normal forms
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the closed numeral
$\mathrm{succ}^n\,\mathrm{zero}$ of type nat does not reduce: there is no closed term $t'$ such
that $\mathrm{succ}^n\,\mathrm{zero}$ reduces to $t'$ in one call-by-name step.

articles.title: Numerals evaluate to themselves
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the closed PCF numeral
$\underline{n} = \mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$ evaluates to itself under big-step call-by-name
evaluation: $\underline{n} \Downarrow \underline{n}$.

articles.title: Environment from a family of values
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a context, that is, a list of PCF
types, and suppose that for every type $A$ and every variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ we are
given a value $f(x)$ in the domain denoted by $A$. The environment built from $f$ is the
environment for $\Gamma$ defined by recursion on $\Gamma$: for the empty context it is the unique
element of the one-point domain, and for the context obtained from $\Gamma'$ by adding a newest
variable of type $B$ it is the pair of the environment built from $f$ on the older variables of
$\Gamma'$ and the value of $f$ at the newest variable. So its entry at every variable $x$ is
$f(x)$.

articles.title: PCF values evaluate to themselves
articles.statement:
For every type $A$ and every closed PCF term $v$ of type
$A$ that is a value, $v \Downarrow v$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation.

articles.title: Least elements of PCF domains
articles.statement:
For every PCF type $A$, the domain denoted by $A$ has a
least element, defined by recursion on $A$: at the ground type it is the undefined element of the
flat domain of partial natural numbers, and at a function type $B \to C$ it is the continuous map
that sends every argument to the least element of the domain denoted by $C$.

articles.title: Plugging into a composite PCF context
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a one-hole context that turns terms of
type $B$ in context $\Delta$ into terms of type $C$ in context $\Theta$, and let $E$ be one that
turns terms of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ into terms of type $B$ in context $\Delta$. Write
$K[t]$ for the term obtained by plugging a term $t$ into the hole of a context $K$, and
$D \circ E$ for the context obtained by replacing the hole of $D$ by $E$. Then
$(D \circ E)[t] = D[E[t]]$ for every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Plugging a term into a PCF context
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a one-hole context that turns terms of type
$A$ in context $\Gamma$ into terms of type $B$ in context $\Delta$, and $t$ a term of type $A$ in
context $\Gamma$. The term $C[t]$ of type $B$ in context $\Delta$ is defined by recursion on $C$:
if $C$ is the hole, $C[t] = t$; if $C$ applies a term former (abstraction, application on either
side, successor, predecessor, the zero test at any of its three arguments, or the fixed point) to
a subcontext $C'$ and fixed terms, $C[t]$ applies the same former to $C'[t]$ and the same terms;
and if $C$ is a subcontext $C'$ carried along a renaming $\rho$, then $C[t]$ is $C'[t]$ renamed
by $\rho$.

articles.title: Contextual approximation in PCF is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every term $t$ of type $A$ in context
$\Gamma$ contextually approximates itself.

articles.title: Contextual equivalence in PCF is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$
is contextually equivalent to itself.

articles.title: PCF renamings
articles.statement:
For contexts $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ (lists of PCF types), a renaming from
$\Gamma$ to $\Delta$ is a map sending each variable of $\Gamma$ of type $A$, for every type $A$,
to a variable of $\Delta$ of the same type $A$; it is the STLC notion of renaming at PCF types.

articles.title: Renaming a PCF term by the identity
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$, type $A$ and term $t$ of
type $A$ in $\Gamma$, renaming $t$ along the identity renaming of $\Gamma$ gives $t$.

articles.title: Renaming after substitution in PCF
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from a context $\Gamma$
to a context $\Delta$ and $\rho$ a renaming from $\Delta$ to a context $\Xi$. For every PCF term
$t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, renaming along $\rho$ the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$
gives the result of applying to $t$ the substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Xi$ that sends each
variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the renaming of $\sigma(x)$ along $\rho$.

articles.title: Renaming of PCF terms
articles.statement:
Given a renaming $\rho$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context
$\Delta$, the renaming along $\rho$ of a PCF term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is the term of
type $A$ in context $\Delta$ obtained by replacing each variable $x$ by $\rho(x)$. Under a
$\lambda$-binder, $\rho$ is replaced by its lift, which sends the bound variable to itself and
the successor of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the successor of $\rho(x)$. Renaming leaves
zero unchanged and commutes with application, successor, predecessor, the zero test and the
fixed-point combinator.

articles.title: Single-variable substitution in PCF
articles.statement:
For a PCF term $a$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$,
this is the substitution from the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$ to
$\Gamma$ that sends the newest variable to $a$ and each older variable $x$ to the variable $x$
of $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Call-by-name reduction step of PCF
articles.statement:
Write $\underline{n}$ for the numeral
$\mathrm{succ}^n\,\mathrm{zero}$, and $b[a]$ for the result of substituting the closed term $a$
for the bound variable of an abstraction body $b$. One-step call-by-name reduction $t \to t'$
between closed PCF terms of the same type is the least relation closed under these rules:
$f\,a \to f'\,a$ whenever $f \to f'$; $(\lambda b)\,a \to b[a]$, without evaluating $a$;
$\mathrm{succ}\,t \to \mathrm{succ}\,t'$, $\mathrm{pred}\,t \to \mathrm{pred}\,t'$ and
$\mathrm{ifz}\,t\,s_1\,s_2 \to \mathrm{ifz}\,t'\,s_1\,s_2$ whenever $t \to t'$;
$\mathrm{pred}\,\mathrm{zero} \to \mathrm{zero}$ and
$\mathrm{pred}\,\underline{n+1} \to \underline{n}$ for every natural number $n$;
$\mathrm{ifz}\,\mathrm{zero}\,s_1\,s_2 \to s_1$ and
$\mathrm{ifz}\,\underline{n+1}\,s_1\,s_2 \to s_2$ for every natural number $n$; and
$\mathrm{fix}\,t \to t\,(\mathrm{fix}\,t)$.

articles.title: Big-step evaluation implies reduction in PCF
articles.statement:
Let $t$ and $v$ be closed PCF terms of
type $A$. If $t$ evaluates to $v$ in the big-step call-by-name semantics, then $t$ reduces to
$v$ in finitely many (possibly zero) call-by-name steps.

articles.title: Multi-step call-by-name reduction of PCF
articles.statement:
For closed PCF terms $t$ and $t'$ of the same
type, $t \to^* t'$ holds when $t$ reduces to $t'$ in finitely many, possibly zero, one-step
call-by-name reductions; that is, $\to^*$ is the reflexive transitive closure of one-step
reduction.

articles.title: Parallel substitutions for PCF
articles.statement:
A substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to a context
$\Delta$ (lists of PCF types) assigns to every variable of $\Gamma$, of any type $A$, a PCF term
of type $A$ in context $\Delta$.

articles.title: Substitution after renaming in PCF
articles.statement:
Let $\rho$ be a renaming from a context $\Gamma$ to a
context $\Delta$ and $\sigma$ a substitution from $\Delta$ to a context $\Xi$. For every PCF term
$t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, applying $\sigma$ to the renaming of $t$ along $\rho$ gives
the result of applying to $t$ the substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Xi$ that sends each variable
$x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\sigma(\rho(x))$.

articles.title: Composition of PCF substitutions
articles.statement:
Write $t[\sigma]$ for the result of applying a
substitution $\sigma$ to a PCF term $t$. Let $\sigma$ be a substitution from a context $\Gamma$ to
a context $\Delta$ and $\tau$ a substitution from $\Delta$ to a context $\Xi$. For every PCF term
$t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, $t[\sigma][\tau] = t[\sigma']$, where $\sigma'$ is the
substitution from $\Gamma$ to $\Xi$ that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to
$\sigma(x)[\tau]$.

articles.title: Substitution in PCF terms
articles.statement:
Given a substitution $\sigma$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a
context $\Delta$, applying $\sigma$ to a PCF term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ gives the term of
type $A$ in context $\Delta$ obtained by replacing each variable $x$ by $\sigma(x)$. Under a
$\lambda$-binder, $\sigma$ is replaced by its lift, which sends the bound variable to itself and
the successor of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the weakening of $\sigma(x)$. Substitution
leaves zero unchanged and commutes with application, successor, predecessor, the zero test and
the fixed-point combinator.

All variables are replaced simultaneously, and since variables are de Bruijn indices the
substitution is capture-avoiding.

articles.title: Termination agrees with definedness of the denotation
articles.statement:
A closed PCF term $t$ of ground
type evaluates to some term if and only if its denotation, an element of the flat domain of
partial natural numbers, is defined.

articles.title: PCF terms
articles.statement:
Write $\mathsf{nat}$ for the ground type of natural numbers and $A \Rightarrow B$
for the type of functions from $A$ to $B$. The intrinsically typed PCF terms of type $A$ in a
context $\Gamma$ (a list of PCF types) are generated by the following rules: every variable of
type $A$ in $\Gamma$ is a term of type $A$; if $t$ has type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended
by a newest variable of type $A$, then $\lambda t$ has type $A \Rightarrow B$; if $f$ has type
$A \Rightarrow B$ and $a$ has type $A$, then $f\,a$ has type $B$; $\mathsf{zero}$ has type
$\mathsf{nat}$; if $t$ has type $\mathsf{nat}$, so do $\mathsf{succ}\,t$ and $\mathsf{pred}\,t$;
if $t$, $s_1$ and $s_2$ have type $\mathsf{nat}$, so does the zero test
$\mathsf{ifz}\,t\,s_1\,s_2$; and if $t$ has type $A \Rightarrow A$, then the fixed point
$\mathsf{fix}\,t$ has type $A$.

articles.title: PCF types
articles.statement:
PCF types are the simple types over a single ground type, the type of natural
numbers.

articles.title: PCF evaluation results are values
articles.statement:
For closed PCF terms $t$ and $v$ of the same type, if
$t \Downarrow v$ under big-step call-by-name evaluation, then $v$ is a value.

articles.title: Values of PCF
articles.statement:
A closed PCF term is a value when it is a $\lambda$-abstraction or the
numeral $\mathsf{succ}^n\,\mathsf{zero}$ for some natural number $n$.

articles.title: PCF variables
articles.statement:
PCF uses the typed de Bruijn variables of the simply typed
$\lambda$-calculus over a single base type: a variable of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ is a
position in the list $\Gamma$ at which $A$ occurs.

articles.title: Weakening of PCF terms
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a context and $A$, $B$ types. Weakening sends a
PCF term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ to the term of type $A$ in the context obtained by
prepending a new variable of type $B$ to $\Gamma$, by renaming every free variable of $t$ to its
successor, that is, by shifting each de Bruijn index up by one.

articles.title: Grover iterates of the uniform state are unit vectors
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite
search space, $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set, and $u$ the uniform amplitude vector, given by
$u(x) = 1/\sqrt{|\alpha|}$ for every $x \in \alpha$. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\psi_k$
be the vector obtained from $u$ by applying the Grover step for $M$ $k$ times. Then
$\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi_k(x)^2 = 1$.

articles.title: Grover iteration preserves the squared norm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite search
space and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set. For every real amplitude vector
$\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\psi_k$ be the vector obtained
from $\psi$ by applying the Grover step for $M$ $k$ times. Then
$\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi_k(x)^2 = \sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi(x)^2$.

articles.title: The uniform amplitude vector is normalized
articles.statement:
For every nonempty finite type
$\alpha$, the uniform amplitude vector on $\alpha$ has squared Euclidean norm $1$.

articles.title: Squared norm of an amplitude vector
articles.statement:
For a finite type $\alpha$ and a real amplitude
vector $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the squared norm of $\psi$ is its squared Euclidean
norm $\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi(x)^2$.

articles.title: Real amplitude vectors
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ (the search space), a real amplitude vector
indexed by $\alpha$ is a function $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, assigning a real amplitude to
each point of $\alpha$.

articles.title: Symmetric Grover state at a given angle
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space and
$M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set with complement $M^c$. For a real number $\varphi$, this is the
real amplitude vector on $\alpha$ whose value is $\sin\varphi / \sqrt{|M|}$ at every point of $M$
and $\cos\varphi / \sqrt{|M^c|}$ at every point of $M^c$.

When $M$ and $M^c$ are nonempty, the marked and unmarked parts of this vector have Euclidean
norms $|\sin\varphi|$ and $|\cos\varphi|$.

articles.title: Inversion about the mean
articles.statement:
For a finite type $\alpha$, the diffusion operator sends a
real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$ to the amplitude vector $x \mapsto 2\bar\psi - \psi(x)$,
where $\bar\psi$ is the arithmetic mean of the amplitudes of $\psi$.

articles.title: Standard Grover iteration count
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite search
space of size $N$, and let $\theta = \arcsin \sqrt{|M| / N}$ be its Grover angle. The standard
iteration count is $\lfloor \pi / (4\theta) \rfloor$, the largest natural number at most
$\pi / (4\theta)$; it is $0$ when $\theta = 0$, that is, when no element is marked.

articles.title: Grover angle
articles.statement:
For a finite search space $\alpha$ and a marked set $M \subseteq \alpha$, the
Grover angle of $M$ is $\theta = \arcsin \sqrt{|M| / |\alpha|}$, where the quotient
$|M| / |\alpha|$ is taken to be $0$ when $\alpha$ is empty.

articles.title: Grover iterate
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked
set. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a real amplitude vector $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the $k$-th
Grover iterate of $\psi$ is the vector obtained by applying the Grover step for $M$ to $\psi$
$k$ times; the $0$-th iterate is $\psi$ itself.

articles.title: Grover phase
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space, $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set and
$\theta$ the Grover angle of $M$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the Grover phase of $M$ after $k$
iterations is the real number $(2k + 1)\theta$.

When $M$ and its complement are both nonempty, this is the phase reached from the uniform
initial state after $k$ Grover steps.

articles.title: Grover step
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a set of marked
elements. Write $O_M$ for the phase oracle, which negates the amplitudes at the points of $M$,
and $D$ for inversion about the mean, which sends an amplitude vector $\varphi$ on $\alpha$ to
$x \mapsto 2\bar\varphi - \varphi(x)$, where $\bar\varphi$ is the arithmetic mean of the amplitudes
of $\varphi$. One Grover step sends a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$ to $D(O_M \psi)$:
phase inversion followed by inversion about the mean.

articles.title: Marked amplitude after a Grover step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite
search space of size $N$, let $M^c$ be the set of unmarked elements, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
With $\mu = (|M^c|\, b - |M|\, a) / N$, the next marked amplitude is $2\mu + a$.

It is the common value at the marked elements after one Grover step applied to the amplitude
vector equal to $a$ on $M$ and to $b$ off $M$.

articles.title: Exact success probability of Grover search
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space and
$M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set such that both $M$ and its complement are nonempty, and let
$\theta = \arcsin \sqrt{|M| / |\alpha|}$ be the Grover angle of $M$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$\psi_k$ be the vector obtained by applying the Grover step for $M$ $k$ times to the uniform
amplitude vector, whose value is $1/\sqrt{|\alpha|}$ at every point. Then the marked probability
of $\psi_k$ is $\sum_{x \in M} \psi_k(x)^2 = \sin^2((2k + 1)\theta)$.

articles.title: Probability of the marked outcomes
articles.statement:
For a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on a type
$\alpha$ and a finite set $M \subseteq \alpha$ of marked elements, the marked probability is
$\sum_{x \in M} \psi(x)^2$. When $\alpha$ is finite and $\psi$ has squared norm $1$, this is
the probability of observing a marked outcome.

articles.title: Mean amplitude
articles.statement:
For a finite type $\alpha$ and a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$,
the mean amplitude of $\psi$ is $\bigl(\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi(x)\bigr) / |\alpha|$, the
arithmetic mean of its amplitudes. When $\alpha$ is empty it is $0$.

articles.title: One Grover iteration suffices when a quarter is marked
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a nonempty set of
marked elements of a finite search space of size $N$ with $4|M| = N$. Starting from the uniform
amplitude vector, one Grover iteration produces an amplitude vector whose marked probability
is $1$.

articles.title: Mean amplitude after the phase oracle
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite
search space of size $N$, let $M^c$ be the set of unmarked elements, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
The oracle mean is $(|M^c|\, b - |M|\, a) / N$.

It is the mean of the amplitude vector obtained by applying the phase oracle to the vector equal
to $a$ on $M$ and to $b$ off $M$.

articles.title: Phase oracle
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ and a finite set $M \subseteq \alpha$ of marked
elements, the phase oracle sends a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$ to the amplitude
vector whose value at $x$ is $-\psi(x)$ if $x \in M$ and $\psi(x)$ if $x \notin M$; that is, it
negates exactly the amplitudes at the marked elements.

articles.title: Symmetric amplitude vector
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a search space
$\alpha$, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The symmetric amplitude vector with marked amplitude $a$
and unmarked amplitude $b$ is the real amplitude vector on $\alpha$ whose value is $a$ at every
element of $M$ and $b$ at every element outside $M$.

articles.title: Uniform amplitude vector
articles.statement:
For a finite type $\alpha$, the uniform amplitude vector on
$\alpha$ is the real amplitude vector whose value at every point is $1/\sqrt{|\alpha|}$, where
$|\alpha|$ is the number of elements of $\alpha$.

articles.title: Unmarked amplitude after a Grover step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite
search space of size $N$, let $M^c$ be the set of unmarked elements, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
With $\mu = (|M^c|\, b - |M|\, a) / N$, the next unmarked amplitude is $2\mu - b$.

It is the common value at the unmarked elements after one Grover step applied to the amplitude
vector equal to $a$ on $M$ and to $b$ off $M$.

articles.title: Shor's order-to-factor reduction, existential form
articles.statement:
Let $N$, $a$ and $r$ be natural
numbers with $N > 1$ and $a \ge 1$. If $a^r \equiv 1 \pmod{N}$, $r$ is even,
$a^{r/2} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{N}$ and $a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod{N}$, then $N$ has a nontrivial
factor: there is a natural number $d$ with $d \mid N$ and $1 < d < N$.

One such factor is $\gcd(a^{r/2} - 1, N)$.

articles.title: Shor's order-to-factor reduction
articles.statement:
Let $N$, $a$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $N > 1$ and
$a \ge 1$. Suppose $a^r \equiv 1 \pmod{N}$, $r$ is even, $a^{r/2} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{N}$ and
$a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod{N}$. Then $d = \gcd(a^{r/2} - 1, N)$, the value computed by the
classical post-processing, is a nontrivial factor of $N$: $d$ divides $N$ and $1 < d < N$.

In the algorithm $r$ is the multiplicative order of $a$ modulo $N$, so the hypothesis
$a^{r/2} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{N}$ is the minimality of the order, and the hypothesis
$a^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod{N}$ is the "good unit" condition. This module assumes that
condition; it does not prove its prevalence among units.

## Sources

- P. W. Shor, Polynomial-time algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms on a quantum computer, SIAM J. Comput. 26 (1997), 1484–1509, Section 5; M. A. Nielsen and I. L. Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information, Cambridge University Press, 2000, Section 5.3.

articles.title: Constant running time on the support gives that expected time
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an algorithm
on inputs of a type $\gamma$ whose running time $T_A(x)$ on each input $x$ is a natural number,
let $D$ be a probability mass function on $\gamma$, and let $c$ be a natural number. If
$T_A(x) = c$ for every input $x$ in the support of $D$, then the expected running time of $A$
under $D$ equals $c$.

Inputs outside the support have probability $0$, so their running times do not contribute.

articles.title: Constant running time on all rearrangements gives that expected time
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an
algorithm on lists whose running time $T_A(y)$ on each list $y$ is a natural number, let
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list of length $n$, and let $c$ be a natural number. If
$T_A(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}) = c$ for every permutation $\sigma$ of
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, then the expected running time of $A$ when its input is $x$ rearranged by a
uniformly random permutation equals $c$.

articles.title: Average formula for the expected time over random orderings, in the reals
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an
algorithm on lists whose running time $T_A(y)$ on each list $y$ is a natural number, and let
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list of length $n$. The expected running time of $A$ when its
input is $x$ rearranged by a uniformly random permutation, converted from $[0, \infty]$ to a real
number, equals

$$\frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\sigma} T_A(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}),$$

the sum running over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and computed in $\mathbb{R}$.

Every term of the average is a natural number, so the expected time is finite and the conversion
loses nothing.

articles.title: Average formula for the expected time over random orderings
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an algorithm on
lists whose running time $T_A(y)$ on each list $y$ is a natural number, and let
$x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a list of length $n$. The expected running time of $A$ when its
input is $x$ rearranged by a uniformly random permutation equals

$$\frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\sigma} T_A(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}),$$

the sum running over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ and computed in
$[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Expected running time
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an algorithm on inputs of a type $\gamma$ whose running
time $T_A(x)$ on each input $x$ is a natural number, and let $D$ be a probability mass function on
$\gamma$. The expected running time of $A$ under $D$ is the extended nonnegative expectation
$\sum_{x \in \gamma} D(x)\, T_A(x) \in [0, \infty]$ of the running time, the sum taken over all
inputs.

Valuing the expectation in $[0, \infty]$ records a divergent expected time as $\infty$; a
real-valued integral would collapse it to $0$.

articles.title: Rearrangements preserve length
articles.statement:
For a list $x$, every list in the support of the uniform
permutation of $x$ has the same length as $x$.

articles.title: Rearrangements are permutations
