articles.statement:
For a list $x$, every list in the support of the uniform
permutation of $x$ is a permutation of $x$, that is, it has the same entries with the same
multiplicities.

articles.title: Uniformly random rearrangement of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$, the
uniform permutation of $x$ is the probability distribution on lists obtained by choosing a
permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ uniformly at random and outputting
$(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)})$.

articles.title: Probability of a Fisher–Yates outcome
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a vector of length $n$, and consider the
draw histories $d$, which assign to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$.
For every outcome $o$ (a vector of length $n$ together with a cost pair), the probability that
the Fisher–Yates output distribution of $x$ assigns to $o$ equals the sum, over all draw histories
$d$ for which the Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$ yields exactly $o$, of
$\prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{n - i}$.

Distinct histories that yield the same outcome (for example when values of $x$ repeat) add up,
and an outcome that no history yields has probability $0$.

articles.title: Fisher–Yates produces a uniformly random permutation
articles.statement:
Let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be a
vector and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ chosen uniformly at random. Then
the Fisher–Yates output distribution of $x$ equals the distribution of the outcome consisting of
the vector $(x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)})$ with cost pair $(n, n)$.

articles.title: Output distribution of the Fisher–Yates shuffle
articles.statement:
For a vector $x$ of length $n$, this is
the probability distribution on outcomes (a vector of length $n$ together with a cost pair in
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$) obtained by choosing a draw history $d$ uniformly at random among
all assignments of a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$ to each position $i < n$, and returning
the result of the Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$.

This models an ideal source of random draws, not an executable pseudorandom generator, and does
not assume that the output permutation is uniform.

articles.title: Fisher–Yates on the empty vector
articles.statement:
For the empty vector $x$ (of length $0$) and its empty
draw history, the Fisher–Yates computation returns $x$ with cost pair $(0, 0)$: it retrieves no
draws and performs no swaps.

articles.title: Fisher–Yates output is a rearrangement of its input
articles.statement:
For every vector $x$ of length $n$
and every draw history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with
$0 \le d_i < n - i$, the list of entries of the vector returned by the Fisher–Yates computation on
$x$ and $d$ is a permutation of the list of entries of $x$. In particular every value occurs
equally often in both, even when values of $x$ repeat.

articles.title: Prefix probabilities of the Fisher–Yates shuffle
articles.statement:
Let $k \le n$ and let
$a_0, \dots, a_{k-1}$ be distinct elements of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. Run the Fisher–Yates
computation on the vector $(0, 1, \dots, n - 1)$ with every draw history $d$, which assigns to each
position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$, and give each history weight $1/n!$.
Then the total weight of the histories whose output vector has entry $a_p$ at position $p$ for
every $p < k$ equals $(n - k)!/n!$.

There are exactly $n!$ draw histories, so this is the probability of the prefix under a uniformly
random history. The cases $k = 0$ and $k = n$ are included.

articles.title: Fisher–Yates on a one-element vector
articles.statement:
For every vector $x$ of length $1$ and every draw
history $d$, the Fisher–Yates computation returns $x$ unchanged with cost pair $(1, 1)$: it still
retrieves the single draw $d_0 = 0$ and performs the self-swap at position $0$.

articles.title: Cost of the Fisher–Yates shuffle
articles.statement:
For every vector $x$ of length $n$ and every draw
history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$, the
Fisher–Yates computation on $x$ and $d$ has cost pair $(n, n)$: it retrieves exactly $n$ draws
and performs exactly $n$ swaps.

When $n \ge 1$, this count includes the final draw $d_{n-1} = 0$ and the self-swap at position
$n - 1$.

articles.title: Fisher–Yates shuffle with supplied draws
articles.statement:
Given a vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ and a
draw history $d$, which assigns to each position $i < n$ a number $d_i$ with $0 \le d_i < n - i$,
the Fisher–Yates computation processes the positions $i = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in increasing order
and at position $i$ swaps the entries at positions $i$ and $i + d_i$ of the current vector. It
returns the final vector together with a cost pair in $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$: each retrieved
draw adds $(1, 0)$ and each swap adds $(0, 1)$.

articles.title: Uniform mass of a Freivalds seed history
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, under the
uniform distribution on histories of $k$ seeds, that is, on $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, every history
has probability exactly $(2^{nk})^{-1}$. This includes the cases $k = 0$ and $n = 0$.

articles.title: Matrix of a Freivalds input
articles.statement:
An $n \times n$ array $A$ of rows over
$\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ determines the $n \times n$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ whose
$(i, j)$ entry is entry $j$ of row $i$ of $A$.

articles.title: The sharp Freivalds example has a wrong product
articles.statement:
Let $A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be
$1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Then $AB \neq C$.

articles.title: Acceptance of the repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices
$A$, $B$, $C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, the
repeated Freivalds test on these seeds accepts if and only if, for every $i < k$, the Freivalds
trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r_i$ accepts.

articles.title: Counting accepted histories of repeated Freivalds trials
articles.statement:
Let $n, k$ be natural numbers
and let $A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The number of histories
$(r_1, \dots, r_k)$ of seeds $r_i \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which the repeated Freivalds executor
accepts equals $a^k$, where $a$ is the number of seeds $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which a single
Freivalds trial accepts.

articles.title: Completeness of the repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be
$n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ with $AB = C$. Then for every $k$, including $k = 0$,
and all seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, the repeated Freivalds test on these
seeds accepts.

articles.title: Repeated Freivalds test on empty matrices
articles.statement:
For $0 \times 0$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/2$ and any number $k$ of seeds (each the empty vector), the repeated Freivalds test
accepts and performs no scalar multiplications or additions.

articles.title: Acceptance probability of repeated Freivalds trials
articles.statement:
Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and
let $A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$. If the history of $k$ seeds is drawn
uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, the probability that the repeated Freivalds executor accepts
is $p^k$, where $p$ is the probability that a single Freivalds trial accepts on a seed drawn
uniformly from $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

articles.title: Completeness of repeated Freivalds trials
articles.statement:
Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and let
$A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB = C$. If the history of $k$
seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, then the repeated Freivalds executor accepts
with probability $1$.

articles.title: Exact acceptance probability of repeated trials on the sharp Freivalds example
articles.statement:
Let
$A = B = (1)$ and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, and let $k$
be a natural number. Run $k$ Freivalds trials on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seeds drawn independently and
uniformly from $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$, accepting exactly when every trial accepts. Then the
run accepts with probability exactly $2^{-k}$.

Since $AB \neq C$, the bound $2^{-k}$ on the probability that $k$ trials accept a wrong product
cannot be improved.

articles.title: Soundness of repeated Freivalds trials
articles.statement:
Let $n, k$ be natural numbers and let
$A, B, C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB \ne C$. If the history of $k$
seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$, then the repeated Freivalds executor accepts
with probability at most $(2^k)^{-1}$.

articles.title: Output distribution of repeated Freivalds trials
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, k$ and
$n \times n$ matrices $A, B, C$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, this is the probability distribution on
$\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ of the result returned by the repeated Freivalds executor on
$A, B, C$ when its history of $k$ seeds is drawn uniformly from $(\mathbb{F}_2^n)^k$.

articles.title: Cost of the repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$,
$C$ over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, the repeated
Freivalds test on these seeds performs exactly $3kn^2$ scalar multiplications and $3kn^2$ scalar
additions.

articles.title: Repeated Freivalds test with no trials
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/2$, the repeated Freivalds test on the empty list of seeds ($k = 0$) accepts and
performs no scalar multiplications or additions.

articles.title: Repeated Freivalds test on fixed seeds
articles.statement:
Given $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{Z}/2$ and seeds $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n$, run the Freivalds trial on
$A$, $B$, $C$ with each seed $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1}$ in order, including the trials after a
rejection, and return the conjunction of their results (true when $k = 0$). The arithmetic cost
of the run is the sum of the costs of the $k$ trials.

articles.title: Uniform mass of a Freivalds seed
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. For every
$n$ and every vector $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the uniform probability distribution on
$\mathbb{F}_2^n$ assigns to $r$ the probability $(2^n)^{-1}$.

articles.title: Acceptance via the product discrepancy
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ and every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$, $r$
returns true if and only if $(AB - C)r = 0$.

articles.title: Acceptance criterion of the Freivalds trial
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ and every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$, $r$
returns true if and only if $A(Br) = Cr$.

articles.title: Soundness of the Freivalds trial
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB \ne C$. Then twice the number of seeds $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which the
Freivalds trial returns true is at most the number of all seeds in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$; that is, at
most half of the seeds accept.

Acceptance is the return value of the same charged run whose cost is counted.

articles.title: Completeness of the Freivalds trial
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ with $AB = C$. Then for every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ the Freivalds trial on
$A$, $B$, $C$, $r$ returns true. This includes the case $n = 0$.

articles.title: Freivalds trial on empty matrices
articles.statement:
For $0 \times 0$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ and the empty seed $r$, the Freivalds trial returns true at zero cost: it performs
no scalar multiplications and no scalar additions.

articles.title: Acceptance probability of the Freivalds trial as a seed count
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be
$n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays. The
probability that the Freivalds trial law of $A$, $B$, $C$ returns true equals the number of
seeds $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r$
accepts, divided by the number $|\mathbb{F}_2^n|$ of all seeds.

articles.title: The Freivalds trial accepts a correct product with probability one
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be
$n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays. If
$AB = C$, then the Freivalds trial law of $A$, $B$, $C$ returns true with probability $1$.
This includes the case $n = 0$ of empty matrices.

articles.title: The sharp Freivalds example is accepted with probability one half
articles.statement:
Let $A = B = (1)$
and $C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. When the seed is drawn
uniformly from $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ accepts with
probability exactly $1/2$.

Since $AB \neq C$, this shows that the bound $1/2$ on the probability that one trial accepts a
wrong product cannot be improved.

articles.title: The Freivalds trial accepts a wrong product with probability at most one half
articles.statement:
Let $A$,
$B$, $C$ be $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays.
If $AB \ne C$, then the Freivalds trial law of $A$, $B$, $C$ returns true with probability at
most $1/2$.

articles.title: Freivalds trial law
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, given as arrays, the Freivalds trial law is the
probability distribution on $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ of the value returned by the
Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r$, where $r$ is drawn uniformly from
$\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

The seeds are exactly uniform; no pseudorandom generator or assumed error probability is
involved.

articles.title: The sharp Freivalds example accepts exactly the zero seed
articles.statement:
Let $A = B = (1)$ and
$C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. For every seed
$r \in (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$, the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$ with seed $r$, which
compares $A(Br)$ with $Cr$, accepts if and only if the single entry $r_0$ of $r$ is $0$.

articles.title: The sharp Freivalds example has exactly one accepted seed
articles.statement:
Let $A = B = (1)$ and
$C = (0)$ be $1 \times 1$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. Exactly one seed
$r \in (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^1$ is accepted by the Freivalds trial on $A$, $B$, $C$.

articles.title: Cost of the Freivalds trial
articles.statement:
For $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ and every seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Freivalds trial performs exactly
$3n^2$ scalar multiplications and exactly $3n^2$ scalar additions.

These counts belong to the same run that returns the acceptance bit and include the additions
into the zero-initialized accumulators.

articles.title: Freivalds trial
articles.statement:
Given $n \times n$ matrices $A$, $B$, $C$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, stored as arrays of rows, and a seed $r \in \mathbb{F}_2^n$, the
trial computes the column vectors $Br$, $A(Br)$ and $Cr$, each by accumulating matrix products
into a zero column, and returns true exactly when $A(Br) = Cr$. Its cost is the pair (number of
scalar multiplications, number of scalar additions), each multiply-add step counting one of each.

The coefficient domain is $\mathbb{F}_2$ by intentional specialization, not by a restriction in
the cited source.

articles.title: Expected number of hires is the harmonic number
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a list of $n$ pairwise
distinct elements of a linearly ordered type, and rearrange its entries by a uniformly random
permutation of the indices. The expected number of hires that the hire-assistant procedure
(interview the entries in order, hiring each one strictly better than every earlier one) makes
on the rearranged list, an element of $[0, \infty]$, converted to a real number, equals the
harmonic number $H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k}$.

articles.title: Expected number of hires as a real harmonic sum
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a list of $n$ pairwise
distinct elements of a linearly ordered type, and rearrange its entries by a uniformly random
permutation of the indices. The expected number of hires that the hire-assistant procedure
(interview the entries in order, hiring each one strictly better than every earlier one) makes
on the rearranged list, an element of $[0, \infty]$, converted to a real number, equals
$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{i+1}$.

articles.title: Expected number of hires under a random permutation
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a list of $n$ pairwise
distinct elements of a linearly ordered type, and rearrange its entries by a uniformly random
permutation of the indices. The expected number of hires, valued in $[0, \infty]$, that the
hire-assistant procedure (interview the entries in order, hiring each one strictly better than
every earlier one) makes on the rearranged list equals $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{i+1}$.

## Sources

- CLRS Section 5.2.

articles.title: Hire-count bounds for the hire-assistant scan
articles.statement:
For every nonempty list of $n$ candidates
in a linearly ordered type, the number of hires $h$ recorded in the cost pair of the
hire-assistant scan satisfies $1 \le h \le n$.

articles.title: The hire-assistant scan hires exactly the strict prefix maxima
articles.statement:
For every list
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, the list of indices hired by the hire-assistant
scan, in chronological order, is the increasing list of all indices $i < n$ such that $x_j < x_i$
for every $j < i$.

articles.title: Strictly increasing input hires every candidate
articles.statement:
For every strictly increasing list
$x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, including the empty list, the
hire-assistant scan hires the indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in that order, and its cost pair is
$(n, n)$.

articles.title: Hire-assistant scan on no candidates
articles.statement:
On the empty list, the hire-assistant scan returns
no manager and an empty list of hires, with cost pair $(0, 0)$.

articles.title: The hire-assistant scan returns the earliest best candidate
articles.statement:
For every list
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type, the manager returned by the hire-assistant scan
is none when the list is empty, and otherwise is the smallest index $i$ such that $x_i$ is a
maximum of the list.

articles.title: Hire-assistant scan on one candidate
articles.statement:
For every element $a$ of a linearly ordered type,
on the one-element list $[a]$ the hire-assistant scan returns manager index $0$ and hire list
$[0]$, with cost pair $(1, 1)$: the single candidate is hired regardless of its quality.

articles.title: Cost of the hire-assistant scan
articles.statement:
For every list of $n$ candidates in a linearly ordered
type, the cost pair of the hire-assistant scan is $(n, h)$, where $h$ is the length of the list
of hired indices that the scan returns.

articles.title: The hire-assistant scan
articles.statement:
Given candidates $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in a linearly ordered type,
the scan interviews them in order while keeping a current manager, initially none, which counts
as below every candidate. Candidate $i$ is hired exactly when $x_i$ is strictly greater than the
value of the current manager, and then becomes the new manager; ties keep the earlier manager.
The scan returns the zero-based index of the final manager (none for the empty list) and the
list of hired indices in the order they were hired, and its cost is the pair (number of
interviews, number of hires).

articles.title: Minimum cut size bounds the number of edges
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid multigraph state with
$n \ge 2$ vertices, $m$ edges (counted with multiplicity) and minimum cut size $k$. Then
$n k \le 2m$: every vertex has degree at least $k$, since its singleton is a cut.

articles.title: Edge contraction
articles.statement:
For a multigraph state $G$ and a pair of vertices $e = (a, b)$, the
contraction of $G$ along $e$ deletes the first occurrence of $b$ from the vertex list, replaces
$b$ by $a$ in both endpoints of every edge, and then deletes every edge whose two endpoints are
equal.

articles.title: Cut sizes under contraction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a multigraph state, $e = (a, b)$ a pair of
vertices and $Y$ a map from vertices to booleans, and let $\rho$ send $b$ to $a$ and fix every
other vertex. The size of the cut $Y$ in the contraction of $G$ along $e$ equals the size of the
cut $Y \circ \rho$ in $G$.

articles.title: Size of a cut
articles.statement:
For a list of edges (pairs of vertices, repeated pairs counted with
multiplicity) and a map $X$ from vertices to booleans, the size of the cut $X$ is the number of
edges $(u, v)$ in the list with $X(u) \ne X(v)$.

articles.title: Cuts distinct as partitions
articles.statement:
Two maps $X, Y$ from vertices to booleans are distinct on a
list of vertices $S$ when some $v \in S$ has $X(v) \ne Y(v)$ and some $w \in S$ has
$X(w) = Y(w)$; so on $S$ neither cut is the other or its complement.

articles.title: Cuts of a multigraph
articles.statement:
A map $X$ from vertices to booleans is a cut of a multigraph state
$G$ when some vertex $v$ of $G$ has $X(v) = \mathrm{true}$ and some vertex $w$ of $G$ has
$X(w) = \mathrm{false}$.

articles.title: Contraction preserves the minimum cut size
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid multigraph state with
minimum cut size $k$, and let $X$ be a cut of $G$ of size $k$. If $e = (a, b)$ is an edge of $G$
with $X(a) = X(b)$, then the contraction of $G$ along $e$ also has minimum cut size $k$.

articles.title: Minimum cut size
articles.statement:
A natural number $k$ is the minimum cut size of a multigraph state $G$
when some cut of $G$ has size $k$ and every cut of $G$ has size at least $k$.

articles.title: Renaming a vertex
articles.statement:
For vertices $a$ and $b$, renaming $b$ to $a$ is the map on vertices
that sends $b$ to $a$ and fixes every other vertex.

articles.title: Repeating Karger's algorithm succeeds with probability at least one half
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
valid multigraph state with $n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut size $k$, and let $t$ be a natural
number with $n(n-1) \le 2t$. Then the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs of
the contraction process returns $k$ is at least $1/2$.

articles.title: Karger's algorithm succeeds with high probability
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with
$n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut size $k$, and let $t$ be a natural number with
$\lceil \log_2 n \rceil \cdot n(n-1) \le 2t$. Then the probability that at least one of $t$
independent runs of the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is at least $1 - 1/n$.

Thus $O(n^2 \log n)$ runs find the minimum cut size with high probability.

articles.title: Amplification with high probability
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$
vertices and minimum cut size $k$, and let $c$ and $t$ be natural numbers with
$c \cdot n(n-1) \le 2t$. Then the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs of the
contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is at least $1 - (1/2)^c$.

articles.title: Success probability of repeated runs
articles.statement:
For a multigraph $G$ with $n$ vertices and
natural numbers $k$ and $t$, let $p$ be the probability that one run of the contraction process
on $G$, with $n$ contractions allowed, returns $k$. The repeated success probability is
$1 - (1 - p)^t$, the probability that at least one of $t$ independent runs returns $k$.

articles.title: Multigraph state of Karger's algorithm
articles.statement:
A state over a vertex type $V$ consists of a
list of current (super-)vertices in $V$ and a list of edges, each an ordered pair of elements
of $V$; repeated pairs are parallel edges.

articles.title: Karger's bound
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices and minimum cut
size $k$. Then the contraction process on $G$, with $n$ contractions allowed, returns $k$ with
probability at least $2 / (n(n-1))$.

articles.title: The success probability is at most one
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, every number of
allowed contractions and every multigraph $G$, the probability that the contraction process on
$G$ returns $k$ is at most $1$.

articles.title: The success probability is nonnegative
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, every number $f$
of allowed contractions and every multigraph state $G$, the probability $P_k(f, G)$ that the
contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ satisfies $0 \le P_k(f, G)$.

articles.title: Success probability of the contraction process
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, a number $f$
of allowed contractions and a multigraph $G$ with edge list $E_G$, the probability $P_k(f, G)$
that the contraction process on $G$ returns $k$ is defined by recursion on $f$. If $f = 0$, or
$G$ has at most two vertices, or $G$ has no edges, then $P_k(f, G)$ is $1$ when $G$ has exactly
$k$ edges and $0$ otherwise. Otherwise
$P_k(f, G) = \frac{1}{|E_G|} \sum_{e \in E_G} P_k(f - 1, G/e)$, where $G/e$ is the contraction of
$G$ along $e$ and the sum runs over the edges with multiplicity.

This models contracting a uniformly random edge while more than two vertices remain and counting
the edges between the last two vertices.

articles.title: Handshake lemma
articles.statement:
For a valid multigraph $G$, the sum over the vertices $v$ of $G$ of the
number of edges crossing the singleton cut $\{v\}$ equals twice the number of edges of $G$.

articles.title: Survival probabilities of distinct cuts sum to at most one
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid multigraph
with vertex list $S$, let $f$ be a number of allowed contractions, and let $X_1, \dots, X_m$ be
Boolean functions on the vertex type that are pairwise distinct as partitions of $S$. Then the
probabilities that the contraction process on $G$, with $f$ contractions allowed, outputs
$X_1, \dots, X_m$ add up to at most $1$.

The survival events are disjoint: a run outputs at most one partition.

articles.title: Each minimum cut survives with probability at least $2/(n(n-1))$
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a valid
multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices whose minimum cut size $k$ is at least $1$, and let $X$ be a
cut of $G$ with exactly $k$ crossing edges. Then the probability that the contraction process on
$G$, allowed up to $n$ contractions, outputs the cut $X$ is at least $2/(n(n-1))$.

articles.title: Probability that a run outputs a given cut
articles.statement:
For a map $X$ from vertices to booleans, a
fuel bound $f$ and a multigraph $G$, this is the probability that the contraction process on $G$
(contract an edge chosen uniformly at random, counted with multiplicity, while more than two
vertices and at least one edge remain, making at most $f$ contractions) never contracts an edge
whose endpoints $X$ separates and ends with exactly two vertices on which $X$ takes both values.

Explicitly: if $f = 0$, or $G$ has at most two vertices, or $G$ has no edges, the value is $1$
when $G$ has exactly two vertices and $X$ is a cut of $G$, and $0$ otherwise. Otherwise it is the
average over the edges $e$ of $G$, counted with multiplicity, of the value for fuel $f - 1$ on
the contraction of $G$ along $e$ when $X$ agrees on the two endpoints of $e$, and of $0$ when it
does not.

articles.title: At most $n(n-1)/2$ minimum cuts
articles.statement:
**At most $n(n-1)/2$ minimum cuts** (Karger; Kleinberg and Tardos, Section 13.2). Let $G$ be a
valid multigraph with $n \ge 2$ vertices whose minimum cut size $k$ is at least $1$. If
$X_1, \dots, X_m$ are cuts of $G$, each with exactly $k$ crossing edges, that are pairwise
distinct as partitions of the vertices of $G$, then $2m \le n(n-1)$, that is, $m \le n(n-1)/2$.

Each of these cuts is output by a run of the contraction process with probability at least
$2/(n(n-1))$, and the runs that output distinct partitions are disjoint.

articles.title: Contraction preserves validity and removes one vertex
articles.statement:
If a multigraph $G$ is valid and
$e$ is one of its edges, then the contraction of $G$ along $e$ is valid and has exactly one
vertex fewer than $G$.

articles.title: Valid multigraph
articles.statement:
A multigraph, given by a list of vertices and a list of edges (pairs of
vertices, with multiplicity), is valid when its vertex list has no repeated entries and every
edge joins two distinct vertices of the list.

articles.title: MinHash, counting form
articles.statement:
The number of permutations of `U` under which `A` and `B` have
the same min-hash, times `|A ∪ B|`, equals `|A ∩ B|` times the number of all permutations.

articles.title: Min-hash of a set under a permutation
articles.statement:
The min-hash of `A` under the permutation `π`: the least element of `π(A)`, or `⊤` if `A` is
empty.

articles.title: MinHash collision probability
articles.statement:
**MinHash collision probability** (Broder 1997): for a uniformly random permutation `π` of
the finite universe `U` (`uniformOn Set.univ` on `Equiv.Perm U`, for any measurable structure in
which singletons are measurable, e.g. `⊤`) and sets `A`, `B` with `A ∪ B` nonempty,
`P(min π(A) = min π(B)) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|`, the Jaccard similarity of `A` and `B`.

articles.title: Array binary search membership test agrees with binary search
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an array with
entries in a type $\alpha$, let $k \in \alpha$, let $\mathrm{lt}$ be any Boolean-valued comparison
on $\alpha$, and let $\ell$ and $h$ be natural numbers. Lean core's Boolean binary search
membership test for $k$ in $A$, with comparison $\mathrm{lt}$ and bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns
true exactly when Lean core's array binary search with the same arguments returns some element.

articles.title: Binary search membership test on a sorted array is correct
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an array with
entries in a linearly ordered type, sorted so that an earlier entry is never greater than a later
one, and let $k$ be an element of that type. Lean core's Boolean binary search membership test
for $k$ over the whole of $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison, returns true if and only
if $k$ is an entry of $A$.

articles.title: Bounded binary search membership test on a sorted array is correct
articles.statement:
Let
$A = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array of length $n$ with entries in a linearly ordered type,
with $a_i \le a_j$ whenever $i < j$. Let $k$ be an element of that type and $\ell$, $h$ natural
numbers. Lean core's Boolean binary search membership test for $k$ in $A$, with the strict order
$<$ as comparison and inclusive bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns true if and only if there is an
index $i < n$ with $\ell \le i \le h$ and $a_i = k$.

articles.title: Binary search on a sorted array fails exactly on non-members
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an array with
entries in a linearly ordered type, sorted so that an earlier entry is never greater than a later
one, and let $k$ be an element of that type. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ over the
whole of $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison, returns no element if and only if $k$ is
not an entry of $A$.

articles.title: Bounded binary search on a sorted array fails exactly when the key is absent
articles.statement:
Let
$A = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array of length $n$ with entries in a linearly ordered type,
with $a_i \le a_j$ whenever $i < j$. Let $k$ be an element of that type and $\ell$, $h$ natural
numbers. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ in $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison
and inclusive bounds $\ell$ and $h$, returns no element if and only if there is no index $i < n$
with $\ell \le i \le h$ and $a_i = k$.

articles.title: Binary search on a sorted array finds exactly its members
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an array with entries
in a linearly ordered type, sorted so that an earlier entry is never greater than a later one, and
let $k$ and $a$ be elements of that type. Lean core's array binary search for $k$ over the whole of
$A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison, returns $a$ if and only if $a = k$ and $k$ is an
entry of $A$.

articles.title: Result of bounded binary search on a sorted array
articles.statement:
Let $A = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an
array of length $n$ with entries in a linearly ordered type, with $a_i \le a_j$ whenever $i < j$.
Let $k$ and $a$ be elements of that type and $\ell$, $h$ natural numbers. Lean core's array binary
search for $k$ in $A$, with the strict order $<$ as comparison and inclusive bounds $\ell$ and
$h$, returns $a$ if and only if $a = k$ and there is an index $i < n$ with $\ell \le i \le h$ and
$a_i = k$.

The requirement $i < n$ reflects the implementation's clamping of an upper bound $h \ge n$ to
$n - 1$.

articles.title: Binary search reports absence exactly when the key is absent
articles.statement:
Let
$a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing
order, and let $k$ be a key. Binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ returns no index
if and only if $a_i \ne k$ for every $i < n$.

articles.title: Binary search returns the first occurrence of the key
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be
an array over a linearly ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, let $k$ be a key and let $i$
be a natural number. Binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ returns the index $i$ if
and only if $i < n$, $a_i = k$, and $a_j < k$ for every $j < i$.

articles.title: Comparison bound for binary search for the first occurrence
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ of length
$n$ over a linearly ordered type and every key $k$, binary search for the first occurrence of $k$
in $a$ makes at most $\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil + 1$ element comparisons.

articles.title: Exact comparison count of binary search for the first occurrence
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array of
length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, let $k$ be a key, and let $\ell$ be the index returned by
lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$. The number of element comparisons made by binary search for the
first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ equals the number made by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$, plus
$1$ if $\ell < n$ and plus $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Binary search for the first occurrence
articles.statement:
Given an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a
linearly ordered type and a key $k$, binary search for the first occurrence of $k$ in $a$ runs
lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$, obtaining an index $\ell$. If $\ell < n$, it makes one further
comparison, charged one unit, and returns $\ell$ when $a_\ell = k$ and no index otherwise; if
$\ell \ge n$, it returns no index without further cost.

When $a$ is sorted in nondecreasing order, the result is the first index $i$ with $a_i = k$, or no
index when $k$ does not occur in $a$. On an unsorted array a present key can be missed and the
result can be no index.

articles.title: Correctness of lower-bound search
articles.statement:
Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be an array over a linearly
ordered type, sorted in nondecreasing order, let $k$ be a key, and let $\ell$ be the index returned
by lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$. Then $\ell \le n$, $a_j < k$ for every $j < \ell$, and
$k \le a_j$ for every $j$ with $\ell \le j < n$.

articles.title: Comparison bound for lower-bound search
articles.statement:
For every array $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly
ordered type and every key $k$, lower-bound search for $k$ in $a$ makes at most
$\lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ element comparisons.

articles.title: Lower-bound search
articles.statement:
Given an array $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ over a linearly ordered type and
a key $k$, lower-bound search maintains a half-open interval $[l, h)$ of indices, starting from
$[0, n)$. While $l < h$, it compares $a_m$ with $k$ at the midpoint
$m = l + \lfloor (h - l)/2 \rfloor$, charging one unit for this comparison, and continues with
$[m + 1, h)$ if $a_m < k$ and with $[l, m)$ otherwise. When $l = h$ it returns $l$.

When $a$ is sorted in nondecreasing order (or at least partitioned at $k$: every entry before the
returned index is $< k$ and every entry from that index on is $\ge k$), the result is the first
index $i$ with $k \le a_i$, or $n$ if every entry is below $k$. On an unsorted array the result is
unspecified: for $a = (2, 1)$ and $k = 2$ the search returns $2$, not the first index $0$ with
$k \le a_0$.

articles.title: Bucket sort on the empty array
articles.statement:
For every linearly ordered field $R$ with a floor
function, bucket sort applied to the empty array of elements of $R$ returns the empty array
at zero cost.

articles.title: Expected occupancy of a bucket in bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on
$[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with
$\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\mathbb{E}[N_i] = 1$.

articles.title: Second moment of a bucket's occupancy in bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on
$[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with
$\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\mathbb{E}[N_i^2] = 2 - 1/n$.

articles.title: Variance of a bucket's occupancy in bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1}$ be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on
$[0, 1)$. For $i < n$, let $N_i$ be the number of indices $j < n$ with
$\lfloor n \omega_j \rfloor = i$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(N_i) = 1 - 1/n$.

articles.title: Bucket sort permutes its input
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor
function. For every array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the array returned by
bucket sort is a permutation of the input: every element occurs in the output exactly as many
times as in the input.

articles.title: Bucket sort sorts
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function. For every
array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the array returned by bucket sort is
nondecreasing: each entry is at most every entry after it.

articles.title: Bucket sort runs in expected linear time
articles.statement:
For each $n$, let
$\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly
distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T_n(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges
on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and
$T_n(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T_n] = \Theta(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Lower bound on the expected time of bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly
distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges
on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and
$T(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $5n \le \mathbb{E}[T]$.

articles.title: Expected time of bucket sort on one input
articles.statement:
Let $\omega_0$ be uniformly distributed on
$[0, 1)$, and let $T(\omega_0)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the
one-element array $(\omega_0)$ if $\omega_0 \in [0, 1)$, and $T(\omega_0) = 0$ otherwise.
Then $\mathbb{E}[T] = 5$.

articles.title: Upper bound on the expected time of bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let
$\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ have independent coordinates, each uniformly
distributed on $[0, 1)$. Let $T(\omega)$ be the number of time steps that bucket sort charges
on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and
$T(\omega) = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[T] \le 5n + (n - 1)/2$.

articles.title: Bucket sort on the empty input has expected time zero
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be the number of time
steps that bucket sort charges on the empty array, the only input of length $n = 0$. Its
expectation under the product of zero copies of the uniform distribution on $[0, 1)$ is $0$.

articles.title: The running time of bucket sort is integrable
articles.statement:
For every $n$, let
$T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ map $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ to the number of
time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if every
$\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and to $0$ otherwise. Then $T$ is integrable with respect to the
product of $n$ copies of the uniform distribution on $[0, 1)$.

articles.title: Bound on the cost of bucket sort via squared bucket sizes
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly
ordered field with a floor function and let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be an array of elements of $R$
that all lie in $[0, 1)$. For $0 \le i < n$ let $c_i$ be the number of indices $j$ with
$\lfloor n x_j \rfloor = i$. Then the cost of bucket sort on this array is at most
$5n + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} c_i^2$.

articles.title: Linear lower bound on the cost of bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with
a floor function. For every array of $n$ elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$, the cost
of bucket sort on this array is at least $5n$.

articles.title: The running time of bucket sort is measurable
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the function
$T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that maps $\omega = (\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ to the
number of time steps that bucket sort charges on the array $(\omega_0, \dots, \omega_{n-1})$ if
every $\omega_j$ lies in $[0, 1)$, and to $0$ otherwise, is measurable.

articles.title: Exact cost of bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function
and let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be an array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$. For
$0 \le i < n$ let $B_i$ be the list of the entries $x_j$ with $\lfloor n x_j \rfloor = i$,
in decreasing order of $j$, and let $T(B_i)$ be the number of comparisons insertion sort makes
on $B_i$. Then the cost of bucket sort on this array equals $5n + \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} T(B_i)$.

articles.title: Bucket sort
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a linearly ordered field with a floor function and let
$x_1, \dots, x_n$ be an array of elements of $R$ that all lie in $[0, 1)$. If $n = 0$, bucket
sort returns the empty array at zero cost. Otherwise it creates $n$ empty buckets indexed by
$0, \dots, n - 1$, visits the entries in order and prepends each entry $x$ to bucket
$\lfloor n x \rfloor$, sorts each bucket with insertion sort, and concatenates the sorted
buckets in increasing order of index. The cost is $n$ for creating the buckets, plus one per
entry placed, plus one per bucket sorted together with the comparisons insertion sort makes on
it, plus one per bucket and one per entry during concatenation.

articles.title: Correctness of counting sort
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number, let $\mathrm{key}$ assign to
each record a key in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $A$ be an array of records. The array that
counting sort returns on $A$ lists its records in nondecreasing order of key, is a permutation of
$A$, and is stable: for every key $q < k$, the records of the output with key $q$, read from left
to right, form the same sequence as the records of $A$ with key $q$.

articles.title: Running time of counting sort
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number, let $\mathrm{key}$ assign to
each record a key in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, and let $A$ be an array of $n$ records. Counting sort on
$A$ with this key is charged at most $7n + 3k$ operations, where one operation is charged for each
counter initialization, key evaluation, counter read, counter write and output write.

articles.title: Counting sort
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a natural number and let $\mathrm{key}$ assign to each record a
key in $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$. Counting sort of an array $A$ of records returns an array together
with a count of charged operations. It starts $k$ counters at zero, counts the records of $A$ with
each key, replaces the counters by cumulative counts so that the counter of key $q$ holds the
number of records with key at most $q$, and then scans $A$ from right to left: for each record it
decrements the counter of the record's key and writes the record at the resulting position of the
output, which starts as a copy of $A$. One operation is charged for each counter initialization,
key evaluation, counter read, counter write and output write.

articles.title: Correctness of heap sort
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, heap
sort returns a list that is sorted in nondecreasing order and is a permutation of $xs$.

articles.title: Heap sort preserves multiplicities
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered
type, the output of heap sort on $xs$ and $xs$ itself are equal as multisets: every value occurs
in both lists the same number of times.

articles.title: Heap sort permutes its input
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type,
heap sort returns a permutation of $xs$.

articles.title: Heap sort output is sorted
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type,
heap sort returns a list sorted in nondecreasing order.

articles.title: Heap sort
articles.statement:
For a list $xs$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, heap sort inserts the
entries of $xs$ one at a time, from first to last, into the empty binary min-heap, and then
extracts the minimum of the heap as many times as the heap has entries, each time continuing with
the remaining heap. The output is the list of the extracted minima in the order in which they
were extracted.

articles.title: Charged comparison
articles.statement:
For elements $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type, this
computation returns the truth value of $x \le y$ and charges one unit of time.

articles.title: Correctness of insertion sort
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, the list
returned by insertion sort is nondecreasing and is a permutation of $l$.

articles.title: Agreement with CSLib's monadic insertion sort
articles.statement:
For a list $l$ over a linearly ordered
type in the lowest universe, the costed insertion sort of $l$ equals CSLib's generic monadic
insertion sort run in the time-counting monad with the charged comparison: the returned lists
agree and the numbers of charged comparisons agree.

articles.title: Cost of a single insertion
articles.statement:
For an element $a$ and a list $l$ over a linearly ordered
type, costed insertion of $a$ into $l$ charges at most $n$ comparisons, where $n$ is the length
of $l$.

articles.title: Costed insertion into a list
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an element of a linearly ordered type. Inserting
$a$ into the empty list returns $[a]$ at no cost. Inserting $a$ into a list with head $b$ and
tail $l$ first charges one unit for comparing $a \le b$; if $a \le b$ it returns $a$ followed by
$b$ and $l$, and otherwise it inserts $a$ into $l$, adding that cost, and returns $b$ followed by
the result.

articles.title: Insertion sort permutes its input
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ over a linearly ordered type, the
list returned by insertion sort is a permutation of $l$; in particular every element occurs in
it exactly as often as in $l$.

articles.title: Insertion sort returns a sorted list
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ over a linearly ordered type,
the list returned by insertion sort on $l$ is nondecreasing.

articles.title: Comparison bound for insertion sort
articles.statement:
On a list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered
type, insertion sort charges at most $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.

articles.title: Insertion sort with comparison cost
articles.statement:
On a list over a linearly ordered type, insertion
sort returns the empty list at no cost when the input is empty. On a list with head $a$ and
tail $l$, it sorts $l$ and then inserts $a$ into the result by costed insertion; its cost is the
cost of sorting $l$ plus the cost of that insertion. Exactly one unit is charged for each order
comparison.

articles.title: Costed insertion returns the ordered insertion
articles.statement:
For an element $a$ and a list $l$ over a
linearly ordered type, the list returned by costed insertion of $a$ into $l$ is the ordered
insertion of $a$ into $l$ with respect to $\le$: $a$ is placed immediately before the first
element $b$ of $l$ with $a \le b$, or at the end of $l$ if there is no such element.

articles.title: Cost-annotated insertion sort returns the standard insertion sort
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$
over a linearly ordered type, the list returned by insertion sort with comparison costs equals the
standard insertion sort of $xs$ with respect to $\le$, which inserts the head into the sorted
tail.

articles.title: Linear search fails exactly when no element satisfies the predicate
articles.statement:
For every predicate
$p$ on a type $\alpha$ and every list $L$ over $\alpha$, linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns no
index if and only if $p(x)$ is false for every element $x$ of $L$.

articles.title: Characterization of a successful linear search
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type
$\alpha$, every list $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $i$,
linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns the index $i$ if and only if $i < n$, $p(x_i)$ is true, and
$p(x_j)$ is false for every $j < i$.

articles.title: Cost recurrence for linear search
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, every
$x \in \alpha$ and every list $T$ over $\alpha$, the cost of linear search for $p$ on the list
with head $x$ and tail $T$ is $1$ if $p(x)$ is true, and $1$ plus the cost of linear search for
$p$ on $T$ if $p(x)$ is false. The head costs one evaluation of $p$, and the tail is searched only
when the head fails.

articles.title: Cost of an unsuccessful linear search
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and
every list $L$ over $\alpha$, if linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns no index, then its cost is
the length of $L$: it evaluates $p$ once for every element of $L$.

articles.title: Cost of a successful linear search
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, every
list $L$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $i$, if linear search for $p$ on $L$ returns the
index $i$, then its cost is $i + 1$: it evaluates $p$ exactly $i + 1$ times.

articles.title: Linear search costs at most the list length
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$
and every list $L$ over $\alpha$, the cost of linear search for $p$ on $L$ is at most the length
of $L$: it evaluates $p$ at most once for every element of $L$.

articles.title: Cost of linear search on the empty list
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$, linear
search for $p$ on the empty list has cost $0$: it evaluates $p$ zero times.

articles.title: Linear search
articles.statement:
Given a predicate $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and a list $L$ of elements of
$\alpha$, linear search scans $L$ from the front and returns the index of the first element of $L$
that satisfies $p$, or no index if no element does, together with a cost that counts one unit for
each evaluation of $p$. On the empty list it returns no index at cost $0$. On a list with head $x$
and tail $T$ it evaluates $p(x)$ at a cost of one unit; if $p(x)$ is true it returns the index $0$,
and otherwise it searches $T$, adds one to the index found there (if any), and adds the cost of
that search.

No cost is charged for list operations, index arithmetic, or control flow.

articles.title: Linear search returns the first satisfying index
articles.statement:
For every predicate $p$ on a type
$\alpha$ and every list $L = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ over $\alpha$, the index returned by linear
search for $p$ on $L$ (ignoring its cost) equals the result of the standard library's
first-index search: the least $i < n$ with $p(x_i)$ true, or no index if $p(x_i)$ is false for
every $i < n$.

articles.title: Correctness of median-of-medians selection on short lists
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list of length
at most $140$ over a linearly ordered type and let $k$ be a natural number. If median-of-medians
selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns an element $x$, then $x$ occurs in $L$, the number of entries
of $L$ less than $x$, counted with multiplicity, is at most $k$, and $k$ is less than the number
of entries of $L$ that are at most $x$.

articles.title: Comparison bound for median-of-medians selection on short lists
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of
length $n \le 140$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians
selection of rank $k$ in $L$ is charged at most $80n$ comparisons.

articles.title: Size budget for the two median-of-medians recursive calls
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $m$ and $p$ be natural
numbers with $n \ge 140$, $m \le \lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor$ and
$p \le \lfloor 7n/10 \rfloor + 6$. Then $20m + 20p + n \le 20n$.

articles.title: Cost budget for one median-of-medians step
articles.statement:
Let $n$, $m$, $p$, $a$, $c_1$ and $c_2$ be
natural numbers with $n \ge 140$, $m \le \lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor$,
$p \le \lfloor 7n/10 \rfloor + 6$, $c_1 \le 20am$ and $c_2 \le 20ap$. Then
$c_1 + c_2 + an \le 20an$.

articles.title: Correctness of median-of-medians selection
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linearly ordered type
and let $k$ be a natural number. If median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns an
element $x$, then $x$ occurs in $L$, the number of entries of $L$ less than $x$, counted with
multiplicity, is at most $k$, and $k$ is less than the number of entries of $L$ that are at
most $x$.

articles.title: Median-of-medians selection agrees with sorting
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a linearly
ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns
the entry at zero-based position $k$ of the insertion sort of $L$ by $\le$ when $k$ is less than
the length of $L$, and returns nothing otherwise.

articles.title: Median-of-medians selection fails exactly on out-of-range ranks
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over
a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$ in
$L$ returns nothing if and only if $k$ is at least the length of $L$.

articles.title: Out-of-range ranks cost no comparisons
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type
and every natural number $k$ at least the length of $L$, median-of-medians selection of rank $k$
in $L$ returns nothing and is charged zero comparisons.

articles.title: Median-of-medians selection is quickselect on short lists
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of length
at most $140$ over a linearly ordered type and every natural number $k$, median-of-medians
selection of rank $k$ in $L$ coincides with timed quickselect of rank $k$ in $L$: both return
the same result and are charged the same number of comparisons.

articles.title: Median-of-medians selection succeeds on valid ranks
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a linearly
ordered type and every natural number $k$ less than the length of $L$, median-of-medians
selection of rank $k$ in $L$ returns some element.

articles.title: Group medians are lower medians of their blocks
articles.statement:
Let $xs$ be a list over a linear
order, and let $g_1, \dots, g_m$ be its consecutive blocks of five elements, the last of which
may be shorter. Then the list of group medians of $xs$ has the same length $m$, say
$x_1, \dots, x_m$, and for each $i$, writing $k_i = \lfloor (|g_i| - 1)/2 \rfloor$ and counting
elements of $g_i$ with multiplicity: $x_i$ belongs to $g_i$, at most $k_i$ elements of $g_i$
are less than $x_i$, and more than $k_i$ elements of $g_i$ are less than or equal to $x_i$.

articles.title: Number of group medians
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear order, the
list of group medians of $xs$ has exactly $\lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor = \lceil n/5 \rceil$
entries.

articles.title: Group medians come from the input
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linear order, every
entry of the list of group medians of $xs$ is an element of $xs$.

articles.title: Comparison cost of the group medians
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear
order, computing the group medians of $xs$ takes at most $2n$ comparisons.

articles.title: Group medians for median-of-medians selection
articles.statement:
Given a list $xs$ over a linear
order, split $xs$ into consecutive blocks of five elements, the last of which may be shorter.
Sort each block $g$ by insertion sort and return, in block order, the entry at position
$\lfloor (|g| - 1)/2 \rfloor$ (counting from $0$) of each sorted block, that is, its lower
median. The cost is the total number of comparisons made by these insertion sorts.

articles.title: Linear solution of the median-of-medians recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $T : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
and $a \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $T(n) \le 20an$ for every $n \le 140$, and that for every
$n > 140$ there are $m, p \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \le \lfloor (n + 4)/5 \rfloor$,
$p \le \lfloor 7n/10 \rfloor + 6$ and $T(n) \le T(m) + T(p) + an$. Then $T(n) \le 20an$ for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Median of medians finds the lower median
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a nonempty list of length $n$ over a
linear order, and let $k = \lfloor (n - 1)/2 \rfloor$. Then median-of-medians selection on $L$ at
zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$ of $L$ such that at most $k$ entries of $L$ are less
than $x$ and more than $k$ entries of $L$ are at most $x$, where entries are counted with
repetition.

articles.title: Set rank of a median-of-medians result
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list without repeated entries over a
linear order and let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. If median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank
$k$ returns an element $x$, then the set $\{y \in L : y \le x\}$ has exactly $k + 1$ elements.

articles.title: Median of medians selects every one-based rank
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list without repeated
entries over a linear order, of length $n$, and let $1 \le i \le n$. Then median-of-medians
selection on $L$ at zero-based rank $i - 1$ returns an element $x$ of $L$, and the set
$\{y \in L : y \le x\}$ has exactly $i$ elements.

articles.title: One-based rank of a median-of-medians result
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list without repeated entries
over a linear order and let $i \ge 1$. If median-of-medians selection on $L$ at zero-based rank
$i - 1$ returns an element $x$, then the set $\{y \in L : y \le x\}$ has exactly $i$ elements.

articles.title: Median of medians makes linearly many comparisons
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ of length $n$ over
a linear order and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, median-of-medians selection on $L$ at rank $k$
charges at most $80n$ comparisons, where $n$ counts repeated entries.

Only order comparisons are charged; list construction, rank checks and recursion are free.

articles.title: Median of medians finds the upper median
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a nonempty list of length $n$ over a
linear order, and let $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Then median-of-medians selection on $L$ at
zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$ of $L$ such that at most $k$ entries of $L$ are less
than $x$ and more than $k$ entries of $L$ are at most $x$, where entries are counted with
repetition.

articles.title: Median-of-medians selection
articles.statement:
Given a list $L$ over a linear order and a zero-based rank
$k$, median-of-medians selection returns either an element of $L$ or nothing, charging one unit
of cost per order comparison. If $k \ge |L|$, where $|L|$ is the length of $L$, it returns
nothing at no cost. Otherwise it runs the following recursive procedure on $(L, k)$ with a budget
of $|L|$ nested calls, returning nothing if the budget runs out. A list of length at most $140$
is handled by deterministic quickselect at the current rank. A longer list is cut into
consecutive groups of five entries, the last possibly shorter; each group is sorted by insertion
sort and its lower median is kept, giving a list $M$ of $m$ medians. The procedure recursively
selects the entry of $M$ at rank $\lfloor m/2 \rfloor$ as the pivot $x$ (returning nothing if
that call does), and splits the list by a three-way partition into the entries below $x$, equal
to $x$ and above $x$, with $b$ entries below and $e$ equal. If the current rank $r$ satisfies
$r < b$ it recurses on the lower part with rank $r$; if $b \le r < b + e$ it returns $x$;
otherwise it recurses on the upper part with rank $r - b - e$.

articles.title: Entries at most the pivot
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an element,
and let $B$ and $E$ be the blocks of entries below and equal to $p$ in the three-way partition
of $L$ around $p$. Then the number of entries of $L$ that are at most $p$, counted with
multiplicity, equals $|B| + |E|$.

articles.title: Entries below the pivot
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an element,
and let $B$ be the block of entries below $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$.
Then the number of entries of $L$ that are strictly less than $p$, counted with multiplicity,
equals $|B|$.

articles.title: Counting through the below block
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an
element, let $q$ be a Boolean predicate on the elements, and let $B$, $E$, $A$ be the blocks of
entries below, equal to and above $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$. If $q$ is
false on every entry of $E$ and on every entry of $A$, then the number of entries of $L$
satisfying $q$ equals the number of entries of $B$ satisfying $q$, both counted with
multiplicity.

articles.title: Counting through the above block
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $p$ be an
element, let $q$ be a Boolean predicate on the elements, and let $B$, $E$, $A$ be the blocks of
entries below, equal to and above $p$ in the three-way partition of $L$ around $p$. If $q$ is
true on every entry of $B$ and on every entry of $E$, then the number of entries of $L$
satisfying $q$ equals $|B| + |E|$ plus the number of entries of $A$ satisfying $q$, all counted
with multiplicity.

articles.title: Correctness of quickselect
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order and let $k$ be a
natural number. If quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns an element $x$, then $x$
is an entry of $L$, and, counting entries of $L$ with multiplicity, the number of entries less
than $x$ is at most $k$ and $k$ is less than the number of entries at most $x$.

Thus $x$ occupies zero-based position $k$ in the sorted order of $L$, also when $x$ is repeated.

articles.title: Quickselect agrees with sorting
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order, let $S$ be the
insertion sort of $L$ in nondecreasing order, and let $k$ be a natural number. If $k < |L|$,
quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns the entry of $S$ at zero-based position $k$;
if $k \ge |L|$, it returns no element.

articles.title: Quickselect fails exactly out of range
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear order and let
$k$ be a natural number. Quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns no element if and
only if $|L| \le k$.

articles.title: Rank inequalities determine the quickselect value
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a list over a linear
order, let $k$ be a natural number and let $x$ be an element. Counting entries of $L$ with
multiplicity, if the number of entries less than $x$ is at most $k$ and $k$ is less than the
number of entries at most $x$, then quickselect on $L$ with zero-based rank $k$ returns $x$.

articles.title: Worst-case comparison bound for quickselect
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a linear order, of
length $n$, and every natural number $k$, quickselect on $L$ with rank $k$ makes at most
$n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.

articles.title: Quickselect
articles.statement:
Deterministic quickselect takes a list $L$ over a linear order and a
zero-based rank $k$ and returns an element or no element, together with its cost, the number
of element comparisons it makes. If $k \ge |L|$, it returns no element at no cost. Otherwise
it runs the following recursion, starting from the list $L$ and the rank $k$. On an empty list
it returns no element. On a list with first entry $p$ and remaining entries $T$, and a rank
$r$, it forms the three-way partition of $T$ around $p$, with blocks $B$, $E$, $A$ of entries
below, equal to and above $p$, at a cost of $|T|$ comparisons. If $r < |B|$, it recurses on
$B$ with rank $r$; if $|B| \le r < |B| + |E| + 1$, it returns $p$; otherwise it recurses on
$A$ with rank $r - (|B| + |E| + 1)$.

The recursion carries a fuel counter that starts at $|L|$ and drops by one per call, and it
returns no element when the fuel is exhausted; since every recursive call is on a strictly
shorter list, the fuel never runs out on a nonempty list.

articles.title: Number of list entries strictly between two values
articles.statement:
For a list $\ell$ over a linear order
and elements $a$ and $b$, this is the number of entries $x$ of $\ell$, counted with multiplicity,
such that $a < x < b$.

articles.title: Correctness of quicksort
articles.statement:
For every list $\ell$ over a linear order, the output of
quicksort on $\ell$ is sorted in nondecreasing order and is a permutation of $\ell$; in
particular every value occurs in the output exactly as often as in $\ell$.

articles.title: Expected comparisons of quicksort on a random permutation, as a real number
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$
be a list without repeated entries over a linear order. Take the expected number of comparisons
made by quicksort on the list obtained by rearranging the entries of $\ell$ by a uniformly random
permutation of their positions, which is an element of $[0, \infty]$, and convert it to a real
number. The result equals the real sum

$$\sum_{a < b} \frac{2}{d(a, b) + 2},$$

where the sum runs over pairs of entries $a < b$ of $\ell$ and $d(a, b)$ is the number of entries
of $\ell$ strictly between $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Expected comparisons of quicksort on a random permutation
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$ be a list without
repeated entries over a linear order. The expected number of comparisons made by quicksort on the
list obtained by rearranging the entries of $\ell$ by a uniformly random permutation of their
positions, computed in the extended nonnegative reals $[0, \infty]$, equals

$$\sum_{a < b} \frac{2}{d(a, b) + 2},$$

where the sum runs over pairs of entries $a < b$ of $\ell$ and $d(a, b)$ is the number of entries
of $\ell$ strictly between $a$ and $b$ (CLRS Section 7.4).

articles.title: Worst-case comparison bound for quicksort
articles.statement:
For every list of length $n$ over a linear
order, quicksort performs at most $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.

articles.title: Quicksort
articles.statement:
Deterministic quicksort on lists over a linear order, using the first entry as
pivot and counting comparisons. The empty list is returned unchanged at no cost. On a list with
first entry $p$ and tail $t$, the algorithm stably splits $t$ into the entries less than $p$, equal
to $p$ and greater than $p$, using one comparison per entry of $t$; it then recursively sorts the
lesser and greater parts and returns the sorted lesser part, followed by $p$, the entries equal to
$p$ in their original order, and the sorted greater part. The cost is the total number of
comparisons.

articles.title: Correctness of radix sort
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ and let every record carry a key that is a vector
$(k_0, \dots, k_{d-1})$ of $d$ digits in $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$, most significant digit first. For
every input array, the output of radix sort is a permutation of the input, is in nondecreasing
lexicographic order of keys, and is in nondecreasing order of the numbers
$\sum_{i < d} k_i b^{d-1-i}$ whose base-$b$ digits are the keys. Moreover it is stable: for every
key vector $v$, the records with key $v$ appear in the output in the same order as in the input.

articles.title: Cost bound for radix sort
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ and let every record carry a key that is a vector
of $d$ digits in $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$. On an array of $n$ records, radix sort uses at most
$d(7n + 3b)$ charged operations, where each counting-sort pass charges one unit for every counter
initialization, key evaluation, counter read, counter write and output write.

articles.title: Radix sort
articles.statement:
Let $b \ge 2$ and let every record carry a key that is a vector of $d$ digits
in $\{0, \dots, b-1\}$, most significant digit first, at positions $0, \dots, d-1$. Radix sort
runs $d$ passes of stable counting sort on the array, the pass for position $i$ sorting by the
digit of the key at position $i$, for $i = d-1, d-2, \dots, 0$, that is, from the least to the most
significant digit. Its cost is the total cost of the $d$ counting-sort passes.

articles.title: Number of differing positions
articles.statement:
For two vectors $a, b \in \mathbb{N}^n$, this is the number of
indices $i < n$ with $a_i \neq b_i$, that is, the Hamming distance between $a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Correctness of the unimodal rearrangement algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $a$ be an array of length $n$ that
is a permutation of $1, \dots, n$, and let $m(a)$ be the value that the program
$\mathrm{minRearrange}$ computes on $a$. Then some unimodal permutation $x$ of
$1, \dots, n$ differs from $a$ in exactly $m(a)$ positions, and every unimodal permutation of
$1, \dots, n$ differs from $a$ in at least $m(a)$ positions. So $m(a)$ is the minimum number of
positions in which $a$ differs from a unimodal permutation of $1, \dots, n$.

## Sources

- NWERC 2025 Problem G, see https://2025.nwerc.eu/problem-set.pdf. Problem `permute_to_unimodal` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Unimodal arrays
articles.statement:
An array $a$ of natural numbers is unimodal if it is the concatenation of a
strictly increasing array $b$ followed by a strictly decreasing array $b'$, where either part may
be empty.

articles.title: Correctness of minimum extraction
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be an element of a linearly ordered type and
$L$ a list over it, and let $(m, r)$ be the pair returned by minimum extraction from $L$ with
initial candidate $c$. Then the list $m$ followed by $r$ is a permutation of the list $c$ followed
by $L$, $m \le c$, and $m \le x$ for every element $x$ of $L$.

articles.title: Cost of minimum extraction
articles.statement:
For every element $c$ of a linearly ordered type and every
list $L$ over it, minimum extraction from $L$ with initial candidate $c$ has cost exactly $|L|$,
the length of $L$; that is, it performs exactly $|L|$ order comparisons.

articles.title: Minimum extraction
articles.statement:
Given an initial candidate $c$ in a linearly ordered type and a list
$L$, minimum extraction returns a pair $(m, r)$ together with a cost. If $L$ is empty, it returns
$c$ with the empty list at cost $0$. If $L$ has head $x$ and tail $L'$, it compares $x$ with $c$
at cost one: if $x < c$, it extracts from $L'$ with candidate $x$, obtaining $(m, r)$, and returns
$m$ with the list $c$ followed by $r$; otherwise it extracts from $L'$ with candidate $c$,
obtaining $(m, r)$, and returns $m$ with the list $x$ followed by $r$. The total cost is one plus
the cost of the recursive extraction.

articles.title: Correctness of selection sort
articles.statement:
For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the list
returned by selection sort on $L$ is sorted in nondecreasing order (each entry is $\le$ every
later entry) and is a permutation of $L$, so it preserves duplicate multiplicities.

articles.title: Comparison count of selection sort
articles.statement:
For every list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered
type, selection sort has cost exactly $n(n-1)/2$ in the model that charges one unit per order
comparison; that is, it performs exactly $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.

articles.title: Selection sort
articles.statement:
Selection sort of a list $L$ over a linearly ordered type is defined
recursively. If $L$ is empty, the result is the empty list at cost $0$. If $L$ has head $x$ and
tail $L'$, minimum extraction from $L'$ with initial candidate $x$ yields a minimum $m$ and the
list $r$ of remaining elements, and the result is $m$ followed by the selection sort of $r$. The
cost is the sum of the costs of all these minimum extractions.

articles.title: The min–max algorithm returns no result exactly on the empty list
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$
over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result on
$xs$ if and only if $xs$ is empty.

articles.title: Characterization of the min–max output
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type
and all elements $lo$ and $hi$ of that type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns
the pair $(lo, hi)$ on $xs$ if and only if $lo$ and $hi$ both belong to $xs$, $lo \le x$ for every
$x$ in $xs$, and $x \le hi$ for every $x$ in $xs$.

articles.title: The min–max algorithm on the empty list
articles.statement:
On the empty list, the simultaneous minimum and
maximum algorithm returns no result and makes no comparisons.

articles.title: Correctness of the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm
articles.statement:
For every list $xs$ over a
linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result on $xs$
when $xs$ is empty, and returns the pair $(\min xs, \max xs)$ of the least and greatest elements
of $xs$ otherwise.

articles.title: The min–max algorithm on a one-element list
articles.statement:
For every element $a$ of a linearly ordered
type, on the list $[a]$ the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns the pair $(a, a)$
and makes no comparisons.

articles.title: Comparisons of the min–max algorithm on even-length lists
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k \ge 1$ and every list of length $2k$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and
maximum algorithm makes exactly $3k - 2$ comparisons.

articles.title: Comparisons of the min–max algorithm on odd-length lists
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$ and
every list of length $2k + 1$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum
algorithm makes exactly $3k$ comparisons.

articles.title: Comparison count of the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm
articles.statement:
For every list of
length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes no
comparisons when $n = 0$ and exactly $\lceil 3n/2 \rceil - 2$ comparisons when $n \ge 1$.

This counts element-order decisions, not full RAM instructions or comparator bit complexity.

articles.title: Simultaneous minimum and maximum
articles.statement:
Given a list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the
paired algorithm returns no result when $xs$ is empty and otherwise returns a pair (a candidate
minimum and a candidate maximum), counting one unit of time for each comparison of elements. On a
one-element list $[a]$ it returns $(a, a)$ without a comparison. On a longer list of odd length
both candidates start at the first element without a comparison; on a list of even length they
start at the smaller and the larger of the first two elements, found with one comparison. The
remaining elements are then taken in consecutive pairs: one comparison orders the pair, its smaller
member replaces the candidate minimum if it is strictly smaller (one comparison), and its larger
member replaces the candidate maximum if it is strictly larger (one comparison).

articles.title: Parallel composition of relabeled comparator lists
articles.statement:
Let $e$ and $e'$ be injective
maps $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with disjoint images, that is, $e(y) \ne e'(y')$ for all
$y$ and $y'$. If the comparator lists $p$ and $q$ both have depth at most $d$, then $p$ with
its wires relabeled by $e$, followed by $q$ with its wires relabeled by $e'$, has depth at
most $d$.

articles.title: The final layer of the odd-even merger has depth at most one
articles.statement:
For every $k$, the
final layer of the odd-even merger on $2^{k+2}$ wires, which compares wires $2i + 1$ and
$2i + 2$ for each $i < 2^{k+1} - 1$, has depth at most $1$: its comparators are disjoint.

articles.title: Depth bound for Batcher's odd-even merger
articles.statement:
For every $k$, Batcher's odd-even merger on
$2^{k+1}$ wires has depth at most $k + 1$.

articles.title: Depth bound for Batcher's odd-even merge sort as a comparator list
articles.statement:
For every $k$,
there is a $d$ with $2d \le k(k+1)$ such that the comparator list of Batcher's odd-even merge
sort on wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$ has depth at most $d$; that is, its depth is at most
$k(k+1)/2$.

articles.title: Relabeling wires preserves a depth bound
articles.statement:
If a comparator list has depth at most $d$
and $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is injective, then the comparator list obtained by
relabeling its wires by $e$ also has depth at most $d$.

articles.title: Last layer of the odd-even merger
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the list of comparators
$(2i + 1, 2i + 2)$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, 2^{k+1} - 2$, in increasing order of $i$. It compares the
neighbouring wires $2i + 1$ and $2i + 2$ and is the last layer of the odd-even merger on
$2^{k+2}$ wires.

articles.title: Lower bound for the depth of Batcher's odd-even merge sorting network
articles.statement:
For all $k$
and $d$, if Batcher's odd-even merge sorting network on $2^k$ wires has depth at most $d$,
then $k \le d$.

articles.title: Size of the odd-even merger
articles.statement:
For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, Batcher's odd-even merger on
$2^{k+1}$ wires consists of exactly $k \cdot 2^k + 1$ comparators.

articles.title: Size of Batcher's odd-even merge sort
articles.statement:
For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the number $L$ of
comparators of Batcher's odd-even merge sort on $2^k$ wires satisfies
$4(L + 1) + k \cdot 2^k = (k^2 + 4) \cdot 2^k$, that is, $L = (k^2 - k + 4) \cdot 2^k / 4 - 1$.

The identity is stated without subtraction or division, and is exact for every $k$.

articles.title: Levels of a relabeled comparator list on the image wires
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a comparator
list and let $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be injective. If two initial level assignments
$\ell$ and $\ell'$ agree on every wire $e(y)$, then the levels after running $p$ with its
wires relabeled by $e$, starting from $\ell$ and from $\ell'$, agree on every wire $e(y)$.

articles.title: Relabeled comparator lists leave the other wires alone
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a comparator list,
let $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be any map and let $\ell$ be an initial level assignment.
For every wire $x$ outside the image of $e$, the level of $x$ after running $p$ with its
