wires relabeled by $e$, starting from $\ell$, is $\ell(x)$.

articles.title: Levels of a relabeled comparator list
articles.statement:
Let $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be
injective, let $p$ be a comparator list and let $\ell$ be an initial level assignment. For
every wire $j$, the level of wire $e(j)$ after running $p$ with its wires relabeled by $e$,
starting from $\ell$, equals the level of wire $j$ after running $p$ starting from
$\ell \circ e$.

articles.title: The odd-even merger merges
articles.statement:
Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f$ assign a Boolean value to
each wire $0, 1, 2, \dots$, with false read as $0$ and true as $1$. Let $a, c \le 2^k$ be such
that wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$ hold $a$ zeros followed by ones (wire $i < 2^k$ holds $0$ exactly
when $i < a$) and wires $2^k, \dots, 2^{k+1} - 1$ hold $c$ zeros followed by ones (wire
$2^k + i$, for $i < 2^k$, holds $0$ exactly when $i < c$). Then after Batcher's odd-even merger
on $2^{k+1}$ wires runs on $f$, every wire $j < 2^{k+1}$ holds $0$ exactly when $j < a + c$.

articles.title: Batcher's odd-even merger
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the odd-even merger on wires
$0, \dots, 2^{k+1} - 1$ is the comparator list defined by recursion on $k$. For $k = 0$ it is the
single comparator $(0, 1)$. For $k + 1$ it is the merger for $k$ with each wire $i$ renamed to
$2i$ (merging the even wires), followed by the merger for $k$ with each wire $i$ renamed to
$2i + 1$ (merging the odd wires), followed by the comparators $(2i + 1, 2i + 2)$ for
$i = 0, 1, \dots, 2^{k+1} - 2$ in increasing order of $i$.

articles.title: Odd-even merge sort sorts every $0$-$1$ input
articles.statement:
Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f$ assign a
Boolean value to each wire $0, 1, 2, \dots$, with false read as $0$ and true as $1$. After
Batcher's odd-even merge sort on $2^k$ wires runs on $f$, there is $z \le 2^k$ such that every
wire $j < 2^k$ holds $0$ exactly when $j < z$: wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$ hold $z$ zeros followed
by ones.

articles.title: Batcher's odd-even merge sort
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, odd-even merge sort on wires
$0, \dots, 2^k - 1$ is the comparator list defined by recursion on $k$. For $k = 0$ it is empty.
For $k + 1$ it is the sorter for $k$ (sorting wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$), followed by the sorter
for $k$ with each wire $i$ renamed to $2^k + i$ (sorting wires $2^k, \dots, 2^{k+1} - 1$),
followed by Batcher's odd-even merger on $2^{k+1}$ wires.

articles.title: Depth bound for Batcher's odd-even merge sorting network
articles.statement:
For every $k$, there is a
$d$ with $2d \le k(k+1)$ such that Batcher's odd-even merge sorting network on $2^k$ wires
has depth at most $d$; that is, its depth is at most $k(k+1)/2$.

articles.title: Batcher's odd-even merge sort sorts every input over every linear order
articles.statement:
For every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every linearly ordered type $\alpha$, Batcher's odd-even merge sorting
network on $2^k$ wires sorts every input over $\alpha$: for every assignment $v$ of elements of
$\alpha$ to the wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$, the output of the network on $v$ is monotone in the
wire order.

The proof goes through the 0-1 principle.

articles.title: Batcher's odd-even merge sorting network
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the comparator
network on the $2^k$ wires $0, \dots, 2^k - 1$ given by the comparators of Batcher's odd-even
merge sort on $2^k$ wires, in the same order, with any comparator that touches a wire $\ge 2^k$
dropped.

articles.title: Relabeling keeps comparators within an interval
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be a list of comparators,
each a pair of natural numbers, that lies within $[l, h)$, and let $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
satisfy $l' \le e(x) < h'$ for every $x$ with $l \le x < h$. Then the list obtained from $ps$ by
relabeling its wires by $e$ lies within $[l', h')$.

articles.title: Relabeling the wires of a comparator list
articles.statement:
Given a map $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
and a list of comparators, each a pair $(i, j)$ of wires in $\mathbb{N}$, the relabeled list
replaces every comparator $(i, j)$ by $(e(i), e(j))$ and keeps the order of the list.

articles.title: Output of the last layer of the odd-even merger
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type,
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ an assignment of values to the wires. Running
the final layer for $k$ on $f$ gives at a wire $x$ the value $\min(f(x), f(x + 1))$ if $x$ is
odd and $\lfloor x / 2 \rfloor < 2^{k+1} - 1$; otherwise the value $\max(f(x - 1), f(x))$ if
$x$ is even, $x > 0$ and $(x - 2) / 2 < 2^{k+1} - 1$; and the value $f(x)$ in all other cases.
In other words, for each $i < 2^{k+1} - 1$ wire $2i + 1$ receives the minimum and wire $2i + 2$
the maximum of the values of $f$ on these two wires, and every other wire keeps its value.

articles.title: Relabeled networks fix the wires outside the image
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered
type, $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ any map and $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ an assignment of
values to the wires. For every list of comparators and every wire $x$ that is not of the form
$e(y)$, running the list relabeled by $e$ on $f$ gives the value $f(x)$ at wire $x$.

articles.title: Running a relabeled network
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let
$e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be injective. For every list of comparators, every
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ and every wire $j$, running the list relabeled by $e$ on $f$ gives at
wire $e(j)$ the same value as running the original list on the input $i \mapsto f(e(i))$ gives at
wire $j$.

articles.title: The bitonic merger sorts every bitonic `0`-`1` input
articles.statement:
Let $k, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f$
assign a Boolean value to each wire $x \in \mathbb{N}$, with Booleans ordered by
$\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$. If the sequence $f(b), f(b + 1), \dots, f(b + 2^k - 1)$ is
bitonic, then running the bitonic merger on the block $[b, b + 2^k)$ on $f$ gives an assignment
$g$ that is sorted on that block: $g(b + i) \le g(b + j)$ whenever $i \le j < 2^k$.

This is the correctness of CLRS's `BITONIC-SORTER`, proved by recursion on the half-cleaner
lemma.

articles.title: Bitonic merger
articles.statement:
The bitonic merger on the block of wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ is the list of
comparators defined by recursion on $k$. For $k = 0$ it is empty. On the block $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$
it is the half-cleaner on $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$, followed by the bitonic merger on $[b, b + 2^k)$,
followed by the bitonic merger on $[b + 2^k, b + 2^{k+1})$.

This is CLRS's `BITONIC-SORTER`.

articles.title: The bitonic sorter sorts every `0`-`1` input
articles.statement:
Let $k, b \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $f$ assign
a Boolean value to each wire $x \in \mathbb{N}$, with Booleans ordered by
$\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$. Running Batcher's bitonic sorter on the block $[b, b + 2^k)$
on $f$ gives an assignment $g$ that is sorted on that block: $g(b + i) \le g(b + j)$ whenever
$i \le j < 2^k$.

articles.title: Batcher's bitonic sorter on a block of wires
articles.statement:
A comparator $(i, j)$ puts the minimum of
the values on wires $i$ and $j$ on wire $i$ and the maximum on wire $j$. Batcher's bitonic sorter
on the block of wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ is the list of comparators defined by recursion on $k$. For
$k = 0$ it is empty. On the block $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$ it is Batcher's bitonic sorter on
$[b, b + 2^k)$, followed by Batcher's bitonic sorter on $[b + 2^k, b + 2^{k+1})$ with every
comparator $(i, j)$ replaced by $(j, i)$, followed by the bitonic merger on $[b, b + 2^{k+1})$.

Reversing the comparators makes the second half sort downwards, so the merger receives a bitonic
sequence. (CLRS's `SORTER` instead sorts both halves up and uses `MERGER`.)

articles.title: Batcher's bitonic sorter sorts every input over every linear order
articles.statement:
For every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ and every linearly ordered type $\alpha$, Batcher's bitonic sorting network on
$2^k$ wires sorts inputs over $\alpha$: for every assignment $v$ of elements of $\alpha$ to the
wires $0, 1, \dots, 2^k - 1$, the output of the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order.

The proof goes through the 0-1 principle.

articles.title: Batcher's bitonic sorting network
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, Batcher's bitonic sorting
network on $2^k$ wires is the comparator network on the wires $0, 1, \dots, 2^k - 1$ made of the
comparators of Batcher's bitonic sorter on the block $[0, 2^k)$ that join two wires below $2^k$
(in fact all of them), applied in the same order.

articles.title: Comparator on natural-number-indexed wires
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For wires
$i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and an assignment $f$ of values in $\alpha$ to the wires $x \in \mathbb{N}$,
the comparator $(i, j)$ applied to $f$ puts $\min(f(i), f(j))$ on wire $i$, puts
$\max(f(i), f(j))$ on wire $j$ when $j \ne i$, and leaves every other wire unchanged.

articles.title: Transported comparator lists agree with the original on Boolean inputs
articles.statement:
Let
$N \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $P$ be a list of comparators on natural-number-indexed wires, each of
which joins two wires below $N$. For every Boolean input $v$ on the wires $0, \dots, N - 1$, run
the network on $N$ wires obtained from $P$ on $v$ and extend its output by $\mathrm{false}$ to
all wires in $\mathbb{N}$; the result equals the result of running $P$ on the extension of $v$ by
$\mathrm{false}$.

articles.title: Extension of a Boolean vector by false
articles.statement:
For $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and a Boolean vector
$v = (v_0, \dots, v_{N-1})$, its extension by $\mathrm{false}$ is the function on $\mathbb{N}$
that takes the value $v_j$ at each $j < N$ and the value $\mathrm{false}$ at each $j \ge N$.

articles.title: The half-cleaner lemma
articles.statement:
Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{2m-1}$ be a
bitonic sequence of Booleans, ordered by $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$. For $i < m$ put
$\ell_i = \min(s_i, s_{i+m})$ and $u_i = \max(s_i, s_{i+m})$. Then either $\ell_i = \mathrm{false}$
for every $i < m$ and $u_0, \dots, u_{m-1}$ is bitonic, or $u_i = \mathrm{true}$ for every
$i < m$ and $\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{m-1}$ is bitonic.

The $\ell_i$ and $u_i$ are the outputs of the half-cleaner on $2m$ wires. This is CLRS Lemma 27.3
for bitonic $0$-$1$ sequences.

articles.title: Half-cleaner
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $m$ and $b$, the half-cleaner on the block of wires
$[b, b + 2m)$ is the list of comparators $(b + i, b + m + i)$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, m - 1$, in
this order: it compares wire $b + i$ with wire $b + m + i$.

articles.title: Bitonic 0-1 sequences
articles.statement:
A sequence $s : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ is bitonic of length $L$
if either $s$ or its complement $1 - s$ is an interval indicator of length $L$; that is, on the
positions $0, \dots, L - 1$ it has the form $0^a 1^b 0^c$ or $1^a 0^b 1^c$. Values of $s$ at
positions $i \ge L$ are unconstrained.

articles.title: Interval indicators
articles.statement:
A sequence $s : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$ is an interval indicator
of length $L$ if there are natural numbers $a \le e \le L$ such that for every $i < L$,
$s(i) = 1$ exactly when $a \le i < e$.

articles.title: Size of the bitonic merger
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $b$, the bitonic merger on
the block of wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ has $k \cdot 2^{k-1}$ comparators; precisely, twice its number
of comparators equals $k \cdot 2^k$.

articles.title: Size of the bitonic sorter on a block of wires
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $b$, the
bitonic sorter on the block of $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires $[b, b + 2^k)$ has $k(k+1)2^k/4$
comparators; precisely, four times its number of comparators equals $k(k+1)2^k$.

articles.title: Comparator count of Batcher's bitonic sorter
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, Batcher's
bitonic sorting network on $2^k$ wires has $k(k+1)2^k/4$ comparators; precisely, four times its
number of comparators equals $k(k+1)2^k$.

articles.title: Size of the half-cleaner
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $b$, the half-cleaner on the
block of wires $[b, b + 2m)$ has exactly $m$ comparators.

articles.title: Restricting comparators to finitely many wires
articles.statement:
For a natural number $N$ and a list of
comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, this is the network on the $N$ wires
$0, \dots, N - 1$ that keeps, in their original order, the comparators $(i, j)$ with $i < N$
and $j < N$, and drops all the others.

articles.title: Constant blocks stay constant
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $l, h \in \mathbb{N}$,
and let $c$ be a list of comparators on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires each of which joins two wires
$x$ with $l \le x < h$. If an input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ takes the same value $a$ on
every wire $x$ with $l \le x < h$, then running $c$ on $f$ gives an output that also takes the
value $a$ on every such wire.

articles.title: Output of the half-cleaner
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $m, b \in \mathbb{N}$, and
let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be an input on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires. Running the
half-cleaner on $[b, b + 2m)$ on $f$ puts $\min(f(b + i), f(b + m + i))$ on wire $b + i$ and
$\max(f(b + i), f(b + m + i))$ on wire $b + m + i$ for every $i < m$, and leaves the value $f(x)$
on every wire $x$ outside $[b, b + 2m)$ unchanged.

articles.title: Locality of comparator networks
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order and let $ps$ be a list
of comparators $(i, j)$ on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires that all lie within $[l, h)$, that is,
$l \le i < h$ and $l \le j < h$ for every $(i, j)$ in $ps$. Then for every input
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ and every wire $x$ with $x < l$ or $h \le x$, the value of wire $x$
after running $ps$ on $f$ is $f(x)$.

articles.title: Reversing the comparators conjugates the network by complement on Booleans
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be
a list of comparators on $\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires and let $ps'$ be obtained by replacing each
comparator $(i, j)$ in $ps$ by $(j, i)$. For every input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$ and
every wire $x$, the value of wire $x$ after running $ps'$ on $f$ is the negation of the value of
wire $x$ after running $ps$ on the complemented input $y \mapsto \lnot f(y)$.

articles.title: Running a comparator network on natural-number-indexed wires
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
linear order. Given a list $ps$ of comparators, each a pair $(i, j)$ of natural numbers, and
an input $f : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ giving the value on each wire, running $ps$ on $f$
applies the comparators of $ps$ to the wire values one after another, from first to last. The
comparator $(i, j)$ puts the minimum of the values on wires $i$ and $j$ on wire $i$ and their
maximum on wire $j$, and leaves the other wires unchanged.

articles.title: Sorted on a block
articles.statement:
A Boolean sequence $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is sorted on
the block $[b, b + L)$ if $g(b + i) \le g(b + j)$ for all $i \le j < L$, where Booleans are
ordered by $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$.

articles.title: Comparators within an interval
articles.statement:
A list $ps$ of comparators, each a pair $(i, j)$ of
natural numbers, lies within $[l, h)$ if every comparator $(i, j)$ in $ps$ satisfies
$l \le i < h$ and $l \le j < h$.

articles.title: Adjacent comparator
articles.statement:
For $n$ wires and an index $i$, this is the comparator on
wires $i$ and $i + 1$ when $i + 1 < n$, and nothing when wire $i + 1$ does not exist.

articles.title: The bubble network sorts
articles.statement: **The bubble network sorts** every input over every linear order.

articles.title: Bubble sorting network
articles.statement:
The bubble sorting network on $n$ wires is the comparator
network obtained by concatenating the bubble passes ending at wires $n - 1, n - 2, \ldots, 0$,
in this order, where the bubble pass ending at wire $k$ consists of the comparators
$(0, 1), (1, 2), \ldots, (k - 1, k)$.

articles.title: Size of the bubble sorting network
articles.statement:
For every $n$, the bubble sorting network on $n$
wires has $n(n - 1)/2$ comparators: twice its number of comparators is $n(n - 1)$.

articles.title: Size of a bubble pass
articles.statement:
On $n$ wires, for every $m < n$ the bubble pass ending at wire
$m$ has exactly $m$ comparators.

articles.title: Effect of one bubble pass
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be an input on $n$ wires with values in a linearly
ordered type, let $m < n$, and let $w'$ be the output of the bubble pass ending at wire $m$
(the comparators $(0, 1), \ldots, (m - 1, m)$) run on $w$. Then $w'_i = w_i$ for every wire
$i > m$; $w'_i \le w'_m$ for every wire $i \le m$; and for every wire $i \le m$ there is a wire
$j \le m$ with $w'_i = w_j$.

articles.title: Bubble pass
articles.statement:
On $n$ wires, the bubble pass ending at wire $m$ is the comparator
network $(0, 1), (1, 2), \ldots, (m - 1, m)$, applied in this order, where a comparator
$(i, i + 1)$ is left out when wire $i + 1$ does not exist (that is, when $i + 1 \ge n$).

articles.title: Successive bubble passes
articles.statement:
On $n$ wires and for a number $m$, this is the comparator
network obtained by concatenating the bubble passes ending at wires $m - 1, m - 2, \ldots, 0$,
in this order; for $m = 0$ it is empty.

articles.title: Settled top wires
articles.statement:
Let $w$ assign to each of $n$ wires a value in a linearly ordered
type, and let $m$ be a natural number. Then $w$ is settled from $m$ when $w_i \le w_j$ for all
wires $m \le i \le j$ (the wires $m, \ldots, n - 1$ are sorted) and $w_i \le w_j$ for all
wires $i < m \le j$ (they hold the largest values). This is the invariant before the bubble
pass ending at wire $m - 1$.

articles.title: Parallel composition of comparator lists on adjacent blocks
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $m$, $b$, $d$ be
natural numbers, and let $p$ and $q$ be lists of comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, where
every comparator of $p$ joins two wires in $[a, m)$ and every comparator of $q$ joins two wires in
$[m, b)$. If $p$ and $q$ both have depth at most $d$, then the concatenation of $p$ followed by
$q$ also has depth at most $d$: the two lists run in parallel.

articles.title: Depth of sequential composition of comparator lists
articles.statement:
If a list $p$ of comparators on wires
indexed by $\mathbb{N}$ has depth at most $d$ and a list $q$ of comparators has depth at most
$e$, then the concatenation of $p$ followed by $q$ has depth at most $d + e$.

articles.title: Batcher's bitonic sorting network has depth at most $k(k+1)/2$
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k$, Batcher's bitonic sorting network on $2^k$ wires has depth at most $d$ for some natural
number $d$ with $2d \le k(k+1)$; that is, its depth is at most $k(k+1)/2$.

articles.title: Influence sets grow at most exponentially with the level
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a list of comparators
on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. Let $S$ assign to each wire a finite set of natural numbers and
let $\ell$ assign to each wire a natural number, such that $|S(x)| \le 2^{\ell(x)}$ for every
wire $x$. For each wire $x$, let $L(x)$ be the level of $x$ after $p$ starting from the levels
$\ell$. Then for every wire $x$, the influence set of $x$ after $p$ starting from $S$ has at most
$2^{L(x)}$ elements.

In particular, a wire at level $l$ depends on at most $2^l$ inputs.

articles.title: Depth bound for a comparator network
articles.statement:
A comparator network on $n$ wires has depth at most
$d$ when its list of comparators, read as pairs of wire numbers in $\mathbb{N}$, has depth at
most $d$: starting with every wire at level $0$ and scheduling each comparator one level after the
later of its two wires, every wire ends at level at most $d$.

articles.title: The bitonic merger has depth at most $k$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $b$, the bitonic
merger on the block of $2^k$ wires $b, b + 1, \dots, b + 2^k - 1$ has depth at most $k$.

articles.title: Depth of the bitonic sorter's comparator list
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $k$ and $b$, the
comparator list of Batcher's bitonic sorter on the block of $2^k$ wires
$b, b + 1, \dots, b + 2^k - 1$ has depth at most $d$ for some natural number $d$ with
$2d \le k(k+1)$; that is, its depth is at most $k(k+1)/2$.

articles.title: The half-cleaner has depth at most $1$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $m$ and $b$, the
half-cleaner on the block of $2m$ wires $b, \dots, b + 2m - 1$ has depth at most $1$: its
comparators join pairwise disjoint pairs of wires.

articles.title: Depth bound for a comparator list
articles.statement:
A list of comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$
has depth at most $d$ when, starting with every wire at level $0$ and scheduling each comparator
one level after the later of its two wires, every wire ends at level at most $d$.

articles.title: Comparators inside $(0, n)$ keep a false value inside $(0, n)$
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural
number, let $p$ be a list of comparators, each joining two wires in $[0, n)$, and let $f$ assign a
Boolean value to each wire in $\mathbb{N}$. If $f(y)$ is false for some $y < n$, then after
running $p$ on $f$ some wire $y < n$ carries the value false.

The smaller value moves to the first wire of each comparator.

articles.title: Tabulated levels agree with levels
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a list of natural numbers of length $N$ and
let $ps$ be a list of comparators all of whose wires lie in $[0, N)$. Extend $t$ to all wires by
setting $t_y = 0$ for $y \ge N$. Then for every wire $x$, the entry at position $x$ of the
tabulated levels of $ps$ starting from the table $t$ (read as $0$ when $x \ge N$) equals the level
of wire $x$ after $ps$, starting from the initial levels $y \mapsto t_y$.

articles.title: Influence sets of wires
articles.statement:
Given a list $ps$ of comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$
and an assignment $S$ of a finite set of natural numbers to each wire, the influence sets after
$ps$ are computed by processing the comparators in order: a comparator $(i, j)$ replaces the
current sets of both wires $i$ and $j$ by their union, and leaves the sets of all other wires
unchanged. Starting from $S(x) = \{x\}$, the set of a wire tracks the inputs it can depend on.

Evaluating this definition directly re-reads both wires' earlier sets at every comparator, a cost
exponential in the depth, so it serves as a proof device only.

articles.title: Batcher's bitonic sorter on $2^k$ wires has depth at least $k$
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers
$k$ and $d$, if Batcher's bitonic sorting network on $2^k$ wires has depth at most $d$, then
$k \le d$.

articles.title: The bitonic sorting comparator list on $2^k$ wires has depth at least $k$
articles.statement:
For all natural
numbers $k$ and $d$, if the comparator list of Batcher's bitonic sorter on the wires
$0, \dots, 2^k - 1$ has depth at most $d$, then $k \le d$.

articles.title: Every sorting network on $n$ wires has depth at least $\log_2 n$
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a comparator
network on $n$ wires and $d$ a natural number. If $C$ sorts every Boolean input (its output is
monotone in the wire order for every input in $\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}^n$, with
$\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$) and $C$ has depth at most $d$, then $n \le 2^d$.

By the 0-1 principle, the hypothesis implies that $C$ sorts every input over every linear order.

articles.title: Sorting comparator lists on $n$ wires have depth at least $\log_2 n$
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be a list
of comparators on wires indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, all of whose wires lie in $[0, n)$, and let $d$
be a natural number. Suppose that for every Boolean input $v$ on the wires $0, \dots, n - 1$,
extended by $\mathrm{false}$ to the wires $\ge n$, the output $w$ of $ps$ satisfies
$w_i \le w_j$ whenever $i \le j < n$ (with $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$). If $ps$ has depth at
most $d$, then $n \le 2^d$.

The smallest output depends on every input, and a wire at level $d$ depends on at most $2^d$
inputs.

articles.title: Levels inside a block depend only on initial levels inside it
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be a list of
comparators all of whose wires lie in $[a, b)$, and let $\ell, \ell' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
be initial levels that agree on every wire in $[a, b)$. Then for every wire $x$ in $[a, b)$, the
level of $x$ after $ps$ starting from $\ell$ equals the level of $x$ after $ps$ starting from
$\ell'$.

articles.title: Comparators inside a block leave levels outside it unchanged
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be a list of
comparators all of whose wires lie in $[a, b)$. Then for all initial levels
$\ell : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every wire $x$ with $x < a$ or $b \le x$, the level of $x$
after $ps$ starting from $\ell$ is $\ell(x)$.

articles.title: Swapping the wires of every comparator does not change levels
articles.statement:
For every list $ps$ of
comparators and all initial levels $\ell : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the levels after the list
obtained from $ps$ by replacing each comparator $(i, j)$ with $(j, i)$, starting from $\ell$, equal
the levels after $ps$ starting from $\ell$.

articles.title: Tabulated levels
articles.statement:
Given a list $ps$ of comparators and a table $t$ of natural numbers
$t_0, \dots, t_{N-1}$, the tabulated levels are computed by processing the comparators in order:
a comparator $(i, j)$ sets both entries $t_i$ and $t_j$ to $\max(t_i, t_j) + 1$, where an entry
outside the table reads as $0$ and a write outside the table is ignored.

Evaluating the levels directly re-reads both wires' earlier levels at every comparator, a cost
exponential in the depth; this computes the same values in time proportional to the network size
times $N$.

articles.title: Comparator levels under earliest scheduling
articles.statement:
Given a list of comparators on
$\mathbb{N}$-indexed wires, each a pair $(i, j)$ of wires, and a starting level $\ell(x)$ for
every wire $x$, process the comparators in order, keeping a current level for each wire, initially
$\ell$: a comparator $(i, j)$ whose wires currently have levels $a$ and $b$ sets the current levels
of both wires $i$ and $j$ to $\max(a, b) + 1$ and leaves every other level unchanged. The result
is the level of each wire after all the comparators, that is, when each comparator runs as early
as possible, one level after the later of its two wires.

articles.title: Outputs depend only on the influence set
articles.statement:
Let $f_0, g_0 : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be two
inputs with values in a linear order $\alpha$, let $S$ assign to each wire $x$ a finite set $S(x)$
of input positions, and let $F, G : \mathbb{N} \to \alpha$ be wire values such that for every wire
$x$, if $f_0$ and $g_0$ agree on $S(x)$, then $F(x) = G(x)$. Then for every list of comparators
and every wire $x$, if $f_0$ and $g_0$ agree on the influence set of $x$ obtained from $S$ through
the comparators, running the comparators on $F$ and on $G$ gives the same value at wire $x$.

articles.title: Comparator list of a network
articles.statement:
The comparators of a network on $n$ wires, in order, with
each comparator $(i, j)$ written as the pair of natural numbers $(i, j)$, forgetting that
$i, j < n$.

articles.title: Comparators commute with monotone maps
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be linear orders, let
$f : \alpha \to \beta$ be monotone, and let $n$ be a natural number. For all wires
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the
comparator $(i, j)$ applied to $f \circ v$ gives $f \circ w$, where $w$ is the output of the
comparator $(i, j)$ on $v$.

articles.title: A comparator permutes its inputs
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order and let $n$ be a natural
number. For all wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and every assignment $v$ of a value in
$\alpha$ to each wire, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the wires such that the output of the
comparator $(i, j)$ on $v$ is $v \circ \sigma$.

articles.title: Comparator
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $v$
assign a value $v(k) \in \alpha$ to each wire $k \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. For wires $i$ and $j$,
the comparator $(i, j)$ sends $v$ to the assignment that has $\min(v(i), v(j))$ on wire $i$,
$\max(v(i), v(j))$ on wire $j$ when $j \ne i$, and $v(k)$ on every other wire $k$.

articles.title: A Boolean input is a threshold of its spread
articles.statement:
For every Boolean input $v$ on $n$ wires,
applying the threshold map that sends a natural number $k$ to true if $n \le k$ and to false
otherwise to the spread of $v$ gives back $v$: for every wire $i$, the spread of $v$ at $i$ is at
least $n$ exactly when $v(i)$ is true.

Since the threshold map is monotone, $v$ is a monotone image of its spread.

articles.title: Comparator network
articles.statement:
A comparator network on $n$ wires is a finite list of pairs $(i, j)$
of wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, each pair standing for the comparator $(i, j)$; the
comparators are applied in list order.

articles.title: The ranking permutation
articles.statement:
For an injective map $w$ from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the natural
numbers, the ranking permutation of $w$ is the permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that sends each
$i$ to the rank of $w(i)$ among the values of $w$, that is, to the number of indices $j$ with
$w(j) < w(i)$. Since $w$ is injective, this map is a bijection.

The ranking permutation has the same relative order as $w$.

articles.title: Rank among the values of an input
articles.statement:
For a map $w$ from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the natural
numbers and an index $i < n$, the rank of $w(i)$ among the values of $w$ is the number of indices
$j < n$ with $w(j) < w(i)$. It is less than $n$, so it is again an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

articles.title: Networks commute with monotone maps
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be linear orders and let
$f : \alpha \to \beta$ be monotone. For every comparator network on $n$ wires and every assignment
$v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of the network on $f \circ v$ is $f \circ w$,
where $w$ is the output of the network on $v$.

## Sources

- CLRS, second edition, Lemma 27.1.

articles.title: The output of a comparator network is a permutation of its input
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear
order. For every comparator network on $n$ wires and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$
to each wire, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the wires such that the output of the network
on $v$ is $v \circ \sigma$.

articles.title: Running a comparator network
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. The output of a comparator
network on an assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each of its $n$ wires is obtained by
starting from $v$ and applying the comparators of the network one after another, in list
order.

articles.title: The Boolean sorting test is correct
articles.statement:
A comparator network passes the Boolean sorting test
if and only if it sorts inputs over the Booleans, that is, for every assignment of a Boolean
value to each wire, the output of the network is monotone in the wire order.

articles.title: Boolean sorting test
articles.statement:
The Boolean sorting test of a comparator network on $n$ wires
returns true exactly when, for every assignment $v$ of a Boolean value to each wire, the output
$w$ of the network on $v$ satisfies $w(i) \le w(j)$ for all wires $i \le j$, where
$\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$.

It is computed by running the network on all $2^n$ Boolean inputs.

articles.title: A network that passes the Boolean sorting test sorts over every linear order
articles.statement:
If a
comparator network on $n$ wires passes the Boolean sorting test, then for every linear order
$\alpha$ it sorts inputs over $\alpha$: for every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each
wire, the output of the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order.

articles.title: The 0-1 principle
articles.statement:
**The 0-1 principle** (CLRS Theorem 27.2): a network that sorts every Boolean input sorts
every input over every linear order.

articles.title: Sorting distinct inputs suffices
articles.statement:
A network that sorts every input with distinct natural
values sorts every input over every linear order.

articles.title: The permutation principle
articles.statement:
A comparator network on $n$ wires that sorts each of the $n!$
permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, viewed as the input whose value on wire $i$ is
$\sigma(i)$, sorts every input over every linear order.

articles.title: Networks that sort
articles.statement:
A comparator network on $n$ wires sorts inputs over a linearly
ordered type $\alpha$ if, for every input $v$ assigning a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the
output of running the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order: for all wires $i \le j$, the
output value on wire $i$ is at most the output value on wire $j$.

articles.title: Spread of a Boolean input
articles.statement:
For a Boolean input $v$ on $n$ wires, the spread of $v$ is the
input with natural-number values whose value on wire $i < n$ is $n + i$ if $v(i)$ is true and $i$
if $v(i)$ is false.

The values of the spread are pairwise distinct.

articles.title: The above list of a three-way partition is a filter
articles.statement:
For every element $p$ of a linearly
ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the above list of the stable three-way
partition of $xs$ around $p$ is the list of the elements $x$ of $xs$ with $p < x$, in their order
in $xs$ and with their multiplicities.

articles.title: The below list of a three-way partition is a filter
articles.statement:
For every element $p$ of a linearly
ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the below list of the stable three-way
partition of $xs$ around $p$ is the list of the elements $x$ of $xs$ with $x < p$, in their order
in $xs$ and with their multiplicities.

articles.title: Correctness of the stable three-way partition
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an element of a linearly ordered
type $\alpha$, let $xs$ be a list over $\alpha$, and let $B$, $E$ and $A$ be the below, equal and
above lists of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$. Then the concatenation $B$, $E$,
$A$ is a permutation of $xs$, every element $x$ of $B$ satisfies $x < p$, every element of $E$
equals $p$, and every element $x$ of $A$ satisfies $p < x$.

articles.title: The equal list of a three-way partition is a filter
articles.statement:
For every element $p$ of a linearly
ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the equal list of the stable three-way
partition of $xs$ around $p$ is the list of the elements $x$ of $xs$ with $x = p$, in their order
in $xs$ and with their multiplicities.

articles.title: Sizes of the three parts of a three-way partition
articles.statement:
For every element $p$ of a linearly
ordered type $\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the lengths of the below, equal and above
lists of the stable three-way partition of $xs$ around $p$ add up to the length of $xs$.

articles.title: Cost of the stable three-way partition
articles.statement:
For every element $p$ of a linearly ordered type
$\alpha$ and every list $xs$ over $\alpha$, the time charged by the stable three-way partition of
$xs$ around $p$ equals the length of $xs$: one unit for each comparison, one comparison per
element.

articles.title: Stable three-way partition
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be an element of a linearly ordered type $\alpha$. The
three-way partition of a list over $\alpha$ around $p$, together with the time it is charged, is
defined by recursion on the list. The empty list gives three empty lists at no cost. For a list
with head $x$ and tail $xs$, one unit of time is charged for comparing $x$ with $p$, the tail $xs$
is partitioned, and $x$ is put at the front of its below list if $x < p$, of its equal list if
$x = p$, and of its above list if $p < x$.

articles.title: Three-way partition record
articles.statement:
A three-way partition over a type $\alpha$ consists of three
lists over $\alpha$, called below, equal and above. They are meant to hold the elements strictly
below, equal to, and strictly above a pivot; the record itself imposes no condition on them.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore agrees with the naive matcher
articles.statement:
For all words $p$ and $t$ over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, the list of offsets returned by the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern
$p$ and text $t$ equals the list returned by the naive matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$,
entry by entry and in the same order. Only the returned lists are compared, not the costs.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore with the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every text $t$ of length $n$ over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, the Boyer–Moore matcher with the empty pattern and text $t$ returns
the list $0, 1, \dots, n$ of all offsets from $0$ to $n$ in increasing order, at cost $n + 1$.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore with a pattern longer than the text
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $t$ be words over the
alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$. If $t$ is strictly shorter than $p$, then the Boyer–Moore
matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ returns the empty list at cost $0$: no preprocessing or
search events are charged.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore returns offsets in strictly increasing order
articles.statement:
For all words $p$ and $t$ over
the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, the list of offsets returned by the Boyer–Moore matcher
with pattern $p$ and text $t$ is strictly increasing: each entry is smaller than every entry
after it.

articles.title: Worst-case cost of Boyer–Moore matching
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $t$ be words over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ of lengths $m$ and $n$. The cost of the Boyer–Moore matcher with
pattern $p$ and text $t$ is at most $n + 1$ if $m = 0$, at most $0$ if $n < m$, and at most
$\sigma + n + 11m - 6 + (m + 4)(n - m + 1)$ if $1 \le m \le n$.

The cost counts the matcher's selected events, not machine instructions. The bound is quadratic
and does not assert linear all-match comparison complexity or machine runtime.

articles.title: Exact Boyer–Moore cost when the pattern repeats one letter and ends in another, which alone makes up the text
articles.statement:
**Exact Boyer–Moore cost when the pattern repeats one letter and ends in another, which alone
makes up the text.** Let $a \ne b$ be letters of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ and let
$m$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $2 \le m \le n$. Write $a^{m-1}b$ for the word of $m - 1$
copies of $a$ followed by one $b$, and $b^n$ for the word of $n$ copies of $b$. The cost of the
Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $a^{m-1}b$ and text $b^n$ equals
$m + n + P + 4\lfloor n/m \rfloor$, where $P$ is the cost of the Boyer–Moore preprocessing of
the pattern $a^{m-1}b$.

On these inputs every alignment makes two character tests and is followed by a shift by $m$.

articles.title: Exact Boyer–Moore cost when pattern and text repeat the same letter
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a letter
of the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers with
$0 < m \le n$, and write $x^k$ for the word of $k$ copies of $x$. The cost of the Boyer–Moore
matcher with pattern $x^m$ and text $x^n$ equals $m + n + P + (m + 4)(n - m + 1)$, where $P$ is
the cost of the Boyer–Moore preprocessing of the pattern $x^m$.

Of this cost, $m(n - m + 1)$ counts character tests: every alignment is a match and compares all
$m$ pattern letters.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore matcher for all occurrences
articles.statement:
Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ and
$t = t_0 \cdots t_{n-1}$ be words over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$. The matcher
returns a list of offsets together with a cost. If $m = 0$ it returns $0, 1, \dots, n$ at cost
$n + 1$, and if $n < m$ it returns the empty list at cost $0$. Otherwise it charges $m + n$ for
converting $p$ and $t$ to arrays, computes the bad-character table $B$ and the strong
good-suffix table $G$ of $p$ with the Boyer–Moore preprocessing and charges the cost of that
preprocessing, and then visits alignments $s$, starting from $s = 0$, as long as
$s + m \le n$. At each alignment it charges $1$ and compares $p_r$ with $t_{s + r}$ for
$r = m - 1, m - 2, \dots, 0$, charging $1$ per comparison and stopping at the first mismatch.
If all $m$ letters agree, it records $s$, charges $2$ and moves to the alignment $s + G_0$. If
the first mismatch is at position $i$, it charges $1$ and moves to the alignment
$s + \max(G_i, B_c - m + 1 + i)$, where $c = t_{s + i}$ and the maximum is taken in the
integers. Finally it charges $1$ for each recorded offset and returns the recorded offsets in
the order they were found.

The result is every occurrence of $p$ in $t$, in increasing order and including overlaps. The
cost counts these selected events, not machine instructions.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore returns exactly the occurrences
articles.statement:
For all words $p$ and $t$ over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ and every natural number $k$, the offset $k$ belongs to the list
returned by the Boyer–Moore matcher with pattern $p$ and text $t$ if and only if $p$ occurs in
$t$ at offset $k$, that is, $k \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the word obtained from $t$ by
deleting its first $k$ letters. In particular, overlapping occurrences are all returned.

articles.title: Bad-character table of Boyer–Moore preprocessing
articles.statement:
Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ be a
pattern over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ and let $B$ be the bad-character table
computed by the Boyer–Moore preprocessing of $p$. For every symbol $c$, either $B_c = m$ and
$p_k \ne c$ for every $k$ with $k + 1 < m$, or there is $j$ with $j + 1 < m$ and $p_j = c$ such
that $B_c = m - 1 - j$ and every $k$ with $k + 1 < m$ and $p_k = c$ satisfies $k \le j$.

Thus $B_c$ is the distance from the last position of $p$ to the rightmost occurrence of $c$
before that position, or $m$ if $c$ does not occur there.

articles.title: The full-match shift is the least period of the pattern
articles.statement:
Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$
be a nonempty pattern over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$ and let $G$ be the good-suffix
table computed by the Boyer–Moore preprocessing of $p$. Then $1 \le G_0 \le m$,
$p_{t - G_0} = p_t$ for every $t < m$ with $G_0 \le t$, and $G_0 \le e$ for every positive
integer $e$ such that $p_{t - e} = p_t$ for every $t < m$ with $e \le t$. That is, $G_0$ is the
least positive period of $p$.

So after a full match the matcher may shift by $G_0$ without discarding overlapping
occurrences.

articles.title: Good-suffix table of Boyer–Moore preprocessing
articles.statement:
Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ be a
pattern over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, let $G$ be the good-suffix table computed
by the Boyer–Moore preprocessing of $p$, and let $i < m$. Call a positive integer $e$ an
admissible shift at $i$ if $p_{t - e} = p_t$ for every $t < m$ with $i < t$ and $e \le t$, and
$p_{i - e} \ne p_i$ whenever $e \le i$. Then $1 \le G_i \le m$ and $G_i$ is the least
admissible shift at $i$.

After a mismatch at position $i$, shifting by $G_i$ keeps the matched suffix
$p_{i+1} \cdots p_{m-1}$ aligned where it overlaps and, when $G_i \le i$, places the symbol
$p_{i - G_i} \ne p_i$ under the mismatched position.

articles.title: Cost of Boyer–Moore preprocessing
articles.statement:
For a pattern of length $m$ over an alphabet of size
$\sigma$, the event cost of the Boyer–Moore preprocessing is at most $\sigma$ when $m = 0$ and at
most $\sigma + 10m - 6$ when $m \ge 1$.

The cost counts the selected events of the preprocessor, including initialization of the
alphabet table; it is not a word-RAM or bit-cost bound.

articles.title: Boyer–Moore preprocessing
articles.statement:
Given a pattern $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, \sigma - 1\}$, this computes a bad-character table $B$ of length $\sigma$ and a
strong good-suffix table $G$ of length $m$. The table $B$ starts with every entry equal to $m$,
and then for $k = 0, 1, \dots, m - 2$ in turn the entry $B_{p_k}$ is set to $m - 1 - k$. For
$G$, let $s_i$ be the length of the longest common suffix of $p_0 \cdots p_i$ and $p$, computed
with the Z algorithm on the reversed pattern. The table $G$ starts with every entry equal to
$m$; then for $i = m - 1, \dots, 0$ in turn, if $s_i = i + 1$, every entry $G_j$ with
$j < m - 1 - i$ that still equals $m$ is set to $m - 1 - i$; finally, for
$i = 0, 1, \dots, m - 2$ in turn, the entry $G_{m - 1 - s_i}$ is set to $m - 1 - i$.

The event cost includes table slots, copies, fill iterations and canonical Z events;
it does not count machine instructions or unbounded-integer bit operations.

articles.title: Backward search returns a genuine row interval
articles.statement:
Backward search always returns a genuine interval of rows, `sp ≤ ep ≤ |L|`, on any list `L`
(so the difference in `backwardSearch_count` involves no truncated subtraction).

articles.title: Counting occurrences
articles.statement:
`ep - sp` is the number of positions `i ≤ |t|` at which `P`
occurs in `t`.

articles.title: Backward-search intervals are suffix-array intervals
articles.statement:
Row `r ≤ |t|` lies in the interval
`[sp, ep)` computed by backward search on `bwt t` exactly when `P` is a prefix of the suffix of
`t` at position `SA[r]`.

articles.title: Backward search is correct
articles.statement:
After processing `P`, the interval `[sp, ep)` is exactly the
set of rows whose rotation starts with `P`.

articles.title: FM-index backward search
articles.statement:
FM-index backward search: the half-open row interval `[sp, ep)` for a pattern, computed from
the last column alone, processing the pattern from its last letter to its first. The interval for
the suffix and `C[c]` are each computed once per letter, so a pattern of length `m` makes `m`
recursive calls.

articles.title: The transform from the suffix array
articles.statement:
`bwt[r] = t$[SA[r] - 1]`, the letter cyclically
before the suffix of row `r` (the sentinel for the row of the whole text, `SA[r] = 0`).

articles.title: Burrows–Wheeler transform
articles.statement: The Burrows–Wheeler transform: the last column of the sorted rotation matrix.

articles.title: Count of smaller letters in the FM-index
articles.statement: `C[c]`: the number of letters of `L` smaller than `c`.

articles.title: Steps of the Burrows–Wheeler inversion walk
articles.statement: `k` steps of the inversion walk from row `r`: the letters `L[r], L[LF r], …`.

articles.title: Inversion
articles.statement: The Burrows–Wheeler transform is inverted by the LF-mapping walk.

articles.title: Inversion of the Burrows–Wheeler transform
articles.statement:
Inversion of the Burrows–Wheeler transform: walk the LF-mapping `|L| - 1` times from row `0`
(the rotation that starts with the sentinel) and reverse the letters read.

articles.title: Length of the Burrows–Wheeler transform
articles.statement: The Burrows–Wheeler transform of `t` has length `|t| + 1` (the sentinel adds one letter).

articles.title: LF-mapping from the last column
articles.statement: The LF-mapping computed from the last column alone: `LF(r) = C[L[r]] + rank_{L[r]}(L, r)`.

articles.title: Step-bounded sampled-suffix-array locate
articles.statement:
`k` steps of sampled-suffix-array locate from row `r`: return the stored value of the first
sampled row reached along the LF-mapping, plus the number of LF steps taken. `sample r` is the
stored value `SA[r]` of row `r`, if any.

articles.title: Sampled-suffix-array locate is correct
articles.statement:
If every stored value is correct
(`sample r = some v → v = SA[r]` for rows `r ≤ |t|`) and every row of text position `0` is
sampled, then `locate` returns `SA[r]` for every row `r ≤ |t|`.

articles.title: Locate takes at most `s - 1` steps
articles.statement:
For `0 < s`, if every row whose text position is
a multiple of `s` is sampled, then from row `r ≤ |t|` locate makes at most `SA[r] mod s` LF
steps (for any amount of fuel `k`). At `s = 0` the `s - 1` bound would be `0` while the
proof only gives `SA[r] mod 0 = SA[r]` steps.

articles.title: Number of LF steps taken by sampled locate
articles.statement: The number of LF steps `locateAux L sample k r` takes.

articles.title: Sampled-suffix-array locate
articles.statement:
Sampled-suffix-array locate (Ferragina and Manzini 2000): the text position of row `r` from
the last column `L` and the samples, with at most `|L|` LF steps.

articles.title: The sentinel stops every prefix match
articles.statement:
A sentinel-free word `P` is a prefix of `u ++ ⊥ :: v` (letters lifted to `WithBot α`) exactly
when it is a prefix of `u`: the sentinel `⊥` stops every match.

articles.title: The reported positions are exactly the occurrences
articles.statement:
`i` is reported for `P` exactly when
`i ≤ |t|` and `P` is a prefix of `t.drop i` (the empty pattern occurs at all `|t| + 1`
positions).

articles.title: Number of FM-index occurrences equals the interval length
articles.statement: The number of reported positions is the length `ep - sp` of the backward-search interval.

articles.title: FM-index reports each occurrence once
articles.statement: Each occurrence is reported once.

articles.title: Occurrences of a pattern reported by the FM-index
articles.statement:
The occurrences of `P` reported by the FM-index: the suffix-array entries
`SA[sp], …, SA[ep - 1]` of the backward-search interval. The BWT and the interval are
bound once with `let` and reused, so one query builds the BWT and runs the backward search
once, not three times.

articles.title: Rows of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix are sorted
articles.statement:
The rows of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix are sorted: the rotations listed by
`sortedRotations t` are in lexicographically nondecreasing order.

articles.title: Rank of a letter in a prefix of the last column
articles.statement: `rank_c(L, r)`: the number of occurrences of `c` among the first `r` letters of `L`.

articles.title: Rotations of `t$` compare as suffixes
articles.statement:
For `i, j ≤ |t|`, rotation `i` of `withSentinel t`
is smaller than rotation `j` exactly when suffix `i` is smaller than suffix `j`.

articles.title: The Burrows–Wheeler matrix is the suffix array of `t$`
articles.statement:
Sorting the rotations of
`withSentinel t` orders the starting positions exactly as sorting its suffixes.

articles.title: The LF-mapping property
articles.statement:
For every row `r`, row `lf (bwt t) r` holds the rotation of
row `r` rotated right by one position, i.e. starting one position earlier in the text.

articles.title: Sorted rotations of a sentinel-terminated text
articles.statement:
The starting positions `0, …, |t|` of the rotations of `withSentinel t`, sorted by their
rotations in lexicographic order: row `r` of the Burrows–Wheeler matrix is
`(withSentinel t).rotate ((sortedRotations t)[r])`.

articles.title: The LF step moves one position left in the text
articles.statement:
`SA[r] = SA[LF r] + 1` when
`SA[r] > 0`.

articles.title: LF in suffix-array terms
articles.statement:
For a row `r ≤ |t|`, `LF r` is a row and
`SA[LF r] = SA[r] - 1` cyclically (`SA[LF r] = |t|` when `SA[r] = 0`).

articles.title: Text with an appended sentinel
articles.statement:
The text `t` with the sentinel `⊥` appended: `t.map (↑) ++ [⊥]`. The sentinel is the unique
occurrence of `⊥` and is smaller than every letter.

articles.title: Running an edit script
articles.statement:
Over a type $\alpha$ with a boolean equality test, running an
edit script on an input list processes the steps from left to right and either fails or
returns an output list. A keep step with value $a$ consumes the next input value $b$ and
outputs $a$; a deletion of $a$ consumes $b$ and outputs nothing; a substitution of $a$ by $c$
consumes $b$ and outputs $c$. Each of these three fails if the input is exhausted or if the
equality test of $a$ against $b$ fails. An insertion of $c$ outputs $c$ without consuming input.
When the script ends, the run succeeds with the outputs in order if the input is used up, and
fails if input values remain.

articles.title: Cost of an edit script
articles.statement:
The cost of an edit script is the sum of the unit costs of its
steps; the empty script has cost $0$.

articles.title: Unit cost of an edit step
articles.statement:
The cost of an edit step is $0$ for a keep step and $1$ for a
deletion, an insertion or a substitution.

articles.title: Table cost of the edit distance algorithm
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a
Boolean equality test, write $|s|$ and $|t|$ for their lengths. The number of table-cell
transitions charged by the dynamic-programming edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ is exactly
$(|s| + 1)(|t| + 1)$, one per pair of a prefix of $s$ and a prefix of $t$.

articles.title: Symmetry
articles.statement: **Symmetry** of unit-cost edit distance.

articles.title: Edit-distance cost counters
articles.statement:
An edit-distance cost record is a pair of natural numbers:
the number of dynamic-programming table cells initialized or transitioned, and the number of
operations emitted while reconstructing an edit script.

articles.title: Edit distance vanishes only on equal lists
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type whose
Boolean equality test agrees with equality, the distance returned by the dynamic-programming
edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ is $0$ if and only if $s = t$.

articles.title: Minimality of the computed edit distance
articles.statement:
Let $s$ and $t$ be lists over a type whose
Boolean equality test agrees with equality. Every edit script that transforms $s$ into $t$ has
unit cost at least the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$.

articles.title: Edit distance from the empty list
articles.statement:
For every list $t$ over a type with a Boolean equality
test, the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm from the empty list to $t$ is the
length of $t$.

articles.title: Edit distance to the empty list
articles.statement:
For every list $s$ over a type with a Boolean equality
test, the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm from $s$ to the empty list is the
length of $s$.

articles.title: Edit distance between distinct lists is positive
articles.statement: Distinct lists are at positive distance.

articles.title: Reconstruction cost bound for edit distance
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a
Boolean equality test, write $|s|$ and $|t|$ for their lengths. The number of reconstruction
steps charged by the edit distance algorithm on $s$ and $t$ is at most $|s| + |t|$.

articles.title: Reconstruction cost of the edit distance algorithm
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with
a Boolean equality test, the number of reconstruction steps charged by the edit distance
algorithm on $s$ and $t$ equals the length of the edit script it returns.

articles.title: Edit-distance result record
articles.statement:
An edit-distance result over a type $\alpha$ consists of a
natural number, the reported distance, and an edit script over $\alpha$.

The record imposes no relation between the two fields; it is meant to hold a minimum edit
distance and a script realizing it.

articles.title: Correctness of the returned edit script
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type whose Boolean
equality test agrees with equality, the edit script returned by the edit distance algorithm on
$s$ and $t$ transforms $s$ into $t$.

articles.title: The returned edit script realizes the distance
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a
Boolean equality test, the unit cost of the edit script returned by the edit distance algorithm
on $s$ and $t$ equals the distance it returns.

articles.title: Edit distance of a list to itself
articles.statement:
For every list $s$ over a type whose Boolean equality
test agrees with equality, the distance returned by the edit distance algorithm from $s$ to $s$
is $0$.

articles.title: Running time of the edit distance algorithm
articles.statement:
For lists $s$ and $t$ over a type with a
Boolean equality test, the total number of events charged by the edit distance algorithm on $s$
and $t$, that is its cell transitions plus its reconstruction steps, equals
$(|s| + 1)(|t| + 1) + k$, where $k$ is the length of the edit script it returns.

articles.title: The triangle inequality
articles.statement: **The triangle inequality** for unit-cost edit distance.

articles.title: Edit distance algorithm
articles.statement:
Given lists $s = s_1 \cdots s_m$ and $t = t_1 \cdots t_n$ over a
type with a Boolean equality test, the algorithm fills a table $D(i, j)$ for $0 \le i \le m$ and
$0 \le j \le n$ by $D(0, j) = j$, $D(i, 0) = i$ and
$D(i, j) = \min(D(i-1, j-1) + c_{ij}, D(i-1, j) + 1, D(i, j-1) + 1)$ for $i, j \ge 1$,
where $c_{ij}$ is $0$ if the test reports $s_i = t_j$ and $1$ otherwise. It then walks back
from $(m, n)$ to $(0, 0)$: on the boundary it deletes the remaining $s_i$ or inserts the
remaining $t_j$; otherwise it takes a move attaining the minimum, preferring the diagonal move
(a keep of $s_i$ if the test reports $s_i = t_j$, else a substitution of $t_j$ for $s_i$),
then a deletion of $s_i$, then an insertion of $t_j$. It returns the distance $D(m, n)$
together with the edit script of the chosen moves in left-to-right order. Each of the
$(m + 1)(n + 1)$ table entries is charged as one cell transition and each emitted operation
as one reconstruction step.

articles.title: Edit script
articles.statement:
An edit script over a type $\alpha$ is a finite list of edit steps over
$\alpha$, applied from left to right.

articles.title: Edit step
articles.statement:
An edit step over a type $\alpha$ is one of four operations, for
$a, b \in \alpha$: keep $a$ (consume the input value $a$ and reproduce it), delete $a$ (consume
$a$), insert $a$ (produce $a$ without consuming input), or substitute $a$ by $b$ (consume $a$
and produce $b$).

articles.title: Composition of edit scripts is subadditive in cost
articles.statement: Two scripts compose into one whose cost is at most the sum of their costs.

articles.title: Every edit script has an inverse of the same cost
articles.statement:
Every script has an inverse of the same cost (swap insertions and deletions, reverse
substitutions).

articles.title: Total edit-distance cost
articles.statement:
The total of an edit-distance cost record is the number of table
cells initialized or transitioned plus the number of operations emitted during reconstruction.

articles.title: An edit script transforming one list into another
articles.statement:
Over a type with a boolean equality
test, an edit script transforms a list $x$ into a list $y$ when running the script on $x$
succeeds and outputs $y$.

articles.title: KMP search agrees with the first-infix split
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $t$ be lists over a type
with a lawful boolean equality, with $p$ nonempty. Let the first-infix split of $t$ by $p$ be
the pair $(u, v)$ with $t = u \, p \, v$ (concatenation) and $u$ as short as possible, or
nothing if $p$ does not occur in $t$. Then the value returned by KMP search for $p$ in $t$ is
the length of $u$ if the split exists, and no offset otherwise.

articles.title: KMP finds no match exactly when the pattern does not occur
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ (the pattern)
and $t$ (the text) over a type with a lawful boolean equality, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ returns
no offset if and only if $p$ is not a contiguous sublist of $t$, that is, there are no lists
$u$, $v$ with $t = u \, p \, v$ (concatenation).

articles.title: KMP finds no match exactly when no offset matches
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ and $t$ over a type
with a lawful boolean equality, write $|t|$ for the length of $t$. KMP search for $p$ in $t$
returns no offset if and only if there is no natural number $i$ at which $p$ matches $t$, where
$p$ matches $t$ at $i$ when $i \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by
dropping its first $i$ elements.

articles.title: KMP returns the first match
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $t$ be lists over a type with a lawful boolean
equality, and write $|t|$ for the length of $t$. For every natural number $i$, KMP search for
$p$ in $t$ returns the offset $i$ if and only if $p$ matches $t$ at $i$ and at no $j < i$, where
$p$ matches $t$ at $i$ when $i \le |t|$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by
dropping its first $i$ elements.

articles.title: KMP search on the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every text $t$, KMP search for the empty pattern in
$t$ returns offset $0$ at cost $0$, that is, without any symbol comparisons.

articles.title: KMP search makes linearly many comparisons
articles.statement:
For any pattern $p$ and text $t$, lists over
a type with a boolean equality, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ makes at most $2|p| + 2|t|$ symbol
comparisons in total, those made while building the prefix table included, where $|p|$ and
$|t|$ are the lengths of $p$ and $t$.

articles.title: Knuth–Morris–Pratt search
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ (the pattern) and $t$ (the text) over a type
with a boolean equality, KMP search for $p$ in $t$ returns either a zero-based offset or no
offset, together with a cost: the number of symbol comparisons it makes. If $p$ is empty, it
returns the offset $0$ at cost $0$. Otherwise it first builds the prefix table of $p$, a list of
entries each pairing a symbol with a failure value. The transition of a table from a state $s$
on a symbol $x$ is defined as follows. If $s$ is less than the number of entries and $x$ equals the
symbol of entry $s$ (counting from $0$), the result is $s + 1$. Otherwise the result is $0$ when
$s = 0$, and when $s > 0$ it is the transition from the failure value of entry $s - 1$ on $x$.
Starting from the empty table, each symbol $x$ of $p$ in turn is appended as a new entry, with
failure value the transition of the current table on $x$ from the state equal to its number of
entries. The search then reads $t$ from the left, starting in state $0$ and moving to the
transition of the table on each symbol read. The first time the state equals $|p|$, after $j$
symbols have been read, it returns the offset $j - |p|$. If this never happens, it returns no
offset. The cost counts every equality test between two symbols, both while the table is built
and while $t$ is scanned. List operations, array access and arithmetic cost nothing.

When the boolean equality is lawful, the returned offset is the least offset at which $p$ occurs
in $t$, and no offset is returned exactly when $p$ does not occur in $t$.

articles.title: The KMP failure function
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a pattern of length $n$ over a type with a lawful
boolean equality, and write $p_{\lt k}$ for its prefix of length $k$. Each entry of the KMP prefix
table of $p$ pairs a symbol of $p$ with a failure value. For every $q < n$, the failure value
$f$ of entry $q$ (counting from $0$) is the length of the longest proper prefix of $p_{\lt q+1}$
that is also a suffix of $p_{\lt q+1}$: $f \le q$, $p_{\lt f}$ is a suffix of $p_{\lt q+1}$, and every
$k \le q$ such that $p_{\lt k}$ is a suffix of $p_{\lt q+1}$ satisfies $k \le f$.

articles.title: Size of the KMP prefix table
articles.statement:
For every pattern $p$, the KMP prefix table of $p$ has
exactly as many entries as $p$ has symbols, one for each symbol of $p$.

articles.title: Correctness of the KMP transition
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a pattern of length $n$ over a type with
a lawful boolean equality, and write $p_{\lt k}$ for its prefix of length $k$. Let $c$ be a list,
$x$ a symbol, and $cx$ the list $c$ followed by $x$. Suppose the state $s \le n$ is the length
of the longest prefix of $p$ that is a suffix of $c$: $p_{\lt s}$ is a suffix of $c$, and every
$k \le n$ such that $p_{\lt k}$ is a suffix of $c$ satisfies $k \le s$. Then the state $s'$ that
the transition of the KMP prefix table of $p$ produces from $s$ on reading $x$ is the length of
the longest prefix of $p$ that is a suffix of $cx$: $s' \le n$, $p_{\lt s'}$ is a suffix of $cx$,
and every $k \le n$ such that $p_{\lt k}$ is a suffix of $cx$ satisfies $k \le s'$.

articles.title: The KMP prefix table stores the pattern
articles.statement:
Each entry of the Knuth–Morris–Pratt prefix
table is a pair consisting of a symbol and a failure length. For every type with a Boolean
equality test and every list $p$ over it, the list of first components of the entries of the
prefix table built from $p$, read in order, equals $p$.

articles.title: Correctness of naive string matching
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type whose Boolean equality
agrees with equality, and write $|t|$ for the length of a list $t$. For every pattern $p$ and
text $t$ over $\alpha$ and every natural number $s$, the naive matcher run on $p$ and $t$
reports the shift $s$ if and only if $p$ matches $t$ at $s$, that is, $s \le |t|$ and $p$ is a
prefix of the suffix of $t$ obtained by dropping its first $s$ symbols.

In particular, the empty pattern is reported at every shift $s \le |t|$.

articles.title: Naive matching with the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every text $t$ of length $n$, the naive
matcher run on the empty pattern and $t$ reports exactly the shifts $0, 1, \dots, n$ in
increasing order and performs no symbol comparisons.

articles.title: Naive matching with a pattern longer than the text
articles.statement:
If the pattern $p$ is longer than
the text $t$, then the naive matcher run on $p$ and $t$ reports no shifts and performs no symbol
comparisons.

articles.title: Naive matching reports shifts in increasing order
articles.statement:
For every pattern $p$ and text $t$,
the list of shifts reported by the naive matcher on $p$ and $t$ is strictly increasing; in
particular, no shift is reported twice.

articles.title: Naive matching on a repeated symbol reports every shift
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type whose
Boolean equality is reflexive, let $x \in \alpha$, and let $m \le n$ be natural numbers. On the
pattern consisting of $m$ copies of $x$ and the text consisting of $n$ copies of $x$, the naive
matcher reports exactly the shifts $0, 1, \dots, n - m$ in increasing order, so all overlapping
occurrences are reported.

articles.title: Output of naive matching
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a pattern of length $m$ and $t$ a text of length
$n$. If $m \le n$, the list of shifts reported by the naive matcher on $p$ and $t$ is the
increasing list of all $s \in \{0, \dots, n - m\}$ such that $p$ is a prefix of the suffix of
$t$ starting at the zero-based position $s$, with symbols compared by the Boolean equality of the
alphabet. If $m > n$, the list is empty.

articles.title: Exact comparison count of naive matching
articles.statement:
Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ be a pattern and
$t = t_0 \cdots t_{n-1}$ a text. If $m \le n$, the number of symbol comparisons performed by the
naive matcher on $p$ and $t$ is

$$\sum_{s=0}^{n-m} \min(m, k_s + 1),$$

where $k_s$ is the least $i < m$ such that $p_i$ and $t_{s+i}$ are unequal under the Boolean
equality of the alphabet, and $k_s = m$ if there is no such $i$. If $m > n$, the naive matcher
performs no comparisons.

articles.title: Upper bound on the comparisons of naive matching
articles.statement:
For a pattern of length $m$ and a text
of length $n$, the naive matcher performs at most $(n - m + 1) \cdot m$ symbol comparisons if
$m \le n$, and no comparisons if $m > n$.

articles.title: Comparison count of naive matching on a repeated symbol
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type whose
Boolean equality is reflexive, let $x \in \alpha$, and let $m \le n$ be natural numbers. On the
pattern consisting of $m$ copies of $x$ and the text consisting of $n$ copies of $x$, the naive
matcher performs exactly $(n - m + 1) \cdot m$ symbol comparisons.

articles.title: Naive string matcher
articles.statement:
Let $p = p_0 \cdots p_{m-1}$ be a pattern and
$t = t_0 \cdots t_{n-1}$ a text over an alphabet with a Boolean equality test. If $m \le n$, the
naive matcher handles the shifts $s = 0, 1, \dots, n - m$ in turn: it compares $p_i$ with
$t_{s+i}$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots$ until a comparison fails or all $m$ symbols are compared, and it
reports $s$ if no comparison failed. It returns the reported shifts in the order found, with cost
the total number of symbol comparisons executed, failed comparisons included. If $m > n$, it
reports no shift at cost $0$.

articles.title: Correctness of Rabin–Karp matching
articles.statement:
For every base $d$, every modulus $q > 0$, all
lists of natural numbers $P$ (the pattern) and $T$ (the text) and every natural number $s$,
Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$ with base $d$ and modulus $q$ reports the offset $s$ if and
only if $P$ matches $T$ at $s$, that is, $s \le |T|$ and $P$ is a prefix of the suffix of $T$
that starts at position $s$ (counting from $0$).

articles.title: Matching cost of Rabin–Karp on repeated-symbol words
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a base, $q > 0$ a
modulus, $a$ a natural number and $m$, $n$ natural numbers with $0 < m \le n$. Let $C$ be the
counted cost of Rabin–Karp matching with base $d$ and modulus $q$ of the pattern $a^m$ in the
text $a^n$ (the lists of $m$ and of $n$ copies of $a$), minus $8m - 1$, with subtraction
truncated at $0$. Then $m(n - m + 1) \le C \le 10\,m(n - m + 1)$.

The subtracted $8m - 1$ is the preprocessing cost, so the bounds do not depend on it.

articles.title: Rabin–Karp matching with the empty pattern
articles.statement:
For every base $d$, modulus $q > 0$ and
list of natural numbers $T$, Rabin–Karp matching of the empty pattern in $T$ returns the list
$[0, 1, \dots, |T|]$ of all offsets from $0$ to $|T|$ in increasing order, at counted cost $0$.

articles.title: Rabin–Karp matching with a pattern longer than the text
articles.statement:
For every base $d$, modulus
$q > 0$ and lists of natural numbers $P$ and $T$ with $|T| < |P|$, Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in
$T$ returns no offsets, at counted cost exactly $1 + 2(|P| - 1) + 6|T|$.

This cost is the work of computing the high-place power and the Horner setup steps attempted
before the text runs out.

articles.title: Rabin–Karp reports offsets in increasing order
articles.statement:
For every base $d$, modulus $q > 0$ and
lists of natural numbers $P$ and $T$, the offsets returned by Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$
form a strictly increasing list; in particular no offset is reported twice.

articles.title: Rabin–Karp and naive matching return the same offsets
articles.statement:
For every base $d$, modulus
$q > 0$ and lists of natural numbers $P$ and $T$, the list of offsets returned by Rabin–Karp
matching of $P$ in $T$ with base $d$ and modulus $q$ equals the list returned by naive matching
of $P$ in $T$.

articles.title: Rabin–Karp offsets on repeated-symbol words
articles.statement:
For every base $d$, modulus $q > 0$, symbol
$a \in \mathbb{N}$ and natural numbers $m \le n$, Rabin–Karp matching of the pattern $a^m$ in the
text $a^n$ (the lists of $m$ and of $n$ copies of $a$) returns $[0, 1, \dots, n - m]$, that is,
every shift in increasing order, including overlapping ones.

articles.title: Exact cost of Rabin–Karp matching
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a base, $q > 0$ a modulus and $P$, $T$
lists of natural numbers with $0 < m \le |T|$, where $m = |P|$, and put $r = |T| - m$. Index
lists from $0$, write $T_{s..}$ for the suffix of $T$ starting at position $s$, and for a list
$S$ with at least $m$ entries put $h(S) = \bigl(\sum_{i\lt m} S_i\, d^{m-1-i}\bigr) \bmod q$. Let
$B$ be the number of offsets $s < r$ with $h(T_{s..}) < (T_s \cdot (d^{m-1} \bmod q)) \bmod q$.
For $s \le r$ let $c_s = m$ if $P$ is a prefix of $T_{s..}$, and otherwise $c_s = j + 1$ for the
least $j$ with $P_j \ne T_{s+j}$. Then Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$ with base $d$ and
modulus $q$ has counted cost exactly

$$(8m - 1) + (r + 1) + 7r + B + \sum_{s \le r,\ h(P) = h(T_{s..})} c_s.$$

The terms count the setup, one hash comparison per alignment, the rolling hash updates, one
extra addition per borrow, and the symbol comparisons that verify hash hits.

articles.title: Cost bound for Rabin–Karp matching
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a base, $q > 0$ a modulus and $P$, $T$
lists of natural numbers with $0 < m \le |T|$, where $m = |P|$, and put $r = |T| - m$. Index
lists from $0$, write $T_{s..}$ for the suffix of $T$ starting at position $s$, and for a list
$S$ with at least $m$ entries put $h(S) = \bigl(\sum_{i\lt m} S_i\, d^{m-1-i}\bigr) \bmod q$. Let
$H$ be the number of hash hits, the offsets $s \le r$ with $h(P) = h(T_{s..})$. Then
Rabin–Karp matching of $P$ in $T$ with base $d$ and modulus $q$ has counted cost at most
$(8m - 1) + (9(r + 1) - 8) + mH$.

articles.title: Exact cost of Rabin–Karp matching on repeated-symbol words
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a base, $q > 0$ a
modulus, $a$ a natural number and $m$, $n$ natural numbers with $0 < m \le n$. Put
$t = \bigl(a \sum_{i\lt m} d^i\bigr) \bmod q$, and let $\beta = 1$ if
$t < (a \cdot (d^{m-1} \bmod q)) \bmod q$ and $\beta = 0$ otherwise. Then Rabin–Karp matching
with base $d$ and modulus $q$ of the pattern $a^m$ in the text $a^n$ (the lists of $m$ and of
$n$ copies of $a$) has counted cost exactly

$$(8m - 1) + (n - m + 1) + 7(n - m) + (n - m)\beta + m(n - m + 1).$$

The last term is $m$ symbol comparisons at each of the $n - m + 1$ alignments.

articles.title: Rabin–Karp string matching
articles.statement:
Given a base $d$, a modulus $q > 0$, a pattern
$P = p_0 \dots p_{m-1}$ and a text $T = t_0 \dots t_{n-1}$, both lists of natural numbers, this
returns the list, in increasing order, of all shifts $s$ with $s + m \le n$ and $t_{s+k} = p_k$
for every $k < m$. For $m \ge 1$ it computes by Horner's rule the residues modulo $q$ of $P$ and
of the first length-$m$ window of $T$, read as base-$d$ numerals, and updates the window residue
by a rolling hash; symbols are compared at a shift only when the two residues agree, from left to
right. If $m > n$ it returns the empty list. The empty pattern returns every shift
$0, 1, \dots, n$ at cost $0$.

The cost counts each executed multiplication, addition, subtraction and modulus in computing
the residues and $d^{m-1} \bmod q$, and each borrow test, residue equality test and symbol
equality test; shift-offset arithmetic and all other operations are free.

articles.title: A pattern occurs in a text iff it matches at some offset
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ and $t$, there
is an offset $k$ such that the pattern $p$ matches the text $t$ at $k$ if and only if $p$ is an
infix of $t$, that is, $t$ is the concatenation of some list $u$, then $p$, then some list $v$.

articles.title: Characterization of a match at an offset
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ and $t$ and a natural number $k$,
the pattern $p$ matches the text $t$ at the zero-based offset $k$ if and only if $k$ is at most
the length of $t$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by dropping its first $k$
entries.

articles.title: Pattern match at an offset
articles.statement:
For lists $p$ (the pattern) and $t$ (the text) over a type
$\alpha$ and a natural number $k$, the pattern $p$ matches the text $t$ at the zero-based offset
$k$ when $k$ is at most the length of $t$ and $p$ is a prefix of the list obtained from $t$ by
dropping its first $k$ entries.

The explicit bound on $k$ excludes offsets beyond the end of the text for an empty pattern.

articles.title: Correctness of the string-matching transition table
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$
over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. For every
state $q \le m$ and symbol $a < A$, the entry at index $qA + a$ of the transition table of $P$
is the greatest $k \le m$ such that $P_k$ is a suffix of the word $P_q a$.

articles.title: Cost bound for the string-matching transition table
articles.statement:
For every pattern of length $m$
over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the cost of computing its transition table is at most
$2A(m+1)^3$.

The cost counts executed candidates, symbol comparisons, failed decrements and table writes.

articles.title: Transition table of the string-matching automaton
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$
over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$. This timed
computation returns a table of $(m+1)A$ entries in $\{0, \dots, m\}$, stored row by row: for
each state $q \le m$ and symbol $a < A$, the entry at index $qA + a$ is found by trying
$k = \min(m, q+1)$ and then each smaller value in turn, and is the first $k$ for which $P_k$ is
a suffix of the word $P_q a$ (the candidate $k = 0$ is always accepted). The cost counts
one unit for each candidate $k$ tried, one for each symbol comparison executed when comparing
$P_k$ with the last $k$ symbols of $P_q a$ (left to right, stopping at the first mismatch), one
for each move to a smaller candidate, and one for each table entry written.

## Sources

- CLRS fourth edition section 32.3, decreasing-candidate row-major construction.

articles.title: Correctness of the finite-automaton matcher
articles.statement:
For every pattern $P$ and text $T$ over the
alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the list of shifts returned by the finite-automaton matcher equals
the list returned by the naive string matcher.

So it is the complete increasing list of zero-based shifts at which $P$ occurs in $T$, including
overlapping occurrences and, for the empty pattern, every boundary.

articles.title: Exact cost of the finite-automaton matcher
articles.statement:
For every pattern $P$ and text $T$ over the
alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, where $T$ has length $n$, the cost of the finite-automaton matcher
on $P$ and $T$ equals the cost of computing the transition table of $P$, plus $2n$, plus the
number of shifts the matcher returns.

articles.title: Finite-automaton string matcher
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a pattern of length $m$ and $T$ a text over
the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$. This timed computation first computes the transition table of
$P$, then runs through $T$ starting in state $0$: on reading the $i$-th symbol $a$ of $T$ in
state $q$ it moves to the state given by the table entry at index $qA + a$, and if that state is
$m$ it reports the shift $i - m$. If $m = 0$, the shift $0$ is also reported before the scan.
It returns the reported shifts in the order found. The cost is that of computing the table,
plus two units for each symbol of $T$ (a table lookup and an acceptance test), plus one unit for
each reported shift.

The table is computed once, before the single pass over the text, and the scan does not reset
after a match, so overlapping occurrences are reported.

articles.title: The string-matching automaton tracks the longest matched prefix
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a pattern of
length $m$ over the alphabet $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$ and write $P_k$ for its prefix of length $k$.
For every word $w$ over this alphabet, the state that the string-matching automaton of $P$
reaches from its start state after reading $w$ is the greatest $k \le m$ such that $P_k$ is a
suffix of $w$.

articles.title: String-matching automaton
articles.statement:
