For a pattern $P$ of length $m$ over the alphabet
$\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, the string-matching automaton of $P$ is the deterministic finite automaton
with states $\{0, \dots, m\}$, input symbols $\{0, \dots, A-1\}$, start state $0$, accepting set
$\{m\}$, and transition from state $q$ on symbol $a$ given by the entry at index $qA + a$ of the
transition table of $P$.

articles.title: Z-values are at most the suffix length
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality
test, not necessarily lawful, and let $s$ be a word of length $n$ over $\alpha$. For every position
$i < n$, the entry at $i$ of the Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on $s$ is at most $n - i$.

articles.title: Z-values are longest common prefix lengths
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean
equality test, let $s = s_0 \dots s_{n-1}$ be a word over $\alpha$, and let $Z$ be the Z-array
computed by the Z-algorithm on $s$. For every position $i < n$ and every natural number $q$,
$q \le Z_i$ holds if and only if $q \le n - i$ and $s_k = s_{i+k}$ for all $k < q$. Hence $Z_i$ is
the length of the longest common prefix of $s$ and its suffix $s_i \dots s_{n-1}$.

articles.title: Z-algorithm cost on a repeated symbol followed by a distinct one
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type
with a lawful Boolean equality test and let $a \ne b$ be elements of $\alpha$. For every $n \ge 1$,
the Z-algorithm run on the word $a^n b$ has cost exactly $3n - 1$, where the cost counts one unit
for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison. In terms of the
input length $N = n + 1$, this is $3N - 4$.

articles.title: Z-algorithm cost on a repeated symbol
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean
equality test, let $a \in \alpha$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The Z-algorithm run on the word $a^n$ has
cost exactly $2(n - 1)$, read as $0$ when $n = 0$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited
position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison. Thus it makes $n - 1$ visits and
$n - 1$ comparisons.

articles.title: Z-array of a repeated symbol
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a lawful Boolean equality
test, let $a \in \alpha$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The Z-array computed by the Z-algorithm on the word
$a^n$ has entry $n - i$ at every position $i < n$.

articles.title: Linear lower bound for the Z-algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality
test, not necessarily lawful. On every word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-algorithm has cost
at least $n - 1$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit
for each symbol comparison.

articles.title: Linear upper bound for the Z-algorithm
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality
test, not necessarily lawful. On every word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-algorithm has cost
at most $3(n - 1)$, read as $0$ when $n = 0$, where the cost counts one unit for each visited
position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison.

articles.title: The first Z-value is the word length
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a Boolean equality
test. For every nonempty word of length $n$ over $\alpha$, the Z-array $Z$ computed by the
Z-algorithm has $Z_0 = n$.

Gusfield leaves this entry undefined; this convention completes it.

articles.title: Z-algorithm
articles.statement:
Given a word $s = s_0 \dots s_{n-1}$ over a type $\alpha$ with a Boolean
equality test, Gusfield's Z-box algorithm returns an array $Z$ of $n$ natural numbers with
$Z_0 = n$. It visits $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$ in turn, keeping a box $[\ell, r)$, initially empty,
that is the rightmost match of a prefix of $s$ found so far. If $\ell \le i < r$ and
$Z_{i - \ell} < r - i$, it sets $Z_i = Z_{i - \ell}$. Otherwise it finds $Z_i$ by comparing
symbols directly, starting at offset $r - i$ if $i < r$ and at offset $0$ if not, and if
$Z_i > 0$ the box becomes $[i, i + Z_i)$. When the equality test is lawful, $Z_i$ is the length
of the longest common prefix of $s$ and its suffix $s_i \dots s_{n-1}$. The cost counts one unit
for each visited position $i \ge 1$ and one unit for each symbol comparison; on the empty word the
result is empty with cost $0$.

articles.title: Sort axioms of CCω
articles.statement:
The axioms say which sort has which sort as its type: $\mathrm{Prop}$
has type $\mathrm{Type}_0$, and $\mathrm{Type}_i$ has type $\mathrm{Type}_{i+1}$ for every natural
number $i$. No other pair of sorts is related.

articles.title: Consistency of CCω
articles.statement:
No closed term has type $\Pi (P : \mathrm{Prop}).\, P$: there is no term
$t$ with $\vdash t : \Pi (P : \mathrm{Prop}).\, P$ in the empty context.

## Sources

- Coquand and Huet, 'The calculus of constructions' (1988); Zhaohui Luo, 'An Extended Calculus of Constructions' (1990); Bruno Barras, 'Sets in Coq, Coq in Sets' (2010). Problem `coc_strong_normalization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Beta conversion
articles.statement:
Beta conversion is the equivalence closure of one-step beta reduction:
every term is convertible to itself, and if $t$ is convertible to $u$ and $u$ reduces to $v$ in
one step, or $v$ reduces to $u$ in one step, then $t$ is convertible to $v$.

articles.title: Shifting de Bruijn indices
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $d$ and $c$, shifting a term $t$ by $d$
above the cutoff $c$ adds $d$ to every variable index $i \ge c$ and leaves every index $i < c$
unchanged. The cutoff goes up by one under each binder, that is, in the body of a $\lambda$ and
in the codomain of a $\Pi$ (not in the type annotation or the domain), and sorts are unchanged.
Thus the free variables of $t$ with index at least $c$ are increased by $d$.

articles.title: Product rules of CCω
articles.statement:
The product rules say in which sort $s_3$ a dependent product
$\Pi (x : A).\, B$ lives when $A$ lives in the sort $s_1$ and $B$ lives in the sort $s_2$. There
are exactly three rules: for every sort $s$, a product with domain in $s$ and codomain in
$\mathrm{Prop}$ lives in $\mathrm{Prop}$ (the impredicativity of $\mathrm{Prop}$); for all natural
numbers $i$ and $j$, a product with domain in $\mathrm{Type}_i$ and codomain in $\mathrm{Type}_j$
lives in $\mathrm{Type}_{\max(i, j)}$; and for every natural number $i$, a product with domain in
$\mathrm{Prop}$ and codomain in $\mathrm{Type}_i$ lives in $\mathrm{Type}_i$.

articles.title: Strongly normalizing terms
articles.statement:
The strongly normalizing terms are defined inductively: a term
$t$ is strongly normalizing when every term to which $t$ reduces in one beta step is strongly
normalizing. Equivalently, classically, there is no infinite chain of one-step beta reductions
starting from $t$.

articles.title: Sorts of CCω
articles.statement:
The sorts are $\mathrm{Prop}$ and $\mathrm{Type}_i$ for every natural number
$i$. In the calculus, $\mathrm{Prop}$ is impredicative and the $\mathrm{Type}_i$ form a
predicative hierarchy.

articles.title: Beta step of the applied polymorphic identity
articles.statement:
The polymorphic identity
$\lambda (A : \mathrm{Prop}).\, \lambda (x : A).\, x$ applied to
$\bot = \Pi (P : \mathrm{Prop}).\, P$ reduces in one beta step to $\lambda (x : \bot).\, x$.

This is an anti-vacuity guard: it pins down beta reduction and substitution.

## Sources

- Coquand and Huet, 'The calculus of constructions' (1988); Zhaohui Luo, 'An Extended Calculus of Constructions' (1990); Bruno Barras, 'Sets in Coq, Coq in Sets' (2010). Problem `coc_strong_normalization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: One-step beta reduction
articles.statement:
One-step beta reduction is the smallest relation on terms that
contains every beta step $(\lambda (x : A).\, b)\, a \to b[a/x]$, where $b[a/x]$ substitutes $a$
for the bound variable $x$ in $b$, and that is closed under every term former: a step inside the
function or the argument of an application, inside the type annotation or the body of a
$\lambda$, or inside the domain or the codomain of a $\Pi$ is a step of the whole term.

articles.title: Strong normalization of CCω
articles.statement:
Every well-typed term is strongly normalizing: if
$\Gamma \vdash t : A$ for some context $\Gamma$ and some term $A$, then $t$ is strongly
normalizing.

## Sources

- Coquand and Huet, 'The calculus of constructions' (1988); Zhaohui Luo, 'An Extended Calculus of Constructions' (1990); Bruno Barras, 'Sets in Coq, Coq in Sets' (2010). Problem `coc_strong_normalization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Subject reduction
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a context and $t$, $t'$, $A$ terms of the calculus
of constructions with universes. If $t$ has type $A$ in $\Gamma$, that is
$\Gamma \vdash t : A$, and $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one step of beta reduction (anywhere
inside $t$), then $\Gamma \vdash t' : A$.

## Sources

- Coquand and Huet, 'The calculus of constructions' (1988); Zhaohui Luo, 'An Extended Calculus of Constructions' (1990); Bruno Barras, 'Sets in Coq, Coq in Sets' (2010). Problem `coc_strong_normalization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Substitution for a de Bruijn variable
articles.statement:
For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and terms $u$ and $t$, the
term $t[k := u]$ is defined by recursion on $t$. For a variable, $\#i[k := u]$ is $\#i$ if
$i < k$, is $u$ with every free variable raised by $k$ if $i = k$, and is $\#(i - 1)$ if
$i > k$. A sort is unchanged, $(f\,a)[k := u] = f[k := u]\,a[k := u]$,
$(\lambda (x : A).\, b)[k := u] = \lambda (x : A[k := u]).\, b[k + 1 := u]$, and
$(\Pi (x : A).\, B)[k := u] = \Pi (x : A[k := u]).\, B[k + 1 := u]$.

articles.title: Terms of the calculus of constructions
articles.statement:
A term is a variable $\#i$ with de Bruijn index
$i \in \mathbb{N}$, a sort $s$ (either $\mathrm{Prop}$ or $\mathrm{Type}_i$ for some
$i \in \mathbb{N}$), an application $f\,a$ of a term $f$ to a term $a$, an abstraction
$\lambda (x : A).\, b$ with domain $A$ and body $b$, or a dependent product
$\Pi (x : A).\, B$ with domain $A$ and codomain $B$.

In the body of an abstraction or the codomain of a product, index $0$ refers to the bound
variable and index $i + 1$ to the variable that has index $i$ outside the binder.

articles.title: Typing the polymorphic identity applied to falsity
articles.statement:
Write $\bot$ for
$\Pi (P : \mathrm{Prop}).\, P$. In the empty context, the application of the polymorphic
identity $\lambda (A : \mathrm{Prop}).\, \lambda (x : A).\, x$ to $\bot$ has type
$\Pi (x : \bot).\, \bot$.

## Sources

- Coquand and Huet, 'The calculus of constructions' (1988); Zhaohui Luo, 'An Extended Calculus of Constructions' (1990); Bruno Barras, 'Sets in Coq, Coq in Sets' (2010). Problem `coc_strong_normalization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Typing the polymorphic identity
articles.statement:
In the empty context, the polymorphic identity
$\lambda (A : \mathrm{Prop}).\, \lambda (x : A).\, x$ has type
$\Pi (A : \mathrm{Prop}).\, \Pi (x : A).\, A$.

This is typable only because $\mathrm{Prop}$ is impredicative: a product over
$A : \mathrm{Prop}$ whose codomain is a proposition is again a proposition.

## Sources

- Coquand and Huet, 'The calculus of constructions' (1988); Zhaohui Luo, 'An Extended Calculus of Constructions' (1990); Bruno Barras, 'Sets in Coq, Coq in Sets' (2010). Problem `coc_strong_normalization` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Typing judgement of the calculus of constructions with universes
articles.statement:
A context $\Gamma$ is a
list of terms whose head is the type of the most recent variable; write $\Gamma, A$ for
$\Gamma$ extended by $A$ at the head. The judgement $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ ($t$ has type $A$
in $\Gamma$) is defined together with well-formedness of contexts as the least relation
closed under the following rules.

* Sorts: if $\Gamma$ is well formed and $s : s'$ is an axiom, namely
  $\mathrm{Prop} : \mathrm{Type}_0$ or $\mathrm{Type}_i : \mathrm{Type}_{i+1}$, then
  $\Gamma \vdash s : s'$.
* Variables: if $\Gamma$ is well formed and its entry at position $i$ (counting from $0$ at
  the head) is $A$, then $\Gamma \vdash \#i : A'$, where $A'$ is $A$ with every free variable
  raised by $i + 1$.
* Products: if $\Gamma \vdash A : s_1$, $\Gamma, A \vdash B : s_2$ and $(s_1, s_2, s_3)$ is a
  product rule, namely $(s, \mathrm{Prop}, \mathrm{Prop})$ for a sort $s$,
  $(\mathrm{Type}_i, \mathrm{Type}_j, \mathrm{Type}_{\max(i, j)})$ or
  $(\mathrm{Prop}, \mathrm{Type}_i, \mathrm{Type}_i)$, then
  $\Gamma \vdash \Pi (x : A).\, B : s_3$.
* Abstractions: if $\Gamma \vdash \Pi (x : A).\, B : s$ for some sort $s$ and
  $\Gamma, A \vdash b : B$, then $\Gamma \vdash \lambda (x : A).\, b : \Pi (x : A).\, B$.
* Applications: if $\Gamma \vdash f : \Pi (x : A).\, B$ and $\Gamma \vdash a : A$, then
  $\Gamma \vdash f\,a : B[a]$, where $B[a]$ replaces variable $0$ of $B$ by $a$ and lowers
  the other free variables of $B$ by one.
* Conversion: if $\Gamma \vdash t : A$, $\Gamma \vdash B : s$ for some sort $s$, and $A$ and
  $B$ are beta convertible, then $\Gamma \vdash t : B$.

articles.title: Well-formed contexts
articles.statement:
A context is a list of terms whose head is the most recent binding.
Well-formedness of contexts is defined together with the typing judgement
$\Gamma \vdash t : A$ as the least predicate such that the empty context is well formed, and
if $\Gamma$ is well formed and $\Gamma \vdash A : s$ for some sort $s$, then the context
obtained from $\Gamma$ by adding $A$ at the head is well formed.

articles.title: Semantic equality is a congruence for application
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base
types. If terms $f$ and $g$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in a context $\Gamma$ are semantically
equal in $I$ (they have the same denotation in every environment), and terms $a$ and $b$ of type
$A$ in $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$, then the applications $f\,a$ and $g\,b$ are
semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Beta is sound for the denotational semantics
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, every term $t$ of type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type
$A$, and every term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the redex $(\lambda.\,t)\,a$ is semantically
equal in $I$ (has the same denotation in every environment) to the instantiation $t[a]$, which
replaces the newest free variable of $t$ by $a$.

The argument $a$ need not be a value.

articles.title: Model-independent beta equality
articles.statement:
For every term $b$ of type $B$ in the variable
context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$, and every term $a$ of type $A$ in
$\Gamma$, the application $(\lambda.\,b)\,a$ is model-equal to $b[a]$, the result of
substituting $a$ for the newest variable of $b$.

articles.title: Associativity of composition of STLC contexts
articles.statement:
Let $E_1$ be a typed one-hole context
whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in
context $\Delta$, $E_2$ one with hole of type $B$ in $\Delta$ producing type $C$ in $\Theta$,
and $E_3$ one with hole of type $C$ in $\Theta$ producing type $D$ in $\Xi$. Then
$(E_3 \circ E_2) \circ E_1 = E_3 \circ (E_2 \circ E_1)$.

articles.title: Composition of STLC contexts
articles.statement:
Let $E_2$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole has
type $B$ in variable context $\Delta$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in context
$\Theta$, and let $E_1$ be one whose hole has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and which produces
a term of type $B$ in $\Delta$. The composite $E_2 \circ E_1$, with hole of type $A$ in
$\Gamma$ and result of type $C$ in $\Theta$, replaces the hole of $E_2$ by $E_1$; by
recursion on $E_2$: $[\,] \circ E_1 = E_1$, $(E_2\,a) \circ E_1 = (E_2 \circ E_1)\,a$,
$(f\,E_2) \circ E_1 = f\,(E_2 \circ E_1)$ and
$(\lambda.\,E_2) \circ E_1 = \lambda.\,(E_2 \circ E_1)$, where $[\,]$ is the bare hole and
$E\,a$, $f\,E$, $\lambda.\,E$ apply a context $E$ to a term $a$, apply a term $f$ to $E$, and
put $E$ under a lambda.

articles.title: Extending a semantic environment in STLC
articles.statement:
Given an interpretation $I$ of the base types, a
value $a$ in the denotation of a type $A$ and an environment $\eta$ for a context $\Gamma$, the
extended environment for the context $A :: \Gamma$ sends the newest variable to $a$ and the
successor $\mathrm{succ}\,x$ of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(x)$.

articles.title: Beta equality inside an STLC context
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole
has type $B$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in context
$\Delta$. For every term $b$ of type $B$ in $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type
$A$, and every term $a$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the term $E[(\lambda.\,b)\,a]$ is
model-equal to $E[b[a]]$, where $b[a]$ is the result of substituting $a$ for the newest
variable of $b$.

articles.title: Eta equality inside an STLC context
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole
has type $A \Rightarrow B$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $C$
in context $\Delta$. For every term $f$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in $\Gamma$, the term
$E[\lambda.\,(f^{\uparrow}\,x_0)]$ is model-equal to $E[f]$, where $f^{\uparrow}$ is $f$
weakened by a newest variable of type $A$ and $x_0$ is that variable.

articles.title: Model equality is a congruence for STLC contexts
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context
whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in
context $\Delta$. If two terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$ are model-equal, then
$E[t]$ and $E[u]$ are model-equal.

articles.title: Denotation of an STLC term
articles.statement:
Given an interpretation $I$ of the base types, the denotation of
a well-typed term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ in an environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ is the
element of the denotation of $A$ defined by recursion on $t$: a variable $x$ denotes $\eta(x)$, an
application $f\,a$ denotes the denotation of $f$ applied to the denotation of $a$ (both in
$\eta$), and an abstraction $\lambda.\,b$ denotes the function sending each value $a$ of
its argument type to the denotation of the body $b$ in $\eta$ extended by $a$ for the newest
variable.

articles.title: Multi-step reduction preserves STLC denotation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, if a term $t$ reduces to $t'$ in zero or more steps of call-by-value reduction, then $t$
and $t'$ have the same denotation in every environment $\eta$ for their context.

articles.title: Big-step evaluation preserves STLC denotation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, if a term $t$ evaluates to $v$ under call-by-value big-step evaluation, then $t$ and $v$
have the same denotation in every environment $\eta$ for their context.

articles.title: One reduction step preserves STLC denotation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, if a term $t$ reduces to $t'$ in one step of call-by-value reduction, then $t$ and $t'$
have the same denotation in every environment $\eta$ for their context.

articles.title: Denotation of an instantiated STLC body
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types,
every term $b$ of type $B$ in context $A :: \Gamma$, every term $a$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$
and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the denotation in $\eta$ of $b$ with its newest variable
replaced by $a$ equals the denotation of $b$ in the environment that extends $\eta$ by the
denotation of $a$ in $\eta$ for the newest variable.

articles.title: Renaming lemma for STLC denotation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every
type-preserving renaming $\rho$ from context $\Gamma$ to context $\Delta$, every term $t$ in
context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the denotation in $\eta$ of the term
obtained by renaming the variables of $t$ along $\rho$ equals the denotation of $t$ in the
environment that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(\rho(x))$.

articles.title: Denotation of an STLC substitution
articles.statement:
Given an interpretation $I$ of the base types, a
type-preserving substitution $\sigma$ mapping each variable of a context $\Gamma$ to a term in a
context $\Delta$, and an environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, this is the environment for $\Gamma$
that sends each variable $x$ to the denotation of $\sigma(x)$ in $\eta$.

articles.title: Substitution lemma for STLC denotation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types,
every type-preserving substitution $\sigma$ mapping each variable of a context $\Gamma$ to a term
in a context $\Delta$, every term $t$ in context $\Gamma$ and every environment $\eta$ for
$\Delta$, the denotation in $\eta$ of $t$ with $\sigma$ applied simultaneously to its variables
equals the denotation of $t$ in the environment that sends each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to the
denotation of $\sigma(x)$ in $\eta$.

articles.title: Weakening preserves STLC denotation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every
term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, every type $B$, every value $a$ in the denotation of $B$
and every environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the weakening of $t$ to the context $B :: \Gamma$ has,
in the environment that extends $\eta$ by $a$ for the newest variable, the same denotation as $t$
in $\eta$.

articles.title: Denotation of simple types
articles.statement:
Given an interpretation $I$ assigning a type $I(b)$ to each
base type $b$, the denotation $[\![A]\!]_I$ of a simple type $A$ is defined by recursion on $A$:
a base type $b$ denotes $I(b)$, and a function type $A \Rightarrow B$ denotes the type of all
functions from $[\![A]\!]_I$ to $[\![B]\!]_I$.

articles.title: Semantic environments for the denotational semantics of STLC
articles.statement:
Given an interpretation $I$
assigning a type to each base type and a typing context $\Gamma$ (a list of simple types), an
environment for $\Gamma$ assigns to every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, of any simple type $A$, an
element of the denotation $[\![A]\!]_I$.

articles.title: Semantic equality is an equivalence relation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, every context $\Gamma$ and every type $A$, semantic equality in $I$ of terms of type $A$
in $\Gamma$ (having the same denotation in every environment) is reflexive, symmetric and
transitive.

articles.title: Eta is sound for the denotational semantics
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types and every term $f$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in a context $\Gamma$, let $f'$ be the
weakening of $f$ to the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable $x$ of type $A$. Then the
term $\lambda x.\, f'\,x$, which binds $x$, is semantically equal to $f$ in $I$ (has the same
denotation in every environment).

articles.title: Model-independent eta equality
articles.statement:
For every term $f$ of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in
variable context $\Gamma$, the term $\lambda.\,(f^{\uparrow}\,x_0)$ is model-equal to $f$,
where $f^{\uparrow}$ is $f$ weakened by a newest variable of type $A$ and $x_0$ is that
variable.

articles.title: Semantic equality is a congruence for lambda abstraction
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of
the base types. If two terms of type $B$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable
of type $A$ are semantically equal in $I$ (they have the same denotation in every environment),
then their lambda abstractions, terms of type $A \Rightarrow B$ in $\Gamma$, are semantically
equal in $I$.

articles.title: Model equality of STLC terms
articles.statement:
Two terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in variable
context $\Gamma$ are model-equal when, for every interpretation $I$ of the base types by types
in the same universe as the type of base types, they are semantically equal in $I$: with
function types interpreted as full function spaces, the denotations of $t$ and $u$ agree at
every semantic environment for $\Gamma$.

Unlike semantic equality in a fixed interpretation, this relation does not choose a particular
model.

articles.title: Single-step evaluation is a semantic equation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, if a term $t$ reduces to a term $u$ in one call-by-value evaluation step, then $t$ and $u$
are semantically equal in $I$: they have the same denotation in every environment.

articles.title: Multi-step evaluation is a semantic equation
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base
types, if a term $t$ reduces to a term $u$ in zero or more call-by-value evaluation steps, then
$t$ and $u$ are semantically equal in $I$: they have the same denotation in every environment.

articles.title: Plugging into a composite STLC context
articles.statement:
Let $E_2$ be a typed one-hole context whose
hole has type $B$ in variable context $\Delta$ and which produces a term of type $C$ in
context $\Theta$, and let $E_1$ be one whose hole has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and which
produces a term of type $B$ in $\Delta$. Then for every term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$,
$(E_2 \circ E_1)[t] = E_2[E_1[t]]$.

articles.title: Plugging a term into an STLC context
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a typed one-hole context whose hole
has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in variable
context $\Delta$. For a term $t$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the plugged term $E[t]$ of type $B$
in $\Delta$ is defined by recursion on $E$: $[\,][t] = t$, $(E\,a)[t] = E[t]\,a$,
$(f\,E)[t] = f\,E[t]$ and $(\lambda.\,E)[t] = \lambda.\,E[t]$, where $[\,]$ is the bare hole,
$E\,a$ applies $E$ to a term $a$, $f\,E$ applies a term $f$ to $E$, and $\lambda.\,E$ puts $E$
under a lambda. No renaming is applied, so a lambda above the hole may bind free variables
of $t$.

articles.title: Pointwise semantic equality of substitutions is reflexive
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$
of the base types and every simultaneous substitution $\sigma$ that replaces each variable of a
context $\Gamma$ by a term of the same type in a context $\Delta$, $\sigma$ is pointwise
semantically equal to itself in $I$: for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, the term $\sigma(x)$
has the same denotation as itself in every environment for $\Delta$.

articles.title: Semantic equality is reflexive
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types, every
term $t$ is semantically equal to itself in $I$: it has the same denotation as itself in every
environment.

articles.title: Renaming preserves semantic equality
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types. If
terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$ (they have the
same denotation in every environment), then for every type-preserving renaming $\rho$ of the
variables of $\Gamma$ into a context $\Delta$, the renamed terms $\rho(t)$ and $\rho(u)$ are
semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Renaming an environment
articles.statement:
Given a renaming $\rho$ from context $\Gamma$ to context
$\Delta$ (a type-preserving map from the variables of $\Gamma$ to those of $\Delta$) and an
environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the renamed environment for $\Gamma$ sends each variable $x$ of
$\Gamma$ to $\eta(\rho(x))$; that is, it is the composite $\eta \circ \rho$.

articles.title: Semantic equality of terms in a model
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types as types.
Two terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type $A$ in the same context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in
$I$ when, for every semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$, the denotation of $t$ in $I$ at $\eta$
equals the denotation of $u$ in $I$ at $\eta$.

articles.title: Semantic equality is a congruence for typed contexts
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of the
base types. Let $t$ and $u$ be terms of type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$ that denote the same
value in $I$ under every semantic environment. Then for every typed one-hole context $C$ whose
hole has type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ and which produces a term of type $B$ in context $\Delta$, the
terms $C[t]$ and $C[u]$ obtained by plugging $t$ and $u$ into the hole also denote the same value
in $I$ under every semantic environment.

articles.title: Pointwise semantic equality of substitutions
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types
as types. Two simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a context
$\Delta$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$ when, for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ (of any
type) and every semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Delta$, the denotation of the term $\sigma(x)$ in
$I$ at $\eta$ equals the denotation of the term $\tau(x)$ in $I$ at $\eta$.

articles.title: Semantically equal substitutions give semantically equal results
articles.statement:
For every interpretation
$I$ of the base types, every term $t$ of type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$, and all simultaneous
substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$ that are pointwise
semantically equal in $I$, the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and the result of applying $\tau$
to $t$ are semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Substitution preserves semantic equality
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types,
if two terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type $A$ in a context $\Gamma$ are semantically equal in $I$,
then for every simultaneous substitution $\sigma$ from $\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, the result
of applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and the result of applying $\sigma$ to $u$ are semantically equal in
$I$.

articles.title: Symmetry of pointwise semantic equality of substitutions
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of
the base types and all simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a context $\Gamma$ to a
context $\Delta$, if $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$, then $\tau$ and
$\sigma$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Symmetry of semantic equality of terms
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types and
all terms $t$ and $u$ of the same type in the same context, if $t$ and $u$ are semantically equal
in $I$, then $u$ and $t$ are semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Typed one-hole contexts
articles.statement:
Fix simple types over a type of base types. A one-hole context
whose hole has type $A$ in variable context $\Gamma$, and which produces a term of type $B$ in
variable context $\Delta$, is built by four rules. The hole itself is such a context, with
$\Delta = \Gamma$ and $B = A$. If $C$ produces type $S \Rightarrow T$ in $\Delta$ and $a$ is a term
of type $S$ in $\Delta$, then the application $C\,a$ produces type $T$ in $\Delta$. If $f$ is a
term of type $S \Rightarrow T$ in $\Delta$ and $C$ produces type $S$ in $\Delta$, then the
application $f\,C$ produces type $T$ in $\Delta$. If $C$ produces type $T$ in the context
$S :: \Delta$ obtained from $\Delta$ by adding a new leading variable of type $S$, then the
abstraction $\lambda C$ produces type $S \Rightarrow T$ in $\Delta$. In every rule the hole keeps
type $A$ in context $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Transitivity of pointwise semantic equality of substitutions
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$
of the base types and all simultaneous substitutions $\sigma$, $\tau$ and $\upsilon$ from a context
$\Gamma$ to a context $\Delta$, if $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$ and
$\tau$ and $\upsilon$ are pointwise semantically equal in $I$, then $\sigma$ and $\upsilon$ are
pointwise semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Transitivity of semantic equality of terms
articles.statement:
For every interpretation $I$ of the base types
and all terms $t$, $u$ and $w$ of the same type in the same context, if $t$ and $u$ are
semantically equal in $I$ and $u$ and $w$ are semantically equal in $I$, then $t$ and $w$ are
semantically equal in $I$.

articles.title: Strict upper bound of a finite set of naturals
articles.statement:
For a finite set $S$ of natural numbers,
this is the number $\max S + 1$, where the maximum of the empty set is taken to be $0$. It is
strictly greater than every element of $S$.

articles.title: Bound-variable supremum of a type scheme
articles.statement:
The bound-variable supremum of a type scheme
$\sigma$ is one more than the largest index $i$ of a bound variable occurring in $\sigma$, and
$0$ if no bound variable occurs in $\sigma$.

articles.title: Extending more general contexts by a binding
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma$ be typing
contexts such that $\Gamma'$ is more general than $\Gamma$, let $x$ be a name, and let $\sigma'$
and $\sigma$ be type schemes such that $\sigma'$ is more general than $\sigma$. Then the context
obtained by putting the binding $x : \sigma'$ in front of $\Gamma'$ is more general than the
context obtained by putting the binding $x : \sigma$ in front of $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Typing context
articles.statement:
A typing context over base types $B$ is a finite list of bindings
$(x, \sigma)$, each pairing a name $x$ (a string) with a type scheme $\sigma$ over $B$. A name
may be bound more than once; the first binding of a name in the list is the visible one.

articles.title: Evaluation of a type scheme
articles.statement:
Given maps $f$ and $g$ from natural numbers to monotypes
over $B$, a type scheme $\sigma$ over $B$ evaluates to the monotype obtained by replacing each
free type variable $x$ of $\sigma$ by $f(x)$ and each bound variable $i$ by $g(i)$, keeping
every base type $b$ unchanged. An arrow $\sigma_1 \to \sigma_2$ evaluates to the arrow from the
evaluation of $\sigma_1$ to the evaluation of $\sigma_2$.

articles.title: Expressions of the λ-calculus with let
articles.statement:
An expression is a variable $x$, an application
$e_1\,e_2$, an abstraction $\lambda x.\, e$, or a let-binding
$\mathsf{let}\ x = e_1\ \mathsf{in}\ e_2$, where $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$ are expressions and variable
names $x$ are strings.

articles.title: Free type variables depend only on visible bindings
articles.statement:
If two typing contexts $\Gamma$ and
$\Gamma'$ give every name $x$ the same visible scheme (or both bind no scheme to $x$), then
$\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ have the same free type variables.

articles.title: Free type variables of a context
articles.statement:
The free type variables of a typing context $\Gamma$
are the type variables occurring free in the visible scheme of some name bound in $\Gamma$.

A binding shadowed by an earlier binding of the same name does not count, so the free type
variables of $\Gamma$ depend only on the visible scheme of each name.

articles.title: Generalization depends only on the free variables of the context
articles.statement:
If two typing
contexts $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ have the same free type variables, then for every monotype
$\tau$ the generalization of $\tau$ in $\Gamma$ equals the generalization of $\tau$ in
$\Gamma'$.

articles.title: Generalizing in a context with fewer free variables
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma$ be typing
contexts such that every free type variable of $\Gamma'$ is a free type variable of $\Gamma$, and
let $\tau$ be a monotype. Then the generalization of $\tau$ with respect to $\Gamma'$ is more
general than the generalization of $\tau$ with respect to $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Renaming step of the substitution lemma
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context, $\tau$ a
monotype and $s$ a type substitution. Write $s\Gamma$ for the context obtained by applying $s$ to
every scheme of $\Gamma$, and let $N$ be one more than the largest free type variable of
$s\Gamma$, with $N = 1$ if $s\Gamma$ has none. Let $\rho$ be the substitution sending a type
variable $y$ to $s(y)$ if $y$ is free in $\Gamma$, and to the type variable $y + N$ otherwise.
Then the generalization of $\rho(\tau)$ with respect to $s\Gamma$ is more general than the scheme
obtained by applying $s$ to the free type variables of the generalization of $\tau$ with respect
to $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Generalization of a monotype
articles.statement:
Given a typing context $\Gamma$ and a monotype $\tau$, the
generalization of $\tau$ with respect to $\Gamma$ is the type scheme obtained from $\tau$ by
turning each type variable $\alpha$ that is not free in $\Gamma$ into the bound variable with
index $\alpha$, while type variables free in $\Gamma$ stay free.

articles.title: `let` generalizes
articles.statement:
For every typing context $\Gamma$, all variable names $f$ and $x$, and
every type variable $\alpha$, the expression $\mathtt{let}\ f = \lambda x.\, x\ \mathtt{in}\ f\, f$
has type $\alpha \to \alpha$ in $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Soundness of type inference for closed expressions
articles.statement:
For every expression $e$ and
monotype $\tau$, if type inference for closed expressions returns $\tau$ on $e$, then $e$ has
type $\tau$ in the empty context.

articles.title: Soundness of Algorithm W
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context, $e$ an expression and $n$ a
natural number. If Algorithm W, run on $\Gamma$ and $e$ with fresh-variable counter $n$,
succeeds and returns a substitution $s$, a monotype $\tau$ and a counter $n'$, then $e$ has
type $\tau$ in the context $s\Gamma$ obtained by applying $s$ to every type scheme of
$\Gamma$.

articles.title: Typing inversion for variables
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context, $x$ a name and $\tau$ a
monotype. Then $\Gamma \vdash x : \tau$ holds for the variable expression $x$ if and only if
there are a type scheme $\sigma$ and monotypes $(t_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that the lookup of
$x$ in $\Gamma$ gives $\sigma$ and $\tau$ is the instance of $\sigma$ at $(t_i)$.

articles.title: Hindley–Milner typing
articles.statement:
The syntax-directed Damas–Milner typing relation
$\Gamma \vdash e : \tau$ between a context $\Gamma$, an expression $e$ and a monotype $\tau$ is the
least relation closed under the following rules, where $\Gamma, x : \sigma$ is $\Gamma$ extended
by the binding $x : \sigma$ in front.

- Variable: if the lookup of $x$ in $\Gamma$ gives the scheme $\sigma$, then
  $\Gamma \vdash x : \tau$ for every instance $\tau$ of $\sigma$, obtained by replacing each bound
  variable $i$ of $\sigma$ by a monotype $t_i$.
- Application: if $\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \tau_1 \to \tau_2$ and $\Gamma \vdash e_2 : \tau_1$, then
  $\Gamma \vdash e_1\, e_2 : \tau_2$.
- Abstraction: if $\Gamma, x : \tau_1 \vdash e : \tau_2$, with $\tau_1$ bound as a scheme without
  bound variables, then $\Gamma \vdash \lambda x.\, e : \tau_1 \to \tau_2$.
- Let: if $\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \tau_1$ and $\Gamma, x : \mathrm{gen}_\Gamma(\tau_1) \vdash e_2 :
  \tau_2$, then $\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{let}\ x = e_1\ \mathtt{in}\ e_2 : \tau_2$, where
  $\mathrm{gen}_\Gamma(\tau_1)$ binds the type variables of $\tau_1$ that are not free in
  $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Completeness of type inference for closed expressions
articles.statement:
If an expression $e$ has a
monotype $\tau'$ in the empty context, then type inference succeeds on $e$ and returns a
monotype $\tau$ of which $\tau'$ is a substitution instance: $\tau' = r(\tau)$ for some type
substitution $r$.

articles.title: Type inference succeeds exactly on typable closed expressions
articles.statement:
Type inference succeeds
on an expression $e$ if and only if $e$ has some monotype in the empty context.

articles.title: Principal types
articles.statement:
The inferred type of a closed expression is one of its types, and
every type of it is an instance of the inferred one.

articles.title: Type inference for closed expressions
articles.statement:
Type inference on an expression $e$ runs
Algorithm W on $e$ in the empty context with fresh-variable counter $0$. If W succeeds with a
substitution $s$, a monotype $\tau$ and a counter $n'$, the inferred type of $e$ is $\tau$;
if W fails, $e$ has no inferred type.

articles.title: Instantiation commutes with substitution
articles.statement:
For every type substitution $s$, every scheme
$\sigma$ and all monotypes $(t_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, instantiating each bound variable $i$ of
$s(\sigma)$ by $s(t_i)$ gives $s$ applied to the instance of $\sigma$ at $(t_i)$. Here $s$ acts on
a scheme through its free type variables only.

articles.title: Instantiation of a type scheme
articles.statement:
Given monotypes $(t_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, the instance of
a scheme $\sigma$ at $(t_i)$ is the monotype obtained from $\sigma$ by replacing each bound
variable $i$ by $t_i$, keeping its free type variables and base types unchanged.

articles.title: The let rule under a type substitution
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context, $s$ a type
substitution, $x$ a variable name, $e_1, e_2$ expressions and $\tau_1, \tau_2$ monotypes, and
write $s\Gamma$ for the context obtained by applying $s$ to every type scheme of $\Gamma$.
Suppose $e_1$ has type $\tau_1$ in $\Gamma$, and $e_2$ has type $\tau_2$ in the context
obtained from $s\Gamma$ by binding $x$, in front, to the type scheme that results from
applying $s$ to the generalization of $\tau_1$ in $\Gamma$. Then
$\mathtt{let}\ x = e_1\ \mathtt{in}\ e_2$ has type $\tau_2$ in $s\Gamma$.

articles.title: Substitutions agreeing on a context give the same lookups
articles.statement:
If two type substitutions $s$
and $t$ agree on every free type variable of a context $\Gamma$, then for every name $x$ the
lookups of $x$ in $s(\Gamma)$ and in $t(\Gamma)$ are equal: both give no scheme, or both give the
same scheme.

articles.title: Context lookup
articles.statement:
The lookup of a name $x$ in a typing context $\Gamma$ is the scheme of the
first binding of $x$ in $\Gamma$ (the visible one), or nothing if $\Gamma$ has no binding of $x$.

articles.title: Typing is preserved in more general contexts
articles.statement:
If $\Gamma \vdash e : \tau$ and $\Gamma'$ is
a context more general than $\Gamma$, then $\Gamma' \vdash e : \tau$.

articles.title: More general context
articles.statement:
A context $\Gamma'$ is more general than a context $\Gamma$ when the
same names are visible in both and, for each such name $x$, the visible scheme of $x$ in $\Gamma'$
is more general than its visible scheme in $\Gamma$. Only lookups matter, so shadowed bindings
play no role.

articles.title: More general type scheme
articles.statement:
A scheme $\sigma'$ is more general than a scheme $\sigma$ when
every instance of $\sigma$ is also an instance of $\sigma'$ and every free type variable of
$\sigma'$ is a free type variable of $\sigma$.

articles.title: No monotype is an arrow out of itself
articles.statement:
For all monotypes $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$,
$\tau_1 \ne (\tau_1 \to \tau_2)$.

articles.title: The abstraction $\lambda f.\, f\, f$ has no type
articles.statement:
For every typing context $\Gamma$,
every variable name $f$ and every monotype $\tau$, the judgment
$\Gamma \vdash \lambda f.\, f\, f : \tau$ does not hold.

The λ-bound variable $f$ is monomorphic, so it cannot be applied to itself.

articles.title: Contexts with the same lookups are related by generality
articles.statement:
If two typing contexts
$\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma$ give the same lookup result for every name $x$ (the same visible scheme,
or none in both), then $\Gamma'$ is more general than $\Gamma$.

Since the hypothesis is symmetric, $\Gamma$ is then also more general than $\Gamma'$.

articles.title: Type schemes
articles.statement:
A type scheme over base types $B$ is a term over the constant set
$B \oplus \mathbb{N}$: its variables $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$ are the free type variables, a constant
$\mathrm{inl}\, b$ is the base type $b \in B$, a constant $\mathrm{inr}\, i$ is the bound variable
$i$, and a node of two schemes is an arrow.

articles.title: Hindley–Milner typing is stable under type substitution
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing
context, $e$ an expression and $\tau$ a monotype with $\Gamma \vdash e : \tau$. Then for every
type substitution $s$, $s\Gamma \vdash e : s\tau$, where $s\Gamma$ applies $s$ to every scheme of
$\Gamma$ and $s\tau$ applies $s$ to $\tau$.

articles.title: Substitution into a scheme depends only on its free variables
articles.statement:
If two type
substitutions $s$ and $t$ satisfy $s(x) = t(x)$ for every free type variable $x$ of a type
scheme $\sigma$, then applying $s$ to $\sigma$ gives the same scheme as applying $t$.

articles.title: Substituting into a generalization is more general
articles.statement:
For a typing context $\Gamma$, a
monotype $\tau$ and a type substitution $r$, the scheme obtained by applying $r$ to the free
type variables of the generalization of $\tau$ in $\Gamma$ is more general than the
generalization of $r(\tau)$ in $r(\Gamma)$: every instance of the latter is an instance of the
former, and every free type variable of the former is a free type variable of the latter.

articles.title: Applying a type substitution to a scheme
articles.statement:
For a type substitution $s$ and a type
scheme $\sigma$, $s\sigma$ is the scheme obtained from $\sigma$ by replacing every free type
variable $x$ with the monotype $s(x)$, read as a scheme with no bound variables. The bound
variables of $\sigma$ are left unchanged.

articles.title: Applying a type substitution to a context
articles.statement:
For a type substitution $s$ and a typing
context $\Gamma$, $s\Gamma$ is the context obtained by applying $s$ to the scheme of every binding
of $\Gamma$, keeping the names and their order.

articles.title: Monotypes as type schemes
articles.statement:
Every monotype $\tau$ is read as the type scheme with no bound
variables of the same shape: a type variable stays the same type variable, a base type $b$
becomes the constant $\mathrm{inl}\, b$, and an arrow $\tau_1 \to \tau_2$ becomes the arrow of the
images of $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$.

articles.title: Monotypes
articles.statement:
A monotype over a set $B$ of base types is a term over the constants $B$: a
type variable $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$, a base type $b \in B$, or an arrow $\tau_1 \to \tau_2$ of
two monotypes (a binary node).

articles.title: Variables below a bound
articles.statement:
A term $t$ has all its variables below $n$ when every variable
$z$ occurring in $t$ satisfies $z < n$.

articles.title: Free type variables of a name's visible scheme
articles.statement:
For a typing context $\Gamma$ and a
name $x$, this is the set of free type variables of the scheme that $\Gamma$ binds to $x$ (the
first binding of $x$ in $\Gamma$), or the empty set if $\Gamma$ does not bind $x$.

articles.title: Completeness of Algorithm W
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context and $n$ a natural number
such that every free type variable of $\Gamma$ is less than $n$. If, for some type substitution
$u$, an expression $e$ has a monotype $\tau'$ in the context $u(\Gamma)$, then Algorithm W
succeeds on $\Gamma$ and $e$ with counter $n$, returning a substitution $s$, a monotype $\tau$
and a new counter $n'$, and there is a type substitution $r$ such that $u(x) = r(s(x))$ for
every type variable $x < n$, and $\tau' = r(\tau)$.

This is the completeness theorem of Damas and Milner.

articles.title: Freshness invariants of Algorithm W
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context and $n$ a
natural number such that every free type variable of $\Gamma$ is less than $n$. If Algorithm W
succeeds on $\Gamma$ and an expression $e$ with counter $n$, returning a substitution $s$, a
monotype $\tau$ and a new counter $n'$, then $n \le n'$, every type variable of $\tau$ is less
than $n'$, and for every type variable $x < n$ every type variable of $s(x)$ is less than
$n'$.

articles.title: Algorithm W
articles.statement:
Given a typing context $\Gamma$, an expression $e$ and a counter $n$,
Algorithm W either fails or returns a substitution, a monotype and a new counter; type variables
$\alpha_m$ with $m \ge n$ serve as fresh. Write $\tau_1 \to \tau_2$ for the arrow type, $s\Gamma$
for $\Gamma$ with the substitution $s$ applied to every type scheme, and $s(\tau)$ for $s$
applied to a monotype $\tau$. Algorithm W is defined by recursion on $e$, and fails as soon
as a recursive call or a unification fails:

- For a variable $x$: if $x$ is unbound in $\Gamma$, W fails; otherwise, with $\sigma$ the
  visible type scheme of $x$, W returns the identity substitution, the instance of $\sigma$
  that replaces each bound variable $i$ by $\alpha_{n+i}$, and the counter $n + k$, where $k$
  is one more than the largest bound-variable index of $\sigma$ ($0$ if it has none).
- For $\lambda x.\, e'$: W runs on the context $\Gamma$ with $x$ bound in front to the
  monotype $\alpha_n$, the body $e'$ and the counter $n + 1$; if this returns
  $(s, \tau, n')$, W returns $(s, s(\alpha_n) \to \tau, n')$.
- For an application $e_1\, e_2$: W runs on $\Gamma$, $e_1$, $n$, giving
  $(s_1, \tau_1, n_1)$, then on $s_1\Gamma$, $e_2$, $n_1$, giving $(s_2, \tau_2, n_2)$, then
  runs unification on the single equation $s_2(\tau_1) = \tau_2 \to \alpha_{n_2}$, giving
  $s_3$; it returns the composite substitution applying $s_1$, then $s_2$, then $s_3$, the
  type $s_3(\alpha_{n_2})$ and the counter $n_2 + 1$.
- For $\mathtt{let}\ x = e_1\ \mathtt{in}\ e_2$: W runs on $\Gamma$, $e_1$, $n$, giving
  $(s_1, \tau_1, n_1)$, then on the context $s_1\Gamma$ with $x$ bound in front to the
  generalization of $\tau_1$ in $s_1\Gamma$, $e_2$ and $n_1$, giving $(s_2, \tau_2, n_2)$;
  it returns the composite substitution applying $s_1$ then $s_2$, the type $\tau_2$ and the
  counter $n_2$.

articles.title: Allocation preserves store typing
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context, $S$ a store
typing and $\mu$ a store that is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$. If $v$ is a value of type
$T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the store obtained by appending $v$ at the end of $\mu$ is well
typed under $\Gamma$ and the store typing obtained by appending $T$ at the end of $S$.

articles.title: The stored recursive function of Landin's knot
articles.statement:
The term
$b_0 = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!\ell_0)\,x$, which applies the contents of store location
$\ell_0 = 0$ to its argument.

It is the function Landin's knot writes into location $0$.

articles.title: The recursive function of Landin's knot, with the cell free
articles.statement:
The term
$\lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,x$, which applies the contents of the reference $r$ to its
argument. Here $r$ is a free variable, de Bruijn index $1$ under the binder $\lambda x$; in
Landin's knot it is bound by the outer $\lambda r$.

articles.title: The knot after allocation
articles.statement:
The term
$(\lambda r{:}\mathrm{Ref}\,(\mathrm{Unit}\to\mathrm{Unit}).\ (\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,
\mathrm{unit})\ (r := \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,x))\ \ell_0$, where $\ell_0$ is store
location $0$: Landin's knot with its allocation $\mathrm{ref}\,(\lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ x)$
replaced by $\ell_0$.

articles.title: Determinism of evaluation with references
articles.statement:
If a configuration $(t, \mu)$ steps to
$(t_1, \mu_1)$ and also to $(t_2, \mu_2)$, then $t_1 = t_2$ and $\mu_1 = \mu_2$.

This relies on allocating each fresh location at the end of the store, at the index equal to the
length of $\mu$; with TAPL's arbitrary choice of fresh location only the result up to renaming of
locations is unique.

articles.title: Well-typed stores hold a typed value at every location
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a typing
context, $S$ a store typing, and $\mu$ a store (a list of terms, whose entry at index $l$ is
the contents of location $l$) that is well typed, $\Gamma \mid S \vdash \mu$. If $S$ assigns
type $T$ to location $l$, then $\mu$ has an entry $v$ at location $l$, $v$ is a value, and
$\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : T$.

articles.title: Retyping a well-typed store under an extended store typing
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable
context, let $S$ and $S'$ be store typings such that $S$ is a prefix of $S'$, and let $\mu$ be a
store that is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$. Then $\mu$ and $S$ have the same length, and for
every location $l$ less than this length, the entry of $\mu$ at $l$ is a value that has, under
$\Gamma$ and $S'$, the type that $S$ assigns to $l$.

articles.title: Store-typing weakening
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and let $S$ and $S'$ be store
typings such that $S$ is a prefix of $S'$. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$,
then $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S'$.

This is TAPL Lemma 13.5.6, with the extension of store typings taken as the prefix order on
lists.

articles.title: Typing judgment for the lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
The judgment
$\Gamma \mid S \vdash t : T$ (TAPL Figure 13-1), where the context $\Gamma$ lists the types of
the free de Bruijn variables (index $0$ first) and the store typing $S$ lists the types of the
locations $0, 1, \ldots$, is the least relation closed under the following rules, in which
$t : T$ abbreviates $\Gamma \mid S \vdash t : T$. A variable $x$ has type $T$ if $\Gamma$
assigns $T$ to index $x$. If $t$ has type $T_2$ in the context $\Gamma$ extended by $T_1$ at
index $0$ (with the same $S$), then $\lambda{:}T_1.\, t : T_1 \to T_2$. If $t_1 : T_1 \to T_2$
and $t_2 : T_1$, then $t_1\, t_2 : T_2$. The term $\mathtt{unit}$ has type $\mathrm{Unit}$. A
location $l$ has type $\mathrm{Ref}\, T$ if $S$ assigns $T$ to $l$. If $t : T$, then
$\mathrm{ref}\, t : \mathrm{Ref}\, T$. If $t : \mathrm{Ref}\, T$, then $!t : T$. If
$t_1 : \mathrm{Ref}\, T$ and $t_2 : T$, then $t_1 := t_2$ has type $\mathrm{Unit}$.

articles.title: The identity on Unit
articles.statement:
The identity function $\lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ x$ on the
unit type.

articles.title: Substitution of a term for variable zero
articles.statement:
For terms $t$ and $s$, the instantiation of $t$
by $s$ applies to $t$ the parallel substitution that sends the de Bruijn index $0$ to $s$ and
each index $x + 1$ to the variable $x$. Thus the free occurrences of variable $0$ in $t$ are
replaced by $s$, with the free variables of $s$ raised by the number of binders crossed, and
every other free variable of $t$ is lowered by one.

This is the substitution of β-reduction, written $\uparrow^{-1}([0 \mapsto \uparrow^1 s]\,t)$ in
TAPL Section 6.3; TAPL's $[0 \mapsto s]\,t$ alone does not lower the other free variables.

articles.title: Instantiating a shifted term
articles.statement:
For all terms $t$ and $s$ of the simply typed lambda calculus
with references, shift every free de Bruijn variable of $t$ up by one (rename by
$x \mapsto x + 1$), then instantiate the result with $s$, replacing variable $0$ by $s$ and
lowering every other variable $x + 1$ to $x$. The outcome is $t$.

articles.title: Substitution lemma for the lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable
context and $S$ a store typing. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $S$ and the context that extends
$\Gamma$ by a new innermost variable (index $0$) of type $A$, and a term $s$ has type $A$ under
$\Gamma$ and $S$, then substituting $s$ for variable $0$ in $t$ (and lowering every other variable
by one) gives a term of type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$.

This is TAPL Lemma 13.5.4 in de Bruijn form.

articles.title: The cycle of Landin's knot
articles.statement:
Write $\ell_0$ for store location $0$, let
$b_0 = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!\ell_0)\,x$, and let $[b_0]$ be the store whose only entry, at
$\ell_0$, is $b_0$. In one call-by-value step, $(!\ell_0)\,\mathrm{unit}$ with store $[b_0]$ steps
to $b_0\,\mathrm{unit}$ with store $[b_0]$, and in one further step $b_0\,\mathrm{unit}$ with store
$[b_0]$ steps back to $(!\ell_0)\,\mathrm{unit}$ with store $[b_0]$.

articles.title: Landin's knot never evaluates to a value
articles.statement:
Starting from Landin's knot with the empty
store, no sequence of zero or more call-by-value evaluation steps reaches a configuration
$(v, \mu)$ in which the term $v$ is a value, whatever the store $\mu$.

articles.title: Landin's knot is well typed
articles.statement:
Landin's knot is closed and has type $\mathrm{Unit}$
in the empty typing context under the empty store typing.

articles.title: The first four steps of Landin's knot
articles.statement:
Write $\ell_0$ for store location $0$ and $[t]$
for the store whose only entry, at $\ell_0$, is $t$, and let
$\mathrm{id} = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ x$ and $b_0 = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!\ell_0)\,x$.
Each of the following is one call-by-value step: Landin's knot with the empty store steps to
$(\lambda r{:}\mathrm{Ref}\,(\mathrm{Unit}\to\mathrm{Unit}).\ (\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,
\mathrm{unit})\ (r := \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,x))\ \ell_0$ with store
$[\mathrm{id}]$; that term with store $[\mathrm{id}]$ steps to
$(\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!\ell_0)\,\mathrm{unit})\ (\ell_0 := b_0)$ with store
$[\mathrm{id}]$; that term with store $[\mathrm{id}]$ steps to
$(\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!\ell_0)\,\mathrm{unit})\ \mathrm{unit}$ with store $[b_0]$; and
that term with store $[b_0]$ steps to $(!\ell_0)\,\mathrm{unit}$ with store $[b_0]$.

articles.title: Landin's knot never gets stuck
articles.statement:
If Landin's knot with the empty store evaluates in zero or
more call-by-value steps to a term $t$ with store $\mu$, then $t$ with store $\mu$ takes a further
step to some term $t'$ with some store $\mu'$. So the evaluation of the knot runs forever.

articles.title: Landin's knot
articles.statement:
The term

$$
(\lambda r{:}\mathrm{Ref}\,(\mathrm{Unit}\to\mathrm{Unit}).\ (\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,
\mathrm{unit})\ (r := \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ (!r)\,x))
\ (\mathrm{ref}\,(\lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\ x))
$$

of the simply typed lambda calculus with references.

It allocates a cell $r$ holding the identity on $\mathrm{Unit}$, overwrites it with a function that
calls whatever $r$ holds, and then calls the contents of $r$ on $\mathrm{unit}$: a recursive knot
tied through the store.

articles.title: Canonical forms for function types
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$ and store typing $S$, if
$v$ is a value and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : T_1 \to T_2$, then $v$ is an abstraction
$\lambda{:}T_1.\, t$ with parameter type $T_1$, for some body $t$.

articles.title: Lifting a renaming under a binder in the lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
Given a
renaming $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of de Bruijn indices, its lift is the renaming that
sends $0$ to $0$ and each $x + 1$ to $\rho(x) + 1$.

articles.title: Lifting a substitution under a binder
articles.statement:
Given a substitution $\sigma$ assigning a term to
each de Bruijn index, its lift is the substitution that sends $0$ to the variable $0$ and each
$x + 1$ to the term $\sigma(x)$ renamed by $n \mapsto n + 1$, that is, with every free variable
raised by one.

articles.title: Canonical forms for reference types
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$ and store typing $S$, if
$v$ is a value and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : \mathrm{Ref}\, T$, then $v$ is a location $l$ to
which $S$ assigns type $T$.

articles.title: Cycle term of Landin's knot
articles.statement:
The term $(!\ell_0)\ \mathrm{unit}$: the dereference of
the store location $\ell_0$ (location $0$), applied to the unit value.

When $\ell_0$ holds $b_0 = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\,(!\ell_0)\,x$, this term steps to
$b_0\ \mathrm{unit}$, which steps back to it; these are the two configurations of the cycle.

articles.title: Values do not step
articles.statement:
If $v$ is a value, then there are no stores $\mu$, $\mu'$ and term $t'$
such that the configuration $(v, \mu)$ steps to $(t', \mu')$: values are normal forms.

articles.title: No value has a base type
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$, store typing $S$ and base type
$b$, there is no value $v$ with $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : b$.

articles.title: Typing is preserved by the embedding of raw STLC terms
articles.statement:
Fix a type $B$ of base types,
and write $\iota$ for the embeddings of simple types and of raw terms of the simply typed
lambda calculus over $B$ into types and terms of the calculus with references over $B$. Let
$\Gamma$ be a context of simple types, $t$ a raw term and $A$ a simple type such that $t$ has
type $A$ in $\Gamma$. Then for every store typing $S$ we have
$\iota(\Gamma) \mid S \vdash \iota(t) : \iota(A)$, where $\iota(\Gamma)$ is the context
obtained by applying $\iota$ to each entry of $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Embedding of raw STLC terms into the calculus with references
articles.statement:
Fix a type $B$ of base
types. The embedding $\iota$ sends a raw (extrinsically typed, binder-annotated) term of the
simply typed lambda calculus over $B$ to a term of the calculus with references over $B$, by
recursion: a de Bruijn variable $n$ goes to the variable $n$, an application $f\,a$ goes to
$\iota(f)\,\iota(a)$, and an abstraction $\lambda{:}A.\,t$ goes to $\lambda{:}\iota(A).\,\iota(t)$,
where $\iota(A)$ is the embedding of the simple type $A$.

The image is reference-free: it contains no unit value, locations, allocations, dereferences or
assignments.

articles.title: Typing of embedded intrinsically typed STLC terms
articles.statement:
Fix a type $B$ of base types, and
write $\iota$ for the embeddings of simple types and of raw terms of the simply typed lambda
calculus over $B$ into types and terms of the calculus with references over $B$. Let $\Gamma$ be
a context of simple types, $A$ a simple type and $t$ an intrinsically typed term of type $A$ in
$\Gamma$, and let $\mathrm{erase}(t)$ be the raw term obtained from $t$ by erasing its typing
information while keeping binder annotations. Then for every store typing $S$ we have
$\iota(\Gamma) \mid S \vdash \iota(\mathrm{erase}(t)) : \iota(A)$, where $\iota(\Gamma)$ is the
context obtained by applying $\iota$ to each entry of $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Embedding of simple types into the calculus with references
articles.statement:
Fix a type $B$ of base
types. The embedding $\iota$ sends a simple type over $B$ to a type of the calculus with
references over $B$, by recursion: $\iota(b) = b$ for a base type $b \in B$, and
$\iota(A_1 \to A_2) = \iota(A_1) \to \iota(A_2)$.

articles.title: Preservation for multi-step evaluation
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and $S$ a
store typing. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, the store $\mu$ is well typed
under $\Gamma$ and $S$, and $t$ with store $\mu$ evaluates in zero or more steps to $t'$ with
store $\mu'$, then there is a store typing $S'$ having $S$ as a prefix such that $t'$ has type
$T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S'$ and $\mu'$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S'$.

articles.title: Preservation for the lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context
and $S$ a store typing. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, the store $\mu$ is
well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$, and $t$ with store $\mu$ takes one evaluation step to $t'$
with store $\mu'$, then there is a store typing $S'$ having $S$ as a prefix such that $t'$ has
type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S'$ and $\mu'$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S'$.

This is TAPL Theorem 13.5.3, with the extension of store typings taken as the prefix order on
lists.

articles.title: Progress
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store typing, $t$ a term of some type $T$ in the empty variable
context under $S$, and $\mu$ a store that is well typed under $S$ in the empty context. Then $t$
is a value, or the configuration $(t, \mu)$ takes an evaluation step to some $(t', \mu')$.

## Sources

- TAPL Theorem 13.5.7.

articles.title: Configurations on the evaluation path of Landin's knot
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be Landin's knot,
$\iota = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\,x$, $b_0 = \lambda x{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\,(!\ell_0)\,x$ with
$\ell_0$ the store location $0$, $a = (!\ell_0)\ \mathrm{unit}$, $b = b_0\ \mathrm{unit}$,
$c_1$ the term $K$ with its argument $\mathrm{ref}\ \iota$ replaced by $\ell_0$,
$c_2 = (\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\,a)\,(\ell_0 := b_0)$ and
$c_3 = (\lambda y{:}\mathrm{Unit}.\,a)\ \mathrm{unit}$; write $[\,]$ for the empty store and
$[t]$ for the store whose only location $\ell_0$ holds $t$. This is the list of the six
configurations (term, store) $(K, [\,])$, $(c_1, [\iota])$, $(c_2, [\iota])$, $(c_3, [b_0])$,
$(a, [b_0])$, $(b, [b_0])$.

Each configuration steps to the next and $(b, [b_0])$ steps back to $(a, [b_0])$; every
configuration reachable from $(K, [\,])$ lies in this list.

articles.title: Renaming the variables of a term
articles.statement:
Given a renaming $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of
de Bruijn indices, renaming a term by $\rho$ replaces each variable $x$ by $\rho(x)$; renames
the body of an abstraction $\lambda{:}T.\,t$ by the lift of $\rho$ (which sends $0$ to $0$ and
each $x + 1$ to $\rho(x) + 1$), keeping the type annotation $T$; leaves the unit value and store
locations unchanged; and acts componentwise on applications, allocations, dereferences and
assignments.

articles.title: Renaming respects pointwise equality
articles.statement:
Let $\rho, \rho' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be
renamings of de Bruijn variables with $\rho(x) = \rho'(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for
every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, renaming $t$ by $\rho$ gives
the same term as renaming $t$ by $\rho'$.

articles.title: Renaming by the identity
articles.statement:
For every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with
references, renaming the de Bruijn variables of $t$ by the identity map of $\mathbb{N}$ gives
back $t$.

articles.title: Composition of renamings
articles.statement:
For all renamings $\rho, \rho' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of
de Bruijn variables and every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references,
renaming $t$ by $\rho$ and then renaming the result by $\rho'$ gives the same term as renaming $t$
by the composite $\rho' \circ \rho$.

articles.title: Substituting then renaming
articles.statement:
Let $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a renaming of de
Bruijn variables, $\sigma$ a parallel substitution sending each index to a term of the simply
typed lambda calculus with references, and $t$ a term. Applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and then renaming
the result by $\rho$ gives the same term as applying to $t$ the substitution that sends each
index $x$ to the renaming of $\sigma(x)$ by $\rho$.

articles.title: Renaming preserves typing
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be variable contexts, $S$ a store
typing, and $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ a renaming of variable indices such that whenever
$\Gamma$ assigns type $A$ to variable $x$, $\Delta$ assigns type $A$ to variable $\rho(x)$. If a
term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the term obtained from $t$ by renaming its
variables by $\rho$ has type $T$ under $\Delta$ and $S$.

articles.title: Assignment preserves store typing
articles.statement:
Let the store $\mu$ be well typed under the variable
context $\Gamma$ and the store typing $S$, and let $l$ be a location to which $S$ assigns the
type $T$. If $v$ is a value of type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the store obtained from
$\mu$ by overwriting the entry at $l$ with $v$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$.

This is TAPL Lemma 13.5.5.

articles.title: Single-variable substitution at index zero
articles.statement:
For a term $s$, the single-variable
substitution for $s$ sends the de Bruijn index $0$ to $s$ and each index $x + 1$ to the
variable $x$.

articles.title: One-step evaluation with references
articles.statement:
One step of call-by-value evaluation
$t \mid \mu \to t' \mid \mu'$, from a term $t$ with a store $\mu$ to a term $t'$ with a store
$\mu'$, is the least relation closed under the following rules, in which $v$, $v_1$ and $v_2$ are
values. If $t \mid \mu \to t' \mid \mu'$, then $t\,t_2 \mid \mu \to t'\,t_2 \mid \mu'$,
$v_1\,t \mid \mu \to v_1\,t' \mid \mu'$,
$\mathsf{ref}\,t \mid \mu \to \mathsf{ref}\,t' \mid \mu'$, $!t \mid \mu \to {!t'} \mid \mu'$,
$t := t_2 \mid \mu \to t' := t_2 \mid \mu'$ and $v_1 := t \mid \mu \to v_1 := t' \mid \mu'$. The
application $(\lambda{:}T.\,s)\,v_2$ with store $\mu$ steps, with $\mu$ unchanged, to the result of
substituting $v_2$ for variable $0$ in $s$. The allocation $\mathsf{ref}\,v$ with store $\mu$ steps
to the location $n$, where $n$ is the length of $\mu$, and the store becomes $\mu$ with $v$
appended at the end. If $\mu$ has an entry $u$ at location $l$, then $!l \mid \mu \to u \mid \mu$.
If $l$ is less than the length of $\mu$, then $l := v \mid \mu \to \mathsf{unit} \mid \mu'$, where
$\mu'$ is $\mu$ with its entry at $l$ replaced by $v$.

## Sources

- TAPL Figure 13-1, with each fresh location allocated at the end of the store.

articles.title: Multi-step evaluation with references
articles.statement:
The relation $t \mid \mu \to^* t' \mid \mu'$ holds
when the configuration $(t, \mu)$ reaches $(t', \mu')$ in zero or more evaluation steps; that is,
it is the reflexive-transitive closure of one-step evaluation on pairs of a term and a store.

articles.title: Well-typed stores
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and $S$ a store typing. A store
$\mu$, a list of terms whose entry at index $l$ is the contents of location $l$, is well typed
under $\Gamma$ and $S$, written $\Gamma \mid S \vdash \mu$, when $\mu$ and $S$ have the same
length and, for every location $l$ less than this length, the entry of $\mu$ at $l$ is a value
that has, under $\Gamma$ and $S$, the type that $S$ assigns to $l$.

Stores here are lists of terms rather than of values, so each entry is required to be a value.

## Sources

- TAPL Definition 13.5.1.

articles.title: Store
articles.statement:
A store $\mu$ is a finite list of terms; each location $l$ less than the length of
$\mu$ holds the term $\mu[l]$, the entry of $\mu$ at index $l$.

articles.title: Parallel substitution in a term
articles.statement:
Given a substitution $\sigma$ assigning a term to each
de Bruijn index, substituting $\sigma$ into a term replaces each variable $x$ by $\sigma(x)$;
substitutes into the body of an abstraction $\lambda{:}T.\,t$ the lift of $\sigma$ (which sends
$0$ to the variable $0$ and each $x + 1$ to $\sigma(x)$ with every free variable raised by one),
keeping the type annotation $T$; leaves the unit value and store locations unchanged; and acts
componentwise on applications, allocations, dereferences and assignments.

articles.title: Substitution respects pointwise equality
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma, \sigma'$ be parallel substitutions,
each sending every de Bruijn index to a term of the simply typed lambda calculus with references,
with $\sigma(x) = \sigma'(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for every term $t$, applying
$\sigma$ to $t$ gives the same term as applying $\sigma'$ to $t$.

articles.title: Substitution by variables is the identity
articles.statement:
For every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda
calculus with references, applying the parallel substitution that sends each de Bruijn index $x$
to the variable term $x$ gives back $t$.

articles.title: Renaming then substituting
articles.statement:
Let $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a renaming of de
Bruijn variables, $\sigma$ a parallel substitution sending each index to a term of the simply
typed lambda calculus with references, and $t$ a term. Renaming $t$ by $\rho$ and then applying
$\sigma$ gives the same term as applying the substitution $\sigma \circ \rho$ to $t$.

articles.title: Composition of substitutions in the lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
For all parallel
substitutions $\sigma, \tau$, each sending every de Bruijn index to a term of the simply typed
lambda calculus with references, and every term $t$, applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and then $\tau$ to
the result gives the same term as applying to $t$ the substitution that sends each index $x$ to
the result of applying $\tau$ to $\sigma(x)$.

articles.title: Parallel substitution preserves typing
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be variable contexts,
$S$ a store typing, and $\sigma$ a substitution sending each variable index to a term, such
that whenever $\Gamma$ assigns type $A$ to variable $x$, the term $\sigma(x)$ has type $A$ under
$\Delta$ and $S$. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the term obtained from
$t$ by applying $\sigma$ has type $T$ under $\Delta$ and $S$.

articles.title: Terms of the simply typed lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
Fix a type $B$ of base types.
The terms are generated by: variables, given as de Bruijn indices $x \in \mathbb{N}$;
abstractions $\lambda{:}T.\,t$, where $T$ is a type over $B$ and $t$ is a term in which index $0$
refers to the abstraction's parameter; applications $t_1\,t_2$; the unit value $\mathsf{unit}$;
store locations $l \in \mathbb{N}$; allocations $\mathsf{ref}\,t$; dereferences $!t$; and
assignments $t_1 := t_2$.

Store locations arise during evaluation, not in source programs.

articles.title: Types of the simply typed lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
Fix a type $B$ of base types.
The types over $B$ are generated by the grammar
$T ::= b \mid \mathsf{Unit} \mid T_1 \to T_2 \mid \mathsf{Ref}\,T$ with $b \in B$: base types,
the unit type, function types, and types $\mathsf{Ref}\,T$ of reference cells holding values of
type $T$.

articles.title: Type safety from the empty store
articles.statement:
A closed term typed under the empty store typing, run
from the empty store, never gets stuck: every term it reaches in zero or more steps, together
with the store reached alongside it, is a value or can take a further step.

articles.title: Type safety
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a store typing, $T$ a type, $t$ a term of type $T$ in the
empty variable context under $S$, and $\mu$ a store that is well typed under $S$ in the empty
context. If the configuration $(t, \mu)$ evaluates in zero or more steps to $(t', \mu')$, then
$t'$ is a value or $(t', \mu')$ takes a step to some configuration $(t'', \mu'')$. So a closed
term that is well typed in a well-typed store never reaches a stuck configuration.

articles.title: Canonical forms for the unit type
articles.statement:
For every context $\Gamma$ and store typing $S$, if
$v$ is a value and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : \mathrm{Unit}$, then $v = \mathtt{unit}$.

articles.title: Values of the simply typed lambda calculus with references
articles.statement:
A term is a value if and only
if it is an abstraction $\lambda{:}T.\,t$, the unit value $\mathsf{unit}$, or a store location
$l$.

articles.title: Weakening of typing
articles.statement:
If a term $t$ has type $T$ in a variable context $\Gamma$ under a
store typing $S$, then for every type $A$, the term obtained from $t$ by shifting each free de
Bruijn variable up by one has type $T$ under $S$ in the context obtained from $\Gamma$ by adding
$A$ in front as variable $0$.

articles.title: Certified canonical terms
articles.statement:
For a context $\Gamma$ and a type $A$, a certified canonical
term of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is a term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ together with a
proof that $t$ is a fixed point of normalization by evaluation: the term underlying the normal
form computed for $t$ is $t$ itself.

articles.title: The identity environment under a binder
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a context, $A$ a type, and
$\Gamma, A$ the context $\Gamma$ extended by a newest variable of type $A$. Transport the identity
semantic environment of $\Gamma$ (which reflects each variable as a neutral value) along the
weakening renaming from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma, A$ that sends each variable to its successor, and
extend the result by the reflection at type $A$ of the newest variable of $\Gamma, A$. The
resulting semantic environment equals the identity semantic environment of $\Gamma, A$.

articles.title: Extending a semantic environment by one variable
articles.statement:
Given a semantic value $a$ of type $A$
in a context $\Delta$ and a semantic environment $\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $\Delta$, the extended
environment is the semantic environment for the context $A :: \Gamma$ (the context $\Gamma$ with a
new innermost variable of type $A$) in $\Delta$ that sends the new innermost variable to $a$ and
sends the successor of each variable $x$ of $\Gamma$ to $\eta(x)$.

articles.title: The identity semantic environment realizes every environment
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$
of the base types and an environment $\eta$ for a context $\Gamma$ in $I$. Then the identity
Kripke semantic environment on $\Gamma$, which reflects each variable as a neutral value,
realizes $\eta$ at $\eta$.

articles.title: The identity semantic environment
articles.statement:
For a context $\Gamma$, the identity environment is the
semantic environment for $\Gamma$ in $\Gamma$ that sends each variable $x$ of type $A$ to the
reflection at type $A$ of the neutral term $x$. Reflection turns a neutral term into a semantic
value of the same type in the same context.

articles.title: Canonical terms have a unique normal form
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in context
$\Gamma$. If $t$ is canonical, then there is exactly one beta-normal, eta-long normal form of type
$A$ in context $\Gamma$ whose underlying term is $t$.

articles.title: Canonical terms are the fixed points of normalization
articles.statement:
A term $t$ of type $A$ in context
$\Gamma$ is canonical if and only if normalization by evaluation maps $t$ to itself, that is, the
term underlying the normal form computed for $t$ is $t$.

articles.title: Normalized terms are canonical
articles.statement:
For every term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$, the
term obtained by normalizing $t$ by evaluation is canonical.

articles.title: Canonical terms
articles.statement:
A term $t$ of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$ is canonical when it is the
underlying term of some beta-normal, eta-long normal form of type $A$ in context $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Equal NbE normal forms imply model equality
articles.statement:
If two terms $t$ and $u$ of type $A$ in
context $\Gamma$ have the same NbE normal form, then $t$ and $u$ are model-equal.

Equality of computed normal forms is thus a sound test for model equality; no converse is
claimed.

articles.title: Realization of environments
articles.statement:
Fix an interpretation $I$ of the base types, contexts
$\Delta$ and $\Gamma$, an environment $\theta$ for $\Delta$ in $I$, a Kripke semantic environment
$\xi$ assigning to each variable of $\Gamma$ a semantic value in $\Delta$, and an environment
$\eta$ for $\Gamma$ in $I$. Then $\xi$ realizes $\eta$ at $\theta$ when for every type $A$ and
every variable $x$ of type $A$ in $\Gamma$, the semantic value $\xi(x)$ realizes $\eta(x)$ at
$\theta$.

articles.title: Evaluation respects pointwise equal environments
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a term of type $A$ in
context $\Gamma$, and let $\xi$ and $\zeta$ be semantic environments interpreting the variables of
$\Gamma$ in a context $\Delta$. If $\xi(x) = \zeta(x)$ for every variable $x$ of $\Gamma$, of any
type, then evaluating $t$ in $\xi$ and evaluating $t$ in $\zeta$ give the same semantic value.

articles.title: Evaluating a neutral term reflects it
articles.statement:
For every neutral term $n$ of type $A$ in context
$\Gamma$, evaluating the underlying term of $n$ in the identity semantic environment of $\Gamma$
gives the reflection of $n$ at type $A$.
